en: *Fayuan zhulin*, Scroll One,
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Daoshi of Ximing Monastery: The Duration of Kalpas,
The Three Realms, The Sun and Moon, The Six Destinies, The Thousand Buddhas, and Reverence for the Buddha.

Revering the Dharma and revering the Sangha; prostrating before the field of merit; laymen and laywomen who take refuge; entering the Way with a sense of shame; encouraging others on the Path; hearing and understanding the teachings; recollecting past lives;
the manifestation of sincerity through spiritual wonders and resonance; the abiding and the hidden; the transformations of spirits and monsters;

awakening merit through sleep and dreams; gathering the mind and making vows; donning the dharma robes; lighting lamps; hanging banners; offering incense, flowers, and hymns of praise; and venerating stupas and monasteries.

Making offerings to the *śarīra*; receiving invitations; [the conduct of] a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*) and his ministers; accepting admonition; examining and deliberating with circumspection; practicing frugality; rectifying transgressions; being harmonious and compliant;

exhorting one another toward loyalty and filiality; [discerning between] unfiliality and gratitude; [distinguishing] between good friends and evil friends; choosing one's associates; evaluating kinsmen; weighing intellectual faculties and eloquence;
[identifying] the dull-witted, the stubborn, the deceitful, and the arrogant; refuting heterodoxy; [considering] wealth and honor versus poverty and lowliness; debts and litigation.
Slander and false accusations; incantations, sacrifices, divination, and prayers for rain; orchards and fruits, fishing and hunting; compassion and releasing life to rescue those in distress;
the karmic causes of resentment and suffering and their resulting retributions of sin and merit; desire covering the four modes of birth; the ten fetters, the ten evils, and the six perfections;

repentance, receiving the precepts, and breaking the precepts; observing the fast and breaking the fast; rewards and punishments, profit and loss; alcohol, meat, filth, and turbidity; illness and suffering; and the renunciation of the body.
*The Essential Biographies of the Dharma’s Extinction at the End of Life*, Volume 1: Chapter on the Duration of Kalpas (I). Chapter One: The Duration of Kalpas.
There are two types of kalpa-disasters: the minor and the major. 1. The Three Minor Disasters. (I) First, an explanation of the three minor disasters. This consists of six sections:
the Section on the General Intent, the Section on Epidemic Disease, the Section on Weapons, the Section on Famine, and the Section on Mutual Generation.
Section One: Introduction to the Meaning of the Title. Section One: Introduction to the Meaning of the Title.
Now, as for the term "kalpa" (劫), it is essentially a designation for recording time, much like a reign title (*nianhao*).
Thus, time has no separate substantial entity;
it is elucidated in relation to phenomena.
This is why the holy teachings are so extensively proclaimed and contain so many diverse accounts.
Although this is not the profound standard for contemplation according to principle,
it is nonetheless a subtle purport for admonishing and encouraging.
If one then crosses the ford of delusion through past consciousness, [one may proceed].
The number of atoms is easily exhausted,
yet one returns to the path of awakening from the initial mind;
the kalpas of asaṃkhyeya are difficult to fulfill.
This is the difference between delusion and awakening.
From within the Avīci Hell, amidst cities as vast as mustard seeds,
one's allotted lifespan must first be exhausted.
In the heavens, those who wear robes of stone receive their forms;
this is the distinction between good and evil.
As for the Sahā world, it regards a mere instant as a hundred years;
in the Kāṣāya lands, even an entire kalpa is treated as a single day.
This is the distinction between defilement and purity.
To summarize it, it does not exceed the categories of the Great and the Small Vehicles.
Within both the great and the small, there are each three types:
the great consist of water, fire, and wind as calamities;
the small consist of weapons, famine, and pestilence as harms.
Thus we know that the Flower Palace of six years' labor was ultimately consumed by fire in a bed of ashes;
and the jade towers of a thousand Brahmā heavens—
In the end, they were swept away by a sudden downpour;
furthermore, medical examinations yielded no signs of recovery,
and the ritual prayers for rain proved ineffective.
Frosty halberds met their blades;
starry swords clashed in combat.
The cruelty and poison took such a toll that living beings were nearly all destroyed.
Fearing the three realms yet remaining unawakened;
sighing over the six paths of rebirth, how tragic!
Section Two: Epidemics. This section on epidemics is based on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
What is meant by the term "kalpa"?
The answer is:
according to the correct phonetics of Western India (Sanskrit), it is called *kalpavarta*.
*Kalpa* is also called *kāpa*;

in the language of Qin, it means "distinguishing time periods. *Bhadra* is in the language of Qin "good existence" (*śubhāstitva*), and is also called "worthy"; because many worthy ones appear in the world, it is named the "Worthy Kalpa" (*Bhadrakalpa*).
Furthermore, the *Lokaprajñapti-abhidharma-śāstra* states:
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, said that one small kalpa (*antarakalpa*) is as follows:
It is called one kalpa.
Twenty minor kalpas are also called one kalpa.
Forty minor kalpas are likewise called one kalpa.
Sixty minor kalpas are also called one kalpa;
eighty minor kalpas are called one great kalpa.
Why is one minor kalpa referred to as "one kalpa"?
At that time, the bhikṣu Devadatta dwelt within hell,
undergoing the retribution for his karmic maturation;
the Buddha declared that he would remain there for one kalpa.
How is it that twenty intermediate kalpas are also called one kalpa?
For example, among the Brahmakāyika devas,
twenty intermediate kalpas constitute their lifespan.
The Buddha stated that his lifespan lasts for one kalpa;
how then can forty minor kalpas also be called one kalpa?
It is like the lifespan of the Brahmakāyika devas.
Forty minor kalpas [constitute] what the Buddha described as one kalpa of lifespan.
How is it that sixty minor kalpas are also called one kalpa?
Just as the lifespan of Mahābrahmā is sixty small kalpas,
the Buddha taught that his own lifespan lasts for one kalpa.
How is it that eighty minor kalpas constitute one great kalpa?
The *Buddha-bhāṣita-kalpa-loka-sūtra* states:
"Twenty minor kalpas [constitute] the period of destruction."
Next, after twenty intermediate kalpas have passed, it is destroyed and remains empty.
Next, after twenty intermediate kalpas have passed, it arises and is formed.
Next, after twenty intermediate kalpas have passed since its formation, it remains in existence.
Regarding these twenty minor kalpas that have arisen, been formed, and are now abiding:
how many have already passed, and how many remain?
Eight minor kalpas have already passed.
Eleven small kalpas remain in the future;
the ninth single kalpa is currently ongoing and not yet exhausted.
This refers to that ninth single kalpa.
How much has already passed and how much remains in the future?

Of the future period, six hundred and ninety years remain until the year Jǐmǎo (1539) at the end of the Liáng dynasty, when this sūtra was translated; this marks the conclusion of the twenty intermediate kalpas.
There are three minor calamities that revolve in succession:
first, the calamity of pestilence;
second, the calamity of weapons.
Regarding these three calamities of famine, the sequence in which they are listed in various sūtras and śāstras differs.
If one follows the *Dīrgha Āgama*, the *Madhyama Āgama*, the *Lokadhātu-vibhāga*, and other such texts:
First, weapons are listed; next, famine; and finally, pestilence.
However, according to the *Abhidharmakośa*, *Vibhāṣā*, *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, and other such treatises, first weapons are listed, then pestilence, and finally famine.
If one follows treatises such as the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Abhidharma*, famine is listed first and the calamity of weapons last;
however, regarding the sequence based on the duration of years and months, it is according to the *Lokaprajñapti-abhidharma-śāstra*. As that text states:
This refers to the ninth intermediate kalpa,
which corresponds to the third calamity;
this kalpa comes to an end because of famine.
The Buddha said:
"During these twenty intermediate kalpas, the world arises and is formed;
this constitutes the first kalpa of its abiding."
When minor calamities arise, there will be great epidemics;
all manner of diseases will break out throughout every land within Jambudvīpa.
All the people were afflicted by a great epidemic,
and all the spirits and deities gave rise to wrathful and evil intentions,
harming the people of the world.
Their lifespan will be brief, lasting for only ten years;
their physical stature will be short and small,
measuring perhaps only two spans (vitasti).
It may be three spans;
by its own measure, it is eight spans.
As for the food one consumes, weeds and barnyard grass are considered superior.
They used human hair and clothing as their primary attire,
adorning themselves only with knives and weapons.
At that time, these people did not practice the True Dharma.
Unlawful greed, attachment, false views, and other such karmas will grow and increase day and night;
various malevolent spirits and ghosts will harm people everywhere;
at that time, the royal lineage of the great king will utterly perish.
All the kingdoms have successively become desolate and abandoned;
only small prefectures and counties remain as their remnants,
situated far apart from one another in various locations.
Such persons suffer from illness and hardship,
yet no one provides them with medicine, food, or drink.
Due to these causes and conditions, their lifespans, though not yet exhausted, end in countless instances of untimely death.
In a single day and night, immeasurable sentient beings die from disease;
this is the retribution they receive due to practicing unwholesome dharmas.
Born within this [world],
they arise during the turbidity of the kalpa;
after their lives have ended, they fall into the three evil realms.
At that time, one district and its counties subsequently became desolate once more;
only a few households remained,
and they were increasingly scattered, each dwelling in a separate location.
Those who died of pestilence were left without anyone to bury them;
at that time, the land was covered with white bones,
until even the households were emptied one after another.
At that time, only seven days remain until the end of the kalpa.
During those seven days, immeasurable sentient beings will perish from pestilence;
those who happen to survive will each scatter to separate locations.
At that time, there was a person who gathered together all the men and women within Jambudvīpa,
leaving behind only ten thousand as the progeny for the future;
these ten thousand alone were capable of maintaining virtuous conduct.
Because various benevolent spirits desire that the human race not be cut off,
they protect these people by causing excellent flavors to enter their pores;
thus, through the power of karma, the human race continues without interruption.
After seven days had passed,
this great epidemic was suddenly extinguished,
and all malevolent spirits departed entirely.
In accordance with the needs of all sentient beings for food, drink, and clothing,
the heavens immediately rain down whatever they require upon their thought;
the yin and yang are harmonized, and exquisite flavors are produced.
Their physical forms are lovely, they dwell in peace and happiness,
and are free from illness. It is like when dear ones who have not seen one another for a long time suddenly meet and give rise to a heart of joy and delight.
They support one another and do not forsake each other.
This was during the previous kalpa when the human lifespan was ten years;
the people of the subsequent kalpa were born from them.
The lifespan is at its maximum of twenty thousand years.
Such merits are spontaneously accomplished,
and one becomes endowed with wholesome dharmas.
Having performed wholesome deeds of body, speech, and mind,
after relinquishing their lifespan,
they will be reborn in the happy realms.
Afterward, when they relinquish their lives, they will be reborn in the human realm,
naturally virtuous and fully endowed with the categories of precepts;
after their lifespan there has ended, they will be reborn again in the heavenly realms.
After a long time, the pestilence was thus exhausted during the middle of the first kalpa;
subsequently, the second kalpa continued for twenty thousand years.
This is the first lifespan during the intermediate kalpa.
These people are born from those whose lifespan was twenty thousand years;
they possess sovereign supernormal powers and are fully provided with the necessities of life.
The lifespan is forty thousand years;
such a long duration of birth in the realms of humans and devas is called the second kalpa.
In the second intermediate period, the lifespan is forty thousand years;
when the necessities of life are fully provided,
the lifespan is sixty thousand years.
When this state has persisted for a long duration in this manner,
it is called the third intermediate kalpa;
during this third intermediate kalpa, the lifespan is sixty thousand years.
From the time when the human lifespan was sixty thousand years until it reached eighty thousand years,
women would only marry at the age of five hundred. At that time,
people suffered from only seven diseases.
This refers to such times as those of defecation, urination, fever, chills, lust, hunger, old age,
and so forth; yet during these times,
all lands are wealthy, noble, abundant, and joyful.
There were no enemies, bandits, rebels, or thieves;
the villages stood close together, their roosters crowing within hearing distance of one another.
Although the cultivation was sparse, the harvest was exceedingly abundant.
He will be fully provided with clothing, wealth, and treasures according to his wishes;
sitting in peace, he will enjoy happiness without any need for striving or seeking.
When his lifespan is eighty thousand years, he will remain for an incalculable number of years (*asaṃkhyeya*).
Until sentient beings, who had not previously committed the ten unwholesome actions, begin to commit them;
because of this, their lifespan decreases by ten years over the course of one hundred years.
Subsequently, over another hundred years, it decreases by another ten years.
The lifespan gradually decreases in succession until it remains at ten years;
once it has reached this final stage of ten years, it stays there and does not decrease further.
Thus, the maximum lifespan is eighty thousand years, and the minimum is ten years.
If a Buddha does not appear in the world, the sequence is as follows:
if a Buddha has appeared and the True Dharma remains,
the lifespan of sentient beings will endure for a time without diminishing.
As the True Dharma gradually declines, the lifespan likewise gradually diminishes.
Third, regarding the Section on Weapons (*Śastra-kalpa*), according to the *Lokasthāna-abhidharma-śāstra*,
the Buddha taught that one minor kalpa (*antarakalpa*) is as follows:
This is called one kalpa.
As before, this continues up until eighty small kalpas, which are called a great kalpa (mahākalpa).
Up to the twentieth intermediate kalpa, the formation [of the world] is completed.
During the second intermediate kalpa of the period of abiding, the calamities arise due to great weapons.
When the human lifespan is ten years, the three poisons and false views grow and flourish day and night.
Parents, sons, brothers, and kinsmen will engage in mutual strife and contention,
let alone with others;
at that time, having given rise to such strife, they will even dance hand-to-hand.
Or they may terrify one another with tiles, stones, swords, or staves;
the various kingdoms of the four quarters may wage war against each other,
killing immeasurable numbers in a single day and night.
Such faults arise spontaneously;
when people perform unwholesome deeds, they obtain this retribution,
and within this birth, the *kalpa-kṣaya* (the turbidity of the eon) arises.
At that time, human dwellings were completely destroyed all at once;
even those that remained were scattered in every direction.
At that moment, seven days of the kalpa’s end still remained.
Within seven days, the grass and trees they grasped in their hands turned into weapons.
Because of these weapons, they slaughtered one another; terrified and exhausted by death, the people at that time fled in fear of the weapons into forests and thickets.
Some crossed the river to hide on solitary islands;
some entered pits and caves to avoid calamities;
and at times, even when they encountered one another, they would still flee in terror, their minds overwhelmed by fear.
At times they fall prostrate on the ground,
like deer or hares encountering a hunter;
in this manner, those who die by the sword in seven days are beyond measure.
Those who remained were scattered in various places.
At that time, a certain person gathered together the men and women of Jambudvīpa until only ten thousand remained.
They were left behind as a seed for future generations.
During that time, everyone practiced what was not the Dharma;
only these ten thousand people were able to practice the wholesome Dharma.
The various benevolent spirits and deities,
desiring that the human lineage not be severed,
shall protect this person by causing wholesome flavors to enter their pores.
By the power of karma,
during the intermediate kalpa, the seeds of humanity are preserved so that they do not naturally perish;
after seven days have passed, [they shall reappear].
This great calamity of weapons shall be extinguished all at once;
all malevolent spirits will depart,
and whatever food and clothing sentient beings require shall be provided accordingly.
Whatever they required would be provided by the gods as rain;
the Yin and Yang were harmonized,
and exquisite flavors emerged.
The physical form becomes lovely and the marks and signs of excellence are restored;
all wholesome dharmas arise spontaneously;
one is cool, tranquil, peaceful, happy, and free from illness.
Arousing a mind of compassion, they harbor no intent to harm one another;
upon seeing each other, they give rise to a heart of joy and happiness,
like dear relatives who have not seen one another for a long time.
Suddenly, they gathered together and gave rise to a heart of joy and happiness;
holding one another’s hands, they did not part,
and from the age of ten, they proceeded to practice virtue in succession.
They are born among humans and devas for up to twenty thousand years,
and even as long as eighty thousand years,
remaining there for incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) years.
The rest is the same as before and need not be repeated.
Section Four: Famine. According to the *Lokasthāna-abhidharma-śāstra*, it ranges from one minor kalpa up to eighty minor kalpas.
During the third aeon within the kalpa of abiding, when the minor calamities arise—
specifically, as the great calamity of famine is about to break out,
and due to celestial drought, all the people suffer from a great epidemic.
All ghosts and spirits give rise to thoughts of anger and malice,
harming the people of the world and causing their lifespans to be short.
They live for only ten years;
their bodies are short and small,
measuring perhaps two or three spans (vitasti) in height.
They eat weeds such as *tí* and *pái*;
they wear human hair as clothing yet consider it their finest raiment;
they arm themselves with swords and weapons, showing no mutual respect.
Poverty, suffering, and the folly of false views increase day and night;
grain becomes expensive, famine ensues,
and people wander about like śarāvakas.
Seeing others with provisions, they would go to seize their food;
by this cause and condition, countless beings perished of hunger.
Thus all sentient beings were born into the kalpa-turbidity.
Spontaneously, they commit evil deeds,
so that for four or five years the heavens do not send down rain.
Due to the great drought, even living grass and vegetables could not be found;
how much less so rice and grain?
All the birds and beasts devoured whatever remained.
In a single day and night, those who died of hunger were immeasurable in number;
the commanderies and counties were completely emptied,
with only a few households remaining.
The distance between them grew ever greater;
they did not practice the True Dharma, and the three poisons increased.
For six or seven years, they were impoverished and distressed, their mouths and minds constantly occupied by such conditions.
The heavens did not send down rain;
because of this great drought, even water could not be found when one desired to see it, let alone food.
During this intermediate kalpa, only seven days remain;
in one day and night, countless beings die of hunger,
and even those who survive are scattered to various places.
At that time, there was one person who, together with the men, women, great and small of all Jambudvīpa numbering ten thousand,
remained to serve as the progeny for future generations;
such a person is capable of practicing goodness.
All the benevolent spirits and deities,
desiring that the human lineage not be severed,
shall protect this person.
By means of exquisite flavors, they cause [the essence] to enter the pores;
through the power of karma,
the human race is not interrupted.
After seven days had passed,
this hunger was suddenly extinguished,
and all the malevolent spirits departed entirely.
Whatever clothing and food were required,
the heavens would immediately rain them down,
and the yin and yang were brought into harmonious balance.
Delicious flavors arise;
their physical forms become lovely and their marks and signs are restored;
all wholesome dharmas spontaneously emerge.
Pure, cool, tranquil, blissful, and free from illness;
with compassion entering the heart, there is no thought of malice or harm.
It is like a beloved person whom one has not seen for a long time.
Suddenly, upon being gathered together, they experience joy and a heart of delight;
they hold one another and do not part.
By practicing wholesome deeds successively from the age of ten,
one is reborn among humans and devas with a long lifespan.
From twenty thousand years up to eighty thousand years,
the external causes and conditions of phenomena are all the same as previously described in the *Lokasthiti* (Establishment of the World).
Each of the three calamities lasts for seven days.

If one follows other sūtras and śāstras, it is said that the famine lasts for seven years, seven months, and seven days; the pestilence lasts for seven months and seven days; and the warfare lasts at most for seven days. Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
It was established only when the human lifespan was thirty years;
it was at that time.
Exquisite food and drink can no longer be obtained;
they can only gather together for banquets by boiling rotten bones.
Should they happen to find even a single grain of rice, wheat, millet, or foxtail millet, [they treat it as a great treasure].
Valuing it as if it were a mani jewel,
they place it within a chest or casket and guard it;
those sentient beings are for the most part devoid of vital energy.
They stumble and fall prostrate on the ground, unable to rise again;
due to this famine and scarcity,
the classes of sentient beings perish almost entirely.
Thus, this calamity of scarcity lasts for seven years, seven months, seven days, and seven nights before it finally passes.
Those sentient beings then gather together once more and give rise to a lesser degree of weary detachment.
By this cause and condition,
the lifespan does not diminish and the calamity of famine is finally stilled.
Furthermore, when the human lifespan is twenty years, [the following occurs].
Having previously given rise to weariness and aversion, they now retreat and abandon them.
At that time, there will be much pestilence and miasmic fevers;
calamities and afflictions will arise in continuous succession.
When those sentient beings encounter these various diseases,
most of them perish.
Such a calamity of disease lasts for seven months, seven days, and seven nights before it finally passes away.
Those sentient beings again gather together and give rise to a moderate sense of weary detachment.
By virtue of this cause and condition,
their lifespan no longer diminishes, and the calamity of disease subsides.
Furthermore, when the human lifespan was ten years,
the original sense of revulsion that had arisen was now abandoned and lost.
At that time, sentient beings looked upon one another.
Each gave rise to a fierce intent to kill;
by reason of this,
they seized whatever grass, wood, tiles, or stones were at hand.
All these become extremely sharp swords and blades,
whereby they slaughter one another until they are completely exterminated.
Thus, this calamity of the swords lasts for a full seven days before it finally passes away.
5. Section on Mutual Arising. Fifth: According to the Madhyama Āgama, in the past there appeared a Wheel-Turning King named Mūrdhaja.
He upheld the precepts of the fast and practiced the giving of alms;
he provided wealth from his own treasury to support the poor within the kingdom.
After a long period of time had passed, [he continued in this way].
However, there were those in the kingdom who were poor and lacked the means to provide relief to the destitute; consequently,
the people became increasingly impoverished and distressed.
Driven by desperation, he stole another's property.
The owner caught him in the act and bound him,
then brought him before King Kṣatriya Mūrdhaja.
He said, "O Heavenly King,
this man has stolen my property."
"May the Heavenly King govern us.
The King asked that man,
"Is it true that you committed the theft?"
He replied,
"I have indeed stolen it. Why is that?"
Because of his poverty,
if he did not steal, he would have no means to support himself;
the king then provided him with wealth and gave it to him.
He said to the thieves,
"Return now and do not commit such acts again.
Because of this, people thought to themselves:
"We, too, should steal the property of others.
Thereupon, they each vied with one another to commit theft.
This is what is meant by being unable to provide relief due to poverty and the lack of possessions.
As his kinsmen became increasingly impoverished, his theft grew ever more frequent.
Consequently, that person’s lifespan decreased and his physical appearance deteriorated.
His father’s lifespan was eighty thousand years.
The son’s lifespan was forty thousand years;
the people there also had a lifespan of forty thousand years.
At that time, another person again stole [the son] and sent him to the king.
Having heard this, the king thought to himself:
"If there are those in my kingdom who steal the property of others,
and I further provide them with even more wealth until their needs are fully met, then by exhausting the treasury in this way, theft will only increase all the more."
"I shall now rather make an extremely sharp sword;
if there is anyone in my kingdom who commits theft,
I will immediately arrest them, place them beneath a high stake, and cut off their heads."
Having formed this thought, he immediately commanded it to be carried out.
Later, that man imitated him with a sharp sword and went about plundering goods.
They seize those owners and cut off their heads;
because of poverty, theft becomes extreme, and killings with the sword increase further.
Consequently, the lifespan of those people decreases and their physical appearance deteriorates.
The father’s lifespan was forty thousand years;
the son’s lifespan was twenty thousand years.
At the time when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years...
Then that thief thought to himself:
"If the king learns the truth,
he may bind and flog me."
"Whether I am banished and fined,
or impaled upon a stake,
I would rather speak falsely to deceive the king."
Having reflected thus, he said to the king:
"I did not steal. This was because of poverty and the lack of anything [to give]."
Unable to provide relief, theft and killing increased;
they then spoke falsely and engaged in double-tongued speech.
Consequently, the lifespan of those people further decreased, and their physical appearance grew increasingly foul.
The father’s lifespan was twenty thousand years;
the son’s lifespan was ten thousand years.
At the time when the human lifespan was ten thousand years...
Consequently, envy and sexual misconduct increased further;
thus, the lifespan of those people decreased and their physical appearance deteriorated.
The father’s lifespan was ten thousand years.
The lifespan of his son was five thousand years.
When the human lifespan was five thousand years,
three phenomena increased further.
Because of unrighteous desires, evil greed, and false teachings,
the father’s lifespan was five thousand years,
while the son’s lifespan was two thousand five hundred years.
When the human lifespan is two thousand five hundred years,
three further phenomena increase:
divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous speech.
Therefore, their lifespan gradually decreased and their physical form gradually deteriorated;
thus, while the father’s lifespan was two thousand five hundred years,
the son’s lifespan was one thousand years.
When the human lifespan was one thousand years,
one phenomenon increased further:
namely, false views.
Because of the increase of this one dharma,
the lifespan of those people gradually decreased and their physical appearance became increasingly degraded;
the father’s lifespan was one thousand years.
The lifespan of his son was five hundred years.
When the human lifespan was five hundred years,
those people were unfilial toward their parents.
They are unable to revere śramaṇas and brahmins;
they do not practice compliant conduct;
they do not perform meritorious deeds.
Because they do not see the retribution for their sins in future lives,
the father’s lifespan is five hundred years,
while the son’s lifespan is two hundred and fifty years.
Or two hundred years;
now, if one has a long life,
it may be a hundred years.
Or perhaps even more than that.
The Buddha again addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"In the distant future..."
When the human lifespan is ten years,
a girl is married as soon as she is five months old;
this is when the human lifespan is ten years.
There is a grain called *priyaṅgu* (millet),
which is considered the foremost of fine foods;
it is like how today people regard refined grain as the highest delicacy.
All ghee, oil, salt, honey, and sugarcane have completely vanished;
only those who practice the ten paths of unwholesome action are honored by others,
for there is no longer any goodness at all.
The mother harbors an extremely harmful intent toward her son;
the son likewise harbors an extremely harmful intent toward his mother.
This is true for fathers and sons, brothers and sisters, and all other relatives.
Turning toward one another, they harbor malicious intent,
just as a hunter, upon seeing a deer, feels an extreme desire to harm it;
this occurs when the human lifespan is ten years.
Then there will arise the flourishing Kalpa of Seven Days of Weapons; at that time,
if one seizes a blade of grass, it immediately transforms into a sword,
and if one seizes firewood, it likewise transforms into a sword.
By means of these weapons, they kill one another.
That kalpa of weapons passes in seven days, and after those seven days it ceases.
At that time, there are still people remaining.
Feeling shame, humiliation, and loathing, they will find no pleasure [in their state].

**II. The Three Great Calamities (1)** This [section] has four parts: the Part on the Measurement of Time, the Part on the Duration of Time, the Part on the Kalpa of Destruction, and the Part on the Kalpa of Formation. **I. The Part on the Measurement of Time** First, regarding the measurement of time, according to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*:
There are three kinds of kalpas:
first, the intermediate kalpa;
second, the kalpa of formation and destruction.
Regarding the three great kalpas,
the intermediate kalpas further comprise three types:
first, the kalpa of decrease.
Second, the kalpa of increase;
third, the kalpa of both increase and decrease.
As for "decrease," it refers to the period when the human lifespan decreases from an immeasurable number of years down to ten years.
The period of increase refers to when the human lifespan increases from ten years up to eighty thousand years.
The periods of increase and decrease refer to when the human lifespan increases from ten years to eighty thousand years,
and then decreases again from eighty thousand years back down to ten years.
In this context, there is one decrease and one increase;
eighteen such cycles of increase and decrease,
totaling twenty intermediate kalpas (antarakalpa), constitute the formation of the world.
The twenty intermediate kalpas during which the world has been formed and remains are collectively termed the kalpa of formation (*vivartakalpa*).
The world undergoes destruction for twenty intermediate kalpas;
having been destroyed, it remains empty for twenty intermediate kalpas.
This combined period is called the kalpa of destruction.
Altogether, eighty intermediate kalpas (antarakalpa) are collectively termed a great kalpa (mahākalpa).
Within the period of abiding after formation, there are twenty intermediate kalpas.
The first [kalpa] consists solely of decrease;
the last [kalpa] consists solely of increase;
the eighteen intermediate [kalpas] consist of both increase and decrease.
Therefore, the Abhidharma-śāstra states:
"By means of these kalpa-numbers,
the lifespans of the various devas in the Form and Formless Realms are revealed."

2. Section on Time and Seasons (Kāla-varga). Second: According to Master Xuanzang’s *Account of the Western Regions*, although the designations differ—such as the movement of the yin-yang cycles and the rotation of the sun and moon—[the underlying principle remains the same].
The seasons do not differ;
they are designated by the names of months according to the lunar mansions (nakṣatras) in which they occur.
The shortest unit of time is called a kṣaṇa.

This was the question concerning the *kṣaṇa* asked previously.
For what reason is giving cited?
Even if one were to explain it in terms of the measure of a *tatkṣaṇa*, the answer is: herein, the coarse is raised in order to illustrate the subtle.
Because it is subtle, difficult to know, and cannot be manifested—
namely, one hundred and twenty kṣaṇas constitute one tatkṣaṇa,
and sixty tatkṣaṇas constitute one lava.
This consists of seven thousand two hundred kṣaṇas.
Thirty lava constitute one muhūrta;
this consists of two hundred sixteen thousand kṣaṇas.
Thirty muhūrtas constitute one day and night;
this [day and night] contains sixty-five hundred thousand kṣaṇas, being slightly less than twenty [muhūrtas] short.
These five aggregates undergo as many instances of arising and ceasing in a single day and night; thus they are impermanent. Some say:
This coarse [measure] is not the duration of a single kṣaṇa.

for as many threads as are severed,
so many moments (kṣaṇa) elapse.
Some say this is not so.
According to my own view,
it is like two strong men pulling apart many fine threads of Kāśī silk.
Suppose there were a strong man who, with a well-tempered steel sword from the country of Cina,
could cut with such swiftness that for every single thread he cuts,

Some say: "It is still coarse and not of the measure of a moment;
the Blessed One did not speak of the actual measure of a moment."
As the Blessed One has said:
"For example, it is like four skilled archers,
each holding a bow and arrow, standing back-to-back and facing the four directions, intending to shoot at all four sides."
There was a swift man who came and said to them,
"You all may now release your arrows at once."
"I can catch them all and prevent them from falling.
What do you think? Is this not swift?"
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
"It is very swift, World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
That person does not equal the terrestrial yakṣas in speed;
the terrestrial yakṣas do not equal the celestial yakṣas in speed;
and the celestial yakṣas do not equal the gods of the Four Great Kings in speed.
The swiftness of that celestial being is not equal to that of the two wheels of the sun and moon;
the swiftness of those two wheels is not equal to that of the Devaputra Dṛḍhavrata.
Thus, he far surpasses the chariots of the solar and lunar wheels.
These various devas move with such rapid succession that the arising and ceasing of their life-span and formations are even more swift than that;
they flow from moment to moment without a single instant's pause.
From this, it is known that the Blessed One did not state the actual measure of a *kṣaṇa*.
Question: For what reason did the Blessed One not explain the actual measure of a *kṣaṇa* to others?
Answer: Because there are no sentient beings capable of knowing it.
Furthermore, the Ānāpāna-sūtra states:
"In the space of a single finger-snap, the mind undergoes nine hundred and sixty [fluctuations]."

Furthermore, the Abhidharma-śāstra contains twelve sections in total.

A day and night consist of thirty *muhūrta*s.
At the time when the days are at their longest, the daytime is eighteen [muhūrta*s] and the nighttime is twelve.

Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

At the time of the equinoxes, day and night each consist of fifteen periods (*muhūrta*).
During other times, they increase or decrease;

In the tenth month, the night consists of eighteen units and the day twelve.

According to Master Xuanzang’s *Record of the Western Regions*, the common secular tradition divides day and night into eight periods—four for the day and four for the night—and each period is further divided into four quarters. The period from the waxing moon until it is full is called the "white fortnight" (*śuklapakṣa*).
The period from the waning moon until the new moon is called the "dark fortnight" (*kṛṣṇa-pakṣa*).
It may consist of fourteen or fifteen days,
depending on whether the lunar month is short or long.
The period from the first day of the waxing moon to the last day of the waning moon constitutes one month;
six months constitute one course.
When the sun travels within [the solstitial limit], it is its northern course.
The sun’s journey outside [the central axis] is its southward course;
these two courses together constitute one year.
Furthermore, one year is divided into six seasons.
From the fifteenth day of the first month to the fifteenth day of the third month, it gradually becomes hot.
From the sixteenth day of the third month to the fifteenth day of the fifth month, it is intensely hot.
From the sixteenth day of the fifth month to the fifteenth day of the seventh month is the period of rain;
from the sixteenth day of the seventh month to the fifteenth day of the ninth month is the period of growth.
From the sixteenth day of the ninth month to the fifteenth day of the eleventh month, it gradually becomes cold.
From the sixteenth day of the eleventh month to the fifteenth day of the first month, it is intensely cold.
According to the noble teaching of the Tathāgata,
the year is divided into three seasons:
from the sixteenth day of the first month to the fifteenth day of the fifth month is the hot season.
From the sixteenth day of the fifth month to the fifteenth day of the ninth month is the rainy season;
from the sixteenth day of the ninth month to the fifteenth day of the first month is the cold season.
Alternatively, there are four seasons:
spring, summer, autumn, and winter.
This is calculated according to the treatises.
The fifteenth night constitutes one half-month;
two half-months constitute one month;
and three months constitute one season.
Two periods constitute one course;
one course is half a year, or six months.
Two courses constitute one year.
Two and a half years constitute one pair;
this is due to the intercalary month,
as the intercalary month is combined with the regular month.
This refers to the "double non-leap month" of the moon.
If one were to calculate by means of two leap months every five years,
there would be one leap month every two and a half years.
How could it stand alone?
Accumulating these periods of time, it is clear that there are four kinds of kalpas:
first, the intermediate kalpa (*antarakalpa*).
Second, the kalpa of formation;
third, the kalpa of destruction;
fourth, the great kalpa.
From a human lifespan of ten years, it gradually increases to eighty thousand years;
after remaining at eighty thousand years for a long period,
it again gradually decreases back to ten years.
It constitutes one *antarakalpa*.
It is called "specific" (*bhedaka*) in contrast to the other [kalpas], which are "general" (*sāmānya*).
If one were to calculate it by way of its actual substance:
According to the *Saṃyukta Āgama*,
a city one yojana in extent has a height and depth equal to that;
it is filled with mustard seeds, from which one seed is removed every hundred years.
Even when the mustard seeds are exhausted, the kalpa is not yet exhausted.
According to this, it constitutes a distinct kalpa (antarakalpa). If one relies on the great kalpa (mahākalpa), [the calculation is as follows].
This takes a city of eighty *yojanas* as the measure.
The *Loutan jing* (Ratnakūṭa Sūtra) states:
"One discusses *kalpas* by means of two matters."
One account states that there is a great city, one thousand *li* from east to west and four thousand *li* from north to south.
It is filled with mustard seeds; even if gods were to descend every hundred years and take away a single seed, they would not exhaust them by the end of the kalpa.
Second, it is said that there is a great rock forty *li* square.
Every hundred years, the devas descend from above;
they take fine gauze garments (*rahuvastra*) and sweep the rock, yet even after an entire kalpa has passed, it is still not exhausted.
This too must be a distinct eon (*kalpa*).
The second period of formation (*vivartakalpa*) lasts forty [eons], and the period of destruction (*saṃvartakalpa*) is likewise.
The reason for this is as follows:
When the world is forming, it takes twenty intermediate kalpas;
when it remains, it takes twenty intermediate kalpas;
and when it is being destroyed, it takes twenty intermediate kalpas.
The period of emptiness lasts for twenty intermediate kalpas (*antarakalpa*).
Within this, the period of abiding is combined with the period of emptiness, and the period of destruction is combined with the period of emptiness;
thus, each consists of forty intermediate kalpas.
Taken together, these eighty intermediate kalpas (antarakalpa) of formation and destruction constitute one great kalpa (mahākalpa).
If this is further expanded, there are another six kalpas.
First, differentiation;
second, formation;
third, abiding.
Fourth, the realm of destruction;
fifth, the realm of emptiness;
sixth, the realm of great space.
If one returns again, there are three kalpas:
first, the small kalpa;
second, the intermediate kalpa.
There are three types of kalpas:
the small is the *antarakalpa* (intermediate kalpa); the medium consists of either the period of formation (*vivartakalpa*) or the period of destruction (*saṃvartakalpa*).
On a grand scale, this encompasses both formation and destruction.
Within the Desire Realm, a lifespan of one kalpa constitutes a minor kalpa (antarakalpa).
In the first dhyāna, the lifespans of the three heavens constitute a middle kalpa (madhyakalpa).
From the second dhyāna upward, a kalpa of lifespan refers to a *mahākalpa*.
According to the secular calculations of foreign lands, there are sixty numerical positions;
beyond these, it can no longer be counted.
It is named asaṃkhyeya.
This number of years constitutes the calculation of kalpas;
from one up to sixty positions, it is called an asaṃkhyeya-kalpa.
This is the measure of a great kalpa (*mahākalpa*).
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that a city of one hundred yojanas is used as the standard of measurement.
Taking a single mustard seed once every hundred years,
it is therefore compared to a kāśī garment of the gods,
which is brushed once every hundred years.
Regarding the measurement of a hundred *yojanas* in stone,
these are all scales for measuring *mahākalpas*.
Specifically, according to the Sahā world (formerly called the Saha world), one thousand Buddhas appear in the course of one *mahākalpa*.
Now, as for the designation "kalpa," it cannot be measured by ordinary units of time;
therefore, it is illustrated through metaphors such as the rubbing away of a stone by a wisp of grass or the destruction of a mustard-seed city.
This is established as the duration of one period;
specifically, it refers to the aforementioned intermediate cycle which fully encompasses the four kalpas of formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness.
As previously described, [the lifespan] increases from ten years up to eighty thousand years.
Furthermore, from eighty thousand years down to ten years,
twenty such cycles constitute one minor kalpa (*antarakalpa*).
Twenty minor kalpas constitute one formation kalpa (*vivartakalpa*).
Calculated by years, this constitutes eight quadrillion, one hundred trillion, eight million years;
this duration alone constitutes one minor kalpa (*antarakalpa*).
Now, the kalpa of formation (*vivartakalpa*) has already passed, and we have entered and abide in the kalpa of endurance (*vivṛttasthāyikalpa*).
After another eight intermediate kalpas,
Śākyamuni Tathāgata will be the fourth Buddha during this abiding kalpa;
nine hundred and ninety-six Buddhas still remain.
It subsequently emerges in the following order.
According to Master Xuanzang’s *Account of the Western Regions*,
regarding the designation for distance and quantity known as *yojana* (formerly translated as *youxun*):
It is also called *yojana*,
and it is also called *youyan*;
both are erroneous abbreviations of *yojanana*.
Since ancient times, it has been the practice of sage-kings to travel one *yojana* in a single day.
According to old traditions, one *yojana* is forty *li*;
however, according to the local custom of the Indian country, it is thirty *li*.
According to the determination of the Noble Teachings, it is exactly sixteen *li*.
Therefore, the Abhidharma-śāstra states that four cubits (*hasta*) constitute one bow (*dhanus*).
Five hundred bows constitute one *krośa*;
eight *krośas* constitute one *yojana*.
One bow is eight feet in length.
Five hundred *dhanus* (bows) in length equal four hundred *zhang*.
Four hundred *zhang* constitute one *krośa*.
One *li* consists of three hundred and sixty paces.
One step measures six chi;
together, two hundred and sixteen zhang constitute one li.
Two li consist of four hundred and thirty-two zhang.
Calculating that five hundred bows equal four hundred *zhang*, this constitutes one *krośa*.
This still falls short by thirty-two *zhang*, not reaching two *li*.
Thus, one *krośa* is calculated as being less than two *li*.
A total of eight *krośas* minus sixteen *li* constitutes one *yojana*.
According to the *Saṃyukta-ratna-piṭaka-sūtra*,
one *krośa* consists of five *li*.
According to the Abhidharma, eight *krośas* constitute one *yojana*, which amounts to forty *li*. Section Three:
The Period of Destruction (*saṃvarta-kalpa*). Based on the *Dīrgha Āgama*, it says:
What is the upper limit of the three calamities?
When the calamity of fire arises,
its limit extends as far as the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
When the time for the calamity of water arrives,
it extends as far as the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven;
when the calamity of wind arises, it likewise extends that far.
Reaching as far as the Fruit-Bearing Heaven (Bṛhatphala),
when the three calamities are about to arise,
the people of the world all practice the True Dharma.
With right view and unerring cultivation of the ten wholesome actions,
when practicing this Dharma, there were those who attained the second dhyāna;
they immediately rose valiantly into the air.
Abiding on the path of the noble ones,
the devas and brahmās cried out in a loud voice: "Virtuous ones,
you should know that the bliss of the second dhyāna, which is without directed thought and without sustained evaluation, belongs to such a person."
Having heard this sound, they immediately cultivated a state free from applied and sustained thought;
upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, they were reborn in the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
At that time, the beings in hell, their retribution exhausted, died and were reborn in the human realm.
Furthermore, by practicing further without vitarka and vicāra,
one attains birth in the Ābhāsvara Heaven;
[likewise] among animals, hungry ghosts, asuras, and even those in the six heavens of the desire realm.
All were reborn in the Ābhāsvara Heaven; at that time, the hells were first emptied,
followed by the animals, and then, in succession,
the hungry ghosts, asuras, and so on, up to the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, were all emptied.
Thereafter, no person remains without exception;
this world is destroyed and thus becomes a calamity.
Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
When not a single sentient being remains in hell,
at that time it is said that hell has been destroyed.
This applies to all those who possess karma for the hells that is fixed to be experienced.
By the power of karma, they are placed in the hells of other directions;
by this analogy, one should understand the realms of animals and hungry ghosts.
At that time, there were no worms within the human body comparable to those in the Buddha’s body.
At that time, when a single person among the human beings of this continent, without a teacher, spontaneously attains the first dhyāna through the nature of reality itself,
they emerge from that dhyāna and utter these words:
"The joy and bliss born of seclusion are exceedingly pleasant and exceedingly tranquil."
Upon hearing this, all other people entered meditative absorption;
when their lives ended, they were all reborn in the Brahma-world until the sentient beings of this continent had completely perished.
These are called those who have already perished in Jambudvīpa.
The two continents to the east and west should be explained by analogy with this.
Those in the northern continent, when their lives end, are reborn in the heavens of the desire realm.
Because those of dull faculties have not yet abandoned desire,
once they are born among the gods of the desire realm, they must first bring meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) into manifestation and attain a superior basis before they are able to abandon desire.
When there is not even a single sentient being remaining in the human realm,
it is said that the human realm has been destroyed.
If, among the celestial realms, any one of the six heavens of the desire realm should, by the natural course of things, attain the first dhyāna;
Eventually, they all attain rebirth in the Brahma-world;
at that time, it is said that the desire-realm heavens have been destroyed.
Thus, not a single sentient being remains in the desire realm.
It is said that sentient beings in the desire realm have already perished.
At that time, when a certain sentient being in the Brahma-world, without a teacher, spontaneously attains the second dhyāna through the nature of things (dharmatā),
he arises from that meditative absorption and utters these words:
The joy and bliss born of concentration are exceedingly pleasant and profoundly tranquil.
Upon hearing this, all the other devas entered that meditative absorption;
when their lives ended, they were all reborn in the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
Until all sentient beings in the Brahma world have completely perished—
this is called the destruction of the world of sentient beings;
only the vessel world remains, vast and empty.
When the karma of all sentient beings in other world-systems that causes them to experience this trichiliocosm is exhausted,
seven sun disks gradually appear here.
All the oceans dry up and the mountain caves blaze forth.
The continents, the islands, and the three wheels were all consumed by the flames.
The fierce fire, driven by the wind, burned upward into the celestial palaces,
until even the Brahma palaces were reduced to nothing but ashes and embers.
The flames of its own level burn the palaces of its own level;
a calamity of another level cannot destroy that of another level.
This statement is made because they are produced by way of their mutual characteristics.
The fire below and the wind blowing from below incinerate the upper realms;
that is to say, the fierce flames of the fire of the desire realm rise upward,
acting as the condition that draws forth the form realm.
The flames and the other calamities are likewise;
they should be understood accordingly.
In this manner, beginning from the gradual reduction of the hells up until the exhaustion of the receptacle world, it is collectively termed the kalpa of destruction (*saṃvarta-kalpa*).
Furthermore, the *Buddhabhāṣita-buddhanusmṛti-samādhi-sūtra* states:
The beginning and end of heaven and earth is called one kalpa.
When the kalpa reaches its end and is destroyed, the calamity of fire is about to arise.
All people turn their backs on the right and face toward the wrong, vying with one another to commit the ten non-virtuous actions.
For a long time there was no rain, so that what was sown did not grow.
The springs and sources, even down to the four great swift rivers, were all completely exhausted.
After a very long time, the wind entered the bottom of the ocean.
It takes up the great city-walls of the sun and places them within the original path on the side of Mount Sumeru. The *Dīrgha Āgama* states:
"Thereafter, after a long time, a great black windstorm arises from the waters of the ocean."
It blows with a depth of eighty-four thousand yojanas, causing [the waters] to part in two.
It takes the sun palace and places it halfway up Mount Sumeru,
at a distance of forty-two thousand yojanas from the earth, within the sun's orbit.
The ritual procedures for taking [the substances] sequentially over the course of up to seven days are likewise the same.
The *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā* states:
"At the time of the destruction of the kalpa, seven suns appear and dwell upon Mount Yugandhara; from there they depart."
Furthermore, it is said that one day is divided into seven days;
it is also said that...
From the Avīci Hell, the sun descends and emerges.
By the power of the karma of sentient beings, when the first sun appears, all the hundred-grass plants and trees wither and fall simultaneously.
When the second sun appears, the waters of the four great oceans recede from within a range of one hundred *yojanas* up to seven hundred *yojanas*.
That water naturally dries up and vanishes.
When the three suns appear, the waters within the four great oceans,
from a depth of one thousand yojanas up to seven thousand yojanas, gradually evaporate until they are completely exhausted.
When four suns appear, the four great oceans, which are one thousand *yojanas* deep, [dry up].
When five suns appear, the four great oceans, which are seven thousand *yojanas* in length and breadth, are completely exhausted. Thus it is said in the *Dīrgha Āgama*.
After the fifth sun has arisen, the waters of the ocean subsequently deepen further, becoming like the water in a cow’s footprint after a spring rain;
they eventually dry up entirely so that they no longer moisten human bodies. When the sixth sun appears, this earth is sixty-eight thousand yojanas thick.
Smoke issued from them all,
reaching from Mount Sumeru throughout the trichiliocosm,
so that not a single one of the eight great hells was not consumed by fire.
When the smoke has vanished without remainder,
the lives of the people come to an end;
they all rely upon Mount Sumeru and the various devas of the six desire realms.
All have reached the end of their lives, and the palaces are entirely empty;
all things are impermanent and cannot endure for long.
When seven suns appear, the great earth and Mount Sumeru gradually crumble away for hundreds of thousands of yojanas.
Nothing remained behind;
the mountains were all completely incinerated,
and the various jewels burst apart.
The smoke and flames shook and reached as far as the Brahma Heaven.
All evil realms were completely cleansed away;
their transgressions ended and blessings arrived.
They all gathered in the fifteenth heaven above;
from the fourteenth heaven downward, everything was completely reduced to ashes and ink.
The newly born devaputra had never before seen such a sight.
All those who were filled with fear were universally comforted; the elder-born devas each came to console them,
saying, "Do not give way to terror."
They never reached this point;
when their lives ended, these people were reborn in the Ābhāsvara Heaven,
where they subsist on the food of mindfulness.
They illuminate themselves with light and travel through the air by means of supernatural power;
they may be reborn in other lands,
or if they are reborn in hell.
When their retribution for hellish offenses is completed, they are also reborn in the heavens;
if their offenses are not yet finished, they are transferred to other regions.
There, there are no sun, moon, or stars, nor is there day or night.
There is only a great darkness called the fire kalpa;
the karmic retribution of the fire calamity brings about this destruction.
When the kalpa is about to be formed, the fire then extinguishes itself.
Furthermore, great clouds arose and gradually released a heavy rain,
with drops as large as chariot axles;
at that time, this trichiliocosm world-system [was inundated].
Water pervades its interior, even up to the Brahma-heaven.
Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"Furthermore, it is due to the predominant power of the karma capable of destroying [the world] of all sentient beings."
Furthermore, due to six kinds of objects to be consumed by fire,
six additional sun-discs appear in succession. These various sun-discs,
compared to the original sun-disc, [are progressively larger].
The intensity of all the heat exceeds that of the previous [levels] fourfold.
Once the seventh has been formed, the heat consequently increases sevenfold.
What are called the six things burned?
The small and large ditches and pits are dried up by the second sun; likewise,
the small and large rivers.
By the third sun, the three great Anavatapta lakes are dried up;
by the fourth sun, [the oceans are dried up].
The four great oceans are dried up by the fifth sun and a portion of the sixth; however,
because the five Sumeru mountains and the substance of the great earth are firm and solid, they remain.
Burned by a portion of the sixth sun and the seventh solar disk,
these very flames, fanned by the wind,
spread and blaze ever more intensely until they reach the Brahma-world.
When these worlds have all been thus consumed by fire,
such that even ashes, soot, and any remaining traces cannot be found,
this is called the destruction of the receptacle world.
It remains satisfied for twenty intermediate kalpas.
Having thus been destroyed, it remains in that state for another twenty intermediate kalpas.
What is the calamity of water?
This means that after seven calamities of fire have passed, there arises simultaneously within the second dhyāna a water element that destroys the receptacle world, just as water dissolves salt.
This water element and the receptacle world both perish at the same time.
Having thus dissolved, it remains for another twenty intermediate kalpas.
What is the calamity of wind?
It occurs when seven calamities of water have passed, followed by seven calamities of fire.
Immediately following this, within the third dhyāna,
there arises a co-emergent wind element that destroys the receptacle world, just as the wind dries out the limbs and joints,
and further causes them to be utterly consumed.
This wind element and the receptacle world perish simultaneously.
Once this destruction has occurred, the world remains in a state of dissolution for twenty intermediate kalpas.
Thus, in brief, the destruction of the world has been described.
Furthermore, according to the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*:
"When these three great calamities of water, fire, and wind arise and oppress sentient beings,
they cause them to abandon their lower realms and gather in the higher heavens."
Regarding the initial arising of the fire calamity, it is said to be caused by the appearance of seven suns.
It is further explained that these seven solar disks travel like a flight of geese, revolving along diverging paths.
Some explain it in this way.
The sun's wheel moves up and down as it traverses its paths, revolving in its course;
the intervals between these paths are each five thousand yojanas apart.
Subsequently, the calamity of water arises through the falling of torrential rain.
Some say that from the void at the edge of the third dhyāna,
hot ash-water suddenly rains down.
Others further say:
from the water-wheel below, surging and boiling waters rise upward, flooding and submerging;
that which is definitively produced is precisely at this edge.
Subsequently, when the calamity of wind arises, it is caused by winds striking one another. Regarding this,
some say that the wind suddenly surges and blows forth from the space at the boundary of the fourth dhyāna.
Others further explain that from the lower wind-circle, the striking winds arise and surge upward, tossing and buffeting;
this is the definitive meaning.
It should be understood as previously explained.
Regarding the sequence in which the three calamities arise:
first, there must be a question concerning the occurrence of seven calamities by fire.
Next, it is certain that one water disaster must arise;
immediately following this, there are again seven fire disasters.
After passing through seven fire disasters, there is once more one water disaster.
In this manner, up until seven calamities of water have been completed,
there again arise seven calamities of fire, followed by a calamity of wind. Thus, in total,
there occur eight cycles of seven calamities of fire, one cycle of seven calamities of water, and one calamity of wind.
The calamities of water and wind arise immediately following the calamity of fire;
after a calamity of water or wind, a calamity of fire must necessarily arise.
Therefore, the principle of the sequence of these calamities must indeed be so.
For what reason do seven fires occur before one water disaster?
It is due to the power of the lifespan of the Ābhāsvara Heaven;
that is to say, their lifespan extends to eight great kalpas.
Therefore, it is only upon reaching the eighth [cycle] that there is a single water disaster.
From this, one should know that it requires passing through seven water disasters and eight cycles of seven fire disasters before there is then a single wind disaster.
Due to the power of the lifespan of the Śubhakṛtsna devas—
meaning their lifespan is sixty-four kalpas—
an eighth wind disaster occurs at the end of every eight intermediate kalpas.
Just as sentient beings, through their cultivation of meditative concentration, gradually become more advanced,
the physical bodies and lifespans resulting from that maturation (vipāka) gradually increase;
consequently, the environments in which they dwell also endure for longer periods.
Therefore, a verse in the Abhidharma-śāstra says:
Seven fires pass in succession, followed by one water disaster;
seven times seven fires and seven waters, and after another seven fires, there is wind.
Furthermore, the Abhidharma-śāstra states:
"In this manner, to the east, there are immeasurable worlds, continuous and uninterrupted."
Some are about to disintegrate;
some are about to form;
some are in the process of disintegrating.
Some abide after having been destroyed;
some are currently being formed;
and some abide after having been formed.
As it is in the eastern direction,
so it is likewise in all the ten directions.
Thus, whether it be the world of sentient beings or the receptacle world.
Because they are produced by the power of karma and afflictions,
and because they arise through the predominance of karma and afflictions,
they are collectively termed the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).
Furthermore, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā* asks:
"For what reason does the kalpa of destruction not reach the fourth dhyāna?
It answers: "Because of the Śuddhāvāsa deities."
Because one who is born in that unsurpassed stage attains parinirvāṇa right there,
they do not descend to lower stages; for those lower stages are not subject to analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
Nor is it the case that those who dwell there remain for the duration of a kalpa of destruction;
for they are born in that place by the power of superior merit,
and because internal disturbances do not exist there.
If there is internal disturbance within that stage, then there will be external calamities.
Within the first dhyāna, there is vitarka and vicāra;
because these are disturbances akin to fire.

Because the second dhyāna is disturbed internally by the water of joy, it is externally swept away by the calamity of water. Because the first dhyāna is disturbed internally by the fire of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), it is externally consumed by the calamity of fire. Because the third dhyāna is disturbed internally by the wind of inhalation and exhalation (*āśvāsa-praśvāsa*), it is externally destroyed by the calamity of wind. Thus, these three dhyānas are each destroyed by their respective external calamities corresponding to their internal disturbances. Furthermore, because the fourth dhyāna is free from such internal disturbances, it is not destroyed by external calamities. Therefore, it is said that the fourth dhyāna is "unshakable" (*akopya*). Because the third dhyāna contains the internal wind of inhalation and exhalation which causes disturbance, it is destroyed externally by the calamity of wind.
One might ask: why is the fourth dhyāna never subject to such disturbance?
How can it not be impermanent?
Answer: Because it is destroyed by momentary impermanence (*kṣaṇānityatā*).
The stage of the fourth dhyāna does not possess a fixed continuity.
The celestial palaces arise simultaneously with those gods;
when the life of a god ends, they likewise perish together.
Section Four: The Kalpa of Formation. According to the *Lokadhātunirdeśa-sūtra*:
At that time, after further immeasurable, vast, and incalculable days and months had passed,
great heavy clouds arose,
eventually covering the entire world-system of the Brahma heavens.
Having completely covered [the world], it pours down a great torrential rain;
its drops are exceedingly coarse,
some as large as chariot axles.
Or again, it may be like a pestle;
after passing through hundreds of thousands of millions of years,
that mass of rainwater gradually increases until the waters completely fill the world where the gods dwell.
However, that mass of water is sustained by four wind-circles. What are these four?
The first is named "Abiding."
The second is named Abiding;
the third, Non-falling;
and the fourth, Firm Lord.
Once that rain has ceased, it recedes of its own accord,
descending for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of yojanas.
At that time, great winds arise simultaneously from the four directions.
That wind is named Anābila; it blows upon that mass of water,
churning it incessantly, and within the water,
great masses of foam spontaneously arise.
A great wind blew the foam and cast it into the air;
from above, it fashioned the palaces of the Brahmā Heaven,
exquisite and lovely, composed of the seven precious gems interspersed.
That is to say, gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, red pearls, conch shells, and agate—
such things as these are produced in this Brahma-world.
That great mass of water then recedes further by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of yojanas.
As before, winds arising from the four directions are named Anābila;
by these great winds blowing and tossing the water-foam, palaces are further formed.
The walls and enclosures of the Māra-body devas abide like those of the Brahmakāyika devas, without any difference.
They differ only in that some possess the color of jewels while others do not, and in their degree of refinement or coarseness.
In this manner, one successively creates the Heaven of Control over Others' Emanations,
proceeding in turn down to the Yāma Heaven.
The six heavens are successively complete and no different from the Brahma Heaven, differing only in their degree of refinement or coarseness.
At that time, that mass of water further diminishes,
receding by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of *yojanas*.
It remains perfectly still and serene.
Within that mass of water, foam floats on all four sides, six hundred and eighty million *yojanas* thick upon the surface,
with an immeasurable circumference.
A great wind blows the foam and further creates Mount Sumeru, which is composed of four precious substances;
it further blows the floating foam upon the water to create the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, which is composed of seven precious substances.
Furthermore, it blows upon the foam of the waters at an altitude of forty-two thousand yojanas on the mid-slope of Mount Sumeru,
forming the palaces of the Sun and Moon Devas, all of which are composed of the seven precious gems.
By these causes and conditions,
there came to exist in the world seven sun-palaces abiding in the present.
Furthermore, they blew the water-foam onto the surface of the ocean to a height of ten thousand yojanas.
For the sake of the *khecaras* (sky-dwelling) yakṣas, he likewise creates crystal palaces and city walls.
Furthermore, he blows the water-foam onto the four sides of Mount Sumeru,
each at a distance of one thousand *yojanas* from the mountain.
Beneath the great ocean, there is a four-sided city of asuras adorned with the seven treasures.
Furthermore, a great wind blows upon the water, gathering the foam to create other great jewel mountains.
In this manner, the wind successively blows the water-foam beyond the four great continents, the eighty thousand small islands, and Sumeru, the king of mountains,
as well as all other great mountains, placing it in a surrounding encircling array outside them.
It is named Mount Mahācakravāḍa.
It is six million eight hundred thousand billion yojanas in height and breadth,
equal in all dimensions, firm and solid.
Formed of vajra and thus difficult to destroy,
this great wind blows upon and excavates the great earth, gradually penetrating deep within it,
until there is placed therein a vast mass of water, clear, still, and accumulated.
By these causes and conditions, there comes to be the great ocean.
Furthermore, the *Qishi jing* (Sūtra on the Arising of the World) says:
"As for this water of the great ocean..."
For what reason is it so salty and bitter as to be unfit for food and drink?
There are three causes and conditions for this.
What are the three? First,
after the destruction by fire has passed through immeasurable time,
great heavy clouds arise, spreading over and remaining densely gathered.
Afterwards, rain falls in torrents, filling the world.
That great downpour washes all the palaces of the Brahmakāyika devas,
and next washes the palaces of the Brahmapurohita devas.
Next, he washes the palaces of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin, Nirmāṇarati, Tuṣita, and Yāma heavens.
When those palaces are washed, all salty, pungent, and bitter flavors flow downward.
Next, he further washes Mount Sumeru, the four great continents, the eighty thousand minor continents, and all other great mountains.
When washing in this manner, they are submerged, drenched, and swept away within it.
For this reason, the waters of the great ocean are salty and unfit for drinking or eating.
Second, there are great beings with immense bodies who dwell within these waters of the great ocean.
All excrement and urine flow into the ocean;
for this reason, its water is salty and bitter, unfit for drinking or eating.
Thirdly, it is because in ancient times various sages once cast spells upon this great ocean water.
It is said that the ocean attained its salty taste, becoming unfit for consumption, due to this very cause;
it was by these conditions that the great ocean became saline and unfit for food or drink.
Furthermore, according to the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*:
What is called the kalpa of formation refers to the period from the arising of the wind until sentient beings first begin to be born in the hells.
This means that once this world has been destroyed by the calamities,
there remains only empty space for twenty intermediate kalpas;
after this long period has passed, there must subsequently again be a period of equal duration for the world’s formation and abiding.
When the kalpa of formation arrives, through the predominant power of the karma of all sentient beings,
subtle winds gradually arise in space;
this is the preliminary sign that the receptacle world is about to be formed.
The wind gradually increases in intensity, forming the wind-circle, water-circle, gold-circle, and so forth, as previously described.
However, when first establishing the palaces of the Great Brahma Heaven up to those of the Yāma Heaven, another wind-circle and the like arise once more.
This is called the establishment of the external receptacle world through the power of sentient beings; that is to say,
it is established by the long-accumulated power of sentient beings in the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
Since the celestial hosts are so numerous and their dwellings are cramped,
those whose merits have diminished should disperse and reside in the lower regions.
At the very beginning of this receptacle world,
a single sentient being passed away from the Ābhāsvara realm and was born within an empty palace in the Great Brahmā abode;
subsequently, other sentient beings also passed away from that same place and were born among the Brahmapurohitas.
