It issues from the Horse’s Mouth and flows through five hundred tributaries into the western sea.
To the north of the lake is the Sītā River,
which issues from the elephant’s mouth and flows through five hundred rivers into the Northern Ocean.
According to Master Xuanzang’s *Record of the Western Regions*,
the central land of Jambudvīpa is Lake Anavatapta (translated into Chinese as "Without Heat");
the old name "Lake Anouda" is a corruption.
It lies south of Mount Gandhamādana and north of the Great Snow Mountains (Himavat),
measuring eight hundred *li* in circumference;
its shores are adorned with gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal.
Golden sands spread everywhere as the clear waves mirror the sky;
by the power of their vows, Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages transform themselves into dragon kings.
Within it lies a hidden dwelling that produces clear, cold water belonging to Jambudvīpa.

Thus, from the silver ox-mouth on the eastern side of the lake flows the Gaṅgā River (formerly called the *Héng Hé*; "Héngjiā" is a corruption), which circles the lake once and enters the southeastern ocean.

From the golden elephant’s mouth on the southern side of the lake flows the Indus River (formerly called the Sindhu River, which is an error), which circles the lake once and enters the southwestern ocean.

From the lapis lazuli horse’s mouth on the western side of the lake flows the Vakṣu River (formerly called the Pakṣu River, which is an error), which circles the lake once and enters the northwestern ocean.

From the lion’s mouth made of crystal on the northern side of the lake flows the Sītā River (formerly called the Xītuó River, which is an error), which circles the lake once and enters the North Sea in the east.
Some say that it flows secretly through the lower realms and emerges from Mount Jishishan (Jyekundo),
where it becomes the current of the Tāo River.
It is the source of the rivers of the Middle Kingdom.
At this time, as no Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin) has appeared to guide the world,
the land of Jambudvīpa is divided among four rulers.
The southern Elephant Lord is warm and hot, suitable for elephants;
the western Treasure Lord borders the sea and abounds in treasures;
the northern Horse Lord is cold and biting, suitable for horses.
The people of the East are harmonious and expansive, and their numbers are great;
thus, the land ruled by the Elephant Lord is characterized by impetuous intensity, yet its inhabitants are devoted to learning and exceptionally skilled in extraordinary arts.
In the region ruled by the Jewel Lord, there is a lack of ritual propriety and righteousness, and they value wealth and bribes above all else.
The customs of the lords of horses are naturally fierce and violent, their dispositions being accustomed to slaughter.
The customs of the lords of men are characterized by sagacity and wisdom, with benevolence and righteousness clearly manifest.
Among the customs of these four lords, those of the East are supreme.
As for his residence, its door opens to the east;
he performs his obeisance facing east during the day.
In the domain of the sovereign, the south-facing position is held as the most honorable.
The diverse customs and differing traditions of various regions constitute the general outline;
as for the rites governing the relationship between sovereign and subject, superior and subordinate,
as well as the ceremonial protocols of laws, statutes, literary culture, and administrative systems.
There is nothing that surpasses the domain of the sovereign:
the instruction on purifying the mind and relinquishing burdens,
and the reckoning of transcending birth and death.
The governance of the Land of the Elephant Lord is excellent;
all of this is recorded in the scriptures and heard from the local customs.
Having extensively familiarized myself with antiquity and the present, and having carefully examined all that I have seen and heard,
I observe that while the Buddha arose in the West, the Dharma flowed to the Eastern lands;
yet in the process of translation, sounds became corrupted and dialects led to errors in expression.
If sounds are corrupted, the meaning is lost;
if words are erroneous, the principle is deviated from.
Therefore it is said:
"It must be that names are correctly established;
this is to ensure there is no contradiction or error.
Furthermore, the *Utpatti-sāgara-sūtra* (Qishi jing) states:
Within the palace of Anavatapta, there is a hall with five pillars.
The Naga King Anavatapta constantly dwells therein.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
For what reason is he named Anavatapta? What is its meaning?
All the dragon kings (nāgarāja) in this Jambudvīpa have three afflictions.
Only the Anavatapta Dragon is free from the three afflictions.
What are these three?

First, all other dragons are afflicted by hot winds and hot sands that strike their bodies, burning their skin and flesh and even burning through their marrow, causing them great suffering and distress.
Only the Anavatapta Dragon is free from these afflictions.
Second, whenever fierce winds suddenly arise within any dragon palace,
they blow through the interior, scattering precious ornaments and garments.
The dragon bodies manifest themselves as a source of suffering and distress;
only the Dragon King Anavatapta is free from such affliction.
Third, when all other dragon kings are each within their palaces enjoying themselves, [the Dragon King Anavatapta is not].
The great golden-winged bird enters the palace to seize and snatch them;
or, having just begun to employ skillful means to capture the nāgas for food,
the nāgas are struck with terror and constantly harbor burning anguish.
Only the Anavatapta Dragon is free from such affliction;
if the King of the Garuḍas conceives the thought of going there, his life immediately comes to an end.
Therefore, he is named Anavatapta.
"Anavatapta" means "Free from Affliction" in the language of Qin. The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"On the right side of the Snowy Mountains there is a city named Kāpiśī.
To the north of that city are seven Black Mountains."
To the north of Mount Kṛṣṇa is Mount Gandhamādana.
This mountain is constantly filled with the sounds of singing, dancing, theatrical performances, and music.
On the mountain are two caves.
The first is named Kṣaya (Exhaustion),
and the second is named Sukhakṣaya (Excellent Exhaustion).
It is composed of the seven treasures of the devas.
It was soft, fragrant, and pure, like a celestial robe.
The Gandharva King Subhāṣitaghoṣa dwelt therein with five hundred gandharvas.
Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
"Among the four continents, only Jambudvīpa possesses the Vajrāsana,
which reaches the surface of the earth above and rests upon the golden wheel below."
All Bodhisattvas in their final existence,
who are about to ascend to unsurpassed, perfect,
and complete enlightenment, sit upon this seat and enter the vajra-samādhi.
By means of the power of firmness residing in the state of nirvana without remainder, as well as in the state with remainder and other locations, one is able to sustain this seat.
Furthermore, the *Dīrgha Āgama* states:
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
There are four great deities. What are the four?
The first is the Earth Deity.
Second is the water deity;
third is the wind deity;
fourth is the fire deity.
Since these four great elements are common to all,
the Earth Deity gave rise to a false view and said:
Within the earth there is no water, fire, or wind.
At that time, I knew what this earth deity was thinking,
so I went to her and spoke.
"Have you ever had the thought that within earth there is no water, fire, or wind?
He replied, "Within earth there is indeed no water, fire, or wind.
At that time, I spoke these words:
Do not give rise to this thought, thinking that within earth there are no water, fire, or wind.
Why is this? Because within earth there are water, fire, and wind.
However, because the earth element is predominant, it receives the name "earth.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus,
"I am that earth deity."
He removed their evil views, instructing, encouraging, benefiting, and gladdening them, so that they attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
Within water there are earth, fire, and wind;
within fire there are earth, water, and wind.
Within wind there are earth, water, and fire;
however, because the former is predominant, it is merely designated by that name.
Section Five: The Measurement of the Elements. According to the *Lokasthāna-abhidharma-śāstra*:
Beyond the Great Salt Ocean there is a mountain named Cakravāḍa (Iron Ring).
It enters the water to a depth of three hundred and twelve yojanas and a half.
It is the same for the emergence from the water.
Its breadth is likewise thus:
it is thirty-six hundred million, ten thousand, three hundred and fifty yojanas in circumference.
From the southern limit of Jambudvīpa to the Cakravāḍa Mountains is three hundred and sixty million, six thousand, six hundred and sixty-three yojanas.
From the center of Jambudvīpa to the center of Pūrvavideha is [the same distance].

Three hundred and sixty million six hundred thousand yojanas from the center of Jambudvīpa to the center of Aparagoyānī; three hundred and sixty million six hundred thousand yojanas [from the center of Jambudvīpa to the center of Pūrvavideha].
From the northern limit of Jambudvīpa to the northern limit of Uttarakuru is four hundred and seven million seven thousand five hundred yojanas.
From the edge of the waters of the Cakravāḍa mountains in the east to the distant edge of the waters of the Cakravāḍa mountains in the west is the same distance.

The circumference of the Iron Ring Mountains (Cakravāḍa) at the edge of the waters is twelve hundred and twenty-eight million two hundred and twenty-five yojanas; the circumference of the mountain itself is thirty-six hundred and eighty-four million seven hundred and seventy-five yojanas.
From the summit of this Mount Sumeru to the edge of the summit of that Mount Sumeru,
it is twelve billion three hundred and forty-five *yojanas*.
From the center of this Mount Sumeru to the center of that Mount Sumeru, it is likewise.
It is twelve hundred and eight thousand three hundred and forty-five *yojanas* from the base of this Mount Sumeru to the base of that Mount Sumeru;
it is twelve hundred and three thousand fifteen *yojanas*.
Regarding this meaning, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, spoke based on the *Dīrgha Āgama*, saying:
"Jambudvīpa is seven thousand yojanas in length and breadth."
Aparagoyānīya: its land is eight thousand yojanas in length and breadth. Pūrvavideha: its land is nine thousand yojanas in length and breadth.
Uttarakuru: [its land is ten thousand yojanas in length and breadth].
That land is ten thousand yojanas in length and breadth.
Section Six: On the Regions. Generally speaking, there are two types of regional characteristics among the various peoples.
There are two types: ordinary beings and sages.
If categorized according to direction, there are four kinds, namely the people of the four continents.
If we speak in terms of dwelling places,
there are four thousand eight locations throughout the four continents, and thus there are four thousand eight types of people.
If we consider only one direction, Jambudvīpa, directly:
As stated in the *Loutan jing* (Ratnāvalī-sūtra),
there are likewise thirty-six people in total for the great kingdoms.
If discussed in detail, however, there are two thousand five hundred small kingdoms.
Human beings are likewise the same.
Furthermore, within each individual country there are various types of people:
Hu, Han, Qiang, Lu, Man, Yi, Chu, and Yue.
Each varies according to the color and type of its respective region;
it is impossible to describe them all in detail.
Thus, the *Loutan jing* (Lokadhātuprajñapti-sūtra) says:
In this Jambudvīpa, there are a total of six thousand four hundred distinct types of human beings;
however, this merely indicates the general number without specifying their individual names.
As stated in the *Dīrgha Āgama*:
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Outside these four continents, there are eight thousand continents surrounding them;
furthermore, a great ocean of water completely encircles those eight thousand continents."
Furthermore, there is a great Vajra Mountain encircling the waters of the great ocean.
Outside this Vajra Mountain is a second great Vajra Mountain.
Between these two mountains, it is profound and pitch-black.
The divine deities of the sun and moon possess great power,
yet they cannot cause their light to reach those eight great hells.
First, as for Uttarakuru in the north:
According to the *Dīrgha Āgama*,
to the north of Mount Sumeru, beneath the heavens, lies the land of Uttarakuru.
That territory is square in shape, measuring ten thousand yojanas in length and breadth.
The human faces are also square.
Resembling the shape of that land, there is a great king of trees named Āmra.
Its circumference is seven yojanas,
its height is one hundred yojanas,
and its branches and foliage extend fifty yojanas in all directions.
There are many mountains and bathing pools,
with flowers and fruits growing in lush abundance;
countless birds sing together in harmony.
The ground grows soft grass that coils and spirals to the right;
its color is like that of a peacock’s throat,
and its fragrance is like that of the vārṣika flower.
It is as soft as celestial garments;
the ground is so supple that when one treads upon it with the foot,
it sinks down four inches.
As soon as he lifts his foot, it returns to its original place;
the ground is level like the palm of a hand, without any elevations or depressions.
On the four sides of that land, there are four Anavatapta lakes.
Each is one hundred yojanas in length and breadth;
from them, four great rivers emerge, paved with the seven treasures,
each ten yojanas in width.
The various birds sing in harmony.
That land has no ditches, pits, thorns, stumps, or brushwood;
nor does it have mosquitoes, gadflies, or venomous insects.
The ground is composed entirely of various precious jewels;
the yin and yang are harmoniously regulated, and the four seasons are in accord.
A hundred grasses grow perpetually, with no distinction between winter and summer.
In that land, there is always natural non-glutinous rice that grows spontaneously without being sown;
it is free of husks and chaff, like a cluster of white flowers,
and its many flavors are as fully perfected as the food of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
In that land, there are always natural cauldrons.
There is a maṇi jewel named Flame-Light;
when it is placed beneath the cauldron, the light extinguishes once the rice is cooked.
It requires neither firewood nor human labor.
On its soil grows a tree named Qugong (Bending).
The leaves overlap one another so that the heavens do not leak rain;
men and women dwell beneath them.
Furthermore, there are fragrant trees seventy li in height.
Flowers and fruits grow in profusion.
When the fruit ripens, its skin cracks and bursts open of its own accord, emitting a natural fragrance.
Some reach heights of sixty or fifty *li*.
The smallest are five *li* in size.
When their fruit ripens, the skin bursts open of its own accord,
naturally producing various kinds of garments or various ornaments for adorning the body.
Some emit various vessels;
some emit various foods;
or there are jeweled boats playing amidst the rivers.
When the people of that region wish to enter it to bathe and sport,
they take off their clothes on the bank,
board the boat in midstream, and after their entertainment is finished, they cross the water and put on whatever clothes they encounter.
Those who come out first shall be clothed first;
those who come out later shall be clothed later.
They shall not seek their original garments.
Next, they arrived at the fragrant trees, which bent down for them.
Those people took musical instruments in their hands and tuned the strings;
then, playing in harmony with exquisite voices, they proceeded to the garden for entertainment.
In that land, during the middle watch of the night, the Nāga King Anavatapta repeatedly gives rise to pure clouds that pervade the entire world and bring down sweet rain.
For as long as it takes a cow to suckle her calf, the eight-flavored water moistens and thoroughly saturates all things.
After midnight, when the sky is pure and free from obscurations and clear and serene,
a cool breeze rises from the sea that gently blows upon the bodies of people, bringing joy to their entire frame.
That land is fertile and abundant, and its population is flourishing.
If food and drink are required, one places naturally husked rice into a cauldron and sets a flame-light jewel beneath it;
the rice becomes cooked spontaneously, and the light of the jewel extinguishes of its own accord.
Whoever came was allowed to eat as much as they desired;
yet even when the host did not rise, the rice was never exhausted.
If the host rose, the rice would then be completely distributed.
The rice was fresh and pure, like a cluster of white flowers;
its flavor was like that of the heavens, free from all ailments.
One’s physical strength was fully restored, the complexion became harmonious and joyful, and there was no further decline.
The people of that land are identical in appearance and cannot be distinguished from one another;
their countenances are youthful, like those of men about twenty years of age in Jambudvīpa.
Their teeth are even, upright, pure white, and without gaps.
His hair is deep blue-black and free from dust or impurity.
It hangs down eight finger-widths, stopping level with his eyebrows;
it is neither too long nor too short.
Whenever the people of that land give rise to a lustful thought,
they gaze intently at a woman and then depart;
she follows them as they go to the groves and gardens.
If that woman is the father, mother, or a blood relative of that man,
such that sexual intercourse would be improper, the tree will not bend to provide shade;
they shall each disperse.
If it was not a relative, the tree would provide a curved shade for them to enjoy as they pleased for one or two days,
or even up to seven days, before they would depart. The *Lokasthāna-abhidharma-śāstra* states:
The people of the Northern Continent do not seek out women nor do they welcome wives;
they neither buy nor sell them.
When a man wishes to marry a woman, he gazes intently upon her.
If a woman desires a man, she must also gaze intently at him.
If he does not look back, another woman will say to her:
"This man is looking at you; you shall immediately become husband and wife."
If a man does not see his woman, she looks at another man and says, "This woman looks at you; let us also be husband and wife.
If they see one another, they immediately follow each other away to another place.
For those with great desire, the number of such occurrences in a single lifetime reaches at most five;
for those of middling capacity, it is either four or three;
and there are also those who practice until death without any desire.
That woman, having conceived due to unwholesome food, gives birth after seven or eight days.
Whether it be a boy or a girl, as soon as it is born, she places it at a crossroads where four great roads meet and departs, leaving it there.
There were practitioners who, passing by its side, would take a finger and rinse their mouth with it;
as they withdrew their fingers, sweet milk flowed forth, filling the child’s entire body.
After seven days had passed, the child grew up to be the equal of those people.
Men [go] toward the assembly of men and women toward the assembly of women.
When those people die, they do not weep for one another;
they adorn the corpse, place it at a crossroads, and depart, leaving it behind.
There is a bird named Ucchuṣmaga that seizes those corpses and carries them away to another region; as stated in the *Lokasthāna-śāstra*,
"that bird pecks at the corpse and takes it away."

Upon reaching the outskirts of the mountain, they immediately partook of food; furthermore, whenever the local people defecated or urinated, the ground would split open, and once they had finished, the earth would close back up of its own accord.
The people of that land were without attachment to anything and possessed no accumulated stores.
Their lifespan is fixed, and upon death they are reborn in heaven.
For what reason is their lifespan fixed?
Because in their previous lives, those people cultivated the ten virtuous actions.
When their bodies perish and their lives end, they are reborn in Uttarakuru.
Their lifespan is one thousand years, neither increasing nor decreasing;
therefore, the lifespans of those people are exactly equal.
If there is anyone who can give to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas,
as well as to the poor, beggars, and those afflicted by illness and suffering,
providing them with clothing, food, vehicles, flower garlands, ointments, beds, and dwellings.
Furthermore, those who construct stupas and temples and offer lamps and candles as worship will,
at the end of their lives, be reborn in Uttarakuru,
where their lifespan is one thousand years, neither increasing nor decreasing.
In that land, one does not intentionally cultivate the ten wholesome actions;
rather, every movement spontaneously accords with them.
Upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, one is reborn in a heavenly realm.
Therefore, that person is called "Victorious" (*jina*).
Among the three continents, his land is the most supreme;
thus, in the language of Qin, it is called "Most Supreme" (*zuishang*).
The *Lishi lun* (Treatise on the Establishment of the World) states: "The inhabitants of that land are all pure white and adorned with ornaments."
His beard and hair were a deep, lustrous black, always appearing as if freshly shaved;
every five days, his hair grew naturally to a length of exactly seven finger-widths, neither more nor less.
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
"The shape of Uttarakuru is like a square seat."
Its four sides are equal in measure,
each side being two thousand [yojanas].
Since it has been stated that the dimensions of each side of the world-system are two thousand [yojanas].
The meaning has already been established.
On its borders are two intermediate continents:
first, the continent of Kuru.
Second is Kaurava Island;
both of these two islands are inhabited by humans.
The second is Pūrvavideha in the east.
According to the *Dīrgha Āgama*,
to the east of Mount Sumeru there is a world called Pūrvavideha.
That land is perfectly circular,
measuring nine thousand yojanas in length and breadth;
the faces of its inhabitants resemble the shape of that terrain.
There was a great king of trees named Kālāmbu,
with a circumference of seven yojanas.
It is one hundred yojanas in height,
with branches and foliage spreading fifty yojanas in all directions.
The *Zao Tiandi Jing* (Sutra on the Creation of Heaven and Earth) states:
The people of the eastern region are superior to those of Jambudvīpa;
in that land, they trade with one another using cotton and silk.
As stated in the *Dīrgha Āgama*:
The lifespan of the people in that land is two hundred years, with few exceeding it and many falling short; the *Loutan jing* (Lokasthāna-sūtra) states that the human lifespan is three hundred years.
Regarding food and drink, they consume fish and meat; this is stated in the *Lishi lun* (Lokaprajñapti-śāstra).
They do not kill living beings themselves,
nor do they cause others to kill.
If there are animals that have died of natural causes, they eat their meat, exchanging it for grain, silk, pearls, and jewels.
Regarding human marriage and the taking of wives, the *Lishi lun* (Treatise on Establishing the World) states:
"Among the people of Pūrvavideha,
those who possess much desire..."
Within a single lifetime, the number reaches up to seven;
for those of middling capacity,
it may reach five or six.
There are also those who practice until death without desire.
The inhabitants of the eastern and western continents lack only the black complexion;
otherwise, they are the same as those of Jambudvīpa, possessing various types of complexions.
That person’s hair is adorned and trimmed so as to cover the front and back;
they wear two garments, one below and one above, with the upper garment merely wrapped around the body. This is in accordance with the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*.
The continent of Pūrvavideha is narrow in the east and broad in the west;
its three sides are equal in measure.
Its shape is like a half-moon.
To the east, there are three hundred and fifty-three sides, each measuring two thousand [yojanas].
This is the eastern edge of Pūrvavideha.
The southern extremity of Jambudvīpa is broad;
thus, its eastern shape is like a half-moon.
On the borders of this continent, there are two intermediate continents (antaradvīpa).
First is Pūrvavideha Island;
second is Aparagodānīya Island.
Both of these islands are inhabited by human beings.
Regarding the third continent, Aparagoyānī:
according to the *Dīrgha Āgama*,
the western subcontinent of Mount Sumeru is named Aparagoyānī.
The shape of that land is like the full moon;
it is eight thousand yojanas in length and breadth,
and the faces of its inhabitants resemble the shape of that terrain.
There was a great king of trees named Kiṃpila,
with a circumference of seven yojanas.
It is one hundred yojanas in height, with branches and leaves spreading fifty yojanas in all directions.
The *Qishi jing* (Sūtra on the Arising of the World) states: "Beneath that tree there is a stone ox."
It is one yojana in height;
for these reasons, it is named Godānīya.
This is called Go-dānīya; the human lifespan there is three hundred years.
They trade with one another using cattle, horses, pearls, and jade.
Both people and things there are superior to those of Jambudvīpa.
The *Lishi lun* (Treatise on the Establishment of the World) states:
"The people of that land either kill living beings themselves or cause others to kill them;
once they have been born [as animals], they eat their flesh, just like the people of Jambudvīpa."
When their kinsmen die, they carry the corpse to the mountains to cremate it and abandon the remains;
or they place it in water,
or bury it in the earth.
Some dwell in open spaces.
The two continents to the east and west are largely similar to Jambudvīpa;
their marriage customs are likewise the same.
Those who desire many reach as many as twelve times in a single lifetime;
those of middling capacity achieve ten times.
There are also those who practice until death without desire.
Those people adorn themselves by letting their hair hang loose and wear garments both above and below.
As stated in the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*:
The western continent of Aparagoyānī is circular like the full moon;
its diameter is two thousand five hundred [yojanas],
and its circumference is seven thousand five hundred.
On the edge of that continent are two intermediate continents:
first, Śāṭhādvīpa; second, Ullaramantridvīpa.
All are inhabited by people.
Regarding the fourth continent, Jambudvīpa,
according to the *Dīrgha Āgama*, it says:
To the south of Mount Sumeru lies a world named Jambudvīpa;
its land is narrow in the south and broad in the north.
It is seven thousand yojanas in length and breadth;
the faces of the people resemble the shape of this terrain.
There is a great king of trees.
It is named Jambudvīpa;
it is seven yojanas in circumference and one hundred yojanas in height.
Its branches and leaves spread out for fifty yojanas; the *Qishi jing* (Sūtra on the Arising of the World) states:
"Beneath this tree, there is a mass of Jambūnada gold."
It is twenty yojanas in height.
From beneath this tree, this superior gold emerges;
it is called Jāmbūnada-tree gold. Furthermore, there is the tree of the King of Garuḍas.
It is named Kūṭaśālmali;
it is seven yojanas in circumference and one hundred yojanas in height.
Its branches and leaves spread fifty yojanas in all directions.
The asura king has a tree named Sujāta.
Its circumference is seven yojanas;
its height is one hundred yojanas;
and its branches and foliage spread fifty yojanas in all directions.
In the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven there is a tree named Pārijāta,
with a circumference of seven yojanas.
It is one hundred yojanas high,
with branches and leaves spreading fifty yojanas in all directions.
This is the Jambudvīpa tree of the people of Jambudvīpa.
The human lifespan is one hundred years,
yet many die prematurely;
during the first ten years, they lack understanding.
At twenty, one has little knowledge and is not yet wise;
at thirty, lustful desires are at their peak;
at forty, one's actions lack coherence.
Fifty: not forgetting what has been practiced.
Sixty: stinginess and attachment.
Seventy: a sluggish physical nature.
At eighty, one is devoid of honor and adornment;
at ninety, one suffers from illness and pain;
at one hundred, the faculties are utterly decayed, having passed through three hundred cycles of winter, summer, and spring.
Within the interval of thirty-six thousand meals,
there may be those who do not complete [the full number].
As stated in the *Lishi apitan lun* (Abhidharmakośa-śāstra):
The clothing and ornaments of the people of Jambudvīpa vary in many ways;
some have long hair divided into two topknots,
while others shave off their hair and beards.
Some leave a single topknot at the crown of the head while removing all other hair;
this is called *cūḍā* hair.
Others pluck out both their hair and their beard.
Some have their hair and beards shaved;
some have their hair braided;
and some have their hair hanging loose.
Some cut their hair at the front and let it grow long at the back to form a circle; some go naked;
others wear clothing.
Covered above and exposed below;
or exposed above and covered below;
or covered both above and below.
Or they may obstruct [the path] before or after;
the many kinds of food consumed by the people of this continent cannot be described in detail.
Matters such as marriage rites and market transactions can be known from present-day occurrences.
However, the treatise states:
"The sensual affairs of the people of Jambudvīpa in a single lifetime are innumerable and immeasurable;
they differ from those of the inhabitants of the other three continents, who have few desires."
There are also those who practice until death without desire.
According to the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*,
there is a peripheral continent within Jambudvīpa.
The first is named Cāmara Island;
the second is named Vāra-cara Island.
Both of these islands are inhabited by human beings.

7. Section on Body Size (Śarīrapramāṇavarga), the Seventh. According to the *Lokasthiti-sūtra*, when the lifespan of the people of Jambudvīpa has decreased to ten years, their physical bodies become short and small.
It may be two or three *vitasti* in length;
thus, upon one's own body, it measures eight *vitasti*.
The Abhidharma-śāstra says:
When the people of Jambudvīpa reach one hundred years of age,
their height will be three and a half cubits,
or perhaps four cubits; as stated in the *Dīrgha Āgama*.
Their height is three cubits, though there are some for whom it is not fixed; speaking in general terms, the people of Pūrvavideha are eight cubits tall,
those of Aparagoyānī are sixteen cubits tall,
and those of Uttarakuru are thirty-two cubits tall.
8. Section on Life Span. Section Eight on Life Span. As stated in the Abhidharma, the life span of humans in Jambudvīpa is indefinite and consists of three categories.
The highest lifespan is one hundred and twenty-five years;
the middle lifespan is one hundred years;
the lowest lifespan is sixty years.
Among them, those who died prematurely are beyond counting.

Furthermore, this category is described according to the period of the kalpa’s decline; if one were to rely on the beginning of the kalpa, when lifespans were immeasurable, [this category would not exist].
Or it may reach eighty-four thousand [years].
According to the *Dīrgha Āgama*,
this refers to the people of Jambudvīpa.
The human lifespan is one hundred and twenty years,
though many die prematurely.
This is the case for the people of Pūrvavideha.
The human lifespan is two hundred years; according to the *Loutan jing* (Ratnakūṭa-sūtra), it is three hundred years.
As for the people of Aparagoyānī:
The lifespan of humans is three hundred years.
The people of Uttarakuru in the north have a lifespan of one thousand years; in the other three continents, there are those who die prematurely.
Only the inhabitants of the Northern Continent have a fixed lifespan of one thousand years.
Section Nine: The Measurement of Garments. According to the *Sūtra on the Origin of the World*, the height of a person in Jambudvīpa is three and a half cubits.
The garment is seven cubits long and three and a half cubits wide;
this is the clothing of the people of Aparagoyānī.
The people of Pūrvavideha wear garments equal in size to those of Jambudvīpa.
The people of Uttarakuru are seven cubits in height.
The robe is fourteen cubits in length,
with seven cubits for both the upper and lower sections.
The body of an asura is one yojana in height.
The robe is two yojanas in length and one yojana in width;
it weighs half a kṛṣṇala, which in the Sui language means half a *liang*.
Other sūtras state that the size of asuras is not fixed;
for example, the asura Vemacitra is four times as high as Mount Sumeru.
10. Section on Superiority and Inferiority. The tenth section on superiority and inferiority states in the *Dīrgha Āgama*:
The Buddha told the bhikṣus, "The people of Jambudvīpa possess three things."
They surpass those of Aparagoyānī in three respects. What are these three?
First, they are courageous, possess strong memories, and are capable of performing karmic actions.
Second, they are courageous, possess strong memories, and diligently practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Third, they are courageous, possess strong memories, and a Buddha appears in their land.
The people of Aparagoyānī excel those of Jambudvīpa in these three respects.
What are the three?
First, many cattle; second, many sheep.
Third, there is an abundance of pearls and jade.
Jambudvīpa excels over Pūrvavideha in three respects.
What are these three?
First, being courageous and possessing a powerful memory, they are able to perform karmic actions.
Second, being courageous and possessing a powerful memory, they are able to cultivate the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Third, being courageous and possessing a powerful memory, a Buddha appears in their land.
Pūrvavideha has three matters in which it excels Jambudvīpa.
What are these three?
First, its land is exceedingly vast.
Second, its land is exceedingly vast;
third, its land is exceedingly wondrous.
Jambudvīpa surpasses Uttarakuru in three respects.
What are the three? First, being courageous and possessing strong memory, one is able to perform karmic actions.
Second, being courageous and possessing strong memory, one is able to cultivate the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Third, there are those who are courageous and possess strong memories; a Buddha appears in that land.
Furthermore, Uttarakuru has three matters by which it excels Jambudvīpa.
What are these three?
First, they have no attachments;
second, they possess no sense of "mine";
third, their lifespan is fixed at one thousand years.
The people of Jambudvīpa also surpass those in the realm of hungry ghosts (preta) by means of the aforementioned three matters.
There are three matters in which the realm of hungry ghosts surpasses Jambudvīpa. What are these three?
First, long life;
second, a large body;
third, that what is done by others is experienced by oneself.
The people of Jambudvīpa also surpass the garuḍas in three aforementioned matters.
Furthermore, the garuḍas surpass the people of Jambudvīpa in three matters.
What are these three?
First, long life;
second, a large body;
third, a palace.
The inhabitants of Jambudvīpa surpass the asuras in three matters;
the asuras, in turn, surpass those of Jambudvīpa in three matters.
What are these three?
First, the palaces are lofty and vast;
second, the palaces are magnificently adorned;
third, the palaces are pure and pristine.
The people of Jambudvīpa surpass the gods of the Four Great Kings in three respects;
furthermore, they surpass the people of Jambudvīpa themselves in three respects. What are these three?
First, long life;
second, physical beauty;
third, abundant happiness.
The people of Jambudvīpa also surpass the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa,
Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, and Paranirmita-vaśavartin heavens by means of the same three matters.
Furthermore, these various gods surpass the people of Jambudvīpa by means of three other matters.
What are the three? First, long life;
second, physical beauty.

Third, the Section on Abundant Joy (Bahusukha). **The Second Part: The Section on the Gods (Devāḥ)** This section is further divided into twenty-two sub-sections: 1. The Section on Distinguishing Positions (*sthāna-vibhāga*) 2. The Section on Assemblies (*parṣad-vibhāga*) 3. The Section on Names (*nāma-vibhāga*) 4. The Section on Karmic Causes (*karman-hetu-vibhāga*) 5. The Section on Rebirth (*upapatti-vibhāga*) 6. The Section on the Dimensions of Realms (*dhātu-pramāṇa-vibhāga*) 7. The Section on the Dimensions of Bodies (*kāya-pramāṇa-vibhāga*) 8. The Section on the Dimensions of Garments (*vastra-pramāṇa-vibhāga*) 9. The Section on the Duration of Life (*āyus-pramāṇa-vibhāga*) 10. The Section on Residences (*āvāsa-vibhāga*) 11. The Section on Extent (*vistāra-saṃkoca-vibhāga*) 12. The Section on Adornments (*alaṃkāra-vibhāga*) 13. The Section on Music and Petitions (*tūrya-yācana-vibhāga*) 14. The Section on Supernormal Powers (*ṛddhi-vibhāga*) 15. The Section on Bodily Radiance (*kāya-prabhā-vibhāga*) 16. The Section on Trade (*paṇya-vikraya-vibhāga*) 17. The Section on Marriage (*vivāha-vibhāga*) 18. The Section on Food and Drink (*bhojana-pāna-vibhāga*) 19. The Section on Servants and Vehicles (*bhṛtya-yāna-vibhāga*) 20. The Section on Retinues (*parivāra-vibhāga*) 21. The Section on Nobility and Meanness (*ārya-anārya-vibhāga*) 22. The Section on Poverty and Wealth (*daridra-adhana-vibhāga*) 23. The Section on Funerary Rites (*mṛta-saṃskāra-vibhāga*) **First: The Section on Distinguishing Positions** As explained in the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*: [The gods of the Desire Realm are divided into six classes. First, the Four Great Kings (*cāturmahārājika*). They reside upon the four sides of Mount Sumeru. Specifically, they dwell on the first terrace of the mountain, which is forty thousand *yojanas* high. On each side, there are four palaces: Vaijayanta, Vaiśravaṇa, Virūḍhaka, and Virūpākṣa. These constitute the Heaven of the Four Great Kings. Furthermore, they have thirty-two cities, such as Sudarśana and so forth. Within these cities, there are various parks, including Caitraratha, Miśraka, Pāruṣyaka, and Nandanavana. In these parks, the gods enjoy themselves with their retinues. There are also four great assemblies of the gods, known as the *Caturmahārājakāyika-deva-parṣad*. Regarding their names, they are called "Great Kings" because they possess great power, great majesty, and great sovereignty over the gods of the Desire Realm. Regarding their karmic causes, they are born there due to having practiced the five precepts and the ten wholesome paths of action with a superior degree of vigor. Regarding their rebirth, they are born from eggs, wombs, moisture, or by transformation. Regarding the dimensions of their realms, the city of Sudarśana is fifty thousand *yojanas* in circumference. Regarding the dimensions of their bodies, they are one-quarter of a *yojana* in height. Regarding the dimensions of their garments, they are half a *yojana* in length and breadth. Regarding the duration of their lives, it is five hundred years, where each day and night is equivalent to fifty human years. Regarding their residences, they dwell within the aforementioned cities and parks. Regarding their extent, the city of Sudarśana is fifty thousand *yojanas* wide and long. Regarding their adornments, they are adorned with various precious jewels, celestial flowers, and fragrances. Regarding music and petitions, they play celestial instruments and present offerings to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. Regarding supernormal powers, they can travel to the heavens of the Thirty-three (*trāyastriṃśa*) and other realms. Regarding bodily radiance, they emit light that illuminates the surrounding mountains and valleys. Regarding trade, they exchange various celestial treasures and garments. Regarding marriage, they marry according to their own customs. Regarding food and drink, they consume celestial nectar and ambrosia. Regarding servants and vehicles, they have celestial beings as attendants and ride on divine chariots. Regarding retinues, each king has a vast number of followers. Regarding nobility and meanness, some are noble while others are common. Regarding poverty and wealth, some are wealthy while others are poor. Regarding funerary rites, when a god passes away, his body transforms and he is reborn elsewhere. Thus ends the first section on distinguishing positions. It is as stated in the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*.
There are thirty-two kinds of devas:
ten in the desire realm and eighteen in the form realm.
The formless realm has four [levels].
Combined, there are thirty-two heavens.
First, as for the ten heavens of the desire realm:
The first is named the Deva of Dry Hands;
the second is named the Deva Who Holds Flower Garlands;
the third is named the Deva of Constant Heedlessness.
The fourth is named the Heaven of the Sun, Moon, and Constellations;
the fifth is named the Heaven of the Four Great Kings;
the sixth is named the Heaven of the Thirty-three, collectively subsumed under the name Trāyastriṃśa; and the seventh is named the Yāma Heaven.
The eighth is named Tuṣita Heaven;
the ninth is named Nirmāṇarati Heaven;
and the tenth is named Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven. These include the first constellation and the latter four.
These five dwell in the void;
the four heavens of Dṛḍhapāṇi, Puṣpamāla, and Pramada reside in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.
These five reside on the mountains.
As explained below in the ninth dwelling place, regarding the second realm, the Form Realm (rūpadhātu), which consists of eighteen heavens:
in the first dhyāna there are three heavens.
The first is named the Heaven of the Brahma-multitude (Brahmapāriṣadya).
The second is named the Heaven of Brahma’s Ministers (Brahmapurohita).
The third is named the Great Brahma Heaven (Mahābrahmā). This Great Brahma Heaven has no separate dwelling place;
rather, within the Heaven of Brahma’s Ministers, there is a tiered terrace that is high, prominent, magnificent, and vast.
Mahābrahmā dwells alone above,
thereby distinguishing himself from the multitudes below.
Among these three heavens, the Brahmakāyika devas are the common people.
The Brahmapurohitas are the ministers,
and Mahābrahmā is the sovereign;
only in this first dhyāna is there such a distinction between ruler, minister, and common people.
From this point upward, none of these exist. Within the second dhyāna, there are three heavens:
the first is named the Heaven of Limited Light (Parīttābha);
the second is named the Heaven of Immeasurable Light (Apramāṇābha).
The third [dhyāna] consists of three heavens of Ābhāsvara;
within the third dhyāna there are also three heavens,
the first of which is called Parīttābha.
The second is named the Heaven of Immeasurable Purity (Apramāṇaśubha);
the third is named the Heaven of Universal Purity (Śubhakṛtsna).
Within the Fourth Dhyāna, there are exclusively these nine heavens.
The first is named the Heaven of Merit-Birth (Puṇyaprasava);
the second is named the Heaven of Merit-Love (Vṛhatphala);
the third is named the Heaven of Vast Fruit (Bṛhatphala).
The fourth is called the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*). This Heaven of Non-conception has no separate location;

it shares the same level as the Heaven of Vast Fruit (*bṛhatphala*) but occupies a distinct region. Because it is the dwelling place of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), it is distinguished by this specific name. The fifth is called the Heaven Without Affliction (*avṛha-deva*).
Sixth is the Heaven of No Heat;
seventh is the Heaven of Good Appearance;
eighth is the Heaven of Good Vision.

The ninth is the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, also called the Color-Culmination Heaven; these constitute the eighteen heavens of the Form Realm in total. Within the third, the Formless Realm, there are four heavens.
First is the Heaven of the Sphere of Infinite Space;
second is the Heaven of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness;
third is the Heaven of the Sphere of Nothingness.
The four heavens of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception—these are called the thirty-two types of heavens in total within the three realms. Question:
It is not yet known how many among these thirty-two heavens are ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and how many are noble ones (*ārya*).
Answer: Two are exclusively the dwellings of ordinary persons;
five are exclusively the dwellings of noble ones.
In the remaining twenty-five heavens, ordinary beings and sages dwell together.
Regarding those two where only ordinary beings reside:
the first is Mahābrahmā, the Great Brahma King of the First Dhyāna.
The second is among the heavens of non-perception within the fourth dhyāna;
these are inhabited solely by non-Buddhists.
Question: [Why is this so?]
Why are these two abodes exclusively for ordinary beings?
The answer is:
because the Great Brahmā King does not understand the causes of karma.
He claimed only he could create all the heavens, earths, people, and things;
relying on this, he became arrogant and held all sages in contempt.
Therefore, [the Buddha] did not dwell with him.
Furthermore, among the gods of the Heaven of No-Thought (asaṃjñisattva), only those non-Buddhists who have cultivated the meditative attainment of non-thought (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) are born there;
they receive the retribution of five hundred kalpas of mindlessness.
Not understanding this, the non-Buddhists claim it to be nirvāṇa.
Once they have finished receiving their retribution, they will inevitably give rise to wrong views and be reborn in hell. For this reason,
no noble one (ārya) is ever born there either.
Regarding what are called the five Pure Abodes where only noble beings dwell:
these refer to the five Pure Abode heavens, such as Avṛha and Atapa, from the Bṛhatphala heaven upward;
they are inhabited solely by non-returners (anāgāmin) and arhats.
Even though ordinary beings are born in that heaven, they must be those who have progressed toward the stage of *anāgāmin* (non-returner);
having attained the four dhyānas, they give rise to untainted (*anāsrava*) states and initiate the karma of perfumed dhyāna,
whether producing one grade up to five grades.
Only then can one be born there.
Since ordinary beings lack this cultivation of meditative karma, they cannot be born there.
If it is said that an Anāgāmin is born there, the principle is beyond doubt.
Question: Since an Arhat is already one who is no longer subject to birth,
for what reason is it also said that they are born in those heavens?
The answer is:
This should be stated as "an Anāgāmin of the desire realm who is born there attains Arhatship," rather than saying that he was already an Arhat before being born there.
As for the remaining twenty-five heavens where ordinary and holy beings dwell together,
they need not be detailed exhaustively.
If one were to provide a general account based on the teachings of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna:
In total, there are four heavens.
Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"There are four kinds of devas."
First, the worldly devas; second, the devas born [in celestial realms];
third, the pure devas.
Fourth, the devas of meaning.
Worldly devas are such as various kings.
Born devas range from the Heaven of the Four Great Kings up to the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception.
The *śuddhadeva* (Pure Heavens) refers to those from the *srotāpanna* up to the *pratyekabuddha*.
The *arthadeva* (Meaning Heavens) refers to the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). For what reason?

Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage are called "Devas of Meaning" (*arthadeva*), because they are able to skillfully understand the meaning of all phenomena and perceive that the nature of all phenomena is emptiness.
Second, the section on the names of the assemblies; within this second section, first, the four heavenly kings.
According to the *Dīrgha Āgama*,
the Heavenly King of the East is named Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
which is translated here as "Ruler of the State. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that Dhṛtarāṣṭra leads the gandharvas and the yakṣa generals.
He protects the people of Pūrvavideha, preventing them from being harmed.
The Heavenly King of the South is named Virūḍhaka;
this is translated as "Lord of Increase. In the *Dazhidu lun* (Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra), he is called Virūḍhakṣa. He governs the Kumbhāṇḍas and the Pretas.
He protects the people of Jambudvīpa.
The Western Heavenly King is named Virūpākṣa, which is translated here as "Lord of Varied Speech.
The *Dazhidu lun* (Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra) states that Virūpākṣa governs all the nāgas and pūtanas.
He protects the people of Aparagoyānī.
The Northern Heavenly King is named Vaiśravaṇa,
which in this [language] means "Lord of Much Hearing."
He leads the yakṣas and rākṣasas to protect the inhabitants of Uttarakuru.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
The title of the Heavenly Lord Śakra, according to the pure Brahma-sound, should be rendered as Devānām-indra.
"Śākya" means "able" in the language of Qin; "deva" means "heaven" and "indra" means "lord. Combining these terms, it is [Devānām-indra].

This is the Lord of the Gods. Suyāma means "Exquisite Goodness" in the language of Qin; Tuṣita means "Exquisite Fulfillment"; Sunirmita means "Delighting in Transformations"; and Vaśavartin means "Mastery over Others' Transformations. The Brahmā King is named Śikhin, which means "Great Crest" in the language of Qin, though it is also called "Great Vessel. Śuddhāvāsa means "Pure Abode" in the language of Qin.
Furthermore, I shall provide an essential commentary based on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
These few [levels] are distinct from the other heavens;
the names of the heavens above these are fully detailed in the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*, but as the text would be too voluminous, they cannot be recorded here in full. The *Madhyama Āgama* states:
At that time, there was a certain bhikṣu who came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet,
and withdrawing to stand to one side, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
by what causes and conditions is he named Śakra Devānām Indra?
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
When Śakra Devānām-indra was formerly a human being, he practiced the giving of alms;
to śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and those who were poor and suffering,
he gave food, drink, money, lamps, and so forth.
He is called Śakra Devānām Indra because of his capability.
For what further reason is he called Puraṃdara?
He replied:
When he was formerly a human being, he frequently practiced giving—
of clothing, food and drink, and even lamps; therefore, he is named Pūraṇa.
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions is he named Mahābrahmā?
He replied:
"In his former life as a human, he was named Maghava."
It was named after its original [source].
For what further reason, then, is it called Sāṃkāśya?
He replied:
In his former life as a human being, he offered and made offerings with robes of *vāsasī* cloth;
therefore, he is named Śakrapūjita.
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions is he named Kauśika?
He said: "When he was originally a human being, his clan name was Kauśika.
For what further reason and by what causes is he named Śacīpati?"
He said: "Śacī is the foremost queen of Śakra, the Lord of Devas.
For what reason and by what causes is she named 'The Thousand-Eyed'?"
He said, "When I was formerly a human being, I possessed intelligence and wisdom;
for in a single sitting, I contemplated, examined, and weighed a thousand kinds of meanings."
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions is he named Indriya?
He replied:
"O Lord of Devas, it is because he is the sovereign over all thirty-two heavens."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Indeed, when that Śakra Devānām Indra was formerly a human being,
he undertook and maintained seven practices by which he attained the status of Śakra Devendra."
What are the seven? They are:
making offerings to one's parents, up to practicing equal generosity.
As stated in a verse of the sutra:
As Śakra, Lord of the Devas.
Section Three: Causes of Karma. Question: What karma must be created to be born as a result within the six realms of existence?
Answer: According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*,
the karma of the six realms of existence does not exceed the categories of good and evil.
Each has three grades: those of the highest grade are reborn in the heavens;
those of the middle grade are reborn as humans.
Those of inferior [virtue] are born into the four evil destinies.
According to this principle, however,
those whose wholesome [roots] are of the highest grade attain rebirth in the heavens.
Are concentration and its non-diffusion distinct?

According to the *Karmavibhaṅga-sūtra*, it is explained in detail that the ten wholesome actions lead to rebirth in the celestial realms; these are distinguished as being either complete, partial, concentrated, or diffused across the three realms.
The Sūtra says:
"Furthermore, there are ten wholesome actions that can cause sentient beings to obtain the retribution of the heavens of the desire realm.
By fully cultivating these superior ten wholesome actions, one obtains birth as a reward in the heavens of the desire realm."
This refers to the scattered wholesome karma of the desire realm.
Furthermore, there are ten karmas that enable sentient beings to obtain the retribution of the heavens of the form realm:
by practicing the ten wholesome paths of action with outflows (*sāsrava*) in association with meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
This refers to wholesome karma of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Furthermore, there are four types of karma that enable sentient beings to obtain rebirth as gods in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

The first is: having transcended all perceptions of form and extinguished all perceptions of sensory resistance, one enters the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana-samādhi*).
Second, transcending the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space, one enters the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite consciousness.
Third, transcending the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite consciousness, one enters the meditative absorption of the sphere of nothingness.
Fourth, transcending the meditative absorption of the sphere of nothingness, one enters the meditative absorption of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
By means of these four karmas, one obtains retribution in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
If this is so, why does one not speak of the ten wholesome actions (*daśakuśalakarma*) in relation to this realm?
One should say that this realm is the retribution of the formless, yet it is cultivated through the distancing of body and speech, which are of mixed nature.
Therefore, based on the [Abhidharma] *Judi* (Grounds), it speaks only of the four types of karma and does not refer to the ten wholesome actions.
Nevertheless, all that has been explained above concerns the Tathāgata’s discernment of how the causes and effects of karma correspond exactly, without any discrepancy.
According to the *Śīla-sūtra*,
monks observe two hundred and fifty precepts,
while nuns observe three hundred and seventy-eight precepts.
This is also karma for rebirth in the heavens.
Thus, a verse in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* says:
"The wise person who can protect the precepts / Shall obtain three kinds of happiness."
"Renown and gain, and upon death, birth in the heavens"—
this refers to the heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Furthermore, as it is said in the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra*:
Alternatively, by observing the precepts— refraining from killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct—
one may also be reborn in heaven due to these three virtues.
This rebirth likewise occurs among the heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
This is based on the teaching regarding a different time;
however, it does not mean that one will definitely be reborn in heaven by performing only these three [actions].
Furthermore, as stated in the *Jentākasūtra*:
The pure karma of making offerings to the Sangha can also result in rebirth in the heavens and the higher realms;
this, too, refers to a different time. It does not mean that one attains rebirth in the higher realms through the mere scattering of good roots from offering water to the Sangha.
However, this is the retribution for those in the heavens of the desire realm.
Furthermore, as stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*,
a compassionate mother rescued her child from the Ganges River.
When both the child and its mother die, they are reborn in the Brahma Heaven;
this is the loving-kindness of the distracted mind,
not assisted by other meditative concentrations or wholesome states.
How could one attain rebirth in heaven?
This refers only to distant causes;
it is not restricted to the case of scattered compassion, for through that one may indeed attain rebirth above.
It is also like how hearing the *nirvāṇa* even once prevents one from falling into the four miserable realms;
the principle is likewise.
Thus, the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* says:
If one refrains from killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct in body, and refrains from false speech, frivolous speech, divisive speech, and harsh speech in speech—
by observing these seven precepts, one shall be reborn in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings.
If one can uphold the seven types of precepts, one will attain rebirth in the heavens of apparitional birth.
These are further divided into superior, middling, and inferior grades.
By upholding the precept against killing, one attains rebirth in the realm of the Four Great Kings.
If one observes the precepts of not killing and not stealing, one will be reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
If one observes the precepts of not killing, not stealing, and not engaging in sexual misconduct, one will be reborn in the Yāma Heaven.

Section Six: Physical Dimensions. According to the *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*:
Seven paramāṇus constitute one *anūpa-rajas* (dust mote on the surface of Lake Anavatapta).
This is the most subtle;
it can be seen by those with the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).
And it is seen by the Bodhisattva-Cakravartin.
Seven *anūcīra* (atoms) constitute one *tāmrapaṃśu* (copper-dust);
seven *tāmrapaṃśu* constitute one *abhrapaṃśu* (water-dust).
Seven particles of water-dust constitute one particle of rabbit-hair dust.
Seven particles of rabbit-hair dust constitute one particle of sheep’s-wool dust.
Seven particles of sheep’s-wool dust constitute one particle of ox-hair dust.
Seven particles of dust on a cow’s hair constitute one particle of drifting dust;
seven particles of drifting dust constitute one nit;
seven nits constitute one louse.
Seven nits make one barleycorn;
seven barleycorns make one finger-breadth;
twenty-four finger-breadths make one cubit.
Four cubits (*hasta*) make one bow (*dhanus*).
Five hundred bows from a village make one *krośa*.
Eight *krośas* [make one *yojana*].
Because it is named one *yojana*, a verse is spoken:
Seven atoms form an *anu*; seven *anus* form a copper atom;
The water-atom, the rabbit-hair atom, and the ox-hair atom— All arise from [the preceding] sevenfold multiplication.
Therefore, in the treatise, the krośa is used as the measure for the bodies of the gods,
ranging from the bodies of the Cāturmahārājakāyika devas up to those of the Akaniṣṭha devas. Thus,
the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
The bodies of the Four Heavenly Kings are one-quarter of a *krośa* in height.

According to the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, the stature of all the gods of the Four Heavens is equal to that of the Kings; this is also consistent with the *Abhidharma*. As for the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, their bodies are half a *krośa* in height.
The body of Śakra is one krośa in height.

The body of a Yāma-deva is two-fourths of a krośa. If one asks why the body of Śakra is taller than that of a Yāma-deva, it is as the sūtra explains: because he cultivated the karma of reverence more extensively in the past, he obtained this exceptional height. The body of a Tuṣita-deva is one krośa in height.
The gods of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, including Śakra and others, are one krośa and one-quarter of a krośa in height.
The gods of the Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven are one and a half krośas in height. Such are the body measurements of the various gods of the Desire Realm.

Regarding the third realm of formlessness (ārūpyadhātu), it is formless and cannot be described; however, according to the Mahāyāna, it also possesses subtle matter (rūpa).
