which corresponds to thirty-six million human years.
This constitutes one day and night in the Kālasūtra Great Hell.
By such days, months, and years, the lifespan in the Kālasūtra Hell is one thousand years;
this corresponds to two hundred human years.
This constitutes one day and night for the Yāma devas.
By such calculation of months, days, and years, the lifespan of the Yāma devas is two thousand years,
which corresponds to fourteen billion four hundred million years by human reckoning.
This constitutes one day and one night in the Saṃghāta Great Hell.
By such reckoning of days, months, and years,
the lifespan in the Saṃghāta Great Hell is two thousand years.
Four hundred human years constitute one day and night in the Tuṣita Heaven;
such is the calculation of its months, days, and years.
The lifespan in the Tuṣita Heaven is four thousand years;
this is calculated as five billion seven hundred and sixty million years in the human realm,
which constitutes one day and night in the hells.
In this manner, four thousand years as reckoned by the days, months,
and years of the hells constitute one day and night for the gods of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven; this corresponds to eight hundred years among human beings.
According to such calculations of days, months, and years,
the lifespan in the Nirmāṇarati Heaven is eight thousand years,
which corresponds to two hundred and thirty billion years by human reckoning.
This constitutes one day and night in the Great Screaming Hell.
Calculated by such days, months, and years, the lifespan in the Great Screaming Hell is eight thousand years,
which corresponds to one thousand six hundred years in the human world.
One day and night of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven is equal to this number of days,
months, and years; thus, the lifespan of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin devas is sixteen thousand years, which,
when calculated by human reckoning, is nine hundred twenty-one billion six hundred million years.
This constitutes one day and night in the Great Saṃjīva (Heating) Hell.
By such days, months, and years, the lifespan in the Great Saṃjīva Hell is sixteen thousand years.
Calculated by the standards of the various Great Saṃjīva Hells, their lifespan amounts to half an *kalpa*.
The lifespan in the Avīci Great Hell is one kalpa;
the maximum lifespan in the animal realm is also one kalpa,
according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
The nāgas, pretas, and others have an extremely long lifespan of five hundred years.
Second, regarding the calculation of the lifespans in the form realm (rūpadhātu),
kalpas are used as the measure.
The lifespan of the gods of the Brahmakāyika heaven is half a kalpa;
the lifespan of the gods of the Brahmapurohita heaven is one kalpa;
and the lifespan of the Mahābrahmā heaven is one and a half kalpas.
The Heaven of Limited Light lasts for four kalpas;
the Heaven of Infinite Light lasts for eight kalpas;
and the Heaven of Limited Purity lasts for sixteen kalpas.
The gods of the Immeasurable Purity Heaven [remain] for thirty-two kalpas;
the gods of the Universal Purity Heaven for sixty-four kalpas;
and the gods of the Merit-Love Heaven for one hundred and twenty-five kalpas.
The gods of Puṇyaprasava dwell for two hundred and fifty kalpas;
those of Bṛhatphala for five hundred kalpas;
and it is the same for the gods of Asaṃjñisattva.
In the Heaven of No-Expectation it is one thousand kalpas;
in the Heaven of No-Heat, two thousand kalpas;
and in the Heaven of Good Vision, four thousand kalpas.
The Śubhakṛtsna Heaven has eight thousand kalpas;
the Akaniṣṭha Heaven has sixteen thousand kalpas.
Third, as for calculating the lifespans of the heavens in the formless realm:
The gods of the Sphere of Infinite Space dwell for twenty thousand kalpas;
the gods of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, for forty thousand kalpas;
and the gods of the Sphere of Nothingness, for sixty thousand kalpas.
The lifespan in the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception is eighty thousand kalpas.
In all three realms, there are premature deaths;
this is the case for all except those in Uttarakuru.
As well as for Bodhisattvas in their final existence in Tuṣita Heaven and those in the Heaven of No-Thought,
their lifespans are fixed and it is not said that they die prematurely.
There are others who meet with untimely death.
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states the same regarding this as well.
However, among those in the human realm, the inhabitants of Uttarakuru possess the strongest power of merit.
Being of dull faculties and having few defilements, they experience much happiness and are free from the fault of grasping.
Upon death, they will certainly be reborn in higher realms; the rest is as previously explained.
Question: When this fire kalpa arises, everything up to the First Dhyāna is completely consumed by the flames.
Why, then, does the treatise say:
Does the Great Brahmā King obtain a lifespan of one and a half kalpas?
The answer is:
this statement of "one and a half kalpas" is based on an accumulation of sixty small kalpas constituting one and a half kalpas.
This does not refer to great kalpas (*mahākalpa*).
If one were to speak according to the great kalpas of water, fire, and wind,
it would still amount to one kalpa composed of eighty minor kalpas (*antarakalpa*).
The minor *kalpas* are still twenty fewer than the [full] minor *kalpas*;
this does not contradict the meaning of their lifespan being one and a half *kalpas*.
How is this known to be so?
In the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (Old Kośa), these are called *antarakalpa*;
in the *Lokaprajñapti-śāstra*, they are called *kṣudrakalpa*;
and in the new *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* and the new *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*, they are called *madhyamakalpa*.
These three names are distinct, but their essence is one and their duration is equal;
as it is said in the Āgama Sūtras.
That is to say, from a human lifespan of eighty-four thousand years,
it decreases by one year every hundred years,
until it reaches ten years.
Then, from ten years, it increases again up to eighty-four thousand years;

one such cycle of increase and decrease constitutes the duration of one intermediate kalpa (antarakalpa). This specific measure is also the same for the minor [kalpas]. According to the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, it is stated as follows:
This refers to heaven and earth;
when the three calamities exhaust one cycle from beginning to end, it is then called a great kalpa (mahākalpa),
corresponding to each occurrence of the calamities of water, fire, or wind.
It requires eighty intermediate kalpas.
Just as one intermediate kalpa is used for destruction and one intermediate kalpa for formation,
nineteen intermediate kalpas are spent with sentient beings dwelling in succession.
The period of abiding lasts for twenty intermediate kalpas;
the period of successive destruction and emptiness lasts for nineteen intermediate kalpas.
This constitutes one intermediate kalpa.
In nineteen intermediate kalpas, they encounter the destruction of the receptacle world by fire, water, or wind; in the [remaining] nineteen,
they encounter the destruction of the sentient-being world by famine, disease, or weapons.
Based on this principle,
the Abhidharma states as follows:
"This is the final abiding place."
This place is empty at the beginning;
that where sentient beings dwell last is the lowest Avīci Hell.
In this place, emptiness is ultimate;
as for where sentient beings first dwell,
that is not fixed.
If based on the fire kalpa, it is the first dhyāna;
if in terms of the water kalpa, it is the second dhyāna;
if in terms of the wind kalpa, it is the third dhyāna.
Based on this analysis, therefore,
within one great kalpa there are sixty intermediate kalpas, together with twenty distinct kalpas of the empty kalpa,
totaling eighty minor kalpas.
The beginning constitutes one great kalpa.
Thus has the exposition of kalpas been presented.
Next, the absence of contradiction will be demonstrated.
Regarding the statement that the lifespan of the first class of gods in the First Dhyāna, the Brahmakāyika devas, is half a kalpa:
it should be understood that this refers to half a kalpa—specifically twenty intermediate kalpas—within one of their own distinct mahākalpas.
Regarding the second, the lifespan of the Brahmā-purohita devas is one kalpa;
this refers specifically to one intermediate kalpa (antara-kalpa) out of the forty intermediate kalpas that constitute a mahā-kalpa.
Regarding the third, the lifespan of the Mahābrahmā devas is one and a half kalpas.
It should be understood that this is stated in reference to sixty intermediate kalpas constituting one and a half great kalpas; for this reason,
there is no contradiction.
The first dhyāna is thus.
From the second dhyāna upward, it should be understood that the lifespans are all explained in reference to the great kalpas of the three calamities,
and not in reference to the intermediate individual kalpas.
Within the second dhyāna,
the lifespan of the first, the Heaven of Limited Light (Parīttābha), is two kalpas; the lifespan of the second,
the Heaven of Immeasurable Light (Apramāṇābha), is four kalpas.
The third, the Ābhāsvara Heaven, has a lifespan of eight kalpas.
If it is said that when the calamity of water reaches the second dhyāna,
how is it that the various devas of the Ābhāsvara Heaven obtain a lifespan of eight great kalpas?
It should be understood that after those seven calamities of fire,
there subsequently arises one calamity of water that reaches as far as the second dhyāna;
this is the time when the beings of Ābhāsvara attain a lifespan of eight great kalpas.
Among the three dhyānas, the lifespan of the first, the Parīttābha (Limited Radiance) Heaven, is sixteen kalpas;
the second, the Apramāṇābha (Immeasurable Radiance) Heaven, is thirty-two kalpas;
and the third, the Ābhāsvara (Universal Radiance) Heaven, is sixty-four kalpas.
If it is asked: "Since the calamity of wind reaches as far as the third dhyāna, how is it that the gods of the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven attain a lifespan of sixty-four great kalpas?
This, too, should be understood.
After sixty-three cycles of calamities by water and fire,
only then does a single calamity by wind arise;
therefore, the Śubhakṛtsna gods attain a lifespan of sixty-four kalpas.
How is this known to be so?
This is as explained in the Abhidharma:
after the seven fire kalpas have arisen in succession, [the world remains empty].
However, when one water disaster occurs,
and likewise when seven times seven— forty-nine— fire disasters have occurred,
there is then one set of seven water disasters; when these are combined, they constitute fifty-six kalpas.
Furthermore, after these fifty-six kalpas have passed,
seven fire-kalpas will arise again;
only after these seven fire-kalpas will a single wind-disaster arise to destroy everything up to the third dhyāna heaven.
Together with the preceding [period], this constitutes sixty-four kalpas. By such reasoning,
the Śubhakṛtsna devas attain a lifespan of sixty-four kalpas.
Therefore, the Abhidharma speaks this verse:
Seven fires pass in succession, Then one water disaster;
Seven times seven fires and seven waters, And after seven more fires, the wind.
Question: Since the lifespan in these four heavens of the sphere of infinite consciousness (vijñānānantyāyatana) is double that of the sphere of infinite space (ākāśānantyāyatana),
one wonders why the lifespans in the latter two heavens do not likewise double those of the former.
The answer is:
As stated in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*,
there were three masters of the treatises who each explained this meaning.
Regarding the first explanation:

it means that in those two spheres of emptiness and consciousness, there are respectively immeasurable modes of practice; because all other practices, such as the "totalities" (kṛtsnāyatana), are abandoned, their lifespans increase twofold.
Because there are immeasurable practices in the sphere of infinite space,
one attains a lifespan of ten thousand kalpas;
furthermore, through other practices, one again attains a lifespan of ten thousand kalpas, and thus together one attains a lifespan of twenty thousand kalpas.
Because the sphere of consciousness possesses immeasurable modes of activity, one attains a lifespan of twenty thousand kalpas;
through further modes of activity, one again attains a lifespan of twenty thousand kalpas.
Since this is double the former, one attains a lifespan of forty thousand kalpas.
In the higher stages, there are no further immeasurable practices;
therefore, the lifespan does not double.
Such is one explanation.
The second master says that because both those realms of emptiness and consciousness each possess the two types of practice— concentration and wisdom—
their lifespans are doubled.
One attains a lifespan of ten thousand kalpas through meditative concentration;
one further attains a lifespan of ten thousand kalpas through the practice of wisdom.
Therefore, combined, one attains a lifespan of twenty thousand kalpas.

Through the practice of the concentration on the sphere of consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana-samādhi*), one attains a lifespan of twenty thousand kalpas; through the practice of wisdom (*prajñā*), one further attains a lifespan of twenty thousand kalpas.
Because this is double the former, one attains a lifespan of forty thousand kalpas.
In the two higher stages above,
there is only the practice of meditative concentration (samādhi) and no practice of wisdom (prajñā);
therefore, their lifespans no longer increase by multiples of one another.
The two [previous] explanations are thus;
as for the explanation of the third master,
he says that it refers to the portion of the life-span and retribution of those four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*).
Each has a lifespan of only twenty thousand kalpas;
because there is the state of being free from desire and the state of not being free from desire,
their lifespans thus differ by being either doubled or not.
In the stage of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), because one has not yet abandoned the desires of that own stage,
those desires have a lifespan of only twenty thousand eons.
In the stage of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), [the lifespan] is twenty thousand eons.
This is their fixed lifespan;
because they have become detached from the desire realm of the sphere of infinite space,
they further obtain twenty thousand kalpas.
Because this is double the previous amount, one attains a lifespan of forty thousand kalpas.
As for the twenty thousand kalpas of the sphere of nothingness,
that is its fixed lifespan.
Because they have abandoned desire for the two spheres of space and consciousness,
their lifespan increases by another forty thousand kalpas;
in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, it is twenty thousand [kalpas].
This fixed lifespan arises from being free from the desires of the three lower stages;
furthermore, one attains a lifespan of sixty thousand kalpas.
By such reasoning, one attains a lifespan of eighty thousand kalpas in the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (Naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana).
Thus it has been stated three times;
the meaning is manifest therein. Section Nine: On Residences. Question:
What is the meaning of "the abodes of the devas"?
The answer is:
As stated in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*,
although there are thirty-two heavens,
their abodes consist of only twenty-eight tiers.
Because those four formless attainments (*ārūpya*) are utterly free from corporeal retribution, they have no distinct location;
they pervade throughout both the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
However, for those beings in the realms of desire and form who have accomplished the karma of the four empty formless attainments,
they receive the retribution of that formless realm immediately upon the end of their life wherever it occurs.
There is no other location where they differ; the Mahāyāna teaches that there is form.
As for the twenty-eight layers, these refer to Mount Sumeru.
The Mūla rises from the earth to a height of four thousand yojanas;
it encircles the mountain with a length and breadth of ten thousand yojanas.
It is there that the devas of the Kṛtānta (Thousand-Handed) dwell.
Ascending another equal distance,
it circles the mountain for eight thousand yojanas;
there the Deva Garland-Holders (Mālādhāra) dwell.
Ascending another double [the previous height], it encircles the mountain for four thousand yojanas;
there dwell the gods who are constantly heedless.
Ascending yet another double, it encircles the mountain for four thousand yojanas.
The celestial deities of the sun, moon, and stars dwell therein.

Ascending another double [the previous height], four thousand yojanas above the mountain, dwell the gods of the Four Great Kings (*Cāturmahārājika*). Within that region there are seven kinds of golden mountains, and all the cities and villages of the Four Great Kings are situated therein.
Ascending further forty thousand yojanas, one reaches the summit of Mount Sumeru, which is forty thousand yojanas in length and breadth.
Within it lies the city of Sudarśana,
ten thousand yojanas in length and breadth.
Each face has its own thousand gates,
and the Trāyastriṃśa gods dwell therein.
From this mountain, one ascends forty thousand yojanas into the void.
There is a place formed of the seven treasures like a cloud;
it is like the great earth,
and the Yāma devas dwell therein.
Ascending another double [the previous height], there is a ground like clouds,
composed of the seven treasures;
this is the Tuṣita Heaven.
Ascending again by another factor of two, there is a ground like clouds,
composed of the seven treasures;
this is the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (Nirmāṇarati).
Ascending again by another factor of two, there is a ground like clouds,
composed of the seven treasures;
this is the Heaven of Mastery over Transformations (Nirmāṇarati).
In this manner, up to the ultimate heaven of the form realm,
there are grounds everywhere like clouds,
all composed of the seven precious jewels.
The distances between them all double successively, so there is no need for a detailed explanation.
According to the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*,
the Heaven of the Thirty-three (*Trāyastriṃśa*) is situated upon the summit of Mount Meru.
Each of its four sides at the summit measures twenty thousand [yojanas].
According to the calculation of its circumference, it totals eighty thousand.
Other masters state:
Each face measures eighty thousand [yojanas].
Its dimensions are no different from those of its four sides at the base.
At each of the four corners of the mountain summit, there is a peak.
Its height and breadth are each five hundred [yojanas].
There dwells a yakṣa deity named Vajrapāṇi,
who resides therein to protect the devas.
In the center of the mountain summit is a palace named Sudarśana;
it measures two thousand five hundred yojanas on each side and ten thousand yojanas in circumference.
The Golden Wall is half a yojana in height;
its ground is level and likewise composed of pure gold.
Both were adorned with one hundred and one varieties of miscellaneous jewels.
The ground was as soft to the touch as tūla-cotton;
when one stepped upon it, it rose and fell according to the movement of the foot.
This is the great capital city where Śakra, Lord of the Devas, resides.
The city has a thousand gates, adorned with magnificent splendor; at each gate stand five hundred yakṣas dressed in blue robes, valiant, handsome, and one yojana in height.
Each [guard] was clad in armor and armed with weapons,
stationed to defend the city gates. Within that city was a magnificent palace,
adorned with every kind of exquisite jewel, its splendor surpassing even the celestial palaces.
Therefore, it is named "Exalted.
It measures two hundred and fifty [yojanas] on each side,
with a circumference of one thousand yojanas.
These are called the delightful things within the city.
Outside the city, on its four sides, are four parks adorned with splendor;
these are the places where those devas sport together.
First is the Garden of Various Chariots (*nānā-ratha-udyāna*), so called because within this garden various chariots appear according to the power of the gods' merit.
Second is the Garden of Coarse Violence (*raudra-udyāna*),
where when the gods desire to wage war, armor, weapons, and other necessaries appear according to their requirements.
Third is the Miśravana Grove;
when the devas enter it, whatever they enjoy therein produces an equally innate and supreme joy.
Fourth is the Nandana Grove.
The most exquisite objects of desire and various species of beings all gather there; one may observe them without ever growing weary.
Thus, these four groves are each situated in a different direction, and each measures one thousand yojanas in circumference.
Each dwelling has its own wish-fulfilling pond, measuring fifty yojanas on each side,
filled with water possessing the eight virtues;
it is adorned according to one's desires by four gardens, flowering groves, birds, and fragrant forests.
The distinctions between the fruits of karma and the celestial blessings are difficult to conceive.
Outside the city, at the southwest corner, there is the Great Hall of Good Dharma (Sudharmā),
where the gods of the Thirty-three Heavens assemble periodically.
To distinguish between matters that are in accordance with the Dharma and those that are not, such as the subjugation of the Asuras and others.
The *Sūtra on the Arising of the World* states:
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
For what reason is the assembly hall of the devas named the Sudharmā Hall? When the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven gather and sit in assembly there, [they discourse on the Dharma].
Within it, one exclusively deliberates upon subtle, virtuous speech and profound meanings, weighing and examining them;
these are all the truly correct principles of the world’s most excellent and essential dharmas.
For this reason, the devas call it the Hall of Good Dharma (Sudharmā).
Furthermore, for what reason is it called the Pāruṣyaka Grove (literally "Roughness" in the Sui language)?
It is because the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven enters therein and sits upon the two rocks named Bhadra and Subhadra.
It speaks only of worldly, coarse, unwholesome, and frivolous speech;
therefore, it is called *pāruṣya*. For what reason is it named the Grove of Variegated Chariots (*citrapuṣpakavana*)?
After the Thirty-three Heavenly Kings had entered,
they sat upon two stones— one variegated and one well-variegated—
and discussed only various worldly matters of diverse appearances and speech.
For this reason, it is called the Park of Variegated Chariots (Citrapuṣpaka).
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions is it named the Park of Confusion (Saṃkīrṇa)?
On the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of every month, the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three (Trāyastriṃśa) always [assemble there].
All the court ladies within the palace enter this garden,
where they mingle and sport with the hosts of the Trāyastriṃśa devas;
without any obstruction arising, they indulge in their pleasures as they please.
Possessing the merit of the five celestial sensual pleasures, they roam about and experience joy.
For this reason, the gods collectively call this garden the Garden of Confusion (Saṃkīrṇa).
Furthermore, by what cause and condition does that heaven have a garden named Joy (Nandana)?
Once the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three have entered therein,
they sit upon the two rocks named Joy and Excellent Joy;
their hearts experience joy and further experience supreme bliss.
For this reason, the devas collectively designate that grove as "Joyful.
Furthermore, by what cause and condition is it named the Pāriyātra-kovidāra tree?
Beneath that tree dwells a son of the gods.
It is named Mada.
Day and night, he constantly enjoys himself in union with the various merits of the five sensory desires of that heaven, playing and experiencing pleasure.
For this reason, the gods subsequently called that tree by that name.
It is considered to be the Pārijāta-kovidāra tree.
Section Ten on Width and Narrowness. Question:
What is the measurement of the width of the heavens?
The answer is:
As stated in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*,
the summit of Mount Sumeru measures eighty-four thousand yojanas in length and breadth.
The area there that is level and habitable is forty thousand yojanas; for the Yāma Heaven,
it is double that, at eighty thousand yojanas.
That ground is eighty thousand yojanas in length and breadth.
In this manner, up to the realm of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods, each successive level doubles the size of the previous one;
that ground is six hundred and forty thousand yojanas in length and breadth.
Regarding the extent of the ground of the fourth dhyāna, it is not fixed;
there are two explanations.
According to the first explanation:
The first dhyāna is as vast as one four-continent world system;
the second dhyāna is like a small thousand-world system;
the third dhyāna is like a medium thousand-world system.
The fourth dhyāna is as vast as the great trichiliocosm.
Regarding the second explanation:
the first dhyāna is like a small chiliocosm.
The second dhyāna is as vast as a medium-thousandfold world system;
the third dhyāna is as vast as a great-thousandfold world system;
and the ground of the fourth dhyāna is so immeasurably broad that its boundaries cannot be described—thus the various masters have evaluated it. Regarding this, it is asked:
The first dhyāna is as vast as a small chiliocosm,
and so on up to the fourth dhyāna stage, which is infinitely vast;
it is not yet known whether [this extends] beyond another great trichiliocosm.
Will they share the Brahma-heaven of the first dhyāna,
and so on up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven?
Or will they [reside] above each of those four continents?
Is there a separate Brahmā Heaven of the First Dhyāna for each [being], and so on, up to a separate Akaniṣṭha Heaven of the Form Realm?
The answer is: Yes.
As stated in the *Loutan jing* (Ratna-kūṭa-sūtra):
"Above each of the four continents, there is a distinct [heavenly palace], and all are entirely different. Thus it is said:
Within a trichiliocosm, there are ten billion sets of four continents, Mount Sumerus, great oceans, Iron Ring Mountains, and the heavens of the Four Great Kings,
up to and including ten billion sets of Akaniṣṭha Heavens, each described individually.
This text clearly elucidates [this point], so there is no need for wearying confusion.
Furthermore, as stated in the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*:
"The term 'small' (*kṣudra*) carries the meaning of being base or inferior."
Because it excludes what has been mentioned above.
Just as a hornless cow is not included when one accumulates small parts to form a remainder, so too it does not include that [other category]. Question:
Since there are, for each of those four continents, even as far as their respective Akaniṣṭha heavens,
would these distinct locations not necessarily obstruct one another?
He replied:
Although there are billions of them dwelling together in one place,
they do not obstruct one another; just as rays of light interpenetrate and pervade each other without obstruction,
so too it is with them.
Because that form is subtle and exquisite,
it is said in the sūtras that the various devas of the form realm descend to listen to the Dharma.

Sixty devas may sit together upon the tip of a single blade of grass, yet they are neither crowded nor obstructed by one another; based on this scriptural evidence, what cause for doubt could there be?
Therefore, the *Yìpì* (Explanatory Parables) says: [text follows].
The first dhyāna is like a village; the second dhyāna is like a district; the third dhyāna is like a province;
the fourth dhyāna is like a kingdom. Section Eleven: Adornment. Section Eleven on Adornment states in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*:
Mount Sumeru is three million three hundred and sixty thousand li in height and is composed of four precious substances;
its eastern face is of gold.
The western side is of white silver;
the southern side is of lapis lazuli;
the northern side is of crystal.
Surrounding the four sides of the mountain range at its midpoint is Mount Yugandhara;
each is forty-two thousand yojanas high,
and the Four Great Kings each dwell upon one of these mountains.
The *Dīrgha Āgama* states:
"The northern face is made of celestial gold;
its light illuminates the north."
The western face is composed of crystal;
its light illuminates the west.
The eastern face is composed of heavenly silver.
The light shines upon the eastern direction.
The southern side is composed of heavenly lapis lazuli;
the light shines upon the southern direction.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"The Four Heavenly Kings each reside in their respective cities. The city in the east is named Uṣita-vīrya;
the city in the south is named Sudarśana."
In the west is a city named Cūḍa.
In the north there are three cities;
the first is named Bhīma.
The second is named Devapūjita (Honored by Gods),
and the third is named Gaṇasammatā (Admired by the Multitude). Furthermore, the *Dīrgha Āgama* states:
Pañcaśikha addressed the Blessed One, saying:
"Once, when the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven had assembled in the Sudharmā Hall for some discussion,
the Four Great Kings sat each in their respective positions according to their quarters."
The Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra sat in the east,
facing west, with Śakra positioned before him.
The Heavenly King Virūḍhaka sat in the south,
facing north, with Śakra before him.
The Heavenly King Virūpākṣa sat in the west,
facing east, with Śakra before him.
The Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa sat in the north,
facing south, with Śakra positioned in front of him.
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings all sat down first, and only then did I sit.
Furthermore, the *Lokasthāna-abhidharma-śāstra* states:
"It is like the Great City of Sudarśana in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven."
It is surrounded by forty-one thousand yojanas and encircled by a city made of pure gold,
ten yojanas in height.
The battlements atop the city walls were half a yojana high;
the gates were two yojanas high,
and the outer double-gates were one and a half yojanas high.
Every ten yojanas there is a gate;
the four sides of the city have a thousand gate-towers.
These city gates are composed of various precious jewels.
Adorned with various kinds of mani jewels,
one-fourth of this great city is the central golden wall, the abode of Śakra.
It measures twelve yojanas and has two main gates;
on its four sides there are four hundred and ninety-nine gates,
plus one small gate, making five hundred gates in total.
The configuration of this city is guarded by the fourfold army;
it features palisades, moats, groves, ponds, and various forests,
as well as palaces where musicians perform songs and instrumental music, along with all manner of external spectacles.
The various jewel adornments cannot be fully described.
In the center of this city is a jeweled multi-storied pavilion named Piśācayanta.
It is five hundred yojanas in length,
two hundred and fifty yojanas in width,
and one thousand five hundred yojanas in circumference.
On the four sides of that pavilion were defensive watchtowers made of jewels;
there were twenty-six on the eastern side and twenty-five on each of the other three sides.
There are one hundred and one such towers in total;
each defensive tower is two yojanas square,
with a circumference of eight yojanas.
Above each bastion there is a jeweled pavilion,
half a yojana in height, serving as a lookout;
on each bastion dwell seven goddesses.
Each goddess has seven handmaidens.
Within the pavilion there are ten thousand one hundred and seventy chambers.
Inside each chamber there are seven celestial maidens.
Each celestial maiden and each female attendant likewise numbered seven;
those celestial maidens were all the principal consorts of Śakra.
Outside the palace, he had four hundred and ninety-four million nine thousand nine hundred principal consorts for warding off enemies,
and three billion four hundred and six million four thousand three hundred female attendants within the various chambers.
The queens and court ladies together numbered three billion nine hundred and fifty-nine thousand two hundred;
at the very center of the multi-storied *piśācayana* pavilion stood a circular chamber.
It is thirty yojanas in width,
ninety yojanas in circumference,
and forty-five yojanas in height.
This is the place where Śakra dwells;
it is composed entirely of lapis lazuli and inlaid with various precious gems.
Furthermore, the *Saṃyukta Āgama* states:
Within the palace of Śakra,
there is the Vaijayanta Hall,
which contains a hundred towers and pavilions.
There are seven layers of walls and seven chambers;
there are seven celestial queens.
Each was later attended by seven female attendants.
As the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana traveled throughout the small chiliocosm,
he found no hall or pavilion as magnificent and dignified as this.
Regarding the Vaijayanta Hall, the *Sūtra on the Arising of the World* states:
"The carvings and decorations within that celestial palace city, and the pleasures of desire experienced therein, are such that they cannot be fully described. Thus it speaks of such a place.
Śakra Devānām Indra dwells together with the Apsaras Śacī, the daughter of the Asuras.
Śakra manifests emanated bodies and dwells together with all his consorts.
All these consorts then reflect as follows:
Śakra dwells together with me;
Satyabhāmā dwells together with Śacī.
These are the residences located on the four sides within this city.
The streets, lanes, and marketplaces are all even and straight.
These celestial cities, according to the merit of their inhabitants, consist of various jewels;
their houses, numerous and vast, are level, upright, and perfectly aligned.
The roads of this celestial city number five hundred;
the four crossroads intersect so that the rows are clearly defined,
all like the lines of a chessboard, with four gates providing thorough access through which one can see from east to west.
In every alley and marketplace, precious goods were filled to overflowing.
Among them, there were seven markets in the heavens:
the first was the market for grain and rice; the second was the market for clothing.
The third is the market for various incenses;
the fourth is the market for food and drink;
the fifth is the market for flower garlands.
The sixth is the marketplace of artisans;
the seventh is the marketplace of courtesans.
In each location, there is likewise a market official.
In these various markets, devaputras and devakanyās come and go, engaging in trade,
deliberating over prices high and low,
and seeking to increase or decrease their value.
They weigh and calculate the number [of items],
fully employing the methods of the marketplace;
though they perform these acts for the sake of amusement and sport.
Without grasping, without giving, and without a sense of "mine," one should take whatever is needed for liberation.
If it accords with one's inclination, one may take it as desired.
If they do not agree, one should say:
"This object is exceptionally precious and is not what I require;
the road through the middle of the marketplace is soft, smooth, and lovely."
Adorned with various jewels,
with celestial garments suspended and banners and streamers erected.
The sounds of music and other such melodies are constantly uninterrupted.
Furthermore, there are voices saying,
"Welcome, welcome!"
"May you wish to eat and drink; I now offer this to you.
This Great City of Sudarśana is the dwelling place of Śakra.

Furthermore, divine districts, prefectures, counties, and villages are spread all around it; beyond these, the various celestial abodes are adorned with jewels, and fragrant music fills every place. The bliss of their retributive enjoyment is beyond all reckoning. Outside the northern gate of the Great City of Sudarśana...
Extending for twenty yojanas, there is a great grove named Nandana,
which is one thousand yojanas in circumference.
Within this [grove] there is also a pond named Nandā (Joy),
measuring one hundred yojanas in extent and likewise in depth.
The four sides are filled with celestial waters,
and their foundations and banks are piled with precious bricks.
Outside the eastern gate of the city, there is a garden.
It is named Saṃkha; there is a pond named Citrā;
outside the southern gate of the city, there is a park.
It is named "Harsh Speech," and the pond bears the same name.
To the west of the city gate, outside the wall, there is a garden named "Miscellaneous Garden."
The ponds are likewise named after them.
The dimensions of the gardens and ponds are all as previously described.
Various flowers, fruits, birds, and groves abound, with the birds wheeling and singing in every variety.
The exquisite adornments and embellishments are beyond description.
Section Twelve: Petitions. As stated in the *Lokasthāna-abhidharma-śāstra*:
At that time, Śakra, leading the hosts of devas,
desired to go to the Sudharmā Hall for recreation in the celestial gardens.
Surrounded by the devas and paying them due respect, he entered the garden.
Within the Hall of Good Dharma (Sudharmā), beside the central pillar, there is a lion throne.
Śakra ascends the throne,
while sixteen heavenly kings on each of the left and right sides sit in rows.
The other devas sat in order according to their respective ranks, from highest to lowest.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, had two crown princes:
the first was named Candana.
The second is named Śubhīra;
these two are the great generals of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven,
who sit on the left and right sides of the Thirty-three Gods.
At that time, King Dhṛtarāṣṭra sat at the eastern gate together with his ministers and military hosts;
having respectfully welcomed the devas who entered, he sat among them.
At that time, the Heavenly King Virūḍhaka sat at the southern gate together with his ministers and military hosts;
having paid homage to the various devas, they were permitted to enter and take their seats within.
At that time, the Deva King Virūpākṣa sat by the western gate, and the Deva King Vaiśravaṇa sat by the northern gate; both did so as before, and they were able to enter and sit within.
These Four Heavenly Kings report the good and evil of the world to Śakra and the Trāyastriṃśa gods in the Hall of Good Dharma; at that time,
the Buddha, the World-Honored One, spoke of these matters.

On the eighth day of this month, the ministers of the Four Great Kings travel throughout the world to observe in succession whether many or few people have undertaken the eight precepts on this very day.
Whether much or little, they all practice giving;
whether much or little, they cultivate meritorious deeds;
and whether much or little, they show reverence to their parents, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and the elders within their households.
It is the same on the fourteenth and fifteenth days of the month.
If there are not many people who observe the eight precepts, practice giving, and show respect,
at that time the Four Kings go to the Hall of Dharma.
Śakra, the Lord of Devas, explained these matters in response to the inquiry.
At that time, having heard this account, all the celestial lords Śakras gave rise to a mind of anxiety and distress.
He spoke these words:
"This matter is not good;
it is not in accordance with the Dharma for the various celestial elders and celestial retinues within the household."
The ranks of the asuras should accordingly diminish,
while their companions increase day by day;
yet if one observes the eight precepts, practices giving, and cultivates merit, [the situation shall change].
They show reverence toward śramaṇas, elders, and others;
the Four Kings consult with them,
and the various devas and Śakra experience joy in their hearts.
He spoke these words:
"This is most excellent.
The assembly of righteous devas is increasing day by day."
The companions of the asuras gradually diminished in number;
therefore, he cites the Buddha’s teaching in a geya verse:
"These ministers of the Four Kings patrol the world on the eighth day."
The Princes of the Four Heavenly Kings, In the fourteenth [assembly], Avalokiteśvara;
In the fifteenth, the Most Victorious One (Jinājit).
Because the Four Kings delight in renown, they themselves travel through the world To observe all that is virtuous and evil.
These people of the world possess minds that accord with the Dharma;
there are many noble ones who practice giving, receive [the teachings],
subdue anger as Bodhisattvas, and are able to cultivate the Path, so that the merit of both men and women increases.
At that time, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, having gained faith, were exceedingly joyful;
they repeatedly gave rise to sympathetic joy. The Four Great Kings, with their retinues, praised the excellence of the discourse;
the various celestial beings increased more and more in number.
May the asura hosts diminish day by day;
may those who follow the mind of the Perfectly Awakened One, the Dharma well-proclaimed, and the Noble Sangha,
dwell in peace and happiness, their hearts ever filled with joy.
The worldly fruit and the supramundane fruit, Which are attainable by those in the human realm who are virtuous toward the Buddha,
Dharma, and Saṅgha; Abiding within the sphere of the Three Jewels,
I now, for your sakes, Proclaim the excellent path of the three types of noble beings.
If a person seeks the truth, abandoning evil and practicing what is good,
they possess such a treasure that from a little they obtain much;
just as the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, by performing small acts of merit, are born in heaven.
Śakra and the other devas, possessing great merit and renown,
have gathered in the Hall of Good Dharma; as well as those men and women of virtuous conduct dwelling in other abodes, they have all been reported by the Four Kings.
Pure and beloved by the devas, its fragrance pervades all the heavens.
Chapter Thirteen: The Section on Supernatural Powers. According to the *Loutan jing* (Lokasthāna-sūtra):
Between the realms of desire and form, there exists a separate palace of Māra.
This Māra harbors jealousy like a stone mill;
he grinds away and destroys all merit.
It is six thousand yojanas in length and breadth;
its sevenfold palace walls are adorned with every ornament, just like those in the lower heavens.
The aforementioned seven heavens all possess these ten qualities.
First, flying hither in infinite numbers;
second, flying thither in infinite numbers;
third, moving without obstruction.
Fourth, they come without obstruction.
Fifth, their celestial bodies have no skin, flesh, sinews, veins, blood, or marrow.
Sixth, their bodies have no impurities, such as excrement or urine.
Seventh, his body never experiences fatigue;
eighth, the celestial maidens do not give birth;
ninth, his heavenly eyes do not blink.
The ten bodies are compliant with one's wishes:
if one desires them blue, they are blue;
if one desires them yellow, they are yellow.
The same applies to the excellence of other colors.
Furthermore, there are ten matters:
first, the infinity of flying through the air.
Second, they travel back and forth without limit.
Third, there are no thieves in the heavens.
Fourth, they do not speak of the good or evil of one another's bodies.
Fifth, his five parts do not protrude;
sixth, the teeth of all his celestial beings are even and closely set;
seventh, his hair is deep blue-black in color, glossy, and eight feet long.
8. If a celestial being desires a blue complexion, their hair shall also be blue.
9. If one desires a white body, the body shall immediately become white.
10. If one desires a black body, the body shall immediately become black.
The *Qishi jing* (Sūtra on the Arising of the World) also says:
"All devas possess ten distinct characteristics. What are these ten?"
First, when the devas travel, their coming and going are boundless.
Second, when the devas travel, their coming and going are unimpeded.
Third, when the devas travel, there is neither slowness nor haste.
Fourth, when the devas walk, their feet leave no tracks.
Fifth, the physical strength of the devas is free from ailment or fatigue.
Sixth, the bodies of the devas have form but cast no shadows.
Seventh, all devas have neither feces nor urine.
Eighth, all devas have neither nasal mucus nor saliva.
Ninth, the bodies of the devas are pure and sublime.
They are without skin, flesh, sinews, veins, fat, blood, marrow, or bone.
Regarding the bodies of the ten classes of devas, whether they wish to manifest them as long or short, blue, yellow, red, or white, large or small, coarse or fine,
they are able to do so entirely according to their will.
All are exquisite, dignified, and peerless, inspiring love and delight in those who behold them.
All the devas possess these ten kinds of inconceivable qualities.
Furthermore, the bodies of the various devas are full and robust;
their teeth are white, square, and closely set;
and their hair is blue-black and neatly trimmed.
Supple and lustrous;
his body emits radiance and possesses supernormal powers.
They soar through the void and travel by flight, their eyes never blinking;
they are adorned with natural necklaces and wear garments free from dust or grime.
As stated in the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*:
The assembly of the Four Great Kings ascends to see the Heaven of the Thirty-three, yet they do not truly belong to the Heaven of the Thirty-three;
their ascent to see the Yāma Heaven and so forth is likewise.
This occurs if they have attained the supernormal powers (abhijñā) produced by meditative concentration (samādhi).
All are able to ascend and behold the realms above; or,
by relying on the power of others, they ascend to see the higher heavens,
namely, by attaining supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) or being led upward by celestial beings.
Going there, they see according to what is appropriate;
they can also see those who have come from above,
or when those from the higher realms descend toward below.
The lower emanation body is not seen by the lower eyes,
because it is not within their range,
just as one does not perceive that touch.
When one descends from the stage of a higher fruit,
one must necessarily transform one's lower body so that those dwelling on the lower stages may see it;
as the *Lokasthāna-abhidharma-śāstra* states:
The people of Jambudvīpa, if they lack supernormal powers or the power derived from others,
cannot see forms that are obstructed by barriers and the like;
as for the people of the other three continents, if they lack the power of others, [they likewise cannot see them].
Consequently, they are unable to see forms beyond obstructions.
Even the various devas of the six desire realms, whether through their supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) or the power of others,
cannot see forms beyond obstructions from within their own abodes.
When looking from afar, one sees only that which is within the Cakravāḍa mountains;
one cannot see the forms beyond the mountains.
Thus it is with Mahābrahmādeva in his own palace.
If one is devoid of supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) or the assistance of others' efforts,
one cannot perceive forms beyond obstructions;
when looking from afar, one sees only within a single thousandfold world-system (*sahasra-lokadhātu*).
14. Section on Bodily Radiance. Regarding the fourteenth section, the Section on Bodily Radiance, according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*:
"As for the bodily radiance produced by the karmic retribution of the various devas, the bodies of all devas in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are constantly luminous."
Because they have practiced giving lamps, candles, bright jewels, and so forth, as well as maintaining the purity of ethical discipline (*śīla*) and meditative concentration (*dhyāna*),
their bodies are constantly luminous and do not require the illumination of the sun or moon.
The gods of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) practice meditation and are free from desire.
Because he practices the fire-samādhi,
his body constantly emits a sublime radiance that surpasses the light of the sun and moon, as well as the retributive light of the heavens of the desire realm that have transcended desire.
To state the essential point:
These various radiances all arise because the mind is pure.
If one were to discuss this according to the commentaries,
the Buddha’s constant radiance extends one zhang from each side of his face.
Although the radiance of the various devas may extend for immeasurable *yojanas*,
it is eclipsed and rendered invisible by the side of a single *zhang* of light.
Furthermore, the *Upāsikā-śīla-saṃvara-sūtra* states:
The Buddha told Viśākhā:
"The Tathāgata possesses six kinds of radiance.
What are these six?"
First, blue light;
second, yellow light;
third, red light.
Fourth, white light; fifth, red light;
sixth, purple light.
These luminous colors shine forth brilliantly.
These are called the six kinds of light of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, the *Dīrgha Āgama* states:
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
The light of a firefly is not equal to the light of a lamp or candle;
the light of a lamp or candle is not equal to that of a torch;
the light of a torch is not equal to that of a massed fire.
The brilliance of accumulated fires is not equal to that of the Four Heavenly Kings;
the palaces, clothing, and bodily radiance of the Four Kings are not equal to those of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Even the radiance extending successively up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven is not equal to the radiance of Maheśvara;
the radiance of Maheśvara is not equal to the radiance of the Buddha.
From the light of fireflies up to the light of the Buddha,
the combined total of all such lights is not equal to the light of the Truth of Suffering, the Truth of the Origin, the Truth of Cessation,
and the Truth of the Path. Therefore, O bhikṣus, those who seek light—
One should seek the light of the Noble Truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
Furthermore, there are seven colors of humans. What are these seven?
Some are golden in color;
some are fire-colored; some are blue.
Some are yellow in color;
some are red in color;
some are black in color.
There are devas and asuras who likewise possess seven colors. Furthermore,
the *Lishi apitan lun* (Abhidharmakośa-śāstra) states:
The physical bodies of sentient beings in Jambudvīpa are of various different types;
so too are those of the people in Pūrvavideha in the east and Aparagoyānī in the west.
Except for the black color, all other colors are the same as those of the people of Jambudvīpa.
As for all the inhabitants of Uttarakuru in the north,
they are entirely white and pure.
The Four Heavenly Kings have four kinds of complexions:
deep blue, red, yellow, and white.
The complexions of all the gods in the realm of desire are likewise the same.
What are the four kinds of colors of the gods?
At the time of their initial birth,
if they see a dark-blue flower, they become dark-blue in color.
The rest is all like this.
Section Fifteen: On Market Transactions. According to the *Utpatti-sūtra*, regarding all market transactions of the people of Jambudvīpa:
Either with money and treasures,
or with grain and silk,
or with sentient beings.
In the commercial transactions of the people of Aparagoyānī,
they use either cattle and sheep or maṇi jewels.
In the markets of the people of Pūrvavideha,
trade is conducted either with wealth and silk or with the five grains.
Or there are mani-jewels;
the people of Uttarakuru no longer engage in buying and selling,
for whatever they desire appears spontaneously.
As the *Qishi jing* (Sutra on the Arising of the World) states:
"The various heavens of the desire realm are like those of the Four Heavenly Kings and the Heaven of the Thirty-three."
They all have markets for trade and places for excursions to delight the spirit;
in reality, they differ from those of the common world as previously described.
16. Section on Marriage: The sixteenth section on marriage states, as recorded in the *Utpatti-sūtra*:
"In the other three continents, there are likewise the customs of marriage between men and women."
The people of Uttarakuru have no sense of "self" or "mine.
When the branches of the trees bend down, men and women unite; there is no further need for marriage.
This is also the case for the various nāgas, garuḍas, asuras, and so forth.
All have the customs for marriage and the rites for men and women,
which are roughly like those of the human realm.
This includes the gods of the six heavens of desire as well as the Māra heavens.
All [the heavens] below have marriage customs,
as briefly described above.
From this point upward, none of the devas engage in marriage anymore.
Because there is no distinction between male and female,
when the people of the four continents engage in sexual desire,
their two organs meet and impurity is emitted.
When all the nāgas, garuḍas, and others engage in sexual desire,
their two organs meet one another.
Merely by emitting wind, they attain satisfaction;
there is no impurity.
This is the manner of sexual desire among the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
When the organs meet and reach satisfaction, they also emit wind;
this is no different from the dragons and birds mentioned before.
In the Yāma Heaven, desire is fulfilled by holding hands.
In the Tuṣita Heaven, desire is fulfilled through recollection;
in the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, it is fulfilled through gazing intently;
in the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, it is fulfilled through conversation.
The various deities within Māra’s body gaze upon one another with desire;
they all attain satisfaction and fulfill their lustful acts.
Furthermore, the *Lokasthiti-śāstra* states:
If the gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings seek a celestial maiden,
they may only receive her after the maiden’s family has granted permission;
she may be taken through either barter or purchase.
The gods of the desire realm are likewise.
The people of Jambudvīpa, as well as those of the other three continents, and the gods of the Cāturmahārājakāyika and Trāyastriṃśa heavens, must necessarily come together to form sexual desire.
In the Yāma Heaven, beings engage in desire by embracing one another;
in the Tuṣita Heaven, they do so by holding hands;
in the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, they do so by laughing together.
The Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods regard one another as objects of desire.
The inhabitants of Aparagoyānī experience various sensual pleasures that are twice as superior to those of the inhabitants of Jambudvīpa.

In this manner, proceeding successively upward, the enjoyment of desire among the gods of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*) is twice as superior as that of the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (*nirmāṇarati*).
Among the inhabitants of the other four continents, there are those who consume unwholesome food and those whose growth occurs within the womb.
Among the goddesses and others in the abodes of the Four Heavenly Kings,
there is no such thing as unwholesome food, nor is there conception or gestation; furthermore,
they do not give birth to children.
Nor does she hold the child;
when a son or daughter is born,
it may rest upon her lap.
Or, if one gives birth at a place where women sleep,
one will give birth to a daughter.
If one is at a woman's dwelling, [the same applies].
The goddess thought to herself,
"This is my son," and the male deity also said, "This is my son."
Thus, if one is born from the lap where a single father and a single mother slept together,
there is only one father,
yet all the wives and concubines may serve as mothers.
There are also those who practice until death without desire.
Among the gods born in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, the matters of desire are immeasurable and incalculable;
yet there are also those who practice until death without desire.
It is the same for all the devas of the desire realm.
Generally, all women find pleasure in touch,
while all men find pleasure when impurity is emitted.
The gods of the desire realm take the emission of vital energy as their pleasure.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states, citing a sūtra: [text follows].
At the beginning of the kalpa, humans lacked the male and female sexual organs;
their physical forms were indistinguishable.
Later, upon consuming the "taste of the earth" (pṛthivī-rasa), the male and female sexual organs arose.
From this, the distinction between male and female arises.
Because the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) is free from edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*), these two faculties do not exist there. Some say:
The two faculties of male and female have utility in the desire realm,
but not in the form realm;
therefore, those two faculties— the nose and the tongue— also lack utility in the form realm, though they do have utility in the desire realm.
Therefore, regarding the question as to whether the celestial beings of the form realm (rūpadhātu) are female or male,
one should respond as follows.
They are all males; although they lack the male organ, they possess other characteristics of a man,
and because they are also able to be free from defilement, they are called males.
17. Section on Food and Drink. As stated in the *Utpatti-sūtra* (Qishi jing):
"All sentient beings have four kinds of nutriment (*āhāra*) by which the great elements (*mahābhūta*) are sustained and maintained."
What are the four?
First, gross material food and subtle food;
second, the food of contact.
Third is the food of mental volition;
fourth is the food of consciousness.
Which sentient beings should consume coarse material food as well as subtle food?
For example, for the people of Jambudvīpa,
rice, parched grain, beans, meat, and the like are called coarse physical food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*);
while massage, bathing, rubbing with ointments, and so forth are called subtle food (*sūkṣmāhāra*).
Those outside of this, including humans of the three continents below and the various devas of the six desire realms,
all take coarse physical matter and subtle [nutriments] as their food. From this point upward,
the devas of the form realm and the formless realm [subsist otherwise].
They take the joy of dhyāna and the delight in the Dharma as their food;
they no longer have coarse or subtle material food. Question:
Which sentient beings take contact as their nutriment?
The answer is:
all those born from eggs take contact as their nutriment because they obtain a body [at birth].
What kind of sentient beings take volition as their nutriment?
Those sentient beings whose mental intentions provide nourishment and moisture,
whereby their sense faculties increase.
Just as fish, turtles, snakes, frogs, *kārakūṭa* and other such beings,
as well as other sentient beings whose sense faculties and life-span are nourished and sustained by mental volition (*cetanā*),
all of these take volition as their food.
Which sentient beings take consciousness as their nutriment?
Namely, the sentient beings of the hells and the gods of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*) and so forth;
all of them use the sustenance of consciousness as their food.
The gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings all consume the essence of *sūdā*;
they eat one pinch in the morning and one pinch in the evening.
Once the food has entered their bodies, it is transformed into their very physical form.
These groves, gardens, ponds, and parks all arise spontaneously with the flavor of ambrosia (*sūdāsa*).
This ambrosial flavor can also transform itself into the eight kinds of food and drink, such as *khādaniya* (solid foods) and so forth.
The food of all the devas in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is likewise of this nature.
The devas of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), from the first dhyāna up to the Universal Purity (*śubhakṛtsna*), take joy as their food.
The devas above the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) take mental activity (*manaskarma*) as their food.
Question: What is the food and drink of the various devas like?
Answer: [As follows].
As it is said in the Sūtra:
among the devas of the desire realm, there are differences according to their nobility or lowliness and their excellence or inferiority;
those whose merit is thick [and abundant].
Whatever they thought of was fully provided;
when they drank, nectar filled their cups,
and when they ate, a hundred flavors arrived together.
Those of meager merit,
though they possess food and drink, never find it to their satisfaction;
because of this insufficiency, they continue to serve themselves more food.
Therefore, a sutra says:
"For example, when the various devas eat from a common precious vessel,
the color of the food differs according to their respective merit."
Those of superior capacity see white;
those of middling capacity see yellow;
and those of inferior capacity see red.
The gods of the form realm take the joy of meditative concentration as their nourishment;
if one speaks in terms of the four kinds of nutriment,
they possess only the nutriment of contact.
18. Section on Servants and Vehicles. Question: What are the servants and vehicles of the various devas?
Answer: [As follows:]
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"Just as the six heavens of the desire realm have servants and vehicles;
'servants' refers to attendants."
"Vehicles" refers to mounts for riding.

This is because among the six heavens of the desire realm, there exist sovereigns and ministers, wives and concubines, and distinctions of honor and status; those of lower rank must necessarily follow those of higher rank.
The lower realms necessarily follow the upper.
As for those who ride [these vehicles], since all six heavens of the desire realm contain various kinds of animals,
the devas may mount them as they please when wishing to travel.
Some ride on elephants and horses;
some ride on peacocks;
some ride on various dragons.
According to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*,
from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven downward, there are elephants, horses, wild ducks, geese, mandarin ducks, peacocks, dragons,
and so forth; however, from the Yāma Heaven upward, there are entirely no elephants, horses, or four-footed sentient beings.
Only the birds known as the "Teaching the Heedless," the "Speaking Truth," and the "Red Water" admonish the devas and warn them against negligence.
It is asked: [Why is this so?]
If there are no four-footed creatures such as elephants or horses,
what do those devas ride when they wish to travel?
The answer is:
As stated in the treatise,
it further explains itself:
"Even though there are no elephants, horses, or various devas who wish to emerge."
By the power of their merit,
elephants and horses immediately appeared,
manifesting according to their will.
The vehicle upon which they ride at will vanishes once the journey is completed.
This teaching for the heedless birds and others exists throughout all six heavens;
it constantly serves as a teacher to the devas, rebuking their negligence.
It is not only above Yama that this exists exclusively.
Question: Since these birds are animals, [how can they be so?]
How could he serve as a teacher for the devas?
As stated in the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra*,
when this bird was formerly a human being, he was a teacher who converted [beings] throughout the three continents.
The various devas were originally sentient beings who were to be transformed.
Because they accepted and believed the transformation,
they now attain birth in the heavens through their practice of generosity and observance of the precepts.
When that bird was formerly his teacher,
he broke the precepts for the sake of fame and profit;
his mind was insincere.
He has now become a celestial bird;
yet, by the power of subtle roots of goodness cultivated through his past teachings,
he is now able to be born in the heavens.
Because he was originally their transformation-teacher,
he acts as a teacher for all the devas;
whenever he sees the devas being negligent, he comes to reprimand them.
Upon seeing and hearing this, the various devas each felt shame and remorse, and they reformed themselves, abandoning negligence. 19. Section on Retinues. Question:
How many are the retinues of the various devas?
Answer: As it says in the treatise:
"The devas of the form realm are so numerous that they cannot be described."
It means that those gods are neither male nor female and have no partners;
they arise through transformation at birth and vanish through transformation at death.
The two retributions— the primary body and the environment— follow him naturally as his palace;
he takes meditative concentration as his joy,
and it is impossible to describe the number of his retinue.
The devas of the desire realm possess males and females who pair with one another.
Thus, the *Mahāmaṅgala-vidyā-mantra-sūtra* states:
"The Four World-Protecting Kings preside over the four directions."
The Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra leads the hosts of gandharvas;
the Heavenly King Virūpākṣa leads the hosts of kumbhāṇḍas;
the Heavenly King Virūḍhaka leads the hosts of nāgas.
The Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa leads a host of yakṣas.
Each of these four kings has ninety-one sons who are handsome in appearance and possess great power.
All are named "Emperor.
This Heavenly King has a total of three hundred and sixty-four sons,
who are able to protect the ten directions.
Śakra Devānām-Indra presides over the four intermediate directions,
while Mahābrahmā Deva-rāja presides over the zenith.
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
All mountains, rivers, trees, lands, cities, and walls,
as well as all ghosts and spirits, belong to the Four Heavenly Kings; therefore,
they all follow and come together with them.
Among these spirits and deities, there are those who have not obtained the scroll of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra;
for this reason, they come to the place where the Prajñāpāramitā is kept to make offerings, prostrate, and likewise seek its benefit.
The retinues of those in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and above increase further and further;
their numbers are such that they cannot be fully recounted.
This is unlike the retinues below the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, which are numerous.
Just as Śakra possesses ninety billion nayutas of celestial maidens,
along with a thousand sons and immeasurable ministers.
They became his retinue.
Thus, a verse in the sutra says:
"Śakra universally responds to all the celestial maidens, numbering nine hundred and twenty billion nayutas."
Each of the goddesses said to herself: "The Heavenly King is sporting with me alone," even among the least of them,
there were still ten thousand goddesses.
They take these as their retinue, and they never fall below this number.
Section Twenty: The Noble and the Base. Question: [As stated above].
Regarding the noble and humble among the various devas:
the answer is that all six heavens of the first desire realm possess both noble and humble ranks,
because there exist distinctions between rulers and ministers, commoners and subjects, and wives and concubines.
Just as among the Śakras of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven,
Śakra is the sovereign and the thirty-two devas are his ministers.
The remaining celestial hosts are the subjects;
among the women, Lady Manoharā is the queen,
and all the other celestial maidens are concubines.
The remaining five heavens are all like this.
Within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), there is distinction between noble and base only among the three heavens of the first dhyāna;
Mahābrahmā is their sovereign.
The Ministers of Brahmā are the ministers;
the Retinue of Brahmā are the common people.
From this point upward, the various heavens receive retributions that are equal.
Furthermore, there is no distinction between noble and base. Section Twenty-one: Poverty and Wealth. Question:
What is the nature of poverty and wealth among the various devas?
Answer: As stated in the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra*,
from the Yāma heaven upward, throughout all the heavens of the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), the gods are equal in both poverty and wealth.
From the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven downward, there are distinctions of retribution ranging from thickness to thinness, and from poverty to wealth.
Those whose merit is thick possess all things in abundance, and their karmic rewards are more than sufficient.
Those of meager merit,
though possessing clothing and palaces made of the seven treasures, always lack sufficient food;
thus it is said in that sutra.
In the past, there were certain devas of meager merit who,
suffering from hunger,
descended here among the people of Jambudvīpa.
He plucked sour jujubes and ate them.
When people saw his extraordinary appearance, they were startled and questioned him; he then replied:
"I am not a human being.
Although we gods of meager merit possess palaces and exquisite garments,
our food is always insufficient."
Therefore, I have come here to pluck and eat these jujubes.
You need not be surprised;
as explained at length in the sūtras, this is due to my prior cultivation of precepts, patience, and so forth, yet my failure to practice generosity.

22. Section on Funerary Rites, Part Two: From the Heaven of the Four Great Kings up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, if a member of one’s retinue dies, they do not perform funeral rites, nor do they cremate, discard, or bury them.
Just as a flame vanishes without leaving a corpse,
for they are born by transformation (*upapāduka*).
The gods of the Four Great Kings kill themselves or cause others to kill them, yet they do not eat meat.
The same applies to the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.
From the Yāma heaven up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven, they neither take life themselves nor cause others to take life.
Upon death, they do not consume flesh, because they are born by transformation;
thus, at death, no physical remains are left behind. The verse says:
The three realms are in turmoil; the six paths are vast and boundless. Coming and going without end, one suffers without respite.
Bound by karmic retribution and pressed from all sides, agonizing pains spread in every direction—this is truly due to evil karma.
Having encountered such peril and ruin, how could one have known of drowning?
How could one know the vessel for crossing? The foundation is built up by successive layers.
Before soaring and wheeling in flight, one should leave this defiled land to travel and rest in the Pure Realm.
With a single thought returning to the Right, may your life-span be boundless. *Fayuan zhulin*, Scroll Three.

It stirs the profound compassion of the Jewel-Mind and awakens the subtle thoughts of auspiciousness;

Manifesting ominous signs to intimidate the wicked,

Section Two: The Department of Constellations. As stated in the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*:
At that time, the Naga King Sagara addressed the Bodhisattva Suciloma, saying,
"O Mahasattva!"
By whom were these constellations originally taught?
Who created the great stars and the small stars?
Who created the sun and the moon?
Within which day does which star appear first in the void of space? Furthermore, by whom was it established?
How do the thirty days, the twelve months, and the years constitute time?
To what are they attached?
What is your clan name and what is your personal name?
What is good and what is evil? What do you eat and what do you give as alms?
How is this day and how is this night?
"How do the sun, moon, and lunar mansions move, and so forth?
You are the foremost and most honored among all holy ones;
we pray that you will compassionately explain this fully for us, O Dragon."
"Having heard this, we shall be liberated from suffering and practice accordingly.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Śuddharaśmi addressed the nāgas, saying:
"In a past life, at the beginning of this Bhadrakalpa, there was a devaputra."
His name was Mahāsammata;
he was handsome beyond compare, possessed of wisdom and intelligence,
and transformed others through right conduct, always delighting in tranquility.
He took no pleasure in sensual attachment and always delighted in maintaining his personal purity.
The king had a consort who was deeply greedy for sexual desire;
since the king had met with misfortune, she found no way to satisfy her heart's wish.
Once, he saw a herd of donkeys manifesting their sexual organs;
his lustful mind was aroused, and he stripped off his clothes and approached them.
When the donkeys saw him, they immediately engaged in intercourse with him.
It subsequently formed a fetus,
and when the months were complete, a son was born whose head, ears, mouth, and eyes all resembled those of a donkey.
They possess only the form of humans,
yet their bodies are coarse, rough, and covered with brindled hair,
no different from those of animals.
When the lady saw this, her heart was struck with terror and fear;
she immediately cast it away into a latrine.
By the power of its merit, however, it remained suspended in mid-air and did not fall.
At that time, there was a rākṣasī named Ass-Face (Kharakarṇī).
Seeing that the child was undefiled, she thought to herself, "This is a blessed son."
He then caught it in mid-air, washed and held it,
and took it to the Snowy Mountains to nourish and raise it with milk,
treating it exactly like his own son without any distinction.
Upon reaching adulthood, he was taught to take elixirs of immortality and roamed day and night with celestial youths;
furthermore, there were great devas who also came to protect him.
As this child consumed sweet fruits and medicinal herbs,

Thus the hosts of devas collectively praised him,
calling him the Great Seer Kakuda Kātyāyana (in the language of Han, Lu-ch'en Da-xian Sheng-ren). Because of these causes and conditions,

within that Snowy Mountain and in all other places, there were produced through transformation various kinds of excellent flowers, fruits, medicinal herbs, and fragrances, as well as various clear streams and various beautiful birds.

Through the causal conditions of nourishment provided by these medicinal fruits,
their remaining coarse physical appearances will all be transformed.
His body was upright and well-proportioned,

O Seer, this Seer of the Donkey-Lips studied the noble Dharma;
for sixty thousand years, he stood upon one foot.
Day and night he did not descend, nor did he feel any weariness.
When the gods beheld the Great Seer undergoing such suffering,

Furthermore, those from the upper realms, such as the desire and form realms,

He never begrudged anything.
At that time, having heard these words, the donkey-lipped one felt joy in his heart.

I recall that in a past kalpa of my former lives,
