Next, Kuī (Revatī) is established as the fifth lunar mansion;
it belongs to the deity Puṣya,
and its clan name is Āśvalāyana.
The constellation Quí (Bharaṇī) consists of one star, appearing like the mole of a woman.
It travels thirty muhūrtas in one day and night.
Those who belong to the Quí lunar mansion are as follows.
One sacrifices to it with curd.
Next, Lou (娄) is established as the sixth lunar mansion;
it belongs to the Gandharva devas, whose clan name is Āhanba.
The constellation Lou (Pūrvaphalgunī) consists of three stars shaped like a horse's head;
it traverses thirty muhūrtas in one day and night.
Those who belong to the Lou star [are as follows].
One should offer it with barley rice and meat.
Next, Wei (胃) is established as the seventh lunar mansion;
it belongs to the deity Yama.
Its constellation name is Bāgavi.
It consists of three stars shaped like the legs of a tripod.
It traverses forty *muhūrtas* in one day and one night.
Those belonging to the lunar mansion Wei (胃) should be worshipped with husked rice, black sesame, and wild jujubes.
These seven lunar mansions above correspond to the northern gate.
Among these twenty-eight lunar mansions,
there are five mansions that traverse forty-five muhūrtas,
namely: Pi (Jyeṣṭhā), Shen (Śravaṇā), Di (Aśleṣā), Dou (Dūḥ), and Bi (Bharaṇī).
Regarding the twenty-eight lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*),
their meanings are so vast and numerous that it is difficult to grasp their profound significance; thus,
they shall not be fully expounded here.
I have now briefly explained this past time;
all the devas who heard it together were filled with joy.
At that time, the rishi Kharoṣṭhī—
Before the great assembly, he joined his palms and spoke, saying:
"In this manner, the days, months, years, and seasons are established. This *Sūtra on the Establishment of Days, Months, Years, and Seasons* consists of one scroll;
as the text is extensive, the details regarding the major and minor constellations are not recorded here.
What are the six seasons called?
The answer is:
the first and second months are called the season of warmth.
The third and fourth months are called the time for sowing and planting;
the fifth and sixth months are called the time for seeking rain;
the seventh and eighth months are called the time when things are about to ripen.
The ninth and tenth months are called the time of cold and freezing;
the eleventh and twelfth months are combined with these,
being the time of heavy snowfall in the twelfth month.
This month of ten days is divided into six periods.
Furthermore, there are eight great lunar mansions (nakṣatras), namely:
Jupiter (Sāvarṇi), Mars (Aṅgāraka), Saturn (Śanaiścara), Venus (Uśanas), Mercury (Budha), the Sun (Āditya), the Moon (Candra), and Rāhu.
Furthermore, there are twenty-eight minor lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*),
namely all the stars from the Pleiades (*Kṛttikā*) to the *Vaiśākha* (胃).
I have established them in this sequential order.
"You all have seen and heard this; what do you think?
At that time, all the devas, humans, ṛṣis, asuras, nāgas, and naras joined their palms and all spoke these words:"
Just as the celestial beings are now the most honored among gods and humans,
such that even the nāgas and asuras are unable to surpass them,
their wisdom and compassion are the foremost.
Because he has not forgotten his compassion for all sentient beings throughout immeasurable kalpas,
he has obtained such meritorious retribution that among all devas and humans, there is no one with wisdom equal to his.
No sentient being whatsoever can perform such a Dharma-deed as this.
May you all rejoice, and may it bring peace and happiness to us.
Excellent, Great Virtuous One! You bring peace and security to sentient beings.
At that time, the Ṛṣi Khaḷuṅka spoke again, saying:
"These twelve months constitute the beginning and end of one year;
such are the methods regarding the large and small stars and so forth."
The exposition of the dharmas of the kṣaṇa has now been completed.
Furthermore, the Four Great Kings are established;
one king is placed at each of the four sides of Mount Sumeru.
In each of these directions there were many sentient beings.
At that time, the entire great assembly all exclaimed, "Excellent!
and rejoiced immeasurably.
At that time, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, and others made offerings day and night.
Furthermore, after the passing of immeasurable kalpas,
there were yet more ṛṣis.
Named Gāla, he appeared in the world; later,
he was further described separately and established among the constellations.

The essential principles regarding the small and large months, as well as the seasons, are briefly presented here as explained in the sūtras. For now, the twenty-eight lunar mansions (nakṣatras) shall be enumerated;
each has its distinct affiliation and is protected by its own spiritual guardians.
Thus, the Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra states:
At that time, the Buddha addressed Mahābrahmā, Lord of the Sahā World, Śakra Devendra, and the Four Great Kings, saying:
"How did the celestial seers of the past arrange the various lunar mansions, planets, and constellations to protect the lands and nurture sentient beings?"
Mahābrahmā and the others addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In the past, celestial seers distributed and established the various lunar mansions, planets,
and constellations to protect the lands and nurture sentient beings."
Within the four directions, each has its presiding constellation.
In the eastern direction, there are seven constellations;
the first is the Horn (Aśvinī) Constellation.
The first is the constellation Jyeṣṭhā, which presides over birds. The second is the constellation Abhijit,
which presides over those who have left the household life to seek the Noble Path.
Third is the lunar mansion Jyeṣṭhā,
which presides over water-born sentient beings.
Fourth is the lunar mansion Mūla.
The fifth is the Heart mansion (Hṛdayā), which presides over women and governs those who travel by vehicle in pursuit of profit.
Sixth is the lunar mansion Mūla,
which presides over sentient beings on islands and marshes.
Seventh is the lunar mansion Pūrvāṣāḍhā.
It presides over potters.
Among the seven lunar mansions of the southern quarter,
the first is the Well (Jing) mansion.
The first is presided over by goldsmiths.
The second is the constellation Ghost (Nakṣatra),
which presides over all kings and great ministers.
Third is the lunar mansion Jyeṣṭhā,
which presides over the dragon of the Snowy Mountains.
Fourth is the lunar mansion Mūla, which presides over those who possess great wealth.
Fifth is the lunar mansion Zhang (Jyeṣṭhā),
presiding over thieves and bandits.
Sixth is the lunar mansion Yi (Pūrvaphalgunī).
It presides over merchants.
Seventh is the lunar mansion Jyeṣṭhā;
it presides over the kingdom of Sūrata.
The seven lunar mansions of the western quarter:
the first is Kṛttikā (Quí),
which presides over those who travel by boat.
The second is the lunar mansion Lou (Revatī),
presiding over merchants.
The third is the lunar mansion Wei (Ārdrā).
The first presides over the country of Varuṇaka;
the fourth is the lunar mansion Mṛgaśiras,
which presides over water buffaloes.
Fifth is the lunar mansion Pi (Bharaṇī),
which presides over all sentient beings.
Sixth is the lunar mansion Zui (Kṛttikā).
The constellation Viśākhā rules over the kingdom of Videha;
the seventh is the constellation Jyeṣṭhā,
which presides over the Kṣatriyas.
The seven lunar mansions of the north:
the first is the Dou mansion,
which presides over the kingdom of Jābūṣa.
The second is the lunar mansion Revatī;
it presides over the Kṣatriyas and the country of Andrapradyota.
The third is the lunar mansion Aśvinī.
The first presides over the kingdoms of Aṅga and Magadha;
the fourth is the lunar mansion Śravaṇā,
which presides over the kingdom of Naṭakara.
Fifth is the constellation Ārdrā;
its presiding deity wears a flower crown.
Sixth is the constellation Mūla.
The first governs the countries of Gandhāra and Sūluna, as well as various dragons, snakes, and other crawling creatures.
The seventh is the lunar mansion Mūla;
it governs the gandharvas who are skilled in music.
"O Great Virtuous Blessed One,
the celestial seers of the past have thus arranged the lunar mansions in the four directions."
He protects the lands and nurtures all sentient beings.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Brahma Kings and others, saying:
"Listen attentively."
Among the world of devas, humans, and ṛṣis,
my knowledge and vision are the most supreme;
I shall also cause the planets and lunar mansions to protect the lands and nurture all sentient beings.
"You must proclaim this so that they may know: regarding the lands and sentient beings assigned by me, each shall protect, sustain, and nourish them according to their respective portions.
The extent of these divided lands belongs individually to the twenty-eight lunar mansions."
Question: What are the shapes and dimensions of these various stars?
Answer: [As follows:]
According to the *Ekottarika Āgama*,
a large star is one *yojana* in size,
while a small star is two hundred paces.
The *Loutan jing* (Lokānuvartana-sūtra) states:
"Large stars have a circumference of seven hundred li;
medium stars are four hundred and eighty li; small stars are twenty li."
The stars are the palaces and residences of the various devas.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"Among the various lunar mansions..."
The largest of those stars are eighteen krośas;
the medium-sized are ten krośas;
and the smallest are four krośas.
The commentary states:
According to the internal scriptures,
these various lunar mansions are all the palatial residences of the devas.
Within, there dwells a deity;
through the power of merit induced by the environment and its rewards, light manifests.
According to secular texts:
Thus it was said that this was a stone;
for when a star fell during the Song period,
the fallen star was like a stone.
Some say it was not a star,
but a celestial stone falling from the Milky Way;
thus, secular texts state:
The celestial river and the terrestrial river are interconnected;
therefore, stones occasionally fall into the [celestial] river.
As stated in the *Sumerukhaṇḍa-sūtra*:
In the sky there is a river named Yamunā that flows through the void;
for a long time it has possessed large boulders and fine sand.
At that time, there was a corruption [of the text] which took it to be a "star"; this is not an authentic scripture.
It is a false composition created by worldly people that has circulated;
it was not spoken by the Buddha.
After the *bingshen* day of the tenth month in the eighteenth year of the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty,
a great thunderclap shook the heavens at the border between Wen-shui County in Fen-zhou and Bing-zhou;
a stone fell from within the clouds in the sky.
It was as large as a pheasant's beak;
its back was high and its belly flat.
Its markings were such that Water County’s Assistant Magistrate Zhang Xiaojing, together with the officials of Fen Prefecture, submitted a memorial concerning it.
At that time, the Master Changnian from the Bodhi Monastery in Magadha, Western Regions, who was widely learned in both Buddhist and secular matters, arrived at the Western Capital.
The Emperor issued an edict to question him.
The answer was:
"This is a dragon; because two dragons were contending with one another, it fell down like a stone."
Judging by this, why must it necessarily be said that what falls from the sky is a star?
For objects in the distant heavens are beyond the measurement of ordinary people.
Nothing is more difficult for people to understand than heaven and earth.
As the common saying goes:
"Heaven is the refined essence."
The sun is the essence of Yang,
and the stars are the essences of the myriad things;
this is what the Confucian teaching accepts as settled truth.
When a star falls, it becomes a stone;
if its essence were such a stone, it could not possess radiance,
and its nature would likewise be heavy and solid.
To what are they attached?
The diameter of a single star is one hundred *li*,
while the distance from the beginning to the end of a single lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) spans tens of thousands [of *li*].
Objects spanning a hundred li are linked together by the tens of thousands;
their width and breadth, whether following the horizontal or diagonal, never exceed or fall short [of their true measure].
Furthermore, the starry bodies are identical in luminous color to the sun and moon.
It is merely that they differ in their respective scales;
yet, would the sun and moon then be made of stone?
Since stone is solid and dense, how could a bird or a rabbit find room within it?
How could a stone within the qi move independently?
If the sun, moon, planets, and lunar mansions were all merely qi,
then because the substance of qi is light and buoyant, they ought to merge with heaven.
Moving back and forth and revolving in cycles, they cannot deviate from their course;
in this regard, the principles governing their speed and slowness must surely be uniform.
For what reason, then, do the sun, moon, five planets, and twenty-eight lunar mansions [move at varying speeds]?
Each possesses its own measure, yet their movements are uneven;
how could it be that the vital energy (prāṇa) should suddenly descend and transform into stone?
Since the earth is already turbid and impure.
The Dharma ought to be profound and substantial.
Yet when one digs into the earth and finds a spring, it floats upon the water;
what else could there be beneath that accumulated water?
From where do the rivers, streams, and hundreds of valleys arise?
Why does the eastern flow toward the sea without overflowing it?
Where do the Guīdāng and Wěilǚ channels reach?
By what force is the Stone of Wujiao ignited?
By whom is the tide regulated as it recedes and returns?
Why does the Milky Way, suspended in the void, not fall away?
The nature of water is to flow downward; for what reason does it rise upward?
When heaven and earth first opened, the constellations already existed, even before the Nine Provinces were delineated.
Before the various states were divided,
when borders were first demarcated and the wilds partitioned,
how were their celestial coordinates established?
Since the establishment of the feudal system, who has ever altered its boundaries?
Though states may increase or decrease in size, the stars neither advance nor retreat;
thus, calamities and blessings, misfortunes and fortunes, do not deviate from their positions therein.
The celestial bodies suspended above are vast,
and the constellations are numerous;
why then are the *fenye* (astrological divisions) restricted solely to the Central Kingdom?
The Pleiades (Mao) constitute the Mao-tou, the station of the Xiongnu.
Why then are the Western Hu, the Eastern Yi, the Diaozhi, and the Jiaozhi alone excluded?
To seek [a solution] on this basis will result in no resolution whatsoever.
How could one take ordinary human affairs as the standard and insist that [the truth] must lie beyond the universe?
For all people, what they believe in are only their ears and eyes;
beyond these, there is nothing else.
Everyone harbors doubts regarding this.

Within the Confucian discourse on Heaven, there are inherently several meanings: sometimes it is described as a vast sphere (hun), sometimes as a canopy (gai); at times it is depicted as a vaulted dome (qiong), and at others as a fixed, level plane (an).
As for calculating the ultimate extent of its enclosures and boundaries,
if one were to witness it directly, there could be no disagreement;
as for what has been measured, how could it possibly serve as a sufficient basis for reliance?
Why do you place faith in the speculative theories of ordinary people and harbor doubts regarding the sublime intent of the Great Sage,
desiring necessarily to deny the existence of kalpas as numerous as the atoms within worlds as vast as the sands of the Ganges?
Furthermore, Zou Yan also had his discourse on the Nine Provinces.
Those from within the mountains do not believe there are fish as large as trees;
those from upon the sea do not believe there are trees as large as fish.
Emperor Wu of the Han did not believe in string-glue;
the people of Wei did not believe in fire-cloth;
and the Hu people, upon seeing brocade, did not believe it was produced by insects that eat trees and spit out silk.
People of Wu do not believe there can be a thousand-person felt tent while they are in Jiangnan;
yet when they come to the north of the Yellow River, they do not believe there can be a two-thousand-stone ship.
Both are matters of practical experience.
Just as there are in the world incantation masters and practitioners of various illusionist arts who can walk upon fire, tread upon blades, plant melons, or shift wells—
performing thousands of transformations and myriad changes in the space of a mere instant.
If human effort can achieve such things,
what hindrance could there be to the inconceivable power of spiritual resonance?
Why should a jeweled banner and its hundred-yojana seat not be transformed into a pure land, with wondrous stupas emerging from them?
Furthermore, the *Record of Wang Xuance’s Journey to the Western Regions* states that in the fourth year of the Xianqing era, the King’s envoy arrived in the kingdom of Pāriyātra.
For the sake of the Chinese visitors, the king staged a performance featuring five women; these five women passed a sword back and forth, increasing the number from three blades to ten.
Furthermore, he performed the art of the tightrope walker, leaping into the air upon the rope while wearing shoes and tossing them;
with his hands, he brandished three weapons: a sword, a shield, and a spear.
There were various acrobatic feats mixed with diverse magical illusions,
such as cutting off tongues and pulling out intestines;
they cannot be described in full detail.
3. The Sun Palace. Third, according to the *Utpatti-sūtra* (Qishi jing), the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The palace of the Sun Deity is exactly fifty-one yojanas in both length and breadth."
The upper and lower levels are likewise so.
Their palaces are constructed from two kinds of substances and are square, like houses.
From a distance, it appears round. What are these two?
They are gold and crystal.
One side and two parts are made of celestial gold,
pure and luminous;
one side and one part are made of celestial lapis lazuli.
It is pure, clean, and radiant.
Five kinds of winds blow upon it, causing it to revolve and move. What are these five?
The first is called "sustaining" (dhāraṇa);
the second is called "abiding" (sthiti);
the third is called "conforming transformation" (anuvartana).
The fourth is named Parāhaka;
the fifth is named Saṃcāra.
They are situated separately before the celestial palace of the Sun God.
Countless devas walk before him;
as they travel, each constantly experiences bliss, and all are called "those who walk firmly.
According to the *Dīrgha Āgama*, the walls and the ground of the Sun God’s palace are as thin as flower petals.
It is sustained by five winds. Furthermore, within the solar palace,
there is a magnificent carriage made of Jambūnada gold,
sixteen yojanas in height.
It was eight yojanas square and exquisitely adorned;
the devaputra and his retinue were seated within that palanquin.
They enjoy pleasures provided by the five celestial desires.
The lifespan of the Sun Deity (Āditya) is five hundred years;
his descendants succeed one another, all ruling there.
The palace remained occupied for the full duration of a kalpa.
The radiance from the body of the Sun Deity shone forth upon the palanquin,
and the light from the palanquin in turn illuminated the palace.
The light, issuing forth in continuous succession, illuminates the four great continents and all the worlds.
The body, chariot, and palace of the Sun Deity possess one thousand rays of light.
Five hundred rays of light shine horizontally,
and five hundred rays of light shine downward.
The celestial palace of the Sun Deity moves constantly without ceasing.
In the sixth month, it travels northward;
within a single day, it gradually shifts six *krośas* toward the north—according to the *Ratnakaraṇḍa Sūtra*, this is five *li*—never for a moment departing from the sun's path.
In the sixth month, it moves southward;
likewise, within a single day, it gradually shifts toward the south by six *krośas*,
without deviating from its solar path.
When the sun palace travels for six months, the moon deity’s palace also travels that same distance within fifteen days.
Section Four on the Moon Palace: As stated in the *Utpatti-sūtra*, the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
The palace of the Moon Deity is forty-nine yojanas in length and breadth, equal on all sides.
Its walls on the four faces are composed of the seven precious jewels.
The palace of the Moon Deity is interspersed with celestial silver and celestial blue lapis lazuli.
Two parts of the celestial silver are pure and stainless, radiating an exceedingly brilliant light;
the remaining one part is celestial blue lapis lazuli,
which is likewise exceedingly pure.
Its interior and exterior are mutually transparent and radiant, shining afar;
it is also sustained and moved by five winds, which function as previously described, just as the celestial palace of the Moon God moves through space.
There are also immeasurable celestial palaces that precede him as he travels, where he constantly experiences bliss;
within this lunar palace, there is likewise a great carriage.
It is made of blue lapis lazuli.
The palanquin is sixteen yojanas high and eight yojanas wide. The Moon Deva-son and his celestial maidens are within this carriage.
Therein, they enjoy pleasures through the various merits of the five celestial sensual desires, moving about as they wish.
The lifespan of those Moon Deities is five hundred years of their own months.
Their descendants succeed one another, all of whom govern there;
yet their palaces remain for the duration of an eon.
The bodily radiance of that Moon Deva-son illuminates that blue carriage.
The radiance of his palanquin illuminates the lunar palace;
the light from the lunar palace illuminates the four great continents.
That Moon Deva-son possesses five hundred rays that shine downward.
There are five hundred rays that radiate sideways and illuminate;
for this reason, the Moon Deity is named "Thousand-Rayed Light" and is also called "Cool and Refreshing Light."
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions does the lunar palace gradually appear?
The Buddha replied:
"This moon has three causes and conditions."
First, they turn their backs [on the world].
Second, the various devas have blue bodies;
their forms, garments, and necklaces are all entirely blue.
During the first half of the month, it constantly obscures the lunar palace;
because of this obscuration, the moon gradually becomes visible.
Thirdly, sixty rays of light stream forth simultaneously from the celestial palace of the Sun God, obstructing the lunar disk.
By these causes and conditions, it gradually appears.
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions is this lunar palace perfectly round and pure?
It is also due to three causes and conditions that it is thus.
First, at that time, the face of the Moon Deity’s palace rotates outward.
Second, all the blue-colored devas become entirely blue and vanish during the middle of the month.
On the fifteenth day, its form is most perfectly full and its radiance intensely blazing;
it is like a torch burning with abundant oil,
before which the light of all small lamps is completely eclipsed.
In this way, on the fifteenth day of the month, the lunar palace is able to eclipse all other lights;
three days later,
its palace emits sixty rays of light.
Regarding the phrase "at one time, that which obstructs the lunar disc flows forth":
this lunar palace is perfectly full on the fifteenth day,
being entirely free from all obscurations in every respect.
At that time, the sunlight cannot be obscured;
for what further reason is this so regarding the celestial palace of the Moon Deity?
On the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight, everything becomes invisible.
On this fifteenth day of the dark fortnight, the lunar palace is closest to the solar palace;
because it is obscured by the rays of that sun, everything becomes invisible.
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions is it called the "Moon"?
During the dark fortnight, from the first day after [the full moon] until the end of the month, this lunar palace—
Its radiance and majestic power gradually diminish.
For this reason, it is called the moon; in the western direction, one month is divided into the dark and the bright phases.
From the first day to the fifteenth day of the initial month.
That which begins from the sixteenth day until the end of the month is called the "white fortnight" (śuklapakṣa).
That which follows is called the "black fortnight" (kṛṣṇapakṣa).
In this system, the dark fortnight is included to form a single month. Furthermore, for what reason do various shadows appear within the lunar palace?
It is because there is a Jambu tree on this continent.
Because of this tree, it is named Jambudvīpa; its great height causes its shadow to appear as the lunar disc.
Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
Because fish, turtles, and other creatures within the great ocean cast their reflections upon the lunar disk,
a dark mark appears therein; thus it is transmitted in the Western lands.
In the past, there was a rabbit who practiced the bodhisattva path.
Śakra, Lord of Devas, tested him by seeking meat for his own consumption.
He cast his body into the fire.
Out of compassion for him, the Lord of Devas took the scorched rabbit and placed it within the moon,
so that all sentient beings of the future might gaze upon it whenever they lift their eyes.
Know that this is the body of a past Bodhisattva practicing loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
Section Five on Cold and Heat: According to the *Utpatti-sūtra*, for what causes and conditions does heat arise during the summer?
The Buddha said:
"For six months, the sun palace travels toward the north;
during this time, it travels six krośas each day."
It never abandons the path traversed by the sun; however,
within that [light], there are ten causes and conditions by which all its radiance strikes those ten kinds of mountains, causing them to become heated.
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions do various colds occur?
After six months, the palace of the Sun Deity gradually moves toward the south.
Moreover, there are twelve dependent origination factors that can produce cold.
Between Mount Sumeru and Mount Khadiraka,
there is the Sumeru Ocean,
eighty-four thousand yojanas in width.
It extends infinitely in all directions,
and it is completely filled with various flowers whose fragrance is exceedingly intense.
The radiance of the Sun Deity shines upon and touches that ocean.
This is the first cause and condition for cold.
Second is Mount Īṣādhara; third is Mount Yugandhara.
The fourth is Mount Sudarśana; the fifth is Mount Aśvakarṇa;
the sixth is Mount Nimindhara;
and the seventh is Mount Vinataka.
The eighth is the Great Cakravāḍa mountain range;
the ninth is all the places where the rivers flow within Jambudvīpa that are touched by the light of the sun deity.
Therefore, there is cold.
In the tenth continent, Aparagoyānī, the rivers are twice as many;
in the eleventh continent, Pūrvavideha, the rivers are twice as many again.
In the twelfth [region], Uttarakuru, the rivers are twice as many.
The flowing waters of these twelve rivers, when touched by the light of the sun, become cold; previously, they were hot. Beyond the eight mountains mentioned before, there are twelve [rivers].
The ninth is ten thousand yojanas above the earth in the sky,
where there are yakṣa palaces.
The tenth is the fourth [heaven].
The Great Continent and the Mountains combined constitute the fourteenth [section].
Furthermore, the *Lokaprajñapti-abhidharma-śāstra* poses the following question:
What is winter cold?
What is spring heat?
What is the cold and heat of the summer season?
This is during the winter season, when the water element is at its maximum and has not yet diminished;
when grasses and trees are still moist and have not yet withered or dried;
and when the earth element is damp and slippery.
The fire element moves downward, while the water element rises upward; this is known because deep water is warmest and shallow water is cold.
Furthermore, when the cold season arrives, the sun travels a long path and its heat shines for only a short time.
When the yang energy is within, food is digested quickly.
For this reason, it is cold during winter.
How is it that at the time of spring heat, the water element increases, and having increased, it is then exhausted?
The grasses and trees wither and dry;
the earth has become parched and cracked;
the moisture of the water sinks downward.
The fire element rises upward.
How is this known to be so?
Because deep water is cold while shallow water is hot.
When winter has passed, the sun travels the inner path and its heat lingers for a long time;
because the internal fire of the body is weakened, there is heat in spring.
Why, then, is it cold and hot during summer?
This great earth is constantly scorched by the midday sun for eight months;
when great clouds send down rain that sprinkles and disperses [the heat], the vapors of the earth rise up in dense steam.
When the wind blows, this steaming vapor is then dissipated.
At that time it is cold;
if the wind does not arise,
at that time it is hot.
Therefore, within the summer there are times that are cold and hot; in the western regions, four months constitute one season.
Because they establish only spring, summer, and winter, they do not establish autumn.
Thus, the Three-Season Hall was established. Furthermore, the *Utpatti-sūtra* states:
"For what reason do the various rivers flow in the world?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus,
"Because there is the sun, there is heat."
Because there is heat, there is roasting;
because there is roasting, there is steaming;
because there is steaming, there is moistening through perspiration. By means of this perspiration, [the body is moistened].
Therefore, among all the mountains, perspiration flows as water to form the various rivers.
Section Six: The Department of Illuminating Function. According to the *Dīrgha Āgama* (Long Discourses):
At the beginning of the kalpa, when beings had grown to maturity, the heavens and earth were in great darkness.
A great black wind blew upon the waters of the great ocean,
opening and taking up the sun to illuminate the world below.
It is situated halfway up Mount Sumeru within the path of the sun,
revolving around the four continents to illuminate sentient beings. Furthermore,
the *Qishi jing* (Sutra on the Arising of the World) states:
At that time, the world became shrouded in darkness.
Then, suddenly, the sun, the moon, and the various constellations appeared;
thereupon came day and night, years, seasons, and times.
At that time, the Sun Deity ascends his great palace and emerges from the east;
he circumambulates the midpoint of Mount Sumeru and proceeds toward the west.
Having set, he emerges again from the east.
At that time, the sentient beings again saw the Sun Deity rising from the east,
and they said to one another,
"O virtuous ones!"
Or it may be the palace of the Sun God, shining with brilliance;
emerging again from the east,
it circumambulates Mount Sumeru to the right and sets in the west.
Having seen this for the third time, they also spoke to one another,
saying, "It is the radiance of a deva that flows here;
therefore, such a name has arisen."
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"The sun and moon are five hundred yojanas in diameter,
yet what we see now does not exceed the size of a fan."
The *Chuchu jing* (Sutra on Various Places) states:
The Buddha said to Ānanda,
"That which is seen by the human eye..."
It is known that [the distance] of four million two hundred thousand yojanas is visible to the human eye.
Furthermore, the *Lokaprajñapti-abhidharma* states:
"What is meant by 'night'?"
What is day? It is night because of the sun;
it is day because of the sun.
The desire realm is dark by its very nature;
because the light of the sun is obscured, it is therefore night.
Because the sunlight is manifest, it is therefore day.
Furthermore, the *Utpatti-sūtra* states:
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"When it is midday in Jambudvīpa,
the sun is just beginning to set in Pūrvavideha."
When the sun first rises over the continent of Aparagoyānī,
it is exactly midnight on the continent of Uttarakuru.
When the sun is at its zenith over Aparagoyānī, [it is midnight on Jambudvīpa].
At this moment, the sun is just setting here in Jambudvīpa;
it is just beginning to rise in Uttarakuru;
and it is exactly midnight in Pūrvavideha.
When it is midday in the continent of Uttarakuru,
the sun is just setting in Jambudvīpa and is just rising in Pūrvavideha.
When it is exactly midnight in Jambudvīpa,
it is midday in Pūrvavideha, and the sun has just begun to set in Uttarakuru.
When it is midday in Jambudvīpa, it is midnight in Aparagoyānī.
Thus the Buddha told the bhikṣus.
What the people of Jambudvīpa call the west, the people of Aparagoyānī consider to be the east;
what the people of Aparagoyānī call the west, the people of Uttarakuru consider to be the east.
What the people of Uttarakuru call the west, the people of Pūrvavideha consider to be the east;
what the people of Pūrvavideha call the west, the people of Jambudvīpa consider to be the east.
The same applies to the two directions of south and north.
Section Seven: The Deficiency and Fulfillment. According to the *Lokasthāna-abhidharma-śāstra*, what is the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*)?
What is the bright fortnight?
It is by means of the sun's dark fortnight;
it is by means of the sun's bright fortnight.
The sun constantly pursues the moon in its course;
every day it draws closer by forty-eight thousand and eighty *yojanas*,
and every day it moves further away by the same amount.
When they are in close proximity, the sun and moon are each covered by three yojanas and one-third of a yojana;
for this reason, on the fifteenth day, the moon is completely obscured.
On this day of the dark fortnight, it is full.
Day by day, the moon also recedes from the sun by forty-eight thousand and eighty *yojanas*,
while the moon opens up [its distance] by three *yojanas* each day.
Furthermore, by another one-third of a yojana,
on the fifteenth day of the month, it becomes clear and perfectly full;
thus, in the world, it is called the "fullness of the white fortnight."
When the sun and moon move at their greatest distance from each other,
the moon is full; at that time,
the world says the bright fortnight is complete.
If the sun and moon were together in one place,
this is called "conjoined movement" (saṃyukta-gati);
in the world, this is said to be the completion of the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇa-pakṣa).
If the sun follows behind the moon, the sunlight illuminates the moonlight;
because the moonlight is coarse, it casts a shadow when illuminated,
and this shadow of the moon then obscures the moon itself.
Therefore, the latter part of the moon is seen as not being full.
By this process, it is gradually obscured until on the fifteenth day the moon is entirely covered.
When it subsequently moves away from that position, this is called the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*).
If the sun moves ahead of the moon,
the daily purification occurs in the same manner;
until the fifteenth day, it becomes fully complete.
When moving forward, it is called the "white fortnight" (śuklapakṣa).
Furthermore, the *Lokadhātunirdeśa-sūtra* asks:
Furthermore, for what reason is the night long and the day short during the winter season?
The Buddha answered the bhikṣus:
After six months have passed, the celestial palace of the Sun God gradually proceeds toward the south,
moving six *krośas* each day without fail.
At that time, the celestial palace of the Sun-god was at the very southern extremity of Jambudvīpa;
because the terrain there was narrow and small, the sun passed through it with great speed.
For this reason, [the days were short].
During the winter season, the days are short and the nights are long.
By what cause and condition, then,
are the days long and the nights short during the spring and summer seasons?
The Buddha replied:
"After six months have passed, the palace of the Sun Deity gradually proceeds toward the north;
every single day it shifts by six *krośas* without any deviation."
It was contrary to the usual way; at that time,
it traveled through the center of Jambudvīpa.
Because the earth is broad and the course [of the sun] is long, the days are therefore long.
By this causal condition,
during spring and summer the days are long and the nights are short.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"As explained in the 'Chapter on the Avaivartika' (Non-retrogressive Stage),
regarding the sun, moon, years, and seasons..."
A "day" refers to the period from dawn to dawn;
it is divided into three parts: the first, the middle, and the last.
The night is likewise divided into three parts.
In one day and night there are thirty periods (*muhūrta*).
During the spring and autumn equinoxes, fifteen periods belong to the day and fifteen periods belong to the night.
At other times there is an increase or decrease:
when it is the fifth month, the days consist of eighteen periods and the nights twelve periods.
In the eleventh month, the night lasts eighteen hours and the day twelve hours;
one month consists of either thirty days or thirty-five days.
Either thirty days,
or twenty-nine and a half days,
or twenty-seven and a half days.
There are four kinds of moons:
first, the sun-moon;
second, the worldly moon.
Third is the month by month;
fourth is the month by lunar mansion.
A month by solar day consists of thirty and a half days.
A worldly month consists of thirty days;
a lunar month consists of twenty-nine days plus thirty-sixty-second parts of a day.
A lunar month by the stars consists of twenty-seven days plus twenty-one sixtieths.
An intercalary month arises from the two factors of the solar month and the worldly month.
This is called thirteen months;
alternatively, thirteen months are termed one year.
This year consists of three hundred and sixty-six days.
It revolves and begins again.
The Bodhisattva knows that at the time of midday,
the preceding portion has already passed.
The subsequent portion has not yet arisen;
the middle portion has no place of abiding;
there is no aspect of the solar portion that can be grasped.
It is empty and void, possessing nothing.
When the thirtieth day arrives,
it is reduced by one on the twenty-ninth day.
How do the sun and moon come together through combination?
Since they do not [inherently] exist, how can they combine to form a year?
For this reason:
The Buddha said,
"Worldly phenomena are like illusions and like dreams;
they are merely phenomena that deceive the mind."
The Bodhisattva is able to know the conjunction of the world’s sun, moon, and years, and is able to know their dissolution and non-existence.
This is called skillful discernment based on the sūtras; those who rely on such people have little merit, and there will be calamities and transformations of the sun and moon.
There may be red suns and red moons,
along with various other evil omens,
as fully described in the sūtras.
8. Section on Rising Clouds, the Eighth. According to the *Utpatti-sūtra* (Qishi jing), there are four kinds of clouds in the world:
first, white; second, black; third, red; and fourth, yellow.
Among these four clouds, those that are white clouds contain a great deal of the earth element;
those that are black clouds...
If there is much of the water element,
it is when there are red-colored clouds;
if there is much of the fire element, it is likewise.
If there are yellow clouds,
there is an abundance of the wind element;
clouds arise from the earth and ascend into the void to a height of one *krośa*.
They abide at distances of two, three, or up to seven *krośas*.
Alternatively, there are clouds that abide in the space above at heights of one *yojana*, up to seven *yojanas*.
Furthermore, there are clouds that abide in the space above at a height of one hundred yojanas,
up to seven hundred yojanas; and furthermore,
there are clouds that rise from the earth into the space at a height of one thousand yojanas.
They remain for as long as seven thousand yojanas,
until the end of the kalpa.
Thus it is said in the *Dīrgha Āgama*.
At the beginning of the kalpa, there were clouds that reached as far as the Ābhāsvara Heaven; according to the sūtras, these clouds are also of many kinds.
Some appear as five-colored auspicious clouds (*kirana-megha*), while others appear as red clouds, black clouds, and various other forms beyond all description.
These details are fully described in such works as the *Ratnaketuparivarta-sūtra* (Renwang jing).
9. The Section on Thunder and Lightning (Zhengléi bù), the ninth, according to the *Lokadhātunirdeśa-sūtra* (*Qishi jing*), states:
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
If any non-Buddhist comes and asks you,
"By what causes and conditions does this sound exist in the midst of space?
you should answer him as follows:
There are three causes and conditions for their mutual contact that produce sound from the gathering of clouds in the sky.
What are these three?
First, because the wind element within the cloud comes into contact with the earth element,
sound is produced. Second,
because the wind element within the cloud comes into contact with that water element.
Even when sound is produced,
it arises because the wind element within the clouds comes into contact with that fire element.
Thus, sound is produced.
Why is this so? It is like fire that arises when tree branches rub against one another;
this is also like that. Furthermore, based on the sūtras, there are many kinds of thunder.
There are thunder-carts with drums struck by spirits and beaten by hand-clappers;
thus, in common parlance, they are called "celestial drums. Among them, there are also those with great sin and evil who die by being struck by lightning.
They are seen receiving their retribution. 10.
The Section on Striking Lightning, the Tenth. According to the *Utpatti-sūtra*, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
If any non-Buddhist comes to ask you,
"By what causes and conditions does lightning suddenly arise in the empty sky?
you should answer him as follows:
There are two causes and conditions for lightning to emerge from the clouds. What are these two?
First, in the eastern direction there is lightning named "Without Thickness."
In the south there is lightning named "Flowing with the Current.
In the west there is lightning named "Falling Light.
In the north there is lightning.
It is called the Hundred-Birth Tree.

Second, there may be a time when the thick and great lightning emerging from the east and the luminous lightning falling from the west strike one another, face one another, rub against one another, and clash.
Because of this, from within that mass of clouds in the void,
there emerged a great radiance named Lightning Flash.
Furthermore, when the Great Lightning of the Southern Current flows and encounters, confronts, rubs against, and strikes the Great Lightning of the Hundred-Birth Tree in the north,
it is because of this that lightning flashes are produced.
It is like two pieces of wood that, when rubbed together by the wind,
suddenly produce fire which then returns to its source. According to the sutras, there may be thunder first without lightning,
or there may be lightning first followed by thunder.
When they strike one another, fire issues forth and thunderbolts strike people and things. 11.
The Section on Causing Rain. Regarding the eleventh section, "Causing Rain," according to the *Vibhaṅga-guṇa-śāstra* (Discourse on the Analysis of Merit), it says:
There are three kinds of rain:
first, celestial rain;
second, dragon rain.
The asuras rain [down stones];
the devas rain fine mist;
the nāgas rain very coarse [stones].
Joy brings harmony and moisture;
anger brings thunder and lightning.
Even when the asuras fight with Śakra, they are able to cause rain to fall.
The coarseness or subtlety [of rain] is not fixed; according to the sūtras, there are also many kinds of rain.
There may be rain without clouds, there may be rain preceded by clouds, and there may be rain caused by dragons.
Alternatively, there are instances where rain falls not by the agency of dragons, but is rather induced solely by the karmic retribution of sentient beings themselves;
this is as fully explained in the sutras.
Section Twelve: On the Loss of Season. As stated in the *Qishi jing* (Sutra on the Arising of the World):
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"There are five causes and conditions that can obstruct the rain,
causing diviners to fail in their predictions and leading them to increasing confusion."
One predicts that it will certainly rain in the heavens, yet it does not rain.
What are the five [signs]?
First, clouds arise and thunder rolls in the midst of the void.
There are sounds such as "gata gata" and "gucchu gucchu," or flashes of lightning appear, or cold winds blow forth.
All such various signs as these are portents of rain;
all diviners and astrologers alike predict that rain will certainly fall at this time.
At that time, Rāhu, the King of the Asuras, emerged from his palace and,
seizing those rain clouds with both hands, cast them into the midst of the ocean.
This is the first causal condition for obstructing the rain.
The diviners did not know [the cause] and consequently it did not rain.
At another time, clouds arose in the sky,
and from within the clouds there also issued sounds such as *gaṭa*.
Lightning also flashed forth,
and a wind blew with cold air. At that time,
the diviners observed these omens and predicted that it would rain from heaven.
At that time, the predominant power of the fire element arises,
whereby rain clouds are consumed by fire;
this is called the second causal condition for the obstruction of rain.
The diviners did not know this,
and consequently it did not rain.
At a third time, clouds arose from within the void.
Within the clouds, there are also sounds such as *gaḍa*,
and lightning flashes forth;
furthermore, winds blow, bringing with them cold air.
At that time, the diviners, having observed this, predicted that it would certainly rain.
However, through the predominant power of the wind element,
the clouds were blown away and cast into that Kalinga desert.
Or it may be placed in the midst of a vast wilderness,
or placed on the sandy plains of Mālava;
this is called the third cause and condition for obstructing rain.
The diviners did not know [the cause] and consequently it did not rain.
Fourth, because there are sentient beings who defile pure conduct through negligence,
the heavens do not send rain at the proper time.
The fifth is for the people of Jambudvīpa.
Because they possess unrighteousness, stinginess, greed, envy, false views, and perversity, the heavens do not send rain;
the ritual procedures for these two cases are both the same as previously explained.
The *Dīrgha Āgama* is also similar in this regard; for these reasons, the physiognomists were confused and their prognostications regarding rain were uncertain.
The *Ekottara Āgama* states:
The sun and moon have four kinds of obscurations that prevent them from emitting their radiance. What are these four?
The first is clouds.
Second, wind and dust;
third, smoke; fourth, asuras.
Just as clouds cover the sun and moon so that they cannot emit their radiance,
so too do monks have four fetters that shroud the human mind,
preventing it from opening and being liberated.
First is the fetter of desire;
second is ill will; third is delusion.
Fourth is gain and honor (lābha-satkāra),
which obscures the human mind so that it cannot attain liberation.
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* also contains four similes identical to those mentioned above.
First, sexual misconduct;
second, drinking intoxicants;
third, handling money and precious objects.
The fourth is wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*).
These four factors likewise cause the Buddha-dharma not to be clear.
Therefore, the verse says:
The rising heat of fire becomes smoke; The gathering vapors form clouds upon the crags.
Cloud-spirits and dragons exhale moisture as mist; Raising up dust that settles upon men.
Wine is the gateway to heedlessness; Lust is the source of birth and death.
The arising of afflictions regarding gold and silver is grave; wrong livelihood destroys the root of the precepts.
13. Section on Earthquakes, the Thirteenth. According to the *Buddha-parinirvāṇa-sūtra*:
Ānanda joined his palms and asked the Buddha,
"I wish to know by how many causes the earth trembles.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
There are three causes and conditions:
first, the earth rests upon water,
and the water rests upon wind.
Wind rests upon space.
When a great wind arises, the waters are disturbed;
when the waters are disturbed, the earth trembles.
Second, it is because the śramaṇas who have attained the Path and the sublime devas wish to manifest a spiritual response;
for this reason, the earth shakes.
Third, by the power of the Buddha, from the time he first resolved to become a Buddha until his final attainment of Buddhahood,
the three thousandfold world system— including its suns, moons, and twelve thousand heavens and earths— was moved such that there was nothing that did not respond with inspiration.
Devas, humans, ghosts, and spirits were for the most part able to hear and understand.
Furthermore, the *Mahāvaipulya Mahāsaṃnipāta Buddhanusmṛti-samādhi Sūtra* states:
"The entire great earth shakes in six ways:
once, all over, and completely all over."
Second, shaking, pervasive shaking, and equal pervasive shaking;
third, surging, pervasive surging, and equal pervasive surging;
fourth, roaring, pervasive roaring, and equal pervasive roaring.
Fifth, arising, universal arising, and so forth, universal arising;
sixth, awakening, universal awakening, and so forth, universal awakening.
These six each have three aspects, totaling eighteen characteristics.
In this manner, the east rose and the west sank;
the west rose and the east sank;
the south rose and the north sank.
The north surged while the south subsided;
the center surged while the periphery subsided;
the periphery surged while the center subsided.
Furthermore, the *Lokaprajñapti-abhidharma-śāstra* states:
The Buddha told Pūrṇa,
"There are also various devas who possess great supernormal powers and majestic virtue."
If one wishes to shake the great earth, one can cause it to move.
If bhikṣus possess great supernatural powers and great majestic virtue,
they contemplate the characteristics of the earth element, making the large small and the small large.
If one wishes to cause the earth to shake, it can indeed be made to tremble.
To cause the earth to shake, there is a wind named Vairambha;
this wind blows constantly, and when they move together, it does not cease.
The power of the wind increases;
there is wind blowing downward,
and there is also movement across.
These winds revolve equally and support one another in a circular motion.
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that there are four kinds of earthquakes.
First, fire; second, nāgas;
third, garuḍas; fourth, the four heavens and the twenty-eight lunar mansions, and so forth.
Furthermore, various Arhats and devas are also able to cause the earth to tremble.
Moreover, the Ekottarika Āgama states that while the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, he addressed the bhikṣus:
There are eight causes and conditions by which the great earth shakes.
This earth is sixty-eight thousand yojanas deep and is supported by water.
Water depends upon space.
Furthermore, at that time, when the wind moves within space, the water also moves;
as the water moves, the earth then shakes greatly.
This is the initial movement.
If a bhikṣu has attained the supernormal powers (ṛddhi) and possesses mastery over his desires,
he perceives the earth as if it were the palm of his hand.
It can cause the earth element to tremble;
this is the second kind of trembling.
Furthermore, if there are devas who possess great supernormal powers and great majestic might, [they may also cause it to tremble].
He can cause the earth to shake;
this is the third shaking.
Furthermore, if a Bodhisattva is in the Tuṣita Heaven...
When he was about to descend his spirit and take birth, the earth shook;
this was the fourth shaking.
If a bodhisattva knows for himself that while he is in his mother’s womb,
the earth undergoes a great shaking—
this is the fifth movement.
If a bodhisattva knows that he shall emerge from his mother’s womb after ten full months,
the earth shakes greatly;
this is the sixth movement.
If a bodhisattva leaves the household life and sits at the site of enlightenment,
they will subdue the hosts of Māra and ultimately achieve perfect awakening.
The earth shook greatly;
this was the seventh shaking.
If he were to attain parinirvāṇa in the realm of nirvana without remainder in the future, [the earth would shake].
The earth undergoes a great shaking;
this is the eighth movement. According to the sutras, there are many kinds of earth tremors;
for instance, there may be an earthquake when a sage appears in the world.
When a mountain shakes, it indicates that the four fruits of sainthood have appeared in the world,
or that various Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have appeared in the world,
or that a single world-system has shaken.

In many worlds, there are also sentient beings of meager merit who experience earthquakes that cause damage and destruction to both their primary and secondary retributions (*āśraya* and *parigraha-vipāka*), as fully described in the sutras. The commentary states:
Below this, I shall briefly set forth the meaning of the secular texts regarding the initial differentiation of heaven and earth and the transformations of the forms of yin and yang.
This refers to five stages:
first, primordial qi;
second, the Great Transformation (Taiyi).
3. Tai-ch'u (The Grand Beginning);
4. Tai-shih (The Grand Commencement);
5. Tai-su (The Grand Essence).
Regarding the first, the primal qi (*yuánqì*):
according to the *Hétú*,
the primal qi is formless, a tumultuous and nebulous mass.
That which lies prostrate is the earth;
that which bows down is heaven.
The *Litong* says:
Heaven and Earth are that from which the primal qi is born and the progenitors of all things.
*The Genealogy of Emperors* (*Dijwang Shiji*) by Huangfu Shian states:
The initial sprouting of the primal qi is called the Grand Beginning (*Taichu*).
The *Sanguo Liji* states:
"Before heaven and earth existed..."
The primordial chaos was like a chicken’s egg;
from the vast and indistinct depths, the nebulous and vast began to differentiate.
In the year of Sheti, the primal qi first commenced its inception.
The Imperial Genealogy states:
When heaven and earth first arose from the vast, chaotic, and nebulous state,
the Heavenly Sovereign was born.
He reigned for eighteen thousand years, ruling as a sovereign by the virtue of Wood.
As Liezi said: "That which has form is born from that which is formless."
"Then from where do Heaven and Earth arise? Zhang Qian’s commentary states:
"Heaven and Earth have no origin from which they arise;
they arise spontaneously. Therefore, there is the Great Ease (Taiyi), the Great Beginning (Taichu), the Great Commencement (Taishi), and the Great Purity (Taisu)."
It transforms into one;
one transforms into seven;
seven transforms into nine.
Ninth, it is the ultimate limit of transformation.
Thereupon, it transforms again into the One.
The One is the beginning of the transformation of forms.
That which is clear and light rises above to become Heaven;
that which is turbid and heavy sinks below to become Earth;
and the harmoniously blended qi becomes Humanity.
Therefore, Heaven and Earth contain the essence, and the myriad things are transformed and born.
Thus, the *Appended Statements* of the *I Ching* say:
"In the *I Ching*, there is the Great Ultimate (*taiji*)."
This gave rise to the Two Polarities.
The Two Polarities gave rise to the Four Images.
The Four Images gave rise to the Eight Trigrams.
The Eight Trigrams determine their good and ill fortune.
The *Spring and Autumn Record of the Symbolic Response to the Essence* states:
"The sovereign shares the same brilliance as the sun and moon."
The four seasons are unified by trust;

thus, Heaven is the father and Earth is the mother, the sun is the elder brother and the moon is the elder sister. Heaven as father is honored at the rite of the Round Mound (Yuanqiu), while Earth as mother is worshipped at the sacrifice of the Square Altar (Fangze).
The sun, as the elder brother, is at the eastern suburb; the moon, as the elder sister, is at the western suburb. The *Chunqiu shuo tici* says:
"The term 'Heaven' (*tian*) signifies 'to fill' (*tian*).
Abiding on high and governing that which is below, it serves as the fundamental principle for humanity and is the essence of all yang."
Contained within, it is the Grand Unity (Taiyi);
divided, it takes on distinct names.
Thus, the character for "one" (yī) and "great" (dà) are established as "Heaven" (Tiān).
The *Fandulu* of the *Chunqiu* states:
"Heaven has ten fundamental principles;
Heaven constitutes one principle."
Earth constitutes one extreme;
Yang constitutes one extreme;
Yin constitutes one extreme.
Earth constitutes one end;
humanity constitutes one end;
and metal constitutes one end.
Wood constitutes one end;
water constitutes one end;
fire constitutes one end.
There are ten points in total.
Heaven also possesses the breath of joy and anger,
as well as the mind of sorrow and pleasure.
To correspond with others,
one unites them through their common nature; thus,
the human and the celestial are one.
In spring, because it is the qi of joy, there is birth.
In autumn, because it is the qi of anger, there is killing.
In summer, because it is the qi of pleasure, there is nourishment.
In winter, the vital energy (qi) is hidden because it is sorrowful;
these four [seasons] are common to both humans and devas.
The *Erya* says:
"Qióngcāng" refers to the Heaven. Lǐ Xún said:
"In ancient times, people of honest character looked up at the form of the sky;
it was vaulted and high, and its color was a deep azure."
Therefore it is said that "qióngcāng" (the high azure) refers to the Azure Heaven (*cāngtiān*) of spring; Lǐ Xún says:
"In spring, the myriad things first come into being, and their color is a deep azure."
Therefore it is said that [the sky] is *cāngtiān* (Azure Heaven). For the Xia dynasty, it was called *hàotiān* (Vast Heaven). Li Xun said:
"In the Xia, the myriad things are flourishing and their qi is vast and expansive (*hào-hào*);

therefore it is called *hàotiān*. For the autumn, it was called *míntiān* (Compassionate Heaven). Li Xun said: [The myriad things are beginning to wither and decline; therefore it is called *míntiān*.]
In autumn, all things reach maturity and each possesses its own patterns;
therefore it is called *min-tian* (the Compassionate Heaven), for "min" signifies "wen" (patterns).
Guo Jingchun said: "Min" is synonymous with "mǐn" (to pity).
It takes pity on the withering and falling of the myriad things; thus, winter is called "the High Heaven" (*shàngtiān*). Li Xun says:

Section Four: The Six Realms (5–7). This Section on the Six Realms consists of six parts.

Part Five: The Realm of the Gods (*deva*). This is further divided into four sections: the Section on Explaining the Intent, the Section on Enumerating Names, the Section on Suffering, and the Section on Requital. 1. The Section on Explaining the Intent. First, regarding the discussion of celestial retribution:

Second, regarding the names of the assemblies: Question:
What are called the six destinies?
According to the Abhidharma-śāstra,
"destiny" (gati) is called "arrival" and is also called "path."
This means that because the path of the causes of those wholesome and unwholesome karmas can transport one to the place of rebirth,
it is called a "gati" (destiny).
Alternatively, it may be understood as the karma itself, once performed, proceeding toward that place of birth.
Therefore, it is called a "destiny" (*gati*).
To have a destiny means the sense of "tending toward";
that is, the karma one has created can lead one toward the heavens or even down to hell.
Question: Are there only these six destinies fixed, or are there further paths?

The six paths are presented first because ordinary beings and sages dwell together, so that they may be transformed by one another.
Regarding "heaven" (*deva*), it is as explained in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* concerning its etymology.

Question: For what reason is that destination called "heaven" (deva)? Answer:

Some say: Having previously performed superior wholesome conduct of body, speech, and mind,

Therefore it is called the heavenly realm (*devagati*).
Some say that it is called "heaven" (*deva*) because light is predominant.
Because that natural light constantly illuminates both day and night,
the etymologists (śabdavādins) say that it is called "deva" because it is able to illuminate.
Because they manifest superior fruits,
illuminating the causes previously cultivated;
furthermore, they are called "devas" (heavenly beings) because of their playful enjoyment.
Because they constantly sport and experience supreme bliss.

Section Three: The Section on Suffering. Now, following the various sūtras, I shall describe in detail the sufferings of the heavenly realms, as well as the sufferings of the form realm and the formless realm.
Although the higher realms are superior, they still possess subtle suffering;
thus, the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states:
"Within the two upper realms, although there is no coarse suffering, there is subtle suffering."
How is this known?
Because within the fourth dhyāna it is said that there are walking, standing, and lying down;
these exist accordingly.
All [beings] should possess suffering.
Furthermore, in the realm of form (rūpadhātu), there exist visual, auditory, and tactile consciousnesses;
all sensations (vedanā) contained within these very consciousnesses [are present].
This is called suffering and pleasure.
From one posture, one seeks another posture;
because one seeks another posture, one knows there is suffering.
Furthermore, there is the suffering of great loss when one fails to understand and becomes attached to what has already been received;
as it is said in the Sūtra:
Only those who have attained the Path exhibit no color of sorrow or suffering at the time of death.

Since you are now merely an ordinary person, how could you be without both sorrow and joy? As for the statement in the treatise that there is no suffering: [it refers to the absence of suffering in that specific context].
Because the characteristic of suffering is subtle, it is said that it does not exist;
this is like saying there is no salt because one has eaten only a small amount of it.
It is not the case that there is exclusively pleasure and no suffering at all.
Because those in the higher realms practice the conduct of tranquility and are unattached, they cannot give rise to coarse greed, anger, or hatred;
therefore, it is called "neither suffering nor pleasure.
Furthermore, because there is no suffering from swords, staves, and the like, it is said to be "without suffering."
It is not that there is no subtle suffering;
thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
"Although the world possesses most excellent and pure gardens and groves..."
However, when a corpse is situated therein, it becomes impure;
everyone collectively abandons it and does not give rise to attachment.
The realm of form (rūpadhātu) is likewise.
Although it is pure and sublime,
because it is possessed of a body,
all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have utterly renounced it.
If one does not perform this contemplation, it is called "not cultivating the body.
Thus, one knows that there is suffering.
Furthermore, the *Dharmapada-avadāna-sūtra* says:
Four bhikṣus were sitting beneath a tree and asked one another:
"What is the most painful thing in all the world?"
One person said,
"Among all the sufferings in the world, none surpasses lustful desire.
Another person said:
There is no suffering in the world greater than hunger and thirst.
Another person said:
"There is no suffering in the world greater than anger."
One person said,
"Among all the sufferings in the world, none surpasses fear and terror.
They then debated the meaning of suffering, their arguments becoming increasingly complex and never ceasing.
The Buddha, knowing their words,
went to where they were and asked the bhikṣus,
"What matter were you discussing just now?"
He immediately rose, paid his respects, and fully reported what he had discussed.
The Buddha said, "Bhikṣu."
What you have discussed does not exhaustively investigate the meaning of suffering.
Among all the sufferings in the world, none exceed having a body.
Hunger, thirst, cold, heat, anger, and fear—these are its manifestations.
Form, desire, enmity, and calamity all originate from the body.
Now, as for this body:
It is the root of all suffering,
the source of calamity and misfortune;
it exhausts the mind and strains the intellect with myriad forms of anxiety and fear.
In the three realms, wriggling creatures harm one another;
bound by the attachment to a self, they do not cease from birth and death—
all of which arises from the body.
Desiring to leave behind the sufferings of the world, one should seek nirvana.
By concentrating the mind, maintaining rectitude, and remaining serene and free from discursive thought, one may attain nirvana;
this is the supreme bliss.
Therefore, one should know that until the noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*) is attained and this body within the triple world (*traidhātuka*) is extinguished,
how could it not be suffering?
[The interlocutor] asks:
It may be so that there is bodily existence and suffering in the realm of form (rūpadhātu).
But in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), where there is no physical form, how can painful sensation (duḥkhavedanā) arise?
The answer is:
That retribution is subtle and refined; it is not seen by ordinary or inferior beings.
While it lacks coarse obstruction, it is not that fine matter does not exist.
An extensive discussion regarding its existence or non-existence is treated in a separate chapter.
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"When dying or falling away from the two higher realms,
one experiences great anguish."
It is even more severe than in the lower realms;
for example, it is like falling from a precipice to be crushed and disintegrated.
Furthermore, the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states:
Suffering and pleasure follow the body up to the fourth dhyāna;
sorrow and joy follow the mind up to the peak of existence (bhavāgra).
Question: [Why is this so?]
Question: Those born in the higher heavens leave behind evil and accumulate merit;
why is it that when their retribution is exhausted, they immediately enter the three miserable realms? Answer:
Ordinary beings have possessed inexhaustible evil karma since beginningless time;
if even for a single day of greed and anger they undergo a thousand forms,
how much more so when their evils are already so numerous?
Having temporarily suppressed the continuity of rebirth,
once the merit of their retribution is exhausted and their past karma ripens,
they fall back into the three miserable realms.
What causes such delusion?
Therefore, the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states:
"Beings in the realm of form and the formless realm take [their state] to be nirvāṇa."
At the moment when life is ending,
one perceives the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of desire and form,
and immediately gives rise to false views.
This means that there is no nirvāṇa;
they slander the unsurpassed Dharma.
One should know that within them there exists unwholesome karma.
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"One may die in the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception and fall into the Avīci Hell.
Thus, one knows that the cycle of transmigration within the three realms is entirely suffering.
Third, explaining the suffering of the various devas in the desire realm:
it refers to the times when they engage in battle within those heavens,

However, they did not see his form.
Later, when others questioned them in wonder,
he revealed the matter.
The jade maiden then sought to depart, saying,
"I am a spirit-person.
Although I have consorted with you, I do not wish for others to see us."
Yet you are by nature careless and negligent.
I have been associated with you for many years, and our bond of affection and righteousness is no small matter.
Once we are separated, how could one not feel sorrow and regret?
Since our time together cannot last long, let us each exert ourselves.
[He] called for his attendants.
While eating and drinking wine,

They remained so until the Taikang period,

On the third day of the third month, the fifth day of the fifth month, the seventh day of the seventh month, the ninth day of the ninth month, and on the fifteenth day of each month,

He was fifty years of age when he passed away in the Mahāyāna Hall of this very temple.
At that time, there was a worthy man from Chengdu named Ying Shifeng.
Due to illness, his breath ceased,
yet his heart remained warm;
he only regained consciousness after five days.

In a brief moment, he arrived.

The official documents were inscribed with the single character for "Great Governance" (大政).
When Yao went outside and sat beneath a tree on a desolate road,

He ordered Yao to record this.
