The Aṭaṭa hell is a place where sentient beings utter cries of "Aṭaṭa" due to the cold. The Hahava hell is a place where sentient beings utter cries of "Hahava" due to the cold. The Huhuva hell is a place where sentient beings utter cries of "Huhuva" due to the cold. The Utpala hell is a place where sentient beings are frozen so that blisters form on their bodies like blue lotuses. The Padma hell is a place where sentient beings are frozen so that their bodies crack like red lotuses. The Mahāpadma hell is a place where sentient beings are frozen so that their bodies crack like great red lotuses. These eight cold hells are located beneath the Avīci hell. Furthermore, there are eight minor cold hells surrounding each of these cold hells. What are these eight? Namely: Śīta, Praśīta, Atiśīta, Śītaka, Praśītaka, Atiśītaka, Uṣṇa, and Prauṣṇa. These eight minor cold hells are all located on the four sides of the Arbuda hell. The other seven cold hells likewise have these same eight minor cold hells situated on their four sides. Furthermore, there are eight intermediate cold hells located between the cold hells. What are these eight? Namely: Śītalika, Praśītalika, Atiśītalika, Śītakara, Praśītakara, Atiśītakara, Uṣṇaka, and Prauṣṇaka. These eight intermediate cold hells are located between the cold hells. Furthermore, there are eight outer cold hells. What are these eight? Namely: Śīta, Praśīta, Atiśīta, Śītaka, Praśītaka, Atiśītaka, Uṣṇa, and Prauṣṇa. These eight outer cold hells are located outside the Arbuda hell. The other seven cold hells likewise have these same eight outer cold hells situated on their four sides. Furthermore, there are eight intermediate outer cold hells located between the outer cold hells. What are these eight? Namely: Śītalika, Praśītalika, Atiśītalika, Śītakara, Praśītakara, Atiśītakara, Uṣṇaka, and Prauṣṇaka. These eight intermediate outer cold hells are located between the outer cold hells. Furthermore, there are eight great outer cold hells. What are these eight? Namely: Śīta, Praśīta, Atiśīta, Śītaka, Praśītaka, Atiśītaka, Uṣṇa, and Prauṣṇa. These eight great outer cold hells are located outside the Nirarbuda hell. The other six cold hells likewise have these same eight great outer cold hells situated on their four sides. Furthermore, there are eight intermediate great outer cold hells located between the great outer cold hells. What are these eight? Namely: Śītalika, Praśītalika, Atiśītalika, Śītakara, Praśītakara, Atiśītakara, Uṣṇaka, and Prauṣṇaka. These eight intermediate great outer cold hells are located between the great outer cold hells. Furthermore, there are eight outermost great cold hells. What are these eight? Namely: Śīta, Praśīta, Atiśīta, Śītaka, Praśītaka, Atiśītaka, Uṣṇa, and Prauṣṇa. These eight outermost great cold hells are located outside the Aṭaṭa hell. The other five cold hells likewise have these same eight outermost great cold hells situated on their four sides. Furthermore, there are eight intermediate outermost great cold hells located between the outermost great cold hells. What are these eight? Namely: Śītalika, Praśītalika, Atiśītalika, Śītakara, Praśītakara, Atiśītakara, Uṣṇaka, and Prauṣṇaka. These eight intermediate outermost great cold hells are located between the outermost great cold hells. Furthermore, there are eight great outermost cold hells. What are these eight? Namely: Śīta, Praśīta, Atiśīta, Śītaka, Praśītaka, Atiśītaka, Uṣṇa, and Prauṣṇa. These eight great outermost cold hells are located outside the Hahava hell. The other four cold hells likewise have these same eight great outermost cold hells situated on their four sides. Furthermore, there are eight intermediate great outermost cold hells located between the great outermost cold hells. What are these eight? Namely: Śītalika, Praśītalika, Atiśītalika, Śītakara, Praśītakara, Atiśītakara, Uṣṇaka, and Prauṣṇaka
Above that is the Hot Hell;
above that is the Great Howling Hell;
and above that is the Howling Hell.
Above that is the Saṃghāta Hell; above that is the Kālasūtra Hell;
and above that is the Saṃjīva Hell.
Each of these hells is ten thousand yojanas in length and breadth;
above that, there remains one thousand yojanas,
five hundred of which consist of white plaster.
Five hundred yojanas below is the mud;
some say that beneath this mud, in its center, lies the Avīci Hell.
The other seven hells surround it on all sides,
just as villages surround a great city.
It is asked:
If that is so, how should one reconcile this with what is stated in the *Prajñapti-śāstra*,
which says: "Jambudvīpa is six thousand and three and a half yojanas in circumference"?
Each individual hell is vast in extent.
How, then, can they all be accommodated beneath this continent?
The answer is as follows:
This Jambudvīpa is pointed at the top and broad at the bottom,
like a heap of grain; therefore,
it is able to contain [the world].
According to this sutra,
it is said that the four great oceans gradually become deeper as one enters them,
and furthermore, each individual great hell has sixteen secondary hells (*utsada*).
That is to say, each has four gates,
and outside each gate there are four additional calamities (*utsada*).
The first is the additional calamity of hot ashes (*kukūla-utsada*).
That is to say, within this [first] increase, hot ashes reach up to the knees.
Second is the increase of corpses and excrement;
that is to say, within this increase, the ground is filled with a mire of corpses and excrement.
Third is the Increase of Razor Blades.
This means that within this increase there are further three types:
first, the Path of Razor Blades.
This refers to the path therein, which is spread out with the edges of blades facing upward;
second, the Forest of Sword-Leaves,
where the leaves above consist entirely of sharp, keen sword-blades.
Third is the Forest of Iron Thorns.
This means that upon this forest there are sharp iron thorns sixteen finger-widths long.
Although the three types, such as the Path of Sword-Blades, differ from one another, they share the same Iron Forest;
therefore, they are subsumed under a single *ūṣmagata* (Heat) hell. Fourth is the *vālukā* (Gravel) *ūṣmagata*.
That is to say, within this [Avīci], there is a hot briny sea;
together with the primary hell itself, these constitute seventeen.
Thus, there are eight great hells along with their various subsidiary realms.
Thus, there are one hundred and thirty-six locations.
For this reason, the Sūtra states that there are one hundred and thirty-six *naraka*s (hells).
Therefore, the *Dīrgha Āgama* states:
"The great hells are eight in number;
each of these eight hells is surrounded by sixteen minor hells."
Just as the four continents are surrounded by eighty thousand continents, and beyond those eighty thousand continents there is a great ocean;

beyond the ocean there is a great Vajra Mountain, and beyond that mountain there is another mountain also named Vajra. The *Loutan jing* (Kāṣāyaprabhāsa-sūtra) states that between these two mountains, the majestic radiance of the deities of the sun and moon does not shine at all.
The eight great hells are:
first, Saṃjīva;
second, Kālasūtra.
Third, the Crushing Hell;
fourth, the Howling Hell;
fifth, the Great Howling Hell.
Sixth, the Hell of Burning and Roasting; seventh, the Hell of Great Burning and Roasting;

eighth, the Hell of Uninterrupted Charring. As for the differences in nomenclature found in other sutras, these are merely variations in translation—some erroneous and some correct—but their general meaning is identical. First, the sixteen hells of the Realm of Perception (*saṃjñā-naraka*).
The sentient beings therein have iron claws growing from their hands.
Driven by mutual hatred and anger, they tear at one another with these claws; as soon as the flesh is torn away, it falls off, and they imagine themselves to be dead.
Therefore, it is named after that perception.
Furthermore, the sentient beings therein harbor thoughts of malice;
grasping swords and blades in their hands, they strike and stab one another.
His body was flayed, split, and hacked until his limbs were shattered upon the ground;
he thought himself dead,
but when a cold wind blew over him, he immediately revived and rose up.
He thinks to himself, "I am now alive"; having long endured his suffering,
he conceives the thought that he has emerged from the hell.
In a state of panic and terror, they cry out for rescue;
unaware, they suddenly arrive at the Black Sand Hell,
where hot winds rise up violently, blowing scorching black sand.
When they enter it, their bodies are scorched from the skin through to the marrow;
flames arise within their bodies, swirling and circling around them,
until their bodies are burned, withered, and rotten.
Because their retribution for that sin is not yet exhausted,
they are not permitted to die; after suffering for a long time,
they emerge from the Black Sand Hell and arrive at the Boiling Excrement Hell.
Boiling excrement and iron balls spontaneously appear before them, driving and pressuring the offenders.
They are forced to grasp the iron balls, which burn their hands and bodies;
they are further made to seize them with their mouths, so that from the throat down to the belly, they are consumed by fire.
Passing through and penetrating downward, there is nothing that is not scorched and roasted.
Iron-beaked insects gnaw at the flesh until they reach the marrow.
The suffering and poison are immeasurable, and the retribution for their offenses remains unfinished.
Still unwilling to die, after having suffered for a long time,
they emerge from the Hell of Boiling Excrement and arrive at the Hell of Iron Nails.
There, the hell-wardens strike them down and lay them supine upon hot iron.
They stretch out his body and drive nails into his hands and feet;
until five hundred nails have been driven all over his body,
he cries out in bitter agony yet still does not die.
Having endured suffering for a long time, they emerge from the Iron Nail Hell and arrive at the Hungry Iron Hell; there,
they are immediately cast upon glowing-hot iron.
Molten copper is poured into their mouths, flowing from the throat down to the abdomen;
it passes through completely, leaving nothing unscorched or rotten.
Yet, as their remaining karma is not yet exhausted, they do not die.
Having long endured suffering, they emerge from the Hungry Hell and arrive at the Thirsty Hell.
There, they are cast upon hot iron and a glowing iron ball is placed in their mouths, burning their lips and tongues.
Passing through [the previous hells] below, there was no place that was not scorched and roasted;
they wailed in bitter agony.
Having endured suffering for a long time, they emerged from the Thirsty Hell (Kṣut-tarpana-naraka) and arrived at the Copper Cauldron Hell (Tāmra-kumbhīpāka-naraka).
The hell-wardens, with eyes blazing with rage, seize the feet of the offenders and cast them headlong into the cauldrons,
where they are tossed about by the surging, boiling broth; spinning up and down,
their bodies are broken apart, decomposed, and cooked until thoroughly rotten.
Because myriad sufferings arrive all at once, they are not permitted to die.
After enduring suffering for a long time, they emerge from one copper cauldron and enter the Hell of Many Copper Cauldrons.
There, the wardens seize the feet of the offenders and cast them headfirst into the cauldrons.
As the boiling broth surges and swirls up and down, their entire bodies are mangled and decomposed;
they are then seized with iron hooks and cast into other cauldrons,
yet they do not die due to the intensity of their piteous cries and bitter agony.
Having endured suffering for a long time, they emerge from the Hell of Many Copper Cauldrons and arrive at the Hell of Stone Grinding.
They seize those offenders and throw them onto hot stones,
stretching out their hands and feet and pressing heavy, scorching stones upon their bodies.
They are turned over and rubbed until their flesh and bones are ground to pulp;
though they suffer such bitter and piercing pain, they are not allowed to die.
After enduring this suffering for a long time, they emerge from the Stone Mill Hell and arrive at the Pus and Blood Hell.
Pus and blood boil and surge;
within it, the offenders run hither and thither,
their bodies, heads, and faces scorched and utterly ruined.
Furthermore, they take pus and blood and eat it, which passes completely through their bodies;
because the bitter torment is unbearable, it prevents them from dying.
After suffering for a long time, they emerge from the Pus and Blood Hell and proceed to the Measuring Fire Hell.
There is a great mass of fire,
its flames blazing fiercely, which drives and coerces the sinners;
with their hands they grasp hot iron measures to measure the mass of fire.
As their entire bodies are scorched by bitter heat and agonizing poison,
they groan and wail, which prevents them from dying.
After enduring suffering for a long time, they emerge from the Hell of Measuring Fire and arrive at the Hell of the Ash River.
It is five hundred yojanas in length, breadth, and depth.
Ashy hot water surges and boils, emitting foul vapors that billow and swirl;
the waves crash against one another with a sound that is terrifying to hear.
From the bottom to the top, iron spikes run both lengthwise and crosswise.
On the banks of that river stands a forest of sword-trees (*asipattravana*),
whose branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits are all swords and blades.
The sinners enter the river and are carried up and down by the waves;
they swirl and sink, and iron spikes pierce their bodies,
penetrating them from both inside and out as pus and blood flow forth.
Because their sufferings are manifold, they are not permitted to die;
thus they emerge from the Ash River and reach the other shore, arriving at the Forest of Sword-Trees,
where their bodies are sliced and pierced by swords until they are mangled and destroyed.
Furthermore, jackals and wolves come to gnaw upon the offenders,
devouring their flesh raw as they flee up the sword-trees.
At that time, the sword-blades turned downward;
when descending from the sword-tree, the sword-blades turned upward.
When raising their hands, their hands were severed; when treading with their feet, their feet were cut off.
The skin and flesh fall away,
leaving only white bones connected by sinews.
At that time, there are iron-beaked crows upon the sword-trees.
Birds peck at their heads and eat their brains;
they wail in bitter agony yet are not allowed to die.
They return to the Ash River, where they sink and drown with the waves.
Iron thorns pierce their bodies with myriad forms of bitter agony;
skin and flesh rot and decay as pus and blood flow out,
until only white bones remain, floating on the surface.
As a cold wind blows, he immediately stands up.
Driven by his past karma, he unwittingly arrives suddenly at the Iron Ball Hell (Ayas-tuṇḍa).
There, hell-wardens with hot iron balls drive him forward and seize him.
Their hands and feet become festering and decayed, and their entire bodies burst into flames.
Because ten thousand poisons assail them simultaneously, they are not permitted to die.
After enduring suffering for a long time, they emerge from the Iron Ball Hell and proceed to the Ax and Hatchet Hell.
They seize this sinner and throw him onto a red-hot iron surface;
with heated iron axes, they hack at his hands, feet, ears, nose, tongue, and body.
He wails in bitter agony, yet they do not allow him to die.
Having suffered these punishments for a long time, they emerge from the Kiln and Axe Hell and arrive at the Wolf and Jackal Hell.
There, a pack of wolves and jackals compete to come and gnaw and bite them;
their flesh falls away, their bones are wounded, and pus and blood flow out.
Because their suffering is manifold, they are not permitted to die.
After enduring suffering for a long time, they emerge from the prison of jackals and wolves and arrive at the Sword-Tree Prison.
Upon entering that forest of swords, a violent wind arises.
The leaves of the sword-tree (asipattravana) are blown by the wind and fall upon their bodies;
there is no part of their heads, faces, or bodies that is not wounded and destroyed.
Iron-beaked crows peck at their two eyes.
Because they wail in agony, they are not allowed to die.
After suffering for a long time, they emerge from the Sword-Tree Hell and arrive at the Cold-Ice Hell.
There, a great freezing wind blows upon their bodies.
Their entire bodies become frostbitten, their skin and flesh fall away,
and they die after uttering cries of bitter agony;
such is the consequence of unwholesome conduct.
The same applies to speech and mind.
Such a person falls into the Saṃjīva Hell;
then, with hair standing on end from fear, they enter the second great hell, Kālasūtra.
It is surrounded on all sides by sixteen minor hells,
each five hundred yojanas in length and breadth.
For what reason is it named "Black Rope"?
The various hell-wardens seize those sinners,
fling them onto hot iron, and stretch out their bodies;
they then mark them with hot iron cords, straightening them.
With a red-hot iron axe, they follow the path of the cord and hack the offenders into hundreds of thousands of pieces.
Furthermore, they mark them with iron cords and saw them apart with saws.
Furthermore, glowing iron ropes are suspended,
crisscrossing in countless numbers, as the offenders are driven and coerced to walk between them;
then, a violent and malevolent wind suddenly arises.
Iron chains are blown onto their bodies, burning through the skin,
penetrating the flesh, scorching the bones, and boiling the marrow;
their suffering and agony are manifold.
Because their remaining karmic retributions are not yet exhausted,
they are not allowed to die; therefore,
it is named Black Rope (Kālasūtra).
After enduring suffering for a long time,
they emerge from the Black Rope Hell and proceed through the Black Sand Hell up to the Cold Ice Hell;
thereafter their lives end, and the details cannot be fully recounted.
Regarding the experiences of suffering and pain in the remaining sixteen hells,
they follow the same principles as previously described;
however, the intensity of the suffering is increased.
By harboring malicious intent toward one's parents, the Buddha, or the śrāvakas,
one falls directly into the Black Rope Hell,
where the suffering is beyond measure; from there, one proceeds to the third great hell, Saṃjīva.
There are also sixteen minor hells surrounding it,
each five hundred yojanas in length and breadth.
For what reason is it named "Crushing" (Pratāpana)?
There are great rocky mountains standing in pairs facing one another;
when a person enters between them, the mountains spontaneously close together and crush their body,
grinding their flesh and bones to dust, after which the mountains return to their original places.
Because of the myriad forms of bitter suffering, they are made not to die.
Furthermore, there are great iron elephants with their entire bodies ablaze,
coming toward them with a roar.
They trample upon the sinners, rolling over them until their bodies are crushed to pieces and pus and blood flow forth;
they wail and cry out in grief, yet are purposely kept from dying.
Furthermore, they seize the offender and lay him upon a large stone, pressing him down with another great stone.
Again, they take the offender and lay him upon the ground, pounding him with iron pestles from his feet to his head.
Their skin and flesh are crushed and mangled, and pus and blood flow forth;
myriad poisons assail them simultaneously, yet because their remaining retributions are not yet exhausted,
they are not permitted to die.
Therefore it is named Raurava.
Having long endured suffering, they finally emerge from the Raurava Hell and proceed to the Black Sand Hell, continuing through to the Cold Ice Hell.
Thereafter, when their lives ended,
because they had committed only the three types of evil karma and failed to cultivate the three types of wholesome conduct,
they immediately fell into the Crushing Hell (Samghāta-naraka).
The suffering there is beyond measure.
The fourth, the Great Hell of Screaming (Raurava),
is likewise surrounded by sixteen minor hells.
Each is five hundred yojanas in length and breadth.
For what reason is it called the Hell of Screaming?
The hell-wardens seize the offenders and hurl them into large cauldrons.
Furthermore, they are placed within a large iron cauldron where boiling hot water surges and seethes,
cooking those sinners who wail and shriek in bitter, agonizing pain.
Furthermore, they seize those sinners and cast them upon a great griddle, roasting them repeatedly from both sides.
After enduring suffering for a long time, they emerge crying out and proceed to the Black Sand Hell, continuing as far as the Cold Ice Hell.
Then, when his life came to an end,
because he had harbored malice and committed various evil deeds out of anger,
he fell into the Raurava Hell.
The fifth is the Great Screaming Hell (Mahāraurava).
It is likewise surrounded by sixteen minor hells, whose dimensions are the same as those previously described. For what reason is it called the Great Screaming Hell?
They seize those sinners and place them within a great iron cauldron;
having left them there for a long time, the boiling hot water surges and seethes as it cooks those sinners.
Furthermore, they cast them upon a great iron griddle, roasting and broiling them repeatedly.
They wail and cry out loudly in bitter pain and anguish;
because their remaining karmic retributions are not yet exhausted, they are prevented from dying.
This is called the Hell of Great Screaming.
Having suffered for a long time, they emerge from the Great Howling Hell and eventually pass away only upon reaching the Cold Ice Hell.
Because they practiced various wrong views, were dragged by the net of craving, and committed base and vile deeds, they fall into the Great Howling Hell.
The sixth is the Hell of Scorching Heat (Tapana).
It is likewise surrounded by sixteen minor hells, the dimensions of which are the same as those previously described. Why is it named "Scorching Heat"?
Because all the offenders are placed within a city of iron.
That city blazes with fire, both inside and out, glowing crimson;
it sears and roasts the sinners,
and they are further placed upon iron towers.
The fire blazes in that tower, making both its interior and exterior crimson;
furthermore, they are cast into a great iron cauldron,
which also blazes with fire, making both its interior and exterior crimson.
The sinners are roasted and scorched;
their skin and flesh are singed and rotted away as ten thousand poisons assail them simultaneously.
Because their remaining retribution is not yet exhausted, they are made not to die.
Therefore it is called the Hell of Burning and Roasting.
After suffering there for a long time, one emerges from the Hell of Burning and Roasting,
and so on until reaching the Hell of Cold Ice, whereupon one finally passes away.
Because they burned and roasted sentient beings, they fell into the Scorching Hell (Tapana),
where they endure this suffering of being scorched and roasted for a long night.
This is the seventh great Scorching Hell.
There are also sixteen minor hells surrounding it, equal in size to the former; why is this called the Great Burning Hell?
It is because all the sinners are placed within a city of iron.
The city blazes with fire, both inside and out glowing crimson.
It scorches and roasts the offenders;
their skin and flesh are singed and rotted away as ten thousand poisons assail them simultaneously.
There is a great pit of fire with blazing flames;
on both banks of the pit are great mountains of fire.
Those sinners are cast into it, impaled upon iron forks, and set upright within the flames.
However, because their remaining retribution is not yet exhausted, they do not die even as fire burns them, scorching and roasting their skin and flesh until it is charred and putrid.
After enduring suffering for a long time, they emerge from the Great Scorching Hell,
and only upon reaching the Cold Ice Hell do they finally pass away.
Because they abandon the karma that yields wholesome fruits and engage in various evil deeds,
they fall into the Great Burning Hell, the eighth Avīci hell.
It is also surrounded by sixteen minor hells, equal in size to the former. Why is it called the Avīci Hell?
This is translated as the "Uninterrupted" (Muzhuan) Hell.
Why is it called "uninterrupted"?
The hell-wardens seize those sinners and flay their skin from their feet to the crown of their heads.
They then wrap that very skin around the sinners' bodies and place them upon fiery chariots,
which roll back and forth over the scorching ground.
Their bodies were shattered and mangled, their skin and flesh fell away;
though myriad poisons assailed them simultaneously, they did not die.
Furthermore, an iron city arose with flames erupting from all four sides.
The flames from the east reach the west, and the flames from the west reach the east;
it is likewise for the south, north, above, and below.
As the blazing flames swirl and circulate, there is not a single empty space between them.
They run to and fro, their bodies scorched and roasted;
their skin and flesh are singed and putrefied, and they endure bitter,
acrid pain as ten thousand poisons assail them all at once.
After the sinners have been there for a long time, the gate is finally opened;
the various sinners rush toward it,
with flames erupting from all their limbs and joints.
As they run toward the gate, the gate closes spontaneously;
because their remaining karmic retribution is not yet exhausted, it prevents them from dying.
Furthermore, whatever these offenders within see when they lift their eyes:
One sees only unpleasant forms,
hears only unpleasant sounds,
and smells only foul odors.
The body experiences painful contact,
and the mind contemplates unwholesome dharmas;
for even the duration of a finger-snap, there is no moment that is not suffering.
Therefore it is called the Avīci Hell.
After suffering there for a long time, one emerges from Avīci;
only upon reaching the Arbuda (Icy) Hells does one finally die.
Because they have committed grave offenses that produce karma leading to the evil destinies,
they fall into the Avīci Hell,
where they undergo unspeakable and incalculable suffering.
These are called the eight great hells; in each,
one passes through sixteen [subsidiary hells],
undergoing punishments as previously described.
Furthermore, the *Buddhāvataṃsaka-samādhi-sāgara-sūtra* states:
"As for the Avīci Hell,
its length and breadth are equal, measuring eight thousand yojanas."
There are seven layers of iron walls and seven tiers of iron nets.
There are eighteen partitions surrounding these seven layers,
all of which consist of forests of swords.
Furthermore, there are seven layers of sword-forests.
At the four corners are four great copper dogs,
forty yojanas in length and breadth.
His eyes are like flashes of lightning; his fangs are like sword-trees;
his teeth are like mountains of knives; his tongue is like iron thorns;
and every hair on his body blazes with fierce fire.
Its smoke is foul-smelling.
There are eighteen hell-wardens whose mouths are like those of yakṣas.
Sixty-four eyes [are on his body],
from which iron balls scatter and fly out;
dog-like fangs protrude upward to a height of four yojanas.
Flames stream from the tips of his tusks, burning the iron chariot before him;
fire and sharp-edged blades emerge from the rims of its wheels, incinerating the city of Avīci,
which is as red as molten copper.
The hell-wardens have eight heads and sixty-four horns;
from the tips of the horns, fire blazes forth, which transforms into steel,
which further becomes blades and wheels.
The wheels follow one another in succession within the midst of the flames, filling the city of Avīci.
Within the city are seven iron pillars;
the fire surges like boiling water.
Molten iron flows and surges forth from the four gates.
Above, eighteen cauldrons of boiling copper overflow and spread throughout the city.
Between the two enclosures dwell eighty-four thousand iron pythons and great serpents.
They vomit poisonous fire that fills the entire city;
they roar and howl like the thunder of heaven,
raining down great iron balls.
There were five hundred yakṣas and fifty billion worms;
from the eighty-four thousand beaks, fire flowed like rain.
It descends and fills the city of Avīci.
When this worm descends, the fierce fire blazes intensely,
illuminating the top of the hell for eighty-four thousand yojanas.
It gushes forth from beneath Mount Jiao (Cakravāḍa) into the waters of the great ocean,
piercing the bottom of the sea with a shape like a chariot wheel.
If there are those who kill their fathers, harm their mothers, or revile their six kin, [they shall fall here].
At the time of death, the copper dogs transform into eighteen chariots shaped like precious canopies,
and all the flames transform into jade maidens.
Seeing them from afar, the sinners felt joy and desired to go toward them.
When the wind-swords cut them, they cried out in the intensity of their cold:
"How wonderful it would be if we could obtain a good fire and place it upon our carts!"
Having lit a fire to expose themselves to it, they immediately die;
those who gaze upon the jade maidens from atop golden chariots have their bodies hacked and severed by all who grasp iron axes.
In the time it takes to bend and extend one's arm, they fall directly into Avīci.
From the upper partition to the lower one, like a whirling firebrand, they reach the lower partition,
their bodies remaining within the partitions.
The bronze dogs barked fiercely,
gnawing on bones and sucking at marrow;
the rakshasa jailers seized them with great iron forks, prying their heads upward.
Flames enveloped his entire body throughout the Avīci Hell.
King Yama shouted out a stern command, saying:
"Foolish man, seed of hell!"
"While you were in the world, you were unfilial toward your parents, arrogant, and unrighteous.
Therefore, you have now been born in the place called Avīci Hell,
where you shall thus undergo great suffering in succession."
It cannot be fully described.
The suffering endured by those in hell for a single day and night is equivalent to sixty minor kalpas in Jambudvīpa.
In this way, for such a great kalpa,
one who commits the five heinous crimes undergoes punishment for five kalpas.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who violate the four grave prohibitions.
They consume the offerings of the faithful in vain, slandering [the Dharma] with false views;
they fail to recognize cause and effect, severing their study of Prajñāpāramitā;
they revile the Buddhas of the ten directions and steal the property of the Saṃgha.
This person, through lustful and unrighteous conduct, coerced and plundered pure-natured bhikṣuṇīs, sisters, and female relatives, committing manifold evil deeds;
such is this person’s retribution when facing the end of life.
These sinners, having passed eighty-four thousand great kalpas,
enter again into the eighteen compartments of the eastern direction,
where they undergo suffering as before.
The same applies to the south, west, and north.
His body fills the Avīci Hell,
and his four limbs further fill the eighteen compartments.
In the Avīci Hell there are eighteen minor hells.
Within each of these minor hells, there are eighteen cold ice hells and eighteen dark hells.
The eighteen minor hot hells;
the eighteen hells of the wheel of knives;
the eighteen hells of the wheel of swords.
The eighteen hells of flaming chariots;
the eighteen hells of boiling excrement;
the eighteen hells of cauldrons of boiling water.
The eighteen Ashigangā (Gray River) hells;
five hundred billion sword-forest hells;
and five hundred billion thorn-forest hells.
There are five hundred billion Copper Pillar Hells,
five hundred billion Iron Mechanisms Hells,
and five hundred billion Iron Nets Hells.
The eighteen hells of iron caves;
the eighteen hells of iron pellets;
and the eighteen hells of sharp stones.
Eighteenth is the Copper-Drinking Hell.
Thus, within this Great Avīci Hell,
there are these eighteen hells.
Within each of these hells,
there are separately eighteen smaller sub-hells,
beginning from the Cold Ice Hell and ending with the Drinking of Molten Copper Hell.
In total, there are one hundred and forty-two compartments of hells.
Each has its own distinct karma;
nevertheless, those who pass through these hells must experience their sufferings in their entirety.
Furthermore, the *Qishi jing* (Sūtra on the Arising of the World) states:
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus,
"In the Avīci Great Hell..."
There are also sixteen minor hells that serve as its retinue,
surrounding it on all sides.
Each is five hundred yojanas wide.
All sentient beings who are born there, emerge there,
or dwell there do so as a result of their evil karma.
Various jailers spontaneously appear,
each seizing the bodies of those sentient beings in hell with both hands and hurling them onto the ground of blazing, red-hot iron.
The flames shoot straight upward,
fiercely blazing as they spread across the ground;
he then takes a sharp blade and [cuts] from above the ankle.
They tear out the sinews of their hands and pull them;
even the sinews at the crown of their heads are all pulled together in succession.
This pierces through to the heart and marrow, such that the suffering is difficult to describe.
Having been dragged in this manner, they are forced to drive iron chariots that gallop away at great speed.
These chariots are extremely hot, with blazing flames,
and the places they travel over are entirely ablaze.
Having departed from the path of glowing iron, they go on and on;
following the will of the hell-wardens, they do not pause for even a moment.
To whichever direction they wish to go, they proceed immediately as desired.
Wherever they go, the hell-wardens drag them along,
never letting them go;
wherever they pass through, they melt and consume the offenders.
The flesh and blood of his body were left with nothing remaining.
He experienced the full retribution for all the karmic actions he had committed in the past when he was a human or a non-human being.
Because of the ripening of these unwholesome deeds, a great mass of fire arose from the eastern direction.
Suddenly it was born, a blazing, crimson,
and immense mass of fierce flames, intensely radiant, extending toward the south, west, north,
the four intermediate directions, and above and below.
Each is thus surrounded by great masses of fire,
which gradually close in upon them as they undergo various agonizing pains.
From the eastern wall, a great flame issued forth;
it shot directly toward the western wall, reached it, and remained there.
From the western wall, a great blaze of light issued forth.
It shines directly upon the northern wall.
From the northern wall, a great flame of light issues forth and shines directly upon the southern wall.
From below to above and from above to below,
they connect horizontally and vertically, shooting up and down in mutual intersection;
the hot light blazes brilliantly as surging flames collide with one another.
At that time, the hell-wardens cast the various offenders into six kinds of great masses of fire,
where they undergo extremely severe and agonizing suffering.
Their life has not yet ended,
and since those unwholesome karmas have not been exhausted or finished,
they experience them fully in the interim.
These sentient beings within this Avīci Great Hell,
due to the retribution of their various unwholesome karmas,
pass through immeasurable time upon the long and distant path.
After having undergone these various sufferings, the four gates of the hell open once again.
When the gates open, all those sentient beings hear the sound and see them opening;
they run toward the gates, thinking thus:
"We shall surely be able to escape while that person is thus running at full speed;
for his body will become even more fiercely and violently ablaze,
like a strong man running against the wind holding a torch of dry grass."
As that torch continues to burn, it becomes even more fiercely blazing;
those sentient beings run on and run again,
and the person's body becomes increasingly ablaze.
When they wish to lift their feet, their flesh and blood disintegrate;
when they wish to set them down, their flesh and blood regenerate.
Upon reaching the gates of hell, the gates close once more.
Unable to escape, his heart became distressed and agitated;
he fell face-down upon the ground, and the fire burned through his skin, then his flesh, and finally his bones.
It penetrates even to the marrow, with smoke and flames blazing intensely;
the smoke billows forth and the flames flare fiercely,
and as smoke and flame intermingle, the torment of heat is doubled.
That person undergoes extremely severe suffering therein;
as long as their evil karma has not been extinguished, they experience it all.
This is the Avīci [Hell].
Within the great hells,
there is not even for a moment, as brief as the snap of a finger, any experience of peace or happiness at any time;
in this manner, they undergo these sufferings in succession.
The World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"You should know this."
Between those worlds, there are ten distinct hells.
What are the ten? First is the Arbuda hell.
2. The Nirarbuda hell; 3. The Ahaha hell; 4. The Huhuva hell.
Fifth, the Aṭaṭa hell; sixth, the Saṃjīva hell;
seventh, the Utpala hell.
The eighth is the Padma hell; the ninth is the Mahāpadma hell; the tenth is the Tāmra hell;
and the eleventh is the Mahātāmra hell. For what cause and for what reason is the [twelfth] named Arbuda hell?
The physical forms of all these sentient beings are like bubbles;
for this reason, it is called the Arbuda Hell.
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions is it named the Nirarbuda Hell?
The physical bodies of these sentient beings are like lumps of flesh;
therefore, this place is called the Nirarbuda Hell.
Furthermore, for what reason is it called the A-hu Hell?
When these sentient beings are oppressed by severe and agonizing suffering, they cry out, saying, "A-hu! A-hu! (Alas! Alas! Thus it is named.
It is a state of extreme suffering;
this is called the A-hu Hell. For what further causes and conditions is it named the Hu-hu-po Hell?
When these sentient beings are oppressed by the extreme sufferings of that hell, they cry out, "Huhuva,
huhuva"; therefore, it is named the Huhuva Hell.
Furthermore, for what reason is it called the Aṭaṭa Hell?
Because these sentient beings are so oppressed by extreme suffering that their bodies can only utter the cry: "Aṭaṭa! Aṭaṭa!"
However, because the sound of their tongues cannot issue forth from their mouths,
it is therefore called the Aṭaṭa Hell. Furthermore,
for what reason and by what causes is it named the Saṃjīva Hell?
Within these hells, the color of the fierce flames is like that of the *sāṅkhatikā* flower;
therefore, it is named the Sāṅkhatikā Hell.
Furthermore, for what reason is it called the Utpala Hell? Within this hell,
the color of the fierce flames is like that of the utpala flower.
For this reason, it is called the Utpala Hell.
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions is it called the Kumuda Hell?
Within these hells, these sentient beings—
The color of its fierce flames is like that of the kumuda flower;
therefore, it is named the Kumuda Hell.
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions is it named the Puṇḍarīka Hell?
Within these various hells,
the color of the fierce flames is like that of the *pāṇḍarīka* flower;
therefore, it is named the *Pāṇḍarīka* Hell.
Furthermore, for what reason is it called the Padma Hell?
Within this hell, the color of the fierce flames of these sentient beings is like that of the padma flower.
For this reason, it is called the Padma Hell.
Furthermore, the *Tridharmaka-śāstra-sūtra* states:
"There are three hells."
First, the hot; second, the cold; third, the peripheral.
Regarding the hot hells, according to the Sarvāstivāda school, there are eight great hells.
The first grade of life;
it is also called "reviving life," or when the hell-wardens proclaim, "You are born."
Alternatively, they may be revived by cold winds;
because these two conditions, though different, both cause them to be revived equally,
it is called the Reviving Hell (Saṃjīva).
The second is named the Kālasūtra Hell,
where one is first marked with lines using cords and subsequently cut with axes.
The third is named the Saṃghāta Hell.
It is also called the Hell of the Colliding Mountains, where two mountains close together to crush the sinners.
Fourth is the Huhu Hell, also known as the Hell of Wailing.
The hell-wardens pursue them, forcing them to run while crying out;
because they utter great cries,
it is also called the Hell of Great Crying (Mahāraurava).
As the fires of the four great elements erupt and there is no way to escape,
it is therefore named the Hell of Great Screaming (Mahāraurava).
The sixth is the Hot Hell (Tapana).
It is also called "The Blazing.
Fire and iron are closely situated within it, and therein one undergoes heat.
Seventh is the hell named "The Mass of Heat" (Pratāpana).
It is also called "Great Conflagration," where mountain fires crackle and spit as they roast the sinners.
The eighth is named the Avīci Hell.
It is also called "uninterrupted" (*ānantarya*),
for once cast into the fires of suffering, there is never an interval of pleasure.
Since the suffering is uninterrupted, what could possibly be chosen?
These eight hells are situated in layers upon Jambudvīpa.
According to the *Tridharmaka-śāstra*,
the first two have presiding rulers.
Next, three [factors] primarily govern the minor [states],
and three govern the absence of primary governance;
however, these eight constitute the foundation.
Each one has sixteen surrounding [enclosures].
There are four on each side;
they combine in groups of four.
In total there are sixteen;
including the fundamental [one], they become seventeen.
Eight times seventeen.
There are one hundred and thirty-six such places in total,
where sinners undergo the suffering of heat and affliction.
The second type, the cold hells, likewise consists of eight.
The first is named Arbuda Hell,
so called because the flesh develops small blisters due to the torment of cold.
The second is named Nirarbuda Hell.
Due to the cold wind blowing upon them, blisters form over their entire bodies;
this is the third, the Aṭaṭa Hell.
Because their lips cannot move, only their tongues can move.
Therefore, they produce this sound.
Fourth is the A-pa-p'o (Āpāpa) Hell;
because the tongue cannot move, only the lips can move.
Therefore, they produce this sound.
The fifth is named the Vessel-of-the-Throat Hell (Kandūrasa-naraka).
Because their lips and tongues cannot move, they can only vibrate air within their throats.
Therefore, they make this sound.
The sixth is named Utpala Hell;
this refers to the blue lotus.
The petals of these flowers are fine, and their fleshy color is cracked like this flower when it blooms under the scorching sun.
The seventh is called the Padma Hell;
this refers to the red lotus.
Because the great patches of flesh color resemble the blooming of this flower,
it is called the eighth, the Pundarika Hell;
this refers to the white lotus.
Because the fissures in those bones resemble the opening of these flowers,
the first two [names] are derived from the characteristics of the body,
while the subsequent three are derived from the characteristics of the sound.
The latter three derive their names from the characteristics of their wounds.
Thus, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states:
"Among these eight, sentient beings are tormented by extreme cold."
This name is established because of the transformation of the body, voice, and sores.
According to the *Tridharmaka-śāstra*:
The first two are subject to calling out;
the next four are not subject to calling out;
from the third [stage] onward, there is no calling out.
These eight [cold hells] are situated at the base of the Cakravāḍa Mountains between the continents;
the sinners dwell there facing upward,
suffering the torments of freezing cold within them.
Regarding the third, the peripheral hells (*pratyantaka-naraka*),
according to the *Tridharmakhaṇḍa-śāstra*,
there are likewise three.
1. Among the mountains;
2. among the waters;
3. in the wilderness.
They receive the retribution of distinct karmas;
this should involve receiving both cold and heat mixed together.
As for the retribution of lifespan, there are variations in its duration, being either extended or shortened.
Furthermore, the *Lokasthāna-abhidharma-śāstra* states:
The World-Honored One said,
"There is a great hell named 'Darkness' (*Kṛṣṇa-andhakāra*)."
On the outer boundaries of each respective world-system, there are [such realms],
all of which are without any covering.
The sentient beings therein cannot see them even by raising their own hands or eyes.
Although the sun and moon possess great majestic power,
their radiance does not illuminate that form;
yet when the Buddhas appear in the world, their great light shines everywhere upon it.
Therefore, by means of this light, they are able to see one another.
Residing between the two worlds of mountains, outside the perimeter of the Iron Wheel, it is called the "Boundary Beyond" (*sīmāntara*);
this is the Cold Hell.
Between the two mountains there are ten names:
the first is Arbuda, and so on,
up to the tenth, which is Padma.
The sentient beings therein move horizontally;
they perceive it as being upward, just like a gecko.
On the outer edge of the iron wheel, they constantly move sideways.
Their bodies are as large as a *ālābu* gourd;
when touched by cold winds, their bodies split and crack like a ripe melon.
Just as a forest of reeds being scorched by a great fire produces a crackling sound,
so too do these sentient beings when touched by the cold wind.
The bones shatter with a loud *ṭha-ṭha* sound that reaches far and wide;
because of this sound, they come to know one another,
and there are sentient beings who take birth therein.
If there are sentient beings who die in this world, many will be reborn there.
The Cold Water Hell (Śītodaka-naraka) lies outside the Iron Wheel.
If there are sentient beings in other worlds who die and ought to be born in the Cold Ice Hell (Himānaka-naraka), [they are likewise reborn there].
Most of that world arises outside the iron wheel;
at its narrowest point between the two realms,
it is eighty thousand yojanas wide.
It has no bottom below and no covering above;
its widest part measures one hundred and sixty thousand yojanas.
Section Four: The Measurement of Time. As stated in the *Lokadhātusamutpāda-sūtra*:
The Buddha said:
"Suppose there were twenty *droṇa* measures of sesame seeds, filling a *droṇa* measure according to the standard of the kingdom of Kośala."
Gao Sheng said: "Suppose there were a man who,
for a full hundred years, took up a single sesame seed every time."
In this manner, after a full hundred years have passed,
he takes another single seed and throws it elsewhere.
He continues until twenty *kho* of sesame seeds have been completely exhausted.
Even if I were to speak for that length of time, I would not yet have finished describing their lifespan.
To calculate it by way of brief summary:
twenty lifespans in the Arbuda hell constitute one lifespan in the Nirarbuda hell.
Twenty *nirarbuda* lifespans constitute one *ahaha* lifespan;
twenty *ahaha* lifespans constitute one *huhuva* lifespan;
twenty *huhuva* lifespans constitute one *ataṭa* lifespan.
Twenty *aṭaṭa* lifespans constitute one *hahava* lifespan;
twenty *hahava* lifespans constitute one *utpala* lifespan;
twenty *utpala* lifespans constitute one *kumuda* lifespan.
Twenty *kumuda* lifespans constitute one *puṇḍarīka* lifespan;
twenty *puṇḍarīka* lifespans constitute one *padma* lifespan;
and twenty *padma* lifespans constitute one intermediate kalpa (*antarakalpa*).
Furthermore, the *Nāgasena-bhikṣu-praśna-sūtra* states:
"The fire of the world is not as hot as the fire in the *niraya* hells.

For instance, if one were to place a small stone in a worldly fire, it would not be consumed by evening; yet if one were to place a large boulder in the fire of the *niraya* hells, it would be consumed immediately."
It is also like a person who commits evil and dies to remain in the hells for tens of millions of years, yet that person does not die;
it is also like great pythons, crocodiles, dragons, and the like, which digest sand and stones as food.
It is like a person who is pregnant; though the child is within the womb, it does not digest [the mother's food].
This is entirely due to the power of good and evil karma, which causes digestion or non-digestion.
Just as the good and evil deeds a person performs follow that person, like a shadow follows the body.
When a person dies, it is only their body that perishes, not their conduct.
It is like writing at night by the light of a fire: when the fire is extinguished, the characters remain; the fire serves as a precursor for what follows.
So too, the deeds performed in this life will be realized in future lives.
Furthermore, it is like the flames in the Padma Hell,
which blaze with such intensity that even when a sinner is a hundred *yojanas* away from this fire,
they are already scorched and roasted by it.
If they are sixty yojanas away,
the ears of the offenders are already deaf, and they hear nothing at all.
If they are fifty yojanas from the fire...
The eyes of that sinner were already blind so that he could see nothing at all,
just as the bhikṣu Kokālika, having harbored an evil mind, slandered Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana.
Upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, one falls into this Padma Hell.
Furthermore, as stated in the *Utpatti-sūtra*:
"The location where the Padma Hell resides..."
If sentient beings are one hundred yojanas away from their location,
they will still be reached by the flames of that hell;
if they are fifty yojanas away, [the same applies].
The sentient beings dwelling there are all熏 (xūn) by that fire and become blind, lacking eyes.
If they are within twenty-five *yojanas* [of it],
the flesh and blood of the bodies of the sentient beings dwelling there are scorched and shattered.
That is to say, because one gives rise to a defiled mind, a harmful mind,
or a poisonous and evil mind toward those who have gone forth in the holy life.
Because of a mind that seeks no benefit,
because of a lack of a compassionate mind,
and because of a lack of a pure mind.
One thus incurs this calamity oneself.
Therefore, toward all fellow practitioners of the holy life,
one should cultivate compassionate actions of body, speech, and mind, and will always experience peace and happiness.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"When people in this world are alive, An axe naturally grows upon their tongues;
That which is called the utterance of various poisons and evils In turn brings decay and harm to their own bodies."

To fail to praise those who deserve praise, and instead to speak of the virtues of those who do not deserve it—this is called a dispute within the mouth. Because of such disputes, there is no experience of happiness.
Even when a person wins wealth through gambling, this is merely a trivial matter of worldly dispute.
To give rise to a turbid mind toward a practitioner of purity—this is called a great and intermediate dispute.
For thirty-six hundred thousand such acts, one falls into the Nirarbuda hell;
for five Arbuda hells, one subsequently falls into the Padma hell.
Because one reviles the sages, such consequences are brought about; this is due to the commission of evil through the karma of speech and mind.
Section Five: The Section on the Masters of the Canon. As stated in the *Yuanwen Diyu Jing* (Sutra on Asking about the Hells) and the *Jingdu Sanmei Jing* (Sutra on the Samadhi of Pure Deliverance):
In total, there are one hundred and thirty-four realms of hell.
First, the names and locations of the presiding lords of these hells are described. As for King Yama:
In the past, he was King Viśākha.
He engaged in battle with King Vitatija,
but his military forces were no match for the enemy.
Consequently, he made a vow to become the lord of hell;
eighteen ministers and attendants led a host of one million,
all of whom had horns upon their heads and ears, and were entirely filled with resentment and rage.
They made a vow together, saying:
"In the future, we shall assist in the governance of these sinful people.
The King Vaiśravaṇa is none other than the present King Yama.
The eighteen great ministers are the various minor kings of today;
the multitude of one million are the various ābhasaras.
Furthermore, the Dīrgha Āgama states:
To the south of Jambudvīpa lies Vajra;
within it is the palace of King Yama, measuring six thousand yojanas in length and breadth. As stated in the *Diyu jing* (Sūtra on Asking about the Hells):
The city of Antarāpura, located within the hells, is thirty thousand li in length and breadth and is composed of gold and silver.
Three times each day and night, a great copper cauldron spontaneously appears before it.
When the cauldron enters the palace, [the hell-beings are cast therein].
The king, seeing this and becoming terrified,
abandoned [the cauldron] and went out from the palace;
if the cauldron went out of the palace, the king would enter the palace.
There are great hell-wardens who lay the king upon hot iron;
with iron hooks they pry open his mouth and pour molten copper into it,
which passes down through his throat without anything remaining unburnt or unscorched.
When the business was concluded, he returned to enjoy himself with his court ladies;
the various ministers who shared in that merit did likewise. As stated in the *Yiqie dizhu jing* (The Scripture on All the Lords of the Hells):
As for the eighteen kings,
they preside over the eighteen hells:
first is Kāyana, who is in charge of Niraya.
Second, the Mount Knife Mountain (Kṣuradhāra-parvata), where they are forced to climb against the grain;
third, the Boiling Sand (Kukūla), where they advance into boiling sand;
fourth, the Boiling Excrement (Kunapa), where they are boiled in excrement.
Fifth, Kaśyapa-dhāraṇī, who presides over Kṛṣṇakarṇī;
sixth, Cakravartin-dhāraṇī, who presides over the Fire Chariot;
seventh, Tapta-dhāraṇī, who presides over the Boiling Cauldron.
8. Ayaḥkāra presides over the Iron Bed;
9. Duḥśīla presides over Mount Kālaśaila; 10.
Śīta (the Cold Ice) [is mentioned], though the king’s name is missing from the sūtra.
Eleventh, the Vicātya [era] of skin-flaying;
twelfth, the Raudra [era] of animals;
thirteenth, the Tairabhukta [era] of weapons.
14. The Great Hell of Grinding with Iron Stones (Ayastāpana).
15. The Hell of the Head-Pressing Water-Earth (Utsada).
16. The Hell of the Iron Bedstead; the name of the king is missing from the sūtra.
Seventeenth, the *Śarīra-sūtra* for the insects;
eighteenth, the *Kāya-vipaśyanā-sūtra* for the molten copper.
Furthermore, the *Jingdu sanmei jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of Pure Deliverance) says:
Furthermore, there are thirty other hells,
each with its own presiding overseer; it is unnecessary to record them all in detail,
but I shall list the names of the five principal officials.
First, the Fresh Official prohibits killing;
second, the Water Official prohibits stealing;
third, the Iron Official prohibits sexual misconduct.
Fourth, the Earth Official prohibits double-tongued speech.
Fifth, the Heaven Official prohibits alcohol.
As the *Diyu jing* (Sutra on the Hell Realms) states:
To the east, south, west, and north of the city of King Yama, various hells are arrayed.
Although there is the light of the sun and moon, it is neither bright nor pure; only the hell of Black Ears (Kṛṣṇakarṇa) is not illuminated by their light.
When a person's life ends, they give rise to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
This intermediate state is that which has already abandoned the aggregates of death but has not yet reached the aggregates of birth.

When such a sinner mounts this intermediate body, they enter the city of Niraya; "Niraya" (in the language of Liang) means the City of Dense Branches, also called the City of Closure. This is the interval during which these various sinners have not yet received their retribution.
Gathering together in this place,
they are blown by the winds of skillful means;
according to the lightness or heaviness of their karma, they receive bodies of large or small size.
Blown by foul winds,
the coarse and ugly forms of sinful persons are produced;
blown by fragrant winds, the subtle bodies of meritorious persons are produced.
6. Section on the Royal Capital. Regarding the sixth section on the royal capital, as stated in the *Sūtra on the Arising of the World*:
"To the south of Jambudvīpa, beyond the two Iron Ring Mountains, lies the palace of King Yama."
The dwelling place is exactly six thousand yojanas in length and breadth,
with sevenfold walls and sevenfold railings.
There are seven layers of bell-nets.
Outside these, seven rows of tala trees encircle it on all sides;
they are composed of the seven treasures and are of variegated colors, beautiful to behold.
On each of its four sides there are various gates;
at every gate there are defensive watchtowers and battlements,
as well as palaces, pavilions, gardens, and flower ponds.
It was filled with various kinds of delicious fruits;
fragrant breezes wafted from afar and flocks of birds sang in harmony.
Yet, because of the king’s evil karma and its unwholesome fruit, [he suffered].
During the three periods of the night and the three periods of the day,
molten red copper spontaneously appears before them,
and their royal palaces immediately transform into iron.
The qualities of the five desires all vanished and were no longer visible.
Upon seeing this, the king was struck with terror and unease;
his hair stood on end, and he immediately went outside.
If he is outside the palace, he immediately runs inside.
Then the wardens seize King Yama, lift him high up,
and dash him down onto the ground of hot iron.
That ground is blazing, exceedingly fierce and intensely radiant with flames.
Having forced them down to lie prostrate, they immediately pry open their mouths with iron tongs and pour molten copper into their mouths.
At that time, King Yama’s lips and mouth were scorched;
next his tongue was burned, followed by his throat;
furthermore, his large and small intestines were consumed by the flames.
It was gradually scorched and emerged from below.
At that time, the king thought to himself:
All sentient beings, having committed evil deeds of body, evil deeds of speech, and evil deeds of mind in the past,
as well as other sentient beings who performed similar actions, all undergo this suffering.
"May it be that from this moment forth, after I have cast off this body,
whenever I obtain another body,
I shall only encounter and take birth among human beings."
Within the Dharma of the Tathāgata, they shall attain faith and understanding, shave off their hair and beard, and don the saffron robes.
Having attained right faith and understanding, they shall go forth from the household life;
once they have gone forth, they vow to realize full penetration.
Birth and death have been exhausted; the holy life has been established;
what was to be done has all been accomplished;
there will be no further rebirth in future lives.
Having given rise to such perfumed wholesome thoughts,
the palace in which he dwells is immediately restored as being made of the seven treasures,
just like those of the devas.
The five objects of desire are fully present before one,
and through the wholesomeness of the three types of action, one attains happiness.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
Question: Are the various hell-wardens included among sentient beings, or are they not included among sentient beings?
Answer: If one considers those who bind the sentient beings newly born in hell with iron chains and lead them before King Yama, [they are sentient beings].
These are included among the category of sentient beings;
however, those various instruments of suffering used within the hells to harm sentient beings are not included among the category of sentient beings.
Beneath Jambudvīpa lies the great hell;
upon Jambudvīpa there are also the borderland hells and the solitary hells.
Sometimes they were in valleys;
sometimes on mountains;
and sometimes in wildernesses.
Or they may exist in the air.
In the other three continents, there are only the peripheral hells and the individual hells, but no great hells. Why is this so?
Only the inhabitants of Jambudvīpa perform wholesome deeds with such intensity;
they likewise commit unwholesome deeds with equal intensity,
for this is not the case in other continents.
Some say that even in Uttarakuru there are no peripheral hells and the like,
because it is a place where one experiences only the fruits of pure karma.
Question: If there are no other great hells,

in what place will those sentient beings who have committed the deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*), severed their roots of virtue (*samucchinna-kuśalamūla*), and so forth, undergo the maturation (*vipāka*)?
Answer: They undergo [retribution] in the great hells beneath this very Jambudvīpa.
Question: What is the physical form of sentient beings in the hells?
Answer: Their form is like that of humans.
Question: What is their speech like?
Answer: At the time of their initial birth, they all speak the noble tongue (ārya-bhāṣā);
however, later, when they experience suffering, although they utter various sounds of pain and agony, [they do not speak intelligibly].
There was not even a single word that could be understood;
there was only the sound of hacking, piercing, breaking, and rending.
7. Section on Karmic Causes. As stated in the *Daśacakrakṣitigarbha-sūtra*:
There are five heinous crimes that are the most extreme evils. What are the five?

They are: intentionally killing one's father, mother, or an arhat; [the remaining three are as follows: [intentionally drawing blood from a Tathāgata with malicious intent, and causing a schism in the Saṃgha.]
Causing a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha of the Śrāvakas,
up to and including shedding the blood of a Buddha with an evil mind—
such acts as these are called the five ānantarya offenses.
If a person commits any one of the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*),
they may not leave the household life or receive full ordination (*upasampadā*).
If they were permitted to leave the household life, they would commit a grave offense.
They should be expelled and sent away.
If there are those who have already left the household life and possess the various dignified demeanors of a monastic,
one must not subject them to whips, staves, or any form of confinement.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of great offenses that are equivalent to the four pārasika (ānantarya) transgressions and constitute root offenses. What are these four?
To kill a pratyekabuddha is called killing a living being and constitutes a root offense.
To engage in sexual misconduct with an arhat bhikṣuṇī [is likewise a root offense].
This is called sexual misconduct that constitutes a root offense.
If a person takes charge of property given to the Buddha, the Dharma,
and the Sangha, and uses it arbitrarily, [they commit a root offense].
This is called stealing and committing a root offense.
If a person, through inverted views, causes schism in the Saṃgha of bhikṣus,
this is called causing a schism in the Saṃgha and committing a root offense.
If a person commits any one of these four root offenses,
they are in all cases prohibited from leaving the household life in accordance with the Buddha’s Dharma;
even if they should leave the household life, they shall not be permitted to receive full ordination.
If one has received full ordination, they should be expelled;
for there exists the dharma of the monastic deportment.
One must not whip, flog, bind, imprison, or deprive them of life.
In this way, all such cases constitute root offenses (*mūlāpatti*), but they are not transgressions against the lineage (*ānantarya*). There are,
however, root offenses that are also transgressions against the lineage.

There are cases where there is an offense of immediate retribution (ānantarya) that is not a fundamental offense (mūlāpatti); there are cases where there is neither a fundamental offense nor an offense of immediate retribution.
Which offenses constitute both an offense of immediate retribution and a fundamental offense?
If one kills a person who has left the household life, received full ordination, and attained the path of seeing the truths (darśanamārga),
this is called a heinous crime (ānantarya-karma);
it is also a fundamental offense (mūlāpatti).
Such sentient beings should be expelled from my disciplinary code.
What constitutes a root offense that is not a heinous crime?
It is when a person has gone forth within my Dharma.
In this way, ordinary worldly beings intentionally take their lives,
whether by means of poison or by causing an abortion.
This is called committing a root offense, though it is not a *ānantarya* (immediate) transgression.
If there are offerings of food, drink, or bedding belonging to the Saṃgha of the four directions,
one must by no means share in the same benefits and gains as them.
If there are sentient beings who give rise to doubt regarding the Buddha, the Dharma,
and the Sangha, and who create obstacles even upon seeing others engaged in renunciation or reciting and chanting [the scriptures].
Even down to a single verse,
this is neither a root offense nor a heinous crime (ānantarya),
yet it is called an extremely evil act that approximates a heinous crime.
If such sentient beings do not repent and eliminate the roots of their offenses,
I shall never permit them to leave the household life within the Buddha-dharma;
even if they were to leave the household life and receive full ordination, [I would still not permit it].
Those who do not repent shall also be driven out.
Why is this? Because they do not believe in the True Dharma, they slander the Three Vehicles, and they destroy the Eye of the True Dharma.
Those who wish to extinguish the lamp of the Dharma and sever the lineage of the Triple Gem,
thereby diminishing the realms of humans and devas without bringing them benefit and falling into the evil paths—
these two kinds of people are called slanderers of the True Dharma and revilers of the noble ones; their lifespans in hell will increase for kalpas.
Such evil karmas as these are already called fundamental major transgressions.
What are the fundamental offenses regarding the laws of improper conduct?
If a bhikṣu intentionally commits sexual misconduct, intentionally kills,
takes what is not given by a common person,
or deliberately utters false speech, he commits [an offense].
Among these four fundamental offenses,
if one commits even a single offense,
one is not permitted to participate in any of the ritual activities performed by the bhikṣus.
The property of the Saṃgha of the four quarters— including food, drink, and bedding—
must not be used or enjoyed in common with them.
Nevertheless, [this does not apply to] emperors, great ministers, and all officials of the state.
One must not apply whips or staves, imprisonment, corporal punishment, or even take their life.
This is called the essential nature and characteristics of the fundamental offense.
For what reason is it called a fundamental grave offense?
If a person acts in such a manner,
at the dissolution of the body after death, they will fall into the evil realms;
to act in such a way is the root of the evil paths.
Therefore, these are called root offenses. For example, just as an iron ball,
though thrown into the air, never remains suspended for even a moment but falls swiftly to the ground,
so it is with the five heinous crimes and the violation of the four grave prohibitions.
Furthermore, among these eleven kinds of offenses— including those two types of sentient beings who destroy the true Dharma and revile the noble ones—
if a person commits even one of these offenses:
When their bodies perish and their lives end, they all fall into the Avīci Hell.
Furthermore, as stated in the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*,
the suffering of the Avīci Hell is a thousand times greater than that of the seven great hells mentioned previously.
Their lifespan lasts for one kalpa;
their bodies are five hundred yojanas tall,
while those who have committed the four ānantarya offenses are four hundred yojanas tall.
One who has committed three of the immediate transgressions [reaches] three hundred yojanas;
one who has committed two of the immediate transgressions [reaches] two hundred yojanas.
The person who has committed one of the five heinous crimes extends for one hundred yojanas.
When that person who has committed the karma of the five heinous crimes is on the verge of death,
they cry out, lose control of their bowels, and gasp with parched throats.
Thus, amidst death and extinction, a form arises that is not seen as its counterpart;
his body is like that of an eight-year-old child.
King Yama binds his throat with a flaming iron noose.
Furthermore, with both hands bound together,
head and face downward and feet above,
they shall travel downward for two thousand years.
The many flaming garlands first burn their heads and then burn their bodies.
When the gods of the six heavens of desire smell the air from within that Avīci Hell,
they immediately all dissolve and vanish. Why is this?
Because the inhabitants of the Avīci Hell emit an extreme and great stench.
Furthermore, the *Buddhanusmṛtisamādhisāgara-sūtra* states:
The Buddha told Ānanda:
If there are sentient beings who kill their fathers, harm their mothers, or revile their six close relatives—
those who commit such sins.
At the moment of death, in the blink of an eye—
like the time it takes a strong man to bend and extend his arm—
they fall directly into the Avīci Great Hell.
The manifested King Yama issued a loud proclamation:
"Foolish person, seed of hell!
When you were in the world, you were unfilial toward your parents, perverse, arrogant, and unrighteous."
"The place where you have now been born is named the Avīci Hell.
Having spoken these words, he immediately vanished and was no longer seen.
At that time, the hell-wardens again drove the sinners forward.
From the lower tier up to the upper tier,
passing through eighty-four thousand tiers in between.
Crouching their bodies, they pass through until they reach the edge of the iron net.
In one day and one night, they travel throughout the entirety of the Avīci Hell.
One day and one night there corresponds to sixty minor kalpas by the reckoning of days, months, and years in this Jambudvīpa.
Thus, their lifespan lasts for one great kalpa;
those who have committed the five heinous crimes shall suffer retribution for a full five kalpas.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who violate the four grave prohibitions, consume the offerings of the faithful in vain,
and slander [the Dharma] with false views.
Failing to recognize cause and effect,
they sever their study of Prajñāpāramitā and revile the Buddhas of the ten directions.
He stole the property of the Saṃgha;
he was lewd and unprincipled,
and he coerced and violated pure bhikṣuṇīs who were his sisters and relatives.
Lacking a sense of shame and remorse, they bring disgrace upon their own kin by committing such evil deeds.
When the retribution for this person's sins approaches at the moment of death, the "sword-wind" shall tear their body apart.
In an instant, his body became like iron flowers,
filling eighteen chambers;
each flower had eighty-four thousand petals.
Each leaf-tip, hand, body, limb, and joint occupies its own separate compartment;
the hell is not large, yet this body is not small.
Pervading this great hell in this manner,
they undergo eighty-four thousand great kalpas;
when this niraya is extinguished, they enter again into the eighteen compartments of the eastern direction.
They undergo suffering as described previously.
To the south, west, north, and east of this Avīci Hell, across eighteen intermediate barriers,
are those who slandered the Vaipulya sūtras.
Having committed the five heinous crimes,
they have destroyed the Saṃgha and defiled bhikṣuṇīs.
Having severed all roots of goodness,
such a sinner, possessed of manifold transgressions,
fills the Avīci Hell with his very body.
The four sides are further filled with eighteen compartments.
This Avīci Hell burns all the various sentient beings within it.
When the kalpa is about to end, the eastern gate opens.
He saw outside the eastern gate a clear spring with flowing water,
and flowering fruit trees;
all appeared together before him.
These sinners run upward from below;
when they reach the upper enclosure, they raise their hand-holds of sword-wheels.
At that time, hot iron balls rain down from the void of space.
He ran toward the eastern gate;
once he reached the threshold,
the hell-warden rākṣasa seized an iron fork and pierced his eyes from above.
The iron dog bites his heart; he faints and dies.
Having died, he is reborn.
Again, he sees the southern gate open, no different from before.
It was likewise at the western gate and the northern gate.
During this period, he spent half an eon passing through the Avīci Hell before being reborn within the Cold Ice Hell.
In the Cold Ice Hell, one dies and is reborn in a place of darkness;
for eighty million years, one’s eyes see nothing.
One receives the body of a great beast, crawling on its belly.
Their faculties are darkened and obstructed, such that they have no understanding or knowledge;
hundreds of thousands of foxes and wolves pull at them and devour them.
After their lives end, they are reborn among the animals.
Five hundred million times they took the forms of birds and beasts;
when they were reborn among humans,
they were deaf, blind, mute, afflicted with leprosy and carbuncles, and impoverished and lowly.
Adorned with all manner of misfortunes,
they undergo this lowly form for five hundred lifetimes;
thereafter, they are reborn once more within the realm of hungry ghosts.
In the realm of hungry ghosts, they encounter virtuous friends and great bodhisattvas,
who rebuke them, saying:
"In immeasurable lifetimes of your previous existence, you committed limitless sins."
Those who slander and lack faith will fall into the Avīci Hell,
where they shall undergo various sufferings that cannot be fully described.
You should now give rise to a heart of compassion.
When the hungry ghosts heard these words, they cried out, "Namo Buddhāya.
By the power of the Buddha’s grace, their lives immediately ended and they were reborn in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings.
Having been born in that heaven, they repented and reproached themselves, giving rise to the bodhicitta.
The heart-light of all Buddhas does not abandon these beings;
they embrace such people as Rāhula,
and instruct them to avoid the hells as one cherishes one's own eyes and ears.
Therefore, in the *Lokadhātu-sūtra*,
the World-Honored One spoke this verse:
"If a person creates karma through body, speech, and mind, having done so, they enter into the evil realms."
Thus one shall dwell in the Reviving Hell, a most terrifying place that makes the hair stand on end;
having experienced countless billions of years there, upon death one is instantly revived again.
Enemies each seek retribution from one another, and by this means sentient beings continue to kill one another.

If one conceives an evil mind toward one’s parents, or toward the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, or the assembly of Śrāvakas, such a person shall fall into the Black Rope Hell. There, they will suffer most intense and fierce torments.
To lead others toward right practice while causing them to become crooked, or to see others developing wholesome roots and necessarily destroying them—[these are the causes for this retribution].

These people shall likewise fall into the Black Rope Hell; Those who delight in committing the three kinds of grave evil karma— Divisive speech, harsh words, and much false speech— And fail to cultivate the sprouts of the three kinds of roots of goodness;
Such deluded persons will surely enter it, Causing them to suffer for a long time in the great hells.
Whether they kill sheep, horses, and various oxen, or various kinds of wild beasts, chickens, pigs, and so forth,
as well as other insects and ants— such a person shall fall into the Saṃghāta Hell,
which possesses many forms of worldly terror; by these means, they oppress and afflict sentient beings.
One shall fall into the Crushing Mountain Hell, Suffering the pains of being pressed, ground, pounded, and thrashed,
Due to the fetters of greed, hatred, and delusion. By perverting the correct principle and making it otherwise,
Judging what is right as wrong and violating the laws and codes, One will be wounded by the turning of swords and blades.
Relying on their power and strength to plunder others, seizing both the powerful and the powerless—
if one inflicts such various oppressions as these, they shall be trampled by iron elephants.
If one delights in killing and harming sentient beings, with hands and body smeared with blood and a heart hardened by evil, [they shall suffer the same fate].
Those who constantly perform such impure deeds will be born in the Raurava hell because they have afflicted sentient beings with various forms of touch and torment. Within that hell,
there is also the Mahāraurava, which arises from a mind of deceit, crookedness, and craftiness.
Enshrouded by the dense forest of various views, Sunk deep within the tightly woven net of craving,
Constantly performing such most base deeds, They shall fall into the Great Howling Hell.
Once they reach such a place of Great Howling, A blazing iron city that makes one’s hair stand on end.
Within those iron halls and iron houses, all who enter are completely consumed by flames.
If they perform various worldly activities, they constantly cause much distress and confusion to sentient beings;
they shall be born in places of burning affliction, where they undergo such torment for immeasurable time.
If one constantly harasses and offends the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas of the world, as well as parents, elders, and the aged,
causing them displeasure, they will all fall into the hell of Heat and Torment.
If one does not delight in cultivating pure karma for rebirth in heaven, one will be forever separated from beloved kinsmen.
Those who take delight in such deeds as these shall enter the hell of Heat (Tapana).
Having acted with malice toward śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, as well as toward virtuous people,
their parents, and other venerable ones, they fall into the hell of Heat, which is perpetually ablaze.
Constantly and frequently committing various evil deeds, Never once giving rise to a single virtuous thought—
Such a person goes straight to the Avīci Hell, Where they shall undergo immeasurable suffering and affliction.
If one proclaims the True Dharma as being false, And proclaims what is not the Dharma as being the True Dharma,
Since they have brought no increase to virtuous deeds, those people shall enter the Avīci hell,
as well as the Saṃjīva and Kālasūtra hells; with the Saṃghāta, Raurava, and others, making five,
along with the Pratāpana and Mahāpratāpana, these together form seven, and the Avīci hell is the eighth.
