These eight are called the Great Hells; Fierce, burning, and agonizing, they are difficult to endure, Produced by those who have committed evil deeds. Within them, there are sixteen minor hells.
Section Eight: Admonitions. As stated in the *Sūtra on the Arising of the World*:
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are three celestial messengers in the world.
What are these three?"
First, old age; second, illness; third, death.
There are those who are heedless and commit evil deeds through the three karmas;
when their bodies perish and their lives end, they are reborn in the hells.
The various jailers shall come at that very moment and drive those sentient beings before King Yama.
He addressed the King, saying: "Great King,
these sentient beings formerly, while in the human realm, were unrestrained and indulged in self-indulgence."
"Due to our three unwholesome karmas,
we have now been born here.
We only pray that Your Majesty will kindly instruct us."
The King questioned the sinner:
"In your former human life, the first divine messenger appeared to you;
he instructed you well and rebuked you well."
"How could one not see the manifestation of birth?
He replied,
"Great Deva."
"I truly did not see it.
The King spoke to him again, saying,
"Did you not see it when you were in human form?"
Sometimes they appear as women, sometimes as men;
the signs of old age manifest, with teeth falling out and hair turning white.
The skin is wrinkled and sagging, with dark moles covering the entire body;
his form is like that of sesame seeds, his shoulders are hunched and his back is bent;
his gait is lame and halting, and his feet do not support his body.
The head tilts to the left and right; the neck is thin and the skin is loose, sagging on both sides like the dewlap of an ox.
The lips and mouth are parched and withered, and the throat and tongue are dry and rasping.
His body was bent and weak, his vital energy and strength were faint and thin;
his labored breathing produced sounds like those of a saw being dragged,
and as he leaned forward about to fall, he relied upon a staff to walk.
In the prime of life, one’s vigor declines and blood and flesh waste away;
emaciated and frail, one sets out upon the path to the next world,
with movements sluggish and no longer possessing a robust form.
"Even to the point that their bodies and minds are constantly trembling;
all their limbs are emaciated and exhausted, difficult to control. Do you see this?"
He replied, "Great King, I truly saw it."
Then the king said:
"You foolish person, devoid of wisdom!
Having already seen such signs as these on a previous day..."
Why does one not reflect in this way:
"I am currently possessed of this nature of aging and have not yet escaped it;
I should perform wholesome deeds so that I may experience benefit, peace, and happiness for a long night"?
That person replied again,
"Great Lord,
I truly did not engage in such reflection."
Because his mind was unrestrained and he acted with negligence,
the king further addressed him, saying:
"You foolish man, you have not cultivated wholesome karma."
One shall fully experience the retribution for the fault of negligence;
this bitter fruit of suffering was not created by another,
but is your own karma.
Now they have gathered once more to undergo their own retribution. Then,
King Yama rebuked them a second time, saying:
"Do you people not see that the second messenger has appeared in the world?
They replied,
"Great King."
"I truly do not see it.
The king spoke again, saying,
"How could you not see it?"
Formerly, while in the world during his time as a human being—
whether in a female body or a male body.
The four great elements, having been in harmony, suddenly fall into discord;
one is assailed by the suffering of illness, becoming prostrate and gravely ill,
perhaps lying upon a large or small bed.
Defiled by excrement and urine,
they wallow therein,
lacking any autonomy.
Whether sleeping, reclining, rising, or sitting,
they depend on others for support and care;
they require others to wash them, wipe them, and hold them.
In providing drink and food,
everyone requires others;
do you not see this?
That person replied,
"Great King, I truly saw it."
The King spoke again:
"Foolish man, you have seen such things;
why do you not reflect upon them?"
I too now possess such a nature that I have not yet escaped the condition of affliction;
therefore, I should perform wholesome deeds so that in the long night of the future I may obtain great benefit and great peace and happiness.
That person replied,
"No. I truly did not engage in such reflection."
Because he acted with negligence due to a lazy mind,
the King said to that foolish man:
"Since you are so indolent..."
"One who does not perform wholesome deeds receives this evil retribution;
it is not created by another that one returns to receive oneself.
At that time, King Yama—
The third [instance] rebuked him, saying:
"O foolish man! When you were formerly a human being..."
"How could one not see that the third divine messenger has appeared in the world?
He replied, "Great King."
"I truly did not see it.
The king spoke again, saying,
"When you were among humans..."
Will they not again see it,
whether in the form of a woman’s body or a man’s body?
When his time has come to die, he is placed upon a bed and covered with cloth of various colors;
he is then carried out of the village,
ascending a decorated pavilion with canopies and various ornaments.
Surrounded by his retinue, he raised his hands and disheveled his hair;
with ashes and dust smeared upon his head, he was overcome with extreme grief and distress,
wailing and weeping while raising his voice in a great cry.
He beat his breast in mournful lamentation, choked with sobs, and writhed in piercing agony.
"Did you see all of this?
he asked. He replied:
"Mahādeva, I have indeed seen it.
Then the king said:
Foolish man, since you have already witnessed such things as these in the past,
why do you not reflect that I too shall die and cannot escape it?
"Now you should perform wholesome deeds for my sake, so that I may obtain great benefit throughout the long night.
That person replied,
"Great Deva!"
"I truly did not have such a thought. Why?
Because of negligence.
At that time, the king said:
Since you were negligent and failed to perform wholesome deeds, you have created this evil for yourself;
it was not created by another that you now receive as its retribution.
"You must receive [the punishment] yourself.
Having thus instructed, admonished, and rebuked him with these three messengers,
he ordered him to be taken away.
At that time, the jailer immediately seized the offender by both feet and both arms,
with the head downward and the feet upward.
They are cast from afar into the various hells. Now,
as for one who seeks to contain its current,
it is not as effective as blocking its source.
Stirring up its boiling water is not as effective as extinguishing its fire;
for what reason? Because its source originates from water.
If the source is not blocked, the water will never cease;
when fire boils in a cauldron,
if the fire is not extinguished, how could the boiling ever stop?
Thus, the guest who seeks to stem the source does not need to dam the current for it to dry up of its own accord;
the visitor who seeks to extinguish the fire does not need to stir the boiling water for it to cease of its own accord.
By discussing matters in this vein, one may gain a detailed understanding.
To weary oneself of the fruits [of suffering] is not as effective as severing their causes;
to fear the pains [of existence] is surely not as wise as restraining oneself from evil.
The cause depends upon the fruit;
though the cause has not yet ceased, the fruit is inexhaustible.
Evil arises from suffering.
If evil is not punished, how can suffering cease?
Thus, those who have severed the causes do not wait for the fruits to ripen before they pass away of their own accord.
The virtuous who punish evil do not wait for suffering to arise before distancing themselves from it;
may all you gentlemen take this to heart and use it as a warning!
The verse says:
Born they come, and at death they are sent away; Days pass and months revolve.
The young and lost are stirred by the winds of delusion, Drifting and wandering as they follow shifting objects.
Foolish and ignorant, one loses the true path, Drifting and sinking into the deep abyss.
Once fallen into the realm of dark obscurity, One treads upon blades and spears for ten thousand kalpas;
Circling through the six realms of existence in suffering, The three karmas have not yet been fully purified.
Following the current with no one to save me, I am moved by sorrow and pity myself;
With sincere devotion I contemplate the forms of things, and only then do I realize they are empty and illusory.
In this sea of suffering, where can one find refuge? I long to board the boat of Prajñā.

Accounts of Resonant Response (Ganying yuan): A brief citation of seven testimonies. 1. Testimony of the Jin layman Zhao Tai. 2. Testimony of the Jin śramaṇa Zhi Faheng. 3. Testimony of the Zhao layman Shi Changhe. 4. Testimony of the Ghost of Hanxian during the Han Dynasty. 5. Testimony of the Wailing in Lujiang County. 6. Testimony of the Cauldron of Boiling Water in the Tubo Kingdom. 7. Testimony of Liu Zhigan’s Judgment of Hell during the Tang Dynasty. Testimony of the Jin layman Zhao Tai. (The repetition of "Jin layman Zhao Tai" appears to be a scribal error or duplication.)
His courtesy name was Wenhé.
He was a native of Beiqiu in Qinghé.
His grandfather had served as the Governor of Jingshao.
The Tai Commandery examined him for the rank of Xiaolian;
he was summoned by a provincial government office but did not accept.
He applied himself with precision to the classical texts and gained renown throughout his local community.
Later in life, he entered official service and served as a Zhong-san Dafu until his death.
When he was thirty-five years old,
he suffered from a sudden heartache and died within a short time.
The corpse was laid upon the ground;
its heart remained warm, and it could bend and stretch according to the person's will.
After the corpse had been left for ten days, there was finally a sound like rain within its throat.
Shortly thereafter, he revived.
He recounted that at the time of his initial death,
he had dreamed of a person coming near his heart.
Furthermore, there were two men riding a yellow horse;
two attendants supported him by his armpits as they proceeded directly east for an unknown distance of several li.
He arrived at a great city that was vast and toweringly high;
the city walls were a dark blue-black, appearing like tin.
Jiang Tai headed toward the city gate and passed through two successive gates.
There were several thousand tiled-roofed buildings,
and several thousand men and women, both young and old, stood in formation.
There were five or six officials wearing black robes;
they listed their names and surnames, saying,
"We shall present this according to the regulations to the Prefect."
Tai’s name was among the twenty.
In an instant, Tai was led forward along with several thousand men and women,
all advancing together at once.
The Prefect sat facing west; having finished inspecting the registers of names, he again sent Tai Nan to enter through the Black Gate.
There was a man wearing crimson robes sitting beneath a large hall.
He called out their names in order and questioned them regarding the deeds they had performed while alive:
what transgressions they had committed and what meritorious virtues they had cultivated.
"Be attentive," he said, "speak your words with truth."
He constantly dispatches six classes of messengers who always remain among human beings to record good and evil deeds in detail;
these reports are thoroughly documented and cannot be false.
Tai replied, "My father and elder brothers all held official posts with the rank of two thousand shi; I, however,
merely stayed at home to cultivate my studies while young."
He had no affairs to attend to,
nor did he commit any evil; consequently,
he was appointed as the Superintendent of the Water Office.
He was appointed as a commander and led more than two thousand men to transport sand and reinforce the riverbanks, laboring diligently day and night.
Later, he was promoted to the position of Commander-in-Chief (Du-du) of the Tai Water Administration.
He was informed of the affairs of the various hells and provided with fine horses and soldiers;
he was ordered to inspect the hells,
whereupon he found that the tortures and poisons in each hell were distinct and varied.
Some have their tongues pierced with needles until blood flows over their entire bodies;
others have their heads shorn and hair disheveled, wandering naked and barefoot.
They lead him along by pulling him together.
One person holding a great staff follows from behind, urging him on toward an iron bed and a copper pillar that are burning with a fierce, glowing heat.
They drive and compel this man to embrace and lie upon it.
As soon as they arise, they are scorched and withered, yet they are immediately reborn.
Or, in vast flaming furnaces and giant cauldrons, sinners are burned and boiled;
their bodies and heads shatter and fall, tumbling and turning as the liquid boils.
A ghost holding a trident leans against its side.
Three or four hundred people stand on one side.
Next, they enter the cauldron, embracing one another and weeping piteously.
Alternatively, there are sword-trees, high and vast, whose limits cannot be known;

According to the tradition of the Western Regions,
Śākyamuni’s entire career of teaching the Dharma consists of three periods.
During the first period, he taught the doctrine of existence with characteristics for the sake of the śrāvakas.
To shatter the attachments of non-Buddhists and cause them to realize the attainment of the Way,
during the second period he taught the Dharma of signlessness (*animitta*) for the sake of bodhisattvas of minor practice;

During the third period, for the sake of bodhisattvas of great practice, he taught both the teachings with marks and the teachings without marks simultaneously;

Those who hear the Dharma and attain the Way are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and beyond counting;

The Buddha addressed Maitreya:

at that time, when the Bodhisattva saw his mother standing on the ground and grasping a tree branch with her hand, [he spoke].

that after the Tathāgata has attained Buddhahood,

Sentient beings are not the same.

"I shall not undergo further existence.

Section Six: On Attending to Parents (9). Section Six: On Attending to Parents; this is divided into three parts: Part One on Expressing the Intent, Part Two on Rearing and Nurturing, and Part Three on Auspicious Signs. Part One: Expressing the Intent. First, the spirit is subtle and wondrous, tranquil and pervasive; perfect wisdom is profound and illuminating.
The Way is severed from the confines of corporeal defilement;
principle is exhausted at the boundary of arising and ceasing. Once the forms and consciousness have long since ceased, [the ultimate state is reached].

how could he possibly require the protection of attendants?
However, the Great Sage’s original vow was to benefit all beings; thus,
he manifests whenever there is a resonance of faith,
and there is nothing hidden that he does not perceive.
The manifestations of their capacities lead to myriad paths, and the teachings received are not uniform:
some attain awakening through the provisional practice of meditative stillness,
while others open their minds through the liberation of wisdom and understanding.
Sometimes he manifests as an infant being supported;
sometimes he appears as one being nourished by nursing.
The conditions for awakening are manifold and cannot be treated by a single rule.
This is the power of inducement;
it is the art of saving the mundane world.
Part Two: The Section on Nurturing. According to the *Buddhacarita-sūtra* (Sutra of the Buddha’s Past Deeds):
At that time, exactly seven days after the Prince’s birth, his mother, Lady Māyā, passed away.

she is capable of tending to and nourishing his body.

bathe [her] at the proper times,

eight women were assigned to bathe the Prince;

Section Three on Auspicious Signs: Furthermore, the *Sūtra of the Buddha’s Past Deeds* (*Buddhacarita*) states that from the time the Prince was born, [there were auspicious signs].

The youth and his compassionate mother always had an abundance of milk, curd, and butter;
even those whose mothers had little milk all obtained it in overflowing quantities.
At that time, all the enemies of King Śuddhodana—
Once they have all naturally given rise to a mind of equanimity,
they gradually develop intimacy and become of one mind;
then wind and rain follow their proper seasons, and there are no calamities such as hail.
There will be no disturbances or turmoil;
there will be much harvest from little sowing,
and all the people will act in accordance with the Dharma.
Through various acts of giving, they cultivate all manner of merit;
no one suffers unjust or violent harm, and all alike rejoice,
just as there is no distinction among those in the heavens.
By the power of the Crown Prince’s majestic virtue,
all such matters were accomplished without exception,
as described in the verse.
In this human world, they follow the Honored One’s teaching; Neither stingy nor parsimonious, they act in every way according to the Dharma.
With a heart of loving-kindness, they do not give rise to killing;

Furthermore, the *Puyao jing* (Sutra of Universal Radiance) states:

Section Seven: Divination and Physiognomy (9) Section Seven: Divination and Physiognomy, divided into eight parts: 1. Section on Stating the Intent; 2. Section on Imperial Decree for Divination; 3. Section on Presenting Reverence; 4. Section on Manifesting Signs; 5. Section on Karmic Causes; 6. Section on Similarities and Differences; 7. Section on Comparative Measurement; 8. Section on the Hundred Blessings. 1. Section on Stating the Intent (First): As for the Most Holy One, he is without fixed form; he manifests or remains hidden according to conditions.

According to the *Ratnāvalī-sūtra* as spoken by the Buddha,
the Ratnāvalī (Jewel Woman) asked the World-Honored One:
The Tathāgata possesses the thirty-two marks of a great man.
What merits did he practice in his past lives that these marks have come to be spread across his entire body?
The Buddha told the Jewel Maiden:
"In ages past, I practiced immeasurable virtues;
by gathering these manifold practices together, I attained these marks that pervade my entire body."
Now, to briefly set forth the essentials:
among the marks of a Tathāgata, his feet stand with level soles;
this is a mark of a Great Man.
In ages long past, he was firm in his exhortations and assistance, never regressing;
because he never concealed the merits of others,
the Tathāgata possesses the mark of a great man consisting of wheels upon his hands and feet.
Because he practiced various kinds of giving in ages long past, the Tathāgata,
the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, possesses the major mark of long and slender fingers.
This refers to his having explained the meaning of the sūtras in detail in ages long past.
Because he rescues and protects sentient beings so that they may be free from affliction,
the Tathāgata possesses the mark of a great man consisting of webbed fingers and toes on his hands and feet;
this is because in ages past he never caused the separation of others' families.
As for the Tathāgata’s mark of a great man consisting of hands and feet that are soft and exquisite,
it is because in ages past he gave various kinds of garments and fine, delicate clothing through the gift of wisdom.
The Tathāgata possesses the mark of a great man characterized by seven parts being full because,
in ages long past, he extensively provided various gifts and offerings to those in need.
The Tathāgata possesses the mark of a great man whose knees are perfectly straight and without joints, and whose calves are like those of a deer.
Because in ages long past he received and upheld the sūtras without violation or loss,
the Tathāgata’s body possesses the mark of a great man known as the sheathed male organ (*kośagatavastiguhyatā*).
Because in ages long past he was circumspect regarding his own person and remained far removed from the ways of sensual desire, [he attained this mark].
The Tathāgata’s body has full, rounded jaws like those of a lion;
this mark of a great man is due to having extensively cultivated pure deeds and perfected his practice in past ages.
As for the Tathāgata’s mark of a great man, the natural *svastika* on his chest,
it is because in ages past he eliminated all defilement and unwholesome conduct.
That the Tathāgata’s limbs are fully endowed with the marks of a great man is because in ages past he bestowed fearlessness and comforted others.
That the Tathāgata’s arms extend beyond his knees is a mark of a great man.
Because in ages long past, people assisted and encouraged him in his deeds,
the Tathāgata’s body is pure and free from blemish, possessing the marks of a Great Man. Because in ages long past,
he practiced the ten wholesome paths of action without satiety, [he has attained these qualities].
As for the Tathāgata’s major mark of having a head filled and well-proportioned like that of a great man:
this is because in ages past, when there were those who were ill, he gave them various kinds of medicine and attended to their treatment.
As for the Tathāgata’s mark of a great man consisting of the emergence like a lion:
it is because in ages long past he planted many roots of virtue and brought them to full completion.
As for the Tathāgata’s mark of a great man consisting of having forty white teeth: [it is likewise due to his past cultivation].
Because in ages long past his disposition was equal toward all sentient beings with benevolence,
the Tathāgata possesses the mark of a great man of having teeth without gaps;
because in ages long past he exhorted those who were disputing to bring them into harmony, [he possesses this mark].
The Tathāgata’s mark of a great man consisting of cheekbones and teeth is due to his having given gifts in past ages that were exquisite and pleasing to the mind.
The Tathāgata’s mark of a great man consisting of pure, white, and beautiful hair and eyebrows is likewise so.
Because in ages long past he well protected his own body, speech, and mind,
the Tathāgata possesses the mark of a great man characterized by a broad and long tongue;
because in ages long past his speech was most sincere and he guarded against faults of the mouth, [he possesses this mark].
The Tathāgata’s tireless marks of a great man are perfected through the ultimate fulfillment of immeasurable merit;
because his mental conduct is benevolent and harmonious, he causes the vows of sentient beings to be fulfilled and protected.
Regarding the Tathāgata’s mark of a great man— the Brahma-voice and the tone of compassionate longing—
it is because in past ages he spoke with gentle words, addressed all people with kindness, guarded his mouth, and restrained his speech.
Because there are countless people who, upon hearing his words, are not without joy.
As for the Tathāgata’s mark of a great man, whose pupils are the color of deep blue,
it is because in ages past he constantly observed all beings with eyes of loving-kindness.
The Tathāgata’s eye, like the new moon, is a mark of a great man because in ages past his will was free from coarseness and violence, and his nature was gentle and harmonious.
The Tathāgata’s white tuft of hair between the eyebrows is a mark of a great man... [because in ages past he honored and served his parents].
Because in ages long past he praised and sang in verse of the virtues of dwelling in seclusion and of various practices,
the Tathāgata possesses the natural mark of a great man consisting of the fleshly protuberance upon his crown.
Because in ages long past he honored and revered the worthy and holy, and paid homage to his elders, [he possesses this mark].
As for the Tathāgata’s mark of a great man consisting of soft and exquisite skin:
it is because in ages long past he gathered the collection of the Dharma-piṭaka through his mental resolve.
As for the Tathāgata’s mark of a great man consisting of a body the color of purple-polished gold: [it is because...]
Because in ages long past he frequently gave away robes, bedding, and seats,
the Tathāgata possesses the mark of a great man in which each hair grows individually.
Because in ages long past he avoided places of assembly and noisy crowds, [he possesses the mark of a great man in which the body hairs curl to the right].
Regarding the Tathāgata’s mark of a great man, whose body hairs curl upward to the right:
this is because in ages past he revered his teachers, accepted the instructions of virtuous friends, and prostrated himself before them.
As for the Tathāgata’s mark of a great man, whose hair is the color of deep blue,
it is because in ages past he took pity on the masses and did not inflict harm upon them with sword or staff.
The Tathāgata’s body is level, square, and perfectly circular, without any curvature;
this mark of a Great Man is due to his having, in past ages, exhorted and settled himself and other sentient beings, causing them to attain concentration of mind.
The Tathāgata’s spine is like a great chain of hooks, possessing a magnificent radiance and the majestic virtue of a mark of a Great Man;
this is because in past ages he established images for the various Perfectly Awakened Ones and restored ruined temples.
He encourages those who are estranged to reconcile;
he bestows fearlessness upon them;
and he transforms those engaged in disputes so that they may become harmonious with one another.
If you wish to know this:
it is because in past lives I practiced the roots of immeasurable and incalculable multitudes of virtues;
thus did the Tathāgata practice in his former existences.
It is precisely through this that one can attain these thirty-two marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*).
Regarding the twenty-second mark, the Brahma-like voice,

The Tathāgata’s mark of the Brahma-voice refers to the presence of a wondrous great element within the Buddha’s throat-cavity,
which is capable of producing a pleasing, harmonious, and sublime Brahma-sound.
Like the kalaviṅka bird,
it utters a deep and far-reaching thunderous sound,
like the drum of Śakra.
Such sounds possess eight qualities:
first, they are profound and far-reaching;
second, they are harmonious and elegant.
Third, it is clear and distinct;
fourth, it is pleasing to the ear;
fifth, it enters the heart.
Sixth, it inspires joy;
seventh, it is easy to understand;
eighth, it never causes weariness.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
The Tathāgata possesses the mark of the Brahma-voice;
like the five kinds of sounds that issue from the mouth of the Brahmā King, [his voice likewise issues forth].
First, it is as profound as thunder;
second, it is clear and heard from afar, bringing joy to those who hear it;
third, it enters the heart with reverence and affection.
The Four Truths are clear and easy to understand;
the five types of listeners desire to hear them without weariness.
The Bodhisattva likewise has these five kinds of sounds that issue from his mouth.
The voice of the kalaviṅka is lovely and pleasing, as deep and far-reaching as the sound of a celestial drum.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* asks:
"What is the meaning of 'mark' (*lakṣaṇa*)?"
Answer: The meaning of a sign (*cihna*) is the meaning of a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).
The meaning of excellence (*viśeṣa*) is the meaning of a characteristic. The meaning of an auspicious omen (*maṅgala*) is the meaning of a characteristic.
Question: For what reason are the marks of a Great Man exactly thirty-two, neither more nor less?
The Venerable Pārśva replied: "If they were increased or decreased," [the result would be as follows].
Both [positions] give rise to doubt, yet neither contradicts the characteristics of phenomena.
That there are thirty-two [marks] is what is commonly accepted in the world.
This is the meaning of auspiciousness;
their number neither increases nor decreases.
If the Buddha’s body is adorned with these thirty-two marks, it is then most supreme and peerless in the world.
If it were to be diminished, there would be a deficiency of power;
if it were further increased, it would become confused and chaotic.
Neither case would be excellent.
Therefore, there are only these thirty-two marks of a great man (*mahāpuruṣa*).
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* asks:
"Among the three types of karma, by which karma are these thirty-two marks produced?"
Answer: This is mental karma, not bodily or vocal karma;
it is because this mental karma is sharp.
Furthermore, among the six consciousnesses, this is of the nature of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and not of the five [sensory] consciousnesses,
because the five consciousnesses lack the capacity for discrimination.
A question is asked:
As for when these thirty-two marks can be brought to fruition as seeds,
the answer is:
at the very longest, one hundred kalpas.
At the fastest, it takes ninety-one kalpas.
The Bodhisattva Śākyamuni practiced for ninety-one great kalpas to accomplish and attain the thirty-two marks,
as stated in the sūtras.
In the distant past, there was a Buddha named Puṣya.
At that time, there were two bodhisattvas:
one was named Śākyamuni.
One was named Maitreya.
When Puṣya Buddha wished to examine whether the mind of the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni had reached full maturity,
he immediately perceived it through his vision.
He knew that his own mind was not yet fully matured,
whereas the minds of all his disciples were already matured,
and furthermore, that the mind of Maitreya Bodhisattva had already reached full maturity.
Yet his disciples were not yet fully matured.
At that time, Puṣya Buddha thought to himself:
"The mind of a single person can be easily and swiftly transformed."
"The minds of the multitude are difficult to cure quickly.
Having reflected thus,
Puṣya Buddha desired to cause the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni to attain Buddhahood swiftly.
On the summit of the Snowy Mountains, he entered a jeweled cave and attained the fire-dhyāna samādhi.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni, acting as a non-Buddhist rishi, ascended the mountain to seek medicinal herbs.
He beheld Buddha Puṣya seated within the jeweled cave, having entered the fire-dhyāna samādhi and emitting a great radiance.
Having seen him, his heart was filled with joy, faith, and reverence;
he stood upon one foot with palms joined toward the Buddha,
gazing at him with single-minded concentration, his eyes never blinking.
For seven days and seven nights, he praised the Buddha with a single verse:
"In the heavens above and the world below, there is none like the Buddha; Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, there is likewise no peer."
"I have seen all that exists in the world, yet there is no one like the Buddha.
For seven days and seven nights, he gazed intently at the World-Honored One without blinking his eyes;
thus, he transcended nine kalpas.
Within ninety-one kalpas, he attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Śākyamuni Bodhisattva valued the intention of the mind and did not value many words;
had he praised the Buddha’s mind with further verses, his mind might have become distracted.
Therefore, for seven nights, he praised the Buddha with a single verse.
It is asked:
Why was the mind of Śākyamuni Bodhisattva not yet fully matured, while his disciples were?
"Is it that Maitreya Bodhisattva’s own mind is pure and mature while his disciples' are not?
He replied,
"Because Śākyamuni Bodhisattva’s mind was more intent on benefiting sentient beings and less so on himself."
Because Maitreya Bodhisattva acts mostly for his own sake and little for the sake of sentient beings.
Section Five: The Department on Karmic Causes. As stated in the *Vimaladattā-paripṛcchā-sūtra*:
The Buddha said:
"A bodhisattva who accomplishes four dharmas attains the thirty-two marks of a great man. What are these four?"
First, scattering handfuls of gold over the Buddha or his stūpas;
second, constantly anointing the Tathāgata’s stūpas with fragrant oil;
third, making offerings of various flowers, incense, and music.
The fourfold retinue followed in attendance to make offerings to their preceptors (*upādhyāya*), ācāryas,
and others. At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
Scattering gold over stupas, Anointing Buddha-stūpas with fragrant oil,
Making offerings of flowers, incense, and music, And reverently making offerings to one's teacher—
By practicing these four dharmas, One attains the thirty-two marks.
He is upright and most wonderful, endowed with all merits.
A Bodhisattva who accomplishes four dharmas attains the eighty secondary marks. What are these four?
First, adorning the Dharma seat with various kinds of exquisite robes;
second, making offerings to others without the mind becoming weary;
third, not creating discord or strife in the presence of the Dharma Master.
Sentient beings of the four teachings cultivate the practices for awakening.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
Adorning the Dharma seat with exquisite robes, making offerings to others without weariness,
teaching sentient beings toward Bodhi, and easily attaining the eighty minor marks—
by practicing these four kinds of merit, a bodhisattva achieves these qualities.
Always, at all times, adorned with superior marks.
The sixth section on similarities and differences, as in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*.
Question: Where do the eighty secondary characteristics reside?
Answer: They reside among the various marks and follow them as they turn;
they adorn the Buddha’s body, making it exceedingly sublime and beautiful.
Question: Do the primary marks (lakṣaṇa) and the secondary signs (anuvyañjana) not obstruct or supplant one another? Answer: No;
rather, the primary marks and the secondary signs mutually manifest and enhance each other.
Just as flowers in a forest cause all the trees to bloom,
so too is the Buddha’s body adorned with such marks and signs;
it is like a mountain of gold embellished with various jewels.
Question: What is the difference between the thirty-two marks obtained by a bodhisattva and those of a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin)?
Answer: The marks obtained by a bodhisattva are superior in four respects.
First, blazing;
second, distinct;
third, complete.
There are four attainments of the place.
Furthermore, there are five matters of superiority:
first, the attainment of the place.
Second, it is extremely sublime;
third, its literary form is profound;
fourth, it accords with supreme wisdom.
5. Conforming to the Abandonment of Defilements.
Section 7: Comparative Evaluation. The *Buddha-abhidharma-sūtra* states:
"The merit possessed by all sentient beings in one thousand asaṃkhyeya worlds [is surpassed by...]"

The merit of attaining a single pore of a Buddha’s body is equal to the merit of attaining all the pores of a Tathāgata’s body; this constitutes the merit of attaining one of the secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*).
In this manner, the merit of accomplishing all eighty secondary marks is achieved.
When increased a hundredfold,
it constitutes the merit for one mark on the body of a Tathāgata; thus,
the merits for all thirty-two marks are accomplished.
Increasing it a thousandfold results in the single white hair-tuft (ūrṇā-kośa) upon the Tathāgata’s forehead;
this is accomplished through the merit of one thousand hair-tufts.
When increased a hundredfold,
it constitutes a single cranial bone mark (*uṣṇīṣa-lakṣaṇa*) of the Tathāgata,
the summit of whose head cannot be seen by any of the flying devas (*vidyādhara*).
In this way, the Buddha-body is accomplished as an inconceivable accumulation of pure merit;
therefore, the Tathāgata is the most honored and supreme among devas and humans.
Section Eight: The Hundred Merits. According to the *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra*:
The Buddha said:
"When a bodhisattva cultivates each individual mark,
it is surrounded by a hundred merits."
Fifty cultivations of the mind and fifty endowments of the mind—
these are called the hundred kinds of merit. Good son!
All the merit possessed by all the worlds does not equal the merit of a single pore of the Tathāgata;
nor does it equal the merit of all the pores of the Tathāgata.
It is not equal to a single mark of excellence (*anuvyañjana*).
The collection of eighty marks of excellence is not equal to a single primary mark (*lakṣaṇa*).
All the merits of the primary marks are not equal to the merit of the *ūrṇā-kośa* (the white tuft of hair between the eyebrows).
The merit of the mark of the white tuft of hair does not equal the merit of the mark of the invisible crown of the head.
Therefore, the Tathāgata has fully accomplished and perfected immeasurable merits;
these are the thirty-two marks.
This is precisely the retributive fruit of great compassion.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* asks:
"As it is said in the *Sūtra*..."
Each of the Buddha’s marks is adorned with a hundred merits.
What are these hundred merits?
Answer: In this context, one hundred volitions are called the hundred merits.
What are the one hundred volitions?
It refers to when a bodhisattva, while performing and increasing the karma that brings about the marks of being well-established,
first gives rise to fifty volitions to purify and make supple the vessel of the body.
Next, one thought arises that directly draws forth that [karma];
subsequently, fifty thoughts arise again to bring it to completion.
This is like a farmer who first prepares the furrows and ridges, then sows the seeds, and finally covers and irrigates them with manure and water.
It is likewise with him:
as the mark of his feet being well-placed is the result of karma,
so too is he adorned by such hundreds of thoughts.
This applies even up to the *uṣṇīṣa* on the crown of the head;
the karma of the *śaśāṅka* [mark] is likewise.
For this reason, it is so stated.
Each of the Buddha’s marks is adorned with a hundred merits.
Question: What are these fifty volitions?
Answer: There are five volitions associated with each of the ten paths of action.
That is to say, based on abstaining from the path of action of killing, there are five volitions:
first, the volition of abstaining from killing;
second, the volition of exhorting others [to do so].
Third is the volition of praise; fourth is the volition of sympathetic joy;
and fifth is the volition of dedication, which means dedicating what has been cultivated toward enlightenment.
This applies up to right view as well;
these are called the fifty volitions (*cetanā*). Some say:
Based on each of the ten paths of action, one gives rise to five grades of wholesome volition— namely, inferior, intermediate, superior, more superior, and most superior—
just as in the case of the mixed cultivation of dhyāna. Some say:
Based on each of the ten paths of action, five types of volition arise:
first, purity of the preliminary application;
second, purity of the fundamental act.
Third, purification through subsequent action;
fourth, not being harmed by discursive thought;
fifth, being sustained by mindfulness.
Some say that fifty moments arise in dependence upon a single mark of the Buddha,
proceeding as a continuous stream of mental engagement with a mark never before cultivated.
Question: What is the measure of each of these hundred merits?
Some say it is the karma that can induce the status of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*).
To exercise sovereign power over the four great continents constitutes one measure of merit;
so it is said by some.
If there is karma capable of bringing about the status of Śakra,
Lord of the Devas, and enabling one to exercise sovereign power over the two classes of devas,
this constitutes a single measure of merit.
Some say: If karma is capable of inducing the status of a king of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven,
one exercises sovereign mastery over all the hosts of devas in the desire realm.
This is the measure of that merit.
Some say it is the karma capable of inducing the status of Mahābrahmā.
To exercise mastery over the first dhyāna and the gods of the desire realm constitutes one measure of merit;
so it is said by some.
The merit of the Great Brahmā King, Lord of the Sahā World, exhorting the Tathāgata to turn the wheel of Dharma constitutes one measure of merit.
Question: At the time of requesting the Buddha, that mind was bound to the desire realm, unobscured and indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
What is called "merit"?
Some say it is when he dwells in the Brahma-world and desires to come to request [the teaching].
First, one should give rise to such a virtuous thought:
"I shall bring great benefit to all sentient beings by requesting the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma.
At that moment, one is said to have attained that Brahma-merit.
This is not reasonable.
Why? Because it is not already accomplished at the time when it has not yet been performed.
Having spoken thus,
he invited the Buddha and returned to the Brahma palace; later,
when the World-Honored One turned the wheel of Dharma, [he came].
The Earth Deity first proclaimed it;
thus, the sound was transmitted in succession until it reached the Brahma palace.
Upon hearing it, the Brahma King rejoiced and congratulated himself.
One generates sympathetic joy with a pure mind.
At that time, one even achieves this merit. Some say:
When the world is formed,
the predominant power of the karma of all sentient beings is able to bring about the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system.
This is the measure of that merit.
Some say that this excludes bodhisattvas who are close to the stage of Buddhahood.
The karma capable of producing all the fruits of wealth and happiness belonging to all other sentient beings constitutes one measure of merit. Some say:
In this regard, the measure of each individual merit should be illustrated by way of analogy.
Suppose all sentient beings were born blind;
there might be one sentient being who, through great skillful means, enables them all to regain their sight.
The merit of that sentient being constitutes a single measure of merit.
Furthermore, suppose all sentient beings were to drink poisonous medicine and become so dazed and distressed that they were on the verge of death.
If there were a sentient being who could cause all others to have their poison removed and their minds awakened,
the merit of that sentient being would constitute one measure of merit.
Furthermore, suppose all sentient beings were bound and imprisoned, facing imminent execution;
yet there were a single sentient being who caused them all to be liberated and simultaneously restored to life.
The merit of that sentient being constitutes a single measure of merit.
Furthermore, suppose all sentient beings were to destroy their ethical discipline and destroy their right view.
If there were a sentient being who could cause both precepts and views to be perfected simultaneously,
the merit of that sentient being would constitute one measure of merit.
The commentary states:
Such explanations and the subjects explained are all skillful means of pure intention (*śuddhāśaya*),
praising the magnitude of the bodhisattva’s merit.
However, none of these have yet reached the actual reality.
According to the true meaning,
the measure of each and every merit generated by a bodhisattva is immeasurable and boundless.
Because the bodhisattva has accumulated and perfected all the pāramitās over three incalculable eons,
and because the volition and aspiration thus induced are exceedingly vast,
only a Buddha can know them.
It cannot be measured by others.
The vast and immeasurable merit thus described is fully sufficient to adorn a single mark [of a Great Man] when perfected a hundredfold.
Proceeding in succession, even the thirty-two marks each possess a hundred merits.
Thus, the Buddha is adorned with these thirty-two marks, each consisting of a hundred merits, as well as the eighty secondary characteristics.
By adorning his body, he is the most honored and supreme among gods and humans. 8. Section on Wandering and Studying (9).

This section consists of four parts: the Section on Stating the Intent, the Section on Summoning the Teacher, the Section on Contending Strength, and the Section on Comparative Measurement. 1. Section on Stating the Intent (First). I have heard in secret that the One of All-Knowledge is named Siddhārtha.
From the beginning of the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*,
the Tree has stood alone in loftiness at the end of the hundred *kalpas*;
it takes the entire Dharma-realm as its wisdom.
He takes all of space as his body;
yet this body is not limited by measure,
extending beyond the furthest reaches of the compass and square.
Wisdom functions in all things;
it transcends the realm of thought and deliberation,
and cannot be fathomed by human affairs.
How can this be discussed merely in terms of physical location?
To open the eyes and ears of the ignorant,
one must demonstrate the traces and manifestations of the Sage.
Or again, he may manifest as dwelling among non-Buddhist practitioners;
or again, he may appear as a child.
One should guide ordinary beings by appearing in their own kind,
and transform sentient beings by assuming various forms;
only then may one be titled the Unsurpassed One, the God among Gods.
This is truly because the connection between the ignorant and the wise is hidden, and the distinction between the ordinary and the sage is difficult to fathom;
thus, the merit of inconceivable virtue is unsurpassed.
2. Section on Summoning Teachers, Part Two. As stated in the *Buddhacarita-sūtra*:

At that time, King Śuddhodana, knowing that his crown prince had reached the age of eight—according to the *Nidāna-sūtra*, he held an assembly of hundreds of officials, ministers, and counselors at the age of seven—addressed them, saying:
"You ministers should know this:
within my realm, who possesses the greatest wisdom?
Who has such thorough mastery of intelligence that they are capable of serving as a teacher for the Crown Prince?"
The ministers replied,
"Your Majesty, you should know that there is now one named Viśvāmitra."
He was most excellent and sublime in his thorough knowledge of all treatises;

such a great master was capable of instructing the crown prince and those below him. Having briefly described this, the King immediately dispatched a messenger to summon him and addressed him, saying:
"Venerable Great Master,
can you teach the Prince all the arts and various treatises?
At that time, Viśvāmitra replied:
"Great King, in accordance with Your Majesty’s command,
I am now able to give rise to a heart of joy."
He immediately arrayed five hundred youths of the Śākya clan to attend him in front, behind, and on both sides;
additionally, there were immeasurable and boundless numbers of boys and girls.
As he followed the Prince toward the hall of learning,
the Great Master saw the Prince from afar;
overcome by the power of his majestic virtue, he could not restrain himself and suddenly rose from his seat.
Bowing his body, he prostrated at the feet of the Prince.
Having risen from his prostration,
he looked around in all four directions and was overcome with great shame and remorse.
At that time, after Maitrāyaṇī had felt shame and remorse,
there was a devaputra in the sky named Viśuddhasūkṣma.
From the Tuṣita Palace, together with immeasurable and boundless great deva kings, they constantly guarded the Prince;
remaining in that void space,
they concealed their bodies and did not appear.
And he spoke in verse:
"Regarding all the arts and crafts of the world, As well as other scriptures and treatises,
This person is able to know them all, And is also able to instruct others."
These supreme beings, in order to conform to the ways of the world,
have long practiced in the past; now they demonstrate that they have learned from teachers all the supramundane wisdom, including the various truths and the powers.
Regarding phenomena produced by causes and conditions— those that have arisen and those that have ceased—
one who does not possess even a single thought of knowing them can still realize and know whether name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) appears or does not appear;
how much more so, then, regarding mere words and letters?
When the devaputra had spoken these verses,
he scattered various kinds of flowers over the Prince and immediately returned to his own palace.
At that time, the Prince first began his studies.
He had a writing slate fashioned from the finest and most exquisite gośīrṣa-candana sandalwood,
its four edges adorned entirely with the seven precious gems.
Having smeared his back with various kinds of extraordinary and wondrous celestial incense,
he took him and went to the presence of the ācārya Viśvamitra,
speaking these words:
"Venerable Teacher, what script did you teach me? The Prince then explained the various scripts in detail, saying:
"There is the script spoken by Brahmā; the current Brāhmaṇa script consists precisely of fourteen vowels, which is the Kharoṣṭhī script—translated in the Sui language as 'Donkey-Lip'."
The *Puṣkarasāri* script, translated into the Sui language as "Flower" (*Huáhuá*);
the *Akkara* script, translated into the Sui language as "Division" (*Jiéfēn*); the *Monggara* script, translated into the Sui language as "Auspiciousness" (*Jíxiáng*);
and the *Yavanānī* script, translated into the Sui language as "Script of the Great Qin Country."
Aṅgulīya script—Sui: "Finger-script";
Yañānika script—Sui: "Yoke-script";
Sāgara script—Sui: "Cow-script."
The *Pārasavanī* script (Sui: "tree-leaf") and the *Pāruṣa* script (Sui:
"evil speech"). The *Pitṛ-lekha* (Letter to the Father) was translated by an unknown translator.
The *Vidada* script (Sui: "Corpse-Rising") is the script of the country of Vidada;
the *Dhīradī* script (Sui: "Southern India") is the script of Jīradī;
and the *Puruṣākṛti* script (Sui: "Human Form") is the script of Puruṣākṛti.
The Dukanāva script, translated into the Sui language as "Right-turning";
the Upaga script, translated into the Sui language as "Fierce Adornment";
and the Sāṃkhya script, translated into the Sui language as "Equal Calculation."
Aparamitā script (Sui: "covering");
Anuloma script (Sui: "following");
Vairasāgara script (Sui: "variegated").
The Āḍhala script is found at the western edge of Mount Vāyavya;
the Aparagoyānī script was translated by Śikṣānanda;
and the Khasa script is found in Śulika.
The characters in the *Mona*, *Koudou*,
and *Matatsakara* scripts, whose translations from the country of Cīna have been lost.
The Pida-siddhi script, the Kharoṣṭhī script,
the Puṣpa-deva script, and the Devanāgarī script.
The Nāga script, the Dragon script,
the Yakṣa script (translated by an unknown translator),
the Gandharva script, and the Celestial Melody script.
The Asura script, the Kinnara script for those who do not drink alcohol,
the Garuḍa script for the Golden-Winged Birds,
and the non-human script for the Kiṃnaras.
The Mahoraga script, the Mahā-uraga script,
the Mṛga-cakra script, the script of the sounds of all beasts,
and the Karkoṭaka script of the sounds of birds.
The Pūrvavideha script is for the gods dwelling on earth;
the Aparagoyānī script is for the gods of the void;
and the Uttarakuru script is for [the inhabitants] north of Mount Sumeru.
The script of Pūrvavideha is written to the east of Mount Sumeru;
the script of Ucchāpā is written as Ūcchāpā;
the script of Kṣepa is written as Kṣepa.
The Sāgara script; the lost translation of the Vajra script;
the Vajrī-pāradigā script; and the script for correspondence.
The Vidyādhara script is "eating the remnants";
the Anubhūta script is "the unprecedented";
the Śāstarāvarta script is "turning like a prostration."
From the Gaṇanāvadā script and others, one transforms into the Utsarāvadā script;
from the Utsarāvadā script, one transforms into the Nikharāvadā script;
from the Nikharāvadā script, one transforms into the Pāṭalīka script, which is the feet.
The Vikṛtara-pota-na-dī script increases by two syllables per line;
the Śyāma-tārā script increases by ten syllables per line;
and the Mātṛ-paśinī script belongs to the middle stream.
The Liśāyavada-paurbhida script is for the *dhāraṇī* of asceticism on the various mountains;
the Picchali script is for contemplating the earth;
the Gaganapilicchanī script is for contemplating space.
The Sāpūṣadīniśānta script, the Sarvauṣadhīnāmamālā script,
the Saṃgrahaṇī script, the Sarvalokadhātu script,
and the Sarvabījaghoṣa script. At that time, the Prince, having spoken of these scripts, [continued].
He further consulted with Ācārya Vimalamitra, saying:
"There are sixty-four kinds of scripts in total;
I do not know which script the Venerable One intends to teach me."
At that time, having heard the Prince speak these words of the scriptures,
Tārā felt joy and gladness in her heart, her countenance bright and serene; yet she secretly harbored a sense of personal shame,
thereby subduing her pride and arrogance.
He addressed the Prince,
speaking in verse:
"O rare one of pure wisdom, you who skillfully accord with all worldly dharmas."
"I ought to master all treatises; yet you have come again to enter my school.
Such writings as these I do not yet know, though I have already recited and mastered their originals.
This is the supreme path of gods and men, yet now you wish to seek a teacher once more. For the divine principle is soundless."
One expresses the intended meaning through words and phrases,
yet words and phrases leave no trace;
one represents the sounds through written characters, yet the characters themselves are merely a means to an end.
Therefore, characters are the tracks for words;
words are the traps for principles.
Sound and meaning form a tally that must not be lost in either part.
Therefore, the application of written characters encompasses the entire universe.
Although their traces are tied to brush and ink, their principle accords with the divine.
This was so even when the masters of calligraphy first created the script.
There are three types of people in total.
The eldest is named Brahmā;
their script runs from right to left.
The next is called Khara;
its script reads from left to right.
Its founder was Cangjie.
As for these scripts, they descend from below.
Brahmā and Kharoṣṭhī reside in India;
the Yellow Historian Cang Jie dwells in the Middle Kingdom.
Brahmā adopted the method from the Pure Heaven (Śuddhāvāsa),
while Cang Jie derived [writing] from the tracks of birds;
though the scripts differ, the principles they transmit are identical.
Looking up to the teachings of the former awakened ones, it is said there are sixty-four scripts.
These include the distinct styles of the *mṛga-lipi* (deer-wheel) and the *cakṣur-āvarta-lipi* (eye-turning) scripts,
as well as the various character forms of the eight classes of beings, such as nāgas and yakṣas.
Based on the Brāhmī and Kharoṣṭhī scripts, which are considered the most excellent among worldly scripts,

The first was named Gopiyā,
a jade-like maiden who was barren;
the second was named Yaśodharā.
When the Bodhisattva had left the household life,
someone spoke at night, saying:
"How could the Prince have become pregnant after leaving home?"
"Seeking to bring disgrace upon our clan, the Śākyas, they wish to burn mother and child in a pit of fire.
Yaśodharā, regretting her innocence, made this great vow:

"I pray that mother and son may be consumed by the fire.

The Buddha then transformed himself into five hundred bhikṣus.
All were like the body of the Buddha.
Rāhula then took the ball and placed it into the Buddha’s bowl,

Furthermore, the *Mahā-upāya-kauśalya-sūtra* states:
Because there were those who doubted that the Bodhisattva was male and instead claimed he was a eunuch,
he took Gopī, the daughter of the Śākya clan, as his wife.
Rāhula was born through transformation upon the celestial transformation;
he did not come into being through the union of parents. Furthermore, the *Buddha-benxing-jing* (Sūtra on the Original Deeds of the Buddha) states:
At that time, Mahāprajāpatī, together with the Śākya woman Yaśodharā,
took Rāhula and prepared extensive offerings.
Carrying various items,
he went to that shrine;
the deity there was named Rudraka.
The name was derived from that deity;
thus, the grove was also named Lumbinī.
Within that grove, [he was born].
In the past, when the Bodhisattva was still living as a householder,
he would frequently engage in massage and recreation within that garden.
Inside that garden, there was a large rock.
In the past, when the Bodhisattva rose from his seat,
Yaśodharā, the daughter of the Śākya clan,
was at that time laying Rāhula down to rest upon that stone.
Thereafter, he seized a stone and threw it into the water, then made this vow:
"I now establish this oath; it is true and not false."
"Except for the Crown Prince, there is no other man who could have fathered this child by me.
The son I have borne is truly the offspring of the Crown Prince's own lineage."
To demonstrate that this is not false,
let this great rock float upon the water without sinking,
remaining just as that mind was settled in its vow.
Upon reaching the water, it immediately floated upon the surface;
just as a plantain leaf floats on water,
neither sinking nor submerging, so too was this.
At that time, when the great assembly had seen and heard this,
they gave rise to a sense of wonder;
they clamored and cheered with unrestrained exultation.
They cried out, leaped about, sang, danced, and whirled their skirts and sleeves;
they also produced various kinds of sounds and musical performances,
specifically for the celebration of Rāhula’s birthday.
At the time Yaśodharā gave birth,
Rāhu, the asura king, seized and devoured the moon;
in a mere instant, he briefly held it and then released it.
For this reason, he was given the name Rāhula;
he was so lovely and handsome that no one who saw him failed to be filled with joy.
His skin was yellowish-white like the color of genuine gold;
his head and neck were shaped like a parasol,
and his nose was high and prominent like that of a parrot.
His two arms are long and supple, hanging down past his knees;
all his limbs and joints are without deficiency,
and his sense faculties are fully developed and complete.
5. Section on Difficulties of Birth. Section Five on Difficulties of Birth. As stated in the *Buddha’s Past Deeds Sūtra* (*Buddhacarita-sūtra*):
Rāhula was born from his mother’s womb only after six years had passed since the Tathāgata’s renunciation of the household life.
On the day the Tathāgata returned to his father’s home,
Rāhula was six years old. He asked:
For what reason did Rāhu remain in his mother’s womb for six years without emerging?
The answer is:
In a former life, Rāhu was a king.
When that seer was brought into the garden,
he did not emerge for six days;
thus, he remained dwelling in his mother’s womb for six years.
The general meaning is the same as before.
Question: For what reason did his mother, Yaśodharā, carry him in her womb for six years?
Answer: The *Pūrvayoga-sūtra* states:
The Buddha said,
"O bhikṣus, I recall that in the past, beyond immeasurable eons..."
There was a herd of cows at a pasture.
The wife of the cowherd took her daughter and went to the herd to milk them for curds and cream.
The two vessels he carried were both filled to the brim;
he sent his daughter to carry the larger one,
while he himself bore the smaller one.
When they reached the middle of the road, he said to his daughter, "Walk quickly;
the path here is treacherous and there is great danger."
At that time, the girl said to her mother,
"This vessel is very heavy;
how can I possibly move quickly now?"
Her mother spoke thus to her two or three times, saying, "Go quickly;
there is great danger on this road.
At that time, the girl thought to herself:
"How can she be sent away carrying such an extremely heavy burden?
Furthermore, she is being urged on and forced to travel with haste.
Because of this, the girl gave rise to anger.
He then said to his mother,
"Mother, please prepare this milk vessel and bring it along;
I wish to relieve myself for a moment."
Then that mother took this large vessel, shouldered it, and set out;
her daughter followed behind at a slow pace.
At that time, the mother was burdened by the heavy load.
He then proceeded for six *krośas*.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"If you have any doubt in your hearts as to whether that woman, out of a mind of ill-will, sent her mother to carry this heavy burden for six *krośas*," [then listen].
Do not harbor any other thought;
it was Yaśodharā, the daughter of the Śākya clan,
who at that time sent her mother to carry a heavy load for six krośas along the road.
Due to those karmic obstructions,
they undergo immeasurable suffering within the afflictions of birth and death; by means of those residual karmas,
[they continue to suffer].
It is said that in this present life, she carried the fetus for six years;
there is also a sutra which states that Rāhula did not emerge for six days because in a past life he had blocked a mouse hole and confined the mouse for six days.
He remained in the womb for six years.

The flowers follow one another in succession like celestial *karpāsa* cloth;

within each of its tiers, there were ten billion lotuses.

We harbored evil intentions and were attached to defiled desires, unaware that they constituted a calamity;
thus we caused the Buddha to hear our reproaches and his loathing for desire and evil,

Four thousand women and others all resolved upon bodhicitta;
two thousand women became free from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye;
and two thousand women will attain the path of a pratyekabuddha in a future age.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"When I first attained enlightenment on the banks of the Hiraṇyavatī River,

Claiming to have attained the Way, he came to where I was;
he circled my body seven times with his physical form,

He then spoke these words:
"Because I am free from desire, my body-faculty is such as this,
like that of Maheśvara."
"My spiritual power now surpasses that of hundreds of thousands of millions of śramaṇas.

When the Tathāgata was practicing the Brahma-faring for kalpas,

He is entirely free from thoughts of desire;
because his mind is unstained by darkness, he receives this retribution.
It is like a precious horse that appears and disappears unpredictably.
"Now I shall manifest a small portion of my body for you.

the Buddha was upon Mount Sumeru,

Flowers followed one after another, ascending as far as the Brahma world.
From the Buddha’s body issued forth ten billion nayutas of lotus flowers made of various jewels,

This lotus flower has one hundred million petals,
each layer containing hundreds of thousands of immeasurable transformation Buddhas.
Each transformation Buddha is attended by ten billion Bodhisattvas and countless Bhikṣus.

The emanated Buddha emitted light that illuminated the worlds of the ten directions; when the Nirgranthas saw this, they were greatly startled and their hearts were subdued, realizing that the Buddha’s marks of pure conduct are thus inconceivable.
His form is not ugly but resembles a lotus flower.
I now prostrate before the ocean of the Buddha’s merits;
those who seek ordination from the Buddha shall all attain the fruits of the Path.

10. Section on Aversion to Suffering (10). This tenth section, "Aversion to Suffering," is divided into four parts: Part One, Expressing the Intent; Part Two, Contemplating the Field; Part Three, The Excursion; and Part Four, Aversion to Desire. 1. Part One: Expressing the Intent. First, to examine in detail the distinctions within the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*).
The four modes of birth possess their respective natures;
they all wander within the burning house and are submerged together in the sea of desire.
These wriggling creatures harbor life, and these clamoring multitudes seek one another.
Therefore, the Dharma King, appearing as an Awakened One during the era of the continents and islands,
responded to the timing of the vehicle of the chariot;
he led those playful children back to this sublime land.
Feeling compassion for the worldly net and joyfully delighting in renunciation,
he viewed the courtesans as if they were corpses lying across his path and realized the palace chambers to be like ruined tombs.
Sighing at the suffering of birth, old age, and illness,
and yearning for the eternal bliss of transcendence,
he abandoned his kingdom and city to take flight into the heights.
Upon the subduing of Māra and the attainment of enlightenment. 2.
Section on Contemplating the Fields (Kṣetrāvalokana-varga), Second: As stated in the *Buddha-carita* (Sūtra on the Original Deeds of the Buddha):
King Śuddhodana, together with many members of the Śākya clan...
The Prince was also taken outside to roam and observe the sowing of the fields;
at that time, all the laborers within that land were working with bare bodies and great toil to plow and till the soil.
The birds preyed upon one another, crying out repeatedly: "Alas! Alas!"
The sentient beings of the world undergo extreme suffering,
namely birth, old age, sickness, and death,
while further experiencing various kinds of afflictions and distress.
Rolling about within it, they are unable to escape;
why do they not seek to abandon these various sufferings?
At that time, King Śuddhodana, having observed the farming work, [returned].
Together with the youths, he returned to a garden.
At that time, the Prince moved with composed dignity,
gazing about as he paced here and there in search of tranquility.
Suddenly, he saw a jambu tree in a certain place,
lush and spreading with foliage, a sight that delights all who behold it;
having seen it, he immediately spoke to those around him.
"You all, depart from me each;
I wish to travel in private.
At that time, the Prince dismissed his attendants.
Having completely dispersed them all, he gradually approached the foot of the tree and sat cross-legged upon the grass,
contemplating with focused attention.
Sentient beings undergo various sufferings such as birth, old age, sickness, and death;
by giving rise to compassion for them, one immediately attains a concentrated mind,
becomes free from all desires, and abandons all unwholesome dharmas.
Upon the exhaustion of outflows in the desire realm, he immediately attained the first dhyāna.
All the celestial lords, including Śakra,
saw the Prince sitting in the shade of the tree.
Having flown to where the Prince was, they paid their respects, spoke verses of praise, and departed.
At that time, King Śuddhodana did not see the Prince for a brief moment;
immediately, a sense of displeasure and lack of joy arose within his heart.
He asked people, saying,
"Where is my crown prince now?
He has suddenly vanished."
At that time, the ministers galloped back and forth in the four directions— east, west, south, and north— searching for the prince, but they did not know where he was. Then,
a certain minister saw from afar the prince sitting beneath the shade of a jambu tree, contemplating while practicing dhyāna.
Furthermore, he saw that the shadows of all the trees had shifted,
yet the shadow of the Jambu tree alone continued to cover the Prince.
At that time, the minister beheld this rare and inconceivable marvel of the Prince.
He was immediately filled with great joy and leaped for gladness, unable to contain himself.
He hurried and ran swiftly to the place where the king was;
having arrived, he knelt down and related the matters exactly as he had seen them.
Then he spoke in verse:
"The Great King’s Prince now sits beneath the shade of a Jambu tree, Seated cross-legged in contemplation, having entered samādhi;
His radiance shines forth like the sun upon a mountain."
This is truly a Great Man; The shadow of the tree stands firm and does not move.
I pray that Your Majesty will observe for yourself: What manner of countenance does the Prince have as he sits?
He is like Mahābrahmā among the various heavenly kings, And also like Śakra, the Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
His majestic power was sublime and his radiance was brilliant, illuminating all those groves of trees.
At that time, King Śuddhodana, having heard this,
went at once to the Jambu tree and saw the Prince from afar.
He sat cross-legged amidst those trees,
appearing like a great mass of fire atop a mountain peak viewed in the dead of night, emitting fierce and brilliant flames;
his majestic power was manifest, shining with towering splendor.
It was like the bright moon suddenly appearing amidst thick clouds,
or like lighting a great, pure lamp within a dark room.
When the king saw this, he conceived a sense of great wonder and marvel.
His entire body trembled with awe and all his hairs stood on end;
he immediately prostrated himself at the crown of his head before the Prince’s feet and,
leaping for joy, spoke these words:
"Excellent, excellent!
This prince possesses great majesty and virtue.
Thus he spoke in verse as praise.
Like a great mass of fire upon a mountain peak at night, or like the autumn moon emerging from behind the clouds—now I see the Prince sitting in contemplation;
unconsciously my hair stands on end and my body trembles with awe.
When King Śuddhodana had finished praising him with this verse, he spoke further.
Again he prostrated at the feet of the Prince and spoke these verses once more:
"Now for a second time I bend this body To prostrate at your sublime and wondrous thousand-spoked feet."
From birth until this very day, I have suddenly beheld him again as he sits in contemplation;
at that time, there was a young boy carrying a fishing trap and a snare who followed the Great King, chattering and laughing.
A certain minister rebuked that young boy,
speaking these words:
"You children, please do not cry out.
Then the children replied to that minister,
"Why do you not allow us to enjoy our clamor?"
At that time, the minister replied to all those children with these verses:
"Though the sun's rays are extremely hot and fierce, They cannot turn back the cool shade of this tree.
Furthermore, there is a most wondrous light one fathom wide; In its majestic power, it has no peer in the world."
Siddhārtha, the Prince, sat in contemplation beneath the tree, as immovable and unshakable as Mount Sumeru;
with a profound inner resolve, he took delight in the shade of this tree and would not depart. As stated in the *Buddha-benxing-jing* (The Sutra of the Buddha’s Fundamental Deeds).
The Bodhisattva addressed King Śuddhodana with these verses:
"Just as a golden house where a fire blazes fiercely, Like delicious food mixed with deadly poison,
Or like a full pond of lotuses infested by a dragon— The pleasures of sovereignty lead to great suffering later."
3. The Section on the Excursion (Nikkhamana-vagga), Part Three. As stated in the *Buddha-carita* (The Life of the Buddha):

At that time, the Devaputra Kumbhakāra, wishing to lead the Prince out toward the gardens to observe the beautiful and the foul so as to arouse a mind of world-weariness (*nirveda*), gradually instructed him in renunciation.
At that time, having heard these sounds,
the Prince immediately called his charioteer and said, "Quickly prepare a fine carriage;
I wish now to go to the park to look about."

issued a proclamation throughout the city of Kapilavastu,

He adorned it with men and women;

At that time, the charioteer decorated the carriage and yoked well-trained horses.
Having completed all the preparations, he addressed the Prince, saying,
"Noble Son, you should know that the carriage is now ready."
At that time, the Prince led the way out through the eastern gate, intending to go to the park to look about.
At that moment, the Devaputra Kumbhakaraka stood right before the Prince at the head of the street.
He transformed himself into an old, decrepit man.
Upon seeing him, the Prince immediately asked his charioteer,
"Who is this person?"
His body was wrinkled, his flesh diminished, and his skin slack;

He then addressed the charioteer with these verses:
"Good charioteer, listen now to me: who is this person before me, whose body is not upright and whose hair is thin—is he thus by birth, or has old age come upon him?
At that time, the charioteer [replied].
