"This time is called one of great suffering and affliction; The beautiful form is destroyed by the slaughter of the kalpa, And the faculties of pleasure are ruined, losing all mindfulness; The movements of the limbs no longer follow the will."
At that time, the prince asked the charioteer, saying:
"Is this person alone whose family law is such as this,
or is it the case that all people are likewise?"
The charioteer replied,
"It is not only this one family that is thus;
this is the law for all the world."
"Though noble and humble differ, none have yet transcended old age.
The Prince said,
"If I cannot escape this old age, it is fitting that I return to the palace at once."
"The law of old age has not yet passed; why do you allow yourself such negligence?
Then King Śuddhodana questioned the charioteer, who answered in full as before, and the King said:
Such a physical appearance as this is rare;
fearing that the Prince might renounce the household life,
they further increased his five sensual pleasures.
The Prince grew weary of and renounced the five desires, contemplating only the suffering of old age.
Later, at another time, he took leave of the King and departed through the southern gate of the city, intending to go to the gardens for an excursion.
The King issued orders to clear and adorn the roads, making them twice as magnificent as before.
At that time, the devaputra Kumbhakāra immediately manifested before the Prince a sick man,
whose bones were joined in agony, whose life hung by a thread,
who lay amidst filth, writhing and groaning, unable to lift himself up.
Crying out, he prostrated himself on his head and begged for support to sit up.
Having seen this, the Prince asked the charioteer,
"Who is this person?"
Their bellies are as vast as great cauldrons;
when they draw breath, their entire bodies tremble violently.
Their grief and anguish are so piercing that they cannot bear to see or hear them.
For these reasons, the charioteer spoke in verse:
"The Prince asked the charioteer: 'For what reason does this person undergo such suffering?'"
The charioteer reported to the Prince: "Because the four elements are out of harmony, illness arises.
Later, at another time, the Prince went out through the western gate of the city to view the gardens and groves.
At that time, the deva Kumbhakāra manifested a corpse lying on a bed before the Prince;
a multitude of people carried it along with immeasurable kinsmen.
They surrounded him weeping,
beating their breasts and striking their heads,
their voices and tears falling like rain.
He wailed and lamented with a great cry;
his bitter sobbing was difficult to hear.
When the Prince saw this, his heart was filled with profound sorrow and compassion.
He asked the charioteer,
"Who is this person being carried along while wailing and crying out?"
He spoke in verse, asking:
"O Prince of exquisite form and upright countenance, ask this skillful driver:
who is this lying upon the bed, carried by four men, surrounded by kinsmen who wail and weep?"
The charioteer addressed the Prince with these verses:
"Having abandoned the mind, the intellect, and all the sense faculties, this corpse is devoid of consciousness, like wood or stone.
Your kinsmen surround it for a moment, wailing aloud; here, love and affection are forever parted."
The Prince asked again,
"Do I too possess this law of death?
He replied with a verse:
For all sentient beings, this karma is exhausted; whether among devas or humans, noble or base, all are equal and uniform.
Though they dwell in various worlds of good or evil, when the time of impermanence arrives, there is no difference.
Later, at another time, the Prince went out from the north of the city.
At that time, the devaputra Kumbhakāra, by means of his supernormal powers,
went not far from the chariot and manifested before the Prince a man who had shaved off his hair and beard and was wearing a saṃghāṭī robe.
With his right shoulder bared and holding a mendicant’s staff in his hand,
he walked along the road with an alms bowl cradled in his left palm.
Upon seeing him, the Prince asked the charioteer:
"Who is this person standing before me,
whose deportment is so dignified and composed, and whose gait is so slow and deliberate?"
He gazed straight ahead for the distance of one fathom without looking to his left or right;
he maintained his mind and conduct unlike any other person.
His hair was shaven, his beard was clipped, and the color of his robes was purely crimson.
Unlike those of laypeople,
the bowl was a deep blue-black color, shining like mineral antimony.
The charioteer said to the Prince:
This is called a person who has gone forth from the household life:
one who constantly practices wholesome dharmas and remains far removed from unwholesome ones;
one who skillfully disciplines the sense faculties and skillfully bestows fearlessness.
He practices compassion toward all sentient beings, refrains from killing, and protects them with mindfulness.
Having heard this, the prince asked his charioteer,
"Drive the chariot now toward that renunciant."
The charioteer received his command and immediately led the Prince toward the place where the renunciant was.
The Prince inquired of him:
"Who are you? he asked.
He replied with a verse:
"Beholding that this world is subject to cessation, I seek the state of inexhaustible nirvāṇa."
Having established a mind of equanimity toward both enemies and kin, they do not engage in worldly desires or such matters;
dwelling instead in mountain forests, beneath trees, or in cemeteries and open spaces,
they renounce all conditioned things and subsist by begging while contemplating true suchness.
At that time, out of reverence for the Dharma,
the prince descended from his carriage and proceeded on foot toward the place where the renunciant was.
He prostrated himself with his head at the feet of that renunciant,
circumambulated him three times, and returned to sit upon his chariot;
he then commanded the driver to turn back toward the palace.
At that time, there was a woman within the palace named Mṛgajā.
From afar, she saw the Prince returning and entering the palace.
Driven by a mind of desire,
he spoke these verses:
"May Great King Śuddhodana enjoy happiness, And may Mahāprajāpatī be free from sorrow."
The palace ladies were exceedingly beautiful; who could withstand the presence of this Holy Son?
Furthermore, according to the *Mahā-upāya-kauśalya-hetu-phala-sūtra* and other texts, at that time the Prince gradually grew older, and the time for his renunciation had arrived.
Therefore, he took leave of his father the King and departed through the four city gates;
having encountered those previously mentioned while traveling and observing, he felt revulsion toward them,
and only rejoiced at the fourth [encounter], which was his renunciation.

All the great physiognomists knew that if the Prince did not renounce the world, after seven days he would attain the rank of a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin) and rule over the four quarters of the world,
with the seven treasures appearing spontaneously.
Each reported what they knew to the King,
who increased the guards at each of the four gates to one thousand men each,
surrounding the city for a distance of one yojana within its walls.
He stationed his people to guard it.
At the eastern gate, an old man recited this verse:
"The city of reeds and plantains is easily breached; The perilous vines are about to bite."
Once the stalk has withered, it will soon be half-decayed;
having bid a long farewell, we shall depart together like white horses in the sun.

9. Section on the Seasons (Kāla-varga). Section Nine on the Seasons. As stated in the *Dvādaśavyūha-sūtra*, the *Ekottarika-āgama*, the *Dīrgha-āgama*, and other texts, he left the household life at twenty-nine.
According to the *Ekottarika Āgama*,
he spent twenty years among the teachings of non-Buddhist paths.
Now, calculating by this general principle, the Tathāgata remained in the world for seventy-nine years.
If he left the household life at twenty-nine and attained enlightenment at thirty-five, the period during which he could have transformed sentient beings would have been only forty-five years.
Furthermore, the *Dhyānārya-sūtra* states:
"Śākyamuni transformed sentient beings with a single body for thirty-nine years."
In most sūtras, the age of nineteen for his renunciation should be taken as the correct version.
Thus, the Adbhuta-dharmaparyāya Sūtra states that Yaśodharā said:
The Tathāgata took me as his attendant less than three years ago;
for the *Ruiying jing* (Sutra of Auspicious Responses) states that the Prince took a consort at the age of seventeen.
Thus, it is correct that he attained realization at nineteen and left the household life;
if he had left the household life at twenty-nine and attained the Way at thirty-five,
there would be fewer years recorded in the sūtras.
Furthermore, it is said that he studied among the non-Buddhists for twenty years and only attained the Way at age fifty;
this is sufficient proof that [the account] is erroneous.
This is truly because the faculties and practices of sentient beings differ, resulting in variations in their perspectives.
Section Ten: On the Concordance of the Sections. The commentary states:

In the books of a single era, successive generations of scholars transmit them to one another;
this has resulted in the confusion of characters such as "hai" for "shi" and the alteration of rhymes such as "yu" for "lu.

how much more so when heterodox practices are easily heard,
yet the True Dharma is difficult to fully comprehend.
Regarding the terms "middle" and "extremes," they were transposed in the manuscript,
and thus [the correct order] was determined through careful examination.
There are no differing explanations.

upon the heads of these two types of beasts—
A separate lotus pedestal arises;
this pedestal serves as the form of the incense burner.
Along the four edges of the burner, six silver pavilions arise separately.
From the towers emerge celestial youths,
each approximately two inches tall;
there are ninety-six such celestial youths in total.
Every time incense was burned,
these youths would each take turns coming forward to hand over the incense burner.
Afterwards, the lion squatted facing outward;
atop the lion’s head, nine dragons coiled around it,
supporting a golden lotus from above.
Within the flower is a golden pedestal;
the pedestal itself constitutes the precious seed.
Within that pedestal and precious seed...
There were one trillion three hundred billion great pearl towers and pavilions,
each filled with various exquisite incenses.
Furthermore, there were one trillion three hundred billion golden tablets of the Vinaya-piṭaka.
Among them was a bhikṣu who had entered the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).
When it came time for the incense offering, [he emerged].
The celestial youths from those various furnaces came to the place of the jeweled terrace;
each one produced songs of incense-burning from their mouths,
and the gates of the terrace opened of their own accord.
The bhikṣus emerged from their meditative concentration;
having taken the incense from the pearl-vision and entrusted it to the celestial youth,
they closed the gate-tower of their own accord.
From the mouths of the nine dragons,
they further held white silver lotuses as attendants for the platform.
Within each of these silver towers,
there are celestial youths who constantly perform divine music, offer praise, and burn incense.
His voice was pure and elegant, beyond compare;
all sentient beings who heard it conceived faith and awakened to the Way.
Whenever the Tathāgata preached the Dharma, [this occurred].
In the presence of the great assembly, he constantly held an incense burner;
a celestial youth took the incense and presented it to the Buddha,
causing him to make offerings.
Furthermore, there was a golden casket containing the Great Perfection of Wisdom Sūtra in its entirety,
comprising thirty billion verses.
The sutra scrolls were made of gold;
the boundary paths were made of white jade;
and the characters were made of silver.
The casket was three inches long;
inside were two bhikṣus, who had likewise entered the meditative absorption of cessation.
This casket and this incense burner were fashioned by Krakucchanda Buddha;
they have been handed down in succession to me, and shall continue until the time of Ruci Buddha.
Whenever the Buddhas wish to appear in the world,
they all open this golden casket and peruse the scriptures;
through the power of Prajñā, they are not disturbed by the heavenly Māras and swiftly ascend to perfect enlightenment.
I now entrust this to you;
exert yourself to protect it and do not let it be lost.
Having received it, I [shall sit] beneath the Bodhi tree.
During his six years of ascetic practice,
he constantly drank the water from this jar,
thereby dispelling hunger and thirst.
The afflictions were likewise extinguished.
Furthermore, when I first desired to attain the Way,
I entered a river to bathe.
Having accepted the milk-rice from the two daughters,
I proceeded to the foot of the Bodhi tree, intending to ascend the Vajra-maṇḍala.
Thereupon, the mountain deity came to my presence and addressed me, saying:
Now that you have attained the Way, you may follow the example of the Buddhas of the past.
If, upon first attaining the Way, you wish to ascend the Vajra-maṇḍala,
you should first hold an incense burner and circumambulate the maṇḍala seven times before the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Each person should hold incense in their hand and place it into that burner.
Now that he has attained the Way, he may follow the example of previous Buddhas;
the Buddha shall follow this method to circumambulate the altar and the tree.
In total, there were thirty-two circumambulations.
The Buddhas of the ten directions likewise came forward to present incense.
Next, they summoned the human kings, celestial kings, Śakra, Brahmā, dragon kings, and Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage.
Each person stepped forward to offer incense.
By the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power,
the fragrance reached throughout the ten directions.
Up to the Peak of Existence,
sentient beings suffering there who smell this fragrance attain liberation;
their sense faculties become complete and their wisdom increases.
The various kinds of miraculous transformations cannot be described in full.
He further addressed the Brahma King, saying:
"Take the water from that dragon-vessel and sprinkle it upon the feet of the World-Honored One."
The human kings, the celestial kings, Śakra, Māra,
and Brahmā each washed his feet in turn,
causing the earth to quake in six ways.
The Tathāgata emitted golden light from beneath his feet and sat upon a seat of golden lotuses;
the Buddhas of the ten directions each came to offer incense.
Within that radiance,
Vairocana Buddha extended his golden hand to stroke the crown of Śākyamuni Buddha’s head and further preached the wondrous Dharma.

I have commanded the Buddhas of the ten directions to perform the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal ritual of a motion followed by three proclamations) to confer upon Śākyamuni Buddha the status of the Unsurpassed Dharma King.
All these Buddhas uphold this *karman* atop the golden altar.
The great assembly of devas and humans, as numerous as the sands of immeasurable rivers,
having heard the Buddha’s *karmavācanā*, became simultaneously silent, like bhikṣus who have entered the fourth dhyāna.
After the Buddhas had presided over the *karmavācanā* and received the station of Dharma King, [the assembly remained thus].
The earth shook in six ways;
the Buddha emitted rays of light that universally illumined the ten directions,
extensively performing buddha-work to benefit both ordinary beings and sages.
It cannot be described in full.
Section Six: The Section on the Grass Seat. As stated in the *Buddha-bhūmi-carita-sūtra*:
At that time, the Bodhisattva had finished bathing in the river, eating the milk-rice, and washing his body.
His physical appearance and majesty were restored to their original state;
his power was sovereign and he proceeded with composure toward the Bodhi tree.
The Bodhisattva reflected:
"What kind of seat should I prepare for this site of enlightenment?
he thought, and immediately he perceived by himself that he should sit upon the grass.
At that time, a deity from the Śuddhāvāsa heaven addressed the Bodhisattva, saying:
"When all Buddhas of the past desired to realize bodhi,
they all spread grass upon it and thereby attained perfect enlightenment."
At that time, the Bodhisattva contemplated, "Who can provide me with such grass?
and looked around in all four directions.
At that moment, Śakra, the King of Gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, [appeared].
Having known the Bodhisattva’s mind through his celestial wisdom,
he immediately transformed his body into that of a grass-cutter and positioned himself neither too near nor too far from the Bodhisattva.
Standing on the right side,
he cut the grass; that grass was green-fringed.
The color is like that of the neck of a peacock king;
it is soft and lustrous, and when touched by the hand,
it is like a fine Kashi cloth.
The form was exquisite and fragrant, curling to the right in graceful spirals.
The Bodhisattva asked that person,
"O virtuous and benevolent one,"
"What is your name?
That person replied,
"My name is Kṣema."
The Bodhisattva reflects:
"I now desire to seek my own welfare,
and likewise seek the welfare of others."
"This is named Kṣema;
it stands before me.
I shall now certainly attain the realization of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"Can you give me some grass?
The transformed person replied,
"I can give you grass."
At that time, Śakra immediately manifested as a man and offered grass for the Bodhisattva to cut.
The Bodhisattva then took a handful and held it in his own hand.
As he was taking the grass,
the earth immediately shook in six ways;
he then set out with this grass toward the foot of the Bodhi tree.
While he was holding the grass along the road,
there suddenly appeared a hundred blue magpies coming from the ten directions to circumambulate the Bodhisattva to the right.
Having completed three circumambulations,
they followed after the Bodhisattva.
Furthermore, there were five hundred *kucīra* birds.
Furthermore, there were five hundred peacocks, five hundred white geese,
and five hundred swans and cranes.
Furthermore, there were five hundred white gulls; five hundred kalaviṅka birds;
and five hundred jīvajīvaka birds.
Furthermore, there were five hundred white elephants,
each with six tusks,
and five hundred white horses.
The heads and ears were jet black, while the manes and tails were entirely crimson;
they were long and flowing.
Furthermore, there were five hundred bull-kings.
Their necks were all draped with [ornaments] resembling black clouds.
At that time, there were also five hundred boys and five hundred girls,
each adorning their bodies with various kinds of exquisite necklaces.
Furthermore, there were five hundred devaputras, five hundred devakanyās, and five hundred precious vases,
all filled with various fragrant flowers and containing diverse kinds of exquisite perfumed water.
Without anyone to grasp it, it naturally moves through the void.
Furthermore, all auspicious things in the world come raining down from the four directions like clouds.
Each stood to the right of the Bodhisattva;
having circumambulated him three times, they followed the Bodhisattva’s path.
All the celestial musical instruments [resounded].
The joyful songs and praises of the bodhisattvas in the air cannot be fully described. Furthermore,
the *Sūtra on the Original Arising of Auspicious Responses* states:
Śakra-devānām-indra transformed himself into an ordinary person and held some clean, soft grass.
The Bodhisattva asked him:
"What is your name? "My name is Śrī.
Upon hearing this, the Bodhisattva’s heart was filled with great joy.
He destroys inauspiciousness to bring about auspiciousness.
Furthermore, the *Buddhabhāṣita-buddhasamādhi-sūtra* states:
"As soon as he spread the grass for his seat upon the ground, the earth shook violently."
The Buddhas manifested eighty thousand Buddha-trees and lion thrones;
some of these Buddha-trees were eight thousand li high, while others were four thousand li high.
Some are a hundred thousand yojanas high;
all the Buddha-trees are complete in number, eighty thousand,
with varying sizes.
Now, the Śāla tree is the shortest;
various celestial garments are spread upon its top.
Furthermore, the *Buddhabhāṣita-buddhasamādhi-sūtra* states:
The Buddha told his father, the King:
"Just as I departed from the palace city..."
Not far from the city of Gayā, he went to the Aśvattha tree.
At that time, the devaputra Śāntamati and hundreds of thousands of other devaputras all had this thought:
"If the Bodhisattva must have a seat-cloth when sitting here,
I should now offer him the celestial grass.
He then took hold of the celestial grass.
That which is pure and supple is called auspicious.
Having received it, the Bodhisattva spread it upon the ground and sat down.
At that time, the devas...
Furthermore, he saw white hair surrounding [the face] for a span of three inches;
it curled to the right in elegant spirals, possessing hundreds of thousands of colors that flowed into all the marks.
Each of these devaputras then had this thought:
"The Bodhisattva now accepts only my grass;
he does not accept your grass.
At that time, within the white hair, there were ten trillion bodhisattvas sitting in the full lotus posture.
Each took a blade of grass and sat beneath this tree.
Each and every devaputra saw such a sign within the white tuft of hair.
At that time, there was a devaputra.
Her name was Manojñā.
Seeing that grass growing from the earth had pierced the Bodhisattva’s flesh and grown up to his elbow,
she addressed the devaputras, saying:
"How marvelous, O man!
Your asceticism is such that you have not eaten for so long."
He did not hear the call,
nor was he aware that grass had grown;
he then extended his white hair with his right hand.
The tips of those white hairs were straight and exactly one zhang, four chi, and five cun in length;
they were like celestial white jewels, hollow both inside and out.
The devas saw within the hair a billion rays of light;
those rays were so subtle and wondrous that they could not be fully described.
Having seen this, the devas marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.
He immediately released the white hair, which curled to the right and returned to its original place;
at that moment, he subdued Māra.
Māra returned to his celestial palace,
while the white hair followed him all the way to the sixth heaven,
accompanied by countless sons and daughters of the gods.
He saw that the pores of his white hair were all hollow within,
round and lovely like the banner of Brahmā.
The Tathāgata possessed immeasurable marks and signs of excellence.
Within each of these marks, there are eighty-four thousand minor marks and signs;
yet such marks and signs do not equal even a small fraction of the merit of the ūrṇā-kośa (the white tuft of hair between the eyebrows).
7. The Section on Subduing Māra. Regarding the seventh section, "Subduing Māra," the *Nidāna-sūtra* states:
On the seventh day of the fourth month, the World-Honored One subdued Māra.
At that time, the setting sun suspended its radiance and the moon shone with penetrating clarity.
The flowers and fruits in the gardens flourish without waiting for spring.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"At that time, the celestial Māra..."
One hundred and eighty thousand hosts of celestial Māras all came to harass the Buddha;
the Buddha, with a subtle light from between his eyebrows, caused them all to fall away.
Furthermore, the *Buddhanusmṛtisamādhi-sūtra* states:
The Māra King’s heart was filled with rage,
and he was about to advance directly forward when his son remonstrated, saying:
The father king, though innocent, has brought this affliction upon himself.
The Bodhisattva’s conduct is pure and as immovable as the earth;
how could it ever be destroyed?
Furthermore, the *Saṃyukta-ratna-piṭaka-sūtra* states:
In the past, beneath a tree, the evil Māra Pāpīyas led a host of eight billion beings, intending to come and destroy the Buddha.
He then said to the Buddha,
"You are all alone; how can you sit here?"
"You must rise and leave at once. If you do not rise,
I shall seize your feet and hurl you across the sea."
The Buddha said,
"I observe that there is no one in the world capable of hurling me.
In a previous life, you..."
In a past life, he observed the eight precepts for one day at a temple and offered a single bowl of rice to a pratyekabuddha;
consequently, he was reborn in the sixth heaven as a great māra king.
And during my three asaṃkhyeya kalpas,
I have also made offerings to incalculable numbers of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Māra said: "You claim that in the past, for one day, I observed the precepts and gave food to a pratyekabuddha; I believe there is indeed truth in this."
I know this for myself, and you also know me.
As for what you have said yourself, who can serve as a witness to verify it?
The Buddha pointed to the ground with his finger and said,
"This earth bears witness to me.
As he spoke these words, [the earth shook].
The entire great earth shook in six ways.
The Earth Deity immediately emerged from the adamantine foundation and,
with palms joined, addressed the Buddha, saying:
I bear witness to this:
from the time this earth came into being, I have always been present within it.
What the World-Honored One has spoken is true and not false.
The Buddha said to Pāpīyas:
"If you can first move this water jar,
only then will you be able to hurl me beyond the sea."
At that time, Pāpīyān and his assembly of eight billion could not cause him to waver.
The host of Māra’s army fell headlong, shattered and scattered like stars.
Furthermore, the *Buddha-benxing-jing* (Sūtra on the Buddha’s Past Deeds) says:
At that time, the eldest son of Māra Pāpīyān, named Śreṣṭhidāraka,
prostrated with his head at the feet of the Bodhisattva and,
seeking forgiveness, spoke these words:
"O Great and Virtuous Noble Son, please listen as your father confesses his faults and offers his apologies.
I am a foolish and shallow person, like a small child lacking in wisdom;
I have now suddenly come to disturb and trouble you, O Noble Son."
The hosts of Māras manifested various forms to terrify the Noble Son.
Previously, with a loyal and upright heart, I had consulted my father, saying: [Please protect him].
"Even though there are wise men who are skilled in all arts,
they still cannot subdue Prince Siddhārtha;
how much less can we?"
I only pray that the Noble Son will forgive my father.
My father was ignorant and did not understand the principles of right conduct;
thus he terrified the Great Holy Prince.
How shall we receive the Great Sage Prince’s birth?
We pray that what you have vowed may be swiftly fulfilled and that you may quickly realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Section Eight: Attaining Enlightenment. As stated in the *Lalitavistara Sūtra*:
The Bodhisattva sat beneath the tree;
when the morning star appeared, he attained sudden and great enlightenment.
At the age of nineteen, he left the household life.
He attained enlightenment at thirty.
Furthermore, according to the *Prajñāparipṛcchā-śāstra*,
he attained Buddhahood within the Uruvilvā forest.
Furthermore, the *Svayaṃpratijñā-samādhi-sūtra* states:
"When he first attained Buddhahood,
the Buddhas of the ten directions each sent him a kāṣāya robe."
The Buddhas combined them into a single robe,
which is now in the Brahma Heaven where it is venerated.
Furthermore, the *Kongxing sanmei jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of the Sky-Walkers) states:
Amitābha Buddha attained the Way four kalpas before me;
Vipaśyin Buddha attained the Way three kalpas before me;
there was also a Buddha named Nengrou.
Kāśyapa Buddha attained parinirvāṇa at thirty; he attained the Way at eighteen.
I attained the Way at twenty-seven.
Now, taking the majority as definitive:
he left home at nineteen and attained enlightenment at thirty;
this textual account should be accepted as correct.
It is also consistent with other meanings.
The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states:
"On the third day after the moon's appearance, one attains all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñatā*)."
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"When the Buddha first emerged and attained the Way,
it was on the eighth day of the fourth month."
This is now established as the correct version.
Section Nine: Hymns to the Devas. As stated in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*:
"At that time, the Tathāgata, by means of his sovereign spiritual power..."
Without departing from his seat beneath the Bodhi tree, nor from the Palace of Sublime Victory atop Mount Sumeru, nor from the Palace of Jewel Adornments in the Yāma Heaven,
he proceeded to the Palace of All Jewel Adornments in the Tuṣita Heaven.
At that time, the Heavenly King Tuṣita,
empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, spoke in verse:
The Tathāgata Unobstructed is like the full moon; the foremost among all auspicious things, he enters the Hall Adorned with All Jewels. Therefore, this place is most auspicious.
As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
At that time, by the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata,
throughout all Buddha-worlds in the ten directions and across all four continents, [the following occurred].
In each and every Jambudvīpa,
there was a Tathāgata sitting beneath a Bodhi tree,
manifesting without exception.
At that time, by the power of the World-Honored One’s majestic spiritual authority,
he rose from this seat and ascended to the summit of Mount Sumeru toward the palace of Śakra.
Then, Śakra spoke these verses:
The seven Buddhas, Dīpaṃkara, and all other Buddhas—among all auspicious things, they are supreme.
Those Buddhas have previously entered this place; therefore, this ground is most auspicious.
At that time, by the majestic spiritual power of the World-Honored One...
Without leaving the Bodhi tree or the palace of Śakra,
he proceeded toward the Jewel-Adorned Hall in the Yāma Heaven.
At that time, the Heavenly King spoke in verse:
The Tathāgata Renowned Name is heard throughout the ten directions; among all auspicious things, he is supreme.
Having entered the Maṇi-Adorned Palace, this place is therefore most auspicious.
(10) Regarding the Tenth Chapter on the Emanation Division (*nirmāṇa-kula*), according to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*:
O Son of the Buddha,
all Buddhas, in every moment of thought,
are able to give rise to ten kinds of inexhaustible wisdom.
What are the ten? In a single thought-moment, one perceives all worlds and the passing away from the Tuṣita heaven.
Within a single thought-moment,
they manifest the birth of Bodhisattvas throughout all worlds.
Within a single thought-moment,
they manifest the renunciation of all bodhisattvas throughout all worlds.
Within a single thought-moment, they manifest all worlds;
they proceed to the site of enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree and attain perfect awakening.
Within a single thought-moment, they manifest all worlds.
They turn the pure wheel of Dharma;
within a single thought-moment, they manifest throughout all worlds, guiding all sentient beings according to their needs and causing them all to attain liberation.
Within a single thought-moment, they do so throughout all worlds.
Manifesting adorned bodies in accordance with sentient beings,
within a single thought-moment,
they fully manifest all the various adornments and countless ornaments of all worlds— the sovereign power of the Tathāgata, the treasury of omniscience.
Within a single thought-moment, they manifest all pure sentient beings in all worlds;
within a single thought-moment, they pervade all worlds and manifest all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
Within a single thought-moment, for the sake of the various faculties, diligence, and dispositions of sentient beings,
they manifest the lineage of all Buddhas of the three periods of time,
attain equal and perfect enlightenment, and guide and instruct living beings.
O Son of the Buddha,
this is how all Buddhas generate ten inexhaustible knowledges in every moment of thought. Furthermore,
the *Dazhidu lun* (Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom) states:
As stated in the Abhidharma:
"At one time, there are no two minds.
This refers to when the emanated Buddha speaks.
The master of the transformation remains silent.
If the master of the transformation speaks,
the manifested Buddha should likewise remain silent.
Question: Why does the Buddha at one time teach all six pāramitās simultaneously?
Answer: This is merely a transformation [displayed] for the sake of non-Buddhists and śrāvakas.
Just as the Buddha’s power of transformation and immeasurable samādhis are inconceivable,
so too when the Buddha speaks himself,
immeasurable thousands of millions of billions of transformed Buddhas also speak simultaneously.
Furthermore, he told the non-Buddhists and the śrāvakas:
"An emanation cannot create another emanation,
unlike the Buddha, the World-Honored One, who can create emanations from his own emanations."
Therefore, the various non-Buddhists and śrāvakas are unable to leave behind emanations after their death,
unlike the Buddha, who, after his parinirvāṇa, was able to leave behind emanations that were no different from himself.
As it is stated in the Abhidharma that there are not two minds at one time,
so it is now with the Buddha as well.
When speaking through transformation,
there is likewise no mind;
the Buddha’s mind contemplates the transformation.
If one wishes to cause them to speak through transformation, they will all immediately speak.

Section Thirteen: The Exposition of the Dharma (11). This section is divided into three parts: the Exposition of Intent, the Discernment of Capacities, and the Exposition of Benefits. Part One: The Exposition of Intent. First, the Exposition of Intent. I have heard that:
The Great Sage adapts his teachings to the capacities of beings, his traces appearing without fixed direction; wherever he manifests, it is invariably for the benefit of others.
Therefore, one must clearly distinguish between the ultimate and conventional truths, so that matters may be resolved and form and mind brought into accord.
Relying on the provisional and the real, one ascends toward the ultimate;
entrusting oneself to the power of skillful means, one descends to accord with the mundane.
This is truly because of birth, old age, sickness, and death.
There will never be a time when one emerges from it on one's own;
yet regarding Bodhi and Nirvana,
there can be the realization attained through cultivation and entry.
However, the internal scriptures (Āgama) are boundless;
they are taught according to the capacities of sentient beings.
Thus, the Wheel of Dharma was first turned in the Jeta Grove.
As for the monks, Kauṇḍinya was the first to be converted;
as for Kāśyapa’s brothers and Maudgalyāyana’s friends,
they were the great leaders of the Western Regions.
Proclamation throughout the East:
To the lords of the twenty-eight heavens and the kings of the sixteen kingdoms.
There was none who did not submit to the Way, inclining their hearts toward it, or who did not partake of its breeze and join their palms in reverence.
Thus, within the Palace of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations,
he laid out the Ten Stages.
On the summit of Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, the three vehicles were assembled;
Subhūti expounded the principle of non-attainment,
and Vimalakīrti revealed the purport of the ineffable.
He subdued the non-Buddhist practitioners of the Ten Immortals and restrained the group of six bhikṣus;
from his chest, he could exhale and inhale the great rivers.
If held in the palm, it would cause the mountains and valleys to tremble;
if discussed in terms of kalpas, even square stones would be exhausted;
if analyzed through calculation, even atoms could be fully enumerated.
This is truly the Great Master of the Three Realms,
the peerless figure of all ages;
how could one of my mediocre talents hope to exhaustively describe him?
Even granted that the Duke of Zhou established the rites and music,
Confucius expounded the *I Ching* and edited the *Shi Jing*,
and that the Duke of Yu and the Marquis of Cai excelled in speech.
As for the literary works of Shang Yan,
as well as those of Zuo Yuanfang, Ge Xianzi, Lao Dan, He Shanggong, Zhuang Zhou, and their peers,
they were all confined within the narrow bounds of the mundane world.
What need is there to speak further?
As for my Master’s Great Dharma,
it is the model for humans and devas, and the standard for the three thousand modes of conduct.
When it reached the Central Lands of China, its benefits became even more profound and far-reaching;
it extensively treated the three poisons and transmitted the illumination of a hundred lamps in an uninterrupted succession.
How can it be fully described?
Section Two: On the Responsive Mechanism (*pratītya-kāraṇa*). As stated in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*:
"When the Tathāgata appears in the world..."
For example, when the sun rises, it first illuminates all the great kings of mountains;
next, it illuminates all the great mountains;
and finally, it illuminates the diamond-jewel mountains.
Thereafter, it universally illuminates the entire earth.
Yet the sun does not form this thought:
"I shall first illuminate the great mountains and only later illuminate the earth."
Because mountains have heights and depths, their illumination occurs in succession;
the Tathāgata is likewise:
he saves all universally and with equanimity.
However, because capacities vary between sharp and dull, and the timing of their response to the Buddha differs— whether before or after his parinirvāṇa—
their perceptions and hearing differ, resulting in distinctions between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
According to the Mahīśāsaka Vinaya, it says:
After the Buddha had attained the Way for seven days and was enjoying the bliss of liberation,
five hundred chariots carrying rock honey, traveling from foreign lands on a journey of trade,
passed by the tree.
The two brothers who were the owners of the chariot were named Nanda and Upananda;
they were the first to offer honey and parched grain.
The Four Kings offered the bowl;
having accepted it, the Buddha preached the Three Refuges for them.
Furthermore, after another seven days, the Dragon King Wenlin (Varuṇa) [offered a bowl].
He offered food to non-human beings.
After seven days had passed, Senaka offered food,
and the four sisters received the three refuges.
After another seven days had passed, the Brahmā King came to request that the Wheel of Dharma be turned.
Furthermore, the *Lalitavistara Sūtra* states:
"At that time, the Brahmā King, together with a retinue of sixty-eight thousand Brahmā kings, came to the place where the Buddha was."
He prostrated at his feet and requested him to turn the Wheel of Dharma.
Having accepted the request,
the Buddha said, "In my past lives, while in Vārāṇasī, I made offerings to six hundred billion Buddhas."
"The Wheel of Dharma should be turned here.
Because he contemplated the tree for seven days to repay its kindness,
he has not yet preached the Dharma."

Regarding the miraculous escape of the stone image from a fire at Panyu during the Jianyuan era of the Qi dynasty: in the Jianyuan period of the Qi, there was an old stone image from the kingdom of Funan in the Viyali Vihāra at Panyu. When the monastery caught fire, the image miraculously rose up lightly. It is said that when the flames reached the image, it suddenly ascended several *zhang* into the air; those who witnessed it were filled with awe. Da’an woke up in alarm and called for the slave.
Those among them who did not rebel had their slaves attempt to draw their blades.

Suddenly, as if in a dream,

Da'an said, "I do not eat pork."

for this reason, the mountain is so extremely cold that no other trees grow there.

He asked again:

What is this matter? The answer is as follows:
This was indeed true and beyond doubt.
King Aśoka’s fourth daughter had an unrefined appearance; though she had been with him for a long time, she had not yet borne a child, and she constantly lamented her own ugliness.

"The statue at Mount Yuhua in Jingzhou, the one at Changsha, the one at Yangdu by Gao Kui, and the image at Chongjing Temple in the capital—

Some have inscribed his halo and pedestal;

King Aśoka, having brought forth this image,

Toward the end of the Western Jin dynasty, the Five Hu rose up in great numbers,

Compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Daoshi of Ximing Monastery. Chapter Six, Part Three: Devotion to the Buddha. Section Four: Amitābha. This section is divided into six parts:

1. The Amitābha Section (15). Sub-section One: Exposition of Intent; Sub-section Two: Collation of Names; Sub-section Three: Discernment of Place; Sub-section Four: The Capable Seer; Sub-section Five: Karmic Causes; Sub-section Six: Citation of Scriptural Evidence. Sub-section One: Exposition of Intent. First, regarding the exposition of intent: Now, all beings seek pleasure and avoid suffering.
This is the natural sentiment of all things;
to loathe the turbid and rejoice in the pure is the ancient principle of all living beings.
It is simply because conduct has its beauty and its evil that lands become coarse or sublime.
In the Sahā world, there are five kinds of suffering;
these arise from the accumulation of evil, which creates mounds and pits.
The seven treasures are perfected in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing; through the cultivation of goodness, the land flourishes in excellence.
Karma is categorized into three grades, and its retribution is divided into nine levels.
Jeweled terraces and rare pavilions stand loftily through the power of sublime contemplation;
jade ponds and crystal lakes [reflect their splendor].
Relying on a virtuous mind, it is pure and bright;
as the flowers bloom and the lotus closes,
one verifies that the Compassionate Father’s words were not in vain.
As the waves surge and the ripples turn back,
the words of the Dharma remain ringing in one's ears.
This could not have been achieved were it not for diligent effort, firm resolve, perfected conduct, and the fullness of causes.
How could one follow a thousand thoughts to ascend the golden terrace, or rely on ten recitations to rise to the Land of Bliss?
Section Two: Explaining the Name of the Assembly. It is stated:
The world is bright and pure;
it is designated as "pure," and it is that which the pure inhabit.
It is therefore called "land.
Thus, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
"The land where one dwells is free from the five turbidities."
Just as crystal and the like are called pure lands,
the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra-śāstra* states:
"The dwelling place of sentient beings free from afflictions is called a pure land."
There are four different types of Pure Lands.
First, the Land of Dharmatā,
which takes True Suchness (tathatā) as its essence.
Therefore, the *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra) of the Liang dynasty states:
"The Lotus King is taken as the basis of the Pure Land,
because it serves as an analogy for the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) and True Suchness (*tathatā*), which constitute the essential substance upon which the Pure Land relies."
Second is the land of true recompense (*sambhoga-kāya*).
According to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*,
it takes the two kinds of emptiness as its gateway.
The three types of wisdom serve as the path for entering and exiting; śamatha and vipaśyanā serve as the vehicle;
and fundamental non-conceptual wisdom serves as the function.
These all define the essential substance [of the Pure Land] by way of its retributive merit;
that is, the three types of pure lands consist of the most exquisite seven treasures.
These five sense objects—form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch—constitute the characteristics of that land.
Therefore, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* states:
"It is the realm of the Buddha’s pervasive radiance, composed of the seven jewels."
Furthermore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"The marks of the realm of all Buddhas are adorned with various intermingled ornaments.
Thus, the *Treatise on the Pure Land* says:
It is replete with all kinds of rare treasures and possesses exquisite, inherent adornments.
Furthermore, the newly translated *Mahābodhisattvapiṭaka Sūtra* states:
"Suppose there were worlds such as these..."
Even if a great fire were blazing intensely and the Tathāgata were in its midst—
whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down.
In that place, water of eight meritorious qualities naturally appears from the earth.
As for the four transformed pure lands (nirmāṇa-kṣetra),
these refer to the bodies of the transformed lands created by the Buddha, consisting of the five sensory objects made of the seven jewels.
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"By the Buddha’s spiritual power, the ground becomes entirely soft and supple,
free from mounds, hollows, soil, sand, gravel, or stones."
This extends even to being like the world of Sukhāvatī of the Buddha Amitāyus in the western quarter.
Furthermore, the *Mahālaṃkāra-śāstra* states:
"By mastery over wisdom, one acts according to whatever is desired."
It can manifest pure worlds such as those made of crystal and lapis lazuli.
Furthermore, the Vimalakīrti Sūtra states that the Buddha pressed the earth with his toe, thereby manifesting purity and other such wonders.
Furthermore, the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* states:
"In order to manifest [himself] according to what sentient beings desire to see in their minds."
What is elucidated in these various sūtras and śāstras is all explained in terms of transformation into a pure land;
it exists because it is manifested through the Buddha’s supernormal power.
Because it is subsumed [within that], it is non-existent;
therefore, it is called a "transformed land" (*nirmāṇa-kṣetra*).
3. Section on Distinguishing the Locations. Third, the section on distinguishing the locations states:
Although it has been explained above that there are four kinds of lands,
the essential points are twofold: first,
the land of retribution (vipākabhūmi).
Second, the transformation lands (*nirmāṇa-kṣetra*). These two comprise both the land of principle (*li*) and the land of phenomena (*shi*).
First, regarding the retribution land (*vipāka-kṣetra*):
This means that the various wholesome entities of the Buddha-Tathāgata’s appearance in the world are untainted (*anāsrava*),
because they are not subsumed within the three realms. As the *Jingtu lun* (Treatise on the Pure Land) states:
Contemplating the characteristics of that world, it surpasses the paths of the triple realm (*tridhātu*). Furthermore, the *Dazhidu lun* (Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom) states:
"There is a wondrous pure land that transcends the triple realm."
However, the Buddha’s dwelling is a non-place that serves as a place;
it transcends the worlds of the ten directions,
or he establishes pure lands based upon the Dharma-body.
Therefore, the treatise states:
"Śākyamuni Buddha further possesses pure worlds such as the land of Amitābha."
That Amitābha Buddha likewise possesses both pure and impure worlds, just as Śākyamuni Buddha does.
Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"I have, in truth, never departed from the realm of Jambudvīpa."
Furthermore, a verse from the Lotus Sūtra says:
"Always dwelling on Vulture Peak Mountain And at other various abodes,
While sentient beings see the end of the kalpa When it is consumed by the great fire."
My land here is peaceful and secure, Constantly filled with devas and humans;
Its gardens, groves, and various halls Are adorned with all kinds of jewels.
Furthermore, the *Huayan jing* (Avataṃsaka Sūtra) says:
The Tathāgata’s pure land may be within the Tathāgata’s jeweled crown,
or it may be within his ear-ornaments.
Sometimes they appear on necklaces,
sometimes in the patterns of garments,
and sometimes within the pores of the skin.
Since worlds are thus contained within a single pore,
we know that the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"When the Buddha takes a single step, he passes through as many trichiliocosms as there are grains of sand in the Ganges."
Regarding the knowledge of that matter:
as for the location of the transformed land (*nirmāṇa-kṣetra*), there is no distinct spatial direction or place where the transformed land resides.
However, based on the land of retribution, coarse characteristics arise;
these may extend throughout the ten directions or be confined to their own realm.
Just as the World-Honored One Amitābha leads forth the multitudes of the three vehicles, including devas and humans,
so too does he lead forth the ordinary and Hinayana beings of this Sahā world and establish them in the Pure Land.
Or, they may manifest purity within impurity, such as when pressing upon the earth manifests it as pure;
this matter is like a celestial palace.
Or, [they manifest it] within the world-receptacle that is shared by sentient beings.
The seeds that are experienced manifest as pure or impure realms therein;
according to the six destinies, each perceives them differently.
All of this arises from the external perfuming of names and expressions (*nāma-vyavahāra*).
Due to the maturation of the seeds of consciousness, the receptacle world is accomplished and its reflected images appear;
these reflected images are the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) of the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*).
Due to the seeds of common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) and the appearance of images,
that consciousness appearing as such serves as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*); this very [consciousness] is the common characteristic.

By the dominant condition of internal retribution, that is, through the power of this common characteristic as a dominant condition of internal retribution, such differences between suffering and pleasure are brought about. 4.
Section on the Capable Seer (Dṛṣṭivāda). Fourth, it is stated:
Just as ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles see Amitābha Buddha within a defiled land,
so too do the various bodhisattvas and others see Amitābha Buddha within a pure land.
According to these two views,
the land of retribution is exclusively pure,
whereas the land of response is both defiled and pure.
Therefore, the *Jingtu lun* (Treatise on the Pure Land) states:
"There are five kinds of lands.
First is the purely pure land."
It exists only in the fruit of Buddhahood.
Second, regarding pure and impure lands:
this means that purity is predominant while impurity is minimal.
This refers to the stages from the eighth bhūmi upward.
Regarding the three types of lands— pure, impure, and intermediate—
it refers to the period from the first bhūmi up to the seventh bhūmi.
Fourth is the impure-pure land, meaning that where impurity predominates and purity is slight; this refers to the stage of the nature-ground prior to the [ten] stages.
Fifth is the mixed-impure land.
That is to say, those who have not yet entered the stage of the spiritual lineage (gotrabhūmi):
the fifth person perceives the latter one but does not perceive the former four;
the fourth person perceives the latter two but does not perceive the former three.
The third person sees the latter three [stages] but does not see the former two;
the second person sees the latter four but does not see the first one;
the first Buddha knows and sees all five stages, both above and below.
Section Five: The Causes of Karma. The commentary states:
Ten different explanations are cited from the sūtras and śāstras;
some state that one is born in the Pure Land through a single practice.
As stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*:
"The King of the country of Yuedi and the bhikṣu Juede,
due to their causes and conditions for protecting the Dharma, were reborn in the Land of Immovability."
Furthermore, the Vimalakīrti Sūtra states: "A straightforward mind is the pure land of a bodhisattva.
When the bodhisattva attains buddhahood, sentient beings who are free from flattery will come to be born in his land," and so forth.
Or it is said that one is born in the Pure Land through two practices.
As the Liang Dynasty *She lun* states:
"Supramundane wholesome dharmas..."

The roots of goodness produced by non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) and subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) serve as the cause for supramundane wholesome dharmas; alternatively,
they take meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) as their vehicle.
Alternatively, it is taught that one is born in the Pure Land through the three practices.
As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"By contemplating the three samādhis—emptiness (*śūnyatā*), wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), and signlessness (*animitta*)—one is born in the Pure Land."
Furthermore, the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra* states:
"To cause all ordinary beings of the future to be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss,
one should cultivate the three karmas."
First, filially supporting one's parents, serving one's teacher, refraining from killing, and practicing the ten wholesome actions;
second, receiving the three refuges, fully observing the various precepts, and not violating the rules of dignified conduct.
Third, to resolve for bodhicitta with deep faith in cause and effect,
to read and recite Mahāyāna sūtras, and to exhort practitioners to advance—
these three matters are called pure karma.
Alternatively, it is taught that one is born in the Pure Land by practicing the four modes of conduct.
As the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* states:
"Practicing the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*) is the bodhisattva’s pure land."
When a Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood,
sentient beings who possess loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity will come to be born in his land;
alternatively, the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) constitute the Bodhisattva’s pure land.
That is to say, generosity, kind speech, beneficial action,
and cooperation are the buddha-field of a bodhisattva. When that bodhisattva attains buddhahood, [these qualities will become his field].
Sentient beings who are embraced by liberation come to be born in that land;
alternatively, it is said that one is born in the Pure Land through the five practices, as stated in the *Jingtu lun* (Treatise on the Pure Land): [text follows].
First is prostration;
second is praise;
third is making aspirations.
Fourth is contemplation;
fifth is dedication.
Alternatively, it is said that one is born in the Pure Land through six practices.
As the Vimalakīrti Sūtra says:
"Generosity is the pure land of a bodhisattva.
When the bodhisattva attains buddhahood,"
All sentient beings who are able to practice relinquishment will come to be born in that land;
even wisdom is a pure land of a bodhisattva. When the bodhisattva attains buddhahood, [these qualities will manifest].
"All beings of wisdom who come to be born in that land," and so forth;
or it is said that one is born in the Pure Land through seven practices,
as stated in the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*:
They spread seven kinds of pure flowers to bathe this stainless person.
First is purity of precepts;
second is purity of concentration.
Third is purity of vision;
fourth is purity of overcoming doubt;
fifth is purity regarding what is the path and what is not the path.
Sixth is the purity of conduct;
seventh is the purity of the knowledge of the abandonment of conduct.
The former two constitute the path of expedient means.
The next three constitute the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*);
the next one constitutes the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*);
and the final one constitutes the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*).
Through these seven purities, the four paths are accomplished;
since the four paths are accomplished, one is reborn in the Pure Land as a reward.
Alternatively, it is said that one is born in the Pure Land by means of the eight practices.
As the Vimalakīrti Sūtra states:
"By accomplishing how many dharmas does a bodhisattva act without blemish in this world and be born in a pure land?
The answer says:
One achieves birth in the Pure Land by accomplishing eight dharmas.
First, to benefit sentient beings without expecting recompense,
and to undergo various sufferings and afflictions on behalf of sentient beings.
Second, they dedicate all the merit they have performed to others.
Third, they treat sentient beings with an impartial mind, remaining humble and free from obstruction.
Fourth, they regard all bodhisattvas as they would the Buddha.
Fifth, hearing sutras never heard before, one does not doubt them.
Sixth, one does not contradict the śrāvakas.
Seventh, one does not envy the offerings received by others nor exalt one's own benefit.
Within this, one should discipline the mind:
eighth, constantly examining one's own faults and not proclaiming the shortcomings of others;
always seeking all merits with a single-minded focus.
Some say that one is born in the Pure Land through nine practices, as stated in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*:
"Briefly, there are three grades; in detail, there are nine classes," as fully explained in the sūtra. Others say that one is born in the Pure Land through ten practices.
As the Vimalakīrti Sūtra states:
"The ten wholesome paths of action are the pure land of a bodhisattva.
When the bodhisattva attains buddhahood,"
One's life shall not be cut short; one will possess great wealth and practice the holy life.
One's words will be truthful and always gentle.
One’s kin and followers will not be separated, and one will skillfully reconcile disputes and litigation.
Their speech is invariably beneficial, free from envy and anger;
beings with right view are born in their land.
Furthermore, the *Maitreya-paripṛcchā-sūtra* states:
If one wishes to be born in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī),
one should practice the ten recollections and will immediately attain rebirth there.
What are these ten?
There are ten:
first, one should constantly give rise to a mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings;
second, one should not disparage the conduct of any sentient being.
If there are those who disparage [this], they shall never attain rebirth there.
Third, one should deeply give rise to compassion for all sentient beings and eliminate any intent to harm them.
Fourth, one should resolve to protect the Dharma, not begrudging even one's own body or life.
Fifth, they do not give rise to slander regarding any phenomena.
Sixth, they develop a mind of certainty within patience.
Seventh, their profound mind is pure and untainted by gain and honor.
Seventh, one should give rise to the mind of omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā-citta*) and constantly maintain mindfulness of it day after day without neglect or forgetfulness.
Eighth, one should conceive a heart of respect toward all sentient beings,
eliminating arrogance and speaking with humility.
Ninth, one does not give rise to defiled attachment toward various conversations;
with a mind close to awakening, one deeply cultivates the causes and conditions for various roots of goodness and does not produce a distracted or agitated mind.
Tenth, one should constantly mindfully contemplate the Buddha and eliminate all signs.
Maitreya, you should know that these are the ten recollections.
They arise one after another in continuous succession;
it is impossible that they would not be born in that land.
Alternatively, it is said that the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment constitute the pure land of a bodhisattva.
When the Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood,
sentient beings who possess the foundations of mindfulness, right efforts, bases of psychic power, faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, and the noble path will come to be born in his land;
or as it is said in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*:

Having made the forty great vows, one is born in the Pure Land; although the explanations given above differ in their detail, if one practices even a single dharma in accordance with the principle, one will attain rebirth in the Land of Peace and Bliss. As the verse in the *Upadeśa-śāstra* says:
Contemplating the characteristics of that world, which surpasses the paths of the three realms and is as utterly exhaustive as space— vast, without limit,
the true path of great compassion, born from the roots of goodness that transcend the world.
"Purified radiance is complete, like the disks of a mirror, the sun, and the moon.
Commentary: This refers to the pure land of actual retribution.
One must cultivate the supramundane, untainted correct cause;
only when this accords with the principles of practice can one attain rebirth.
If one is of inferior capacity and lacks the fundamental correct karma, [rebirth cannot be achieved].
If one practices even a single method,
or if the ten recitations are accomplished at the moment of death,
one will surely be reborn in a Land of Transformation; however, one will not yet be able to see the Land of Ultimate Reward.
The visualization methods are fully described in the ten-fascicle *Dhyāna-gate of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna*.
Section Six: Citing Scriptural Evidence. From the *Amitābha-drum-sound-king-dhāraṇī-sūtra*: [text follows]
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"In the western direction, there is currently a Buddha in the world-realm of Sukhāvatī, named Amitābha."
If there are members of the fourfold assembly who can correctly receive and uphold the name of that Buddha,
by virtue of this merit, when they are about to pass away,
Amitābha will come with his great assembly to that person's place and cause them to behold him.
Having seen this, he immediately gives rise to joy and his merit increases manifold.
By virtue of these causes and conditions, in whatever place he is born,
he will forever be free from the impure form of the womb and from carnal desire.
They are spontaneously born within pure and exquisite lotus flowers of rare jewels,
endowed with the six supernormal powers and radiant brilliance.
Amitābha Buddha is there together with his śrāvakas.
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha resides there;
his kingdom is named Qingtai (Pure Peace),
where the Holy King dwells.
That city is ten thousand yojanas in length and breadth,
and it is filled with members of the Kṣatriya caste.
Amitābha Buddha’s father was the noble Cakravartin King named Candracchattra.
His mother was named Viśeṣacāritramukhā;
his son was named Candraprabha;

As they received and carried him toward the funeral pyre for interment,
the characters "Puguang Tang" (Hall of Universal Radiance) and others appeared spontaneously upon his feet.
He returned and sent [the remains] to the cave he had excavated at Hanling Mountain;
after spring had passed, they remained undecayed, and his seated posture was as firm as it was at the beginning.
Furthermore, on the night he ascended the lecture hall...
At that time, it was dark and gloomy, with no lamps or candles at all;
when he raised his palm high to show it,
a wondrous light suddenly emanated.
The hall was brilliantly illuminated.
The great assembly, beholding this auspicious marvel, wondered from where it originated.
Daowang said:
This light is constantly present within his hands;
what is there to marvel at?
Were it not for one who has personally attained the Way through the numinous scriptures and whose practice of talismans borders on that of the sages, how could this be?
How could such auspicious responses as these have been manifested?
The Tang Dynasty śramaṇa Shanzhou— Shi Shanzhou of Jingying Monastery in the Western Capital of the Tang—
was a native of Yingzhou.
He was well-versed in the sutras and śāstras, specializing particularly in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.
In the art of discourse and spiritual awakening, he was foremost in the land.
He reached the age of seventy-one.
At the onset of his illness, as he approached the end of his life, he said to his disciples:
"Throughout my life, I have maintained right faith in my heart;
regarding the principles and teachings of the Buddha, I never had the slightest thought of neglect or disregard."
Without even considering whether he would be reborn in the Pure Land,
[the master] immediately had the rooms swept and cleaned, burned incense, and waited with solemn reverence.
The patient had been ill for many days, lying prostrate and unable to rise.
Suddenly, sitting down by himself, he joined his palms and said to his attendant,
"Arrange for the World-Honored One to be seated," and added,
"The World-Honored One has arrived."
The youth now repented with shame and remorse.
After a long while, he said,
"The World-Honored One has departed."
He lowered his body as if to see her off.
Then, lying down, he said,
"Just now, Amitābha Buddha came."
"Do you not see? Before long, I shall depart.
Having spoken these words, he passed away instantly.
These three accounts of verification are extracted from the *Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Tang Dynasty*.
