2. Maitreya Section (16). Chapter Six, Part Four: Reverence for the Buddha. Maitreya Section, Part Five. This section is divided into five parts:

Expressing the Intent, Receiving the Precepts, Praising, Karmic Causes, and Making Vows. 1. Expressing the Intent. First, Expressing the Intent: Only the Great Awakened One, the Hero of the World, benefits sentient beings according to their capacities.
He skillfully manifested the teachings of expedient means to rescue those in urgent need of the future; yet now,
as the final age has passed, life is as fragile as a candle in the wind.
To seek the essential benefit of sentient beings, there is no better way than to see the Buddha;
for this is the final instruction left by the World-Honored One Śākyamuni: that those who practice within my Dharma [should do so].
He entrusted Maitreya with this so that he might awaken to the fruits of sagehood;
the Great Sage’s earnestness is firm and surely not false.
To encounter [the teaching] for even a single thought-moment prevents one from being forever separated by the four currents of existence.
He formed sublime vows amidst the Flower Forest;
he was moved by the compassionate countenance in Tuṣita Heaven.
Able to strike the hidden mechanism, the clouds and dragon met in harmony.
Therefore, the *Ūrdhvamśa-jātaka-sūtra* states:
"All these people have planted various roots of goodness within the Dharma;
Śākyamuni Buddha has sent them here to entrust them to me."
Reflecting on these words, it is indeed truly worthy of prayer.
This sutra first began to be transmitted from the end of the Jin dynasty;
by the time the Song dynasty flourished, this assembly was inaugurated.
He manifested a majestic form a thousand feet high and modeled it after the Way-tree of ten-thousand fathoms;
offerings were prepared in the Upper Garden as the great assembly gathered like scales of fish.
Thereupon, the fourfold assembly rejoiced with devotion and propagated the teachings extensively;
every year, on auspicious days, the three assemblies were held without fail.
Since the Qi dynasty took control of the calendar, the conditions for the Dharma have expanded and flourished.
The Emperor Wenxuan propagated virtue and instruction, encompassing this great undertaking.
Since that time, however, grand assemblies have rarely been convened and practitioners have become few and far between;
even those who do engage in study lack the method for settling the mind.
I now compile these various sutras so that you may rely upon them for practice.
I hope that by attaining the Eightfold Noble Path, [the Dharma] will be arrayed in splendor within the Purple Palace;
and that as the transformation of the Ten Wholesome Deeds flows forth, it will shine brilliantly throughout Tuṣita Heaven.
The merit covers those born in later ages, and the benefit is equal for the first assembly.
Part Two: The Section on Receiving Precepts. It is stated:
If one is a layperson in the household who has not yet received the precepts...
First, one receives the Three Refuges for the Reversal of Heresy;
this is received at any time during the six periods of each day to manifest refuge in the Triple Gem.
One should vow not to turn back, for one will certainly attain rebirth in the higher realms.
If one belongs to the fivefold monastic community and has already received the precepts,
one need only rely upon their practice.
There is no need to receive it separately;
yet if one lacks preceptual conduct and merely pursues empty recollections of goodness,
rebirth [in that realm] will likewise not be attained.
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"I, [Name], for as long as life shall last, take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṃgha. Thus it is recited three times. "I, [Name], have completed taking refuge in the Buddha for as long as life shall last."
The taking of refuge in the Dharma is completed.
The taking of refuge in the Saṃgha is completed. Thus it is said three times. Furthermore, in the *Garbhāvakrānti-sūtra*, the Buddha addressed Maitreya in verse, saying:
Those in your three assemblies are those whom I previously transformed—
nine hundred and sixty million people who received my five precepts,
followed by nine hundred and twenty million people who received the three refuges.
"By reciting 'Namo Buddha' even once, all shall attain the Way of the Buddha.
Commentary: This extensively clarifies the power and efficacy of the Three Refuges.
This is as fully explained in the three fascicles of the *Gongyang lun* (Treatise on Reverence and Merit).
Having already received the Three Refuges,
one must next receive the dharma of the ten wholesome precepts.
If one does not practice the ten wholesome actions,
one will certainly not attain rebirth in the higher realms;
therefore, one should fully cultivate proper deportment.
Approaching a renunciant, one should admonish one's own mind and perform a sincere repentance;
thereafter, one receives [the precepts], saying:
"I, [Name], for as long as life lasts..."
Toward all sentient beings, without discriminating between high and low or ordinary and noble, I shall not give rise to the intent to kill.
Thus, up to the tenth [vow]:
I, [Name], for as long as life lasts.
"Regarding all sentient beings, high and low, without discriminating between ordinary persons and noble ones, I shall not give rise to wrong views"—
thus he says three times. "I, [Name], for as long as life lasts,
regarding all sentient beings, high and low, without discriminating between ordinary persons and noble ones, shall never again give rise to the intent to kill."

"Up to the tenth [vow], I, [Name], for as long as life lasts, shall not give rise to wrong views regarding any sentient being—whether superior or inferior, ordinary or noble. Having thus recited this three times, these ten wholesome precepts prevent the three physical transgressions of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct.
The four verbal transgressions are false speech, frivolous speech, divisive speech, and harsh speech;
the three mental transgressions are greed, malice, and wrong view.
These constitute the ten [unwholesome paths of action].
This is the root of all virtues.
To abide [in it] is to maintain;
to act [against it] is to transgress.
Violating these constitutes the root of the ten evils and the calamity of ten thousand misfortunes.
Section Three: Praise. As stated in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-sūtra* (The Sutra on the Original Acts of the Bodhisattva):
Even if one were to transform countless billions of people into pratyekabuddhas,
and someone were to provide them with the four requisites for a hundred years,
their merit would be exceedingly great.
It is not as good as someone, with a heart of joy, praising the immeasurable merits of the Tathāgata with a single four-line verse.
Furthermore, as the *Sukhavihāra-sūtra* states:
"To offer the treasures of the four continents to the Buddha..."
Furthermore, the merit of praising the Tathāgata with a sincere heart is equal to these two [other merits], without any distinction.
Moreover, the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra* states:
Whoever utters the name "Namo Buddha" once,
by virtue of this root of goodness, shall enter the realm of nirvana and never exhaust it.
Furthermore, if one can recollect the merits of the Buddha with a heart of utmost sincerity, [the same result shall be attained].
Even for one who scatters but a single flower into the air,
their merit shall not be exhausted throughout the future ages of all the devas and Brahmā kings.
Because they do not reach the ultimate end of nirvana.
Furthermore, in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*,
Kāśyapa praised the Buddha with a verse, saying:
Out of great compassion for sentient beings, you cause me to take refuge;
Because you have skillfully extracted the arrows of all poisons, you are called the Great King of Physicians.
The treatments administered by worldly physicians, though they may bring recovery, lead to illness arising once again.
That which was treated by the Tathāgata never arises again;
the World-Honored One bestows the ambrosial medicine upon all sentient beings,
and once they have taken it, they neither die nor are they born.
The Tathāgata now expounds for me the Great Nirvāṇa;
when sentient beings hear this secret treasury, they immediately attain the state of neither arising nor ceasing.
Furthermore, from the Mahāvaipulya Dhāraṇī Sūtra:
At that time, the Bodhisattva Puṣpaketu praised the Buddha, saying:
"The World-Honored One’s body and color are like a mountain of gold;
Like the light of the sun illuminating the world, you are able to uproot all suffering and affliction. I now prostrate myself before the Great Dharma King."

The Lord of the World, the Dharma King, is most rare; such a wondrous Dharma as this is even more difficult to see, difficult to hear, and difficult to encounter. Should anyone behold it, they shall attain perfect enlightenment.
At that time, the Asura praised the Buddha with these verses.
The World-Honored One’s countenance is like the sun and moon, Able to extinguish all darkness;
Now he further delivers us— We take refuge in the Honored One among Gods.
In the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra*, Mañjuśrī spoke these verses in praise of the Buddha:
I pay homage to all Buddhas, the peerless Tamer of men,
whose true Dharma-body is sixteen cubits tall; I also pay homage to the Buddha-stūpas at the place of birth,
the place of attaining the Way, the place of turning the Wheel of Dharma, and the place of Parinirvāṇa.
Whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, I pay homage to all of them.
The Buddhas are inconceivable; the wondrous Dharma is likewise so.
Those who can believe in it, as well as those who grasp its fruits, are also inconceivable.
Whoever is able to praise the Tathāgata with this geya shall not fall into any of the evil realms for thousands of millions of billions of kalpas.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Mañjuśrī, excellent, excellent!
The Tathāgata is inconceivable.
Then he spoke these verses:
The Buddha was born of the Ikṣvāku clan; Once extinguished, he is not born again.
If a person takes refuge in the Buddha, They shall not fear the suffering of hell. Thus it was said three times.
Furthermore, a verse from the Avataṃsaka Sūtra says:
"Better to endure all suffering Than to receive all pleasure Without hearing the name of the Buddha."
Therefore, for immeasurable kalpas, they have endured these various sufferings while transmigrating within birth and death, because they did not hear the name of the Buddha.
Furthermore, the *Maitreya-paripṛcchā-pūrvapraṇidhāna-sūtra* states:
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"It is not only now that Maitreya praises me with verses.
In the past, ten incalculable kalpas ago,"
At that time, there was a Buddha named King of Flaming Radiance and Resounding Action (Jvalanaprabhā-nirghoṣakārakarāja Tathāgata).
Among all the brahmins and householders [there],...
His name was Bhadrapāla.
Under this Buddha, he had already attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
At that time, the brahmin Bhadrapāla...
"This is none other than the present Bodhisattva Maitreya.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying,
"It has been so long since Maitreya attained the patience of the Dharma (dharmanidhyānakṣānti)!"
"Why do you not swiftly attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path and achieve supreme perfect enlightenment?
The Buddha said to Ānanda,
"A bodhisattva does not take up perfect enlightenment by means of four dharmas."
What are the four?
First, purifying the land;
second, protecting the land.
Third, purifying all;
fourth, protecting all.
These are the four matters.
When Maitreya was originally seeking Buddhahood,
he did not accept it for four reasons.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
When I originally sought Buddhahood, I also possessed these four qualities;
however, Maitreya conceived the aspiration for enlightenment forty-two kalpas prior to me.
It was only after that that I first resolved my mind upon the Way.
Through great diligence in this Bhadrakalpa, I transcended nine kalpas and attained the unsurpassed,
true, and correct path, achieving supreme perfect enlightenment.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "I have attained supreme perfect enlightenment by means of ten matters. What are these ten?
First, to possess nothing whatsoever that one does not give away with complete non-attachment."
Second, wives and concubines;
third, sons; fourth, leaders and subordinates.
Fifth, hands and feet;
sixth, lands; seventh, rare treasures and wealth.
Eight, marrow and brain;
nine, blood and flesh;
ten, not sparing one's body or life.
"I shall swiftly attain the Way of the Buddha through ten matters.
Furthermore, the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra* states:
The Buddha told Ānanda, "Observe, Ānanda, when the Tathāgata was walking along the road."
He can cause high places on the great earth to become low and low places to become high,
making all uneven areas perfectly level; once the Tathāgata has passed,
the ground immediately returns to its original state.
All the groves of trees leaned toward the Buddha;
the tree deities manifested their forms and bowed their heads in worship.
Once the Tathāgata had passed by, the trees immediately returned to their original positions.
All hills, mounds, pits, chasms, latrines, foul impurities, thickets,
and rubble were entirely swept away, leveled, and purified;
fragrant and potent scents arose, and various flowers were strewn upon the ground.
When the Tathāgata stepped upon them with his feet and passed over,
even insentient objects all leaned and tilted;
how much more so would sentient beings not show reverence?
For what reason?
When I was originally practicing the bodhisattva path,
there was no one among all people to whom I did not incline my body, humble myself, and pay respectful homage.
Having attained Buddhahood through these virtuous deeds,
whenever the Tathāgata walks, both sentient and insentient beings do not fail to incline themselves, bow their heads, and pay him homage. In the past,
I once offered pure, exquisite, and pleasing assets.
With a sincere mind, he personally bestowed gifts upon all sentient beings.
By the karmic retribution of this deed,
the great earth becomes level and even whenever the Tathāgata walks.
I have swept and sprinkled it clean,
and there are no shards or debris.
When I travel along the roads where immeasurable noble sages reside, [it is likewise so].
In the past, I swept and cleaned roads and plastered the floors of dwellings.
With a mind of equanimity, free from notions of high or low, I swept them clean.
At all times, I have constantly sought awakening for the benefit of sentient beings.
By virtue of these roots of goodness,
wherever the Buddha-Tathāgata travels, at the head of every path he treads,
the ground naturally becomes pure and level as the palm of a hand.
Even Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, which is eighty-four thousand yojanas high and likewise deep within the great ocean,
as well as the Cakravāḍa mountains, which are one hundred and sixty-eight thousand yojanas high.
It is also as firm and solid as a vajra.
When the Buddha enters parinirvāṇa, there is nothing that does not lean over and bow its head in reverent salutation.
If one wishes to avoid it from afar so as not to lean over, [it will still do so].
Nor is it possible that this occurred otherwise;
it was because of praising the Tathāgata.
Thus, Śāriputra heard from another the verses in praise of the Buddha.
They also attain the fruits of the Path.
Thus, in the *Puyao jing* (Sutra of the Universal Radiance), a bhikṣu from Anlu replied to Śāriputra in verse, saying:
My Teacher, the God among Gods, the Supreme Honored One of the Three Realms,
possesses a body sixteen feet tall with the marks and signs of perfection; his supernormal powers are like the sky,
he has eliminated the five aggregates through perfuming, and has uprooted the twelve fundamental [causes].
Not coveting the positions of gods or worldly rulers, his mind purified, he opened the gateway to the Dharma;
at that time, Śāriputra was filled with joy and delight, as if one in darkness beheld the light.
He spoke with his mouth, saying, "Excellent!
For a long time I have harbored doubts.
Furthermore, I am fond of learning; at the age of eight, I followed a teacher."
By the time he reached the age of sixteen, there was nothing he had not mastered.
He traveled throughout the sixteen great kingdoms of the world, believing himself to have attained perfection.
Now, having heard of this extraordinary, unsurpassed, and true-and-right path, he has realized his original vow.
Because the Tathāgata’s past mind was pure, free from attachment, and non-harming toward sentient beings,
wherever he walked, his feet were not soiled and insects or ants were not harmed.
Thus, it is said in various sūtras:
There are three reasons why the Buddha does not wear footwear:
first, to cause practitioners to have few desires;
second, to manifest the wheels on the soles of his feet.
Third, it causes those who see him to rejoice.
There are three reasons why the Buddha’s feet remain four inches above the ground as he walks:
first, because he sees insects and ants on the ground.
Because there was growing grass on the second stage;
because he manifested supernatural powers on the third;
and also because he wished to cause people’s minds to come to rest.
There are three causes and conditions why the ground where the Buddha walks becomes level regardless of its natural elevations and depressions:
first, because he has practiced the four immeasurable minds throughout his past lives, desiring that all beings be secure and at ease;
second, because the earth rests upon water; and third, because there are deities within the water.
All insects and moths that come into contact with the Buddha’s feet find peace and security,
becoming one in mind and intent. Therefore, the lowly become high, and the high become low.
Second, the devas and spirits performed meritorious deeds to level the ground for the Buddha’s removal of it.
Third, when the Buddha was a bodhisattva, he cleared and opened roads and paths, providing bridges to ferry people across.
Therefore, one obtains merit from this;
thus, the high and low become perfectly level.
This is intended so that the human mind may likewise be so.
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"The World-Honored One’s body possesses the mark of fine, thin skin upon which dust and soil do not adhere;
his body is like a lotus leaf, receiving neither dust nor water."
If a bodhisattva walks upon a mountain of dry earth,
the dust does not adhere to his feet;
yet when a *laṇa* wind arises and blows, it shatters the earthen mountain, reducing it to dust.
Not even a single speck of dust adheres to the Buddha’s body.
When a bodhisattva raises food to his mouth,
at that moment, there are two locations on either side of the throat.
It flows with nectar, blending all flavors;
because these flavors are pure,
it is called "attaining the supreme flavor among all flavors."
Furthermore, the *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
"Those who lack a heart of reverence toward the Buddha shall be reborn among dragons and snakes."
Because he has come from the past with this [nature],
even now he remains without respect, prone to sleep, and deluded.
Furthermore, a verse in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* says:
Those who revere their elders and seniors are able to protect the Dharma;
they will gain renown in the present life and be reborn in the good realms in the future.

Therefore, I prostrate to Maitreya Buddha; I pray that the Compassionate Honored One will deliver all sentient beings, and that together with all living beings, we may ascend to Tuṣita Heaven to behold Maitreya Buddha in person.

The World-Honored One’s precious crown contains many emanated Buddhas, their number exceeding hundreds of thousands;

That this is so for Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, How much more so for my own original teacher, Śākyamuni!

All Buddhas eternally dwell in pure lands, Enjoying retributive bodies of infinite magnitude;
Ordinary beings with their fleshly eyes have never known them, Yet for our sake, he manifests this single golden body a thousand feet tall.
Sentient beings gaze upon him without ever being satiated; He causes them to know that the fruits of karma manifest here in Jambudvīpa.
If one can listen to the sutras and diligently recite the Dharma, One will roam at ease and surely proceed to the Tuṣita Palace.

Section Four: Causes of Karma. As stated in the *Adbhuta-dharma-sūtra*:
"The lower grade of the ten wholesome actions refers to [the duration of] a single thought-moment."
The medium grade of the ten wholesome actions refers to a duration of one mealtime; the superior grade of the ten wholesome actions refers to [a longer duration].
That is to say, from dawn until noon,
if during this time one contemplates the ten wholesome deeds in the mind and refrains from the ten unwholesome deeds,
one shall likewise attain rebirth there.
Therefore, the jackal contemplated the ten wholesome paths of action;
after seven days of fasting, he was reborn in Tuṣita Heaven.
Furthermore, the *Śūramgama-samādhi Sūtra* states:
After my parinirvāṇa,
if members of the fourfold assembly or the eight classes of beings wish to be reborn in the fourth heaven,
they should do so within one day up to seven days [after hearing this teaching].
Fixing their mindfulness upon those devas, they uphold the Buddha’s prohibitive precepts, contemplate the ten wholesome deeds,
and practice the path of the ten wholesome actions.
By means of these merits, they dedicate them toward the vow to be reborn in the presence of Maitreya Buddha.

Regarding the statement that one is reborn there after seven days, this is merely spoken from the perspective of a short duration; if even such a brief period can induce rebirth in that heaven, how much more so for a single lifetime—how could one not achieve it? Furthermore, the *Sūtra on Rebirth Above* states:
If there are those who pay homage and respect to Maitreya Buddha,
they shall eliminate the sins of birth and death accumulated over ten billion kalpas;
furthermore, in a future age, beneath the Dragon-flower Tree, they shall also behold the Buddha.
It further states:
"After my parinirvāṇa,
the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings who hear my name and pay homage [shall attain liberation]."
At the end of their lives, they will be reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven.
Should there be men or women who have violated various prohibitions and precepts or committed manifold evil deeds,
if they hear the name of this Bodhisattva of Great Compassion, [they shall be purified].
Prostrating with the five limbs touching the ground and repenting with a sincere heart,
all evil karma will swiftly be purified. If there are those who take refuge in Maitreya Bodhisattva, [their transgressions shall likewise be cleansed].
One should know that such a person attains non-retrogression;
upon Maitreya’s attainment of Buddhahood, they will behold the Buddha’s radiance and immediately receive their prediction of enlightenment.
Furthermore, the *Sūtra on Rebirth Above* states:
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa,

if there are those who diligently cultivate all manner of meritorious virtues, whose majestic deportment is never lacking, who sweep the stupas and smear the ground with plaster, making offerings of flowers and incense,
who practice various samādhis and recite the sūtras—
Although such persons have not severed their fetters, they are as if they had attained the six supernatural powers;
they should maintain constant mindfulness by visualizing the image of the Buddha and reciting the name of Maitreya.
If for even a single moment they receive the eightfold precepts and cultivate various pure deeds, [they shall attain liberation].
At the time of death, one will immediately attain rebirth upon a lotus pedestal in the Tuṣita Heaven.
There, one shall behold the light from the Buddha’s ūrṇā-kośa at that very moment and transcend the karmic offenses of birth and death for ninety billion kalpas.
According to their past affinities, he preaches the sublime Dharma for them so that they may attain non-retrogression.
Furthermore, the *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
"Sentient beings create evil through the three karmas."
Those who, at the time of death, bring to mind the merits of the Tathāgata will certainly leave the evil realms and attain rebirth in the heavens;
this holds true even for those who are extremely wicked.
By means of mindfulness of the Buddha, one may also attain rebirth in the heavens.
Furthermore, the Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra states:
"If one cultivates loving-kindness..."
At the moment of relinquishing body and life, one shall see the Buddhas of the ten directions place their hands upon one's crown.
By virtue of being touched by those hands, the mind becomes peaceful and joyful,

Section on Expressing the Intent: I have heard that...
Quiescent and unmoving,

May it be that on a freezing, still night,

The characters are distinct and the flavor of the words flows with beauty;
the phrasing and rhythms are interconnected, suiting the hearts of the multitude.
It benefits sentient beings and promotes goodness, sufficiently causing the spirits to rejoice and their minds to be delighted.

through reverent and earnest recitation, one moves the divine with sincere devotion.
Thus, one comes to know with certainty that the merit and benefit of upholding even a single verse are vast and profound.

Section on Hearing the Dharma. Section Two on Hearing the Dharma, as stated in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya-śāstra* (The Sutra on the Entrustment of the Dharma-treasury):
The Buddha said:
"All sentient beings who wish to emerge from the great ocean of birth and death within the triple world must rely upon the Dharma-boat to attain deliverance."
The Dharma is refreshing, removing the fever of afflictions;
the Dharma is a sublime medicine, capable of curing the diseases of the fetters;
the Dharma is the true spiritual friend of sentient beings.
They bring about great benefit and deliver all from suffering and affliction. Why is this so?
Because of all sentient beings.
The nature of one's resolve is not fixed;
it follows whatever one is habituated to.
If one draws near to the good, one becomes good.
To associate with the evil leads to evil;
if one associates with evil friends, one will create evil karma and wander through birth and death without end.
If one draws near to virtuous friends and gives rise to a mind of faith and reverence,
listening to and receiving the sublime Dharma will surely enable one to leave behind the suffering and affliction of the three miserable realms;
through this merit, one shall experience the most supreme bliss.
The King of the country of Pāṭaliputra possessed a white elephant capable of destroying his enemies;
if anyone committed a crime, he would have the elephant trample them to death.
Later, the elephant stable was consumed by fire,
and the elephants were moved closer to the monastery.
Hearing the bhikṣus reciting verses from the Dhammapada, the elephants said:
"By doing good one is born in heaven;
by doing evil one enters the abyss.
Having heard this Dharma, the elephant's mind immediately became gentle, and he gave rise to a heart of loving-kindness and compassion.
Afterward, when criminals were brought before him, he would merely sniff them with his nose and lick them with his tongue before departing;
he was utterly unwilling to kill them.
When the king saw this, his heart was filled with great terror.
He immediately summoned his ministers to deliberate on this matter.
A wise minister said to the king,
"This elephant has been near the temple and must have heard the sublime Dharma."
"It is indeed so. You may now move him to be tied up near the slaughterhouse.
The king followed his advice.
When the elephant saw it being slaughtered, its malevolent mind blazed fiercely and its cruelty increased even further.
Therefore, one should know that the dispositions and natures of all sentient beings are not fixed.
If even animals are thus—
giving rise to compassion upon hearing the Dharma and increasing their malice when witnessing slaughter—
how much more so should humans not be subject to such defilements?
Therefore, the wise should awaken to this understanding:
when they see evil, they must abandon it;
when they behold the good, they should draw near to it.
One should diligently listen to the sutras and the Dharma. Furthermore, in the past,
there was a brahmin who carried a great many human skulls.
He went into the city of Pāṭaliputra and traveled about everywhere hawking his wares,
but after a long time had passed, there was no one at all who would buy them.
At that time, the brahmin became extremely enraged.
He shouted with a loud voice, reviling them:
"The people of this city are foolish, ignorant, and dull-witted!
If you do not come to me to buy skulls," he continued.
"I shall bring him a bad reputation.
At that time, the lay disciples (*upāsaka*) in the city,
hearing this and fearing slander, purchased it for money.
He would then pierce their ears with copper skewers;
if they were completely passed through, he would give them a high price,
but for those that were only half-pierced, the payment was proportionally less.
"If you cannot pass through at all, I will give you no payment whatsoever.
The brāhmaṇa said,
"This skull of mine is entirely without difference [from yours]."
"Why is it that the prices offered differ so unequally?
The upāsaka replied, "The former one was completely beyond [the price]."
When this person was born, they heard and received the sublime Dharma, and their wisdom was lofty and superior;
they were esteemed as such and given a high price.
As for those who have partially penetrated it:
Although they have heard the sutras and the Dharma, they have not yet skillfully distinguished them;
therefore, they are given a small amount of payment.
As for those who do not understand at all:
Because this person had never listened to the Dharma in the past,
he did not pay for it.
At that time, the upāsaka took this skull.
They went outside the city to erect stupas and make offerings;
after their lives ended, they were all reborn in the heavens.
By this cause and condition, [the merit was established].
One should know that the sublime Dharma possesses great merit.
This upāsaka, by erecting a stūpa for the skull of one who had heard the Dharma and making offerings to it,
was even reborn in heaven.
How much more so for those who can listen to and receive the sutras with a sincere heart,
and who offer worship and respect to those who uphold the sutras;
the karmic reward of this is truly difficult to exhaust.
In the future, they will certainly attain the unsurpassed path.
Therefore, the wise who desire to obtain unsurpassed peace, security, and happiness [should practice this].
One should listen to the Dharma of the sutras with a sincere and diligent mind.

Section on Seeking the Dharma. Third: As stated in the *Saṃyukta-ratnapiṭaka-sūtra*:
In the past, there was a woman who was intelligent and wise, and who possessed deep faith in the Triple Gem.
She would regularly invite two bhikṣus from the monastic roster to her home to receive offerings.
Later, there was an elderly bhikṣu who arrived at her house in turn; being old,
his faculties were dull and he had never been knowledgeable.
When the meal was finished, the woman earnestly requested him to preach the Dharma;
she spread her seat before him and sat in quiet meditation with her eyes closed.
The bhikṣu knew for himself that he did not understand how to preach the Dharma.
She closed her eyes, fled, and returned to the monastery;
yet this woman, with deep reflection, contemplated that conditioned phenomena are impermanent, suffering, empty, and devoid of self-mastery.
Observing with a profound mind,
he immediately attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*.
Having attained this fruit, he went to the monastery to seek him out, wishing to repay his kindness.
However, this bhikṣu, realizing for himself that he was ignorant,
abandoned the others and fled,
feeling redoubled shame and humiliation.
He again tried to hide and avoid her,
but as this woman pressed him relentlessly,
he finally appeared before her.
Having seen this, the woman recounted in detail the causes and conditions by which she had attained the fruits of the Path;
she presented offerings as an expression of gratitude.
Upon hearing this, the elderly bhikṣu felt profound shame and remorse.
He severely reproached himself and likewise attained the fruit of Srotāpanna.
Therefore, a practitioner should seek the Dharma with a sincere and earnest mind.
If one is sincere, that which is sought will certainly be obtained.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
The Buddha said,
"I recall that in the past I was a brāhmaṇa."
While practicing the bodhisattva path in the Snowy Mountains,
there was at that time no Buddha, nor were there any scriptures or Dharma.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, observed the Bodhisattva practicing various ascetic austerities alone in the mountains.
He immediately descended to test him,
transforming his own body into the form of a rākṣasa,
which was most terrifying.
Standing before the Bodhisattva, he spoke half a verse with his own mouth:
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; this is the nature of arising and ceasing.
Having spoken this verse, he gazed intently in all four directions.
Upon hearing the verse, the Bodhisattva felt great joy in his heart.
He immediately rose from his seat, lifted his hair with his hand,
and looked in the four directions, but saw no other person.
Seeing only a rākṣasa,
he immediately went to him and asked,
"Great Being, where did you obtain this half-verse?"
The meaning of this half-verse is the true path of all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
The rākṣasa replied,
"You need not ask."
"It has been many days since I last ate.
Having searched everywhere, I have been unable to find anything.
Afflicted by the suffering of hunger and thirst, my mind is disordered and I speak incoherently."
"This is not something my own mind can know.
The Bodhisattva spoke again:
"If you will finish reciting this verse for me."
"I shall serve as your disciple for the rest of my life.
The rākṣasa replied,
"Your wisdom is excessive."
"He is only concerned with his own person and does not show any regard for me.
Now, pressed by hunger, I truly cannot speak.
The Bodhisattva spoke again:
"What do you eat? The rākṣasa replied,
"My food is exclusively the warm flesh of humans."
That which he drinks is nothing but the warm blood of humans.
Upon hearing this, the Bodhisattva immediately said to the rākṣasa,
"Simply complete the recitation of this verse."
"I shall offer my own body as a gift for your worship.
The rākṣasa replied,
"Who would believe you?"
"For the sake of eight words, I have abandoned my beloved body.
The Bodhisattva replied,
"I now have a witness."
"Brahmā, Śakra, the Four Kings, and all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas can bear witness for me.
Upon hearing this, the rākṣasa commanded that he be granted leave to speak.
The Bodhisattva, filled with joy, immediately removed his deerskin garment and spread it out as a seat for the Dharma.
He addressed him, saying,
"Preceptor, please sit upon this seat and explain it well for me.
The rākṣasa then spoke.
"When birth and death have ceased, nirvana is bliss.
Having spoken this verse, the Bodhisattva reflected deeply;
thereafter, he inscribed this verse everywhere upon stone walls and at the foot of the Bodhi tree.
Having climbed to the top of a tall tree, he threw himself down.
Before he had reached the ground, various sounds issued from the midst of space;
at that moment, the rākṣasa returned to his original form as Śakra.
He received the Bodhisattva, placed him on level ground,
repented, apologized, prostrated himself, and departed.
By virtue of this cause and condition of sacrificing his body for half a verse, he transcended twelve kalpas.
One shall attain the unsurpassed path before Maitreya.

he wished to make an offering, yet being poor and lacking material wealth,

"I wish to sell myself."
“Can you buy it? The man replied, “In my household,
there is no one capable of performing this work.”
"I have a malignant disease for which a skilled physician has prescribed medicine;
one should take three *liang* of human flesh daily.
If you are able to provide me with three *liang* of your own body's flesh every day,"
"I shall give you five gold coins.
Having heard this, I spoke with joy:
"Grant me seven days; once my business is concluded, I shall return to join you."
The man replied,
"I will grant you one day.
I shall take the money and go at once to where the Buddha is."
Having performed the prostrations and made offerings,
I then listened to and received this sutra with a sincere heart.
At that time, being dull-witted and slow of understanding, I received only a single verse.
"The Tathāgata has realized nirvāṇa, Forever severing birth and death;
If there are those who listen with a sincere heart, They shall always obtain immeasurable bliss.
Having recited this verse, he went to the house of the sick person.
Although he was given three *liang* of meat every day,
because he kept the verse in mind, he did not consider it a hardship;
he did not cease this practice daily for a full month.
That person’s illness was cured and his sores were healed.
At that time, I saw my own body fully restored;
I immediately made a bodhicitta vow, praying that when I attain Buddhahood in a future life, my name shall likewise be Śākyamuni.
By these causes and conditions, he has now attained Buddhahood.

Section Four: On Receiving Merit. As stated in the *Lalitavistara Sūtra*:
"If there are worthy persons who, upon hearing this sūtra, join their palms in self-refuge..."
One immediately abandons the eight matters that are the roots of indolence and accomplishes the eight meritorious virtues. What are these eight?
First, one obtains a handsome and upright countenance.
Second, they attain powerful and flourishing spiritual strength;
third, they attain a flourishing and abundant retinue;
fourth, they attain immeasurable eloquence.
Fifth, one quickly attains the state of a renunciant through training.
Sixth, one’s conduct is pure.
Seventh, one attains the concentration of samādhi.
Eighth, one attains the light of wisdom that illuminates all things without exception.
If there is a Dharma master who spreads out a seat and recites this sutra, they shall obtain the merit of eight seats.
What are these eight?
First, one obtains the seat of a householder;
second, one obtains the seat of a universal monarch (cakravartin);
third, one obtains the seat of a celestial lord (devendra).
Fourth, one attains the seat of the sovereign devas;
fifth, one attains the seat of the arhats;
sixth, one attains the seat of the bodhisattvas.
Seventh, they attain the seat of the Tathāgata.
Eighth, they attain the seat of turning the wheel of Dharma to deliver all sentient beings.
If there is a Dharma master who proclaims this Dharma, [they shall likewise attain these seats].
There are those who praise [this] as "well said," and they shall attain eight pure practices. What are these eight?
First, their conduct and speech are in accord, free from contradiction or error.
Second, their verbal expressions are sincere and devoid of falsehood.
Third, within the assembly, they abide in the ultimate truth without deception.
Fourth, those who hear what he says believe him and do not abandon or distance themselves from him.
Fifth, his speech is gentle and supple, never coarse or harsh.
Sixth, his voice is mournful and harmonious, like that of a grieving phoenix.
Seventh, his body and mind are timely, and his voice is like that of Brahmā;
those among the assembly who hear it all receive his teachings with reverence.
Eighth, the resonance of his voice is like that of a Buddha, conforming to the minds of sentient beings.
If one writes down this sutra, one shall obtain the eight great treasuries.
What are these eight? First, the treasury of attaining the meaning, which is never abandoned through delusion.
Second, they attain the treasury of the mind that understands and discerns all sūtras and dharmas without exception;
third, they attain the treasury of coming and going that universally comprehends all the sūtras and dharmas of all Buddhas;
fourth, they attain the treasury of dhāraṇī, whereby they are able to recognize and remember everything they have heard.
Fifth, they attain the treasury of eloquence, proclaiming the scriptures for all sentient beings so that all receive them with joy.
Sixth, the profound treasury of the Dharma never ceases, ensuring the continuity of the teachings of the Triple Gem.
Eighth, by practicing in accordance with the Dharma-treasury, one immediately attains the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

"O son of good family..."

first, copying [the scriptures];
second, making offerings.
Third, giving [the teaching] to others;
fourth, listening with single-minded attention when others recite or chant it;
fifth, reciting it oneself.

Furthermore, Śāriputra,
these sons and daughters of good family who uphold this sutra,

Furthermore, Śāriputra:

On the day of his initial death,

There they saw a monk; the King first called for the Master.
A question was asked:

The Master replied:
"Since my birth, this poor monk has recited nothing but the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*.
Upon hearing these words,
the King suddenly rose in alarm, joined his palms, and praised him, saying:"
Excellent, excellent!
Master, if you truly recite the Prajñāpāramitā,
you shall surely ascend to heaven and transcend the world.
"For what reason have you come here by mistake?
Before the King had finished speaking,
a celestial robe suddenly descended from above, leading the Master up to heaven.
The king later summoned a man from Suizhou before him and asked,
"Since your birth, what meritorious deeds have you cultivated?
The man replied to the king:
"Your servant has, throughout his entire life, not cultivated the Buddhist scriptures;
he has only been fond of collecting and recording the literary works of Yu Xin.
The King said:
"That Yu Xin is a person of great transgression;
he is currently undergoing this suffering. Do you recognize Yu Xin?"
The man replied, "Although I have read his writings, I do not know him personally.
The King immediately dispatched someone to bring out Yu Xin and show him to that man.
Then he saw a tortoise with one body and many heads.
After the tortoise had departed for a short while, a man appeared.
He spoke, saying:
"I am Yu Xin. Because I was fond of composing literary works during my lifetime,"
He falsely cited Buddhist sutras and mixed them with secular books to slander the Buddha-dharma,
claiming that it did not equal the teachings of Confucius and Laozi.
Now he undergoes the retribution for his sins in the form of a tortoise, enduring such suffering.
After this man had recovered,
he related everything in detail to his relatives.
It so happened that the people of Suizhou were fond of hunting and trapping birds, beasts, insects, and fish.
Those who heard or saw this, both far and near,
exhorted one another to reflect and forever sever the karma of killing;
each gave rise to a sincere heart and received and upheld the Prajñāpāramitā.
It has continued without interruption until the present day.
Liu Bi, County Assistant of Penglzhou during the Tang Dynasty: In the first year of the Zhenguan era of the Tang Dynasty, Liu Bi served as the County Assistant of Yilong County in Penglzhou.

One night, he dreamed of a monk who praised the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* extensively and instructed him to recite it one hundred times.

Suddenly, a great wind arose from the northeast.
He pulled this bird from the tree, crossed over the house, and threw it far into the alley;

Afterwards, one observes the direction from which the wind comes;

When the wind ceases, they rise again as before.

Section Two: Citing Evidence. As stated in the Brahmajāla Sūtra:
The dharma for those who have left the household life does not permit prostrating before kings, parents, or six types of relatives,
nor does it require revering or serving ghosts and spirits.
Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
Those who have left the household life do not pay homage to those still in the household life.
Furthermore, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:
"The Buddha commanded the bhikṣus to perform prostrations to one another according to their seniority."
One should not pay obeisance to any laypeople (*avadātavasana*).
Furthermore, the *Buddha-mūla-pratipatti-sūtra* states:
"King Śuddhodana, together with his retinue and hundreds of officials..."
Having paid homage to the Buddha in due order,
the Buddha said,
"O King, you should now pay homage to the bhikṣu Upāli and the other bhikṣus."
Upon hearing the Buddha’s instruction, the king immediately rose from his seat,
prostrated at the feet of the five hundred bhikṣus and other renunciants,
and paid them homage in due order.
Furthermore, the Satyaka-nirgrantha-sūtra states:
"If one slanders the Dharma of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and the Mahāyāna, or disparages and obstructs it, one commits a root offense.

To cause the Saṃgha to rely on the sūtras of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna by not prostrating to rulers and parents is to follow the Buddha’s teaching; yet now, by making them perform prostrations, one contravenes the Buddha’s teaching and causes them to bow and kneel before worldly persons. Because this leads to a lack of faith in the Buddha’s words, one commits a root offense."
Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
"The various hosts of devas do not dare to seek the prostrations of those who have received the five precepts,
just as [subjects do not prostrate] to a sovereign."
Nor does he seek prostrations from bhikṣus, for fear that such acts might diminish his merit and lifespan.
Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
If there are those who establish and uphold the true Dharma,
such persons should be entreated;
one should sacrifice even body and life to make offerings to them.
As I have taught in this Mahāyāna sūtra:
"Whoever knows the Dharma, whether old or young, should be honored, revered,
and prostrated to, just as Brahmins serve the sacrificial fire."
"Whosoever knows the Dharma, whether old or young, should therefore be honored,
revered, and prostrated to, just as the devas serve Śakra.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
If there is an elder who upholds the prohibitive precepts and receives instruction on what he has not yet heard from a junior,
how should this person be treated with respect?
If one were to pay homage [to them],
this would not be called upholding the precepts.
If a youth protects and maintains the prohibitive precepts...
Should one pay homage to those long-established persons who have broken the precepts when consulting them for teachings not yet heard? Furthermore,
if a renunciant consults a householder for teachings not yet heard, [should they pay homage?]
"Should one still pay homage?
Indeed, those who have left the household life should not pay homage to those who remain in the household life.
Nevertheless, within the Buddha-dharma, even those who are young and immature [in years] are [to be honored]."
One should revere the elders and seniors.

Furthermore, the Madhyama Āgama states:
"How does one know who is superior? It is said that a bhikṣu knows there are two kinds of persons:
those with faith and those without faith."
If one has faith, they are superior;
if one lacks faith, they are inferior.
Furthermore, those who possess faith are of two kinds.
There are those who go frequently to see bhikṣus,
and there are those who do not go frequently to see bhikṣus;
those who go frequently to see bhikṣus are superior.
It is inferior not to go frequently to see the bhikṣus.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of people who go frequently to see the bhikṣus:
those who pay homage to the bhikṣus, and...
There are those who do not pay respect to bhikṣus;
those who pay respect to bhikṣus are superior,

Regarding the paying of respect to bhikṣus, there are further two types:

"Where else is there one more venerable than the Venerable One who is superior even to Śakra,
now facing directly toward the east with palms joined in reverent salutation?
At that time, Śakra spoke this verse in reply:
I am indeed the most honored lord among all the great and small kings of the world,
the four World-Protecting Kings, and the hosts of the Heaven of the Thirty-three;
therefore, they have all come to pay me homage.
Furthermore, there is one in the world who accords with perfect enlightenment and is named the Great Teacher; therefore,
having prostrated in salutation to the Charioteer, I spoke again.
He must be the most excellent in the world, for which reason Śakra, the Heavenly King, pays him homage with palms joined. Facing east, he bows his head in salutation;
I too shall now pay homage to that one whom the Heavenly King honors.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "Even Śakra, the Lord of Devas and sovereign king, still reveres the Buddha, the Dharma, and the rest.
How much more so should a bhikṣu who has left the household life to study the Path!"
In this same way, one should also revere the Buddha. Śakra,
Lord of the Devas and husband of Śacī, pays homage to the Dharma and the Saṅgha,
and likewise praises those who pay homage to the Dharma and the Saṅgha.
"Since you have been able to leave the household life out of right faith to study the Path,
you should likewise praise and pay homage to the Dharma and the Saṃgha.
At that time, Śakra descended from the Vaijayanta Palace.
He faced all directions with palms joined in reverent salutation.
At that time, the charioteer saw Śakra, Lord of the Devas, descending from the palace and standing in the central courtyard, facing all directions with palms joined in reverent salutation.
Having seen this, he was struck with terror; his horse-whip fell to the ground again, and he spoke this verse:
"For what reason, Kauśika, do you so greatly value the homeless life?"
"Please explain its meaning to me; I am parched with thirst and wish to hear it.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, replied in verse:
"I hold him in the highest reverence—he who is able to go forth from the household life."
He wanders freely through all directions, Without calculating his coming or staying;
The colors of cities, towns, and kingdoms Cannot burden his mind.
He does not store up the necessities of life; Once gone, he remains in desireless concentration.
In going forth, there is nothing sought; Only non-action is taken as joy.
In speech, one speaks only words of certainty and goodness; In silence, one remains in tranquil stillness.
The devas and asuras Each oppose one another.
Human beings contend with one another, and their mutual opposition is likewise.
Only those who have gone forth from the household life are free from contention amidst all disputes.
Toward all sentient beings, they lay aside the sword and the staff.
Detached from wealth and from sensual forms, neither intoxicated nor dissolute,
having distanced himself from all evil— for this reason,
I pay homage to him. At that time, the charioteer spoke again in verse:
"Since he is revered by the Heavenly Kings, he must be the most excellent in the world;
therefore, from this day forth, I shall pay homage to those who have left the household life.
Furthermore, the *Pudawang jing* (Sūtra of King Pūrṇa) states:
At that time, there was a king of the country of Fuyan,
named Puda, who ruled over various nations to which tribute was offered from all four directions.
The King personally honored the Buddha-dharma, never once acting with partiality or injustice.
He constantly maintained a compassionate heart, pitying the ignorant masses who did not know the Triple Gem.
Whenever it was time for the fast and purification, he would ascend a high terrace to burn incense.
He turned his head to the ground and prostrated himself in salutation.
The ministers and citizens of the kingdom marveled at the King’s behavior and deliberated among themselves, saying:
The King occupies the most honored position among the myriad people; those far and near revere and submit to him, and when he speaks, they follow his words.
What desire could there be that would lead one to disparage his majestic demeanor by prostrating with head and face upon the ground?
The ministers deliberated among themselves many times, wishing to remonstrate but not daring to do so.
The King commanded his subordinates to prepare the carriage;
he was about to depart when he set out from the palace with several thousand officials and commoners.
Before long, he suddenly saw a practitioner of the Way.
The king immediately descended from his carriage, set aside his parasol, and halted his retinue.
He prostrated himself with his head to the ground to pay homage to the practitioner.
He immediately turned back to provide food and drink,
and consequently the journey was not carried out.
Thereupon, the ministers remonstrated, saying:
"Great King, Most Honored One,
why should you, on this road, act as a beggar for a mendicant by prostrating yourself with your head to the ground?
Of all that is noble and precious in the world, there is nothing more so than one's own head."
Furthermore, as the sovereign of the nation, he was unlike others.
The King then issued an edict to his ministers, commanding them to seek out the heads of dead humans, as well as the heads of oxen, horses, pigs, and sheep.
The ministers immediately went everywhere to search for them.
After many days, he finally obtained them and returned to report to the king, saying:
"Previously, I was instructed to seek the heads of a dead man and the heads of six types of domestic animals."
"Now I have obtained them all.
The king said,
"Sell them in the marketplace."
The minister then had people put them up for sale;
oxen, horses, pigs, sheep, heads, and so forth were all sold,
but human heads remained unsold.
The king said, "Sell it to whoever is willing, whether they be lowly or noble;
simply ensure that it is sold."
If it does not sell, he shall give it to a beggar.
Thus, as the days pass, if it neither sells nor is taken by a beggar, [he shall do so].
Their heads were all swollen and so foul-smelling that one could not even approach them.
The king then became greatly enraged and said to his ministers,
"You officials previously offered this counsel:"
The human head is most precious;
one must not defile or insult it by placing the head upon the ground to prostrate before a practitioner of the Way.
Even when selling livestock, their heads are all sold separately.
"Why is it that no beggars take this human head?
The King immediately commanded his ministers to prepare the carriage and set out for the wilderness marsh beyond the city walls.
Whenever the king had something to inquire about, the assembled ministers and the common people were all struck with awe and trepidation.
The king then addressed the ministers,
saying, "Do you know of that young boy who, during the time of my late father, was constantly in charge of holding the parasol?"
The minister replied,
"I truly am aware of it.
The King said:
"Where is this young child now?
He replied, "He has been gone for a very long time; seventeen years have already passed."
The king asked,
"As for this child's character, how is he in terms of good and evil?
They replied:
We, your servants, have often observed him serving the former king;

he maintained himself with fasting and ritual purity, was reverent and solemn, and remained steadfast in his sincerity and faith. He never spoke of anything that was not in accordance with the Dharma.
The king said to his ministers,
"If you were now to see the clothes this child wore when he was alive,
would you recognize them?"
The ministers replied,
"Although it has been a long time, we have known him personally.
The king looked back at them and sent him along as an attendant.
He hurried back to the inner treasury to retrieve the clothes of his previously deceased son.
In a short while, the clothes arrived,
and he said, "Is this it?"
He replied,
"It is indeed his robe.
The king said:
"Now, would you recognize the child's body if you were to see it?
The ministers below remained silent for a long while.
"I myself am dull-witted and ignorant; having suddenly beheld him, I could not distinguish him."
Just as the king was about to relate his origins,
he saw a man of the Way arrive at his location;
the king was filled with great joy.
He rose, prostrated himself with his head to the ground to pay homage to the practitioner,
and among the ministers and subordinates, there was none who did not rejoice.
The practitioner then took his seat.
The king joined his palms and fully related the preceding circumstances:
"I have now solemnly come forth wishing to reveal the beginning and end of this matter.
I pray that you will guide the ignorant ministers and subjects of this kingdom, enabling them to know the True Dharma."
The practitioner then explained to his subordinates the king’s original transformation:
"If you wish to know the king,
he was originally a young boy who held a parasol for a former king."
He constantly followed the former king in observing the fasts and precepts for one day without transgression.
Subsequently, after passing away from that life, his soul was reborn as the son of a king.
That he now attains such high honor and nobility is entirely due to his past conduct.
The high and low among the subjects were all of one mind, saying:
"We are fortunate to have encountered and beheld this man of the Way.
We pray that you will grant us your compassion."
"I beg to become your disciple.
The practitioner replied,
"My teacher is titled Buddha."
His body is fully endowed with the primary and secondary marks;
he walks alone through the three realms, and his teachings are never in vain.
The Buddha is now six thousand li from here.
In the brief span of a moment’s speech,
the practitioner flew to the kingdom of Śrāvastī and reported everything in detail to the Buddha.
The people of that land are most pitiable;
they now all sincerely desire to see the Buddha.
We only pray that you will bestow great compassion and reveal the true path.
The Buddha granted his permission.
The following day, he arrived at the kingdom of Vatsa.
There, the Buddha preached the Dharma for the king, his ministers, and the common people, saying:
"Do you wish to know the origins and history of King Puhada and the practitioner?
Ānanda replied,
"I pray that I may hear of these matters."
The Buddha said:
"In the past, during the time of Mahāmaṇi Buddha,
the king was the son of a prominent family."
His father made offerings to the Triple Gem.
When the father commanded his son to pass the incense,
there was at that time an attendant.
In his mind he held her in contempt and did not give her any incense;
because transgressions and blessings respond to one another, he incurred this calamity.
Although he was briefly made to serve as her servant, he served the Dharma without falsehood.
Now that you have become a king,
the practitioner was originally your servant;
at that time, he could not obtain incense.
Although he did not obtain the incense, his mind felt no resentment;
he immediately made a vow, saying,
"If I attain the Way, I shall deliver this person."
The convergence of merit, vows, and karmic fruit has now brought him here to deliver the King and the people.
Upon hearing the Buddha’s account of its origins and conclusion,
the King attained understanding and immediately realized the stage of Srotāpanna.
The people within the kingdom, having heard the sutra,
all received the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions as their constant practice.
Furthermore, the Aśokarāja-sūtra states:
In the past, King Aśoka saw a seven-year-old śrāmaṇera and, leading him to a secluded place, prostrated before him and said to the śrāmaṇera:
"Do not tell anyone that I have paid you homage.
At that time, there was a water jar before the śrāmaṇera;
the śrāmaṇera immediately entered into it.
Emerging once more from the bathing jar, he spoke, saying:
"Your Majesty, please do not tell anyone that the śrāmaṇera entered the bathing jar and emerged again.
The King then said to the śrāmaṇera:
I must now speak this openly to others so that it can no longer be concealed.
For this reason, all the sūtras state:
"A śrāmaṇera, though small, must not be treated with contempt."
Though a prince may be young, he must not be disregarded;
though a dragon’s son may be small, he must not be disregarded;
though a śrāmaṇera may be young, he can deliver others.
Though the prince is small, he is capable of killing;
though the dragon’s son is small, he is capable of raising clouds.
Because he raises clouds, rain, thunder, and lightning are brought forth.
One should be moved by how even that which is small cannot be treated lightly.
Furthermore, the *Dharmapada-śāstra* (付法藏經) states:
"In the past, one hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there was King Aśoka."
With faith and reverence for the Triple Gem, he regularly held great *pañcavārṣika* assemblies.
On the day of the assembly, the king bathed in fragrant water, donned fresh and clean garments,
and ascended a high pavilion to prostrate toward the four directions.
He invited the assembly of monks from afar;
twenty thousand holy beings flew there.
The King’s faith was profound and immeasurable.
Whenever he saw any śramaṇas— whether old or young, ordinary or noble— he would always go out to greet them,
inquire after their well-being, and pay them respectful homage.
At that time, there was a certain minister.
His name was Yaśas.
Possessing fierce wrong views and lacking faith or reverence,
he saw the king prostrating and spoke these words:
The king was utterly lacking in wisdom;
he personally humbled his noble virtue to prostrate before a mere child.
Having heard this, the king immediately issued an edict to his ministers.
Each was dispatched to search for and find one hundred animals that had died of natural causes;
each person was required to provide one head,
with the sole exception of Yaśas, who was ordered to seek out only human heads.
Having obtained them, he commanded each of them to go to the market and sell them.
All the other heads were sold,
but as for the head of Yaśas, those who saw it despised it as something loathsome.
There was no one at all who would buy it;
after several days, it was about to rot.
When the people saw this, they all gathered together to revile and insult him.
He spoke to him, saying:
"You are not a candāla, nor a yakṣa, nor a rākṣasa;
why then do you seize the head of a dead man and sell it?"
At that time, having been thus reviled,
Yaśas approached the king and addressed him, saying,
"I have sold human heads, yet I have instead been subjected to insults."
"I do not even wish to see it,
much less buy it.
The king spoke again, saying:
"If there is no one to buy it, you should simply give it away for free.
Yaśas followed these instructions and went back into the market with the item, announcing to the crowd:
"If there is no one with money to buy this, I shall now give it away for free."
Having heard this, the citizens reviled him all the more and none were willing to take it.
Nayasā felt ashamed and returned to the king, where he joined his palms and addressed the king.
"This head is difficult to sell.
Even if offered for nothing, it would only bring me insults;
how much more so if there were someone actually willing to buy it?"
The king asked Yaśas:
"What thing is most precious?
Yaśas replied to the king:
"A human being is most precious.
The king said,
"If they are so precious, why are they not sold?"
Yaśas replied to the king:
"Though a person is noble in life, they are base and lowly at death.
The king then asked Yaśas:
"If my head were to die, would it not be just as base as this?
Nayasena was terrified and afraid, and did not dare to answer.
The king then spoke to him, saying:
"I grant you fearlessness;
you should answer truthfully.
Yaśas, trembling with fear, looked up and down before answering the king.
"O King, even if my head were to die, it would likewise be as base as this.
The King said to Yaśas,
"If my head were to die, it would likewise be as base as this."
"Why do you wonder at my paying homage to the Sangha?
If you are truly my spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), you ought to have exhorted me to trade this fragile head for a firm one; why instead do you stop me from prostrating today?"
At that time, upon hearing these words from the king, Yaśas repented his own faults,
abandoned evil for the right, and took refuge in and honored the Triple Gem.
By this cause and condition, all sentient beings who hear it [shall likewise do so].
If one sees the Triple Gem, one should with a sincere heart pay homage and prostrate.
Furthermore, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:
"The Arhat Piṇḍola..."
Originally a minister of King Udayana,
he attained the fruit of arhatship after leaving the household life through diligent ascetic practice.
Thereafter, whenever the king went out of the city to pay his respects,
the monastery was twenty *li* from the city.
Seeing that Piṇḍola did not rise to greet him, the various sycophantic ministers [reported this to the king].
With an evil mind, he admonished the king.
Later, the king took a sycophantic minister who had advised him on dangerous matters and intended to kill him.
Piṇḍola saw the king approaching and entering the gate.
He immediately descended from his bed and walked seven paces to meet him.
The King said in anger,
"Great Virtue, you have always been difficult to move."
"Why do you now leave your seat to welcome him?
He replied, "Previously,
when the King arrived with a benevolent heart, I did not rise to welcome him."
"He has now come with an evil mind in his heart;
if I do not rise to greet him, I fear he will kill me.
The King sighed and said:
"Excellent! Your disciple was foolish and ignorant, rashly accepting the words of flatterers and failing to distinguish between the ordinary and the holy."
Although the King was spared from hell after being invited to repent for his transgression,
Piṇḍola predicted to him that because the monks had risen to greet him, he would inevitably lose his royal throne seven days hence.
Just as recorded: he was attacked by a neighboring state that sent troops to capture him;
for twelve years he remained imprisoned with his feet in shackles, and so forth.
The commentary states:
For this reason, one must be especially reverent and cautious;
one must not exalt oneself, for fear of damaging future retribution.
Recently, I have observed that when laypeople receive even minor official positions, they fail to give rise to faith;
instead, they falsely harbor arrogance, reviling and scolding monks and nuns,
subjecting them to all manner of insults and humiliation.
Or, standing in the hall before them on high beds, they have people drag them away and unjustly humiliate and beat them.
No greater cause for the destruction of goodness and the increase of evil exists than these practices;
even if they violate the king’s laws, they must still act with reason.
Although one may practice external dharmas, one must inwardly reflect with a sense of shame.
Both monastics and laypeople are ordinary beings dwelling within the three realms;
until one has attained entry into the state of a sage, who among us is without fault?
However, although those who have left the household life may lack actual practice within,
they outwardly manifest the shaving of their hair and wear the dharma robes upon their bodies.
Those who perceive his physical form give rise to wholesome views and develop reverence;
even monks and nuns who have broken the precepts can ascend the seat and preach the Dharma in various ways to benefit all sentient beings,
such that those who hear or see him cultivate and uphold the six perfections.
Transforming one another through successive stages,
they cultivate wholesome deeds so that in their future places of birth, [they may attain liberation].
Nearing the attainment of the states of humans and devas,
and ultimately achieving the fruits of sainthood;
having attained this sainthood, one further proceeds to bring about infinite benefit for others in succession.
It is like a single lamp that kindles hundreds of thousands of lamps, yet its light never comes to an end.
Measuring this inexhaustible Dharma,
one sees that it all results from the great benefit obtained through the merit of preaching and transforming others by monks and nuns who previously broke the precepts.
Since there are these benefits, each person must exercise self-restraint.
Even if one were to deceive hundreds of thousands of monastics,
one could not obtain even a hair’s breadth of benefit in this present life.
One will only have the spread of an evil reputation throughout the four seas and undergo calamities for kalpas in future places of birth.
Thus, the Sūtra says:
A single thought of evil can open the gates to the five unwholesome paths,
as will be described below.
Furthermore, the *Saṃyukta-ratna-piṭaka Sūtra* states:
The King of the Yuezhi, named Candana-Kaniṣka,
heard that there was a venerable Arhat in the kingdom of Kaśmīra.
His name was Jñānadhara;
he possessed great renown and desired to meet him.
He then set out with his ministers to go to that country;
on the way, a thought arose secretly in his mind:
"I am now the king."
There was no one among all the people under the king’s dominion who did not revere and submit to him.
[The Bodhisattva thought: "Were it not for his possession of virtue, how could he be capable of receiving my offerings?
Having formed this thought, he then proceeded forward.
A person from that country said to the Venerable One,
"King Moṭṭāla (Yuezhi), together with his ministers, has come from afar to meet you.
We pray only that you will adjust your robes so that we may welcome and receive him."
The Venerable replied:
"I have heard the Buddha’s words:
for one who has left the household life, the Way is honored above the secular world."
"One should devote oneself solely to virtue;
how could one go out to receive others with finery and ornaments?
He then remained silent and sat upright, refusing to come forth.
Thereupon, the King of the Yuezhi went to the Venerable’s dwelling.
Upon seeing the Venerable Jīvaka and beholding his majestic virtue, his reverence and faith increased twofold.
He immediately prostrated himself before him and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, the Venerable One was about to sleep;
King Moṭṭāyana, unaware, stepped forward and offered him a spittoon.
At that time, the Venerable One spoke to the king, saying:
"This poor monk is not yet worthy to serve as a field of merit for Your Majesty.
Why have you deigned to trouble your divine carriage and come here in person?"
At that time, the King of the Yuezhi felt profound shame and remorse, thinking:
"I previously harbored a secret, trivial thought, yet he already knew my mind.
Were it not for his divine virtue, how could this be so?"
Even though I have briefly explained the Dharma for the sake of the King,
the path is favorable when the King comes,
but it is like that when he departs.
Having heard these instructions, the king immediately returned to his kingdom.
Upon reaching the middle of the road, his ministers spoke with grievance, saying,
"We have followed our Great King from afar to that distant land."
Having heard nothing at all, he returned to his country empty-handed.
Then the king said to him,
"The Venerable One has just now preached the Dharma for me."
"When they came, they spoke well;
when they departed, they were like those who have come. Do you not understand this?"
"Because I maintained the precepts, practiced generosity, and cultivated merit in the past, I planted the seeds for this royal lineage;
thus I now enjoy this position and continue to accumulate further goodness."
"In a future age, you shall surely receive great blessings.
Therefore, he cautioned me, saying:
'When the King comes, let the road be good; when the Tathāgata departs, let it be as it was.'"
Having heard this, the ministers bowed their heads in prostration and apologized, saying:
"We, your humble and ignorant subjects, have privately given rise to erroneous interpretations.
Your Majesty’s divine virtue is wondrously in accord with the profound essence."
"Because he has cultivated merit, he enjoys this position.
Having spoken thus, the ministers withdrew in joy.
Furthermore, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke to the bhikṣus regarding the causal conditions of a past life:
"In times long past,
there were three birds and beasts dwelling together near the foot of the Snowy Mountains."
First, a francolin partridge;
second, a monkey;
third, an elephant.
These three birds and beasts initially treated one another with contempt and lacked respectful conduct;
they thought to themselves,
"For what reason do we not show each other respect?"
"If you were born before us, you should have honored, respected, and instructed us.
At that time, the francolin partridge and the monkey asked the elephant,
"What do you remember from the past?"
At that time, there was a large *piṇḍīta* tree at that spot.
The elephant said,
"When I was small, I walked beneath this tree, which passed under my belly."
The elephant and the francolin asked the monkey,
"What do you remember?
He replied:
"I recall when I was young, sitting on the ground and seizing the top of this tree, pressing it down until it reached the earth.
The elephant said to the monkey: [Continue as in the source].
"You are older than I;
I shall respect you and ask you to teach me the Dharma.
Thus the elephant and the monkey asked the partridge.
"What do you remember? He replied,
"There was a large pippala tree."
"I ate its fruit; from this excrement,
this tree has grown."
"It grew to such a size;
this is what I remember.
Thus the monkey spoke to the francolin.
"You are older than I;
I shall provide for you,
and you should preach the Dharma to me."
At that time, the elephant respectfully listened to the monkey as he taught the Dharma,
and then explained it to the other elephants.
The monkey paid respectful homage to the francolin bird;
having listened to and received the Dharma from him,
he preached the Dharma for the other monkeys.

The francolin birds taught the Dharma to the other francolins; according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, the birds rode upon monkeys, and the monkeys mounted elephants, traveling everywhere to convert and teach the Dharma. These three species of birds and beasts had previously delighted in killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and false speech.
Thereafter, they admonished one another to cease [these acts].
They immediately abandoned this transgression, and at the end of their lives, they were all reborn in the heavens.
At that time, the people of the world saw that the beasts extensively practiced wholesome dharmas and did not encroach upon human grain.
They admonished one another, saying,
"If even animals are capable of such reverence,
how much more so should we?"
At that time, the people of the world all respected one another and practiced the five precepts;
after their lives ended, they were all reborn in the heavens.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
At that time, the partridge was none other than myself;
the monkey was Śāriputra;
and the elephant was Maudgalyāyana.
The Buddha said:
"Even animals, though lacking knowledge,
still respect one another for their own benefit and for the benefit of others."
How much more so for you,
who have left the household life out of faith yet do not show mutual respect!
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
If a person does not revere the Buddha and the assembly of his disciples,
they will be reviled by people in the present life and fall into the evil realms in future lives.
If a person knows to revere the Buddha and the assembly of his disciples...
Having praised and venerated the Dharma through various causes and conditions— praising it as being lauded by people of the present world and leading to rebirth in the heavens in future lives—
the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus.
From now on, even for as long as a great muhūrta,
this person should sit first, receive water first, and receive food and drink first.
3. Section on Reverence and Benefit. Section Three on Reverence and Benefit: As stated in the *Ratnagotravibhāga*, the Three Jewels possess six meanings;
therefore, they must be revered.
First is the meaning of rarity:
just as worldly treasures cannot be obtained by those who are impoverished,
so it is with the Triple Gem.
Sentient beings with meager merit cannot encounter it for hundreds of thousands of millions of lifetimes;
therefore, it is called a "jewel.
Second is the meaning of being free from defilement.
Just as the substance of the world’s true jewels is free from flaws and impurities,
so too are the Three Jewels;
they are utterly detached from all outflows (*āsrava*).
Therefore, it is called a "jewel.
Third is the sense of "powerful efficacy.
Just as worldly precious jewels have great power and efficacy in eliminating poverty and removing poison, [so too does this].
The Three Jewels are thus.
Because they possess the inconceivable power of the six supernormal knowledges (*ṣaḍabhijñā*),
they are called "Jewels."
Fourth is the meaning of adornment.
Just as worldly precious jewels can adorn the body and head, making the person beautiful,
so too are the Three Jewels.
Because it can adorn the practitioner’s pure body,
it is called a "jewel.
Fifth is the meaning of supreme excellence.
Just as worldly rare treasures are superior among all things,
so too are the Three Jewels;
they are the most preeminent in all the world.
Therefore, it is called a treasure.
Sixth is the meaning of being unchangeable:
just as true gold of the world cannot be altered by burning, grinding, or polishing.
The Three Jewels are thus;
they cannot be altered by the eight worldly dharmas,
and for this reason they are called "Jewels."
Furthermore, one must pay respect because [the Buddha] possesses six qualities. First,
the Buddha is able to provide instruction and guidance.
The Dharma is a potent medicine;
it can be transmitted and communicated,
and it brings benefit to me in every way.
One pays respect out of gratitude for their kindness;
secondly, as the Dharma is difficult to transmit during this degenerate age,
I entreat you to bestow your majestic protection.
Therefore, one must pay respect.
Third, it is out of respect for inspiring faith in sentient beings so that they may receive and uphold [the teachings].
Fourth, it is to demonstrate the proper ritual for monks and nuns to show reverence.
Fifth, it is out of reverence so that the dharmas conducive to joyful offerings may endure for a long time;
sixth, it is out of reverence to manifest a mark of excellence.
Thus, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states:
The Triple Gem is most auspicious;
therefore, I place it at the beginning of this sutra.
