The Śramaṇa Shi Tanshi of the Wei Dynasty: During the reign of Emperor Taiwu of the Former Wei.
The śramaṇa Tanshi possessed extraordinary spiritual powers and wonders.
For more than fifty years, he remained constantly seated without lying down,
and his feet never touched sandals.
Walking barefoot through mud and filth, his feet would become clean as soon as he stepped;
their color was white like his face,
so the common people called him the "White-Footed Āraṇyaka."
When Helian Chang conquered Chang’an,
he did not believe in the Buddha-dharma and persecuted monks and nuns;
yet when he first encountered the white blade, [the Master] remained unhurt.
Consequently, many monks and nuns were spared from death.
Emperor Taiwu held him in such high esteem that more than ten years after his passing, his physical appearance remained unchanged.
The Jin dynasty śramaṇa Shi Daokai (also known as Shan Daokai) was a native of Dunhuang.
He left the household life and resided in the mountains.
He wore hempen garments for thirty years,
after which he consumed nothing but small pebbles;
his gait was as swift as flight.
Unable to endure the company of others,
he delighted in seclusion and lived on Mount Baofu for many years.
During the reign of Shi Hu, he came from Xiping.
Traveling seven hundred li a day,
he reached Ye, where he traversed the towns and countryside, relieving all who suffered from affliction and pain;
whatever wealth he obtained, he immediately distributed.
He traveled on foot alone.
As the Shi clan was nearing its end,
he came to Jianye with his disciples.
Furthermore, he passed away at his mountain retreat on Mount Luofu to the south.
During the Xingning era, Yuan Yanbo ascended the mountain to pay respects to his skeletal remains.
He Chong, the Minister of Works of the Jin dynasty (the He Chong who was Minister of Works during the Eastern Jin), was devoted to the Dharma from his youth. For several years,
he maintained a seated posture during his fasts,
awaiting the arrival of the divine sages, and he hosted assemblies at his own home.
The assembly of both clergy and laity was very grand.
Among them sat a monk whose robes were soiled and whose countenance was humble and unrefined;
he rose from the crowd to take his seat, remaining merely silent with hands clasped in reverence.
The assembly found this strange and deemed it erroneous;
Chong also showed his displeasure on his countenance.
When it was time for the midday meal, he sat with the monks to eat.
When the meal was finished, he took up his bowl and left the hall,
looking back at Chong and saying:
"What is the Marquis of He doing with such diligent effort?
he asked, whereupon he tossed his alms bowl into the air and departed, soaring through the void.
Sengchong, along with the monastics and laypeople, watched him as he vanished toward the horizon.
I subsequently shared in my regret and remorse for many tens of days. The above three accounts of verification are taken from the *Liang Dynasty Biographies of Eminent Monks*.

He was a meditation master (dhyāna-ācārya) of Liangzhou.

Regarding the śramaṇa Shi Huiming of the Qi: on Mount Chicheng in Shifeng, Qi, there was the śramaṇa Shi Huiming.

Section on Fields of Merit (21) This section consists of three parts: the Part on Stating the Intent, the Part on Superiority and Inferiority, and the Part on Equality. 1. Part on Stating the Intent (First Sub-section) In the first part, "Stating the Intent," it is said that since the Great Awakened One entered Nirvana, merit has been dedicated to the assembly of sages.

Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-amṛta-rasa-sūtra* states:

1. The field of great virtue;
2. The field of poverty and suffering; 3.
The field of both great virtue and poverty and suffering.
What is the field of great virtue?
It refers to the Buddha, the pratyekabuddhas, and those who have attained the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
What is the field of poverty and suffering?
This refers to animals, the elderly, the sick, and so forth.
What is the field of the noble ones who suffer from poverty?
This refers to the elderly, the sick, and so forth among the noble ones (*ārya*).
If one gives to a field of great virtue with a mind of reverence, one obtains a great reward.
If one gives to a field of poverty and suffering with a mind of compassion, one obtains a great reward.
If one gives to a field that is both of great virtue and subject to poverty and suffering, with a mind of both reverence and compassion, one obtains a great reward.

What constitutes excellent things?
It is obtaining goods without killing, stealing, plundering, or deceiving.
To give whatever pure things one has, whether many or few, as an offering—

If one gives to the Buddha, one immediately obtains all blessings.
If one gives to the Sangha,

12. Chapter on Laymen and Laywomen (21). Chapter Twelve: Laymen and Laywomen. This consists of two sections: the Section on Laymen and the Section on Laywomen. 1. Section on Laymen. Section One on Laymen. This is further divided into three parts: the Part on Stating the Intent, the Part on Admonishing the Laity, and the Part on Exhorting and Guiding. 1. Part on Stating the Intent. Part One on Stating the Intent. Now, among laymen living at home, there are two categories of noble and humble.
First, noble; second, lowly.
First, wealthy; second, poor.
Those who possess wealth and nobility often become heedless.
They are arrogant and haughty, treating those beneath them with contempt and disdain.
Some, riding upon their power and relying on their influence, exalt themselves and oppress others;
others, possessing extensive learning and keen intelligence, rely on their talent to look down upon others.
Some possess eloquent speech and sharp rhetoric, speaking fluently to overbear others;
some boast of their nobility and luxury, treating others with contempt and arrogance;
and some rely on their beautiful appearance and graceful demeanor, using their physical charms to overbear others.
Some ride fat, galloping horses and rely on their mounts to overbear others;
some possess wealth, servants, and slaves, and rely on their riches to insult others.
Such instances are so numerous that they cannot be fully described.
Sentient beings are deeply pitiable for their ignorance;
unaware that impermanence is approaching,
they falsely give rise to arrogance.
They wait for you to come, prepared to roast you in boiling water or scorching coals;
the hell-wardens have held their pitchforks in attendance for a long time.
Yet, you do not worry about this matter, but instead openly indulge in joy and pleasure.

How different from flies that greedily delight in corpses!

Birth and death pass each other like the shifting of one's arm; the noble and the base alike mingle with the dust.

Since one knows that both the noble and the humble are equally reduced to ashes,

Therefore, intimacy and estrangement are not fixed, and nobility and meanness are not constant.
The shifting of suffering and pleasure refers to the mutual alternation between rising and sinking.
2. Section on Admonishing the Laity, Part Two: As stated in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, there are ten types of arrogant actions that one should avoid.
First, to fail to show respect, reverence, and provide offerings to those who are fields of merit— namely one’s preceptors (upādhyāya), teachers (ācārya), parents, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas—
is the karma of pride.
Second, there are Dharma masters who have attained the supreme and wondrous Dharma;
they understand the profound teachings of the Mahāyāna and know the path for transcending birth and death;
they have attained dhāraṇīs and achieved great learning.
To possess the treasury of wisdom and be well-able to expound the Dharma,
yet not believe, accept, revere, or make offerings to it— this constitutes the karma of pride.
Third, when listening to and receiving the Dharma...
If, upon hearing the profound Dharma, one should give rise to a mind free from desire and experience immeasurable joy,
yet fails to praise the Dharma teacher so as to bring delight to the assembly,
this constitutes an act of pride.
Fourth, giving rise to pride, exalting oneself and disparaging others,
failing to examine one's own reality and failing to discipline one's own mind—
this constitutes the karma of pride.
Fifth, they give rise to the conceit of self.
When they see those with merit and wisdom, they do not praise their excellence;
when they see those without merit, they conversely speak of them as good.
If, upon hearing praise of another, one gives rise to a mind of envy toward that person,
this constitutes the karma of pride. Sixth,
if there is a Dharma teacher who knows that "this is the Dharma, this is the Vinaya, this is the truth, this is the word of the Buddha."
Out of malice and envy, one declares that it is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, not the truth, and not the word of the Buddha,
desiring to destroy the faith of others;
this constitutes the karma of pride.
Seventh, one should personally prepare a high seat;
as a Dharma teacher, one should not perform menial services,
nor should one pay homage or make offerings to others who practice the holy life.
To think, "Elders and those of virtuous qualities should all respect, honor,
and provide for me," is an act of pride.
Eighth, one should avoid frowning or looking at others with malicious eyes.
One should always regard sentient beings with a serene countenance;
one's speech should always be gentle and free from coarseness or harshness, remaining devoid of anger and resentment,
and one must not seek out the faults or evils of that Dharma teacher.
This constitutes the karma of pride.
Ninth, with a mind of self-conceit,
one does not go to those who are learned to pay them respect or to listen to the Dharma.
They do not consult even when facing obstacles, nor do they inquire:
"What is wholesome and what is unwholesome? What should be done and what should not be done?"

**Section Two: Laywomen** This section is divided into two parts: Part One, "Expressing the Intent," and Part Two, "Deceit and Fraud. **Part One: Expressing the Intent** Laywomen living at home suffer from many afflictions and transgressions.
The Buddha taught that deceit and flattery are more severe than those of men;
they may falsely apply cosmetics and rouge to their faces and heads for adornment,
or wear flowery silks and elegant robes to deceive and entice the foolish.
Some flirtatiously moved their lips and mouths, casting sidelong glances while singing and laughing;
some sighed and recited verses while gazing intently at people;
some bared their chests and exposed their hands, shielding their faces or hiding their heads.
Sometimes they walk slowly or move with deliberate steps, swaying their bodies and playing with their shadows;
sometimes they open and close their eyes, suddenly appearing sorrowful and suddenly joyful,
deluding foolish men and causing their minds to become falsely attached.
Such deceptive and false phenomena are ultimately difficult to describe in full.
Ordinary people, intoxicated by delusion, are all ensnared by them.
They are like treacherous bandits who employ all manner of guile.
It is like a painted jar filled with excrement used to deceive people;
it is like a high net that causes flocks of birds to fall;
it is like a dense net into which shoals of fish cast themselves.
It is like a blind person falling into a dark pit;
it is like a moth seeing fire and throwing itself into it;
it is like a fly craving the stench of a corpse.
If approached closely, it ruins the state and destroys the family;
if touched, it is like grasping a venomous serpent.
Its outward words are like honey, but its inner heart is like aconite.
Family poverty and suffering all stem from women;
losing one's life abroad also stems from women;
domestic disharmony likewise stems from women.
Patriarchal rebellion between men and women arises because of women;
the estrangement of brothers arises because of women;
and the alienation of kinsmen arises because of women.
Falling into the evil realms is also due to women;
not being reborn among humans or devas is also due to women;
obstructing the path of wholesome karma is also due to women.
Even failing to enter the fruits of sainthood is due to women.
Such faults and calamities cannot be fully discussed.
Sentient beings who act in this way are truly to be pitied.
Constantly burned by the fire of desire, they are unable to leave it;
thus they undergo calamity and suffering that continues without end to this day.
2. Section on Deceit and Fraud, Part Two. As stated in the *Udānavarga* (Chuyao jing):

Driven by desire, one lets the mind run wild and cannot find peace;

Section Two: On Rejoicing and Loathing. As stated in the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra*:
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"All merits are not equal to the mind of renunciation. Why is this?"
Because those who live at home have immeasurable faults and afflictions,
while those who have gone forth possess immeasurable merits; thus,
living at home involves obstacles.
Those who have gone forth are free from obstacles;
those who dwell at home practice various unwholesome dharmas,
whereas those who have gone forth are detached from all unwholesome dharmas.
The householder dwells in a place of dust and defilement;
the renunciant dwells in a place where dust and defilement are removed.
The householder is submerged in the mire of desire.
The one who has gone forth emerges from the mire of desire;
the one who lives at home follows the ways of fools;
the one who has gone forth stays far removed from the ways of fools.
Those who live as householders cannot attain right livelihood;
those who have gone forth from the household life attain right livelihood.
Those who live as householders dwell in a place of sorrow, lamentation, and affliction.
The life of one who has gone forth is a place of joy;
the life of one who dwells at home is a place of fetters;
the life of one who has gone forth is a place of liberation.
The householder’s life is a place of harm;
the life of one who has gone forth is not a place of harm.
The householder possesses craving for gain and pleasure.
Those who have left the household life are free from the pursuit of gain and pleasure;
those who dwell at home are in a place of clamor,
whereas those who have left the household life are in a place of tranquility.
The householder’s life is a lowly state;
the life of renunciation is a sublime state.
The householder is consumed by the afflictions.
Those who have gone forth extinguish the fire of afflictions;
those who dwell at home constantly act for the sake of others,
whereas those who have gone forth always act for their own sake.
Those who live at home take suffering for pleasure;
those who have gone forth take renunciation for pleasure.
Those who live at home increase the thorns.
Those who have gone forth are able to extinguish thorns;
those who dwell at home accomplish minor dharmas,
whereas those who have gone forth accomplish the Great Dharma.
Those who live as householders have no use for the Dharma;
those who have gone forth do have use for the Dharma.
Those who live as householders are disparaged by the followers of the Three Vehicles.
Those who have left the household life are praised for the sake of the Three Vehicles;
those who dwell at home are never content,
whereas those who have left the household life are always content.
Those who dwell at home are cherished by Māra;
those who have gone forth cause Māra to tremble with fear.
Those who dwell at home are largely negligent.
Those who have left the household life are free from negligence;
those who dwell at home are servants to others,
whereas those who have left the household life are masters over servants.
Those who live at home dwell in darkness;
those who have gone forth dwell in light.
Those who live at home increase pride.
Those who have gone forth extinguish the basis of pride;
those who dwell at home have little fruit, while those who have gone forth have much fruit.
Those who dwell at home are full of guile and crookedness.
Those who have left the household life are upright in mind;
those who dwell at home are constantly beset by sorrow and suffering,
whereas those who have left the household life always cherish joy and happiness.
The householder’s life is a deceptive dharma;
the life of one who has gone forth is the true dharma.
The householder’s life is full of distraction.
Those who have gone forth are free from distraction;
those who dwell at home are in a place of saṃsāra,
whereas those who have gone forth are not in a place of saṃsāra.
Living at home is like poison;
going forth from home is like nectar.
Those who live at home lose internal reflection.
The one who has gone forth attains internal reflection;
the one who lives at home has no place of refuge,
whereas the one who has gone forth has a place of refuge.
Those who live at home have much anger;
those who have left the home life practice much compassion.
Those who live at home bear heavy burdens.
The one who has gone forth has laid down the heavy burden;
the one who lives at home is subject to faults,
whereas the one who has gone forth is free from faults.
Those who live as householders wander through birth and death;
those who have left the home life have a limit to their journey.
Those who live as householders regard material wealth as treasure.
Those who have left the household life take merit as their treasure;
those who dwell in the household flow with the current of birth and death,
whereas those who have left the household life go against that current.
The householder dwells in the great ocean of afflictions;
the renunciant possesses the great vessel of liberation.
The householder is bound by the fetters.
Those who have left the household life are free from entanglements;
those who dwell at home are subject to the instructions of kings,

Furthermore, it is said in the Śuka-sūtra:"
The Brahmin son Śuka addressed the Buddha, saying:
"That a layperson in white robes can cultivate merit and roots of goodness superior to those who have gone forth— how is this so?"
The Buddha said,
"In this matter, I do not give a definitive answer.
Among those who have left the household life, there may be some who do not cultivate roots of goodness."
In that case, it would not be as good as remaining at home;
if one can practice while at home, it is superior to leaving the household life.
Furthermore, the *Three Thousand Dignified Manners* (*Sānqiānwēiyí*) states:
The duties performed by those who have left the household life are two:
first, sitting in meditation;
second, reciting the Dharma.
Third is the encouragement and transformation of various matters.
If one fully performs these three types of actions,
this accords with the dharma of those who have left the household life.
If one does not practice,
it is a life lived in vain and a death met in vain;
there will be nothing but the causes for undergoing retribution.
Furthermore, the *Śatavarga-avadāna* (Hundred Similes Sūtra) says:
Once there was a man who required both fire and cold water for his use;
he therefore kept a fire burning overnight.
He filled a water jar with water and placed it over a fire; later,
when he wished to take the fire, the fire had completely gone out.
If one wishes to take cold water but the water is instead hot,
both purposes— the fire and the cold water— are lost.
So it is with people of the world who enter into the Buddha-dharma, leaving the household life to seek the Way.
Having already left the household life,
he still dwells upon the pleasures of his wife, children,
and the five desires; for this reason, he loses the fire of his merit.
Furthermore, they lose the water of their upheld precepts.
It is the same for those who dwell on sensual desires.
Also, from the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*:
The Buddha said:
"After my parinirvāṇa, there will be śrāvaka disciples who are ignorant,
violate the precepts, and delight in inciting strife."
They abandon the twelve divisions of the sūtras and the reading and recitation of various non-Buddhist texts, verses, and writings;
they accept and store all kinds of impure things,
claiming that these are permitted by the Buddha.
Such a person would trade fine sandalwood for tiles and wood.
Exchanging gold for brass;
exchanging silver for white tin;
exchanging silk for coarse woolen cloth.
Exchange the bitter poison for ambrosia.
Furthermore, the *Śāsanānuśāsanī-sūtra* states:
"During the day, cultivate wholesome dharmas with a diligent mind, ensuring that no time is wasted."
Do not neglect the practice during the first and last watches of the night.
During the middle watch, recite the sutras to regulate yourself.
Do not allow sleep to cause this one life to pass in vain, resulting in nothing attained.
By practicing the path in reliance upon this, one may attain the four fruits of śrāmaṇya up to bodhi.
A practitioner who acts in this manner is fit to be a teacher and model;
as a true and excellent field of merit, they are capable of consuming offerings given in faith.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"Just as a person's vision becomes unclear when looking at the sun,
so too when one contemplates and seeks [truth] according to the treatises of non-Buddhists, it causes the eye of wisdom (*prajñā-cakṣus*) to become impure."
Just as when a person gazes at the moon, their eyes become clear and bright,
so too when one contemplates and seeks the meaning of the Buddha’s sūtras and śāstras, the eye of wisdom becomes clear and bright.
If one seeks external, worldly things,
it is like beating a monkey, which results in nothing but impurity;
if one seeks the Buddha-dharma, [it is otherwise].
Just as refined gold becomes increasingly pure the more it is smelted,
so too the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* states:
"A bodhisattva does not fail to read or recite the authentic scriptures of the Tathāgata."
One incurs an offense by reading, reciting, or commenting upon secular texts, verses,
or commentaries. There is no offense if one does so for the purpose of debating doctrine and refuting false views.
If one divides the Buddha’s scriptures into two parts and the non-Buddhist texts into one part,
for what reason?
It is for the purpose of knowing that the external scriptures are false teachings while the Buddha-dharma is the truth;
it is for the purpose of knowing worldly affairs;
and it is so as not to be treated with contempt by worldly people.
Based on this textual evidence,
if a student of the Buddha-dharma were to exclusively abandon internal cultivation to seek externally, they would incur fault;
even if they understand the principles and practice, such study may only be undertaken temporarily.
In order to subdue non-Buddhists,
one must still cultivate a sense of weary detachment and advance in the practice of internal tasks so as to ensure their excellence;
if one is excessively attached, it will destroy the True Dharma.
Therefore, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"If a bodhisattva abandons what has been taught by the Buddha and does not study it,
instead practicing the heterodox treatises of non-Buddhists or worldly scriptures."
This is called committing many offenses;
it is an offense arising from defilement.
However, one who possesses superior intelligence can quickly receive and study [the teachings] to attain unshakable wisdom.
If one constantly studies the Buddha-dharma with two parts during the day and night, and one part of non-Buddhist texts,
this is called non-offense. However,
regarding worldly treatises or the heterodox teachings of outside paths—
To cherish it and not relinquish it, nor to form the thought of discarding it—
this is called a transgression of many offenses;
this is a transgression arising from affliction.
The verse says:
In winter, the fox coats itself in thick fur; In spring, the silkworm spins light silk.
Yet the physical form becomes an obstacle, And the mind-consciousness deceives itself once more.
From childhood, we sang and drummed with joyful bellies;
in our youth, we drove carriages in pursuit of chivalrous knights and quaffed wine while dallying with seductive beauties.
We cared only for what was good before our eyes, unaware of the sorrows of future generations.
Startled, I am filled with shame, forever parting from worldly affection;
may I recognize the root of truth and delusion, so that defilement and purity may naturally separate.
Ashamed of lingering under the five hindrances, how could I know how to accord with the four reliances?

Section Fifteen: Encouragement and Guidance (23). Section Fifteen: Encouragement and Guidance. This consists of four parts: the Part on Stating the Intent, the Part on Citing Evidence, the Part on Generating Faith, and the Part on Karmic Causes. Part One: Stating the Intent. First, regarding the statement of intent: the status of noble and base is not constant, and wealth and poverty are not fixed.
It is like water and fire alternating, or cold and heat coming one after another;
thus, one sees wealth and property, a warm dwelling, abundant clothing, and sufficient food for people arrive spontaneously without the need for laborious seeking.
Furthermore, he saw others who were impoverished, suffering from hunger and exhaustion, laboring and rushing about in their quest for sustenance;
they rose at dawn and slept at night until their physical forms were withered and haggard,
and their minds were weary and disturbed.
Even if one should acquire something, it is lost through a hundred means;
though one prays for wealth and abundance all day long, it has never been possessed even for a moment.
Because of this suffering, [one seeks liberation].
Therefore, one should encourage and commend them to practice the power of giving and diligently cultivate merit.
Furthermore, if there are those who possess clothing, furs, garments, and playthings that are fresh, brilliant, fragrant, and clean,
which provide against the seasonal shifts of spring and autumn, and the variations of cold and heat;
Although the four seasons change and transform according to necessity without deficiency,
one still sees that there are pieces of cloth not even a cubit long, and bolts of silk worn out and tattered—
filthy, stained with dust and ink, foul-smelling and greasy, decayed and putrid.
In the heat of summer, they were unaware of fine linen;
in the ice and snow, they knew nothing of silk or cotton padding.
To such an extent that their very bodies remained uncovered.
The impurities of men and women are not only shameful, but are indeed a source of remorse.
Seeing such suffering, how could one not distance oneself from it?
Therefore, I exhort and encourage them to cultivate merit.
One should provide clothing and dwellings;
for do you not see that while all others possess these, I alone am destitute?
Therefore, one must practice with courageous diligence.
Furthermore, suppose there is a person who,
when eating, is served sweet flavors with all manner of delicacies presented in full;
tables are set in rows and benches piled high, filling the beds and extending across the mats.
Fragrant oils and aromatic incenses were displayed in full abundance;
yet, there was still insufficient coarse grain for rice,
and the soup of wild herbs and greens was often lacking.
Salt and pickled plums were long ago absent both;
fish and vegetables have for a long time been missing in pairs.
It has even reached the point where we eat only once every two days, with gruel and porridge following one after another.
Mixed with various fruits and supplemented with herbs and vegetables,
he was so emaciated and gravely ill that he had no means of sustaining himself.
If one perceives this suffering, how could one not distance oneself from it?
Therefore, I exhort you to cultivate merit;
you should provide food, drink, and water. How can it be that while all others are satisfied, I alone am in distress?
Therefore, one must practice with courageous diligence.
Furthermore, suppose there is a person who holds a high and distinguished rank, riding in fine carriages and wearing light, elegant garments, living in comfort and autonomy.
When walking, they were gazed upon with reverence by devas and humans;
when standing still, they were honored and esteemed by ghosts and spirits.
Yet, there were also those seen who were so base, vulgar, and lowly that they were not even mentioned among the ranks of men.
In life they do not know their living;
in death they do not know their dying.
They lie smeared like charcoal in the side of a ditch.
While sitting or lying within the borders of Qi,
though there were shouts of "shame! and "scold!",
it resulted instead in the suffering of being beaten and struck.
It is not only that gods and ghosts show no respect;
even dogs and hounds inflict poison upon them.
Seeing such suffering, how could one fail to keep a distance?
Therefore, one should be encouraged and exhorted to cultivate merit;
one ought to extinguish arrogance and practice humility and respect.
How could it be that others are always noble while I am always base?
Therefore, one should practice with courageous diligence.
Furthermore, if there is a person whose physical appearance is upright and handsome, and whose speech and voice are elegant and refined.
He constantly maintains broad benefit for others;
his benevolence and compassion are vast, and his speech does not harm living beings.
Yet there was another man whose appearance was haggard and ugly, and whose words were treacherous and violent.
One knows only how to benefit oneself and pays no heed to others;
because that person practices patience, they achieve excellence,
whereas because one harbors much anger, one invites evil.
If one perceives this suffering, how could one not distance oneself from it?
Therefore, I exhort and encourage you to cultivate merit;
you should extinguish anger and practice patience.
How can it be that while the multitude constantly dwell in superior states, I am forever separated from pure conditions?
Therefore, one must practice with courageous vigor.
Furthermore, if there is a person whose mental power is robust and who suffers little from illness, [they should likewise apply themselves].
One is always capable of practicing the Path without obstruction;
yet there are others who are emaciated and afflicted by many ailments, their physical strength exhausted and debilitated,
such that they become increasingly distressed at every movement and find no peace whether lying down or sitting.
Seeing that these evils truly exist, they ought to be abandoned and distanced.
Therefore, one should encourage and exhort others to cultivate merit;
one should provide medical treatment and offer timely relief.
How can it be that while the multitude are constantly free from illness and exhaustion,
I alone am forever beset by stagnation?
Therefore, one must practice with courageous vigor.
In all such matters, one should truly offer the most earnest exhortation;
if one does not so exhort them, [it is a fault].
Thus, students will not apply themselves with diligence.
Section Two: Quotations from Scriptures. As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"Living at home is like being in a prison."
Wife and children are like shackles;
wealth and possessions are like heavy burdens;
relatives are like enemies.
Furthermore, they were able for one day and one night to observe the pure prohibitions and practice the Way during the six periods;
additionally, throughout the year they observed the three long months, and throughout each month they observed the six days of fasting.
They maintained a vegetarian diet and restrained their flavors.
He examined his body, speech, and mind so that they did not wander outward;
with single-minded devotion, he revered the transcendent and held the Buddha-dharma in high esteem.
Whether looking up or down, he was without deficiency; whether sitting or reclining, he was without error.
At night one contemplates the sign of light, and by day one reflects upon pure dharmas;
one deeply reveres śramaṇas and benefits the world with a compassionate heart.
If one can act in this way, [one will attain success].
Even while dwelling in the household life, one may attain liberation from suffering;
thus a sutra says:
"When the Buddha-dharma is about to perish, those in white robes shall protect the Dharma."
Cultivating goodness and ascending to the heavens is like snow falling from the sky;
a bhikṣu who violates the precepts falls into the evil realms like rain descending from heaven.
One should know that cultivating merit while in suffering yields the greatest merit;
committing evil while amidst merit results in no light transgression.
Therefore, one proceeds from suffering to happiness.
One does not yet know the bliss within bliss;
only when one passes from pleasure into suffering does one finally come to know the suffering within suffering.
These words may be verified;
I hope you will examine them.
Furthermore, a verse from the *Dharmapada* says:
"No heat exceeds lust; no poison exceeds anger; no suffering exceeds the body;
no bliss exceeds cessation. Having spoken this verse, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"In the distant past, incalculable aeons ago..."
There was a bhikṣu possessing the five supernormal powers named Vīryabala,
who sought the Way in the seclusion beneath a tree in the mountains.
At that time, there were four birds and beasts that relied upon him on his left and right, always finding peace and security.
The first was a pigeon.
Second, crows;
third, venomous snakes;
fourth, deer.
These four beasts went out to seek food during the day and returned to their lodging at evening.
One night, the four beasts questioned one another, saying:
"Among the sufferings of the world, which is the most severe?
The crow replied,
"Hunger and thirst are the most severe."
At times of hunger and thirst, the body becomes emaciated and the eyes grow dim, while the consciousness remains restless.
One casts oneself into nets and disregards sharp blades;
it is for this reason that we lose our lives.
Speaking from this perspective, hunger and thirst are suffering.
The pigeon said,
"Sensual desire is the greatest suffering."
The fire of sensual desire blazes so fiercely that one has no regard for anything;
there is nothing that does not lead to the endangerment of the body and the extinction of life.
The venomous snake said:
Hatred is the most grievous suffering;
once a poisonous intent arises, one spares neither friend nor foe.
It can kill others and likewise lead to one's own suicide.
The deer said,
"Fear and terror are the greatest suffering.
While I am in the wilds of the forest, my heart is constantly anxious and apprehensive."
Terrified by the hunters and the jackals and wolves,
they fled toward a ditch as if at the sound of a phantom;
mother and child abandoned one another, their hearts trembling with dread.
Speaking thus, [he said,] "Fear and terror constitute suffering.
Upon hearing this, the bhikṣus immediately replied to him,
"What you are discussing is merely the branches."
One does not investigate the root of suffering.
Among all sufferings in the world, none exceeds having a body;
the body is a vessel of suffering, with immeasurable grief and fear.
For this reason, I have abandoned worldly life to study the Way, extinguishing mental activity and severing conceptualization;
I do not crave the four great elements, desiring only to cut off the source of suffering.
With one's resolve set upon *nirvāṇa*, one therefore knows that the body is the root of great suffering.
Thus, a book says:
"Nothing is as great a calamity as the body."
3. Section on Generating Faith. Third: As stated in the *Nāgasena Bhikṣu Sūtra* (The Questions of King Milinda):
At that time, there was King Milinda, who questioned the Arhat Nāgasena Bhikṣu, saying:
If a person commits evil while in the world,
yet at the point of death after reaching a hundred years of age recollects the Buddha,
they will be reborn in heaven after death.
"I do not believe these words.
Furthermore, you say that upon killing a single living being, one immediately enters hell;
I also do not believe this."
The Bhikṣu Nāgasena asked the king:
"Suppose a person were to take a small stone and place it upon the water;
would the stone float or sink?"
The king said,
"That stone has sunk.
Nāgasena said:
"If one were to place a hundred large stones upon a boat,
would that boat sink?
The King said, "No."
It does not sink. Nāgasena said:
"A hundred large stones in a boat do not sink because of the boat."
Although a person may possess inherent evil,
if they recite the Buddha’s name for even a single moment, they will thereby avoid falling into hell and instead be reborn in the heavens.
Why do you not believe this?
Those small stones that sink are like people who commit evil deeds and do not know the Buddhist scriptures;
after death, they immediately enter hell.
"Why do you not believe?
The King said,
"Excellent, excellent!"
The Bhikṣu Nāgasena said:
"It is like two people who die together;
one is reborn in the seventh Brahma-heaven."
One person was born in the kingdom of Kaśmīra;
although these two were far apart in distance,
they both arrived at death at the same time.
It is like a pair of birds flying together:
one perches upon a high tree,
while the other perches upon a low tree.
"The two birds fly together at the same time,
and their shadows reach the ground together.
Thus spoke the bhikṣu Nāgasena.
When a fool commits evil, the calamity they incur is great;
when a wise person commits evil, the calamity they incur is small.
It is like iron that has been heated and placed on the ground: one person knows it to be heated iron.
One person did not know,
while two people both took [the fruit].
However, the hand of the one who did not know became large and raw, whereas that of the one who knew was small.
It is the same with committing evil;
because the fool is unable to repent for himself,
his calamity becomes great.
When a wise person commits an evil deed, they know it is improper;
they repent of their transgressions daily,
and thus their calamities are few.
Furthermore, the *Sishipin Xuejing* (Scripture on Training in the Four Categories) states:
"Among ordinary worldly people,
there are some who are even worse than animals."
Animals may even be superior to humans.
Why is this? Because humans commit sins without ceasing and, upon death, enter hell.
When their retribution for these sins is completed, they first become hungry ghosts;
when their retribution as hungry ghosts is completed, they turn into animals;
and when their retribution as animals is completed, they return to being human.
Having completed their retribution among the animals, they shall then obtain human birth.
For this reason, one should perform good deeds and reverently uphold the teachings of the Triple Gem,
so as to remain forever free from the three evil realms.
After receiving the blessings of devas and humans, one will subsequently attain long-term liberation.
Furthermore, the Sutra in Forty-two Sections states:
The Buddha said:
There are five difficulties in the world:
it is difficult for the poor to practice giving;
it is difficult for the wealthy and noble to study the Way.
It is difficult to master one's life and avoid death;
it is difficult to behold the Buddha’s sutras;
and it is difficult to be born in an age when a Buddha dwells in the world.
Furthermore, the *Saṃyukta-avadāna-sūtra* states that there are eighteen matters that are extremely difficult to encounter in the world.
First, it is difficult to encounter the era of a Buddha.
Second, even if one encounters a Buddha, it is difficult to attain human birth.
Third, even if one becomes a human being, it is difficult to be born in a central land.
Fourth, even if one is born in a central land, it is difficult to be born into a family of noble lineage.
Fifth, even if one is born into a family of noble lineage, it is difficult for the four limbs and six sense organs to be fully intact.
Sixth, even if one possesses the four limbs of the noble ones and has all six sense faculties complete, it is difficult to acquire wealth and property.
Seventh, even if one acquires wealth and property, it is difficult to encounter a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra).
Eighth, even if one encounters a virtuous friend, it is difficult for that person to possess wisdom.
Ninth, even if one possesses wisdom, it is difficult to possess a virtuous mind.
Tenth, even if one possesses a virtuous mind, it is difficult to be able to practice generosity.
Eleventh, even if one is able to practice generosity, it is difficult to encounter a person who is noble, excellent, and endowed with virtue.
Twelfth, even if one encounters a worthy and virtuous person, it is difficult to go to their place.
Thirteenth, even if one reaches their place, it is difficult to find what is suitable and appropriate.
Fourteenth, even if one finds what is suitable and appropriate, it is difficult to receive and hear the teaching.
Fifteenth, even if one hears and understands, it is difficult to attain the wisdom of correct realization.
Sixteenth, even if one attains understanding, it is difficult to be able to receive profound sūtras.
Seventeenth, even if one receives profound sūtras, it is difficult to practice according to what is taught.
Eighteenth: Even if one is able to receive profound sutras, practice according to what is taught, and attain realization of the fruits of sainthood, it is difficult.
These constitute the eighteen difficulties.
4. Section on Karmic Causes. Section on Karmic Causes, Part Four. The *Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on Prince Śuddhodana* states:
The crown prince of King Ajātaśatru, named Śuddhoda,
addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By what causes and conditions does a bodhisattva obtain such upright and handsome features?"
By what causes and conditions does one not enter a woman’s womb but instead undergo miraculous birth within a lotus?
By what causes and conditions is one able to know the matters of past lives?
The Buddha told the prince:
"Because you are able to practice forbearance, you are truly beautiful;
because you do not engage in lustful excess, you are able to be born through transformation."
Having lived for only seven days, he immediately came to know his past lives and countless events of former worlds.
By what causes and conditions did his body come to possess the thirty-two marks?
And by what causes and conditions did he come to possess the eighty secondary characteristics?
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions is it that those who behold the Buddha’s body never tire of gazing upon it?
The Buddha told the Prince:
"In the past, as a bodhisattva, he delighted in giving various kinds of diverse goods to the Buddhas, bodhisattvas, teachers, parents, and the people, providing whatever they required."
Therefore, one attains the thirty-two marks.
One should possess a heart of compassion and take pity upon all wriggling creatures of the ten directions,
regarding them as one would an infant.
Desiring to deliver all beings from suffering,
he has attained the eighty minor marks;
he regards his enemies as he would his own parents.
With an impartial mind free from differentiation,
they gaze upon the Buddha without weariness.
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions do they come to know the wisdom of the profound sūtras and the practice of dhāraṇīs?
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions is it known that the concentrated mind of the three times attains peace and security?
Moreover, by what causes and conditions is it that all who hear the excellence spoken by the Buddha rejoice, believe, and accept it with faith?
The Buddha told the prince:
"A bodhisattva delights in writing, receiving with joy, reciting, and studying.
For this reason, one knows the wisdom of the profound sutras and attains the practice of dhāraṇī."
Furthermore, by constantly focusing the mind and its functions,
one attains the peace and stability of samādhi; thus,
what is spoken is most sincere.
Therefore, all those to whom one speaks believe and turn toward them, and those who hear it rejoice.
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions does one not take birth in evil realms?
And by what causes and conditions does one attain birth in the heavens?
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions does one not crave sensual desires?
The Buddha told the Prince:
"The Bodhisattva, in lifetime after lifetime, has faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha."
For this reason, one is not born in the eight unfavorable states.
Because one maintains the precepts without deficiency,
one is therefore born in the heavens.
Because they know that the fundamental nature of the sūtras and dharmas is empty,
they are without craving or desire.
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions are the thoughts and actions of a bodhisattva’s body, speech, and mind all pure?
"Furthermore, by what causes and conditions does Māra find no opportunity?
And by what causes and conditions does he not dare to slander the Triple Gem?
The Buddha told the Prince:
The Bodhisattva cherishes the Three Jewels;
therefore, he attains purity through diligent and tireless effort.
Therefore, Māra finds no opportunity;
all that they do is performed with utmost sincerity.
Consequently, the multitude dares not slander the Triple Gem.
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions does a bodhisattva obtain a fine, lofty voice like the voice of Brahmā?
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions are there eight kinds of vocal qualities?
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions is he able to know the thoughts of all people and respond to them all?
The Buddha told the prince:
"A bodhisattva is sincere and non-deceptive from lifetime to lifetime;
for this reason, he attains a fine, lofty voice like the voice of Brahmā."
Because he refrained from harsh speech throughout successive lifetimes,
he obtained the eight qualities of his voice.
Because he refrained from divisive speech and false speech throughout successive lifetimes...
Therefore, one is able to repay all that people think of one.
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions does one obtain a long life?
And by what causes and conditions does the body attain freedom from illness?
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions are family members harmonious and not separated?
The Buddha told the prince:
"It is due to abstaining from taking life."
Therefore, one is long-lived when born as a human.
Because one does not wield weapons or strike others,
one is free from illness in a future life when born as a human.
Because one reconciles those who are fighting and causes them to rejoice,
one will not suffer separation when born as a human in a future life.
Furthermore, by what cause and condition does one obtain wealth without it being lost?
"Furthermore, by what causes and conditions does one not become a thief?
And by what causes and conditions does one attain a position of high honor?
The Buddha told the Prince:
Because they do not covet the wealth of others,
they are thus wealthy and happy;
they delight in giving and are not stingy.
Therefore, one does not lose wealth or property,
and the mind is free from envy;
consequently, one is born with high status and honor.
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions does one obtain the divine eye for clear vision?
By what causes and conditions does one obtain the divine ear for penetrating hearing?
And by what causes and conditions does one know the matters of death and birth in the world?
The Buddha told the prince:
"Because you lit a lamp with a virtuous intention as an offering before the Buddha,
you have thereby attained the divine eye of clear vision."
Because he joyfully offered musical instruments before the Buddhist temple,
he obtained the divine ear for far-reaching hearing;
because his mind was settled in meditative concentration through joy.
Therefore, one knows the transformations of death and birth in the world.
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions does one attain the power of flight and the four dhyānas?
Again, by what causes and conditions does one know the events of countless kalpas from previous lives?
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions does one attain the three bodies of a Buddha and then enter parinirvāṇa?
The Buddha told the prince:
"It is because of joyfully giving chariots, horses, boats, and so forth for the use of the Three Jewels and other persons."
Therefore, one attains the four bases of supernormal power (ṛddhipāda) for flying through the air;
by constantly and single-mindedly recollecting the samādhis of all Buddhas and joyfully teaching others,
one thereby attains the recollection of events from incalculable kalpas in past lives.
Because the bodhisattva attains the path of non-retrogression (avaivartika),
he is able to sever the root of birth and death.
Having attained the Buddha-way, he then enters parinirvāṇa.
The verse says:
Vast and boundless is the universe; Stupefied and deluded are sentient beings. Dwelling in suffering, they call it pleasure;
Neither diligent nor striving, They do not follow the fundamental principle, But vainly transmit their delusive thoughts.

Externally complying with sensory objects, internally at variance with the clarity of the mind; Compassionately guiding those who have turned back from delusion, their sincerity strikes a resonance of freshness.
The numinous penetrates and emits radiance; the hidden provides aid through wondrous sounds.
Returning the heart to perfect enlightenment, one crosses the ford of awakening and receives the reward of merit. When one caresses this, there is a profound realization.

The karmic conditions for response transcend those of the past; I shall briefly cite three such accounts of response. First is Zhu Changshu of the Jin, Xing Huaiming of the Song, and Wang Shuda of the Song. Regarding Zhu Changshu of the Jin: Zhu Changshu of the Jin... [text continues].
His ancestors were people from the Western Regions.
For generations, they had possessed wealth and goods, making them a wealthy family.
Zhu Ju moved inland to Luoyang during the Yuankang era of the Jin dynasty.
Changshu served the Dharma with the utmost sincerity and was particularly fond of reciting the Avalokiteśvara Sūtra.
Later, a fire broke out in his neighborhood.
The Changshu family’s home was entirely thatched;
moreover, it was directly downwind.
He calculated to himself that the fire had already drawn near.
The fire spread further, and there was almost nothing left of the property;
he then commanded his household members not to remove any goods,
nor was there anyone to provide water for extinguishing the flames.
He simply recited the sutra with a sincere heart.
After a short while, the fire burned down his neighbor's house;
although it was separated from Changshu’s by a fence, the wind suddenly turned back on its own.
The fire also stopped at the edge of the house.
At that time, everyone considered it a miracle.
Among those in the village were four or five youths who were frivolous and reckless.
They all mocked it together, saying:
"The wind turns of its own accord;
what divine power is there in this?"
"Wait for a clear and dry evening, and you shall set fire to his house.
You may consider your task accomplished if you can prevent it from burning.
Subsequently, the weather became extremely parched and dry, and the winds arose with great speed.
The youths secretly bound torches together and threw them onto the roof of the house;
though they threw them three times, they were extinguished three times.
Thereupon, they were greatly alarmed and fled home in haste.
The next morning, they led one another to the house of Changshu.
They recounted the events of the previous day and bowed their heads to the ground in apology. Changshu replied:
"I am utterly devoid of spirit.
It is surely through the protection of the majestic power of Avalokiteśvara that we have been saved.
You gentlemen need only purify your hearts and place your faith in him."
From then on, his neighbors and fellow villagers all respected and marveled at him.
Xing Huaiming of the Song dynasty was a native of Hejian.
He served as a military aide to the Grand General of the Song dynasty.
He once accompanied Zhu Xunzhi, the Governor of Nanjun, on a northern expedition,
and both were captured and perished.
Thereupon, while waiting for an opportune moment, they all attained the Way and returned home.
Traveling by night and concealing themselves by day,
three days had already passed, yet they still feared pursuit.
He then dispatched men ahead to scout for the enemy outposts;
several days passed without their return.
One night, as rain was imminent, the sky grew dark and overcast.
The person who had been sent arrived unexpectedly at dawn and said in surprise, "Just now,
from afar, I saw a firelight that was extremely bright."
Therefore, he came to seek refuge with them.
How could he have arrived and yet returned in darkness?
Xuṇ and the others were filled with wonder and alarm.
Huai-ming had previously served the Dharma;
since the military expedition, he has constantly worn the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra* upon his head,
reciting it without ceasing.
That evening, he likewise recited it correctly from memory.
Everyone suspected this was due to the spiritual power of the scripture,
and from then on, they constantly directed their prayers toward it with sincere hearts.
Consequently, he was spared and resided in the capital.
In the seventeenth year of the Yuanjia era,
a śramaṇa came to Huiming and said:
"I, a poor monk, have observed that there is a distinct aura of blood and qi within this alley and in your home;
you should move and take refuge elsewhere.
Having finished speaking, he departed.
Huaiming pursued him and watched as he vanished upon exiting the gate;
Huaiming felt a profound sense of aversion toward this.
After twenty days had passed, a neighbor named Zhang Jingxiu injured his father and killed his father’s concubine;
Huaiming considered this a sign of the presence of blood-qi and hoped that, consequently,
no further calamities would occur.
At that time, [he] was with Liu Bin and Liu Jingwen;
their residences were adjacent, sharing the same alleyway.
In that year, they were both members of Liu Zhan’s faction.
It is said that they were all executed together.
Song Wang Shuda— Song Wang Qiu, whose courtesy name was Shuda—
was a native of Taiyuan.
He served as the Governor of Fuling.
In the ninth year of the Yuanjia era, he lost the defense of the commandery and was imprisoned in a penal facility,
where he was bound with a single heavy chain secured by solid iron plates.
Sengqiu first applied himself with diligent effort;
having been placed in prison, his resolve became even more earnest.
Of the more than one hundred people in the jail, most were suffering from hunger.
Every time he ate, he would divide his food to give it away.
He observed the fast daily and,
with a sincere heart, called upon Avalokiteśvara in meditation.
In a dream at night, he ascended a high seat and saw a śramaṇa who gave him a scroll of scripture titled "The Chapter on the Radiant Inspection."
Along with the names of all the bodhisattvas,
he obtained and read them, yet he forgot the name of the first bodhisattva;
the second was Avalokiteśvara.
Third, Mahāsthāmaprāpta again saw a wheel of a chariot, and a śramaṇa said:
"This is the wheel of the five destinies.
Once awakened, all fetters are severed and cast off."
Qiu Xin, knowing of the divine power, increased his single-minded devotion even further.
Consequently, he personally repaired the locks and scriptures himself for three days, after which he was granted amnesty.
These three accounts of miraculous response originate from the *Mingxiang ji* (Records of Miraculous Auspiciousness).

Section Sixteen: On Preaching and Listening (23–24) This section consists of eight parts: the Part on Stating the Intent, the Part on Citing Scriptural Evidence, the Part on Ritual Procedures, the Part on Selecting the Assembly, the Part on Gradual and Sudden Approaches, the Part on the Gift of Dharma, the Part on Repaying Kindness, and the Part on Benefits. **Part One: Stating the Intent** Regarding the relationship between teacher and disciple, the meaning is profound; among the various studies, the study of wisdom is supreme.
Cultivation through righteous principles takes extensive learning as its excellence; thus,
Aśvaghoṣa shook the纲 (guiding ropes) that were on the verge of being severed,
and Nāgārjuna gave rise to the dialectical expositions of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
Your wisdom is brilliantly clear and your elegant discourse is preeminent;
it is truly capable of encompassing technical categories and cleansing long-standing doubts.
Yet, as Confucius lamented, "To learn without speaking is what I fear."
Because they do not understand the meaning of the World-Honored One’s admonition,
the Sūtra says:
"The offering of the Dharma surpasses all other offerings."
Therefore, an external text says:
"The good person is the teacher of the bad person; the bad person is the resource of the good person.
When one receives this teaching without contradiction, the principle transcends the depths of the emotions.
As it is said, if one's listening deviates from the fundamental tenets, it will be difficult to achieve understanding and reconciliation.
Thus, if a single image is deficient, the six lines of the hexagram collapse;
if a single word is erroneous, one shall suffer calamity for kalpas on end.
Thus we know that transmitting the Dharma is not easy and receiving its teachings is extremely difficult.
This is truly because a long time has passed since the Sage departed and his subtle words have gradually become obscure;
consequently, for one person to explain and another to receive is inherently hard to accomplish.
I fear that fame and profit will preoccupy the mind, making it difficult for the afflictions of emotion to be purified.
2. Section on Citing Evidence, Part Two: As a verse in the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states:
"Because the true Dharma, its speaker, and its listener are difficult to find."
In this way, saṃsāra is neither finite nor infinite.
Furthermore, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"Because both the speaker and the listener do not accord with the Dharma, each incurs two faults."
First, the fault of speaking what is unjust;
second, the fault that the Buddha does not rejoice [in it].
Thus, a verse in the Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra says:
If there are sentient beings who lack the vessel of the Dharma, the Tathāgata cultivates equanimity toward them;
employing great skillful means, he awaits the proper time. This is as stated in the *Mahālaṃkāra-śāstra*: "In order to enable them to attain true liberation..."
One attains awakening through what one has heard; one should carefully refrain from disparaging what one has not yet heard.
There is an immeasurable amount remaining that one has not heard; those who slander it create the karma of delusion.
As stated in a verse from the *Ratnagotravibhāga*:
Those who are deluded and full of pride, who delight in practicing inferior dharmas,
and who slander the Dharma and its teachers, are rebuked by all the Buddhas;
though they outwardly manifest the appearance of following the proper rites, they do not understand the Tathāgata’s teaching.
"To slander the Dharma and the Dharma masters is to be rebuked by all the Buddhas.
Now I see those who have only recently begun their studies— both the virtuous and the unvirtuous, the young and the immature— who set out upon the path only to remain steadfast in their delusion.
They develop a sense of complacency regarding the words and their meanings;
relying on themselves and disparaging others, they become increasingly arrogant and contemptuous.
Thus, the *Bhūmivastu-śāstra* states:
There are five faults in interpreting the meaning according to the literal phrasing:
first, the absence of right faith;
second, the regression of courageous effort.
Third, deceiving sentient beings;
fourth, disparaging the Dharma;
fifth, slandering the Dharma.
If the person who speaks still has defilements in their own mind,
how much less can those who listen give rise to faith? If one preaches the Dharma with a pure mind, [others will likewise believe].
Even if birth-and-death were transformed into nirvana,
if spoken with a defiled mind,
even nirvana would be transformed into birth-and-death.
Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"The Mahāyāna is nectar;
it is also called a poisonous drug."
That which can be digested is nectar;
that which cannot be digested becomes poison.
It is like placing poison in milk, which then becomes capable of killing a person.
Thus, a verse from the *Ratnagotravibhāga* states:
"Those who lack knowledge and lack wholesome discernment, who harm right practice through evil friends, are like a spider fallen into milk; that milk then becomes poison."
Furthermore, the *Daśacakrakṣitigarbha-sūtra* states:
"Just as a Kṣatriya-cāṇḍāla and others,
upon seeing those who have gone forth within my Dharma— whether they be śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or even Mahāyāna Dharma-preachers who expound the teachings— "
They slander, revile, and deceive the True Dharma,
creating obstacles and causing distress to the Dharma Master;
by these causes and conditions, they fall into the Avīci Hell.
If one sees someone who has gone forth within my Dharma,
and repeatedly feels anger toward that person,
reviles them, and refuses to believe or accept the Dharma I have taught;
By destroying stupas, monasteries, monastic quarters, and halls, and by killing bhikṣus,
all previously cultivated roots of goodness will be utterly extinguished.
When his life is about to end, all his limbs ache as if being burned by fire;
the root of his tongue feels as if it were bound,
and for many days he is unable to speak.
After his life ends, he will fall into the Avīci Hell.
Section Three: Rituals. As stated in the *Sānqiānwēiyí* (Three Thousand Dignified Manners):
There are five matters regarding ascending the high seat to recite the scriptures.
First, one should first pay homage to the Buddha.
Second, one should pay homage to the Sūtras, the Dharma, and the elders.
Third, one should first step onto the *āsanasthiti* seat with one foot and then sit upright upon it.
Fourth, one should return to the seat of the senior monk (upādhyāya).
Fifth, one should first press down the seat with the hand before sitting upon it.
Once seated, there are five matters [to attend to].
1. One should properly don the dharma robe and take one's seat.
2. When the sound of the *ghanṭī* has ceased, one should first recite verses of praise and chant.
3. One should read according to the specific circumstances.
Fourth, if there is an unpleasant person, one must not harbor anger while on one's seat.
Fifth, if there is someone bringing an offering to give, one should set it aside and place it before [the teacher].
Furthermore, he asked about five matters concerning the sutras.
First, one must descend from the bed in accordance with the Dharma before questioning;
second, one must not question while sitting together on the same seat;
third, if there is someone who understands, one must not question them directly.
Fourth, one must not maintain thoughts directed toward external conditions.
Fifth, even if one has attained understanding, one should prostrate with the head touching the ground; having performed this salutation, one should turn back and exit the door.
Furthermore, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
When the Dharma Master occupies the lion throne, there are four dharmas. What are these four?
First, when about to ascend the high seat:
First, one should respectfully pay homage to the assembly before ascending the seat.
Second, if there are women in the assembly, one should contemplate their impurity.
Third, one’s deportment and gaze should possess the marks of a great man (*mahāpuruṣa*).
When expounding the sounds of the Dharma with a serene and joyful countenance, all people will believe and accept them;
one does not speak of the scriptures of external paths, and one’s mind is free from fear or timidity.
Fourth, when faced with malicious words or difficult challenges, one should practice patience.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas:
first, conceiving the thought of benefiting all sentient beings;
second, not giving rise to the notion of a self toward any sentient beings.
Third, one does not give rise to the notion of dharmas regarding any written characters.
Fourth, one vows that all sentient beings, having heard the Dharma from me,
shall never regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas:
first, not disparaging oneself;
second, not disparaging those who listen.
Third, not disparaging what has been taught;
fourth, not acting for the sake of gain and offerings.
Furthermore, the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra* states:
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"At what time should the fourfold assembly not make any sound—
whether by body or speech, or any other sounds such as those of wood, stone, or the like?"
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"During the six periods of the day, one must not make any sound while paying homage to the Buddha."
When listening to the Dharma;
when the assembly is in harmony;
and when going on almsround.
When eating, and when defecating or urinating,
for what reason must one not make a sound at these times?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"At that time, there were various devas who came.
Those devas possessed minds that were constantly pure, undefiled, empty, in accordance with the pāramitās, and contemplating the Buddha-dharma."
Because of those sounds, their minds became unsettled;
because they were unsettled, they all returned.
Because the devas had departed, the various malevolent spirits arrived.
Performing acts that are unbeneficial and unstable,
they enter this birth and give rise to various calamities like flames;
the people suffer from famine and further violate one another.
Therefore, Mañjuśrī, you should pay homage to the Buddha with tranquility.
The Buddha spoke in geya:
Not producing sounds of body, speech, or voice— like wood or stone,
with all other sounds stilled— the one who pays homage to the Buddha is praised by the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, the *Buddha-mūla-pratipatti-sūtra* says:
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, I establish a rule for my disciples:
you must not request those whose faculties are dull and obtuse, or who have broken or incomplete precepts, to preach the Dharma to them."
From this time forward, if you are requested to preach the Dharma,

you should request one who is endowed with sublime conduct, who has achieved excellence among the assembly, who is well-versed in the Sūtras, who understands the Vinaya, and who understands the Mātṛkā.
One should select those who possess clear characters and complete eloquence to preach the Dharma.
These bhikṣus shall be dispatched from the lower seats in successive order to preach the Dharma for the assembly.
If the first one becomes exhausted, he should invite a second;
if the second becomes exhausted, he should invite a third;
if the third becomes exhausted, he should invite a fourth.
If the fourth person becomes fatigued, one should invite the fifth,
and so on, until as many capable preachers as there are have been invited in succession to preach the Dharma for the assembly.
At that time, when the multitude saw that Dharma Master possessed such eloquence and was able to expound the Dharma,
they immediately took fragrant flowers and scattered them over him. However,
the bhikṣus did not accept his teaching and instead gave rise to feelings of revulsion and detachment.
Why is this? Because the Buddha has prohibited it.
Those who have left the household life must not carry or possess scented ointments, powdered incense, or various flower garlands.
At that time, when people heard of and saw this matter, they spoke in disparagement,
saying: "These bhikṣus are not even worthy of receiving such offerings."
How much more so for those who are superior.
At that time, the bhikṣus went to the Buddha and reported these matters in detail.
Then the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"O bhikṣus, if there are lay donors who,
with a joyful heart..."
For the sake of auspiciousness,
those who hold various kinds of incense, flowers, ointments, powdered incense, and flower garlands to scatter over the Dharma Master should accept them.
Thereupon, these lay followers and donors presented various kinds of wealth, treasures, goods,
and monastic robes as offerings to the Dharma Master.
Those bhikṣus, filled with fear and shame, did not accept those items.
Consequently, the people of the world spoke in disparagement, saying:
"These śramaṇas, these sons of the Śākyas, [act in such a manner]."
"If they cannot even bear the weight of some light objects,
how much less so those that are superior?
When the bhikṣus heard this matter, they went together to inform the Buddha.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "O bhikṣus,
if there are laypeople who offer various goods, including monastic robes and the like, as gifts to a Dharma teacher."
For the sake of joy, I permit you to give as alms.
If anyone requires it, let them receive and take it;
if they do not require it, I permit you to send it back.
At that time, the bhikṣus extracted the essential meanings and flavors from the sūtras and preached for the sake of conversion without following the proper sequence.
Thereupon, the bhikṣus felt ashamed and were filled with fear.
Concerned that they were deviating from the sūtras and the vinaya, they reported the matter to the Buddha in full detail.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"I permit you to select essential meanings from among the various sūtras as the occasion demands, and to arrange the phrasing accordingly when preaching the Dharma for others."
One should simply adopt the meaning from the middle [of the texts] without destroying the original wording of the sūtra.
Furthermore, the *Buddhacarita-sūtra* states:
"At that time, the bhikṣus gathered within a single hall."
There were two bhikṣus who also expounded the Dharma;
because they obstructed one another,
he then constructed two halls for them.
Within the two halls, each was preaching the Dharma separately,
yet they continued to obstruct one another.
Therefore, within this hall, he led the bhikṣus to proceed to that hall.
There were bhikṣus at that hall who, mutually encouraging one another, led people to this hall;
as they came and went in such confusion, the assembly became disordered.
Some people came and went, and the Dharma activities were interrupted.
Furthermore, there were some bhikṣus who took no pleasure in hearing or speaking of this Dharma-gate.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported all of this in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, two persons shall not preach the Dharma in the same hall.
Furthermore, two halls must not be situated so close together that their sounds overlap and interfere with one another."
Furthermore, one must not go from this assembly to that assembly, nor from that assembly to this assembly.
One must also not harbor hatred toward śramaṇas or take no pleasure in hearing their teachings. If one does harbor such hatred, they must be dealt with according to the Dharma.

Moreover, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* does not permit two Dharma masters to sit together on high seats in close proximity within the same hall to preach the Dharma; singing, chanting in unison, or performing *bhāṣya* in a blended melody are all forbidden. Other vinayas likewise do not permit a Dharma master on a high seat to receive flowers scattered by laypeople; if the flowers should touch his body, he must immediately shake them off. Furthermore, the *Sudarsana-vinaya* states:
If a Dharma master preaches the Dharma for others who listen,
and a woman among the listeners uses a fan to shield her face,
she must take care not to expose her teeth while smiling.
If there are those who laugh, drive them out. Why is this?
Because he is the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
"What has been spoken from the golden mouth out of compassion for sentient beings—
you all should listen with a sense of shame and remorse.
Why do you laugh at it and drive him out?"
*Fayuan zhulin*, Scroll 23, Section 4: Contrary to the Dharma (*Vi-dharma-varga*). As stated in the *Buddhapiṭaka-sūtra*:
The Buddha said, "Śāriputra..."
In the future, there will be bhikṣus who delight in reading non-Buddhist scriptures.
When they preach the Dharma, they will embellish their prose and rhetoric to entertain the assembly.
At that time, Māra the Evil One will assist in deluding the multitude and obstructing the wholesome Dharma.
If there are those who are greedily attached to sounds, speech, and cleverly adorned rhetoric,
or if there are others who delight in reading the scriptures of non-Buddhists,
Māra will delude them all, causing their minds to lack peace and stability.
These people have been deluded by Māra;
their eye of wisdom is obscured and they greedily crave gain and offerings.
They study various external texts like a herd of blind men being deceived by a charlatan.
They cause all of them to fall into a deep pit and die.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
one who preaches the Dharma impurely...
Not understanding the Tathāgata’s intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*),
one who explains it to others based on their own poor comprehension incurs five faults in this present life. What are these five?
First, when preaching the Dharma, they harbor fear in their hearts, apprehending that others might challenge them.
Second, they preach the Dharma to others while inwardly harboring anxiety and dread.
Third, they are ordinary worldlings who lack true wisdom.
Fourth, that which he preaches regarding impurity consists merely of empty words.
Fifth, his speech lacks sequence, being a mere jumble of excerpts gathered from here and there;
for this reason, those in the assembly harbor fear in their hearts.
In this way, ordinary persons lack wisdom and their minds are not resolved; they seek only fame and reputation.
With doubt and regret in their hearts, they preach to others.
For this reason, Śāriputra, [it is so].
If one occupies a high seat without having personally realized the Dharma,
and teaches others while remaining ignorant themselves,
they shall fall into hell.
Furthermore, the Ekottarika Āgama states:
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying,
"You should know that there are these four kinds of birds."
What are the four? First, there are some birds whose voices are beautiful but whose forms are ugly;
the *kukkuṭa* bird is an example of this.
Second, there are some birds whose forms are beautiful but whose voices are ugly;
these are, for example, birds of prey.
Third, there are some birds whose voices are ugly and whose forms are also ugly.
This refers to the owl.
Fourth, there are birds whose voices are beautiful and whose forms are also beautiful;
this refers to the peacock.
In this world, there are also four kinds of persons whom one should observe and understand. What are these four?
First, there may be a bhikṣu who is handsome in appearance and perfected in his deportment.
However, they are unable to recite or chant the various dharmas that are excellent in the beginning, middle, and end;
this is called a person whose form is beautiful but whose voice is not beautiful.
Second, there are some people whose voices are beautiful but whose forms are ugly.
In their coming and going, their deportment is not perfected;
yet they delight in extensive preaching, being diligent in observing the precepts, excellent in the beginning, middle, and end, and profound in their underlying principles.
This is called a person whose voice is fine but whose form is ugly.
Third, there are some whose voices are ugly and whose forms are also ugly;
that is to say, there are people who violate the precepts, lack diligence,
and have not heard much of the Dharma.
What one hears is immediately lost.
This is called a person whose voice is ugly and whose form is also ugly.
Fourth, there are some whose voice is beautiful and whose form is also beautiful.
That is to say, a bhikṣu is handsome in appearance and perfect in deportment;
furthermore, he is diligent in practicing wholesome dharmas, possesses great learning without forgetting it,
and is well able to recite that which is good in the beginning, middle, and end.
This is called a person whose voice is excellent and whose form is also excellent.
Furthermore, the *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus.
There are four kinds of clouds. What are the four?
First, there are some clouds that thunder but do not rain.
Second, there may be clouds and rain without thunder;
third, there may be clouds, rain, and thunder;
fourth, there may be clouds with neither rain nor thunder.
These four kinds of clouds correspond to four types of persons in the world.
First, there is the cloud that thunders but does not rain.
This refers to a certain bhikṣu who recites the twelve divisions of the scriptures with a loud voice, chanting them without losing their meaning.
However, when one does not extensively preach the Dharma to others,
this is called "thundering without raining.
Second, what is meant by "raining without thundering"?
There may be a bhikṣu whose countenance is upright and handsome, and who is fully endowed with dignified deportment;
yet he has not heard much and does not recite the twelve divisions of the scriptures aloud,
nor does he receive them from others or retain them without forgetting.
It is good to associate with virtuous friends and also good to preach the Dharma to others;
this is called "rain without thunder."
Third: Why is there no rain and no thunder?
It is because there are some people whose countenances are not upright and whose deportment is not complete;
they do not cultivate wholesome dharmas nor are they learned.
Furthermore, he does not preach the Dharma to others.
This is called a person who neither rains nor thunders.
Fourth, what is it to both rain and thunder?
There may be someone whose physical appearance is upright and whose deportment is complete;
who delights in learning and also delights in expounding the Dharma to others,
exhorting them to accept and uphold it.
This is called a person who both rains and thunders.
*Fayuan zhulin*, Volume 24, compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Daoshi of Ximing Monastery.
Section Sixteen, Part Two: On Speaking and Listening;
Chapter Five: Selecting the Assembly (24). Regarding the fifth section on selecting the assembly:
when a Dharma Master ascends the seat, he must first pay homage to the Triple Gem and purify his own mind.
Observing the time and selecting the person, one should possess a mind of compassion,
save living beings, and benefit all things;
only then should one preach for them.
Therefore, the *Bao'en jing* (Sutra on Requiting Kindness) states:
"If the listener is seated and the speaker is standing, one should not preach to them;
likewise, if the listener seeks out the faults of the speaker, one should not preach."
One should not preach it to those who rely on the person rather than the Dharma,
or who rely on the letter rather than the meaning.
One who relies on sutras of provisional meaning rather than sutras of definitive meaning,
and who relies on consciousness rather than wisdom, should not be taught [this].
Why is this? Because such a person is unable to revere the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and the pure Dharma.
If one speaks of honoring the Dharma, [one must act accordingly].
Those who hear the Dharma also give rise to reverence and respect;
