he conceived a profound sense of reverence and respect, and having completed his prostrations with his head at [the Buddha's] feet, he withdrew.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for them;
fifteen of those people attained the purity of the Dharma-eye and sought ordination.
The Buddha said, "Welcome."
Their hair and beards fell away naturally and dharma robes appeared upon their bodies;
[the Buddha] preached the Dharma to them again, and they became arhats.
Among the sixteen people—
At that time, there was a man named Piṅgiya,
who was the nephew of the Elder of Pāvā;
he was immediately dispatched to deliver the news.
He returned to his own country and recounted in detail everything he had heard and seen. When Pāpā heard this,
they were filled with joy.
He immediately rose from his seat, knelt with palms joined,
and with sincere heart entreated the Buddha toward the city of Rājagṛha, saying:
"I only pray that you will deign to come and receive me with your compassion."
The Tathāgata, knowing this from afar, arrived before him in the time it takes to bend and extend one's arm.
Having prostrated, he raised his head and saw the Buddha; filled with wonder and joy, he was struck with amazement.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he attained the stage of Anāgāmin.

At that time, the World-Honored One immediately returned to Vulture Peak; only Maitreya alone did not take the lesser fruit, but instead made a great vow, setting his mind upon Bodhi. The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus:
In a future age, this land of Jambudvīpa will be square and regular,
level and vast, and free from mountains and rivers.
The ground grows soft grass like celestial garments.
At that time, the people have a lifespan of eighty-four thousand years and a height of eight zhang;
they are upright, exquisite, and wonderful.
Human nature will be harmonious and benevolent, and all will practice the ten wholesome deeds.
At that time, there shall be a Wheel-Turning Sage King named Śaṅkha (in the Jin language, this means "Possessed"). At that time, there will also be a Brahmin.
A son was born to the family, named Maitreya.
His body was the color of purple-gold, endowed with the thirty-two marks and all the secondary characteristics in full perfection; his radiance was exceptionally brilliant.
Having left the household life to study the Way, he attained supreme perfect enlightenment.
He extensively turned the sublime wheel of Dharma for the sake of sentient beings;
in his first assembly, he delivered nine hundred and thirty billion classes of sentient beings.
In the second assembly, he delivered ninety-one billion beings;
in the third great assembly, he delivered ninety billion.
Thus, through these three assemblies of preaching the Dharma, those who were able to receive deliverance were saved.
"All those sentient beings who have planted roots of merit through my bequeathed Dharma shall all be present within those three assemblies.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha:
"I do not understand from what this name 'Maitreya' originated.
The Buddha said:
In the distant past, he practiced the Samādhi of Loving-kindness;
his mind was settled in composure, supple, and free from any intent to harm.
Therefore, he is named Maitreya (in Sanskrit, Maitreya).
This "Maitreya" or "Cishi" is also his clan name.
Other sutras state:
In the past, there was a Buddha already named Maitreya.
Encountering that Buddha, [the practitioner] made a vow to be named Maitreya as well.
As for the one named Ajita:
This is called "Invincible" (Ajita).
Because his wisdom surpasses that of ordinary people, he is called Invincible.
The Verse says:
The Sage’s Path, the Source, and the Deliverance; The Youthful Wanderer Ascends to the Void and Transmigrates.
The Master Penetrates and Provides for Others; The Spirit-Light Illumines Those with Karmic Connection.
Adapting to circumstances, each distinct and unique, The sacred records match the numinous chapters.
Riding the Qian hexagram by means of the ninth and fifth lines, Resonant echoes resound through the three thousand worlds.
The Dharma drum vibrates with the profound teaching; The Dragon soars, responding to humans and devas.
Tranquil wisdom merges with the subtle boundary; in vast and ethereal tones, one chants the profound mystery.
For seven times seven cycles, the world has been winding and turning;
now that the auspicious destiny arrives at its midpoint, this form of thirty-two marks emerges. It shines brilliantly, adorning the Huālínyuán Garden.

Regarding the conditions for spiritual resonance (*ganying yuan*): there were many eminent masters such as Sengsheng and Sengzhao, as well as Fotudeng and Daoan; their accounts are appended to separate sections and are not recorded here at length to avoid redundancy. Furthermore, I shall briefly cite two testimonies: those of the Jin dynasty śramaṇa Kumārajīva and the Song dynasty śramaṇa Shi Faxian. As for the Jin dynasty śramaṇa Kumārajīva: during the Jin dynasty, in Chang’an, there was Kumārajīva.
This person is known as Tongsou (Dharmakṣema).
He was a native of India, whose family had served as prime ministers for generations.
Kumārajīva’s grandfather, Datta, was unconventional and stood out from the crowd; his reputation was esteemed throughout the kingdom.
His father, Kumārayāna, was intelligent and possessed virtuous qualities.
When he was about to succeed his father to the position of minister, he declined the appointment and left home to become a monk.
Crossing the Pamir Mountains to the east,
the King of Kucha heard that he had renounced his glory and felt profound admiration for him.
He went out from the outskirts of the city to welcome him and invited him to serve as the National Preceptor.
The King had a younger sister who was twenty years of age;
she possessed such brilliant intelligence that she could master anything upon a single reading.
Upon hearing it once, he recited it;
moreover, there was a vermilion mole on his body,
a sign that the Son of Wisdom had been born.
Various states sought her hand in marriage, but she refused them all.
Upon seeing Yan, however, her heart desired him,
and so he was compelled to take her as his wife.
Soon after, she conceived Kumārajīva;
while he was in her womb,
his mother’s wisdom and understanding became twice as great as usual.
Having heard that the great temple of Kukkutārāma possessed many renowned virtues and also monks who had attained the Way,
[he] immediately [sent] noble ladies of the royal clan along with nuns of virtuous conduct.
They prepared offerings for an entire day,
inviting him to a vegetarian feast and to hear the Dharma;
at that time, Kumārajīva’s mother suddenly understood the language of India by herself.
His responses to difficult questions invariably exhausted their profound depths,
and the assembly all marveled at him.
An arhat named Dharmaghoṣa said:
"This woman must be carrying a child of wisdom.
He spoke thus to provide proof that Śāriputra had been in her womb;
however, after Kumārajīva was born, he forgot his previous words.
Shortly thereafter, Śīkṣānanda’s mother desired to leave the household life,
but her husband did not grant her permission;
consequently, she gave birth to another son.
His name was Puṣyadeva. Later,
while going out of the city for an excursion,
he saw withered bones scattered here and there among the burial mounds.
Thereupon, he deeply contemplated the root of suffering and resolutely sought to leave the secular world.
He vowed to shave his hair and abstain from food and drink;
by the sixth night, his physical strength had become utterly exhausted.
He remained in doubt until dawn.
The man then became fearful and gave his consent;
however, because he had not yet shaved his head, he still did not partake of the food.
He immediately ordered someone to shave his hair,
then provided him with food and drink;
on the following morning, he received the precepts.
He continued his practice of the dhyāna methods with such focused diligence that he attained the first fruit of the path.
When Kumārajīva was seven years old, he also entered the monastic life;
studying under his teacher, he recited a thousand verses daily.
The verses consist of thirty-two characters;
in total there are thirty-two thousand words.
Having already completed the recitation of the Abhidharma, [he proceeded].
The Master taught him its meaning, whereupon he attained thorough understanding himself; there was nothing obscure that he could not clarify.
At that time, there was a man from Kucha.
Because his mother was the daughter of a king and received immense offerings,
they took Kumārajīva with them to avoid them.
When Kumārajīva was nine years old, he followed his mother across the Indus River.
Upon arriving in the kingdom of Kaśmīra, he encountered the eminent and virtuous Dharma Master Bandhudatta,
who was the younger cousin of the King of Kaśmīra.
He was profound and pure, possessed of great capacity, and his brilliant talent and vast learning were peerless in his time.
He was thoroughly proficient in all three baskets and nine divisions of the scriptures.
From morning until noon, he would transcribe a thousand verses by hand;
from noon until evening, he would likewise recite a thousand verses.
His fame spread throughout many countries, and those both far and near took him as their teacher.
Upon Kumārajīva’s arrival, [the King] honored him with the rites due to a teacher.
From him, he received the *Saṃyukta-āgama*, the *Madhyama-āgama*, and the *Kṣudraka-piṭaka*, totaling four million words.
Dharmadatta constantly praised Kumārajīva’s divine brilliance,
and his reputation eventually reached the King.
The King immediately invited him to enter.
The masters of the non-Buddhist schools gathered together to debate and challenge one another;
as their words first began to clash,
the non-Buddhists looked down upon him because of his youth.
His words were quite insolent.
Kumārajīva took advantage of this opening to defeat him;
the non-Buddhist was humbled and, filled with remorse, remained speechless.
The King’s respect and admiration for him increased further.
Daily, he was provided with a pair of goose carcasses, three *sheng* each of bran and flour, and six *sheng* of ghee;
these were the highest-quality offerings from foreign lands.
The monks of the monastery where he resided then dispatched five senior monks and ten śrāmaṇeras to attend to him,
sweeping and cleaning as if they were his own disciples.
He was thus held in such high esteem.
When he reached the age of twelve,
his mother took him back to Kucha.
The various kingdoms all offered him positions of high honor,
but Kumārajīva took no notice of them at all.
At that time, Kumārajīva’s mother took him to the Northern Mountains of the Yuezhi.
An arhat saw this and marveled at it;
he said to his mother,
"You must always protect her."
If this śrāmaṇera does not break the precepts by the age of thirty-five,
he shall greatly propagate the Buddha-dharma and deliver countless people, no different from Upagupta.
If one's precepts are not complete, they are incapable of achieving anything;
at best, such a person can only be a learned and talented Dharma Master.
Kumārajīva proceeded to the kingdom of Kāśyapa (Śāle).
Placing the Buddha’s almsbowl upon his head, he thought to himself, "The shape of this bowl is immense; how can it be so light?
Immediately, it became so heavy that he could not bear its weight, and he let it fall with a cry.
The mother asked him the reason for this,
and he replied,
"It is simply that my mind makes distinctions, while the bowls have varying weights."
He remained in Śākala for one year.
That winter, he recited the Abhidharma,
specifically the various chapters on the cultivation of wisdom in the *Daśamukha* (Ten Gates).
Without having received instruction from anyone, he fully mastered its subtleties.
Furthermore, he encountered no obstacles regarding the various gates of the six *pādas*.
The King of Śālukya had a *tripiṭaka* śramaṇa named Priyadarśana.
He said to the king,
"This śrāmaṇera must not be treated with contempt;
Your Majesty should invite him."
The initial opening of this Dharma gate provides two general benefits:
first, the śramaṇas within the kingdom will feel shame at their own shortcomings and will surely exert themselves;
second, the King of Kucha will surely say that [the teaching] originated in his own country and thus honor it.
"He regards me with honor;
he will surely come to establish friendly relations.
The King granted his permission.
He immediately organized a great assembly and invited Kumārajīva to ascend the seat and preach the *Dharmacakra-pravartana-sūtra*.
The King of Kucha indeed sent an envoy to reciprocate his personal friendship.
During the intervals between his preaching, Kumārajīva—
He then sought out and investigated the scriptures of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas),
becoming well-versed in the Vedas and Śāstras;
he was particularly proficient in the composition of literary works, including the art of debate and question-and-answer exchanges.
He had extensively studied the four Vedas and the various treatises on the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*).
He mastered the principles of yin-yang, astrology, and mathematics without exception;
he was exquisitely proficient in discerning auspiciousness and misfortune, his words coinciding with reality like the joining of tally-sticks.
He was by nature straightforward and perceptive.
Kumārajīva initially studied the Hīnayāna,
but later devoted himself exclusively to the Mahāyāna (Vaipulya) scriptures.
He then sighed and said:
"In the past, I studied the Hīnayāna;
it was like a person who does not recognize gold and mistakes brass for something exquisite."
He extensively sought out the essential meanings of the teachings and received and recited the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*, the *Śata-śāstra*, the *Dvādaśamukha-śāstra*, and other treatises.
Shortly thereafter, he followed his mother.
He proceeded to the kingdom of Wensu,
which was the northern border of Kucha.
At that time, there was a Daoist master in Wensu.
Divine in debate and brilliant in talent, his fame resounded throughout all lands.
He struck the royal drum with his own hand and made this vow:
"Should anyone defeat me in debate, I shall behead myself as recompense."
Once Kumārajīva arrived, he examined [the matter] through these two principles;
immediately, [the king] became bewildered and lost his composure, bowing his head in refuge.
Thereupon, his fame filled the region east of the Pamirs, and his reputation spread beyond the Yellow River.
The King of Kucha went in person to Wensu to welcome Kumārajīva back to his kingdom.
There, he extensively expounded various sutras;
those who studied under his school from all directions were unable to challenge him.
At that time, there was a royal princess who had become a bhikṣuṇī named Ajātaśatru;
she had extensively studied the various sūtras and possessed particularly profound mastery of the essentials of dhyāna.
Having declared that he had already realized the second fruit [of the path],
he was filled with joy upon hearing the Dharma;
he then further organized a great assembly to inquire about the profound mysteries of the Vaipulya sutras.
Kumārajīva analyzed and expounded how all phenomena are empty and devoid of self,
distinguishing that the aggregates and elements are merely provisional designations and lack substantial reality.
Among those present in the assembly, there was none who did not feel moved by sorrow.
In their mourning, they all lamented that his realization had come so late.
At the age of twenty, he received the full precepts in the royal palace and studied the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* under Vimalākṣa.
After a short while, Kumārajīva’s mother took her leave to travel to India.
She said to Bai Chun, the King of Kucha:
"Your kingdom will soon decline; it is time for me to depart."
While traveling in India, he advanced to attain the third fruit of arhatship.

As his mother was about to depart, she said to Kumārajīva, "The profound teachings of the Vaipulya (Vaipulya-sūtras) should be extensively propagated in China; you must transmit them to the Eastern Land."
"Your strength alone will bring no benefit to yourself;
what can be done about that?
Kumārajīva said:
The path of the Great Being benefits others even at the cost of his own life.
If one can ensure that the Great Transformation spreads and enlightens the ignorant masses,
he would have no regrets even if his body were cast into the cauldrons of hell.
Thereupon, he remained in Kucha and stayed at the New Temple.
Later, within the old palace adjacent to the temple, he first obtained the *Prabhāsa-sūtra* (The Scripture of Radiant Light).
He then began to open and read it.
Māra came and concealed it,
so that he saw only a blank slip of paper;
Kumārajīva, knowing this was Māra’s doing, vowed with even greater resolve.
The character "Mó" (Māra) disappeared,
yet he continued to recite it.
Again, he heard a voice from the air saying:
"You are a wise man; why do you need to read this?
Kumārajīva said, "You are a minor Māra; you should depart at once."
"My mind is like the earth, unshakable.
He remained there for three years,
extensively reciting Mahāyāna sūtras and śāstras until he thoroughly penetrated their profound mysteries.
The King of Kucha had a golden lion throne constructed for him and spread it with brocade cushions from Da Qin;
he then ordered Kumārajīva to ascend it and preach the Dharma.
Kumārajīva said,
"My master has not yet realized the Mahāyāna;
I wish to go in person to welcome and pay my respects to him, so I cannot remain here."
Before long, the Great Master Pāṇḍuvadana arrived from no great distance away.
The King said,
"Great Master, how have you been able to come here?"
Dharmatāta said:
"First, I heard that what my disciple has realized is extraordinary;
second, I heard that Your Majesty extensively praises the Buddha-way."
Therefore, braving hardships and dangers, he traveled from afar to gather at this divine land.
Upon the arrival of the Master, Kumārajīva was filled with joy as his original aspiration was fulfilled;
he then preached the *Sūtra on the Questions of the Virtuous Woman*.
The *Pratītyasamutpādahṛdaya-śāstra* and the *Śūnyatāsaptati* were both previously disbelieved by the Master;
therefore, he spoke of them first.
The Master said to Kumārajīva:
"What distinct characteristics do you perceive in the Mahāyāna that you wish to hold it in such high esteem?
Kumārajīva replied, "The Mahāyāna is profound, pure, and clear; it reveals that all phenomena are empty."
The Hinayana is partial and narrow, often stagnating in names and forms.
The Master said:
"You say that all things are empty."
This is truly terrifying.
Why would one abandon existence and yet love emptiness?
It is like that madman of old who ordered a weaver to spin thread, demanding it be spun as fine and beautiful as possible.
The master weaver applied himself with such care that the work was as fine as a mote of dust;
yet the madman still complained that it was too coarse.
The master weaver was greatly incensed.
He then pointed to the sky and showed it, saying,
"This is the fine thread. The madman asked,
"Why can I not see it?"
The Master said,
"This thread is extremely fine; even with my skillful craftsmanship,
it still cannot be seen."
"How much more so for others!
The madman was overjoyed and entrusted it to a weaver.
The Master also imitated this;
both received rewards from the sovereign, yet in reality they possessed nothing.
Your "empty dharma" is likewise derived from this.
Kumārajīva then presented his arguments by drawing parallels between similar cases;
he debated with such earnest persistence that it took more than a month before [the opponent] was finally convinced.
The Master sighed and said, "I was unable to reach the truth, yet you have instead awakened to its intent; this is now proven.
Thereupon, he paid homage to Kumārajīva as his teacher and spoke thus.
"The Upādhyāya is my teacher of the Mahāyāna;
I am his teacher of the Hīnayāna. Thus it was that the various kingdoms of the Western Regions were all subdued by Kumārajīva’s divine brilliance and excellence.
Every time he gave a lecture,
the various kings would all kneel long at the side of his seat and have Kumārajīva step upon them to ascend;
such was the esteem in which he was held.
Once Kumārajīva’s teachings had spread to the West and his fame resounded throughout the East, Fu Jian was usurping the title of Emperor in Guanzhong.
At that time, there were the King of the Eastern Frontiers of the foreign lands and the younger brother of the King of Kucha.
Both came to pay court to Fu Jian.
Jian received them in audience,
and the two kings addressed him as follows:
The Western Regions produce many rare and precious things;
I request that troops be sent to establish order there so that they may submit to our rule.
This was in the first month of the thirteenth year of Jian’s Jianyuan era, the year of Dingchou.
The Grand Historian reported, saying:
"A star has appeared in the celestial division corresponding to foreign lands;
there shall surely enter to assist the Middle Kingdom a man of great virtue and wisdom."
Fu Jian said,
"I have heard that there is Kumārajīva in the Western Regions."
"In Xiangyang there is a śramaṇa named Dao'an; could it not be him?
He immediately dispatched an envoy to seek him out.
In the second month of the seventeenth year,
the King of Shanshu and the King of Qianbu again spoke with earnest entreaty,
requesting that troops be dispatched for a western expedition.
In the ninth month of the eighteenth year, Fu Jian dispatched the General of the Light Cavalry Lü Guang and the General Who Crosses Rivers Jiang Fei,
leading Wang of the Former State, the King of Cheshi, and others.
He led seventy thousand troops to the west to campaign against the kingdoms of Kucha and Uḍḍiyāna.
As he was about to depart, Yao Xian saw off Lü Guang at the Jianzhang Palace and said to him:
Now, emperors and kings respond to Heaven in their governance;
they take cherishing all living beings like their own children as their fundamental principle.
How could they covet their lands and wage war against them?
This is precisely because he is a person who cherishes the Way.
I have heard that in the Western Regions there is Kumārajīva.
He possessed a profound understanding of the characteristics of phenomena and was well-versed in the principles of Yin and Yang;
he served as a model for later students.
I, the Emperor, reflect upon this with great longing.
The wise and sagacious are the great treasure of a nation.
Had he subdued Kucha, he would have immediately dispatched an express courier to send Kumārajīva; however, before the vanguard of the army had even arrived, [the situation changed].
Kumārajīva said to the King of Kucha, Bai Chun:
"The destiny of your kingdom is declining;
you shall soon face a formidable enemy."
A man from the land under the sun arrived from the east.
It was appropriate to receive him with hospitality and not oppose his advance; [Kumāra]jun was not compliant and instead fought.
Guāng subsequently defeated Kucha and killed [Kumāra]jun.
He established Shun’s younger brother, Zhen, as the leader.
Having already obtained Kumārajīva,
Faguan had not yet gauged the extent of his wisdom and capacity.
Seeing that his age was still young,
[the opponent] treated him as an ordinary man and mocked him.
Kālaya returned and stationed his army on the mountain slope along the way.
When the officers and soldiers had finished their rest,
Kumārajīva said,
"We must not remain here."
"You will certainly find yourself in a state of distress;
it would be best to move the army to the heights of Long.
Guang did not accept this advice.
When night fell, it indeed rained heavily, and a sudden flood surged forth;
the water reached several zhang in depth,
and thousands died.
Fayuan began to feel secretly uneasy about this.
Kumārajīva said to Fayuan, "This is a place of ill omen; it is not appropriate for you to remain here long."
"By calculating the movements and reckoning the numbers, it is clear you should return quickly.
Along the way, there will surely be a blessed land where you may dwell.
Guang followed his advice.
Upon arriving in Liangzhou, he heard that Fu Jian had already been killed by Yao Chang.
Fuguang donned white mourning garments and held a great funeral ceremony south of the city.
Thereupon, he usurped the title of ruler outside the Passes and styled his era "Tai'an."
In the first month of the second year of the Tai’an era, a great wind arose in Guzang.
Kumārajīva said, "This is an inauspicious wind; there will surely be treacherous rebellion."
However, it was not necessary for him to determine this himself;
later, Kumārajīva’s words were proven correct.
Kumārajīva remained in Liangzhou for many years.
Since Lü Guang and his son did not propagate the Way,
they retained their profound understanding without being able to proclaim its transformative teachings;
and since Fu Jian had already perished, they never met one another.
When Yao Chang usurped power over Guanzhong,
he too admired Kumārajīva’s eminent reputation and respectfully invited him with an open mind;
because Lü [Falu] knew that Kumārajīva possessed many insights and skills in strategy, he [recommended him].
Fearing that Yao might plot against him, he did not permit [Dun] to enter the east. When Yao Chang passed away, his son Yao Xing succeeded to the throne and again sent envoys to invite Dun.
In the third month of the third year of Hongshi, a tree with interlocking branches grew in the courtyard of the temple.
In the Xiaoyao Garden, the scallions transformed into garlic;
this was regarded as an auspicious omen,
signifying that a wise person should enter.
In the fifth month, he dispatched Shiduo, Duke of Longxi, on a western expedition against Lü Long; Long’s army was utterly defeated.
By the ninth month, Long submitted a memorial offering his surrender, and only then was it possible to welcome Kumārajīva into Guanzhong.
On the twentieth day of the tenth month of that year, he arrived in Chang’an.
Emperor Xing treated him with the etiquette due to a National Teacher and showed him great favor and honor.
When engaging in conventional discourse, one might linger for an entire day;
yet when investigating the subtle and penetrating the ultimate truth, one exhausts a whole year without weariness.
Since the Great Dharma first spread to the East during the reign of Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty, [the tradition has continued].
Having traveled through the Wei and Jin dynasties, his familiarity with the sūtras and śāstras gradually increased.
However, many of the translations produced by Zhi Qian and Zhu Foshuo were hindered by archaic phrasing and reliance on *geyi* (conceptual matching).
Daoxing had revered the Triple Gem since his youth.
Liu Rui subsequently invited Kumārajīva to reside at the Ximing Pavilion and the Xiaoyao Garden, where he requested him to translate various scriptures.
Kumārajīva had memorized and recited most of the scriptures, exhausting every detail;
he was moreover highly proficient in translating them into Chinese with fluent and elegant diction.
Upon examining the older translations, he found that their meanings were frequently erroneous and deviant.
All of these resulted from previous translations that missed the essential meaning and thus did not correspond with the Sanskrit original. Consequently,
Xuánzàng dispatched over eight hundred people, including the śramaṇas Sēngqiè, Sēngqiān, Fǎqīn, Dàoliú, Dàocháng, Dàobiāo, Sēngruì, and Sēngzhào.
He consulted with and received the instructions of Kumārajīva, who was then commissioned to produce a new translation of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
Kumārajīva held the Sanskrit manuscript.
Daorong took up the old edition of the sutra to collate it with the new;
those passages where the phrasing differed from the old version were all found to be perfectly coherent in meaning.
The hearts of the multitude were satisfied and submissive;

there was none who did not rejoice and offer praise. He [Dongxing] believed that the Buddha-way is profound and subtle, its practice consisting solely of goodness, and that faith is the excellent ford for escaping suffering.
This is the grand principle for governing the world.
Therefore, he entrusted his intent to the Nine Classics and let his mind roam through the Twelve Divisions of Scripture,
subsequently composing the *Tongsanshi Lun* (Treatise on the Three Times) to exhort and demonstrate the law of cause and effect.
From the princes and dukes downward, all admired and praised his character.
General of the Left, the Duke of Changshan, Xian, and General of the Left, the Marquis of Ancheng, Song,
both possessed deep faith in the principle of causes and effects.

He repeatedly invited Kumārajīva to the Great Monastery in Chang’an to lecture on the newly translated scriptures; in total, he continued the translation of Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras and śāstras numbering more than three hundred and ninety fascicles, the titles of which are recorded in a separate biography.
He fully elucidated the divine source and brought forth its profound subtleties;
at that time, scholars from all quarters gathered from ten thousand *li* away.
His magnificent achievements have long been vast, and we now look up to them with reverence.
Among the monastics and laypeople from all quarters, such as the eminent and wise Śramaṇa Huìyuǎn and others,
their learning permeated the various scriptures,
and they served as pillars and beams for the enduring legacy of the Dharma.
At that time, as the Sage had been gone for a long period, doubts regarding various meanings remained unresolved;
he therefore sealed the texts and consulted Kumārajīva.
Whenever one has an audience with a king, there must necessarily be praise of his virtues.
The ritual for beholding the Buddha takes the chanting of hymns as its essence;
the gāthās found throughout the sūtras are all of this form.
However, by transcribing the Sanskrit into the Qin language, their elegant refinement has been lost.
Although you have grasped the general meaning, it is vastly removed from the literary style;
it is like chewing food for someone else—
not only does it lose its flavor, but it is also improper.

Part One: Exposition of the Intent. First, Exposition of the Intent: I have respectfully investigated the teachings of the Buddha.
Beginning from the reign of Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty and ending with the Great Tang,

there are none who do not scale the mountains to offer tribute or gaze toward the sun to acknowledge the King.
Yet, the records transmitted from past to present differ and contradict one another.
His deeds are rarely misunderstood, yet his titles and designations cause much confusion.
Although he has been moistened by the residual grace [of the Dharma], the profound intent remains incomplete;
while the sounds differ between the Central Kingdoms and the barbarian lands, the literary meanings are largely complete.
The traces of the Sage are so profound that it is difficult to exhaustively investigate them;
for this reason, the monks of this land each harbored feelings of resentment and frustration.
At that time, there was the Dharma Master Xuanzang, a śramaṇa from the Great Tang.

in the third month of the final spring of the third year of the Zhenguan era, [proceeded].

Starting from the capital city, he gradually reached Shazhou,
traversing treacherous passes and fortresses all by himself.

what auspicious signs did you encounter, bhikṣu? He replied:

2. Section on Punishment. Section Two on Punishment: Since the Great Sage’s Western disappearance and the eastward flow of the True Teaching, the Buddha-dharma was entrusted to kings, commanding them to provide protection and support.

If one hears these teachings expounded, one is instead subjected to humiliation.
Because the distinction between the clergy and the laity has long been blurred and their dispositions have diverged,
if one intends to administer punishment to reform the wicked and lead them toward goodness,
those who rely on official power will instead use it to oppress pure individuals.
The monastic community lacks the power to counteract this and instead defiles their pure minds;

Consequently, the Great Teaching’s practical application has ceased, and its remaining traditions have fallen into corruption and replacement.
Therefore, the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states:
"If, in the future, kings and members of the four castes, for the sake of protecting the Dharma, should be able to sacrifice their own bodies and lives,

there will be many bhikṣus of evil conduct at that time."
Not knowing the subtle and secret treasury of the Tathāgata,
they are indolent and lax, unable to read, recite,
proclaim, or analyze the true Dharma of the Tathāgata.
It is like a foolish thief who abandons genuine jewels to carry a load of straw;
because he does not understand the subtle and secret treasury of the Tathāgata,
he is indolent and lacks diligence regarding this sutra.
Alas, what a great peril!
The future age will be most terrifying.
How bitter it is for sentient beings!
They do not diligently listen to or receive this Mahāyāna scripture,
the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra; only the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and those like them are able [to do so] regarding this sūtra.
One should grasp the true meaning and not cling to the words;
one should teach for the sake of sentient beings in accordance with the truth and without opposition. Furthermore, good son:
It is like a cowherd woman who, wishing to sell milk and desiring a greater profit,
adds two parts of water to it before selling it to another cowherd woman.
Having acquired that woman, he added two more parts to her price and sold her to a woman living near the city;
having acquired her, she in turn added two more parts to her price.
He then sold it again to a woman in the city;
having obtained it, she added two more parts to the price and went to the market to sell it.
At that time, there was a man who had taken a wife for his son.
He required good milk to provide for his guests,
so he went to the market intending to purchase some.
At that time, the milk seller asked for a high price; the man replied,
"Your milk contains much water and is not worth that much."
"Since I am currently hosting guests,
you should take it. Having taken it,
return home and boil it to make gruel."
It has no flavor of milk at all;
yet, although it lacks flavor, it is a thousand times superior among bitter flavors.
Why is this? Because of the nature of the flavor of milk.
The most excellent among all flavors. Good son,
after my parinirvāṇa, when eighty years remain before the True Dharma has perished.
At that time, this sutra shall be widely disseminated throughout Jambudvīpa.
At that time, there will be many wicked bhikṣus who will plunder this sutra and divide it into many parts.
They are able to destroy the color, fragrance, and exquisite flavor of the True Dharma;
although these evil persons may read and recite such scriptures, they destroy the profound and secret essential meanings of the Tathāgata.
They arrange worldly ornaments and embellish meaningless speech,
excerpting what precedes and attaching it to what follows.
Place what was collected behind in front;
place what was in front in the middle;
place what was in the middle behind and in front.
You should know that such evil bhikṣus are the companions of Māra;
they accept and store all kinds of impure things,
yet claim that the Tathāgata has permitted them to possess them all.
Just as a cowherd woman adds excessive water to milk,
so too are the wicked bhikṣus;
they merely use worldly language to erroneously determine this sutra.

They cause many sentient beings to fail to obtain correct exposition, correct transcription, and correct comprehension [of the teachings], and they prevent them from receiving respect, praise, offerings, and veneration;
for the sake of gain and support, these evil bhikṣus act in this way.
They will be unable to widely proclaim and disseminate this sutra;
what little they do manage to spread is not worth mentioning,
like that poor cowherd woman.
Though it becomes increasingly insipid and lacks flavor,
even this lack of flavor is still a thousand times superior to other flavors by comparison with the taste of that milk.
It is a thousand times superior to all other bitter flavors.
Why is this? Because it is the Mahāyāna scripture, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra.
It is the most preeminent among the Śrāvaka sūtras,
just as cow’s milk is the most excellent among all flavors; for this reason.
It is named Great Nirvāṇa.
Section Four: On Preaching and Listening. As stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*:
"Furthermore, good son..."
If my disciples receive, uphold, recite, copy, and expound this Nirvana Sutra,
they must not speak at improper times,
nor must they speak with obstinacy.
Do not preach unless requested;
do not preach with a轻慢 mind (a disrespectful or contemptuous attitude); do not preach in every place.
Do not lament for yourself;
do not disparage others;
do not speak at a time when the Buddha-dharma is being extinguished.
Do not engage in worldly discourse with excessive fervor. Good son,
if my disciples uphold this sutra and preach it at an improper time, [they will incur fault].
"Even those who speak with such fervor in the world will be disparaged by others, who will say:
'If the Buddha’s Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, the Secret Treasury, possessed any power,' [it would not have come to this]."
"How is it that you speak at an improper time, even to the point of speaking while the world is ablaze?
If those who uphold the sūtras speak in such a manner,
one should know that this sūtra possesses no power."
If one lacks majestic power, even if one upholds [this sutra], it will be of no benefit;
because of this slighting and disparaging of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*,
it causes immeasurable sentient beings to fall into hell.
Such individuals are evil friends to sentient beings;
they are not my disciples,
but rather the retinue of Māra.
If one preaches the sutras for the sake of gain, the five desires, or fame,
it is equivalent to bartering for profit and will swiftly cause the True Dharma to perish.
Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
How could one trade sandalwood for common wood?
It is like my disciples who,
for the sake of making offerings, [act in such a manner].
When preaching the sutras and the Dharma to laypeople,
the laypeople are indolent in mind and take no pleasure in listening;
moreover, the laypeople sit on high while the bhikṣus remain below.
Furthermore, he provided him with various kinds of delicacies and food and drink,
yet [the other] still refused to listen.
This is called "trading sandalwood for common wood."
Why is it said that one trades gold for brass?
Brass is a metaphor for form, sound, smell, taste, and touch;
gold is a metaphor for the precepts.
My disciples, on account of form, break the precepts they have received;
this is called exchanging gold for brass.
Why is silver used as an exchange for white tin?
Silver is a metaphor for the ten wholesome actions;
white tin is a metaphor for the ten unwholesome actions.
If my disciples abandon the ten wholesome actions and practice the ten unwholesome dharmas,
this is called trading silver for white tin.
Why is silk used as a trade for coarse woolen cloth?
Coarse woolen cloth is used as a metaphor for a lack of shame and a lack of dread of blame;
silk is used as a metaphor for shame and dread of blame.
"My disciples abandon shame and modesty and cultivate shamelessness; this is called trading fine silk for coarse woolen cloth.
What is it to trade ambrosia for poison?"
Poisonous drugs are used as a metaphor for various kinds of offerings;
ambrosia is used as a metaphor for all untainted dharmas (anāsrava-dharma). My disciples—
For the sake of gain and offerings, one speaks to laypeople,
falsely praising oneself by saying that one has attained the outflows-free state;
this is called trading ambrosia for poison.
Furthermore, the Lotus Sūtra states:
"Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not associate with kings, princes, ministers, or high officials;
they do not associate with various non-Buddhists, such as brahmans and Nirgranthas."
Furthermore, they compose secular writings and verses in praise of non-Buddhist texts;
they engage in all manner of evil disciplines, such as hunting and fishing;
and they do not associate with those who seek the state of a śrāvaka.
Furthermore, one should not preach the Dharma while perceiving signs in a woman’s body that could give rise to thoughts of desire,
nor should one take pleasure in seeing her.
If one enters another's home, one should not converse with young girls, virgins, widows, or the like.
Furthermore, one should not associate with the five kinds of impotent persons as friends or companions.
One should not enter another's house alone;
however, if there is a necessary reason to enter alone, [one should proceed].
Simply focus the mind single-mindedly on the Buddha.
When preaching the Dharma to women,
do not smile with bared teeth.
They do not reveal their innermost thoughts;
they do not even become intimate for the sake of the Dharma,
much less for other matters.
He did not delight in keeping young disciples, śrāmaṇeras, or children, nor did he delight in having the same teacher as them.
He always preferred to practice dhyāna in secluded places, cultivating and collecting his mind.
Furthermore, the *Buddhapiṭaka-sūtra* states that there are five kinds of impure preaching of the Dharma.
The first is to claim for oneself that one fully knows all the Buddha-dharma.
Second, when expounding the Buddha’s sutras, one points out contradictions and faults within those scriptures.
Third, one harbors doubts and lacks faith regarding all phenomena.
Fourth, one considers what one knows for oneself to be superior to the teachings of other scriptures.
Fifth, those who preach the Dharma to others for the sake of gain and offerings—
I say that such persons shall fall into hell and shall not attain nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, it says:
"For a long time I have diligently undergone hardships seeking this Dharma-treasure,
yet these wicked people have abandoned it and failed to preach it."
They merely rely on words that contradict the meaning of the sūtras,
asserting right and wrong against one another in a manner that does not accord with the True Dharma;
within the Noble Dharma, they harbor a mind of self-aggrandizement.
If one speaks at will for the sake of seeking gain and offerings,
or if a bhikṣu preaches the Dharma while intermingling it with the doctrines of external paths,
virtuous bhikṣus should depart from their seats.
If it were not so, one would not be a virtuous bhikṣu,
nor would one be called a follower of the Buddha’s teachings. Thus it is said.
I say that such a person is called a disciple of the non-Buddhist Nirgrantha,
not a disciple of the Buddha;
they are what I call beings of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts.
Why is this? Because one occupies a high seat without having personally realized the Dharma,
teaching others while remaining ignorant oneself.
Such a person shall fall into hell.
Furthermore, there will be bhikṣus in the future who take pleasure in reading non-Buddhist scriptures;
when preaching the Dharma, they will embellish their prose and rhetoric merely to entertain the assembly.
At that time, Māra will assist in deluding the multitude and obstructing wholesome dharmas.
Whether it be those who are greedily attached to sounds, speech, and cleverly adorned rhetoric,
or those who take pleasure in the scriptures of external paths— [Māra will hinder them].
Māra causes all to be deluded, yet he makes their minds peaceful and secure.
Furthermore, it is like a group of blind men who, having abandoned the goods they had obtained, wish to go to a great distribution of alms but fall into a deep pit. My disciples are also like this.
Abandoning coarse food and clothing, they pursue great offerings and seek fine sustenance;
for the sake of worldly profit, they lose their great wisdom and fall into the deep pit of the Avīci Hell.
It is further said:
"To preach the Dharma with impurity incurs extremely grave offense;
it also makes one an evil friend to sentient beings."
They also slander the Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
If someone were to take the lives of all sentient beings in a trichiliocosm, the sin of preaching the Dharma impurely would be greater than that.
Why is this? Because these people all destroy the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of the Buddhas, acting as an aid to the works of Māra,
and they also cause sentient beings to undergo various decays and afflictions for hundreds of thousands of lifetimes.
One who can only create bondage and cannot bring about liberation should be known as an evil friend to all sentient beings;
such a person is a speaker of falsehood.
Within the great assembly, they slandered and reviled the Buddhas;
by these causes and conditions, they fell into the great hells.
They taught many sentient beings the matters of false views.
For this reason, they are called those with evil and false views.
Furthermore, it says: "Śāriputra,..."
At that time, monks who have broken the precepts will even preach the Buddha-dharma to laypeople for the sake of obtaining a single cup of wine.
What do you think? Those who possess much greed,
anger, and delusion, who take great pleasure in reciting scriptures,
and who are attached to gain and offerings while practicing impurity— [are they to be considered wise?]
Śāriputra, if there is a bhikṣu who is advanced in years and possessed of virtue.
Among the bhikṣus, there are dragon-like ones who possess profound wisdom;
such persons are able to believe in the dharma of selflessness and the absence of a person, which is empty of intrinsic characteristics and devoid of anything existing.
Why is this? Because such a person does not delight in crowds or idle chatter, nor do they delight in sleep or many worldly affairs;
they do not engage in business or administrative tasks on behalf of laypeople.
One shall not act as a messenger to carry documents;
one shall not practice medicine;
and one shall not study medical prescriptions.
They do not engage in buying and selling;
they take no pleasure in discussing worldly talk,
but rather delight in preaching the supramundane Dharma.
Śāriputra, I now clearly inform you: when seeking one's own benefit, bhikṣus who are well-established in their practice should,
at such a time, not enter a crowd, nor even stay there for a single night.
Except for Arhats whose afflictions have already been severed,
and for sick bhikṣus who have a specific need for it. Why is this?
Śāriputra, at that time,
the poisons of greed, hatred, and delusion will be rampant among people.
They will be constantly oppressed by the fear of being unable to survive.
Those seeking benefit and virtue should always dwell in small forests and empty, quiet places, remaining there until the end of their lives, dying like wild animals.
It is further said: "This True Dharma of mine will not remain for long."
For what reason is this?
Because the merit and roots of goodness of sentient beings have been exhausted,
and a turbid world is drawing near.
Furthermore, the Mahāsaṃnipāta-candragarbha-sūtra states:
"If there are sentient beings who,
relying solely upon recitation, desire to seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi..."
Such persons mostly take great pleasure in worldly attachments;
because of these worldly attachments,
they are not even able to subdue the afflictions of their own minds.
How can one subdue the afflictions of others?
Good son, those who delight in attachment to recitation while seeking bodhi—
They immediately give rise to jealousy and seek fame and profit;
with haughty minds, they rely on themselves, showing contempt for and disparaging others,
such that they cannot even attain the roots of goodness of the desire realm.
How much more so, then, can they attain all the wholesome roots of the form and formless realms?
Furthermore, the Mahāyāna Mahāratnakūṭa-sūtra says:
"It is, for example, like a physician who travels about carrying medicine."
Yet one cannot cure one's own illness.
It is the same for a person of great learning who suffers from the disease of afflictions (*kleśa*):
although they possess much learning, if they do not restrain their afflictions, they cannot benefit themselves; it is all in vain and of no use.
It is like a dead man wearing a golden necklace;
likewise, one who is learned but violates the precepts, yet wears the Dharma robes and accepts the offerings of others, is just the same.
Furthermore, the *Vaipulya Daśacakra Sūtra* states:
If there are sentient beings who give rise to coarse, base, foolish, and evil speech,
yet consider themselves wise;
They do not even abandon wrong views;
they give rise to envy in their pursuit of the benefit of others;
they crave fame, exalting themselves and disparaging others, and are unable to guard their body, speech, and mind.
Their minds constantly dwell on evil and they always utter such words,
yet they claim for themselves to be followers of the Mahāyāna,
and they also teach others to read and recite it.
However, having praised themselves, they disparage others.
For this reason, though they extol the Mahāyāna, they remain undisciplined themselves.
Desiring to instruct others in the Mahāyāna path and lead them to practice the Mahāyāna—
up to the point of saying that it is difficult to obtain a human body—
one would also cause them to lose the vehicles of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha and constantly fall into the evil realms.
Not wishing to associate with those who possess wisdom,
they utter these words and let out a lion’s roar.
I am a son of good family of the Mahāyāna.
It is like a donkey wearing a lion’s skin that considers itself a lion;
someone seeing it from afar would also call it a lion.
Before the donkey has made a sound, no one can distinguish it;
once it has let out its voice,
everyone far and near knows it is not a real lion.
All who saw them spat upon them and said,
"Is this a wretched, evil donkey, not a lion?"
Even those who violate the prohibitive precepts and engage in evil conduct are not suitable vessels for the Dharma in any respect.
If they should say of themselves:
I am the Mahāyāna. I am able to shatter the great battle arrays of the afflictions and defilements of all sentient beings,
and I also cause sentient beings to abide in the Eightfold Noble Path.
It is impossible for one who has entered the city of fearlessness to be in such a state.
Furthermore, the *Buddhapiṭaka Sūtra* says:
In a past age, there were five bhikṣus:
the first was named Pūrvakāla (Universal Service),
and the second was named Duḥkha-tīra (Banks of Suffering).
The third was named Sādhaka;
the fourth, Nandika;
and the fifth, Upananda.
These five bhikṣus were teachers of the great assembly;
those who served them universally understood the Buddha’s teaching on the true meaning of emptiness and the dharma of non-attainment.
The other four bhikṣus all fell into heterodox paths and frequently asserted the existence of a self. Consequently,
the Bhikṣu Pǔshì was held in contempt by the fourfold assembly.
They will lack power and influence;
many people will treat them with hatred and contempt—
these four types of evil bhikṣus.
They teach many people by way of false views;
because they do not show mutual respect within the Buddha-dharma,
they act in opposition to it.
They cause the extinction of the Buddha-dharma; it even says:
"These evil people extinguish the True Dharma of the Buddha."
Furthermore, it brings great ruin and suffering to many people;
moreover, after such an evil person’s life ends,
they will fall into the Avīci Hell.
He lay on his back for nine hundred trillion years;
he lay prone for nine hundred trillion years;
and he likewise lay on his left and right sides for the same duration.
Upon glowing red-hot iron, they are scorched and seared;
from there, having died and been reborn, they enter the Tapana Hell and the Pratāpana Hell.
In the Reviving Hell and the Black Rope Hell,
they all undergo various sufferings for the same number of years as mentioned above.
After dying in the Kālasūtra Hell, they are reborn again in the Avīci Great Hell. ...
[and so on] ... until it says:
"One who associates with such a person..."
Together with spiritual friends and various donors,
there were six hundred and forty trillion people who lived and died together with these four teachers.
They undergo various forms of burning and boiling in the great hells,
even to the point that it is said:
"In this manner, they successively undergo suffering for the duration of one kalpa."
Because the great kalpa is about to burn, they remain in hell.
Furthermore, it is said that the great kalpa burns these four types of evil persons.
And six hundred and four trillion people were transferred from this Great Avīci Hell to other regions within the great hells.
Why is this? Śāriputra,
one who is fully possessed of grave offenses will receive no small retribution.
They shall undergo great suffering for countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of years in other worlds,
until those worlds are once again formed;
this applies to these four criminals as well as six hundred and forty trillion people.
Furthermore, those others whose offenses are not yet exhausted,
when their lives there end, will return to be born here again within this great hell.
It is also said:
After a long time, although he escapes the sufferings of hell and is reborn among human beings,
he remains blind from birth for five hundred lifetimes;
only thereafter does he encounter the Buddha Sarvākṣa.
It continues, saying:

"He went forth in that Buddha-dharma and practiced with diligent effort for ten trillion years as if his head were on fire, yet he did not attain the patient acceptance of conformity (*anulomikī kṣānti*)."
How much more so for one who has attained the fruits of the Path?
Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"The bhikṣu Sunakṣatra had mastered the twelve divisions of the scriptures."
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Devadatta left the household life to study the Way and mastered sixty thousand dharma-aggregates.
Commentary says:
These two individuals both fail to cultivate the true Buddha-nature within the path of skillful means,
nor do they contemplate the practices of the four foundations of mindfulness and other such dharmas.
Having observed that the five aggregates are impermanent, suffering, empty, and without self or what belongs to a self,
yet having become greedily attached to the view of a self, the view of a person, and the view of a sentient being,
they commit the great crime of parricide by slandering the Tathāgata.
For this reason,
the physical bodies of these two individuals sank into the Avīci Hell to undergo inexhaustible suffering.
Such precedents and examples are too numerous to describe in full.
5. Bodhisattva Section, Part Five. As stated in the *Kāśyapa Sūtra*:
At that time, the Buddha addressed Mahākāśyapa:
"The Tathāgata will soon enter parinirvāṇa."
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One, we only pray that the World-Honored One [will explain this]."
He shall remain in the world for one kalpa,
or slightly less than a kalpa,
to protect and uphold the True Dharma.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Even if a thousand Buddhas were to appear in the world and teach the Dharma through various supernormal powers to instruct and transform such a foolish person,
that foolish person's evil desires could not be made to cease."
Kāśyapa, in the future final age, during the last five hundred years,
there will be sentient beings who are endowed with roots of goodness and whose minds are pure.
"They will be able to repay the Buddha's kindness and protect my Dharma.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One,"
I have cultivated but little practice and my wisdom is shallow;
like one carrying a heavy burden, I am unable to sustain it.
Only a bodhisattva can.
They are capable of bearing such a heavy burden. It is,
for example, like a person who is extremely old, one hundred and twenty years of age,
whose body is afflicted by a grave illness and unable to rise or move.
At that time, there was a man of immense wealth and abundant riches who,
carrying various precious treasures, went to the place where the sick person was and spoke to him, saying:
I have a matter of karmic connection that requires me to travel to another region.
I entrust these jewels to you;
please guard them for my sake.
"When I have returned, you should come back to me.
That old, sick man had no children;
he was all alone.
Not long after that person had departed, he fell gravely ill and passed away;
all the wealth he had entrusted was completely lost,
and when the traveler returned, he sought it but found nothing.
World-Honored One,
it is likewise with the śrāvakas;
their wisdom is slight and shallow, and their practice is very limited.
Furthermore, lacking companions,
one cannot remain long in this world;
if the True Dharma is entrusted [to others], it will not soon perish.
The Buddha praised Kāśyapa:
"I already understood this, yet I have entrusted it to you so that those deluded people, upon hearing it, may give rise to a mind of remorse."
At that time, Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
I shall now further speak a second parable."
For example, suppose there is a person whose physical strength is robust and vigorous, free from all ailments and suffering,
with a lifespan of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of years,
born into a great lineage and fully endowed with wealth and treasures.
He upholds the pure precepts well;
possessing great compassion and inward joy,
he benefits many people and brings them peace and happiness.
At that time, there was a man carrying precious goods who came to his place and said to him,
"I have a matter requiring my presence in another region."
I entrust these precious seals to you; please guard them well.
Whether they are returned in ten years or in twenty years.
"When I return, you shall see the signs and restore it.
That person obtained the treasure and guarded its accumulation;
when that man returned from his journey, he immediately gave it back to him.
World-Honored One,
it is likewise for the bodhisattva-mahāsattva:
if the Dharma-jewel is entrusted to these bodhisattvas.
For immeasurable thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas, it shall never perish;
it shall benefit immeasurable and boundless sentient beings and ensure that the Three Jewels are never interrupted,
World-Honored One.
"I am unable to uphold such matters;
only a bodhisattva is able to endure them,
World-Honored One."
This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya is present here in this assembly;
the Tathāgata entrusts him with [this teaching] for the future age, during the final five hundred years when the Dharma is about to perish.
They are fully able to protect, propagate, and extensively expound the Dharma collected by the Tathāgata. Why is this?
This Bodhisattva Maitreya shall, in a future age, realize unexcelled perfect enlightenment.
He will be like the eldest crown prince of a king,
who shall attend to the affairs of state and govern the world according to the Dharma.
Maitreya Bodhisattva shall likewise do so,
governing the rank of the Dharma King and protecting the True Dharma.
At that time, the Buddha praised Kāśyapa.
"Just as you have said," he said,
and extending his right hand, he stroked Maitreya’s head and spoke these words.
Maitreya, I entrust you with this:
in the future final age, during the last five hundred years when the True Dharma is extinguished,
you must protect the Triple Gem and ensure that it is not severed.
At that time, when the Tathāgata touched Maitreya’s crown,
this trichiliocosm shook in six ways, and a radiance filled the entire great trichiliocosm.
At that time, the devas of the earth and the devas of the sky,
up to those of the Akaniṣṭha Heaven,
all joined their palms and addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, saying:
The Tathāgata has entrusted the Dharma to you,
O Noble One. We pray that you will accept all these sentient beings for the sake of benefiting all devas and humans.
They would still undergo suffering for immeasurable billions of kalpas;
how much more so, then, could one not accept the True Dharma entrusted to me by the Tathāgata?
World-Honored One,
at that time I shall receive and uphold the Dharma of unexcelled bodhi accumulated by the Tathāgata over immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, so as to proclaim it in future ages.
When Maitreya Bodhisattva spoke these words,
the trichiliocosm shook in six ways.
Furthermore, the Mahāsannipāta Sūtra says:
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the foremost Maitreya and all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the Bhadrakalpa, saying:
"O sons of good family, in the past,
when I was practicing the bodhisattva path..."
In the past, they made such offerings to the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas;
by these roots of goodness, may they become the cause for my attainment of *samyak-saṃbodhi*.
It is because I now have compassion for all sentient beings.
Divide this fruit of retribution into three parts.
Set aside one part for oneself to receive.
As for the second part:
After my parinirvāṇa, may the śrāvakas who are firmly established in dhyāna, liberation,
and samādhi have nothing lacking.
This is the third section.

Maitreya, you should ensure that those who have shaved their heads and donned the kashaya— who, though they may break the precepts, are associated with the study and recitation of the sutras, and who belong to the period of the True Dharma or the Semblance Dharma— are not lacking in anything.
I now further entrust to your hands the assembly of śrāvakas—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—who are endowed with the three karmas.
Do not allow them to pass away in poverty, destitution, or solitude.
Furthermore, those who, during the period of the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma, have violated the prohibitions and precepts yet wear the kāṣāya—
entrust them to your hands.
Do not allow them to pass away in want of any necessary provisions.
Furthermore, do not allow any Cāṇḍāla kings to cause mutual affliction and harm, so that they may suffer in body and mind.
I now entrust those donors into your hands once again.

7. The Section on Monks and Nuns (Sengni-bu), the Seventh. As stated in the *Vinayamātṛkā-sūtra*:
"If monks and nuns who have left the household life possess five causal conditions, they can cause the True Dharma not to disappear prematurely."
First, regarding the sūtras one recites and studies:

"A person such as this is capable of causing the Buddha-dharma to abide long in the world."
Second, they have extensively studied the texts and meanings of the Tripitaka such that they are fully proficient;
furthermore, they are able to instruct the fourfold assembly according to their own understanding.
Although their physical bodies perish, they cause the True Dharma to continue in succession without interruption for future generations.
Such persons as these are able to prevent the True Dharma from falling to the ground.
Third, if within the Saṃgha there is a virtuous elder (sthavira) who is esteemed by the fourfold assembly,
and who is able to diligently cultivate the three karmas while renouncing worldly affairs,
his disciples and followers will succeed one another in succession.
All are likewise so.
This also causes the True Dharma to abide for a long time.
Fourth, if there is a bhikṣu whose nature is gentle and mild, and whose speech is free from contradiction or opposition.
When hearing of the good, follow it;

If there are those of lofty talent, wisdom, and virtue, [one should honor them].
To receive their instructions and teachings with reverence and practice them accordingly;

Fifth, if bhikṣus are mutually harmonious and do not form factions based on status or gain to assist one another in disputing right from wrong.
These five matters are able to cause the True Dharma to circulate without interruption;

Chapter Twenty-three: On Hiding and Escaping;

Chapter Twenty-four: On Monstrosities. 23. Chapter on Hiding and Escaping (31): This chapter consists of two sections. Section One: Exposition of the Intent. First, Exposition of the Intent: I have heard that when sages and worthies respond to the world, their traces and manifestations are not confined to any single place.
In whatever country one dwells, there is nothing that does not bring benefit.
Worldly people fixate upon their auspiciousness and misfortune;
those of superior wisdom remain serene amidst both good and evil.
If one rectifies the mind and awaits [the natural course], then one's measure will be equal to that of Heaven.
Formerly, during the reign of Emperor Wu of Jin,
there was a physician from India named Jīvaka.
At the beginning of the reign of Emperor Wu of the Song dynasty, there was Bei-du of Pengcheng,
who manifested various auspicious signs to awaken the common people.
During the Qi and Liang dynasties, there was a śramaṇa named Baozhi who first appeared at the beginning of the Yongming era.
He concealed his wisdom as if he were mad, and his physical form was like withered dust.
He could store away the past and know the future;
his insights were consistently accurate and efficacious, his countenance and words moved others,
and he rarely failed in his strategic counsel.
Scholars and commoners rushed to him from all quarters like clouds;
though his physical traces were constrained by worldly defilements, his spirit wandered in profound stillness.
Neither water nor fire could scorch or moisten him.
Neither snakes nor tigers can inflict their venom upon him;
though his body may be confined by the nine gates of hell, he ultimately remains unimpeded.
From the perspective of Buddhist principle, he ranks as a śrāvaka or above.
Regarding their reclusion, they are transcendents and lofty gentlemen who have hidden themselves.
Because the world possesses that which is good, they emerge to respond with goodness;
because the world possesses that which is evil, they emerge to respond with evil.
It may be said that [this merit] hangs as high as the sun and moon and outlasts metal and stone;
boundless blessings are seen therein.

Section Two: On Transformation and Change. As stated in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*:
"O Son of the Buddha, it is as if a single Tathāgata were to manifest a single transformation-body."
Such unspeakable clouds of wheels of Dharma, illustrated by these and other metaphors,
pervade all worlds throughout the entire realm of phenomena and the realm of space,
even when measured exhaustively with the tip of a single hair.
At the tip of every single hair,
in every moment of thought, they manifest bodies as numerous as the atoms within unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields,
continuing thus until the end of all future kalpas.
Each and every transformed Buddha has as many heads as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields;
each head has as many tongues as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields.
From each tongue there issued forth sounds equal in number to the atoms of unspeakably unspeakable Buddha-fields;
each sound proclaimed sutras equal in number to the atoms of unspeakably unspeakable Buddha-fields.
In each and every sūtra, there are explained unspeakably unspeakable numbers of dharmas equal to the atoms of a buddha-field;
within each and every dharma, there are explained unspeakably unspeakable numbers of word-bodies (*padakāya*) and syllable-bodies (*vyañjanakāya*), equal to the atoms of a buddha-field.

Furthermore, for as many eons as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable Buddha-fields, one might speak with various bodies of phrases, bodies of meanings, and sounds that fill the entire Dharma-realm;

Section Two: The Three Natures. Second, according to the *Sudarsana-vinaya*, there are four kinds of dreams.
First, dreams caused by the disharmony of the four great elements;
second, dreams resulting from prior perceptions;
third, dreams of gods and humans.
Fourth is the dream of perception.
What is the dream of the disharmony of the four great elements?
Answer: During sleep, one sees in a dream a mountain collapsing.
Whether one soars through the void or sees oneself pursued by tigers, wolves, lions, or bandits—
these are dreams of the disharmony of the four great elements;
they are empty and unreal.

Whether male or female,

Answer: If a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) or a deva manifests a virtuous dream for them.
It causes people to attain what is wholesome.

What is meant by "one who perceives a dream"?
The answer is: this person, in a previous life, may have possessed merit.
There may be those with karmic obstructions;

For example, when a bodhisattva first intends to enter his mother’s womb, he dreams that a white elephant descends from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and enters his right side; this is a dream of conceptualization (*saṃjñā*).
If one dreams of paying homage to the Buddha, reciting sutras, observing the precepts, practicing giving, or performing various meritorious deeds, these are also dreams of conceptualization.
Question: Are dreams wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate?
Answer: They may be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
For instance, if one sees in a dream paying homage to the Buddha, listening to the Dharma, or preaching the Dharma.
These are virtuous merits. If one sees killing,
stealing, or sexual misconduct in a dream,
these are unwholesome dreams.
If one sees in a dream colors such as blue, yellow, red,
or white, this is an indeterminate dream. Question:
If that were so, one would have to undergo karmic retribution.
The answer is: one does not undergo retribution. Why is this?
Because the mental karma was weak, no retribution was incurred.
Therefore, the Vinaya states:
"Except for that which occurs in dreams, there is no offense."
Furthermore, the *Kātyāyanīputra-śāstra* asks:
"In what sense is everything associated with sleep?
It answers:
Or it may be associated with sleepiness or lack of sleep;
as when one has not yet fallen asleep,
the body is not supple and the mind is not supple.
The body is heavy and the mind is heavy;
the body is lethargic and the mind is lethargic;
the body is agitated and the mind is agitated.
When the body is drowsy and the mind is drowsy,
and one is enveloped by drowsiness,
this is called being associated with drowsiness but not with sleep.
What is sleep associated with non-waking?
The answer is:
sleeping in dreams with an undefiled mind.
This is called being associated with sleepiness but not with drowsiness.
What is meant by being associated with both sleepiness and drowsiness?
The answer is:
A defiled mind during sleep or dreaming is called "associated with sleep.
What is "neither sleeping nor dreaming"?
Answer: Excluding the aforementioned matters.
Question: Should sleep be described as wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate?
Answer: Sleep may be wholesome or unwholesome.
Or it is indeterminate. What is wholesome?
The answer is:
If a wholesome mind sleeps or dreams,
how can it be unwholesome?
The answer is:
Regarding unwholesome states of mind during sleep and dreams,
how are they indeterminate?
The answer is:
Setting aside the aforementioned matters,
it is like performing acts of giving, cultivating merit, observing the precepts, and maintaining the fast within a dream;
it is like the merit produced when one sleeps with a virtuous mind.
It should be said that other merit is redirected;
this is called "wholesome.
Why is it that the non-merit produced during sleep should be said to be redirected?
Answer: It is like killing, stealing, and so forth within a dream;
it is like an unwholesome mind or other non-meritorious minds revolving while one is asleep.
This is called unwholesome.
Why is it that the merit or demerit performed during sleep should not be said to be "transformed"?
The answer is:
Just as when one is asleep, neither a non-meritorious mind nor a non-non-meritorious mind arises,
so it is with an indeterminate mind during sleep.
The merit or non-merit that has been performed should not be said to be "turned over";
this is called the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Question: What kind of phenomenon is called a dream?
Answer: It is the hindrance of ignorance (*avidyā-nīvaraṇa*) among these five hindrances.

The tree deity, filled with grief and fear, reported this to the Four Heavenly Kings.
The King informed Śakra.
Śakra observed that there was no one in Jambudvīpa capable of being that son;
he then went to Brahmādeva and extensively proclaimed the aforementioned matter.
The Brahmā King, using his divine eye, surveyed everywhere and saw a Brahmā deity on the verge of death;
he immediately went to him and spoke,

Having received these instructions, Brahmā descended to take birth.
When ten months had passed, he gave birth to a son whose countenance was upright and handsome, and whose body was the color of pure gold.
A brilliant radiance shone forth, illuminating a distance of forty li.
A physiognomist divined and said,

Upon hearing this, his parents were filled with great sorrow and distress.
The husband and wife consulted one another, saying,

He reflected to himself:
