I shall betroth him to an upright and beautiful maiden to sever his passion."
When he reached the age of fifteen, his parents wished to arrange a marriage for him.
He spoke to them, saying, "My aspiration is for purity; I have no need for a wife."
The parents would not listen.
Knowing he could not escape, the son devised a stratagem and said to his parents:
"If you can obtain for me a daughter of purple-golden complexion, upright and surpassing the world,
I shall take her as my wife.
His parents immediately summoned various brahmins and sent them everywhere to seek a bride.
The brahmins cast a golden image of a woman, exquisite and extraordinary in appearance.
They carried it through the villages on a palanquin, proclaiming in a loud voice:
"If there is any woman who beholds this golden deity and pays her homage,"
When she later marries, she will surely obtain an excellent husband;
her body will be of true golden color, upright and most exquisite.
Upon hearing this, the girl emerged from her seclusion.
There was only one daughter whose body was golden in color, upright and exceptionally beautiful;
she was none other than the girl who had offered gold in the past.
It was because of those superior conditions from the past that she possessed such a wondrous body.
Her mind delighted in purity and she alone refused to go out.
The other women forcibly took her along to see the Golden Deity.
As soon as this woman arrived, [the deity appeared].
Her golden radiance outshone the Golden Deity (Suvarṇadeva).
Upon seeing her, the Brahmin immediately betrothed her to him.
Once she arrived at her husband's home, she...
The husband and wife, facing one another, were both pure and entirely free from desire;
they made a mutual agreement to each occupy a separate room.
Once their parents learned of this, they demolished one of the rooms.
He had them share a single room and place a single bed between them.
Kāśyapa said to his wife,
"When I am sleeping and resting, you should practice walking meditation."
"If you sleep and rest, I shall practice walking meditation.
Later, the second wife lay down with her hand hanging over the edge of the bed.
A venomous snake entered the room, intending to bite her hand.
Having seen this, Kāśyapa wrapped his hands in his robe and placed them upon the bed.
His wife woke up again in alarm and reproached him, saying,
"We made a vow together that we would never have sexual relations with one another."
"Now for what reason have you secretly raised your hand?
Kāśyapa replied, "A snake came in; I feared it might injure your hand."
Thus, he merely raised it up.
He then pointed to the snake and showed it to his wife, whereupon she regained her senses.
The husband and wife, their integrity firm, grew deeply weary of the world.
Kai took leave of his parents, seeking to renounce the household life.
Upon seeing this, his parents granted him permission.
Thereupon, husband and wife together renounced the world and came to the place where the Buddha was.
The Buddha shared his seat with him and preached the Dharma for him;
he immediately attained arhatship while still upon that seat.
Later, the wife also attained arhatship.
While Kāśyapa was still in the world,
she constantly sat facing the Tathāgata as he preached the Dharma.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, he entrusted the entire Dharma treasury to Kāśyapa.
Later, having completed the compilation of the Tripiṭaka,
he entered parinirvāṇa at Mount Kukkuṭapāda.
With the entire body remaining undispersed,
one shall emerge from the mountain at the time when Maitreya Buddha appears in the world.
In the midst of the great assembly, he performed eighteen miraculous transformations,
delivering immeasurable numbers of people,
and thereafter extinguished his physical body.

He will attain Buddhahood in the future, and his name shall be Guangming (Radiance). Regarding the sixty baskets of gold dust, this is recorded in the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra* (*Sapoduo zhuan*). That he will attain Buddhahood in the future is stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says:
Formerly, when the Buddha was in the world,
there was Nanda, the son of King Śuddhodana and younger brother of the Buddha, residing in the city of Kapilavastu.
His body was upright and possessed thirty marks of excellence.
The king took him a wife named Sundarī,
whose countenance and features were so upright and beautiful that they had few equals in the world.
Because Nanda cherished and respected his wife day and night, he did not wish to leave the household life.
The Buddha used skillful means to transform him and cause him to go forth.
Once he had gone forth, he attained arhatship.
Having seen this, a bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What merit did the bhikṣu Nanda plant in past lives that he was born together with the Buddha and possesses thirty marks?
His body is upright and handsome, peerless in the world."
Furthermore, having renounced his noble status and left the household life, he attained the Way.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"In the distant past, ninety-one kalpas ago..."
After Vipaśyin Buddha had entered nirvana,
Nanda was at that time a great householder;
within the stūpa and temple of a pratyekabuddha, he...
He smeared the walls with indigo and painted images of Pratyekabuddhas upon them,
and thereupon made this vow:
"May I be born into a noble family in every lifetime."
He shall always obtain a handsome physical form with a golden complexion;
meeting a Buddha, he shall attain the Way through the merit of his vows and these roots of goodness.
From that time forward, for ninety-one kalpas, he did not fall into the evil realms.
Among gods and humans, his body was upright and possessed thirty marks;
he was noble, honored, wealthy, and his happiness was boundless.
Thus, even until this day, you have been born with me, left the household life together, and attained the Way.
Section Six: On Almsgiving (*Kṣiṇa*). As stated in the *Sūtra on the Five Paths of Transmigration like a Wheel*:
The Buddha said:
"In performing meritorious deeds as part of one's daily conduct,
burning incense and lighting lamps yields exceedingly great blessings."
When burning incense to cultivate merit or reciting sutras,
one must not employ others without giving them a reward (dakṣiṇā).
How could one hope to satisfy oneself by merely employing others for their food?
They maintained it as their regular practice to burn incense for purification,
light lamps to maintain constant illumination, offer incense and vegetarian meals, and recite scriptures and give alms.
Through giving, one obtains merit;
the devas will welcome and escort them;
all manner of evils are repelled, and the multitudes of māras are subdued.
Those who are indolent are unable to practice with diligence.
When suddenly stricken by illness or encountering an inauspicious omen,
they then desire to burn incense before finally performing meritorious deeds.
The various devas have not yet descended, and the various māras stand before you,
vying with one another to harass and disturb you by manifesting all manner of strange portents.
For this reason, you must always practice with diligent perseverance.
Sin and merit follow a person like a shadow follows a form.
Cultivating the field of merit is like the nyagrodha tree:
from planting a single seed, it gradually grows larger and larger.
"The gathering of disciples is limitless.
The Buddha said, "Ānanda."
The saying that "giving once yields ten thousandfold" is not false.
At that time, the Buddha spoke this verse:
"The wise person delights in giving; the celestial deities themselves support and guide them."
Giving once, one gains ten thousandfold; peace, joy, and a long life are attained.
Giving today to virtuous people, the merit thereof is immeasurable;
all shall attain the Way of the Buddha and deliver all beings throughout the ten directions.
7. Section on Miscellaneous Merit (Saṃkīrṇapuṇya-varga), the Seventh. As stated in the Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra:
"If one constructs monasteries, stupas, or images;
or constructs wells along desolate roads, as well as bridges and boats."
The merit of this person arises at all times and constantly benefits the donor,
except under three conditions:
first, when the previous object [of the gift] has been destroyed.
Second, if this person dies;
third, if they give rise to evil and heterodox views.
If these three causes and conditions do not exist, [then one may teach].
Merit is constantly produced.
Furthermore, the *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus.
There are five kinds of giving that do not yield merit. What are these five?
First, giving a blade to another person.
Second, giving poison to others;
third, giving wild oxen to others;
fourth, giving courtesans to others.
Fifth, constructing shrines for deities.
These are the five kinds of giving that do not yield merit.
Furthermore, there are five other kinds of giving through which humans and devas obtain merit.
What are the five?
First, constructing parks and gardens;
second, planting groves and trees.
Third, constructing bridges;
fourth, constructing large ships;
fifth, providing dwellings and residences for those of the future and the past.
This is called obtaining merit now through these five things.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke this verse:
"By giving pleasure gardens for cool retreats, And by constructing fine bridges,"
He ferries people across the river and builds fine dwellings for them;
throughout day and night, that person shall constantly receive its blessings.
Having perfected the precepts and meditative concentration, this person will surely be reborn in heaven.
Furthermore, in the Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya,
there were certain devaputras who questioned the Buddha in verse.
"What kind of person proceeds toward goodness? What kind of person is born in heaven?
What kind of person, day and night, nurtures virtuous merit?
At that time, the World-Honored One [spoke].
He replied in verse:
"By digging fine wells on desolate roads, by planting orchards and giving groves of trees,
and by providing cool shade, bridges, and boats to ferry people across."
By practicing generosity and cultivating pure precepts, and through wisdom abandoning stinginess and greed, one’s merit increases day and night; one will constantly be reborn among gods and humans.
Furthermore, the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states:
If there are sentient beings who give others fine water,
or who cover up wells and springs,
fearing that venomous snakes might fall into them.
The practitioner drinks it and experiences suffering;
at the end of his life, he is reborn in the Heaven of the Three Emptinesses (Trayastrimsha), where he enjoys the pleasures of the five senses.
From there, his life comes to an end.
If one has obtained a human body and is held in high esteem by kings,
and if one sees another who is suffering from illness, with a voice emerging from their throat and their life-force not yet exhausted;
They give them drinks or provide them with wealth to sustain their lives.
Upon the end of his life, he was reborn in the Heaven of Deep Waters,
where his happiness was like that of Śakra.
When his life there ended, he transmigrated according to the flow of his karma.
They shall not fall into the three miserable realms but will obtain a human body;
from birth to birth, they shall not encounter the suffering of illness.
There shall be no affliction or disturbance. If there are sentient beings who uphold the precepts,
and seeing the community of bhikṣus, they offer fans so that they may attain coolness while reciting and studying the Dharma.
Upon the end of their lives, they will be reborn in the Heaven of Wind Travel (Vāyujavana),
where fragrant scents waft and blow with incomparable joy. Furthermore,
if there are sentient beings who construct bridges or boats at river crossings and ferries, [they shall likewise attain such merit].
With a virtuous mind, they ferry across those who uphold the precepts,
as well as other people who refrain from committing various evils.
At the end of their lives, they are reborn in the Mālyavad (Holding-Garland) Heaven, where they enjoy the pleasures of the five senses.
When his life ended, he became the royal treasurer among humans.
Furthermore, the *Piyū jīng* (Sutra of Parables) states:
"In the past, there were three mother and sons who constantly performed three tasks."
First, he constructed a great ship and placed it in the river to ferry the common people across.
Second, he established fine wells in the marketplace to provide for the myriad subjects.
Third, he built latrines at each of the four gates to provide for the convenience of the people.
By virtue of these meritorious deeds,
after their lives come to an end, they shall all be reborn in the heavens where they naturally receive blessings;
when subsequently reborn among humans, they will be wealthy, noble, and long-lived.
In whatever place one is born,
one shall not pass through the three miserable realms;
even for such a minor merit, one shall yet obtain a sublime and immeasurable karmic reward.
How much more so for those who extensively cultivate merit,
erecting stupas and temples, practicing the giving of alms, and performing various meritorious deeds;
such merit is hundreds of thousands of millions of times superior to this, beyond all calculation.
Therefore, the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* quotes a verse from a sutra:
"If one plants trees and groves, Or constructs wells, bridges, and the like,
The merit performed by such a person Constantly increases day and night."
Furthermore, the *Puṣpamālā-sūtra* states:
The Buddha told Śāriputra,
"There are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva never regresses from unsurpassed bodhi."
What are the four? First,
if one sees that a stupa or temple is dilapidated, one should repair it,
whether by using clods of earth, mud, or even a single brick.
Second, if one establishes a stūpa or constructs an image at a crossroads or a place where many people gather,
it serves as a favorable condition for the wholesome merit of mindfulness of the Buddha. Within the stūpa,
one should depict [scenes such as] the Turning of the Wheel of Dharma or the appearance of renunciation.
Up until the manifestation of his entry into parinirvāṇa between the twin trees.
Third, if one sees the two divisions of the bhikṣu-saṃgha in dispute,
one should diligently seek skillful means to bring them into harmony.
Fourth, if one sees that the Buddha-dharma is about to perish, one should read, recite, and explain it,
even if only a single verse, so as not to let the Dharma be interrupted;
for the sake of protecting the Dharma, one should respectfully provide for and support the Dharma-teacher.
Dedicating oneself to protecting the Dharma without regard for body or life—
if a bodhisattva accomplishes these four dharmas,
they shall become a wheel-turning sage king (cakravartin) in every lifetime.
He shall obtain great physical strength like that of Nārāyaṇa;
he shall renounce the four continents to go forth into homelessness,
and be able to practice the four Brahma-vihāras at will.
At the end of his life, he will be reborn in heaven as a Great Brahmā King,
and eventually attain the unsurpassed path. Therefore,
a wise person who seeks the Buddha-way should train in this manner.
Furthermore, the *Gopālaka-sūtra* (The Cowherd Sūtra) is translated separately as a distinct chapter within the *Ekottarika-āgama*.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are eleven dharmas."
A cowherd boy does not know the advantages of tending cattle and is ignorant of how to raise them.
What are these eleven?
First, the cowherd boy does not know their color.
Second, not knowing the signs [of healing];
third, not knowing how to cleanse;
fourth, not knowing how to protect the wound.
Fifth, not knowing how to produce smoke;
sixth, not knowing how to choose the path for travel;
seventh, not knowing where to station cattle.
Eighth, not knowing which path to take to cross the water;
ninth, not knowing how to seek out good grass and water;
tenth, not knowing how to milk the cow without leaving any residue.
Eleventh, he does not know how to distinguish between what is suitable and what is unsuitable for feeding.
These are the eleven matters regarding which a cowherd boy who does not understand how to care for his cattle remains ignorant.
The cow never reproduces, and its numbers diminish day by day;
this is a metaphor for the bhikṣus,
who likewise experience eleven kinds of loss and gain that cannot be described in detail.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"The cowherd was discerning; The owner of the cattle possessed merit.
Six cows for six years Yielded sixty without diminishing."
The cowherd boy is wise, Knowing how to distinguish various characteristics;
Like this cowherd boy, he was praised by the Buddhas of past ages.
Chapter Eight: Washing the Sangha. As stated in the *Dṛṣṭānta-sūtra* (Piyu jing): [Text follows].
On the eighth day of the twelfth lunar month, the Buddha, through his supernatural powers, subdued the six heretical teachers.
The six teachers were unable to prevail and threw themselves into water and died.
Thereupon, the Buddha extensively preached the Dharma to deliver all the non-Buddhists.
The non-Buddhist practitioner, having been subdued and converted, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Buddha has washed the defilements of my mind with the water of the Dharma.
I now request that the Sangha bathe so as to remove the impurities of my body."
This remains a constant practice. On the eighth day of the twelfth month, when monks bathe, only this scriptural passage is cited.
Furthermore, the *Mahāsthavira-sūtra*, also titled the *Sūtra on Bathing the Buddha’s Image*, states:
The Buddha told the people of the world:
"The Buddhas of the ten directions were all born at midnight on the eighth day of the fourth month.
They all left their homes and studied the Way at midnight on the eighth day of the fourth month."
All attained the Way of the Buddha at midnight on the eighth day of the fourth month.
All entered *parinirvāṇa* at midnight on the eighth day of the fourth month.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
The reason for using the eighth day of the fourth month is that it marks the transition between spring and summer, when all calamities and transgressions have come to an end,
all things are universally brought forth, and no toxic vapors have yet circulated.
When it is neither cold nor hot, the seasonal climate is harmonious and pleasant.
Today is the Buddha’s birthday;
therefore, the people of the heavens and the world together contemplate the Buddha’s meritorious virtues and bathe his physical image.
Just as when the Buddha was in the world,
he showed it to all people under heaven.
The Buddha said:
When I was a bodhisattva, I served as Śakra, the king of gods, thirty-six times;
I served as a universal monarch with a golden wheel thirty-six times.
Thirty-six times he became a Universal Monarch (Cakravartin).
Today, among you virtuous ones, who possesses a benevolent heart that contemplates the grace and virtue of Śākyamuni Buddha?
Who seeks the foremost merit by bathing the images of the Buddha with incense and flowers?
This is witnessed and known by all the devas and spirits.
On the eighth day of the fourth month, the time for bathing the Buddha,
one should take three kinds of incense.
First, do-liang incense;
second, huoxiang incense;
third, ainara incense.
Combine these three types of fragrant grasses, press them, and soak them;
this constitutes the blue-colored water.
If the fragrance is insufficient, one may temporarily substitute with indigo, antimony, or *qinpi* (Eucommia bark).
Furthermore, take saffron and press it into water with the hand to soak it;
by pressing it, one creates "red water.
Once the water has become pure, use it to perform the consecration (abhiṣeka) upon the image.
Wipe it with white silk.
After cutting [the thread], perform a divination for oneself and then re-consecrate it;
this is called "purification. Its merit is supreme.
Furthermore, the *Jentāka-sūtra* states:
The Buddha told the elder Jīvaka,
"In the method of bathing, one should employ seven substances to eliminate seven ailments."
One obtains seven kinds of meritorious rewards.
What are these seven things?
The first is lighting a fire.
Second, pure water;
third, cleansing beans;
fourth, ghee and ointments.
Fifth, coarse ash;
sixth, a tooth-stick;
seventh, an inner garment.
This is the method for bathing.
What is meant by "removing the seven ailments"?
First, the four great elements are brought to peace and stability.
Second, it eliminates wind;
third, it eliminates dampness and numbness;
fourth, it eliminates cold and ice.
Fifth, it removes heat.
Sixth, it removes impurities.
Seventh, the body becomes light and agile, and the eyes become clear and bright.
This constitutes the elimination of the seven ailments and the attainment of the seven blessings.
The first is that the four great elements are free from disease, resulting in constant peace.
Second, those born [to them] will have pure faces and upright features.
Third, their bodies will always be fragrant and their clothing clean and pure.
Fourth, their skin will be soft and lustrous, and their majestic radiance and virtue will be great.
Fifth, many people will follow him to wipe away his dust and grime.
Sixth, his mouth and teeth will be fragrant and fine, and what he speaks will be solemn and effective.
Seventh, in whatever place he is born, clothing will appear spontaneously.
Furthermore, the *Śāriputra Vinaya* states:
"Bathing yields five benefits:
first, the removal of dust and impurities."
Second, it treats the skin of the body, making it uniform in color.
Third, it dispels cold and heat.
Fourth, it regulates and expels wind-energy (vāyu).
"Śāriputra, there was once a hired laborer during the height of the summer heat who suffered from slight illness."
While drawing water in the garden to irrigate the trees,
he saw Śāriputra and conceived a slight faith;
he called out to Śāriputra and told him to strip off his clothes beneath the tree.
By bathing his body with water, he attained lightness and coolness;
after his life as a human ended, he was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven,
where he possessed great majestic power.
Although his merit was small,
because he encountered a fertile field, the reward he obtained was very great;
he then went down to where Śāriputra was and scattered flowers as an offering.
Śāriputra, taking advantage of his faith, expounded the essential points of the Dharma for him,
whereby he attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*.
Furthermore, the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* states:
At that time, the Śuddhāvāsa devas descended to Jambudvīpa and went to the place where the World-Honored One was;
they requested the Buddha and the Saṃgha to bathe and offered them sustenance.
The World-Honored One silently gave his consent.
He immediately prepared food and drink, and provided bathing facilities and a warm chamber;
hot water, properly tempered ghee, and cleansing herbs were all fully supplied.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One and the bhikṣus accepted his offerings; having bathed together,
they partook of a generous meal.
The food was sweet and delicious, such as the world rarely encounters.
When they had finished eating and rinsed their mouths, each returned to his original place.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha.
What meritorious deeds did this deva perform in the past,
such that his physical form is so exquisite, his majestic appearance so extraordinary,
and his radiance so brilliant as a great mountain of jewels?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"In the distant past, during the time of Vipaśyin Buddha,
this deva was the son of a poor family in that world."
He constantly performed manual labor to provide for his own body and mouth.
Upon hearing the Buddha speak of the merit of washing the Sangha,
he felt great joy in his heart and immediately applied himself diligently to his work.
Having obtained a small amount of money and grain, he used it to provide washing utensils,
as well as food and drink, to invite the Buddha and the assembly of monks,
offering them all. By virtue of this meritorious deed, after his life came to an end...
Those born in the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven possess this radiant mark.
From the time of the seven Buddhas of the past up until the appearance of the thousand Buddhas of the future, it has been thus: they wash both the Buddha and the Saṅgha.
The Buddha bestowed this prediction:
In a future age, after two hundred asaṃkhyeya kalpas, he shall attain Buddhahood,
with the name Śuddhakāya,
fully endowed with the ten titles.
Furthermore, the *Saṃyukta-avadāna-sūtra* states:
"In the past, Nanda, the younger brother of the Buddha,
was a person during the time of the Tathāgata Vipaśyin."
Having washed away the merit and virtue of the assembly of monks,
he was reborn by his own karma in the body of one of the Śākya clan;
adorned with the marks of a five- or six-year-old child, his divine countenance shone brilliantly with a golden hue.
Riding upon his prior merit, he was born in the same world as the Buddha;
by refining his essence at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), he immediately attained the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā).
Since even the ancients received vast rewards for giving a single thing, how much more so for such great merit!
How much more so for a donor today who is able to practice extensively;
through such universal and impartial conduct, they will surely attain the Honorable Title,
increase their joy, and broadly deliver all beings.
Furthermore, the *Puṇyakṣetra-sūtra* states:
There was a bhikṣu named Ānanda who addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
I recall my past life when I was born as the son of a commoner in the kingdom of Rājagṛha.
A malignant ulcer broke out on my body, and though it was treated, it would not heal.
A spiritual friend who was a practitioner of the Way came and said to me:
When the assembly of monks bathes, take some of that bath-water;
by using it to wash the ulcer, it may be healed,
and one may also obtain merit.
I was immediately filled with joy and went to the monastery.
With increased reverence and a sincere heart,
I further prepared a new well, fragrant oil, and bathing requisites to bathe the assembly of monks.
By washing the ulcer with this decoction, it was immediately healed.
Due to these causes and conditions,
he became handsome, with a golden complexion that shone brilliantly and remained free from dust and grime.
For ninety-one kalpas, he constantly obtained pure blessings and vast, far-reaching auspicious protection;
now, having encountered a Buddha once more, the defilements of his mind were extinguished, and he attained arhatship.
Furthermore, the *Śāriputra-paripṛcchā-vinaya* (Ten Recitations Vinaya) states:
The diagram of the foreign-style bathhouse is shaped like a circular granary.
A door is opened to allow smoke to escape, and a hidden conduit is constructed below.
On the exterior, three tiers of platforms are installed, reaching as high as a person can reach.
Water was placed in jars to fill three tiers of pavilions;
as the heat of the fire rose upward,
the water in the upper pavilion became hot.
The water in the upper chamber is warm;
the water in the lower chamber is cold.
Use it as appropriate according to your needs, without separately preparing hot water.
Therefore, it is said that this is merely pure water.
Furthermore, the Ekottarika Āgama states:
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus.
There are five merits in constructing a bathhouse. What are the five?
First, it dispels wind.
Second, one’s illnesses are healed;
third, dust and impurities are removed;
fourth, the body becomes light and agile.
Fifth, one obtains a plump and radiant complexion.
If there is an assembly of the fourfold community that desires to seek these five merits, [they should apply themselves accordingly].
One should seek to construct a bathhouse.
Furthermore, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"When one wishes to bathe, one should have the monastery attendants (*ārāmika*) sweep and sprinkle [the area]."
Having had the firewood and charcoal prepared cleanly so that it is warm and appropriate,
one should strike the *gandī* to signal that it is time to enter the bathhouse.
Each person shall tie their robe with a waistband to mark it and place it upon the clothing rack.
When entering, one must not enter with both arms swinging;
rather, one should enter with one hand covering the front.
If one wishes to rub the teacher’s body, [one should do so]...
One should first announce this, and there shall be no offense.
One must not raise both hands simultaneously;
rather, one should first have one arm rubbed and then cover the front with one hand until it is finished.
Next, having rubbed one arm, one hand, and the rest of the body both internally and externally,
close the door and sit until perspiration breaks out from the body.
One must calculate the amount of water used and not use too much.
If one washes oneself with water from a pond, there is no offense.

Second, the mind of the path of practice;
third, the mind of non-retrogression;
fourth, the mind of being one birth away from Buddhahood.
The initial aspiration serves as the causal condition for the mind that practices the path;
the mind that practices the path serves as the causal condition for the mind of non-retrogression;
and the mind of non-retrogression serves as the causal condition for the mind of the stage of one birth remaining before Buddhahood.
Furthermore, the initial arousal of the mind of enlightenment is like sowing seeds in a field;
practicing the path is like the growth of those seeds;
and the mind of non-retrogression is like the initial formation of flowers and fruit.
The mind of one in the stage of succession is like a flower or fruit that is useful;
the mind of the initial aspiration is like a carpenter assembling materials;
and the mind while practicing the path is like hewing and treating timber.
The mind of non-retrogression is like timber laid out for construction;
the mind of one who is in their final birth before Buddhahood is like a completed carriage ready for transport.
Furthermore, the initial resolve for awakening is like the newly risen moon.
The mind practicing the Path is like the moon on the fifth day;
the mind of non-retrogression is like the moon on the tenth day;
the mind of one who is to be reborn in the next life for enlightenment is like the moon on the fourteenth day.
The wisdom of the Tathāgata is like the moon on the fifteenth day.
Furthermore, the initial aspiration for enlightenment can surpass the stage of the śrāvaka,
and the mind that practices the path can surpass the stage of the pratyekabuddha.
The non-retrogressive mind is able to transcend the stage of uncertainty;
the mind of one in their final birth before Buddhahood dwells securely in the stage of certainty.
Furthermore, the initial aspiration for enlightenment is like a sick person seeking medicine.
The mind practicing the path is like the discernment of medicine;
the mind of non-retrogression is like taking medicine for an illness;
the mind of the stage of succession is like the recovery from an illness.

It is that which distinguishes the practitioner from the world and that which causes one to be revered by gods and humans. If one treats it with disrespect, one will instead incur calamities and obstacles. It is not that the moon takes away the light of the sun; rather, it is because the sun has departed that the moon appears. His spiritual resonance was such that he could move both the divine and the human. [The text continues with his various miraculous responses.]

he prayed for an immediate response.

On the seventh day, he felt a sudden sense of clarity within his throat;
he immediately asked for water to wash his face and rinse his mouth, saying:
"I have a response.

one should first select an excellent site intended for the location of the stūpa;
it must not be situated to the south.
One must not sit to the west;
one should sit to the east or to the north.
One must not encroach upon the grounds of the Buddha or the grounds of the Saṃgha.
Monastic quarters should be constructed to the west or the south;
the stūpa for the Buddha should be built in a high and prominent location.
One must not wash, dye, or dry clothes within the precincts of a stūpa courtyard, nor spit upon the ground.
One may construct niches on the four sides of a Buddha stūpa and decorate them with various colorful paintings of lions, birds, and other animals.
With banners and canopies suspended within,
it may be established as a Buddha-stūpa;
on its four sides, one should plant various groves of gardens with flowers and fruits.
Among these, flowers that grow thereon should be used to make offerings to the stūpa.
If the donor who planted the tree personally offers these flowers from the center [of the grove] as an offering to the Buddha, they may be given as food to the Saṃgha.
The Buddha said,
"One should follow the words of the donor.
If there are many flowers,"
He gave some flowers to a garland-maker and spoke to him.
"Make a garland with that much of this flower;
give me the remainder,
and give me such-and-such a price for it."
If one obtains money, it may be used to purchase lamps, incense, and other offerings for the Buddha;
furthermore, it may be used to repair stupas. If the amount of money is large, it may be placed within the "Inexhaustible Treasures" (akṣaya-nīvi) dedicated to the Buddha.
If someone says that the Buddha is free from greed, anger, and delusion, yet merely adorns himself with these flowers and fruits to experience pleasure,
they incur a grave retribution for their offense.
The Buddha said:
It may also be made into a caitya.
That which contains relics is called a stūpa;
that which contains no relics is called a caitya.

At these various caityas— the place where the Buddha was born, the place where he attained enlightenment, the place where he turned the wheel of Dharma, the place where the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa, the images of bodhisattvas, the images of pratyekabuddhas, and the footprints of the Buddha—
one may offer worship by placing Buddhist flower canopies.
Among those who make offerings, the superior ones offer to the Buddha-stūpas,
while the inferior ones offer to the caityas.
If a sudden wind or rain should arise, one should collect the offering implements.
One should settle them according to their proximity.
One must not say, "I am a senior elder," "I am a forest-dweller," "I am a practitioner of alms-gathering," or "I am a virtuous one (bhadanta)";
to do so constitutes an offense against the Vinaya.
If bandits arrive in an emergency, one must not hide or discard items belonging to the stupa or the Sangha.
However, items belonging to the Buddha— such as ornaments for the Buddha image and the seating mats of the Sangha— may be hidden.
One should arrange and set out various kinds of food and drink so that the bandits may see them;
perhaps they will then give rise to a heart of compassion.
If bandits ask a bhikṣu to come out, he should not be afraid; a junior monk should be sent to look after things.
If the bandits arrive suddenly and it is impossible to hide one's belongings, one should say:
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent."
Having spoken these words, he departed.
This is called a "difficult dharma" (dharmanigraha).
Section Four: On the Attainment of Merit. As stated in the *Cūḍāmaṇi-avadāna* (The Sutra of Minor Marvels):
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Suppose there were a person who took all the grasses and trees filling the four continents under heaven and turned them all into human beings."
They attained the fruits of the four paths and the state of a pratyekabuddha.
Throughout their lives, they were fully provided with the four requisites for sustenance.
After their parinirvāṇa, a stūpa was erected for each of them.
They made offerings of incense, flowers, banners, flags, and precious canopies.
Furthermore, they constructed a Great Adorned Palace for Śakra,
utilizing eighty-four thousand jeweled pillars.
There were eighty-four thousand jeweled windows,
eighty-four thousand skylight jeweled windows,
and eighty-four thousand watchtowers and pavilions.
It was surrounded by four exits and adorned with various jewels.
If there were sons or daughters of good family who were to construct hundreds of thousands of billions of such great palaces of magnificent adornment, [the merit would be even greater].
Although the merit from using [this] to give to the Sangha of the four directions is great,
it is not equal to that of someone who, after the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, [acts as follows].
One might build a stūpa for a relic the size of a mustard seed, as large as an *āmalaka* fruit,
with a spire like a needle and a parasol placed upon it.
It is like the leaf of a jujube tree;
even if a Buddha image were as large as a barley grain,
it would not equal even a hundredth part of the merit of the former [offering], which remains fully satisfied.
It cannot be reached by a thousandfold, ten-thousandfold, or even a hundred-thousand-ten-thousandfold; it is beyond measure.
Ānanda, you should know that such is the Tathāgata.
Immeasurable merit:
the factors of morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation—these constitute immeasurable merit.
They possess great supernormal powers, transformations, and the six pāramitās.
Such are his immeasurable merits.
Furthermore, the *Anuttaraśrayasūtra* states:
Ānanda joined his palms toward the Buddha and spoke these words:
Today, as I entered the city of Rājagṛha to beg for alms,
I saw a great multi-storied pavilion that had been newly constructed and was magnificently adorned, with both its interior and exterior being perfectly finished and secure.
If there were a person of pure faith who were to offer it to the Saṃgha of the four directions, providing them with all four requisites.
If, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, one were to take a relic of the Buddha as small as a mustard seed and enshrine it within a stūpa,
constructing a stūpa as large as an āmalaka fruit.
One constructs a *cakra* as large as a needle,
a *ghaṇṭā* as large as a jujube leaf,
and a Buddha image as large as a grain of wheat.
"Between these two merits, which is superior?
The Buddha told Ānanda,
"Suppose there were as many noble ones who have attained the four fruits and pratyekabuddhas as there are beings filling the four continents."
Suppose there were a grove of sugarcane, a bamboo thicket, a field of hemp, or the like,
and a single person were to provide for it throughout their entire life with all four requisites in full abundance,
and after its entry into nirvana, were to erect great stupas for it all.
They made offerings of lamps, incense, robes, banners,
and streamers. Ānanda, what do you think?
"Is this person's merit great?
Ānanda replied, "It is exceedingly great."
World-Honored One,
let us set aside Ānanda for a moment;
it is also like the dwelling place of Śakra’s celestial palace.
There is a great flying pavilion named the Hall of Constant Victory,
adorned with eighty-four thousand varieties of precious jewels.
If there are faithful men or women, [who...]
One constructs such a perpetually superior jeweled palace and bestows hundreds of thousands of koṭis of them upon the Saṃgha of the four directions. Furthermore,
if there is another person who, after the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa...
One takes a relic as large as a mustard seed,
constructs a stupa as large as an āmalaka fruit,
and erects a *cakra* (spire) as large as a needle.
If one were to create a *stūpa* with a parasol as large as a jujube leaf,
or fashion an image of the Buddha as large as a grain of wheat,
this merit would surpass that previously described; the former does not equal even a hundredth part of it.
It does not approach even one part in ten million billion, nor even one part in an incalculable number (*asaṃkhyeya*). Why is this?
Because the Tathāgata possesses immeasurable merit.
Even if one were to shatter the Sahā world-system into atoms, and if each of these atoms were,
in turn, a person who had attained one of the four fruits of śrāmaṇya or the state of a pratyekabuddha,
and if faithful men and women were to provide them with offerings for as long as they lived—
Furthermore, even after my parinirvāṇa, building stupas to make offerings is not as [meritorious] as taking up a relic the size of a mustard seed,
or even fashioning an image the size of a grain of wheat.
This merit cannot be matched by even a hundredth, a thousandth, or ten millionth part of what was previously described;
it is beyond reach even through calculation or analogy.
Thus it is, Ānanda.
In the past, when all Tathāgatas were on the stage of the causal ground,
they knew that the realm of sentient beings is pure by nature,
yet defiled by adventitious afflictions.
Yet, without entering the realms of sentient beings,
they are able to preach the profound and wondrous Dharma for all sentient beings,
thereby eliminating the hindrance of afflictions.
One should not give rise to a base mind,
because of its vast magnitude;
one should maintain a mind of reverence toward all sentient beings.
Arouse reverence for the Great Teacher; arouse prajñā; arouse jñāna.
Arousing great compassion,
by relying on these five dharmas,

a bodhisattva attains entry into the stage of *avaivartika*— here translated as "non-retrogression. Relying on such knowledge of reality as it is, they realize great skillful means and attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"If one makes an offering of even a single incense stick or lamp to the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha,
or even presents a single flower, one will be reborn in the Land of Immovability."
One should carefully guard the property of the Buddha and the Sangha, sweep and plaster the grounds of the monasteries and temples,
and fashion images and stupas even as small as a thumb,
always giving rise to a heart of joy.
They are also reborn in the Immovable Land (*Acalā*).
This is precisely the Pure Land, eternally adorned and unmoved by the three calamities.
Furthermore, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
While the Buddha was traveling through the kingdom of Kosala,
a brahmin who was plowing a field saw the World-Honored One passing by;
leaning his ox-goad against the ground, he paid homage to the Buddha.
Having seen this, the World-Honored One smiled.
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying,
"For what cause and condition did you smile?"
"I only wish to hear it.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"This brāhmaṇa is now paying homage to the two Buddhas."
The bhikṣus asked, "Which two Buddhas?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Under my staff is a stūpa of Kāśyapa Buddha.
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha,
"We wish to see the stūpa of Kāśyapa Buddha."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus,
"Go from this brahmin and ask for a clod of earth along with the earth itself.
They then asked for it immediately.
Then the brahmin gave it to him.
Having received it,
the World-Honored One immediately manifested the seven-jeweled stupa of Kāśyapa Buddha.
It was one yojana in height and half a yojana in width.
When the brahmin saw it, he...
He then addressed the Buddha, saying,
"My clan name is Kāśyapa.
This is my Kāśyapa mound."
At that time, the World-Honored One immediately constructed a stūpa for Kāśyapa Buddha at that very spot.
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying,
"May we receive the clay [for the construction]?"
The Buddha said,
"You may receive it," and then spoke this verse:
To take hundreds of thousands of loads of pure gold and use them to practice giving is not as good as using a single lump of clay to respectfully repair a Buddha-stūpa;
at that time, one honors the Buddhas of the past.
He then prostrated himself.
The bhikṣus also paid homage to the Buddha and spoke this verse:
"Even if one were to take hundreds or thousands of gold pieces And use them to practice giving as alms..."
It is not equal to a single virtuous mind that reverently pays homage to a stūpa of the Buddha.
At that time, the bhikṣu immediately brought incense and flowers to offer to the World-Honored One,
out of reverence for the Buddhas of the past.
He then took it and offered it to the stūpa.
The Buddha then spoke this verse:
“Though one were to take hundreds of thousands of carts of pure gold and use them to practice giving in charity...”
It is not equal to a single virtuous thought of offering incense and flowers to a stūpa.
At that time, the great assembly gathered like clouds.
The Buddha addressed Śāriputra:
"You shall preach the Dharma for all people.
The Buddha spoke in verse:
"Even if one were to give as alms the Jambudvīpas, numbering in the hundreds of thousands, filled with pure gold..."
It is not equal to a single gift of Dharma that leads others to practice accordingly.
At that time, there were those among the assembly who had attained the Way.
The Buddha spoke these verses:
Giving filled worlds numbering in the hundreds of thousands of true gold is not equal to the gift of a single Dharma;
furthermore, it accords with the vision of the True Truth.
Moreover, the *Dharmapada-avadāna-sūtra* says:
Formerly, when the Buddha was in the world,
he dispatched an arhat named Sumana.
Taking the Buddha’s hair and nail relics, he traveled to the Southern Mountains of Jibin and constructed a Buddhist stupa.
Within the monastery, there were always five hundred arhats who,
morning and evening, burned incense and circumambulated the stupa in worship.
At that time, there were five hundred monkeys in the mountains.
Seeing the monks circumambulating the stupa, prostrating, and making offerings,
they immediately began carrying stones together to learn from the monks how to build a stupa and circumambulate it in worship.
At that time, as the heavens rained and mountain streams surged in flood,
five hundred monkeys perished simultaneously and were reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
The palaces of the seven treasures were towering and immeasurable;
food, clothing, and drink appeared spontaneously, and their happiness was boundless.
Having been born in heaven, they each thought to themselves:
"By what cause and condition have we been reborn here?
They then used their divine eye to observe their previous lives and saw that they had been monkeys.
Because he had played with the assembly of monks while constructing a stupa,
he was swept away by mountain torrents and, at the end of his life, was reborn here;
they immediately took him together and brought offerings of incense and flowers.
Descending from heaven, they came to make offerings to the corpse;
then they proceeded to the Buddha’s dwelling to pay homage and inquire after his well-being.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for them.
Five hundred devaputras simultaneously attained the fruit of srotāpanna;
having attained this fruit, they returned to the heavens.
A monkey, imitating the monks' play, built a stūpa for them.
If one can still obtain such magnificent and sublime rewards for merit,
how much more so for a person who builds a stūpa with a faithful heart— how could there not be a karmic fruit?
Furthermore, the *Piyavāda-sūtra* (Analogies Sūtra) says:
Long ago, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa,
there was a householder in King Aśoka’s kingdom whose merit and virtue were rare in the world.
Whatever he required would arrive the very moment he thought of it.
His residence was composed of the seven precious gems,
and the women within the inner chambers were of such exquisite beauty that they had few equals.
Day and night he enjoyed pleasures beyond measure.
With a heart of faith, this man constantly made offerings to more than twenty thousand monks.
When King Aśoka heard of this, he summoned him for an audience.
He then spoke to him, saying, "I have heard that you are a man of great wealth; what possessions do you have?
He immediately replied to the king.
The house contained nothing at all.
The king did not believe him and sent someone to investigate.
When the envoy arrived, he saw only seven successive layers of gates and pavilions,
with houses and halls adorned with the seven treasures, towering and immeasurable.
When the envoy entered the inner chamber, he saw no other objects.
He saw only a woman of such exquisite beauty that she was peerless;
upon seeing her, he immediately returned and reported the matter in detail to the king,
who’s mind was gradually appeased.
At that time, the householder, knowing that the king understood,
pointed eastward with his hand before the king; immediately,
immeasurable rainfalls of the seven treasures descended from the sky.
He pointed out that it was likewise so in the other three directions.
Upon seeing this, the king realized he possessed great merit.
The king then went to the monastery to inquire about this matter.
In the monastery there was a senior elder (*sthavira*) who had attained arhatship, possessing the three knowledges (*trividyā*) and the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*).
The king asked the elder,
"What merit did this householder plant in his past lives?"
Whatever was required arrived spontaneously as soon as it was thought of.
The Elder replied to the King:
"In the distant past, ninety-one kalpas ago..."
After Vipaśyin Buddha entered nirvana,
the householder at that time constructed a stupa together with four others,
applying himself with exceptional devotion.
Once the stūpa has been completed,
one should further take the seven precious gems and excellent flowers and place them upon the summit of the stūpa,
scattering them down from all four sides as an offering.
He made a vow, saying:
"May my enjoyment of merit be natural and never cease throughout all my successive lives.
By virtue of this merit..."
From that time forward, for ninety-one kalpas, he did not fall into the evil realms.
Among gods and humans, he enjoyed natural bliss and inexhaustible happiness.
At that time, he merely wished for his enjoyment of merit to be endless; he did not wish for liberation.
Therefore, up to the present day, they have only received superior merit but have not yet attained the traces of the Path.
Furthermore, the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra* states:
The Buddha told Ānanda:
If a person, being attached to the retributive fruits of the three realms of existence,
practices giving to the Buddha as a field of merit or performs other roots of goodness,
they may vow: "May I not enter nirvana in every lifetime."
It is impossible that one would not enter parinirvāṇa by means of these roots of goodness.
Although such a person does not seek nirvāṇa with delight, [they will nonetheless attain it].
However, regarding those who have planted various roots of goodness under the Buddha,
I say that such persons will certainly enter nirvana. Furthermore,
the *Śatavarga-vyākaraṇa-sūtra* (*Bai yuan jing*) states:
Long ago, when the Buddha was in the world,
there was an elder in the city of Śrāvastī whose family was immensely wealthy,
possessing immeasurable treasures and riches beyond calculation.
A son was born, handsome and exquisite, such as is rarely seen in the world.
In each of his two hands he held gold coins;
having taken them, they were produced again without end.
His parents were filled with joy and gave him a name,
calling him Ratnapāṇi (Jewel-Hand).
As he gradually grew up, he was compassionate and filial.
He delighted in giving alms.
When someone came to beg, he would extend both hands and take out fine gold coins,
bestowing them upon them immediately.
Later, he went out of the city with several others to sightsee.
Upon arriving first at the Jetavana, he beheld the Buddha’s marks and signs of excellence;
his heart was filled with joy, and he prostrated himself, inviting the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus.
"I pray that you will accept my offering. Ānanda said,
"To prepare an offering requires wealth."
Thereupon, Ratnapāṇi extended his two hands,
and a rain of gold and silver coins fell,
filling the ground in an instant.
His accumulation [of merit] surpassed that of others.
The Buddha commanded Ānanda to provide him with offerings.
When he had finished eating,
the Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
He then returned home to take leave of his parents, requesting permission to go forth into the religious life.
Having already left the household life, he attained the fruit of arhatship.
Seeing this, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By what merit did the bhikṣu Ratnapāṇi plant seeds in his past lives that he was born into a noble family?"
From his hand, he produced money that was inexhaustible.
Furthermore, he encountered the World-Honored One, who had left the household life and attained the Way.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
In the past, after Kāśyapa Buddha entered nirvana,
there was a king named Kāśī who collected his relics and constructed a stupa made of the four precious substances.

At that time, there was an elder who, upon seeing the erection of the stupa and temple, gave rise to a mind of sympathetic joy; he placed a single gold coin beneath the stupa, made a vow, and departed.
By virtue of this merit, he did not fall into the evil realms.
In the heavens and among humans, they constantly received blessings and experienced happiness with gold and money;
even until now, having encountered me, they have left the household life and attained the Way.
Furthermore, the *Śatavarga-vyākaraṇa-sūtra* says:
When the Buddha was in the world,
there was an elder in the city of Kapilavastu whose wealth and treasures were immeasurable.
His wife became pregnant and gave birth to a son whose appearance was so upright and handsome that it was rarely seen in the world.
At the time of his birth, a *maṇi* jewel canopy spontaneously appeared above his head, covering the entire city.
The parents were filled with joy and,
because of this, gave him a name,
calling him Ratnacchattra.
As he gradually grew up, he encountered a Buddha, left the household life, and attained the fruit of Arhatship.
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
"In the past, ninety-one kalpas ago..."
There was a Buddha who appeared in the world named Vipaśyin. After his parinirvāṇa,
there was a king named Bandhumat.
Having collected the relics, he constructed a stupa made of the four precious substances,
one yojana in height,
and made offerings to it.
At that time, there was a merchant who entered the sea to gather treasures and returned safely.
He immediately covered the top of the stupa with a maṇi jewel, made a vow, and departed.
By virtue of this merit, for ninety-one kalpas he did not fall into the evil realms.
In the heavens and among humans, there was always a precious canopy that arose together with him;
even until now, he has encountered me, left the household life, and attained the Way.
Having heard what the Buddha had spoken, they rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Furthermore, the *Śatavarga-vinaya-sūtra* states:
During the time when the Buddha was in the world, in the city of Kapilavastu...
There was a householder whose wealth and treasures were immeasurable and beyond calculation.
His wife gave birth to a son who was handsome and exquisite, a rarity in the world.
A *maṇi* jewel appeared spontaneously upon his head.
At that time, his parents gave him a name,
calling him "Jewel-Ball" (*Ratnaka*).
As he gradually grew up, he saw the Buddha, left the household life, and attained the fruit of arhatship.
When he entered the city to beg for alms,
the precious jewel was still upon his head.
The people within the city marveled at the reason for this and vied with one another to come and see it;
they were deeply ashamed and returned to their respective dwellings.
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
this precious gem upon my head cannot be made to depart."
"Now, as I beg for alms, I am ridiculed by others.
I pray that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, will accept and set aside this jewel.
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
"You need only say to the jewel:
'My life-portion is now exhausted; I have no further need of you.
If you say this three times, the jewel will depart of its own accord."
When the bhikṣus had received the instruction, the precious jewel did not appear.
At that time, the bhikṣus requested the Buddha to explain the causes and conditions of their past karma.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
In the past, ninety-one kalpas ago,
there was a Buddha who appeared in the world named Vipaśyin.
After he had entered nirvana, [the following occurred].
At that time, the king of that country was named Bandhumatī;
he collected the relics and constructed a stupa made of the four precious substances,
one yojana in height.
And they made offerings to it.
At that time, the king entered the stupa to pay his respects and tied a mani-jewel to the top of its spire.
Having made this vow, he departed.
By virtue of this merit, for ninety-one kalpas he did not fall into the three miserable realms.
Throughout his births among gods and humans, he always possessed a precious jewel.
Atop that [peak], he experienced celestial bliss.
Having now encountered the Buddha and gone forth into homelessness, he attained the fruit of arhatship.
Upon hearing this, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
5. Section on Circumambulation. Fifth. As stated in the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra*:
"In the past, when the Buddha was in the world, the Buddha and Ānanda entered the city of Śrāvastī to go on their almsround."
At that time, there was a brahmin in that city who came from outside and saw the Buddha emerging from the city, his radiant marks majestic and sublime.
At that time, the brahmin was filled with joy and leaped for gladness;
he circumambulated the Buddha once, paid his respects, and departed.
The Buddha then smiled and addressed Ānanda, saying:
This brahmin, seeing the Buddha, was filled with joy;
with a pure mind, he circumambulated the Buddha once.
By virtue of this merit,

From this point forward, for twenty-five kalpas, he shall not fall into the evil realms; enjoying unsurpassed happiness among devas and humans, at the end of those twenty-five kalpas, he shall attain the state of a pratyekabuddha.
It is named Dhāraṇī-guhyaka.
By this causal condition, if a person circumambulates a Buddha or a Buddhist stupa,
they will obtain immeasurable merit in whatever place they are born.
Furthermore, the *Tie-wei jing* states:
The elder Tie-wei addressed the Buddha, saying, "I scatter flowers,
burn incense, light lamps, and pay homage."
"This is what constitutes making offerings.
What kind of merit is obtained by circumambulating a stūpa?
The Buddha said:
There are five merits in circumambulating a stūpa:
first, one will obtain a handsome and beautiful appearance in future lives;
second, one will obtain a pleasant voice.
Third, one attains rebirth in the heavens;
fourth, one attains rebirth in the family of a king or noble;
fifth, one attains the path of nirvāṇa.
By what causes and conditions does one obtain a handsome and upright appearance?
It is because of seeing the image of the Buddha with joy.
By what conditions does one obtain a beautiful voice?
Because of circumambulating the stupa and preaching the sutras,
for what reason is one reborn in the heavens?
It is because at the time of circumambulating the stupa, one’s mind does not transgress the precepts.
By what cause was he born into the family of a king or noble?
It was because he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet.
By what cause did he attain the path to Nirvana?
Because there was still further merit remaining,
the Buddha said:
"There are three dharmas for circumambulating a stūpa."
First, when lifting a foot, one should be mindful of lifting the foot.
Second, when lowering a foot, one should be mindful of lowering the foot.
Third, one must not look left or right or spit upon the ground within the monastery.
Regarding circumambulation: within the Sūtras and Vinayas, it is prescribed that one should circumambulate keeping the object to one's right.
To circumambulate by keeping it to one's left is censured by the deities.
Even to the point where those who circumambulate to the left among piles of grain are rebuked by the laity;
such is the conduct of their followers today.
Aligning oneself with the celestial timing, turn toward the northwest;
baring the right shoulder and facing the Buddha with reverence,
circumambulate him either one hundred times, ten times, seven times, or three times.
Each has its own symbolic significance.
To discuss, for instance, the practice of circumambulating three times:
it symbolizes making offerings to the Triple Gem and bringing the three poisons to rest.
Purifying the three karmas extinguishes the three evil realms because one encounters the Three Jewels.
As a verse in the Avataṃsaka Sūtra says:

When first wishing to circumambulate the stupa, one should wish that all sentient beings practice the bestowal of blessings and merit so as to fully realize the intent of the Way. When circumambulating the stupa three times,
one should wish that all sentient beings attain a single-minded resolve and forever sever the three poisons.
Furthermore, the *Bhadra-pañcaśīla-sūtra* states:
"Circumambulating a stupa three times symbolizes reverence for the Three Jewels:
first, the Buddha; second, the Dharma; and third, the Saṅgha."
One should also contemplate the extinction of the three poisons:
first, greed; second, hatred; and third, delusion.

Section Six: On Ancient Stūpas. According to the *Sūtra on Resolving Doubts Regarding the Semblance Dharma*, it says:
