Furthermore, the *Aśokarāja-sūtra* states:
"In the past, King Aśoka desired to take the relics that had been enshrined by King Ajātaśatru."
King Ajātaśatru placed a great iron sword-wheel in the Ganges River and caused the wheel to revolve at the location of the śarīra;
despite employing various skillful means, he was unable to retrieve it.
He asked the bhikṣu Padma,
"How can this be attained?
The bhikṣu replied:
"If one throws several thousand *hu* of pears into it, the wheel can be stopped.
He immediately followed these words and placed the pears into the water.
He happened to try a single crabapple;
as the fruit fell into the opening of the mechanism,
the wheel of swords immediately stopped and ceased to revolve.
However, the great dragon kings' protection was entirely unobtainable.
The king then asked,
"By what means can it be obtained?"
The Dragon King’s merit is so supreme that it cannot be fathomed.
He asked: "How can one know that his merit is superior?"
Cast images of a dragon and of the king out of gold,
and weigh them on a scale;
whichever is heavier possesses superior merit.
Immediately, when the statue was weighed, it was found to be twice as heavy.
Upon witnessing this event, the king diligently cultivated merit;
having cultivated merit, he further cast another statue.
He weighed them once more;
the image of the king and the image of the dragon were exactly equal in weight.
The king further cultivated merit and cast another image.
As he lifted it to look at the king’s image, it became increasingly heavy. The king,
realizing the image was heavy, led his troops to the water's edge.
The Dragon King came forth in person and offered various kinds of jewels.
The King said to the dragon,
"King Ajātaśatru has sent me these relics."
"I now wish to take it.
The Dragon King, realizing his own power was insufficient,
immediately led the king to the site of the śarīra.
The door was opened and the śarīra were given to him.
Just as the oil lamp prepared by King Ajātaśatru was about to go out,
once the śarīra had emerged, the lamp also went out completely.
The king, finding this strange, questioned the Bhikṣu Padma:
"How is it that King Ajātaśatru measured out the oil for the lamp,
and it was only when he had taken up the śarīra that it finally went out?"
The Venerable One replied:

"At that time, there was a skilled mathematician who calculated that such an amount of oil would be used over the course of a hundred years; by calculating in this manner, it has lasted until the present day."
5. Section on Receiving Merit. Section Five on Receiving Merit. As stated in the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra*:
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda:
"After my parinirvāṇa..."
If there is anyone who makes offerings even to my relics as small as a mustard seed,
honoring, respecting, and reverently making offerings to them with humility—
I declare that by this root of goodness, such a person shall entirely attain the realm of nirvana and reach the ultimate limit of nirvana.
If there are those who construct images, stupas, or temples,
and possess the faith to contemplate the merit of the Buddha's mindfulness,
even to the extent of scattering a single flower into the air;
"I say that by these roots of goodness, all such persons shall attain the realm of nirvāṇa and reach the ultimate limit of nirvāṇa.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"If there are sentient beings who, because they practice mindfulness of the Buddha..."
Even if one scatters but a single flower into the air,
the karmic fruit obtained from such merit is inexhaustible. If there are sentient beings who,
with a heart of utmost sincerity, recollect the merits of the Buddha and scatter even a single flower into the air, [the reward is likewise boundless].
In future lives, one shall become a Śakra-devendra, a Brahmā-devendra, or a Cakravartin king;
even their meritorious rewards cannot be exhausted.
When giving to the Buddha as a field of merit, such rewards cannot be limited or exhausted by any conditioned fruit.
I declare that such a person will certainly attain *nirvāṇa* and reach the very limit of *nirvāṇa*.
Even if there is an animal that can give rise to a thought of the Buddha, the World-Honored One,
I likewise declare that its roots of goodness and karmic reward shall lead it to attain *nirvāṇa* and reach the very limit of *nirvāṇa*.
Suppose there were a trichiliocosm filled with those who have attained the four fruits of śrāmaṇya and pratyekabuddhas, as dense as a field of sugarcane, bamboo, or reeds;
and suppose someone were to erect stupas for them, whether during their lifetimes or after their parinirvāṇa, and make offerings to them.
Whether for an entire kalpa or slightly less than a kalpa,
one might offer worship, honor, and humble service with all manner of pleasing articles of enjoyment;
yet if another person, in the presence of the Buddhas, were to join their palms but once or utter the name of the Buddha but once—
Compared to the former merit, this merit does not equal even one hundredth part;
it does not equal one thousandth,
nor one hundred-thousandth, nor one billionth part.
It does not even approach a single *kalā* [of merit]. Why is this?
Because the Buddha-Tathāgata is the most supreme among all fields of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*).
Therefore, making offerings to the Buddha brings about great merit, supernatural powers, and majestic authority.
The verse says:
The golden body was dispersed as relics; Stupas of jewels fill the realms of gods and dragons.
He first established ten stupas, which ultimately became eighty thousand;
The jeweled canopies transformed into numinous light, and the pillars of the *kṣetra* spat forth lotus flowers.
Repeatedly opening amidst the morning mists and dew, they frequently revealed the traces of his spiritual awakening.
Red and rainbow hues reflect and shine upon one another; the wind stirs their resonance in harmony with the bells.
Immortal cranes are frequently seen, and divine monks follow in succession.
Transcending all sages alone, they inspire universal reverence among all conscious beings.
Though struck with a mallet upon a grindstone, it does not shatter; only then does one know the lofty resonance of the Sage’s virtue.

A brief listing of sixteen generations of such responsive conditions follows. During the Sui dynasty, there were fifty-three prefectures. Regarding the Han monk Daojue, the *Fahanzhongneizhuan* (Inner Biography of the Dharma of Han) states:
Since Emperor Ming had extensively propagated the Buddha-dharma,
established monasteries, and ordained monks,
the various Daoist practitioners at the mountain retreats of the Five Peaks [were likewise accommodated].
He requested a contest to determine the relative superiority of the Daoists and Buddhists;
he took his Daoist scriptures and subjected them to a fire test,
whereupon they were consumed by the flames and reduced to ashes.
Fei Cai, the leader of the Daoist community, was filled with shame and self-reproach, dying in the presence of the assembly.
Zhang Yan awakened them to the truth, and they vied with one another to leave the household life.
At that time, the śarīra brought from the Western Regions—
Five grains of five colors ascended straight into the air,
revolving in circles like a canopy.
He eclipsed the sunlight.
The Arhat Madhyāntika leaped up and soared high;
he dwelt in the air as if on the ground, and walked upon the earth as if in the sky.
He manifested divine transformations with sovereign ease to preach the Dharma for the assembly.
Heavenly rain poured down jeweled flowers, scattering over the Buddha and the Sangha;
celestial music played in diverse melodies, heard by the entire multitude together.
He saved immeasurable people.

During the Wei dynasty, a foreign śramaṇa from the Western Regions stored śarīra relics in a golden dish; five tongues of flame leapt upward, as described in detail in the "Refuting Heresies" (Poxie pian).
In the city of Luoyang during the Wei dynasty, there were originally three monasteries.
One was located to the west of the palace;
whenever a śarīra was tied atop a banner or a stūpa spire,
it would suddenly appear within the palace grounds.
The Emperor was troubled by this and intended to demolish and destroy it.
At that time, there was a foreign śramaṇa residing in the monastery who brought a golden basin filled with water.
The water held the śarīra,
and five-colored lights surged and blazed without ceasing.
When the Emperor saw this, he sighed in admiration and said:
Were it not for divine efficacy, how could such a thing have been achieved?
Thereupon, he constructed one hundred rooms with surrounding galleries to the east of the road,
which was named the Official Buddhist Monastery (Guān Fótú Jíngshè).
The Monk Kang Hui of Wu Prays for Sarira Relics: In the fourth year of the Chihu era of Sun Quan of Wu,
the foreign śramaṇa Kang Senghui first arrived in the region south of the Yangtze River,
where he established images and performed religious practices.
The people of Wu regarded this as a strange anomaly.
They reported the circumstances to Sun Quan,
who summoned them to an assembly for questioning.
"What numinous omens does the Buddha possess?
He replied, "The Buddha’s numinous traces are obscured, yet his relics—the śarīra—manifest without fixed direction. Quan said:
"Where is it? [Hui] said, "It is a divine marvel that responds through resonance; one may obtain it by means of prayer. Quan said:
If one obtains the relics, one should establish a temple for them.
After three weeks of earnest supplication,
they were finally obtained within a bottle.
At dawn, he presented it to Sun Quan;
its light illuminated the palace.
Sun Quan took the vessel and poured its contents onto a bronze basin.
The śarīra fell and struck the tray, which immediately shattered.
Huiquan was greatly startled by this rare and auspicious omen.
Huìjin then said:
The Buddha’s sacred relics are adamantine and imperishable;
they are not consumed even by the fires at the end of an eon.
The mallet and the anvil did not shatter.
Even when those who were capable exerted all their strength to strike them,
both the mallet and the anvil were dented, yet the śarīra remained undamaged.
The radiance spread in all directions, dazzling the eyes.
Furthermore, as the fire burned, its light surged upward, forming a great lotus flower.
One should then skillfully give rise to great faith.
He then established a monastery for him, naming it Jianchu (Beginning of Construction), and changed the name of the district where they resided to Fotuo Li (Buddha Village).
During the reign of Sun Hao, the Dharma was destroyed; as his tyrannical administration sought to eliminate Buddhism, he burned the scriptures and leveled the stupas.
A person of faith remonstrated with him, saying:
"Be patient for a while.
Once it is known that there is no divine efficacy, it will not be too late to execute those responsible."
Sun Hao followed his advice.
He summoned Hui and said,
"If you can manifest proof before my very eyes, I will assist you in establishing [the Dharma]."
"If he cannot be brought to submission, we shall execute him.
Hui said, "The Buddha responds to conditions through resonance; his influence must surely reach him."
He then hoped that it would not be difficult to request leave to offer his services.
Huìhào granted him a three-day period.
At that time, more than a hundred monks gathered together at the monastery.
Senghao deployed his troops to surround the monastery, and executioners with blades and saws arrived in full force.
With the date for their execution fixed,
some monks, fearing that [the deity] lacked spiritual power, hanged themselves beforehand.
Hui addressed the assembly, saying:
"The Buddha has left behind his relics for our present time.
Since there have already been manifestations in the past, how could there not be such now?"
At the appointed time,
he obtained it and presented it to Sun Hao,
saying: "This is the adamantine bone of the Tathāgata."
Zhicheng said, "Even if struck with a pestle weighing a hundred *jin*, it will ultimately suffer no damage whatsoever.
Hao replied:
"Metal and stone may be worn away, but how could dry bones be firm?
This śramaṇa has deceived me with his face; he shall merely die quickly.
He then placed him upon an iron anvil.
He struck it with a golden mallet;
while both the gold and the iron were dented, the śarīra remained as it was.
He then washed it with clear water.
Śāriputra emitted light and scattered radiance that illuminated the entire hall;
thereupon Hào was filled with joy, accepted the faith,
and transformed his sincerity to embrace the teaching.

During the Jin dynasty, Zhu Changshu cast a śarīra into the water, whereupon five-colored light appeared. At the beginning of the Jin dynasty, Zhu Changshu had previously possessed a śarīra which he revered;
his son became a śramaṇa named Fayen.
Whenever he wished to return to secular life,
he would laugh and say,
"The śarīra are nothing but sand and stones."
"What is there to be so precious about?
His father threw it into the water;
it circled three times with five colors, its light spreading upward for a foot.
Having seen these signs, he conceived faith and consequently did not return to secular life;
however, as his end approached, he again gave rise to worldly thoughts,
whereupon he immediately fell ill and became utterly exhausted.
He eventually became a śramaṇa.
He enshrined the śarīra within a stupa in Jiangxia.
During the Taixing era of the Jin dynasty, the wooden image of the Dong family, which had been kept in secret, emitted light from its śarīra.
At Yuqian, Dong Wangxin had a statue made of *shangmu* wood.
At night, it emitted a brilliant light.
Later, a sound was heard beside the statue as something fell to the ground.
Upon looking at the śarīra,
they were seen floating and sinking in the water, shimmering with five colors,
and circling three times to the right.
Later, the śramaṇa Fachang watched it;
the bird then leaped up to a height of four or five chi and alighted upon Chang’s chest.
Chang said:
If one were to cause temples and monasteries to be constantly established, one would again behold his majestic spiritual power;
thus, he leaped forward once more,
and [the Emperor] immediately and permanently constructed temples and stupas for him.
Those who secretly entered the Dharma at Yuqian numbered ten per day.
During the Daxing era of the Jin dynasty,
as Northern Chinese people fled to Guangling, they arrived there by the thousands each day.
There was one who took the śarīra and established a small temple, erecting a stūpa pillar;
the śarīra emitted light that reached the peak of the pillar.
This moved people both near and far.
During the Xianhe era of the Jin dynasty, the northern monk An Fakai arrived in Yuhang, where he sought śarīra relics to establish a temple.
Wishing to establish a monastery but lacking the necessary funds,
he went about with his hands searching for strings of coins to trade.
After many years, he had accumulated thirty thousand coins.
He built a dwelling on city land and constantly used thread and needles as his means of livelihood;
he wished to erect a stupa, but there were no relics.
There was one named Luo You who already possessed it himself;
when [the Master] requested it from him, he refused.
When Kai arrived at the monastery to pay homage to the Buddha,
he saw the young Śāri’s bag already before the seat.
He immediately informed the young man.
When he was young, he followed [the Master] to see him;
the Master was delighted and opened his mind to him,
and together they established a monastery in Yuhang.
During the Xiankang era of the Jin dynasty, Meng Jing, the Governor of Jian’an,
desired to establish a monastery and construct a temple; consequently, he obtained three śarīra relics.
At night, he heard a tinkling sound by his bedside;
upon looking, he found three śarīras.
Consequently, he established a temple and a stupa there.
In the sixth month of the sixteenth year of the Yuanjia era,
the śarīra emitted light that illuminated everything from above to below;
it ceased only on the seventh day of the seventh month.
Everyone saw it all.
In the first year of the Yixi era of the Jin dynasty, a śarīra spontaneously divided itself into three.
In the first year of the Yixi era of the Jin dynasty, there was a man from Lin-yi who once possessed a śarīra.
On every fast day, there was a light.
The śramaṇa Huìsuì was in the south with Diāo Kuí, the Regional Inspector of Guǎngzhōu;
admiring this manifestation of light, he wished to invite him [to the capital].
Before he had even had time to speak,
the śarīra spontaneously divided into two parts;
upon hearing this, Sengquī was filled with joy.
Furthermore, he requested that [the image] be retained with reverence; subsequently, it was divided into three parts.
Daogui wished to copy the image from Changgan Temple.
The temple master stubbornly refused, not permitting it.
That night, he dreamed of a person several *zhang* tall who told him, "This image is precious for its power to guide and transform others; why are you so parsimonious?"
Mingbao listened and felt it with his hands.
Once the statue was completed, he placed the śarīra within the usnīsa of the image.
Among the various images brought from the West, many emit light.
This was due to a *śarīra*.
In the sixth year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, Jia Daozi obtained a *śarīra* within a lotus flower while traveling along the Jing River.
Jia Daozi was traveling up the Jing River.
Seeing clearly that the lotus was just beginning to bloom,
he took it home; upon hearing a sound from within the flower,
he investigated with wonder and found a śarīra relic.
White as a pearl, its flames illuminated the beams and rafters;
he venerated it, placed it upon a chest and desk, and suspended it on the wall of his house.
Whenever members of his household saw Buddhist monks coming from outside,
they would take off their robes and sit upon the dining table;
those who stayed overnight as guests were unaware of this irreverent behavior.
Then, in a dream, a person told him:
"The true body of Śākyamuni is here;
the assembly of sages has come to pay their respects. Why do you commit evil?"
"After death he will fall into hell, and upon emerging, he will become a slave. How can he not be afraid?
The man was struck with great terror.
Not long after, he died of an epidemic.
Lotus flowers sprang up from the ground where the śarīra-house stood;
they grew to eight branches and withered after sixty days.
After more than a year, they were lost;
it was unknown where they had gone.
In the eighth year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, Qianzai of Anqian, who was a devoted follower of Buddhism, obtained śarīra relics.
An Qianzai of Kuaiji was a family that had long venerated the Buddha.
One night, there was someone knocking at his door.
He went out and saw more than ten people dressed in red garments transporting wealth and piling it up inside the gate, saying,
"The government is commissioning the construction of a Buddhist temple.
Suddenly, they vanished without a trace.
When Ming arrived at another household,
he obtained a purple-gold *śarīra* while the meal was being served;
it could not be crushed even when struck with a hammer.
Illuminated by the radiance of the water-movement,
it spontaneously inspires reverence;
there is always a sublime fragrance.
Later, when he went out wishing to pay his respects, he suddenly lost him.
He searched for him exhaustively and returned only after half a day.
At that time, the Prince of Linchuan was stationed at Jiangling.
They went forward to meet him,
and various rays of light emerged intermittently;
the attendants and śramaṇas all saw different things.
The King held up the water vessel and made a vow, saying [as follows].
Immediately, a radiant light issued forth.
At night, he saw more than a hundred people circling the śarīra chamber, burning incense and holding flowers, appearing as if a Buddha were emerging.

Furthermore, in the ninth year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, several dozen *śarīra* relics were obtained from atop flowers before a statue at the home of Zhang Xuyuan. Both the flowers and the *śarīra* were lost to sight.
At the home of Zhang Xuyuan in Xunyang, an eight-day *gāṇḍī* vegetarian feast was held.
Several dozen monastics and laypeople saw what appeared like ice and snow upon the flowers before the image;
upon inspection, they found dozens of *śarīra*.
He then used water to perform the rite until the flames became continuous,
but subsequently lost them.
After several days, he opened the storehouse and looked again, and recovered the tusks.
Within the casket were ten śarīra relics wrapped in white cotton cloth,
emitting a radiant glow that reached the heavens.
People from all quarters came to request them.
In the fifteenth year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, Liu Ningzhi of Nanjun,
who lived in seclusion at Mount Heng and declined all summons, obtained two śarīras from beneath his chin.
He followed the Way of the Five Pecks of Rice and did not believe in the Buddha-dharma.
He dreamed of a person who was several zhang above the ground, who said:
Your doubts were then resolved.
He suddenly awoke from his trance and,
from morning until evening, practiced with diligent devotion for half a year, prostrating before the Buddha.
Suddenly, he saw a purple light beneath his forehead;
feeling for the source of the light, he found two śarīras,
which remained undamaged even when cut or struck.
A light emerged from the water.
Again, at mealtime, he concealed his teeth within his mouth and spat out a radiant object, which his wife and children obtained as another gem.
There were five pieces in total.
Later, they were lost again,
but were soon thereafter found once more.
Xu Chūn of Sòng reads scriptures and obtains two śarīras. In the nineteenth year of the Yuánjiā era of the Sòng dynasty,
Xu Chūn of Gāopíng was reading scriptures when he obtained two śarīras while eating.
He placed them in a large jar.
Later, he observed that they gradually increased until there were twenty.
Subsequently, he entrusted them to Liu Fu, the Magistrate of Guangling.
Fusi opened an empty jar,
and Chun, while in the capital, suddenly obtained it for himself;
later, when they both regressed, they lost it entirely.
Those who encounter the śarīra relics are exceedingly numerous;
all who honor them obtain them,
while those who are arrogant lose them.
Since the founding of the Buddhist stūpa for the śarīra by Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty, the relics have flowed eastward through successive dynasties.
What has been recorded in historical chronicles represents but a mere fraction of the whole;
because such manifestations occurred repeatedly due to the convergence of various circumstances, they ceased to be considered extraordinary.
That the Buddha’s transformative influence remains hidden is indeed its ultimate purpose; yet,
among all nations where stupas have been erected, none surpasses that of the Sui dynasty,
with more than one hundred sites within a single reign.
The divine portents that were manifested have been set forth in various separate biographies;
now, I shall briefly extract them here.
This was done to manifest the attainment [of merit]. Thus it is said, and so forth.

Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty established Buddha-relic stupas. Stupas were erected in twenty-eight prefectures, and auspicious omens were manifested in fifty-three prefectures. These included Xianyou Temple in Yongzhou, Fengquan Temple in Qizhou, Sijue Temple in Huazhou, Daxingguo Temple in Tongzhou, Daxingguo Temple in Jingzhou, Xiyan Temple in Puzhou, Daie Temple in Taizhou, Wuliangshou Temple in Bingzhou, Changyue Temple in Dingzhou, Songyue Temple in Songzhou, Daci Temple in Xiangzhou, Lianyunyue Temple in Kuozhou, Hengyue Temple in Hengzhou, Daxingguo Temple in Xiangzhou, Jushenshan Temple in Mouzhou, Huikeshan Temple in Wuzhou, Huqiu Mountain Temple in Suzhou—these seventeen temples in the aforementioned prefectures erected stupas using materials from the *dacha* (stupa-founding) funds and the main treasury to construct them.

In the eleven prefectures of Qinzhou, Guazhou, Yangzhou, Yizhou, Bozhou, Guizhou, Jiaozhou, Ruzhou, Fanzhou, Jiangzhou, and Zhengzhou—namely, in the mountains, waters, prefectures, counties, and monasteries of these regions that are pure and serene—one shall erect stupas and provide offerings as previously described.
Your Excellencies, we look up to you with reverence.
The Perfectly Enlightened One, with great kindness and great compassion, rescues and protects all sentient beings and serves as a bridge for the myriad classes of creatures.
We, the Emperor, take refuge in the Triple Gem and seek to restore the holy teachings.
I contemplate all the people within the four seas,
that they may together resolve for Bodhi and collectively cultivate meritorious deeds.
May this serve as a perpetual cause of goodness for those currently living and for future generations alike,
so that all may ascend together to the sublime fruit.
It is appropriate to invite thirty śramaṇas who are well-versed in the characteristics of the Dharma and capable of providing instruction,
each accompanied by two attendants,
with one lay official assigned to each.
One hundred and twenty *jin* of frankincense and five horses were provided for the distribution of the śarīra along the various routes to erect stupas in the aforementioned prefectures.
As for riverside or land temples, they shall follow the previous precedent regarding the construction of stupas at mountain-side or waterside temples.
In cases where there was no temple on a mountain in the past,
the stupa shall be established at a pure and quiet temple site within that same province.
The relevant authorities fashioned models and sent them to the local prefecture.
There were three hundred and sixty monks of the highest rank,
and two hundred and forty of the next.
Next, as for the one hundred and twenty persons—
if the number of monks is small, let all see the Sangha—

for the sake of my Empress, the Crown Prince, the various princes and their descendants, as well as all officials, both internal and external, and all commoners, sentient beings of the hidden and manifest realms, and all living souls.
Each person shall practice the Way and perform repentance for seven days.
On the day the practice begins, strike the *kṣa* (the ritual gong).
This applies regardless of whether one resides in the same province or a different province.
Leave the giving of alms to others;
as for money, it shall be limited to ten coins or less,
and must not exceed ten coins.
The money offered shall be used for the construction of the stupa;
if it is insufficient to cover the laborers' expenses,
treasury funds may be utilized.
The monks and nuns from all the provinces throughout the realm shall collectively observe a vegetarian feast for the sake of the śarīra relics,
limited to the hour of noon on the fifteenth day of the tenth month,
at which time they shall all descend together to place them within the stone casket.
From the Regional Commanders and Prefectural Governors down to the County Magistrates,

except for matters of military emergency, they shall suspend their regular duties for seven days to specialize in inspecting the roads and performing the rites of striking the sacrificial posts (*yaṣṭi*).
Strive to exhaust your utmost sincerity and reverence to accord with My intention.
Let the presiding authorities carry this out.
The thirteenth day of the sixth month, the first year of the Renshou era.
Proclaimed by the Director of the Inner Secretariat, the Prince of Yuzhang, Your Servant Jian.

*Records of the Miraculous Responses of the Śarīra*, twenty fascicles, compiled by Wang Shao, Court Historian of the Sui Dynasty. When His Majesty was formerly in the state of a hidden dragon (prince),...
A certain brahmin ascetic came to the house,
brought out a bundle of relics, and said:
Because the donor had a sincere heart, he kept [the bowl] to offer in worship;
once the śramaṇa had departed,
he searched for it but did not know where it was.
Thereafter, the Emperor and the śramaṇa Tánqiān each placed the śarīra in their palms and counted them;
whether they were few or many, neither could reach a definitive number. Tánqiān said:
I have heard it said by the Brahmins that the Dharma-body transcends all measure and number,
and cannot be fathomed by the world.
Thereupon, a casket made of the seven precious gems was first fashioned to house it.
The divine nun Zhixian said,
"The Buddha-dharma is about to perish."
"All the deities have now departed to the west.
You, my son, shall act as a compassionate father to all under heaven to restore the Buddha-dharma.
All the deities shall then return."
Subsequently, the Zhou dynasty indeed extinguished the Buddha-dharma.
When the Sui house received the Mandate, they restored it; the Emperor frequently spoke of the Divine Nun, saying, "My rise was due to the Buddha."
Therefore, within the śarīra stupas throughout the world,
images of the divine nun were each fashioned;
and the Emperor and Empress [commissioned one] at the Fajie Nunnery in the capital.
He constructed a stupa upon the foundation to fulfill his former vow,
enshrining śarīra relics within it.
On a night in the final month of autumn in the fifteenth year of the Kaihuang era, he...
A divine light rose from its base,
circling the dew-dish to the right with a brilliance like the flames of a smelting furnace;
within a single ten-day period, this occurred four times.
On the thirteenth day of the sixth month in the first year of the Renshou era,
the Emperor presided over the Renshou Hall of the Renshou Palace;
this was the anniversary of his own birth.
Year after year, on this very day, he would with profound sincerity and constant mindfulness cultivate merit and perform virtuous deeds to repay the kindness of his parents;
for this reason, he would invite eminent śramaṇas of great virtue to discuss the ultimate Way.
Thirty sites throughout the various provinces within the realm shall be selected for their lofty, bright, and pure tranquility,
and at each a śarīra-stūpa shall be erected.
Thereupon, the Emperor personally provided a casket made of the seven precious gems.
He respectfully brought forth thirty śarīras from within and placed them upon the table of the imperial throne;

38. Chapter on Offerings (41). Chapter on Offerings, Part Three-Eight; Chapter on Accepting Invitations, Part Thirty-Nine.
This [Chapter on Offerings] consists of two sections. Section One: Exposition of the Intent. First, Exposition of the Intent: Now, the Three Jewels are equal and vast as empty space.
In principle, there is no distinction between enemy and kin, and in practice, there is no separation between noble and base.
Therefore, one should offer worship with sincere devotion according to one’s capacity, universally providing for both internal and external needs;
one must strive to eliminate the sense of duality, hoping thereby to give rise to universal benefit.
Therefore, in the past, when the mother Viśākhā separately invited five hundred arhats,
the Tathāgata rebuked her and proclaimed the principle of equality. Thus,
one knows that because the mind is limitless, it pervades the ten directions.
When wealth is neither excessive nor deficient, the mind pervades the Dharma-realm.
Section Two: Quotations from Scriptural Authority. As stated in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra*:
"The Bodhisattva makes offerings to the Tathāgata."
Briefly stated, there are ten kinds:
first, bodily offering; second, limb-offering.
Third, making offerings in one's presence;
fourth, making offerings in one's absence;
fifth, making offerings by oneself.
Sixth, offerings made by others;
seventh, offerings of material wealth;
eighth, superior offerings.
Ninth, the undefiled offering;
tenth, the offering of the path that leads to the destination.
If a bodhisattva makes an offering to the Buddha’s form body (rūpakāya),...
This is called bodily offering.
If a bodhisattva, for the sake of the Tathāgata, makes offerings at a stūpa,
or at a cave, or at a dwelling, or at an old site.
If it is new,
this is called offering to a shrine (caitya).
If a bodhisattva, seeing the Buddha’s body or a shrine face-to-face, makes an offering.
This is called manifest offering.
If a bodhisattva, toward the Tathāgata or a caitya,
performs a manifest offering with a mind of longing and a mind of mere joy, [this is also such an offering].
As it is for one Tathāgata, so it is for those of the three periods of time;
and as for making offerings before the caityas of the Tathāgatas,
so it is for those in immeasurable worlds throughout the ten directions of the three periods of time.
Whether new or old,
this is called the bodhisattva’s common offering made in the presence [of the object].
If a bodhisattva [makes offerings] to a Tathāgata, a Śrāvaka, or to Nirvāṇa when they are not present;
One should erect stūpas for the Buddha’s relics—
whether one, two, or even hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, millions, or billions—
as far as one’s means and capacity allow.
This is called extensive worship performed without being present in person.
By these causes and conditions, one attains immeasurable great fruits and constantly gathers the merit of Brahma.
Throughout immeasurable great kalpas, they shall not fall into the evil destinies and will fulfill all the requisites for unsurpassed bodhi.
If a bodhisattva makes offerings in their presence, they shall obtain great merit.
Making offerings when not present yields great merit;
making offerings both when present and when not present yields the greatest of all merits.
If a bodhisattva, toward the Tathāgata or a caitya...
To personally perform offerings without relying on indolence or causing others to perform them—
this is called a bodhisattva’s own personal offering.
If a bodhisattva does not offer to the Tathāgata or to a caitya alone, [but rather encourages others to do so], this is also their own personal offering.
He causes all his relatives, both those living at home and those who have gone forth, to make offerings together.
This is called "offering by oneself and others together.
If a bodhisattva possesses even a small amount of goods...
With a mind of compassion, one gives to those impoverished and meritless sentient beings,
causing them to make offerings to the Tathāgata and the caityas,
so that they may attain peace and happiness, rather than for one's own sake.
This is called making offerings on behalf of others.
Making offerings by oneself yields great karmic fruit;
as for making offerings on behalf of others:
One obtains a great fruit of retribution;
one who makes offerings by performing them oneself or having others perform them obtains the greatest and most supreme fruit of retribution.
If a bodhisattva makes various offerings of clothing, food, and assorted jewels to the Tathāgata or to a caitya,
this is called material offering.
If a bodhisattva has long since made offerings of material wealth,
whether in great or small measure,
whether in the presence of the recipient or not.
Whether performed by oneself or by others,
one should make offerings with pure and sincere faith,
dedicating these roots of goodness toward unexcelled bodhi.
This is called the supreme offering.
If a bodhisattva personally makes offerings to the Tathāgata and the caityas, does not treat others with contempt, and remains free from negligence, [this is the supreme offering].
Without indolence,
with a sincere heart of reverence,
and with an undefiled mind.
Not manifesting flattery toward those of superior faith in order to seek wealth,
nor making offerings with various impure things—
this is called undefiled offering.
If a bodhisattva makes offerings to the Tathāgata or to a caitya with excellent, undefiled wealth that they have acquired through their own effort, [this is a supreme offering].
Whether seeking from others,
or obtaining wealth as one desires,
or manifesting a transformed body.
Whether as two, three, or even hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of bodies,
they all prostrate to the Tathāgata;
from each of those bodies, they manifest hundreds of thousands of hands.
With each of their hands, they offered various flowers and incense to the Tathāgata and the caityas;
with their entire bodies, they all praised the true merits of the Tathāgata.
They bring benefit to sentient beings.
Such as these are called offerings through the power of sovereign mastery of intention (*vaśitā-vaśitva*).
They do not depend upon the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world.
Why is this? Because a bodhisattva dwelling on the stage of non-retrogression has never encountered any obstruction regarding any buddha-field.
If a bodhisattva does not obtain wealth through their own power,
nor seek it from others for the purpose of making offerings,
yet [acts] toward other sentient beings...
Even unto the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions,
regarding all offerings made with superior, middling, or inferior minds,
the Bodhisattva [responds] to all those offerings.
With a mind of pure faith and a mind of supreme understanding, they universally rejoice.
By means of these few expedient means, this bodhisattva performs a great offering and embraces great bodhi.
Even for as long as it takes to milk a cow,
one cultivates the four immeasurable minds and so forth toward all sentient beings;
this is called the "cultivation of the path leading to the destination" (yānīya-mārga-pūjā).
The Tathāgata is the foremost and most supreme;
compared to the aforementioned offerings of material wealth,
he cannot be equaled even by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, or by any calculation, analogy, or metaphor.
These ten matters are called the bodhisattva’s offerings in all their aspects to the Tathāgata;
the same applies to the Dharma and the Saṅgha.
One should know that one performs these ten kinds of offerings to this Triple Gem.
A bodhisattva gives rise to six kinds of pure minds toward the Tathāgata: namely,
the unsurpassed mind regarding him as a field of merit,
and the unsurpassed mind regarding his benevolent virtues.
With a supreme mind toward all sentient beings,
a mind as difficult to encounter as the udumbara flower,
he dwells alone with a single-minded focus throughout the trichiliocosm.
With a mind that fully possesses all mundane and supramundane qualities and relies upon their true meaning,
one who offers even a small amount of thought as an offering to the Saṃgha of those who practice according to the Dharma will obtain immeasurable merit.
How much more so for many?
Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* asks:
"How does a bodhisattva make offerings to the Tathāgata in the presence of the Tathāgata?"
It should be known that there are briefly ten kinds of offerings:
first, offering to the śarīra;
second, offering to the caitya.
Third, making offerings in one's presence;
fourth, making offerings in one's absence;
fifth, making offerings by oneself.
Sixth is making offerings by instructing others; seventh is making offerings with respect through the seven types of wealth;
eighth is vast offerings;
ninth is untainted offerings.
The commentary on the ten modes of correct practice and offering is largely identical [to the preceding].
Furthermore, the *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra* states:
The Buddha said:
"Good son, if a lay bodhisattva wishes to receive and uphold the upāsaka precepts,
he must first, in due order, make offerings to the six directions."
To speak of the "east" refers to one's father and mother.
If there is anyone who can provide their parents with clothing,
food and drink, bedding, medicinal decoctions, housing, and wealth;
If one reverently bows to, praises, and honors them,
that person will thereby be able to make offerings to their parents in the eastern direction.
Those parents, in turn, will repay them with five things.
First, to love and cherish them with a single mind;
second, never to deceive or mislead them;
third, to relinquish wealth and give it to them.
Fourth, they marry them into noble families;
fifth, they instruct them in worldly affairs.
Those from the south are like teachers and elders.
If there is anyone who can provide offerings to their teachers and elders—
namely, clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites—
and who honors, praises, respects, and prostrates before them.
Rising early and retiring late, one receives and practices the good teachings;
such a person is then able to make offerings to the teachers of the southern direction.
These teachers, in turn, repay them with five matters.
First, to teach swiftly so as not to let the opportune moment pass;
second, to teach exhaustively so as not to leave anything incomplete;
third, to refrain from giving rise to jealousy toward those superior to oneself; and fourth, to entrust [the student] to a strict teacher and virtuous friends.
Fifth, at the time of death, one gives away one's wealth to them.
"The Westerner" refers to the wife.
If there is someone capable of providing for their wife and children...
Robes, food and drink, bedding, medicinal decoctions,
necklaces, ornaments, and articles for adorning the body—
such a person is able to provide these offerings to their wife and children in the Western Quarter.
The wife and children, in turn, repay him with fourteen matters:
first, they attend to whatever he does with all their heart;
second, they always act without ever becoming indolent or negligent.
Third, one must ensure that what is undertaken is brought to completion.
Fourth, one acts with promptness so as not to miss the proper time.
Fifth, one constantly attends to guests and visitors.
Sixth, one purifies their dwelling and bedding.
Seventh, one uses words of affection and respect that are gentle and soft.
Eighth, one instructs servants and attendants with mild speech.
Ninth, he is well able to guard his wealth and possessions.
Tenth, he rises at dawn and retires at night.
Eleventh, he is able to provide pure food.
Twelfth, they are able to endure instruction and admonition.
Thirteenth, they are able to conceal others' misdeeds.
Fourteenth, they are able to attend to those suffering from illness.
The north is none other than the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra).
If there is anyone who can make offerings to such a virtuous friend,
they should give according to their capacity.
If one respectfully follows the teachings, speaks with gentle words, prostrates, and offers praise,
that person will be able to make offerings to the spiritual benefactor of the north.
That spiritual benefactor, in turn, will repay them with four things.
First, they teach the cultivation of wholesome dharmas;
second, they cause one to abandon unwholesome dharmas;
third, when there is fear or terror, they are able to provide rescue and deliverance.
The four [types of] negligence can be abandoned through this means.
Those who are "below" are servants and slaves.
If there is someone who can provide for these servants and slaves...
Providing food, clothing, and medicine for those who are ill or emaciated;
not reviling or striking them—
such a person is able to support the servants and slaves below.
These servants and slaves, in turn, repay him with ten matters:
first, they do not commit transgressions;
second, they act without waiting for instruction.
Third, one must ensure that what is undertaken is completed.
Fourth, one acts with promptness so as not to miss the proper time.
Fifth, even if the master is impoverished, one never abandons them.
Sixth, rising early;
seventh, guarding possessions;
eighth, repaying even small kindnesses with great gratitude.
Ninth, to revere and mindfully recollect with a sincere heart;
tenth, to cover over evil deeds with good.
"The ones above" refers to śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and others.
If there are śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas above who are provided with offerings of robes,
food and drink, lodgings, bedding, and medicines for the sick and infirm,
and who are able to rescue them when they are afraid.
In times of famine, one gives food;
upon hearing evil, one is able to restrain it;
and one performs prostrations, shows reverence, respects, and praises [others].
Such a person is then able to make offerings to the śramaṇas and others of the upper direction.
These renunciants, in turn, repay them with five things:
first, they are able to inspire faith in this life.
Second, he teaches the cultivation of wisdom;
third, he teaches the practice of giving;
fourth, he teaches the observance of ethical discipline.
The fifth instruction is to cultivate extensive learning.
If one makes offerings to these six directions,
that person will be able to increase their wealth and lifespan.
One is able to receive and uphold the Upāsaka precepts.
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Because the Buddhas revere the Dharma, they make offerings to the Dharma."
Take the Dharma as your teacher.
Why is this? Because all Buddhas of the three periods of time take the true reality of all phenomena (dharmas) as their teacher.
Question: If the Buddha does not seek merit,
for what reason does he accept offerings?
The answer is:
Throughout immeasurable kalpas, the Buddha cultivated all manner of merit and constantly practiced all forms of goodness, not merely seeking a reward.
Out of reverence for his merit, he made this offering.
It was as when the Buddha was still in the world,
before Aniruddha had attained the divine eye.
Being blind, he could see nothing;
yet with his hands he sewed clothes.
At that time, the needle and the seam came loose.
He then said, "Who loves merit? Let them serve as my needle-puller.
At that time, the Buddha went to his location and spoke to the bhikṣu, saying:
"I am one who loves merit;
I have come for your sake.
This bhikṣu recognized the voice of the Buddha.
He rose quickly, put on his robes, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet,
and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Buddha’s merit is already complete."
"Why do you say that one should cherish merit?
The Buddha replied,
"Although my merits are already fulfilled,"
Because I deeply understand the power of repaying the kindness of merit,
I have attained the state of being foremost among all sentient beings.
Furthermore, for the purpose of teaching and transforming my disciples, I spoke these words to them.
I still perform meritorious deeds;
why do you not? It is like an old man of a hundred years from a troupe of performers who still dances.
Someone rebuked him, saying, "Old man,
you are already a hundred years old;
what use is there for this dancing?"
The old man replied, "I have no need for dancing myself; it is only because I wish to teach my sons and grandsons.
The Buddha is also like this.
Although his own merit was already complete,
he made this offering for the sake of creating merit for his disciples through the act of teaching them.
Therefore, when the Buddha’s foster mother Mahāprajāpatī passed away,
the Four Heavenly Kings carried her on a bed to the funeral pyre.
The Buddha went before them, holding an incense burner and burning incense as an offering.
Out of gratitude for the kindness received,
one performs equal offerings even without seeking a specific result; indeed,
only a Buddha is worthy of making offerings to a Buddha.
Other people do not know the virtues of the Buddha.
As it is said in a verse:
"The wise can revere the wise; through discourse with the wise, one becomes skilled in wisdom."
The wise can know wisdom, just as a snake knows its own feet.
Furthermore, the *Sūtra on King Bimbisāra Going to the Buddha for Offerings* states:
At that time, Bimbisāra (Bimbi meaning "color" and sāra meaning "handsome") of the Magadha kingdom went to the place where the Buddha was and addressed the World-Honored One.
"I possess all the wealth and resources within this kingdom;
I am capable of providing whatever is required.
I wish to make offerings to the Tathāgata and the community of bhikṣus for as long as my life lasts."
You should also exhort and lead your ministers and subjects so that they may receive these provisions— robes, food and drink, bedding and seating,
and medicines for the sick and infirm— and thereby attain deliverance, leave the three miserable realms behind, and dwell forever in peace and security.
Having accepted the invitation, the Buddha spoke these verses:
"Sacrificing to the Great One is foremost; poetic hymns are likewise foremost."
The king is the foremost among men; the ocean is the foremost among all streams;
the moon is the foremost among the stars; and the sun is the foremost among luminaries.
Throughout the zenith, the nadir, and the four quarters, he is the sovereign over all created things.
In the heavens and throughout the world, the Buddha is supreme and without superior;
those who wish to cultivate merit should seek the Three Buddhas.
Furthermore, the *Saṃyukta-ratna-piṭaka-sūtra* says:
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"There are eight kinds of persons to whom one should give with certainty and no longer harbor doubt.
The first is one's father."
Second, the two mothers;
third, the Buddhas;
fourth, the disciples.
Fifth, those who have come from afar;
sixth, those who are departing for afar;
seventh, the sick.
Eighth, regarding the caregiver:
furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that all bodhisattvas have accomplished immeasurable and inexhaustible merits.
With a single meal, they make offerings to the Buddhas and the Sangha of the ten directions;
all are fully satisfied, yet it is not exhausted,
just like a gushing spring that flows forth without ever being depleted.
For example, Mañjuśrī once offered a single bowl of *modaka* cakes to eighty-four thousand monks;
they were all fully satisfied, yet the food was not exhausted.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva offers a single bowl of food to the Buddhas of the ten directions,
before each of those Buddhas, a complete array of food and drink appears.
For example, it is like a ghost or spirit who, upon receiving a single mouthful of food from a human, produces ten million times more.
Furthermore, the *Old Sutra of Miscellaneous Parables* states:
"In the past, there was a brahmin."
He was one hundred and twenty years old.
From his youth, he had never married and possessed no lustful desires.
He dwelt in deep mountains, in places where no other people lived.
They made their huts from *má* grass,
their mats from *péng* and *jiǎo* grass,
and took wild fruits as their food.
He did not accumulate wealth or treasures.
When the king sought to recruit him, he did not go to comply with the intent.
He dwelt in stillness and non-action in the mountains for several years, enjoying the company of birds and beasts and cutting himself off from the paths of men.
On the mountain there were four beasts:
the first was named fox;
the second was named macaque.
The third was a otter,
and the fourth was a rabbit;
these four animals went daily to the place of the practitioner to listen to the recitation of the sutras and the exposition of the precepts.
Thus, after a long time had passed,
all the fruits and melons he ate were completely exhausted.
Subsequently, the practitioner intended to depart.
The four beasts were deeply distressed and their hearts were not at ease;
they consulted one another, saying,
"Let us each go out to seek offerings for the practitioner."
The monkey went to another mountain, obtained sweet fruit,
and returned to offer it to the practitioner, saying,
"I pray that you will stay and not depart."
A wild fox, having transformed its appearance to become a human,
obtained a bag of rice and flour and brought it to offer to the practitioner.
"You may be granted a month's provisions;
we pray you stay and do not depart.
The otter likewise entered the water and caught a large fish.
"O practitioner of the Way,
we provide you with a month's worth of provisions;
we pray that you will stay and not depart."
The hare thought to himself,
"With what shall I make an offering to this man of the Path?
He then reflected that he should offer his own body as an offering.
He then gathered firewood to kindle a fire and produce charcoal.
He went to inform the practitioner, saying,
"Now I have become a rabbit."
"Please enter the fire to roast yourself and offer your body to this practitioner;
it will provide him with a day's worth of provisions."
He then threw himself into the fire,
but the flames would not ignite.
When the practitioner saw the rabbit, [he realized its intent].
Moved by his benevolence and righteousness,
and feeling pity and sorrow for him,
he then stayed there of his own accord.
The Buddha said,
"The brahmin at that time was the present Buddha Dīpaṃkara;
the rabbit at that time was my own self."
The monkey of that time was the present Śāriputra;
the wild fox of that time was the present Ānanda; and the otter of that time was the present Maudgalyāyana.
Furthermore, the Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya states:
The Buddha was staying by the banks of the Rohiṇī River.
At that time, the World-Honored One’s bowl and the bowls of the bhikṣus were together in an open place.
At that time, there was a monkey who,
while walking, saw ripe honey free of bees within a tree;
it came and took the World-Honored One’s alms bowl.
The bhikṣus tried to stop him.
The Buddha said,
"Do not stop him."
Having no ill intent,
he took his bowl, fetched some honey, and offered it; however,
the World-Honored One did not accept it.
He had to wait for the water to become clear.
The monkey, not understanding the Buddha’s intention,
thought there were insects in it.
Seeing honey flowing from the edge of his bowl,
he went to the water’s edge to wash it;
having rinsed the bowl with water, he brought it back to offer to the Buddha.
The Buddha accepted it.
Having received it, the monkey was filled with great joy;
he retreated several paces and danced.
He fell into a pit and died,
whereupon he was immediately reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
At that time, the bhikṣus spoke these verses:
The Hero of the World, endowed with the ten powers, was in a thicket; the Buddha’s bowl and the monks’ bowls were in an open place.
Wild animals, having cultivated virtue and possessing intelligence, saw that the honeycomb was ripe and excellent;
they went straight forward to take the World-Honored One’s bowl. The bhikṣus wished to stop them, but the Buddha did not permit it.
Having obtained a bowl filled with honey, he came to offer it to the Buddha. Out of compassion, the Tathāgata accepted it;
his heart was filled with joy and delight, and as he retreated, he danced. His feet stumbled on the bank and he passed away, immediately being reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Later, descending to be born in the human world, he left the household life and became an Arhat.
Furthermore, the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra* states:
"A bodhisattva may possess wealth for the purpose of making offerings to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, as well as to one's parents, brothers, and sisters."
If one accepts gold, silver, or wealth for the purpose of building monasteries, constructing shrines, or making images as an act of giving,
there is no offense.
The verse says:
Far-reaching is the long stream; Distant is the extended rein. Trapped within the dark confinement of affliction, it is difficult to achieve liberation;
Were it not for the Great Vehicle, By what other high station could one ascend?

Making Offerings to the Triple Gem: The Fruit Surpasses the Ten Stages (39) Section on Accepting Invitations (41–42), Section Thirty-Nine This section consists of nine parts: the Part on Explaining the Intent; the Part on Inviting the Sangha; the Part on the Noble Sangha; the Part on Bestowing Food; the Part on the Time of Eating; the Part on the Method of Eating; the Part on Concluding the Meal; the Part on Reciting Vows; and the Part on the Merit of Giving. 1. Part on Explaining the Intent (First): Regarding the method of making offerings and assemblies, its fundamental principle is non-limitation.
Having no preference for this nor aversion to that, one accords with the mind of giving;
thus, with a profound disposition that dispels all signs,
one reaches the ultimate limit of emptiness.
Acting according to the time and following conditions,
it is equal in measure to the dharma-realm;
since the cause is inexhaustible, the fruit is likewise endless.
Furthermore, those who follow worldly ways are frugal with their wealth and poor in resources, thus limiting the objects they give as offerings.
Since the objects are limited, their minds are likewise constrained by attachment.
They may even calculate the number of people to determine their provisions.
Or perhaps one selects those of virtue before making a request;
yet the finite blessings have not been relinquished,
while the infinite retribution has not yet been received— such is the case for those who practice the foolish giving of the Dharma.
Although things may be abundant while the distribution is meager,
one who possesses skillful means and compassion ensures that even when things are few, the distribution is universal.

For this reason, when foreign lands establish fasts, they generally do so on a vast scale as "unrestricted" (*amogha*) assemblies, directing their minds toward the ten directions to encompass the entire Dharma-realm. 2.
Section on Inviting Monks: The second part, regarding the section on inviting monks, is as stated in the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* (*Xiányú jīng*).
At that time, the Buddha’s maternal aunt Mahāprajāpatī,
after the Buddha had already left the household life,
personally spun and wove a single piece of golden-colored cotton cloth to create a great robe (*saṃghāṭī*), which she then offered to the Tathāgata.
The Buddha ordered that this be taken to be offered to the assembly of monks.
The maternal aunt, however, harbored thoughts of him and waited for the Buddha with longing in her heart.
"I only pray that you will look upon me with compassion and accept it from me.
The Buddha knew that his mother’s intention was solely to offer it to him;
however, because her mind was still bound by affection, the merit would not be vast.
If one gives to the Sangha, the retribution obtained is even greater;
knowing this, I exhort you accordingly.
If there is a donor who makes a specific invitation for the sixteen kinds [of monks], it is complete.
Although they obtain the retribution of merit, it is not yet considered much.
What are the sixteen?
There are eight classes each among the bhikṣus and the bhikṣuṇīs.
