Fifth, the body attains peace and stability.
Nor does it cause illness.
For this reason, the śramaṇa knows the nature of merit and does not eat.
[The commentary] states:
If greed for food increases and gives rise to further afflictions,
one must contemplate it with revulsion and form the perception of impurity.
Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
Regarding the contemplation of the repulsiveness of food:
one should observe that this food arises from impurity;
for example, meat arises from semen, blood, and the urinary tract.
This is the dwelling place of pus-worms;
it is formed from the transformations of ghee, milk, curd, and blood, and is no different from putrid pus.
It is defiled by the filth of the kitchen and various kinds of impurities.
If it enters the mouth, the brain produces putrid saliva that flows down through two channels; this mingles with the spittle and then forms flavor.
Its appearance is like vomit, entering through the gateway of the abdomen.
The earth supports them, water rots them, wind agitates them, and fire boils them,
like porridge being cooked in a cauldron;
the dregs and impurities sink to the bottom.
The pure rises to the top.
It is like brewing wine:
the dregs and turbidity become excrement.
The clear portion becomes urine.
The backbone has three apertures;
when the wind blows upon the oily secretions, they disperse and enter the hundred vessels.
Combined with the prior blood, it coagulates and transforms into flesh;
from this new flesh, fat is produced,
and the marrow arises from within it.
From the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), produced by the union of new and old flesh, the five sense-faculties (*pañcendriya*) arise.
From these five faculties, the five consciousnesses (*pañcavijñāna*) arise. Following the five consciousnesses, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises in succession.
One discriminates and grasps at signs, weighing their beauty and ugliness;
thereafter, various afflictions such as the mind of "I" and "mine," as well as various sinful karmas, arise.
Furthermore, one reflects that the labor expended for this food is exceedingly great.
He calculated that for a single bowl of rice,
his laborers had sweated until they were exhausted;
he then gathered them together to measure the total amount.
One eats little but perspires much;
such is the bitterness of this food that it becomes impure as soon as it enters the mouth.
Within a single night, it transforms into excrement and urine;
what was once a delicious flavor becomes something loathsome that one does not wish to behold.
The practitioner reflects to himself:
"If I were to become greedily attached to such wretched food as this,"
One will fall into the three miserable realms.
Contemplating food in this way, one should cultivate revulsion for the five desires.
It is, for example, like a certain Brahmin who practices the dharma of purity.
Due to certain circumstances, he arrived in an impure land.
He thought to himself, "How may I avoid this impurity?
Only by eating dry food can I attain purity."
He saw an old woman selling cakes of white marrow and said to her,
"I have a reason to stay here for one hundred days."
"I will always make cakes for you and give you a generous price.
The old woman made cakes every day and sent them to him;
the Brahmin, greedily attached to eating his fill, was filled with joy.
When the old woman first made the cakes, they were pure white;
later, they turned colorless and tasteless.
He then questioned the old woman.
"For what reason?
The mother replied,
"Because the abscess has healed."
The brahmin asked, "What does this mean?
His mother replied:
A boil developed in the private parts of my mistress.
I applied flour and ghee to it;
when the boil ripened, pus emerged, mixing with the ghee and flour.
It was thus every day.
I made cakes with this and gave them to you;
that is why the cakes were so excellent.
"Now that the noble lady's abscess has healed,
where shall I find another?
When the brahmin heard this, he [was moved].
He struck his head with both fists, beat his chest,
and retched dryly, saying, "How can I ever violate this pure Dharma?
I have already fulfilled my purpose."
Abandoning the objects of attachment, he hastens back to his native land;
the practitioner is likewise attached to these foods and drinks.
Delighting in eating while failing to contemplate impurity, what can one do when the retribution of suffering arrives later and regret sets in?
Section Seven: On Finishing the Meal. As stated in the discourse of Upāli:
When the ordained monks and nuns, as well as laypeople, have finished their meal,
if they do not use powdered soap, *kumuda* powder, or similar substances to cleanse their mouths,
their fast is not considered complete.
In the past, there was a bhikṣu named Liandi who observed the fast and precepts for sixty years without fail;
on the single day he took food, he maintained his fast with only coarsely ground mung bean flour and the like.
If it were not so, the fast would not be accomplished at all;
this sūtra lacks a specific definition.
The *Vinayamātṛkā* states: "Gomaya refers to cow dung."
If one follows this sutra,
how could one use cow dung to purify the mouth?
According to the *Biography of Dharma Master Yashas*, it says:
The laypeople and non-Buddhists of the western regions take Brahmā and the ox as their objects of veneration,
for they believe these two can produce all things and nourish the people.
Therefore, one uses cow dung to purify the ritual site (*maṇḍala*).
The Buddha, following worldly conventions, likewise used it for purification.
However, this does not apply to the purification of the mouth; if one follows the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* and other such texts, [the procedure differs].
One merely maintains the four modes of deportment—walking, standing, sitting, and reclining—and consumes the five kinds of formal food;
provided these four aspects do not conflict with the precepts, the method of the fast (*upavāsa*) is accomplished.
It is not necessary to wash the mouth with cleansing powder (*kṣāra*) to complete the fast.
If the proper time has passed or if one’s deportment (*īryāpatha*) has been lost,
even if one uses bath powder, the fast (*upavāsa*) is not accomplished.
Furthermore, the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states:
If, after having fasted, one has vomited food that has not yet passed the throat and swallows it again, there is no offense.
If it has passed the throat and is swallowed again, one commits an offense.
Furthermore, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
If one becomes thirsty after eating,
the Buddha permitted that one may take all grains, beans, and wheat that have been boiled until they are soft but not broken, and drink their juice at improper times.
This also applies to ghee, oil, honey, rock sugar, and various fresh fruit juices.
One must drink only water that has been purified;
however, if the residual water at the bottom of a vessel is washed by rain,
it is likewise considered pure.
The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"The clarified juice of *śālūka* fruit may be drunk outside of the permitted time; this refers to the root of the lotus (*utpala*).
The *Mahādeva-lakṣaṇa-śāstra* states that molasses syrup may also be drunk outside of the permitted time."
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"A person has four hundred and four diseases;
one hundred and one of these are caused by the wind element (*vāyu-mahābhūta*) and are treated with vegetable oil."
One hundred and one types of fever caused by the fire element (*tejo-dhātu*) are treated with ghee (*sarpis*).
One hundred and one types of water-related diseases (*jala-roga*) are treated with honey (*madhu*).
One hundred and one types of miscellaneous diseases are treated using whichever of the three aforementioned medicines is appropriate.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"Stone honey (śarkarā) may not be consumed at improper times.
There are five types of persons who are permitted to eat it at improper times."
That is to say: those traveling far away,
those who are ill,
and those who have not received food.
There are few people who eat.
If at a place where water is offered, one mixes it with water, it may be drunk.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:

Since it is permitted to drink [medicinal liquids] during the two times of hunger and thirst, one knows that when not ill, even substances such as rock honey, ghee, or oil may not be consumed at improper times. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"Black pepper, long pepper, ginger, and *harītakī*, etc."
It is permitted to take this medicine at improper times when it is mixed with food;
furthermore, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:
"All [medicines] that are bitter, pungent, salty, sweet, and so forth..."
Regarding those that cannot be used as food:
it is permitted to take them as medicine at non-authorized times (vikāla) for as long as one lives.
The *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra* (Shanjian lun) states:
All trees, fruits, roots, stalks, branches, leaves,
and so forth that are not fit to be eaten may all be used as medicines to be taken for as long as one lives.
The commentary states:
Recently, I have observed that many people consume "timely food" (kālāhāra) outside of the permitted time.
What, then, constitutes such food?
This refers to monastics and laypeople in frontier regions who,
upon hearing that the Vinaya permits the consumption of fruit juices and syrups,
immediately consume the juice of dried dates or raw pears, grapes, and pomegranates.
Do not drink the juice after crushing [the fruit];
eat both the pulp and the seeds together.
Although there is crushed juice, [do not consume it].
It was not that he made the turbid clear;
rather, he took the thick,
muddy broth along with the dregs and ate it.
Some, having heard that drinking a decoction of śleṣmātaka fruit would cure fever, took raw lotus roots along with their fibers and ate them raw;
others took clear rice-gruel and drank it.
Some claim that the body is free from hunger and thirst and thus do not eat at improper times, consuming ghee, oil, honey, rock sugar, and the like;
others use apricot kernels boiled into a thick broth.
Instances of such impropriety are numerous.
It cannot be described in full detail.
According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*,
those who have not previously traveled on long journeys and the other four types of persons mentioned are not permitted to eat [the food] indiscriminately.
Eating [after the meal] breaks the fast.
Seeing that many people commit this offense,
I have therefore separately recorded this in my notes.
Section Eight: Benedictions. As stated in the *Buddhacarita* (The Life of the Buddha):
At that time, the World-Honored One was in the eastern direction when the sun rose.
Having donned his robes and taken up his alms bowl,
surrounded on all sides by the community of bhikṣus,
with the Buddha as their leader, he arrived at the palace of King Śuddhodana.
Having arrived, he sat upon the Buddha’s seat that had been prepared.
The community of bhikṣus each sat down in their respective order according to the Dharma.
At that time, King Śuddhodana...
With the Buddha at their head,
when the assembly of bhikṣus had taken their seats in order,
he personally served them all varieties of exquisite food and drink until they were exhausted.
Having finished his meal, at that time the World-Honored One taught and transformed King Śuddhodana;
having caused him to awaken and give rise to joy,
he rose from his seat and returned to his own abode.
Furthermore, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"There was a bhikṣu who, having accepted an invitation for a meal from another,
entered in silence and departed in silence."
The laypeople rebuked them, saying,
"We do not know whether the food is good or not.
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"From now on, during mealtime, one should perform a *bhāṣya* (chant) and offer prayers of blessing for the donor.
[The monks] did not know who should perform this."
The Buddha said:
"Let the Elder perform it;
if the Elder is unable, [let another do so]."
Those who are capable should perform [the duties] in sequence;
therefore, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"The elder (sthavira) should take cognizance of this."
Whatever kind of offering the donor has made,
one should offer a corresponding aspiration for them.
If it is an offering made for the merit of the deceased, [one should recite the following].
One should offer this prayer:
"All classes of sentient beings, As long as they possess life, shall return to death;
According to their various deeds, good or evil, They themselves shall receive their retribution."
Those who commit evil enter hell; those who do good are born in heaven.
Those who are able to skillfully practice the Path attain Nirvāṇa through the exhaustion of outflows.
If one gives birth to a son and establishes merit for him...
One should offer this prayer of aspiration as follows:
The youth takes refuge in the Buddha: Tathāgata Vipaśyin, Śikhin, Viśvabhū, Krakucchanda, and Kanakamuni.
Kāśyapa and Śākya, these seven generations of Great Holy Honored Ones,
are like the parents of a person; with compassionate thoughts for their children,
they desire that all the joys of the world be obtained by them.
May the son receive all blessings; moreover, he shall surpass the kinsmen of every household,
and his enjoyment of happiness shall likewise be boundless,
as if one were entering a new house and establishing offerings there.
One should offer this aspiration as follows:
"May the noble and holy assembly, having received this gift of a roofed dwelling, enjoy it at their pleasure and attain auspiciousness."
In this world, there are wise people who understand this:
by observing the precepts and the holy life, by cultivating merit and providing food and drink,
and by making oral prayers for the Saṅgha, the deities of the household will always be joyful.
With a well-born mind, one maintains protection and dwells therein throughout the long night;
whether entering a village or staying in a wilderness,
by day or by night, the devas will always follow and protect them.
If a merchant intends to set out on a journey and wishes to perform a merit-making rite, he should offer this prayer:
"May all directions be peaceful and secure; may the devas grant auspiciousness."
Having heard this, their hearts rejoice; they obtain everything they desire.
Those with two feet dwell in peace, and those with four feet likewise dwell in peace.
They find peace when departing, and they find peace when returning.
Peaceful by night and peaceful by day, may the devas always protect and assist you.
May all your companions be virtuous and good; may everyone be entirely secure, healthy, and well-disposed, with hands and feet free from ailment.
Throughout the entire body and all its members, there is no place of sickness or suffering;
if one has any desire, one shall attain what the heart wishes for.
If one gives [this] for the sake of taking a wife, [one's wish shall be fulfilled].
One should make this aspiration as follows:
A woman who faithfully upholds the precepts, And whose husband likewise does so,
By virtue of their faith, Is able to practice the giving of alms.
When two people both uphold the precepts and cultivate right view, they find joy in practicing together and performing meritorious deeds. The devas will constantly follow and protect them;
such is the fruit of this karma, like traveling without provisions.
If one gives alms to those who have left the household life,
one should offer this aspiration:
"Holding their bowls, they beg from house to house, Encountering anger or meeting with joy."
To protect their intentions, one should act accordingly; for it is difficult to practice giving after having left the household life.
Thus, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"When the Elder presides over a meal, he should gauge the circumstances of those present and offer prayers of blessing on behalf of the donor (*dānapati*)."
By giving food as a gift, one obtains the fruit of fulfillment.
Furthermore, in the *Ekottarika Āgama*,
when the World-Honored One was offered a garden by a woman, he made this aspiration:
By giving garden fruits, one bestows coolness; by building bridges, one ferries people across;
by constructing latrines near the roads, people find rest and obtain peace and security day and night—their merit is immeasurable.
Those who achieve the precepts of all dharmas will, upon death, certainly be reborn in the heavens.
Section Nine: The Merit of Giving. As stated in the *Śatavāraṇa-sūtra*:
During the time when the Buddha was in the world...
In the city of Rājagṛha, there was an elder whose wealth and treasures were immeasurable and beyond calculation.
His wife gave birth to a daughter who was able to speak immediately upon birth.
Within the house, a hundred flavors of food and drink were naturally provided in full.
When his parents saw this,
they thought it was a non-human *piśāca* demon.
Terrified, she did not dare approach. Seeing her fear,
the girl joined her palms toward her mother and spoke this verse:
I pray that my mother will listen to my words; I shall now speak according to reality.
I am truly not a piśāca nor any other kind of ghost;
I am truly a human being, pursued and driven by the consequences of my own karma.
"By the causal conditions of wholesome karma, she has now obtained such a reward.
At that time, when her parents heard the girl’s verse,
they were overcome with joy beyond measure.
He immediately went forward, took her up in his arms, and nurtured her by suckling her at his breast;
consequently, he established a name for her,
calling her Shan'ai (Good Love).
At that time, seeing her mother’s joy, the girl joined her palms and said to her mother,
"Please invite the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus for my sake.
Her mother immediately accepted the invitation.
They were fully provided with food and drink of a hundred flavors.
Thereupon, before the Buddha, they yearned to hear the Dharma;
the Buddha then preached for them, and they attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
Later, she sought to leave the household life.
The Buddha said to her, "Come, Bhikṣuṇī," and her hair fell away of its own accord.
Having donned the dharma robes upon her body, she became a bhikṣuṇī.
Through diligent cultivation, she attained the fruit of arhatship and was revered and honored by devas and worldlings alike.
At that time, the World-Honored One was accompanied by one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
He traveled to another land and arrived in the midst of a wilderness;
the time for the meal had already come.
She addressed the nun Śuklā, saying,
"You should now prepare food and drink to offer as alms to the Buddha and the Sangha.
She then immediately took the Buddha’s bowl and threw it into the air.
Food of a hundred flavors spontaneously filled [the bowls].
In this manner, he successively took the alms bowls of the one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus;
the rice likewise filled them all, making everyone fully satisfied.
Having seen this, Ānanda marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence and requested that the Buddha explain its original causes and conditions.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
In this Bhadrakalpa,
there was a Buddha who appeared in the world named Kāśyapa.
Wearing his robes and carrying his alms bowl, he entered the city with his bhikṣus to beg for food.
Next, he arrived at the house of a great elder who had prepared various delicacies intending to invite guests;
while the guests had not yet arrived, there was a maidservant.
Seeing the Buddha and the Sangha standing outside the gate begging for alms,
she did not inform her mistress; instead,
she took all the food and drink and offered it entirely to the Buddha and the assembly of monks.
Later, when a guest arrived and sat down,
he commanded the maidservant, saying,
"Prepare and bring food."
The maidservant replied to her mistress,
"There is now a Buddha and his Sangha standing outside our gate begging for alms.
I have already given all of this food as an offering."
Having heard this, everyone was immediately filled with joy and said to the maidservant,
"We have now encountered a field of merit."
"It is beyond words how wonderful it is that you are able to take this food and offer it as alms.
I now release you to pursue whatever you seek according to your own will."
The maidservant replied to her mistress,
"If you permit me to leave, I shall join the ranks of those on the road.
She was granted permission immediately.
She became a bhikṣuṇī and practiced with diligent effort for ten thousand years without ceasing;
when her life came to an end, she did not fall into the evil realms.
"Food and drink of a hundred flavors from among the heavens and humans shall arrive as soon as they are thought of.
Now that you have encountered me, you may leave the household life and attain the Way.
Having heard this, the bhikṣu rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Furthermore, the *Śatavāraṇa-sūtra* states:
When the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park,
it was the conclusion of the summer retreat.
As the bhikṣus were about to travel to another country,
King Bimbisāra, accompanied by his ministers, went out of the city and gazed from afar at the Tathāgata as he approached to accept his offerings.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing from afar that the king’s mind was filled with deep longing and that the community of bhikṣus was gradually preparing to travel,
set out for the kingdom of Magadha, where he encountered a flock of birds.
Within it was a king of śuka parrots who, seeing the Buddha approaching from afar, soared into the air and went out to meet him on the road, saying:
"I pray that the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus will,
out of compassion and pity, come to my grove and accept my invitation for one night."
The Buddha then granted his consent.
Knowing that permission had been granted, the King of Parrots returned to his original forest.
He commanded all the parrots to come individually to welcome him.
At that time, the World-Honored One, accompanied by the bhikṣus, [proceeded].
They went to the Śuka Grove and each spread out their sitting mats beneath the trees.
While he was sitting in meditation and contemplation,
the King of Parrots saw that the Buddha and his bhikṣus were sitting in serene stillness;
he felt profound joy.
Throughout the night, the bhikṣu circled the Buddha in flight;
looking in the four directions, he saw no lions, tigers, wolves, birds, beasts, or thieves to disturb the World-Honored One or the community of bhikṣus.
When it was dawn the following morning, the World-Honored One proceeded forward,
led by the joyful parrot as his guide toward Rājagṛha.
He addressed King Bimbisāra, saying,
"The World-Honored One is now approaching with his bhikṣus and has arrived nearby.
We pray that Your Majesty will [attend to this]."
He prepared various delicacies and went out to welcome him against the grain of protocol.
Upon hearing these words, the king issued an edict to prepare the delicacies.
Carrying banners, streamers, incense, flowers, and musical instruments,
the various ministers went out to meet him on the road to welcome him.
At that time, King Śuka passed away during the night and was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Suddenly, he grew to the size of an eight-year-old child and thought to himself:
"By what merit have I been born in this heavenly realm?"
Upon investigating this for myself, I realized that it was because the parrot had requested the Buddha to stay for one night that I was able to come and be born here.
I must now go back and repay the World-Honored One’s kindness.
Wearing a celestial crown upon his head and adorned with various necklaces,
he beautifies his body.
Carrying incense and flowers,
they made offerings to the Buddha and withdrew to sit on one side.
The Buddha then preached the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths for him;
his mind was opened and his understanding attained, and he realized the fruit of Srotāpanna.
He circumambulated the Buddha three times and returned to the heavens.
Then the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What karma did this son of heaven create in his past lives to be born among the parrots?
And what merit did he cultivate to attain birth in the heavens?"
They came to make offerings to the Buddha, heard the Dharma, and attained the fruits [of the path].
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"In this Bhadrakalpa, in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, a Buddha appeared in the world."
He was named Kāśyapa.
Within that Dharma, there was an elder who observed the five precepts.
Thus, at one time, he violated a single precept and was consequently reborn among the parrots;
the other four precepts remained intact.
Now he has encountered me, left the household life, and attained the Way.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If you wish to know who that upāsaka was at that time,"
This present parrot is that very one.
Having heard what the Buddha taught, he rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Furthermore, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya-śāstra* (付法藏經) states:
In the past, ninety-one eons ago, after the Buddha Vipaśyin had entered parinirvāṇa,
there was a bhikṣu who suffered greatly from a headache.
At that time, Bakula was a poor man.
Seeing a sick bhikṣu, he immediately took an *harītakī* fruit and offered it to the sick bhikṣu.
Once the bhikṣu had consumed it, his illness was immediately cured.
By virtue of this gift of medicine, for ninety-one kalpas, he dwelt among gods and humans.
He experienced happiness and blessings, never having been ill;
in his final birth, he was born into a brahmin family,
and his mother died early.
The father took another wife. Kula was young,
and seeing his mother making cakes, he asked her for some.
The stepmother, filled with jealousy,
seized Kuṇāla and threw him onto a hot griddle; yet,
although the griddle was scorching hot, it could not burn or harm him.
The father, returning from outside, saw Bakula on the hot griddle and immediately took him down and embraced him.
Later, the mother was boiling meat in a cauldron.
At that time, Bakula asked his mother for some meat.
His mother became even more incensed;
she immediately threw it into the cauldron, yet it was neither burned nor decomposed.
The father could not find him and called out to him;
Kula heard the call and responded from within the cauldron.
The father immediately took him out in his arms, and he was restored to his former state.
Later, the mother went toward the river and pursued him.
Subsequently, the mother, filled with anger and resentment, spoke these words:
"What kind of ghost, demon, or ominous creature is this?
Even though we burn and boil it, we cannot cause its death.
Thereupon, they seized it and threw it into the river.
He encountered a large fish and immediately swallowed it;
yet, due to his karmic merit, he did not die.
A fisherman caught this fish.
He went to the market to sell it; however,
because the price he demanded was so high,
no one would buy it.
By evening, it was about to smell.
When Vakkula’s father saw this, he immediately purchased it.
He brought it back home.
As he cut open the belly with a knife,
the child within the fish’s belly cried out in a loud voice,
"I pray that my father remain calm and do not harm me."
The father opened the fish’s belly and took up the child, who was neither injured nor harmed.
As he gradually grew older, he sought the Buddha and left the household life, attaining the fruit of Arhatship.
From birth until his old age at one hundred and sixty years, he never once suffered from illness.
Furthermore, they shall experience neither bodily fever nor headaches;
by virtue of giving medicine, they shall attain such long life as to not die in any of the five locations.
Roasted on a grid, one is not scorched;
boiled in a cauldron, one is not decomposed;
drowned in water, one does not die.
The fish swallowed it but could not digest it;
the knife cut it but could not wound it.
For these reasons, [it is so].
The wise should perform such deeds.
Furthermore, the *Śāriputra-vinaya* states:
At that time, there was a lay devotee (*gṛhapati*) in the city of Rājagṛha.
His name was Śrīkumāra; he was immensely wealthy and possessed great riches.
He was a disciple of a non-Buddhist Brahmin.
This man constantly harbored doubts,
wondering whether the śramaṇa Gautama possessed omniscience.
He went to where the Buddha was and said to him:
"The śramaṇa Gautama shall take his meal at my house tomorrow.
Because the Buddha saw that he was one who should be delivered, he accepted the invitation by remaining silent.
At that time, the householder returned to his home.
Between the outer gates, he had a great fire pit prepared, with flames that were smokeless;
he covered it over with sand.
He then entered the house and spread out an un-woven sitting mat, and mixed poison into the food.
He spoke these words with his mind and mouth:
"Gautama, if you are an omniscient person, you should know this matter;
if you are not an omniscient person, you shall fall into this pit and die from the poison."
He sent a messenger to inform the Buddha, saying,
"The food and drink are prepared.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
He commanded that none of the bhikṣus should go before the Buddha.
Then the Buddha, having put on his robes and taken up his bowl, proceeded ahead.
The bhikṣus followed behind as they entered the house of Śrīgupta.
The Buddha transformed the fire pit into a lotus pond filled with pure water, both sweet and cool;
various kinds of lotuses completely covered the surface of the water.
At that time, the Buddha and the Sangha all walked upon lotus petals to enter the house.
Upon sitting down, the un-woven bed was transformed into a woven one.

40. Chapter on the Wheel-Turning Kings (43). Chapter Forty of the Chapter on Wheel-Turning Kings. This consists of five sections:

the Section on the Intent, the Section on the Assemblage of Names, the Section on the Seven Treasures, the Section on Mūrdhaja, and the Section on King Aśoka. 1. Section on the Intent. First, the Section on the Intent. I have heard it said:

and when he led and transformed others through the ten wholesome deeds, a thousand sons appeared in response.
Encompassing both the distant and the near, he alone dwells in the Central Plains;

Having lived for a long time in this world, their greed and indolence became increasingly rampant;

Thereupon, they exercised the fierce might of a *cakravartin*.
He aspired to ascend to the palace of Śakra;

he fell and lost the rank of a Cakravartin king.
Bearing this sorrow with poignant intensity,
it is as grievous as the calamity of being submerged in fire and water;
how lamentable and painful this is!
How deeply lamentable! Section Two:
On the Names of the Assemblies. According to the Tripitaka Master Paramārtha, during the period of formation (vivartakalpa), the lifespan of human beings was immeasurable years.
During the kalpas of abiding and destruction, when the human lifespan is eighty thousand years,
a Wheel-Turning King appears in the world;
if it decreases, he does not appear.
There are three types of wheel-turning kings (cakravartin):
first, the military wheel-turning king;
second, the wealth wheel-turning king.
Third, regarding the Wheel-Turning Kings:
when the human lifespan is less than eighty thousand years, a Wealth-Wheel-Turning King does not appear in the world. This is because:
The merit and lifespan of this king are long and far-reaching;
because he is contrary to the conditions for longevity, he does not appear in the world.
If a Wheel-Turning King of diminished merit were to appear in the world, [the same would apply].
The reason for this is that the Tathāgata,
out of great compassion, appeared in the world so that all sentient beings might recognize suffering and impermanence, thereby becoming easily transformable.
Thus, the treatise says:
Buddhas appear in the world during the period of kalpa-decrease;
at the beginning of the kalpa, there are universal monarchs (cakravartin);
it is only when Maitreya Buddha appears that [these three occur together].
The people possess merit;
thus, two kings appear together in the world.
There are four kinds of wealth.
A golden-wheel-turning monarch has his transformative influence extend over the four continents;
a silver-wheel-turning monarch governs three continents, excluding the northern continent of Uttarakuru.
A copper-wheel-turning king rules over two continents, excluding Uttarakuru in the north and Aparagoyānī in the west;
an iron-wheel-turning king, however, is restricted solely to Jambudvīpa.
When the lifespan of the world is less than eighty thousand years, a Wheel-turning King by means of military force appears and subdues the realm through his military might.
Ruling over the whole world refers to King Aśoka and others;
the Tathāgata is the Wheel-Turning King of the Dharma (Dharmacakravartin).

Regarding the statement that a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin) appears during the period of increase (*utsarpiṇī-kalpa*), this refers specifically to the wheel-turning monarch of wealth (*dhanacakra-rāja*).
If one discusses the wheel of military power (*balacakra*), however, it applies throughout all periods of decrease (*avasarpinī-kalpa*).
The iron wheel has two hundred and fifty spokes;
the copper wheel has five hundred spokes;
the silver wheel has seven hundred and fifty spokes.
The golden wheel has a thousand spokes.
Thus, the *Ratnaketuparivarta* (Renwang jing) states:
"The King of Firm Virtue in the Seed of the Path (*Mārgajātadṛḍhaguṇa-rāja*) mounted the golden wheel and ruled over the four continents."
A king of the nature-seed lineage (prakṛti-gotra) becomes a silver-wheel-turning monarch (rājā cakravartī) who rules over three continents;
a king of the practice-seed lineage (śikṣā-gotra) becomes a copper-wheel-turning monarch who rules over two continents.
These kings attain their sovereignty through the ten wholesome paths of action.
Ruling over a single world-system as an Iron Wheel-Turning King.

This refers to the four divine virtues:
first, long life without premature death, such that none can equal it;
second, physical strength free from ailment, such that none can equal it.
Third, his countenance was upright and handsome, such that none could equal him.
Fourth, his treasuries were overflowing with jewels, such that none could equal him.
When the King traveled, he treated the people with compassion, nurturing all creatures as a father loves his children.
The people admired the king as sons look up to their father;
all their rare and precious treasures they offered to the king,
praying that he would graciously accept them and bestow upon them whatever he saw fit.
Then the king replied, "Cease, all of you!
I have my own treasures; you may use them yourselves."
The king’s realm was peaceful, prosperous, and joyful, as level as the palm of a hand.
Food and clothing were provided spontaneously without the need for seeking or labor;
its inhabitants practiced only the ten wholesome deeds and committed no unrighteous acts.
It is like the northern continent of Uttarakuru, which cannot be described in full detail.
Furthermore, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"There is the Lake Anavatapta."
It is fifty yojanas in length and breadth;
surrounding the four sides of the pond are various fruit trees,
and there stands the palace residence of the Elephant King Supratiṣṭhita.
He has eight thousand elephants as his retinue.
When a Wheel-Turning Sage King appears in the world,
even the smallest among those eight thousand elephants [is of such quality].
When it emerges, it serves as the Elephant Jewel for the Universal Monarch to ride.
Furthermore, within the great outer ocean and on the continent, there is Mount Candraprabha (Moon-Bright Mountain),
the dwelling place of the palace of the Brahman Horse-King.
He has eight thousand horses as his retinue;
when a Wheel-Turning King appears in the world,
even the smallest among those eight thousand horses [is of such quality].
When brought forth, it serves as the Horse-Jewel for the Wheel-Turning King to ride.
Furthermore, the *Lokadhātunirdeśa-sūtra* states:
"This Elephant-Jewel and Horse-Jewel, within a single day, are temporarily tamed and become capable of performing all tasks."
To test the elephant and horse, at the break of dawn when the sun first rises,
he mounts this precious elephant and other [vehicles] to travel in circuitous rounds,
traversing all the shores of the ocean until reaching the very limits of the earth.
Having completed this universal circuit,
the Wheel-Turning King returns to his original palace and partakes of a light meal.
Furthermore, the Mahāsāṃghika-lokadhātu-sūtra (Daluotan jing) states:
There are four kinds of Wheel-Turning Kings (cakravartin rāja).
First, regarding great wealth, precious treasures, fields, houses, slaves, servants, and so forth,
there is no one in the world who can equal the King.
Second, the king is most handsome and his complexion is incomparably beautiful;
there is no one in the world who can equal the king.
Third, the king is always peaceful and secure, free from illness, and likewise free from the afflictions of cold and heat.
All food and drink consumed will bring peace and security.
Fourth, the king shall always enjoy peace and longevity;
there is no one in the world like this king.
This constitutes the Cakravartin King’s possession of the four virtues and the seven treasures in accordance with the Dharma.
Furthermore, the *Satyaka-nirgrantha-sūtra* states that the Buddha said:

Great King, you should know that the Wheel-Turning Sage King further possesses seven kinds of so-called "soft jewels," whose meritorious qualities are slightly inferior to those of the previous seven jewels.
What are the seven?
First, the sword-treasure;
second, the leather-treasure.
Third, the treasure of couches;
fourth, the treasure of gardens;
fifth, the treasure of dwellings.
Sixth, the jewel of garments;
seventh, the jewels for use on foot.
Regarding the first, the sword-jewel:
Within the realm ruled by the Wheel-Turning King,
if there should be anyone who violates the king’s command,
that sword-treasure immediately flies through the air to them.
When the various minor kings see it, they immediately submit and prostrate themselves.
As for the second precious treasure, the skin-treasure:
this is the skin of the dragon king of the ocean.
Emerging from the great ocean, it was five yojanas wide and ten yojanas long;
its substance was pure and bright, shining with the brilliance of the sun.
Fire cannot scorch it;
water cannot rot it;
and even a violent wind cannot move it.
Its substance contains both warmth and coolness, capable of warding off cold and heat.
Wherever the King goes, the skin-treasure follows him;
it can accommodate a host of soldiers extending for ten *yojanas*.
It covers it entirely above,
capable of forming a separate chamber without any obstruction.
As for the third bed-jewel:
The bed used by the king is able to remain level and upright, soft and appropriately comfortable.
When the king enters dhyāna, he immediately enters the samādhi of liberation,
whereby he is able to extinguish greed, hatred, and delusion.
When the women saw the king seated upon the precious throne,
they all immediately became free from the minds of greed, hatred, and delusion.
This was the fourth treasure-grove.
Upon entering that garden, he immediately attains a concentrated mind.
When the king wishes to enjoy the pleasures of the five senses,
it is by virtue of the merit of the wholesome karma performed by the king.
All the flowers, fruits, ponds, rivers, and articles for play and enjoyment found within the various celestial realms naturally vanished and appeared before the king.
Fifth is the precious house.
The king entered that house desiring to see the sun, moon, and stars;
all manner of extraordinary treasures, curiosities, and musical instruments were heard within the house,
and he was immediately freed from sorrow, affliction, and all fatigue.
He experiences supreme bliss while sleeping.
As for the sixth treasure, that of clothing:
among all the garments possessed by the king, there are none made of the silks, fabrics, or threads found in the world.
Its patterns are unsurpassed in their breadth and length, and it is exceedingly soft;
no dust or impurities can stain it.
Upon wearing that precious robe, one is immediately freed from cold and heat, hunger and thirst, and all mental distress.
Furthermore, it cannot be harmed by water, fire, blades,
or the like. The seventh requisite of treasure consists of items such as boots.
If the king wears it,
he will not sink when crossing water,
nor will he be burned when entering fire.
Even when traveling a distance of hundreds of thousands of yojanas, he does not feel exhausted;
this is called the seventh minor treasure of the wheel-turning monarch,
which is a portion of the merit from the habitual tendencies of the ten wholesome paths of action.
They do not fully possess the ten paths of wholesome action.
Furthermore, the Madhyama Āgama states:
"When a Wheel-Turning King appears in the world..."
One should know that these seven treasures appear in the world.
Likewise, when a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha appears in the world,
one should know that there also appear in the world seven kinds of precious limbs.
What are the seven? First, the jewel of the awakening factor of mindfulness;
second, the jewel of the awakening factor of discrimination of phenomena.
3. The jewel of the awakening factor of energy;
4. The jewel of the awakening factor of joy;
5. The jewel of the awakening factor of tranquility.
Sixth is the jewel of the concentration factor of enlightenment (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga-ratna*). Seventh is the jewel of the equanimity factor of enlightenment (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga-ratna*).
Section Four: The Mūrdhaja Section. As stated in the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* (*Kṣudrakavastu*): [The Fourth Section on Mūrdhaja].
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"In the past, immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago,
there was a great king in this Jambudvīpa."
His name was Gosāla; he presided over this world,
which consisted of eighty-four thousand small kingdoms.
He had twenty thousand queens and concubines, and ten thousand ministers.
At that time, a swelling suddenly appeared on the crown of the king’s head,
shaped like a silkworm cocoon.
It was clean, pure, and transparent, and there was no pain.
Later, it became as large as a gourd;
he then split it open to look inside.
I have obtained a young boy who is exceedingly handsome;
the Great King has already passed away.
Mūrdhagata became king;
he was possessed of the seven treasures,
and food, clothing, and music provided themselves as natural delights.
After eighty-four thousand years had passed,
a yakṣa suddenly leaped forth before the palace and cried out in a loud voice:
"In the east there is a land named Pūrvavideha;
its abundance, joy, and excellence are beyond compare.
Great King, you may go there."
The king was immediately filled with joy and desired to set out.
The golden wheel turned once more, and he advanced through the air,
followed by his ministers and all seven precious jewels.
Having arrived in that land,
all the minor kings came to pay their respects and offer congratulations.
For eight thousand years, the king indulged himself in the five desires within that kingdom.
The yakṣa spoke again:
"In the western direction there is a land named Aparagoyānī;
Your Majesty may go there."
They returned as they had gone before.
After fourteen billion years had passed,
the yakṣa sang once more.
In the north there is a land named Uttarakuru.
Your Majesty may go there and return just as you went before.
After eighteen hundred million years had passed,
the yakṣa proclaimed again:
"There are the abodes of the Four Heavenly Kings, whose pleasures are immeasurable."
"The King may go and visit it.
The King, together with his ministers and the fourfold army, ascended into the air.
The gods of the Four Heavenly Kings saw them from afar and were filled with great terror.
He immediately assembled his armies and went outside to resist him,
but in the end, they could do nothing.
Māndhātṛ remained there, dwelling at ease and enjoying pleasures.
After ten billion years had passed,
he again thought within his mind that he wished to ascend to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
He then ascended into the void together with his ministers;
at that time, five hundred rishis were dwelling within the belly of Mount Sumeru.
The elephant and horses of the king dropped their dung, urine, and sweat upon the bodies of the rishis.
The various rishis asked one another,
"By what cause has this occurred?"
Among them, a wise man said to the crowd,
"I have heard that King Mūrdhaja wishes to ascend to the Heaven of the Thirty-three;
this filth must surely have been dropped by his elephant or horse."
The rishi, filled with resentment, then bound a divine incantation that caused King Mūrdhaja and his entire retinue to come to a standstill and be unable to move.
The king became aware of this as well.
He immediately made this vow:
"If I possess merit, may all these rishis come, moved by the majesty of the king.
Then, five hundred rishis all arrived at the king's side.
Supporting the divine horse, they traveled together toward the heavens.
Before they had yet arrived, they gazed afar upon the celestial city named Sudarśana.
Its color is brilliant white, lofty, prominent, and extraordinary.
This city of Sudarśana has one thousand two hundred gates;
out of fear, the devas have closed all these gates and secured them with threefold iron bolts.
The troops of Mūrdhaja advanced straight ahead without hesitation.
The king then took up his lute, blew it, drew his bow, and struck its strings;
all one thousand two hundred gates opened simultaneously.
Śakra immediately came forth to meet him;
he invited him into the palace and shared his seat with him.
The appearance of the Heavenly Lord and the human king were of one kind.
Those who first see them cannot distinguish between them;
they can only know their difference by observing the speed of their blinking.
The king enjoys the pleasures of the five senses in the heavens.
Having reached the summit of the Heaven of the Thirty-three,
he finally desired to harm Śakra alone, finding solace in his own solitude;
as soon as this evil thought arose, he immediately fell.
When he was exhausted and on the verge of death before the main hall,
people came and questioned him;
Mūrdhaja replied:
He ruled over the four continents for thirty billion years, during which it rained jewels for seven days;
yet because he remained unsatisfied even while dwelling in the two heavens, he fell into ruin.
Ānanda asked again,
"By what merit did this King Mandhātṛ plant in his past lives to obtain such a great reward?
The Buddha told him:
In the distant past, incalculable eons ago, there was a Buddha in the world named Puṣya,
who traveled through the world with his retinue to teach and transform sentient beings.
At that time, the son of a brāhmaṇa was about to marry a wife;
he held a handful of black beans in his hand, intending to scatter them over the bride,
according to the ancient domestic customs of his family.
Encountering the Buddha on the road, his heart was filled with joy;
he immediately took these beans and scattered them as an offering over the Buddha.
Four grains entered the bowl, while one remained upon the Buddha’s crown.
By virtue of these causes and conditions, one receives immeasurable merit:
four grains enter the bowl, and the king rules over the four continents;
one grain remains upon the crown of the head, whereby one experiences bliss in the two heavens.
Furthermore, the *Sūtra on the Story of King Mūrdhaja* states:
"At that time, as soon as King Mūrdhaja conceived this thought,
he fell from the seat of Śakra Devendra back down to Jambudvīpa."
When the fourfold army retreated and lost its supernormal powers,
their entire bodies were racked with pain as if they were about to die;
even the seven treasures and the rest likewise met their end.
At that time, the relatives from the five regions all gathered together.
They went to where King Mūrdhaja was and said to him:
"After the Great King’s life has ended, suffering will be all-encompassing."
At that time, King Mūrdhaja was none other than myself.
You should know that even regarding the five sensual desires, there is no satisfaction;
one is never satiated by attachment, accumulation, and the hoarding of desires.
What is called "sufficiency" is that which is attained only upon reaching the path of the noble ones; it is then sufficient.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
Not for the sake of wealth or occupation, but through awakening,
one perceives that sensual desire brings little joy and much suffering; thus the wise do not engage in it,
nor do they find delight therein even amidst the five objects of desire.
When craving is exhausted, one attains bliss;
yet these disciples of the Buddha are gripped by a surging abundance of greed. In the end, they enter hell;
though their original desire was for peace, their lives are now tormented by suffering.
All phenomena are entirely impermanent; that which is born must inevitably decay.
All that is born returns to extinction; its cessation is the supreme bliss.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda heard what the Buddha had spoken.
They joyfully received and practiced [the teaching].
Furthermore, the *Lokasthāna-sūtra* states:
"When a Wheel-turning King (cakravartin) passes away, he will certainly be reborn in the heavens."
He dwelt together with the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;
only after his life had ended and seven days had passed did the seven treasures all vanish.
Section Five: King Aśoka. As stated in the *Saṃyukta Āgama*:
At that time, the World-Honored One, having dressed in the morning and taken up his bowl, entered the city of Rājagṛha together with the bhikṣus to beg for food.
At that time, the World-Honored One, his radiant appearance illuminating everywhere like the blaze of a thousand suns,
proceeded through the town.
At that moment, there were two young boys there.
First, those of noble lineage;
second, those of secondary lineage;
they all played together in the sand.
One was named Jayā and the other was named Vijayā;
they saw the World-Honored One approaching from afar.
His body was adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man.
At that time, the youth Jayanta thought to himself,
"I shall offer him a handful of parched barley."
Fine sand fell into the World-Honored One’s alms bowl.
At that time, Viśākha joined his palms in sympathetic joy and made this aspiration:
By means of the merit of his wholesome giving, he shall become a universal monarch (cakravartin) with a parasol over the entire world;
furthermore, in this very life, he shall make offerings to the Buddha,
and ultimately attain unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
The World-Honored One manifested a smile.
At that time, Ānanda, seeing the World-Honored One smiling,
immediately joined his palms toward the Buddha and addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One,
it is not without cause or condition that you manifest a smile.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
Ānanda, you should know that there is a cause and condition for my smile now.
"One hundred years after my parinirvāṇa,
this youth shall rule over a region in the city of Pāṭaliputra as a Cakravartin king;
his clan name shall be Kauśika."
He shall be named Aśoka;
he will rule according to the True Dharma and further distribute my relics far and wide.
By constructing eighty-four thousand stūpas for the Dharma King, one shall bring immeasurable peace and happiness to sentient beings,
as stated in the verse:
"After my parinirvāṇa, such a person shall become a king."
The name of the peacock was Yù (Yuk).
Just as King Mūrdhaja reigned alone over this Jambudvīpa and was honored by the world, the Buddha told Ānanda: [it was the same].
"Take the sand offered here in this bowl and place it where the Tathāgata walks, so that they may be reborn in that place.
Ānanda received these instructions;
he immediately took the sand from the bowl and placed it at the walking path.
Ānanda, you should know that in the city of Pāṭaliputra there will be a king named Candraprabha;
that king shall have a son born to him.
His name was Bimbisāra;
he shall rule that kingdom.
He, in turn, shall have a son.
His name was Śūrasena.
At that time, there was a Brahmin woman in the kingdom of Campā who was exceedingly beautiful.
She was a joy for all to behold and was highly prized by the kingdom.
When the various physiognomists observed her physical marks, they [were struck with wonder].
He then prophesied that she would become a queen consort and would give birth to two sons:
one who shall rule over a celestial realm, and the other who shall rule over a human kingdom.
"Secondly, she shall leave the household life to study the Path and attain the traces of the Noble Ones.
When the brahmin heard what the physiognomist had said, he was filled with immeasurable joy and immediately adorned his daughter and gave her in marriage to this king.
When the king saw that his daughter was upright and possessed of virtue,
he immediately made her his queen;
the former queen and all the court ladies [were demoted].
Seeing his wife approaching, he thought to himself:
"This woman is so beautiful that she is a treasure of the kingdom;
yet the king has abandoned us, not even casting a glance our way, and has instead caused her to train in the profession of a barber."
Having mastered all these skills, she attended to the king’s hair and beard.
While she was grooming him, the king was greatly delighted and immediately asked her:
"What do you seek? the woman replied to the king,
"I only wish that Your Majesty would hold me dear in your heart."
Thus he made this proclamation three times. Then the king said,
"I am a Kṣatriya, an anointed king."
"You are a barber; how can I love you?
The woman said to the king:
"I was not born of a low caste;
I am the daughter of a noble Brahmin.
A physiognomist said to my father:"
"This girl ought to be married to the king;
that is why she has come here.
The king said:
"If that is so, who has caused you to practice such a base craft?
The woman replied to the king,
"It was the former queen and her attendants who made me learn this."
The king immediately issued a decree, saying,
"From this day forward, do not again engage in such lowly occupations.
He then established her as his first consort.
The king constantly took pleasure with her,
and she subsequently conceived.
When the months were complete, she gave birth to a son.
At the time of his birth, he was peaceful and his mother was free from anxiety or distress;
after seven days had passed, they established his name as Aśoka.
Furthermore, another son was born.
He was named Viśoka. As for his being "without sorrow," it was because his body was coarse and rough;

as a result of his past giving of sand, he obtained a corresponding fruit. His father the king did not hold him in high regard or affectionately embrace him, as he was not what the king cherished in his heart.
Furthermore, the king, wishing to test his two sons,
called the brahmin Piṅgala-Āśīva and said,
"Preceptor, observe my sons."
"After my passing, who shall become king?
The brahmin replied,
"Take these sons out of the city to the golden palace gardens."
One should observe its signs there;
even as he went out toward that garden,
King Aśoka’s mother said:
"Having heard that the King has gone out toward the Golden Palace Garden to observe which of the princes shall become king,
why do you not go now? Aśoka replied:
Since the King neither remembers me nor takes pleasure in seeing me,
his mother spoke again, saying:
"Simply go to that place.
Aśoka then addressed his mother again,
saying, "I shall go now."
"I pray that my mother will bring me food.
His mother said, "So be it."
As he was leaving the city gate,
he encountered a high minister named Anurādha.
The minister asked Aśoka,
"Where has the prince gone now? Aśoka replied:
"I have heard that the Great King has gone out from the golden palace garden to observe the princes and consider who shall become king after my passing;
I shall now go to him.
The King first commanded his ministers.
"If Aśoka comes, he should be made to ride an old, sluggish elephant,
and moreover, he should have an old man as his attendant."
Then Aśoka, riding that old elephant, arrived at the park pavilion and sat upon the ground among the princes.
Thereupon, each of the princes served him food.
Queen Asoka’s mother sent curd-rice in a clay vessel to Asoka.
In this manner, each of the princes ate their respective meals.
Then, the father king asked his preceptor:
In this matter, who possesses the marks of a king to succeed to my throne?
At that time, the physiognomist examined the princes and saw that Aśoka possessed all the royal marks and was destined to succeed to the throne.
"If I speak, the King will become sorrowful and unhappy. He then said,
"I shall now give a general summary."
The king replied,
"As the teacher has instructed.
The teacher said:
In this regard, if there is one who rides upon a fine vehicle,
that person shall become a king.
At that time, the princes heard what he said.
Each thought to himself,
"I am riding in a fine vehicle. Then Aśoka said:
"I rode an old elephant and thus attained the status of king.
He further said,
"In this assembly, there is one who occupies the foremost seat."
"He shall become king.
Then the princes said to one another,
"I shall sit upon the foremost seat!"
Aśoka said, "I am now sitting upon the earth;
this is my superior seat."
"I shall become king. He further said, "Among these,
the one who eats from the superior vessel..."
"This one shall become king. ...
Up to this point, Aśoka thought to himself:
"I possess superior vehicles, superior thrones, and superior food."
When the king had finished observing his son’s marks, he immediately returned to the palace.
At that time, Aśoka’s mother asked Aśoka,
“Who shall become the king?”
"Brahmin, whom did you prophesy? Aśoka replied,
"The one who is the highest vehicle,
the highest seat, the highest vessel, and the highest food shall become king."
The prince saw for himself that he was to become king;
the old elephant served as his mount,
and the earth as his throne.
He served food from an unadorned vessel:
rice mixed with husks and curd.
At that time, the brahmin knew that Aśoka was destined to become king.
He frequently paid his respects to his mother,
who in turn provided generous offerings to the brahmin.
If the son becomes the teacher of a king, he shall attain all that is good and auspicious.
He provided offerings for as long as he lived.
At that time, Takṣaśilā, a border kingdom of King Bindusāra, rebelled.
Then the king spoke to Aśoka.
"You shall lead the fourfold army to invade that kingdom.
When the prince was about to depart, he did not provide them with armor or weapons at all.
Then his attendants said to the prince:
"Now we are going to attack that country.
Since they have no military weapons, how can it be subdued? Aśoka said:
"If I were to become a king as a result of the ripening of my roots of goodness, let weapons and armor appear spontaneously.
As soon as he spoke these words, [they appeared].
Upon hearing the sound, the ground opened and an army emerged from it;
he then led these four divisions of troops to invade that kingdom.
At that time, the people of those various kingdoms heard that Aśoka was coming.
They immediately leveled the roads and adorned the city walls.
Carrying jars of auspicious water and various offerings, they went out to welcome the prince,
saying these words:
"We do not rebel against the Great King nor against Prince Aśoka;
however, various ministers are hostile toward us,
and for this reason we have gone contrary to Your Majesty’s holy transformation."
He immediately provided various offerings and invited the prince to enter the city.
Having pacified this kingdom,
he again dispatched an envoy to the kingdom of Kāśa.
At that time, those two great strongmen were leveling the roads for the king.
The devas issued a proclamation:
"Aśoka shall rule this world."
"Do not harbor rebellious thoughts.
The king of that country then submitted;
in this manner, he brought the whole world under his control, reaching as far as the shores of the ocean.
At that time, the father king fell gravely ill.
The king said to his ministers,
"I now wish to establish Śūrasena as king."
They sent Aśoka to that kingdom.
At that time, the ministers wished to have Aśoka installed as king;
they therefore smeared yellow substances upon Aśoka’s body, face, hands, and feet.
The ministers addressed the king, saying,
"Prince Aśoka has now fallen gravely ill. Thereupon,
the ministers adorned Aśoka and brought him to the king's presence.
"For now, let us install this son as king;
later, we shall gradually install Śūrasena as king.
When the king heard these words, he was deeply displeased.
He remained silent and did not respond.
At that time, Aśoka thought to himself and spoke aloud:
"I shall rightfully obtain the throne."
The various devas spontaneously arrived and poured water over my crown, binding a plain silk cloth around my head.
When the king saw this phenomenon, he was overcome with extreme grief and distress,
and immediately passed away.
After King Aśoka had performed the funeral rites for his father according to the prescribed dharma,
he immediately appointed Anuruddha as his chief minister.
At that time, there was Prince Susīma.
Hearing that his father had passed away and that Aśoka had now been established as king,
he felt unbearable resentment;
he immediately assembled his various troops and came to wage war against Aśoka.
Among the four gates of King Aśoka’s palace,
two strongmen were stationed at two gates,
and a high minister was stationed at the third gate.
He himself guarded the eastern gate.
At that time, Āniruddha fashioned a great mechanical wooden elephant and also created an image of King Aśoka.
He immediately mounted an elephant and stationed it outside the eastern gate;
furthermore, he prepared a smokeless fire pit and covered it with objects.
When Śūrasena arrived, [he saw this].
The minister Anuruddha said to Prince Susīma,
who desired to become king:
"Aśoka is at the eastern gate."
"You may go and attack him;
if you can capture this king, you will naturally become king yourself.
At that time, the prince immediately proceeded toward the eastern gate.
He immediately fell into a fire pit and died on the spot.
There was a great strongman named Bhadrasena.
Having heard this, Śramaṇa died without further attachment to the world;
together with countless followers, he went forth from home within the Buddha-dharma to study the Path and attained arhatship.
At that time, the ministers said, "We shall jointly establish Aśoka as king."
Consequently, they treated the king with contempt and failed to observe the rites due to a sovereign and his ministers.
The king, perceiving that his ministers were likewise showing him disrespect, spoke to them, saying:
"You all may cut down the trees bearing flowers and fruit and plant thorny brambles instead.
The ministers replied,
"We have never seen or heard of anyone removing trees that bear flowers and fruit to plant thorny trees in their place."
He should instead cut down the trees with thorns and brambles and plant those bearing fruit;
yet even after being commanded to cut them down two or three times,
they still did not comply.
At that time, the king was enraged with his ministers and immediately took up a sharp sword and slew five hundred of them.
On another occasion, the king, accompanied by his retinue of court ladies, went out to play in a park.
He saw a single *aśoka* tree in full bloom;
seeing that this flowering tree shared the same name as his own,
the king felt great joy in his heart.
The king’s physical form was ugly and his skin coarse and rough;
the ladies of the court did not love the king,
and because they detested him, they used their hands to break off the flowers of the *aśoka* tree.
The king woke from his sleep and saw the flowers of the *aśoka* tree strewn in disarray upon the ground; filled with rage, he bound the female attendants and burned them to death.

Section Two: On Royal Virtue. Second, according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*:
"Great King, you should know that there are briefly ten kinds of royal merit.
If a king accomplishes such merit as these,"
Although they possess no great treasuries, no great ministers, and no great armies,
they are worthy of being taken as objects of refuge and veneration. What are these ten?
First, one's lineage is noble and eminent;
second, one attains great sovereignty;
third, one's nature is not violent or malevolent.
Fourth, the arousal of indignation is slight;
fifth, the bestowal of grace is intense;
sixth, one receives the true mantra.
Seventh is the volition that reflects upon what is to be done in accordance with the proper rules of conduct;
eighth is the longing for wholesome dharmas;
ninth is the volition that understands distinctions and knows what is to be done.

There are ten ways of not being self-indulgent and not practicing heedlessness, which are the opposites of the aforementioned ten [faults]. Although one may possess great treasuries, great ministers, and a great army, they cannot be relied upon for refuge; Your Majesty, you should know this.
The king’s skillful means are briefly of five kinds. What are these five?
First, he skillfully examines and receives his ministers.
Second, he is able to perform acts of grace and sublime deeds at the proper time.
Third, he is free from negligence and focuses exclusively on state affairs.
Fourth, he is free from negligence and skillfully guards the treasury and granaries.

The five [factors] of non-negligence consist in the exclusive cultivation of the practice of Dharma; conversely, if one reverses these five practices, they become the five gates of decline, whereby one falls away from the present life and loses the benefits of the Dharma. Great King, you should know this.
Briefly, there are five kinds of desirable qualities.
What are these five? First, being respected and loved by the world.
Second, mastery and supremacy;
third, the ability to crush enemies;
fourth, the skillful cultivation of the body.
Fifth, one is able to go to the happy realms.
Furthermore, there are five kinds that can lead to what is desirable. What are these five?
First, nourishing the world with kindness;
second, being fully endowed with heroic valor;
third, possessing skillful means and expedients.
Fourth, the sphere of right reception (*samyak-samādāna*).

Fifth, the diligent cultivation of the practice of Dharma (*dharmapratipatti*), which is the opposite of the aforementioned five types and is thus called "unpleasant. Furthermore, kings possess three kinds of perfection:
first, the perfection of karmic fruition (*vipākasaṃpad*); [and so forth].
Second, the perfection of human effort;
third, the perfection of merit.
This refers to those kings who are born into families of wealth and nobility.

If kings uphold the True Dharma, they are called Dharma Kings;

Planting roots of merit, observing the fast, and firmly upholding the prohibitive precepts—

Furthermore, as for being "Perfected in Retribution":
The fulfillment of human effort consists of enjoying the karmic fruit of pure deeds from previous lives,
as well as enjoying the desirable fruits of the present life.
One whose merit is perfected will likewise,
in the future, enjoy the full fruition of the results of pure karma.
If there is a king who lacks three things, [he shall not do so].
Such a person is called an inferior individual (*hīnapuruṣa*).
If, however, there is perfection of the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*),
or perfection of human effort (*puruṣakāra*), or both, [then one is a superior individual].
One who possesses three [of these] is called a person of middle capacity; one who possesses all three is called a person of superior capacity.
Furthermore, the Madhyama Āgama states:

There are five protocols for governing the great earth: first, the sword;

If, however, one is neither loyal nor trustworthy, possesses no skills or talents, and lacks wisdom,

3. Section on the King’s Transgressions, Part Three. As stated in the *Yixiangfa jueyi jing* (Sutra on Resolving Doubts Concerning the Semblance Dharma):
"Furthermore, no layperson, regardless of their status as noble or humble, shall beat or strike the servants or animals belonging to the Triple Gem."
Furthermore, receiving prostrations from slaves belonging to the Three Jewels will result in calamity and guilt for all involved.

If one destroys a stupa or monastery, or takes the property of the Buddha;
or if one instructs others to do so or rejoices in their doing;
or if there is a śramaṇa wearing dyed robes [and one harms them].
There may be those who observe the precepts or violate them;
they may be imprisoned, beaten, bound,
or compelled to return to lay life.
Or they may take his life.
If one commits such a fundamental grave offense,
one will certainly fall into hell and undergo the sufferings of the Avīci Hell.
Because this unwholesome conduct was practiced within the king’s realm,
the various sages and holy men departed from the country,
and the powerful deities no longer protected it.
Ministers vied with one another and strife arose in all four directions.
Floods and droughts were不调 (irregular), winds and rains missed their seasons,
the people suffered from hunger, and bandits ran rampant.

people did not realize that they acted as the cause themselves, yet they resented the various heavens.
Furthermore, the *Ratnarāśi Sūtra* (Renwang jing) states:
The king and his ministers, relying on their own noble status, have destroyed my Dharma.
They have established restrictive laws to govern my disciples,
forbidding them from leaving the household life and forbidding the creation of Buddha images.

He mandated that bhikṣus stand while laypeople (avadātavasana) sit on high seats.
Furthermore, the king and crown prince arbitrarily enacted such laws and regulations.
Not relying on the Buddhist teachings regarding the causes and conditions for schism in the Saṃgha,
the Director of Music takes charge of the monks and the Registrar of the Saṃgha maintains them with diligent care.
The Buddha-dharma will not endure for long.
Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"Great King, you should know."
A king has ten faults. What are these ten?
First, his lineage is not noble.
Second, lack of self-mastery;
third, an inherently violent and cruel nature;
fourth, the intense outburst of fierce anger.
Fifth, meager gratitude for favors received;
sixth, accepting the words of the wicked and sycophants;
seventh, acting without reflection and failing to conform to established protocols.
Eighth, disregarding wholesome dharmas.
Ninth, lacking discernment and forgetting the kindness one has received.
Eleventh, being self-indulgent and exclusively practicing negligence.
Furthermore, the *Śatadharma-upama-sūtra* states:
Once there was a man who spoke of the king’s transgressions and faults.
He spoke these words:
"The king is exceedingly tyrannical and governs without principle.

The King believed the sycophants and seized a virtuous minister,

The king’s heart was filled with regret, and he requested a thousand *liang* of flesh to mend his spine.
During the night, he groaned and cried out in great agony.
Hearing his voice, the king asked:
"Why are you distressed?

is your desire still not satisfied?"
"Why do you distress those beside you? he asked.
They replied, "Great King, it is like cutting off a son's head;
though one were to obtain a thousand heads, one cannot avoid the death of the son."
Even if one obtains ten times more meat, one cannot escape suffering;
so it is with the foolish,
who do not fear future lives and, out of greed and corruption, crave present pleasure.
He oppresses sentient beings and coerces the common people,
thereby acquiring great wealth;
he hopes that by doing so he may extinguish his sins and obtain meritorious rewards.
For example, it is like that king who cuts a person’s spine and takes their flesh, hoping to fill the void with the remaining flesh so as to prevent pain;
such a thing is impossible.
Furthermore, the *Saṃyukta-avadāna-sūtra* says:
In the past, there was a king who delighted in eating human flesh.

Taking this as their constant practice,
the ministers all became aware of it and together expelled him, casting him beyond the borders.
He further selected a virtuous and worthy man to serve as king;
thus, after thirteen years had passed since the reign of the man-eating king, two wings grew upon his body.
Flying about and devouring people regardless of distance,

The king then flew through the air to seize them;
having captured four hundred and ninety-nine people,

At that time, there was a king who,
