The king immediately granted his permission.
He intended to bestow gold and silver upon returning to the palace.
At that time, the king entered the pond, wishing to bathe.
That man-eater flew through the air,
seized the king, and carried him away back to the mountains.
When the King saw the Man-eater King,
he was neither afraid nor terrified, his countenance remaining as it had been before.
The Man-eater King said:
"I originally feared that I must offer human sacrifices to the gods.
I have already obtained four hundred and ninety-nine people;
now that I have obtained you, one person, the required number is complete. I shall kill you to sacrifice to the gods."
"Why do you not fear? The king replied,
"Human birth is subject to death."
All things that come into being must perish;
all unions must end in separation;
all oppositions result in division.
"Why need you grieve?
When I departed from the palace at dawn, I encountered a practitioner on the road who recited a verse for me."
"I have already consented to give the gift, but it has not yet been delivered;
this is my regret. Now, may Your Majesty’s great compassion grant me the grace of an extension."
"Once the almsgiving is concluded, I shall return; I dare not dare violate my promise.
He was granted permission to depart, and [the king] addressed him, saying:
"I grant you a period of seven days;
if you do not return, it will be no difficulty for me to go and fetch you myself.
The king then returned to his palace.
Throughout the capital, both within and without, there was no one who did not rejoice.
They immediately opened the treasuries to bestow gifts upon those far and near,
and they enthroned the Prince as King.
The common people took their leave with earnest farewells and departed.
King Manuṣyabhakṣa encountered them as they were coming and thought to himself:
"Could this be none other than that man?
Having returned to life after death, he has come back here.
He then asked:
Body and life are what people of this world cherish and love most dearly;
yet you, sir, have renounced life, which is exceedingly difficult to do.
I wonder not what your aspirations and pursuits are.
"I pray you, explain its meaning.
The king replied,
"I shall give it this very day."
With utmost sincerity, he made this vow: "May I attain the state of an *anuttara-samyak-saṃbuddha* and may I deliver all beings throughout the ten directions.
The king then asked:
Regarding the meaning of seeking Buddhahood,
what are its practices?
The king then explained for him at length the five precepts, the ten wholesome actions, the four immeasurables, and the six perfections.
His mind opened wide and clear;
he received the five precepts and became a lay follower (*upāsaka*).
Consequently, he released four hundred and ninety-nine people, each allowing them to return to their own countries.
The various kings went together to that country, moved by his sincere oath and having their lives saved;
none of them wished to return to their own lands,
but instead remained and settled in this country.
For each of these kings, a premier residence was established,
exquisitely carved and adorned with intricate ornamentation, magnificent and orderly.
Their food, drink, clothing, and vehicles were no different from those of the king.
People from the four quarters came and asked,
"Why is there this? It is like the palace and residence of a king."
Throughout the entire kingdom,
the people replied,
"These are all the dwellings of various kings."
His fame spread far and wide;
from that time forth, it was called the City of Rājagṛha (the King’s Abode).
After the Buddha had attained the Way, he himself recounted its origins and details.
The king who established the Dharma was my own self;
the man-eating king was Aṅgulimāla.
Returning to Rājagṛha to preach the Dharma, he brought immeasurable beings to liberation.
All of them were people who, in their past lives, had established the causal conditions for kingship.
Section Four: The Kingly Enterprise. As stated in the *Rājanirdeśa-sūtra*:
When the Buddha was in the world...
There was a king named Udayana who, while traveling through his realm,
passed by the place where the Buddha was.
He paid homage to the Buddha, took a seat, and sat down.
The Buddha told the king:
"A king should govern by means of the True Dharma without losing proper measure;
he should always nurture the people with a heart of compassion."
That one is able to attain the governance of a kingdom as a sovereign is entirely due to the performance of wholesome deeds in past lives.
In administering civil affairs, one must not be partial or unjust.
The various officials, high ministers, and subordinate functionaries, down to the common people, all voiced grievances.
Because the King’s governance was unjust, all within the realm were indignant;
when his life ended, his spirit entered the Tai Shan Hell.
Later, although he may regret it, it will be impossible to remedy.
When a king governs a state,
he must always maintain moderation in his administration.
The subjects and citizens sighed in admiration of his virtue, and the hearts of all within the four seas turned toward him.
Devas, nāgas, and spirits alike heard of the King’s goodness;
having died to ascend to heaven, he would have no regrets thereafter.
May Your Majesty not indulge in lewdness and dissipation to bring about your own ruin;
may you not, out of a wrathful mind, commit acts of cruelty or destruction.
You should instead accept the loyal and upright admonitions of your ministers.
When speaking with others, one should always be broad-minded and detailed;
there should be no scorching words, but only discourse on filial piety,
obedience, and the compassionate nurturing of one's two parents.
One should serve śramaṇas of lofty conduct and pure virtue;
upon seeing any elderly person, one should respect them;
and whatever wealth and treasures one possesses, one should share in joy with the common people.
One should bestow kindness upon the people with a virtuous mind.
Do not harm the lives of the people with slanderous words.
As the law of a king, one should proclaim the teachings of the sages and instruct the people in doing good.
"Only by maintaining a single mind and keeping the Three Honored Ones in heart can a king be such as this;
thus do all the sages praise him."
Devas, nāgas, and spirits will protect that land;
those born there will possess honor and fame, and upon death will ascend to heaven.
Worldly rank and position are like illusions and dreams, incapable of being maintained for long.
When a person is about to die, people gather around them both inside and outside the house; they beat their breasts and cry out to Heaven, all saying, "Alas! What can be done?
as tears flow down in profusion.
Alas, how painful!
The divine spirit has departed alone, abandoning me.
Among those who hear this, there are none whose hearts are not grieved.
Those who beheld him could not help but feel compassion.
He was carried out of the city and abandoned in the wilderness,
where flying birds and running beasts tore at and devoured him.
Worms within the body devour its own flesh;
scorched by the sun and buffeted by the wind, the bones become completely parched.
In former times, one was honored, illustrious, and noble, with a presence as vast and resonant as the rolling of thunder.
It is just as with Your Majesty:
now it has suddenly vanished and can no longer be seen.
This is a clear proof of impermanence.
If it was thus even in antiquity,
how much more so today? Your Majesty,
reflect upon this deeply and do not harbor thoughts of lustful excess.
Do not accept sycophantic words.
When witnesses have committed offenses, one should accept loyal admonitions and govern them with moderation.
One should fear the agony of being punished and tortured in hell.
All sentient beings crave life;
one must not kill them.
When the Buddha had finished preaching the sutra,
the king’s mind was immediately liberated,
and he wished to become a disciple.
He immediately received the five precepts,
prostrated with his head to the ground,
and paid homage to the Buddha.
Furthermore, the *Mādavya-rāja-sūtra* states:
During the time when the Buddha was in the world,
there was a king named Mādavya.
At that time, the king was about to mobilize his army for a military expedition.
There was a bhikṣu who had already attained the path of arhatship;
he arrived in the kingdom to beg for alms.
He was also included in the records.
As he was about to arrive at the gate of the royal palace,
the king had a stable for his horses.
He ordered the bhikṣu to tend to the king’s horses for seven days of strenuous labor. Later,
the king personally went to inspect the military formations.
When the bhikṣu saw the king, he immediately rose up lightly before him and flew into the air, manifesting his majestic spiritual power. The king was struck with fear;
he prostrated himself, knocking his head to the ground, and repented of his transgressions.
"I am truly foolish and unable to distinguish between the true and the false.
I have inquired throughout the kingdom:
who commanded this divine being to tend these horses?"
"Now we shall execute him.
The bhikṣu said to the king,
"This is not the fault of the king or the people of the country."
Since my past lives, I have always practiced the Way by constantly making offerings to my teachers.
On one occasion, I prepared a meal for my teacher,
and the teacher said to me:
"Furthermore, you must first wash your hands before you may eat with me.
The fool thought to himself,
"The Master does not even keep official horses."
"Why did you not first wash your hands?
The teacher then said to me,
"You now think this matter is trivial."
"What will happen later?
When I heard these words, I became sorrowful.
The Master, perceiving his intention, thought to himself:
"I shall enter parinirvāṇa.
Why cause others distress?
Thereupon, during the third watch of that very night, he entered parinirvāṇa.
Since time immemorial, each has undergone birth and death;
now, for this reason, they must suffer the retribution of their past karma.
They shall tend horses for seven days.
Indeed, every act of good or evil is immediately followed by retribution or blessing,
just as a shadow follows a form.
Upon hearing this, the king took refuge in the Triple Gem, seeking protection from his transgressions and merits.
Having received the five precepts and become an upāsaka,
the Buddha then preached the Dharma for the king and the people, and they attained the stage of srotāpanna.
Furthermore, the *Dharmapada-avadāna-sūtra* states:
In the past, there was a king who governed according to the True Dharma, and the people admired his transformation. Yet,
because he had no crown prince, he was filled with sorrow and anxiety.
When the Buddha came into the kingdom,
she respectfully received the five precepts and honored him with unwearied devotion.
There was an attendant, eleven years of age, who constantly served as the king's messenger;
he was loyal and faithful, observed the Dharma, and did not consider his service a burden.
He eventually contracted a grave illness and passed away;
his spirit returned to become the king's son.
When he reached the age of fifteen, he...
He was established as the crown prince.
Upon the death of his father, the king, he succeeded him;
however, being arrogant and self-indulgent, he neglected the affairs of state.
The ministers and officials were dismissed from their posts and the people suffered from their oppression.
The Buddha, knowing that their conduct was inconsistent with fundamental consciousness,
led his disciples and traveled to that kingdom.
The Buddha said to the king,
"Do you now know from where you originally came?
The king replied:
Foolish and ignorant, he did not understand nor know his previous lives.
The Buddha said to the Great King:
"Originally, one becomes a king by means of five matters."
What are the five? First, by practicing generosity, one becomes a king;
the myriad people offer palaces, pavilions, and resources to him in infinite abundance.
Second, he shall establish temples and shrines to provide offerings for the Three Honored Ones, including beds, couches, curtains, and canopies;
by means of this, he shall rule the kingdom from the throne in the main hall as king.
Third, he shall personally pay homage to the Three Honored Ones and all those of venerable virtue.
By virtue of this, he becomes a king;
among all the myriad people, there are none who do not pay him homage.
Fourth, he practices patience: his body and speech are free from the four [unwholesome acts], and his mind harbors no evil.
He serves as king because all who see him are without fail filled with joy.
Fifth, he studies and constantly seeks wisdom.
By means of these, he becomes a king;
whatever state affairs he decides and adjudicates, there are none that are not carried out.
These five matters ensure that he shall be a king for generation after generation.
In a previous life, this king was an attendant to a great king;
he served the Buddha with faith and served the Dharma with love.
Serve the Sangha with reverence;
serve one's parents with filial piety;
serve the sovereign with loyalty.
He constantly practiced single-minded diligence and generosity,
toiling his body and exhausting his flesh without ever becoming weary;
this merit followed him and enabled him to become a prince.
Purakṛt was the younger brother of the king.
Now that he has attained wealth and status, he has instead become indolent.
As a king, one ought to practice five duties.
What are the five? First, governing the myriad people without any injustice or excess.
Second, nourishing and supporting the generals and soldiers by providing them with provisions according to the season.
Third, one should mindfully cultivate one's fundamental deeds so that merit and virtue are never interrupted.
Fourth, one should trust the loyal and upright admonitions of faithful ministers,
and not accept slanderous words to the detriment of the upright.
Fifth, one should moderate desire and greed for pleasure, keeping the mind free from negligence.
Practicing these five matters will cause one's fame to spread across the four seas and blessings and prosperity to come naturally.
If these five matters are abandoned, the many essential principles will not be upheld.
When the people are impoverished, they contemplate rebellion;
when the scholars are exhausted, their influence cannot be exerted;
and when there is no merit, the spirits and deities do not provide assistance.
If one acts solely according to one's own will, one loses the Great Principle.
If loyal ministers do not dare to offer admonition, their minds become dissolute and unrestrained.
If the ruler of the state does not attend to the affairs of the people, resentment will abound.
"If it be so, one loses one's reputation in this life and shall have no merit hereafter.
Thereupon the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"One who acts as a leader in the world Cultivates rectitude and avoids crookedness."
With a mind tamed, he surpasses all evils; thus he is a Dharma King.
Seeing correctly, he is able to cultivate wisdom; being benevolent and loving, he delights in benefiting others.
Having benefited them with impartiality, the multitude thus attaches themselves to him with affection.
When the Buddha had spoken these words,
the king was filled with great joy;
he prostrated himself with his five limbs to repent and offer his apologies.
The Buddha heard the Dharma and attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
Furthermore, the *Bimbiṣāra-rāja-sūtra* (or *Udāyana-rāja-sūtra*) states:
"In the past, there was a son of a prime minister named Bimbasāra Arhat."
For King Udayana, he spoke this verse: "The afflictions of birth,
old age, sickness, and death— within these, you have not yet attained liberation."
The poisoned arrows of ignorance and craving have not yet been extracted;
O Lord of Men, how can you conceive thoughts of pleasure and attachment,
like an elephant dwelling in a forest while great fires break out on all four sides?
Abiding in this place of urgent distress, how could there be any joy?
Great King, you should know that positions of honor and rank are but momentary;
the wise observe this deeply and should not be attached to such things.
Yet you give rise to thoughts of rarity; why do you misinterpret this and remain unliberated from the womb of birth and death?
While the thieves of desire plunder the sense faculties, you recklessly give rise to thoughts of fearlessness. You recklessly give rise to thoughts of fearlessness.
Impermanent and not solid, like a plantain tree, a bubble on water,
or a dispersing cloud; the exalted and sovereign position of a heavenly king is likewise precarious and fragile— thus should the Lord of Men understand.
Greed for gain rushes with extreme speed, like water pouring down a deep valley;
craving is exceedingly swift and light, tossing and turning like a dangling rope.
When the foolish are stained by desire, they do not realize that they are being led to their downfall.
The Venerable One said,
"Great King,
I shall now provide a brief analogy for Your Majesty."
"O King, listen with a sincere mind.
In the past, there was a man traveling on a desolate road who encountered a great, wicked elephant and was pursued by it."
Driven by frantic fear, he fled in haste, finding no one to rely upon.
Seeing a dilapidated well, he immediately sought out the roots of a tree and entered the well to hide.
Above him, a black and a white mouse were gnawing at the tree root in turn.
On the four sides of this well are four venomous snakes wishing to bite that person;
beneath the well are three great poisonous dragons.
[The person] is terrified of the four snakes on the sides.
Below, he feared the venomous dragon;
the tree upon which he clung shook,
and five drops of honey from the tree fell into his mouth.
At that time, he shook the tree, knocking down the honeycomb;
the swarms of bees flew out in disorder and stung him.
A wild fire broke out and came to burn the tree as well.
Great King, you should know that the suffering and affliction of that person are beyond measure;
that person obtains very little flavor, while their miseries are exceedingly many.
That which they savor is like the water in a cow’s footprint;
their suffering and affliction are like the great ocean,
while their delusion is as minute as a mustard seed.
Mount Sumeru is like a glowworm in comparison to its taste, and as bitter as the sun and moon;
it is like comparing the holes in a lotus root to the vast void of space.
"It is just like comparing a mosquito to a garuḍa;
such is the difference between the bitterness of suffering and its magnitude," the Venerable One said.
"Great King."
The wilderness is a metaphor for birth and death;
that man is a metaphor for an ordinary person;
and the elephant is a metaphor for impermanence.
The well in the pit is a metaphor for the human body;
the tree roots are a metaphor for human life;
and the white and black rats are metaphors for day and night.
The gnawing at the tree root is a metaphor for the moment-to-moment cessation of thoughts;
the four venomous snakes are metaphors for the four great elements;
and the honey is a metaphor for the five sensual desires.
The swarm of bees is a metaphor for evil discursive thoughts (*vitarka-vicāra*); being burned by a wild fire is a metaphor for old age;
and the three venomous dragons below are a metaphor for death and falling into the three evil destinies.
Therefore, you should know that the flavor of desire is extremely slight while its suffering and afflictions are exceedingly many;
birth, old age, sickness, and death exercise their power over all people.
The people of the world suffer physical and mental exhaustion and have no place of refuge.
Harassed by manifold sufferings, they pass away as swiftly as lightning;
this is a cause for sorrow and one should not be attached to it.
5. Section on the King’s Merit (Rājan-puṇya). Fifth. As stated in the *Sūtra of Miscellaneous Parables of Old*:
Once, there was a king who returned from hunting.
Passing by a monastery, he circumambulated the stupa and paid homage to the śramaṇas.
The ministers all laughed at him.
When the king realized this, he asked his ministers,
"If there were gold in a boiling cauldron, could one take it with the hand?"
He replied,
"It cannot be obtained.
The king said:
"If you were to pour cold water into it, would it be possible to retrieve [the object]?
The minister replied to the king,
"It would be possible."
The king said,
"I perform the duties of a king;
my hunting excursions are like boiling water."
To burn incense, light lamps, circumambulate stupas,
and pay homage to the Sangha is like pouring cold water into boiling soup. Indeed,
a king who performs both virtuous and non-virtuous deeds [will experience their respective fruits].
"Why is it that there is only evil and no goodness?
Furthermore, the *Kāśyapa-sūtra* states:
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
In the past, incalculable asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Subhūṣita.
At that time, there was a wheel-turning monarch named Nimi.
Ruling the four continents as a sovereign who governs according to the Dharma,
the Great King then saw two spontaneously born youths who had already renounced the household life;
he immediately appointed his crown prince to succeed him on the throne.
The king, together with his nine hundred and ninety-nine sons,
eighty-four thousand consorts,
five thousand ministers, and all the people.
With pure faith, they all went forth together into homelessness.
At that time, seven days after the prince had ascended the throne,
he reflected within himself:
"I shall never abandon the mind of omniscience (sarvajñā-citta).
Of what use is royal sovereignty?
Having formed this thought, he resolved to leave the household life and go forth.
On the fifteenth day, while traveling through the four continents,
he spoke this verse:
"My father and all my kinsmen have already gone forth into the homeless life."
Countless billions of sentient beings have likewise left the home life for the sake of the Dharma;
I too now delight in leaving the home life. I take no pleasure in dwelling among the five desires, but seek the path of the Buddha with a single mind, wishing to go to the presence of the Teacher.
If you have resolved to leave the home life and depart from the fires of all desires,
you should quickly follow me; for it is extremely difficult to escape from hardships,
and one who has not given rise to the mind of renunciation will not remain far from the fires of desire.
"Finding peace while living at home, Kāśyapa, dwell securely in the true Dharma.
At that time, as the youth spoke this verse, [the earth shook].
Among the four continents, there was not a single sentient being who took pleasure in the household life;
they all resolved their minds and vowed to seek renunciation.
Once they had renounced the world, there was no need for them to engage in cultivation or planting.
In that land, non-glutinous rice grows spontaneously;
all trees produce garments spontaneously;
and all the devas serve as attendants and messengers.
All sentient beings shall attain the fruits of the Path.
Section Six: The Royal Capital. As stated in the *Dvādaśavyākaraṇa-sūtra* (Twelve-Part Scripture):
"As for King Prasenajit..."

The kingdom of Śrāvastī;

four thousand five hundred species of birds,

eight thousand species of grasses,

Furthermore, the Madhyama Āgama states:
In meditation, sound is a thorn;
the World-Honored One has also said that sound is a thorn. Why is this so?
I have indeed spoken thus: for one who practices dhyāna, there is a thorn;
for one who maintains the precepts, breaking the precepts is the thorn;
for one who guards the sense faculties, adorning the body is the thorn.
For one who cultivates the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), the perception of purity is a thorn;
for one who cultivates loving-kindness (*maitrī-citta*), ill-will is a thorn;
for one who has renounced fermented liquor, drinking alcohol is a thorn.
For one who practices the holy life, the sight of female form is a thorn;
for one who has entered the first dhyāna, sound is a thorn;
for one who has entered the second dhyāna, applied and sustained thought (vitarka-vicāra) are thorns.
For one who enters the third dhyāna, joy is the thorn;
for one who enters the fourth dhyāna, inhalation and exhalation are the thorn;
for one who enters the sphere of infinite space, the perception of form is the thorn.
For one entering the sphere of consciousness, the perception of the sphere of infinite space is a thorn;
for one entering the sphere of nothingness, the perception of the sphere of consciousness is a thorn;
for one entering the sphere of non-perception, the perception of the sphere of nothingness is a thorn.
For one who enters the meditative attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-samāpatti*), perception and feeling are considered thorns.
Furthermore, there are three other thorns:
the thorn of desire, the thorn of ill-will, and the thorn of delusion.
These three thorns have been abandoned and fully understood by the Arhat whose taints are exhausted;
their roots have been uprooted, they are extinguished and will not arise again.
This is the Arhat who is "thornless"; one who removes these thorns is called "one who accepts admonition."

Investigation (Catvāriṃśattrayottaraśatatamaḥ paricchedaḥ) This chapter consists of four sections: the Section on Stating the Intent, the Section on Investigating Anger, the Section on Investigating Transgressions, and the Section on Investigating Training. 1. Section on Stating the Intent (Prathamam abhiprāyaparicchedam) First, as for the sages who benefit sentient beings, they investigate objects and contemplate the mind.
One regulates consciousness and emotion at the place of the Treasure, and mobilizes the provisional and the real within the realm of delusion and sincerity.
Therefore, one must examine them closely; without wisdom, there is no means to exhaustively fathom their reality.
Without wisdom being critical and discerning, there would be no means to examine its illumination.
Thus, the source of illumination and examination is the essential point of critical determination;
therefore, there is no phenomenon that it does not take as a condition, and no object that it does not examine.
Thereafter, by taking dharmas as conditions and examining their objects, one comes to know that they all converge toward profound efficacy (*xuan-gong*) and mutually nourish the myriad phenomena.
Section Two: Examining Anger. As stated in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*:
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"In a past age, there was a brahmin who was poor.
He had a wife, but she did not bear children."
In his home there was a nākulī insect that gave birth to a son; because he had no children,
the brahmin raised him with the thought that he was his own son.
Nakula’s son regarded the brahmin as his father. Subsequently,
his wife became pregnant and, when the months were complete, gave birth to a son.
He then thought: "By means of Naḍakūlaka,
a son of auspicious birth has been produced,
so that I now have a son."
At that time, the brahmin wished to go out to beg for alms,
so he instructed his wife, saying,
"If you go out, you must take the child with you."
"Be careful not to stay long.
After the wife had given food to her child, she went to a neighboring house to borrow a mortar and pestle to husk grain.
At that time, the child had the fragrance of ghee and curd.
A venomous snake, drawn by the scent, came there, opened its mouth,
and spat poison, intending to kill the child.
The Naṅgula insect then thought to himself:
"My father has gone abroad and my mother is not at home;
how can this venomous snake wish to kill my younger brother?"
He then killed the venomous snake, cut it into seven pieces,
and stood at the gate with his mouth smeared with blood, thinking, "If my parents find out, they will surely reward me."
Wishing to cause her parents to see her with joy,
at that time the brahmin returned from outside;
seeing his wife at the entrance of the house, he spoke with anger:
"When I go to practice my religious duties, I shall take my son with me;
why should I go alone?
As the father was about to enter the gate, he saw that there was blood in Nākulika’s mouth.
He then thought to himself:
"While my husband and I are away, will they not kill and eat my son?
It is in vain that I nourish this creature."
He immediately struck and killed it.
Having entered inside the gate, he saw his own son playing while sucking his finger,
and he also saw the snake’s body divided into seven pieces lying on the ground.
At that time, the brahmin reproached himself deeply, thinking:
"Nāṭakura was well-versed in human affairs and saved my son's life;
yet, because I failed to examine him properly, I killed him so abruptly."
Piteous and lamentable,
he fell to the ground in a state of confusion and distress.
A deity appeared in the sky.
Then he spoke in verse:
"You should observe with careful discernment; Do not act with sudden violence or anger.
To separate a good friend from their loved ones Is to wrongfully harm and injure the virtuous."
It is, for example, like the Brahmin who killed that Nākulī.

"This child will surely be ridiculed by other countries.

though outwardly upright, he harbors inauspicious intent within.

"He cannot be raised;

One minister said,

dig a deep pit in the ground and bury him alive."

"I alone am without [auspicious] signs.

he said, "Prince,
why do you not speak? Are you to be buried alive?"

Thereupon, they escorted the Crown Prince to the upper chamber of the outer palace.
Five hundred ministers came to visit the prince;
seeing that the prince was upright, handsome, and pure,
they hurried back to inform the Great King.
"This son is not a mute;
let him stay for a moment.
He will speak before long."
"The Brahmin teacher cannot be trusted.
The King said,
"This is a matter of state affairs, not something you know."
Having finished preparing the treasury, he came to summon the Prince.
The King said to his attendant,
"Have the Prince mount the four-sided elephant chariot."

the Prince would then speak.
If he spoke, they were to carry him back.
Thereupon, as the Crown Prince traveled along the road in his carriage,

The Prince insisted that they speak at least one word.
"If you do not speak, I shall split my chariot and drive over you.
Although the various dragon-like warriors supported and escorted him,

Flying birds and running beasts circled the treasure three times and then blocked the entrance to the treasury;

He then raised his hand and remained silent,

He was about to speak,
but fearing he would fall into hell,

Because I deliver beings from suffering, I remain silent;
yet you believe deceitful words and claim that I am deaf and blind.
He was truly mute. At that time,
when the people heard the Prince’s exquisite voice,
those who were traveling stopped in their tracks.
Those who were seated rose;

Upon hearing this, the servant was filled with joy and leaped for gladness.
I hastened to inform the Great King:
"The Prince has already spoken;
his words reach from the azure heavens above down to the yellow springs below."

"Can my parents truly know my suffering?

I hope to escape beyond the dust and grime of the world;

3. Section on Examining Transgressions. Section Three. As stated in the *Dharmaguptaka-vaṃśa-nidāna-sūtra*:
At that time, in the city of Śūrasena, there was a merchant leader who organized a great *pañcavārṣika* assembly for the sake of the Saṃgha.
There was a bhikṣuṇī who had attained arhatship.

and she further reflected upon who the leader of the saṃgha might be.
He saw that the arhats and those still in training had long since severed their afflictions and were worthy of receiving offerings.
He observed a bhikṣu named Aśvala, who,
though not yet having attained liberation, stood at the very head of the assembly.

Section 44: On Reflection and Caution (46). Section on Reflection and Caution, Number Forty-four;

Section on Frugality and Economy, Number Forty-five. This section on Reflection and Caution consists of five parts: the Part on Stating the Intent, the Part on Careful Use, the Part on Heeding Calamity, the Part on Heeding Objects, and the Part on Heeding Transgressions. 1. The Part on Stating the Intent (First): Regarding the intent of this section: the principle is that through reflection and caution one prevents transgressions and remains free from affliction.
To seal the mouth and stifle anxious thoughts is to depart from the source of evil;
to admonish oneself at the beginning and be cautious until the end is the "salt and plum" seasoning of the gentleman.
To revere the beginning and protect the end is the essential path for nourishing life;
may you thus awaken to the arising of causes and conditions.
Discerning that arising and ceasing are impermanent;
recognizing that suffering and emptiness are without self;
illuminating the wondrous gate of equality.
Thus, one preserves the principle while discarding the traces;
one avoids calamity and invites fortune.
This is the way to harmonize with the spirit of the divine and accord with the Way of all things.

If I were now to see my father and the great assembly and rise to go and welcome them,

"If I were to remain here now maintaining my majestic deportment,

The Tathāgata forms these three kinds of reflections.
Having observed that there are these three kinds of causes and conditions,

Furthermore, the Brahmajāla Sūtra states:
O sons of the Buddha,

those who received the precepts first shall sit in the front.

one does not inquire whether they are senior or junior bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs, nor whether they are nobles, kings, princes, or even eunuchs and slaves.

those who have received them later should sit in successive order.
Do not act like the deluded followers of external paths.
Whether old or young, there is no priority or sequence;
they sit without order according to the custom of soldiers and slaves.

If a Bodhisattva does not sit in the proper order,
they commit a minor offense.
O Disciples of the Buddha!
One should constantly engage in teaching and transformation.
When entering the homes of wealthy patrons or among all assemblies with a heart of great compassion,

The fourfold assembly of listeners sat in lower seats as if they were filial toward their parents;
they venerated and obeyed the teacher’s instructions as fire-worshipping Brahmins serve their sacred fires.
Yet, if the one who preached the Dharma was not in accordance with the Dharma...
One commits a minor offense (āpatti).

Question: Regarding the four modes of bodily deportment— sitting, standing, walking, and reclining—

The answer is:
One should not walk for the sake of visiting,

One should not lie down for the sake of making offerings.
Furthermore, the *Three Thousand Dignified Postures* (*Sānqiānwēiyí*) states:
"There are five matters to attend to when wishing to ascend to one's bed."

Second, one must not crawl up onto it.
Third, one must not allow the bed to make any sound.
4. One must not vigorously sweep or wipe the bedding so as to make a sound.
5. If the feet have been washed and are not yet dry, one should wipe them.
There are five matters regarding being on the bed.
1. One must not blow loudly.
2. One must not scold, hiss, or belch.
3. One must not sigh or dwell upon worldly matters.
Fourth, one must not lie down to sleep with a pack of dogs.
Fifth, when wishing to rise from sitting, one should do so at the proper time;
if the mind wanders and is unsettled, one should reproach oneself for the original cause of its arising.
Furthermore, there are five matters regarding lying down:
first, one should have one's head directed toward the Buddha;
second, one must not lie down looking at the Buddha.
Third, one must not extend both feet together.
Fourth, one must not lie facing a wall, nor must one lie prostrate.
Fifth, one must not keep the knees upright; rather, one should clasp the hands and restrain the feet, stacking the knees one upon the other.
Furthermore, there are five matters regarding rising from bed and wishing to exit the door:
first, when rising from the bed, do not allow the bed to make a sound;
second, when putting on sandals, one should first shake them out.
Third, one should properly wear the dharma robes.
Fourth, when wishing to open a door, one should first snap the fingers three times,
ensuring that the door makes no sound.
Within the five doors, one must not exit with one's back turned toward the Buddha image;
rather, one should turn back toward the door when leaving.
Once outside, one must not stand still to converse with others.
Furthermore, the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states that the Bodhisattva Peacock expounded the Dharma of subduing for the assembly of devas,
whether they be householders or renunciants.
Whether old or young,
they are adorned by this discipline of self-mastery.
Just as one who has left the household life first disciplines themselves with the *kāṣāya*,
they should practice seven matters.
The first is to receive discarded rags (*pāṃsukūla*) in accordance with the laws of the land.
If there is clothing discarded by householders,

one should not take it if it has been stepped upon by a corpse.
If one obtains a tattered robe from among the graves, it should be used;
this is called the method of discipline regarding the kāṣāya.
Second, when entering a village, one should walk while observing the ground.
Gazing forward at a distance of one fathom,
one should contemplate the image of the Buddha with single-minded right mindfulness,
keeping the sense faculties undisturbed, and not looking at any necessary articles.
One should not engage in conversation with women;
one should not embrace small children;
and one should not move the feet repeatedly.
He did not move his arms or his seat;
he did not rub his head with his hands, nor did he repeatedly adjust his robes or shake out his *kāṣāya*.
One should not rub one's hands,
nor snap one's fingers;
this is called the second method of self-discipline.
Third, when entering the home of a donor,
one should wash one's hands up to the wrists at the time of the meal;
and when receiving food, one should not extend the hand too far.
The food should be one fore-arm's length away;
it should not fill the mouth, nor should it be too small.
The morsel of rice should be neither too large nor too small.
Do not open the mouth wide;
do not allow sounds to be made.
Of the food that should be eaten, eat only two parts.
One should know moderation and sufficiency in eating;
one should not look at another's bowl and give rise to a covetous mind,
nor harbor improper thoughts regarding the food received.
One observes one's own bowl and does not look left or right;
this is called the third method of self-discipline.
Fourth, at the time of eating:
If, in a village or a city,
one does not give rise to thoughts regarding food previously seen.
He does not engage in frequent speech nor harbor expectations;
he accepts and possesses bedding and requisites in accordance with the Dharma,
seeking nothing superior or more excellent.
This is called the fourth method of subduing.
The fifth is that in all one's actions, one is neither dependent nor attached, does not cherish even body or life,
and does not accumulate many possessions for use.
One should not travel to frontier regions that are perilous or fearful;
one should not wear unconventional clothing;
and one should not habitually frequent or dwell exclusively in a single household.
This is called the fifth method of subduing.
The sixth is not to cut grass or trees, nor to dig the earth;
one should not wear sandals of variegated leather or garments of variegated colors.
They do not violate the precepts of others;
they do not slander or speak ill of them;
and their minds harbor no expectations.
The king’s food does not please his heart;

This is called the sixth method of subduing.
Seventh, if there are those who share the same intention and the same Dharma,

Constantly practicing emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—

If there is a bhikṣu who can practice in this way, [he shall attain liberation].
Thus, one is able to cast off all fetters and attain liberation.
Furthermore, the *Saṃyukta-ratna-piṭaka-sūtra* states:
"On the night the Buddha first left the household life..."

She disregards right and wrong, acting with reckless ease.
"You were not careful in loving yourself,

Prince Siddhārtha has long since left the household life."
Now she has suddenly given birth to a son;

"What is this weeping?

"How do you kill with bitter poison?

"The fire shall be extinguished and shall never burn or harm me and my son.

Chapter on Harmony and Accordance (47) Chapter Forty-seven on Harmony and Accordance consists of five sections: the Section on Stating the Intent (*Shùyì bù*), the Section on Citing Evidence (*Yǐnzhèng bù*), the Section on Bestowing [Gifts] (*Shī bù*), the Section on the Country (*Guó bù*), and the Section on Affairs (*Shì bù*). 1. Section on Stating the Intent (*Shùyì bù*) Section One: Now, good and evil are contrary to one another, and speech and action may diverge from each other.
Calamities and provocations arise from this, and the bitterness of resentment grows ever heavier.
Thus, it is easy to speak of such things,
but difficult to put them into practice.
Therefore, when the firm and the yielding attain the mean, one accords with nature whether in opposition or compliance.
It is like forging a sword: if it is too firm, it will snap; if it is too yielding, it will curl.
To ensure the sword does not snap, one must add tin to it.
If one wishes to forge a sword without scrolls, one must add gold to it.
Why? Because the nature of gold is hard while the substance of tin is soft;
when hardness and softness are balanced, it becomes excellent.
To possess a nature of peace and harmony is truly excellent.
Thus, Rāhula practiced his conduct in secret to discipline himself;
therefore, the Sage praised him with words of renown.
Because Deva’s conduct was coarse and his nature was fierce and evil,
the multitude reviled him and his transgressions became manifest.
As a secular text says:
Ximen Bao was impetuous by nature;
he wore a girdle of cowhide to restrain himself and become more relaxed.
Dong An-yu was slow by nature.
By attaching strings to tighten them for oneself,
one brings harmony to Yin and Yang and attains the concord of Heaven and Earth;
by balancing hardness and softness, one accords with the nature of humans and things.
Section Two: Quotations from Scriptural Authorities. As stated in the *Guhyakapada-vajrapāṇi-paripṛcchā-sūtra*:
King Ajātaśatru asked the Buddha, "How many qualities does a bodhisattva possess who is harmonious and gentle?"
In all his comings and goings and interactions, he always maintains gentleness and refinement, never giving rise to coarse thoughts.
The Buddha said:
"There are eight dharmas of benevolence and harmony for a bodhisattva."
What are the eight? First, his disposition is upright and straightforward, free from flattery and deceit.
Second, his nature and conduct are harmonious and elegant, always devoid of sycophancy and falsehood.
Third, the mind remains pure and matured, forever free from falsehood.
Fourth, the mental conduct is firm and essential, without any weakness or inferiority.
Fifth, there is no delusion, as the will is set upon benevolence and harmony.
Sixth, he receives their virtuous conduct as one who is the benefactor of the world’s multitudes.
Seventh, his mental activities are thoroughly realized and free from attachment.
Eighth, he contemplates demerit and merit with a mind that harbors no conceptualizations.
These are the eight matters.
Thereupon, King Ajātaśatru addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How many dharmas must a bodhisattva practice to attain such power and infinite majesty?"
The Buddha said,
"There are ten dharmas. What are these ten?"
First, one should rather sacrifice body and life than fail to diligently receive the True Dharma;
second, one should never be self-important, but remain humble and reverent, lowering one's mind to pay respect to all sentient beings;
third, upon seeing sentient beings who are stubborn and difficult to transform, one should establish oneself in patience toward them.
Fourth, seeing those suffering from famine, one provides them with excellent and delicious food as alms.
Fifth, upon seeing those who are terrified, one encourages, consoles, and brings them peace.
Sixth, if there are sentient beings afflicted by a grave illness, one treats them with efficacious medicine.
Seventh, if there are those who are weak and inferior and are treated with contempt by others,
one should honor, cherish, and be devoted to them so that they are not neglected or disregarded.
Eighth, one should smear the temples of the Tathāgata with pure mud and water to repair whatever is deficient or damaged.
Ninth, seeing those who are orphaned, suffering, impoverished, and distressed, constantly burdened by heavy loads,
he causes them to be freed from their hardships and most grievous calamities.
Tenth, if there are those who have no protector and no one to turn to for refuge, he shall always deliver them.
What is spoken is consistent with what was said and does not deviate or change;
these are the ten dharmas.
Furthermore, the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states:
If there are sentient beings who, seeing others' friends and relatives destroying one another and harboring resentment in their hearts,
are able to bring them into harmony, they will,
at the end of life, be reborn in the Heaven of Desire-Love.
Whatever one’s mind desires, one immediately obtains the five sensory pleasures for one's own enjoyment.
If there are sentient beings who see others ruined and plundered by others, they rescue them and enable their liberation;
or, in dangerous places, they instruct people on the correct path.
Or, by causing others to find peace and security in places of doubt and fear,
one is reborn after death in the Heaven of Right Practice (Suyāma),
where one is honored by celestial maidens and enjoys the pleasures of the five senses.
If one is born among humans, one will be born into the family of a great elder with right view.
If there is anyone whose mind is supple and profound, free from all defilements,
for them nirvana and liberation are as if already in their hands.
The mind of one with a gentle heart is like white tin;
practicing virtuous deeds, such a person is trusted by all.
The mind of one who is coarse and fierce is like a diamond.
Constantly harboring a heart of resentment without forgetting it,
one acts with lack of self-discipline and becomes detested by the masses; thus,
one is neither loved nor trusted.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Peacock spoke these verses in the style of Buddhist sūtras:
If a person’s mind is supple, Like refined and purified gold,
And they are virtuous both within and without, They will swiftly be liberated from all suffering.
If a person’s mental vessel is harmonized, all things become supple;
such a person plants seeds of goodness, like an excellent field of merit.
Furthermore, the *Kātyāyanāvavāda-anāgāmi-sūtra* says:
The Anāgāmin has eight matters that he does not wish others to know.
What are these eight?
First, he makes no requests and does not wish others to know them.
Second, out of faith, one does not wish for others to know [one's faults].
Third, out of shame (*hrī*), one does not wish for others to know them.
Fourth, out of self-reproach (*apatrāpya*), one does not wish for others to know them.
Fifth, one practices diligence without desiring others to know it.
Sixth, one observes oneself without desiring others to know it.
Seventh, one attains dhyāna without desiring others to know it.
The eight forms of wisdom do not wish to be known by others.
The reason they do not wish to be known by others is that they do not wish to cause disturbance or vexation to people.
3. The Third Section on the Harmony of Giving and the Division of Giving. As stated in the *Buddha-spoken Sūtra on the Dānapāramitā Practiced by All Donors*, the Buddha said:
"In the remote past, incalculable kalpas ago..."

At that time, there was a great king of the world named Sāvadha (in the Jin language, meaning "Universal Giver"). At that time, he practiced giving such that whenever anyone requested anything, he did not refuse their wishes.
At that time, there was a son of a brahmin in another country who had lost his father at a young age;
he lived alone with his mother and sister.
His family home was poor and humble.
His mother told her son,
"Our household is in such dire straits that we have nothing with which to provide for ourselves."
"If your father were still alive,
you would go to King Śānta to beg for what you need to sustain yourself.
Why do you not now go to that king's place and seek money and jewels from him?"
The son replied to his mother, saying,
"I do not yet possess any knowledge;
first I must study and learn, and only then shall I act."
The mother said to her son,
"Now there is nothing at all in your house;
yet you possess learning, so you must go forth."
"If you leave after you go, this place will be empty and destitute;
how shall we sustain ourselves?
The son then spoke to his mother.
"I shall first borrow one *tǐng* of gold;
it will suffice to provide for a year's provisions.
His mother immediately granted him permission.
He then went out and borrowed one *liang* of gold to return to his mother.
Thereupon, he left the household life to practice and study.
When one year had passed, he returned home.
When the mother saw her son returning, she immediately asked him,
"Have you already gone to the place of King Sarvamdada?
The son replied to his mother:
"If what you have studied has not yet been mastered, you must study further.
His mother said, "The previous gold is already exhausted; what plan should we make?"
The son replied to his mother,
"I shall go again to borrow.
He then went once more to the house where he had previously borrowed the gold.
He spoke to his master, expressing his intention to borrow another ounce of gold.
The owner of the gold said to the boy,
"You have already taken gold from me before."
Since you have not yet returned it to me,
you now wish to demand it back once more.
If you truly intend to have that gold again, [then...]
"You must take your mother and your sister and brother; only with the superior vouchers can you obtain them.
If they are not paid for by the appointed time," [the remainder of the sentence follows].
"I shall enslave you, your mother, and your siblings. They then gave their consent;
he immediately drew up a contract, took it with him, and handed it over to his mother.
He again left the household life to pursue his studies,
and after another full year,
his knowledge was roughly complete.
Desiring to return and speak with his mother, he went to the presence of King Viśvāmitra.
On the way, he was pursued by creditors;
furthermore, when he returned with his mother, sister, and brother, they were bound at the feet with fetters.
The Brahmin’s son said to the creditor,
"Even though you bind me, it would be of no benefit to me even if I were held for the rest of my life;
it would be better to release me."
"I shall go to King Viśvantara to beg for goods, and with what I obtain, I will repay you.
The king reflected on this and then released the brahmin youth, allowing him to depart.
At that time, the army of a certain foreign king raised troops, intending to go and seize the kingdom of King Sarvadatta.
Then the ministers addressed the king,
saying, "Now, a foreign nation has mobilized its forces and entered our borders."
"I do not know what plan Your Majesty should adopt.
At that time, the king thought to himself:
"The life of a human being is exceedingly short; one must ultimately return to impermanence."
Furthermore, since my youth, I have delighted in practicing generosity;
I have been compassionate, benevolent, and patient, harboring no intent to harm,
and have never wished to oppose or resist others.
Why is this? It is merely because of my single person that the military host has been stirred up;
were I to be struck, it would truly not be fitting for me.
He then issued an edict to his ministers: "There is no need for preparations. Do not be afraid.
Simply prepare a formal reception and send-off to pay him due honor."
They respectfully served him and received his instructions, placing him above themselves.
The ministers further addressed the king, saying,
"An enemy has entered our borders."
"Why is it not complete?
The king remained silent and did not respond.
This was repeated up to three times.
The King said,
"There is no need to resist;
it shall be as I previously stated."
All the ministers said,
"The King has commanded that we not prepare for it; we all agree."
The King said, "Excellent!
Each of you may now settle in peace; be careful not to cause any disturbance."
At midnight, that king removed his seals and insignia and departed in silence.
Upon entering the kingdom, the other king immediately assumed the throne and then issued a proclamation to search for King Sarvamdada.
The reward was extremely generous.
The king then departed from the kingdom and traveled more than five hundred li,
when he saw the son of a brahmin in the distance.
The king thought to himself:
"This son of a brahmin will surely come now to demand me; of this there is no doubt."
At that time, the son of the brahmin also thought to himself,
"Could this person perhaps be King Sarvamdada?
The two men approached each other, met, and then stood still.
The king asked the son of the brahmin,
"From where have you come?
Where do you intend to go now?"
The son of the brahmin replied,
"I wish to go to the place where King Sarvamdada resides.
The king asked again:
"I wish to go to the place where King Sarvamdada resides.
What do you seek to obtain?
The Brahmin's son replied:
Having lost his father at a young age, he lived in extreme poverty.
He had pawned his mother, elder sister, and younger brother as collateral for a debt;
wishing to beg money and treasures from King Sarvamdada to redeem them and thereby save himself as well, he set out.
The king then spoke to him, saying,
"I am indeed the King who Gives All.
The Brahmin's son asked the king:
"While your attendants are present,
why do you travel alone?
the King asked.
"A kingdom from another land has come wishing to seize my domain;
therefore, I am avoiding it. Why is this so?"
Because he did not wish to harm living beings with weapons,
the son of the brahmin, upon hearing what the king said,
immediately fell to the ground and wept bitterly, unable to restrain himself.
The king then stepped forward, took hold of the brahmin’s son, and exhorted him,
urging him to rise and saying,
"There is no need to weep any longer."
"That which you seek, I shall now give to you.
The Brahmin’s son said,
"Your Majesty has now lost your kingdom."
"What should one carry to provide for those who beg?
The king then replied,
"The reward offered by that kingdom for the capture of the king is very heavy."
"You may now cut off my head and take it to him;
whatever he seeks shall be obtained.
Thereupon, the Brahmin’s son spoke a verse in reply:
In this world, those who kill their parents At the end of their lives fall into hell;
Now you inflict harm upon the King— The sin is no different.
I truly cannot bear To do evil against the Great King.
"Rather let my life come to an end than ever harbor a rebellious thought.
Then King Viśvantara spoke again to the son of the brahmin:
"If you do not wish to take my head,"
"You may simply cut off my nose and ears and send them;
you will thus receive a reward.
It is only for fear that [the whole person] might not suit the King's purpose."
The son of the brahmin replied to the king,
"As for me, today I cannot bear to do such a thing.
The king spoke again to the son of the brahmin:
If it is not so, you may simply bind me and send me to him;
thus you will also gain much.
The Brahmin’s son was able to recognize him; the king returned once more to his kingship and was not harmed by him.
The Brahmin’s son said, "If Your Majesty truly intends this, we may return together."
Upon reaching their own country, they were to bind one another.
Thereupon, the king and the son of the brahmin took each other with them and returned together to their native land for more than twenty li.
The king, intending to depart,
turned his hands behind his back and said to the son of the brahmin,
"You may bind me."
The son of the brahmin then bound the king;
the people of the entire kingdom all heard and knew that the king, who had practiced universal giving, had been captured and sent to another country by the son of a brahmin.
People, both great and small, upon seeing the king, could not help but weep;
they fell prostrate on the ground as if struck by a sudden calamity, like those who have lost their parents.
They then proceeded forward to the palace gate.
The ministers immediately entered and informed the king:
"The former king, Sarvamdada, who was sought out by recruitment,
has been seen and bound by the son of a brahmin and sent here."
"He is now at the palace gate.
The king then said, "Go and seize him! and they saw him.
King Sarvamdada then proceeded forward into the palace.
Upon seeing King Sarvamdada, the king, his ministers,
and all the officials fell to the ground in prostration, weeping without exception.
The king of men in that kalpa also shed tears and asked his ministers,
"Why are you all weeping?"
The ministers addressed him, saying,
"We have seen King Viśvantara abandon his kingdom for the sake of the king,
and furthermore, give even his own body as a gift to the son of a brahmin."
"What he has done brings no regret;
that is why he weeps.
When the king of men heard each of his ministers speak thus, [he was moved].
Even as he fell to the ground and wept bitterly,
unable to restrain himself,
he asked the brahmin’s son: "How have you now become this king?"
The son of the brahmin fully explained the origins and circumstances to the king.
Upon hearing what the son of the brahmin had said,
that king of the world immediately fell to the ground, weeping and saying:
He commanded his ministers to hasten to untie the king's bonds,
bathe him, clothe him in robes, and restore him to the throne with the investiture of his seals and insignia.
He immediately returned to his seat and administered the affairs of state according to former custom.
Thereupon, that king knelt for a long time with palms joined in reverence, and praising him, spoke these verses:
"When I was in my own kingdom, I heard from afar of the Great King’s virtue."
Now I have come here and behold the Honored One, far exceeding what I had heard of;
his towering accumulation of merit is like a mountain of gold,
and his power is so firm that none can shake him.
Now I behold the conduct of Your Majesty, which is truly peerless in this world.
I pray that you return the kingdom and its ministers, and grant me back my own realm.
May I return to my native land and perform the rites of a subject to pay my respects.
"I did not dare to be arrogant again, serving the king as if he were a World-Honored One.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"At that time, the King Sarvamdada was none other than myself."
The king of that country was Śāriputra;
the son of the brahmin was Devadatta.
He brought to fulfillment for me the marks and signs of the six pāramitās and their meritorious qualities.
"All these are the kindness of Devadatta.
Devadatta is my spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) and also my good teacher."
Devadatta shall, after an incalculable number of kalpas (asaṃkhyeya-kalpa), attain Buddhahood;
his name shall be T'i-ho-lo-ye (Dīpaṃkara), which in the Jin language means "King of Gods and Men.
4. Section Four on the *Huó-guó* (Kauśāmbī) from the *Zá-bǎo-zàng-jīng* (Saṃyukta-ratnapiṭaka-sūtra) states:
The Buddha said:
"In the distant past, there were two kings.
One was the King of Kāśī."
The second was the King of Videha.
King Videha possessed a great fragrant elephant, and by the power of that fragrant elephant, he crushed and subdued the army of the King of Kāśī.
The King of Kāśī then thought to himself:
"How shall I now obtain a fragrant elephant to crush and subdue the army of King Videha?
At that time, someone said,
"I have seen a white fragrant elephant in the mountains."
Having heard this, the king immediately issued a proclamation:
"Whoever can capture the fragrant elephant,
I shall grant them a generous reward."
Someone issued a recruitment call, saying,
"Gather a great multitude of troops and go to seize that elephant.
The elephant reflected and thought:
"If I were to go far away,
my parents would be blind and old;
it would be better for me to tame myself and go to the king's presence."
At that time, the people brought the fragrant elephant themselves to the king's side.
The king was greatly delighted and had a fine house built for it;
he provided it with fine woolen blankets and spread them beneath it.
He entertained him with various courtesans playing the lute and the harp;

yet, when given elephant fodder, the elephant refused to eat it. Then the elephant keeper came and addressed the king, saying: [The elephant] will not eat the food. At that time, the elephant keeper came and reported to the king, saying:
The elephant refused to eat.
The king went to where the elephant was;
in ancient times, animals were all able to speak human language.
The king asked the elephant,
"For what reason do you not eat?
The elephant replied to the king:
"I have parents who are old and blind, to whom no one provides water or food.
If my parents do not eat, how can I eat?"
The elephant said to the king,
"If I wish to depart,
none of Your Majesty's armies will be able to obstruct me."
"It is only because my parents are blind and aged that I have come here in accordance with the King's command.
Now that you permit me to go and provide for my parents until the end of their lives,
I shall surely return."
Upon hearing these words, the king was filled with great joy,
saying, "We are but men with the heads of elephants;
this elephant, however, is a man with the head of an elephant."
Previously, the people of Kāśī were wicked and contemptuous toward their parents, lacking any heart of filial support;
it was because of this elephant that [the situation changed].
The king immediately issued a proclamation throughout the entire kingdom:
"Whoever fails to filially support their parents shall be punished with a great crime."
He immediately released the elephant and returned to his parents' abode,
where he served them for the duration of their lives.
When his parents passed away, he returned once more to the king's presence.
The king was greatly delighted upon obtaining the white elephant.
He immediately prepared for an expedition to conquer that kingdom.
The elephant spoke to the king, saying:
"Do not give rise to strife.
Generally, the nature of strife causes much harm.
The King said:
"He is bullying me.
The elephant said, "Listen; let me go there."
"May it cause those enemies to dare not insult or humiliate you.
The King said,
"If you go, it is possible that you will not return."
He replied,
"There is no one capable of obstructing me so that I do not return.
Thereupon, the elephant proceeded to that kingdom.
When King Bhīmaratha heard that the elephant had arrived,
he was filled with great joy and went out in person to welcome it.
Having seen the elephant, he spoke to it, saying,
"Stay here in my kingdom.
The elephant addressed the king, saying:
I may not remain here.
Since I first established myself in this body, I have never violated my word or vow;
I previously promised that king that I would return to his kingdom.
"You two kings should eliminate enmity and evil.
Would it not be joyful for you to bring peace to your own kingdoms?
Then he spoke this verse:
Victory increases enmity; defeat adds further sorrow and suffering.
For one who does not contend for victory or defeat, that joy is the foremost.
At that time, having spoken this verse, the elephant—
He immediately returned to the kingdom of Kāśī.
From that time forward, the two kingdoms were at peace.
At that time, the king of the kingdom of Kāśī...
The King of Poṣadha is now King Prasenajit; the King of Videha is now King Ajātaśatru.
The white elephant of that time was my own self in this present life.
Because I filially supported my parents at that time,
I have caused many sentient beings likewise to filially support their parents.
At that time, he was able to bring about peace and harmony between the two nations;
today, too, it is well. 5.
