Section 48: Admonitions (48). Section 48: Admonitions. This section contains six parts: Part on Stating the Intent; Part on Admonishing Horses;

Part on Admonishing Study; Part on Admonishing Theft; Part on Admonishing Offenses; and Part on Miscellaneous Admonitions. Part 1: Stating the Intent. First, regarding the statement of intent: Images are established to represent the Truth and serve as the standard instruction for transforming worldly customs.
Pointing at the finger, using the trap, or following the moon are but the conventional paths;
yet, due to deluded thoughts and inverted sentiments, people follow the current and solidify their habits.
Without the thought of reforming themselves, they drift and sink along with the force of their karma.
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"Performing good leads to ascension, comparable to the soil on one's fingernails;
performing evil leads to sinking and stagnation, analogous to the dust of the earth."
This is truly because the six thieves have arrived together and the ten fetters are entangling one another;
it is comparable to a painted jar used as a latrine,
or like a fragile earthen vessel at a besieged city.
Therefore, as one approaches the collapse of this decaying house, the three fires are constantly burning;
as one flees to hide in the empty village, the five swords are constantly in pursuit.
These are the metaphors of the well and the river.
The physical forms are constrained within a single kṣaṇa;
like oxen and sheep at a butcher’s stall,
their lives are severed in a mere moment.
It is also like a mouse entering a horn of fat;
when it reaches its end, where can it go?
How much more so when the five turbidities intersect and the four mountains constantly press in from all sides!
Yet one is able to practice patience and give rise to neither sorrow nor regret.
For this reason, when the Great Sage bestowed his instructions,
the ultimate purpose of both the teachings and the parables lay solely in admonition and restraint.
With body and mind free from indulgence and desire,
one should examine oneself with vigor and diligence, remaining focused and mindful of one's transgressions.
One will see that at the moment of death, the light of the eyes fades away.
Relatives gather in crowds, yet they cannot save one by their very presence.
Alas! With tears and sobs, I lament their sinking into the depths of suffering.
Since you are already subject to such misery, why do you not admonish yourself?
My transgressions arose from myself and were rectified without depending on others;
yet there remains a slight merit whose retribution resides within me.
Furthermore, I have encountered the bequeathed Dharma and personally beheld the Triple Gem.
Once one has been reborn in the evil realms, it will be beyond one's power to know [the truth] face-to-face.
Therefore, out of this sorrow, there is no reason for indolence or negligence.
2. The Section on Admonishing Horses, Part Two. As stated in the Madhyama Āgama:
At that time, there was a horse trainer named Jīvaka who came to where the Buddha was,
prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and paid his respects.
Withdrawing to sit on one side, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
I observe that the world is exceedingly trivial and shallow."
They are like a flock of sheep.
In this world, I alone am capable of taming horses that are wild, unruly, and evil.
By employing skillful means, I shall cause all their vices and ailments to manifest in an instant.
He tamed him through skillful means according to his temperament and illness.
The Buddha said to the horse trainer:
"Village headman," [he continued].
"By how many kinds of skillful means do you tame horses?
The horse trainer replied to the Buddha,
"There are three methods for taming a wicked horse."
What are the three? First, softness;
second, coarseness.
"Third, they may be supple or coarse.
The Buddha said to the village headman:
'You train horses by means of these three methods.'"
"What should be done with those that remain untamed?
The horse trainer replied to the Buddha,
"Those that are untamed should simply be killed."
"Why is this? So that they do not bring me disgrace.
The horse trainer said to the Buddha:
"The Blessed One is the unsurpassed tamer of men.
By how many kinds of skillful means does he tame men?
The Buddha told the village headman:
I also discipline men of noble character through three kinds of skillful means. What are these three?
The first is being consistently gentle.
Second, those that are exclusively coarse and rough;
third, those that are both soft and coarse-rough.
The Buddha told the village headman:
As for what you have called "exclusively gentle," this is what you refer to as virtuous conduct of the body.
This is the result of wholesome bodily conduct;
this is wholesome verbal and mental conduct;
this is the result of wholesome verbal and mental conduct.
These are called devas;
these are called humans;
these are called those born by transformation in the happy realms.
This is called nirvana;
this is what is meant by "supple.
As for the second, which is consistently coarse and harsh:
It is as you have said:
this is bodily misconduct;
this is the retribution for bodily misconduct.
Virtuous and non-virtuous actions of speech and mind,
and the retribution for those non-virtuous actions of speech and mind— this is called hell.
These are called animals;
these are called hungry ghosts;
these are called evil destinies.
This is called falling into the evil destinies;
this is called the Tathāgata’s harsh teaching.
Third, as for those who possess both the gentle and the harsh:
That is to say, at times the Tathāgata speaks of wholesome bodily conduct;
at times he speaks of the retribution for wholesome bodily conduct;
and at times he speaks of wholesome verbal and mental conduct.
Sometimes it speaks of the retribution for good verbal and mental conduct;
sometimes it speaks of bodily misconduct;
and sometimes it speaks of the retribution for bodily misconduct.
At times he speaks of the misconduct of speech and mind;
at times he speaks of the retribution for the misconduct of speech and mind.
Thus he describes what it means to be a deva and what it means to be a human being.
Such is called a happy rebirth;
such is called nirvana; such is called hell.
These are called animals and hungry ghosts;
these are called the evil destinies;
these are called falling into the evil destinies.
This is called the Tathāgata’s teaching that is both gentle and harsh.
The horse trainer addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One,"
"If one employs three kinds of skillful means to discipline sentient beings,
what should be done regarding those who remain undisciplined?
The Buddha told the village headman:
"You should also kill him.
Why? So that he does not bring me dishonor."
The horse trainer said to the Buddha,
"If one kills a living being,
it is considered impure within the Dharma of the World-Honored One."
"In the Dharma of the Blessed One, one likewise does not kill living beings.
What then is the meaning of the statement that one 'kills'?
The Buddha told the village headman:
In the Dharma of the Tathāgata, there is likewise no killing of living beings.
Nevertheless, within the Dharma of the Tathāgata, those who are not disciplined are taught by means of three kinds of instruction.
If one no longer speaks with them,
nor instructs or admonishes them, is this not death?
The horse trainer said to the Buddha,
"It is indeed so, World-Honored One;
he no longer speaks with me."
Never to receive instruction is truly to be dead.
For this reason, [it is said].
"From this day forth, I shall abandon all evil and unwholesome deeds.
Having heard what the Buddha had spoken, he departed with joy.
Furthermore, the *Dharmapada-avadāna-sūtra* says:
The Buddha asked the elephant trainer,
"How many methods are there for training an elephant?
He replied:
There are three. What are the three?
First, a stiff hook with a curved mouth that catches its bit and tether.
Second, they reduce their food so that they are constantly hungry and emaciated.
Third, they inflict pain upon them with beatings and staffs.
Because their mouths are pried open with iron hooks, this serves to restrain their voracious appetite.
"By not providing food and drink, he restrains his body's wildness;
by applying the whip and staff, he subdues his mind.
Thus the Buddha told the householder.
I also have three applications for disciplining all things,
and by means of them I have disciplined myself to reach the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
The first is to control the afflictions of speech through utmost sincerity.
Second, by means of compassionate integrity, they subdue physical rigidity.
Third, by means of wisdom, they extinguish the delusive veil of the mind.
By maintaining these three matters, they deliver all beings and cause them to leave the three evil realms.
3. Section on Admonitions for Study, Part Three. As stated in the Ekottarika Āgama:
within a single verse, one gives rise to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the meanings of all dharmas.
Kāśyapa asked, "What is it?
Then the Venerable Ānanda spoke this verse:
Refrain from all evil, practice all good, and purify one’s own mind:
this is the teaching of all Buddhas. As for why it is so:
refrain from all evil.
One observes the prohibitions of the complete precepts and practices pure conduct.
One should practice all that is good and maintain a pure mind.
"Purify your own minds and eliminate false inversions;
this is the teaching of all Buddhas."
One should eliminate deluded thoughts.
Kāśyapa, what is meant by purity of ethical discipline?
Is the mind not pure?
That which is pure is free from inversion.
Because the deluded perceptions of inversion have been extinguished,
the fruits of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are accomplished; through the accomplishment of these fruits of the path, [liberation is attained].
Is this not indeed all phenomena?
Section Four: Admonitions on Stealing. As stated in the *Saṃyukta Āgama*:
At one time, there was a certain bhikṣu.
While staying in a forest grove among the people of Kosala,
that bhikṣu suffered from an eye ailment.
He received instruction from his teacher, which said:
"One should smell the padma flowers.
Then that bhikṣu, having received his teacher's instruction,
went to the side of the Padma Lake.
He sat on the bank of the pond with his back to the wind,
sniffing the fragrance as it drifted with the breeze.
At that time, there was a deva who presided over this pond.
He said to the bhikṣu,
"Why did you steal these flowers?
You are now nothing but a thief of incense."
At that time, the bhikṣu answered in verse, saying:
"Neither destroyed nor taken away, dwelling afar yet following the scent you smell—
why do you now say, 'I am a thief of fragrance'?"
At that time, a celestial deity spoke again in verse:
"Neither seeking nor abandoning—this is what the world calls a thief.
You now take for yourself exclusively that which others have not given."
This is what is called the "worldly thief who truly steals the fragrance.
At that time, there was a man who took those lotus roots, carried them away on his back, and departed.
At that time, the bhikṣu spoke these verses for the sake of that deva:
"Just as that man, having severed the *puṇḍarīka* lotus,
uproots it and carries it away under a heavy burden— such a person is indeed a deceitful rogue."
"Why do you not stop me? he asked. "I am stealing the incense," she replied, answering him with this verse as the celestial deity had spoken:
"O mad, deluded, and deceitful man, you are like a nurse’s garment."
What need is there to address him further? He is merely fit for conversation with you.
A stained *kāṣāya* does not show its impurity; black clothing is not defiled by blackness.
The world does not converse with those who are treacherous, deceitful, and cruel.
As fly-spots defile pure white silk, so do even minor transgressions appear like ink spots on a conch shell; though small, they all become manifest.
That bhikṣu then spoke another verse:
"Excellent, excellent is this teaching! It comforts me with its meaning.
You should constantly and repeatedly recite this verse for me.
Then that celestial deity spoke another verse:
I am not a slave bought by you, nor was I given to you by another;
why then do you constantly follow me? You should now understand for yourself that I repeatedly speak to you for your own benefit in each and every matter.
5. Section on Admonishing Transgressions. Section Five on Admonishing Transgressions. As stated in the *Yanluowang Wushi jing* (The Scripture of the Five Messengers of King Yama):
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, "When humans are born into this world..."
They were unfilial toward their parents,
disrespectful toward śramaṇas,
and failed to practice benevolence and righteousness.
Those who do not study the sutras and precepts and do not fear future lives will,
upon the death of their bodies, fall into hell.
The presiding official, holding the records of conduct, reports the transgressions and evils to King Yama,
stating such various faults as this person’s lack of filial piety and their absence of merit.
They do not fear death;
they await only the king’s punishment.
King Yama always first speaks with calm composure and words of loyalty and integrity.
He manifested as the five messengers and asked:
"First, do you not see how people in this world begin as infants?"
Lying stiffly in excrement and urine, unable to protect oneself;
the mouth cannot speak, nor can one distinguish between what is good and what is evil. Do you see this?
The man replied, "I have already seen it.
The king said,
"You yourself say that it is not so."
However, as the spirit of man follows its conduct until the end, there will inevitably be rebirth.
Although you have not yet seen this clearly, you ought always to do good and rectify your three karmas;
how can you allow your mind to run wild and your will to be unrestrained, thereby committing transgressions?
The man replied,
"I am ignorant and do not know.
The king said:
"You were yourself foolish and acted wickedly according to your own will;
this was not the fault of your parents, teachers, elders, sovereign, deities, śramaṇas, or practitioners of the Way.
Your transgression arises solely from you."
"How could one not rejoice?
One should now accept this.
This is the first divine messenger manifested by King Yama."
The second King Yama asked again:
"When you were a human being,
the celestial messengers arrived in succession."
"Are you able to perceive it?
The man replied, "I do not perceive it.
The king said:

"Do you not see that among the people of the world there are those who are old, with white hair and fallen teeth, emaciated and hunched over, walking with a stoop and rising from their seats only with the aid of a staff?
The man replied, "Indeed, there are.
The King said:
You think that you alone can escape and avoid aging;
yet for all ordinary people, once born, the law of aging and decrepitude prevails.
You should always do good, rectify your body, speech, and mind, and reverently practice the sutras and precepts.
"How can you act so wantonly?
The person replied,
"It is because of my ignorance."
The king said, "You committed evil because of your own ignorance;
it was not the fault of your parents, your sovereign, the devas, the śramaṇas, or the practitioners.
Your transgression is of your own making."
"How could one not rejoice?
Now you shall receive it.
This is the second divine messenger manifested by King Yama."
The third King Yama asked again:
"When you were a human being,

did you not see that among the men and women of the world there were those whose bodies were afflicted by disease, whose physical pain made them restless in sitting or rising, whose lives were near their end in urgent distress, and whom no physicians could cure?"
The man replied, "I have.
The king said,
"Can you avoid being ill?"
Since one has grown old in life, the law is that all shall fall ill.
Hearing that your body is currently strong and healthy, you ought to strive to do good and practice the sutras and precepts, rectifying your body, speech, and mind.
How can you indulge yourself?
The man replied,
"It is because of my ignorance and delusion.
The king said:
"You consider yourself foolish for committing evil;
it is not the fault of your parents, your sovereign, the deities, śramaṇas, or practitioners of the Way.
Your transgression arises solely from yourself."
"How could one not rejoice?
You shall now receive [the fruits of your actions].
This is the third divine messenger manifested by King Yama."
The fourth King Yama asked again:
"When you were a human being,
did you not see the various deaths that occur in the world?"
Some bury their corpses,
while others cast them away;
by the seventh day, the flesh and muscles have rotted and decayed.
Foxes and all manner of birds flock to feed upon it.
When an ordinary person has died, their body becomes foul and putrid;
have you not seen this?
The man replied, "Yes.
The king said,
"Do you think that by striving alone you can avoid death?"
All people who have been born must die.
Having heard that one should constantly perform good deeds while in this world,
they command their body, speech, and mind to practice the sutras and precepts.
"How is it that you act so wantonly?
The person replied,
"It is because of my ignorance and delusion."
The king said,
"You have committed evil yourself;
it is not the fault of your parents, your sovereign, the heavens, the śramaṇas, or the practitioners of the Way."
Your transgressions are forgiven;
how could you not rejoice?
You shall now receive [the fruit of this].
This was the fourth divine messenger manifested by King Yama.
The fifth time, King Yama asked again:
"When you were a human being..."
One does not see the wicked people or evil sons of the world being seized by officials, interrogated for their crimes, and subjected to legal punishments—
such as having their hands and feet severed,
or having their noses and ears cut off.
Some have their bodies burned and their heads hung out in the scorching sun;
others are slaughtered, dismembered, and subjected to various forms of agonizing pain.
He replied, "There are."
The king said:
"Do you believe that evil alone can be understood?
With one's own eyes, one sees the distinctions between sin and merit in the world with clarity."
"Why do you not maintain goodness by restraining your body, speech, and mind, and practice the sutras and precepts?
Why do you seek only your own pleasure?
The person replied:
"It is because of your ignorance and folly.
The king said,
"You have acted with a mind of your own, committing acts of disloyalty and injustice."
This is not the fault of one's parents, sovereign, devas, śramaṇas, or practitioners;
it is now this calamity and sin that must necessarily be experienced by oneself.
This was the fifth divine messenger manifested by King Yama.
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra,
all the disciples received his instructions and admonitions.
Each person prostrated before him and joyfully practiced [the teaching].
Section Six: Miscellaneous Admonitions. In the sixth section on miscellaneous admonitions, the verses of the *Dharmapada* contain eleven admonitions in total.
The person who possesses faithful conduct is praised by the sages; one who delights in non-action has all fetters released.
When comparing worldly profit to this, faith and generosity are the light;
they are the supreme treasure among riches. Family wealth is impermanent; if one wishes to see the Truths, one must practice them.
Delighting in listening to the Dharma, Able to abandon stinginess and envy— This is called faith;
one without faith does not practice it. One who loves to refute and correct others Is like a clumsy man drawing water:
he digs the spring and stirs up the mud. The virtuous man practices wisdom And delights in looking up toward purity.
Just as one who skillfully draws water must have it cold and undisturbed, so too faith that is untainted by others is most excellent.
Like a well-trained elephant, one who trains oneself is supreme.
Faith is a treasure, as are the treasures of ethical discipline, shame, and dread of blame; learning is a treasure, and generosity is a treasure.
Wisdom is the seventh treasure; those born with this treasure—whether man or woman—will ultimately be free from greed.
The wise recognize the truth that all things are impermanent, for they are subject to the law of arising and decaying: whatever is born must inevitably die.
This cessation is bliss; like the swift current of a river, life passes away and does not return.
Thus is the human lifespan: that which has departed does not come back.
For the living, day and night, life is as if being carved away by a razor; the exhaustion of one’s longevity is like water in a shallow pit.
That which is constant comes to an end; that which is high must also fall. There is separation from those who meet, and death for those who are born.
Sentient beings harm one another, thereby losing their lives and falling according to their actions.
They themselves receive calamity and misfortune, even if they live for a hundred years.
One dies and passes away, weary of old age; sickness suddenly arrives, and this day has already gone by.
Life accordingly diminishes, like a fish in shallow water—what joy can there be in this?
With old age, one’s complexion fades; what is afflicted naturally decays.
The form decays and rots; when life ends, it is just so. Of what use is this body, which is constantly leaking and foul-smelling?
It is beset by disease and plagued by the afflictions of old age and death.
There is no reliance on sons, nor on father or elder brother, when one is pressed by death.

Having no kinsman to rely upon, being negligent day and night, not ceasing lust in old age, and having wealth yet not practicing giving—these four obscurations cause one not to accept the words of the Buddha.
To practice benevolence by not killing, and to always be able to restrain the body: in such a state, there is no death.
Wherever one goes, there is no distress; by not killing, one practices benevolence. Guarding speech and maintaining the mind, this is the way to dwell in immortality.
Wherever one goes, there is no distress; when others are in disorder, one maintains composure through compassion and benevolence.
Being able to endure anger when provoked—this is called the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
With utmost sincerity and tranquility, one’s speech is free from coarse words;
not being angry at what others hold to be right—this is called the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
With hands folded and effortless, not harming living beings and causing them no affliction—this is called the holy life. Always with compassion and pity...
Pure as the Buddha’s teaching, Contented and knowing when to stop, Thus one crosses over birth and death;
universally loving the virtuous and beautiful, Bestowing compassion upon all sentient beings, Constantly practicing a heart of loving-kindness, wherever one goes there is peace.
Day and night recollecting loving-kindness, The mind is free from injury or aggression.
Not harming living beings, one practices without enmity; sleeping in peace and waking in peace, one sees no evil dreams.
Protected by devas and loved by humans, one is not harmed by poison, weapons, water, or fire, nor suffers loss.
Whatever one encounters, one gains profit; at death, one ascends to the Brahma Heaven.
Experiencing happiness naturally, the benevolent one has no distracted mind; practicing supreme compassion, he takes pity on sentient beings. This merit is immeasurable.
Even when reviled with evil words or treated with arrogance and contempt, he gives rise to this practice.
When resentment arises, speak with humility and use compliant words;
by honoring others and abandoning enmity while enduring evil, resentment will naturally perish.
For a person’s birth is as if an axe were held in their mouth; it is by means of their own evil speech that they cut themselves down.
To strive for small gain is like losing one's wealth; from that, disputes arise, causing the mind to turn toward evil.
The mind is the foundation of all phenomena; the mind is the master, the mind is the messenger.
When one harbors evil thoughts within the mind, suffering follows as its own consequence. The mind is the foundation of all phenomena.
The mind is the lord, the mind is the driver; if one dwells upon goodness within the mind, happiness and merit follow of their own accord.
But following the conduct of a distracted mind, one is bound by folly and enters darkness.
If one is self-important and lacks the Dharma, how can one understand well-spoken words? By following the conduct of a right mind, one attains clarity and understanding.
Do not harbor jealousy; be quick-witted and discerning regarding virtuous speech. One who harbors resentment toward those who resent them will never be free from resentment;
by not harboring resentment, resentment is naturally eliminated. This path is worthy of veneration:
do not take pleasure in blaming others, but strive to examine yourself. If there is one who understands this—
To take the true as false and the false as true is wrong view; one shall not obtain the true benefit.
To know the true as true and to perceive the false as false is right view;
one will certainly obtain the true benefit. If the walls and roof of one's house are not sealed tight, [the rain shall leak in].
When it rains, the leak occurs; when the mind does not contemplate what is right, evil dharmas pierce it like a wall.
When a house is well-sealed, rain does not leak in; by restraining the mind and dwelling only in what is right, evil is hidden and does not arise.
A base person who defiles others is like being near a foul-smelling object.
Gradually one becomes fully habituated to what is wrong, Unaware that one has become evil.
A virtuous person is influenced by others like being perfumed by incense; Advancing in wisdom and practicing the good, One’s conduct becomes pure and right mindfulness constantly arises.
Evil dharmas naturally perish as one masters the True Dharma through self-restraint.
May your goodness increase daily; you should contemplate the Path. Firmly maintain right conduct;
the steadfast shall attain deliverance. This is the unsurpassed auspiciousness: subdue yourself, discipline your mind, and practice without negligence.
Through generosity, precepts, patience, diligence, concentration, and wisdom, may you always be clear-sighted.
Not troubled by birth, nor grieving at death; the paths of calamity and fortune diverge.
The ignorant are attached to birth and death and do not know the True Dharma. Foolish and lacking wisdom, they are like those dwelling in a dark room;
their minds are clouded and distracted by every occurrence, unable to distinguish between cold and heat.
Though one has practiced for a long time, one still does not know the Dharma;
though one performs acts of giving, it brings affliction to the body. One who delights the mind in committing evil brings upon oneself heavy calamity.
That which the fool hopes for is not called "satisfying," yet he falls into a place of peril.

he still yearns for the meal of wild herbs and beans, wishing to carry rice for his parents as he once did;
that can never be regained.
Every time I reflect on these words,
though I am alive, it is as if I were dead;
such is the debt of gratitude owed to one's parents.
How could it be possible to repay such kindness?
One's compassion is as deep as the rivers and seas,
while one's filial piety is but a speck of dust.
Forever longing for you and wailing aloud,
my grief pierces through my heart and head.
In worldly parlance, it is said that you suckled me at your breast and gave birth to this physical body of mine.
The kindness of a single lifetime is already difficult to repay;
how much more so the Great Compassion of the Tathāgata, which universally moistens all beings equally as if they were his only child,
uprooting them from the three miserable realms and enabling them to attain liberation from the four modes of birth.
Having bid farewell to the eight sufferings and forever guided [beings] by means of the Three Vehicles, I reflect silently upon the weight of their kindness;
how could it be like that of ordinary people? My inner heart collapses in ruin, as if burning and searing.
My feelings are more urgent than reason and my grief is sharper than a blade cutting through me.
Though I have gazed upon you with reverence throughout kalpas and constantly offered you rare delicacies,
I have still been unable to repay even a moment’s kindness.
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"The Buddha possesses a single flavor of great compassion;
he regards all sentient beings with pity as if they were his only son."
Sentient beings do not know that the Buddha can save them;
they slander the Tathāgata, as well as the Dharma and the Saṅgha.
Section Two: Quotations from Scriptural Authority. As stated in the *Malla-rāja-sūtra*:
A person asked the World-Honored One,
"What constitutes the power of one's parents?
The Buddha replied:
That is to say, receiving the physical body from one's parents,
the kindness of nursing and nourishing with breast milk,
or gathering precious treasures from the earth.
Even if one were to give everything up to the twenty-eighth heaven as an offering to others,
it would not equal making offerings to one's parents.
This is the power of parents.
Furthermore, the *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus.
There are two dharmas by which an ordinary person attains great merit and achieves a great karmic fruition:
first, making offerings to one's parents;
second, making offerings to a Bodhisattva in his last birth before Buddhahood.
Giving to these two persons yields great merit and brings about a great karmic fruit.
Furthermore, if there were another person who placed their father upon their left shoulder...
Placing his mother upon his right shoulder,
he provided her with clothing, food, bedding, seats, and medicinal requisites for the sick for a period of ten million years.
If one were to discharge excrement and urine upon their shoulders,
even then one would still be unable to repay their kindness; thus,
one should know that the debt of gratitude owed to one's parents is profound.
When providing nourishment, one should protect [the recipient] so as not to miss the proper timing;
one should also offer sustenance with filial devotion.
Furthermore, the *Niraya Sūtra* states:
If one, as a disciple, speaks of the faults of one's preceptor,
even if those faults are real, the preceptor will surely enter hell after death and devour that person's tongue.
Furthermore, if [the disciple] obtains fine food, delicious fruits, or the like, [they shall lose them].
If one eats and drinks before one's parents, teachers, or monastics,
one will fall into the realm of hungry ghosts;
subsequently, if reborn as a human, one will be poor.
If a person harbors malice toward their teachers or elders, they will enter the Iron Stake Hell and later be reborn among venomous snakes.
If one learns the words of one's parents, teachers, or elders with an evil mind, one will enter the Melted Copper Hell.
In a future life, one will be born as a human being who stammers.
Furthermore, the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states:
"It would be better to destroy a stūpa or damage an image than to speak of another's gross transgressions."
If one speaks [of such matters], it destroys the Dharmakāya.
Regardless of whether the aforementioned bhikṣu is guilty or innocent,
one must not speak of it at all.
Furthermore, the *Jingshi jing* (Sutra on Reverencing the Teacher) states:
"Three times each day, one should attend to the teacher’s movements and conduct.
If one attends upon the teacher and does not see him at that time,"
One should carry clods of earth, grass, or wood as tokens of remembrance.
If the weather is hot, one should fan the teacher three times each day with a fan.
If there is a bhikṣu who, in the presence of that teacher or his preceptor (upādhyāya),...
Those who speak of others' faults without a mind of respect will,
in a future age, be reborn in a separate minor hell called "The Striking Down."
When one falls into that place as described in this sutra, one’s body— with four heads— becomes completely scorched;
furthermore, there are various insects within that hellish realm.
It is named Hook-Mouth;
it constantly devours the root of the tongue.
If one hears even a single four-line verse from another, [it is immediately destroyed].
For each of those thousands of kalpas, he took his preceptors and ācāryas upon his shoulders,
or at times carried them on his back or bore them upon his head.
Yet even this cannot repay [the Buddha's kindness].
Furthermore, the Abhidharma-śāstra states:
"If a patient, a Dharma-preacher, those near the Buddha, or various Bodhisattvas receive offerings, they shall obtain a great reward."
Furthermore, the *Six Perfections Compendium Sutra* (*Liudu ji jing*) states:
"In the past, the Bodhisattva was born as a crane and had three sons."
At that time, the country suffered a great drought and there was no means to feed them.
He tore the flesh from beneath his own armpits to sustain their lives.
His three sons questioned him, saying:
"The flavor and scent of this meat are exactly like the scent of our mother's body;
could it be that our mother has fed us with her own flesh?
At these words, the three sons were overcome with profound sorrow and intense grief.
He further said,
"I would rather lose my own life than harm my mother's body.
Thereupon, he closed his mouth and refused to eat.
When the mother saw that he would not eat and sought it out again,
a celestial deity sighed in praise, saying:
"The mother's compassionate wisdom is beyond compare."
Your filial piety is rare indeed.
May the various devas protect you;
may your wishes be fulfilled immediately according to your heart's desire.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The mother crane was I myself;
the three sons were Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and Ānanda."
The Bodhisattva’s practice of the perfection of giving through loving-kindness and wisdom is thus.
Furthermore, the Sutra in Forty-two Sections says:
The Buddha said:
Feeding a hundred ordinary people is not as meritorious as feeding one virtuous person; feeding a thousand virtuous people is not as meritorious as feeding one person who has attained the Path.
Feeding ten thousand people who observe the five precepts is not as meritorious as feeding a single *srotāpanna*.
Feeding one million stream-enterers (srotāpanna) is not equal to feeding a single once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin);
feeding ten million once-returners is not equal to feeding a single non-returner (anāgāmin).
It is not as good as providing a meal to a single *anāgāmin*.
Providing a meal to one hundred million *anāgāmins* is not as good as providing a meal to a single *arhat*.
Feeding ten billion arhats is not equal to feeding a single pratyekabuddha;
feeding ten billion pratyekabuddhas is not equal to [feeding a single buddha].
It is not as good as using the teaching of the Triple Gem to deliver one’s parents of this life;
nor is it as good as teaching a thousand billion people.
It is not as good as offering a meal to a single Buddha and making a vow to seek Buddhahood.
To "raise a vow" means to seek Buddhahood with the desire to deliver sentient beings.
Feeding virtuous people brings the greatest and most profound merit.
It is like ordinary people serving Heaven, Earth, and the spirits.
It is not as good as being filial toward one’s parents.
One’s two parents are the most divine.
Furthermore, the *Saṃyukta-ratna-piṭaka-sūtra* says:
In the distant past, long ago,
there was a parrot in the midst of the Snowy Mountains whose parents were both blind.
He would always take choice fruits and first offer them to his parents.
At that time, there was a landowner who,
when first sowing grain, made this vow:
"The grain that is sown must be shared and eaten together with all sentient beings.
At that time, the parrot, because the field-owner had previously possessed a mind of generosity,
would regularly take some of the grain to provide for his parents.
As the field owner was walking through the grain, he saw that insects and birds had stripped the ears of grain.
Filled with anger and resentment, he set a net and captured a parrot.
At that time, the parrot spoke to the field owner, saying:
"O Landowner,
because you previously gave with a benevolent heart,
I venture to come and take [this]."
"How is it that you have now been caught in the net?
The landowner asked,
"For whom did you take this grain?"
The parrot replied, "I have blind parents; I wish to offer them [this gift].
The landowner said to him:
From this day forward, always obtain [the medicine] from here; do not harbor doubts or difficulties.
If even animals act thus, how much more so should one filially support one's parents?
How much more so for a human being!
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"In the past, there was a parrot."
I am that very person now;
the master of the field at that time was Śāriputra.
The blind parents were my own parents of the present, King Śuddhodana and Queen Māyā;
because of their filial care in the past, they have now attained Buddhahood.
3. Section on the Prince. Section Three. As stated in the *Baoen jing* (Sutra on Gratitude):
The Buddha told Ānanda, "In the distant past, immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) kalpas ago, a Buddha appeared in the world."
He was named Vipaśyin.
After he entered nirvana,
during the period of the Semblance Dharma, there was a king of Vārāṇasī named Rāja.
That king ruled over sixty minor kingdoms.
The king had a crown prince who served as the ruler of one of these minor kingdoms.
He had a chief minister named Rāhula.
In his heart he conceived a rebellious intent and murdered the Great King along with two of the crown princes.
The King’s youngest son became the king of a frontier realm;
by nature he was gentle and well-disciplined, and the heavenly deities held him in reverence and affection.
A crown prince was born named Sujāti;
he was seven years of age,
intelligent, compassionate, and filial.
The king cherished him deeply.
At that time, a deity said to the king:
"The minister Rāhu plots to seize the throne."
He has imprisoned and killed the father king and slain his two elder brothers;
before long, his army shall come to kill you, O King.
Hearing these words, the king’s heart was struck with terror and his hair stood on end.
He looked up and asked,
"Who are you, sir?
I hear only your voice but do not see your form."
"What you have declared is not true," he replied to the king,
"for I am the guardian deity of the palace."
"Because Your Majesty governs the kingdom with the merit of virtue and the True Dharma, never wronging the people, we have come first to inform you.
You should depart quickly; misfortune will arrive before long."
Having heard this, the king immediately entered the palace and reflected within himself that he wished to seek refuge in another kingdom.
At that time, there were two routes leading to a neighboring country.
One route was calculated to take seven days to reach;
the other route was calculated to take fourteen days to reach.
The king immediately procured provisions for seven days and departed, carrying his son with him;
the queen followed behind.
As they traveled in great haste, their minds became disordered and confused, and they mistakenly took a fourteen-day path.
The road is perilous and lacks both water and grass;
when first setting out, we took provisions for only one person,
yet now three people must share them.
After several days, their provisions were exhausted, yet the road ahead remained long.
The King and his consort raised their voices and wept bitterly, exclaiming, "How strange! How bitter!"
"Since my birth, I have never heard of such suffering and distress.
Why is it that today I must experience it myself?
All manner of calamities have come upon me at once."
Throwing their entire bodies to the ground, they repented, saying,
"What evil deeds did we commit in our past lives that we now suffer this calamity?
Having thought this, they wept bitterly and fell to the ground in a swoon.
He further reflected to himself:
"It is not fitting that three lives perish together at this death.
It would be better to kill the lady, take her flesh to sustain my own life, and thereby continue the life of my son."
Having thought this, he drew his sword, intending to kill the queen.
When her son saw that the king wished to kill his mother,
he stepped forward, seized the king’s hand, and asked for the reason.
The king immediately wept, his eyes filling with tears of grief;
in a low voice, he said to his son,
"I wish to kill your mother to take her flesh and blood so as to sustain my remaining life."
"If they do not kill me, I shall also die of my own accord.
It is the same with my own body.
Now, as for life and death, where exactly do they reside?"
"To save my son's life, I wish to kill your mother.
The son said to his father,
"If Your Majesty kills my mother, I shall likewise not eat."
Where is there a son who eats the flesh of his own mother?
Since the son would die along with his parents if he did not eat the flesh,
it is now fitting for Your Majesty to kill the son, take his flesh, and save the lives of the parents.
Upon hearing his son's words,
the king immediately fainted, rolled about, and fell to the ground,
saying to his son:
"You are like my own eyes.
What person would ever pluck out their own eyes to eat them?
I would rather lose my life."
He would never kill his son to eat his flesh.
The son spoke again to his father, saying,
"If my life were cut short, my flesh would soon become putrid and rotten."
It has not been many days since I left you.

I only pray that my parents will come to my side every day and cut three jin of flesh from my body, dividing it into three portions: two portions to offer to my parents and one portion for myself to eat, thereby sustaining our lives.
The father followed his son’s words;
he cut three jin of flesh from his own body to sustain his life as he proceeded on the road.
After two days, he had not yet arrived, and the flesh of his body was completely exhausted.
With his joints still connected and his remaining life-force not yet severed,
he immediately fell to the ground.
Upon seeing this, his parents rushed forward to embrace him and wailed aloud with a loud cry.
And they spoke these words:
"We have acted without cause, devouring your flesh and causing you such agony."
The road ahead is still long and we have not yet reached our destination.
Your flesh is now exhausted;
let us now end our lives together and gather our corpses in one place.
Having already eaten my son’s flesh at the urging of his words, I have now reached this point on my journey;
calculating the distance traveled, only one day's journey remains.
My body now lies here, having surrendered its life.
I pray that my parents will not, like ordinary people, perish together in this one place;
rather, you may cut away all the remaining flesh from the various limbs and joints of my body.
"By using this to save your parents, you shall reach their location.
Following these words,
the parents cut off a small amount of flesh and divided it into three portions.
He gave one part to his son and ate two parts himself;
having finished eating, he departed.
The son rose and stood watching as his parents departed.
At that time, the parents raised their voices and wept bitterly as they followed the road;
once they had gone far away, the Crown Prince could no longer see them.
Longing for his parents, he did not cast his gaze away for even a moment;
after a long while, he fell prostrate upon the ground,
blood flowing from his body as mosquitoes and gadflies fed upon him.
The agonizing pain was beyond description;
with his remaining life-force not yet severed, he raised his voice and made a vow:
"May the calamities and evils from my past lives be completely eradicated from this moment on."
From this day forward, I shall never again dare to do so.
Now, I offer my own flesh as sustenance for my parents;
may my parents always obtain further blessings.
Sleeping in peace and awakening in peace,
one sees no evil dreams;
protected by the heavens and loved by humans.
The secret plots of local officials and bandits shall be extinguished;
may there be auspiciousness in all undertakings.
I offer my remaining flesh and blood to these various insects, so that they may all be fully satiated.
"May I attain the path of Buddhahood in a future life;
by bestowing upon you the food of the Dharma, may I eliminate your hunger, thirst, and the grave illness of birth and death.
When he made this vow, [the earth shook].
Heaven and earth shook violently, and the sun lost its brilliant light.
Having seen this, Śakra immediately manifested as lions, tigers, and wolves,
intending to terrify the Prince and come to devour him.
The Prince said,
"If you wish to eat me, take as much as you please;
why are you afraid of me?"
Śakra then spoke, saying:
"I am not of the species of lions, tigers, or wolves;
I am Śakra, the Lord of Devas."
"Therefore, I have come to test you.
Having heard this, the Prince was filled with immeasurable joy.
Śakra then questioned the Prince.
At this moment, you are able to relinquish what is difficult to relinquish;
you are able to offer your own flesh as an offering to your parents.
Regarding such merit, what do you wish it to become?
"Are you a Heavenly King, a Human King, a Brahmā King, or a Māra King?
The Prince replied, "I do not desire these;
I seek the Way of the Buddha to deliver and liberate all beings."
The Heavenly King Śakra said,
"The path of the Buddha is long and distant;
one must undergo diligent suffering for a long time."
Only then will it be accomplished.
How can you endure such suffering?
The Prince replied:
"Even if a wheel of fire were placed upon the crown of my head,
I would never retreat from the path of the Buddha because of suffering.
Śakra, Lord of Devas, said:
"Your words are mere empty talk;
who would believe you?
The Prince immediately made a vow, saying:
If I have deceived Śakra, the Lord of Devas,
may the wounds on my body never heal from beginning to end;
if it is not so, [may they heal].
"May my body be restored and my blood turn into milk.
Once the Prince had made this vow,
his body immediately returned to its former state.
The blood turned white and became milk;
his physical form and features became more upright and excellent than ever before.
Śakra then praised him, saying:
"If you attain the Way of the Buddha, I pray that you will deliver me first.
At that time, the parents, having reached a neighboring kingdom,
related the aforementioned matter in detail to the king of that country.
"My son has provided filial support with his own flesh; such was the nature of his service.
When the neighboring king heard this, he was moved by his compassionate filiality and immediately dispatched troops to escort him back to his own country.
He went to wage war against Rāhu.
His father, leading his host of soldiers, returned along the road and passed by the place where he had parted from his son.
He then thought to himself:
"My son is dead! I must collect his remains and return to my native land.
Raising her voice in mournful wailing, she searched for him along the road.
Seeing from afar that the Prince’s body had recovered and was more upright and handsome than ever before,
he immediately went forward to embrace him, his heart filled with a mixture of grief and joy,
and spoke to the Prince, saying:
"Is my son alive now?
At that time, the prince related all these matters in detail to his parents.
His parents were filled with joy, and together they mounted a great elephant and returned to their native land.
By the power of the Prince’s merit, compassion, and filial piety, he reclaimed his own kingdom.
His father, the King, immediately installed the Prince as king.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
The father at that time is now my present father, Śuddhodana;
the mother at that time...
The one who was my mother, Queen Māyā, is now present here.
The Prince is now my own self.
The Śakra of that time is now Ājñātakauṇḍinya.
Section Four: The Section on Śyāma. As stated in the *Śyāmaputra Sūtra*:
In a past age, there was an elder in the kingdom of Kāśī.
Having no children, the husband and wife lost their sight;
they resolved in their hearts to enter the mountains to seek the unsurpassed path.
Cultivating pure resolve and delighting in seclusion,
there was at that time a bodhisattva named Sarvadarśanaviśeṣa who thought to himself:
This person’s resolve is subtle and profound;
his eyes see nothing.
If he enters the mountains, he will surely encounter wrongful harm.
When the Bodhisattva’s life came to an end, he vowed to be reborn into the family of a lay elder;
his name was Śyāma.
He was filially pious and benevolent, and he practiced the ten wholesome deeds.
Day and night he served his parents with diligence,
as if a person were serving the heavens.
When he was over ten years old,
Śyāma knelt upright and addressed his parents, saying,
"I originally conceived the great resolve to enter the deep mountains to seek the aspiration for emptiness, tranquility, and unsurpassed, true,
and correct awakening. How could I abandon my fundamental vow merely because of you, my parents?"
Taking their parents' words, Śyāma immediately entered the mountains.
He gave all the household wealth and possessions to the poor,
then went into the mountains and made a hut of grass.
He provides beds and bedding that are neither cold nor hot,
always ensuring they are appropriate.
Having entered the mountains for one year,
the various fruits were abundant and delicious, all of which tasted sweet;
springs gushed forth, their water clear and cool.
The ponds were filled with five-colored lotuses, birds, beasts, and music;
all beings faced one another with hearts of loving-kindness, free from any intent to harm.
Śyāma, in his supreme filial piety and compassion, stepped upon the ground fearing it might cause pain.
The gods and mountain deities constantly assumed human forms to comfort him day and night.
Śyāma, wearing a deer-skin garment and carrying a water jar, went to fetch water;
the deer and various birds likewise went there to drink.
They did not fear or hesitate.
At that time, there was a king of the Kāśī kingdom who entered the mountains to hunt.
Seeing a herd of deer by the water’s edge, the king drew his bow and shot at them;
the arrow mistakenly struck Śāṇa in the chest.
Pierced by the poisoned arrow, Śāṇa raised his voice and cried out:
"Who was it that shot and killed three practitioners of the Way with a single arrow?
Upon hearing these words, the king immediately dismounted his horse and went before Śyāma.
Śyāma said to the king:
The elephant perishes because of its tusks;
the rhinoceros dies because of its horn;
the peacock comes to its end because of its plumage.
"The deer provide their skin and flesh;
why am I now sitting here doing nothing, dying for no reason?
The King asked Śyāma:
"What kind of person are you?
Wearing a deer-skin garment, you are no different from a beast.
Śyāma replied:
I am a native of Wangguo.
I have come here with my blind parents to study the Way for more than twenty years.
Never before have we been harmed by tigers, wolves, or venomous insects.
Now I have been shot and killed by the king.
At that very moment, a violent wind suddenly arose in the mountains, blowing and breaking the trees,
while hundreds of birds wailed in grief.
The lions, bears, brown bears, and other species of wild beasts all let out great cries;
the sun lost its brilliance, and the flowing springs ran dry.
The various flowers withered and died, and a thunderous earthquake shook the earth.
At that time, the blind parents rose in alarm and said to one another,
"Śyāma has been gone for a long time fetching water and has not yet returned."
"Perhaps he has been harmed by venomous insects;
the birds and beasts are crying out unlike their usual state.
When winds rise and trees break, there must be some calamitous anomaly."
At that time, the king was struck with terror and deeply reproached himself,
saying, "I have committed a heinous act;
intending to shoot a deer, my arrow has mistakenly struck and killed this practitioner of the Way."
The sin is extremely grave;
because of coveting a small piece of meat, one undergoes heavy calamity.
I now [possess] all the rare treasures of the kingdom.
The palace courtesans, mounds, walls, cities, and towns all cried out to save the life of his son.
Then the king reached out with his hand and pulled at the arrow in Śyāma’s chest;
it was so deep that it would not come out.
Birds and beasts gathered from all four directions, their cries shaking the mountains;
the king became even more terrified,
his three hundred and sixty joints trembling.
Every joint moved. Śyāma said,
"This is not the King's fault."
"This is brought about by my own past transgressions.
I do not begrudge my body or life;
I only pity my blind parents."
Now that my years have reached old age and both my eyes have become blind,
I shall one day pass away without a self and without anyone to look after me; for this reason, I am filled with anguish.
"It is not for the sake of poison or pain.
The king spoke again with renewed emphasis:
"I would rather enter the hells and undergo punishment for a hundred kalpas."
"If Śyāma is restored to life,
should my son's life end, I shall not return to my kingdom;
instead, I will remain in the mountains to provide for your parents."
Do not harbor such thoughts as you did when you were alive;
all the devas, nāgas, and spirits shall bear witness to this.
"I shall not fail this vow.
When Śyāma heard the king's oath,
his heart was filled with joy and gladness.
Though I die, I shall have no regrets.
I leave my parents to rely upon Your Majesty;
by supporting these practitioners of the Way, their present offenses will be extinguished and they shall obtain immeasurable merit.
The king said,
"Tell me where my parents are;
let me know this before you die."
Śyāma immediately pointed out the path:
"From here, follow this trail;
not far from here, you will surely see a thatched hut."
"My parents are inside;
Your Majesty, please proceed slowly so as not to cause my parents any fear."
Using skillful means and expedient wisdom, awaken his mind and convey my deepest apologies:
impermanence has now arrived;
I must depart for the next world.
"I do not begrudge my own life, but I only think of my parents.
They are old and both blind;
were I to die suddenly, they would have no one to rely upon. It is for this reason that I am filled with anguish."
Having used extreme cruelty against myself, I have died as my constant habit;
this is brought about by the offenses of past lives, from which there is no escape.
Now I repent of it myself.
May my transgressions be extinguished and merit arise.
May we meet one another in every lifetime and never be separated.
May my parents live out their full natural lifespan.
May there be no sorrow or affliction.
Devas, nāgas, and spirits shall constantly follow,
protect, and assist you, so that all calamities are extinguished.
Upon hearing these words, the king took several attendants and went directly to his parents' dwelling.
After the king had departed, Śyāma suddenly passed away.
Birds and beasts wailed and circled around Śyama’s corpse, licking the blood on his chest with their mouths.
Hearing these sounds, the blind parents became even more filled with loathing and terror.
As the king traveled with such haste, he brushed against and shook the grasses and trees.
A human voice was heard from within the coffin.
His parents were startled and said, "Who is this? This is not the conduct of our son."
The king said,
"I am the King of Kāśī.
Having heard that a man of the Way was practicing the Path in the mountains, I have come to make offerings."
The parents said,
"Welcome, Great King! We are honored that you have condescended to travel so far from your majesty to visit this humble wilderness."
Is Your Majesty’s person in good health?
Are the palace ladies, the crown prince, the officials, and the citizens all well?
Are the winds and rains harmonious, are the five grains abundant, and do neighboring states refrain from mutual aggression?
The king replied to the practitioner, saying,
"I have received your grace, O practitioner, and all is well.
The king then inquired after the blind parents, saying:
Having come to these mountains, you have labored with great diligence and hardship.
Among the trees, have the birds and beasts caused you no harm?
In these mountains, have you remained at ease as the cold and heat shifted with the seasons?
The blind parents said,
"We have constantly lived in peace and security, having received the King's great kindness.
We have a filial son named Śyāma."
I always gather fruits and melons for you, and the spring water is naturally abundant.
The winds and rains in the mountains are harmonious and temperate, never lacking in anything.
I have grass mats upon which you may sit and fruits and melons which you may eat.
When Śyāma was out fetching water and was about to return at dawn,
the King heard of this and his heart was grieved; tears fell from him as he spoke.
I am a wicked and lawless man who entered the mountains to hunt.
Seeing a herd of deer by the water's edge, I drew my bow and shot at them;
my arrow mistakenly struck Śāṇa, and thus I have come to speak with you.
Upon hearing this, his parents threw themselves to the ground,
their bodies collapsing like a great mountain crumbling; the earth then shook.
The king then stepped forward himself to support and lead him.
His parents wailed and wept, looking up to heaven and saying, "Our son was filial and compassionate;
he would have feared that treading upon the earth would cause it pain."
"For what offense did you shoot and kill him?
Just now, when the wind rose and the trees shook, a hundred birds cried out in sorrow all at once;
I suspected my son had died."
His mother wept and cried out,
but his father said,
"Stop for now."
In human life, death is inevitable and cannot be averted.
For now, let me ask the King: where did you shoot Śyāma?
Is he dead or alive?
When the King recounted Śyāma’s words,
his parents were overcome with grief,
saying, "If we lose our son even once, both of us shall surely die."
According to the *Saṃyukta-ratna-piṭaka-sūtra*,
the king then wept and spoke this verse:
"I am the king of this land, And I have come to hunt upon this mountain."
Desiring only to hunt birds and beasts, I did not realize that I was harming others.
I now renounce the royal throne To serve my blind parents;
They are no different from your own children— Be careful not to give way to grief or suffering.
The blind parents replied to the king in verse:
"My son is compassionate, filial, and obedient; Among gods and humans, there is none like him.
Though Your Majesty shows us pity, How could anyone equal my son?"
"May Your Majesty have compassion on us; we pray that you will show us the place where our son is, so that we may be at his side and share in his life and purpose.
Thereupon, the king led his parents toward the child's location.
Beating their breasts in anguish, they wailed and said:
"My son was compassionate, kind, and filial beyond compare. Then the gods of the heavens, the mountains, the trees, the rivers, the ponds, and all the various deities spoke verses to them, saying:
Śakra, Brahmā, and the World-Rulers—why do you not assist me, a filial son? Let him see such profound suffering;
moved by my filial devotion, quickly save his life!
Furthermore, the *Śyāmaka-putra Sūtra* states:
"I pray that Your Majesty will lead us two to the side of the corpse.
The King then led the blind parents to the side of the corpse.
The father held his feet,
and the mother held his head;
they looked up to heaven and cried out loudly.
The mother then licked the wound on Śyāma’s chest with her tongue, praying:
"May the poison enter my mouth;
I am already old and my eyes see nothing."
I have substituted my own body for my son;
Śyāma lives and I die.
In death, I have no regrets.
Śyāma was so profoundly filial that it was known even to Heaven and Earth;
the arrow should be pulled out and the poison removed,
for Śyāma shall be restored to life.
Thereupon, the throne of the second Heavenly King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven immediately shook.
With his divine eye, he saw two practitioners of the Way embracing their child and wailing;
then, the fourth Tuṣita Heaven Palace was heard to shake as well.
Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Heavenly Kings, immediately following the Fourth Heavenly King, descended before Śyāma in the time it takes a person to bend and extend their arm;
they then poured divine medicine into Śyāma’s mouth.
The medicine entered Śyama’s mouth and the arrow was drawn out by itself;
he returned to life as before,
and his parents were filled with joy and wonder.
Seeing that Śyāma had died and then returned to life, with both eyes wide open,
the birds and beasts were all filled with great joy;
the wind ceased, the clouds dispersed, and the sun shone with renewed brilliance.
Springs gushed forth, and various flowers of five colors bloomed;
the trees flourished with blossoms twice as profusely as usual.
The king rejoiced greatly, unable to contain his joy.
He paid obeisance to Śakra Devendra, then returned his salutations to his parents and to Śyāma.
He wished to offer the wealth of the kingdom to the ascetic.
Śyāma said, "If Your Majesty wishes to repay this kindness,"
"Your Majesty, please return to your kingdom and bring peace and security to the people, ensuring that all observe the precepts.
Do not resume hunting and shooting, which causes the premature injury and death of insects and beasts;
in this present life, your own person will find no peace."
When one's lifespan is exhausted, one shall enter the hells.
While people dwell in this world,
the bonds of affection are but temporary.
Parting lasts for a long time;
nothing can be preserved forever.
Your Majesty possessed merit in past lives, and by that merit you have now attained the status of king.
"Do not become negligent on account of having attained self-mastery.
Your Majesty, you should reproach yourself;
from this day forward, you shall act according to the instructions of Śyāma."
The several hundred attendants all leaped for joy and received and upheld the five precepts.
The King took his leave and returned to the palace,
ordering that throughout the kingdom, all those whose parents were blind, such as Śyāma, [should be provided for].
All should provide offerings;
one must not abandon them.
To violate this is a grave offense.
Thereupon, throughout the kingdom, all followed the King’s instructions;
they upheld the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions,
so that upon death they were reborn in the heavens and none entered the three evil realms.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"The son Śyāma of a former life was I myself;
the blind father was the present King Śuddhodana."
The blind mother was Queen Māyā;
the King of the Kāśī country was Ānanda;
and the Lord Śakra at that time was Maitreya.
That I have swiftly attained the unsurpassed, true, and correct path is entirely due to the virtue of filial piety.
Section Five: Causes and Conditions of Karma. As stated in the *Saṃyukta-ratna-piṭaka-sūtra*:
The Buddha said:

In the distant past, during a long-elapsed age,
I was born in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī as the son of a householder.
Her name was Maitrakanyā.
Her father had died early, and she lived with her mother.
As their family was poor, she sold firewood daily, earning two coins to provide for her mother's support.
His schemes became increasingly successful;
he obtained four coins daily to provide for his mother.
Subsequently, his condition gradually improved, and he obtained eight coins daily to make offerings to his mother.
Later, as people flocked to him seeking profit,
he earned sixteen coins daily to provide for his mother.
When others saw his intelligence and merit, they were filled with admiration.
They all came to urge him to go to sea to gather treasures.
Having heard this, he informed his mother;
seeing his filial piety and compassion, she thought he would not be able to leave.

Your son has already given his word to another; I fear he will prove unfaithful to his promise."
He then pulled himself out by his own hand, tearing off dozens of his mother's hair strands and wounding her.
He subsequently departed for the sea, where he obtained much treasure and returned.
On the way back, his traveling companions were already ahead of him.

Upon reaching a mountain, she saw a city of lapis lazuli;

Holding four wish-fulfilling jewels and performing music,

for forty thousand years, he experienced great happiness.
Again, a mind of revulsion arose within him, and he abandoned them and departed.
He saw a city of crystal where eight jade maidens,

For eighty thousand years he experienced the utmost great joy;
later, becoming weary of it, he departed.
Upon reaching the city of Silver, there were sixteen jade maidens.
Sixteen *cintāmaṇi* jewels are held aloft to welcome them as before;
they enjoy great happiness for one hundred and sixty thousand years,
after which [the jewels] again depart.
Upon reaching the Golden City, thirty-two jade maidens bearing thirty-two wish-fulfilling jewels came forward to welcome them as before;
there they enjoy great bliss for three million two hundred thousand years.
Later, becoming weary and leaving that place,
he arrived at an iron city.
Upon entering, he saw a man wearing a wheel of fire upon his head.
Having cast it upon the head of the girl Maitrakanyaka, he departed.
Then the girl Maitrakanyaka asked the warder:
"When may I be released from this wheel that I bear?"
The wardens replied,
"In this world there are people who perform deeds of both sin and merit,
just as you have entered the sea and traveled through various cities."
"Then one shall come in the future to receive the retribution for your offenses on your behalf.
If there were no such substitute, you would never fall to the ground.
He asked again:
"What sins or merits did I commit in the past?
The warder replied,
"Because you formerly made an offering of two coins to your mother."
He obtained a city of lapis lazuli, four wish-fulfilling jewels, and four jade maidens;
for forty thousand years he enjoyed their pleasures,
while using four coins to provide for his mother.
He obtained the eight wish-fulfilling jewels and eight jade maidens of the city of Vaiḍūrya,
and for eighty thousand years he enjoyed every pleasure;
with eight coins, he made offerings to his mother.
He obtained a city of white silver, sixteen wish-fulfilling jewels, and sixteen jade maidens;
for one hundred and sixty thousand years he enjoyed happiness.
Because he offered sixteen coins to his mother, he obtained a city of gold.
He possessed thirty-two wish-fulfilling jewels and thirty-two jade maidens,
and for three hundred and twenty thousand years he enjoyed great happiness. Yet,
because he cut his mother’s hair, he has now received this retribution of the iron city and the wheel of fire.
"If someone were to take your place, you might be able to escape.
He then asked the wardens,
"Are there any others in this prison who suffer punishments like mine?"
He replied,
"It is immeasurable and beyond calculation.

may all those who ought to suffer [the consequences] gather here upon my body.
Having formed this thought, the iron wheel immediately fell.
When the hell-wardens saw him, they struck his head with iron forks;
he died immediately and was reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
The girl Maitrī of old was my very self in this present life. For this reason,
even small deeds of good or evil performed toward one's parents yield immeasurable retribution.
Therefore, one should diligently make offerings to one's parents.
Furthermore, the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states:
"The Tathāgata [is superior] to all sages, as well as to one's parents and others."
When one gives rise to wholesome or unwholesome karma, one receives the retribution in the present life.
Furthermore, in the Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra,

How much more so for the Buddha’s great kindness, which universally saves without end!
To repay this grace and virtue, how could one fail to devote one’s person with utmost devotion?

Regarding Wang Qianshi and his sense of mourning for his ancestral tombs: Wang Qianshi of Danyuan served as the Regional Inspector (*Cishi*) of Cizhou during the Tang dynasty.
By nature he was benevolent and filial, and was renowned for his profound prudence.

In the sixth year of the Zhenguan era, he observed the mourning period for his father’s death with an intensity that exceeded the prescribed rites.

Every time the sound of the chime was heard, it was exceptionally clear and penetrating, accompanied by a strange fragrance that extended for several li.

50. Chapter on Filial Piety (49). Chapter Fifty: On Filial Piety. This consists of four sections: the Section on Stating the Intent, the Section on the Five Heinous Offenses, the Section on the Offense of a Wife, and the Section on Abandoning One’s Father. 1. Section on Stating the Intent. First, regarding the establishment of loyalty and the establishment of filial piety: it is said that one who is loyal and filial is called a superior man. If one is not loyal or filial, they are called a petty person. Therefore, the sages established the Way of Filial Piety as the foundation for the governance of the world. It is the root of all virtues and the source of all righteousness. Because it is the root of all virtues, it is honored above all things; because it is the source of all righteousness, it is the most fundamental of all principles. Thus, the *Classic of Filial Piety* says: "Filial piety is the beginning of virtue and the root of humanity. Furthermore, the *Analects* says: "The Master said, 'If one does not serve their parents with filial piety, how can they serve their ruler with loyalty? And: "If one does not serve their elder brothers with fraternal respect, how can they serve their ruler with loyalty? These passages demonstrate that loyalty and filial piety are fundamentally one and the same. Therefore, the sages established the Way of Filial Piety as the basis for governing the world. Although Devadatta constantly sought to harm the Buddha, the Buddha always gave rise to great compassion toward him. Thus the Buddha said:

in the past, there was a merchant leader in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.

"These are the five hundred brahmins who have left the household life and attained the Way.

There was a great sandalwood tree.

The fragrance was perceived from afar as a marvel of the world;

Not long thereafter, the king fell ill with a headache.

A renowned physician examined him and found that only sandalwood could cure his illness.
The king immediately sought it throughout the populace, but none possessed any.

having cut it down, smear it with human blood and cover it over with liver and intestines.

Thereupon, the messenger consulted with his attendants, saying:

"This person has now died;
let him serve as the substitute.

The physician immediately administered the King of Medicines, and the illness was cured.
The entire nation rejoiced, and the king commanded all the people within the kingdom who were ill: [to take this medicine].

Ānanda withdrew to his seat, bowed his head in prostration, and addressed the Buddha with these words:
"This man is wretched.

The Buddha replied,
"In the distant past, during the time of Vipaśyin Buddha,
there was a father and two sons."
His father observed the fasts and precepts without ever being remiss.
The eldest son constantly burned incense in the open courtyard to make offerings to the Buddhas of the ten directions.
The youngest brother was foolish and ignorant of the Triple Gem.
He immediately covered the incense with his robe.
His elder brother said to his younger brother,
"This matter is of great importance."
"Why did he commit this?

His younger brother conceived an evil intent and wished to sever his elder brother's feet;

Now, having become a tree spirit,

Later, they suffered from headaches;
each received their own retribution.
The Buddha said:
The retribution for sins and blessings follows one like a shadow follows a form.
A verse says:
His great compassion brings salvation; His virtue is as vast as heaven and earth; His kindness is deeper than that of parents.
The Venerable Master Yiyue was loyal and filial, exhausting his very life; yet even so, it was difficult to repay his kindness.
Should one violate this principle, both soul and spirit shall perish together. *Fayuan zhulin*, Scroll 50.

Section 53: On Good Friends (*Sakhibandhu*).

Chapter 54: On Evil Friends; Chapter 55: On Discerning Companions. 53. Chapter on Good Friends (51). This chapter consists of two sections. Section One: Exposition of the Intent. As for the ultimate limits of principle, they are found only in good and evil.
Reflecting upon these two paths, they are clearly and easily distinguished:
in the hidden realm there are transgressions and blessings, suffering and joy;
in the manifest realm there are the wise and the foolish, honor and disgrace.
To love honor and loathe disgrace, to seek pleasure and turn away from suffering—
this is what all sentient beings inevitably share.
Yet now, while loving honor, they do not know to admire the worthy.
To seek blessings while remaining ignorant of how to avoid calamity is like sowing chaff and husks yet hoping for a harvest of fine grain each year,
or driving a team of sluggish, lame horses while hoping to gallop far beyond the reach of others.
Is this not delusion?
Even the intelligence of birds, beasts, insects,
and vipers knows to rely on the wind, borrow the momentum of waterfowl, and take advantage of height to accomplish their ends.
How much more so for a human being—how could one not rely on friends to achieve goodness?
Therefore, if one relies on virtuous friends, one’s person will endure and virtue will be perfected;
if one is intimate with the ignorant and obscured, one’s person will be exhausted and one’s reputation will be foul.
Thus, the essence of the profound path emerges from the lofty model;
this is the intent of constant refinement and polishing.
The matter rests with my friend.
It is like a gadfly on an ox that can fly only a hundred paces;
yet if it clings to the tail of a phoenix, it soars ten thousand li in a single flight.
Is this not because they rely on the swift power of the artisan of wings?
They are likewise like ordinary beings who drown and perish in the ultimate realms, unable to transcend the human and celestial worlds;
yet if they rely upon the majesty of the Great Sage, [they may do so].
Then one ascends high to the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and is born together in the pure realm.
Section Two: Citing Scriptural Evidence. As stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*:
"O Bhikṣu Ānanda..."
It is said that half of the holy life (brahmacarya) is called a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra). The Buddha said: "Not so."
One who is fully endowed with the holy life is called a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
It is also said:
"A spiritual friend..."
To speak according to the Dharma and to act according to what one has spoken:
what is meant by speaking according to the Dharma and acting according to the Dharma?
It is to refrain from taking life oneself.
He teaches others not to kill,
up to and including practicing right view himself and teaching others to practice right view.
If one can act in this way, they may be called a true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra).
They cultivate enlightenment for themselves and are also able to teach others to practice enlightenment.
For these reasons, they are called "virtuous friends" (kalyāṇamitra).
They are able to practice themselves in faith, precepts, generosity, learning, and wisdom,
and they are also able to teach others to practice faith, precepts, generosity, learning, and wisdom.
Furthermore, for this reason they are called "virtuous friends" (kalyāṇamitra).
A virtuous friend is so called because they possess wholesome qualities (kuśaladharma).
What are the wholesome dharmas?
They are those actions performed without seeking one's own happiness,
but always seeking happiness for the sake of sentient beings.
When seeing the faults of others, one does not proclaim their shortcomings;
one’s mouth constantly proclaims only matters of pure goodness.
For these reasons, they are called a "virtuous friend" (kalyāṇamitra).
"Good son, just as the moon in the sky gradually waxes from the first day until the fifteenth day,
so too is it with a spiritual friend."
This causes all students to gradually distance themselves from unwholesome dharmas and increase wholesome dharmas.
Good son, if there are those who draw near to virtuous friends (kalyāṇamitra), [they shall likewise attain this].
Originally there was no concentration, wisdom, liberation, or the knowledge and vision of liberation;
now they have come into being,

Thus, one shall attain increase and expansion.
Furthermore, it says:
"A virtuous friend should observe."
Regarding this person’s thoughts of greed, hatred, and delusion,

for those with much malice,

For those with excessive discursive thought and vitarka,
teach them to practice counting the breaths. For those with excessive attachment to a self, [teach them to practice mindfulness of the body].
One should analyze the eighteen elements and so forth;
having heard this, one practices in sequence to attain the four foundations of mindfulness,
contemplating the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena.
Having attained this contemplation, one next contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*).
Having contemplated in this manner, one next attains the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*).
From the attainment of the stage of Heat, one gradually proceeds until attaining the fruits of Arhatship or Pratyekabuddhahood.
The bodhisattva path, the Mahāyāna, and the fruit of Buddhahood all arise based upon this;
there is no further doubt or obstruction.
It brings about both self-benefit and the benefit of others.
One who does not add water or milk [to the pure teaching] is called a true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) in the rank of a Dharma teacher.
If one does not possess these qualities, they are not a spiritual friend.
The method of adding water cannot be followed as a precedent.
Therefore, the *Buddhatva-śāstra* quotes a verse from a sutra:
"Lacking knowledge and lacking wholesome discernment, an evil friend destroys right practice."
When a spider falls into milk, the milk turns into poison;
therefore, one must truly benefit sentient beings.
First subdue yourself, and only then teach others.
There is no fault of limited learning; no fault of regression;
no fault of distraction.
There is no fault of contemptuousness; no fault of inversion;
no fault of greedy seeking.
There is no fault of ill-will;
there is no fault of misconduct;
there is no fault of attachment to a self.
There is no loss in minor practices.
One who possesses these ten qualities is called a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Thus, a verse in the *Śrī-saṃghāṭa-sūtra* (or *Mahāyāna-sūtrālaṃkāra*) says:
"One who is learned and has seen the truth, who is skillful in exposition and compassionate,
