fifth, they conceal each other's faults;

Seventh, not despising those who are poor and lowly.

Furthermore, the *Vyavahāra-śāstra* quotes a verse spoken by the Buddha:

Furthermore, the *Kāla-vyūha-ṣaḍ-abhimukha-namaskāra-sūtra* states:
"There are four types of virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*)."
First, though appearing like an enemy on the outside, they harbor deep affection within.
Second, they offer direct admonition in his presence but speak of his virtues to others.
Third, when he is ill or facing official scrutiny, they relieve his anxiety and distress.
Fourth, seeing a person who is poor and lowly, one should not abandon them in mind, but should instead cultivate the wholesome intention of wishing for them to become wealthy.
Furthermore, there are four types of kinsmen and friends:

Third, when one's acquaintances have died, one attends to their encoffining and burial.
Fourth, when one's acquaintances have already died, one continues to dwell upon their households.

Having spoken these words,
King Brahmadatta spoke in verse:
"If there is such a minister as this, he should be granted a heavy reward of food and stipends;
he must be like a fierce and strong crow that seeks food for its master without sparing its own life.
After King Brahmadatta had spoken this verse, [the crow said:]
He spoke again to the crow, saying:
"Excellent, you crow!
From now on, you shall come here constantly to take fragrant and delicious food."
If anyone should obstruct you and refuse to give you food,
come and inform me;
I myself will give you my own allotted portion of food.
And he was about to depart.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"You should all know this."
That king of crows was I myself;
the crow who at that time acted as master and stole food was none other than the bhikṣu Udāyin.
King Brahmadatta was none other than King Śuddhodana;
at that time, there was the bhikṣu Udāyin.
Just as he caused him to rejoice and take food for me, so it is now;
he causes King Śuddhodana to feel joy in his heart and likewise brings food for my sake.
The verse says:
Washing the body and bathing in virtue, The furnace of the mind is tempered firm. When spring comes, ice melts;
when autumn arrives, orchids wither. The wise person becomes enlightened; The foolish companion increases entanglement.
Aspiring to ascend the Jewel Ground, may I encounter virtuous conditions.

(54) Chapter Fifty-four: On Evil Friends (51). This chapter consists of two sections. Section One: Exposition of the Intent. Now, when the Great Sage bestowed his transformative teachings, he rightly gathered and guided the minds of all beings.
The two gates of good and evil are employed to mark the ultimate tenet:
those of the good class ascend to purity, while those termed evil descend downward.
This is truly because karma and delusion have not yet collapsed, causing one to be caged within the three realms.
The passions and sensory objects remain unquiet, obscuring and clouding the five fires;
one stagnates in the drowning depths of the eight inversions and toils under the fetters of the four modes of birth.
Therefore, by following false teachers and placing trust in evil companions,
one causes afflictions and delusions to become difficult to restrain and leads to constant agitation.
The horse of the mind runs wild, and the monkey of the emotions is hard to control.
Those who cultivate merit and mind the good rarely fail to hear of them;
yet those who commit offenses and harbor transgressions increase day by day. Because of this, the cycle of birth and death continues without end.
How could the Great Sage not feel heartache when he pities them?
Section Two: Quotations from Scriptural Sources. As stated in the *Śikṣānanda-ṣaḍdiśapraṇāma-sūtra*:
"There are four types of evil associates (*pāpamitra*).
The first are those who harbor enmity within while outwardly pretending to be an associate."
Second, they speak pleasant words in the presence of others but speak ill of them behind their backs.
Third, when in distress, they appear sorrowful and suffering in the presence of others but rejoice behind their backs.
Fourth, they appear outwardly affectionate and close while inwardly hatching schemes of malice.
Furthermore, there are four types of evil associates:
first, those who become greatly enraged at even a slight offense;
second, those who, when asked to perform a task on their behalf, refuse to do so.
Third, seeing someone in distress, they flee to avoid them.
Fourth, seeing a person die, they abandon them and do not look back.
Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
A bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates that there is no duality between a wicked elephant and a wicked spiritual friend. Why is this?
Because their bodies will both perish,
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has no fear or dread toward evil elephants and the like.
One should give rise to a mind of fear and dread toward evil associates. Why is this?
Because such evil elephants and the like can only destroy the body, but cannot destroy the mind.
Because an evil associate ruins both [the self and others].
While such evil elephants and the like ruin only a single body,
an evil associate ruins immeasurable virtuous bodies and immeasurable virtuous minds.
These evil elephants and the like can only destroy the impure and foul body;
however, an evil spiritual friend (pāpamitra) can destroy both the pure body and the pure mind.
These evil elephants and the like can only destroy the physical body.
A bad friend destroys the Dharma-body;
being killed by a wild elephant does not necessarily lead to the three evil realms,
but being killed by a bad friend inevitably leads to the three evil realms.
While such wicked elephants and the like are merely enemies to the body,
a bad spiritual friend is an enemy to the wholesome dharmas;
for this reason, the bodhisattva—
One should always remain far removed from all evil associates.
Furthermore, in the *Ekottarika Āgama*,
the World-Honored One spoke this verse:
Do not associate with evil companions, nor follow the ways of fools;
you should draw near to virtuous friends, those who are the most excellent among men.
Among men there is no such thing as evil; it is like associating with poison that one becomes familiar with evil.
In the future, one will surely plant the roots of evil and forever walk in darkness.
Furthermore, the *Madhyama Āgama* states:
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus.
There are seven types of enemies;
the Dharma acts as an enemy.
First, it does not wish for the enemy to possess a beautiful appearance.
Although they delight in bathing and anointing their bodies with famous perfumes,
for the sake of physical form,
their minds are shrouded by anger and they act as enemies toward one another.
Second, one does not wish for an enemy to sleep in peace, even though they lie upon a bed with pillows covered in fine brocades;
nevertheless, their anxiety and suffering do not cease,
for their mind is shrouded by hatred as they act as an enemy.
Third, one does not wish for an enemy to obtain great benefit.
Although they ought to obtain benefit, they do not;
although they ought not to obtain benefit, they do.
These two parties, being mutually antagonistic, have their minds shrouded by hatred and act as enemies toward one another.
Fourth, one does not wish for the enemy to have friends;
yet if they do have relatives and companions, [the enemy] abandons them and flees from them.
One becomes an enemy to others because the mind is shrouded by hatred.
Fifth, one does not wish for the enemy to have a good reputation; rather, their evil name and foul fame spread in all directions because the mind is shrouded by hatred.
Thus, one becomes an enemy to others because the mind is shrouded by hatred.
Sixth, one does not wish for an enemy to possess extreme wealth.
Should that great rich man happen to lose his property,
he might allow anger to cloud his mind and thus become an enemy.
Seventh, one does not wish for an enemy, having already committed evil deeds of body, speech, and mind, to go to a good destination after death; rather, upon the end of life,
they will certainly go to an evil destination.
They are born in the hells and act as enemies.
Furthermore, the *Buddha-benxing-jing* (Sutra on the Buddha’s Past Deeds) says: At that time, the Buddha told [them]:
The bhikṣus said:
"I recall that in the distant past,
at the foot of the Snowy Mountains, there were two-headed birds."
They shared a single body and dwelt there;
one head was named Garuḍa.
One head is named Upakāruṇḍa; as for those two birds,
whenever one head sleeps, the other immediately wakes.
Once, when that garuḍa was asleep,
there was a fruit tree named mātuluṅga near his head as he lay awake.
When the flowers of that tree fell,
the wind blew them to the side of his head as he was waking;
at that time, his head had this thought:
Although I now eat these flowers alone,
once they enter my belly, both heads simultaneously obtain color and strength, and both are relieved of hunger and thirst;
yet that waking head does not allow the sleeping head to wake.
Without informing him,
he silently ate those flowers.
Later, when the one with the sleeping head awoke, [he realized what had happened].
His belly became full, and as he belched and gasped for breath, he spoke thus to that head:
"Where did you obtain this fragrant, delicious, and exquisite food and drink that you have eaten?"
"May my body be peaceful, secure, and well-satisfied;
may the sounds I produce be subtle and exquisite. Thus spoke Baudhu.
While you were asleep,
not far from this spot at the side of my head,
there was a tree bearing the fruit of the mādhuka flower.
At that time, a single flower fell onto the side of my head.
At that moment, I thought to myself:
"Now I shall eat this flower all by myself."
If it enters the belly, one simultaneously obtains physical strength and is relieved of hunger and thirst;
for this reason, at that time, I did not cause you to awaken,
nor did I inform you of it.
He immediately ate this flower.
At that time, having heard these words,
his head gave rise to a mind of anger, resentment, and malice.
He formed this thought:
"The food he has obtained,
he does not inform me of."
Without calling me to wake up,
he simply ate by himself.
If it is like this...
From this day forward, regarding whatever food and drink I obtain, I shall not call out to them to wake them and inform them;
yet those two heads will at one time travel and wander about together.
Suddenly encountering a poisonous flower,
he thought to himself:
"I shall eat this flower."
"I wish that both heads may die at the same time.
Then he spoke to that garuḍa:
"While you are now asleep, I shall remain awake. When the garuḍa heard these words from the head of Upagaruḍa, [he remained silent].
He immediately fell asleep.
Then, that Garuḍa-king sought out and ate poisonous flowers.
Once the Garuḍa-king had awakened, [he saw...]
Coughing and gasping for breath,
he immediately realized there was this poisonous vapor and addressed the headman with these words:
"What evil food did you eat just before you woke up that has caused my body to find no peace and brought me to the brink of death?"
Furthermore, it causes my speech to become coarse and harsh,
and creates obstacles that hinder the production of sound, making it ineffective. Thereupon,
the head of awakening replied to the head [of delusion], saying:
"While you were asleep, I ate poisonous flowers;
I pray that both our heads may die at the same time.
Then, that head spoke to the other head, saying:
"What is this haste you have shown?
Why have you committed such an evil deed?
Then he spoke in verse:
While you were sleeping in the past, I ate exquisite flowers of sweet and delicious flavor;
when the wind blew those flowers toward me, you instead gave rise to such great anger.
May I never see such foolish people, nor may I ever dwell together with the ignorant.
"Dwelling with delusion brings no benefit; it harms oneself and harms the bodies of others.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If you have any doubts in your hearts..."
At that time, the garuḍa bird who ate the beautiful flowers—
do not entertain any other thought—
he was none other than myself.
At that time, the bird Upakāruṇḍa who ate the poisonous flowers was none other than this Devadatta;
at that time, I acted for his benefit.
On the contrary, they give rise to anger;
now it is the same again.
I teach for their benefit.
On the contrary, they have instead treated me as an enemy. Furthermore, the *Buddha-benxing-jing* (Sutra on the Original Deeds of the Buddha) states:
"At that time, the World-Honored One..."
Accompanied by Nanda, he entered the city of Kapilavastu.
Having entered, they gradually arrived at a fishmonger’s shop.
At that time, the World-Honored One saw that upon a bed of straw within the shop lay one hundred stinking, putrid dead fish.
Having set aside that grass mat and seen it, he addressed the Elder Nanda, saying: "Nanda!"
"Come, take this handful of grass for the fish-stall.
Then Nanda addressed the Buddha, saying,
"As the World-Honored One has instructed."
Having spoken these words, he immediately drew out a handful of foul-smelling,
putrid *kuśa* grass from beneath the fish stall in that shop.
Once he had grasped it, [he departed].
The Buddha spoke again, saying:
"Elder Nanda, hold him for a short while, then release him back to the ground."
Nanda replied, "As the World-Honored One has instructed," and immediately grasped the grass and held it still.
At that time, Nanda seized the grass,
and after a short while, he dropped it to the ground.
Then the Buddha again addressed Nanda, saying:
"Smell your own hand.
At that time, Nanda immediately smelled his hand.
Then the Buddha again addressed Nanda, saying:
"What is the scent of your hands?
The Elder Nanda replied,
"World-Honored One."
There is nothing but impure, putrid, and foul-smelling odors.
At that time, the Buddha said to the Elder Nanda: "So it is, so it is."
If a person associates with evil friends,
becoming their companion and dwelling together with them,
even though they may follow one another's lead for a short time;
Later, because of the habitual conditioning of his evil karma,
his ill repute spread far and wide.
At that time, the World-Honored One...
On account of this matter,
he spoke these verses:
"Just as one standing beneath a fish stall Takes up a handful of straw with their hand."
The hands of such a person will smell like fish; associating with evil friends is just like this.
The verse says:
Lofty is the city of Rājagṛha, Lush is the Gṛdhrakūṭa Bamboo Grove.
Within this world, there are spirits who manifest as elders, Skillfully luring people into the darkness of ignorance.
The virtuous admire them and receive blessings; Evil companions delight in enmity and resentment.
The paths of good and evil diverge, leading to ascent or descent; As with the fragrance of incense and the stench of rancid herbs, their destinies part ways.
Chapter 55: On Choosing Friends (51). This chapter consists of two sections. Section One: Exposition of the Intent. Now I have heard it said:
The Sūtra states that one must not be separated for even a moment from a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra),
nor from an evil friend (pāpamitra).
One must not approach it even for a moment.
However, the consciousness-mind of an ordinary person is like unbleached silk;
it changes according to conditions, and the colors it receives differ.
When objects come to permeate the mind, the mind responds to those objects; as the mind and its objects mutually reinforce one another, the karma of good and evil manifests.
Thus we know that what the Triple Gem relies upon for sustenance is the material object, which is therefore held in high esteem.
Since their virtue is vast and their merit is great,
they wish that you abandon evil friends and draw near to virtuous people;
thus not only will your own practice be perfected, but others will also be benefited.
This also causes those in both the hidden and manifest realms to turn their hearts [toward the Dharma].
Section Two: Citing Scriptural Evidence. As stated in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*:
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
In a past age, at the base of Cloud Mountain, within a valley of winding peaks where there was a sunlit spot,
a great multitude of birds gathered together and deliberated, saying:
"Today we should elect one bird as king so that the multitude will stand in awe and refrain from unrighteous conduct.
The birds deliberated, saying, "Excellent! Who ought to be king?"
One bird said, "We should drive away the cranes.
Another bird said:
This matter is not permissible. Why?
Because birds with long legs and long necks might inadvertently peck at our brains.
The assembly all said, "So be it.
Then another bird spoke, saying,
"We should elect the goose as king."
Its color was a pure white, revered by all the birds.
The birds spoke again, saying,
"This is also not acceptable."
Although his countenance is fair, his neck is long and crooked;
since his own neck is not straight,
how can he correct others?
Therefore, it is not possible.
Furthermore, the multitude said:
"There is indeed a peacock."
His garments and hair were adorned with colorful decorations that delighted the eyes of those who beheld him;
it seemed he should be made king,
yet they again said it was not possible.
Why is this? Although their feathers and fur are beautiful, they lack a sense of shame and remorse;
every time it is time to dance, their hideous forms appear.
Therefore, it was not possible.
There was a bird who said,
"Let the earth-owl be king."
Why is this? Because he remains tranquil by day and diligently keeps watch at night to protect us;
he is fit to be a king.
The assembly all agreed that this was so.
There was a parrot living in a certain place.
Possessing great wisdom,
he thought to himself:
"It is the nature of birds that they should sleep at night."
Seeking food during the day is the nature of this earth-owl;
it does not sleep at night.
During the day he was prone to sleep,
yet the various birds attended him on all sides;
they kept watch day and night, no longer slumbering.
"It is a most painful matter.
If I were to speak now,
they would surely become enraged and pluck out my feathers."
I was just about to remain silent,
but these various species of birds have suffered distress throughout the long night;
it would be better for me to endure the plucking of my feathers than to transgress the path of righteousness.
He then went before the assembly of birds, raised his wings in reverence, and addressed them, saying: "I pray you, listen;
I shall speak as before."
At that time, when he had expressed his opinion,
the various birds immediately spoke in verse as a reply.
The wise who possess broad knowledge of meaning need not be old;
though you are young in years, O wise one, you should speak at this time.
At that moment, the parrot heard what the birds were saying.
Then he spoke in verse:
"If you follow my will, do not let the king of the owls see your face when he is joyful;
always cause the other birds to be terrified."
How much more so when, in a state of anger, his face is unbearable to behold;
at that time, all the birds said,
"It is truly as you have said."
They immediately gathered together to deliberate on the matter:
"This parrot is clever, wise, and capable of being king.
They then installed him as king.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"That owl at that time was none other than the bhikṣu Channa now."
The parrot was none other than Ānanda in the present life.
Furthermore, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"In times past, there was a flock of chickens that lived in dependence upon a stick forest."
There was a wildcat that preyed upon the roosters until only the hens remained;
later, a crow came and covered them over.
They cohabited and had a son.
When the son made a sound, the father spoke this verse:
"This child is not mine; The father is from the wilds, the mother is from the village."
Together they mated and produced a single offspring, who was neither a crow nor a hen.
If one wishes to learn the father’s cry, it is born of the mother-hen;
if one wishes to learn the mother’s call, its father is the crow.
Learning to crow like a rooster, yet making the sound of a crow when learning to be a rooster—learning both the crow and the rooster, neither of these two succeeds.
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* asks: "How does giving give rise to the *dāna-pāramitā*?"
The Bodhisattva reflects:
"Sentient beings do not know that poverty will result in future lives from their failure to practice generosity;
because of this poverty, the mind of robbery arises."
Because of theft, there is killing;
because of poverty, one lacks sufficient material goods;
because of the lack of material goods, one engages in sexual misconduct.
Because of poverty, one becomes lowly and base;
being base and fearing others, one gives rise to false speech.
In this way, such impoverished persons practice the ten unwholesome paths of action.
If one practices giving,
one will be born with wealth and possessions that are not acquired through unrighteous means. Why is this?
Because the five desires were fully satisfied and nothing was lacking,
as in the case of Devadatta,
who in a previous birth was once a snake.
He gave a frog and a tortoise;
they lived together in a single pond,
forming a close friendship.
Thereafter, the water in the pond dried up, leaving them hungry, destitute, and exhausted,
with no one to whom they could appeal.
At that time, the snake sent the tortoise to summon the frogs.
The frog spoke a verse to dismiss the tortoise, saying:
"If one encounters poverty and loses their original resolve, They do not contemplate the fundamental meaning, but prioritize food.
You must carry my voice and speak it to the snake; A frog shall never come to your side."
If one cultivates generosity, one will have merit in future lives and lack nothing;
thus, one is able to maintain the precepts and remain free from these various evils.
This is how generosity can give rise to the śīlapāramitā.
If one can practice giving to break the mind of stinginess,
then precepts, patience, and so forth will easily become possible to practice,
as was the case with Mañjuśrī.
In the distant past, many eons ago,
he was once a bhikṣu who entered a city to beg for alms.
He obtained a full bowl of joyous pills of a hundred flavors.
Within the city, there was a young boy.
He pursued him and begged for them,
but [the man] did not give them to him immediately;
eventually, the Buddha took two pellets in his own hand.
To state the essential point:
if you can eat one pill yourself and give one pill as an offering to the Sangha, [then you shall attain it].
"I shall give it to you. They both agreed,
and he offered a single *modaka* to the assembly of monks.
Thereafter, in the presence of Mañjuśrī, they received the precepts, generated the bodhicitta, and resolved to become Buddhas.
Such generosity is able to cause one to receive the precepts, generate the bodhicitta, and resolve to become a Buddha.
The verse says:
Good and evil are inherently opposed; light and darkness do not abide together.
The Sage takes pity on deluded beings and enters the cycle of birth and death according to their capacity.
Those who admire his virtue dispel worldly clamor; by disciplining the mind, they perceive the ultimate truth.
Choosing [whom] to associate with determines whether one ends in evil or attains the beginning of deliverance from suffering.

Regarding the conditions for karmic response, I shall briefly cite three accounts: those of the Wei śramaṇa Shi Chaoda, the Wei śramaṇa Shi Senglao, and the Qi śramaṇa Shi Daofeng. As for the Wei śramaṇa Shi Chaoda, he was a monk from Yingyang in the Wei dynasty.

He possessed extensive knowledge and understanding, and was skilled in incantations and esoteric arts.
The Emperor’s prohibition against *tu* (diagrams) and *chan* (prophecies) was particularly strict;
search parties were dispatched everywhere to investigate,
and someone falsely accused Da.

He bound wheels from a carriage around [the man's] neck and placed him under strict guard.
Realizing he had no hope of survival, the man focused his mind exclusively on Avalokiteśvara.
When the fourth watch of the night arrived, the wheel suddenly vanished.
Seeing that the guards were all in a deep, heavy sleep,
he ran outside, intending to flee to a distant place.
Because the prisoner had been incarcerated for a long time,
his legs became cramped and he was unable to travel far.
At dawn, the barbarian cavalry went out in all directions to pursue him.
Da hurriedly prostrated himself and lay down amidst the grass;
as the soldiers and cavalry trampled the grass, it was completely crushed everywhere.
Facing the pursuers so closely that he could not see them, he looked up at the faces of the barbarians.
He had his eyes completely covered with leather.
With single-minded devotion, he submitted to death and focused his sincere faith solely on reciting [the Buddha's name].
During the night, the captors departed, and he was immediately able to escape.
Furthermore, there was the monk Mingdaoren,
who served as the abbot of the Shikusi (Stone Cave Temple) on the Northern Terrace.
During the Wei dynasty’s rule over the world, he presided over the monastery.
Suspecting that the śramaṇas were thieves,
the authorities arrested several hundred monks and bound them all with fivefold fetters.
Sengming was made the leader and bound tightly with ropes from head to foot; at dawn,
he was executed by beheading.
The monk Ming was greatly terrified;
with single-minded devotion, he called upon Avalokiteśvara.
At midnight, he awoke to find that the rope had become slightly loose.
I felt profound joy and my sincerity grew ever more earnest.
At dawn, when I searched for the rope, it was found to be completely severed;
thus, by this means, I escaped.
He fled and ran into the mountains.
When the prison warden came to search for him the next morning, he was nowhere to be seen; there were only severed ropes lying on the ground.
He realized that this was due to the intervention of supernatural power.
"This does not concern human affairs," he said,
and immediately reported it to the Emperor.
The Emperor, believing that the Daoist practitioners had not rebelled, subsequently released them all.
The Śramaṇa Shi Senglang of the Wei dynasty; Shi Senglang of Liangzhou during the Wei period.
When the Wei barbarians attacked Liangzhou, the population within the city was small.
They forced the monks to ascend the city walls;

When the King’s army was about to reach the location of the Wei ruler,

When the appointed time arrived for the meal,
a crimson vapor several zhang in length pierced the sun and passed straight through it.

He replied, "The descent of this extraordinary being from Heaven was solely for the sake of the Way;

The officials suppressed him and ordered him to be brought forward;
he prayed that he need not be killed.
The Emperor then released him.

only Senglang and a few other monks were separately attached to the imperial guard and escorted back east with the Emperor.
When the Wei army returned to the east,
Faling and his fellow student, longing for their native land,
deserted him together along the way.
However, it was strictly guarded with no way to escape;
the sheer cliffs to the east and west were unfathomable in depth,
and large trees hung down from above toward the edge of the bank.
He then tied the drum-flagpole rope to a tree and lowered himself down.
At that time, the night was pitch black;
the base of the cliff was covered entirely with thorns, leaving no place to set foot.
Desiring to climb to the top of the precipice, he feared the army would discover him;
in his panic, he devised a plan and seized a rope to hang himself there,
but his situation could not endure for long.
They said to one another,
"Now that this calamity has suddenly arrived,
we can do nothing but call upon Avalokiteśvara."
He struck his head against the rock with single-minded concentration;
in a brief moment, a brilliant light issued from the sun, illuminating heaven and earth,
and he was finally able to see a place where he could descend through the thorns.
As the light reached the ground, it suddenly vanished into darkness;
only then did he realize that this was the power of the Sage and had nothing to do with the clarity of day.
They congratulated one another on their fortunate encounter, and feeling at ease, they soon fell asleep.
After a long while, at dawn,
he first heard the military drums and horns signaling the army’s departure;
yet the mountains and valleys were so layered and winding that it was as if they stretched for ten thousand li.
Not knowing the way out,
he traveled by waiting for the moonlight.
On the road, he encountered a large tiger that emerged directly before him.
They looked at one another and said,
"Though we have escaped the calamity of being captured by the barbarians, it is difficult to escape from the tiger's mouth.
Lang spoke to the monk, saying:
"It is not as you say.

Now we have encountered this tiger."
"Could it be that a sage is showing us the way?
Thereupon, the two men went straight to where the tiger was.
The tiger then moved forward ahead of them.
If Lang was slightly delayed, the tiger would also pause for a moment;
by dawn he emerged,
but the tiger's tracks had vanished.

after seven days, he reached Quchi.

His ultimate end is unknown.
Shi Daofeng of Mount Gu in Xiangzhou during the Qi dynasty;
his clan and lineage are not detailed.
The world acclaimed him as one who had attained the Way.
He lived with three disciples on Mount Gu in Xiangzhou,
seeking no gain or sustenance.
Some say that he understood all the worldly arts and crafts, such as the elixir of immortality (yellow and white), medicine, and physiognomy;
he traveled between the Qi capital and Ye.
The Emperor frequently visited him to question him;
he would respond without hesitation, answering each matter directly as it was raised.
On one occasion, the Emperor commanded wine and a steamed pig to be served.
The Emperor issued an edict to provide him with food from Fengxian Commandery and sent it for his consumption.
Feng ate to his heart's content without offering any refusal or modesty.
The Emperor then laughed heartily.
He did not speak with him either.
After the carriage had departed, he said to his disciples,

56. Chapter on Retinues (52): This chapter consists of four sections: the Section on Stating the Intent (*Shùyì bù*), the Section on Lamentation (*Āiliàn bù*), the Section on Transformation (*Gǎiyì bù*), and the Section on Severing Attachment (*Lízháo bù*). 1. Section on Stating the Intent (*Shùyì bù*): First, I have privately investigated that retinues are as transient as floating plants, revolving through the cycles of the new and the old.
Departure and remaining are difficult to predict, and meetings are but temporary;
this is truly because good and evil conditions diverge, leading to different destinies of ascent or descent.
As for the virtuous, they are like Nanda, who abandoned glory and desire to follow the Way.
Rāhula abandoned the royal throne and severed the fetters;
like a sandalwood grove surrounded by sandalwood trees,
he delivered beings according to their needs.
The excellence of his mastery as a tamer can be seen herein.
Though [his disciples] were as evil as Devadatta, who split the Saṃgha, or King Ajātaśatru, who murdered his father—
men who constantly harbored poisonous intentions and maintained deep-seated enmity— [the Buddha remained steadfast].
Since they are as alike as a thorny forest,
they are also similar to the species of venomous snakes;
the paths of good and evil diverge, and fortune and calamity can thus be foreseen.

The assembly of monks vied with one another to go to the room and look;
there, the silk was upon the bed,
and on its leg was a burnt wound as large as a coin.
He recovered after more than a hundred days and passed away at the beginning of the Wude era.
Zhenji Temple is the present-day Huadu Temple. The above account is one verification from the *Mingbao ji* (Records of Miraculous Retribution).
The Layman Wang Huishi of the Tang Dynasty: In the northern shop of the Western Market in the capital of the Tang, there was a man named Wang Huishi.
His mother had passed away previously, and he had already completed the period of mourning.
In the second year of the Xianqing era,
his family gave birth to a dog that was both green and yellow;
it happened that the Master’s wife had its food stolen by this dog.
He then struck it several times with his staff.
The dog then spoke in human speech, saying,
"I am your paternal aunt."
"The bride struck me; I was greatly mistaken.
Because I was excessively severe toward my family members, I have consequently received this retribution."
Having now been beaten, he felt ashamed to face your family and immediately fled.
When Master Hui heard of this, he wept with tears streaming down his face and took him back to his home.
He then departed again,
and this occurred four or five times in total.
Eventually, the Master perceived that his intention was resolute, so he yielded and invited him to the main street north of the market.
This was precisely the northern wall of his own shop.
Later, he built a small shed there to house him and provided food for him every day.
The townspeople and travelers who came to observe were extremely numerous;
those who threw cakes to it were beyond counting.
This dog never left this house.
After the time for the midday meal had passed, she refused to eat;
after one or two years, no one knew where she had gone.
This was the lay devotee Li Xin of the Tang dynasty. As for the lay devotee Li Xin:
He was a native of Taipingli in Wenxian County, Bingzhou.

It was during the winter of the Xianqing era that—
I followed the established custom and traveled to Shuozhou for military duty,
riding one horse of red grass-patterned coat along with a foal.
At that time, late in the year, the cold shadows gathered and the wind and snow were thick and heavy.
After traveling ten or so li, the horse suddenly stopped moving.
Because the deadline for his term of service was drawing near, Xìn struck it several dozen times with his whip.
The horse then spoke in human speech and said to Xin,
"I am your mother."
"Because you avoided your father throughout your life and begged for a few stones of rice from a woman, you have received this retribution.
This colt is your younger sister;
she has now repaid her debt through her labor."
"Why do you press me so hard with such distress?
Xìn heard this and was struck with such alarm that his tears flowed uncontrollably;
he then bowed in gratitude and took his leave.
He personally loaded the saddle and bridle and said to her,
"If you are truly a faithful lady, you should return home on your own.
Thereupon, the horse proceeded forward.
Xin took up the saddle and bridle and followed him to his home.
When Xin’s brothers and others saw him, they wept in sorrowful mutual regard.
They built a separate stable for him to graze and feed, and he lived there together with his mother.
He invited monks to perform a vegetarian feast;
the entire family was diligent in their practice,
and both the laity and clergy of the local community all marveled at this extraordinary feat.
At that time, Wen Wuyin, Vice Minister of Works, and Zhang Jinting,
Judicial Officer of Qizhou, were both observing the mourning period for their parents;
hearing of this, they marveled at it from their homes.
Therefore, he went to visit the faithful family and saw that the horse was still there;

The two preceding accounts of miraculous responses are as transmitted in the *Mingbao Shiyi* (Supplement to Accounts of Karmic Retribution).

57. Chapter on Comparative Measurement (52), the Fifty-seventh Chapter on Comparative Measurement. This consists of seven sections: the Section on Stating the Intent, the Section on the Field of Giving, the Section on the Ten Grounds, the Section on Meritorious Deeds, the Section on Sinful Deeds, the Section on Miscellaneous Practices, and the Section on Regions and Lands. 1. Section on Stating the Intent, Part One. I have heard that while sagely wisdom is of a single principle, its schematics and calculations encompass myriad ends.
Karmic actions are black or white, resulting in retributions of ascent or descent;
there are distinctions of large and small, regional accents, and long and short durations across different domains.
Virtue may be hidden or manifest, and conduct may be shallow or profound.
Therefore, when the multitude of sages descend to manifest their traces, they respond to conditions and stimuli;
at times they display extraordinary wonders and manifest their physical forms, and at other times they conceal their appearances and obscure their tracks.
Although their methods differ, the propagation of the Way is no different.
If one does not compare and evaluate them, it is rare that one will know which is superior or inferior.
Section Two: The Field of Merit. As stated in the *Bodhisattva-pūrva-caryā-sūtra*:
The Buddha told Sudatta:
"In a past age, there was a brahmin named Pilinda."
He was of incomparable physical beauty and possessed supreme intelligence;
his wealth was immeasurable and beyond calculation.
All the riches and treasures of Bimbisāra were, by comparison, utterly impermanent.
"I do not use it myself;
I wish to bestow it upon the destitute.
He then immediately established a great altar.
The people gathered in great numbers and all came to where he was.
At that time, Pilinda wished to wash himself and tilted his water jar with his own hand,
but no water came out.
He was greatly distressed with anxiety,
thinking, "What fault has occurred now in my great sacrifice that the water does not flow?
At that moment, a celestial being spoke from the midst of the sky to Bimbisāra, saying:
The gift you have bestowed is most excellent and unsurpassed; however,
those to whom you have given are all members of a faction of the heterodox, the false, and those with inverted views,
who are incapable of receiving your respectful offering.
For this reason, the water could not emerge. Thereupon,
upon hearing the meaning of the celestial being’s words, Piliyakkha attained understanding and immediately made this vow:
"If my application of this gift shall now bring about the attainment of unsurpassed, perfect,
and true enlightenment, and if it is indeed as I have prayed,
may this water I pour down now fall into my hand."
Having made his vow, he tilted the water from his ritual flask, but it immediately fell back into his hand.
The devas praised him, saying:
"According to your vow, you shall attain Buddhahood before long."
At that time, Viśvantara gave alms of clothing and food to the poor for twelve years;
he exhausted all his resources in giving and had nothing left to store away.
The Buddha said to Sudatta:
The Brahmin Bilamba of that time was my very self;
both my gift was excellent and my intention was excellent.
Such recipients are not worthy;
though one may give much, the reward obtained is very small.
But now, my Dharma is truly sublime and pure, and my disciples are genuine.
Although the gift given was small, the reward obtained was exceedingly great;
it surpassed the merit of all the almsgiving performed over twelve years,
as well as that of all the people of Jambudvīpa.
If one calculates its merit, it does not equal that of giving to a single *srotāpanna*;
its blessings are far greater and surpass the former.
This is even more so than the combined merit of giving to a hundred *srotāpannas* along with the aforementioned rewards.
It is not equal to giving to a single Sakṛdāgāmin.
The merit from giving to a hundred Sakṛdāgāmins, together with the aforementioned rewards,
is not equal to giving to a single Anāgāmin.
Giving to one hundred *anāgāmins* along with the aforementioned merit does not equal giving to a single *arhat*.
Giving to one hundred *arhats* along with the aforementioned merit...
It is not equal to giving to a single pratyekabuddha;
nor is it equal to giving to a hundred pratyekabuddhas, a hundred arhats, a hundred anāgāmins, a hundred sakṛdāgāmins, or a hundred srotāpannas.
Furthermore, the merit obtained by giving to the people of Jambudvīpa is not equal to that of erecting stūpas,

monasteries, and vihāras, or providing offerings such as food, clothing, and other necessities to the Saṃgha of the four quarters— past, present, and future— providing them with all that they require.
If one calculates its merit, it surpasses all previously performed meritorious deeds;
indeed, the previously accumulated merit is not equal to making an offering to a single Buddha.
The merit is so vast that it cannot be calculated.
Even the merit from making offerings to the Buddha and the previous acts of giving do not equal that of a person who,
within a single day, takes the three refuges, observes the eightfold precepts of the *upavāsa*, or maintains the five precepts.
The merit thus obtained exceeds that of the former by hundreds of thousands of millions of times, beyond all comparison;
furthermore, this is through the blessing of upholding the precepts.
Even if one were to combine all the merit from those previous deeds,
it would not equal the merit obtained by sitting in meditation with thoughts of loving-kindness toward sentient beings for the duration of a single meal;
the latter exceeds the former by hundreds of thousands of millions of times.
Furthermore, even if one were to possess the aforementioned merits,
they would not equal those of one who hears the Dharma, takes it to heart, and contemplates the Four Noble Truths;
compared to the former merits, this is most honored, foremost, and unsurpassed.
Thereupon, upon hearing the Dharma, Sudatta leaped for joy;
his body and mind were purified, and he attained the stage of Anāgāmin.
Section Three of the Ten Stages (Daśabhūmika): Like the Vajra-samādhi, it is indestructible and imperishable.
The sutra says:
The Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva,
"I shall now, for your sake, expound the dharmas of the stages of merit practiced by bodhisattvas."
A Bodhisattva on the first stage is like the new moon, whose radiance is not yet manifest;
nevertheless, its marks of luminosity are entirely complete.
A Bodhisattva on the second stage is like the moon on the fifth day.
A Bodhisattva of the third stage is like the moon on the eighth day;
a Bodhisattva of the fourth stage is like the moon on the ninth day;
a Bodhisattva of the fifth stage is like the moon on the tenth day.
A Bodhisattva of the sixth stage is like the moon on the eleventh day;
a Bodhisattva of the seventh stage is like the moon on the twelfth day;
a Bodhisattva of the eighth stage is like the moon on the thirteenth day.
A Bodhisattva of the ninth stage is like the moon on the fourteenth day;
a Bodhisattva of the tenth stage is like the moon on the fifteenth day, fully visible and complete with all its radiant marks.
Their mind is serene, dwelling in imperturbable stability.
"Neither sinking nor regressing,
one abides in the Śūraṅgama-samādhi.
Furthermore, the *Vyākhyāyukti* (Commentary on the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*) states:
This means that when one penetrates the dharma-realm at the first stage (*bhūmi*),
one is able to thoroughly penetrate all stages.
This refers to the time when one correctly penetrates the first stage.
Because it is of such a nature, one is able to swiftly penetrate all subsequent stages.
As it is said in a verse:
Just as when the first node of a bamboo is split, the remaining nodes can be quickly split;
so too, having attained the true wisdom of the first stage (*bhūmi*), all the stages shall be swiftly attained.
(4) Section on Meritorious Deeds. Section Four on Meritorious Deeds, based on the *Ekottarika Āgama*, states:
The merit of all the people of one Jambudvīpa is equal to the merit of one Cakravartin King;
the merit of one Cakravartin King is equal to the merit of one person of Pūrvavideha;
the merit of one person of Pūrvavideha is equal to the merit of one person of Aparagoyānī.
The merit of one person from Godānīya is equal to the merit of one person from Uttarakuru;
the merit of one person from Uttarakuru is equal to the merit of one deity of the Cāturmahārājika heaven;
and the merit of one deity of the Cāturmahārājika heaven is equal to the merit of one deity of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.
The merit of thirty-two heavenly kings is equal to the merit of one Śakra;
the merit of one Śakra is equal to the merit of one Suyāma deva.
In this manner, they are successively compared and measured up to the merit of the Naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana heaven.
It is inconceivable. Furthermore, the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states:
"Just as the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three experience the pleasures of the five senses."
It is like the pleasure experienced by a Cakravartin King of Gold;
compared to celestial bliss, it does not equal even one-sixteenth part of it.
The celestial body they receive is devoid of bone and flesh.
Furthermore, they are free from defilement,
do not give rise to envy,
and their eyes do not blink.
Their robes were free from dust and grime;
there was no smoke or mist,
nor was there any affliction of excrement or urine.
The radiance of his body can shine afar,
a quality which the Universal Monarch (Cakravartin) entirely lacks;
furthermore, he does not show partiality toward his own wife and children.
Free from jealousy, they possess mastery over food and drink;
they are without the sufferings of sleep, exhaustion, and the like—
things which universal monarchs (cakravartin-rājas) and others entirely lack.
When these devas are first born, their singing,
dancing, and music are performed without anyone to instruct them;
they do not learn from others.
Due to their wholesome karma, they naturally possess all knowledge;
when they fall, because their wholesome karma is exhausted, they forget everything.
Even in the heavens below the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, there is still great bliss.
Moreover, the bliss of the heavens above is difficult to compare with;
thus, by successive comparison from the lower realms upward,
it remains incomparable even when reaching the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception.
5. Section on Karmic Offenses. Section Five on Karmic Offenses. As stated in the *Daśacakrakṣitigarbha-sūtra*:
The Buddha said, "If there should be a kṣatriya who is a caṇḍāla king..."
If one gives rise to an evil mind toward the Triple Gem,
no Buddha can save them; it is like pressing oil from seeds.
Within each and every sesame seed, various worms arise;
they are pressed by means of an oil-pressing wheel,
and immediately the oil comes forth.
For this oil-presser, throughout that day and night,
there are a certain number of sentient beings who ought to be killed; yet,
if another person were to press oil using these ten wheels, [the merit would be far greater].
If a single wheel presses one thousand *hu* of oil in one day and night,
and this continues until a full thousand years have passed,
how much sin does that oil-presser incur?
Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva said,
"It is very much so, World-Honored One;
no one is able to know the measure of this person's transgressions."
The exact number is known only to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"For example, the sin of ten wheel-turning [karmas] is equal to the sin of visiting a single courtesan's house."
In that house there are a thousand women, all seeking sensual desire;
ten such brothels are equal in sin to one tavern.
Ten such taverns are equal to one butcher’s shop.
In this way, the sins of ten butcher’s houses are equal to those of one *kṣatriya-cāṇḍāla* householder;
and the sins of ten such *cāṇḍāla* houses are equal to the sin of one king’s wheel for a single day and night within the "Ten Wheels" [sūtra].
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Ten offenses equal to those of the ten wheels are equal to one offense of visiting a brothel; ten offenses of visiting a brothel are equal to one offense of drinking alcohol;
ten offenses of drinking alcohol are equal to one offense of being a butcher; ten offenses of a butcher’s shop are equal to one offense of a brahmin household."
6. Section on Miscellaneous Karmas, Part Six. As stated in a verse from the *Jyotiṣka-sūtra*:
"What is higher than the sky? The conceit of self (*asmimāna*) is higher than the sky.
What is heavier than the earth? Virtue born of ethical discipline (*śīla-guṇa*) is heavier than the earth."
What is more abundant than grasses and trees? Discursive thoughts are more abundant than grasses and trees.
What is swifter than the wind? The movement of the mind is swifter than the wind.
By what means does one attain rebirth in heaven? Through the ten wholesome actions, one attains rebirth in heaven.
What is it that clothes the human body? The five precepts clothe the human body.
What is it that casts one into hell? The ten unwholesome actions cast one into hell.
What is it that causes one to fall among animals? Colliding and goring cause one to fall among animals.
What is as firm as a diamond? The unattached mind is as firm as a diamond.
What is as soft as a crane’s down? A gentle heart is as soft as a crane’s down.
What is fragrant? Sandalwood is fragrant. The fragrance of upholding the precepts is like sandalwood.
What are the sun and moon? The radiance of the Buddha is the sun and moon.
What rests upon the mountains? One who sits in meditation rests upon the mountains.
What moves upon the earth? The three realms move upon the earth.
What is most pure? Nirvana is most pure.
What is most defiled? Saṃsāra is most defiled.
What is most exalted? Harmony within the family is most exalted.
Which mountain is most luminous? Sumeru is most luminous.
Which country is most blissful? Śrāvastī is most blissful.
Which country abounds in people? The country of Kāśi abounds in people.
What plays in the deep mountains? The deer plays in the deep mountains.
What delights in the thickets? The fox and the marten delight in the thickets.
What falls into the wind and dust? Sand and gravel fall into the wind and dust.
"What creature sports in the deep abyss? "The carp sports in the deep abyss.
Furthermore, the *Saṃyukta Āgama* states that a certain devaputra spoke a verse asking the Buddha:
"What are the precepts? What is the deportment? What is attained? What constitutes their activity?
How does the wise one abide? And how is rebirth in heaven achieved?
At that time, the World-Honored One answered in verse:
Abstaining from taking life, guarding oneself through the precepts,
and harboring no intent to harm living beings— this is the path to rebirth in heaven.
Abstaining from taking what is not given, one finds joy in giving.
Abandoning the mind of theft is the path to heaven;
Not coveting what others hold dear is the path to heaven. Staying far from sexual misconduct and knowing contentment for oneself is the path to heaven.
One should not speak falsehood for one's own sake or for the sake of another, nor for the sake of wealth or in jest; this is the path to heaven.
One should sever double-tongued speech and never alienate the friends of others.
Constantly maintaining harmony between oneself and others— this is the path to rebirth in heaven.
Avoiding unkind speech, speaking gently without harming others,
and always uttering pure and beautiful words— this is the path to rebirth in heaven.
One who does not speak what is unestablished or unproven, whose words are meaningful and beneficial,
and who always speaks in accordance with the Dharma— this is the path to heaven,
whether in a village or in the wilderness. When seeing profit, he says, "This is mine."
Not indulging in these thoughts of greed is the path to rebirth in heaven;
with a mind of loving-kindness and non-injury,
not harming living beings and always free from resentment, this is the path to rebirth in heaven.
Regarding suffering, karma, and their retribution— When one gives rise to pure faith in both and upholds right view, This is the path to rebirth in heaven.
Such wholesome dharmas as these are the ten tracks of pure karma.
"Equanimity is the firm sustenance; this is the path to rebirth in heaven.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra spoke a verse and asked the Buddha:
"What dharma does life not know? What dharma does life not perceive?"
"By what dharma is life fettered? By what dharma is life bound?
At that time, the World-Honored One answered with a verse:
"Form does not know life; The conditioned formations do not perceive life."
"The body is shackled by its life-force; the one who possesses life is bound by craving.
Furthermore, the *Saṃyukta Āgama* states:
At that time, the World-Honored One took a lump of earth in his hand, as large as a pear fruit.
He addressed the bhikṣus:
"Which is more: the lump of earth in my hand, or the earth and stones within the Great Snowy Mountains?"
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One."
What is in my hand is but a tiny fraction;
the earth and stones of that Snowy Mountain are so vast that even calculation cannot compare with them.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Those sentient beings who know the Four Noble Truths— suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—
are like the lump of clay I have held in my hand."
Regarding those who do not know things as they truly are:
it is like the earth and stones of the Great Snowy Mountains.
At that time, the World-Honored One took up some soil with his fingernail and addressed the bhikṣus.
What do you think?
Is the soil on my fingernail more,
or is the soil of this great earth more?
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha,
"World-Honored One,
the dust upon the fingernail is exceedingly small."
"The soil of this great earth is exceedingly vast;
it cannot even be compared by means of calculation.
Thus the Buddha told the bhikṣus.
If those sentient beings whose forms are visible were like the dust on a fingernail,
those whose forms are so subtle as to be invisible would be beyond measure.
Just as with the soil of the great earth,
and just as with dry land,
so too is it with the nature of water.
Those who attain the human realm are like the soil on a fingernail;
those who fall among non-humans are like the soil of the great earth.
Such is the case for those born in a central land.
Those born in the borderlands are like the soil on a fingernail; those born in the central lands are like the soil of the great earth.
Those who have thus perfected the noble eye of wisdom are like the soil upon a fingernail;
those who have not perfected it are like the soil of the great earth.
Those who know the Dharma and Vinaya are like the soil of the great earth;
those who do not are like the soil upon a fingernail.
Those who do not know the law are like the soil of the great earth;
those who thus know that there are parents [are few].
Those who do not know their parents are like the soil upon a fingernail; those who do know them are like the soil of the great earth.
Those who know how to observe the precepts of the fast are like the dust upon a fingernail;
those who do not know how to observe the precepts of the fast are like the earth.

Those who, having passed away from the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts, are reborn among humans, are like the soil on the surface of the great earth; those who pass away from there to be reborn among humans are like the soil upon a fingernail.
Those who, having passed away from hell, are reborn again in the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts,
are as numerous as the soil of the great earth.
Those sentient beings who, having passed away from the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts, are reborn in the heavens are likewise [as few].
Those who return to birth as hell-beings, animals, or hungry ghosts are like the soil on one's fingernail;
those who do not are like the soil of the great earth.
Those who, having passed away from the heavenly realms, are reborn again in the heavens are like the dust upon a fingernail; those who, having passed away from the heavenly realms,
are reborn in the hells, the animal realm, or the realm of hungry ghosts are as numerous as the earth itself.
Like the soil of the great earth.
Section Seven: The Regional Divisions of the Earth. As stated in the *Qishi jing* (Sūtra on the Arising of the World):
"Jambudvīpa excels in five matters over Aparagoyānī, Pūrvavideha, Uttarakuru, the world of Yama, all the nāgas, garuḍas, and asuras."
What are the five? First, valor;
second, right mindfulness.
Three are the places where Buddhas appear in the world;
four are the grounds for cultivating practice;
five are the places for practicing the holy life (brahmacarya).
The continent of Aparagoyānī excels the continent of Jambudvīpa in three respects:
first, it abounds in oxen;
second, it abounds in sheep.
Third is the *nirmāṇa* maṇi jewel.
Pūrvavideha has three matters in which it excels:
first, the continent is vast and expansive.
Second, it universally encompasses all the continents;
third, the three continents are exceedingly superior and wondrous.
The continent of Uttarakuru is superior in three respects.
First, that person is devoid of self and what belongs to a self;
second, their lifespan is most excellent;
third, they possess superior spiritual practices.
In the realm of Yama, there are three things that are superior:
first, a long lifespan;
second, a large physical form.
The three realms of existence naturally provide clothing and food.
All nāgas and garuḍas possess three things by which they excel:
first, a long lifespan.
Second, their physical forms are large;
third, their palaces are vast and expansive.
Among the asuras, there are three matters in which they excel.
First, a long lifespan;
second, superior physical form;
third, abundant enjoyment of pleasure.
The gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings excel in three respects:
first, their palaces are lofty;
second, their palaces are exquisite.
The three palaces possess superior radiance.
The Heaven of the Thirty-three has three things that are superior:
first, longevity.
Second, their physical forms are superior;
third, they experience much pleasure.
The remaining four heavens above, as well as the Māra-body heavens and others, are equal to the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
There are three prior excellences;
furthermore, Jambudvīpa has five things by which it excels.
Regarding the other heavens, as stated above, the verse says:
Evil is so vast it defies calculation; good is so slight it can barely be recounted.
Those in the realms of humans and devas are as few as stars, while those in the turbid destinies are like dust motes. Noble and base trade places; the causes of poverty and wealth differ.
When weighing their merits and demerits, one sees the rise and fall between pleasure and suffering.
*Fayuan zhulin*, Scroll 52, Part 1: The Merit of Humans of the Two Lower Continents, etc.
One portion of the merit of a Cakravartin King of Copper equals one portion of the merit of a person of Kuru (Kūyāni).
The merit of the people of the three upper continents is equal to the merit of one silver-wheel-turning monarch (*rājā cakravartin*).
The merit of one silver-wheel-turning monarch is equal to the merit of one person from Uttarakuru.
The merit of the people of the four continents above is equal to the merit of one gold-wheel-turning monarch.
The merit of one universal monarch (*cakravartin*) is equal to the merit of one deity of the Four Great Kings (*cāturmahārājakāyika*).
The merit of one deity of the Four Great Kings is equal to the merit of one deity-king.
The merit of one deity-king is equal to the merit of one deity of the Heaven of the Thirty-three (*trāyastriṃśa*).
The merit of thirty-three gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven is equal to the merit of one Śakra;
the merit of one Śakra is equal to the merit of one god of the Yāma heaven;
the merit of one god of the Yāma heaven is equal to the merit of one heavenly king.
*Fayuan zhulin*, Scroll 53, Compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Daoshi of Ximing Monastery,

Chapter Fifty-nine: On Folly and Stupidity (58) Section Fifty-three: On Eloquence and Wit (Ji-bian-pian) This section consists of three parts: the Exposition of Intent (Shu-yi-bu), the Bodhisattva Section, and the Arhat Section. **1. Exposition of Intent (Shu-yi-bu)** First, the Exposition of Intent: Alas! The Three Piṭakas are vast and expansive; the seven classes of practitioners are manifold and complex.
The established teachings and prepared expedients are brilliantly elucidated for thorough understanding.
Upon hearing of suffering and its accumulation, one’s emotions are moved by poignant sorrow;
upon hearing of cessation and the path, one is joyfully awakened through equanimity.
The pure and limpid resonance is as lush as *zhīlán* (orchids),
and its lofty purport, like the notes of *gōng* and *shāng*, opens and guides the ears and eyes;
thus, Aśvaghoṣa illuminated its profound doctrine.
Nāgārjuna revitalized its severed lineage;
Āryadeva refuted the systems of enumeration;
and the Arhats synthesized its structural principles.
Together they assisted and propagated the sublime scriptures and vanquished those of external teachings;
those lost at the crossroads beheld the main thoroughfare, and those in the long night encountered the dawn,
thereby continuing the lofty model of the Buddhist canon.
That the teachings and arts of master and disciple are now embodied herein—
this may truly be called magnificent!
If Jetavana were still present and the Deer Park could be beheld as it was,
one would truly be close to attaining the fruit and approaching Buddhahood.
