64. Chapter on the Poor and Lowly (56). Chapter Sixty-four on the Poor and Lowly. This consists of five sections: the Section on Stating the Intent, the Section on Citing Evidence, the Section on Sudatta, the Section on the Poor Boy, and the Section on the Poor Woman. 1. Section on Stating the Intent. First, regarding the Section on Stating the Intent: Poverty, wealth, nobility, and lowliness all arise from past karma.
Gain and loss, existence and non-existence, all arise from past actions.
Thus, a sutra says:
"If you wish to know past causes, you should observe present effects."
If you wish to know the fruits of the future, you should observe the causes of the present.
This is why the homes of Yuan Xian and Qian Lou had doorways with rope pivots and windows made from jars;
they lacked coverings to shield them from wind and dust.
Their mats and doors, made of reeds and rushes, offer no protection against frost and dew;
sometimes they weave rice stalks to serve as mats,
and at other times they cut lotus leaves to provide clothing.
When he folded his elbows, both sleeves were worn through;
when he tucked in the threads, both lapels were equally torn.
His mouth and belly were sustained by the provisions of An-yi.
When resting, he dwells within the spirit-platform;
upon his head he wears a cap of ten years' age,
and upon his body he is clad in garments of a hundred tattered threads.
Having neither fields nor houses in my hometown,
and lacking a host in Luoyang as well,
I drifted about according to the times, passing my days in a state of restless wandering.
Although I am ashamed of the conduct of Lingzhe,
I still suffer the misfortune of Yi Sang;
yet I am even more ashamed of Bo Yi, which leads inevitably to the bitterness of Mount Shouyang.
My furs and robes are suddenly exhausted;
how can I see through the spring? With not even a bushel or a pint left, how shall I survive the year?
The reason it has come to this is that,
due to not practicing generosity in the past and constantly harboring stinginess and greed,
the retribution has resulted in one's wealth being utterly exhausted in a single day.
Therefore, practitioners should practice giving.
Section Two: Citing Scriptural Evidence. As stated in the *Dīpāṅgulī-sūtra*:
"One should know that poverty is comparable to hell."
Having lost their support and refuge, they dwell nowhere;
the fire of anxiety blazes, and they are withered and scorched by grief.
As their radiant complexion fades, their appearance becomes increasingly impaired.
The body is emaciated and wasted by hunger and thirst;
the eyes are sunken deep, and the joints stand out like bones;
thin skin envelops the frame, and the sinews and veins are laid bare.
Their hair is disheveled and their hands and feet are emaciated and thin;
their complexion is ashen white and their entire bodies are cracked and split.
Furthermore, they lack clothing and [crawl] into filth and excrement.
Gathering together coarse and tattered rags,
they stitched them together to barely conceal their human forms, leaving their four limbs bare;
they leaned and lay upon heaps of filth, with no mats or bedding at all.
His former relatives and acquaintances saw him but did not recognize him;
as he wandered through the streets begging for food like a starving crow,
he arrived at the side of a close friend, intending to beg for alms from him.
The gatekeeper blocked him and would not let him enter;
whenever he found an opportunity to enter, he was again repulsed and insulted.
When the master of the house came out, he intended to whip and beat him.
Bowing his head low and bending his body, he prostrated twice to apologize for his offense.
The host treated him with contempt and did not deign to look back;
even if he were permitted to enter the dwelling, it was because of such disdain that he would neither speak to him nor engage with him.
Furthermore, they do not spread out seats for them;
they give them meager food and drink, tossing it into their bowls and vessels, hoping that these small offerings will suffice to satisfy them,
or that they might happen upon a great assembly where they can beg for leftover scraps.
Because he was treated with contempt, they did not call him to sit,
but instead drove him away.
Such is the lot of the poor.
For example, when a forest tree has no flowers, the swarms of bees depart;
when the blades of grass are struck by frost, they wither and curl up of their own accord;
and when a pond is parched and dry, the geese do not frequent it.
Deer do not frequent a forest that has been burned;
when the grain in the fields has been harvested, no one gathers the remains.
Today, being impoverished, you speak of your former wealth and happiness.
It is merely empty talk; who would be willing to believe it?
Because of my poverty, there is no path for me to turn, like a vast wilderness consumed by fire.
People find no joy in them;
they are like withered trees that provide neither shade nor refuge for those who seek shelter,
and like crops struck by frost and hail that are cast aside and not harvested.
Like a venomous snake that harms people and is therefore shunned by all;
like food mixed with poison that no one will taste;
like an empty tomb to which no one approaches.
It is like a foul latrine overflowing with stench and filth;
it is like a butcher, loathed and despised by all people,
such that even when he speaks pleasant words, others consider them wrong.
If one performs wholesome deeds, others consider them contemptible;
if one's actions are quick and nimble, they are again found wanting as being frivolous and fickle;
yet if one is slow and relaxed, they say it is overly grave and rigid.
Furthermore, if one praises them, people will call it flattery;
if one does not offer praise, they will instead slander them,
saying, "This poor man never has anything good to say."
If one further instructs others, they are said to be deceitful;
if one speaks extensively, people call one garrulous;
if one remains silent, people say one is hiding one's true feelings.
If one speaks straightforwardly, they say it is coarse and harsh;
if one seeks to please others, they say it is sycophantic and crooked;
if one associates with them frequently, they say it is deceptive and delusive.
If one does not associate with them, they say it is outlandish and hypocritical;
if one follows what others say, they say it is a pretense to seize their intentions;
if one does not comply, they say it is self-willed.
If one bends one's will to accommodate them, they revile one as cold and lowly;
if one does not bend one's will, they say, "This poor man still relies on me";
if one slightly relaxes oneself, they say he is foolish and lacks restraint.
If he restrains himself, they say he is empty, stingy, and hypocritical, though he appears upright and resolute;
if he is again joyful and carefree, they say he is boastful and dissolute, appearing like a madman;
if he is again sorrowful and distressed, they say he harbors malice and has no heart for joy from the start.
If one hears another's speech that is incomplete and provides an explanation for it,
they say that everyone is rushing toward folly in place of wisdom, which is the height of shamelessness.
Yet if one remains silent, they further say that one is stubborn and ignorant, not understanding the principles of reason.
If they engage in trivial frivolity, they claim they do not believe in the retribution of sin and merit.
If they seek something, they say they obtain it by chance and are unaware of shame.
If they seek nothing, they say that although they do not ask for it now, they hope to obtain much later.
If one cites scriptures, they say one is feigning cleverness;
if one speaks with plain simplicity, they find it dull and clumsy;
if one discusses facts according to public consensus, they claim one is merely forceful in one's assertions.
If one speaks truthfully in private, they further call one a slanderer and a sycophant;
if one wears new clothes, they further say they are borrowed and merely for show;
if one wears tattered clothes, they further say one is wretched, impoverished, and emaciated.
If one eats and drinks excessively yet claims to be hungry and destitute, it is gluttony;
if one eats only a little yet says the belly is full while feigning integrity, it is hypocrisy;
if one expounds upon sutras and treatises yet speaks only to display what one knows while exposing one's own ignorance and shortcomings, it is self-aggrandizement.
If one does not speak of the sutras and śāstras, saying they are foolish and ignorant and fit only for tending cattle;
or if one speaks of one's own past deeds to boast and praise oneself;
or if one remains silent and sullen, claiming that one's family background and resources are meager.
For all those who are impoverished,
every movement— whether coming or going, advancing or halting, speaking or looking up and down—
is entirely a transgression.
For those who possess wealth and status, the commission of various unrighteous acts carries no fault or calamity;
whatever they undertake or do, all is deemed appropriate.
For those who are poor, even the arising of a corpse-demon inspires total terror.
It is like encountering a terminal illness that is difficult to cure; like being in a desolate wilderness where water and grass are utterly absent;
like falling into the great ocean and drowning in a surging torrent;
or like a person whose throat is being squeezed so that they cannot draw breath.
It is like a cataract over the eye, by which one cannot discern where things go;
it is like thick filth and impurity that is difficult to wash away;
and it is like an enemy who, though sharing food and clothing, does not abandon their malevolent intent.
It is like a person entering a well during a summer torrent who loses consciousness;
it is like sinking into deep mud where one is stuck and cannot emerge;
it is like trees being blown and swept away by the violent currents of a mountain torrent.
Poverty is likewise thus:
it is fraught with many hardships.
As for those who possess wealth and honor—
He possesses noble majesty;
his appearance is composed and his disposition is broad and expansive.
Rites and righteousness flourish in competition, and he is able to give rise to wisdom and courage.
The family estate will increase, the kin and retinue will be harmonious and yielding,
and one's good reputation will spread far and wide; observe this accordingly.
The wealth, nobility, and splendor of all worldly people are not worth coveting or clinging to.
One should not seek idle pleasure in the honor and dignity held by humans and devas;
one must know that poverty is a great mass of suffering.
If one wishes to sever poverty, one should not be stingy or greedy.
Therefore, it is said in the sūtras that being poor is a most grievous suffering.
Section Three: Sudatta. As stated in the *Saṃyukta-ratna-piṭaka-sūtra*:
Formerly, when the Buddha was in the world,
the elder Sudatta reached the end of his life in poverty and suffering, his wealth entirely exhausted.
He obtained four *śē* of rice by working as a hired laborer, which he blew upon to cook for his meal.
It happened that Aniruddha came there to beg for alms;
the wife immediately took his bowl, filled it with rice, and gave it to him.
Later, Subhūti, Kāśyapa, Maudgalyāyana, Śāriputra, and others [did the same].
He gave alms to everyone who came to beg in succession until each had a full bowl.
Finally, the Buddha arrived,
and he likewise gave him a full bowl.
Sudatta, having gone out on business, returned home and asked his wife for food.
His wife then spoke to him, saying:
"If the Venerable Aniruddha were to come,
would you eat yourself or would you give it as an offering to the Venerable One?
Sudatta replied:
"It would be better for me not to eat at all than to give it to the Venerable One.
The wife spoke again,
saying, "Even if Kāśyapa, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Subhūti, Śāriputra, and others, up to the Buddha himself, were to come..."
"What shall you do? the husband replied to his wife,
"I would rather not eat myself than give it away entirely."
The wife then said to her husband,
"This morning all the holy ones came to beg for food;
I gave them all the food and drink we had."
The husband heard this and was filled with joy;
he spoke to his wife, saying,
"Our transgressions are exhausted, and our merit should now lead us to rebirth."
He immediately opened the storehouses, and they were filled to overflowing with grain, silk, food, and drink;
as these were used up, they would be replenished once more. Such karmic rewards are beyond description.
Furthermore, the *Saṃyukta-avadāna-sūtra* states:
"In the past, the elder Sudatta was poor seven times;
later, his poverty became most extreme."
He had not even a single coin.
Later, he found a wooden ladle amidst the refuse;
it was actually made of sandalwood.
He went out to the market and sold it, obtaining four *sheng* of rice.
He told his wife, "Cook one *sheng* together;
I shall go to seek some vegetables."
When returning, they ate together.
The Buddha thought to himself:
"I shall deliver Sudatta so that his merit may increase further."
Just as the rice was being cooked until it was fully done, Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and Kāśyapa came;
the four *śē* of rice were cooked away one after another.
After he had departed, Fu further invited the Buddha and the Sangha for offerings until they were exhausted.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he attained the Way.
Furthermore, the *Bodhisattva-pūrvacaryā-sūtra* states:
At first, the householder Sudatta was poor and distressed;
having received the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma, his body and mind became pure and he attained the stage of Anāgāmin.
He possessed only five gold coins.
One day he took one coin and gave it as an offering to the Buddha;
one coin he gave as an offering to the Dharma; and one coin he gave as an offering to the Sangha.
He ate one coin for himself and used one coin as capital;
he did this every day in this manner.
He always had a single coin that was never exhausted.
He then received the five precepts, and his lustful mind was severed.
The women each followed their own inclinations.
There was a woman who was parching grain to make roasted flour.
She lost control of the fire, which spread widely and burned people and livestock.
King Prasenajit commanded his ministers to establish a boundary around the area.
"From this day forward, you must not kindle fires or use lamps and candles at night.
Any who violate this shall be fined one thousand taels of gold.
At that time, Sudatta had attained the Way while remaining a householder.
He sat in meditation and entered samādhi day and night.
At midnight, when the cock crowed, he lit a lamp and sat in meditation;
[the thieves] then observed him and captured him.
The one who seized the lamp said to the King,
"I must pay the penalty.
Sudatta said to the King:
"Now I am so poor that I have not even a hundred coins;
with what shall I pay?
The king, enraged, ordered his officers to cast him into prison.
Just as he was about to hand Sūḍatta over to the prison guards,
the Four Heavenly Kings descended during the first watch of the night and said to Sūḍatta:
"We shall give you money."
By paying the king's fine,
he may be released.
Having preached the sutra for the Four Heavenly Kings, he then departed.
At midnight, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, came again to see him.
After Sudatta had finished preaching the Dharma for him, Śakra departed.
Next, during the latter part of the night, Brahmā descended again to see him.
After the Brahmā Deva had departed,
the King saw a light atop the prison from his observation tower one night.
The next day, the King immediately dispatched a messenger to speak with Sudatta.
While sitting by the fire, he was confined and felt no shame;
he continued to kindle the fire.
Sudatta replied:
"I do not kindle fire.
If one were to kindle fire, there would necessarily be smoke and ash.
He then spoke again to Sudatta.
During the first watch of the night there are four fires;
during the middle watch of the night there is one fire,
which is twice as large as the previous fires.
In the latter part of the night, there was yet another fire,
twice as large as the previous one.
He asked, "What is this fire that has been lit?"
Sudatta replied, "This is not fire.
During the first watch of the night,
the Four Heavenly Kings came to see me."
At midnight, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, came to see me;
at the latter part of the night, Brahmā came to see me.
This was the radiant blaze of light from their bodies.
"It is not fire. When the official heard these words, he immediately went to inform the king.
Upon hearing this, the king was struck with alarm, his hair standing on end.
The King said,
"This man’s merit and virtue are so exceptionally distinguished;
how could I now humiliate him?"
He immediately commanded his officials,
saying, "Release him quickly;
do not allow any delay."
He was then released and allowed to depart.
Sudatta managed to escape and went to the Buddha's dwelling, where he paid homage to the Buddha and listened to the Dharma.
King Prasenajit immediately prepared his carriage and went to where the Buddha was.
When the people saw the king, they all rose to avoid him;
however, Sudatta alone remained seated, his mind dwelling on the flavor of the Dharma, and did not rise when he saw the king.
The king felt a slight resentment in his heart.
"This is my subject," he thought, "who harbors such contempt as to see me and not rise.
He then conceived a mind of indignation.
The Buddha, knowing his intention, refrained from preaching the Dharma.
The king addressed the Buddha, saying,
"I pray that you will preach the sūtras and the Dharma."
The Buddha said to the king:
"Now is not the time for me to preach the Dharma to you, O King.
Why is it not the right time?"
When people give rise to anger and resentment, harboring knots of enmity that they do not untie;
when they crave the beauty of women, becoming arrogant and disrespectful;
and when their minds are defiled and turbid such that they cannot understand the sublime Dharma upon hearing it—[they are lost].
For this reason, it is not the proper time now to preach the Dharma to the king.
When the king heard the Buddha’s words, [he understood].
He thought to himself:
"Because of this man,
I have today suffered two reductions."
Furthermore, having given rise to anger, he was unable to hear the Dharma;
he paid homage to the Buddha and departed.
Having gone outside, he commanded those around him:
"If this man comes out, I shall simply strike off his head.
Having spoken these words, at that very moment, tigers, wolves, lions, and other venomous and harmful beasts came from all four directions and surrounded the king.
The king, seeing this, was struck with fear and returned to the place where the Buddha was.
The Buddha asked the Great King,
"Why have you come back?"
The king said to the Buddha,
"I saw him and returned.
The Buddha told the king:
"Do you know this person?
The king replied, "I do not."
The Buddha said,
"This person has already attained the stage of Anāgāmin; because he harbored an evil intention toward this man while sitting or rising,
it was for that reason that such a thing occurred."
"If he does not return, the King will surely be in peril and shall not be fully saved.
Upon hearing the Buddha's words, the King was immediately seized with great terror;
he then turned toward Sudatta, confessed his transgressions, and prostrated before him.
The four classes of people were spread out before Sudatta, and the king said,
"These are my subjects, yet they have been subjected to such humiliation."
"This is indeed most difficult.
Sudatta spoke again,
"Yet I am poor and still practice giving."
This, too, is extremely difficult.
Śīlavant was captured by bandits while acting as a judge to settle a legal dispute for his country;
yet, at the moment of death, he did not commit the offense of lying.
The bandits then released him;
this was indeed extremely difficult.
Furthermore, there was a deity named Śakali.
While he was lying on a high tower, celestial jade maidens came to him; yet,
because he maintained his prohibitive precepts, he did not accept them—
this is truly most difficult.
Thereupon, the four men each spoke a verse before the Buddha:
"It is difficult for the poor to practice giving; It is difficult for the wealthy and noble to practice patience;
It is difficult for those in peril to maintain the precepts; It is difficult for the young and strong to renounce desire."
After the Buddha had spoken these verses,
the king, his ministers, and the common people were all greatly rejoiced;
they paid their respects and departed.
4. Section on the Poor Boy. Section Four. As stated in the *Sūtra of the Elder’s Son Vimaladatta*:
At that time, the elder’s son Vimaladatta paid homage to the Buddha.
With palms joined, he addressed the Buddha, saying,
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will pass through my poor village."
He further invited the entire assembly for a meal at his residence on the following day.
At that time, the World-Honored One granted his consent by remaining silent.
The sons of the elders prostrated before the Buddha and departed.
Upon arriving at his residence, he prepared a full meal.
The following day, the World-Honored One, together with the great assembly,
went to that place and sat down with solemn dignity.
Vimalacitta addressed his parents and kinsmen, saying,
"Let us first prostrate at the Buddha’s feet and each attend to him.
Vimalacitta rose and went to fetch water for washing, then respectfully presented the food.
Before the serving of food was finished, a beggar came forward and went from seat to seat begging;
since the Buddha had not yet offered his blessing, no one dared to give him anything.
Finding nothing at all, he departed in anger and gave rise to an evil thought:
"These śramaṇas are indolent, foolish, and deluded."
"What kind of path is this?
When the poor man begged from him, he had no intention of giving;
yet the elder, in his foolish delusion, used it as if it were sweetmeat."
"Without any thought of compassion,
I shall become a king and crush his head with an iron-rimmed chariot.
Having said this, he departed.
When the Buddha had finished bestowing his alms,
another beggar came in to beg for food;
everyone in the assembly gave him something.
Having received a great amount of food and drink,
he departed with joy and immediately thought to himself:
"These śramaṇas all possess a heart of compassion."
"Out of pity for my poverty and cold, you have given me food to satisfy my hunger.
I have been sustained for several days.
Excellent, excellent!"
"Elder, you are indeed able to serve these great beings;
your merit shall be immeasurable."
"If I were to become a king,
I would provide offerings to the Buddha and his disciples;
yet even after seven days, I would still not have repaid the kindness of relieving my hunger and thirst today."
Having spoken thus, he departed.
After the Buddha had finished his meal and delivered his discourse, he returned immediately to the vihāra.
The Buddha addressed Ānanda:
From this day forward, after the distribution of alms is concluded, food shall be served; let this be the constant rule.
At that time, the two beggars wandered from place to place begging for alms until they reached another kingdom, where they lay down amidst the thick grass by the roadside.
At that time, the king suddenly passed away, leaving no successor. The royal astrologer,
who was well-versed in the science of physiognomy,
stated in his records of prophetic omens:
When there was a man of low status who ought to be king,
the ministers, officials, and the retinues of thousands of chariots and ten thousands of horses traveled throughout the borders of the kingdom to determine who should be king.
Looking back toward the deep grass by the roadside, he saw a cloud-canopy above it.
A physiognomist examined the signs and said,
"There is a divine person within."
He then saw that the beggar had become the king;
the ministers prostrated themselves before him, each addressing him as their sovereign.
The beggar was struck with astonishment.
They themselves claimed to be of low birth and not of royal lineage;
they all said that their physical marks were not those of one who attains power by force.
They bathed in fragrant water and donned the robes of a king.
The majestic radiance of his countenance was solemn and his excellence was immeasurable;
escorted by attendants before and behind, he turned his carriage and entered the kingdom.
At that time, the man of evil intent lay sleeping in deep grass, unaware of what was happening.
The chariot crushed his head.
When the king arrived in the kingdom,
the yin and yang were harmonized and the four seasonal energies flourished brilliantly.
The people were peaceful and happy, praising the virtue of the king.
At that time, the king thought to himself:
"In the past, there was a poor man."
By what causes and conditions did he become a king?
Formerly, while practicing alms-gathering, he received the Buddha's grace and obtained a great amount of food;
thereupon, a wholesome thought arose that he might become a king.
The merit of having made offerings to the Buddha for seven days has now borne fruit.
He immediately summoned his ministers and, facing toward the kingdom of Śrāvastī from afar, burned incense and paid homage.
He immediately dispatched a messenger to invite the Buddha, saying:
"Having received the World-Honored One’s gracious favor, I have become a king of men;
I pray that you will deign to humble your divine majesty and come to transform this land."
Foolish and ignorant people have now received this instruction.
Thereupon, the Buddha told his disciples:
"You should accept his invitation."
The Buddha, together with an immeasurable multitude of disciples,
traveled to that kingdom.
At that time, the king came out to welcome him and paid homage to the Buddha.
Having entered the palace and finished his meal,
the king requested the World-Honored One to explain the karmic conditions for his attainment of kingship.
The Buddha explained it in full, recounting the causes and conditions as previously described.
The one who gave rise to the wholesome thought is the present king.
At that time, the one with the evil thought was not only crushed to death;
after dying, he entered hell again, where he was crushed by a flaming chariot.
"Only after a hundred million kalpas shall he emerge.
Your Majesty has now invited the Buddha, and your fulfillment of your vow is exceedingly great;
you shall receive blessings in every lifetime without end."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The human mind is the root of poison; The mouth is the gateway to calamity.
What the mind conceives, the mouth speaks; The body then receives the retribution."
Do not dwell on the good or evil of others; One reaps the suffering one has created for oneself.
If you intend to harm another, you will not realize that your own head is being crushed by a carriage wheel.
The Dharma of the Nectar of Immortality causes people to be born in the heavens.
Mentally contemplating and verbally reciting, one’s body receives that merit;
for those who mindfully contemplate both good and evil, they create the foundation for their own peace through their own actions.
By intending all that is wholesome, one is like a king who has attained his royal station.
At that time, the king heard the sutra and rejoiced;
the ministers and citizens of the entire kingdom attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
Furthermore, the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* says:
The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Śrāvastī together with his disciples, numbering one thousand two hundred and fifty.
Within the kingdom, there were five hundred beggars.
Constantly relying on the Tathāgata and following the community of monks to beg for his livelihood,
a sense of renunciation arose within him and he sought to go forth.
Together, they addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The appearance of a Tathāgata in the world is extremely rare to encounter.
We, who were lowly and base, have been granted our very lives through his aid.
Now that we have left home in poverty, we do not know whether you will permit it or not. The Buddha said to the beggars:
My Dharma is pure and possesses no distinction between noble and base.
It is like clear water that washes away all impurities,
whether they belong to the noble or the base.
There is nothing that water cannot cleanse when it washes it.
Likewise, wherever a great fire reaches,
there is nothing that it does not burn to cinders.
Furthermore, just as within empty space those who enter— whether poor or wealthy, noble or humble— may act as they please according to their own will,
so too when beggars hear this teaching, they all rejoice; their faith redoubles,
and they take refuge by leaving the household life.
The Buddha said, "Welcome.
His hair fell away of its own accord and dharma robes appeared upon his body;
thus, he was fully endowed with the appearance of a śramaṇa.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for them, and they became arhats.
At that time, the prominent elders and wealthy men of the country,
hearing that the beggars had been ordained, all gave rise to feelings of arrogance.
"How is it that the Tathāgata permits this low-born person to take his place in the assembly of monks?
We have cultivated merit by inviting the Buddha and the Sangha for a meal;
now this low-born man sits upon our couches and mats and grasps our eating vessels."
At that time, Prince Jeta invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha,
and sent a messenger to inform the Buddha:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will graciously accept my invitation for tomorrow."
As well as the community of bhikṣus and the beggars whom I have delivered;
I did not invite them.
"Be careful not to bring it.
At the time of the meal the following day,
the Buddha said to the beggar:
"I have accepted his invitation; you are not included in this instance.
You may now go to Uttarakuru, fetch naturally ripened husked rice, and return to his house.
Sit wherever you please and eat the husked rice yourself."
The bhikṣus followed his command and,
by means of their supernormal powers, went to that world;
each took a bowl filled [with offerings] and returned, restoring their dignified deportment.
They came through the air,
arriving like flying geese,
and sat in Jeta’s house to eat according to their respective order.
At that time, the Prince beheld the majestic deportment, the movements, the supernormal powers, and the merit of the bhikṣus;
with a heart of reverence and joy, he marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I do not understand from what direction these worthy sages and saints have come.
The Buddha told Jeta,
"If you wish to know, they are precisely those whom you did not invite yesterday."
He related the circumstances of the matter in detail to the Prince.
At that time, when Jeta heard these words, he felt profound shame and remorse, thinking:
"I have been so foolish and deluded that I could not distinguish between light and darkness."
I do not understand what kind of wholesome deeds these people have cultivated that they now encounter the World-Honored One and receive such extraordinary grace. Yet,
what fault have they committed that they must beg for their livelihood?
The Buddha told Jeta:
"In the distant past, there was a great kingdom named Vārāṇasī.
There was a mountain there called Ṛṣi."
In ancient times, many Buddhas resided therein.
When there were no Buddhas, two thousand pratyekabuddhas constantly dwelt within it.
There was a householder named Sandhāna.
At that time, there was a drought and famine;
since his family was immensely wealthy,
he immediately questioned the treasurer.
"I now wish to invite a Great Being, but I do not know whether my storehouse contains sufficient grain and rice to provide for them."
The Tibetan official replied,
"I have sufficient provisions.
He then invited two thousand pratyekabuddhas to partake of a meal as an offering.
Five hundred messengers were dispatched to provide and prepare the food and drink.
At that time, weariness arose in the minds of those messengers,
and they thought, "The reason all of us are undergoing such hardship..."
All this was due to those beggars.
At that time, the elder always had one person announce when the time for the meal had arrived;
he also raised a puppy that went along with him every day.
At that time, the messenger happened by chance to forget one day to go and inform them.
When the time arrived, the puppy went alone to its usual place and barked loudly toward the great beings.
When the pratyekabuddhas heard the dog barking,
they immediately knew that the time had come;
they came and sat down, receiving the food according to the Dharma.
He informed the elder, "The heavens shall now send rain; it is fitting that you sow and plant.
Following these words, the elder plowed and sowed.
Whatever seeds were sown all transformed into gourds.
Seeing this as strange, the elder irrigated them according to the season;
later, when they ripened, they were all large.
He immediately split it open,
and within it was found a full measure of well-tilled, excellent barley, exactly as the seeds he had planted.
The elder was filled with joy.
His household was filled to overflowing, and he further distributed [the wealth] among his kinsmen;
all throughout the kingdom received his grace and favor.
At that time, the five hundred food-preparers thought to themselves:
That we have obtained this fruit is due to the grace of the Great Being.
How could we address him with such harsh words?
We shall go at once to his place and request his forgiveness for our repentance.
They further made this vow: "May we, in future lives,
encounter the worthy and holy ones and attain liberation."
For this reason, he was constantly a beggar for five hundred lifetimes;
however, because he repented and again made a vow,
he has now encountered my era and attained deliverance.
"Prince, you should know that at that time,
the great wealthy man Sandhāna was none other than myself;
the treasurer at that time is now Sudatta."
The one who arrived at the time of the daily white [meal] was none other than King Udayana;
the five hundred food-preparers were these five hundred arhats;
and those who were Jeta and the assembly at that time—[are likewise present here].
Beholding his miraculous transformations, all attained the four fruits [of the śramaṇa].
Section Five: The Poor Woman. As stated in the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish*: "Long ago, when the Buddha was in the world..."
The Venerable Kātyāyana was staying in the country of Avanti.
At that time, there was a householder in that country who was very wealthy and possessed great riches.
The householder had a maidservant who committed a slight transgression;
the elder beat her with a whip.
Day and night he ran on errands;
his clothing did not cover his body,
and his food did not fill his mouth.
Old and worn out from hardship, he longed for death but could not find it.
Having just taken a water jar to the river to fetch water,
he raised his voice and wept aloud.
At that time, the Venerable One heard the sound of her weeping;
he went to where she was, inquired about the circumstances,
and spoke to her as follows:
"If you are poor, why do you not sell it?
The old woman replied,
"Who would buy from one who is poor?"
Kātyāyana said, "The poor man can indeed be sold.
The old mother replied:
"If poverty can be sold,
how would you sell it? Kātyāyana replied:
"If you are selling it, follow my words and tell them first to wash it.
Once it has been washed, instruct them to offer it to the Mother, saying:
'Venerable One, I am now so poor that not even a hair's breadth of clothing remains upon my body.'"
"There is only this jar, which belongs to the entire community. With what,
then, shall we make our offering?"
He immediately took the bowl and instructed him to fetch water for the offering;
having received it, he offered a blessing.
Next, he conferred the precepts upon him.
After he had finished instructing her in the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha, he asked her, "Where do you reside?
The maidservant immediately replied:
Having no fixed dwelling place,
they stay wherever they happen to be when pounding grain, cooking, or grinding;
sometimes they even stay upon dung and soil.
The Venerable One spoke, saying:
"Serve with a diligent mind and respectful care;
wait until the master of the house and all others have finished sleeping."
He quietly opened the door and entered;
inside the door, he spread grass and sat down,
contemplating and meditating upon the Buddha.
Having received these instructions, the mother went to her seat at night;
she passed away inside the door and was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
At dawn, the mistress of the house saw this and spoke with indignation.
"This maidservant was never permitted to enter the house;
why has she suddenly died here?
He then immediately sent someone to tie grass around her feet.
She was placed in the śītavana forest cremation ground.
This maidservant has been reborn in heaven,
where she now has five hundred devaputras as her retinue.
Having observed with his divine eye the causes and conditions for those beings to be born in heaven,
he immediately took those five hundred devaputras,
carrying incense and flowers, and went to the Śītavana forest.
They burned incense and scattered flowers as offerings to the corpse,
emitting a celestial radiance that illuminated the village and its forests. When the villagers saw this,
they were struck with wonder and alarm.
He made a public proclamation far and near,
and people came to the forest to observe;
having seen it, they spoke.
"This maidservant has already died; why do you offer worship?
The devaputra replied, "This was my former body."
He then explained in detail the causes and conditions for rebirth in heaven.
Afterwards, they all went to Kātyāyana to pay their respects, make offerings, and listen to his teaching on the causes and conditions of the Dharma.
Five hundred devaputras all attained the fruit of srotāpanna;
having attained this fruit, they returned to the heavens.
By reason of these causes and conditions...
The wise should all train in this manner.
Furthermore, the *Buddhabhāṣita-mahākāśyapa-tārayati-daridra-mātṛ-sūtra* states:
The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Śrāvastī.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa traveled alone to teach and transform others, arriving at the city of Rājagṛha;
he constantly practiced great compassion and bestowed blessings upon all sentient beings.
He renounced all wealth and nobility to beg from the poor.
When he was about to go on his alms-round, he first entered samādhi, [thinking]:
"Which poor person shall I bring to fortune?"
He then entered the great city of Rājagṛha and saw a solitary mother who was extremely impoverished.
He was situated amidst a great heap of excrement in the streets and alleys;
having carved a cave out of the side of that heap of filth,
he remained there, emaciated and diseased, constantly lying within it.
Lonely and destitute, with neither food nor clothing,
he then constructed a small fence around a mountain cave to shield his body from the five elements.
By means of the Kāśyapa-samādhi, he knew that this person had not planted roots of merit in past lives,
and was therefore poor in the present; he also knew that his mother’s life would end soon.
"If I do not deliver her, she will lose the hall of merit forever.
At that time, the mother was starving and exhausted;
the elder’s servant girl had discarded the rice-water.
The stench was foul beyond words.
His mother begged him for it,
and he immediately placed it in a broken tile shard to his side.
Kāśyapa went to where she was making her vow and begged from her, saying, "Give me however much you can; by doing so, you will obtain great merit.
At that time, the old woman spoke this verse:
With his entire body afflicted by disease, how can his solitary poverty even be described?
The poorest man in the land, with food and clothing barely covering his form—
yet even such a person, if he were unkind, would still be met with compassion and pity.
What is called compassion? It is to be unaware of this calamity—the cold suffering of the entire world—and to think, "Nothing surpasses my own body;
I pray you show me mercy and forbearance. Truly, it is not out of benevolence that one cherishes [the self].
Mahākāśyapa immediately replied in verse:
"The Buddha is the Honored One of the three realms; I am fully contained within them."
To remove your hunger and poverty, I therefore beg from you in this state of want;
if you can diminish what you have for body and mouth to give even a fraction as an offering,
you shall attain liberation through the long night and be reborn with great wealth.
At that time, the old woman heard the verse and was filled with joy.
She thought to herself, "The other day I had some foul-smelling rice gruel;
I wished to give it as an offering, but it could not be drunk."
He called out from afar to Kāśyapa,
"Will you have pity on me and accept [this]? Kāśyapa replied:
"Very well.
The mother then crawled into the cave to retrieve it;
however, as its body was naked, she was unable to carry it out.
Bending his body and leaning over the fence,
he handed it to him; Kāśyapa accepted it,
and the Honored One offered a blessing for him to receive merit and peace.
Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"If I take this away and drink it elsewhere,
my mother will not believe me and will say that I have discarded it."
He then finished drinking in front of his mother, rinsed the bowl,
and returned it to the bag;
thereupon, the old woman’s genuine faith was further strengthened.
Kāśyapa thought to himself,
"I must manifest my supernormal powers so that this woman may surely attain great peace.
He then immediately displayed a vast array of miraculous transformations in mid-air.
At that time, the woman saw this and leaped for joy;
with single-minded devotion, she knelt on one knee and gazed afar at Kāśyapa.
Kāśyapa addressed her, saying:
"What is it that you now desire in your heart, Mother?
she asked. She then replied to Kāśyapa, "I wish, by means of this small merit, to be reborn in the heavens."
Thereupon Kāśyapa suddenly vanished. After several days,
the old woman’s life came to an end, and she was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven,
her majestic virtue so magnificent that it shook heaven and earth.
The radiance was so exceptionally brilliant that it was as if seven suns had risen simultaneously;
its dazzling brilliance illuminated the celestial palaces,
causing Śakra to tremble with alarm.
"Whose merit has moved [the gods] more than mine?
He then used his divine eye to observe the merit of this goddess that had caused this to happen,
and he immediately knew the place from which the goddess had originally come in her previous life.
At that time, the goddess thought to herself:
"This karmic reward is due to my having made offerings to Kāśyapa in a previous life.
Even if I were to bestow upon Kāśyapa hundreds of thousands of various kinds of celestial jewels, it would not compare."
Before he had yet repaid even a moment’s kindness,
he suddenly descended, bringing with him a maidservant holding celestial incense and flowers.
They scattered [flowers] from the void above Kāśyapa, and then descended,
prostrating themselves with their five limbs touching the ground. Having completed their salutation, they stood back, joined their palms,
and sighed in praise, saying:

Chapter Sixty-five: On Debts; Chapter Sixty-six:

On Litigation. 65. Chapter on Debts (57): This chapter consists of two sections. Section One: Exposition of the Intent. The first section, the Exposition of the Intent, states: Encouraging virtue and punishing transgression is the constant mind of the Great Being (*mahāsattva*).
To abandon evil and cultivate merit is the constant aspiration of a bodhisattva;
thus, the workings of good and evil karma are as mutually dependent as form and shadow.
The calamities and transgressions of debt and obligation plant the bitter fruits of the three retributions;
some may incur present debts and receive present retribution.
Some may experience retribution in the present life; some may experience retribution in the next life; and some may experience retribution in subsequent lives.
Thus, in these three periods of time, one may incur even a single hair’s breadth of debt.
If one refuses to return it, one will certainly suffer;
therefore, the Sūtra says:
"A person who steals first enters the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts."
When one subsequently attains a human body, two kinds of retributive fruits are obtained:
first, one constantly dwells in poverty;
second, although one obtains a small amount of wealth, it is always seized by others.
These words have evidentiary proof when one reflects upon oneself as a person.

During the Daye era of the Sui dynasty, there was a man named Wang Wujie from Luozhou.

Weeping, he said:
He lost his father at an early age, and his mother became a widow.
She raised a son and a daughter; the daughter was married, and twenty years have passed since the mother’s death.
On the day of Han Shi, he carried wine and food to sacrifice at his grave.
This man went there riding a donkey;

On that day, his younger sister was alone at her elder brother's house.

I have come to inform you:

While she was at home, her mother made offerings to her.

Having now decorated it for domestic offerings,
the mother said to her daughter:
"It was solely because of this scripture that I have undergone such suffering."
"In the midst of the dark paths of hell, the wardens struck my back until it was broken.
Look at how emaciated my body is.
The prison official spoke these words.
For what reason have you taken the scriptures of another school and treated them as your own?
What merit do you possess?
"You have committed a great transgression.
When the daughter saw her mother speak thus,
she wrote out another copy of the Lotus Sūtra for her mother.

the woman again saw her mother in a dream coming to urge her on with the text;

For what reason do you come again to press me so urgently?
Wait until it is finished; why such haste?
Later, when the copying of the sutra was completed,
the mother came to inform her daughter:
"It is because of you that I have had this sutra copied for me."
Now that I have emerged from the dark path and attained birth in a favorable realm,
I come to repay you for the power of your kindness.
"You should dwell well;
perform the rites of a wife properly,
taking faith as your foundation."
Having finished speaking, they wept with sorrow as they parted.
Later, when he investigated the former owner of the *Lotus Sūtra* who had ransomed it,
he found that his surname was indeed Fan.
Although the Fan family did not obtain the sutra,

Liu’s wife obtained a small measure of merit by ransoming [the child], yet her deceased mother could not benefit from it;

66. Chapter on Disputes and Litigation (57). Chapter Sixty-six on Disputes and Litigation consists of two sections. Section One: Exposition of the Intent. First, Exposition of the Intent: Now, when a single word of compassion is uttered, humans and devas smile with joy.
Once vulgar words are made public, both the hidden and the manifest will feel resentment;

The following [texts] are all from the *Catalogue of the Collection of Miscellaneous Dhāraṇīs*, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of the Later Wei. At that time, when the Tathāgata had first attained perfect enlightenment...
There was a Great Brahmā King who came to where the Buddha was, paid homage at the Buddha’s feet,
and spoke these words:
Namo buddhāya. Namo dharmāya. Namo saṃghāya.
I pay homage to the Buddha, the World-Honored One, the Great Dharma King who illuminates the world, who dwells in Jambudvīpa.
First, he spoke this divine mantra: The nectar-like, pure, and supreme Dharma, And the homage to the Sangha of those free from attachment.
Having paid homage at the feet of the Muni, he immediately spoke these verses: "O World-Honored One, all Tathāgatas..."
The śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, the various sages, world-protecting kings,
powerful nāgas, devas, and other such multitudes—
all are born among human beings; there are also yakṣas and rākṣasas.
Constantly delighting in devouring human fetuses,
this realm of the non-human king cannot be restrained by force;
it can cause people to be childless and bring harm to the womb at the time of the union of man and woman.
They cause their minds to become deluded and confused, and prevent the pregnancy from reaching fruition;
or they affect the *kalala* and *arbuda* stages, causing infertility or injury to the fetus,
and even taking life at the time of birth— all these are various malevolent spirits.
To those who inflict harm upon them, I shall now declare their names;

may the Buddha listen as I speak. First is Mīcuka; second is King Miga; third is Khanda; fourth is Apasimara; fifth is Mocika; sixth is Macika; seventh is Jamika; eighth is Kāminī; ninth is Revati; tenth is Pūtanā; eleventh is Mandanandi; twelfth is Śakunī; thirteenth is Kaṇṭhapānī; fourteenth is Mukhamanda; fifteenth is Lambā—these are the fifteen spirits.
Constantly wandering through the world, they cause terror among infants and small children.
I shall now describe the terrifying forms of these spirits,
by which forms all small children are made to feel alarm and fear.
As for Mīcuka, his form is like that of an ox. As for King Mīgā,
[his form is like that of a deer].
Their forms are like those of lions.
As for the Khaṇḍas,
their forms are like those of the god Kumāra.
The apasmāra is shaped like a wild fox.
The mukhacchedaka...
Its form is like that of a monkey.
As for the macika,
its form is like that of a rākṣasī.
Jāṃghika has a form like that of a horse; Kāminī—
Their forms are like those of women.
As for the Lipeṭis,
their forms are like those of dogs.
Pūrṇa was shaped like a pig; Māndhātṛ—
Its form is like that of a cat.
As for the Śākuṇikī,
its form is like that of a crow.
*Kaṇṭhapāṇi* is shaped like a cock;
*Mukhamanḍa* is... [as above].
Her form is like that of a *khuṅ-khu* fox. As for Lambā,
her form is like that of a snake.
These fifteen spirits afflict young children, causing them to tremble with fear.
I shall now further describe the signs of fear in children when they are possessed by these spirits.
As for those possessed by the Mīchuka spirit:
It causes the eyes of small children to roll back;
when possessed by the Mīka-rāja ghost,
it causes small children to vomit repeatedly.
When possessed by a Skanda ghost,
it causes the child’s two shoulders to move.
When possessed by an Apasmāra ghost, [it causes the child to fall prostrate].
If a child is possessed by the Mucilinda spirit, it causes froth to emerge from the mouth;
if possessed by the Mukhacchedaka spirit,
it causes the child to clench its fists and refuse to open them.
One possessed by the Māṭṛkā spirits causes the child to bite its own tongue.
One possessed by the Jāṃbhika spirits...
If possessed by the Kāminī spirit, it causes small children to weep and laugh excessively,
and makes them take pleasure in women.
One possessed by the Rīpudhi spirit causes a child to manifest various miscellaneous forms.
One possessed by the Pūtana spirit...
They cause young children to cry out in terror while asleep.
When possessed by the *mandanati* spirits,
they cause children to weep and laugh excessively.
One possessed by the Śākinī demon will cause a young child to refuse to nurse.
One possessed by the Kaṇṭhapānī demon...
If seized by the Mukhamanda spirits, it causes the throats and voices of children to become obstructed;
it also causes childhood fevers, heat-illnesses, and diarrhea.
As for those possessed by the Lambā spirits,
they cause young children to belch and retch repeatedly.
These are the fifteen malevolent spirits.
I have already described such forms used to terrify small children, as well as the manner in which those children react with fear.
Furthermore, there is a great king of the ghost-spirits named Candana-gandharva.
He is the foremost among all spirits and ghosts.
One should take a five-colored thread and recite this dhāraṇī once for each knot.
Tie one hundred and eight knots and write down the names of the gods and ghosts upon it;
have a person carry this written cord.
He said to that messenger:
"Go now with haste; travel as swiftly as the wind."
They went to the four quarters,
following the places where those fifteen spirits resided,
together with the Gandharva Mahāyakṣa King Candana.
One should cause those spirits and deities to be bound with the five fetters,
while simultaneously making offerings to the King of Spirits with various delicious foods and drinks, incense, flowers, lamps, and milk porridge.
At that time, the Great Brahma King again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
if there is a woman who does not give birth to sons or daughters..."
Some perish and fall away while still in the womb;
others have their lives taken after birth.
For those women who seek to obtain offspring and ensure their longevity, [this practice is prescribed].
One should constantly maintain mindfulness and practice wholesome dharmas.
On the eighth and fifteenth days of the month, one should observe the eight precepts,
bathe for purification, and put on new, clean clothes.
One should pay homage to the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Then, at midnight, one should place a few mustard seeds upon the crown of one's head and recite the dhāraṇī mantra spoken by me.
May this woman have her wishes fulfilled immediately;
may the son she bears be secure and free from affliction,
and may he live out his full natural lifespan without meeting an untimely death.
If there are ghosts or spirits who do not comply with my incantation,
I shall cause their heads to split into seven pieces,
like the branches of an *ari* tree.
Then he spoke the dhāraṇī-mantra for protecting all children, saying:
Tadyathā | agarā | gani | nāgagani | salūre | jile | gabale | bale | bure | raśude | surabhe | carabhe | vadhani | parāhaliṣani nayi | minayi | svāhā || World-Honored One.
I shall now proclaim this dhāraṇī mantra for the purpose of protecting all boys,
enabling them to attain peace and security and to obtain long life.
At that time, the World-Honored One, the Omniscient One, spoke the mantra as follows:

Tadātā | Buddha Buddha Buddha | Anumate | Bodhi Bodhi | Māre | Śikṣāyaśāri | Sthāne | Sarati | Dhūre dhūdhere | Paratadhūre | Śamane | Cāpe cāle | Parate cālaśame | Bandha bandhe | Pāhane | Jīmāne | Dāpane | Svāhā | Nepalane | Svāhā. Fifteen spirits constantly consume blood and flesh.
By the power of this dhāraṇī-mantra,
they shall all remain far removed from it and never give rise to evil thoughts;
it shall cause these youths to be free from fear, secure, and without affliction.
When dwelling in the womb and at birth, there shall be no calamities or difficulties.
For those who recite this mantra,
whether in cities, towns, or villages, [no such misfortunes shall occur].
Wherever they dwell, they shall also enable those infants and young children to grow up in peace and security,
preserving their lives unto the end of their natural term. Homage to the Buddha!
By accomplishing this mantra, all children shall be protected;
they shall not be harassed or harmed by malevolent spirits or ghosts,
and all calamities and all terrors shall be entirely dispelled.

For one who practices this ritual application:
Recite the mantra seven times over a cord made of black sheep’s wool and tie it on the left arm.
If sheep’s wool is unavailable, black thread may also be used.
This is for those suffering from fever lasting three or four days.
Tie a black thread with a mantra around the left arm.
If one suffers from a headache,
recite the mantra seven times.
Rub it with the hand.
If one suffers from deafness,
recite the mantra over a piece of wood seven times and insert it [into the ear].
If one suffers from toothache, recite the mantra over a willow branch seven times and chew it.
If one suffers from abdominal pain, recite the mantra over salt water seven times and drink it.
If one suffers from difficult labor, recite the mantra over a black thread seven times and tie it around the neck.
A child will then be easily born.
If one suffers from indigestion due to residual food, by chanting mantras over the hands and rubbing them [on the abdomen],
the person will immediately vomit and purge.
If one suffers from other calamities, one will immediately be able to protect oneself;
one will not fear water, fire, weapons, or venomous beasts,
and none of these evils shall be able to cause harm.
Except for those who do not apply their minds with care regarding flavors,
and who are defiled, evil, and impure— for them,
there will be no divine efficacy.

The Dhāraṇī for Great Learning and Strong Memory, Spoken by the Buddha. *Bhūta-vibha | Māna-jau | Ādhi-śūru | Nama-piṭa | Dāra | Jambū-bha | Saiman | Piṭa-parātus-kāri-sita | Dhyādi-siddhi | Nasati | Asanti | Kaci-picaci | Puccha-vayara-ti | Agati-samakhiti | Siddhi-samabiti.* The Buddha addressed Ānanda: [This is the dhāraṇī for great learning and strong memory.]
If you practice this rite,
take these three substances— pāramitā, śvetaharītakī, and pippalī—
and recite the mantra over them together at dawn for one thousand times.
Take it by mixing with ghee and honey;
then one will be able to hear, receive, and uphold [this spell] upon hearing it but once.

The *Dhāraṇī-mantra for the Practice and Petition of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva*: *Namo radana dharaye | namo ārya varakite śavaraye bodhisatvaye mahābodhisatvaye mahāsādhaye mahākāruṇika tāḍha usumeśadhataye sumivadevadhataye sugiriśadhataye subhiśadhataye ismisicchaniparaye svāhā.* This is the method for this practice.
Before an image of Avalokiteśvara,
smear the ground with fragrant mud and make offerings of incense and flowers.
Recite it six times throughout the day and night,
completing one hundred and twenty recitations during each session. Then,
according to whatever you seek, [invoke] Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
Because this practitioner manifests their body in response to others, allowing them to see it;
whatever they seek shall be fulfilled according to their original wishes.
Regarding the *Varṣāpana-dhāraṇī*, the *Mahāmegha-sūtra* states: [The *Varṣāpana-dhāraṇī*] ... [The *Varṣāpana-dhāraṇī*] ... The *Mahāmegha-sūtra* says:
At that time, by the supernatural power of the World-Honored One,
four black clouds arose;
together with sweet rain, they spread everywhere as three kinds of clouds emerged.
That is to say, there arose sounds of sweet rain falling in low, medium, and high tones,
like the music of the devas, which all sentient beings delighted in hearing.
At that time, the World-Honored One—
He then spoke the mantra:

*Kṛte parikṛte saṃkṛte parisaṃkṛte pare parāyaṇe saparāyaṇe sārasārapasārapasāra māñjamañjacāracāre cāracāre pracāracāre pracāracāre saparacāracāre vitīhe he he sariṣi sariṣi phuru phuru svāhā.* If there are any nāgas who, having heard this mantra, do not send down sweet rain, [they shall be punished].
May [the head] shatter into seven pieces.
Dharani for Stopping Toothache. Dharani for Stopping Toothache.
Namo Buddha. Namo Dharma.
Homage to the Sangha of Bhikṣus. Homage to Śāriputra. Tulu.
The bhikṣu Mahāmaudgalyāyana pays homage to the Venerable One whose awakened mind is renowned throughout the ten directions;
he dwells in the north on Mount Gandhamādana.
There is a king of worms there named Xiūxiūwude (Xiuhui Wude),
which resides within his teeth.
He shall dispatch a messenger [with this command]:
"None shall dare eat its teeth—whether they be at the roots, within them, or by their sides.
If the insects do not quickly descend into the vessel, their heads shall split into seven pieces."
Just as Kaurukullā was aided by Brahmā,
so may this incantation now be fulfilled according to my wish through homage to the Buddha.
If one practices this rite, one should take pure water, recite the mantra over it once, and then spit it into a vessel, whereupon the [pestilence] will cease.

To prevent locusts and grasshoppers from arising when sowing grain seeds, one should recite this dhāraṇī mantra over the seeds. The dhāraṇī mantra for preventing locusts and grasshoppers from arising when sowing grain seeds is: *Tadyathā | Paravati | Nāśavati*. When one wishes to sow, [one should do so].
Take one *śeṣa* of seeds,
recite the mantra twenty-one times over them,
and cast them into the great seed-vessel.
At the end of its growth from the seed within,
it is not eaten by insects,
nor does it suffer from any calamities or pests.

The Dhāraṇī for Blessing Fields and Soil. Namo buddhāya. Namo dharmāya. Namo saṃghāya. Namo mīlūkṣpe. Bodhisattvānāṃ tathāgatānāṃ bhagavatāṃ. Virūḍhakāya bhagavate. Kūṭadikāya virūḍhakāya bhagavate. Meruśāpe. Kṣemāya bhagavate. Hume anivartāya bhagavate. Mārābhaṭāya bhagavate. Hume bubhagavate. If one fears that the crops will not flourish, [one should recite this].
Recite this dhāraṇī over one *hu* of soil twenty-one times,
and scatter the soil upon the grain.
Furthermore, it shall cause all malevolent spirits to be unable to suck the essence of these grains and crops;
those who eat such grains shall have their heads split into seven pieces.
It can eliminate all disasters and locusts, ensuring that no evils arise.

Dhāraṇī for Subduing the Poison of Snakes and Scorpions. Dhāraṇī for Subduing the Poison of Snakes and Scorpions: *Namo ratnāmbareṇa tadyathā hulu phuni phulu ha ri ha ri ha svāhā*. *Namo gurukeṇayam ratna tadyathā ilu rili philu phulu svāhā*. With this dhāraṇī, one should recite it twenty-one times, or seven times.
Give one mouthful of water.
Recite the mantra three times and give three mouthfuls of water;
[the patient] will be healed immediately.

Dhāraṇī Mantra for Healing All Hundred Diseases and Poisons. Homage to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. Tadyathā: āraṇi, tāraṇi, sarvadaṭa, varāṇi, sarvadaṭa, bandhami, śarvadharī, namucami-sidantatu, mantapata, svāhā. For those who practice this rite:
One should use white thread and tie one knot while reciting the mantra once;
recite it seven times and tie seven knots.
If there is anyone suffering from illness, tie it around their throat.
All hundred diseases and various poisons shall be entirely eliminated and healed.

This is the *Dhāraṇī Mantra Spoken by Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva for the Extinction of Sins and the Fulfillment of Wishes*. *Namo lecang lishesheshe* *Namo alishesheshe* *Poluqidi shafuoshashe* *Bodhisattvashe* *Mahāsattvashe* *Tadhyatha* *Dudhulu dudhulu* *A si* *Masimolimi* *Shibamolili* *Doudoupi* *Namunamu* *Svāhā* If one practices this method:
Before an image of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva,
burn high-quality agarwood incense and perform repentance with a sincere mind;
throughout the six periods of the day, engage in prostrations, recitation, and circumambulation.
If one recites this three times at each session,
all sinful karmas accumulated since beginningless time will be extinguished, and one will attain inconceivable great merit.
Whatever one seeks or desires shall surely be obtained according to one's wishes.

The Dhāraṇī-Mantra Spoken by Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva for Eliminating Sudden Abdominal Pain. *Namo le nang li she she | Namo a li she | Ba lu ji ti | She bu lo she | Bo di sa tuo she | Mo he sa tuo she | Ta che ta | Jiu zhi jiu zhi | Luo zhi luo zhi | A na san po tuo ni yi | Svāhā.* If a person suddenly contracts the disease of abdominal pain and becomes distressed, [they should recite this].
One should quickly recite the mantra over salt water three times and have the person suffering from abdominal pain drink it;
their pain will then be immediately relieved.

The Dhāraṇī Mantra Spoken by Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva for Eliminating Poison, Even for Those Already Dead. *Namo lecang li she she* *Namo ali she* *Polu jidi* *Shefuluo she* *Puti sata she* *Mahāsattva she* *Tad yathā* *Sari sari* *Viśari viśari* *Sarvaviṣa-nāśani* *Svāhā* If a person is afflicted by various poisons and is on the verge of death, [they shall be saved].
If [the person] has already died,
quickly recite this mantra into their ear.
He was immediately cured.
Even if he had died from violence, he would have revived.

The Dharani-mantra Spoken by Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva for Eliminating Various Forms of Leprosy and Even Wounds and Injuries. Namo lecana-leśe-śe | Namo arileśe | Varoṣiṭi | Śavaraśe | Bodhisattvaśe | Mahāsattvaśe | Tadyathā | Sumukhe | Vimukhe | Hūle | Hūle | Sumule | Vi-sumule | Sunande | Vi-sunande | Masitapadumasure | Madanti | Babati | Tapasu | Sadhu | Svāhā. If a person suffers from leprosy...
Whether one suffers from white leprosy or red leprosy,
if they repent with utmost sincerity, practice the Way, and constantly recite [this scripture], they will be cured.
If one gnashes the teeth in madness;
if there is a wound or disease on the body;
or if one has been wounded by a blade or arrow such that the wound is torn open.
By means of this divine mantra, one should consecrate earth and smear it upon [the patient];
then they will immediately recover.

The Dhāraṇī Spell Spoken by Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva for Obtaining the Power of Hearing and Retention Without Forgetting through the Ingestion of Five-Colored Acorus Calamus. *Namo le nang li she she* *Namo a li she* *Ba lu ji ti* *She bu lo she* *Bodhisattva she* *Mahāsattva she* *Tad yathā* *Kien t'i pu na li* *Pa lo pa li* *Svāhā* [Recite this] before an image of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
Burn aloeswood incense and, with utmost sincerity,
recite the mantra over white calamus root eight hundred times;
by consuming it, one will attain the power of hearing and retaining all without forgetfulness.
Apart from these, there are also separate mantras for the four types of *chāmbu*—black, red, blue, and yellow;

however, the text is too voluminous to describe them here. The Mantra for Healing Axillary Odor: 1. *Yathā nu jñe hū hū hū hū yathā nu jñe* 2. *Bhū lu lu lu lu yathā nu jñe* 3. *Mālāte yathā nu jñe* 4. *Anānā yathā nu jñe* 5. *Svāhā* If one performs this rite:
Take three sheng of lime and three sheng of bitter wine;
place them upon a platter and recite the mantra over them twenty-one times.
Form them into balls, alternating and replacing them one after another.
For a man, place it under the left armpit;
for a woman, place it under the right armpit.
He will immediately recover.
The Incantation for Healing the Demons of Malaria: 1. Sumedha, 2. Anīta, 3. Kacinita, 4. Uhuṇasumeda, 5. Cīvahusumeda, 6. Icinitathasumeda, Svāhā. If one performs this rite:
Take five-colored thread and, having recited mantras over it, tie seven knots.
If the pain descends from the head, first tie the topknot; then tie the hands and feet, causing the pain to become acute.
Chant the mantra over water three times and sprinkle it;
the illness will be cured immediately.

For the treatment of the "ghost who prevents food from being swallowed," chant the mantra: *Huma-dhu-uśahau-hu huma-dhu-aṇu 1; kapi huma-dhu kapi huma-dhu 2; prapara huma-dhu 3; svāhā 4*. One must then chant this over water seven times.
Give it to the patient to drink;
after no more than three or five doses,
they will recover.

The Scripture on the Divine Water Mantra for Healing All Diseases, Spoken by the Buddha. Homage to the Buddha. Homage to the Dharma. Homage to the Sangha of Bhikṣus. Homage to the Seven Buddhas of the Past. Homage to all Buddhas. Homage to the disciples of all Buddhas. Homage to all noble and holy teachers. Homage to all noble and holy disciples. (Recite the names of the Seven Buddhas: First, Vipaśyin Buddha; Second, Śikhin Buddha; Third, Viśvabhū Buddha; Fourth, Krakucchanda Buddha; Fifth, Kanakamuni Buddha; Sixth, Kāśyapa Buddha; Seventh, Śākyamuni Buddha. This is the divine mantra spoken by the Buddha.
Recite the mantra three times over a well, pond, river, or spring.
Those who drink from it shall have all their hundred ailments eliminated.

The Dhāraṇī of Fulfilling Wishes Spoken by Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. Homage to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva! *Tantidhā khuravada khuravada gahavada gavada gavada svāhā.* For those who practice this rite:

One must purify the three karmas, stay in a clean place such as a Buddha hall or a stūpa courtyard, and with single-minded devotion perform prostrations and circumambulations while reciting this dhāraṇī twelve thousand times.
When one beholds Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, all one’s wishes shall be fulfilled according to one’s desire.

This is the *Dhāraṇī for Smearing Mud upon Soldiers* spoken by the Buddha: *Dhāraṇī for Smearing Mud upon Soldiers*: *tadyathā | ilili phuli phuli phulenti | āvau | māvau | bhāvau | bhiñjivau | bhisitau | macchitau | uśravāvau | svāhā*. If there is anyone who wishes to enter among a band of thieves...
Recite the mantra three times over clay and smear it upon one's body.
If one smears it upon banners, standards, flags, drums, horns, or musical instruments,
one will certainly achieve victory.
If one is bitten by a venomous insect,
or if one has been poisoned,
or if there is a swelling on the body;
Having smeared it with mud enchanted by mantra,
one uses blue pigment to draw a circle upon it; then [the patient] is immediately cured.
The verse says:
A chronic ailment has indeed persisted for long; This deep-seated malady is truly difficult to cure.
The four Māras constantly harass me, And the six thieves vie with one another to drag me away.
Trapped in distress with no one to save me, I rejoice only in your great compassion and pity;
From afar you look upon my mind caught in the net, and shaking your mendicant's staff, you travel through the mists.
Bestowing this medicine of nectar, you ensure that no false path can precede it.
Eliminating calamities and eradicating the burden of karma, Rescuing those tormented by suffering,
the flow of grace vibrates through the profound teachings; Benefiting all equally throughout the great trichiliocosm,
Were it not for the power of divine mantras, how could one’s years be extended?

Chapter Sixty-Eight, Part Two: Incantations and Arts; Accounts of Responsive Manifestations.

A Brief Citation of Eight Testimonies of Responsive Manifestations: Ge You of the Former Zhou; Shi Qicheng of the Jin; Zhu Fotucheng of the Jin; Zhu Fayin of the Jin; Shi Baoyi of the Song; Shi Beidu of the Song; Shi Xuanchang of the Song; Miscellaneous Secular Illusions and Arts. Ge You of the Former Zhou. Ge You of the Former Zhou.
He was a Qiang person from Shu.
During the time of King Cheng of Zhou,
he delighted in carving wood to make sheep and selling them.
Once he mounted the wooden ram and entered Shu,
the kings, lords, and nobles of Shu pursued him up Mount Suishan.
Mount Suishan is located to the southwest of Mount Emei.
Its height is infinite.
Those who follow it do not return;
they all attain the Way of the Immortals.
The *Guli lun* says:
"To obtain even a single peach from Mount Suishan,
though one cannot thereby become an immortal, is sufficient to make one feel exalted."
According to the *Sou Shen Ji* (Searches for the Divine), there were dozens of shrines established at the foot of the mountain.
During the Jin dynasty, there was a monk named Qi Yu in Luoyang;
he was a native of India.
He traveled extensively among the Chinese and the barbarians, having no fixed abode;
yet he was bold and extraordinary, following his own nature while disregarding worldly conventions,
such that his traces and conduct were never constant.
The people of the time were unable to fathom him.
From his departure from India until his arrival in Funan,
he traveled along various seacoasts.
Thereupon he traveled through the regions of Jiaozhi and Guangzhou, where there were many miraculous manifestations;
having reached Xiangyang, he arrived.
He wished to be carried across the river by boat;
however, seeing that the Venerable’s saṃghāṭī was tattered and worn, the boatman treated him with contempt and would not take him aboard.
The boat reached the northern bank;
Daoyi had already crossed over.
As he walked forward, he saw two tigers with their ears flattened and tails wagging.
Fayou stroked its head with his hand;
the tiger descended the path and departed.
Those who witnessed this on both banks followed after it in great crowds.
At the end of the reign of Emperor Hui of the Jin dynasty, he arrived in Luoyang.
All the monastics there prostrated themselves before him,
yet Fotudeng knelt in the Hu fashion, remaining composed and unmoving in expression.
At times, he would inform others of his previous incarnations,
stating that Zhi Fayuan had come from among sheep,
while Zhu Faxing had come from among humans.
Furthermore, he criticized the various members of the Sangha,
saying that their clothing was too ornate and did not accord with the simple dharma.
Upon seeing the palace city of Luoyang, he remarked:
It appeared vaguely like the palace of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;
the only difference was that what is natural there is not so with human affairs.
Daoyi said to the śramaṇa Jīvamitra:
The one who built this palace came from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;
once it was completed, he returned to the celestial realm.
Beneath the roof tiles of the ridge, there should be fifteen hundred crafted objects.
At that time, everyone said,
"In the past, we have heard that this craftsman actually used to place his tools beneath the tiles.
They also said:
After the palace was completed,
he was subsequently killed.
Teng Yongwen of Nanyang, the Grand Governor of Hengyang, [recorded this].
While residing at Mansui Temple in Luoji, he fell ill;
the condition did not improve for a year,
and his two legs became so contracted that he was unable to rise or walk.
Zhiyu went to see him and said,
"Do you wish for your illness to be cured?
Thereupon, he took a cup of pure water and a branch of willow.
He then brushed the water with a willow branch and raised his hand toward Yongwen, reciting a mantra.
He did this three times.
Thereupon, he grasped Yongwen’s knee with his hand and caused him to rise.
He immediately rose and walked as before.
In this monastery, there were several dozen withered *cintāmaṇi* trees;
Fayu asked Yongwen about them.
"How long has it been since the tree died?
Yongwen replied,
"It has been many years."
Yu then recited incantations over the tree,
following the ritual methods used for the Yongwen [trees].
Immediately, the tree burst forth with blossoms, its branches spreading wide and flourishing in lush abundance.
In the Shangfang Bureau, there was a man who was ill and about to die.
Bo Yi placed a metal vessel upon the patient's abdomen and covered him entirely with a white cloth.
He recited thousands of words of incantations and prayers,
whereupon a foul odor immediately permeated the entire room.
The patient said:
"I am alive. Yu then ordered someone to lift the cloth;
inside the alms bowl were several liters of what appeared to be silt and mud.
The stench was such that one could not approach it;
the patient subsequently recovered.
At that time, there was unrest in Luoyang.
He took his leave and returned to India.
Zhu Faxing, a śramaṇa from Luoyang,
was a monk of eminent standing.
At that time, the people requested Daoyi, saying,
"Venerable Sir, you are a monk who has already attained the Way.
We pray that you will leave behind a single word as a perpetual admonition."
Fayou said,
"We may assemble the multitude. Once the assembly had gathered, he spoke.
Kāśyapa ascended the high seat and spoke these verses:
Guarding the mouth and restraining body and mind, Be careful not to commit any evil;
Practice all that is wholesome— In this way, one attains deliverance from the world.
As soon as he finished speaking, he entered meditative silence.
Xing bowed again and requested, saying,
"I pray that the Venerable Master will grant me teachings I have not yet heard."
The meaning of such verses as these is already familiar to an eight-year-old child through recitation;
it is not something one would expect from a person who has attained the Way.
Yu Xiu said: "Though one may recite [the scriptures] at eight years of age, if one does not practice them for a hundred years, what benefit is there in such recitation?
Everyone knows to revere those who have attained the Way."
They do not realize that by practicing they will naturally attain the Way.
How tragic! Though my words are few, those who practice them will be many.
Thereupon, they took their leave,
saying that several hundred people each invited Daoyi to a meal at their own homes;
Daoyi consented to go to them all.
At dawn the next day, each of the five hundred houses had a beggar;
at first they thought he was alone, but as he came,
they addressed one another with questions.
Only then did they realize that he had manifested his divided body and descended.
Once he departed, the various practitioners escorted him as far as Henan City;
Kṣemaṅkara walked slowly, and those who pursued him could not catch up.
Fayou then drew a line on the ground with his staff and said, "We part here.
On that same day, someone arrived from Chang'an.
Jianyu was in that monastery.
Furthermore, on the very same day, as evening drew near, the merchant Hu Shideng arrived.
He encountered Fēngyù in the midst of the shifting sands;
calculating the distance traveled, he had already journeyed over nine thousand li.
Having returned to the Western Regions, [he reported his findings].
His final whereabouts are unknown.
During the Jin dynasty, there was a man named Zhu Fotucheng in Ye.
He was a native of the Western Regions.
His original surname was Bo.
Having left home to become a monk in his youth, he maintained pure integrity and devoted himself to study,
reciting several million words of the sutras.
He was adept at understanding both the literal text and its underlying meaning;
although he had not yet read the Confucian histories of this land,

Section 70: On Physiognomy (62). This section consists of two parts: the Exposition of Intent and the Citation of Evidence. 1. Exposition of Intent. First, the Exposition of Intent: Now, the Great Teaching is impartial.
Supreme virtue evokes a shared resonance,
yet ordinary sentiments are separated by conditions;
the forces of creation fashion diverse forms.
The mind and its objects interact;
the retributions of suffering and pleasure differ accordingly,
like a wax seal pressed into clay.
The seals manifest as written characters;
their forms may be divined,
thereby enabling humans and animals to distinguish their respective sounds.
The Hu and Han dwell together yet are distinguished by their physical forms;
the noble and the humble differ in their degrees of clarity and obscurity;
the sages and the ordinary differ in their purity and turbidity.

Chapter on Praying for Rain (63): This chapter consists of four sections: Section One: Exposition of the Intent; Section Two: Ritual Offerings for Prayer; Section Three: The Occurrence of Rainfall; Section Four: Rivers and Seas. Section One: Exposition of the Intent. First, as the Holy Way is empty and tranquil, it is able to respond perfectly and universally to all places.
Because its responses are without fixed direction, there is nothing to which it does not appropriately respond.
Recently, as the Yin and Yang have been out of harmony and the weather has remained parched for many months,
the rites at the Northern Wall have long been performed.
The rains in the western suburbs have not responded.
