Looking upward, I reflect that the torch of wisdom shines in secret obscurity.
Nothing hidden remains unilluminated;
its divine efficacy is unfathomable;
there is nothing that does not respond to those who feel its presence.
Therefore, we rely upon the Triple Gem to propagate the One Vehicle and recite these subtle words.
May this great merit be cultivated here;
may the teachings of the Dharma first begin to unfold,
and may the clouds of compassion spread far and wide.
Once the profound words were expounded,
their nourishing grace spread far and wide;
auspicious grains grew in continuous clusters across the fields and plains.
Auspicious fruits grow everywhere upon the trees;
for clothing, one wears only the products of eight silkworms;
for food, one relies necessarily upon the harvest of seven crops.
The world is as lush as the Land of Many Fragrances;
all living beings are as if in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī).
There is no request that is not harmoniously fulfilled.
Prayers are invariably answered;
all alike bathe in these waters of meditative concentration,
continuing the source of sagely wisdom.
This opens up the net of craving and transcends the realm of existence and non-existence.
2. Section on Prayers and Sacrifices (Prayajī-bhāga), Part Two. As stated in the *Mahāmegha-vṛṣṭi-saṃprayukta-sūtra* (*Da yun lun qing yu jing*):
The Buddha said:
"If you wish to invoke great rain or the method for stopping rain,
listen attentively now."
The presiding master for the rite of requesting rain shall give rise to a mind of compassion toward all sentient beings and observe the eightfold precepts.
In an open, unsheltered space,
one should spread out a blue canopy and suspend ten blue banners;
having thoroughly purified the ground, one should smear the site with cow dung.
Please request the mantra-reciter to sit upon a green seat.
If he is a layperson, he should observe the eight precepts;
if he is a bhikṣu, he should maintain his monastic vows.
All were dressed in pure, clean garments;
they burned excellent,
famous incense and further scattered powdered incense over the Dharma Master’s seat.
One should consume three kinds of pure foods:
namely, cow's milk, curd, and rice with the husks.
While reciting this "Chapter on the Great Cloud Wheel," [one should do so].
Facing east, sit and with a sincere mind throughout the day and night, let the sound not cease,
making offerings to all Buddhas.
Furthermore, place pure water in new flasks and install them in the four intermediate directions.
According to one's financial means, prepare various kinds of food offerings for the nāgas.
Additionally, scatter fragrant flowers throughout the site of practice (maṇḍala).
Furthermore, for the four sides of the Dharma-seat, one should use exclusively fresh, pure cow-dung juice to paint the forms of nāgas.

To read and recite this sutra for one day, two days,

He went hunting again and once more saw the man who had previously been wearing a white sash;
he spoke to him, saying:
"I tell you, do not come here again;
you have failed to heed my words,
and your enemy's son has already grown large."
"I must certainly repay my lord; this is not something I can bear to leave unaddressed.
Hearing him shoot at the man, the latter was terrified and wished to flee.
He then saw three men dressed in black robes,
each eight feet tall,
all opening their mouths toward him.
If one shoots a person, they die immediately.
The *Lüshi Chunqiu* says:
"When Tang saw a hunter setting up a net, spreading it out on all four sides, he addressed him, saying:"
Those who come from the heavens,
those who emerge from the earth,
and those who arrive from the four quarters.
"All have been caught in my net.
Tang said, "Alas!
They are all gone."
Who other than Jie could have been like this?
Regarding Song’s Ruan Zhizong, who was fond of hunting and manifested the retribution of suffering:
Song’s Ruan Zhizong was a native of Hedong.
In the sixteenth year of the Yuanjia era, Ruan Yin was serving as the Governor of Zhongli under the Sui dynasty.
Yin dispatched Zizong to travel to a distant village,
accompanied by the local officials Ge Gou and Bian Ding.
He arrived at a commoner's house;
he was dazed as if asleep,
and did not wake up again.
The people thought he was dead and carried him out through the outer gate to prepare the funeral equipment;
after a night had passed, he was able to speak.
Previously, about one hundred men had bound Zizong and taken him away.
After traveling several tens of *li*, he arrived at a Buddhist monastery (*buddhastūpa*).
The offerings provided by the monastic community were no different from those in the secular world. A certain monk said:
"You who were fond of fishing and hunting must now receive your retribution.
He then took the skin of a young deer, flayed it, and cut it into pieces,
following exactly the method used for treating sacrificial animals.
He then placed it back into deep water and fished it out again;
he sliced and minced it until it was shaped like sashimi.
Furthermore, they are boiled in cauldrons and roasted on furnaces;
though their bodies are first completely disintegrated, they are restored to their original state as soon as they are replaced.
The agonizing pain and bitter suffering reached their peak three times before ceasing.
He asked, "Do you wish to live?
Zhizong then prostrated himself, entreating for his life.
The practitioner had him squat on the ground and pour water over him, saying:
"Each pouring removes five hundred offenses."
Zhizong earnestly requested many more initiations.
The śramaṇa said,
"Only three will suffice."
Seeing several ants, the practitioner pointed at them and said,
"Although these are minute creatures, they must not be killed."
Furthermore, whatever is of such a nature— even large fish or meat that has died of its own accord—
may indeed be eaten.
On the day of the vegetarian assembly, everyone wore new clothes; since there were no old ones available, there was nothing to wash.
Zizong then asked:
"I am a traveler with three companions;
why am I alone beset by suffering?
The practitioner said:
Those two individuals know for themselves their transgressions and blessings;
knowing this, they intentionally commit offenses.
Only you, O fool, are ignorant and fail to recognize the retribution of causes and conditions.
Therefore, they admonished one another.
Consequently, he immediately regained consciousness and was able to rise after several days.
Consequently, he then abandoned fishing and hunting. The above account is one verification from the *Mingxiang ji*.
Liu Zhenli of Liangzhou made his living as a butcher and suffered great calamity as a manifest retribution at the Xiao Zhuangyan Temple.
It was located in Dingyin Ward in Jiankang.
Originally the site of the Temple of King Lingling of the Jin Dynasty,
it was established by Master Tandu in the sixth year of the Tianjian era.
At that time, there was a man named Zou Wenli who made his living by slaughtering animals for meat.
He once intended to kill a deer.
The deer knelt and shed tears, deeming it an ill omen;
he immediately proceeded to disembowel and dissect it.
The deer was carrying a fawn.
She was soon about to give birth;
when she approached the kitchen, her grief was so intense that she felt a heartbreak at the thought of harm,
and because of this, she fell ill.
His eyebrows and beard fell out, and the sores on his body completely rotted away.
Consequently, he felt shame and gave rise to deep remorse and self-reproach.
He then sought out Master Dudo to confess his transgressions and perform a solemn repentance.
He established a great vow and completely relinquished his family wealth to purchase this land.
Regarding the establishment of the monastery, the *Jiǎngjīng sì jì* (Record of the Temples of the Liang Capital) states:

During the Sui dynasty, there was a General of the Household for the Cavalry who was fond of hunting; his wife was as flighty as a rabbit. At the end of the Kaihuang era of the Sui, he was a man from Dàizhōu.
Surnamed Wang, he served as General of the Flying Cavalry.
He was stationed at Puzhou,
where his fondness for hunting led him to kill countless creatures.
He had five sons and no daughters.
Later, he gave birth to a daughter who was so beautiful that all who saw her loved and marveled at her.
His parents cherished him with a care unlike that of ordinary people.
Once he had returned to his hometown,
the villagers and his kinsmen provided him with clothing and together nurtured and loved him.
The girl was seven years old;
one day she was lost,
and there was nowhere to seek her.
Suspecting that a neighbor had played a game of hiding him,
they searched for him but could not find him;
only when his elder brothers rode their horses out to search further did they finally see him.
He had traveled more than thirty li from home;
his horse could not catch up with him.
Only after his elder brothers surrounded him with several dozen riders did they finally capture him.
He made sounds from his mouth like the cry of a rabbit;
with thorns covering his feet up to the knees, he died of starvation after more than a month had passed.
His parents were so overcome by grief that they could not bear the pain.
This was truly because the father’s hunting had brought calamity upon his daughter, who received its retribution;
consequently, the entire family observed the fasts and practiced ascetic discipline without ceasing.
Cai Xuanming, Vice Director of the Court of Judicial Review, [recorded this].
He once served as a legal officer (fǎcáo) for the Dai Commandery, where he expounded the teachings to them.

Jang Lue, a General of the Flying Eagles (Yīngyáng lángjiàng) of the Sui dynasty, was fond of hunting; seeing a flock of birds being hunted to death, [he was moved]. Jang Lue of Tianshui was a General of the Flying Eagles of the Sui.
In his youth, he was fond of hunting and skilled at releasing hawks and dogs.
Later, while suffering from an illness, he saw a flock of birds numbering in the thousands, all of which were headless;
they circled his bed and shrieked, saying:
"Quickly return my head to me!
He then suddenly suffered a headache and fainted; after a long time he revived.
Thereupon, he requested the assembly of monks to urgently perform merit-seeking rites for the sake of the birds.
Having granted this permission, they all departed.
Subsequently, he was healed;
once recovered, he vowed for the rest of his life to abstain from wine and meat and to refrain from killing living beings.
While stationed in Longyou, I met Jiang Lue,
who was already about sixty years old;
he told me this himself.

In a district outside Jizhou during the Sui dynasty, there was a young boy who ate roasted chicken eggs and received immediate retribution. At the beginning of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, in a district outside Jizhou, there was a young boy thirteen years of age.
He constantly stole the eggs of his neighbor’s chickens to roast and eat them.
One morning, before the villagers had risen,
someone knocked on his door and called out the boy's name.
The father ordered his son to go out and respond;
he saw a man who said,
"The official summons you."
The boy said,
"Call my servant; enter and fetch my clothes and provisions."
The messenger said,
"There is no need.
He then led the boy out.
To the south of the village was formerly a mulberry field;
after the plowing was finished but before the seeds had been sown,
this young boy suddenly saw a small city to the right of the road.
The gate-towers on all four sides were extremely magnificent, both in their vermilion and white colors.
The boy marveled, saying,
"When did this city come to exist?"
The messenger rebuked him, telling him not to speak,
and then proceeded to the north gate of the city, ordering the boy to enter first.
As the boy crossed the threshold, [the earth shook].
The city gates suddenly closed;
not a single person was to be seen,
for it was nothing but an empty city.
The ground was entirely hot ashes and embers, deep enough to just submerge the ankles.
A young child suddenly cried out and ran toward the southern gate;
as he was about to reach it, the gate closed.
Furthermore, as he ran toward the east and west, it was likewise in all cases:
before he had arrived, the gates opened;
once he reached them, they closed.
At that time, many villagers went out to gather mulberry leaves;
both men and women were numerous,
and they all saw this boy in the middle of the plowed field.
With a voice like that of one weeping, he ran about in all four directions;
everyone said to one another,
"This child is mad."
From dawn until now,
he has played thus without ceasing.
When the time for his midday meal arrived, [he...]
When the mulberry gatherers had all returned,
the boy’s father asked,
"Did you see my son?"
The man from Sang replied,
"My father and son were playing and running about south of the village;
I called for them, but they refused to come."
The father went outside the village;
seeing his son running from afar,
he called out his name loudly.
At the sound of a single cry, he came to a halt.
The city's ashes suddenly vanished.
Seeing his father, he collapsed.
He wailed aloud as he spoke of it.
He saw that from the midpoint of his feet upward, the flesh and blood were scorched and withered;
from his knees downward, they were festering and raw like roasted meat.
He carried him back to nurse and treat him;
the flesh above his thighs returned to its former state,
but from the knees downward, they became withered bones.
When the neighbors heard of this, they vied with one another to ask for the reason.
He answered them as before.
When the people examined the place where he had run, the footprints were clear and distinct.
There was not a trace of ash or fire;
it was truly because their karmic offenses caused them to see hells wherever they looked.
Thereupon, among the men and women of the town, regardless of whether they were old or young, there was no exception.
They all observed the fasts and precepts until death without fail.
There was a monk of great virtue, the Dharma Master Daohui,
who was originally a native of Jizhou.

I have related this in full for you as it occurred. It was similar to the case of his neighboring district. Regarding the Tang General Li Shou, Duke of Suian, who was fond of hunting and was sued by a dog over the flesh he had torn from a living animal: Li Shou, Duke of Suian, served as the Governor-General of Jiaozhou during the Tang dynasty. He was an avid hunter. Once, while out hunting, he encountered a dog that had been chasing a wild boar. Seeing the dog exhausted and unable to catch its prey, the Duke took pity on it and commanded his attendants to release the beast. However, the dog instead turned upon the Duke’s own horse and bit it severely. The Duke, enraged, ordered his men to kill the dog. But the dog then began to howl piteously, shedding tears as it looked toward the Duke. Moved by this, the Duke asked his attendants, "Why does this dog weep so bitterly? They replied, "This dog has been chasing a wild boar for some time now; it is exhausted and cannot catch it. Your Honor released it, yet it has come to bite your horse. It fears that you will kill it, and thus it weeps. The Duke sighed and said, "If even a mere dog can understand human sentiment, how could I be so cruel as to kill it? He then ordered his attendants to cut a piece of flesh from his own thigh and give it to the dog. The dog immediately devoured it. The Duke further instructed them to provide the dog with food and drink and to release it back into the wild. From that day forward, the Duke no longer hunted. This account is recorded in the *Zizhi Tongjian*. It is a matter of great significance that one should not harm living beings. Furthermore, there is the story of the dog that was sued for the flesh it had torn from a living person. In the past, there was a man named Wang Zhi who lived in the region of Xiangyang. He was a man of integrity and virtue. One day, while walking along the road, he saw a dog chasing a rabbit. The dog caught the rabbit, but before it could devour it, a hawk swooped down and snatched the rabbit away. The dog then turned to bite the hawk. The hawk fled, dropping the rabbit. The dog then went to the man and barked at him. The man, seeing this, felt compassion and picked up the rabbit to give it to the dog. The dog, however, would not take it. The man then asked the dog, "Why do you not take this? The dog replied, "I was originally going to eat this rabbit. Now that I have obtained it, I must not give it away. The man said, "I am giving it to you out of compassion; why do you refuse? The dog then said, "If you truly wish to give it to me, you must first cut a piece of flesh from your own body and give it to me. Only then will I take it. The man, moved by the dog's sincerity, took a knife and cut a piece of flesh from his thigh to give to the dog. The dog then ate it and departed. Later, when the man returned home, he told his wife and children what had happened. His family members were all astonished. The man said, "The dog’s spirit is such that it understands human righteousness. How much more so should I, a human being, act with integrity! From that time on, the man became even more diligent in his conduct. This account is recorded in the *Shishuo Xinyu* and other historical texts. It serves as a warning that one must not be unkind to animals. These two stories illustrate the principle that the Way of Heaven and Earth is fundamentally one and the same, and that one should treat all living beings with compassion. Thus, it is said: "To harm living beings is to oppose the Way of Heaven; to cherish life is to accord with the Way of Heaven. This is the meaning. It is also said: "The Great Way is impartial; it gives life to all things. This is the ultimate truth. Therefore, one should practice benevolence and extend it to all creatures. This is the teaching of the sages. It is also said: "The sage regards all things as equal. This is because the sage perceives that the nature of all things is identical. Thus, he treats others as he treats himself. This is the foundation of the Way of Humanity. It is also said: "The Way of Heaven is constant, and the Way of Man is the same. This means that the principles governing the heavens and the earth are consistent with those governing human affairs. Therefore, one must cultivate oneself through moral cultivation and apply this to the governance of the world. This is the way of the sages. It is also said: "The Way of Heaven is vast and far-reaching; the Way of Man is subtle and profound. This means that while the heavens and earth are immense in scale, the principles of human conduct are subtle and difficult to fathom. Therefore, one must study the classics and histories to understand these principles. This is the path of learning. It is also said: "The Way of Heaven is silent and inactive; the Way of Man is active and transformative. This means that while the heavens and earth operate silently without effort, human beings must exert themselves to transform the world. Therefore, one must be diligent in one's duties and never cease in one's efforts. This is the way of the worthy. It is also said: "The Way of Heaven is impartial and just; the Way of Man is harmonious and balanced. This means that the heavens and earth do not show favoritism, and human beings should strive for harmony and balance in their relations. Therefore, one must be fair and equitable in all matters. This is the way of the virtuous. It is also said: "The Way of Heaven is eternal and unchanging; the Way of Man is adaptable and responsive. This means that while the heavens and earth remain constant throughout the ages, human beings must adapt to changing circumstances. Therefore, one must be flexible and responsive to the times. This is the way of the wise. It is also said: "The Way of Heaven is clear and bright; the Way of Man is dark and obscure. This means that while the heavens and earth are luminous and manifest, human affairs are often hidden and difficult to perceive. Therefore, one must be discerning and insightful in all matters. This is the way of the sagely. It is also said: "The Way of Heaven is high and distant; the Way of Man is low and near. This means that while the heavens and earth are sublime and remote, human beings live in the mundane world. Therefore, one must ground oneself in the practical affairs of daily life. This is the way of the common people. It is also said: "The Way of Heaven is expansive and inclusive; the Way of Man is narrow and exclusive. This means that while the heavens and earth encompass all things, human beings often harbor biases and prejudices. Therefore, one must strive to eliminate partiality and embrace all. This is the way of the universal ruler. It is also said: "The Way of Heaven is simple and plain; the Way of Man is complex and intricate. This means that while the heavens and earth are straightforward and unadorned, human affairs are often convoluted and complicated. Therefore, one must simplify one's actions and return to the essence. This is the way of the true sage. It is also said: "The Way of Heaven is spontaneous and effortless; the Way of Man is deliberate and striving. This means that while the heavens and earth act spontaneously without exertion, human beings must strive diligently to achieve their goals. Therefore, one must be persistent and resolute in one's endeavors. This is the way of the diligent practitioner. It is also said: "The Way of Heaven is natural and uncontrived; the Way of Man is artificial and contrived. This means that while the heavens and earth operate naturally without artifice, human beings often rely on cleverness and deception. Therefore, one must abandon artifice and return to nature. This is the way of the Daoist. It is also said: "The Way of Heaven is eternal and inexhaustible; the Way of Man is finite and limited. This means that while the heavens and earth are infinite and everlasting, human life is brief and transient. Therefore, one must seek the eternal and abandon the transient. This is the way of the immortal. It is also said: "The Way of Heaven is pure and serene; the Way of Man is turbid and chaotic. This means that while the heavens and earth are pure and tranquil, the human world is often muddled and disordered. Therefore, one must cultivate purity and tranquility within oneself. This is the way of the recluse. It is also said: "The Way of Heaven is vast and boundless; the Way of Man is narrow and confined. This means that while the heavens and earth are limitless in scope, human understanding is often restricted by boundaries. Therefore, one must expand one's mind and transcend limitations. This is the way of the transcendent. It is also said: "The Way of Heaven is impartial and non-discriminating; the Way of Man is biased and discriminatory. This means that while the heavens and earth treat all things equally, human beings often favor some and exclude others. Therefore, one must practice impartiality and eliminate discrimination. This is the way of the bodhisattva. It is also said: "The Way of Heaven is empty and void; the Way of Man is substantial and solid. This means that while the heavens and earth are empty and formless, human beings cling to material existence. Therefore, one must realize emptiness and detach
He was initially enfeoffed as a prince of the imperial clan.
At the beginning of the Zhenguan era, he resigned from his office and returned to his residence in the capital.
By nature, he was fond of hunting.
He constantly kept several pairs of hawks in cages;
he would kill other dogs to feed the hawks.
Subsequently, the Duke fell ill.
Seeing five dogs coming to claim their lives,
the Duke said to them,
"The one who killed you was a slave."
"This error of failing to penetrate [the truth] is not my fault.
The dog said:
"How could one who has attained mastery fail to be free?
Moreover, since we did not steal your food,
we simply passed by your gate."
"Since you have unjustly killed us, we must surely seek retribution; it shall never cease. We beg you to offer prayers for our merit on our behalf.
The official apologized and consented to perform the funeral rites for them.
The four dogs granted this request.
The white dog refused once;
he said, "I am innocent, yet you have killed me.
Furthermore, while I am not yet dead—"
"You have cut my flesh into pieces;
as I contemplate this agony,
how could I release you?"
Suddenly, he saw a man who pleaded on behalf of the dog, saying,
"Killing him will bring you no benefit."
"If we release him to allow you to perform meritorious rites for his benefit, would that not be well?
The dog then gave its consent.
After a short while, the Duke regained consciousness, but he subsequently suffered from hemiplegia such that his limbs no longer responded to his will.
Thereupon, he performed meritorious rites for the sake of the dog,
yet the Duke’s illness ultimately did not improve.
Du Youyan, Duke of Gong, stated that this was merely what the wife’s younger brother told him in jest.
The above four proofs are taken from the *Mingbao ji* (Records of Miraculous Retribution).

Fang Shan-kai, a native of Chaozhou during the Tang dynasty, was fond of hunting and experienced retribution for his actions in this life. Fang Shan-kai, a native of Chengwu in Chaozhou during the Tang dynasty,
was skilled with the bow and arrow from his youth and was particularly fond of hunting.
He made this his profession and killed countless people.
He died in the eleventh year of the Zhenguan era.
After one night had passed, Su said:
"At the time of my initial death, I was led away by two people.
We traveled for about ten li or so."
They immediately ascended the aforementioned mountain;
the three ghosts together drew it open, and they climbed the ladder to advance.
As they were about to reach the summit, [the mountain closed again].
Suddenly, a large white hawk with an iron beak and talons flew in,
tore open his left cheek, and departed.
Furthermore, there was a black hawk with iron-like beak and talons that seized his right shoulder and flew away.
Upon reaching the mountain peak,
he was led into the main hall,
where he saw an official.
Wearing crimson robes and a black cap on his head, he said to Shan Kai,
"What meritorious deeds have you performed throughout your life?
You should recount them all in detail."
He replied,
"Since I first established myself in life, I have not cultivated meritorious deeds.
The official said:
"You may lead me southward for a while to observe.
The two men then led him south,
arriving at a city.
It was extremely steep and precipitous.
The two men knocked on the north gate several times,
and the gate then opened immediately.
He saw that within the city it was all ablaze with fierce fires,
and by the side of the gate were several venomous snakes,
each more than ten zhang in length.
His head was as large as a five-dǔ block of earth;
from his mouth he spat fire,
as if intending to shoot at people.
Terrified, the mountain opened up and he did not know where to go;
he knew only to prostrate himself and recite the Buddha's name.
The gate then opened of its own accord.
Upon returning, he saw an official intending to sentence him to punishment.
An attendant remonstrated, saying,
"If the mountain opens and does not close again, you will die immediately."
"I only fear that once he enters this city, he will not be able to leave again.
It would be better to release him for now so that he may cultivate merit.
The official released him.
He ordered the two men before him to escort him down by the same path as before;
however, as they descended, a soaring hawk attempted to seize him.
Fortunately, thanks to the assistance of these two men, he escaped and was delivered from danger.
Upon descending the mountain, he saw a pit that was utterly filthy;
while he hesitated, he was suddenly pushed into it by two men.
In a brief moment he revived;
the nail marks were extremely deep and did not fade throughout his life. Later, the mountain opened, whereupon he finally abandoned his wife and children.
He converted his residence into a Buddhist monastery and made the constant recitation of scriptures his primary occupation.
Liu Mo’er, a native of Fenzhou during the Tang dynasty, was fond of hunting and consequently suffered retribution in his present life in Xiaoyi County, Fenzhou.
Liu Mo’er, a native of Xianquan Village,
passed away on the twenty-seventh day of the eighth month in the fourth year of the Xianqing era.
The next day, his son’s tutor also died.
Throughout their lives, the conduct of both father and son had been treacherous and perverse.
To their north lived Qi Longwei.
While gathering firewood, he was run over by a cart and died.
After several days,
he revived and saw that Moe-er-nan-si-pao was in a cauldron of boiling water for a brief moment.
The skin and flesh were completely worn away;
no human form remained,
and only white bones were visible.
After remaining thus for a long while, he returned to his original form.
Longwei asked him the reason for this,
and he replied:
"It was for the sake of hunting for me that he incurred this punishment.
He then asked Bao, "Where is your father?"
He replied,
"My father’s transgressions are grave and cannot be seen all at once.
Once you have returned, my lord, [I shall show him to you]."
He informed his family that he was to perform a vegetarian feast for merit;
having finished speaking, he was urged on by the messengers.
He proceeded to the official residence and saw that the buildings were lofty and imposing;
more than twenty men stood there holding weapons.
An official asked him,
"What meritorious deeds have you performed recently?
He replied:
In the first month of last year, Longwei was reading the *Sarvadharmaparyāya* at Duku Village.
He offered a shirt as a gift and also received the five precepts.
To this day, he has not committed any offense.
The official then said, "If it is as you say..."
"Your merits are immeasurable;
why must you come here?
He then requested the register for inspection, and upon seeing the register, he said:
It is not without reason that such a person should die;
however, the marginal note states:
"By receiving the precepts and performing acts of giving, the merit and assistance thereof should further extend their lifespan."
He then sent someone to escort him back, whereupon he immediately revived.
Li Zhili of Longxi in the Tang dynasty was fond of hunting and received retribution for his deeds in this life. Li Zhili of Longxi in the Tang dynasty...
He was agile from his youth,
skilled in archery,
capable of riding horseback, and proficient in the art of throwing slingshots.
The number of those killed was extremely great;
at times, the fish caught in his nets were beyond counting.
In the nineteenth year of the Zhenguan era, he fell slightly ill.
After three or four days he died and saw a ghost,
who was leading a horse that was larger than any horse commonly ridden in the secular world.
Zhili said, "King Yama is pursuing you.
He then ordered Zhili to mount the horse.
In a mere moment, he suddenly appeared before the king,
who addressed him with these instructions:
"I am sending you to suppress the rebels;
you must not suffer defeat. Should you fail, I shall put you to death."
There were twenty-four companions who looked toward the northeast;
they could see no end to the bandits.
Heaven and earth were completely shrouded in darkness;
dust fell like rain.
Zhili and the others knew they had been defeated.
He said to his companion,
"The King’s commands are severe;
it would be better to die advancing than to return in defeat."
Zhili turned his horse and shot three arrows;
thereafter, the bandits seemed to retreat slightly.
When the number of shots reached five, the bandits were finally defeated and dispersed.
When the business was concluded, he went to pay his respects to the king. The king rebuked him, saying, "I know you are well-versed in propriety;
yet though your enemy has retreated, why did you lose at the very beginning of the battle?"
He braided his hair with hemp,
bound his hands and feet,
and lay down upon a stone.
They used a large stone to press down and grind him;
the bodies of four people, both before and after him, were completely rotted away.
When it was Zhi-li’s turn, he cried out with a resolute voice:
The rebels' defeat earlier was entirely due to the power of knowing propriety;
yet they were subsequently killed by the king.
Lest it fail to encourage future generations,
the King then released him without further instructions,
allowing him to travel and roam at will.
After three days had passed,
he headed toward the northwest and entered a walled courtyard where a herd of birds and beasts filled more than three mu of ground.
Coming together to claim his life, they gradually drew near;
having once killed a female dog,
one now came straight forward and bit him in the face.
Next, his entire body was wounded without exception.
He saw three great ghosts,
each one chiang and five chi in height.
The surrounding area was treated in the same manner.
Together they flayed them, knowing the proper ritual for skin and flesh;
in a brief moment, everything was completely finished.
Only the face, eyes, and white bones remained;
furthermore, he saw his own five viscera,
and with this flesh, he gave alms to birds and beasts.
Their flesh falls off and grows back again;
once grown, it is flayed once more.
This continues for three days.
The bitterness of his suffering was so extreme that it could not be fully recorded.
When the ordeal was over, the great ghosts, birds, beasts,
and the rest suddenly vanished without a trace.
Zhilü looked back but saw nothing;
he then immediately leaped over the wall and fled southward,
not knowing where he was going.
In his mind, it was as if he had leaped a thousand li in an instant.
Again, he saw a ghost pursue Zhili and catch him,
then enclose him within an iron cage.
Countless fish vied with one another to come and devour it.
After a long while,
the ghost finally returned.
The fish were no longer seen.
His family had previously supported a monk,
who had died some time ago.
He came to release Zhili from his confinement and said to him,
"The donor is suffering from a great famine."
He gave him three white pills, each the size of a jujube fruit,
and instructed him to prostrate and eat them;
immediately, he was greatly satiated.
He spoke to him, saying,
"When you, donor, return home, the monks shall also depart separately.
Upon arriving at the residence, he saw a large pit to the north of the house.
Within it were various spears and lances bristling together so that one could not pass through.
He saw his elder brother’s daughter and a maidservant carrying a chest,
along with money, silk, and a vessel of food and drink, located to the northeast of the pit.
Zhilü perceived in his mind that [the monk] intended to dally with this maidservant and his niece, and he found this deeply strange.
Turning his head to look north, he immediately saw a ghost advancing straight toward him, brandishing a sword.
Zhili, filled with fear and trepidation, threw his body into the pit and immediately regained consciousness.
From the moment of his initial death until his rebirth, [he experienced...]
After six days had passed,
he questioned his family,
and it was discovered that his niece had been carrying paper money and silk.
Upon being escorted and informed of the situation,
what he saw at that time were copper coins,
silk, and cloth. These three pieces of evidence are extracted from the *Mingbao ji* (Records of Miraculous Retribution).
A Case of Miraculous Retribution for a Butcher Who Slaughtered Pigs in Jinzhou during the Tang Dynasty. In the third year of the Xianqing era of the Tang,
while Xu Yu was serving as the Prefectural Governor of Jinzhou,
there was a butcher in the eastern alley of the marketplace.
A pig was slaughtered;
its life severed, it was scalded in boiling water,
and its skin and hair fell away all at once.
He died halfway through the day;
still craving to kill the remaining pigs,
he had not yet reached a state of liberation.
At dawn, he slit open his own belly with a knife,
making a long incision beneath it;
yet one blade still had not entered his abdomen.
The pig suddenly rose and ran out the door,
heading straight for the western wall of the marketplace.
It went to the shop of a certain worthy man and lay down beneath his bed.
The city folk vied with one another to go and see him.
The butcher continued to pursue him with his knife in hand.
Those who were watching asked him the reason for his actions.
The butcher replied,
"In all my life of slaughtering pigs, I have never heard of or seen such a thing. Yet,
I still wish to take it away."
Several hundred onlookers all rebuked the butcher with indignation and vied with one another to offer money to redeem him.
The people together built a hut to house him.
After a long time, his body hair finally began to grow;
however, the sores on his neck and abdomen, having healed, became large fleshy warts.
It was as large as an arm;
it came and went and entered and left its dwelling without ever soiling it.
By nature pure, it was unlike other pigs.
He passed away in his forty-fifth year. Wang Tongren, a native of Jinyang County in Bingzhou and a secretary to the Xu Prince, personally witnessed and recounted these accounts.

74. Chapter on Compassion (64). Chapter on Compassion, Number Seventy-Four. This consists of five sections: the Section on Stating the Intent, the Section on Bodhisattvas, the Section on Kings, the Section on Animals, and the Section on Contemplating Suffering. 1. Section on Stating the Intent (First): As for all sentient beings who have received vital breath, they all possess spiritual intelligence.
All that stirs and soars knows the dread of death; thus,
it is the foremost concern for Bodhisattvas to practice salvation,
and the great compassion of the Buddhas appearing in the world is its very foundation.
Therefore, as the saying goes, "To stand by the river envying the fish is not as good as weaving a net.
To observe others receiving blessings is not as good as practicing the causes for them.
Thus, if one seeks their reward, there is nothing better than first giving rise to goodness.
One should practice impartial giving toward the noble and the lowly, maintaining an even mind toward both the virtuous and the non-virtuous.
One must equally revere the Triple Gem as a field of merit and show respect to all four modes of birth.
Furthermore, one must provide timely relief and assistance by granting food and clothing to those in need.
They exhaust the treasures held in their fists and withdraw the objects of pleasure for their ears and eyes;
they renounce what they possess to offer as gifts, following this act with joy.
Truly, chests and caskets are used to encourage one's intent,
while jade and silk are employed to manifest one's sincerity;
even one’s own flesh, marrow, and bones are not cherished or clung to.
How much less, then, could one give rise to attachment toward external wealth?
When a bodhisattva practices the various deeds, they do not even wait for them to be solicited;
yet while their mind does not wait for material things, those things nevertheless serve as a means (snares) to reach the mind.
Mind and matter are both fully present, and merit and wisdom are practiced in tandem.
2. Bodhisattva Section, Part Two. As stated in the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, the Buddha said:
In the past, for the sake of all sentient beings,
I cultivated the practices of a bodhisattva in order to establish this Dharma-eye.
He gave rise to a heart of great compassion for all sentient beings and sacrificed his own bodily blood,
as vast as the great ocean.
To all beggars, he gave away his head, eyes, and ears like Mount Vipula;
he gave away his nose, tongue, and so forth like ten *tulunas*.
He gave away his hands, feet, and other limbs like Mount Vipula;
he gave away his skin and other parts sufficient to cover the entire Jambudvīpa;
and he also gave away immeasurable elephants, horses, male and female slaves, wives, children, as well as royal thrones, kingdoms, lands, cities, palaces, villages, and so forth.
Together with all beggars,
they upheld the prohibitive precepts in the presence of all Buddhas without any transgression,
making immeasurable offerings at the abode of each and every Buddha.
At each and every Buddha-field, I received and accepted immeasurable hundreds of thousands of nayutas of Dharma-gates;
I upheld, recited, and skillfully cultivated samādhi.
I also reverently honored immeasurable noble ones of the three vehicles and four fruits, as well as my parents, teachers, elders, and those suffering from illness.
To those without protection, he provides protection;
to those without refuge, he provides refuge;
to those without a destination, he provides a destination.
I have thus caused them to dwell securely throughout those three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
Out of compassion for all suffering sentient beings,
he gave rise to a great, firm, and courageous mind,
and long cultivated the practice of unsurpassed bodhi.
Now, in this blind and dark world, at a time when there is no Great Teacher and the Dharma is diminished,
you have resolved your mind among such sentient beings to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
I desire that they may not regress from the enlightenment of the three vehicles;
furthermore, I vow to rescue and deliver sentient beings of the three evil realms,
establishing them in the good paths and the bliss of nirvana.
Furthermore, the *Saṃyukta-ratna-piṭaka Sūtra* states:
"At that time, the Tathāgata was pierced in his foot by a kaṇṭaka thorn;
blood flowed and would not stop."
Though he was anointed with various kinds of medicines, he could not be cured.
The Arhats took medicine from Mount Gandhamādana and applied it to treat him,
yet it still did not remove his ailment.
Daśabala Kāśyapa went to where the World-Honored One was and spoke these words: "If the Buddha,
the Tathāgata, possesses a mind of equality toward all sentient beings..."
"If there were no difference between Rāhula and Devadatta,
the blood from my feet should stop.
Immediately, the blood ceased.
Since the ulcer was also healed, we know that the great compassion of all Buddhas is equal and without distinction toward all sentient beings.
Furthermore, in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*,
the Buddha said:
In the distant past, there was a king named Prajñāpradīpa (Wisdom Lamp),
who commanded all men and women in Jambudvīpa who were able to speak.
All practiced the ten wholesome deeds.
When the king was first born, eighty-four thousand treasuries spontaneously emerged.
At the crossroads, he gave everything to whoever came seeking it. Then,
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, thought to himself:
"This King Jñānapradīpa grants everything that is requested of him;
fearing that he might seize my seat in a future life,
I should now go to test him."
"Is this giving for the sake of the unsurpassed path,
or is it for the sake of falling back?
Thereupon, he transformed himself into a man.
They said to one another,
"King Prajñāpradīpa has instructed us to practice the ten unwholesome deeds,
from killing up to wrong view."
Then all the ministers went to inform the king.
The king replied, "No;
I have already said this previously."
"I shall become king so that all beings in Jambudvīpa who are capable of practicing [virtue] may practice the ten wholesome actions—
from refraining from taking life up to refraining from wrong views."
Therefore, such words are not appropriate.
You all should now prepare the elephant carriages;
I wish to go in person to teach and transform the people of the country.
When the celestial omen had appeared,
the king immediately mounted it.
The king said, "Show me [the way]."
That man said, "I taught the people of my country to practice the ten unwholesome actions," and he immediately pointed them out to the king.
The king asked:
"Did Prajñāpradīpa instruct you to commit the ten unwholesome deeds?
He replied, "It is true."
The king asked again,
"Is there a skillful means by which one may practice the ten wholesome paths of action?
He replied, "There is."
He asked, "What is it?
He replied, "If one attains the accomplishment of a Bodhisattva, one may eat their flesh and drink their blood."
Thus one is able to practice the ten wholesome deeds.
At that time, King Prajñāpradīpa (Wise Lamp) had this thought:
"Since beginningless time, I have [been subject to...]"
Having experienced manifold sufferings while transmigrating through the five realms,
one may undergo the amputation of hands and feet, the cutting off of ears and noses, the gouging out of eyes, or the decapitation of the head;
yet in the end, what benefit is there?
He immediately took a sharp knife and cut flesh from his own thigh.
He placed it in a vessel, gave it to the man along with his blood, and said to him:
"Good son, you may eat and drink this flesh and blood and practice the ten wholesome deeds.
At that time, that man could not endure the majestic power of King Prajñāpradīpa.
He immediately vanished and was no longer seen.
Suddenly, a devaputra appeared standing before him and asked the king:
"Does Your Majesty now give this gift for the sake of one world-system, or two, three, or four world-systems?
Is it for the sake of the sun, the moon, Śakra Devendra, Māra, or Brahmā?
The King replied:
I practice giving not for the sake of the world, nor even for the sake of Māra or Brahmā;
rather, I direct my mind toward seeking unsurpassed, perfect, and true all-knowledge,
in order to deliver those who have not yet been delivered.
To liberate those who are not yet liberated;
to cause those who have not attained nirvāṇa to attain nirvāṇa;
and to deliver them from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction—such as these.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, thought to himself:
"It would be most improper for King Prajñāpradīpa to die from this wound.
Therefore, I shall pour celestial nectar (amṛta) over his body."
Even when he poured [the medicine] upon it, the wound was immediately restored to its former state.
The Buddha said to King Bimbisāra:
"The one who was the King Benefiting Sentient Beings at that time..."
Could this have been anyone else?
It was none other than our present father, King Śuddhodana.
As for the king’s first queen at that time:
The mother Māyā is she;
the King Prajñādīpa at that time was none other than myself.
In a previous life, I taught and transformed several people in Jambudvīpa, causing them all to practice the ten wholesome paths of action.
By virtue of these causes and conditions, the thousand-spoked wheels with their rims have been perfected upon the soles of my feet.
The brilliant light shone forth, illuminating the trichiliocosm.
Furthermore, the *Mahākaruṇāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states:
The Buddha addressed the sons of good family:
In the past, beyond immeasurable asaṃkhyeya great kalpas,
at that time this land was named Vimalamerudhvaja. During that great kalpa,
when the lifespan of humans was one hundred years, within the Semblance Dharma of the Tathāgata Padmagandha, there appeared...
I was a universal monarch of Jambudvīpa named Ajita;
I and my thousand sons all resolved upon bodhicitta.
They all went forth together and fully cultivated the holy life within the Dharma of the Tathāgata Padmagandha; however,
only six sons did not wish to go forth and did not resolve upon bodhicitta.
"I have repeatedly instructed you;
why do you not go forth into the homeless life?
The six sons then replied to the king:
"I cannot leave the household life.
The king asked again,
"Why do you not resolve to attain bodhicitta?"
He said, "If you can give all of Jambudvīpa to us, we shall then resolve upon bodhicitta."
Having heard this, I was filled with great joy;
I established all the people of Jambudvīpa in the Three Refuges and the Eightfold Precepts,
and further exhorted them toward the Three Vehicles.
I divided this Jambudvīpa into six parts and gave them to my six sons, exhorting them toward bodhi;
I then left the household life and fully practiced the holy life.
Those six princes were not in harmony with one another;
they raised armies and engaged in battle, each finding no peace for themselves,
causing a period of extreme famine throughout Jambudvīpa.
Heaven does not send down rain;
the five grains do not ripen;
grasses and trees do not grow.
I then reflected: "Now is precisely the right time;
I ought to give my body as an offering."
With his flesh and blood fully restored,
he departed from the forest and traveled to the Central Land, where he ascended Mount Upagaṅgā and made a great vow.
At that time, the entire palace of the asuras trembled violently.
Mount Meru trembled and shook, and the waves of the ocean surged;
the devas and all the spirits wept in sorrow.
At that time, I immediately cast myself down from the mountain peak.
By virtue of his original vow, it immediately became a mountain of flesh,
one yojana in height,
with its length and breadth being exactly equal.
People, birds, and beasts came to eat their flesh and blood;
yet, by virtue of their original vows, they grew day and night until they gradually reached a height of one thousand yojanas.
The same applies to the four corners; they all have human heads,
each fully possessing hair, eyebrows, eyes, ears, noses, tongues, mouths, and teeth.
Those people raised their voices and cried out:
"Ho! You sentient beings, each according to your desire, take as much as you wish!"
Their flesh, blood, and six sense faculties were fully restored;
they obtained whatever they desired from their minds.
There are those with the minds of the three vehicles, even down to those seeking the blessings of gods and humans;
some consume flesh and blood;
and some take away eyes, ears, noses, lips, teeth, and tongues.
By virtue of his original vow,
it immediately returns to its former state,
neither exhausted nor diminished.
For as long as ten thousand years,
he filled all the people of Jambudvīpa, as well as the yakṣas, birds, and beasts, with the flesh and blood of his own body;
for those ten thousand years, he gave away eyes as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
He gave blood equal to the four great oceans;
he gave the flesh of his own body as vast as a thousand Mount Sumerus;
and he gave his tongue to others like Mount Cakravāḍa.
I gave my ears as a gift like Mount Meru;
I gave my nose as a gift like the Great Mount Meru;
I gave my teeth as a gift like Vulture Peak Mountain.
I have given my own skin as a gift throughout the Sahā world-system. Good son,
observe how for ten thousand years I have thus given away my body and life in such immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* numbers.
Because immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings did not give rise to a single thought of regret for even a moment,
they immediately established a great vow.
If my intention to attain unexcelled bodhi is thus fulfilled,
may I likewise universally relinquish as many [worlds] as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River in the ten directions.
If, within five turbid Buddha-lands, I do not fulfill my vow to provide the flesh of my own body to those sentient beings for as many great kalpas as there are sands in the Ganges,
may I never attain enlightenment.
May I never behold the Buddhas of the ten directions and fail to attain Bodhi;
may I also never hear the sounds of the Triple Gem or the Three Vehicles;
and may I always dwell in the Avīci Hell.
Furthermore, the *Mahākaruṇāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states:
The Buddha said,
"I recall that during immeasurable kalpas ago..."
This buddha-field is named Sun-Moon Radiance.
During a time of the five turbidities,
I shall be a wheel-turning monarch here in this Jambudvīpa.
His name was Dīpaṃkara.
He skillfully exhorted and transformed all sentient beings.
At that time, I went out to wander and observe the gardens.
He saw a man with both arms bound behind his back most tightly and urgently,
and he immediately asked his ministers,
"What crime has this man committed?"
The ministers replied,
"This is the deceptive law of kings;
how could it possibly apply to the subjects of heaven?"
He regularly paid his taxes,
contributing one-sixth of his produce.
This man has now disobeyed my command.
He immediately commanded his ministers:
"Release this man at once.
Do not press him harshly for provisions, ghee, or oil."
The minister replied to the king,
"In the end, there is no one who can offer various goods to Your Majesty with a virtuous heart.
As for those things provided daily for the royal consort and her attendants— "
All that was required for the kitchen offerings came from the people;
without the power of the king, it could never have been obtained.
At that time, I was filled with sorrow and anxiety, and withdrew to reflect within myself.
"To whom shall this royal throne now be entrusted?
I have five hundred sons, all of whom I have exhorted toward Bodhi.
He then divided this Jambudvīpa into five hundred portions and bestowed them upon his sons.
He immediately renounced his former life and went to the forest to seek the holy life of an ascetic.
To the south, near the great ocean, he sat in meditation within the Udumbara grove,
sustaining his life by eating fruits and roots.
Before long, he gradually attained the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*).
At that time, there were five hundred merchants in Jambudvīpa who went out to sea to gather treasures.
They obtained a great mass of various jewels.
Among them was a merchant leader named Nakṣatrarāja (Host of Constellations),
who, by virtue of his minor merit, obtained a wish-fulfilling maṇi jewel.
From that jewel island, he took a great quantity of various gems and mani-jewels.
As he first set out on his journey, the waters of the sea surged with waves;
the nāgas were distressed and the sea deities wept.
Among them was a dragon-seer named Aśvajit,
who was in fact a bodhisattva.
By virtue of their original vows, they are born therein;
those mahāsattvas protect the merchants, enabling them to cross the ocean in safety,
and then return to their own abodes.
A malevolent rākṣasa followed those merchants,
constantly pursuing them from behind and watching for an opportunity;
during the daytime, he unleashed violent winds and rain.
They caused the merchants to lose their way;
not knowing where they were headed, they were overcome with extreme terror,
raising a great clamor as they wailed and wept in grief.
They supplicated the various heavenly deities, the spirits of wind and rain,
and even called out with voices like those of their own beloved children.
At that time, I heard those sounds with my divine ear.
He immediately offered words of consolation: "O merchants, do not be afraid.
I shall show you the way and guide you so that you may reach Jambudvīpa in safety."
At that time, I immediately bound my own hands with silk cloth,
placed them inside oil, and set them on fire,
uttering these words of utmost sincerity:
For thirty-six years in the forest, I dwelt in the four Brahma-abodes.
For the benefit of sentient beings, I ate various fruits.
Having thus transformed eighty-four thousand nāgas and yakṣas, I established them in the stage of non-retrogression.
"By this root of goodness, may my hand remain burning so that these merchants may reach Jambudvīpa;
thus may my hand remain burning for seven days and seven nights."
Those merchants reached their destination in safety and immediately made this vow:
"If these rare treasures are such that I shall attain unexcelled bodhi, [may they remain as they are]."
May I become a leader of merchants and hold the wish-fulfilling jewel,

raining down various treasures throughout this buddha-field and within all the empty buddha-fields of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, which are afflicted by the five corruptions.
In each and every direction, various kinds of precious jewels rained down seven times,
satisfying all according to their wishes.
He caused immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* sentient beings to abide in the Three Vehicles.
Furthermore, in the *Mahāpuruṣa-śāstra*, the Bodhisattva Deva spoke this verse:
"A virtuous man of merit, with hands of compassionate charity,
pulls those out of the mire of poverty who are unable to emerge on their own."
Just as when a bodhisattva practices giving,
all those who are poor and destitute come to seek refuge in him;
just as when there is a tree in a wilderness, all travelers in the heat of the day go to it for shelter.
A bodhisattva who delights in this is said to have attained supreme liberation.
Suppose someone were to come and say to the bodhisattva:
"A beggar has arrived."
The Bodhisattva, filled with joy, immediately rewarded the messenger with wealth;
he then gave the remaining items to the beggars,
treating them with affection, love, and respect.
When one says "beg" to a petitioner,
one should do so with a mind of compassion toward any who come to ask.
Not knowing that the Bodhisattva’s nature is one who delights in giving,
the Bodhisattva takes his hand and speaks to him with joy,
just like a close friend.
He destroys that which others do not recognize as such, causing them to perceive it as knowledge;
when bystanders see this, they likewise rejoice.
If he sees a beggar...
He addressed him with comforting words, saying, "Come, tell me what you require; take whatever you wish."
"Welcome, worthy one; do not be afraid.
I shall act as your refuge so that the mind of that beggar may attain coolness."
If one gives in this manner, it is called giving by a living person;
if not in this manner, it is called giving by a dead person.
If [the recipient] does not come, one should go there oneself to give.
If one would even sacrifice body and life to those who come seeking,
how much more so material wealth?
If there is no heart of compassion, it cannot be called giving.
If one gives with a compassionate heart, that itself is liberation;
even one who is very wealthy is called "poor" [in spirit] if they lack compassion when giving.
On the other hand, a wealthy person who gives without a heart of pity is likewise destitute.
Although one may be called a donor or not called a donor,
it is one who gives with a heart of compassion that is truly named a donor.
If one who gives seeking a reward were called a "giver," then merchants and traders could also be called givers;
yet even for such giving with expectation of reward, the karmic fruit would still be immeasurable.
How much more so for one who gives with a compassionate heart and seeks no recompense—
how could the resulting merit be measured?
If one gives seeking recompense, it can only bring personal gratification.
One who cannot provide relief merely exhausts themselves;
one who gives with a compassionate heart is able to provide relief,
which brings great benefit when the future fruit is attained.
Those who cultivate generosity attain wealth;
those who cultivate meditative concentration attain liberation;
and those who cultivate compassion attain unsurpassed enlightenment.
The Bodhisattva reflects: "It is through that beggar that I shall attain supreme enlightenment."
I now obtain incomparable bliss because of this giving;
if the bliss of giving even during the causal stage is thus,
how much more so will that of unsurpassed bodhi!
Such a petitioner’s kindness is exceedingly great;
there is no way to repay it.
If material wealth is insufficient to repay their kindness,
one should bestow upon them unsurpassed bodhi;
through my merit, may this be so.
May those who beg likewise become great donors in future lives and attain unsurpassed bodhi, just as I have now;
for those who do not acknowledge kindness possess no compassion.
If there is no compassion, there is no practice of giving;
if one does not give, one cannot deliver sentient beings from birth and death.
If one does not practice giving, it obscures the mind of compassion.
Just as one knows the true from the false by inscribing upon stone, so too should one treat even an enemy as a close friend.
Section Three: The Chapter on Kings. As stated in the *Buddhabhāṣita-sūryaprabha-bodhisattva-sūtra*:
The Buddha said:
"In the past, there was a king in Jambudvīpa named Jñānabala."
He constantly performed the works of a Buddha and had deep faith in the Triple Gem.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Zhicheng (Utmost Sincerity).
His mind constantly maintained samādhi and felt compassion for all sentient beings;
the king never grew weary of beholding this bhikṣu.
On the bhikṣu’s thigh, a large and malignant ulcer had grown.
The physicians of the kingdom could not cure him.
The King was filled with sorrow and great distress, and tears immediately flowed from his eyes.
At that time, twenty thousand ladies of the court simultaneously felt deep grief.
At that time, as the king was lying down,
a celestial being came to him in a dream and said to him,
"If you cure this bhikṣu’s illness..."
"If one could obtain human flesh and blood to eat and drink, one would immediately be cured.
Upon waking, the king was startled and distressed;
he thought to himself that the bhikṣu’s illness was grave.
Since that medicinal method was difficult to obtain,
he issued an edict to inquire among his ministers regarding the king’s eldest son.
His name was Zhizhi.
He said to the king, "Do not grieve, do not sorrow or worry over this;
flesh and blood are the most base and insignificant things."
He returned to his meditation chamber, took a knife,
cut the flesh from his thigh, and brought the meat and blood to the bhikṣu, who then consumed it.
The abscess was immediately healed,
and his body attained peace and security.
When the king heard that he had recovered, he was filled with great joy and delight.
The bhikṣu kept his mind on the Dharma and did not dwell upon the pain of his son.

Maintaining this joy with each person’s utmost sincerity, the elder son also recovered naturally; this was truly because his practice accorded with the Buddha-mind, whereby the sores on his body were restored.
Furthermore, the *Saṃyukta-ratna-piṭaka-sūtra* states:
"In the past, there were two brothers who were princes; they were driven out of their country and reached a desolate wilderness where their provisions were completely exhausted."
The younger brother immediately killed his wife, divided the meat, and gave it to his elder brother and sister-in-law.
The sister-in-law then ate it.
When the elder brother received this meat, he hid it away and did not dare to eat it.
He cut flesh from his own leg for his wife and they ate it together.
When the younger brother’s wife had finished the meat and wished to kill her sister-in-law,
the elder brother said, "Do not kill her."
He took the meat he had previously hidden and gave it to his younger brother to eat.
Having passed through the wilderness, they arrived at the dwelling place of a divine seer.
They gathered flowers and fruits to provide for their own sustenance.
Later, the younger brother fell ill and died,
leaving only the elder brother remaining.
At that time, the prince saw a man whose hands and feet had been severed;
compassion arose in his heart,
and he gathered flowers and fruits for him.
He restored that amputated man to life.
The prince was one who had few desires;
he would go out to gather flowers and fruits.
His wife was behind him;
she had an illicit affair with a man who had lost his feet and,
due to her deep attachment to this paramour, harbored intense hatred for her husband.
During the course of a single day, she followed her husband as he gathered flowers;
upon reaching the riverbank, she spoke to him, saying,
"Pick the flowers and fruits from the tops of the trees."
As the husband speaks and the wife replies,
there is a deep river below;
one might fall into it.
The wife said,
"Tie a rope around my waist;
I shall pull the rope."
They drew near to the riverbank;
the wife pushed her husband so that he fell into the river,
yet by the power of his benevolence, he was carried away by the current without drowning.
Downstream from that river, a king had passed away.
The state astrologers of that kingdom searched throughout the land to determine who was worthy to be king.
From afar, he saw a yellow cloud-canopy over the water. Having observed it,
the physiognomist divined that beneath the yellow cloud-canopy there must surely be a divine person.
He dispatched men into the water to go and receive him,
establishing him as king.
The former wife of the king carried that amputated man upon her back.
Traveling from place to place begging for alms, they arrived at the kingdom of the prince.
All the people there spoke of a virtuous woman who carried her husband—who had had his feet cut off—reverently and with filial devotion.
This news eventually reached the king’s ears.
Having heard this, the king immediately dispatched a messenger to summon her to the presence of the palace.
The king asked his wife,
"Is it true that this man who has had his feet cut off is indeed your husband?"
He replied, "It is indeed so.
The King then said,
"Do you recognize me?"
He replied, "I do not know him.
The king said,
"Do you know so-and-so?"
He looked intently at the king,
and then felt ashamed. The king,
out of his compassionate heart, sent someone to provide for his sustenance.
The Buddha said,
"If you wish to know who that king was, it was I myself."
As for that woman, she was the brahmin woman Ciñcā who slandered me while carrying a wooden bowl;
as for those whose hands and feet were severed at that time, [they are now these people].
Now, because Devadatta [is such], we know that good and evil have manifest evidence through direct observation.
Furthermore, the *Bodhisattvapūrvacaryā-sūtra* states:
The Buddha said to the king:
In a past age, in this Jambudvīpa, there was a country named Aparāntaka,
and its king was named Bhandin.
The lady’s name was Bhadrā-Māṭhara.
At that time, grain was expensive and the people were suffering from famine;
moreover, there was a plague.
At that time, the king was also ill.
The queen went out herself to sacrifice to the gods.
Beside the steps, there was a household.
Now, her husband was away from home when his wife gave birth to a child,
and she had no maidservants to assist her.
After giving birth, she was famished and had no food;
she then thought to herself,
"Now death is imminent."
Having no other recourse,
she desired to eat her own child;
she immediately took up a knife and was just about to kill him.
Her heart was moved by compassion, and she raised her voice and wept aloud.
At that time, as the lady was about to return to the palace,
she heard the sound of this woman’s piteous and piercing lamentation.
Filled with sorrow and pity, he stopped to listen.
At that moment, the woman was about to raise her knife to kill her son,
when she thought to herself:
"How can I bear to eat the flesh of my own child?
Having had this thought, he wept once more.
The lady then entered his house and approached him to question him.
"Why do you weep? What do you wish to do?
The wife answered him in detail.
Upon hearing this, the lady felt deep compassion and said,
"Do not kill her son."
"I shall go to the palace and bring food for you.
The woman replied,
"The lady is of noble rank."
Furthermore, there may be delays,
or one might forget;
yet today my life hangs by a thread, not to last beyond this very moment.
"It would be better to eat my own child to sustain my life.
The lady asked, "Could we not instead obtain other meat to eat?"
He replied, "I have obtained this by means of my daily task to sustain my life;
I do not inquire whether it is good or foul. Thereupon, the lady immediately took a knife and cut off her own breast.
He then made this vow:
"I now offer this milk as a gift to relieve these beings from their perilous distress;
I do not wish to become a Wheel-Turning King, Śakra, Māra, or Brahmā."
He resolved to employ these merits to achieve the path of unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment;
he then took the milk and gave it to this woman.
Just as he was about to raise his knife and cut off one breast, [the Buddha said: "Stop!"
At that moment, the trichiliocosm shook violently. Śakra, Lord of Devas,
observed this and saw that his wife had cut off her own breast to relieve him of his perilous distress.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas,
and countless other devas immediately descended and remained in the air;
they all stood before the lady, weeping with grief.
He then asked: "The generosity you have now displayed is truly beyond compare;
what vow do you seek?"
The lady replied,
"I shall take these merits and use them to seek the unsurpassed, true, and correct path,
in order to deliver all sentient beings from suffering and calamity."
The Heavenly Lord replied,
"By what means shall you provide proof of this vow you seek?
Thereupon, the lady immediately made a solemn oath.
"If the merit of my current offering truly results in the attainment of perfect enlightenment,
may my breast immediately return to its former state.
At that very moment, her breast returned to its former state.
The Heavenly Lord praised him, saying,
"He will attain Buddhahood before long.
All the devas rejoiced.
Even as he manifested his form, he addressed the lady, saying,
"In the gift you have now bestowed, do you feel no regret or sorrow?
She replied:
"May my female body be transformed into that of a man by this merit I now apply, seeking the path to Buddhahood without regret or pain.
Having made this vow, she was instantly transformed into a man.
The devas praised him, saying,
"He will attain Buddhahood before long.
At that time, all manner of diseases within the kingdom were eliminated.
Grain was abundant and cheap, and the people lived in peace and happiness.
Later, when the king passed away,
he was immediately appointed as king.
"The people flourished and the kingdom subsequently prospered.
The Buddha said to the king,
"As for that queen at that time..."
"I am that very person now.
Having not begrudged my own body or life, I have now attained Buddhahood.
The great assembly rejoiced, prostrated, and departed.
4. Section on Animals (Tiryagyoni-varga). Section Four. As stated in the *Sarvajñajyotisṛṣi-maitracittā-māṃsābhakṣaṇa-sūtra*:
"The Buddha was staying at the Śiva-temple monastery in the village of Mṛgāramātṛ near the site of enlightenment in the kingdom of Magadha."
At that time, there was a son of the brahmin Kapila named Maitreya,
whose body was golden in color.
Endowed with the primary and secondary marks of excellence and possessing immeasurable majestic radiance,
he came to where the Buddha was.
At that time, there were five hundred brahmins with matted hair who,
seeing Maitreya from afar, addressed the Pure Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
The radiance of this youth is thus immeasurable,
no different from that of a Buddha.
Under which Buddha did he first resolve his mind upon the path?
"Whose sutra do you uphold?
Explain it for me.
The Buddha told the brahmin Śreṇika:
Listen attentively now;
I shall explain it for you.
In the past, immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago.
At that time, there was a world named Supuṣpita;
the Buddha there was named Maitreya.
He constantly teaches and transforms all beings with a mind of loving-kindness.
That Buddha’s discourse is titled "The Great Ocean Cloud of Compassion and the Light of the Samādhi of Loving-Kindness.
Should anyone hear it, [they shall attain liberation].
One will immediately transcend the sins of birth and death for ten billion koṭis of kalpas and will certainly attain Buddhahood.
At that time, there was a great brāhmaṇa in that country.
Named Sarvajñāprabha (Light of All-Knowledge),
he was intelligent, possessed great wisdom, and had extensively heard many sūtras. Upon hearing that the Buddha had appeared in the world and preached the *Maitrīsamādhi-sūtra*,
he immediately believed and submitted, becoming a disciple of the Buddha.
Generating the bodhicitta,
he spoke these words:
"I now recite and uphold the Mahāmaitrī-samādhi Sūtra."
"May I surely attain Buddhahood in the future and be named Maitreya. Thereupon,
he left his home and entered the deep mountains.
For eight thousand years, he lived with few desires and no worldly affairs, sustaining himself by begging for alms;
he recited and upheld this sutra with single-minded concentration, free from distraction.
At that time, continuous rain did not cease, and the floodwaters rose suddenly and violently.
The rishi sat upright and was unable to go begging for food;
seven days passed.
At that time, there were five hundred white rabbits in that forest.
There was a hare king with his mother and three other animals;
seeing that the rishi had not eaten for seven days,
they spoke these words.
Now this seer, for the sake of the Buddha-way, has not eaten for many days;
his life is not far from its end,
and the banner of the Dharma is about to fall.
"The ocean of Dharma is about to be exhausted;
I shall now, for the sake of the Unsurpassed Dharma, ensure its long endurance even at the cost of my own body and life.
He then addressed the rabbits:
All conditioned phenomena are entirely impermanent.
Sentient beings cherish their bodies, yet they are born empty and die empty,
never having acted for the sake of the Dharma.
"I now wish to act as a great bridge for all sentient beings,
so that the Dharma may endure for a long time and the Dharma-preachers may be honored.
At that time, the King of Hares addressed the hares, saying:
"I now wish to offer my own body as an act of worship to the Dharma Master.
You all should each rejoice accordingly.
At that time, the mountain deities, tree spirits, and others—
He immediately piled up fragrant wood and set it ablaze.
The hare king and his mother circumambulated the feet of the seer seven times and said:
"Great Master,
I now offer this Dharma-offering to the Venerable One.
The Rishi replied:
"You are a beast. Although you possess a compassionate heart, by what means could you possibly accomplish this?
The hare said to the seer:
"I offer my own body as an offering to you, O Noble One,
so that the Dharma may endure for a long time and all sentient beings may obtain great benefit.
Having spoken these words, he immediately said to his son:
"You may seek out water and grass as you please, while binding your mind in contemplation and maintaining right mindfulness of the Triple Gem.
At that time, having heard what his mother said, the rabbit knelt and addressed her, saying:
"Regarding the unsurpassed Great Dharma as spoken by the Honored One, which you wish to make offerings to, I too aspire to it.
Having said these words, he threw himself into the fire.
The mother followed after him.
At the moment the Bodhisattva relinquished his body,
heaven and earth shook violently.
Even as far as the realm of form and all the devas,
they all rained down celestial flowers to make offerings.
After the flesh had been cooked...
Then the mountain tree deity said to the seer:
"The hare king and his mother, for the sake of making an offering,
have cast themselves into the fire."
"The meat is now cooked;
you may eat it. At that time, the seer heard the words of the tree deity.
Overcome with grief, she was unable to speak.
She placed the scriptures she had been reciting upon the leaves of a tree and further spoke these verses:
It would be better to burn one’s own body and gouge out one’s eyes than to bear to commit killing and eat living beings.

In the *Compassion Sūtra* taught by all the Buddhas, it is said therein that those who practice loving-kindness would rather have their marrow broken and their brains exposed than bear to eat the flesh of living beings.
As the Buddha has said: "One who eats meat does not fulfill their practice of loving-kindness;
lost and submerged in birth and death, they shall not attain Buddhahood. After that seer had spoken this verse, he made a vow.
May I, in every lifetime, never give rise to the thought of killing;
may I never eat meat;
and may I enter the white-light samādhi of loving-kindness.
He continued until he attained Buddhahood, at which point he established the precept prohibiting the consumption of meat.
Having spoken these words, he threw himself into a fire pit and perished along with the rabbit.
At that moment, the heavens and earth shook in six ways.
By the power of the devas, the trees emitted a brilliant light;
its golden radiance shone forth, illuminating a thousand lands.
At that time, those people of the country who beheld this light—
They all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, true, and right path to enlightenment.
The Buddha told Śikhaṇḍin:
"You should now know this."
The White Rabbit King of that time was my very self;
the rabbit cub was... [the present one].
The one who was Rāhula at that time is this very person.
The seer who recited the sūtras then is Maitreya Bodhisattva, the son of a brāhmaṇa, within this assembly now.
The five hundred rabbits of that time are now the five hundred bhikṣus, headed by Mahākāśyapa.
The two hundred and fifty mountain tree spirits of that time...
The two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, such as Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana,
are these very ones. The thousand kings, such as Bhadrapāla and others,
are these very thousand bodhisattvas.
"From my appearance in the world until that of Ruci,
those among them who have received the Dharma and attained the Way are these disciples.
Thus spoke the Buddha to Śāṇakavāsin.
When Bodhisattvas seek the Dharma, they undergo diligent suffering throughout kalpas, not sparing even their own bodies or lives;
by casting themselves into a pit of fire as an offering,
they immediately transcend the transgressions of nine hundred trillion kalpas of birth and death.
At that time, five hundred brahmins, including Śvāśka and others,
sought ordination under the Buddha and became arhats.
Then those rishis, having cast themselves into the fire pit, were reborn in the Brahma world.
Until they attain Buddhahood,
those who eat meat violate the grave prohibitions;
in their future rebirths, they shall constantly drink molten copper.
Furthermore, the Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra states:
The Buddha said,
"O son of good family."
In a past age, there was a lion king who dwelt in a cave deep in the mountains.
He constantly thought to himself:
"I am the king among all beasts."
The Bodhisattva was able to look after and protect all the beasts.
At that time, there were two monkeys on that mountain who had fathered two sons together.
Then the two monkeys said this to the lion king:
"If you, O King, can protect all animals,
we now entrust our two children to you."
"I wish to go elsewhere to seek food and drink.
The lion king then granted his permission.
Thereupon, the monkey left behind his two young ones.
He entrusted him to the king of beasts and immediately departed.
At that time, there was a king of vultures in the mountains.
His name was Lijian (Beneficial Sight).
While the lion king was sleeping,
he immediately seized two young monkeys.
While dwelling in that perilous place,
the king awoke and immediately turned toward the King of Vultures.
And he spoke in verse:
"I now entreat you, Great Vulture King, I pray that you will graciously accept my words with a sincere heart;
I beg you to release him for my sake, Do not let him lose his faith and be filled with shame."
The King of Vultures spoke this verse in reply to the Lion King:
"I am able to fly and roam through the void; I have already passed beyond your domain and my mind is fearless.
