If you must protect these two children, For my sake, you should sacrifice this body."
Then the Lion King said:
"Now, for the sake of protecting these two sons, I shall sacrifice my body without regret, as if it were withered grass.
If I were to protect my own life by speaking falsely, how could I be called one who acts according to his word?"
After the Lion King had spoken this verse,
he immediately went to a high place, intending to cast off his body.
At that time, the Vulture King spoke another verse:
If one sacrifices body and life for the sake of others, that person shall immediately receive unsurpassed bliss.
I now give this monkey to you; I pray that the Great Dharma King will not harm himself, O son of noble family.
The lion king was none other than myself;
the male monkey was... [the Buddha].
He was none other than Kāśyapa.
The female macaque was the bhikṣuṇī Sārthavāhī, and those two macaque offspring were... [the two śrāmaṇeras].
The one who was Ānanda at that time is none other than the present Ānanda;
the one who was King Gṛdhra is none other than the present Śāriputra.
Therefore, for the sake of protecting those who rely [on the Dharma], one does not spare even body or life.
Section Five: Contemplating Suffering. As stated in the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra*, the Bodhisattva Peacock spoke thus to the various devas:
If one possesses a heart of compassion, that person is not far from Nirvana and is said to possess "Great Adornment.
If one gives rise to compassion toward sentient beings within the five realms of existence, one is able to destroy the afflictions.
How can one give rise to a compassionate mind toward beings in the hells?
These beings are deceived by their own karma; they are created by this enemy.
They undergo various incomparable sufferings in one hundred and thirty-six locations, such as the great hells;
when sentient beings fall into these places, the earth splits and gapes open.
Being cut, severed, burned, and boiled, they have no rescue and no refuge;
though they run hither and thither seeking pity for their own deliverance, they cannot escape.
To give rise to a heart of compassion toward them causes one's immeasurable Brahma-merit to increase.
If a person benefits sentient beings,
they contemplate the various forms of hunger and thirst among the hungry ghosts,
seeing their own bodies as if burning like a forest fire.
They run about in all directions, trampling and goring one another;
as flames consume them, their entire bodies blaze with fire,
and though they seek protection, there is no one who can save them.
"When will these sentient beings ever be freed from their various sufferings and afflictions?
This is called contemplating ghosts and giving rise to compassion, whereby one is reborn in the Brahma Heaven.
If a person contemplates animals...
One should give rise to a heart of compassion,
reflecting upon the immeasurable suffering and afflictions therein, where beings kill one another,
and the ways of death by air, water, and land are infinite.
They harm one another and devour one another.
When shall these sentient beings ever be liberated?
This is called contemplating the suffering of animals and giving rise to a mind of compassion.
If one can give rise to such a thought, one will be reborn in the Brahma Heaven.
If a person contemplates the various devas of the six heavens of desire and gives rise to a mind of compassion...
They experience celestial pleasures in the six heavens of the desire realm that are beyond analogy;
amidst various valleys, mountain peaks, and groves,
they enjoy every form of happiness.
Once they have experienced that pleasure, their karma being exhausted, they fall back and are reborn in places of suffering,
undergoing great anguish; they fall into the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals, running hither and thither.
Being distracted and ignorant, they undergo great suffering and affliction;
this is called contemplating the heavens and giving rise to compassion, whereby one is born in the Brahma Heaven.
If a person contemplates those among humans and gives rise to compassion...
Through various karmas, they are born among human beings and experience the fruits of suffering and pleasure;
they possess diverse mental dispositions and diverse inclinations.
Some are impoverished and must rely upon others for their own survival.
Having thus observed that beings in the five realms of existence undergo these five kinds of suffering, one gives rise to a heart of compassion.
Such a person attains supreme peace and security, and thereby achieves nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, the *Saṃyukta Āgama* states:
At that time, the World-Honored One took some soil from under his fingernails and addressed the bhikṣus,
saying, "What do you think?"
"Is the soil on my fingernail more, or is the soil of the great earth more?
The bhikṣu replied to the Buddha,
"World-Honored One, the soil on Your fingernail is very, very little indeed."
The soil of that great earth is immeasurable, incalculable, and beyond comparison.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If such sentient beings were to do so repeatedly, even for as little as the snap of a finger..."
Their cultivation of a mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings is like the amount of soil upon a fingernail;
those sentient beings cannot be counted, even for as little as the duration of a finger-snap.
Those who cultivate a mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings are like the soil of the great earth. Therefore, O bhikṣus.
One should constantly and repeatedly cultivate a mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings.
Furthermore, a verse from the *Caryā-melāyana-sūtra* says:
"One should set forth with a mind of loving-kindness, regarding an enemy as a virtuous friend."
Wandering through the cycle of birth and death, all have once been our kin;
just as a tree produces flowers that subsequently ripen into fruit without distinction,
so too are parents, wives, children, friends, and kinsmen.
Those who practice a mind of loving-kindness maintain an even mind free from hatred or attachment,
regardless of distance or proximity; they should thus cultivate great loving-kindness and impartiality,
as well as great compassion, extending it even to all beings within the three realms.
For one who practices loving-kindness in this way, their virtue surpasses that of Brahmā;
neither the blade of a sword can harm them, nor can officials, fire, enemies,
those of evil intent, various rākṣasas, snakes, vipers, lightning, or thunderbolts.
Lions, elephants, tigers, and all other harmful creatures do not dare to approach; none are able to cause him injury.
Furthermore, the *Sudarsana-vinaya* states:
If a dwelling place contains tigers, wolves, or lions,
down to the smallest ant, one must not reside there;
even if there is an anthill, [one must not stay].
The ants roam about,
seeking food and driving away others,
until they find a place to settle.
Furthermore, the *Saṃyukta Āgama* states:
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus,
"In times past, the devas and asuras drew up battle lines and fought."
The asuras were victorious and the devas were defeated.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, seeing his army shattered, retreating, and scattering, was filled with extreme terror;
he mounted his chariot and fled northward back to the celestial palace.
At the foot of Mount Sumeru, there are paths and groves;
beneath these groves are nests of garuḍas,
where many young garuḍas dwell.
At that time, Śakra, fearing that the chariot and horses might pass over and trample the fledglings to death, said to the charioteer:
"Turn the chariot back; do not kill the fledglings."
The charioteer addressed the king:
"The army of the asuras is pursuing us from behind;
if we turn back, we shall be beset by them."
Śakra declared:
"It would be better to turn back and be killed by the asuras than to trample and kill sentient beings with this army."
The charioteer on the path turned the vehicle southward.
When the asura army saw Śakra from afar turning his mount to return,
they assumed it was a tactical maneuver and immediately retreated in flight.
The host was struck with great terror;
their ranks were broken and they fled in dispersion,
returning to the palace of the asuras.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"That Śakra, Lord of the Devas, is the sovereign king of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
By the power of his compassion, he subdues the armies of the asuras through his majestic might."
One should also praise the merits of a compassionate mind.
Furthermore, the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra* states:
The Buddha told Ānanda:
Furthermore, if there is a person whose mind abides in loving-kindness and compassion,
they shall obtain eleven kinds of meritorious benefits. What are these eleven?
First, one sleeps in peace and wakes with a joyful heart;
second, one does not see evil dreams.
Third, they are beloved by humans and non-humans alike.
Fourth, they are protected by the various devas.
Fifth, they cannot be harmed by poisons.
Sixth, they cannot be harmed by knives or arrows.
Seventh, they cannot be burned by fire.
Eighth, they cannot be drowned by water.
Ninth, one constantly obtains fine clothing, delicacies, food and drink, bedding, seats, and medicinal decoctions for the treatment of illness.
Tenth, one attains the qualities of a superior person (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*).
Eleventh, at the dissolution of the body after death, one is reborn in the Brahma Heaven.
Furthermore, the Ekottarika Āgama states:
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying,
"There are six powers common to ordinary people."
What are the six? Infants have crying as their power;
women have anger as their power.
The bhikṣu takes patience as his strength;
the king takes arrogance as his strength;
the arhat takes diligence as his strength.
All Buddhas take great compassion as their power.
Therefore, bhikṣus, you should mindfully cultivate the power of great loving-kindness and compassion.
The Verse says:
The Muni pities the suffering of illusion; The Sage’s mind commiserates the deep darkness.
In pity for the ignorant, he opens the gates of skillful means To provide compassionate guidance and reception.
The Dharma-body pervades the entire Dharma-realm; Relying on transformation, it points to the Jeta Grove.
Together we dissolve the bonds of the five paths, And jointly resolve the enmity of the four maras.
Through the three trainings, the horse of craving is driven away; With the six recollections, the monkey of the mind is stilled.
The meditation pool is clear with the water of concentration; The awakening mind stirs amidst the clamor of sound.
The wind of wisdom blows upon the Dharma drum, Shaking the roots of my ignorance.
One must always stay close to virtuous friends, To open up words never before spoken.

Accounts of Resonant Response (*Ganying yuan*): Briefly citing five verifications. 1. The Sui Dynasty Śramaṇa Shi Huiyue. 2. The Tang Dynasty Śramaṇa Shi Daoji. 3. The Tang Dynasty Śramaṇa Shi Cizang. 4. Lu Yuanli, County Magistrate of the Tang Dynasty. 5. The Biography of Master Xuanzang’s Journey to the Western Regions during the Tang Dynasty. 6. The Sui Dynasty Śramaṇa Shi Huiyue (of the Sui Huiri Monastery).
A native of Lingnan,
he resided on Mount Luofu. By nature,
he was broadly affectionate and compassionate, seeking to save all living beings.
He dwelt in a secluded and remote place where tigers and leopards caused him no disturbance.
Once, a herd of wild beasts came before him,
and he preached the Dharma for them.
The tiger then rested its head upon its knee;
Yue immediately stroked its whiskers,
his facial expression showing no fear whatsoever.
The multitude beheld him all together.
His transformative teachings spread across the Five Ridges,
and his reputation flowed throughout the Three Chu regions.
At the end of the Kaihuang era, he was summoned to Huiri Monastery.
On his way back to Yangzhou, he fell ill and passed away;
his corpse remained on the bier as if still alive.
At night, he saw a flaming light issue from his feet,
enter the crown of his head,
and then emerge again from the crown.
The light entered through his feet and continued unabated throughout the entire night;
both monastics and laypeople marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.
The Śramaṇa Shi Daoji of the Tang Dynasty. Shi Daoji of Fugan Temple in Yizhou of the Tang Dynasty was a native of Shu.
He recited the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* in its entirety.
This is the constant and eternal practice of his life.
Whenever he intends to preach, he first washes away bodily impurities and dons clean robes;
only then does he ascend the seat.
He was by nature grave and circumspect, compassionate and benevolent, and diligent in all affairs.
Whenever there were those afflicted with leprosy, pus, blood, or foul odors,
he would gather them together in great numbers to wash and mend their clothing for them.
He treated them as food and ate them without revulsion.
When people of the time marveled and questioned him, he replied:
Objects have neither defilement nor purity;
purity and impurity arise from the mind. Since the mind does not arise, [there is no defilement or purity].
How could love or hatred arise?
He passed away at his own temple in the fifth month of the first year of the Zhenguan era,
at the age of seventy.
At that time, as the season was hot and humid, the corpse neither smelled nor decayed.
After a hundred days had passed, he remained sitting cross-legged just as he was at first.
Monastics and laypeople marveled at this marvel and subsequently applied lacquer to the body.
He inspired reverence throughout Ba and Shu.
Regarding the Tang dynasty śramaṇa Shi Cizang: he was the Great Sang-tong of the Tang dynasty’s Silla kingdom, whose secular surname was Kim.
A native of Silla, he was over fifty years of age; his spiritual insight was profound and lucid.
Disgusted with worldly glory, his heart delighted in the life beyond the mundane world.
He practiced meditation in solitary stillness, not avoiding even tigers and rhinoceroses;
he upheld the precepts without seeking companions, prioritizing compassionate salvation.
Dwelling in deep mountain seclusion, he was cut off from all provisions as people ceased coming and going.
Thereupon, various exotic birds each brought fruits in their beaks to present to his hands;
the birds would place them in his hands, and they would eat them together.
This occurred whenever the time came, never failing its appointed season.
His practice elicited such profound spiritual responses that few have been able to succeed him;
yet he constantly harbored a deep sense of sorrow and compassion for all sentient beings,
wondering what skillful means might be employed to enable them to escape birth and death.
Thereupon, while sleeping, he saw two men who said, "You are in a secluded and hidden place; what benefit do you seek?
Zang replied:
"Exclusively for the sake of benefiting sentient beings," he said, after which he conferred the five precepts of the treasury and declared:
"You may employ these five precepts to benefit sentient beings."
He further addressed Zang, saying,
"I have come from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, therefore I have conferred the precepts upon you. Having said this,

Regarding Lu Yuanli, the County Magistrate of Tang: he was Lu Yuanli of Fanyang, Tang.

Once, having fallen into a deep stupor due to a severe illness,

after a long while, he rose and proceeded to a separate courtyard.

from these stoves, vapors were rising.

the tumultuous sound of boiling was as loud as that of several tens of thousands of people.
Yuanli looked upward.

it was said to be the place where sinful people were steamed.

he then stripped off his clothes, stood naked, and threw himself into the cauldron.

The *Record of the Master of the Dharma Xuanzang’s Journey to the Western Regions* (also known as the *Biography of the Master of the Dharma Xuanzang*) states:
Within the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, there is the Lake of the Arrayed Heroes;
to the west of the lake is the Stūpa of the Three Animals.

Long ago, at the beginning of the kalpa, there were foxes,

They took pleasure in one another despite their different species.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, wishing to test those practicing the bodhisattva path,
descended as a spirit and transformed himself into an old man.
He addressed the three beasts, saying:
"O you three, are you dwelling in peace and security? Are you free from alarm and fear?"
It is said that they traverse the waters and lush grasses of the Feng River, sporting in the dense forests;
though of different species, they share in joy,
being both secure and happy.
The old man said,
"I have heard that you gentlemen’s affection is deep and your intentions sincere, such that you have forgotten my age and infirmity; therefore,
I have come from afar to seek you."
"I am currently suffering from hunger and exhaustion.
With what can you provide me with food?
He replied, "Please stay here for a short while."
I personally hurried there to visit him.
Thereupon, we sought him out with one mind;
a fox, following along the riverbank, carried a fresh carp in its mouth.
The monkeys gathered fruit from the trees in the forest and all came back together, while only the rabbit returned empty-handed.
The old man said to him:
As I observe you,
you are not yet in harmony;
though the monkeys and foxes share the same purpose, each is able to employ its own mind.
Only the rabbit returned empty-handed, alone and without any gift.
From this, it can truly be known.
Upon hearing the criticisms,
the rabbit said to the monkey and the fox,
"Only when we have gathered a great quantity of firewood can we proceed with our task."
The monkey and the fox raced against each other, carrying grass and dragging wood.
Once they had piled it up high and the fierce flames were about to blaze forth,
the hare said:
“O Benevolent One, my body is lowly and what I seek is difficult to fulfill;
I venture to offer this humble person as a single meal.
Having finished these words, he entered the fire and immediately died.
At that time, the old man resumed his form as Śakra.
Gathering the remaining ashes and collecting the remains, he lamented for a long while and said to the fox and the monkey:
"How is it that he has come to this?
Moved by his sincere heart, I shall not let his traces vanish;
I entrust them to the lunar disc to be transmitted to future generations."
Therefore, they all say that the hare within the moon has existed since this time;
later generations erected a stūpa at this site.

Section on Releasing Living Creatures, Number Seventy-Five; Section on Relieving Calamities, Number Seventy-Six. 75. Section on Releasing Living Creatures (65). This section consists of two parts: Part One: Exposition of the Intent. Regarding this exposition of intent: [The text continues with the standard opening formula for the "Exposition of Intent" (*shuyibu*): Generally speaking, the practice of releasing living creatures is a profound means of cultivating merit and extending compassion. It is a fundamental virtue that accords with the Way and aligns with the teachings. By liberating beings from the peril of death, one generates vast roots of goodness; by sparing them from suffering, one manifests the heart of universal benevolence. Furthermore, it serves as a remedy for the karmic retribution of killing, a method for accumulating blessings, and a way to repay the four debts of gratitude. Therefore, those who wish to cultivate the path must first prioritize this practice. [End of Part One: Exposition of the Intent. [The text proceeds to the second part, the "Citation of Scriptural Evidence" (*zhengjuebu*), which quotes various sutras and treatises concerning the merits of releasing life. [End of Section on Releasing Living Creatures, Number Seventy-Five. 76. Section on Relieving Calamities. [This section follows, detailing methods for averting misfortunes through ritual, repentance, and spiritual cultivation. [End of Section on Relieving Calamities, Number Seventy-Six.]
Among the myriad classes of beings, there is none that does not cherish life;
even the ignorant and deluded know to fear death.
Thus, when a tiger loses its forest and is driven to desperation, it [will do anything].
He then surrendered his life within the thatched hut;
like a startled bird with its wings clipped,

yet, as the hidden destiny did not fail, this noble reward has now arrived.
Thus we know that the workings of cause and effect are as clear as the sun.
Furthermore, the transformation of great compassion takes the salvation from suffering as its primary aim;
such is the nature of the mind of the great vow.
Saving living beings is the fundamental principle.
Yet, those of the five lineages and noble clans all vie with one another in ostentation,
as if their sacrificial tripods were displayed in rows.
In the three markets,
none failed to ply their butcher knives to carry out their tasks;
what crime had the multitude of living beings committed?
Injustice leads to physical mutilation;
all sentient beings harbor resentment.
To be needlessly subjected to being minced as meat causes the vengeful soul to remain unextinguished, resulting in bitter retribution that is paid back in kind.
I now exhort you, O virtuous one,
to practice compassion together;
set aside all fear and anxiety, entrusting them to equanimity.
"Let them soar or dive as they please for food and drink;
I shall ensure that those with purple scales and vermilion tails shall gaze upon one another across the rivers and lakes,
while those with brocade-like breasts and emerald plumage likewise do so."
Wandering freely through the Milky Way,
some hear the Three Refuges and awaken to the Way;
how are they any different from the blind dragon?
Having heard the Four Noble Truths and been reborn in heaven,

This likewise invites the fruit of eternal life.
Section Two: Citing Scriptural Evidence. As stated in the Brahmajāla Sūtra:
"If a son of the Buddha..."
By means of a compassionate mind, one brings about the karma of releasing living beings. All men have been my fathers;
all women have been my mothers.
Throughout my successive births, there has never been one from whom I did not receive birth.
Therefore, all sentient beings of the six realms have been my parents.
To kill and eat them—
They have killed my parents;
they have also killed my former body.
All earth and water were my previous bodies.
All fire and wind are my fundamental essence; therefore,
I constantly practice the release of living beings,
receiving birth after birth.
If you see people of the world killing animals,
you should employ skillful means to rescue and protect them, liberating them from their suffering and distress.
You should constantly teach and preach the Bodhisattva precepts to save and deliver sentient beings.
On the anniversary of the death of one's parents or siblings,
one should invite a Dharma Master to lecture on the Bodhisattva Precepts Sūtra and Vinaya,

One shall attain the sight of the Buddhas and be reborn among humans or in the heavens;
if one does not do so,
one commits a minor offense.

examine it thoroughly. While examining it,

he instructed those who were trustworthy to filter the water,

76. Section on Saving from Calamity (65). Section on Saving from Calamity, the Seventy-sixth. This consists of five parts: the Part on Stating the Intent, the Part on Bodhisattvas, the Part on Flowing Water, the Part on the Merchant Leader, and the Part on the Beast King. 1. Part on Stating the Intent, the First. Regarding the practice of compassion and the power of magnanimity:
Petitions for blessings and the alleviation of calamities can truly move the divine when the sincerity is profound;
this has been the consistent practice of successive sagely emperors.
Yet the Great Being Avalokiteśvara alone has seen and heard [of this]; therefore,
he cast himself into the fire,
possessing a body that was destined to be consumed by it.
For one drifting at sea, there is no certainty of survival;
yet if, for even a mere instant, one speaks of or thinks of taking refuge [in the Buddha],
then the vast ocean may be exhausted.
Fierce flames fly over them with coolness;
some stand with blades at their throats, yet the white-edged weapons do not wound them;
others fall into deep pits, yet their entire bodies remain unharmed.
Or they may be subjected to shackles and fetters that constrain their bodies;
such powers as these are difficult to fully discern, even with exhaustive scrutiny.
If one is sincere and self-disciplined, one will surely receive spiritual responses;
if one is superficial, idle, and negligent, it will be difficult to save them from peril.
2. Bodhisattva Section, Part Two: As stated in the *Saṃgharakṣa-sūtra*:
At that time, there was a bodhisattva dwelling on a mountain, sitting upright in meditation with a mind of loving-kindness, unmoving in contemplation.
A bird nested upon his head; he became aware of the bird on his head.
Fearing that the eggs might fall, he did not move his body;
he walked with careful steps, remaining motionless at each spot until the birds grew wings.
However, he was unable to fly away and ultimately did not depart.
Furthermore, the *Maitreya-paripṛcchā-pūrvapraṇidhāna-sūtra* states:
The Buddha said,
"Ānanda, when I originally sought the Way, I underwent immeasurable hardships."
In a past age, there was a prince named Ratnakusuma,
who was handsome and of exquisite beauty.
As he was leaving the park and coming out onto the road,
he saw a man suffering from leprosy.
Seeing him, he asked the sick man:
"With what medicine shall I treat your illness?
The patient replied,
"I would receive the marrow and blood from the King's own body to anoint my body."
The illness was thereby cured.
Upon hearing this, the Prince immediately broke his own body, taking marrow and blood to give to the sick man.
He gave with a sincere heart, his mind free from regret.
That prince was none other than myself.
The waters of the four great oceans may yet be measured with a peck; however,
the marrow, bones, blood, and other fluids of my own body cannot be reckoned,
for the sake of seeking perfect enlightenment.
Furthermore, the Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra states:
"At that time, the Bodhisattva Āṭavaka manifested in the form of a ghost,
and the Bodhisattva Saṃjñeya manifested in the form of a deer."
The Bodhisattva Prajñāpradīpa manifested in the body of a monkey;
the Bodhisattva Vigatarāga manifested in the body of a billy goat;
the Bodhisattva Āsravakṣaya manifested in the body of a king of geese.
In this way, these five hundred bodhisattvas each manifested various kinds of bodies,
from all of which issued forth great fragrant light.
Each and every bodhisattva held a lamp in their hand to make offerings to the Buddhas of the ten directions, who,
since the time of the seven Buddhas, have shared in being their kinsmen and retinues.
He upholds the five precepts and gives rise to the bodhicitta.
He assumes this body for the purpose of subduing all sentient beings and causing them to give rise to the bodhicitta.
Furthermore, the *Saṃyukta-ratna-piṭaka Sūtra* states:
In the past, there was an arhat practitioner who kept a śrāmaṇera as a disciple.
He knew that this śrāmaṇera would surely reach the end of his life in seven days.
He took leave to return home.
When the seventh day arrived,
the imperial messenger came back again.
The śrāmaṇera took leave of his teacher and departed immediately.
On the way, he saw a swarm of ants.
As he drifted with the current and his life was about to end,
he gave rise to a heart of compassion;
he removed his own kashaya robe, filled it with earth, and used it to dam the water.
He then took the ants and placed them in a high, dry location,
whereupon they all survived.
On the seventh day, he returned to his teacher's place.
The Master found this very strange.
He immediately entered meditative concentration and,
observing with his divine eye, realized that the man had no further merit remaining to account for such a state.

By reason of saving even a single ant, one shall not die for seven days and shall obtain the prolongation of life; furthermore, by repairing an old stupa, one shall also obtain the prolongation of life;
and by mending the mud-holes in the walls of a monastery, one shall likewise obtain the prolongation of life.
3. Section on the Elder Jalavāhana. Third: As stated in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*:
At that time, the Elder Jalavāhana was within the kingdom of King Devendraprabha.
He treated the ailments of all sentient beings,
causing them to recover.
At that time, the elder’s son had a wife.
His name was Suikū Ryūzō (Water-Space Dragon-Treasury),
and he begot two sons;
the first was named Suikū (Water-Space).
The second was named Water-Treasury.
Then the elder’s son led these two sons on their journey in succession until they reached a vast, desolate marsh.
Seeing various birds and beasts devouring much flesh and blood while running frantically in one direction,
the elder thought to himself,
"For what cause and condition are these birds and beasts running away so frantically in one direction?"
The son of the householder then followed after him and saw a pond whose water had dried up;
within that pond there were many fish.
When the elder saw the fish, he conceived a heart of great compassion.
At that time, a tree spirit manifested half its body and spoke these words:
"Excellent, noble son!
These fish are pitiable;
you should give them water."
For this reason, you shall be named Flowing Water.
The elder asked the deity:
"How many fish heads are there?
The tree deity replied,
"Their number is exactly ten thousand."
At that time, having heard these numbers, the Flowing Water (Jalavāhana) felt a twofold increase in his compassionate heart.
Then this empty pond was scorched by the sun,
and those ten thousand fish were on the verge of entering the gateway of death.
At that time, the elder searched for water in the four directions but was unable to find any.
Seeing a large tree, he immediately took its branches and leaves and returned to the pond to provide shade and coolness.
Having created this shade, he again ran swiftly to another distant place,
where he saw a great river named Jālodaka.
There were some wicked men who, in order to catch these fish,
dammed up and diverted the water so that it would not flow downstream;
however, the breach they had made was situated on a steep precipice and difficult to repair.
Then the son of the elder went quickly to the king's presence and explained the circumstances, saying:
"I only pray, Great King..."
"Please lend me twenty great elephants so that they may carry water and save these fish from death.
At that time, the Great King immediately commanded his ministers to provide them with the utmost speed.
"Choose from among them as you please.
At that time, Shrotas and his two sons led twenty great elephants.
He borrowed a leather bag from the city maintenance workers,
went to a place where the upper reaches of the river were dammed,
filled it with water, and had an elephant carry it on its back.
He galloped swiftly to an empty marsh and pond,
poured it into the water, and the pool was immediately filled to overflowing.
At that time, as the son of the householder wandered about the four sides of the pond,
the fish followed him,
moving along the bank.
At that time, the son of the elder again had this thought:
"For what reason do these fish follow me?
Surely they must be tormented by the fire of hunger and are seeking food from me."
At that time, Flowing Water told his son:
"Go home and inform your father regarding the food available in the house."
They loaded everything onto the elephants and returned with great haste.
At that time, the two sons followed their father’s instructions;
upon arriving home, they informed their grandfather of all that had occurred, exactly as described above.
At that time, the two sons gathered the food, loaded it onto the elephant,
and returned to their father's place;
the elder felt great joy in his heart.
He took some food from his son, scattered it into the pond,
and after feeding the fish until they were full,
he further reflected on a passage in the sutras: "If there are sentient beings who are at the point of death..."
Having heard the name of the Tathāgata Ratnottama,
they were immediately reborn in the heavens;
thereupon, they entered the water and spoke these words.
Homage to the Tathāgata Ratnaśrī of the past,
whose name comprises the ten titles.
Furthermore, for the sake of these fish, he expounded this most profound and wondrous Dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination.
At that time, the Flowing Water and his son returned home.
Later, while their guests were lying drunk,
the earth suddenly shook violently.
At that time, ten thousand fish died on the same day and were immediately reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Having been born there, they reflected upon how to repay his kindness.
At that time, ten thousand devaputras descended from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to the house of the elder.
At that moment, the elder’s son was sleeping on the upper floor of the building.
These ten thousand devaputras—
He placed ten thousand strings of exquisite celestial pearl necklaces at the head of the bed;
another ten thousand at the foot of the bed;
and another ten thousand at the right side of the bed.
Furthermore, ten thousand [flowers] were placed at the left side of his ribs,
raining down *māndārava* flowers and *mahāmāndārava* flowers.
The accumulation reached up to his knees.
Various celestial musical instruments produced exquisite sounds.
Among those in Jambudvīpa, there were some who were asleep.
They all awoke, and the Elder Jalavāhana also awakened from his sleep.
These ten thousand devaputras then traveled through the air.
Within the king’s realm, celestial flowers rained down everywhere;
proceeding further to a marshy pond, celestial flowers rained down once more.
Then, vanishing from that place, he returned to his palace in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
4. The Chapter on the Caravan Leader (Sārthavāha-varga). Fourth. As stated in the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra*:
The Buddha addressed Ānanda:
"In a past age, there was a great caravan leader."
For the sake of gathering jewels, he led a company of merchants into the great ocean.
Their ship was filled with all manner of treasures,
but when they reached the middle of the sea, the vessel suddenly broke apart.
At that time, those merchants were filled with fear and gave rise to extreme distress;
among them, some managed to grasp a plank from the ship,
while others floated upon the water.
There was one whose life had come to an end;
at that time, I was the leader of that merchant caravan in the great ocean.
Using this as a life-preserving float, they crossed over in safety.
At that time, five men called out to the caravan leader,
saying, "O Great Being, Caravan Leader, we pray only that you grant us fearlessness."
Having spoken these words,
the caravan leader then addressed them, saying:
"O noble men, do not give way to fear."
"Do not be afraid.
Ānanda, I shall cause you all to cross this great ocean safely."
At that time, the merchant leader, carrying a sharp sword, had this thought:
"The nature of the great ocean is such that it does not harbor corpses."
"If I now sacrifice my own life,
these merchants will surely be able to cross over the perils of the great ocean.
Having formed this thought, he [acted].
He immediately summoned the merchants,
placed them upon his own body, and instructed them to hold on firmly;
among those merchants were some who rode upon his back.
Some embraced his shoulders,
while others grasped his thighs.
At that time, the merchant leader, desiring to bestow upon them freedom from fear, [proceeded].
Arousing a heart of great compassion and manifesting great valor,
he immediately severed his own life-faculty with a sharp sword and quickly brought about his death. At that time, the great ocean carried his corpse and cast it upon the shore.
Then the five merchants were able to cross the sea;
they experienced peace and happiness,
and returned safely and auspiciously to Jambudvīpa without any misfortune.
Ānanda, do you think that the caravan leader at that time was someone else? It was I myself.
The five merchants are these present five bhikṣus.
These five bhikṣus were delivered and liberated in the great ocean in the past.
Now, once again, one attains liberation from this great ocean of birth and death and is established on the fearless shore of nirvāṇa.
Section Five: The Lion King. As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*:
In the distant past, immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago,
there was a great forest abounding in birds and beasts.
A wild fire broke out, burning from three sides simultaneously.
There was only one side [of the mountain] separated by a single body of water.
The various beasts were driven to desperation, having no place to flee for their lives.
The Buddha said:
At that time, I was a large-bodied, powerful deer;
with my forefeet spanning one bank and my hind feet spanning the other bank.
He caused the various beasts to tread upon his back as they crossed over;
though his skin and flesh were completely destroyed,
he endured it until death through the power of his compassion.
The last rabbit arrived;
its strength was already exhausted,
yet it exerted itself with all its might to endure until it could pass through.
Having passed over it, its back was broken, and it fell into the water and died.
This has been so for a long time;
it is not merely a case of today.
Those who attained deliverance previously are now these various disciples;
the last rabbit was Subhadra. Throughout his successive lifetimes, the Buddha delighted in practicing diligence.
Even now it does not cease.
Furthermore, the *Sūtra on the Wise and the Foolish* states:
"In the distant past, during a long-ago age, the Buddha..."
At that time, there was famine in the world.
Out of compassion while practicing the path as a bodhisattva, the Tathāgata saved sentient beings by manifesting as the body of a great fish.
It was five hundred yojanas in length.
Those in the country who required its flesh—
whether humans or animals— would all come to take and eat it.
Having taken [the flesh], it was reborn;
he gave his flesh and blood for twelve years.
Furthermore, the *Shousheng jing* (Sūtra on Receiving Birth) states:
In the past, the Bodhisattva was once a king of turtles.
Born and raised in the great ocean, he transformed his fellow species;
all the subjects of his realm practiced benevolence and virtue.
The King himself practiced compassion and provided protection;
he took pity upon sentient beings as a mother loves her child.
That ocean was deep and vast, its limits difficult to fathom.
He traveled everywhere until there was nowhere he had not traversed.
At that time, the King of the Turtles emerged from the outer sea and lay down to rest on the shore.
Having accumulated for days and months, its back became hard and dry, like dry land;
merchants traveling from afar stopped there upon it.
They split firewood and lit fires to cook rice and food;
they tethered their oxen and horses, and loaded their carts with stones,
placing them all upon them.
The king of turtles wished to enter the water,
yet he feared falling into unrighteousness;
just as he intended to endure it by force, the pain became unbearable.
He then devised a skillful stratagem to enter a shallow-water area,
extinguishing the poisonous fire so that the merchants would not be endangered;
yet the merchants remained terrified.
That is to say, as the tide suddenly surged,
he wailed and sighed in grief,
taking refuge in the various devas.
Seeing only this as a means of rescue,
the King of the Turtles felt even greater compassion for him and said to the merchant:
Do not be afraid. It was because I was being consumed by fire that I abandoned it and entered the water,
desiring to let the pain cease.
"I shall now ensure your safety;
you shall never again be endangered.
When the merchants heard this, they knew there was hope for their survival.
Simultaneously, they raised their voices and said, "Namo Buddha.
The turtle, moved by great compassion, carried the merchants back and set them down on the shore.
All those who were freed from their plight were filled with joy;
they called out from afar to the King of Turtles,
praising his virtue and honoring him as a bridge that delivers many across.
"By means of the great boat of conduct, one transcends the three realms.
Once the Way of the Buddha is attained, one shall further rescue and liberate others from the perils of birth and death.
The King of the Turtles replied:
"Excellent, excellent!
It shall be as the Tathāgata has spoken. Having said this, they each departed for their respective places.
The Buddha said,
"At that time, I myself was the king of the turtles."
The five hundred merchants were the five hundred disciples, Śāriputra and the others, of the present day.
Furthermore, the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states:
If there are sentient beings who see one who has committed a crime and deserves the suffering of death,
they should ransom that person's life with wealth.
Causing them to attain liberation,
he does not seek any reward for his kindness;
at the end of his life, he is reborn in the Heaven of Constant Joy.
Descending from the heavens, they receive human birth and do not encounter the calamities of kings.
If there are sentient beings who maintain the precepts and see a great fire arising that burns other beings,
they extinguish the fire with water to rescue those beings.
At the end of his life, he was reborn among the Heaven of Those Who Practice the Path and experienced various kinds of bliss.
Furthermore, as stated in the *Juguzi jing* (Sutra on Saving the Puppy):
"In the past, there was a certain kingdom."
Grain and rice became exceedingly expensive,
and the people suffered from hunger.
At that time, there was a śramaṇa who entered the city to beg for alms.
He searched throughout the gates and houses but obtained nothing at all.
Next, he went to the gate of a wealthy and noble elder and received some coarse and unpalatable food;
just as he was about to leave the city, [the story continues].
At the gate, he encountered a butcher who had been hunting;
the man was carrying a puppy back home intending to kill it.
Upon seeing the śramaṇa, he rejoiced and came forward to pay him homage.
The śramaṇa offered a blessing:
"May you live long and enjoy longevity.
The śramaṇa knew there was a dog and suspected he intended to kill it.
Therefore, he asked the man,
"What have you brought with you now?
He replied:
The śramaṇa further asked: "I have already seen it. The practitioner replied: "It is empty; there is nothing to be grasped or maintained. The śramaṇa asked again:
"I have already seen it."
"Why do you conceal it?
The sin of killing is extremely unwholesome.
I pray that you take my food in exchange for this puppy."
"May your life be saved.
Your merit is immeasurable. The man replied:
"We cannot share [this] with you;
therefore, I have gone out to seek it so that our household may eat together."
"How can this meager meal of yours suffice?
The śramaṇa earnestly exhorted him and invited him [to stay],
but the man was obstinate and refused to comply with his words.
The śramaṇa spoke again:
"If you are unwilling,
you may show it to me."
The man immediately brought it out to show the śramaṇa.
The śramaṇa lifted the rice to feed the puppy;
as he stroked it with his hand and offered prayers, tears fell from his eyes.
"It is due to your own transgressions that you have obtained this canine body;
you lack self-mastery and are seen being slaughtered and devoured."
May your sins be extinguished and merit arise in every lifetime;
may you leave behind the body of a dog and be reborn as a human being,
wherever you may be, naturally encountering the Dharma and the Triple Gem.
When the dog obtained food, a wholesome mind arose within him;
he leaped for joy, knowing that he had found refuge.
Yet, when people were about to take him home to slaughter and eat him, [he realized his error].
The dog’s life having ended, he was immediately reborn into the family of a wealthy and noble great householder.
As soon as he was born and fell to the ground, he possessed a heart of compassion.
At that time, the śramaṇa, while on his almsround, arrived at the gate of the householder's residence.
While on his almsround, the elder’s son saw that śramaṇa;
recollecting their past connection, he approached, prostrated at the śramaṇa’s feet,
and invited him forward to offer food and drink of a hundred flavors as an act of worship.
He then addressed his parents, saying:
"I now wish to follow this great Upādhyāya and receive the sūtras and precepts as his disciple."
My parents, out of great affection and esteem, were unwilling to grant my request.
"In this entire family, you are my only son;
you must continue the lineage as the future head of our house."
"For what reason do you wish to abandon your home and depart?
This child weeps and refuses to eat or drink;
he does not wish to hear of it and would rather die himself."
When his parents saw this, they granted him permission to depart.
Following his teacher to study the Way, he shaved off his beard and hair,
donned the three dharma robes, and recited the Buddhist sutras.
Having deeply understood its meaning, they immediately attain samādhi;
established in non-retrogression, they transform and enlighten all beings,
giving rise to the aspiration for the Great Way.
A Buddha’s appearance in the world is difficult to encounter;
the Way of the Sūtras is difficult to hear.
Those who are able to meet with them will all, without exception, receive deliverance.
If even animals can attain the Way,
how much more so can humans?
How could they fail to obtain the fruit?
Even if one has committed transgressions, if one subsequently gives rise to shame and remorse,
the black defilements will naturally perish once purity has been restored.
Furthermore, the *Saṃyukta Āgama* states:
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "In a past age,
there was a bird named Rāva."
Seized by a hawk, he soared into the void,
crying out in the sky:
"I was unaware that I had suddenly encountered this calamity."
"I sat apart from the domain of my parents and wandered elsewhere;
for that reason, I encountered this calamity.
How is it that today I have been imprisoned by another?"
"You have no autonomy," the hawk said to Rāva. "In what place could you possibly possess your own domain and attain autonomy?"
Rāva replied, "I have my own domain within the furrows of the plowed field;
it is sufficient to avoid all calamities."
"This is the domain of my parents.
The hawk spoke with arrogance toward Rāva:
"I release you to go back and plow the furrows."
"Can you escape? Thereupon,
Rāva escaped from the hawk's talons and returned to the base of a large clod of earth beneath a furrowed field.
He remained settled in his place,
yet he still desired to fight the hawk over the lump of meat;
the hawk then became greatly enraged.
"That it is but a small bird that dares to fight me!
His anger reached its peak;
he soared upward and swooped down directly upon him.
Thereupon, Rāva entered beneath a clod of earth;
as the hawk’s flight carried its breast against the hard clod,
its body was shattered and it died instantly.
At that time, the lapwing bird crouched deeply beneath a clod of earth and spoke this verse, looking up:
"The hawk has come with great force; The lapwing relies upon its own clod."
Riding upon the force of intense anger, you brought about calamity that shattered your own body;
yet I, possessing full realization, rely upon my own domain to subdue the mind of enmity,
and with sympathetic joy, I observe my own power with delight.
Even if you possess a hundred thousand beasts of prey,
their strength is not equal to even a sixteenth part of my wisdom;
behold the excellence of my superior intelligence, which destroys the fierce hawk.
The verse says:
All conscious beings fear death; Those with life dread peril and danger, Like fish trapped in a drying pool, Longing for the edge of flowing water.

Whether kin or strangers, all are one’s parents; how can one ever presume to deceive them? Through compassion, one rescues others from calamity and suffering, and the retribution of merit follows naturally.

[The first account] of the Qin śramaṇa Shi Daojiong. [The second account] of the Qin śramaṇa Shi Daojiong.
His native village and clan have already been recorded in previous accounts.
In the eighteenth year of the Hongshi era of the Yao Qin dynasty,
Shi Daoyi was dispatched to Mount Huo in Henan to collect stalactites.
He traveled together with four fellow students, including Daolang,
carrying torches to investigate the site. After entering about three li,
they encountered a deep stream which they crossed by means of a wooden beam laid across it.
Jiong was the first to rescue his junior, who fell from the wood and died;
at that moment, the fire was extinguched again, leaving everything in pitch-black darkness.
Jiong, realizing his efforts were in vain, wept bitterly with utter grief.
He continued to single-mindedly invoke the name of Avalokiteśvara and his vow.
Having escaped from his confinement, he held a feast for a hundred people to express his gratitude for the deity's majestic power.
After one night had passed, a small light was seen, shining brilliantly.
It appeared like a firefly;
in an instant, the cave was completely illuminated.
Thereupon, the path became visible, and he emerged from beneath the cliff.
Because of this, his faith and awakening grew ever deeper,
and he repeatedly witnessed spiritual wonders.
In the nineteenth year of the Yuanjia era.
When the Prince of Kang of Linchuan was stationed at Guangling,
he invited Sengjiong to provide offerings.
In the ninth month of that year, after holding a ten-day *Avalokiteśvara* fast within the western chamber, [the following occurred].
Having attained [this state], at the end of the fourth watch on the ninth night, when the assembly of monks had all fallen asleep,
he rose and paid homage;
then, returning, he desired to sit in meditation.
Suddenly he saw countless śramaṇas on the four walls,
all with their upper bodies half-emerged.
He clearly and distinctly beheld one Buddha with a conch-shell-shaped topknot (śaṅkhacakrābha-jaṭā).
There was a tall man wearing a flat-topped cap (*pingshangxi*),
with trousers and tunic made of *jian* cloth, and holding a long sword with a fur grip;
his appearance was exceedingly majestic and extraordinary.
When [the Master] was about to offer incense and transmit the Way to [Wang] Jiong,
Jiong at that time refused to accept it.
A śramaṇa from within the wall spoke, saying:
Master Jiong may accept this incense to provide protection for the host.
In an instant, everything vanished and nothing could be seen again.
At that moment, none of the assembled monks were visible; one beheld only the image of Śākyamuni that had been placed there.
Lü Sǒng of the Jin dynasty, courtesy name Mào Gāo,
was a lay devotee from Guǎnzhōu who resided in Shǐfēng.
The mountain stream to the south of this county flows rapidly with steep banks;
it winds and curves like a coil and abounds with large boulders.
Even those traveling in broad daylight still harbor feelings of peril and apprehension.
Song himself recounted that his father was once crossing a mountain stream when he encountered this.
After traveling about ten li from home,
as the sun was setting toward dusk,
the sky suddenly became dark as lacquer due to wind and rain.
No longer knowing east from west,
they were about to drown;
they could do nothing but turn their hearts in devotion to Avalokiteśvara.
As he recited and contemplated,
in a brief moment a firelight came ashore like someone holding a torch.
Illuminating and seeing clearly within the stream,
one attains the home from afar;
the fire constantly leads the way before.
He went about ten paces from the boat.
Later, Song associated with Xi Jabin;
what was transmitted by Xi is as follows.
Regarding Xu Rong, the lay devotee of the Jin dynasty:
Xu Rong was a native of Langya.
While returning from Dongyang, he passed through Mount Ding.
The boatmen were unaccustomed to the waters;
they mistakenly fell into a whirlpool,
tossing and dancing upon the waves until they were on the verge of being submerged.
Having no further concerns,
he called upon Avalokiteśvara with a sincere heart;

It is difficult to distinguish the blades of grass and counting-sticks; the mounds and hollows of the great earth are none other than my former bodies, and the currents of the vast oceans are all the same as my tears and blood.
Viewed from this perspective, [all things are one].
Who is not a kinsman or friend?
Though humans and ghosts differ,
their arising and ceasing are fundamentally the same.
The sentiments of affection and love occasionally manifest like shadows and echoes;
yet the masses of the wicked remain ignorant and darkened.
Failing to recognize kinship or distance,
they instead cause the loss of one's physical form to nourish their own lives; thus,
they slaughter and carve one another, sharing in a common abode of enmity.
Through kalpas of mutual enmity, the retribution of suffering is difficult to exhaust.
Reflecting quietly upon this matter, how could it not cause one’s heart to ache?

or they may fall into the realms of hell-beings, animals, or hungry ghosts.
The flowing out of marrow and blood is likewise so.

they may take on the forms of horses, camels, donkeys, oxen, birds, beasts,

surpassing the waters of the four great oceans.

As evil associates, we have wandered through the long night of beginningless birth and death,

throughout the long night of saṃsāra’s cyclic revolution,
they were shrouded by ignorance.

thus they revolve through the long night,

"Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:
'With diligence and skillful means, we shall sever the great elements so that they do not increase.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:"

yet for the noble disciples who possess right knowledge and see the Truths.

one cultivates the eightfold path; proceeding directly toward parinirvāṇa,

The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Sentient beings have been wandering through the long night of birth and death since beginningless time."
One does not know the ultimate limit of suffering;
there is not a single place where one is not born and does not die.
Thus, this long night of beginningless birth and death continues on.
One does not know the ultimate limit of suffering.

with craving binding their necks,
they revolve through the long night, unaware of the ultimate limit of suffering.

just as the heavens rain everywhere over the world without cessation.

it is like throwing a staff into the air:
either its head will fall to the ground.

Some fall into hell;
some fall among the animals;

immediately knelt down and turned toward the realm below.

one becomes a true son of the Buddha for as long as life lasts;
it is not by means of being a celestial king.
Thus it was repeated up to three times.
Having spoken these words, he no longer entered the womb of a pig,
but was instead born into the family of a householder.
At that time, the deva-son, according to the length of his lifespan, was reborn in the household of a great elder in the city of Rājagṛha.
At that time, the elder’s wife knew she was pregnant;
when the ten months were nearly complete, she gave birth to a son.
He was of peerless beauty, a rarity in the world.
When he reached the age of ten,
his parents took him to the presence of the Buddha.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for them;
immediately upon these seats, all defilements were exhausted and they attained the purity of the Dharma-eye,

Furthermore, the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states:
"At that time, the King of the Yāma Heaven..."
To summarize for the assembly of devas:
among gods and humans, there are sixteen kinds of suffering.
What are these sixteen?
Among gods and humans, those comprised within the good realms experience two kinds of suffering:
first, the suffering of the intermediate state (antarābhava);
second, the suffering of dwelling in the womb.
Third is the suffering of birth from the womb;
fourth is the suffering of fear regarding food;
fifth is the suffering of association with the disliked.
Sixth is the suffering of separation from the beloved;
seventh is the suffering of cold, heat, and so forth;
eighth is the suffering of illness.
Ninth is the suffering of being employed as a servant by others;
tenth is the suffering of being sent to perform labor;
eleventh is the suffering of associating with evil associates.
Twelfth is the suffering of decline and affliction caused by one's wife, children, and kinsmen;
thirteenth is the suffering of hunger and thirst;
fourteenth is the suffering of being despised and reviled by others.
Fifteenth is the suffering of old age;
sixteenth is the suffering of death.
These are the sixteen great sufferings among human beings.
In the human world, from birth until the end of life and through all other sufferings,
one cannot endure the cycle of birth and death;
within conditioned existence, there is not even the slightest happiness.
"All things are impermanent;
all things are subject to decay.
At that time, the King of the Yāma Heaven spoke in verse:
In the world of humans, all aggregates are suffering;
those who are born must inevitably die. Where there is death, there is necessarily birth;
if one dwells within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), one suffers the afflictions of one's own karma.
The suffering of traveling far through the long night— this suffering is beyond description;
submerged in excrement and urine, scorched by the heat of gases,
such is the suffering of dwelling in the womb, which cannot be fully told.
Constantly craving the flavors of food, their minds always longing for tastes lead to great suffering; this suffering is beyond description,
as the small mind constantly hopes and desires, never knowing satisfaction with its cravings.
The various sufferings one undergoes— this suffering is beyond description:
the meeting with those one hates and dislikes, and the sufferings born of great fires and poisons— this suffering is beyond description.
In the separation from those one loves, sentient beings undergo great suffering,
great evil, and what is unbearable; this suffering cannot be described—
it is the fear of great suffering through cold and heat, giving rise to immeasurable kinds of pain.
Sentient beings undergo this suffering; this suffering is beyond description.
The suffering of illness harms human life; illness acts as the messenger of the King of Death.
Sentient beings undergo this suffering; this suffering is beyond description.
Driven by others, they always lack self-mastery;
sentient beings undergo this suffering which is beyond description.
Scorched by the poison of craving, they are sent to seek out great suffering.
From this sequence up to death—this suffering is beyond description.
If one draws near to evil associates, all sufferings will never cease;
one shall undergo the sufferings of the evil realms, which are beyond description.
When one's wife and children suffer decline and distress,
seeing them gives rise to great agony exceeding even that of hell; this suffering is beyond description,
as hunger and thirst burn the body like a fierce, blazing fire.
That which can destroy both body and mind—this suffering is beyond description.
Constantly treating others with contempt, one gives rise to grief, lamentation, and pain toward kinsmen and friends; this suffering is beyond description.
When a person is oppressed by old age, the body becomes frail and the mind weakens;
bent over and reliant on a staff to walk, this suffering is beyond description.
When a person is seized by death, they depart from this world for the next.
This death is a great suffering that cannot be fully described.
Furthermore, the *Sūtra on the Nine Untimely Deaths* states:
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
There are nine classes [of people].
Due to nine causes and conditions, their lives may end prematurely even before their allotted lifespan is exhausted.
The first is eating food that one should not eat.
Second, not measuring the rice;
third, not practicing with the rice;
fourth, not producing [the result].
Fifth is for the sake of bringing [the faculties] to maturity;
sixth is for the sake of not maintaining the precepts;
seventh is for the sake of associating with evil associates.
Eighth, entering a village at an improper time and being ignorant of the rules of conduct.
Ninth, failing to avoid what should be avoided.
These nine causes and conditions lead to the untimely end of a person's life.
First, that which is unfit for consumption is called "unpleasant food," as it also causes the stomach to become unbalanced and indigestible.
Second, "not measuring the rice" means not knowing moderation and eating more than is sufficient.
Third, "unaccustomed to the rice."
This is called "not knowing the proper time.
Having traveled to another country during winter or summer,
one does not know the local customs regarding meals and has not yet become accustomed to them.
Regarding the four types of "non-arising" (anutpāda) food:
it refers to consuming more food before the previous meal has been digested,
or failing to take medicine for emesis or purgation.
Because it has not yet been digested.
Fifth, regarding "stopping for digestion":
when the urge to defecate or urinate arises, one does not go immediately.
Sighing, belching, sneezing, and when the wind blows downward—these are the six [conditions] for restraint.
Those who do not uphold the precepts are said to have transgressed the five precepts: killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, double-tongued speech, and drinking alcohol.
They cause them to enter the custody of the authorities, where they are beaten with canes and staves,
hacked, and pierced; some die at the hands of their enemies,
while others die of terror, recollecting their sins and filled with anxiety.
Seventh is being close to evil associates;
because one does not distance oneself from evil associates while sitting, one fails to discern good and evil.
Eighth is entering villages at improper times.
This is called "stealthy conduct. Furthermore,
there are disputes within the village,
and the local officials and magistrates pursue them without regard for their own safety.
First, entering the houses of others in an improper manner.
Ninth, failing to avoid what should be avoided:
being disturbed by wicked elephants, horses, oxen, carts, snakes, vipers, wells, water, fire, weapons, staves, or intoxicated and malicious persons.
These are the nine untimely deaths by which one's life-span, though not yet exhausted, comes to an end through such circumstances.
Furthermore, in the *Pañcopādānaskandhopama-sūtra*, the Buddha spoke this verse:
"The aggregate of foam is a metaphor for form; Sensation is like a bubble upon the water."
Perception is like a mirage in the heat; Volitional formations are like the core of a plantain tree;
Consciousness is illustrated by a magical illusion— Thus have the Buddhas taught;
one should contemplate this as the essential point, Examining it thoroughly and reflecting upon it.
To examine emptiness thoroughly, one does not perceive its permanence;
yet when one wishes to see the subtle, it is thus. All that is taught by true wisdom is likewise so:
when these three things are severed, one knows the body has no inherent value.
When life ends and warmth and breath depart, the body is cast aside and passes away.
As one lies dead upon the ground, they are as insentient as grass.
Observing their condition thus, it is but an illusion; yet the foolish are greedy for it.
Cessation is without rest, and there is likewise no firm solidity;
knowing the five aggregates to be thus, a bhikṣu should apply himself with diligence.
Therefore, day and night, he should awaken himself through mindfulness and right wisdom.
Practicing the path of tranquility, the practice of elimination is the supreme bliss.
Section Three: The Five Aggregates. As stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*:
It is like a king who keeps four venomous snakes in a basket.
I entrust it to one person,
commanding you to look after and nourish it;
were you to cause even a single snake to give rise to anger, [it would be a grave offense].
"I shall execute him in the marketplace according to the law.
Upon hearing this, the man was seized with terror at the king's stern resolve; he abandoned his basket and fled.
At that time, the king again dispatched five caṇḍālas who followed behind him with drawn swords.
When the man looked back and saw the five men behind him,
he immediately abandoned his departure and fled.
At that time, the five men, using evil means,
concealed the knives they held and secretly dispatched one man to feign intimacy and friendship.
He then said to him, "You may return.
But the man did not believe it.
He entered a village intending to hide himself;
once inside the village, he peered into the various houses,
but saw no one at all.
He took up his jars and vessels, finding them all empty and devoid of anything;
seeing no one and failing to obtain any goods,

"Alas, O man! This place is desolate and devoid of inhabitants.
Tonight, six great bandits shall arrive."
"If you should encounter them, you will die;
how then can you now hope to escape them?
At that time, the man's fear increased even further.
He departed again, leaving that place.
On the road he encountered a river;
its current was so swift and turbulent that there were no boats or rafts, and he was filled with fear.
He immediately gathered various kinds of grass and wood to construct a raft.
He then reflected further:
"If I remain here, I shall surely be harmed by the venomous snake, the five caṇḍālas, the one who feigns intimacy, and the six great thieves."
If one attempts to cross this river, the raft cannot be relied upon;
one will surely sink and die.
It would be better to sink and die than to be harmed by those serpent-thieves.
He immediately pushed the grass raft into the water,
leaned his body against it,
and held onto it with his hands while pressing down with his feet.
Having cut across the stream,
he went forth and immediately reached the other shore, secure and free from affliction;
his mind was at ease, and all fear and dread were eliminated.
The four venomous snakes are the four great elements (mahābhūta).
The five caṇḍālas are...
These are the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
First, the one who feigns intimacy is craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
The "entrance into a single village" refers to the six internal sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*).
The "arrival of the six great thieves" refers to...
These are precisely the external objects;
they are the six great thieves.
Only kings are capable of restraining them.
Only Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are able to restrain these six great thieves;
even if various kings were to cut off their hands and feet, they would not be stopped.
Even so, they are still unable to cause the mind to find rest.
The evil thieves of the six sense-objects are likewise;
even if one attains the four fruits of śrāmaṇya and cuts off their hands and feet, they remain as such.
Nor can they prevent one from being robbed of wholesome dharmas.
Just as a valiant and strong man is able to subdue these six great thieves,
