One is thus able to destroy and annihilate the evil thieves of the six sense-objects.
Section Four on the Eight Sufferings: As stated in the *Pañcarājopadeśa-sūtra* (The Scripture of the Five Kings), the Buddha preached the Dharma for the five kings.
In this life, there are constantly immeasurable sufferings that cut to the very core of one's being.
Now, for your sake, I shall briefly explain the eight types of suffering.
What are these eight sufferings?
First is the suffering of birth;
second is the suffering of old age;
third is the suffering of illness.
Fourth is the suffering of death;
fifth is the suffering of separation from those one loves;
sixth is the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks.
Seventh is the suffering of association with the disliked;
eighth is the suffering of grief and lamentation.
These constitute the eight sufferings.
What constitutes the suffering of birth?
When a person dies, they do not know toward which realm their spirit is heading,
as they have not yet attained a place of rebirth.
They universally assume the form of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Upon reaching the twenty-first day,
when the parents are in union, they immediately come to enter the womb.
In the first week, it is like thin curd;
in the second week, it is like thick curd;
in the third week, it is like solidified butter.
In the fourth week, it is like a mass of flesh;
in the fifth week, five vesicles are formed,
and the wind of skillfulness enters the womb.
It blows upon its body,
causing the six sense-faculties to open and expand;
it dwells within the mother's womb, below the raw viscera and above the cooked viscera.
When the mother ate a cup of hot food, it felt as if her body were being plunged into a cauldron of boiling water;
when she drank a cup of cold water, [it felt like being immersed in ice].
It is as if coldness cuts through the very marrow of one's bones.
When the mother is full, her body is constricted with an unspeakable pain;
when the mother is hungry, there is a gnawing sensation within her belly, as if she were being suspended upside down.
They undergo immeasurable suffering.
When the full moon arrives and they are about to give birth,
their heads are pressed against the birth canal with an intensity like being squeezed between two mountain crags.
When one is about to be born, the mother is in peril and the father is terrified.
Upon being born and falling onto the grass, the body is so delicate and soft that the contact of the grass with it is like walking upon swords and blades.
Suddenly, he lost his voice and cried out loudly,
"Is this suffering? Everyone said:
This is great suffering.
What is meant by the suffering of old age?
It refers to when one’s parents have nurtured and raised one until reaching adulthood.
Relying on one's own strength and vigor, one carries light and heavy burdens without self-restraint; thus,
one loses the proper measure regarding cold and heat.
In old age, the hair turns white and the teeth fall out;
the eyesight grows dim and the hearing dulls.
Vigor departs and decay arrives; the skin slackens and the face wrinkles.
The hundred joints ache and pain, making every step exceedingly bitter;
sitting or rising, he groans with grief and sorrow, his mind distressed.
His spiritual consciousness diminishes further until he immediately forgets.
Life’s days are hastening to their end;
as he speaks, his tears flow down his face, and he requires assistance for every movement, whether sitting or rising.
"Is this suffering? He replied, "It is great suffering.
"What is meant by the suffering of illness?"
A person is composed of the combination of the four great elements.
If one element is out of harmony, one hundred and one diseases arise;
if all four elements are out of harmony, four hundred and four diseases manifest simultaneously.
When the earth element is disturbed, the entire body becomes heavy;
when the water element is disturbed, the entire body becomes swollen;
when the fire element is disturbed, the entire body becomes feverish and hot.
When the wind element is disturbed, the entire body becomes rigid and stiff;
the hundred joints ache as if struck by a staff.
As the four great elements fluctuate, the hands and feet become useless.
Their vital energy is utterly exhausted, such that they require assistance to sit or rise;
their mouths are parched and their lips are withered, their tendons snap, and their noses run;
their eyes no longer perceive forms, and their ears no longer hear sounds.
Impure fluids flow from his body as he lies upon it;
harboring bitter anguish in his heart, he constantly utters lamentations.
His six kin remain by his side, watching over him day and night.
From the very beginning there was no rest;
whatever delicacies and fine foods entered the mouth were all bitter. Is this not suffering?
He replied,
"It is indeed a great suffering.
"What is meant by the suffering of death?"
At the time of a person's death, the four hundred and four diseases arise simultaneously.
The four elements seek to disperse and the soul-spirit becomes restless.
At the moment of death, the "sword-wind" (kṣurapra-vāyu) dissolves the physical form.
There is no place that does not ache;
white sweat flows forth as both hands grasp at empty space.
Family members, both inside and outside the house, stand at his left and right.
Grief and sorrow caused him to weep with tears streaming down, the pain piercing to his very marrow;
unable to sustain himself,
he was left behind by the deceased.
The wind-movement ceases and the breath is cut off;
the fire is extinguished and the body grows cold.
The wind comes first, followed by the fire.
The spirit has departed;
the body remains upright and motionless, no longer possessing any consciousness.
Within ten days or a month, the flesh decays and blood flows.
Swollen, putrid, and foul-smelling, it was utterly unbearable to approach.
Abandoned in the wilderness, it was devoured by various birds;
once the flesh was gone and the bones dried, the skull lay in a separate place.
"Is this suffering? "He replied,
'Indeed, it is great suffering.'"
What is the suffering of separation from loved ones?
It refers to when members of a household— parents, siblings, wives, and children— are bound together by mutual affection,
yet in a single day their home is destroyed or plundered by others.
They dispersed in their respective directions:
the father to the east and the son to the west;
the mother to the south and the wife to the north.
It is not in only one place;
as slaves and servants, they each wail in grief,
their hearts and flesh severed, left in utter darkness and obscurity.
"There is no prospect of seeing one another again. Is this not suffering?
He replied:
This is indeed great suffering.
What is meant by the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks?
It is the dispersal and expenditure of the family's wealth and property in pursuit [of further gain].
High officials and those esteemed by the people attain wealth and honor;
through diligent and unremitting effort, they eventually encounter and obtain it,
serving as governors and magistrates on the borders.
Before long, he greedily seized the property of the people.
When he was accused by others,
one day he was taken away in a cangue-cart on account of his offenses.
At the moment one is about to be killed, there is immeasurable sorrow and suffering;
one does not know whether death or life will come on what day. Is this not suffering?
He replied,
"It is indeed a great suffering.
What is meant by the suffering of association with the disliked?"
The people of this world are base and vulgar, dwelling together amidst love and desire;
they contend over matters that are not urgent,
and further kill and harm one another.
Consequently, they became bitter enemies.
Each sought to avoid the other, yet there was no place to hide;
each sharpened their blades, notched their arrows, slung their bows over their shoulders, and took up their staves.
They feared meeting one another;
they encountered each other on a narrow path, with bows drawn and arrows raised, facing each other with double-edged blades,
not knowing who would emerge victorious.
At that time, one experiences immeasurable fear and dread. Is this suffering?
He replied: "It is."
This is indeed great suffering.
What is meant by the suffering of sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair?
It refers to human life as it exists in this world.
Those with long lives may even reach a hundred years;
those with short lives suffer miscarriage or abortion.
As for those with long lives, they are granted a full hundred years.
Half of the night has passed, and fifty years remain of his life;
yet, intoxicated by wine and afflicted by disease, he is unaware of what he does as a man—
thus five years have been diminished.
In my youth I was ignorant;
by the age of fifteen, I still did not understand propriety and righteousness.
Now that I am over eighty years old, I am senile, dull-witted, and devoid of wisdom.
Deaf and blind, lacking all sense of order,
another twenty years were subtracted;
thus ninety years had already passed.
During the remaining ten years,
there was much sorrow;
he also grieved when the world was about to fall into chaos.
When there is drought in the world, he is also distressed.
When there is a great flood in the world, he is also distressed.
When there is frost in the world, he is also distressed.
One worries that the harvests throughout the world will not ripen;
one worries that there are many illnesses and ailments within the household and its members;
and one worries that the family’s wealth and property, as well as their livelihood, may be lost.
I am also distressed that the government has not yet received my hundred installments of tax.
I am also distressed that my family members have been seized by the authorities and imprisoned, with no known date of release.
I am also distressed that my brothers have traveled far away and have not yet returned.
He was distressed that his household was impoverished and cold, lacking both food and clothing;
he was distressed by troubles in his neighboring villages;
and he was distressed that the local deities could not be properly propitiated.
When family members die, they have no wealth for their funeral rites and are thus distressed;
when spring arrives and it is time for sowing, they have no oxen or plows and are likewise distressed.
In this way, amidst various kinds of sorrow and grief, there is never a moment of happiness.
On this festival day, when you should have gathered together in joy,
instead you are weeping and wailing at one another; is this not suffering?
He replied,
"It is indeed a great suffering.
Furthermore, the *Suvarṇavarṇa-rāja-sūtra* states:
On one occasion, a celestial maiden addressed King Suvarṇavarṇa with these verses:
What dharma is called suffering? Of all sufferings, what is the most grievous?
It is said that the suffering of poverty and the suffering of death—these two sufferings are equal and no different.
It would be better to undergo the suffering of death than to be born into poverty.
Furthermore, the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"The five fears are..."
First, the fear of lacking a livelihood;
second, the fear of ill repute;
third, the fear of death.
The fear of the four miserable destinies and the fear of timidity—
these five fears are all completely abandoned upon realizing the stage of pure intentionality (*śuddhāśayabhūmi*).
Furthermore, in the *Sūtra on the Demise of King Prasenajit’s Queen*, the World-Honored One spoke this verse for the king:
"All people return to death; there is none who does not die."
Following one's actions, one reaps the seeds of calamity or fortune; One personally obtains the fruits of good or evil.
Hell is for those of evil conduct; The virtuous will surely be born in the light.
Clear wisdom can distinguish between them; Only merit can restrain evil.
In this way, Great King,
there are four terrors that cannot be avoided:
old age is a great terror.
When the fatty flesh has been consumed,
illness becomes a source of great terror;
one lacks the will for strength and vigor.
Death is a great terror;
there is no end to the exhaustion of life.
Parting from those one loves is a great terror.
One should not seek to dwell therein.
These four great elements are terrifying; they cannot be redeemed by any swords, staves, incantations, medicinal herbs, elephants, horses, people, treasures, or fortified cities.
For example, when a great cloud arises with thunder and lightning, it disperses in an instant.
Human life is extremely short; though the maximum lifespan is a hundred years, those who reach it are few.
By cultivating only the perception of impermanence and eliminating affection and attachment,
one may attain liberation from suffering.
Section Five: Miscellaneous Difficulties. As stated in the *Furen yu gu jing* (Sutra on a Woman Encountering Calamity):
When the Buddha was in the world, there was a man who had no wife.
He traveled to the kingdom of Śrāvastī to take a wife;
his own country already had two sons,
the eldest of whom was seven years old.
The second son was still an infant in her arms, and his mother was again pregnant; she wished to return to her family's estate.
According to the customs of India, it is the custom for women to return to their parents' country.
At that time, the husband and wife were traveling in a carriage with their two children toward Śrāvastī;
midway, they stopped to rest and tended to their cattle.
At that time, a venomous snake was coiled around the ox's leg;
the ox consequently broke free from its bonds.
Her husband took the ox, intending to prepare it for departure.
She saw that the ox had been killed by a venomous snake;
the snake then left the ox and coiled around her husband to kill him.
Seeing this from afar, the wife was struck with terror and trembled with fear.
They wept and wailed, crying out to Heaven;
there was no one to provide protection or rescue.
The sun was then about to set.
Not far from where he was going lay a river.
Opposite the river stood a house where a woman lived;
she feared that as night fell, she would be robbed by bandits.
He abandoned the carriage and took his two sons to the water's edge;
he left the elder son by the bank and carried the younger son across the water.
Just as she reached the middle of the stream, the wolf devoured her child.
As the child cried out to its mother, she looked back and saw that it had been eaten by the wolf.
In her shock and terror, she lost the child she was holding in her arms.
Falling into the water, she was carried along with the current;
her mother became increasingly distressed, bewildered, and lost her composure,
stumbling in the water and causing the child she carried to fall.
He then crossed the water and asked a traveler on the road,
"Is my father and mother at home safe and well?
The traveler replied:
"Last night a fire broke out and completely consumed my parents' home, leaving nothing behind.
She then asked the traveler, "Is my husband's family well? Are my father-in-law and mother-in-law at peace?"
The traveler replied,
"Yesterday there was a bandit who plundered and destroyed his home;
both my paternal aunt and her husband died, and nothing remains intact."
Upon hearing this, his mother was filled with sorrow, anxiety, and dread;
her mind became bewildered and her senses confused, such that she could not distinguish east from west.
She stripped off her clothes, stood naked, and wandered about in a state of delusion and madness.
Travelers on the road saw this and were greatly alarmed,
saying it was a demonic affliction caused by malevolent spirits.
At that time, the Buddha was staying at the Anāthapiṇḍika Monastery in Śrāvastī.
Then the woman ran toward him. At that time, the World-Honored One was preaching the Dharma to the great assembly.
Such is the law of all Buddhas.
The blind who saw the Buddha all had their vision restored; the deaf regained their hearing;
the mute were able to speak;
and those afflicted by disease were healed.
The weak and feeble become strong and healthy;
those afflicted by poison are unable to move,
yet their distracted minds attain concentration.
At that time, when the woman saw the Buddha, her mind immediately attained concentration and she was no longer distressed.
Seeing herself naked, she felt ashamed and prostrated herself on the ground.
The Buddha called for Ānanda.
He took the robe and gave it to him.
Having put it on, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.
The Buddha then preached the sutra for them, manifesting the nature of sin and merit:
human life is impermanent;
those who meet must eventually part.
Their minds were opened and their intentions liberated through these various essential teachings;
they immediately resolved upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path and attained the stage of non-retrogression.
Furthermore, the Abhidharma-śāstra states:
Why is birth itself suffering?
Because it is oppressed by manifold sufferings and because it serves as the basis for other sufferings.
Furthermore, at the time of emerging from the womb, one undergoes the great suffering of the oppression of the limbs.
As for being the basis for other sufferings,
it means that various sufferings such as birth, old age, sickness, and death follow after one.
Why is old age suffering?
Because it is the suffering of transformation and decay over time.
Why is illness suffering?
Because the great elements undergo transformation and change, they are suffering.
Why is death suffering?
Because the life-force undergoes decay and destruction, it is suffering.
Why is association with the disliked suffering?
Because meeting [with them] gives rise to suffering. Why is separation from the beloved suffering? Because parting [from them] gives rise to suffering.
Because suffering arises at the time of separation from what is loved;
for what reason is not obtaining what one seeks suffering?
Because suffering arises when the sought-after result is not achieved.
Briefly summarized, for what reason are all five aggregates of clinging suffering?
It is because of the suffering of *dauṣṭhulya* (coarseness).
Furthermore, the *Saṃyukta-avadāna-sūtra* says:
In the past, there was a man of the world who entered the sea to gather treasures and encountered seven perils.
First, great winds arose simultaneously from all four directions, blowing the ship until it was overturned.
Second, the ship was about to break apart and began to leak.
Third, when a person was about to fall into water and die, he managed to reach the shore.
Fourth, two dragons came ashore, intending to devour him.
Fifth, having reached level ground, three venomous snakes pursued him, intending to devour him.
Sixth, the ground is covered with hot sand upon which one must run; this burns and sears the feet.
Seventh, looking upward, one cannot see the sun or moon; it is perpetually dark, and one does not know east from west—this is extremely difficult.
The Buddha told his disciples,
"You all likewise have seven matters.
The first is when great winds arise from the four directions."
That is to say: birth, old age, sickness, and death;
and second, the boundless craving of the six sense-faculties, which is like a boat that is overflowing.
Third, falling into water and wishing for death,
which is said to be being seized by Māra.
Fourth, the two nāgas coming ashore to devour [them].
This refers to the life-force being eclipsed by the sun and moon.
Fifth, the three poisonous snakes on level ground refers to the three poisons within the human body.
Sixth, those whose feet are scorched and blistered by hot sand refers to the fires within the hells.
Seventh, those who look upward and cannot see the sun or moon.
This refers to the place where one undergoes retribution—a realm of profound darkness and gloom from which there is no time of escape.
The Buddha spoke these words to his disciples:
"You should take note of this."
Do not associate with such people.
By diligently practicing the six matters, one may attain liberation.
Furthermore, the Nirvāṇa Sūtra says:
If non-Buddhists were to attain the Way through the ascetic practice of self-starvation,
then all animals should likewise attain the Way. Therefore,
non-Buddhists undergo the method of self-starvation.
They threw themselves into deep abysses and rushed into fires;
they leaped from high cliffs and constantly stood on one leg.
They scorch their bodies with the five fires of heat;
they constantly lie upon ashes, soil, thorns, wooden stakes, tree leaves, coarse grass, or cow dung;
and they wear coarse garments of hemp, rags from dust heaps, woolen blankets, or *kambala* cloths.
They eat vegetables, fruits, lotus roots, and the dregs of oil.
When going on almsrounds, they limit themselves to a single household;
if the host says there is nothing, they immediately depart.
Even if called back, he would never look behind him;
he abstained from salt, meat, and the five pungent roots,
and constantly consumed filtered molasses and boiling decoctions.
To claim that these can serve as causes for unsurpassed liberation is impossible;
for one does not see any bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing such dharmas who attains liberation.
Therefore, one must first discipline the mind;
it is not by excessively tormenting the body that one attains the fruit of the Way.
Furthermore, the *Xiuxing daodi jing* (Sutra on the Stages of Cultivating the Path) says:
It is like a small child who catches a sparrow and holds it so as to distress it;
he then ties it with a long thread and releases it to fly away,
thinking to himself that it has escaped.
No longer encountering misfortune,
they went to the trees and ponds to drink as they pleased, living in peace and security.
When the thread was exhausted, they were pulled back and subjected to torment and suffering as they were handled and toyed with.
It is just as it was originally, without difference;
one practices in this manner and reflects within oneself, saying:
"Even if one reaches the Brahma Heaven, one must return to the Desire Realm to suffer as before.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Just as a sparrow with its feet bound by a cord, Soars briefly until the string is spent and is pulled back again."
Practicing such cessation, one dwells in the Brahma-heaven; continuing in practice within the desire realm, one does not depart from the dharma of suffering.

Section Six: The Realm of Worms (67). Section Six: The Realm of Worms. As stated in the *Dhyānaguhya-uttama-sūtra*:
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when a practitioner enters meditative concentration,
if the wind of sensual desire arises from thoughts of longing, [it must be counteracted].
The four hundred and four channels,
from the eyes to the body-faculty,
all tremble simultaneously.
The various sense-faculties are obstructed, causing the wind of the mind to stir and drive the mind into madness.
Consequently, one becomes possessed by mad spirits and demons,
thinking of sensual desires day and night as if putting out a fire on one's head.
One should treat this with urgency.
As for the method of treatment,
one instructs this practitioner to contemplate the womb.
The fetal receptacle is located below the stomach and above the large intestine;
it consists of ninety-nine layers of membranes, resembling the bladder of a dead pig.
The four hundred and four channels originate from the womb,
like the roots of a tree;
they spread throughout the various sense organs like a bag filled with excrement.
It has one thousand nine hundred joints resembling the leaves of a plantain tree.
It is surrounded on all sides by eighty families of worms, as well as four hundred and four channels and the womb,
which is like the small intestine of a horse.
The birth canal extends as far as the shape of a bracelet on the forearm;
it is circular in circumference and size, rounded at the top and tapering to a point at the bottom,
resembling the teeth of a shell.
There are ninety-nine layers.
Between each layer there are four hundred and four worms,
and each worm has twelve heads.
When twelve people drink water,
the essence of the water enters their channels and spreads throughout the various worms;
it reaches the crown of the *vīra* worm and proceeds directly to the birth canal.
Every half-month, impure water issues forth,
and various worms each vomit it up like putrid pus,
which enters the mouths of ninety kinds of worms.
From within the twelve worms and six apertures, there issues forth a liquid like spoiled crimson dye.
Furthermore, there are various worms smaller than an autumn hair that frolic therein.
Due to the evil karmic offenses of these men in their past lives,
four hundred and four channels spread from the eye-organ to the four limbs,
flowing through the various intestines to the area below the stomach (āmāśaya) and above the large intestine (pakvāśaya).
On both sides of the vessels of the lungs, spleen,
and kidneys, there are sixty-four worms each;
each has twelve heads and twelve mouths.
They are entwined and adhered to one another like finger-rings;
they contain blue pus as thick as wild boar semen,
foul-smelling and immense, even reaching into the private parts.
It branches into three parts;
the two upper groups of nine are like the leaves of a plantain tree,
containing twelve hundred channels.
Within each and every vessel, wind-insects are produced;
they are as fine as the down of an autumn hair and resemble the beaks of the *vilanda* bird.

Among the various worms, there is the *jinse* (sinew-colored) worm; this worm’s body resembles a chopstick, it supports the womb, can move the various vessels, and absorbs the essence as it enters and exits. There are seventy-eight thousand male worms, which are blue-white, and female worms, which are red-brown, all of which entwine one another.
Its appearance is like a stack of rings, resembling the eyes of the *gośīrṣa* bird;
ninety-eight channels surge upward from the heart to the crown of the head.
All men [possess this].

the wind moves the faculty of the mind.

Eighty types of worms simultaneously open their mouths;
pus issues from the eyes and flows into the various channels,
until the very tops of the worms tremble and collapse.
The madman, being unaware,

and these are the tears of various worms.
The female essence is yellowish-red;
it consists of various worms and pus,
a dharma cultivated as perfumed by the ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*).
The eighty types of worms and the movements of earth, water, fire, and wind all proceed from this.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

Those who seek liberation and wish to transcend the suffering of the world should study this Dharma,

Even down to the various large and small insects within the female and male sexual organs and other parts of the body,
they open their mouths, prick up their ears,

Turn the hand over and place it at the edge of the left knee.

Having seen these things,

like the appearance of a *śarabhaṇḍala* ghost from hell;

Do you know now?

If one takes this medicine, one is a great man,

They are exempt from the mud of desire;

nor are they afflicted or harmed by the inauspicious, illusory forms of seductive demons.

yet their body is as fragrant and pure as the *utpala* flower,
surpassing anything achieved by human beings, fragrant elephants, dragon kings, powerful warriors, or Maheśvara.
A man of great power, revered by devas and humans.

Furthermore, the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states:

He observes the body in its entirety, from head to foot,

Observe within the skull that there are naturally moving worms called "brain-walkers."

whether moving or stationary,

Furthermore, there are various worms that dwell within the skull;

Furthermore, by means of the wisdom derived from hearing:

When they circulate within the blood, they cause the body to become coarse and rough,
stiff, numb, and devoid of sensation.
If the *dhyānāndumāraka* worms circulate within the blood, [the same occurs].
Sometimes they are in the nose,
and sometimes in the mouth,
causing both the mouth and nose to become utterly foul-smelling.
If those red worms give rise to anger and move within the blood,
they can cause sores to form in a person's throat.
If the *rasaja-kṛmi* (juice-insect) gives rise to anger while circulating within the blood,
it causes the person's body to suffer from a bluish wasting disease,
or a blackish or yellowish wasting disease.
If the *roma-kīṭa* (hair-insect) gives rise to anger,
it circulates within the blood and causes the onset of illness and suffering,
such as sores, scabs, erysipelas, leprosy, and cracked skin.
If there are blood-worms of anger,
because of their hatred they circulate within the blood and may cause diseases such as jaundice.
Women have red secretions;
their bodies itch, and they suffer from scabies, sores, and festering pus.
If blood-eating insects become enraged, they give rise to illness and affliction.
The head spins and turns;
sores arise within the throat and in the mouth;
sores arise at the lower gate.
If the *gaveṣa* worms circulate within the blood, one will fall ill;
becoming emaciated and utterly exhausted, one has no desire for food or drink.
If the *ācva* worms become enraged, [the same occurs].
It also causes that person to contract such a disease.
Furthermore, one observes ten kinds of worms moving within the *dhātus*. What are these ten?
The first is named the ulcer-producing worm;
the second is named the piercing worm;
the third is named the muscle-constricting worm.
The fourth is named the moving-bloodworm;
the fifth is named the skin-eating worm;
the sixth is named the fat-moving worm.
The seventh is named the *saṃghāta* worm;
the eighth is named the *pūtika* worm;
the ninth is named the *saṃsvedaja* worm.
The tenth is named the "Heat-Worm.
This is known either through the wisdom derived from hearing or by means of the divine eye.
One sees worms at the ulcer,
or at the site of the ulcer,
with various worms surrounding and devouring this ulcer.
Or sores may arise in the throat;
or one may see thorny insects.
If anger arises, it causes diarrhea in the person.
It is as if one were being burned by fire;
the mouth becomes parched and food and drink are not digested.
When a person is afflicted by grief and distress, these worms rejoice.
They bite the blood vessels of people to cause decline and affliction;
or they cause red blood to flow downward,
or indigestion and diarrhea.
Alternatively, one may see the *bandhanaka* worms moving through the coarse sinews or the fine sinews;
if one perceives the movement of these worms within the sinews, it causes pain.
If one is unaware of the movement of the sinews, they do not ache;
yet all the flesh and bones likewise wither away, while pain persists within the sinews.
If the worms become enraged, the person is unable to eat.
If they dwell within the sinews and drink human blood, they cause people to lose their strength;
if they eat human flesh, they cause people to become emaciated.
Or one may see the *dhamanī-kṛmi* (vein-worms).
This worm circulates throughout all the channels;
its body is so subtle that it moves without obstruction.
If the worm dwells within the food-carrying channels of a person, it causes the affliction of disease.
It causes the body to become parched and one to have no desire for food or drink.
If the worms reside within the water-vessels (*jaladhātu*),
then illness arises that causes the mouth to become dry.
If it enters the sweat-vessels,
it causes all the pores of the body to be without perspiration;
if it enters the urine-vessels, it causes the disease of dysuria.
It may cause the semen to be corrupted,
or it may cause suffering;
if the worm is provoked by anger, it moves through the lower orifice.
It causes the person's bowels to become obstructed and impassable,
leading to such suffering that they are on the verge of death;
or they may see "skin-eating worms."
Because of excessive eating, the worms become enraged;
this causes a person's facial complexion to become ugly or leads to the growth of malignant sores.
It may cause itching, or redness, or yellowness, or sores;
it may also cause the falling out of one's hair and nails,
and bring about loathsome diseases in people.
Either the skin is torn and damaged,
or the flesh is putrid and decayed,
or one sees the moving fat-worms.
It resides within the fatty vessels inside the body.
It arises when food is consumed in excess or when one sleeps too much.
This worm becomes angry and prevents the digestion of food and drink;
it may cause scabies or eruptions,
or produce malignant swellings and diseases of the hair follicles.
Some may develop goiters or tumors;
some may suffer from swollen veins;
others may contract the disease of emaciation.
Either the body emits a foul odor,
or one perspires while eating,
or one sees two kinds of insects gathering upon the body.
First is the conscious body;
second is the unconscious body, consisting of skin,
flesh, blood, and so forth.
This is called the conscious body.
Hair, nails, teeth, and so forth are called the unconscious body.
Because of overeating, the worms lose their strength,
and the person likewise loses their strength.
One cannot move swiftly back and forth;
one is drowsy and lethargic,
or suffers from excessive heat and thirst.
The skin, flesh, bones, blood, marrow, and vital essence are diminished;
or one sees stinking insects dwelling within the flesh and amidst the excrement and urine.
Because of overeating, the worms become enraged; the flesh of the body,
excrement, urine, saliva, and nasal mucus all become foul-smelling,
and putrid pus flows from within the nostrils.
Or their tears may become putrid and foul-smelling;
wherever the insects crawl, everything becomes utterly stinking and filthy,
whether it be their clothing or their bedding.
If food remains stuck between the teeth,
because of the stench of the worms, the food also becomes foul-smelling,
and even the clothing and bedding become entirely malodorous.
There is much white plaque upon the tongue, foul and filthy;
the body's impurities are likewise malodorous;
or one may see moisture-walking insects.
It travels through the flesh of the back;
once it knows the food has been digested, it enters the three apertures of the waist and takes up human excrement.
The liquid becomes urine;
the dregs become feces,
which are made to enter the lower gate.
Furthermore, the practitioner of contemplation observes the body within the body by following its course.
He contemplates ten kinds of worms moving within the sense organs;
all human bodies emerge from these.
What are the ten? First is the *kṣudrakṣudraka* worm;
second is the *tanutanuka* worm.
The third is named the Vermilion Flower Insect;
the fourth is named the Great Deceitful Insect;
the fifth is named the Black Insect.
Sixth is the worm named Great-Eater;
seventh is the worm named Warm-Mover;
eighth is the worm named Heat-Producer.
The ninth is named Fire-Worm;
the tenth is named Great Fire-Worm.
These various worms dwell within the yellow matter of the *dhātu*.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye,
he sees the *gṛhīta* worms.
Because of overeating, these worms become angry;
they feed on the eyelashes of humans, causing the eyes to itch and producing an abundance of discharge and tears.
If these minute worms move within the eyes, the eyes will become afflicted with many diseases,
or even cause the eyes to be destroyed.
If it enters the pupil, white spots appear in the eye;
these worms are red in color.
If the worms are not provoked to anger, this disease does not occur.
Or one may see a withered insect dwelling within a person's body, moving amidst the aggregates (skandhas),
its yellowish excrement covering the body.
If it enters into the bones, it causes a steaming heat within the person.
If it moves within the skin, there is constant heat day and night, and both hands and feet are hot.
If it enters between the layers of the skin, the body then perspires.
Or one may see insects with sharp beaks and short legs,
their bodies like repositories of fire, moving or dwelling within the shadows of the sprouts and flowers.
They have no desire for food or drink;
wherever they go, they are scorched and boiled by great heat.
Their bodily blood increases, and their bodies are steaming with feverish heat.
If the worms move in their proper direction, these ailments do not occur.
Alternatively, one may see the Great Deceit Worm,
which dwells within the body and moves through the yellow channels.
Whether in a state of well-being or ill-health,
because of excessive eating, the worms become enraged;
they move from the crown of the head to the feet without obstruction.
It causes all the warm blood within the body to produce hot sores;
whether as blood or as pus,
it flows out from the mouth and the ears.
If the worm does not become angry, this disease will not occur.
Alternatively, one may see black worms residing within the body, moving through the yellow channels.
Whether it be settled or unsettled,
because of excessive eating, the worms become enraged, causing the person's face to wrinkle or giving rise to many dark spots.
Some are black, some yellow, or some red;
some cause the body to smell foul,
while others cause the eyes to become inflamed.
Alternatively, sores may arise in the mouth,
or sores may arise at the openings of the large and small intestines;
if the worms do not become angry, these ailments will not occur.
Or one may see the "Great-Eating" worm;
because of excessive eating, it gives rise to anger and dwells within the yellow constituent (pīta-dhātu),
consuming and digesting as it goes along.
If the worms do not become angry, this disease does not occur.
Alternatively, one may observe "warmth-moving" worms that always crave warm food and loathe cold food.
If I eat cold insects,
my mouth produces much saliva due to anger,
and I become either indolent or drowsy.
Either the mind is clouded and dull,
or the body is aching and stiff,
or again, there is excessive nasal discharge.
Or there may be excessive salivation,
or diseases of the throat;
if the worms do not become angry, these ailments will not occur.
Or one may see "hot insects" dwelling within the human body;
due to dietary excesses, the impurities of disease increase.
It obstructs the inhalation and exhalation, causing the body to become coarse and large;
or it causes the throat to become constricted, making both urine and feces entirely white in color,
and one no longer craves cold things.
It does not delight in bland food.
Or it is seen as the fire-worm (*khadyota*),
which dwells within the body, moving about among the aggregates (*skandha*).
This worm rejoices when it is cold and withers and weakens when it is hot; because it rejoices in the cold,
[it is called "Joyful"].
Humans, however, remember food;
when it is hot, their fire increases and they have no desire for food,
whereas in the cold of winter they do.
In coolness, it is refreshing;
when hot, the coolness manifests.
Or one may see fire-insects.
If a person’s nature is not accustomed to a certain food and they force themselves to eat it,
the worms within become enraged due to this overeating;
they devour the internal organs, causing the person’s intestines to ache.
Alternatively, there may be pain in the hands and feet;
wherever the parasites reside within the food, all those areas will ache.
If the parasites are not provoked to anger, there will be no such symptoms as described above.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body by means of the wisdom derived from hearing.
Alternatively, by means of the divine eye,
one observes ten kinds of worms within the bones. What are these ten?
The first is named the *cīgu* worm;
the second is named the bone-biting worm (*asthibhakṣaka*);
the third is named the joint-severing worm (*parvavicchedaka*).
The fourth is named the red-mouthed stinking worm;
the fifth is named the putrid worm;
the sixth is named the red-mouthed worm.
Seventh is the *pāṭhama* worm;
eighth is the skin-eating worm;
ninth is the wind-blade worm.
The tenth is named the Sword-Mouth Worm (*kṣuramukha*).
These ten types of worms move within the bones;
their ways are contrary to one's nature and they damage the body, such that they cannot be described in full detail.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body by means of the wisdom derived from hearing.
Or, by means of the divine eye,
one sees ten kinds of worms moving within the urine.
What are the ten? First is the "birth-worm" (jāti-kṛmi);
second is the "needle-mouthed worm" (sūcīmukha-kṛmi).
Third, the Three-Jointed Worm;
fourth, the Footless Worm;
fifth, the Juice-Discharging Worm.
Sixth is the *trikaṭuka* worm;
seventh is the *antra-bhedin* worm;
eighth is the *saṃvṛta* worm.
The ninth is named the Good-Color Worm;
the tenth is named the Foul-Orifice-Wound Worm.
Its color is loathsome, and it dwells within excrement and filth.
These ten kinds of worms,
if provoked by contrary natures or anger, also harm the human body;
this is fully detailed in the scriptural text.
It cannot be described in full detail.
Furthermore, the practitioner contemplates the body within the body.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing or with the divine eye,
he sees ten kinds of worms moving within the marrow.
Within the essence of the moving worms,
what are the ten? The first is named the Hair-Worm (roma-kīṭa).
The second is named Black-Mouth Worm;
the third is named Powerless Worm;
the fourth is named Great-Pain Worm.
The fifth is named the *kṛmi-udvega* (distress-worm);
the sixth is named the *agni-kṛmi* (fire-worm);
the seventh is named the *snigdha-kṛmi* (smoothness-worm).
The eighth is named the Downward-Flowing Worm;
the ninth is named the Body-Faculty-Arising Worm;
the tenth is named the Mindful-Joyful Worm.
These ten types of worms,
if they act contrary to their nature and become angry, will likewise harm the human body,
as explained in detail in the sutras.
It cannot be described in full.
Section Seven: The Hell Section. Seventh, as stated in the *Jièzuòbàoyìngjiàohuàdìyùjīng* (Sūtra on Teaching and Transforming Hells According to the Retribution of Karmic Offenses):
At that time, the Bodhisattva Śraddhālinga, acting as an initiator for the sake of all sentient beings, addressed the Buddha, saying:
World-Honored One,
there are currently sentient beings undergoing retribution who are being crushed by mortars and having their bodies hacked to pieces by various hell-wardens.
From head to foot, and even unto the crown of the head,
he had finished cutting them all away.
The skillful wind blew him back to life, yet he was cut down again.
What sin caused this?
The Buddha said:

In a previous life, because he sat in disbelief toward the Triple Gem, was unfilial to his parents, and was a butcher or executioner who slaughtered and dismembered sentient beings, he incurred this retribution.
Second, there are further sentient beings.
The body becomes withered and shriveled, the eyebrows and beard fall out, and the entire frame festers and rots.
It becomes a place where birds perch and deer lodge, forever severed from human tracks;
it defiles one's kin, and people take no pleasure in seeing it.
"It is called leprosy.
By what offense was this caused?
The Buddha said:
In a previous life, he sat in disbelief toward the Triple Gem,
was unfilial toward his parents,
and destroyed stupas and monasteries.
They plunder and strip those who follow the Path;
they hack and shoot at the worthy and holy;
they injure and harm their teachers and elders.
They are constantly devoid of reciprocity;
they turn their backs on kindness and forget righteousness,
always acting with mere expediency.
He transgressed the bounds of propriety between the noble and the humble, showing no sense of restraint or shame; therefore,
he has incurred this retribution.
Third, there are further sentient beings whose bodies are large and who are deaf and mute; having no feet, they crawl on their bellies,
subsisting on nothing but eating earth to sustain their lives.
They are devoured by various small insects,
constantly enduring this unbearable suffering.
What offense has caused this?
The Buddha said,
"In a previous life, when he was a human being,
he was self-opinionated and did not believe the good words and virtuous speech [of others]."
They are unfilial toward their parents and rebellious toward their sovereign.
Whether they serve as emperors, chief ministers, governors of the four frontiers, regional lords, or officials such as magistrates, district heads, or military inspectors, they act in this manner.
Relying on their power and influence, they encroach upon and seize the property of the people;
acting without any sense of propriety, they cause the people to wither and waste away as they go about their business, sighing in lamentation.
Therefore, they incur this retribution.
Fourth, there are further sentient beings whose two eyes are blind and sightless, seeing nothing at all.
Some strike against trees;
others fall into ditches and pits.
Having died at that time, they receive another body once again in this very same manner.
"By what offense was this caused?
The Buddha said,
"In a previous life, you sat [in judgment] without believing in the retribution of sin and merit."
It obstructs the Buddha’s radiance,
sews shut the eyes of hawks,
and cages and binds sentient beings.
Because his head was contained within a leather bag, he could not see; therefore,
he incurred this punishment.
Fifth, there are further sentient beings who are stammering,
mute, or unable to speak; if they have something to say,
they close their eyes and raise their hands, yet cannot finish speaking.
"By what offense was this caused?
The Buddha said,
"In a previous life, he sat in slander against the Triple Gem."
They disparage the Noble Path,
discuss the merits and faults of others,
and seek out the shortcomings of others.
He falsely accused the virtuous and harbored hatred and envy toward the worthy; therefore,
he has incurred this retribution.
The sixth [type of being] further has a large abdomen and a thin neck, such that they cannot swallow food;
whatever they do eat turns into pus and blood.
"By what offense was this caused?
The Buddha said,
"In a previous life, he stole the food of the Sangha."
Or they may secretly steal and eat from the merit-food provided at great assemblies;
they are stingy with their own possessions yet covet the wealth of others,
constantly harboring evil intentions and administering poison to people.
Because their breath was obstructed,
they incurred this transgression.
Seventh, there are again sentient beings.
They are constantly subjected to being driven by hell-wardens with glowing iron nails through the joints of their hundred bones;
once the nails have been driven in, fire spontaneously arises,
burning their bodies until they are completely scorched and rotten.
"By what offense was this caused?
The Buddha said,
"In a previous life, while serving as a physician of acupuncture and moxibustion, he performed treatments on people's bodies but was unable to cure their illnesses."
Deceiving others to take their wealth leads only to the experience of suffering and pain;
because one causes others distress,
one incurs this retribution.

Eighth, there are furthermore sentient beings who constantly dwell within boiling cauldrons, where the ox-head *ābhangas* impale them with three-pronged iron forks and thrust them into the boiling cauldrons to cook them until they are disintegrated.
"He was blown back to life and then boiled again.
What karma caused this?
The Buddha said:
In a previous life, they believed in heterodox and inverted views,
performing sacrifices to spirits and deities by slaughtering sentient beings—
scalding them with boiling water, plucking their feathers, and cooking them in cauldrons of boiling brine.
It is immeasurable; therefore, they incur this transgression.
Ninth, there are furthermore sentient beings.
They constantly dwell within a city of fire where glowing embers reach their hearts; all four gates stand wide open,
yet whenever they wish to approach a gate,
the gate immediately closes.
They ran hither and thither, unable to escape, and were utterly consumed by the fire.
"By what karma was this brought about? [the beings asked].
The Buddha said:
In a previous life, while sitting by a fire that burned mountains and marshes, they roasted chickens and boiled sentient beings, causing their bodies to rot and their skin to be flayed;
therefore, they have incurred this retribution.
Tenth, there are further sentient beings.
"Constantly dwelling amidst the snowy mountains, blown by cold winds that peel away his skin and flesh, he seeks death but cannot find it.
By what sin has this been brought about?
The Buddha said:
In a previous life, while sitting by the side of the road, he committed robbery and stripped people of their clothing,
causing others to die of cold during the winter months.
He also flayed living cattle and sheep, inflicting unbearable pain upon them.
Therefore, they incur this retribution.
Eleventh, there are further sentient beings who constantly dwell atop mountains of blades and trees of swords.
"If whatever one grasps immediately cuts and wounds the limbs and joints, severing and destroying them,
by what offense is this caused?
The Buddha said:
In a previous life, he made his livelihood as a butcher,
slaughtering and harming sentient beings by cutting,
carving, flaying, and tearing them apart.
Flesh and bone were separated;
head and feet were scattered about,
suspended from high racks.
They sell them by weight,
or else they hang living beings up,
causing them to endure unbearable suffering.
Therefore, they incur this retribution.
Twelfth, there are further sentient beings who are deficient in their five sense faculties.
"By what offense was this caused?
The Buddha said,
"In a previous life, he sat idly watching hawks fly and dogs run as they shot and speared birds and beasts."
Some have their heads severed;
some have their feet severed;
others have the wings of birds grown upon them.
Therefore, they incur this retribution. Thirteenth,
there are further sentient beings who are born twin-legged,
with crippled backs, hunched waists and hips that do not move in coordination, lame feet, and constricted hands, such that they are unable to grasp or travel.
"By what offense was this caused?
The Buddha said,
"In a previous life, while walking along a path through the wild fields of others, you sat upon a wooden stake that had been driven into the ground."
Some set up bird-nets and lay out snares and pits to trap and fell sentient beings.
Their heads were shattered and their legs broken;
the injuries sustained were manifold,
and thus they incurred this retribution.
Fourteenth, there are furthermore sentient beings who are constantly shackled by the wardens of hell, unable to escape.
By what offense is this brought about?
The Buddha said,
"In a previous life, you sat by a net catching sentient beings and imprisoned humans and livestock in cages."
Stricken by hunger, poverty, and suffering,
some act as lords, officials, or magistrates,
greedily seizing wealth and money while unjustly imprisoning the virtuous and good.
The cruel and vast heavens do not permit one to follow their own desires; therefore,
this retribution has been incurred.
Fifteenth, furthermore, there are sentient beings who are either dazed or insane,
or deluded or idiotic.
"He cannot distinguish between the beautiful and the ugly.
What sin has caused this?
The Buddha said:
In a previous life, while sitting and drinking alcohol, he became intoxicated and confused, committing thirty-six transgressions.
Furthermore, his deluded body was like that of a drunkard;
he did not recognize the honorable from the lowly, nor could he distinguish between the beautiful and the ugly.
Therefore, they incur this retribution.
Sixteenth, there are further sentient beings whose bodies are extremely small while their private organs are exceedingly large.
When he attempts to pull it away, his own skin is drawn along with it;
whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, it acts as an obstruction.
What sin has caused this?
The Buddha said:
"In a previous life, while engaged in trade, he sat selling living beings;
he praised his own goods while disparaging the wealth of others."
They deceive people by manipulating the scales with a rattle and a counterweight, cheating them from both ends;
therefore, they incur this retribution.
Seventeenth, there are further sentient beings who...
"If one lacks the male organ and becomes a eunuch, unable to marry a wife,
what offense has caused this?
The Buddha said:
In a previous life, because he sat upon elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, pigs, and dogs that died and then revived,
he has incurred this retribution. Eighteenth, there are further sentient beings who,
from birth until old age, have no sons and remain solitary and alone.
"By what offense was this caused?
The Buddha said,
"In a previous life, you were violent and wicked toward others and did not believe in the retribution of sin and merit."
At the time when various birds were laying their eggs, he would carry vessels with him and,
following the banks of large bodies of water, search for and collect the eggs and shells of swans, cranes, parrots, geese, and wild ducks;
he would then carry them back home, boil them, and eat them.
Various birds, having lost their young, wail with such piercing cries that blood flows from their eyes;
thus they incur this retribution.
Nineteenth, there are further sentient beings who have been orphaned and destitute since childhood.
Having no parents or brothers,
they serve as laborers for others,
sustaining their lives through bitter toil.
Having grown up and reached adulthood,
they were caught in calamities and misfortunes,
and bound by the local authorities.
Imprisoned in a dungeon,
with no one to bring him food,
he suffers from hunger, destitution, and misery.
"There is no one to whom he can appeal.
What offense has caused this?
The Buddha said:
In a previous life, he delighted in capturing and seizing eagles, vultures, hawks, falcons, bears, brown bears, tigers, and leopards, keeping them in captivity with shackles and chains,
thereby severing these sentient beings from their parents, siblings, and kin.
They are constantly filled with grief and sorrow, their lamentations piercing and rending;
their pathos moves the hearts of men, yet they are unable to provide for them.
They suffer perpetually from hunger, their bones standing out as skin and flesh cling together.
Seeking death, they cannot find it;
thus they incur this transgression.
Twenty: furthermore, there are sentient beings.
Its form was exceedingly ugly;
its body was black as lacquer,
and its two eyes were blue.
The cheeks were both swollen and protruding;
the face was pockmarked and the nose flat;
the two eyes were yellowish-red.
Teeth are sparse and missing;
breath is foul and rancid;
one is short of stature and corpulent.
The belly is large and protruding, the hips are prominent;
the legs are further twisted and crooked,
the spine is hunched, and the ribs are distorted.
Wasting away of clothing, body, and food;
malignant sores with pus and blood;
dropsy and consumption.
Scabies, leprosy, carbuncles,
and various other evils will all gather upon their bodies.
Although they may be close to others, people will hold them in no regard;
if others commit sins, they will be falsely implicated in the calamity and shall never see the Buddha.
They shall never hear the Dharma and never recognize the Sangha.
What sin has caused this?
The Buddha said: "In a previous life, when I was a son, I was unfilial toward my parents;
when I was a minister, I was disloyal to my sovereign;
and when I was a ruler, I was disrespectful toward my subordinates."
Friends do not prize his trustworthiness;
his local community does not respect him for his seniority;
the court does not honor him for his rank.
Deceitfully practicing guile,
their minds are inverted and lack all measure;
they do not believe in the Triple Gem.
They assassinate their sovereign and harm their teachers;
they invade states and plunder the people;
they besiege cities and destroy watchtowers.
The evil karmas of theft, pilfering, and robbery are manifold;
they exalt themselves while disparaging others,
and they oppress the solitary and the elderly.
Slandering the noble and holy, showing contempt for elders and superiors,
and deceiving those of low station—
all such sinful karmas.
They have committed them all; as the retribution for the accumulation of manifold evils,
they have thus incurred this punishment.
At that time, all the sentient beings undergoing retribution for their offenses,
hearing the Buddha speak thus, wailed with grief,
causing the earth to tremble.
Tears fell like rain,
and he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will remain for a long time to preach the Dharma."
"May we and our like attain liberation.
The Buddha said,
"If I were to remain for a long time..."
Those of meager virtue do not plant roots of goodness;
they think, "I shall always exist," and fail to contemplate impermanence. Good son!
For example, when an infant’s mother is always by its side, it does not conceive the thought that she is difficult to encounter;
however, if the mother departs, the child immediately gives rise to a heart of longing and yearning.
Only when the mother returns does it feel joy.
Good son, I am now likewise thus: I know the good and evil karmic conditions of all sentient beings and how they receive retributions, whether beautiful or ugly.
Therefore, he attained parinirvāṇa.
At that time, the World-Honored One [acted] for the sake of these sentient beings undergoing retribution.
And he spoke in verse:
"The flow of water is not ever full; A blazing fire does not burn for long;
The sun sets in an instant; The moon, though full, wanes once more."
Those who are honored, illustrious, and noble—impermanence exceeds even this.
One should reflect thus and diligently apply oneself with vigor; one should prostrate to the Unsurpassed Honored One.
Furthermore, the *Old Miscellaneous Parable Sūtra* (*Jiu za piyu jing*) says:
In the past, there were six people who committed offenses as companions;
