it is as when a certain brāhmaṇa said:
"All things that exist upon the entire great earth."
"It belongs to me alone.
Why? Because that king previously bestowed it upon me."
Because I lack the power,
my resources have been seized by others of different lineages;
therefore, what I take is indeed my own property.
This is not called stealing;
it is said to arise based on a mind of delusion,
just as one who commits sexual misconduct based on the three poisons [does so].
If it arises based on a mind of greed,
it may involve giving rise to a mind of lustful attachment toward sentient beings,
failing to practice according to reality, and so forth.
This is called arising based on greed.
If it arises based on a mind of hatred,
it may be directed toward another's protected means of subsistence.
It arises based on a mind of hatred; for instance,
one may commit adultery with the wife or concubine of an enemy,
or commit adultery with someone beloved by that enemy, and so forth.
This is called arising based on hatred.
As for that which arises based on a mind of delusion, some people say:

For example, there is no offense in engaging in sexual intercourse with women who work at a mill or mortar, those who prepare flowers, fruits, food, or drink, those who tend rivers, or those who work on roads; or as in the case of Prasenajit and others,
who committed sexual misconduct with their own mothers and so forth.
This is called arising based on delusion (*moha*).

Just as those who utter false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*) based on the three poisons can be understood through these three, so too are double-tongued speech (*paiśunya*), harsh speech (*pāruṣya*), and frivolous speech (*saṃbhinnapralāpa*) likewise [to be understood]. As for those arising from a mind of greed (*lobha*): [the following applies].
Arising in dependence on the fetter of greed,
a second moment of mind subsequently manifests;
this is called "arising in dependence on greed."
That which arises based on the fetter of hatred is called "arising based on hatred"; that which arises based on the fetter of delusion is [called "arising based on delusion"].
It is said that this arises based on the fetter of delusion (*moha-saṃyojana*).
One should know that greed, hatred, and false views are all likewise. Question:
Why is it not stated whether the characteristics of performing, not performing,
or non-performing exist definitively within which karmas and do not exist within others?
The answer is:
With the sole exception of sexual misconduct,
among the remaining six courses of action, all are indeterminate.
What is the meaning of this?
If it were self-made,
it would entail both the performance of action and the non-performance of action.
If one causes another to act,
there is only non-acting; there can be no acting.
Regarding sexual misconduct, there is certainly the act of doing it;
it cannot be that one does not do it. Why is this?
Because this sexual misconduct is ultimately committed by oneself and not caused to be committed by another, the Sūtra says:
"Is it possible for the offense of killing to be accomplished without physical action?
He replied, "It is."
For example, one may cause another to commit the offense of killing through speech.
Again, he asked:
"Is it possible to incur the offense of lying without performing an action of verbal karma?"
He replied: "There is.
For example, by means of bodily action, one may commit the offense of lying, which is a verbal action."
He asked again:
"Is it possible that without performing physical action or verbal action, one nevertheless accomplishes physical and verbal karma?
He replied:
There is. For example, due to the resentment of a rishi, even with a physical body belonging solely to the desire realm,
there exists within the wholesome courses of action both the manifest (*vijñapti*) and the unmanifest (*avijñapti*).
In dhyāna and the untainted (anāsrava) precepts, there is no non-informative (avijñapti) precept. Why?
Because they depend upon the mind.
The intermediate dhyāna is indeterminate.
If one performs bodily and vocal actions with a profound mind and a mind of ultimate reverence,
one accomplishes both manifest action and non-manifest action.
If one performs bodily or vocal karma with a profound mind that binds the heart,
one accomplishes both manifest action and non-manifest action; however,
this is not the case when one performs bodily or vocal karma with a mind that is neither profound nor characterized by ultimate reverence.
There is only active karma and no inactive karma. Furthermore,
if bodily or vocal karma is initiated by a mind that is not driven by deep-seated fetters (saṃyojana),
there is likewise only active karma and no inactive karma.
Regarding one who performs an action through skillful means but subsequently regrets it:
there is only the performance of the action, but no non-performance of the action.
[The questioner] asks:
Among the paths of action,
which are the preliminary attendants and which are the subsequent attendants?
The answer is:
If one initiates the means for taking life,
such as a butcher killing a sheep.
Or they purchase them with goods and take them to the slaughterhouse;
when the first stroke of the blade is applied, or the second or third.
Before the sheep's life has been severed,
all its evil karma is called its "preceding retinue";
whichever blade is brought down upon it follows accordingly.
When their life-faculty is severed,
at that very moment of thought,
whatever karma they have performed [comes to fruition].
And non-action; these are all termed the fundamental courses of action (*mūlakarmapatha*).
Following these, there is the bodily activity of performing actions.
This is called the preliminary karma of taking life.
This applies likewise to all [the other verbal misdeeds] up to frivolous speech.
It should be understood that among the remaining karmas of greed, hatred, and wrong view, there are no such preliminary stages.
At the very moment the initial thought arises, the fundamental path of action is immediately accomplished.
Furthermore, all ten unwholesome paths of action of body, speech,
and mind possess preceding and following attendants.
What is the meaning of this?
It is like a person who, having conceived the intention to take the life of one being,
subsequently takes the life of another being as well.
Just as when one desires to sacrifice to the heavens, one slaughters sentient beings and seizes the property of others,
wishing to kill those people.
He further committed adultery with his wife.
He conceived such a thought as to cause that wife to take her own life, and he further used various words of discord and strife.
He destroys their kinsmen;
there is no time when he does not speak untruths;
and he gives rise to a mind of greed toward the destruction of material things.
They then give rise to further anger toward that person;
for the sake of killing them, they produce such wrong views,
and by increasing those wrong views, they take their life.
Furthermore, he wishes to kill his wife, children, and others.
In this manner, he sequentially fulfills the ten unwholesome paths of action (*daśākuśalakarmapatha*).
Such actions as these are termed the "preliminary associates" (*pūrvamgamaparivāra*).
It should be understood that all ten unwholesome paths of action are likewise so.
Furthermore, to be apart from the wholesome paths and not practice the wholesome paths through skillful means is [unskillful],
because it lacks the fundamental basis for such skillful means.
And regarding those who are far removed from skillful means:
as for what is called "skillful means," it is like that novice monk who wishes to receive the full precepts.
He was about to proceed to the ordination platform to pay homage at the feet of the assembly of monks;
he immediately requested his preceptor to accept the three robes,
and began by making the first formal announcement (*jñapti*).
It is the same when making the second proclamation;
all are designated as the preceding retinue.
This continues from the third proclamation until the conclusion of the *karmavācanā*.
The actions performed and the non-performed actions associated with that mindfulness are all termed the fundamental paths of action (*mūlakarmapatha*).
Next, the four reliances are explained, up to the point of not abandoning them.
The wholesome bodily and vocal actions one has undertaken,
as well as non-actions—
these and all such things are collectively termed the subsequent retinue.
Question: One should explain the fruits of the ten unwholesome courses of action as well as their corresponding causes. Answer:
There are three kinds of fruits:
first, the fruit of retribution;
second, the fruit of habitual tendencies.
Third, the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*).
Each and every course of action (*karmapatha*) possesses these three kinds of fruits.
What is the meaning of this?
The ten unwholesome courses of action possess lower, middling, and superior degrees.
If one is born in the hells, this is the fruit of retribution (*vipākaphala*).
As for the fruit of habitual tendencies (*vāsanāphala*):
Descending from the hells to be born among humans,
one experiences the fruit of short life due to killing,
and the fruit of lacking the means of subsistence due to stealing.
Due to sexual misconduct, one cannot protect one’s wife;
due to lying, there is the fruit of being slandered by others;
and due to divisive speech, one’s retinue is broken apart.
Due to harsh speech, one does not hear pleasant sounds;
due to frivolous speech, one is not trusted by others;
and due to fundamental greed, the greedy mind increases.
Based on fundamental hatred, the mind of hatred increases;
based on false views, the mind of delusion increases.
All such cases are termed the fruits of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
Regarding the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*):
based on those ten types of unwholesome courses of action (*akuśalakarmapatha*),
all external objects lack power and majesty.
That is to say: the terrain being high or low;
sparrows, mice, hail, and thorns;
dust, soil, and foul odors.
There are many snakes and scorpions;
grain and fine grain are scarce;
fruits and fine fruits are scarce.
And as for the fruit of suffering—
all such [results] are called the sovereign fruit (*adhipatiphala*).
Furthermore, there is the fruit of resemblance (*niṣyandaphala*).
Just as a killer inflicts various kinds of suffering upon the sentient beings he harms, so too,
because of that suffering, he is born in the hells to undergo various kinds of suffering;
yet, after ending another's life, he may later be born among human beings.
One receives the retribution of a short life and severs the warmth of others;
consequently, all external material resources for sustenance lose their vitality.
In this way, one should understand that among all ten paths of action,
the explanations are to be applied according to their respective meanings,
such as seizing the property of others or committing sexual misconduct with the wives of others.
Although they do not produce intense suffering of oppression in others,
they destroy the mind;
for this reason, they undergo punishment.
Although one does not destroy, does not become angry, and does not speak harsh words,
because it arises from an evil mind,
one nevertheless incurs guilt.

4. Section on the Ten Wholesome Actions (Daśakuśala). Section Four: If one distinguishes according to the ten wholesome actions, as explained in the Abhidharma, within that realm of hell-beings there are only three wholesome courses of action belonging to the mental ground.
However, they are merely accomplished and do not manifest;
the same applies to the northern direction. All others possess all ten meanings.
The meaning is clear and can be understood.
As stated in the *Sūtra on the Questions of Maitreya Bodhisattva* (Maitreyaparipṛcchāsūtra-śāstra):
"This bodhisattva practices the ten unwholesome paths of action."
Through the accumulation of causes and conditions, one falls into the three evil realms;
through the accumulation of causes and conditions for practicing the ten paths of wholesome action, one is born among humans or devas.
Furthermore, these are the aforementioned ten paths of wholesome action.
Practicing in conjunction with the contemplation of wisdom,
his mind is humble and narrow;
he feels weary of the triple world.
They are far removed from great compassion because they attain realization by hearing sounds from others;
having understood the meaning through hearing sounds, they establish themselves in the Śrāvaka vehicle.
Furthermore, because these superior ten paths of pure wholesome action are realized through one's own correct awakening without hearing them from another,
and because they lack great compassion,
one penetrates the profound law of dependent origination and accomplishes the vehicle of the pratyekabuddha.
Furthermore, these are the supreme and most excellent ten paths of wholesome action;
they are pure and complete, and his mind is vast and immeasurable,
as he gives rise to compassion for all sentient beings.
Because one cultivates all aspects [of practice] to bring them to complete purity,
one thus accomplishes the Bodhisattva Vehicle.
It is asked:
What is the meaning of "paths of action" (*karmapatha*)?
The answer is:
the seven actions of body and speech constitute their essential nature (*svabhāva*).
These are called the paths of action;
the other three are associated with the mind.
Furthermore, they are that very same karma.
Because they can act as the path,
they are called "paths of action" (*karmapatha*). Question:
If the paths were identical to the actions themselves,
such that all could give rise to rebirth in hell and so forth,
why are the other three not considered courses of action (*karmapatha*)?
The answer is:
Just as with those seven types of karma,
these three are able to serve as their foundation.
Because they are associated [with the mind],
yet cannot function in the same manner as that karma,
they are not termed "paths of action" (karmapatha).
Question: All exquisite flavors, drinking alcohol, eating meat, clapping with the hands, striking others, all forms of frivolous laughter—
such evil deeds as these [are forbidden].
Why are such virtuous practices as prostrating to all, making offerings, showing respect,
and abstaining from drinking alcohol not designated as courses of action (*karmapatha*)?
The answer is:
Abstinence from drinking alcohol and so forth is solely a mental action;
it can give rise to the seven [other] actions, but is not itself a physical or vocal action.
Therefore, it is not a path of action (*karmapatha*).
If that which is performed is associated with the mind, it is also a path of action. Question:
If those very karmas that can act as a path are designated as "paths of action" (karmapatha),
then all phenomena would be called paths of action in relation to the mind.
Why, then, are only ten types of paths of action taught?
It does not mention immeasurable courses of action.
The answer is:
because they are superior and grave.
Because among all evil and wholesome actions, the ten paths of karma are the most significant, while the others are not;
therefore, they alone are designated as "immeasurable.
Furthermore, seven of these karmas are invariably and extremely grave.
The three mental [actions] are both light and heavy,
whereas drinking alcohol and so forth are not;
for this reason, only ten are designated as paths of action (karmapatha).
The non-mentioning of others is called a path of action (*karmapatha*). Question:
Regarding one who abstains from taking life...
How should the association with killing and so forth be explained?
The answer is:
there are eight types of killing.
First, one's own mind;
second, others;
third, the characteristics of sentient beings who are either fixed or unfixed.
Fourth, doubt;
fifth, the undertaking of the means to end one's life;
sixth, the actual performance.
The seventh is the characteristic of non-action;
the eighth is the characteristic of non-manifestation. These are termed the bodily karma of killing.
The actions of body, speech, and mind are called "killing.
Question: For what reason is it called "intentional"?
The answer is:
If the offense of killing were incurred without intentional thought,
then Arhats would not attain nirvana.
Since Arhats have severed the causes of the mundane world,
even if they were to kill sentient beings without intending it,
they should likewise be reborn in the mundane world.
But in reality this is not so.
For this reason, one who kills without intentional thought does not incur the retribution of sin.
Question: For what reason is it called "other"? Answer:
Because it is not one's own life-force.
If there is another person who is subject to being killed,
the one capable of killing that person incurs the offense of taking life.
Because one who commits suicide lacks an object to be killed,
they do not incur an evil retribution for taking their own life.
Furthermore, when an Arhat destroys his own body...
Because he has taken his own life, he incurs no fault.
Why is this? Because he has already abandoned thoughts of hatred and the like.
In this case, one who commits suicide does not incur the karmic offense of killing. Question:
What is meant by the characteristics of sentient beings who are "fixed" or "unfixed"?
The answer is:
To determine the characteristic of a sentient being is,
for example, when a hundred thousand people form the intention within their minds to kill a particular person among them.
This constitutes the offense of killing.
If one kills another person, it does not constitute the offense of killing.
As for that which is indeterminate:
Because one has abandoned all [sentient beings], one incurs the offense of killing accordingly;
this is because in that state, the perception of sentient beings is not yet absent. Question:
Why is it called "killing with doubt"?
The answer is:
even if one kills with a doubting mind, one still incurs the offense of killing.
Because that being is also a sentient being, one incurs the sin of killing;
because one has abandoned the mind of compassion, one incurs the sin of killing. Question:
Why is it called "initiating the means of taking life"?
The answer is:
if the killer gives rise to an unwholesome mind toward that act.
To desire to take a life is not a mind of compassion;
it constitutes the preparation for killing.
This is called "arising. Question:
Why are they named the "characteristic of doing," the "characteristic of not-doing," and the "characteristic of non-doing"?
The answer is:
An agent performs an action;
that which is not an agent is designated as "action."
Their activities arise together;
although the karma performed ceases, the continuity of wholesome and neutral dharmas remains uninterrupted,
as stated in the Sūtra.
One who possesses faith practices ten kinds of meritorious deeds;
whether walking, standing, sleeping, or waking,
they constantly generate merit day and night.
[It would mean] that merit increases.
If there were no non-informative action (*avijñapti*) apart from bodily and vocal actions,
how could it increase as something distinct from mental factors (*cittadharma*)?
Therefore, one should know that there exists an unmanifest action (avijñapti) apart from bodily and vocal karma;
furthermore, it is not produced by one's own performance, nor by causing another to perform an action.
If non-manifestation (avijñapti) did not exist, how could this be established?
If there were no dharma of non-manifestation,
it would be apart from the Prātimokṣa.
There would also be no such thing as non-informative (avijñapti) precept;
therefore, one should know that there exists the phenomenon of non-informative action.
Question: What is meant by "one who has distanced themselves from stealing"? Answer:
There are nine types of stealing:
first, that which is protected by another;
second, the perception of it as such.
Third, doubt; fourth, knowing and not following others;
fifth, the desire to seize.
Sixth, perceiving another's property and giving rise to the thought of "mine.
Seventh, the aspect of performing [an action]. Eighth, the aspect of not performing [an action].
The ninth is the characteristic of non-manifestation (*avijñapti*). These are called the bodily actions of stealing. Question:
What is meant by "protected by another"?
The answer is:
this clarifies the taking of objects protected by another.
Question: What is meant by "that perception"? Answer:
If one does not give rise to the notion of "self" and does not say,
"This is my possession," then one incurs no offense.
This is called "that perception. Question:
What is meant by "one with a doubting mind"?
The answer is:
If there is doubt in the mind as to whether it is one's own property.
Is it another's property?
Furthermore, both that object and the other person's property must be recognized.
It is asked:
What is meant by "knowing not to follow others"?
It is knowing that when another's property arises in one's mind, one follows the notion of "mine.
[The questioner] asks:
What is meant by "one who seeks to seize"?
The answer is:
one who gives rise to a mind of harm.
Question: What is meant by "arousing the thought of 'I' with respect to the property of others"? Answer:
If one perceives no difference,
or if one takes hold in the dark,
or if one takes hold too hastily.
If one takes another object,
or takes the property of another,
or takes it with the perception that it is one's own property.
Question: What are the characteristics of the performed, the unperformed, and the unmanifest? Answer:
These three are as previously explained in the section on killing. Question:
What is meant by abstaining from sexual misconduct?
The answer is:
There are eight kinds of sexual misconduct.
The first is protected women.
Second, that perception;
third, doubt; fourth, the path and what is not the path.
1. The five things that need not be guarded; 2. Unrighteousness and untimeliness; 3. Action.
The eighth is the perception of non-action.
These are called the bodily karma of sexual misconduct. Question:
What is meant by "those who protect women"?
The answer is:
so-called protection by parents and others.
Question: What is meant by "that perception"? Answer:
If one knows that the girl is protected by her parents and others,
and perceives her as being protected rather than unprotected,
it is asked:
What is meant by "one with a doubting mind"?
The answer is:
if one gives rise to a doubting mind regarding one's own daughter.
A woman who belongs to another;
a woman protected by her parents;
and a woman who is unprotected, and so forth.
Each and every one of these constitutes sexual misconduct.
It is asked:
what is meant by "the path" and "that which is not the path"?
The answer is:
The Way refers to all that constitutes the Way;
that which is not the Way is not the Way.
This refers to what is not the proper way. It is asked:
What is meant by "that which is neither the proper way nor the proper time regarding a woman who is unprotected"?
Answer: This is also called sexual misconduct. Question:
What are the characteristics of the performed, the unperformed, and the unmanifested?
The answer is:
these three are as explained in the section on killing.
However, regarding the "non-performance" aspect within this context, there is no such non-performance regarding sexual misconduct; it must be accomplished through one's own actual action.
[The questioner] asks:
What is meant by "one who has distanced themselves from false speech"?
The answer is:
there are seven kinds of false speech.
First, matters such as seeing for the first time;
second, matters of perversion and non-perversion;
third, doubt.
Fourth, the thought of concealment arises;
fifth, the performance [of the offense]; sixth, the appearance of not having performed it.
The seventh is the characteristic of non-action (*avijñapti*). These are called the verbal karmas of false speech. Question:
What are the objects of seeing and so forth?
The answer is:
they are what is seen, heard, sensed, and known.
Question: What is meant by "perverted" and "non-perverted" matters? Answer:
Regarding "perverted matters," they are as they are heard; that which is not perverted is said to be "as it actually is.
[The opponent] asks:
What is meant by one who has a doubting mind?
The answer is:
if one gives rise to doubt as to whether it is thus or not thus.
Is it invariably thus? Or is it invariably not thus?
[The questioner] asks:
What is meant by "conceiving the thought of concealment"?
The answer is:
it is to conceal the actual fact and, while abiding in a different characteristic, to speak of that which has a different characteristic.
The characteristics of performing, not performing, and non-performing [of actions] are as explained in the section on killing. Question:
How does one distance oneself from divisive speech?
The answer is:
There are seven types of divisive speech (*paiśunya*).
First, it arises from an unwholesome intention (*akuśalacitta*).
Second, they are real yet false;
third, they destroy the mind;
fourth, they first shatter the intention for harmony.
Fifth, the mark of action;
sixth, the mark of non-action;
seventh, the mark of non-manifestation.
These are called the verbal karma of divisive speech. These seven [types of verbal karma] are easy to understand, so there is no need to trouble oneself with further explanation. Question:
What is meant by "abstaining from harsh speech"?
The answer is:
There are seven kinds of harsh speech.
First, that which is based on an unwholesome intention.
Second, giving rise to a mind of affliction and disturbance;
third, relying on a disturbed mind;
fourth, speaking to others.
The five acts of commission,
the six acts of non-commission,
and the characteristic of non-manifestation (*avijñapti*); these seven are also easy to understand and need not be explained at length.
Question: What is meant by one who is far removed from frivolous speech? Answer:
Frivolous speech is of seven kinds:
first, that which is based on an unwholesome intention;
second, that which is meaningless.
Third, at an improper time;
fourth, associated with unwholesome states;
fifth, performed.
Sixth, the characteristic of non-action;
seventh, the characteristic of non-manifestation. Question:
What is meant by "based on an unwholesome intention"?
The answer is:
that which is associated with the mind of afflictions cultivated through the path of meditation in the desire realm is called frivolous speech.
Question: What is meant by "that which is meaningless"? Answer:
Because it deviates from the true meaning. Question:
What is meant by "untimely"?
The answer is:
Although speech may possess meaning, if it is spoken at an inappropriate time, it constitutes frivolous chatter (*saṃbhinnapralāpa*).
Furthermore, even if spoken at the appropriate time, if one speaks to those who are self-indulgent within a great assembly, it also constitutes frivolous chatter.
Question: What is meant by "one associated with unwholesome dharmas"? Answer:
This refers to all frivolous speech, such as improper singing and dancing,
and all that is associated with unwholesome states;
these are all idle chatter.
Regarding the characteristics of action (*kṛta*), non-action (*akṛta*), and non-manifestation (*avijñapti*):
as previously explained in the section on killing, the following passages concerning greed, hatred, and wrong view are easy to understand and need not be elaborated upon.
Furthermore, the treatise states:
As the Tathāgata said in the *Sāgaranāgarājaparipṛcchā-sūtra*:
"Nāga King, by abstaining from killing, one attains ten kinds of dharmas that are free from the heat of afflictions and are cool."
What are the ten? First, bestowing fearlessness upon all sentient beings.
Second, abiding in the state of great loving-kindness.
Third, it eliminates the afflictions, faults, and habitual tendencies;
fourth, it attains the fruit of freedom from illness;
fifth, it increases the seeds of longevity.
Sixth, they are constantly protected by non-human beings and others.
Seventh, they are peaceful and secure whether sleeping or awake.
Eighth, they do not see evil dreams and are free from a mind of resentment.
Ninth, not fearing any non-Buddhists;
tenth, being reborn in the heavens after passing away.
These are called the ten dharmas that are free from the heat of afflictions and are refreshing and cool.
Nāga King, if one does not kill living beings and dedicates those roots of goodness toward unexcelled bodhi,
that person will attain mastery of mind upon attaining bodhi.
Therefore, their lifespan is immeasurable.
Just as the Bodhisattva Dragon King, by abstaining from taking life, was able to practice giving,
he thereby attained the accomplishment of great wealth and the necessities of life.
They shall be indestructible,
attain long life,
and practice the bodhisattva conduct.
Just as one transcends all the afflictions and misfortunes of the world, O Dragon King,
so too it is with the ten paths of wholesome action.
Because it accomplishes the adornment of great benefit.
Section Five: Citing Scriptural Authority. As stated in the *Saṃyukta-ratna-piṭaka-sūtra*:
"In the past, when the Buddha was in the world..."
King Prasenajit had a daughter named Śubhā,
who was intelligent and beautiful.
The parents felt compassion for her, and the entire palace loved and revered her.
The father said to his daughter,
"It is by my power that you are loved and revered by the entire palace."
The daughter replied to her father, "I possess the power of karma; it does not depend on you, O King.
Upon hearing this, the king spoke to her with fierce indignation.
"I shall now test whether you possess the power of your own karma.
He then dispatched his attendants to seek out the lowliest and most impoverished beggar and gave his daughter as a wife to him.
The king said to the woman,
"Your own karma does not depend on mine; from this day forward,
you may verify it for yourself."
The woman replied,
"I have the power of karma.
She then went out together with the poor man.
The wife asked her husband,
"Do you have parents?
Her husband answered his wife.
"My parents were formerly the foremost elder in this city of Śrāvastī.
Now that my parents and all those living in our household have died, I have no one to rely upon; for this reason, I beg for alms."
The wife asked again,
"Do you know where that old house is located?
He replied:
Knowing the location,
as the walls and house had collapsed, leaving only an empty space,
the husband and wife went together to the old dwelling and walked about it, inspecting it thoroughly.
Wherever he went, hidden treasures spontaneously emerged.
He immediately used these precious gems to hire craftsmen to build a residence;
before a month had passed, the palace was completely finished.
His palace women, musicians, slaves, and servants were beyond counting.
The king suddenly remembered his daughter,
Sunetra, wondering, "How is she living?"
Someone answered the king:
"The wealth and palace of the maiden Suprabhā are no less than those of the king.
That very day, the king sent his daughter away with her husband.
He invited the king to his residence.
The king accepted the invitation and,
upon arriving, beheld the magnificence of the palace and its inner quarters.
Marveling at this unprecedented occurrence,
the king went to question the Buddha:
"What meritorious deeds did this girl perform in her previous lives?"
He was born into a royal family and his body possessed radiance.
The Buddha replied to the king:

The Buddha said, "There are four dharmas for a bodhisattva."
All who see him are filled with joy. What are these four?
First, anger does not arise.
1. To regard enemies as virtuous spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra).
2. To always maintain a mind of loving-kindness toward all beings.

Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva attains the supernormal powers (ṛddhipāda) to travel from one buddha-field to another.

third, seeing others practicing giving, assisting them with joy;
fourth, seeing whatever deeds the bodhisattvas perform, not engaging in slander.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas of a bodhisattva by which those who hear their speech believe and follow them, receiving and practicing it with joy.

Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva cannot be taken advantage of by Māra.

There are five practices by which one may be reborn in the heavens. What are these five?
First, with a compassionate mind, one does not kill,
showing mercy and nurturing all living beings so that the multitude may attain peace.
Second, being virtuous and upright, one does not steal the property of others.
Through generosity free from greed, one relieves all who are destitute.
Third, through purity, one refrains from sexual misconduct with men or women outside of marriage;
one guards the precepts, observes the fasts, and exerts diligence.
Fourth, one should be sincere and truthful, not deceiving others, and guard against the four faults of speech.
Fourth, one must not covet or practice deception.
Fifth, one should not drink alcohol and ensure that it does not pass through the mouth.
By practicing these five things, one attains birth in the heavens.
The Buddha told Bianyi:
"Furthermore, there are five things by which one attains birth among human beings."
What are the five? First, benefiting the poor through the moisture of generosity;
second, observing the precepts without committing the ten non-virtuous actions.
Third, practicing patience so as not to disturb the assembly or succumb to afflictions.
Fourth, exerting diligence in exhortation and transformation without any laziness.
Fifth, serving with single-minded devotion and exhausting one's loyalty.
These are the five matters by which one is born among humans as one who is wealthy, long-lived, handsome, majestic, and becomes a lord over whom all show respect and service.
The Buddha told Bianyi:
Furthermore, there are five things that cause one to enter hell upon death and remain there for billions of kalpas before emerging.
What are these five? First, not believing in the existence of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
First, they slander and disparage the Noble Path;
second, they destroy Buddhist temples and sacred shrines;
third, members of these three groups further slander one another, taking no account of their calamities or transgressions.
First, there is no mind of reverence and compliance.
Second, there are four kinds of rebelliousness, wherein there is no distinction between superior and inferior, and rulers, ministers, fathers, and sons do not accord with one another.
Third, in the future, there will be those who wish to practice the Way.
Having attained the path, they do not follow the teacher’s instructions and admonitions;
instead, they become arrogant, treat the teacher with contempt, and slander them.
These are the five matters by which one dies and enters hell, transmigrating from hell to hell without any prospect of release.
Furthermore, there are five things that cause one to fall among the hungry ghosts. What are these five?
First, being stingy and greedy, having no desire to practice giving.
Second, they commit theft and are unfilial toward their two parents.
Third, they are ignorant and dark, lacking any heart of compassion.
Fourth, they hoard wealth and refuse to provide for their own food or clothing.
Fifth, not providing for one's parents, siblings, wife, children, or servants.
These five matters cause one to fall among the hungry ghosts (*preta*).
Furthermore, there are five matters of practicing the conduct of animals that cause one to fall among the animals (*tiryagyoni*).
What are the five? First, violating the precepts by secretly committing theft;
second, owing a debt and refusing to repay it.
Third, one must repay the taking of life with one's own body.
Fourth, one does not properly listen to or receive the sūtras and the Dharma.

Fifth, one constantly uses the hardships of causal conditions as pretexts for observing fasts, maintaining precepts, and attending assemblies, thereby making worldly concerns one's primary motivation.
These are the five matters by which one is born among animals.
Furthermore, there are five matters by which one attains nobility and is honored by the multitude. What are these five?
First, the wisdom of giving is universally vast.
Second, one pays homage to the Triple Gem and the assembly of elders.
Third, one practices patience and is free from anger.
Fourth, being gentle and humble;
fifth, being widely learned in the sūtras and precepts.
These five matters enable one to become noble and respected by others.
Furthermore, there are five things that cause one to be constantly born in lowly and base circumstances as a servant or slave. What are these five?
The first is arrogance and a lack of respect.
Second, they are stubborn and defiant toward their two parents and lack a sense of reverence.
Third, they are negligent and do not pay homage to the Triple Gem.
Fourth, they engage in theft as their means of livelihood.
Fifth, fleeing one's debts without repaying them.
These five matters cause one to be constantly born among lowly slaves and servants.
Furthermore, there are five other matters by which one may be born among human beings.
One's breath will be fragrant and pure, one's body and mind will always be at peace,
one will be praised by others and not subjected to slander. What are these five?
First, to be single-mindedly sincere and not deceive others;
second, to recite the sutras without partiality toward this or that;
third, to protect the precepts and not slander the Noble Path.
Fourth, one instructs others to distance themselves from evil and turn toward the good.
Fifth, one does not seek out the faults of others.
These five matters lead to birth among human beings with fragrant and pure breath, constant peace of body and mind, praise by others, and freedom from slander.
Furthermore, there are five matters: if one is among human beings, they will constantly be slandered and loathed by others;
their physical form will be ugly and repulsive, and their mind will remain restless.
They constantly harbor fear and apprehension. What are the five?
First, they are perpetually devoid of sincerity and deceive others.
Second, when there are those preaching the Dharma among the assembly at the two great gatherings, one slanders them.
Third, upon seeing fellow students, one treats them with contempt and subjects them to trial.
Fourth, without having witnessed another's transgression, one falsely accuses them of committing an offense.
Fifth, engaging in strife and divisive speech between this side and that;
these are the five matters.
If one is among human beings, they will constantly be subject to slander.
One will be detested by others, have an ugly physical form, and experience mental and physical unease, constantly harboring fear.
Furthermore, there are five other matters regarding the places where one is born:
one will always be in the company of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha.
At first, he did not deviate from his purpose;
upon seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dharma, he conceived a virtuous mind.
If he were to become a śramaṇa, he would immediately attain his wish.
What are the five? First, to personally serve the Three Jewels and exhort others to do so.
Second, to create images of the Buddha and ensure they are fresh and clean.
Third, they constantly uphold the Buddha’s teachings and do not transgress what they have received.
Fourth, they universally love all beings with respect and equanimity, as if cherishing their own infant children.
Fifth, they recite the sutras and dharmas they have received day and night.
These are the five matters from which one’s place of birth arises;
one will always be present in the assemblies of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha,
never failing to do so from the very beginning.
Upon seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dharma, he immediately conceived a virtuous mind.
He thought that if he were to become a śramaṇa, he would surely attain his aspiration. Thereupon, the elder’s son Bianyi—
Upon hearing the Buddha explain the meaning of these fifty essential dharmas,
they were filled with joy and delight, attaining the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*).
All five hundred elders attained the pure Dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣur viśuddham*).
Furthermore, each member of the assembly attained their respective aspirations.
A verse says:
Mind and objects mutually multiply; Karmic bonds entangle and ensnare; The seven consciousnesses arise and manifest.
The eight consciousnesses act as causes and conditions; within the three realms one receives retribution.
Wandering through the six destinies, one initiates karma according to circumstances, becoming entangled wherever contact occurs.
The five aggregates bring weariness, and the nine afflictions cause distress. Were it not for the compassionate and holy ones, how could they benefit my means of liberation?
Sentient emotions are universally moistened; the faculties are awakened to the profound mystery. When extended, they benefit all things;
when withdrawn, they return to spontaneity. *Fayuan zhulin*, Scroll Sixty-eight;
*Fayuan zhulin*, Scroll Sixty-nine.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Daoshi of Ximing Monastery.
Section 79: Receiving Retribution (69–70). Section on Receiving Retribution, Number Seventy-Nine. This section consists of twelve parts:

the Part on Stating the Intent, the Part on Citing Evidence, the Part on Conception, the Part on the Intermediate State (*antarābhava*), the Part on Retribution Seen in the Present Life, the Part on Retribution Received at Birth, the Part on Retribution in Future Lives, the Part on Fixed Retribution, the Part on Indeterminate Retribution, the Part on Good Retribution, the Part on Evil Retribution, and the Part on Dwelling Places. 1. Part on Stating the Intent, Number One. Regarding the functional operation of the karma of good and evil:
This is truly a sign and omen of the three types of retribution,
as indispensable to one another as form and shadow;
it serves as a clear verification of the six realms of existence.
As for these three forms of retribution,
they serve to delight the ears and eyes of the Empress of Heaven and repay her profound grace of nine colors.
I, alone, surrendered my life to the King of Birds;
together we endured the extreme cruelty of the five sufferings.
This is the retribution manifest in this very life.
The multitudes sink in secret into the abyss of darkness;
the spirit ascends and drifts through the cycles of rebirth without ceasing.
The body endures the calamities and transgressions of successive generations.
They do not understand the principle of the Prince’s passing as a retribution for his past life; thus,
the non-Buddhists have unleashed calamity upon those in the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception who are deluded regarding the Dharma.
Perpetually deluded from beginning to end,
one becomes like a violent raccoon dog with wings;
whether soaring or diving, one encounters distress that is difficult to calculate.
This constitutes their retribution in a future life.
One who possesses profound discernment observes the currents of those in the Three Dynasties who were submerged in the loss of their integrity;
they deeply record the transformations to come and the burdens of this fragile physical form.
It causes one to awaken to the chamber of the Four Truths and the Threefold Knowledge, and leads one out of the darkness of the three retributions and five sufferings.
Part Two: Citing Testimonies. As stated in the *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra*:
The Buddha said,
"Good son, there are four kinds of karma created by sentient beings."
First is retribution in the present life: when one performs extremely good or evil deeds in this very body, one receives the fruit in that same body.
This is called retribution in the present life. Second is retribution in the next life: when one creates karma in this body, one receives the fruit in the body immediately following.
These are called the three types of retribution for birth: first, immediate retribution;
second, subsequent retribution, which refers to karma created in this life that has not yet been experienced, but will be experienced from the second or third birth onward.
This is called "retribution in a subsequent life. Fourth, there is "no retribution," such as neutral (avyākṛta) karma and so forth. This karma of no retribution further has four types:
first, that which is fixed in time but indefinite in its retribution; this is determined across three periods of time and cannot be altered.

First, because karma can be transformed, its retribution is not fixed; second, because although the retribution is fixed, the time is transformable, the timing is not fixed—yet since the power of karma is fixed, the retribution itself cannot be changed;

third, both time and retribution are fixed because the karma is fixed, and thus the time of its fruition is also fixed; fourth, both time and retribution are not fixed because the karma is not determined, and thus neither the time nor the retribution is fixed. Sentient beings' performance of karma may be complete or incomplete.
If one first forms the intention and subsequently performs the act, it is called "fulfillment through performance.
If one performs the act directly without prior intention,
it is called "non-fulfillment through performance."
Furthermore, there are those whose actions are incomplete,
meaning that although the action has been performed, its retribution is not fixed.
There are also those whose actions, once performed, are complete.
This refers to karma that, once performed, is certain to yield its retribution.
Furthermore, there is karma that, though performed, is not fully completed;
while its fruit and retribution are certain, the timing of their manifestation is uncertain.
Furthermore, there are those who have performed [the action] and are also complete [in their result],
being fixed in both time and circumstance.
There are also those who have performed [the action] but are not complete.
There are those who maintain the precepts and hold right view;
furthermore, there are those who, having performed [actions], are likewise complete [in their practice].
There are also those who violate the precepts and hold wrong views.
Furthermore, there are those who, having acted, do not fulfill [the deed], and thus give rise to regret at three times.
There are also those who, having acted, do fulfill it,
and thus feel no regret at the three times.
As it is with evil, so it is with good. Section Three:
On Entering the Womb. As stated in the *Sudarsana-vinaya*:
When a woman is about to conceive,
the menstrual fluid (puṣpa-vāri) flows out.
As for this "flower-water":
This is the name for blood.
When one is about to conceive,
a mass of blood arises at the site of the embryo.
It will break open of its own accord after seven days and emerge from there.
If the blood flows out without ceasing, [the patient will die].
The male semen does not remain;
it flows out together with [the female fluid].
If it is completely discharged, [then...]
The male seed returns to its original place,
and only then does the embryo form;
therefore, once the blood has been exhausted, the male seed can remain.
Even when there is a womb,
furthermore, there are seven conditions by which a woman conceives:
first, physical contact.
Second, taking up clothing;
third, emitting semen;
fourth, rubbing with the hands.
Fifth, seeing forms;
sixth, hearing sounds;
seventh, smelling odors.
Question: What is meant by conception through physical contact?
Answer: When a woman experiences the desire for a man during her fertile period, and the man touches her body with his own body.
That is, one conceives while being attached to desire.
Question: What is meant by "taking up clothing" and "receiving conception"?
Answer: It is as in the case of Udāyin, who went forth into homelessness together with his wife.
Their sensual desire not ceasing, they each questioned one another;
when the semen soiled her robe,
the nun took it and licked it.
Furthermore, when the internal faculties are taken up, one immediately becomes pregnant.
Question: What is meant by "the inferior semen receiving conception"?
The answer is: Just as a doe, smelling the semen of a practitioner,
drinks it with a lustful mind and subsequently becomes pregnant, giving birth to a fawn-practitioner.
Question: What is meant by "receiving conception through the hand's touch"?
Answer: It is like the case of the Bodhisattva Śyāma, whose parents were both blind;
Śakra, knowing this from afar, descended to their location.
Since husband and wife had both left the household life to practice the Way,
they were no longer subject to the union of yin and yang;
he rubbed his hand below her navel.
Even though she conceived and gave birth to the son Śyāma, [the Buddha] asked, "What is meant by 'conceiving upon seeing a form'?
He replied: "There was a woman."
Candraprabhā was unable to conceive because she lacked union with a man;
her desire was so intense that she could only gaze upon men,
just as it was with the women of the royal palace.
Even though they conceive, it is asked:
what is meant by "conceiving upon hearing a sound"?
The answer is: for example, the white heron has only females and no males.
By the time of the Spring Festival, the yang energy begins to spread and the thunder first resounds;
upon hearing this sound, the female egret conceives with single-minded focus.
Even chickens can become pregnant upon hearing the crowing of a rooster.
Question: What is meant by "conceiving through smelling the fragrance"?
Answer: It is like the mother of a Qin ox, who becomes pregnant merely by smelling the scent of her calf.
Furthermore, the *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus,
"There are three causes and conditions by which consciousness comes to enter the womb."
If the mother has desire and the father has desire, and the parents come together in one place,
yet the external consciousness does not descend to enter,
then conception does not occur.
If consciousness approaches but the parents do not unite, an embryo will not be formed.
Second, if the mother has no desire while the father’s desire is intense...
If the mother is not intensely ardent, conception does not occur.
Third, if the parents come together in one place,
but the mother’s desire is intense while the father is not intensely ardent, [conception does not occur].
Thus, conception does not occur.
Furthermore, there are three conditions:
first, if the father and mother come together in one place; [and so forth].
If the father has a wind disorder and the mother has a cold disorder,
conception will not occur.
Second, if the mother has a wind disorder and the father has a cold disorder,
conception will not take place.
Third, if the father’s body has an excess of watery humors while the mother does not have this affliction,
then conception will not occur.
Furthermore, there are three types.
First, if parents gather in one place,
the father possesses the signs for having a son, while the mother lacks the signs for having a son.
Then conception does not occur.
Second, if the mother’s physical characteristics indicate she will have a child while the father’s characteristics do not,
then conception does not occur.
Third, if both parents lack the necessary conditions for procreation,
then conception does not occur.
Furthermore, there are three other types [of cases].
First, if at the time when the consciousness and spirit enter the womb,
the father is away on a journey,
then conception does not occur.
Second, if at some time the father and mother ought to assemble in one place,
yet the mother travels far away and is not present,
then conception does not take place.
Third, when both parents have come together but this [union] does not occur, one then takes conception.
Furthermore, there are three types.
First, if at some time the parents should come together in one place.
However, if the father’s body encounters a grave illness,
and his consciousness occasionally returns to it,
then conception does not occur.
Second, if the mother’s body suffers from a grave illness, conception does not occur.
Third, if both the father and the mother’s bodies are afflicted by illness,
conception does not occur.
If the parents are free from illness and the consciousness-principle (*vijñāna*) descends,
and the parents are both physically capable of conceiving a child, then conception occurs.
Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
Furthermore, regarding the distinctions among the eight stages of this embryonic development (garbha), what are these eight?
They are as follows: the stage of kalala.
The stage of arbuda,
the stage of peśī,
and the stage of ghana.
The stage of *praśākhā* (the limbs),
the stage of hair, body hair, and nails, the stage of the sense organs (*indriya*), and the stage of physical form (*ākṛti*).
If it has already coagulated internally while remaining thin, it is called *kalala*.
If it is like curd both on the surface and within, but has not yet reached the stage of flesh, it is called *arbuda*.
If it has already become flesh yet remains extremely soft, it is called *peśī*.
When it has become firm and thick enough to be slightly touched, it is called *kaṇa*.
When this mass of flesh further increases and the characteristics of the limbs appear, it is called *praśākhā*.
From this point onward, when hair, body hair, and nails appear, that stage is so named.
From this point onward, the arising of the sense faculties such as the eye is called the stage of the faculties (*indriya-avasthā*).
From this point onward, the distinct manifestation of their respective bases is called the stage of form (*saṃsthāna-avasthā*).
Furthermore, within the womb,
either due to the power of past karma or due to winds that arise from the mother’s failure to avoid unwholesome conditions,
the hair, complexion, skin, and other limbs of this embryo undergo transformation and develop.
Regarding the transformation of the hair:
this occurs due to unwholesome and evil karma created in previous lives that brings about such a result,
as well as because the mother has frequently consumed flavors such as ash and salt.
If, through drinking or eating,
the hair and body hair within this womb become sparse and the complexion undergoes a change, [it is known as such].
This means that due to the causes of prior karma as previously described,
and due to the present conditions of the mother’s exposure to smoke and heat,
a dark and murky complexion is produced within that fetal womb.
Furthermore, if the mother habitually stays in extremely cold rooms and the like,
it causes that fetal body to become an extreme white color.
Moreover, it is due to the mother consuming excessive amounts of hot food [that this occurs].
It causes that fetal matrix to become intensely red;
as for the transformation of the skin,
this occurs due to the causes of past karma, as previously described.
Furthermore, due to the present condition of the mother’s habitual indulgence in sexual desire,
it causes that fetal development to emerge with an abnormal skin condition, such as scabies, ringworm,
or leprosy; thus, the limbs are born deformed.
This means it is due to the causes of prior karma as previously described,
as well as because the mother frequently practiced the postures of running and leaping,
and failed to avoid uneven conditions in the present circumstances.
It causes that embryo to be born with deficient sense organs and limbs.
Furthermore, if that embryo is to become a female...
He dwells leaning against the mother's right flank, with his back toward her spine and facing her abdomen if he is to be male; if he is to be female,
he dwells leaning against her left flank, with his abdomen toward her spine and facing her back.
Furthermore, when this embryo has reached full development,
the mother is unable to sustain this heavy fetus;
internal winds then arise, producing great suffering and distress.
Furthermore, this embryonic state, impelled by karmic retribution,
gives rise to the "wind of birth" which causes the head to turn downward and the feet to turn upward;
enveloped by the fetal membrane, it proceeds toward the birth canal.
When it emerges properly, the fetal membranes then tear and separate at the two armpits as it passes through the birth canal.
This is called the stage of "actual birth.
After birth, one gradually encounters the contacts pertaining to birth,
namely, eye-contact through to mind-contact.
4. The Section on the Intermediate State (antarābhava). The fourth [chapter] of the Section on the Intermediate State states, as it says in the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra*:
"There are seventeen kinds of phenomena pertaining to the intermediate state;
you should fix your mindfulness and practice the path of cessation."
Whether gods or humans, those who contemplate this path will never fear the harm inflicted by the messengers of Yama.
What are the seventeen types of intermediate existence (*antarābhava*)?
First, if one dies among humans and is reborn in the heavens,
one perceives the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) as having the appearance of bliss,
like a white woolen cloth about to fall.
It was fine, soft, white, and pure;
furthermore, he saw gardens and flowering ponds,
and heard the sounds of singing, dancing, and laughter.
Next, they smell various fragrances;
they experience all manner of pleasures from immeasurable kinds of objects,
combined with subtle tactile sensations.
He was immediately reborn in the heavens;
by virtue of his wholesome karma, he presently experienced celestial bliss,
smiling with joyful serenity and a pure countenance.
His kinsmen and brothers wept and wailed with grief; yet,
because of his auspicious marks, they neither heard nor saw him,
nor did their minds even take notice of him.
At the time of death, one will first be born in a happy realm;
a celestial body, resembling a seal impression, will form,
and upon seeing the superior abodes of the devas, one will immediately give rise to a state of craving for that object.
Therefore, one receives a celestial body;
this is called the first intermediate existence (*antarābhava*).
As for the second intermediate existence:
If a person from Jambudvīpa,
at the end of their life, is reborn in Uttarakuru,
they will see the lovely color of fine, soft, red cotton cloth.
Immediately, a mind of greed arose;
he grasped it with his hand and raised it up,
but it was like grasping empty space.
His kinsmen are said to be like two hands groping in empty space.
Furthermore, there is a wind blowing;
if this patient is in the midst of winter's cold, [it will be unbearable].
A warm breeze comes to blow away their cold and suffering.
When it is hot and scorching, a cool breeze comes to blow,
dispelling the stifling heat and causing their hearts to rejoice.
Because the mind is focused elsewhere, one does not hear the sounds of lamentation and weeping;
yet if the mind were to gather and stir, it would also move,
and hearing those sounds of grief would cause one to be blown away to another place.
Therefore, the weeping and wailing of one's kinsmen at the time of death is a great hindrance; yet,
if it does not constitute such an obstacle, one may be reborn in Uttarakuru.
In the interim, auspicious signs appeared in succession:
he saw a pond of blue lotuses,
filled with geese, ducks, and mandarin ducks.
He immediately ran toward and entered the middle of it to sport;
desiring to enter his mother’s womb,
he emerged from the lotus pond onto dry land.
Seeing one's parents in union through lustful passion,
one perceives the father’s body with a perverted view due to the impurity [of the seed].
He was indeed a male goose,
while his mother was a female goose;
had it been a male child born, [he would have been the father].
If one is born as a male, one sees oneself as a male goose;
if one is born as a female,
one sees oneself as a female goose.
If a male is born, he conceives aversion toward his father and affection toward his mother.
If a female is born,
she conceives love for her father and aversion toward her mother.
This is called the second intermediate state existence (*antarābhava*) for those born in Uttarakuru.
As for the third intermediate state existence:
it is when one dies in Jambudvīpa and is reborn in Aparagoyānī.
Then signs will appear.
If, at the time of death,
one sees houses and dwellings appearing entirely yellow in color.
It was like the color of gold,
covering everything like a cloud;
one saw the appearance of yellow cotton cloth within the void of space.
He raised his hands and grasped at them.
His kinsmen and brothers said,
"The patient is grasping at empty space with both hands."
At that time, as this person’s lifespan was drawing to a close,
they saw their own body like an ox and saw herds of oxen as if seen in a dream.
If one is to be born as a male,
he sees his parents in union performing the act of impurity;
he also perceives himself as having a human body with many dwellings.
Seeing her father’s appearance as being like that of a bull,
she removes him from his union with her mother;
if a daughter is born, [she does so].
She saw her own body as being like a milch cow and thought to herself:
"For what reason does the bull mate with that one and not with me?"
Having formed such a thought, one receives a female body;
this is called the third intermediate state (antarābhava) arising in Aparagoyānī.
As for the fourth intermediate state:
If a person from Jambudvīpa dies and is reborn in the realm of Pūrvavideha, then a sign appears:
one sees the appearance of blue woolen cloth.
Everything was entirely blue,
pervading and covering the void;
he saw his own dwelling as being completely like empty space.
Fearing that the blue cotton cloth would fall,
he caught it with his hand;
his kinsmen said, "He has died while shielding empty space."
He sees the intermediate state (antarābhava) as having the form of a horse;
he sees his own father as being like a stallion.
The mother is like a mare;
when the father and mother unite in passionate union, if it is a male being that is to be born, [the consciousness enters].
He formed this thought:
"I shall mate with this mare; if a female child is born," [he will take her as his wife].
He saw his own body in the form of a stallion and thought to himself:
"Why does this mare not mate with me?"
Having formed this thought, he immediately received a female body.
This is called the fourth intermediate state existence (antarābhava) in Pūrvavideha.
As for the fifth intermediate state existence:
If a person of Uttarakuru is at the point of death,
they see upward-moving signs;
if their mind is dominated by great karma, they will be reborn in the heavens.
He grasps empty space with his hand as if seeing it in a dream;
the fragrance of exquisite flowers and supreme perfumes,
along with the most sublime colors and scents, are held within his hand.
Seeing the flowers, he conceived desire for them. Thinking, "Now that I see this tree,
I shall climb it," he immediately ascended the great tree.
"This is indeed ascending Mount Sumeru;
I shall behold the celestial realms adorned with flowers and fruits,
and I shall wander therein."
This is called the fifth intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of inferior rebirth for the people of Uttarakuru.
As for the sixth intermediate state:
if it is a person of Uttarakuru...
Due to these intermediate karmas,
at the time of death,
they desire to be reborn in the heavens.
Then a sign appeared:
he saw a lotus pond that was exceedingly delightful,
adorned with swarms of bees, all of which were fragrant.
Ascending this lotus flower, they fly through the air in an instant,
as if born in the heavens within a dream.
He forms this thought:
"I shall now go to the excellent Lotus Pond.
This is called the sixth intermediate state (*antarābhava*) for those born among the people of Uttarakuru in the middling degree.
Regarding those in the seventh intermediate state:
because of the excellence of their karma, people from Uttarakuru are born in the Hall of Good Dharma and other realms within the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
At the time of death, one sees a magnificent hall, adorned with exquisite splendor;
at that moment, the person ascends that superior hall and is born within this celestial palace.
He is regarded as the Son of Heaven.
This is called the seventh intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) of superior birth experienced by those born in Uttarakuru when they are reborn in the heavens.
As for the eighth intermediate existence:
When a person of Uttarakuru is approaching the end of life,
signs appear; they see themselves in places for sporting in gardens and groves.
Fragrant, pure, and lovely;
hearing it brings joy and delight,
with little suffering or distress.
Their minds are not turbid;
with a pure mind, they ascend to the palaces and see the hosts of devas traveling through the sky.
It is just like being in a dream:
the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven is supremely wonderful and lovely,
with all five objects of desire fully present.
Dying in Uttarakuru and being born in this celestial realm—
this is called the eighth intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of a person from Uttarakuru who, having been habituated to and sporting in this heavenly abode, dies.
Regarding the ninth intermediate state being:
if a person from Aparagoyānī dies and is reborn in the heavens, there are two kinds of karma. What are these two?
First is residual karma;
second is generative karma,
by which one is born in the heavens.
When that person approaches the end of life, signs will appear because of their wholesome karma as they are about to relinquish their life.
The breath is not turbid;
the pulse is neither interrupted nor broken;
and the sense faculties are pure.
He saw a great pool of water;
its waters were temperate and flowed in vast, surging currents.
He floated to the other shore.

5. Section on Immediate Retribution (Pañcamaḥ sadyaḥ-phala-vargaḥ). From the *Saptakṛtvābhavapratyaya-sūtra* Spoken by the Buddha:
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying, "There are seven kinds of persons."
They are worthy of service and worthy of veneration;
they are the unsurpassed field of merit in this world.
What are these seven kinds of persons?
First, practicing loving-kindness;
second, practicing compassion;
third, practicing sympathetic joy.
Fourth is the practice of protection;
fifth is the practice of emptiness;
sixth is the practice of signlessness.
Seventh is the practice of wishlessness.
Any sentient beings who practice these seven dharmas will obtain their karmic fruit and reward within this present life.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"For what reason do you not speak of the srotāpanna and the sakṛdāgāmin?"
Anāgāmin, Arhat, and Pratyekabuddha.
"Why then do you speak of these seven matters?
The World-Honored One replied,
"There are seven types of persons who practice loving-kindness."
Their practice is equal to that of the *srotāpanna* up to the Buddha,
yet their circumstances differ.
Although one makes offerings to those such as the *srotāpanna*, no immediate retribution is obtained.
However, those who make offerings to such a person will receive their reward in this very life;
therefore, Ānanda, you should diligently and vigorously accomplish these seven dharmas.
Furthermore, the *Saṃyukta-ratna-piṭaka-sūtra* states:
"In the past, in the kingdom of Gandhāra,

10. Section on Good Retribution (Śubhavipāka). As stated in the *Sūtra on the Questions of Maitreya Bodhisattva* (*Maitreyaparipṛcchāsūtra-śāstra*):
Question: What is the fruit of giving?
Answer: Briefly stated, there is one kind of fruit for giving.
What is called the fruit of enjoyment.
The fruit of enjoyment further consists of two kinds of fruits:
namely, the fruit experienced in the present.
Regarding the future experience of results,
there are again three kinds of results;
that is, these two kinds with the addition of *prajñā*.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of fruits. What are the four?
First, there is that which has a fruit but lacks utility.
Second, there is that which has utility but no fruit;
third, there is that which has both fruit and utility;
fourth, there is that which has neither fruit nor utility.
First, there are cases where a gift has a fruit but lacks utility;
this refers to giving without a sincere mind or not giving with one's own hands.
One gives with a frivolous mind;
although such a person obtains various immeasurable fruits of retribution through that giving, [it is not supreme].
Yet they are unable to enjoy them,
just as the Lord of the Gods in Śrāvastī, though he obtained immeasurable varieties of rare treasures, was unable to enjoy them.
Second, there are those that have utility but no fruit.
This means that although one does not give oneself,
one gives rise to a mind of sympathetic joy upon seeing others practicing generosity;
it is for this reason.
Although they obtain and enjoy them, there is no fruit for themselves.
It is like the property of a celestial king: although all śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and others may obtain food, clothing, and their enjoyment, there is no fruit for themselves.
Furthermore, it is like the fourfold army of a wheel-turning sage king:
although they obtain food and clothing, they do not obtain the fruit;
likewise, there are those who possess both the fruit of the three realms of existence and its utility.
This refers to giving with a sincere mind and not giving with a contemptuous mind,
as was the case with the elder Jyotiṣka and others.
Regarding the fourth point, that there is neither fruit nor utility:
it means that once the gift has been used, it is immediately extinguished;
or else, because it acts as an obstacle to the supramundane noble path.
It is like a noble one who has distanced himself from afflictions.
Furthermore, there are five kinds of fruits, namely:
the attainment of life, physical form, strength, happiness, and eloquence.
Because life is obtained through causes,
giving food is equivalent to giving life;
by this causal condition, one will obtain long life hereafter.
In this same way, giving beauty, giving strength, giving happiness, giving eloquence, and so forth,
are all likewise. Furthermore,
there are five kinds of superior fruits.
It is said that giving to one's parents, the sick, and Dharma-preachers results in supreme karmic rewards for a Bodhisattva.
Since parents provide the kindness of nurturing and raising one’s life and body,
therefore, one who gives...
They shall obtain superior karmic rewards.
Furthermore, those who are ill are solitary and pitiable.
For this reason, one who gives to the sick should arouse a mind of loving-kindness and compassion.
One attains superior karmic rewards.
Furthermore, the Dharma-preacher is able to give rise to the Dharma-body.
It increases the Dharma-body,
eternally guiding both good and evil,
and brings to equilibrium that which is balanced and that which is unbalanced.
Because it is neither inverted nor non-inverted,
the donor thereby attains a superior karmic fruit.
Furthermore, all bodhisattvas are able to gather in and benefit sentient beings;
they give rise to a mind of loving-kindness and compassion in order to gather in the causes for the non-interruption of the Three Jewels. For this reason:

One who gives to a bodhisattva obtains a superior karmic fruit; for the power of a bodhisattva’s resolve, characterized by courageous compassion and vows, is vastly different from other merits, whose minds are narrow and inferior.
Furthermore, the Ekottarika Āgama states:
The World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus,
"I shall now expound the four merits of the Brahma-world."
What are the four? First,
if there is a faithful son or daughter of good family who has never established a stūpa where one had not previously existed.
Among these, one can undertake the second:
the restoration of old monasteries;
and the third: the harmonizing of the noble Saṃgha.
Fourth, when a Tathāgata first turns the wheel of Dharma,
the devas and people of the world entreat him to turn the wheel of Dharma;
this is called the fourth kind of merit for receiving Brahma-hood.
A bhikkhu addressed the Blessed One, saying,
"How much, Blessed One, is the merit of Brahmā?
The Blessed One replied:
All the merit possessed by the sentient beings within the land of Jambudvīpa is exactly equal to the merit of a single wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin).
The merit of the people of Jambudvīpa and that of a single universal monarch is equal to the merit of one person from Aparagoyānī.
The combined merit of the two regions, Jambudvīpa and Aparagoyānī, [is equal to the merit of one person from Videha].
Therefore, the merit of those three regions is not equal to the merit of a single person in Pūrvavideha;
and the merit of those three regions is not equal to the merit of a single person in Uttarakuru.
The merit of the people of the four continents is not equal to the merit of the Four Heavenly Kings;
even the merit of the people of the four continents [is not equal to that].
And the merit of the six heavens of the desire realm is not equal to the merit of a single Brahmā king.
If there are good men or good women who seek such merit, [they should practice accordingly].
This is its measure. Furthermore, the Madhyama Āgama states:
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus.
If one can uphold these seven kinds of dharmas,
one will be born in the abode of Śakra.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
Make offerings to one's parents and the elders of the family;
speak with gentle and respectful words; abandon harsh speech and double-tongued talk;
subdue the mind of stinginess; and always cultivate truthful speech.
The gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, seeing those who practice these seven dharmas, each spoke thus: "In the future, you shall be born in this heaven.
(From the *Ratnakaraṇḍaka Sūtra*, verse).
When the fruit of meritorious deeds ripens, one does not attain the human vehicle through divine sacrifices;
rather, by maintaining the chariot of precepts, one is certain to be reborn in the heavens.
Just as one knows for certain when a lamp is extinguished, so too shall one reach the unconditioned state (*asaṃskṛta*).
All is attained through practice; what is the use of seeking heaven?
