Section on Receiving Retribution, Number Seventy-nine. Part Eleven:
The Section on Evil Retribution (70). Part Eleven: The Section on Evil Retribution. Now, where there is form, its shadow appears.
When there is a sound, there is an echo.
It has never been seen that while the form remains, the shadow perishes,
or that while the sound continues, the echo diverges.
The principle that good and evil are reciprocated is clear and evident.
I hope you will believe this deeply and refrain from doubting or deriding it.
The various degrees of suffering and retribution are detailed below as described.
For example, there are those who physically commit acts of killing,
such as flaying, carving, mincing, roasting, or boiling shellfish like clams and oysters;
or those who use flying hawks and running dogs to hunt living beings.
Those who slaughter, tear apart, hack, and mince sentient beings shall fall into the Hell of Butchery and Carving;
those who boil, steam, burn, and roast sentient beings shall fall into the Hells of Boiling Cauldrons and Burning Charcoal.
Because of this killing of living beings,
one shall dwell within the hells for years without end and for the duration of kalpas.
They undergo intense suffering;
once that suffering is exhausted,
they fall again into the realm of animals.
They are born as various oxen, horses, pigs, sheep, donkeys, mules, camels, chickens, dogs, fish, birds, frogs, crabs, and snails, being slaughtered by people;
such creatures as these do not attain a natural end of life.
They even offer their own flesh as provisions for the sacrificial tables;
thus they remain among these birds and beasts through immeasurable births and deaths.
If there were not even a slight root of goodness, there would never be a time of escape.
Should they have even a fragment of merit remaining, they may obtain an inferior human body;
yet they may fall from the womb,
or perish shortly after birth.
Some for ten or twenty [eons] have not yet attained any knowledge;
they pass from darkness into darkness.
What people hold dear and cherish, one should know,
all results from taking short lives due to the killing of living beings.
Furthermore, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states:
The sin of killing causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms;
if they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retributive fruits.
First is a short lifespan;
second is much illness.
Such are the ten unwholesome actions.
Each of these is fully endowed with five kinds of retributive results.
First, for what reason does one who kills receive the suffering of hell?
It is because by killing, they cause suffering to sentient beings.
Therefore, when the body perishes and life ends, the manifold sufferings of hell all come to press upon one's person.
Second, for what reason does the taking of life lead to rebirth as an animal?
It is because killing lacks compassion and mercy, and its conduct deviates from human ethics.
Therefore, when their retribution for hellish offenses is exhausted, they receive the body of an animal.
Thirdly, as for why those who kill living beings are further reborn as hungry ghosts:
it is because their acts of killing are invariably motivated by a mind of stinginess and an attachment to flavors.
Furthermore, they become hungry ghosts.
Fourth, why is it that those who kill living beings are born as humans yet obtain a short lifespan?
It is because they killed and harmed the lives of creatures that they obtain a short lifespan.
Fifth, as for why taking life results in contracting many diseases:
because the act of killing violates the harmony of living beings, causing a multitude of afflictions to converge, one suffers from many illnesses.
One should know that taking life is a great suffering.
Furthermore, the *Saṃyukta-ratna-piṭaka-sūtra* states:
At that time, there was a hungry ghost who addressed Maudgalyāyana, saying:
I always have eyes on my two shoulders and a mouth and nose upon my chest;
I am perpetually without a head.
"For what reason?
Maudgalyāyana replied,
"In a previous life, you..."
"You have always served as my executioner's apprentice.
Whenever I killed a person, you always felt joy in your heart.
You would bind the victim's hair with a rope and pull it tight."
For this reason and by these causes, they undergo such retribution.
This is but the "flower-retribution" for their evil conduct;
the bitter fruits of hell lie yet ahead.
Furthermore, there was another ghost who said to Maudgalyāyana:
"My body is always like a lump of flesh."
They lack hands, feet, eyes, ears, noses, and so forth;
they are constantly devoured by insects and birds,
enduring the unbearable suffering of their transgressions.
"For what reason is this so?
He replied, "In a previous life, you..."
She constantly administered abortifacients to others to cause them to miscarry their fetuses;
for this reason, she undergoes such retribution.
This is the "flower reward" (the immediate karmic result).
The bitter fruits of hell will only manifest in future lives;
furthermore, because their killing and greedy malice have increased so greatly,
and because they have increased so greatly...
Thus, lacking any sense of propriety or yielding,
one commits robbery and theft;
in this very life, one steals— that is, one takes what is not given.
Upon death, one shall fall into the Iron Cave Hell and undergo various sufferings for many eons;
once those sufferings are exhausted, one will fall among the animals.
Their bodies are constantly burdened with heavy loads and subjected to driving, urging, and beating;
they have no remaining breath for anything else, and the only flavors they consume are water and grass.
Amidst these immeasurable births and deaths,
by virtue of past causes and conditions,
one may encounter even a slight good deed and again obtain an inferior human body.
They are constantly servants and slaves,
driven and dispatched as messengers,
never attaining autonomy.
As long as their debts are not fully repaid,
they shall not be permitted to hear the Dharma;
because of this, they will suffer and transmigrate through saṃsāra without end.
One should know that all this suffering arises from theft:
in this life, one obscures the light of others and fails to offer light as an offering to the Triple Gem.
On the contrary, they take the radiance of the Triple Gem to illuminate themselves;
yet upon death, they shall fall into the Black-Ear, Black-Rope, and Dark Earth hells,
where they will undergo various sufferings for distant eons.
Having finished undergoing that suffering, they fall among lice and fleas;
unable to endure the light,
they undergo immeasurable births and deaths therein.
Due to these original causes and conditions,
even if one encounters a slight merit and attains an inferior human body,
its appearance will be dark-complexioned, filthy, and impure.
One dwells in a foul and loathsome place, detested and shunned by others;
one is born blind with both eyes, unable to behold heaven or earth.
Know that such concealment of light is likewise caused by the karmic condition of stealing.
Therefore, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"The sin of stealing also causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms."
If one is born among humans, two kinds of retribution are obtained: first, poverty;
second, being unable to exercise mastery over shared wealth.
Why do those who commit robbery fall into hell?
Because by robbing, plundering, and stealing the wealth of others, they cause suffering to sentient beings;
thus, upon the death of their bodies, they immediately enter the Cold Ice Hell.
They endure manifold sufferings.
Why do those who plunder and steal become animals?
Because they fail to practice the way of humanity, they receive the retribution of an animal.
His body constantly bears heavy burdens and provides his flesh for others to repay his karmic debts from past lives.
For what reason has he further fallen among the hungry ghosts?
It is because, driven by stinginess and greed, he committed robbery and theft.
Therefore, when their retribution as animals is exhausted, they become hungry ghosts.
As for why they are born poor among humans,
it is because they robbed others and left them destitute.
This is why they are impoverished.
For what reason do they lack mastery over their shared wealth?
It is because of their past acts of plundering, stealing, and seizing by force.
If one possesses wealth, it is shared among the five families and cannot be controlled;
one should know that both robbery and theft are great sufferings.
Furthermore, the *Saṃyukta-ratna-piṭaka Sūtra* states:
At that time, there was a hungry ghost who addressed Maudgalyāyana, saying:
"Venerable Sir,
my belly is as vast as a jar, while my throat,
hands, and feet are exceedingly slender like needles."
"You may not eat or drink.
For what reason and by what causes do you undergo such suffering?
Maudgalyāyana replied:
In a previous life, you were the head of a village.
Relying on your own wealth and nobility, you lived with unrestrained indulgence in food and drink,
treating others with contempt and deceit.
They deprive sentient beings of food and drink;
by reason of these causes and conditions, those beings become hungry and exhausted.
One undergoes such retribution;
this is merely the provisional blossoming of the fruit, while the bitter fruits of hell await later.
Furthermore, there was another ghost who said to Maudgalyāyana:
"There are always two hot iron wheels revolving beneath both my armpits."
"Their bodies are scorched and putrefied.
For what cause and condition is this so?
Maudgalyāyana replied:
In a previous life, while you were making cakes for the community of monks,
you stole two portions and tucked them under both your armpits;
therefore, you have received this retribution.
This is the preliminary retribution;
later, one will undergo the retribution of suffering in hell.
Furthermore, because of this theft, the mind becomes neither upright nor correct.
To indulge in lust and lewdness according to one's desires brings danger and peril in this present life.
She is constantly filled with fear and alarm,
lest her husband or relatives discover her,
causing her to suffer calamity at that time.
Blades and clubs are brought to bear upon their bodies;
their heads and feet are severed,
even unto the loss of life.
Upon death, they enter hell;
they lie upon iron beds or embrace copper pillars.
The hell-guardians kindle fires to burn their bodies;
when their retribution in hell is exhausted, they shall receive the form of an animal.
As chickens, ducks, birds, sparrows, dogs, pigs, and moths—
thus undergoing immeasurable births and deaths,
they experience various sufferings and afflictions throughout distant eons.
Once the suffering has been fully endured,
due to their original causes and conditions,
if they encounter even a slight merit, they may again obtain a human body of inferior quality.
Within the inner chambers, there is lewd disorder and the wives and concubines are unchaste;
if one has a favorite who is seized by another,
they will constantly harbor fear and anxiety.
There is much peril and little peace;
one should know that this peril and suffering all stem from sexual misconduct.
Thus, the *Bhūmivastu* (Dichilun) says:
The sin of sexual misconduct likewise causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms.
If they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution:
first, their wife will not be chaste.
Second, one obtains a retinue that does not comply with one's wishes.
Why does sexual misconduct lead to rebirth in hell?
Because such misconduct involves violating what is not one's due and encroaching upon the property of others, thereby causing suffering.
Therefore, at the end of life, one undergoes the suffering of hell.
For what reason does sexual misconduct lead to rebirth as an animal?
It is because such misconduct does not accord with human principles.
This is why they emerge from hell to receive the body of an animal;
for what reason does sexual misconduct further lead to rebirth as a hungry ghost?
It is because such lustful behavior arises entirely from stinginess and craving.
Due to the sin of stinginess and attachment, one further becomes a hungry ghost (*preta*).
Why is it that women commit sexual misconduct and fail to be chaste?
It is because they have violated the wives of others.
The wives one obtains will never be chaste or upright.
Why is it that those who engage in sexual misconduct do not obtain a retinue according to their wishes?
It is because through sexual misconduct they have stolen away the affection and favor of others.
Therefore, his retinue cannot act according to their will,
and for this reason, they are further seized by others.
One should know that harboring lust constitutes three great sufferings.
Furthermore, the *Saṃyukta-ratna-piṭaka-sūtra* states:
Once, there was a hungry ghost who said to Maudgalyāyana:
I cover my head with objects to conceal myself,
and I am constantly afraid that someone will come to kill me;
my mind is perpetually terrified and overwhelmed by fear beyond endurance.
"For what reason is this so?
He replied, "In a previous life,
you committed sexual misconduct with another's wife."
She is constantly afraid of being seen by others;
she fears her husband might seize, bind, beat, or kill her,
or that the laws of the state might execute her in the marketplace.
Constantly harboring fear and with fear perpetually continuing,
they thus undergo such retribution;
this is the "flower-retribution" for their evil conduct.
In the future, one will undergo the retribution of suffering in the hells.
Furthermore, because of that sexual misconduct, all speech becomes false.
If one speaks falsely in this life, one causes suffering to sentient beings.
Upon death, one shall fall into the Wailing Hell (Raurava),
where one will undergo various sufferings for many eons.
Once these sufferings are exhausted, one will fall among the hungry ghosts (preta).
Having undergone immeasurable suffering within the cycle of birth and death,
due to past causes and conditions,
they may encounter some slight merit and again obtain an inferior human body.
Afflicted by many diseases, emaciated and weak,
suddenly exhausted and tormented by pain, they are beset by bitter suffering and are not loved or cared for by others.
One should know that all this suffering is conditioned by false speech.
Thus, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states:
"The transgression of false speech also causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms."
If one is born among humans, two kinds of retributive fruits are obtained:
first, being frequently slandered;
second, being deceived by others.
For what reason does one who speaks falsely fall into hell?
It is because that false speech is unreal;
it causes people to undergo suffering in vain.
Therefore, upon death, one undergoes the sufferings of hell.
For what reason does one who speaks falsely emerge as an animal?
It is because such deception and falsehood violate human integrity and trust.
This is why, upon leaving prison, one receives the retribution of an animal;
and for what reason does one become a hungry ghost due to false speech?
It is because such false speech arises entirely from greed and deception.
Due to the sins of stinginess and deception, one further becomes a hungry ghost (*preta*).
For what reason is one frequently slandered by others?
It is because of speaking falsehoods and lacking sincerity.
For what reason is one deceived by others through false speech?
It is because one uses false speech to deceive and entice others.
One should know that false speech is the greatest of the four sufferings.
Furthermore, based on false speech, one then resorts to divisive speech;
in this present life, one's words lack compassion and love,
and one engages in slander, defamation, harsh speech, and confused chatter.
Upon death, one shall fall into the hell of the Ploughed Field of Molten Copper with Severed Tongues,
where one will undergo various sufferings for many kalpas.
Once these sufferings are exhausted, one falls among the animals.
They consume filth and excrement like cormorants,
even though they possess the faculty of the tongue.
Within this, throughout immeasurable births and deaths,
by virtue of original causes and conditions,
if one encounters even a slight good deed.
Furthermore, they obtain an inferior human body;
their faculty of the tongue is incomplete,
and their breath is foul and putrid.
Mute, stammering, and halting in speech;
teeth neither even nor white;
hair thin, sparse, and scanty.
Even if one has wholesome words,
if people do not trust and accept them,
one should know that such slanderous discord arises entirely from double-tongued speech.
Therefore, the *Bhūmivastu-viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* states:
"The sin of divisive speech also causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms.
If they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retributive results."
First, one obtains wicked kinsmen;
second, one obtains discordant kinsmen.
For what reason does one who engages in divisive speech fall into hell?
Because of divisive speech that separates the affection between people,
one undergoes the suffering of hell due to the pain of being parted from loved ones.
For what reason does divisive speech lead to rebirth as an animal?
Because of their divisive speech and incitement of strife,
they share the same fate as the jackal that received the body of an animal;
for what reason do those who engage in divisive speech further become hungry ghosts?
Because of their double-tongued speech, they are also driven by stinginess and envy;
due to the transgression of stinginess and envy, they further become hungry ghosts.
For what reason does double-tongued speech cause one to obtain wicked and evil associates when reborn as a human?
Because of divisive speech, one causes virtuous companions to harbor ill will toward one another.
For what reason does divisive speech lead to a lack of harmony among one's retinue?
Because of divisive speech, one separates people from their close friendships and prevents them from being united.
One should know that divisive speech is one of the five great sufferings.
Furthermore, because of such divisive speech, one's words will invariably become coarse and evil;
thus, in this present life, one suffers on account of harsh speech.
They engage in strife, disorder, and mutual injury;
they invade and attack one another,
slaughtering all living beings.
Upon death, one shall fall into the Hell of Swords and Weapons,
where one will undergo various sufferings throughout distant eons.
Once these sufferings are exhausted, one falls among the animals.
With their feet torn out, their arms sold away, their thighs lost,
and their shoulder blades forfeited, they undergo various sufferings throughout distant kalpas; once these sufferings have been exhausted, [they may attain liberation].
Within this, there are immeasurable births and deaths due to fundamental causes and conditions.
If one encounters even a slight good deed,
yet obtains an inferior human body that lacks its four limbs.
Their hands were cut off, their feet amputated, their noses slit, and their lips gashed; their physical forms were mutilated and destroyed,
and neither ghosts nor spirits would protect them.
One should know that being despised and abandoned by others arises from harming sentient beings through harsh speech.
Thus, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states:
The sin of harsh speech also causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms; if they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution:
first, they constantly hear unpleasant sounds;
second, whatever they say is always met with contention and litigation.
Why does harsh speech lead to rebirth in hell?
Because those who speak harshly all intend to harm others,
and for people to hear such words is a source of suffering.
Therefore, at the end of life, they undergo the sufferings of hell.
For what reason do those who speak evil words become animals?
It is because they used evil speech to insult others by calling them animals.
This is why, upon leaving prison, one becomes an animal;
and for what reason does one who uses harsh speech further become a hungry ghost?
It is because of their stinginess and their habit of reviling others whenever they encounter them.
Thus, when the suffering of the animal realm has ended, one becomes a hungry ghost.
For what reason does one who speaks harshly always hear evil sounds as a human?
It is because their speech was coarse and vulgar that what they hear is always evil.
For what reason is it that whatever is spoken with harsh speech is always accompanied by contention?
It is because such harsh speech opposes all virtues;
whatever words are uttered thereby invariably lead to dispute and litigation.
One should know that harsh speech constitutes six great sufferings.
Furthermore, because of such harsh speech, one's words are invariably frivolous and ornate,
providing no benefit or meaning whatsoever.
Because it is without benefit or profit, one gives rise to arrogance in this present life;
upon death, one shall fall into the Binding Hell and undergo various sufferings throughout distant eons.
Having finished undergoing such suffering, they fall among the animals;
there they think only of water and grass, unaware of the kindness of their parents' nurturing.
Within this state, they undergo immeasurable births and deaths.
Due to these original causes and conditions,
even if one encounters a slight good deed,
one will again obtain an inferior human body.
Born in a borderland,
they do not know loyalty, filial piety, benevolence, or righteousness,
nor do they see the Three Jewels.
If one were in China and was short,
ugly, and stunted, one would be treated with contempt and disdain by others.
One should know that arrogance arises entirely from meaningless frivolity and a lack of restraint.
Thus, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states:
"The transgression of meaningless speech also causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms."
If one is born among humans, one receives two kinds of retribution:
first, people do not believe or accept whatever one says;
second, one is unable to speak with clarity when making a statement.
For what reason does one who speaks meaningless words fall into hell?
Since such speech does not accord with reality and causes harm to others,
one consequently undergoes the suffering of hell at the end of life.
For what reason does one who utters meaningless speech become an animal?
Because their speech lacks meaning, they violate human ethics;
therefore, they fall into hell and receive the body of an animal.
For what reason does one who speaks meaningless words become a hungry ghost?
Because their speech is meaningless, they are obstructed by the delusion of stinginess;
because of that delusion of stinginess, they further become a hungry ghost.
For what reason does one who has committed the offense of idle speech, upon being reborn as a human,
have their words disbelieved and not accepted by others?
It is because their speech was meaningless and thus not worthy of being received.
For what reason is speech that is meaningless indistinct?
Because such speech lacks meaning, it is entirely based on obscurity;
due to this retribution of obscurity, it cannot be clear.
One should know that idle speech constitutes seven great sufferings.
Furthermore, because of idle speech, one cannot be modest or yielding,
causing greed and desire to become insatiable.
If one is stingy and greedy in this present life and does not practice giving,
upon death one shall fall into the Hell of Boiling Excrement,
where one will undergo various sufferings for many eons.
Having finished suffering these torments, they fall among the animals and hungry ghosts;
lacking clothing and food, they depend upon humans for their sustenance and consume excrement and filth.
If one does not give, one shall not obtain;
within this state, there are immeasurable births and deaths due to original causes and conditions.
If one encounters even a slight good deed,
yet obtains an inferior human body,
one will suffer from hunger, cold, and nakedness.
They were constantly in a state of exhaustion; since others would not give to them,
they could find nothing even when they sought it.
Even if one possesses but a tiny fraction [of wealth], one will immediately encounter plunder and seizure;
guarding against suffering becomes impossible, leading to the loss of body and life.
One should know that this failure to practice giving is entirely due to the cause of greed and desire.
Therefore, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"The transgression of covetousness also causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms.
If they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retributive fruits."
First, having many desires;
second, lacking contentment.
For what reason do those with covetous desire fall into hell?
Because they are moved by greed, they act through body and speech and suffer over material things; therefore,
when their bodies die, they undergo the suffering of hell.
For what reason does one who gives rise to covetous desire become an animal?
Because this covetous desire causes movement that violates human ethics;
therefore, upon emerging from prison, one becomes an animal.
For what reason are those with covetous desire further reborn as hungry ghosts?
Because of this covetous desire, they inevitably become greedy and stingy;
due to the transgression of greed and stinginess, they are further reborn as hungry ghosts.
For what reason is there greed and yet an abundance of desire?
Because of this greed, that which is desired becomes ever more abundant.
For what reason is there no satiety in greed?
Because of this craving, one seeks with insatiable greed;
know that craving is the eighth great suffering.
Furthermore, because craving leads to what is disagreeable.
Then, being provoked to anger, one gives rise to hatred.
If one is full of hatred in this present life,
upon death one shall surely fall into the Niraya hell.
Throughout successive kalpas, they undergo manifold sufferings;
once these sufferings are exhausted, they fall among the animals,
becoming venomous snakes, vipers, tigers, leopards, or jackals.
Within this, the wolf has undergone immeasurable births and deaths;
yet, due to past causes and conditions, if it encounters even a slight bit of goodness, [it may be liberated].
Furthermore, they obtain an inferior human body;
moreover, they are prone to much anger and their facial features are ugly and hideous.
He is loathed by others;
not only do they not provide him with food for his kinsmen and friends,
but even his sight is unpleasant to behold.
One should know that anger and resentment all have their source in hatred and vexation.
Thus, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states:
"The transgression of hatred also causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms."
If one is born among humans, one will receive two kinds of retribution:
first, one will constantly have others seeking out one's faults;
second, one will constantly be troubled and harmed by the masses.
For what reason does one who is angry and afflicted fall into hell?
Because of this anger and affliction, one harms others with resentment;
thus, one undergoes the sufferings of hell.
For what reason does one who is prone to anger and resentment fall among the animals? It is because,
due to this anger and resentment, one is unable to practice benevolence and forbearance.
This is why, upon leaving prison, he received the body of an animal;
for what reason did his anger and affliction further cause him to become a hungry ghost?
It was because this anger and affliction arose from a mind of stinginess.
Due to the sin of a stingy mind, they further become hungry ghosts.
Why do they harbor anger and vexation,
constantly seeking out the faults and shortcomings of all?
Because of this anger and resentment, one cannot be包容 (inclusive/forbearing);
thus, everyone seeks out one's faults.
For what reason is one who is angry and resentful constantly harmed by others?
Because of this anger and resentment, one harms others,
and others also harm one;
know that anger and resentment constitute nine kinds of great suffering.
Furthermore, because of their anger and vexation, they harbor heterodoxy and do not believe in the Right Path;
in this present life, their wrong views prevent others from hearing the Dharma.
If one recites the sutras while not eating the [offered] food,
upon death one shall fall into the Hell of Deafness and Ignorance,
where one will undergo various sufferings throughout distant kalpas.
Having finished suffering their retribution, they fall among the animals;
though they hear the sounds of the Triple Gem and the Four Noble Truths,
they do not know them to be wholesome.

12. Section on Abodes (Vihāra-varga), the Twelfth. This section is further divided into four parts: the seven abodes of consciousness (*vijñāna-sthiti*), the nine abodes of sentient beings (*sattva-nikāya-sthiti*), the twenty-five states of existence (*bhava*), and the forty-two places of residence. 1. The Seven Abodes of Consciousness. Regarding the first, the seven abodes of consciousness, as explained in the *Abhidharma*: it is said—
Within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), only the two fortunate destinies (*sugati*)—those of humans and devas—are taken as one;
together with the first three stages of each of the two higher realms, there are thus seven.
As the treatise states:
For what reason are the four types of evil destinies, the fourth dhyāna, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception not established as stations of consciousness?
This is explained in the treatise as follows:
"If consciousness were to dwell in bliss therein..."
Thus, the stations of consciousness are established;
however, that which is not of the nature of abiding in pleasure is not so established.
This means that because they are oppressed by suffering within those four evil destinies, consciousness does not delight in dwelling there.
Furthermore, because the gods of the Pure Abodes within the fourth dhyāna delight in entering nirvāṇa, consciousness does not delight in dwelling there either.
Because the beings in the realm of non-perception lack a mind, it cannot be described as a station of consciousness;
the same applies to the rest of the fourth dhyāna,
which is likewise indeterminate.
Because some seek the formless realm,
some seek the Pure Abodes,
and some seek the state of non-perception, consciousness likewise does not delight in dwelling there.
In the existence of the first dhyāna, because it is obscure and lacks agility, consciousness does not delight in dwelling there;
for this reason, it is not established [as a realm].
Furthermore, it is said that if there were factors that destroy consciousness,
then those would not be established as stations of consciousness;
this refers to the four miserable destinies, wherein consciousness is afflicted and destroyed by the sensation of suffering.

For this reason, it is not established [as a basis for consciousness]. Furthermore, within the fourth dhyāna, because there is the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and the non-conceptual heavens (*asaṃjñika*), which sever and destroy consciousness,
it is likewise not established in each of those cases.
In the stage of non-perception,
there exists that samādhi of cessation;
because it harms the conscious mind.
For this reason, consciousness does not abide in any of these three locations.
Thus is the brief analysis of the seven stations of consciousness.
II. The Nine Abodes of Sentient Beings. Second Question: What is the distinction between the nine abodes of sentient beings?
The answer is:
As it is stated in the Abhidharma,
namely, above the seven stations of consciousness (vijñānasthiti).
Including the Heaven of Non-conception and the Heaven of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception,
these constitute the nine abodes of sentient beings.
If one speaks of the miserable realms and the remainder of the fourth dhyāna, [they are not included].
Why are the abodes of sentient beings not established?
This is as explained previously in the treatise:
if those sentient beings delight in dwelling [therein], [then they constitute an abode].
One establishes dwellings for sentient beings;
however, for those who delight in dwelling in what is improper, no such establishment is made.
This means that because those four evil destinies involve much suffering and affliction,
sentient beings do not delight in dwelling there.
Within the fourth dhyāna are the five Pure Abode heavens.
Because they hasten toward the bliss of nirvāṇa, they do not delight in remaining there;
as for the other fourth dhyānas, they are as previously described.
For these reasons, they are not established as abodes of sentient beings.
3. The Twenty-five Abodes of Existence. Chapter Three on the Twenty-five Abodes of Existence. Question:
How are the twenty-five existences distinguished?
Answer: [As follows:]
As stated in the *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra*,
within the desire realm there are fourteen existences (*bhava*),
and in the form realm there are seven.
There are four formless [realms].
Because they are discussed in combination with the three realms, there are twenty-five [categories] in total.
Regarding the fourteen in the desire realm:
That is to say, the four evil destinies constitute the first four;
furthermore, one takes the people of the four continents.
Furthermore, these are divided into four;
combined with the preceding, they become eight.
Again, the six classes of gods of the desire realm are taken as six.
The aforementioned constitute the fourteen realms of existence (*bhava*).
Regarding the seven [realms] of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*),
they are the so-called four dhyānas.
These are thus taken as four:
furthermore, from within the first dhyāna, the Great Brahmā Heaven is taken;
and from within the fourth dhyāna, the five Pure Abodes together with the Heaven of Non-conception are taken.
These constitute the seven [realms].
Adding these seven to the previous fourteen makes twenty-one realms of existence.
The four within the formless realm refer to the four formless absorptions (ārūpya-samāpatti);
these four are appended to the preceding [categories].
This constitutes the twenty-five realms of existence (bhava).
Therefore, a verse in that treatise says:
The four continents and the four evil destinies, The Brahmā kings and the six heavens of desire.
The five Pure Abodes of the Non-conceptual, the four Emptinesses, and the four Dhyānas.
Question: It is not yet known for what reason the Brahmā King is separately singled out from within the first dhyāna.
Within the fourth dhyāna, the Unconscious Heaven (asaṃjñisattva) and the five Pure Abodes (śuddhāvāsa) are separately extracted and established as the three realms of existence;
this distinguishes them from the first four dhyānas.
What is the meaning of this?
The answer is:
it is because that Great Brahmā of the First Dhyāna is so designated.
The non-Buddhist practitioners and others constantly reckon this [ātman] to be the fundamental source that gives rise to the myriad things;
they hold that by opposing it one undergoes birth and death,
while by conforming to it one attains liberation.
Furthermore, that Brahmā King likewise reckons himself to be the creator and lord of all things,
asserting that he is both unique and eternal.
This is true liberation.
Because the Tathāgata wishes to shatter that emotional and intellectual clinging to views,
he specifically designates it and speaks of it as "existence."
The second is the Heaven of Non-conception (asaṃjñisattva-deva).
This refers to those in that heaven who have all attained a fixed lifespan as the retribution for their state of mindlessness for five hundred great kalpas.
The non-Buddhist practitioners do not understand this;
instead, they falsely reckon it to be true nirvana.
For this reason, they delight in cultivating the concentration of non-perception (asaṃjñi-samādhi) in order to seek birth in that realm.
The Tathāgata, wishing to shatter their emotional views,
therefore specifically designates and declares them to exist.
Third, as for the five Pure Abodes (Śuddhāvāsa):
Within that [realm] is the abode of the celestial king Maheśvara;
non-Buddhist practitioners likewise reckon that this celestial king is the fundamental source of creation.
By returning to [the truth], one attains liberation.
To shatter this view,
the Tathāgata specifically designates and teaches that [the self] exists.
The meaning of the separate explanation is revealed herein.
It is asked:
It is not yet known which among those six realms of existence [is meant].
The four types of evil destinies each establish one existence (*bhava*);
among humans, four are established;
and among devas, seventeen existences are established.
For what reason is this so?
The answer is:
It is because, among those four evil destinies, there are certain [conditions].
Because of their manifold sufferings,
sentient beings do not become attached;
their inclination toward dwelling in bliss is faint.
Therefore, one existence (bhava) is established for each realm of rebirth (gati).
Among them, the human realm is superior;
sentient beings take pleasure in dwelling there.
Because the mind is already deeply attached,
they are accordingly described as four according to their respective directions.
The celestial realms are the most excellent;
the state of dwelling in bliss is supreme and unsurpassed.
Therefore, they are described as seventeen according to their respective locations.
Thus has the brief exposition of the twenty-five states of existence been presented.
4. The Forty-two Abodes. Fourth Question: [The text continues: "The forty-two abodes... [Question: ...asked:
It is not yet known how the forty-two abodes are differentiated.
Answer: As stated in the *Loutan jing* (Ratna-kūṭa Sūtra).
That is to say, within the desire realm there are twenty abodes;
within the form realm there are eighteen; and within the formless realm there are four.
Taken together across the three realms, there are forty-two places of abode.
Regarding the twenty [realms] of the desire realm:
these consist of the eight great hells, along with animals and hungry ghosts,
which together constitute ten.
Furthermore, taking the inhabitants of the four continents and the six heavens of the desire realm,
these are again made into ten;
together they constitute twenty dwelling places.
Regarding the eighteen [realms] within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*):
this refers to the eighteen heavens existing within the four dhyānas,
which constitute eighteen places of residence.
Within the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu),
there are four stages of the meditative attainments of emptiness (ākāśānantyāyatana, etc.), which together constitute forty-two places of residence.
Question: For what reason, among the six realms of existence,
is it that [the teaching] is found within three of them— the hells, humans, and devas?
Each [of the five destinies] establishes many places of residence;
why is it that the two destinies of ghosts and animals each establish only one,
while the destiny of asuras is not established at all?
The answer is:
"Dwelling" refers to a place of peaceful abiding.
One who has a fixed location [is so called].
It is established wherever it follows;
that which has no fixed location is not established.
That is to say, those hells definitely have eight locations;
humans have four locations;
and the heavens definitely have twenty-eight locations.
Therefore, within these three destinies,
many distinct dwelling places are established for each; however,
for the two destinies of hungry ghosts and animals, there are no fixed or distinct locations for their many dwellings.
Therefore, one is established for each destination (gati).
Since the asura destination is subsumed within other realms,
it is not discussed separately.
Question: According to the explanation in the Abhidharma,
those four formless attainments (ārūpya-samāpatti) pervade both the desire realm (kāmadhātu) and the form realm (rūpadhātu).
Furthermore, there is no fixed distinction;
moreover, since it has no form,
it has no place of abode or reliance.
Why can it be said that there is a place of abiding?
The answer is:
according to the Hīnayāna.
It is indeed so. If one speaks according to the Mahāyāna,
those [atoms] also possess subtle form and shape.
Each has its own palaces,
and there are four distinct locations within the triple world.
Each maintains its own single realm without being mixed with the other two;
therefore, they are said to be the four abodes.
Question: According to the Abhidharma,
that Brahmā King and the Brahmā-purohita devas share the same dwelling place without distinction.
Regarding the gods of the Heaven of No-Thought within the fourth dhyāna:
they share the same level as those of the Vast Fruit (Bṛhatphala) and have no separate location. If this is so, then...

The answer is:
because the Brahmā King exists within the first dhyāna.
Although there is no separate heaven,
within the second Brahmā-purohita Heaven,
there is a distinct tiered terrace, lofty, vast, and magnificent.
Mahābrahmā dwells above; he does not share the same level as the Brahmā-purohita devas,
because the sovereign is superior while his ministers are subordinate.
As for the Heaven of Non-conception (asaṃjñisattva),
although it is the same as the Heaven of Vast Fruit (bṛhatphala),
their respective abodes are distinct from one another.
It is similar to the prefectures and counties here;
they are distinguished in this way,
and for this reason, they are described as two types of dwellings.
The verse says:
Form and mind defile one another; Karmic obstacles entwine and bind. The seven consciousnesses arise and activate, while the eighth consciousness is pulled along;
Receiving retribution within the three realms, The suffering of the six paths extends endlessly.
Unless one cuts off delusion, how can one attain firm and stable resonance?

2. Section on Karmic Actions (Karmapatha-varga). Second:
It is stated that these actions are called "indeterminate" by the Noble Ones (*ārya*).
That is to say, they are the unwholesome actions (*akuśala-karma*) mentioned in various sūtras.
Some describe it as "black-and-black karma" and "unwholesome karma," while in various sūtras concerning the meritorious conduct of ordinary worldlings,
it is described as "black-and-white karma" and "wholesome karma."
Although their names are diverse, the essence of their activity is not different.
What is the essence of this activity?
As stated in the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*:
Killing and so forth are unwholesome karmas;
giving and so forth are wholesome karmas.
This is what is meant by the two courses of action: transgression and merit.
Regarding the mention of "killing and so forth," the term "and so forth" includes the ten unwholesome actions;
these are collectively designated as "actions of transgression."
Regarding the phrase "generosity and so forth," the term "and so forth" includes such activities as ethical discipline and meditative concentration;
these are likewise mundane virtues.
These are all called meritorious formations (*puṇyābhisaṃskāra*).
Among the wholesome states of this world,
there are eight dhyāna-concentrations.
In relation to the distracted wholesome states of the desire realm,
it is called "unwavering conduct" (*āneñjya-saṃskāra*); however, in relation to the wisdom of supramundane contemplation of principles, it is not so termed.
When these conditions dwell upon the objective basis, they are called meritorious formations (*puṇyābhisaṃskāra*),
as described in the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*).
The meditative concentrations (dhyāna) contained within the first five perfections are also generally termed merit; however,
the conduct of those who practice various sinful or meritorious deeds differs.
Some exclusively cultivate merit;
some commit only transgressions;
and yet others practice both transgression and merit together.
One who exclusively cultivates merit is one whose mind is pure,
practicing generosity, ethical discipline, and so forth for the benefit of others.
Only those who commit offenses—
meaning they lack the moisture of compassion—
are such that every movement of body, speech, and mind serves only to harm others.
Regarding "those who possess both sin and merit":
this refers to when one cultivates merit while the internal mind is impure.
Alternatively, it may involve harming other beings;
this is because such karma in the desire realm is mixed rather than purely wholesome,
and is therefore also termed "impure."
If one discusses sinful actions,
they are coarse and manifest, and thus easily known;
if one discusses mixed karma, however, it is not so.
The commonalities and differences between [this] and the practice of pure merit are somewhat obscure and difficult to discern.
That is to say, regarding the cultivation of merit, if one relies on its external appearances,
the actions performed out of faith and devotion within those matters are all the same;
however, if one relies on the internal mind, there is the distinction of whether it is for oneself or for others.
Their respective aspirations differ;
their diligence and coarseness are unequal.
This is because, while their cultivation of merit is outwardly identical, it is inwardly different.
Therefore, there are two distinct types of karma: pure and mixed.
If one can discipline the mind with compassion and pity for all beings, then whatever actions one performs will all become great goodness.
If one does not maintain mindfulness while observing signs and cultivating merit—
being coarse within and subtle without— one merely accomplishes mixed karma,
which accords with the sentiments of the foolish.
Although it is said that this pertains to past lives, in reality it contradicts the Path and is not pure merit;
for when cultivating merit, one does not contemplate the emptiness of birth.
I, however, constantly practice pervasively through all three natures;
all my activities correspond with inversion and are of a nature that is falsely grasped.
Therefore, this contradicts the Way;
for with an unwholesome mind, one seeks much worldly reward and also seeks much fame.
Therefore, it is not pure merit.
Because ordinary people are largely deluded regarding the mixture of the pure and the mundane,
I shall now briefly discuss this one-sidedly.
This causes people to recognize their conduct:
first, the discussion of mixed karma;
afterwards, the clarification of pure merit.
However, among various mixed karmas, there are naturally coarse and subtle types.
The coarse ones constitute evil deeds that also harm others;
the subtle ones are performed for oneself alone, seeking only worldly retribution.
First, we shall discuss the coarse and impure. Regarding giving,
there may be those who give wealth acquired through unrighteous means.
If one steals another's property to use for giving,
this will result in a retribution of constant decline and depletion.
Likewise, if one feels regret after having given, the fruit obtained will be the same.
Therefore, the *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra* states:
"If a person, having already given a gift, gives rise to a mind of regret;
or if they take the wealth of others by force and hold it as an act of giving."
Although such a person may acquire wealth in the future, it will always be dissipated and never accumulate.
Or, they may even cause harm to others while practicing giving;
that is to say, when giving, they do not maintain right mindfulness of what is wholesome.
One may give rise to anger or conceit,
and shall consequently fall into the evil realms.
Although one may receive the retribution of merit, it is experienced specifically within the animal realm and does not induce birth among humans or devas.
Thus, a verse from the *Vibhaṅga-karmavipāka-sūtra* says:
Practicing great generosity, yet impetuous and prone to anger,
failing to rely on right mindfulness— later, having assumed the body of a great nāga,
he was able to practice great generosity, yet remained haughty and looked down upon others with contempt.
From these karmic actions, the mighty garuḍa is born.
If one seeks worldly rewards by cultivating merit,
it is like the time when one gives away wealth.
They seek a reward for themselves;
or they renounce out of fear that their body and wealth are impermanent;
or they seek exclusively their own benefit for the sake of fame.
This is not compassion for the sake of relieving poverty and suffering;
it is like a commercial transaction and is not a purely wholesome deed.
Therefore, it is called "impure giving" in the sūtras.
As stated in the *Śata-śāstra*:
"To give as an act of almsgiving is called impure;
such giving is like a commercial transaction."
Therefore, there are two kinds of retribution.
Immediate retribution refers to such things as reputation, honor, and affection.
Regarding "retribution in a future life": this refers to wealth, status, and so forth in subsequent existences,
which is termed "impure giving."
For example, it is like a merchant who travels far to another land;
although he carries various goods that bring great benefit,
he does not do so out of compassion for sentient beings.
Because it is for the sake of seeking one's own profit,
this karma is impure;
seeking a reward through giving is likewise so.
By this it is proven that there is no genuine compassion;
they seek only their own reputation.
Or if it is for the sake of future retribution,
then even though one may practice extensive giving,
none of it constitutes pure karma.
Because karma is not pure, the retribution obtained is not refined.
Thus, the *Vibhaṅga-karmavipāka-sūtra* says: "If one gives for the sake of being born in heaven..."
Or again, they may seek fame and renown;
they may give out of gratitude for favors received or in hope of a reward;
or they may practice giving out of fear.
The fruits obtained will not be pure;
what one receives will be mostly coarse and harsh.
Such is the case with the practice of giving.
The same applies to all other wholesome qualities such as the precepts, which are likewise impure.
Thus, the *Śata-śāstra* says:
"One who maintains the precepts with impurity..."
Seeking a pleasant retribution for oneself,
if one maintains the precepts seeking rebirth in the heavens,
one will enjoy themselves with celestial maidens.
If one among humans is wealthy and noble, enjoying the pleasures of the five senses,
yet for the sake of sexual desire acts like a deceptive person.
To harbor internal desire for the forms of others while outwardly feigning intimacy and kindness is called impurity;
this refers to the external, subtle mental impurity of maintaining the precepts.
As Ānanda spoke this verse to Nanda:
"Just as two rams butt each other, Advancing only to retreat again,
So too is the matter of your maintaining the precepts for the sake of desire."
When one gives with a joyful mind solely for the benefit of others,
the merit obtained is great.
Furthermore, regarding the recipients of the gift, there are those who are poor and those who are sick.
There may be those who understand the Dharma yet lack what they require;
if one gives to them so that they may obtain benefit and increase their wholesome qualities,
and if the gift is appropriate such that much merit is gained, then [the giving is fruitful].
Therefore, the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* states:
"The Buddha praised five kinds of giving,
through which one obtains immeasurable merit."
That which is called giving to those who have come from afar,
to those who are departing for distant places,
and to those who are ill and emaciated.
When there is famine,
one gives food and drink;
one gives to those who know the Dharma.
Thus, these five kinds of giving yield blessings in the present life.
This giving is such that it may appropriately yield abundant blessings in the present;
it differs from giving for the sake of fame, which, though not restricted to improper objects, fails to obtain pure retribution despite much sacrifice.
Furthermore, regarding one who rejoices in the giving of others:
compared to those who commit extremely coarse unwholesome deeds,
even their minor transgressions may be termed "wholesome."
If one aspires for detachment from desire or acts solely for the sake of others,
such mixed karma constitutes a fault. Therefore,
the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
Coarse people commit coarse transgressions;
subtle people commit subtle transgressions.
Therefore, these mixed karmas involve both offenses and merits acting together.
The aspiration of the mind is not purely impure karma.
Thus far, it has been clarified that sin and merit are practiced together;
this concludes the discussion on the impure mixed karma of the desire realm.
If one discusses mixed karma, it can be understood by reversing the preceding [explanation].
Thus, the *Śata-śāstra* says:
"Regarding pure giving..."
If one loves, respects, and benefits others, one will likewise obtain great merit.
Thus, a verse in the *Karmaprajñapti-sūtra* says:
"If there is a person who is poor, having no wealth to give as alms..."
When seeing others practicing generosity, one should give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*).
The karmic reward of this sympathetic joy is equal to that of the act of giving itself and no different.
Furthermore, a verse from the *Puruṣa-śāstra* says:
The merit of giving with a compassionate heart to a single person is as vast as the earth;
the reward for giving everything for one’s own sake is like a mustard seed.
To rescue a single person from calamity is superior to all other forms of giving.
Though the many stars possess light, they do not equal that of a single bright moon;
likewise, when ordinary beings create their own sins and merits,
they do not understand that cause and effect, as well as good and evil, lack inherent nature.
This constitutes delusion regarding phenomena and grasping at their intrinsic nature;
thus one is perpetually bound to the three realms of existence.
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
For example, a fly has no place it will not alight upon, except for a flame;
the craving and attachment of sentient beings is just like this.
They are attached to all wholesome and unwholesome dharmas,
even up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
they are attached to everything, except for the great fire of the emptiness of intrinsic nature of the *prajñāpāramitā*.

By this evidence it is known that those who lack the nature of good or evil and perpetually cycle through the five realms of existence are precisely those sentient beings who possess no Buddha-nature.
This concludes the brief clarification that ordinary beings’ two types of conduct—sinful and meritorious—are delusions regarding phenomena and their grasping at intrinsic nature.
The relevant sutras and treatises are hereby finished.
3. Section on Sinful Conduct. Third, the section on sinful conduct states:
This clarifies that when the Noble One speaks of "faulty conduct" with reference to subsequent meritorious actions,
it refers merely to the defilement of the object through false views.
By fixating on a self and others and becoming attached to what is favorable or unfavorable,
one causes both oneself and others to commit evil karma.
Therefore, a sutra says:
Greed neither arises nor ceases;
it cannot afflict the mind.
If a person possesses the notion of a self, [then greed will arise].
Furthermore, those who behold [this] will,
out of greed and desire, enter into hell.
Therefore, although there are no separate objects apart from the mind,
due to that deluded state of mind, one forcibly perceives them and gives rise to defilement,
just as one experiences various attachments and aversions upon seeing objects in a dream.
To say that those dreamers perceive reality and not falsehood is logically incorrect;
in truth, there are no external objects, and it is merely the deluded vision of the mind.
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
Just as in a dream, one experiences joy despite the absence of anything joyful,
anger despite the absence of anything provoking anger,
and fear despite the absence of anything to be feared.
The sentient beings of the three realms are likewise.
Because they sleep in ignorance, they become angry when they ought not to be angry, and so forth.
Thus, one knows that although there are no separate objects external to the mind.
It is said that based on their deluded emotions and false perceptions, they give rise to defilement;
although there are no phenomena such as hells existing outside the mind,
when their evil karma matures, they falsely perceive themselves undergoing suffering.
As the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states:
"The Yama-wardens are not sentient beings;
yet when sinners see them, they take them to be sentient beings."
Holding flaming iron tongs in his hand,
once that hell-being’s evil karma is exhausted and his life there has ended, he shall no longer behold the jailers of Yama.
Why is this? Because they do not belong to the category of sentient beings.
It is like a lamp: when the oil and the wick are exhausted, the light ceases to exist.
When karma is exhausted, it is likewise;
one no longer sees the jailers of Yama.
It is just as when the light of the sun appears in Jambudvīpa, there is no more darkness.
When their evil karma is exhausted, the jailers of Yama are likewise so;
their evil eyes and evil speech, which appeared according to the characteristics of sentient beings,
and their terrifying forms shall all be completely extinguished.
Just as when a painted wall is destroyed, the painting also perishes accordingly, so too is it with the wall of evil karma;
one no longer beholds the terrifying forms of the jailers of Yama.
Based on this textual evidence,
those sentient beings who ought to suffer due to their evil karma naturally perceive a hell within what is actually non-existent.
Question: As for those who see the hells, the hell-wardens,
tigers, wolves, and so forth that they perceive might be illusory visions.
In that place of hell, Yama presides therein to judge all the sinners;
such is the realm.
Why do you say they do not exist?
The answer is:
even that perception of a jailer is a false perception.
It is simply that the evil karma of the sinner has permeated their mind, causing it to undergo a transformation;
thus they falsely perceive what does not exist.
In reality, there are no hells nor Yama within.
Therefore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"Just as there is no master of hell within the hells,
yet the sentient beings in hell [suffer] based on their own natural karma."
Seeing the lord of hell and various forms of suffering, he gives rise to the thought and perceives: "This is the place of hell;
this is the time of night."
This is daytime; yet because of my evil karma, I see dogs and crows,
or I am seen being crushed by mountains.
Based on this textual evidence,
good and evil permeate the mind,
causing the mind to perceive things differently.
In reality, there are no hells.
Therefore, although there are no hells external to the mind,
when evil karma is actualized, one forcibly and delusively perceives them as such.
Question: Since this retribution for unwholesome karma is not a virtuous matter,
why not simply teach what is wholesome so that it may be practiced?
"Why is it necessary to speak of suffering and karma according to one's circumstances?
He replied,
"The dharmas of cause and effect for good and evil must correspond."
If one does not state that greed and the like are faults,
by what means can it be shown that giving and the like are wholesome?
If one does not proclaim that the three miserable realms are suffering...
Without this means, one cannot manifest the bliss of humans, devas, and so forth; therefore,
it is necessary to explain the transgressions of ordinary beings,
so that people may recognize them, develop weary detachment, and turn toward what is wholesome.
If those of dull faculties,
upon hearing of this suffering and karma, give rise to revulsion and detachment,
they immediately seek worldly pleasures.
Therefore, one turns the mind and cultivates various meritorious deeds.
If one possesses sharp faculties,
upon hearing of these karmas of suffering, they give rise to weary detachment.
One immediately seeks liberation.
Because of this transformation of the mind, one is able to cultivate the contemplation of the path;
thus, within the midst of afflictions, one gives rise to the cause for emergence.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"All afflictions are the seeds of the Buddha.
Thus, one knows that they are the root of revulsion toward suffering and karma, and the condition for the arising of wholesome states.
Therefore, it must be explained;
for if these evil karmas and transgressions were not explained,
sentient beings would remain ignorant of them and would continue to practice them without interruption.
Although one may describe various faults and evils according to one's perceptions and views,
in reality there are no karmic sufferings apart from the mind;
for consciousness alone exists without external objects, and the essence of the mind is eternally pure.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"Although one speaks of the faults of sensual desire,
one does not perceive any phenomenon that is worthy of being desired."
Although he speaks of the faults of anger,
he does not perceive any phenomenon that is worthy of being angry toward; although he speaks of the faults of delusion, [he does not perceive any phenomenon that is worthy of being deluded about].
He knows all dharmas without delusion or obstruction.
Although he manifests to sentient beings the suffering of fear from falling into the three evil realms,
he does not perceive the characteristics of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, or animals.
By means of this textual evidence,
one knows that the causes and effects of virtuous and non-virtuous actions exist solely within the mind and have no external reality;
yet ordinary, deluded people do not understand this.
According to the circumstances and through skillful means,
one must explain the suffering of karma;
thus far, these have been the two gates.
According to the ultimate teaching, the essence of transgression is explained as being truly non-existent;
there is nothing distinct that can be destroyed.
Because the ignorant have not yet understood,
it is necessary to definitively explain their transgressions;
this is a separate clarification of how the ignorant are deluded regarding the truth and produce false interpretations.
Therefore, it is necessary to definitively explain the nature of unwholesome actions.
Section Four: On Wholesome Actions (Puṇyakriyāvastu). The commentary states:
This clarifies the practitioner of wholesome actions.
Regarding the aforementioned unwholesome actions, this is called "meritorious conduct.
First, it clarifies that when ordinary beings cultivate wholesome states of the desire realm,
they merely cause a distracted mind to cultivate various forms of worldly merit.
Karma that is definitely produced in the lower realm is called "karma of the desire realm" (*kāmadhātu-karman*).
It arises within all five destinies (*gati*).
First, regarding its description in relation to the hells:
According to the Abhidharma,
beings in the hells also possess three types of wholesome karma;
these are the three wholesome roots of the mental faculty.
This is merely accomplished and not manifest;
because this is a difficult place where the Dharma is rarely heard and one must rely on reflection to pursue the path,
there is no manifestation.
If we discuss roots of goodness acquired at birth,
they exist even in the hells;
for example, King Rāvaṇa (Śrīyaśas) killed five hundred brahmins and was reborn in hell.
When faith arises, one is born in the Land of Ambrosia (Amṛta).
Thus, we know that [this refers to] actual manifestation (*samudācāra*). If one follows the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*:
It is also taught that there are instances of wholesome conduct in the hells;
although they lack the power to exert effort through skillful means to cultivate and attain the Noble Path,
they nonetheless give rise to innate wholesome roots and produce wholesome states.
This means that since beginningless time, sentient beings have practiced worldly faith, diligence, mindfulness, and so forth,
and have not yet given rise to wrong views that deny cause and effect.
This wholesome [state] does not perish;
it is acquired upon birth, and is thus called "wholesome acquired at birth" (upapatti-pratilambhika-kuśala).
Based on these roots of goodness, wholesome states of mind arise.
If there are strong conditions for the ripening of past karma,
the Great Sage manifests transformations to cause suffering to cease.
It explains that one attains the cultivation of skillful means through the Dharma of the Path;
furthermore, secondly, even animals such as nāgas can cultivate goodness,
as stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
When the Buddha taught this meaning,

81. Chapter on the Desire to Conceal (71). Chapter Eighty-one: The Desire to Conceal. This consists of two sections: Section One, the Five Desires (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*); Section Two, the Five Hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*). 1. Section on the Five Desires. This section contains four sub-sections: Sub-section One, Explaining the Intent; Sub-section Two, Bondage by Desire; Sub-section Three, Obstructions of Desire; Sub-section Four, Rebuking Desire. 1.1. Sub-section Explaining the Intent. First, I have privately examined the sūtras and śāstras.
Practitioners cultivating the Path all say that the five desires are the root obstacle to the Path;
if one does not train in their abandonment, there is no way to realize sainthood.
If one wishes to know the fundamental [conditions], they are briefly described as threefold:
first, the five internal sense faculties;
second, the five external sense objects.
The five consciousnesses arise from these three;
because of these three, one is able to give rise to defiled desire.
Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
Good son, it is like a wild elephant whose mind has not yet been tamed;
if someone mounts it, it will not go according to his will.
Just as one who has departed from towns and cities to dwell in desolate places cannot properly restrain themselves,
so too it is with these five faculties.
They lead people away from the city of Nirvana and bring them to the wilderness of birth and death,
O son of good family.
For example, just as a sycophantic minister instructs a king to commit evil,
so too are the five sense-faculties like sycophantic ministers;
they constantly instruct sentient beings to create immeasurable evils.
For example, just as a wicked son who does not obey the instructions of his teachers, elders,
and parents will commit every kind of evil,
so too it is with one who fails to discipline the five sense faculties.
They do not accept the kind words, instructions, and admonitions of their teachers and elders,
and there is no evil they will not commit. Good son.
Ordinary worldlings do not restrain their five sense faculties;
they are constantly harmed by the marauders of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts,
just as enemies and thieves harm virtuous people.
Furthermore, the *Sutra of the Bequeathed Teaching* states:
"The calamities of the thieves of the five faculties bring misfortune that extends through successive generations;
their harm is exceedingly grave."
One must not fail to be cautious.
Therefore, the wise person restrains them and does not follow after them.
One should treat them as if they were thieves;
even if one were to release them,
they would all not last for long.
One observes its wearing away and extinction. Now,
as for the term "canopy" (lun gai),
it carries the meaning of providing shade and protection.
That is to say, they obstruct the practitioner, causing their will and nature to become dull and heavy;
they obscure concentration and wisdom, and cause the virtuous to vanish.
Because they are obstacles to the cultivation of the Right Path, they are called "hindrances" (nīvaraṇa).
Therefore, the Abhidharma-śāstra states:
"This is indeed that which prevents wholesome qualities from becoming manifest;
this is the meaning of 'hindrance' (nīvaraṇa)."
They obscure the mind and obstruct all wholesome qualities so that they cannot proceed;
thus, they have the meaning of "hindrances" (*nīvaraṇa*).
As for the five desires mentioned previously:
These five hindrances arise from the five external sense objects;
they are produced from within the five internal faculties.
2. Section on the Bonds of Desire (Kāma-bandhana). Second part. It is stated:
Regarding the discussion of the five desires, once their roots exist, the five desires are then aroused.
They bind sentient beings so that they cannot attain liberation.
Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
"Ordinary persons are bound by the five desires."
He will allow Māra Pāpīyān to take him away at his own will,
just as that hunter seized the monkey, carried it on his shoulder, and returned home.
O son of good family!
For example, just as a king dwells in his own realm with peace and happiness of body and mind,
yet encounters manifold sufferings when he enters another's realm, so it is with all sentient beings.
If one can abide within one's own domain, one will attain peace and happiness;
if one enters another's domain,
one will encounter evil Māras and undergo various sufferings and afflictions.
One's own domain refers to the four foundations of mindfulness;
another's domain refers to...
This refers to the five desires.
The five desires are the forms,
sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles found upon the bodies of men and women.
This refers to the meaning of longing for the five desires (*pañca-kāma-guṇa*).
Attachment to the five sense objects is called "desire" (*kāma*).
Furthermore, the objects conditioned by the contact of the mental consciousness are called "dharma-dust" (dharmāyatana).
These six dusts are not merely called "dust" in name only.
Furthermore, wherever one goes, one incurs the reputation of being a wicked thief.
Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
"Just as six great thieves can plunder all the wealth and treasures of the people."
The six objects of sensory desire, which are like wicked thieves, are also like this;
they can plunder all the wholesome wealth of sentient beings,
just as when the six great thieves enter a person's house.
It can then plunder all that currently belongs to the household,
making no distinction between the good and the bad,
causing even those of immense wealth to suddenly fall into poverty.
These thieves of the six sense objects are likewise:
once they enter the faculties of a person, they are able to plunder all wholesome dharmas;
when wholesome dharmas are exhausted, [the person falls].
Destitute and exposed,
one becomes an icchantika; therefore,
the bodhisattva contemplates the six sense objects as being like six great bandits.
3. Section on the Obstacles of Desire. Third in the section on the obstacles of desire, it is stated:
Regarding the discussion of the faults of desire, this refers to the five sensual desires as the depraved Māra and the six sense-objects as the evil bandits.
The Buddha judged these to be false delusions because they obscure and obstruct the Buddha-nature.
As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
Although the five consciousnesses of sentient beings are not of a single moment,
they are nevertheless outflowing (sāsrava) and moreover characterized by perversion and inversion.
They increase the various outflows for the sake of all ordinary beings;
they grasp at form and so on, up to grasping at consciousness.
Because of this attachment to form, a mind of craving arises.
Because they give rise to a mind of craving, they are bound by form,
and so on, up to being bound by consciousness.
Because they are thus bound, they cannot attain liberation.
Regarding birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, and all great sufferings and afflictions,
it is further said:
"If there is a bodhisattva who claims for himself that his precepts are pure..."
Although he does not associate with women, nor engage in conversation or jesting with them,
nor listen to their voices,
yet when he sees a man pursuing a woman, [he feels aversion].
Or, when seeing a woman following after a man,
he immediately gives rise to greedy attachment;
in this way, the bodhisattva accomplishes the dharma of desire.
They violate the pure precepts,
defile the holy life, and cause their moral discipline to become defiled and impure.
One cannot be said to be fully endowed with pure precepts.
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"The bodhisattva contemplates various forms of impurity."
Among all forms of decay, the decay of a woman is the most grievous.
Even weapons, fire, thunderbolts, lightning, enemies,
and venomous serpents may yet be approached for a brief moment.
Women are stingy, envious, wrathful, deceitful, and depraved;
they are quarrelsome, greedy, and jealous, and thus should not be approached. Why is this?
Women and those of small mind have shallow hearts and meager wisdom;
they desire only intimacy and do not regard wealth, nobility, wisdom, virtue, or renown.
Those who exclusively practice desire and evil destroy the roots of goodness in others;
they are bound with shackles and fetters and confined in prisons.
Though such bonds are said to be difficult to untie, they are still relatively easy to open.
The female fetter binds people so that their defilement is deeply rooted;
there is no way to escape it.
It is the most severe among all maladies.
As the Buddha said in verse:
"Better to have glowing iron Twisted and turned within one's eyes, Than with a defiled mind to gaze upon female forms,
Smiling with coquettish gestures, Conceiving thoughts of pride and attachment."
Turning her face and casting sidelong glances, she speaks with sweet words while harboring jealousy and anger;
her gait is seductive and defiling, intended to delude others. Within the net of lustful desire, all people—whether sitting, lying, walking, or standing—are submerged.
With sidelong looks of artful coquetry, she ensnares those of meager wisdom and foolish minds.
One who is intoxicated may be made to hold a sword against an enemy; this can still be overcome.
But a female thief who harms others—this cannot be restrained.
A venomous serpent may still be grasped by hand; but the passions of a woman that delude men—these must not be touched.
That which a person of wisdom should not look upon—if one wishes to observe it, one should do so as one would toward a mother or a sister.
Even if one gazes at it with careful scrutiny, it is filled with impurities;
the fire of lust is not extinguished, but is instead incinerated by it.
Since this is the case for visible forms,
the same applies by analogy to the remaining objects— odors, tastes, tangibles, and so forth.
Thus it has been for all sentient beings since beginningless time.
That they sink forever into birth and death and are unable to escape is truly due to female form;
bound by it, they are difficult to release.
Blind and lacking the eye of wisdom,
they see the pit of birth and death and fall into it;
now, both monastics and laypeople alike fail to contemplate the afflictions of desire.
Having galloped away just now,
on what day shall I return to avoid this transgression?
The mind is constantly defiled and cannot be relinquished even for a moment;
since even the precepts do not remain, how can there be concentration and wisdom?
How can one contemplate the Buddha-nature?
Thus, a verse in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
"Committing evil, one does not receive the retribution immediately, Just as milk does not instantly become curd,
Or like embers covered by ashes— The fool lightly treads upon them."
4. The Section on Rebuking Desire (Kāma-nindā-varga). Fourth: As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the practitioner should rebuke the five desires, saying:
"Alas for sentient beings!"
Constantly tormented by the five desires,
they seek them without ceasing;
they are about to fall into a great pit.
When one obtains them, they only become more severe,
like roasting a scab with fire;
the five desires are of no benefit.
Like a dog gnawing at a bone,
the five desires increase contention;
like birds competing for meat.
The five desires burn a person like holding a torch against the wind;
the five desires harm a person.
Like treading upon a venomous snake,
the five desires are without reality;
they are like what is obtained in a dream.
The five desires are not long-lasting;
they are like a temporary loan for a mere moment.
Yet worldly people, deluded by ignorance, greedily cling to these five desires.
They do not abandon them until death,
whereby they undergo immeasurable suffering in future lives;
these five desires provide but a momentary pleasure when obtained.
To lose [the opportunity] at the proper time is a great suffering.
It is like licking honey from a blade; the one who licks it craves the sweetness and does not realize it will wound their tongue.
Such is the nature of the five desires.
These are called form, sound, smell, taste, and touch.
These five objects are the primary obstacles for those of the Chan school;
if one wishes to cultivate meditative concentration, one should abandon them all.
First is the refutation of the faults of desire for form (*rūpa*).
For example, King Bimbisāra, because of his attachment to form,
entered the territory of an enemy state with his own body.
He was alone in the chamber of the courtesan Āmrapālī. King Udayana,
due to his attachment to sensual beauty, cut off the hands and feet of five hundred rishis.
Through various causes and conditions such as these,
this is called the condemnation of the faults of desire for form.
Second, the condemnation of the faults of desire for sound:
Just as the characteristic of sound does not abide,
being extinguished as soon as it is briefly heard,
foolish people do not understand that the characteristic of sound is impermanent, subject to change, and lost.
Therefore, one falsely gives rise to attachment and delight within sounds;
one recollects and becomes attached to sounds that have already passed away.
It is like the five hundred sages who dwelt in the mountains.
The Kinnarī women were bathing in a pool within the Snowy Mountains when they heard the sound of his singing;
they immediately lost their meditative concentration,
their hearts became intoxicated and wild, and they could not restrain themselves.
One loses all merits and subsequently falls into the evil realms.
A person of wisdom contemplates the arising and ceasing of sound;
as the preceding and succeeding moments do not coexist, there is no characteristic that can reach another.
One who understands in this way will not be defiled by attachment. Such a person—
Even the music of the devas cannot disturb it,
let alone the voices of humans.
For such various reasons as these.
This is called the fault of desiring the sound of scolding.
Therefore, the treatise says:
"For example, when five hundred rishis were flying through the air, they heard the singing voice of a kinnarī."
Their minds became intoxicated and deluded, and they all lost their supernormal powers (ṛddhi-pāda),
falling to the ground all at once,
just as when the Śrāvakas heard the sound of the Kinnara king Tuṇḍurumanta playing the lute and singing.
They praised the Buddha by means of the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
