The reason why delusions regarding the principles differ is truly because sentient beings, since time immemorial, have transmigrated through birth and death, being unable to sever outflows and failing to attain supramundane fruits;
this results in the ten afflictions (*daśa-kleśa*) becoming the very obstacles to karma.
The Dharma of the Four Noble Truths is the principle that constitutes the object of obstruction.
Regarding the "Four Truths":
first is suffering (*duḥkha*).
Second, accumulation;
third, cessation;
fourth, the path.
Regarding the detailed explanation of the sequence of cause and effect within the Four Noble Truths and the similarities and differences between the Great and Small Vehicles,
I fear that the text would become too cumbersome,
so I shall not describe it here. For now, I will briefly explain their names so that one may understand cause and effect.
The principle that arising and ceasing are impermanent is in truth suffering;
that which oppresses the practitioner is called the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).
"Truth" (*satya*) has the meaning of reality.
Since this is examined and found to be without error,
it is called a "truth" (satya).
The meaning of the three subsequent truths is explained in the same manner.
All contaminated wholesome and unwholesome states are capable of producing results;
by principle, the accumulation of these causes is termed the Truth of Origination (samudaya-satya).
The state wherein afflictions are exhausted is termed Cessation (nirodha).
In truth, non-arising is called the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
Contemplating this principle to remove obstructions is truly not in vain;
it is called the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*).
If one discusses the Four Noble Truths with respect to a single individual,
it means that this body and mind, along with their suffering and pleasure as aspects of tainted retribution,
constitute the Truth of Suffering.
If one does not contemplate the principles regarding the arising of good and evil,
up to and including the eight dhyānas,
this constitutes the truth of origination (samudaya-satya).
If one contemplates the arising and ceasing of body and mind as being without self,
this very wisdom of contemplation is the Truth of the Path.
Therefore, when the path-knowledge perceives non-self,
the point at which the afflictions are severed is the Truth of Cessation.
Regarding the statement "delusion concerning principle," the treatises offer differing explanations.
According to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, it says:

The view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) are deluded only regarding the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*). This means that ordinary worldlings all grasp at the retribution of suffering as being a self;
therefore, the view of a self-identity arises taking the truth of suffering as its object.
Based on the retribution of bodily suffering, one calculates it as either annihilation or permanence;
therefore, the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) also arises in delusion regarding suffering.
Thus, the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* says:
Because these two views arise from the fruit of their respective positions,
they are exclusively delusions regarding the Truth of Suffering.
Generally, one reckons that "sin and merit are what I have created."
One does not take wholesome or unwholesome karma as being the self;
therefore, the view of a self-identity does not rely upon or arise from that accumulation.
Knowing that the accumulation is not the self is what is meant by not being deluded regarding the accumulation.
The view of extremes does not rely upon the body, nor does it rely upon origination;
furthermore, it does not take cessation or the path as a self, nor does it conceive of them as annihilation or permanence.
The principle is the same for all [the other views].

Therefore, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) are said to be delusions regarding the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), as they rely solely upon the designation of "suffering. As for the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), it is a delusion regarding both suffering and the path.
This refers to a foolish person who, upon merely hearing such an explanation, [misunderstands].
They do not understand the teaching that diligent asceticism can sever birth and death; thus,
they exert their minds day and night.
Only by diligently contemplating suffering and emptiness can one sever birth and death; thus,
it is said that within the realm of phenomena, the body of suffering is itself the Way.
Not knowing that bodily suffering is not the Noble Path,
one thus gives rise to the delusion of clinging to precepts regarding the Truth of Suffering;
or, some do not take bodily suffering to be the Path.
To directly grasp meritorious practices such as the precepts and so forth as the path,
and to take that which is merely a cause for the accumulation [of merit] as the path—
this is called the delusion regarding the truth of the path.
In reality, ordinary fools do not recognize the cause of origination;
they falsely grasp it as the path,
which must therefore be a delusion regarding origination.
However, because that deluded mind does not reckon meritorious conduct as the cause for accumulation,
it subsequently transforms into the Path;
therefore, it cannot be called "delusion regarding accumulation."
Those who do not reckon suffering as the path,
yet take suffering to be the path,
are therefore said to be deluded regarding suffering.
Therefore, regarding the clinging to precepts and observances,
there are those who are deluded about suffering and those who are deluded about the path.
One is not deluded regarding the origin [of suffering].
Cessation is the noble fruit sought by sentient beings.
One does not grasp at the cessation of delusions as the causal practice for the Path; therefore,
the clinging to precepts and observances is not termed "delusion regarding cessation."
If one discusses wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*),
these three all universally delude regarding the Four Noble Truths;
that is to say, as for wrong view:
To slander the existence of cause and effect encompasses both the ordinary and the noble; therefore,
this constitutes universal delusion.
If one discusses the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*),
taking one's own karmic retribution as supreme constitutes delusion regarding suffering (*duḥkha*).
To regard worldly meritorious deeds as supreme is called delusion regarding the origin [of suffering].
To take rebirth in the Brahma heavens or the realm of non-perception as nirvana is likewise so called.
To call this "delusion regarding cessation" means that one takes the path described by those who cling to precepts and observances as being supreme;
this is called "delusion regarding the path."
Therefore, the grasping at views is universally deluded regarding the four truths. As for doubt,
it concerns both ordinary beings and noble ones, as well as causes and fruits.
Not knowing whether [it] exists or not,
one gives rise to doubt and fails to reach a decision;
thus, one is likewise deluded regarding the four [truths].
The five views and doubt previously explained are exclusively delusions regarding the principle of the Truths (satya);
they are not termed delusions regarding phenomena (vastu).
Because one is deluded regarding the principle,
when one contemplates and perceives that principle, one knows there is no self or person;
only then does one sever the mind of "I" and realize the wisdom of contemplation.
One is able to sever the afflictions, the causes and effects of ordinary beings, and the suffering and origin that are not the Path.
Only by recognizing and contemplating this as the Path does one then sever the clinging to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). One correctly recognizes the cessation of the Path as supreme.
One does not regard that which is tainted as superior or excellent;
knowing the world is to be reviled, one then severs the grasping to views.
By seeing the Four Truths, one gives rise to neither doubt nor slander.
Only through the certainty of realization can one sever perverse doubt; therefore,
the [afflictions of] self-view, views regarding extremes, precept-and-vow adherence, views,
and perverse doubt arise from delusion regarding principle and are themselves severed by seeing that principle.

One does not take the objects of the sensory realms, such as forms and sounds, to be the basis for conceiving of a self, a person, or for reckoning in terms of annihilationism and eternalism. Therefore,
although one correctly cognizes objects such as forms and sounds,
one does not sever the mind of "I" nor even the underlying tendencies of doubt.
If one discusses the four underlying tendencies of greed, hatred, delusion, and pride,
they universally obstruct both the paths of seeing and cultivation, as they are all delusions regarding both principle and phenomena.
That is to say, if it arises based on views, it is called delusion regarding principle;
if it arises based on phenomena, it is called delusion regarding phenomena.
As for that which arises based on views:
If one discusses its nature as greed,
it is precisely named "greed" (rāga);
because of this attachment to the view of self (satkāyadṛṣṭi), the mind becomes increasingly deluded.
When one contemplates the emptiness of beings and realizes there is no self,
one then comes to loathe the view of self;
thus, this craving is severed.
As for their anger: when they possess the notion of a self,
hearing the teaching of non-self gives rise to resentment.
Later, when one contemplates non-self and realizes there is no person,
one rejoices upon hearing the teaching on the emptiness of arising;
thus, when the principle is perceived, that anger is severed.
Based on views, delusion arises such that one does not recognize the faults of those views;
later, when one perceives the truth, that delusion is severed.
Based on views, conceit arises, whereby one relies on those views to hold oneself in high esteem.
When one later perceives the truth, that pride is severed.
Therefore, those [afflictions] such as craving that arise based on views are likewise delusions regarding the truth.
It is only upon seeing the principle that [false views] are severed; they arise based on other views.
Other cases may be understood by analogy with this.
Regarding the statement that greed and the like arise based on objects:
this refers to the sensory objects of form, sound, fragrance, and so forth;
it is upon these that greed arises, becoming entangled and difficult to sever.
Therefore, even when one perceives the truth, there are still [afflictions] that have not been severed;
subsequently, by further practicing the path, they are gradually eliminated through repeated cultivation.
This applies to all cases where anger, pride, ignorance, and so forth depend upon specific objects.
This clarifies that the ten proclivities (daśa-ānuśaya) differ in their delusions regarding the principles [of the truths].
There are ten types of delusion concerning suffering (duḥkha),
and eight types of delusion concerning the path (mārga).
Regarding delusion concerning origination and cessation, there are seven latent dispositions (anuśaya) for each;
regarding delusion concerning phenomena, there are four.
Altogether, there are thirty-six.
This explains the mind of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
If one discusses the mind of an ordinary person in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), it possesses thirty-one [mental factors],
because anger (*vyāpāda*) is absent there.
Within the five categories of practice (*pañca-kṛtya*), one is excluded from each.
The four truths and the path of cultivation are termed the five categories of practice;
therefore, there are only thirty-one proclivities (*anuśaya*).
The ordinary minds of the formless realm are likewise thirty-one.
When considering all three realms together,
there are ninety-eight in total.
There are eighty-eight [afflictions] regarding delusion concerning the principle of the Four Noble Truths;
there are ten types combined regarding delusion concerning the phenomena of the three realms.
This is a brief explanation based on the Abhidharma.
According to the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, all ten latent afflictions (*anuśaya*) possess the nature of grasping (*upādāna*),
as they all thoroughly penetrate the principle;
that is, they are deluded regarding the emptiness of the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) of the Four Noble Truths.
Therefore, when one contemplates the truths as being empty of intrinsic nature in their entirety,
the severing of the coarse grasping at intrinsic nature is called the Path of Seeing;
the subsequent severing of the subtle [grasping] is called the Path of Cultivation.
This is called the ten proclivities (daśa-anuśaya), which differ according to their delusion regarding the principles [of reality].
Section Four: Severing Obstructions. The commentary states:
Regarding these ten proclivities of affliction, there are those that are difficult and those that are easy to sever.
Generally speaking, ordinary people inherently possess [the capacity for] cultivation;
now, because we clarify the entry into the Way, we shall describe its difficulties and ease.
However, among the various afflictions of views, they are difficult to recognize but easy to sever.
The four underlying tendencies (anuśaya), such as greed and the rest, are easy to recognize but difficult to eliminate.
As for those views that are difficult to recognize,
this refers to the ordinary person who is constantly deluded.
That which is easy to sever according to principle is exhausted upon seeing that principle;
that is to say, if one can learn to contemplate non-self.
When one first realizes the principle,
it is called the First Fruit; that is,
one has previously severed the eighty-eight latent proclivities (*anuśaya*).
However, regarding the initial vision of the truths, there are those of sharp faculties and those of dull faculties. If one possesses sharp faculties,
they contemplate all phenomena as a whole.
All are conventionally designated and devoid of intrinsic nature;
one perceives neither self nor person.
Within a single thought-moment, one cuts off the eighty-eight [delusions].
This single moment of thought is called the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*).
For those of dull faculties,
the Four Truths are observed separately.
The eighty-eight afflictions (*āsrava*) are gradually severed in successive stages.
Therefore, the *Buddhatva-śāstra* states:
"If a person of sharp faculties, within a single thought-moment, contemplates the Four Noble Truths in their totality."
The eighty-eight afflictions (*āsrava*) are severed all at once;
these are all termed "seeing the truths" (*satyadarśana*).
If a person of dull faculties practices sequential contemplation, [the process is as follows].
Thus, at the initial moment of contemplation, one contemplates suffering and does not perceive the other three truths;
one merely severs the afflictions associated with suffering.
Based on this textual evidence,
one may enter the Way through both the general and specific methods of contemplation.
One must not hold to a biased attachment.
If one relies on the various sutras to teach people how to enter the Path,
they mostly speak directly of contemplating birth-and-death and non-self.
Thus, one severs all fetters and departs from birth and death.
As stated in the *Dìchí jīng* (Bodhisattvabhūmi-sūtra):
"All births in the world arise from attachment to a self."
If one is free from attachment to a self, there will be no worldly place for receiving a body or being born.
Furthermore, as it is said in a sutra:
"A person of the pratyekabuddha lineage does not understand even the names of the dharma-gates of the Four Noble Truths."
Directly observing the conditions of the aggregates as being devoid of self,
one severs all fetters and surpasses the śrāvakas;
within this very practice of the contemplation of non-self, [one proceeds].
Although one does not analytically discern the four truths individually,
when observing in this manner, all four truths are present.
That is to say, the observed impure retribution-body (sāsrava-rūpakāya) arises and perishes from moment to moment.
This principle consists of suffering and its origination. What was previously termed "suffering" is,
when it gives rise to what follows, termed "origination."
When one knows non-self, that is the vision of suffering.
At that time, the non-self state severs the accumulation of phenomena.
That which is severed so as not to arise is the realization of cessation.
This wisdom of contemplation is itself the Noble Path.
Therefore, when one directly contemplates non-self,
one possesses the Four Truths and attains liberation by severing the fetters.
One need not wait for a separate contemplation of the Four Noble Truths before emerging [from concentration].
Therefore, the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* cites a sūtra, stating:
"As it is said in the *Kiṃśuka-sūtra*, there are various causes and conditions for attaining the Path."
One does not attain the Way merely through the Four Noble Truths;
therefore, it is known that entering the Way does not necessarily require separate contemplation.
It can also be attained by contemplating the single practice of non-self as a whole.
If one can clearly perceive that body and mind are without self,
this is the path of seeing (darśana-mārga),
which severs all delusions of view.
However, when the delusions of view are categorized according to the truths,
there are eighty-eight in total for the three realms combined; yet,
if one discusses them from the perspective of a single individual’s deluded mind:
In summary, these consist solely of the five views and doubt.
These six, when compared to delusion (*moha*), are termed "difficult to recognize";
yet when compared to the wise, they are further termed "easy to sever."
This refers to those ordinary, foolish practitioners who cultivate virtue;
they mostly all feel revulsion toward greed, hatred, delusion, and pride,
as well as toward their own sense of self and their attachment to precepts and the like.
One does not perceive this as a fault;
therefore, it is difficult to recognize. Because it is difficult to recognize, [it is hard to abandon].
The Sūtra states that these are grave,
as explained in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*: namely,
the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīla-vrata-parāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*), among others.
Because it is constantly aroused by all sentient beings,
and because it is difficult to awaken from;
just as a disease that constantly manifests is called a "severe illness."
Furthermore, because it is difficult to recognize,
it is also called a "severe illness.
Moreover, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states:
People of the world do not perceive the fault within the attachment to precepts and rituals;
therefore, it causes them to be bound by fetters.
Thus we know that ignorant people of sharp faculties do not recognize it.
Regarding the statement that for those who aspire to wisdom it is "easy to sever," this means that if one trains in contemplating the arising and ceasing of body and mind,
one will come to partially perceive non-self.
When the afflictions are attenuated,
one immediately knows that the wisdom of contemplation is the path for severing the dharmas;
within the mind, the six latent tendencies naturally and eternally cease to exist.
That is to say, when one knows that the arising and ceasing of form and mind are not the person,
then the view of self and the view of extremes are naturally severed;
for by contemplating and seeing the principle, one recognizes the Noble Path.
With right faith and no doubt,
slander will naturally cease;
wisdom is the path.
If precepts and the like were not superior,
there would be no grasping at precepts;
grasping at views would be spontaneously severed.
Therefore, the six underlying tendencies (anuśaya) are difficult to recognize but easy to sever.
Because they are difficult to recognize,
one has been deluded since beginningless time.
Because they are easy to sever, once the principle is understood, they are completely eliminated;
this is unlike greed and other afflictions, which are easy to recognize but difficult to sever.
Because they are easy to recognize,
most people do not cling to them;
because they are difficult to sever, [they remain].
The Anāgāmin also possesses [this].

Therefore, the sharp faculty of wrong view, being deluded regarding principle and characterized by a perverse mind, closely conceals the noble understanding; thus, although the practice is joined, one does not emerge [from saṃsāra].
Unlike greed and other afflictions, which arise from specific objects and merely obstruct the cultivation of insight (*vipaśyanā*) without directly deluding one regarding the principles [of reality],
the minor sages (*śrāvaka*), despite possessing greed and hatred,
are nonetheless able to attain certainty in their understanding of the principles.
Therefore, those wise people who study and practice cultivation should exclusively cultivate contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) to dispel delusion and enter the Path.
Even if one studies contemplative practice but remains dull-witted, such a person is still called an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*).
When one has a slight understanding of principle, there is no longer false grasping;
yet if one does not study to achieve understanding, one will remain perpetually deluded regarding the Way and its teachings.
Thus, although one may cultivate various virtues, one will not eliminate perverse attachments.
Not only are they unable to emerge from their own false attachments,
but they frequently slander the True Dharma and those who practice the Way;
this is because their deluded minds have not yet distinguished between the heterodox and the orthodox.
Not realizing that the other is not in accord with oneself,
one immediately claims oneself to be right and declares the other to be wrong.
Therefore, the minds of those who are deluded lack the path and Dharma;
they mostly rely on worldly virtues and falsely cling to signs as being real.
Thus, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* says:
Householders engage in conflict with one another because they grasp at the five sensory objects;
renunciants do so because they grasp at various differing views.
They engage in disputes with those who have left the household life.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states:
"If a person upholds the precepts and takes them to be purification..."
This is called the fetter of clinging to precepts and observances;
it refers to taking that which is clung to as being truly real.
All other [views] are false speech;
this is called the fetter of adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa-saṃyojana*). These two are the root of strife for those who have left the household life.
This is also called "conforming to the end of suffering.
Furthermore, based on this clinging to precepts and observances, one is able to abandon the Eightfold Noble Path,
[thinking] that this is not the true path.
It is not the path of purification;
it follows after the faults of suffering.
Furthermore, attachment to precepts is a bond for those who have left the household life.
All sensual desires are the fetters of householders.
Furthermore, as for the clinging to precepts and rituals, although one may practice various forms of the ascetic life, [one remains bound].
Emptiness is non-apprehensible.
Furthermore, due to this clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), one can slander the true path and those who practice the true path.
Moreover, clinging to precepts and observances is the basis from which all non-Buddhists give rise to arrogance.
One should form this thought:
"I am superior to other people.
This is known through the evidence of such passages.
The clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) and the like are merely mundane virtues that produce the fruits of birth and death; therefore,
they are called "conforming to suffering" (*duḥkha-anuvartin*),
for they are not the true Dharma of the Path.
Fools are often deluded and cling to false attachments, thereby giving rise to transgressions.
Therefore, although all ten afflictions (*daśa-āsrava*) are unwholesome,
when considering their role as obstacles to the Path and the source from which faults arise, [the first five are the primary concern].
Thus, it is solely the six underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) that take delusion of the mind as their root;
if one cannot sever them,
not only will one fail to emerge [from saṃsāra].
Because of committing a grave offense, one shall be reborn in the evil realms.
This concludes the explanation on the ease or difficulty of severing the ten proclivities (*anuśaya*).
The verse says:
Far distant is the city of the King of Love; towering high is Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.
Karmic bonds form the prison of the three realms; the ten fetters, sharp or dull, bind the necks [of beings].
Following the turbid and evil, one descends to the lower destinies; by severing outflows, one ascends to the highest peak.
Attached to the retribution of pleasure and pain, I feared like an elephant falling into a mountain well.
Longing for the ranks of those transformed, I vowed in every thought to remove the tumor of the mind.
By the grace of past blessings, I encountered the Buddha Śākyamuni; I look up with high admiration to the eminent Great Sage.
Having already shattered the fetter of ignorance, one returns to the true awakening;
bearing this with joy, the profound mind is tranquil.
Wherever one rests, there is no lack of stillness. *Fayuan zhulin*, Volume 72.
*Fayuan zhulin*, Scroll 73, Compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Daoshi of Ximing Monastery. Section 84:
The Ten Evil Deeds (73–79). Section Eighty-Four: The Ten Evil Deeds. This section contains thirteen parts.

Section on Stating the Intent; Section on Karmic Causes; Section on Retributive Results; Section on Killing; Section on Stealing; Section on Sexual Misconduct; Section on False Speech; Section on Harsh Speech; Section on Divisive Speech; Section on Frivolous Speech; Section on Covetousness; Section on Anger; Section on Wrong Views. 1. Section on Stating the Intent (73). First, the Section on Stating the Intent: Alas! How tragic it is that these deluded followers are heavily obstructed.
They cast aside the three chariots and do not mount them;
drifting and sinking in the sea of suffering,
they endure being scorched and withered without weariness.
It is like gadflies and flies delighting in a putrid corpse,
or like moths throwing themselves into a mass of fire;
this is truly because they have been mired in delusion for many kalpas and have undergone every kind of hardship.
Having endured manifold sufferings until now, they continue to be scorched and boiled;
therefore, the Tathāgata’s great compassion cannot bear to abandon them forever,
as He demonstrates both suffering and pleasure to inspire in them a sense of aversion and aspiration.
Therefore, in this chapter, the two courses of action—ten unwholesome deeds and merit—are briefly elucidated. Section Two:
Causes of Karma (73). Section Two on the Causes of Karma: Only ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) create karma, and there are many varieties thereof.
There are instances where the mind accords with body and speech,
and there are also instances where body and speech contradict the mind;
it is based on this that we speak.
All movements of body and speech are instigated by the mind.
If the mind is not good, it can only cause harm to things;
if there is goodness within, one can only accord with merit.
Although benefit and harm differ,
the three types of karma are fundamentally rooted in the mind as their source.
Therefore, the arising of karma differs;
this requires a brief analysis.
As the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states:
There were three people walking together around a stupa:
one was doing so to contemplate the merit of the Buddha’s virtues,
while the second was there for the purpose of theft.
Third is "coolness.
Although their physical actions may be identical, they differ according to the three natures: wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral.
One should know that transgression and merit arise from the mind;
the characteristics of physical and verbal karma are not fixed as either good or evil.
For this reason, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* and the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* state: [that the nature of action depends on the intention].
If one is without the intent [to kill],
even if one mistakenly kills one's father or mother,
one does not incur the crime of immediate retribution.
It is also like an infant grasping its mother’s breast with its body;
it incurs no offense because there is no defiled mind.
According to the Abhidharma,
it is said that the materiality of the basis for retribution gives rise to the materiality of skillful means,
which constitutes bodily action.
Sound constitutes vocal karma;
the mind is the essence of transgression and merit,
yet it remains hidden and is not spoken of.
If one follows the definitive teaching of the Mahāyāna,
the physical forms and vocal sounds of body and speech are eternally neither sinful nor meritorious;
if it is said that good and evil are both solely of the mind.
When the mind, having deliberated as it desires, initiates action of body and speech,
this very volition is the substance of the karma of body and speech.
If one merely intends in the mind without wishing to initiate action through body or speech,
it is designated only as mental karma (*manas-karma*).
Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
As people of the world say:
"The bandits burned the mountain forests, villages,
and cities," rather than saying "the fire burned them."
This principle is likewise:
it is solely by depending upon the mind that wholesome and unwholesome karma is established.
Thus, a verse in a sutra says:
"All phenomena have the mind as their basis; all phenomena have the mind as their sovereign.
Apart from the mind, there are no phenomena; they are merely mind, designated as body and speech.
Thus it is said in the Commentary on the Treatise.
There is only mental consciousness and no bodily or vocal karma;
as for bodily and vocal karma,
they exist merely as names.
In reality, this is mental karma;
bodily and verbal actions are merely called "explanations.
It is also like when, at the moment of death, one gives rise to a mind of wrong views and consequently falls into hell.
When the mind of right view arises, one is immediately born in a favorable realm.
Therefore, the treatise states:
"Apart from the mind, there is no volition; thus, there is no karma of body or speech."
Furthermore, the *Śāriputra-parivarta Sūtra* (The Sūtra of the Bequeathed Teaching) states:
"To indulge this mind is to lose one's wholesome deeds."
When controlled and concentrated in one place,
there is nothing that cannot be accomplished.
Furthermore, the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states:
There are five causes and conditions by which one commits no offense despite killing.
The first is when one is traveling on a road with a neutral state of mind (*avyākṛtacitta*).
Second, unintentionally killing the lives of crawling insects, ants, and the like;
third, unintentionally severing the life of a living being by throwing iron or other objects;
fourth, a physician administering medicine to a patient for the sake of healing, whereby the patient’s life ends as a result of the treatment.
Fifth, a firefly enters [the flame].
Without the intention to kill the insect,
the insect enters the fire and dies.
Thus, although these five types involve the taking of life, they do not incur the offense of killing.
Therefore, one knows that the initiation of all karmic actions created arises from the mind.
Furthermore, this is as in the case of killing, where it is distinguished according to the object and the mental state.
The mental states differ as superior, middling, or inferior;
the first [classification] is based on the object.
For example, killing an animal.
A bhikṣu incurs a pāyattika offense;
killing an ordinary person or a trainee (śaikṣa) incurs a pārājika offense;
killing one's father, mother, or an arhat incurs the five grave offenses of immediate retribution (ānantarya).
Killing a person who holds wrong views and has severed their roots of goodness incurs the lightest offense;
it is not as grave as the offense of killing an animal.
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"The Bodhisattva knows that there are three types of killing:
namely, inferior, middling, and superior."
The lower ones range from ants to all animals,
with the sole exception of those bodhisattvas who manifest birth [in such forms].
These various animals possess subtle roots of goodness.
Therefore, the killer fully receives the retribution for the sin; as for the one who kills moderately, [he likewise receives it].
This refers to those ranging from ordinary worldlings up to the stage of Anāgāmin. As for "superior killing," it refers to killing one's father,
mother, an Arhat, a Pratyekabuddha, or a Bodhisattva who is fixed in the certainty of enlightenment.
If one is able to kill an icchantika, one does not fall into any of these three types of killing.
It is, for example, like digging the earth, cutting grass, felling trees, or chopping up a corpse; there is no retribution for sin.
The icchantika is also like this: it is said that they lack the retribution for grave offenses, but it is not that they lack minor suffering. Second, regarding the mind:
the determination of an offense depends on the mind;
thus, karma has degrees of lightness and gravity.
Just as when hatred is heavy, the offense is heavy;
when hatred is light, the offense is light.
Therefore, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* says:
Or, because the matter is grave, there is a fixed retribution,
as in the case of the Buddha and his disciples,
whether one makes offerings to them or does not.
If there is a mind of contemptuous disparagement,
or because the mind is grave, there will be a fixed retribution;
it is like a person who, with deep-seated and intense fetters of malice, kills insects and ants.
It is a grave offense to kill out of a light-minded state;
however, if there is no anger in the mind,
even though one kills a superior object such as one's parents, it is not so.

Furthermore, the offenses against those below oneself, such as parricide and so forth, vary in gravity; as the text would be too cumbersome to recount them all, they may be understood by analogy. Moreover, the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* asks:
"What is non-killing?"
If rice, millet, or wheat contains minute insects,
one should not pound or grind them,
knowing that they contain insects.
Protect the life of this insect;
do not give it away to others,
nor kill living beings.
If worms arise within the sores on the backs of oxen, horses, camels, or donkeys carrying loads,
and one washes these sores with a decoction of grain-water,
one must not use medicinal herbs to sever the lives of these worms.
He washed and wiped away the worms with bird feathers,
placed them among other stinking, putrid, and decayed meat,
thereby ensuring their survival while simultaneously protecting these donkeys and oxen.
Fearing that their own lives might be harmed, they further protect the lives of insects, even down to ants,
whether by day or by night.
One does not practice heedlessness;
the mind does not harbor thoughts of killing.
Even if one sees sentient beings wishing to eat their insects...
He used what he had eaten as currency to trade for [the captive],
thereby enabling him to escape.
3. Section on Retribution (73). Section Three on Retribution: As stated in the *Maitreya-paripṛcchā-sūtra-śāstra*, there are three types of the ten unwholesome paths of action.
First, the fruit of retribution;
second, the fruit of habitual tendencies;
third, the dominant fruit.
Regarding the fruit of retribution:
if one is born within the hells, it is called the fruit of retribution.
Regarding the fruit of habitual tendencies:
If one emerges from hell and is reborn among humans,
due to the act of killing there is the result of a short lifespan;
due to the act of stealing there is the result of lacking the means of subsistence.
Up to the point where, due to false views, deluded states of mind increase—
such as all these are called the fruits of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
Furthermore, as the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* says:
For example, the monk Gomayapiccha was constantly chewing like a cow because he had come from among cattle in successive lifetimes; likewise, there was a certain bhikṣu who,
although he had attained the destruction of the outflows (āsravakṣaya), [continued to act in such a manner].
Yet she constantly uses a mirror to look at herself,
because in every lifetime she has come from among courtesans,
just like the bhikṣu Maudgalyāyana.
Although he has attained supernormal powers, he still habitually leaps and bounds about because,
in a previous life, he had once been among the monkeys.
As for the fruit of dominance:
Due to those ten kinds of unwholesome paths of action,
all external objects lack vitality and power;
that is to say, the land is uneven with highs and lows, frost and hail, thorns, dust, foul odors, and there are many snakes and scorpions.
There is little grain and meager grain;
little fruit and meager fruit,
as well as bitter fruit.
All such as these are called dominant fruits (*adhipatiphala*).
Furthermore, there is the fruit of similarity (*niṣyandaphala*);
for example, in the case of a killer.
Therefore, one inflicts various kinds of suffering upon the sentient beings who are harmed;
because of that suffering,
one is born in the hells and undergoes various kinds of suffering.
Because of taking life, one will receive the retribution of a short lifespan when reborn among humans.

This is due to severing the nature of another's "warmth" (*uṣman*). The rest may be inferred accordingly; it is also as explained in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* within the section on receiving retribution.
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* asks:
"What is meant by the residual retribution of afflictions?
If there are sentient beings who habitually associate with and indulge in sensual desire..."
Because this retribution has ripened, they fall into hell. Emerging from hell, they receive the bodies of animals—
such as pigeons, sparrows, mandarin ducks, parrots, green pigeons, fish, turtles, monkeys, and deer.
If one obtains a human body but takes on the form of a eunuch, a woman with two sexual organs, one without sexual organs, or a prostitute;
or if one leaves the household life and violates the first grave precept—
these are called residual retributions.
If there are sentient beings who, with a mind of intense earnestness, cultivate and associate with anger,
they will fall into hell due to the ripening of that retribution;
having emerged from hell, they will receive the body of an animal.
What is called a venomous snake possesses four kinds of poison:
first, the poison of sight;
second, the poison of touch.
Third, the poison of biting;
fourth, the poison of stinging.
This includes tigers, wolves, lions, bears, brown bears, wildcats, foxes, hawks, falcons, and their like.
If one obtains a human body yet remains fully possessed of the twelve types of evil disciplinary codes (*duḥśīla*),
or if one leaves the household life and violates the second grave precept (*ānantarya*),
these are called residual retributions (*avaśeṣa-vipāka*).
If one associates with foolish people,
when that retribution ripens, one falls into hell;
emerging from hell, one receives the body of an animal.
That is to say, the forms of elephants, pigs, cattle, sheep, water buffaloes, fleas, lice, mosquitoes, gadflies, ants, and so forth.
Even if one obtains a human body, it may be deaf, blind, mute, stammering, crippled, or hunchbacked.
Those with impaired faculties cannot receive the Dharma;
even if they manage to leave the household life, their faculties are dull and dark,
and they frequently violate the third grave precept.
This is called the residual retribution.
If there are those who cultivate arrogance,
when this retribution ripens, they will fall into hell.
Emerging from hell, they undergo the bodies of animals—
namely, dung-worms, camels, donkeys, dogs, and horses.
If they are born among humans, [they are born into lowly states].
Some enter the bodies of slaves or servants,
or become impoverished beggars; others manage to leave the household life and become renunciants.
They are constantly held in contempt and despised by the multitude and take pleasure in violating the fourth grave precept;
this is called the residual retribution.
The general meaning of the latent tendency of doubt is the same as that of delusion;
there is no need for a separate explanation.
It is also called the retribution of the five dull latent tendencies (*pañca-mṛdu-anuśaya*).
Furthermore, the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra* states:
"Moreover, householder,
I observe the world."
All sentient beings,
by means of the ten unwholesome paths of action,
are able to establish themselves and remain settled upon wrong paths.
They mostly fall into the evil destinies. What are these ten?
The first is taking life.
Second, taking what is not given;
third, sexual misconduct;
fourth, false speech.
Fifth, divisive speech;
sixth, harsh speech;
seventh, frivolous speech.
Eighth is greed and attachment;
ninth is anger and hatred;
tenth is wrong view.
"O Householder,
I see that sentient beings, because of these ten kinds of unwholesome karma,
travel upon deviant paths."
They follow many paths and take many directions,
mostly falling into the evil realms;
it is for the sake of realizing unexcelled bodhi and transcending all false paths that [this is taught].
With pure faith, he renounced the Śākya clan and set out upon the unsurpassed path.
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
The Buddha said to the upāsaka Nandika that there are ten offenses for taking life.
What are the ten? First, their minds constantly harbor poison that persists without end through successive lifetimes.
Second, sentient beings loathe them and take no pleasure in seeing them.
Third, they constantly harbor evil thoughts and contemplate wicked matters.
Fourth, sentient beings fear them as if seeing a snake or a tiger.
Fifth, their hearts are terrified while sleeping, and they remain uneasy even when awake.
Sixth, one constantly experiences evil dreams.
Seventh, at the time of death, one dies a mad, terrified, and miserable death.
Eighth, one plants the causes and conditions for a short life.
Ninth, upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, one falls into the hells.
Tenth, if one emerges as a human being, one will invariably be short-lived.
Thus, the Buddha taught that there are ten offenses for taking what is not given.
What are the ten? First, the owner of the goods is constantly angry;
second, he gives rise to suspicion in others.
Third, acting at improper times and in improper places without due deliberation;
fourth, associating with wicked people and distancing oneself from the virtuous and good;
fifth, destroying the signs of goodness.
Sixth, one incurs punishment from the authorities;
seventh, one's wealth and property are confiscated by the authorities;
eighth, one plants the karmic causes and conditions for poverty.
Ninth, upon death they enter hell.
Tenth, if they emerge as humans,
they labor painfully to seek wealth and are treated with contempt by others.
Whether it be kings or thieves,
water or fire, or even if it is used by those who are not one's beloved children.
The same applies even to burying [the body].
As the Buddha taught, there are ten offenses for sexual misconduct. What are these ten?
First, the husband who commits adultery will constantly seek to harm her.
Second, the husband and wife will lack harmony and constantly engage in quarreling and strife.
Third, all unwholesome dharmas will increase day by day.
First, all wholesome dharmas diminish day by day. Second, one fails to protect one's body, wife, children, orphans, and widows.
Third, one’s wealth and property are exhausted daily. Fourth, one does not guard one's body, wife, children, orphans, and widows.
Fifth, one’s assets and property waste away each day.
Sixth, one will constantly be suspected by others due to various evil deeds.
Seventh, one will not be loved or cherished by relatives and friends.
Eighth, one plants the karmic causes and conditions for enmity with enemies.
Ninth, when their bodies perish and their lives end, they die and enter hell.
Tenth, if they emerge [from that state] as women, many will share a single husband;
if they emerge as men, their wives will not be chaste.
Not committing various acts such as these for any of these reasons is called abstaining from sexual misconduct.
As the Buddha taught, there are ten faults in false speech. What are these ten?
First, one's breath is constantly foul-smelling.
Second, benevolent deities distance themselves while non-human spirits find an opportunity to cause harm.
Third, even when one speaks words of truth, people do not believe or accept them.
Fourth, he is never consulted or involved in the deliberations of wise men.
Fifth, he is constantly subjected to slander,
and his foul reputation spreads throughout the world.
Sixth, one will not be respected by others;
even when one issues instructions, people will not accept or follow them.
Seventh, one will constantly experience much sorrow and anxiety.
Eighth, they plant the karmic causes and conditions for slander.
Ninth, when their bodies perish and their lives end, they shall fall into hell.
Tenth, if they emerge from there to be born as humans, they will constantly be subjected to slander.
To refrain from such various [actions] is non-false speech;
it is called "excellent restraint" (*susaṃvara*).

As the Buddha taught that there are thirty-six faults in drinking alcohol—as detailed below in the exposition of the five precepts—to refrain from these four transgressions constitutes bodily excellence.
Abstaining from false speech constitutes the oral discipline (*vāksaṃvara*) of the five precepts.
Furthermore, the *Karmavibhaṅga-sūtra* states:
Furthermore, there are ten karmas that can cause sentient beings to receive external evil retributions.
If there are sentient beings who...
Because of the frequent cultivation of the ten unwholesome courses of action,
one experiences external objects that are entirely deficient. What are these ten?
First, because of the karma of killing,
the external retribution causes the great earth to become saline and barren,
and medicinal herbs to lose their potency. Second, because of the karma of stealing...
First, due to [the karma of] external frost, hail, locusts, and other such pests, they cause famine in the world.

Second, due to the karma of killing, they experience being struck by weapons and suffering from diseases. Third, due to the karma of sexual misconduct, they encounter adverse winds and rains as well as various types of dust and grime.
Fourth, because of their karma of false speech,
they experience external objects that are entirely foul and putrid.
Fifth, because of their karma of divisive speech...
Sixth, because of their evil verbal karma, they experience external retribution in the form of uneven ground with high and low elevations,
mountains, hills, mounds, stumps, and ruins; as well as coarse, harsh,
and foul objects such as tiles, stones, sand, and gravel that are unpleasant to touch or approach.
Seventh, because of their karma of frivolous speech,
all grasses, trees, dense forests, branches, and thorns [become sharp]. Eighth,
because of their karma of excessive greed.
The external retribution arising from this causes all crops and seeds to become minute and insignificant.
Ninth, because of the karma of anger,
it causes the fruits of all trees to be bitter and astringent.
Tenth, because of the karma of false views,
one experiences external retribution such that the crops do not ripen and the harvest is meager.
Thus, through these ten types of karma, one receives external evil retribution.

4. Section on Killing (73). Section on Killing, Part Four. This is divided into two sub-sections. 1. Sub-section on Stating the Intent. Sub-section on Stating the Intent, Number One: Now, those who have received physical forms within the six realms of existence...
There is none who does not cherish their existence and crave life;
having received their physical forms from the two polarities of Heaven and Earth, all alike feel a deep sense of urgency and fear of death.
Although beings may rise or sink through ten thousand categories, and their capacities for folly or wisdom may vary in a thousand ways,
when it comes to avoiding suffering and seeking peace,
how does this fundamental sentiment differ?
Thus, a startled bird seeking refuge in a tower still entreats for its life from the Lord of Wei;
a cornered beast entering a thatched hut then prays for survival from the family of Qiu.
The Han Prince cast away the bait and was thus moved by the reward of the bright pearl;
Yang Bao bestowed the flowers.
Thus, one receives the reward of the white ring;
even a novice monk who saved ants saw his life extended,
and Liu-shui (Jalavāhana) who rescued fish had heaven send down precious jewels.
How could such instances as these be fully recounted?
How can it be tolerated that you indulge in this insatiable craving to provide for those who depend on you?
They cut off his life-force and severed his physical aggregates,
causing him to embrace suffering until his end and to depart this world with grief;
though the great earth is vast, there is no place for him to flee or hide.
The heavens being so high, there is no one from whom one may offer a plea.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"All beings fear the sword and the staff."
There is no one who does not cherish their own life;
use this as a metaphor for yourself.
Do not kill, and do not wield the rod of punishment.
Whenever ordinary people, driven by inverted views, false perspectives, and ignorance,
perform sacrifices for good or ill fortune— whether for public or private purposes—
or when they entertain guests and manage the kitchen;
The bodies of various creatures were slaughtered and cooked to provide meals for the multitude; yet,
as the years passed and the seasons advanced, there came times of leisure and intervals from affairs.
The heavens grew bleak as frost descended;
the wilds blazed as fires spread across them.
Thereupon, he mounted swift horses that could chase the wind.
He held a fine falcon as swift as a flash of lightning;
his swords were the Gujuai and the Qianjiang;
his bows were the Wuhao and the Fanruo.
Consequently, all the marshes were emptied and the thickets of the forests exhausted;
their tree-dwelling nests were overturned and their cave-dwellings torn asunder,
while nets and snares stretched across the wilds.
They cast a net over Mount Mucilinda;
some were entangling from the front while others blocked from behind,
luring from the left and intercepting from the right.
Dust clouds swelled until they obscured the sun,
and smoke and fire pierced the heavens;
consequently, even birds lost their companions and flew off in alarm.
The beasts bolt away, fleeing from their herd;
the wild geese, hearing the twang of the string, compete to fall;
the monkeys embrace the trees and wail in lamentation.
There was none who did not wail in grief upon facing precipitous valleys,
nor cry out in despair while confronting lofty forests;
thus, arrows were never discharged in vain.
His bow never missed its mark;
it pierced the armpit, penetrated the chest, severed the head, and crushed the brain.
At other times, he cast his line upon turbid shallows or scattered bait in clear depths.
I studied the art of fishing for carp at the river ford;
together we shot for minnows in the well-gully.
Now, the crimson scales have already hung upon the hook.
There is no longer any capacity for relying on faith;
since the pure nature is already suspended,
the auspicious omen of leaping upon the boat shall forever cease.
The fei-kuai spirits, with their emaciated forms,
gather like clouds on a platter and scatter like rain;
or again, the Xianyun may burn fiercely.
It is fitting to issue a decree for a punitive expedition;
as the frontier regions are being ruthlessly ravaged,
the task must rely upon divine prowess.
Even though there have been worthy emperors and sagely rulers who still moved their weapons of war,
as well as enlightened sovereigns and wise monarchs—
Yet military expeditions must still be undertaken;
it was for this reason that during the campaign at Shêr,
he established his great reputation.
The army at Muye is justly celebrated for its magnificent virtue;
among its ranks, there may even be those who command a million troops and advance with reckless audacity.
Leading five thousand men, he advanced deep into the enemy lines;
he shattered Cao Cao at the Red Wall and struck down Emperor Xiang Yu at the River Wu.
The heads of Mangshou were suspended from a high tower,
and corpses were laid out across the marketplace;
both were once heroes of sudden majesty and prowess.
At that time, such as these were beyond counting;
there was not one who did not pile up bones into mountains and flow blood into oceans.
Now the King’s army moves like thunder to sweep away the demonic rebels;
raising troops and bearing the ceremonial staffs, they bring blessings to the borders and moisten the frontiers.
Having joined the vanguard, I have humbly taken my place among the rear forces.
Beneath the cloud-banners, how could one dare to seek personal security?
Amidst the frosty blades, there is indeed much peril.
Thus, one strikes one's head in supplication beneath the sword and begs for life beneath the spear.
Such offenses cannot be fully recounted.
Whenever sentient beings harm one another, creating enmity and discord,
[they incur this retribution].
One who neglects their life-force and neglects their body may create the causes for a short lifespan and consequently invite the fruit of much illness.
I vow that from this day forth, I shall forever sever the continuity [of afflictions] and serve as a retinue for Bodhi until the end of the future,
never breaking these excellent conditions and remaining as an equal companion within the city of Dharma.
Section Two: Quotations from Scriptural Authority. As stated in the Vinaya of the Piṇḍola:
Formerly, when the Buddha was in the world, there was a brahmin in the kingdom of Śrāvastī.
He constantly made offerings to Kālodāyin.
That brahmin had an only son, whom he raised until he was grown and took a wife for him.
At that time, the brahmin, as he was approaching death, instructed his son:
"After I have passed away, you shall attend upon the Venerable Kālodāyin just as you do today."
"Let there be no lack of anything.
After his parents passed away,
the son followed his parents' instructions and returned once more to provide offerings to Kālodāyin.
It was no different from when his father was still alive.
Later, at another time, the brahmin’s son went out and was away.
He entrusted his wife with the task of making offerings.
On that very day, there were five hundred bands of bandits;
among them was one bandit whose face and head were handsome.
The wife saw him from afar and sent a messenger to summon him;
they then engaged in illicit intercourse together.
Kālodāyin went to that woman's house frequently.
Fearing that the śramaṇa might divulge their secret,
she later conspired with this thief to kill him.
When King Prasenajit heard that the Venerable Kālodāyin had been killed by bandits,
he remembered the Venerable one and was filled with anger and distress;
he immediately executed the members of the Brahmin family.
He also killed eighteen other families on his left and right.
He captured five hundred bandits, severed their hands and feet, and threw them into a ditch.
When the bhikṣu saw this, he said to the Buddha:
What evil did Kāḷodāyin commit in the past that he was killed by the wife of a brahmin?
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
"In the distant past, Kālodāyin was a master of a great celestial shrine."
There were five hundred men who led a single sheep,
cut off its four legs, and were about to take it to a celestial shrine where they made a collective prayer.
Having received them, the master of the sacrifice immediately slaughtered them.
Because of killing the sheep, he fell into hell and underwent immeasurable suffering.
The master of the sacrifice in the past was none other than Kāḷudāyin now.
Although he had attained arhatship, his remaining karmic retribution was not exhausted,
and thus he now receives this reward.
The sheep of that time is none other than his current wife.
Those five hundred people who once severed the feet of sheep are these very five hundred thieves who today have their hands and feet cut off by the king.
Thus the Buddha told the bhikṣus.
If a person commits killing,
the retribution they receive will never decay or perish.
Furthermore, the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* states:
Long ago, when the Buddha was in the world,
there was an elder in the city of Śrāvastī named Revata.
He had seven sons,
all of whom were married;
the wife of his youngest son was named Vaiśālī.
He was exceedingly wise and virtuous;
there was nothing he did not know.
At that time, Reṇu entrusted his entire household estate to him.
Because of her wisdom and virtue,
King Prasenajit paid her homage and treated her as his sister.
At one time, she became pregnant.
When the moon was full, thirty-two eggs were produced.
From one of these eggs emerged a young man,
whose countenance was upright and handsome, and whose valor and strength were extraordinary.
The strength of one man is equal to that of a thousand men.
His many wives are all daughters of the eminent and virtuous within the kingdom.
At that time, Vaiśālī invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha to provide offerings at their residence.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for them,
and the entire family attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*;
only the youngest son had not yet attained the path.
While riding an elephant on an excursion,
he encountered the son of a high minister riding a carriage across a bridge;
he immediately seized him and threw him into a ditch beneath the bridge.
With his body wounded and torn,
he came and informed his father.
The minister said to his son:
That man is strong and is a relative of the state;
it would be difficult to contend with him for victory.
He should consider this secret report.
He then had thirty-two horse-whips fashioned from the seven precious gems,
with swords made of pure steel placed within them.
Someone presented him with one.
Everyone loved it and joyfully accepted it;
he would always hold it in his hand as he entered and left to see the king.
According to the laws of the kingdom, one may not carry a sword when appearing before the king.
When the minister saw this, he immediately slandered the son of Vaiśālī to the king. The son of Vaiśālī...
"In their prime and full of vigor, each man could have faced a thousand;
yet now they harbor treacherous schemes, intending to kill the king.
Each has fashioned a sharp blade and concealed it within his horsewhip."
The matter was clearly established.
The King immediately had it examined,
and it was indeed as he had said.
The king believed this to be true and had them all executed.
Having completed the executions, he took thirty-two heads.
He placed [the relic] inside a casket,
sealed and stamped it, and sent it to his younger sister.
On that very day, Vaiśālī invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha.
He went to the monastery to offer his support.
Seeing that the king had sent a casket,
he assumed the king was providing assistance for the offerings.
He immediately wished to open it and look inside,
but the Buddha stopped him, not permitting it,
until the monks had finished their meal.
When the meal was finished, the Buddha preached the Dharma to him on impermanence, suffering, and so forth;
at that time, Viśāla attained the fruit of Anāgāmin.
After the Buddha had departed, he opened the casket and saw his son with thirty-two heads.
Because they have severed the craving for sensual desire, they do not fall into affliction;
they merely utter these words:
"Alas! How tragic!"
Human life is subject to death and cannot endure forever.
Why do you toil so bitterly, rushing through the five realms of existence?
You have thirty-two sons, along with their wives' families and kinsmen.
Hearing of these matters, he was filled with anguish and cried out,
"The Great King is unrighteous!
He has unjustly slain a virtuous man!"
Gathering their troops together, they intended to go and take revenge.
At that time, the king, struck with fear, fled to the place where the Buddha was.
The men led their army and surrounded the Jetavana Monastery.
Ānanda saw that King [Ajātaśatru] had killed the thirty-two sons of the Licchavis;
their wives' families and kinsmen, wishing to take revenge,
joined their palms and questioned the Buddha.
"For what cause and condition were the thirty-two sons killed by the king?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
In the distant past, thirty-two men stole another's ox and together led it to the house of an old woman,
intending to kill it there.
The old woman joyfully prepared the implements for slaughter.
As the blade was brought down, the ox knelt and begged for its life;
yet, because the men’s intent was so fierce, they killed it nonetheless.
The Cow’s Vow of Enmity:
"You have killed me now;
in a future life, I shall never let you go."
After she had died, they ate her together.
When the old mother was full,
she spoke these words of joy:
"From the past until now, there has never been a guest as well-received as you today.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
The ox at that time was the present King Prasenajit;
the man who stole the ox was the present thirty-two sons of Vaiśālī;
and the old woman was the present city of Vaiśālī.
Because of killing the cow,
he was constantly slaughtered for five hundred lifetimes;
the old woman rejoiced.
For five hundred lifetimes, she was always my mother.
When her son was killed, she felt extreme anguish;
now, having encountered me, she has attained the fruit of Anāgāmin.
When the relatives of the wife's family heard what the Buddha had said,
their resentment subsided,
and each of them spoke these words:
This person now receives the retribution for what he himself sowed.
If such is the case even for killing a single ox,
how much more so for many?
"King Prasenajit is my king.
Why do you harbor resentment and seek to kill me?
She immediately threw herself before the king, seeking mercy and repenting her transgression.
The king was also relieved and did not question her regarding her crime.
Ānanda asked the Buddha,
"What further merit did she cultivate?"
A man of noble status, courageous and strong, encountered the Buddha and attained the Way.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"In the distant past..."
During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha,
there was an old woman who gathered various kinds of incense.
He mixed it with oil,
intending to go and smear it upon a stūpa;
on the way, he encountered thirty-two people.
Thereupon, he exhorted him,
and they went together to plaster the stupa.
When the plastering was finished, he made a vow.
In every place where she was born, she was honored, noble, and wealthy;
she was always mother and child together, meeting the Buddha and attaining the Way.
From that time forward, for five hundred lifetimes, she was always born into a state of supreme nobility.
They were always mother and son.
Now, having encountered the Buddha, each has attained the fruit of the Path.
The verse on their retribution says:
In jest, they take the lives of others; Wailing in grief, they enter the foul-smelling hells.
Putrid stench and molten copper Pour down upon them in an unceasing stream.
They rush toward blades and leap into flames; Torn apart and crushed by agonizing torments.
For billions of years, suffering has been manifold; its heart-wrenching details cannot be fully recorded.
The verse on the retribution of habitual practice says:
By killing, one enters the four realms of existence; One undergoes suffering until the three miserable paths are exhausted.
Though one may be born among humans, with a short life, much sorrow,
illness, pestilence, and the hardships of infancy; with a brief lifespan and constantly submerged in suffering—
if there is a wise and discerning person, they would surely not give way to a murderous mind or negligence.

Yi verified that after Song Gaozu (Emperor Wu) had defeated Huan Xuan,
he appointed Liu Yi as General Who Pacifies the Army and Governor of Jingzhou.
Upon arriving at the province, Yi immediately arrested the abbot of Niumu Monastery, saying:
Zang Huan’s son was ordained as a śrāmaṇera;
he subsequently killed four practitioners of the Way.
Later, during the night, he saw this monk in a dream, who said:
"Why do you wrongfully seek to kill this poor monk?
I have already informed the Heavenly Emperor;
I fear that you, too, shall not live long."
Consequently, he fell ill and ceased eating;
day by day he grew emaciated.
This was when they were about to set out for Yangdu.
There were many internal conflicts and usurpations against the ministers.
Emperor Gaozu of the Song dynasty consequently dispatched troops to subdue him.
When Huiyi was defeated, he fled alone on horseback at night and sought refuge at Niumu Temple.
The monk addressed the General of the Pacification Army:
"In the past, you wrongfully executed my master, a man of the Way.
By nature, there is no principle for me to harbor a grudge."
However, why should he come here?
This deceased master has frequently manifested spiritual efficacy,
saying that the Heavenly Emperor will summon his army to the temple to kill him.
Yi then sighed in lamentation.
After leaving the temple, he climbed a large tree on the rear ridge and hanged himself to death. This first account of evidence is from the *Yuanhun zhi* (Record of Vengeful Spirits).
During the Liang dynasty, there was a person who used chicken egg whites for washing his hair; it is verified that during the Liang dynasty,
there was someone who constantly mixed chicken egg whites with his wash,
saying it caused the hair to shine.
Whenever he bathed, he would invariably break twenty or thirty eggs.
At the moment of his death, there was heard only the chirping of several thousand chicken chicks from within his hair.
During the Liang dynasty, there was a man who made his living selling eels; this was verified by the case of the Liu family of Jiangling during the Liang period.
He made his living by selling eels.
Later, he fathered a son whose head was complete with an eel.
From the neck downward, it was clearly human.
During the Liang dynasty, there was a guest who ate roasted meat and verified that King Wengong of Liang had served as the Governor of Yongjia.
Someone had sent him a sheep.
The guests had gathered, intending to hold a banquet,
when a tethered sheep broke its rope and came to throw itself upon one guest,
first kneeling and performing two prostrations.
He then entered into his robes;
the guest did not say a word at all and made no effort to offer any plea for help.
In a short while, a sheep was slaughtered to roast its meat.
When the first slice was served to the guest and entered his mouth,
it immediately fell into his skin.
As he wandered about, his entire body was racked with pain and he wailed aloud;
only then did he speak again,
whereupon he died making the bleating of a sheep.
During the Liang dynasty, there was a man who killed an ox and tied it beneath a pillar at a monastery gate; later, it was verified that this man had served as a county magistrate.
During the time of Liu Jinggong, his county yamen was burned down, and he took up residence in a temple.
The people presented oxen and wine as offerings to the County Magistrate;
they tied the ox to the stupa pillar,
removed the religious images, and prepared couches and seats.
While he was receiving guests in the hall,
before the animal had been slaughtered, the ox untied itself and came straight forward;
it reached the steps and bowed.
The magistrate laughed loudly and ordered his attendants to slaughter him.
Having eaten and drunk his fill, he lay down beneath the eaves.
Upon waking, he immediately felt his body itch;
as he scratched the itchy rash,
in a mere moment it turned into a great affliction.
After more than ten years, he died.
During the Liang dynasty, there was a subordinate who cut off the hands of a bandit as evidence; Yang Sidai of Liang served as the Governor of Xiyang Commandery during the rebellion of Hou Jing.
At that time, there was again a drought and famine.
Starving people stole wheat from the fields,
so Sthavira dispatched a subordinate soldier to guard them.
Those caught stealing were immediately severed at the wrist; in all,
more than ten people were executed in this manner.
A later-born son of a subordinate military unit was naturally born without hands.
At that time, there was a person who killed an ox for food; it was verified that at that same time, there was one who held the rank of *fengchaoqing*.
His family was extremely wealthy and extravagant;
he would not find it delicious unless he had slaughtered the ox with his own hands.
When he was about thirty years old, he fell gravely ill.
A large ox saw [the man] coming;
its entire body felt as if it were being pierced by knives,
and it died with a loud cry.
During the Qi dynasty, there was a man catching fish who saw a fish biting a tally-stick. During the Qi dynasty,
Gao Wei of Jiangling followed the Wu people into the Qi state for several years.
He was traveling toward Youzhou when he caught fish in a marsh.
Later, while ill, he repeatedly saw flocks of fish biting him before he died. These seven accounts of verification are taken from the *Hongming zhuan*.
The Case of Yin Anren of Tang: Stopping a Guest and Killing a Donkey for Inspection. During the Tang dynasty, Yin Anren of the capital city of Jingzhao was a man of great wealth.
He had long supported the monks of Cimen Temple.
At the beginning of the first year of the Yining era, a guest arrived and stayed at his residence.
A guest stole another's donkey from his house and killed it;
the donkey skin was left at the home of An Ren.
This occurred in the third year of the Zhenguan era.
Anren then saw a man on the road who said to him,
"I have been sent to summon you; you shall arrive tomorrow."
"You shall die. Fearing this, Anren went straight to Cimen Temple;
he sat within the Buddha hall and did not emerge for the entire night.
The next day, three horsemen along with several dozen foot soldiers,
all bearing weapons, entered the temple.
Seeing Dao’an from afar, they called him out.
Anren did not respond, but his recitation of the mantras progressed even further.
The ghosts said to one another,
"We did not seize him immediately yesterday."
"Today we have cultivated such merit;
by what means could this have been obtained?
Thus they departed together.
He left one person to guard it.
The guard said to Anren,
"In the past, you killed a donkey."
"The donkey now accuses you;
we have come specifically to seize you,
for in the end, we must face him together."
"What benefit is there in not going?
Anren replied from afar:
"In the past, another thief committed suicide on his donkey."
"Give me only the hide; it was not I who killed it.
Why do you pursue me?"
"I beg you to return and speak for me to the donkey:
'I originally did not kill you;
however, I shall now also perform merit-seeking rites on your behalf.'"
"It will be to your benefit;
you should abandon me.
That person gave his promise, saying:
"If you do not permit it,
I shall come again tomorrow;
if you do permit it," [he said].
"I shall not come.
Having finished speaking, he departed.
The next day, he did not return.
Thereupon, Anren performed meritorious rites for his donkey,
and his entire family observed the precepts and maintained a vegetarian diet;
thus spoke Lu Wenli.
Anren is currently alive.

Regarding Du Guī, the Duke of Zan who served as the Regional Inspector (Dudu) during the Tang dynasty: he was fond of killing. [Note: This repeats the phrase "Examining Du Guī, the Duke of Zan who served as the Regional Inspector of Luozhou during the Tang dynasty" for emphasis.
By nature, he delighted in slaughter.
Initially serving as the Vice President of the Administration Commission for Yizhou,
he killed many generals and soldiers,
and furthermore murdered Wei Yunqi, the Minister of the Administration Commission.
In the winter of the second year of the Zhenguan era,
while residing in Luozhou, he became severely ill and exhausted.
Suddenly, he spoke of his own accord:
Someone brought me some melons as a gift.
My attendants reported that there are no melons in the winter months.
The Master said:
"A plate of fine melons— why are they not here?
He then looked on in astonishment and said:
These are not melons;
they are all human heads seeking their lives from me.
He spoke again, saying,
"Support me up and let me see Minister Wei."
Having finished speaking, he passed away.
During the Tang dynasty, Pan Guo killed Yangshe Suo; this was verified by a person in the Tang capital named Pan Guo.
Before reaching the age of twenty,
during the Wude era, he served as a minor official in the Department of Waterways.
Upon returning home, he went out to the fields with several youths to play.
While passing by a cemetery, he saw a sheep that had been left behind by its herder,
standing alone and grazing on grass.
Guo Yin and the youth seized him and were leading him home;
on the way, the sheep bleated and cried out.
Fearing that her husband would hear of it, Guo then extracted the sheep's tongue;
she subsequently killed and ate it during the night.
After one year had passed, Guo’s own tongue gradually withered and shrank away until it was completely gone.
He submitted a formal petition to release the official.
Zheng Yuping, the Magistrate of Fuping County,
suspecting it was a fabrication, ordered him to open his mouth to verify the matter.
He then saw that his tongue was entirely absent;
its root was barely the size of a bean and not yet fully gone.
The official questioned him regarding the circumstances.
Guo took paper and wrote a reply to the original petition.
The officials immediately admonished him, instructing him to perform meritorious deeds for his deceased parents by reciting the Lotus Sūtra and other scriptures.
Guo then gave rise to a mind of faith and reverence, maintaining the precepts without interruption.
He performed meritorious deeds on behalf of the sheep;
after one year had passed, its tongue gradually grew back and was restored to its former state.
He went again to the government offices to submit a petition;
the county magistrate appointed him as a village head (li-zheng).
Yu Qing served as a Censor-in-Chief until the eighteenth year of the Zhenguan era.
I have related these accounts myself. The three preceding testimonies are from the *Mingbao ji* (Records of Miraculous Retribution).
Regarding the case of He Yue of the Tang dynasty, who was cured of his tongue-tied muteness after having a cow's tongue severed:
during the Wude era of the Tang, He Yue of Daping in Xin Prefecture was from Yongxing.
Because a neighbor’s ox had damaged his crops,
he tied a rope around the ox’s tongue and cut it off.
Later, in Yongxing, three sons were born to him.
They were all mute and unable to speak.
Regarding Lu Xiaozheng of Yongzhou during the Tang dynasty:
during the Zhenguan era, Lu Xiaozheng served as the Left Fruit-Yi (left *guòyì*) of the Xichuan Commandery in the Right Guard (*Yòuwèi*).
Xiaozheng was by nature impetuous and prone to cruelty.
Within his residence, there had previously been a hive of honeybees.
They divided and flew to gather upon a tree to the south of the residence.
At that time, Xiaozheng sent someone to move them to a separate niche;
while the bees had not yet departed, [the following occurred].
Xiaozheng was greatly incensed; he then boiled a basin of hot water and poured it over the bees on the tree,
whereupon they all died.
He was nearly about to lose his son.
In the fifth month of the following year,
Xiaozheng was taking a nap in the hall during the day.
Suddenly, a bee stung his tongue,
which immediately became swollen and blocked his mouth;
he died after several days.
During the Tang dynasty, there was a man who was murdered by his enemies; the case was investigated by Li Yiyen of Longxi.
During the Zhenguan era, Li served as the County Magistrate of Hua Prefecture.
Suddenly, one person went missing from this county, and no one knew where they had gone.
His father and elder brother suspected that he had been killed by an enemy or a vengeful kinsman,
so they went to the county office to present their plea.
Fayian investigated the case but was unable to reach a definitive conclusion.
During the night, he held a candle and questioned him in great detail.
By the second watch, Yiyen was leaning over his desk with his head bowed, unaware that the dead man had already arrived, still bearing the marks of his wounds. He said:
A person named So-and-so, whose character was wounded,
has been beaten to death and placed in a well at such-and-such a location.
Your Excellency should investigate this promptly.
"Otherwise, I fear he will be moved elsewhere and can no longer be found.
Yiyen then went there in person to search for him.
It was exactly as described.
Shortly thereafter, the vengeful family submitted their full confession.
Those who heard and witnessed it at that time—
All were filled with wonder and admiration.
During the Tang dynasty, there was Qi Shiwang, a native of Wuchang in Wuwei, who was renowned for his ability to burn chicken eggs.
He died in the twenty-first year of the Zhenguan era.
After seven days, he revived.
He said of himself:
"Immediately after my death, I was led before the King."
He was immediately handed over to the judicial authorities and dispatched for separate interrogation.
After four or five days, the examination of the registers revealed that he shared the same name as those slated for execution.
However, he did not die immediately.
The judge said to Shi Wang, "Throughout your life,
you were fond of roasting chicken eggs."
"You ought to accept your punishment and depart.
He immediately ordered men to escort him out the gate;
they traveled about one or two *li* from the office.
He then saw a city and heard the sound of drums and musical instruments within it.
The officer, filled with joy, hurried forward and entered.
Once they had entered, the city gates were already closed;
within, there were no dwellings at all,
and the ground was entirely covered with hot ashes.
Shi Wang was flustered and did not know what to do.
His feet were scorched and burned, causing him extraordinary agony.
Shi Wang looked around and saw that the city gates were all wide open.
When he rushed toward the gate and its doors were already closed,
a full day had passed.
Someone then commanded the gatekeeper, saying:
He opened the gate and released the criminals from the previous day.
