and from each nail a great flame burst forth. Furthermore,
a bhikṣu in charge of monastic affairs had repeatedly received property belonging to the Saṃgha, which he then begrudged and hoarded.
Or they may give to the Saṃgha at an improper time;
or they may give with difficulty;
or they may give out of distress.
Or they may give a little;
or they may not give at all;
or there may be those who do give.
Or, if they do not give,
because of these unwholesome roots,
they will become foul and loathsome hungry ghosts who constantly eat balls of excrement.
When this person’s life ends, they shall be reborn therein;
for hundreds of thousands of years, they will constantly be unable to obtain food,
and even when they do eat, it turns into excrement and urine.
Or it may turn into pus and blood.
For this reason, Kāśyapa,
a bhikṣu who manages affairs...
It would be better to eat one's own flesh than ever to use the property of the Triple Gem for clothing, bowls, food, or drink.
Section Six: On Ordinary Objects. As stated in the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā-śāstra*:
If one carefully guards and protects the property of others, including that of the Three Jewels,
by securing it with firm locks and concealing it within the rooms;
Yet thieves may steal from within the house through a hole,
or take it by force;
these are not things that a guardian can prevent or restrict.
One should merely seek to charge the original owner with the offense;
in all such cases, it is improper to demand restitution.
This applies even if the custodian was negligent and failed to diligently guard the property.
If an item is stolen by a thief,
the person in charge of the goods must compensate for it,
so as to hold the guardian accountable for the offense.
Therefore, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"If one receives another's entrusted property from a distant place and it is damaged or destroyed while on the way..."
If it was caught and broken through good intentions,
there should be no compensation;
if it was caught and broken through malicious intent, [there must be compensation].
It must be repaid.
If one borrows another's property,
it does not matter whether the intention was good or evil.
If one destroys anything, it must be compensated.
Furthermore, the *Śāriputra Vinaya* states:
"When thieves come to steal property..."
Either one gives out of a good heart,
or one gives because one takes [the object] due to fear of being pursued by another;
in either case, one becomes the owner of the object.
However, do not beg from bandits;
you may take what they give of their own accord.
Once you have taken it, dye it a ruined color and wear it.
If there is an owner who recognizes it, it should be returned.
Furthermore, the *Madhyama-āgama* (*Maudgalyāyana-vinaya*) states:
"If a madman personally takes an object and gives it as a gift..."
If it is unknown whether they are one's parents or relatives, one may take it;
however, if they are known to be one's parents and they do not give it with their own hands, one must not take it.
Furthermore, the *Śāriputra-paripṛcchā-vinaya* states:
"If one takes the remains of meat left over by a tiger, one commits a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*),
because it does not sever the craving for such things."
If one takes the leftovers from a lion, there is no offense,
because the expectation [of ownership] has been severed.
Furthermore, the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:

To steal the remains of birds or beasts constitutes a minor offense (*dukkaṭa*). In this present age of scarcity, there are many laypeople who destroy the burrows of others' rats to take their stored millet, walnuts, various fruits, and so forth; such acts constitute an offense according to this principle. The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states: [as cited above].
If one takes it with the perception of "mine," with the perception of "my own possession," with the perception of "rags from a dust heap," or with the perception of "temporary use."
There is no offense in cases such as taking [an object] with the thought that it belongs to a friend. As for what constitutes a "friend": [the following applies].
According to the Vinaya, one must possess seven qualities to be designated as a "true friend":
first, being able to perform what is difficult to do.
Second, being difficult to give to and able to give;
third, being difficult to endure and able to endure;
fourth, confiding secret matters to one another.
Fifth, they conceal each other's faults;
sixth, they do not abandon one another when encountering suffering;
seventh, they do not treat those who are poor or lowly with contempt.
These are the seven dharmas;
whoever among people can practice them is a true and virtuous friend.
One may take [them] without committing an offense.
Furthermore, the *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
If a person commits theft by stealing another's property and is seized by the owner,
they are bound and delivered to the king.
He was punished for his crime of theft.
The king immediately dispatched men to cast him into prison,
where he was either imprisoned or had his hands and feet cut off.
Some have their ears and noses cut off;
some have their skin flayed;
some have their tendons pulled out.
Some are hung upside down;
some are sawn apart;
others are roasted with fire.
At times they are boiled in cauldrons;
at other times their heads are bound and lashed with raw hide;
or again, molten copper is poured over their bodies.
Some were impaled through the hips with long stakes;
some were trampled to death by fierce elephants;
and some had their bellies ripped open and their entrails pulled out like bundles of straw.
At times, they were bound hand and foot and beaten with drums of evil sound;
they were led to the marketplace and executed by decapitation beneath a banner,
or else their bodies were dismembered limb by limb.
Some are split with knives;
some are pierced by arrows;
in such various ways they are tormented and killed.
Due to the causal conditions of this evil karma of stealing,
after the end of life, one is born in hell,
where fierce fires burn the body and molten copper is poured into the mouth.
In the boiling cauldrons and burning charcoal, on the mountains of blades and the trees of swords,
amidst the glowing embers, excrement, and urine, and being ground by millstones or pounded in mortars—
they undergo all such various sufferings as these.
The bitter, acrid, and poisonous pains are beyond measure;
though hundreds of thousands of millions of years pass, there is no end in sight to their release.
Once the retribution for their hellish offenses is exhausted, they are reborn among the animals.
As elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, camels, donkeys, dogs, and so forth,
they must repay their debts to others for hundreds of thousands of years;
once their karmic retribution as animals is exhausted, they are born among the hungry ghosts.
The suffering of hunger and thirst is beyond description;
for hundreds of thousands of years, they endure such agony without ever hearing the names of water or drink.
When their retribution for offenses in the evil realms is exhausted, they are reborn among human beings.
If born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution: first, poverty.
Their clothing does not cover their bodies,
and their food does not fill their mouths;
furthermore, they are constantly plundered by kings, thieves, fire, water, and wicked bandits.
Furthermore, the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* says:
"What is called stealing?
It is when a person thinks:"
He constantly harbored such unwholesome thoughts, wishing that while he alone should achieve success in various grains and wheat, the people of the world should fail to produce the five grains.
At another time, however—
Sentient beings have meager merit;
their fields and crops will not be harvested.
Such are these evil people.
Seeing the world suffering from famine,
his heart gave rise to joy, thinking,
"It is just as I had intended."
Selling grain in the marketplace with a crooked mind and crafty deceit,
they measure out the various grains and wheat.
Deceiving and deluding others,
one ultimately completes the karma;
if one contemplates this with the mind.
That which is called the karma of volition;
when one performs deception,
it is called the karma of deception.
Once the act of deception has been committed, it is termed "culminating karma" (*niṣṭhita-karman*).
Section Seven: On Bequeathed Objects. As stated in the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*:
If one sees items left behind along the roadside—
whether gold, silver, or other treasures— one should take them and announce it aloud.
To whom does this belong?
If someone were to say, "This is my possession," [one would respond:]...
One should inquire about its characteristics;
if it is indeed his, he shall return for it.
If no one claims it, [it shall be kept].
Maintain this practice for seven days,
chanting it every day. If no owner comes forward to claim it, [it shall be considered abandoned].
These precious objects are entrusted to the kings, great ministers, and governors of provinces and districts.
If these kings, great ministers, and governors of provinces and districts do not take these objects from those who possess merit and virtue.
In the future, one shall protect and uphold the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha;
this is called non-stealing.
Furthermore, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
If one sees abandoned clothing or belongings,
one should announce it aloud.
If there is no owner, one should hang it in a high and conspicuous place so that people may see it.
If one says, "This is my property," one should ask:
"Where did your property go missing?"
Answer: If there is someone suitable, give it to them.
If there is no one with the necessary knowledge, you should wait until three months have passed.
If it is obtained within the precincts of a stūpa,
it shall be used for the stūpa; if it is obtained within the precincts of the Saṃgha, [it shall be used for the Saṃgha].
Regarding the property for the Sangha of the four quarters: as for items of high value,
such as gold, silver, or necklaces, they must not be displayed openly.
When the proclamation "treasure has been found" is made,
people should examine it with careful scrutiny;
they must repeatedly look at what its characteristics are before lifting it up.
When someone comes to claim [the item], give it to the one who corresponds [to the description].
Give it before a multitude of people;
do not do so in a private place, and furthermore, instruct them to receive the Three Refuges.
Regarding speech:
that which the Buddha did not prohibit as a precept,
you may not look upon with your own eyes.
If no one comes forward to claim it,
let it remain for three years; thereafter,
it shall be used by the local community of that district as previously prescribed.
If one discovers a treasure trove while repairing a stūpa,
it shall be used for the stūpa itself;
the same applies to land belonging to the Saṃgha.
Therefore, the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states:
"There is no offense in taking and using hidden treasures when the Buddha was still in the world."
The Elder Anāthapiṇḍada was a noble being;
since he also accepted these items,
one should know that there is no fault.
Furthermore, naturally obtaining objects is not termed robbery.
Moreover, the Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya states:
"In a human settlement, there may be lost or abandoned items."
One must not take it.
If it is given to a bhikṣu, he may take it;
that person is then the donor.
In a village, one must not take clothing that has been blown there by the wind;
it may be taken only with the perception of it being discarded refuse.
On a desolate road in an uninhabited place, it may be taken.
Furthermore, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"If a robe has been set aside for twelve years and has not been returned,
the community of monks shall assemble to appraise it and put it to use for the sake of the Sangha of the four directions."
If he later returns, he should repay it with property belonging to the Saṃgha;
it is well if he does not accept [the debt].
The verse on the primary retribution says:
"Those who plundered the property of others for their own use Shall sink alone into the *niraya* hell;
There, the *jvaka* bird with its adamantine beak Will peck at their brains and split open their hearts."
Their mouths are doused with molten copper; crushed by iron mallets and anvil, they flee in terror and panic, only to return to the forest of swords and blades.
The verse on the ripening of their karma says:
The retribution for those who plunder and steal is to be melted down in hell;
when their offenses are exhausted and they are reborn among humans, they end their lives in hunger and poverty,
their shared wealth seized by others— how is this any different from being among the lowly and base?

I address those who cherish integrity: you must contemplate how to remain steadfast even in poverty. Regarding the conditions for response and resonance, I shall briefly cite six instances of verification: 1. Gong Shou, a village head (ting-chang) of Cangwu Commandery during the Han dynasty. 2.

A village head of Li Village in Mei County, Qizhou, during the Han dynasty, who stole and killed another’s daughter. 3. A man surnamed Huangfu named Qian in Yizhou during the Sui dynasty. 4. Wei Qingzhi, a Grand Master of the Household (Changshi) to the Prince of Wei during the Tang dynasty, whose daughter died. 5. Zhao, a woman from the brush-seller family in the Eastern Market of the Western Capital (Xi'an) during the Tang dynasty. 6. Zhou Ji, a District Magistrate (Zhubu) during the Tang dynasty, who was stolen and killed by an official. [These accounts are followed by] Gong Shou, a village head of Cangwu Commandery during the Han dynasty; and He Chang of the Han era.
Acting as the Regional Inspector (Cishi) of Jiaozhi,
he traveled through the provinces and arrived at Gaoyao County in Cangwu Commandery,
where he stayed overnight at Queben Pavilion.
The night was not yet half over when a woman came out from below the tower and said of herself:
I am a concubine named E, with the surname Su and the courtesy name Yishu.
I was originally from Xiu Village in Guangxin County.
At an early age, I lost both my parents and have no brothers.
He had been dead for a long time.
There were one hundred and twenty bolts of various silks and a maidservant named Zhifu.
I am a widow, destitute, frail, and weak, unable to support myself.
I wish to go to a neighboring county to sell my silk,
and have gone to Wang Bo, a man from the same county.
He hired one carriage and ox,
for which the price was twelve thousand coins;
he loaded his concubine along with silks upon it and ordered Zhifu to hold the reins.
I arrived outside this pavilion on the tenth day of the fourth month of last year.
At that time, as evening had fallen and all travelers had ceased their journey,
I did not dare proceed further.
He remained there for that reason.
Soon after, he suddenly developed abdominal pain.
His concubine went to the house of the village headman to beg for some gruel and firewood.
The village head, Gong Shou, wielding a blade and grasping a halberd,
came beside the carriage and asked the lady:
"From where has this lady come?
What is being carried in the carriage? Where is the man?"
"Why do you travel alone?
His wife replied to him,
"Why do you ask this?"
Śouyin seized his concubine by the arm and said, "Do you not love this beauty? Could we not enjoy each other's company?
At that time, the concubine was terrified and refused to comply.
Shou immediately stabbed himself in the side with a knife; he died instantly.
Furthermore, he killed Zhifu.
Shou then dug beneath the tower and buried his concubine along with her maidservant.
He took the property and departed.
He slaughtered an ox and burned the chariot,
placing the chariot’s axle-bolt and the ox bones inside an empty well to the east of the pavilion.
"The grief of my death is so bitter that there is no one to whom I may appeal.
Therefore, I have come to seek refuge with you, Illustrious Lord. Chang said:
"Now I wish to cause your corpse to rise up in terror.
What shall serve as the proof?
The girl said:
"The maidservant was dressed entirely in white garments from head to foot;
her green silk sandals were still not decayed.
When they dug it up, it was indeed as he had said.
Chang then dispatched an official to arrest Shou;
under interrogation, Shou fully confessed.
He was sent down to Guangxin County for further examination.
His conversation with E was the same [as before].
He arrested Shou’s parents and brothers, all of whom were imprisoned.
Chang submitted a memorial stating that Shou had committed murder.
Under the eternal law, one does not incur the penalty of clan extermination;
however, if one lives out a life of evil in secrecy for many years,
it is something that the royal law cannot reach.
"Among the ghosts and spirits, there has not been one in a thousand years who has brought such a plea.
We pray that you execute them all,
thereby assisting the secret execution."
The Emperor approved of the report.

At that time, there was a man named Wang Xun, courtesy name Shaolin, who served as the Magistrate of Mei County in Qizhou under the Han dynasty. A village headman from Liting in Mei County had stolen and murdered another person’s daughter.
Wang Xun was then serving as the Magistrate of Mei County.
He arrived at Liting in that commandery.
The pavilion was constantly haunted by ghosts,
which had killed people on numerous occasions.
Tun was staying on the upper floor of the tower when,
at night, a woman appeared,
claiming she wished to appeal her grievance.
He had no clothes to cover himself.
Tún gave him his own garment,
whereupon the man stepped forward and said:
"I am originally the wife of the Magistrate of Fuyang.
I was traveling to take up my official post and stayed overnight at this pavilion."
The head of the watch killed his concubine and more than ten other people, both old and young,
and buried them beneath the tower.
They plundered his clothes and property.
The station chief was now serving as a patrolman at the county gate. Dun said:
"I shall inform you of this;
do not again recklessly kill the virtuous and good.
Having said this, the ghost threw down his garment and departed.
Tun then arrested the patrol officers;
upon interrogation, they immediately confessed.
He arrested more than ten co-conspirators and put them all to death.
He excavated the various graves, returned the remains to their homes, and performed the encoffining and burial rites.
Thus, eternal peace and tranquility were established.
The people sang this folk song:
How true it is that Shaolin has no peer in the world!
Flying cloaks and galloping horses, conversing with ghosts.
Flying cloaks and galloping horses.
These are separate matters and are not recorded here;
the two preceding accounts of evidence are taken from the *Yuanhun zhi* (Record of Vengeful Spirits).
During the eighth year of the Daye era of the Sui dynasty, there was a man in Yizhou named Huangfu Qian.
More than forty li to the southeast of the city of Yizhou,
there was a household surnamed Huangfu.
There were four brothers living together in the family.
The eldest brother and the youngest brother both diligently attended to their livelihoods;
they were benevolent, kind, loyal, and filial.
The second younger brother was named Qian.
Associating with evil friends and not attending to his livelihood,
at a later time his mother was inside the hall;
she took sixty coins, intending to have him go shopping.
He was placed upon a bed.
His mother went to the back of the house,
while his younger brother came in from outside and entered the hall.
Looking around to left and right, he saw no one;
he then stole the money and took it out for his private use.
When his mother returned and searched for the money, she could not find it.
Not knowing where the child had gone,
he then interrogated the entire household;
both the masters and servants alike said they had not seen him.
The mother, resentful that the entire household had not been purified,
proceeded to whip both the adults and the children; all,
both great and small, harbored resentment.
In the following year, he passed away.
He was conceived in the womb of a sow within the household;
after three or five months had elapsed, she gave birth to a single piglet.
When he was two years old,
the village festival arrived in the eighth month;
needing money, his family sold him to a household from a distant village and received six hundred cash.
The shrine official was about to depart.
At the first watch of the night,
he then roused the entire family, both great and small.
First, he touched his wife with his nose;
while she was sleeping, she said in a dream: "I am your husband."
For the sake of taking sixty coins from an old woman,
you unjustly implicated my entire family and subjected us to needless torture,
causing me to be reborn as a pig.
"I have now come to repay my debt.
I am now being sold to the village shrine;
the shrine attendants have bound me, intending to kill me."
"You are my wife. How could you bear not to tell your son and daughter to ransom me?
This was the wife's first dream.
Suddenly waking up, his heart was startled;
yet he still did not believe it.
He fell back asleep and again dreamed thus.
The pig again touched the woman with its snout;
she was startled, put on her clothes, and went toward the hall to inform her mother-in-law.
Her mother-in-law had already risen and was sitting up.
He again dreamed of being with his new wife;
he also dreamed of his children as before, dressing them for the night and taking his elder brother along,
while carrying one thousand two hundred coins.
The mother replied to her son,
"If the village official is unwilling to release it,
we shall seek to give him double the price."
Fearing that it would grow light and he would be killed,
he galloped away in haste;
he traveled more than thirty li from his dwelling.
Once the son arrived there,
he did not mention his own relatives,
fearing he might bring disgrace upon his family.
He merely said, "There is no need to kill it;
I now wish to redeem this pig.
However, the village headman was unwilling to agree.
"The time for my sacrifice to the Earth God has now arrived;
I will not give the pig to you.
Though you entreat me repeatedly and with great earnestness, I shall not release it."
The elder brother’s son was terrified and in haste,
fearing that he would be killed.
He secretly relied upon a man of learning and understanding who possessed faith and respect, and who had formerly served as a county magistrate.
He related the full details of the actual circumstances.
Only after this was the pig eventually ransomed;
once it had been recovered, he drove it toward the wild fields.
The elder brother said to the pig,
"If you are truly my younger brother,
you should quickly go forward and return home."
The boy spoke again to the pig,
saying, "If it is truly my father,
you too should come forward and return home."
Upon hearing these words, the pig ran ahead and returned home.
After some time had passed, the entire village became aware of the matter, and the children were filled with shame and humiliation.
Neighbors who harbored mutual resentment began to mock and revile them, attributing the incident to the pig.
The children secretly told the pig, "Father,
because you performed unwholesome deeds, you have received this body as a pig;
we, your sons and daughters, cannot emerge from our heads."
Throughout his life, my lord was always on very close terms with the worthy man Xu;
my lord [was well-disposed] toward the Xu family.
The children brought food and went there to offer it to their father;
when the pig heard these words, [he was moved].
Shedding tears, he hurried toward the Xu family home.
The Xu residence was more than forty li from his own dwelling.
This occurred during the eleventh year of the Daye era.
Zhu Xu passed away at his home.
Xìn realized that karmic retribution does not distinguish between the close and the distant, as clearly as if it were before one's eyes.
How could one not be cautious?
Dharma Master Jinglin of Hongfa Temple in Chang’an was a neighbor of Xian;
he personally saw that pig.

During the Qi dynasty, Wang Huan, who served as the Left Vice-Director of the Department of State Affairs, was jealous and murdered his concubine; this was a strange instance of karmic retribution.
Wang Huan of Langya served the Qi dynasty until he attained the rank of Left Vice-Director of the Department of State Affairs.
He had profound faith in the Buddhist scriptures,
yet his jealousy was so deep that he forgot the virtue of broad magnanimity.
Once, while he was inside his quarters having a favorite concubine trim his mustache,
a crow suddenly flew across the courtyard with a yellow plum in its beak and dropped it.
Seng-huan remarked that the bird must have seen the concubine’s secret appointment and had dropped the fruit as a playful offering.
He sent a slave out to scout;
the slave encountered a man wandering privately toward a fence and immediately went to seize him.
When this man spoke words of anger, defilement, and insult,
he immediately fled in haste;
the slave returned and reported this to him.
Huan said, "I believe you have the truth.
Please undergo further interrogation.
The concubine then related her account in full.
In the end, he did not investigate her;
he immediately ordered her down the stairs to be flogged to death.
As she was being stripped of her clothes, she made a vow, saying:
This death today is truly unjust and premature.
If there is such a thing as the Way of Heaven, [may it take its course].
He then informed the authorities.
Thereafter, he frequently saw the concubine come to him to recount her grievances.
Shortly thereafter, he was appointed as the Governor of Yongzhou.
His disposition gradually became deranged and strange,
as if possessed by a spirit;
for no apparent reason, he beat and killed a minor official.
The Regional Secretary Liu Xingzu falsely accused him of intending to rebel.
He was then impeached by Kong Zhigui, the Palace Aide to the Censor-in-Chief.
Emperor Shizu dispatched the Secretariat Drafter Lü Wenxian and the Commander of the Guard Cao Daogang.
He led the ceremonial guards and troops to capture Liu Huàn.
Huàn’s son, Liu Biāo, was already notorious for his cruelty and ferocity;
so too was his son-in-law, Yīn Ruì.
He then urged Huian, saying,
"Cao and Lü have now arrived,
yet we have not seen the authentic imperial edict."
"Fearing this may be a plot for treachery,
it is appropriate that you record it and dispatch it immediately for the Emperor's report.
Huàn accepted his advice.
He then assigned more than a thousand men to guard the gates with weapons to hold them in defense.
Piao subsequently engaged the government troops in battle.
Liu Biao was defeated and fled.
Pei Shuye, the Regional Inspector for Pacifying the Barbarians,
raised troops within the city.
Gong Huan cut him down.
People of the time considered this to be the retribution of the concubine. The two preceding accounts of evidence are from the *Mingxiang ji*.
During the Qi dynasty, there was a man surnamed Xu of Donghai in Song who was jealous of his wife; he castrated the son of his former wife, and a strange karmic retribution followed.
His first wife was Lady Xu,
who bore him a son named Tiejiu; subsequently,
Lady Xu passed away.
So-and-so remarried Chen;
Chen was cruel and tyrannical, intent on destroying the iron mortar.
Chen gave birth to a son.
Upon his birth, he made a vow, saying:
"If you do not eliminate the iron mortars,
you shall not be my son."
For this reason, it was named the Iron Pestle.
He intended to use the bell to pound within the iron mortar;
thereupon, he struck the iron mortar.
They were exposed to all manner of suffering and poison;
when hungry, they were not provided with food,
and when cold, they were not given quilted clothing.
I am by nature dull-witted and weak,
and moreover, I am often absent.
My wife thereafter acts as she pleases, committing acts of violence and cruelty.
Tiejiu eventually died from the pain of chronic hunger and beatings;
he was sixteen years old at the time.
More than ten days after his death, [the following occurred].
The ghost suddenly returned home,
climbed onto Chen’s bed, and said,
"I am an iron mortar."
"In truth, I have committed not the slightest offense, yet I am being unjustly subjected to this cruel slaughter.
My mother has appealed her grievance to Heaven,
and she has received a warrant from the Celestial Office to fetch an iron pestle."
I shall cause the iron pestle and the illness to suffer the same misfortune as I do when my time to depart arrives; for that day is certain.
For now, I shall remain here and wait.
The voice was as if produced by a living person;
family members and guests did not see his form, yet they all heard his speech.
Thereupon, he constantly resided upon the rafters of the house.
The Chen family knelt in thanks and struck their cheeks in grief as they prepared offerings for the memorial service.
The ghost said,
"There is no need for this."
"I am starving to death;
how could a single meal possibly compensate for this?
I shall speak of it in secret during the night. Thus he spoke.
The ghost said in a harsh voice,
"How dare you speak of me?
Now I shall cut through the ridgepole of your house."
Then he heard the sound of a saw;
shavings fell accordingly,
and there was a loud creaking noise.
It was as if the ridgepole had truly collapsed;
the entire family rushed out and used a bright candle to illuminate the scene.
Nor was there any difference.
The ghost then cursed the iron pestle, saying,
"Since you have killed me..."
He sat peacefully upon his house, considering it a source of pleasure, thinking,
"I shall burn down your house.
Immediately, he saw the fire blazing.
The smoke and flames were fierce and violent, causing great distress both inside and out;
yet in an instant they extinguished themselves,
and the thatched cottage remained intact without any damage.
Day after day he reviled him,
and at times he would sing:
"The peach and plum trees are in full bloom."
Frost has fallen; what can be done?
The seeds of peach and plum are already hardened. The frost fell early.
The sound was extremely poignant,
as if lamenting that he would not grow up.
At that time, Tiechu was six years old.
When the ghost arrives, the person immediately falls ill;
the body aches, the abdomen swells,
there is shortness of breath, and eating is obstructed.
The ghosts struck him repeatedly;
his body was covered in bruises everywhere.
After more than a month, he died.
The ghost then became silent. [This is] the first account from the *Yuanhun zhi* (Record of Vengeful Spirits).
During the Tang dynasty, Wang Zhi of Qizhou experienced a haunting involving a nuptial marriage with a spirit.
In the third year of the Xianqing era of the Tang, Wang Zhi was serving as the magistrate of Qishan County in Qizhou. He was subsequently appointed as the county magistrate of Yizhou.
Upon the completion of his term of office, he returned to his hometown.
There was a maiden living in her father’s house whose countenance was upright and beautiful.
Before his marriage could take place, he passed away while traveling and was staying in Mianzhou;
his body was encoffined and interred in a temple.
He stayed for several months.
There was already a student in the temple who resided in one of the rooms.
Early in the night, he saw this deceased daughter enter his room;
she was elegantly adorned and offered him her respects with full courtesy.
Desiring to pursue one another,
the student was received; they became acquainted over the course of several months.
The woman gave the student a single bronze mirror, a towel, and a comb, each one.
Thinking of ascending the Path,
the woman was together with the student.
They expressed their grief in full and took their secret leave;
the family members searched for this object but could not find it,
so they were ordered to search every room.
He found it in the student’s room and ordered his attendants to bind and beat the man,
treating him as a private thief.
The student related the matter in detail, saying,
"I have obtained not only this object from my wife."
Furthermore, he left two robes, one for the upper body and one for the lower, along with a parting message addressed to [the deceased],
to serve as tokens of his sincerity;
he then dispatched people to open the coffin and search for them.
As it turned out, there was no such garment;
moreover, he saw that the woman’s body resembled that of a human being in a fortunate state.
Having observed this omen, [he understood].
He dispatched people to release him and questioned the man:
"Where do you reside?"
He replied,
"I am originally from Qizhou. Because my father was appointed to a southern post, I followed him there."
Both his parents having passed away,
Quan traveled through various provinces to pursue his studies;
he would soon be returning.
He provided him with clothing and a horse;
they set out together,
intending for him to become her husband.
Out of profound affection, he related these matters in detail to the monk Fayun of Ximing Monastery, who was originally from his home province of Zizhou.
During the Tang dynasty, a woman in India violated her vows by engaging in illicit affairs with outsiders; she subsequently received a strange karmic retribution during the Wude era of the Tang.
The Indian man’s surname was Wei.
He made a vow with a woman that they would not betray one another.
After many years, her favor declined;
the woman became resentful and vengeful.
Fearing she would turn against him, Wei strangled her to death.
A few days later, Wei’s entire body became itchy;
he subsequently broke out with leprosy sores and died.
Wei Xiaoxie recounted this to Lin.
This is the first of the right-hand proofs from the *Mingbao ji* (Records of Karmic Retribution).

Section Seven: On False Speech (75). Section on False Speech, Number Seven; this is further divided into two parts. Part One: Exposition of the Intent. First, Exposition of the Intent: Now, as for those who have received a physical form within the human realm...
Encountering such a time of defilement and turbidity,
one receives a false physical form and constantly creates illusory and deceptive realms.
Therefore, they falsely construct delusive thoughts,
harbor confusion and perversity within their hearts, and turn their minds away from reality while turning their backs on the objective realm.
The words uttered are all false;
they deceive and delude those before them,
causing others to misunderstand.
This causes myriad sufferings to entangle one another and a hundred anxieties to converge,
sowing the seeds of delusion.
One reaps the retribution of being treated with contempt;
the heavy sufferings of hell are further intensified by boiling water and glowing coals.
That one becomes deluded regarding the Dharma and confuses the true for the false is truly due to false speech.
Section Two: Quotations from Scriptural Authority Furthermore, a verse from the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* says:
Those who speak with false words Afflict all sentient beings;
They are always like darkness, And though they possess life, they are as if dead.
If one speaks words that cut oneself with a knife, why would the tongue not fall out?
If one utters false speech, one loses genuine merit;
if a person speaks falsely, there is a poisonous snake within their mouth.
The sword dwells within the mouth; the blazing fire burns within the mouth.
Poison is the poison; the poison upon the earth is not the true poison.
The poison of the mouth cuts through sentient beings, causing them to fall into hell at the end of their lives.
If a person speaks false words, pus will emerge from their own mouth and their tongue will become like hell;
their tongue will also be like a blazing fire.
If a person slanders falsely, that person will quickly be held in contempt.
Those who abandon virtuous people, whom the heavens do not protect;
those who constantly harbor hatred and envy toward others,
and who employ evil means to afflict and disturb other sentient beings— because of these causes, they enter hell.
Furthermore, a verse from the *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra* says:
"If there is another person who delights in false speech, That person will, in this present life, obtain harsh words and an ugly appearance;
Even though what they say is true, people will not believe or accept it."
All people detest them and take no pleasure in seeing them; this is called the retribution for evil karma in the present life.
After casting off this body, they enter hell and undergo great suffering—hunger, thirst, and the torment of heat; this is called [the retribution] in future lives.
As the retribution for evil karma, even if one obtains a human body, one's mouth shall be incomplete;
though what one says is true, people will not believe or accept it. Those who see one will find no pleasure;
though one preaches the True Dharma, people will take no delight in hearing it—such is this evil person.
By the power of causes and conditions, all external objects and the necessities of life diminish;
by this one may know for certain that those who speak falsehoods suffer in the three periods of time.
Furthermore, the *Dhyāna-guhyaka-sūtra* states:
"If there are members of the fourfold assembly who,
within the Buddha-dharma, act for the sake of gain and offerings..."
Greedy and insatiable,
they feign virtue and commit evil deeds for the sake of a good reputation.
In truth, they do not practice meditation;
their bodies and speech are negligent, and they engage in heedless conduct.
Out of greed for gain and offerings, they falsely claim to be practicing meditation.
In this way, a bhikṣu commits a sthūlātyaya;
having passed the time without confessing it and without reforming his ways,
within a mere moment he commits a thirteenth saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If it lasts for one day, or even two days,
you should know that this bhikṣu is a thief among gods and men.
A rākṣasa executioner will inevitably fall into the evil realms and commit a grave and heavy transgression.
If a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī,
having not actually seen white bones,
claims to have seen white bones.
Even down to the practice of ānāpānasmṛti,
these bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs deceive and delude the devas, nāgas, spirits, and so forth.
These wicked people are of the lineage of Pāpīyān;
for the sake of falsehood, they speak of themselves thus.
"I have attained the contemplation of impurity,
up to the stage of the Peak Dharma"—
this is a person who speaks falsely.
After their lives have ended, they will fall into the Avīci Hell faster than a flash of lightning or a rain shower;
their lifespan there shall be one kalpa.
Emerging from hell, they fall among the hungry ghosts;
for eight thousand years they consume hot iron balls.
Emerging from the realm of hungry ghosts, they fall among the animals.
In life they constantly carry heavy burdens;
in death, their skin is flayed.
This continues for five hundred lifetimes.
They will be reborn among humans,
yet will suffer from deafness, blindness, muteness,
lameness, and a hundred other ailments.
They use them as clothing.
Such sufferings endured therein cannot be fully described.
Furthermore, a verse from the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* says:
Ambrosia and poison both reside within the human tongue;
ambrosia is called truthful speech, while falsehood is poison.
If a person requires ambrosia, that person must abide in truthful speech.
If a person requires poison, that person speaks falsely when saying it will not certainly kill;
yet if one speaks falsely, they are certain to be called a dead man.
False speech brings no benefit to oneself, nor does it profit others;
if neither self nor others find joy in it, why speak such falsehoods?
If a person engages in evil discrimination and delights in speaking false words—
Falling upon flaming swords, though such suffering and poisonous harm are extremely terrible, they can destroy but a single body;
yet for one who commits the evil karma of lying, hundreds of thousands of bodies shall be ruined.
Furthermore, the *Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on Sūrata* states:
The Buddha said, "Now,
as for those who speak falsely..."
Deceiving oneself and also deceiving others,
the liar causes one's body to emit a foul odor.
Lacking sincerity in thought and speech,
one causes the mind to suffer;
such is the nature of false speech.
It causes their breath to be foul-smelling,
their bodies to be endangered,
and they to be abandoned by the celestial deities.
Those who speak falsely lose all roots of goodness; being ignorant and deluded within themselves,
they lose their way on the path of virtue.
False speech is the root of all evils;
it severs the foundation of virtuous conduct and solitary dwelling.
Furthermore, in the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, King Yama reproaches the transgressors with these verses:
"By truthful speech one attains peace and happiness; by truthful speech one attains nirvāṇa."
False speech produces bitter fruits, which one now experiences here;
if one does not abandon false speech, one will undergo all manner of suffering.
Truthful speech need not be purchased; it is easily obtained and not difficult to attain.
It truly does not come from another country, nor is it sought from another person.
Why, then, do you abandon truthful speech and take delight in speaking falsehoods?
To speak words of falsehood is the very cause and condition for hell.
The causal conditions were already established in the past; what benefit is there in crying out now?
False speech is the foremost fire; it can even burn the great ocean, let alone the person who utters such falsehoods—just as it burns grass and wood.
If a person abandons truthful speech and utters false words,
such a foolish and evil person discards jewels to take up stones;
if a person does not love themselves, they will love hell.
The fire of one’s own lying burns the self in this place;
truthful speech is very easy to obtain. Yet, abandoning truthful speech to speak falsely for the sake of adorning oneself, one arrives at this place through delusion.
Furthermore, a verse from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says:
Truthful speech is the foremost precept; Truthful speech is the ladder for ascending to heaven.
Though small, truthful speech is as great [as the heavens]; False speech leads one into hell.
Furthermore, the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states:
"Regarding non-false speech:
if one speaks the Dharma, engages in debate, or transmits messages concerning all matters of right and wrong,"
Do not claim [this] for yourself;
always ensure that you can trace it back to its source,
and then there will be no fault.
Otherwise, the axe is in one's own mouth.
Furthermore, the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* states:
"If one says to a person of high birth that they are low-born..."
If one with two eyes says to another who has one eye that they have only one,
it constitutes a lie; likewise,
if one says to a person with one eye, "You are blind," it also constitutes a lie.
One also incurs the offense of lightly annoying others.
The verse on the primary retribution says:
"Deceitful in lying to others, one suffers punishment clumsily in hell."
Flaming saws dismember their forms; hot iron plows their tongues and douses them with molten copper. They are ground by hard steel;
their grief shatters their very marrow, as they groan and weep in constant sobs.
The Verse on the Retribution of Habitual Practice says:

Those who speak falsehoods enter the three miserable realms; Once their punishment in those realms is settled, Their residual karma leads them to rebirth in the human path, Where they are constantly beset by slander and the knots of anxiety.
Yet one is again deceived by others; The fire of resentment burns like heat.
A wise person should not resent others; One must extinguish it by examining the fruit through its cause. *Fayuan zhulin*, Scroll 75.

Section 8: Harsh Speech (76). Section Eight on Harsh Speech is divided into two parts. Part One: Exposition of Intent. First, the Exposition of Intent: In ordinary persons, the poison is fierce and the fire of anger burns constantly.
When encountering conditions that give rise to obstacles and contacting objects that provoke anger,
one’s words burst forth in a fit of rage, burning the heart.
This harms others as painfully as being cut by a blade and violates the benevolent mind of a Bodhisattva.
Because they violate the compassionate instructions of the Tathāgata,
there are differences in karmic retribution.
As a verse in the *Karma-vibhaṅga-sūtra* says:
Harsh speech that offends and vexes others, A fondness for exposing the private faults of others, And being stubborn and difficult to subdue— These lead to rebirth as a *jvālāmukha* hungry ghost.
Section Two: Quotations from Scriptural Authority As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*:
There are some hungry ghosts who,
in previous lives, were malicious in speech and delighted in using coarse language.
Furthermore, those sentient beings will harbor hatred and loathing for him,
regarding him as an enemy whenever they see him.
Because of these transgressions, one falls among the hungry ghosts.
Furthermore, the Dharmapada states:
"Though one may be a śramaṇa..."
They do not restrain their body or speech;
they speak crudely and wickedly,
causing much injury and harm.
That which the multitude does not love,
the wise do not cherish;
when the body dies, the spirit departs.
They revolve through the three miserable realms,
undergoing birth and death by themselves,
experiencing immeasurable suffering and affliction.
The Buddhas and noble sages do not spare [anyone] from this.
Even if sentient beings have no faults in their physical actions,

10. Section on Frivolous Speech (76). Section Ten on Frivolous Speech, which is divided into two parts. 1. Part One: Exposition of the Intent. Regarding the exposition of the intent: Now, the purpose of loyal speech is to manifest the principle.
Frivolous speech deviates from the truth because it lacks sincerity;
through sincerity there is reality,
and through reality virtue arises.
Because virtue arises, one becomes a sage;
because of frivolous speech, there is falsehood;
because of falsehood, sin arises.
Because sin arises, one undergoes suffering;
therefore, know that those who seek the principle and the noble must speak the truth.
To say that what is false is ultimately contrary to reason—
that all improper speech is termed frivolous talk (*sambhinna-pralāpa*)— is correct;
however, such frivolous talk merely fails to benefit oneself or others.
Only increasing negligence and growing all manner of unwholesome states,
they fall into the three miserable realms at death;
when later reborn as humans, [they will suffer].
Even when one speaks correct words, if others do not believe them,
and whatever one says is indistinct and unclear,
this is also called frivolous speech (*saṃbhinnapralāpa*).
Therefore, the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states:
"Even if one's words are true, if they are spoken at an improper time,
they also fall under frivolous speech (*sambhinna-pralāpa*)."
Section Two: Citing Scriptural Authority. As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, a verse says:
"Those who fall among the hungry ghosts (*preta*) Have flames issuing from their mouths;
They cry out in all four directions with a great sound— This is the retribution for verbal transgressions."
Though one may have heard much and seen much, preaching the Dharma in the midst of the great assembly does not constitute the karma of inspiring faith; if all people do not believe and accept it,
yet one desires wide renown and to be trusted and accepted by others— [one must practice accordingly].
Therefore, one should be sincere and must not engage in frivolous speech.
Furthermore, the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states that the four verbal transgressions, when combined with one another, each form four permutations.
First, there may be double-tongued speech that is neither false speech nor harsh speech.
For example, suppose there is a person who conveys the words of one person to another;
because they speak what is true, it is not false speech.
Because it is spoken with gentle words, it is not harsh speech (*pāruṣya*).
Because it is motivated by a mind intent on causing division, it is called divisive speech (*paiśunya*).
Second, there may be cases where divisive speech is also false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*) but not harsh speech.
Suppose there is a person who conveys the words of one person to another;
because it is done with a mind of separation, it is divisive speech (*paiśunya*);
because it is spoken falsely, it is lying (*mṛṣāvāda*).
Because it is spoken with gentle words, it is not harsh speech (*pāruṣya*).
Third, there may be divisive speech (*paiśunya*) that is harsh speech but not false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*).
For example, when one person conveys the words of this person to that person.
Because it involves a mind of separation, it is divisive speech; because it is spoken with harsh words, it is abusive speech.
Because it is spoken according to reality, it is not false speech.
In the fourth case, there may be divisive speech that is both false speech and abusive speech.
Suppose there is a person who conveys the words of one person to another;
because it is done with a mind of separation, it is divisive speech (*paiśunya*);
because it is spoken falsely, it is lying (*mṛṣāvāda*).
Because one speaks with harsh sounds, it is called *pāruṣya* (harsh speech).
Apart from these, the four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) for *mṛṣāvāda* (false speech) and *pāruṣya* are likewise established.
As for *saṃbhinnapralāpa* (frivolous speech), each of these types is inseparable from the others.
Therefore, they are not explained separately.
Thus, the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states:
"The remaining three types of vocal karma..."
While some may be combined or separated,
the single type of frivolous speech is necessarily never dissociated from them.
The verse on the direct retribution states:
Frivolous speech is devoid of meaning and principle, Causing the human mind to become deluded and confused;
It destroys the roots of others' goodness, And molten copper is poured into one's split mouth.
Blazing iron burns their tongues, and their internal organs are all scorched and rotten;
this pain is unbearable, and they wail and shriek in constant lamentation.
The verse on the ripening of karma says:
Idle rumors obscure the true Dharma; because of this, one sinks into the evil realms.
Those who have departed from that state and returned for a time as humans speak words that lack clarity, and being devoid of faith and devotion, they are constantly ridiculed by others.

11. Section on Avarice and Greed (77). Section Eleven on Avarice and Greed is divided into two parts. Part One: Exposition of the Intent. Regarding the affliction of delusion among sentient beings, attachment to the self is its primary cause.
Generally, the delusions of ordinary beings are rooted in stinginess and greed;
thus they regard even a hair’s breadth of good as light, yet view a mountain of evil as heavy.
Their merit is as thin as spring ice, while their poverty is like the incessant autumn rains.
The net of the six sense-faculties is not easily transcended;
the ford of the three poisons provides no means of crossing.
The body is heavy and remains perpetually submerged.
They are like fish in a river that flap their fins in an attempt to fly;
they cannot be compared to birds in the heavens.
This causes poverty to follow upon poverty as they compete to encroach and oppress,
and suffering to follow upon suffering as they strive to inflict harm;
it is like a moth fluttering into a flame, bringing about its own incineration.
Just as a silkworm makes its cocoon to bind itself, one is not entangled by anything else;
it is truly due to the obstacle of stinginess and greed that one undergoes the suffering of hunger and cold.
Generosity is the cause of wealth, constantly inviting abundance and joy.
Section Two: Quotations from Scriptural Sources. As stated in a verse from the *Karmavipāka-sūtra*:
"One who constantly delights in cultivating wisdom, yet does not practice giving, will be born ever-intelligent and discerning, yet remain impoverished and destitute of wealth."
Those who delight solely in practicing generosity, yet do not cultivate wisdom,
will obtain great wealth in their future lives; those who are foolish, dark, and lacking in insight,
should practice both generosity and wisdom, so that in their future lives they shall possess both wealth and wisdom.
Those who cultivate neither of the two will dwell in poverty and low status for a long night;
as the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
"Avarice is an obstacle to abundant wealth."

Regarding the tenth case: Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty wished to construct a monastery atop the tomb of Emperor Wen. He sent for Master Huiyuan of Mount Lu to perform the consecration rites. When the Master arrived at the site, he saw that the ground was filled with wild grass and thorns, and the tomb was overgrown with weeds. He remarked, "This place is not auspicious. The Emperor then ordered the construction of a monastery on Mount Zhong, where the Master resided. Later, when Emperor Wu fell ill, he dreamed of a monk who said, "The spirit of the deceased Emperor Wen has come to take you away. Upon waking, the Emperor summoned the Master to inquire about his dream. The Master replied, "The spirit of the deceased Emperor Wen is indeed powerful; it is likely that he has come to summon Your Majesty. The Emperor then asked, "Is there any way to avert this? The Master replied, "If Your Majesty can build a monastery on the site of the late Emperor’s tomb, the calamity may perhaps be averted. The Emperor followed this advice and built the monastery. Afterward, the Emperor’s illness gradually subsided. This is proof that the spirits of the dead possess supernatural power and can respond to human sincerity. Thus, one must be cautious in selecting burial sites. One should avoid locations where the geomancy is unfavorable, as such places will surely bring misfortune to the descendants. Furthermore, if one performs meritorious deeds such as building monasteries or stupas on the site of a grave, one can transform the inauspiciousness into auspiciousness and ensure that the descendants will enjoy peace and prosperity. This is why the ancients were so diligent in selecting gravesites and why they emphasized the importance of filial piety and merit-making. These accounts demonstrate that the principle of karmic retribution is inexorable and that the spirits of the dead truly exist and can manifest their influence. Chapter on the Ten Evil Deeds, Section Thirteen on False Views (79). This is divided into two parts. Part One: Exposition of the Intent. First, regarding those who have newly entered the Buddha-dharma:
One must take faith as the foremost requirement.

"Foolish people do not recognize cause and effect;

There is neither misfortune nor fortune, even unto neither good nor evil;

nor is there the birth of sentient beings in this life or in future lives.
Such a person, by destroying both wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, is said to have severed their roots of goodness;
they will certainly fall into the Avīci Hell.
Section Two: Citing Scriptural Authority. As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*:

Section Four: Universal Bestowal. As stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*:

Furthermore, although one does not perceive the giver,

Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

Why is this? Because material giving is limited,
whereas the gift of Dharma is immeasurable.
The gift of material wealth yields retribution within the desire realm;
the gift of the Dharma yields retribution beyond the three realms.
The gift of material wealth cannot sever the outflows.
The gift of Dharma leads one to ascend to the further shore;

whereas the gift of Dharma universally elicits the fruits of the three vehicles.
The gift of material wealth is accessible to both the foolish and the wise;
the gift of Dharma is restricted solely to the wise.
Through the gift of material wealth, only the donor obtains merit.
The gift of Dharma benefits both the giver and the recipient;
the gift of material wealth can be received even by the ignorant and animals,

The gift of material wealth benefits only the physical body;

and if one goes out to beg for alms,
one will quickly obtain food.
Reading the scriptures is sufficient; however,
if one is late in begging for alms,
the reading will not be complete.
If the sutra is insufficient, he shall be subject to reproach;
harboring grief and distress, he departs weeping.
At that time, an elder sees him shedding tears and mucus.
He called out to him from a distance and asked,
"Why are you so distressed?
The śrāmaṇera replied:
"Elder, you should know that my teacher is strict and difficult to serve; he commands me to recite the scriptures,
setting daily quotas for my studies."
If they are complete, one should rejoice; if they are not sufficient,
[one should seek them].
"I am being severely reproached.
When I go out to beg for alms,
if I obtain it quickly, my recitation of the scriptures will be sufficient."
If I request [a scripture] and receive it late, it will not suffice;
if I do not obtain the scripture at all, I am rebuked.
It is for these reasons that I am sorrowful.
At that time, the elder spoke to the śrāmaṇera:
"From this day forward, you shall come to my house regularly;
I will provide you with food so that you need have no anxiety."
Having finished eating, he applied himself with single-minded diligence to the recitation of the scriptures.
Upon hearing these words, the śrāmaṇera focused his mind and applied himself with diligent effort to the recitation of the scriptures.
The daily limit was not reduced,
and the teacher and his disciples were both filled with joy.
The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus:
The teacher at that time was Dīpaṃkara Buddha;
the śrāmaṇera was my own self in this present life;
and the great householder who made offerings then was Ānanda.
It is because of having performed such practices in the past that one now attains dhāraṇī without any forgetfulness.
