First, there are ten benefits to begging for food as long as one lives.
First, that which is used for sustaining life belongs to oneself and not to others.
Second, when sentient beings give me food, I shall cause them to abide in the Three Jewels before I eat.
Third, if there are those who give me food, I shall generate a heart of compassion toward them.
I shall apply myself with diligence so that [the recipient] may be well-established in giving;
only after this has been done will I eat.
This is for four reasons that accord with the Buddha’s teaching.
Fifth, he is easy to satisfy and easy to support.
Sixth, he practices the dharmas that destroy pride.
Seventh, he possesses the roots of goodness of the invisible crown of the head.
Eighth, seeing me beg for alms,
others who cultivate wholesome dharmas should likewise follow my example.
Ninth, I do not engage in any causal affairs with men, whether young or old.
Tenth, because of begging for food in successive order,
one generates a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings, thereby planting the seeds that assist the attainment of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
Second, there are also ten benefits in accepting the life of a forest-dweller (*āraṇyaka*).
First, coming and going with mastery;
second, being without self or what belongs to a self;
third, dwelling wherever one intends without obstruction.
Fourth, the practice of delighting in dwelling in forest hermitages through the transformation of the mind;
fifth, dwelling with few desires and few concerns;
sixth, not sparing one's body or life for the sake of fulfilling meritorious qualities.
Seventh, by staying far removed from clamorous speech;
eighth, by practicing meritorious deeds without seeking recompense;
ninth, by conforming to meditative concentration so that single-mindedness is easily attained.
Tenth, dwelling in an empty place makes it easy to give rise to the perception of non-obstruction.
Third, there are also ten benefits to wearing rag-robes (*pāṃśukūla*):
first, one does not associate with householders for the sake of clothing.
Second, one does not manifest the appearance of begging for robes for the sake of clothing.
Third, one does not employ expedient means to speak of obtaining robes.
Fourth, one does not seek or solicit in the four directions for the sake of clothing.
Fifth, if one does not obtain robes, one does not grieve;
sixth, even if one obtains them, one does not rejoice;
seventh, as these are inferior items that are easy to obtain, they are free from faults and afflictions.
Eighth, he practices in accordance with the four reliances received at the outset;
ninth, he enters among those who wear coarse clothing;
tenth, he is not greedily attached to by others.
The fourth practice, eating in a single sitting, also has ten benefits:
first, there is no seeking for more;
second, there is no exhaustion from the hardship of eating; third, what is received is light and small in amount.
Third, there is no exhaustion or suffering from uselessness.
Fourth, there is no exhaustion or suffering before meals.
Fifth, one enters into the practice of the rules for refined eating.
Sixth, food is digested after eating.
Seventh, there is little prevention of calamities.
Eighth, there is little illness.
Ninth, the body becomes light and agile.
Tenth, the body experiences happiness.
The fifth [practice], constant sitting, likewise has ten benefits.
First, not craving the pleasure of the body;
second, not craving the pleasure of sleep;
third, not craving the pleasure of bedding.
Fourth, there is no time for lying down, as one suffers from the side pressing against the mat.
Fifth, one does not follow the desires of the body.
Sixth, it is easy to engage in seated meditation.
Seventh, one easily reads and recites the sūtras;
eighth, one sleeps little;
ninth, the body is light and rises easily.
Tenth, the mind becomes detached from seeking bedding, seating, and clothing.
Regarding the sixth [precept], not accepting food at improper times after the midday meal also has ten benefits.
First, one does not eat excessively.
Second, eating until one is no longer hungry;
third, not craving delicious flavors;
fourth, having few desires and aspirations.
Fifth, few obstacles or afflictions;
sixth, little illness;
seventh, easy to satisfy.
Eighth, being easy to support;
ninth, knowing contentment;
tenth, not becoming physically exhausted while practicing seated meditation or reading the scriptures.
The seventh [category] consists of having only the three robes, which likewise possesses ten benefits:
first, there is no exhaustion from seeking or receiving anything beyond the three robes;
second, there is no exhaustion from guarding [possessions].
Third, the possessions one maintains are few;
fourth, one is content with only what is worn on the body;
fifth, one practices the precepts with meticulous care.
Sixth, one comes and goes without entanglement.
Seventh, the body is light and agile.
Eighth, one dwells in accordance with forest hermitages (āraṇyaka).
Ninth, one goes to various places without any sense of regret or attachment.
Tenth, one proceeds in accordance with the Path.
Eighth, there are also ten benefits to receiving robes made of coarse wool.
First, wearing coarse clothing;
second, having few desires and seeking little;
third, being able to sit according to one's inclination.
Fourth, it is easy to lie down upon;
fifth, it is easy to wash;
sixth, it is also easy to dye.
Seventh, it is slightly damaged by insects;
eighth, it is difficult to repair;
ninth, one shall not accept any other robe.
The tenth is not losing the quest for the Way.
Regarding the ninth, sitting according to [the rules], there are also ten benefits:
first, one does not seek to dwell in fine monasteries, thereby avoiding the exhaustion and suffering [of such pursuits].
Second, not seeking out fine bedding and seating that causes fatigue and distress;
third, not troubling those of senior standing;
fourth, not causing those of junior standing to feel sorrow or distress.
Fifth, having few desires;
sixth, having few affairs;
seventh, using only what is obtained as it comes.
Eighth, by using little, one has few concerns.
Ninth, one does not create the causes and conditions for disputes or litigation.
Tenth, one does not deprive others of what they use.
Sitting under a tree as the tenth [practice] also has ten benefits:
first, there is no weariness from seeking a dwelling;
second, there is no weariness from seeking bedding and seating.
Third, there is no exhaustion from that which is cherished;
fourth, there is no exhaustion from sensory enjoyment;
fifth, there is no locus for names.
Sixth, there is no matter of strife or contention.
Seventh, one accords with the four reliances (*catur-śaraṇa*).
Eighth, it is meager yet easily obtained and free from fault.
Ninth, conformity with the path of cultivation;
tenth, freedom from the conduct of worldly clamor.
Eleventh, there are also ten benefits in dwelling among those who have died.
First, one constantly maintains the perception of impermanence;
second, one constantly maintains the perception of death;
third, one constantly maintains the perception of impurity.
Fourth, they constantly attain the perception that all worlds are not to be relished.
Fifth, they constantly attain the state of being separated from all those they love.
Sixth, they constantly attain a heart of compassion.
Seventh, to remain far removed from frivolity and restlessness;
eighth, to maintain constant detachment in the mind;
ninth, to practice with diligent vigor.
Tenth, it can eliminate fear and dread.
Twelfth, sitting in an open space also has ten benefits.
First, one does not need to seek out the shade of a tree.
Second, being far removed from the sense of "mine";
third, being free from contention;
fourth, departing elsewhere without any lingering attachment or regret.
Fifth, they engage in little playful dalliance.
Sixth, they are able to endure wind, rain, cold, heat, mosquitoes, gadflies, venomous insects, and the like.
Seventh, they are not pierced by the thorns of sound.
Eighth, they do not cause sentient beings to feel anger or resentment.
Ninth, they themselves are free from sorrow and resentment.
Tenth, they have no place of conduct involving worldly clamor.
Furthermore, the Ratnarāśi Sūtra states:
The Buddha told Kāśyapa,
"If a bhikṣu wishes to go to an araṇya dwelling..."
One should contemplate eight things. What are these eight?
First, "I shall relinquish this body."
Second, one should relinquish life;
third, one should relinquish gain and honor;
fourth, one should depart from all places of attachment and delight.
Fifth, when dying among the mountains, one should die like a deer.
Sixth, in a forest hermitage (āraṇya), one should practice the conduct of a forest-dweller.
Seventh, one should sustain oneself by means of the Dharma.
8. Not using afflictions to govern oneself.
Section Four: On Benefit. As stated in the *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*:
"There are ten further dharmas for a bodhisattva practicing meditative concentration that are not shared with the followers of the two vehicles."
What are the ten? First,
cultivating meditative concentration without a sense of self,
because of being fully endowed with the various dhyānas and samādhis of the Tathāgata.
Second, one cultivates meditative concentration without relishing it or becoming attached to it,
relinquishing defiled states of mind and not seeking one's own pleasure.
Third, one cultivates meditative concentration to master the various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
For the sake of knowing the various mental activities of sentient beings,
one cultivates the fourth concentration in order to know the minds of all beings and to deliver and liberate them.
Fifth, one cultivates meditative concentration for the sake of great compassion,
because it severs the fetters of affliction in all sentient beings.
Sixth, one cultivates meditative concentration through the various dhyānas and samādhis.
Because they skillfully know how to enter and emerge from the three realms;
seventh, because they constantly attain mastery in the cultivation of meditative concentration and are fully endowed with all wholesome dharmas.
Eighth, by practicing meditative concentration, one’s mind attains quiescence,
for it surpasses the various dhyānas and samādhis of the two vehicles.
Ninth, by practicing meditative concentration, one constantly enters into wisdom.
Because it transcends all worlds and reaches the other shore;
and because the tenth, the cultivation of meditative concentration, can cause the True Dharma to flourish,
thereby ensuring that the Three Jewels continue without interruption.
Such concentration is not shared with śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Furthermore, the *Ṣaṭpāramitā-samuccaya-sūtra* states:
Furthermore, there are four kinds of meditative concentration that are fully endowed with wisdom. What are these four?
First, always delighting in dwelling alone.
Second, they always delight in single-mindedness.
Third, they seek meditative concentration and supernormal powers.
Fourth, they seek the unimpeded wisdom of a Buddha.
Furthermore, the Candrapradīpa-samādhi-sūtra states:
The Buddha said,
"If there is a bodhisattva..."
There are ten benefits for one who dwells in meditative seclusion. What are these ten?
First, their minds are not turbid;
second, they abide in heedfulness;
third, all Buddhas cherish and protect them.
Fourth, practicing with faith in the perfect enlightenment;
fifth, having no doubt regarding the Buddha's wisdom;
sixth, recognizing kindness.
Seventh, not slandering the true Dharma.
Eighth, being well able to maintain prohibitions and restraints.
Ninth, reaching the stage of subduing.
This verifies the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
Furthermore, the Buddha said:
"If there is a bodhisattva who delights in solitude, there are ten kinds of benefits."
What are the ten? First, reducing worldly affairs;
second, distancing oneself from clamor and bustle.
Third, there is no conflict or dispute;
fourth, one dwells in a state free from affliction;
fifth, one does not increase the outflows (*āsrava*).
Sixth, not giving rise to disputes or litigation;
seventh, abiding in tranquil silence;
eighth, conforming to the continuity of liberation.
Ninth, they swiftly realize liberation.
Tenth, they attain samādhi through the application of effort.
Furthermore, the Buddha said:
If there is a bodhisattva who is able to be in accord with dhyāna, there are ten kinds of benefits. What are the ten?
First, abiding securely in the ritual protocols.
Second, practicing the sphere of loving-kindness;
third, being free from the fever of remorse;
fourth, guarding the sense faculties.
Fifth, obtaining the joy and bliss of food;
sixth, distancing oneself from craving and desire;
seventh, practicing meditation so that it is not in vain.
Eighth, the snare of Māra’s liberations;
ninth, abiding securely in the realm of the Buddha;
tenth, liberation through maturation.
Furthermore, the Buddha said:
"If there is a bodhisattva who delights in the dhūta practice of begging for food, there are ten kinds of benefits. What are these ten?"
First, to demolish the banner of self-conceit;
second, not to seek intimacy or affection;
third, not to act for the sake of fame or reputation.
Fourth, they abide in the noble lineages;
fifth, they are without flattery, without deceit, and do not manifest artificial appearances, nor are they arrogant.
Sixth, not exalting oneself;
seventh, not disparaging others;
eighth, severing attachment and aversion.
Ninth, when entering a person's home, one does not go for the sake of food and drink, but practices the gift of Dharma.
Tenth, whatever Dharma one preaches is accepted with faith by others.
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
There are two kinds of samādhi:
first, that of the Buddha;
second, that of the bodhisattva.
These bodhisattvas have attained mastery within the samādhis of bodhisattvas,
but not within the samādhis of buddhas.
As it is said in the *Sarvabuddhaparṣadupasaṃkramaṇa-sūtra*:
Mañjuśrī wished to see the assembly of the Buddhas but was unable to reach it;
each of the Buddhas had returned to their respective abodes.
Mañjuśrī then went to the place where the Buddhas had gathered.
There was a woman sitting near that Buddha who had entered into samādhi. Mañjuśrī,
having entered and prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, [proceeded].
She said to the Buddha,
"Why is it that this woman is permitted to sit near the Buddha, while I am not?"
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī,
"Awaken this woman and cause her to rise from samādhi;
you yourself shall question her."
Mañjuśrī then snapped his fingers to awaken him, but he could not be awakened;
he called out to him with a loud voice, yet still could not awaken him;
he took him by the hand and pulled him, but he could not be awakened.
Furthermore, even when he moved the great trichiliocosm with his supernormal power, they remained unaware of it.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One..."
I am unable to awaken them.
At that time, the Buddha emitted a great radiance that illuminated the worlds of the lower direction.
Within those worlds was a bodhisattva.
Named Abandoner of All Veils (Sarvāvaraṇaprahāṇa),
he immediately emerged from below and approached the Buddha.
He prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet and stood to one side.
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Apagatasaṃvara: "Awaken this woman.
Immediately, he snapped his fingers.
This woman arose from samādhi.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha:
"By what cause and condition was it that although I shook the trichiliocosm, I could not cause this woman to arise?"
The Bodhisattva Prajñākūṭa rose from samādhi with a single snap of his fingers.
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī,
"It was because of this woman that you first conceived the aspiration for awakening."
This woman first conceived the aspiration for enlightenment because of her abandonment of the various hindrances by the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin; for this reason,
you are unable to awaken her.
"Your merit within the samādhis of all Buddhas is not yet fulfilled.
This Bodhisattva Abandoning All Coverings has attained mastery within samādhi.
It is simply because you have only recently entered the Buddha’s samādhis to a small degree and have not yet attained mastery."
5. Section on Dhyāna (Meditative Concentration). Section Five. As stated in the *Dhyānaguhya-uttama-sūtra*:
"A bhikṣu practicing in an araṇya (forest hermitage) may become insane due to five kinds of causes.
The first is due to distracting sounds."
Second, due to ill repute;
third, due to gain and offerings;
fourth, due to external winds.
Fifth is the internal wind.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke this incantation:

*Namo buddhāya | namo dharmāya | namaḥ saṃghāya | namo mahāriṣaye | vijarāja | kṣudhadadha | samanta | vajrāśi | dhara-kūṭa-śīta-carī carī | mahā-carī umari umarake | siddhāmbi-jambhi | ajambhili | jugujuki | sarvadhāraṇi | aśanti mocaya mocaya | mahā-moha-svāhā.* At that time, having spoken this incantation, the World-Honored One [ceased].
I tell you, Śāriputra:
this divine mantra was spoken by immeasurable Buddhas of the past;
I, too, now in the present, speak this mantra.
In the future, the Bodhisattvas of Maitreya’s Bhadrakalpa shall likewise proclaim this.
The merit of such a divine mantra is like that of Maheśvara;
it can cause the evil bhikṣus of the five-hundred-year period in later ages to attain purity of mind.
It harmonizes and properly regulates the increase and decrease of the four great elements;

it also cures the four hundred and four diseases and the four hundred and four pulses within the mind, as well as the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), the seeds of desire-nature, and the disordered realms.
It also cures karmic obstructions and exhausts all evils of transgressing the precepts without remainder.
This is called the Dhāraṇī for Thoroughly Treating the Seventy-two Kinds of Diseases and Sorrowful Afflictions;
it is also called the Dhāraṇī for Uprooting the Root of Ignorance within the Five Aggregates.
He is also called "Manifestly Seeing All Buddhas and Śrāvakas Preaching the True Dharma to Break the Fetters of All Dharmas.

Regarding the conditions for resonance and response, six instances of verification are briefly cited: the Jin dynasty śramaṇa Zhi Tanlan; the Song dynasty śramaṇa Shi Xuangao; the Song dynasty śramaṇa Shi Puchang; the Qi dynasty śramaṇa Shi Sengchou; the Sui dynasty śramaṇa Shi Fajin; and the Tang dynasty śramaṇa Shi Huirong. As for the Jin dynasty śramaṇa Zhi Tanlan: on Mount Chicheng in Shifeng during the Jin dynasty, there was Zhi Tanlan.
A native of Qingzhou,
he maintained a vegetarian diet, delighted in meditation, and recited three hundred thousand words of scripture.
During the Taiyuan era of the Jin dynasty, he traveled to Shan.
Later, he rested at Mount Chicheng in Shifeng and,
seeing a place where the woods and springs were pure and expansive,
he took up residence there. Several days passed.
Suddenly he saw a man several zhang tall who called out to Lan, ordering him to leave.
He also saw various strange-shaped birds and beasts attempting to terrify Lan.
Seeing Lan appearing composed and self-satisfied,
[the king] knelt and prostrated, saying,
"Zhūqī Wáng is my maternal uncle."
He ordered [the monk] to go to Mount Weihang to join him,
offering that place as a gift.
Three years later, the sound of a carriage and horsemen was suddenly heard.
The attendants reached Mount Mi.
Suddenly, a man wearing a *zhè* cap appeared, claiming to be the King of Zhūqī.
He came forward with twenty-three people, including his wife, children, and grandchildren.
Her physical appearance was upright and handsome, surpassing that of those in the world.
Once she had arrived at Lan’s residence and finished exchanging greetings, Lan asked where she lived.
He replied,
"I have long admired your reputation from Mount Weihang in Weixiang County, Leyuan."
Now, accompanied by my family, I look up to you for refuge;
I beg that you grant me the lay precepts.
Lan immediately conferred them upon him.
Having completed the reception of the Dharma,
he was presented with a donation of ten thousand coins and two vessels of honey;
then, taking his leave, he departed.
Suddenly, they heard the sound of whistling flutes and the vibration of wind instruments shaking the mountains and valleys;
Lan’s assembly of over ten people all witnessed and heard this.
He passed away in his mountain cell during the Yuanxi era of the Jin dynasty.
He was eighty-three years of age.
Among the śramaṇas of the Song dynasty was Shi Puchang; in the Pingcheng of the illegitimate Wei dynasty of the Song, there was also Shi Xuangao, whose secular surname was Wei.
His original name was Lingyu.
He was a native of Píngyì Wànnián.
His mother, of the Guān clan, had originally been a believer in non-Buddhist paths.
When she first married into the Wei family,
she conceived her first child,
a daughter, who was the elder sister of Gao.
Upon birth, he immediately placed his faith in the Buddha and made a vow on behalf of his mother:
"I pray that our family may be free from sectarian views and that we may serve the Great Dharma."
In the third year of the Hongshi era of the pseudo-Qin dynasty,
her mother dreamed that a foreign monk scattered flowers until they filled the room;
upon waking, she immediately conceived.
On the eighth day of the second month of the fourth year, a son was born.
Suddenly, a wondrous fragrance filled the house,
and a brilliant light illuminated the walls.
At dawn, they finally ceased their labor.
Because his mother perceived auspicious omens at the time of his birth,
she named him Lingyu (Divine Nurturing).
The people of the time held him in high esteem and called him Shigao.
At the age of twelve, he took leave of his parents and entered the mountains.
After a long time, he still did not grant permission.
On another day, a scholar came to stay overnight at the Gao household and said that he intended to go into seclusion on Mount Zhongchang.
His parents then placed him upon a high seat.
That evening, everyone saw the villagers gathering together to see him off.
At dawn the next morning, the villagers all came to visit Gao.
The parents said,
"We already sent you off yesterday;
why are you seeking us again today?"
The villagers said,
"We have no knowledge of it at all;
how could we possibly have sent it?"
Only then did his parents realize that those who had come to welcome and escort him the previous day were divine beings.
Since Hui-gao had turned his back on worldly conventions and departed from secular life,
he changed his name to Xuangao.
Endowed with keen intelligence and innate wisdom, he required no further reflection to master learning;
by the age of fifteen, he was already expounding the Dharma to mountain monks.
After receiving the precepts, he devoted himself exclusively to the cultivation of dhyāna and the Vinaya.
Hearing that the Dharma Master Buddhabhadra was propagating the Dharma at Shiyang Temple in Guanzhong,
Senggaō went to him as his teacher.
Within ten days, he attained a profound mastery of the methods of Chan.
Bhadra sighed in admiration and said,
"Excellent, Son of the Buddha!
You are truly able to awaken so profoundly to this."
Thereupon, he lowered his countenance and declined with humility, refusing to accept the rites of a teacher.
Daogao then took up his staff and retired to the Maiji Cliff in Western Qin,
where he had a hundred disciples.
He revered their righteous teachings and received their methods of meditation.
At that time, there was a śramaṇa from Chang’an named Shi Tanhong.
Gaozu of the Qin region was dwelling in seclusion on this mountain when he met Gao;
they were companions in their shared practice.
At that time, Qifu Chibian controlled the region of Longxi,
which bordered the territory of Liang to the west;
he constantly maintained more than three hundred disciples.
There was one named Xuanshao,
a native of Longxi in Qinzhou, who had thoroughly mastered the various methods of Chan meditation.
His supernormal powers were sovereign;
from his fingers he drew forth water to provide for the high-ranking official’s washing and rinsing,
the water being fragrant and pure, far surpassing anything ordinary.
Whenever he obtained non-worldly flowers or incense, he would offer them to the Triple Gem.
There were eleven others, such as Shao, who manifested such spiritual wonders.
Later, Shao entered Tangshu Mountain and passed away by casting off his mortal shell like a cicada.
Later, together with Tanhong, he proceeded toward Henan.
The king, his ministers, and the people came out along the road to welcome him;
both within and without the court, they paid him reverent homage and honored him as their National Teacher.
After Huabi had completed his work in Henan, he traveled to the Liang territories.
Juqu Mengxun treated him with profound respect and service,
gathering eminent guests to inspire in them lofty and superior resolve.
At that time, there was Fan Sengyin of the Western Sea,
who also studied under Huiyao; however,
his aspirations were narrow and his capacity limited, and he considered himself satisfied with having acquired but little.
He then claimed that he had already attained arhatship and had suddenly exhausted the gates of dhyāna.
Baogao then secretly employed his supernatural powers to cause Huiyin,
while in meditative concentration, to fully perceive the various different dharma-gates being preached by the Buddhas in the infinite worlds of the ten directions.
During a single summer, I searched for what I had seen and could never exhaust it;
only then did I realize that the waters of meditative concentration are bottomless,
and I was filled with great shame and trepidation.

The first is repentance based on phenomena by means of a deluded mind.

Therefore, this is a partial teaching.

If there were no suffering, ignorance and volitional formations would not arise below it;

The Arhats are likewise so.
Thus, one should know that contemplating the principle is true repentance.
Therefore, a verse in the Avataṃsaka Sūtra says:
The entire ocean of karmic obstructions arises entirely from deluded thoughts;
if one wishes to repent, one should seek the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, the *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra* says:
Karmic fetters and afflictions practiced over hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas are all extinguished by means of the contemplation of the single reality (*eka-tattva*).
Furthermore, the *Sarvadharmāpravṛttinirdeśa-sūtra* states:
If a bodhisattva can perceive that the nature of all sentient beings is itself the nature of nirvāṇa,
they will be able to utterly extinguish the karmic obstructions and transgressions.
Therefore, the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-sūtra* states:
Contemplate that the mind is no-mind;
it arises from the marks of inversion.
Such a mind, characterized by these marks, arises from delusive thoughts.
Just as wind in the sky has no place of dependence,
one should know that the grasping at the nature of good and evil and the formation of signs arise because the principle has not yet been awakened;
it is not that deluded karma does not exist.

since no dharma remains to abide,
it does not produce rebirth.
When contemplating the principle correctly,
one should reflect that all obstacles are fundamentally empty and quiescent,
and that they are eternally of the same true nature as all Buddhas.
The myriad virtues, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, are no different from the Dharma-realm;
yet, because the veil of ignorance is thick, one is unable to perceive them.
Failing to see them, one constantly breaks the precepts and violates the Way even while standing before the Buddha.
There is no transgression among the ten evil deeds or the five rebellious acts that they will not commit.
It is like a banquet hall where both ordinary people and sages are seated together for offerings,
and there are many blind men present.
Because he was without eyes, he subsequently committed all manner of evils in the presence of the multitude.
At that time, a wise person, feeling unceasing compassion for him,
spoke to the blind man, saying:

Upon hearing this, the blind man was filled with shame, remorse, and fear.

"Your disciple has had little merit; since early youth, I have been blind.

Now, through the guidance of a virtuous friend,
I have only just come to know that there is a teacher.

for all Buddhas possess the supernatural wisdom of the three knowledges and the clear illumination of the five eyes.
Knowing all things without exception,

Responding to conditions as they arise without missing the proper time;
furthermore, knowing that the causes and conditions of offenses have no inherent nature,
existing only through the causal conditions of deluded thought.
To receive [existence] in vain is suffering.
Thus, the Vimalakīrti Sūtra says:

Because the mind is pure, sentient beings are pure.

The nature of sin is not within, not without, and not in between.
The mind, likewise, is not within, not without, and not in between.

One then kindles the fire of wisdom to burn away the darkness of ignorance.
The various evils committed since beginningless time are like a dark room;

It is like a bright lamp.

From time immemorial, clarity has dispelled delusion;
yet since the beginningless past, beings have been lost due to causes of error and have produced all manner of non-virtuous effects.
These matters are like darkness.
Now, wishing to repent and eliminate [these faults],
one relies on the power of the Buddha-nature to give rise to the fire of right view;
this matter is like a bright lamp.
When the lamp arises, darkness is dispelled;
when understanding is born, delusion perishes.
There is no meaning that is not extinguished.
It is like frost and snow that wait for the sun to be dispelled;

therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
For example, a thousand catties of cotton flowers are not equal to a single ounce of pure gold;
though one's transgressions may be many, they are not equal to even a small amount of goodness. Since one has committed an offense in the presence of the Buddha, [the consequences are grave].

offenses have no inherent nature and are extinguished through conditions.

Once one knows what is true and what is false, one then knows that the karmic offenses which serve as objects of perception arise from one's actions;
these deluded emotions obstruct liberation.
Deluded and lacking awakening,
one thus incurs these transgressions;

when understanding dawns, delusion perishes,
just as light extinguishes darkness.

Through long and uninterrupted cultivation, the seeds of karma naturally perish.

The arising of wholesome states in the final moments of mind is like a torch dispelling darkness.
Furthermore, the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* says:
"Just as a garment soiled for a hundred years may be washed in a single day until it becomes bright and clean."

Thus, all the unwholesome karma accumulated over hundreds of thousands of kalpas can be entirely extinguished in a single day and a single moment through the power of the Buddha-dharma and by means of correct reflection.
Section Five: The Ritual Procedures. Regarding this first gate, when a practitioner wishes to perform repentance, they must do so before the superior objective conditions of the Triple Gem.
They should bare one shoulder, expose the upper arm, and remove their headcloth and footwear.
Women need not trouble themselves by baring their shoulders; they should maintain full decorum and,
with palms joined in reverence,
invite a single virtuous elder— one who is advanced in years, long-established in the path, and whom they respect from the depths of their hearts.
First, one should respectfully invite the Triple Gem of the ten directions to serve as a virtuous condition.
Thus, a person has composed a verse that says:
I take refuge in all Buddhas of the ten directions; I prostrate to the boundless ocean of pure awakening.
I also pay homage to the wondrous Dharma, inconceivable, the naturally pure *tathatā*-store,
who dwells in the stage of supreme love for all beings as an only son; to all the noble ones who have attained the Path and its fruits,
I bow my head in prostration, with body, speech, and a pure mind, and take refuge in each and every one of them.
Thereupon, one requests the master of confession, saying:
"Virtuous One, please attend to me with single-minded mindfulness.
I, your disciple [Name],..."
I now request the Venerable One to serve as my preceptor for confession.

Out of compassion, it is well to perform this once, or even three times.
Second, regarding the confession: the master first instructs [the practitioner] to recognize the nature and gravity of their previous offenses, as detailed in the initial instructions.
According to the treatise, there are four general types of repentance.
The first is the repentance of mutual exchange and release;
this is the inferior-grade repentance method for ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
Second is the repentance for the permanent severing of the continuity [of afflictions];
this is the repentance method for superior-grade ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
Third is the repentance for the three types of karmic action.
This is the method of repentance for worthy persons (*satpuruṣa*).
The fourfold repentance for extinguishing karma is the method of repentance for noble ones (*ārya*).
The first two are ritual confessions (*pratideśanā*) that eliminate the opposing factors;
however, they cannot extinguish karma, but merely suppress it so that it does not arise.
This is because, by not relying on contemplation according to the principle, one has not yet entered the stage of the noble ones (*ārya*).
Although one may escape [retribution] and not enter the evil realms in the future, the nature of this karma remains constantly present, having been perfumed to form a seed.
Thus, it is like a person cutting down a tree: though the branches and twigs are removed, the root still remains.
Regarding the latter two types of repentance, one must necessarily take emptiness as the object and awaken to the principle so that the mind and its objects become empty and harmonious.
One must constantly maintain this perception and gradually cultivate the realization of the Truth; only then can they be extinguished.
Now, let us first rely on the second method of repentance for ordinary beings to permanently sever the continuity [of karma],
thereby subduing karmic actions so they do not manifest.
One should constantly rely on virtuous friends and give rise to great vows.
At the time of death, one will likewise attain rebirth in the pure lands of the ten directions according to one's vows, forever leaving behind the three evil realms;
yet, because one dwells in this Sahā world, the mind may become timid and weak, unable to remain steadfast.
For one who intends to retreat,
there are five dharmas that should assist in attaining the fruit of non-regret:
first, faith.
Second, shame;
third, remorse;
fourth, virtuous friends.
The Five Reverences for the Precepts:
First, faith is the source of the Way and the mother of merit;

Second is shame (*hrī*),
which is not committing transgressions oneself.
Third is remorse (*apatrāpya*).
Not teaching others to commit transgressions.
Furthermore, as for "shame" (hrī),
it is inwardly feeling shame before oneself.
As for "shame" (*hrī*),

it is the feeling of shame before the heavens. Because one possesses shame and remorse (*apatrāpya*), one is able to show reverence toward parents, teachers, elders, and all ordinary and noble beings.
A virtuous friend is the entirety of the holy life;
because the precepts are your great teacher;
and because the Three Jewels are that upon which both ordinary beings and sages rely.
Therefore, one must pay homage and take refuge.

This section is divided into six parts: Part One: Exposition of the Intent; Part Two: Prohibitions and Exceptions; Part Three: The Method of Receiving; Part Four: The Characteristics of the Precepts; Part Five: Gains and Losses; Part Six: Divine Protection. Part One: Exposition of the Intent. Regarding that which is esteemed by the mundane world:
Benevolence, righteousness, propriety, wisdom, and trustworthiness are what humanity possesses. That which sentient beings rely upon are non-killing,
non-stealing, non-lust, non-falsehood, and non-intoxication.
Although the ways of the secular and the monastic diverge,
the gradual teaching applies to both; thus,
when it issues forth from the benevolent person, there is no killing.
One who honors righteousness does not steal;
one who respects ritual propriety does not engage in sexual misconduct;
one who values trustworthiness does not speak falsely.
The Master did not drink wine in the presence of those who were wise;
this was likely intended for the purpose of guiding and transforming people at that particular time,
rather than being a teaching concerning the fundamental practice itself.
Those who cultivate the fundamental teachings are said to practice the True Dharma.
To propagate the Way through internal instruction must begin with its causes.
The causes are killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, and intoxication.
This, then, resides in the actual phenomena (*dharmas*).
It points directly to the facts and speaks plainly;
therefore, it does not rely on ornate rhetoric or resort to metaphorical names to manifest its meaning.
Cultivating causes in this manner,
the fruit is realized without being sought,
and bliss is manifested without being craved.
If one neglects what is near to gaze at what is distant,
or abandons the small to preserve the great,
then there will be no place of refuge or destination.
Thus we know that by taking up the cause of non-killing,
one personally realizes the fruit of benevolence and righteousness;
this is how we know it to be so.
Now, seeing that you uphold the precepts and refrain from killing,
benevolence manifests without your seeking it;
you maintain the precepts and abstain from stealing.
Without seeking after righteousness, righteousness spreads;
one observes the precepts without succumbing to lust.
Without praying for ritual propriety, propriety is established.
He observed the precepts without falsehood;
he did not seek fame through faith, yet his faith was manifest.
Having received the precepts, he renounced alcohol.
Without practicing for wisdom, wisdom becomes luminous.
Such is the reality;
it may be called "shaking the net and holding the main cord so that the myriad meshes open wide."
Shaking the mechanism to govern the realm and thereby transcending cold and heat—
what further merit could be added to this,
and what virtue could possibly surpass it?
Had it not been for their cultivation being obscured by what they desired,
they would have merely exhausted their deliberations over forms and names,
and toiled their minds over the hundred schools of thought.
To weary one's body and spirit through the nights,
and to lose one's hearing and sight during fair days—
how far removed is this from the Way!
Is it not that they have passed away before reaching their goal?
If one attains the fundamental source, there will be no desire and no disputation.
Only then does one realize the truth of the fish that swallows a boat.
The waters of the ditches and canals do not produce [great creatures].
How could birds as vast as the Peng and Kun soar within the groves of a mere sparrow?
2. Section on Obstacles (Āvaraṇa-varga), Part Two. When a person wishes to receive the precepts, the preceptor must first inquire regarding their obstacles.
Thus, the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* asks about these obstacles.

Those who have committed a heinous crime (*ānantarya*), those who live as thieves among the monastic community, those who have defiled a bhikṣuṇī, and others such as these are not permitted to become bhikṣus;
yet, if such persons become lay followers (*avadātavasana*), they may obtain the wholesome restraint (*kuśala-saṃvara*).
This does not preclude the practice of wholesome deeds such as giving and loving-kindness;
however, there is only mundane morality,
because such a person is defiled by their karma and also obstructs the Noble Path.
He did not permit him to go forth [into homelessness].
Furthermore, the Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra states:
The Buddha said:
If one wishes to receive the upāsaka precepts in order to increase wealth and longevity, one should first consult and inform one’s parents;

next, notify one’s wife, children, slaves, and servants; and finally, report to the king. This requirement to report exists because the king may impose prohibitions that would not permit the reception of the precepts; however, if he has not previously imposed such prohibitions, reporting is required for other reasons.
There is no need for further deliberation; once you have asked and received permission,
whoever among them has left the household life and resolved to attain bodhicitta,
go to that person's side and prostrate yourself at their feet.
He addressed him with gentle words of greeting, saying:
"Venerable Sir."
I am a man, possessing a male body, and I wish to receive the Bodhisattva Upāsaka precepts.

I only pray that the Virtuous One, out of compassion, will grant me this single request; for even if one has not previously generated the aspiration [for enlightenment], one may still receive the Śrāvaka Prātimokṣa precepts.

If a person who possesses the bodhicitta merely gives rise to the mind of the Hīnayāna and receives the precepts from among the five groups of renunciants, they likewise obtain the precepts. At that time, the bhikṣu should speak as follows:
"Does your father, mother, wife, children, servants, and the ruler of the country all consent? If they say they do,
you should further ask:"
"Have you never misappropriated the property of the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Sangha, nor the property of others?
If you say you have not,
you should further be asked:"
"Within your body now, do you perhaps have any illness of body or mind, either internal or external?
If you say there is none,
you should further be asked:"
"Have you not committed an unrighteous act toward the bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs?
If he says he has not, one should further ask:
Have you not committed any of the five heinous crimes?
Have you not stolen the property of the Sangha?
Are you not a person without sexual organs or with dual sexual organs?
Have you not failed to observe the eightfold precepts and fast, nor committed a grave offense?
Have you not abandoned your parents or teachers when they were ill?
Have you perhaps killed someone who had resolved to attain bodhicitta?
Have you not stolen property belonging to the Saṃgha present before you?
Have you not become a wicked person through double-tongued speech and harsh words?
Have you not committed unrighteous acts toward your mother, daughter, or sister?
"Have you not uttered a falsehood before this great assembly?
If you say 'no,' you should further be told:"
Good son, this precept is extremely difficult;
it serves as the foundation for the ten precepts of a śrāmaṇera, the precepts of a mahābhikṣu, the bodhisattva precepts, and even for awakening itself.
If one receives and maintains these with a sincere heart, one will obtain such immeasurable benefits as these precepts provide.
However, if there are those who violate such precepts,
they will dwell within the three evil realms throughout immeasurable and boundless lifetimes, undergoing great suffering and affliction.
Do you now wish to obtain immeasurable benefit?
Can you receive this with a sincere mind?
If you say you can, [then proceed].
Next, instruct them in the three refuges.
Furthermore, one should ask:
"These precepts are extremely difficult."
Once one has taken refuge in the Buddha,
one would rather sacrifice body and life than ever rely upon Īśvara or other such deities.
Once one has taken refuge in the Dharma...
One would rather sacrifice body and life than rely upon the scriptures of non-Buddhist paths;
once having taken refuge in the Sangha, one would never, even at the cost of body and life, rely upon the heterodox assemblies of non-Buddhists.
Are you able to thus take refuge in the Triple Gem with a sincere heart?
If one says they are capable,
they should be made to attend upon and serve a wise person who has gone forth for a full six months.
That wise person, in turn, should with a sincere mind observe the four modes of deportment of that individual's body.
If it is known that this person can act according to the instructions,
then after six months have passed, the Saṃgha should assemble;
with a quorum of twenty persons, they shall perform the formal motion (*jñapti-karman*) as follows:
Venerable Saṃgha, listen. This person,
so-and-so, having now requested from the Saṃgha to receive the upāsaka precepts,
has maintained the four dignified postures with purity for six months.
With a sincere mind, one should receive and uphold the Ground of Pure Adornment.
Such a person is a true man, endowed with a male body.
If the Sangha grants its permission:
The monks all remained silent.
For one who does not listen, it suffices to speak once.
This applies unless they are those who hold false views.
For those who have possessed correct faith from of old,
there is no need for them to undergo this six-month trial of the three refuges for converting heretics;
one should simply inquire about their impediments and obstacles, and instruct them to perform repentance.
Having done so, one may immediately receive the five precepts, the eight precepts, or the three refuges and thereby attain them;
this is not the same as the present case.

Section Three: The Method for Receiving [Precepts]. Regarding the third section on the method for receiving [precepts]: if one wishes to receive the precepts, one must fully cultivate dignified deportment.
One receives [the precepts] before a group of five ordained persons.
Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says:
"I, [name], take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, take refuge in the Saṃgha"—this is recited three times. "I, [name], have completed taking refuge in the Buddha."
The refuge in the Dharma is completed.
The refuge in the Saṅgha is completed. Having recited this three times, I declare: "May you, the Śākya-muni Buddha, as a laywoman (*upāsikā*), bear witness to me.
I, [name], from this day forth for as long as life lasts, take refuge."
The preceptor should say: "Listen, you upāsaka.
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha knows persons and perceives persons."
Thus have I explained the five precepts for the upāsaka.
You should receive and uphold them all. What are these five?
First, to refrain from killing for as long as one lives is a precept of the upāsaka.
Within this, for as long as one lives, one should not intentionally kill living beings.
If one can say "I am able" regarding this matter, then although the formal discourse uses the term "I agree," there is no fault in changing "I agree" to "I am able.
Second, for as long as life lasts, one shall not steal.
This is the Upāsaka precept.
Within this, for as long as life lasts, one must not steal.
Regarding this matter, if you are able [to observe it], you should say "I am able."
Third, for as long as life lasts, one shall refrain from sexual misconduct;
this is a precept of the upāsaka.
Regarding this, for as long as life lasts, one must not engage in sexual misconduct.
If one is able to do so, one should say "I am able.
For as long as life lasts, one shall not speak falsely;
this is the precept of an upāsaka.
Within this, for as long as life lasts, one should not speak falsely.
Regarding this matter, if you are able [to observe it], you should say "I am able.
Fifth, for as long as life lasts, one shall not drink alcohol.
This is the Upāsaka precept.
Within this, one must not drink alcohol for as long as life lasts.
If you are able to observe this matter, you should say, "I am able."
Having explained the characteristics [of the precepts], one should further say:
"This upāsaka fully receives and maintains the five precepts."
One should make offerings to the Triple Gem and diligently cultivate merit;
seeking the Buddha-way from afar, one may realize the states of humans and devas nearby.
If one can observe the three long months and the six monthly fast days, [great benefit shall follow].
One must act accordingly for each case.
If one is receiving only a single precept,
the phrase "one of the five" should be removed from the text.
Simply say: "I am a lay follower (*upāsaka*) who observes the precept of refraining from killing.
The remaining text is as before for the three refuges.
Once the third repetition is complete, one then formally undertakes the five precepts.
At a later time, the three fetters were directly entrusted [to him]. Therefore,
the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states:
Question: If one does not receive the three refuges, can one obtain the five precepts?
Answer: One cannot.
One must first receive the Three Refuges;
only afterwards may one obtain the precepts. Receiving the Eight Precepts below follows this same method.
Section Four: The Characteristics of the Precepts. According to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra*:
Question: Among the five precepts, how many are actual precepts? Answer:
The first four are actual [prohibitions],
while the last one is a prohibitive [denial].
The reason they are collectively concluded as such is:
Because this negligence is the root by which one may transgress the four precepts,
it was as in the time of Kāśyapa Buddha,
when there was a lay follower (upāsaka).
Due to drinking alcohol, he committed adultery with another's wife, stole another's chicken, and killed another person.
When others came to question him about these acts, he replied that he had not done them.
One would then commit false speech and could also create the four pārājika offenses; however,
one alone cannot cause a schism in the Saṃgha if one has received the precept against killing.
Furthermore, one must not inflict harm upon any sentient being, whether stationary or moving;
nor should one ever consume meat, pungent vegetables, or other strong-smelling foods.
All such transgressions are strictly forbidden.
Therefore, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:
The Buddha told Mahāmati,
"There are immeasurable causes and conditions for which a bodhisattva should not eat meat."
I shall now briefly explain ten kinds of causes and conditions.
First, all sentient beings have, from the very beginning, been related to one another through successive causes and conditions;
because they have always been one's own kin, one should not eat meat, as one regards them with the thought of kinship.
Second, because the flesh of donkeys, mules, camels, foxes, dogs, oxen, horses, humans, and other domestic animals is sold mixed together by butchers;
third, because it grows from impure vapors and elements;
and fourth, because all sentient beings give rise to fear upon smelling its odor.
Like a caṇḍāla, because dogs see them with loathing and fear and bark at them in a pack;
fifth, because they prevent the arising of a compassionate mind in the practitioner.
Sixth, because it is foul-smelling, impure, and lacks a good reputation, which the six classes of ordinary, deluded beings crave;
seventh, because it causes various incantations and arts not to succeed;
and eighth, because when people see the form of one who kills living beings, they give rise to perceptions and become stained by attachment to its flavor.
Ninth, those who eat meat are abandoned by the devas; their breath becomes foul because of the abundance of evil.
Tenth, tigers and wolves in secluded forests will catch their scent.
I have often said this.
In all eating and drinking, one should conceive of it as the flesh of one's own child,
or as taking medicine.
For this reason, in the past, there was a king.
He was named Siṃhasūtaputra;
he ate various kinds of meat,
eventually reaching even human flesh.
The subjects and citizens could not bear it and immediately plotted rebellion,
as described in the *Banzu Wang Jing* (Sūtra of King Banzu).
Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"Those who eat meat sever the seeds of great compassion."
Whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, all sentient beings who smell the scent of its flesh will give rise to terror,
just as if a person were near a lion.
When the multitude saw him,
they smelled the stench of the lion and were likewise struck with terror.
It is like a person who eats garlic; being foul-smelling and loathsome,
others see him and depart upon smelling the odor,
and even from afar they say they do not wish to look at him.
How much more so when they draw near;
those traveling by water, land, or air all abandon them and flee,
saying in unison:
"This person is our enemy;
for this reason, a bodhisattva does not practice eating meat.
Thus it is said in meaning.
The upāsakas who observe the five precepts and others are like the well water of a lay household,
which contains many tiny insects.
One must strain [the water] thoroughly, examine it, and then return it to its original place.
If one intends to move about, one must also carry a strainer with oneself at all times.
This applies unless one has received the precept against stealing.
One must not take even as much as a single blade of grass or a single grain of rice; therefore,
the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
Kauṇḍinya, try seeing whether a single grain of rice is raw or cooked and return it to its original owner;
yet for violating the path of karma, one will still become an ox for five hundred lifetimes.
Even after attaining the state of an Arhat, he still continued to chew his food.
Regarding the precept against sexual misconduct,
as stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*:
Except for one's own wife,
engaging in sexual intercourse with any other man, woman, spirit,
or animal constitutes entirely wrong conduct.
Although one does not commit an offense with one's own wife,
one must nevertheless avoid improper places; that is,
engaging with one's own wife in an improper manner or after she has conceived.
One must also refrain from it,
for fear of harming the fetus.
Within three years after giving birth, one must likewise avoid and exercise caution.
This refers to preventing the exhaustion of breast milk.
If there were a separate wet nurse who was not subject to these restrictions, it would also be so;
furthermore, the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states:
One's own wife in an improper place—
namely, the mouth or the anus—
and all women who are protected by their parents or children.
For nuns and other women who have left the household life, sexual misconduct is also defined as occurring for the sake of protecting the Dharma.
However, if a woman without a husband comes forward of her own accord before a group of people to become one's wife,
doing so in accordance with the Dharma constitutes no offense.
Furthermore, the *Tiewei jing* states:
"There are three long months and six monthly fast days (*upoṣadha*), as well as the three periods of brightness— day, moon, and lamp— and below these, the eight *rājan* days,
which are also called the eight seasonal festivals."
Furthermore, one must strictly observe the prohibitions on the eight *rājadina* days as described below. If one has received the precept against false speech,
it constitutes an offense regardless of whether the object is actually false or not, provided that the mind is insincere.
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* asks:
"For what reason does a lay follower (upāsaka) observe the restraint of speech and maintain a pure livelihood?"
The answer is:
Laypeople living at home enjoy worldly pleasures while simultaneously cultivating merit and virtue.
One cannot fully practice all the precepts;
therefore, the Buddha enjoined the observance of the five precepts.
Furthermore, among the actions of speech, false speech is the most grave.
Because of false speech, one is able to commit other transgressions,
whether intentionally or unintentionally; yet,
even if it were merely false speech, it would already encompass these three matters.
If one speaks truthful words,
all four kinds of right speech are thereby fully encompassed;
among all virtues, truthfulness is indeed the greatest.
Furthermore, the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states:
"Even though these are true words,
because they are spoken at an improper time, they are termed frivolous speech (*sambhinna-pralāpa*)."
Or, at times, it may be because it conforms to decline and affliction and is thus without benefit;
or, even if it is beneficial,
it may be because the words lack a fundamental basis and the principles are disordered.
Because they are spoken with an afflicted mind, all such instances are termed frivolous speech (*saṃbhinnapralāpa*).
Furthermore, the *Mahālaṅkāra-śāstra* states:
"To convey insults on behalf of another constitutes both merit and demerit."
Furthermore, the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states:
regarding the false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*), divisive speech (*paiśunya*), and harsh speech (*pāruṣya*), when they are combined, each forms four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
The first is that which is false speech but not divisive or harsh speech.
To repeat these words of his to another because they are untrue constitutes lying;
it is not slander, as there is no intention to cause division.
Because they speak with gentle words, they do not engage in harsh speech;
the remaining phrases may be understood by analogy with one another.
Furthermore, the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states:
"The remaining three karmas may be combined or separated."
The single type of frivolous speech (sambhinna-pralāpa) is necessarily inseparable from it.
Furthermore, the *Śraddhākaravarman-sūtra* states:
"If one were to speak falsely..."
This also encompasses the meanings of frivolous speech, divisive speech, and harsh speech.
Furthermore, the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states:
"One who does not speak falsely..."
When expounding the meaning of the Dharma or discussing various doctrines, whether right or wrong,
do not claim for yourself that you alone are correct.
If one always examines whether there is a fundamental basis [for one's conduct], then one will be without fault.
Otherwise, the axe is in one's own mouth.
This applies even to one who has vowed not to drink alcohol.
As stated in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*:
"If one drinks alcohol,
one must not even place a drop of alcohol on a blade of grass and put it into the mouth."
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that there are thirty-five faults in drinking alcohol.
What are these thirty-five?
The answer is:
First, one's wealth and possessions in the present life are exhausted. Why is this?
Because drinking alcohol causes the mind to become intoxicated and chaotic, lacking all restraint,
and because one spends without moderation,
it is the gateway to the two kinds of illness.
Third, it is the root of strife and contention.
Fourth, one is exposed and shameless.
Fifth, one acquires an ugly reputation and foul exposure, such that people do not respect them.
Sixth, one no longer possesses wisdom.
Seventh, one does not obtain the objects one ought to obtain,
and the objects one has obtained are lost.
Eighth, one reveals all hidden matters to others.
Ninth, various undertakings are abandoned and not brought to completion.
Tenth, intoxication is the root of sorrow; why is this so?
11. In intoxication one commits many errors, yet upon sobering up, one feels shame, remorse, and sorrow.
12. One’s physical strength diminishes further.
13. One’s physical complexion deteriorates.
Thirteen, not knowing how to revere one's father;
fourteen, not knowing how to revere one's mother;
fifteen, not revering śramaṇas.
Sixteenth, he does not respect brahmins.
Seventeenth, he does not respect uncles, paternal aunts, or elders. Why is this?
Eighteenth, because they are intoxicated, stupefied, and afflicted by delusion such that they cannot distinguish anything, they do not revere the Buddha.
Nineteenth, they do not respect the Dharma.
Twenty: not respecting the Saṃgha.
Twenty-one: associating with evil persons who form cliques.
Twenty-two: distancing oneself from the wise and virtuous.
Twenty-three: becoming a person who breaks the precepts;
twenty-four: lacking shame and remorse;
twenty-five: failing to guard the six sense faculties.
Twenty-sixth, they indulge in sensual pleasures and negligence.
Twenty-seventh, they are loathed by others and no one delights in seeing them.
Twenty-eighth, they are collectively cast out by their honored relatives and all their acquaintances.
29. Practicing unwholesome dharmas;
30. Abandoning wholesome dharmas;
31. Not being trusted or respected by wise and learned men.
Why is this? Because alcohol leads to heedlessness,
and it is thirty-two ways far removed from nirvāṇa.
Thirty-three kinds of causes and conditions for madness;
thirty-four [kinds of karma] whereby, at the dissolution of the body and the end of life, one falls into the evil destinies and the hells;
and thirty-five: even if one is born among humans, one will always be insane and deluded.
Because there are various faults such as these,
one does not drink alcohol.
Furthermore, the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states:
It is permitted for a lay follower (upāsaka) who observes the five precepts to engage in trade; however, they must not perform five types of business.
First, they must not trade in livestock.
If one possesses [such items] oneself, one may sell them directly;
however, they must not be given to butchers.
Second, one must not trade in bows, swords, arrows, or spears.
If one possesses [such property] oneself, it may be sold directly;
however, it must not be given to butchers or those who engage in slaughter.
Third, one must not make a profession of selling liquor.
Those who possess their own [means] are permitted to sell [oil] directly.
Fourth, one must not take the pressing of oil as a profession;
this is because there are insects within foreign sesame seeds, and thus it constitutes an offense.
According to this principle, one should not commit an offense when there are no insects present.
Fifth, one must not dye [robes] with the five primary colors,
as this results in the killing of many insects.
For example, in the land of Qin, indigo dyeing also involves killing many insects and is thus included among the five primary colors.
Furthermore, the *Susheng jing* (Sūtra on Good Birth) states:
"Regarding those who receive the precepts..."
There are five places where one should not go:
namely, the dwellings of butchers, prostitutes, taverns, kings, and *caṇḍālas*.
There are five kinds of actions that one should not perform.
That is to say, one must not engage in selling poisons, brewing alcohol, gambling with animal skins or *chūpú* dice, playing *wéiqí* or *liùbó*,
or performing songs, dances, and theatrical acts; nor should one associate with such people.
Furthermore, the *Ratnamegha Sūtra* states:
"One who maintains the precepts must not go to the homes of those who have broken the precepts to beg for alms.
Additionally, the *Āgama Sūtras* state:
There are four dharmas for distancing oneself from evil and drawing near to the good;
one should flee from them as swiftly as possible for a distance of one hundred yojanas—
where one yojana equals forty li.
One hundred yojanas is four thousand li.
As for the four factors:
the first is an evil friend.
Second, evil assemblies;
third, excessive speech and laughter;
fourth, anger or quarreling.
Furthermore, the *Upāsaka-śīla-lakṣaṇa-sūtra* states:
The Buddha told the bhikṣus,
"There are three ways of committing the offense of killing that take human life."
First, doing it oneself;
second, instructing another;
third, dispatching a messenger.
"Committing it oneself" means taking the life of another with one's own hand.
"Instructing others" means...
He instructs others, saying:
"Seize this person, bind them, and take their life," and he dispatches messengers.
He says to another person:
"Do you know so-and-so?
Seize this person, bind him, and take his life."
When one causes another to take that life by following their words,
the upāsaka commits an offense of non-atonement. Furthermore,
there are three types [of such offenses].
First, employing internal form;
second, employing non-internal form;
third, employing both internal and non-internal form.
First, regarding killing by means of one's own internal physical form:
this refers to using one's hands to strike,
or using one's feet or other parts of the body to cause another to die.
This constitutes an offense of irreparable transgression (*ānantarya*).

If one does not die immediately, but later dies as a result of this [act], it likewise constitutes an offense of irreparable transgression. If, however, one does not die later, [it is still an offense].
This constitutes a middling offense that may be expiated through confession.
Second, regarding killing by means of external matter:
if one causes another to die by using wood, stones, swords, spears, bows, arrows, or the like.
The offense is the same as before.
Third, regarding killing by using internal or non-internal matter:
this refers to striking with one's hand, wood, stones, or the like, causing death.
The offense is the same as before.
Furthermore, there are those who do not kill by means of these three methods,
but instead combine various poisons and apply them to the eyes, ears, nose, body, food, bedding, and so forth.
If one causes that person to die,
they likewise incur the same offense as before. If it is an upāsaka...
Or if one creates a pit of fire with a deceitful mind to harm others:
if a human falls into it and dies, they commit an offense of irreparable transgression;
as do non-humans, ghosts, spirits, and the like, who die within it.
Committing a middle-grade offense is subject to confession;
killing an animal is committing a minor offense subject to confession.
If no one dies at all, one incurs three light offenses of the preparatory stage that are subject to confession.
If one resolves in one's heart to create a fire pit specifically for a certain person and does not extend it to others, [the offense is likewise determined].
If a person dies, one commits an offense that cannot be remedied; if they do not die, one commits an offense of preliminary preparation (*prayoga*).

so shall I now, for one day and one night, sever sexual misconduct, remain far removed from worldly pleasures, and purely cultivate the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Following and training in these dharmas according to the noble ones:
Just as the noble ones always abstain from false speech and speak words that are true and straightforward,
I now, for one day and one night, shall abstain from false speech and speak words that are true and straightforward.
One should train in accordance with the noble ones through such dharmas as these.
Just as the noble ones always remain far removed from intoxicants,
for intoxicants are the source of heedlessness.
Today, for one day and one night, I shall abstain from alcohol.
By means of such a practice, I shall train in accordance with the noble ones.
Just as the noble ones always abstain from singing, dancing, music, and from using flowers, perfumes, garlands, and ornaments to adorn the body.
For one day and one night, I shall now distance myself from singing, dancing, music, perfumes, incense, garlands, and ornaments for adorning the body;
by such means, I shall train in accordance with the noble ones.
Just as all noble ones constantly remain far removed from high, wide, and large beds, dwelling instead upon small couches or seats of grass and straw,
so shall I now, for one day and one night, remain far removed from high, wide, and large beds, dwelling instead upon a small couch or a seat of grass and straw.
I shall train in accordance with the noble ones by means of such dharmas.
Just as the noble ones always abstain from eating past midday and avoid traveling or eating at improper times,
so too shall I now, for one day and one night, abstain from eating past midday and avoid traveling or eating at improper times.
One should train in accordance with the noble ones by means of such dharmas.
As it is said in verse:
"Killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, drinking intoxicants, and [using] flowers and perfumes..."
Necklaces, songs, dances, and the like, high beds, eating past midday—
these things abandoned by the Noble Ones, I now likewise renounce.
By the causal conditions of this merit, may all together attain Buddhahood.
Furthermore, the *Buddha-bhāṣita-upoṣadha-sūtra* states:
The Buddha was staying in the palace of the Prime Minister’s residence to the east of Śrāvastī;
the Prime Minister’s mother was named Viśākhā.
Rising early, she bathed and donned her colorful robes.
Together with her sons' wives, she went forth, prostrated at the Buddha's feet, and sat to one side.
The Buddha asked Vīrā:
"Why are you bathing so early?
He replied,
"I wish to receive the precepts for fasting together with my sons' wives."
The Buddha said,
"There are three grades of fasting.
Which kind of fast do you prefer?"
Vaiśravaṇa knelt on his right knee and said,
"I wish to hear what is meant by the three fasts.
The Buddha said:
First is the cowherd’s fast;
second is the Nirgrantha’s fast;
third is the Buddhist fast.
Regarding the "Cowherd’s Meal":
it is like a cowherd who seeks out fine water and grass to feed his cattle, and at evening,
as he returns home, he reflects upon them.
In which field is there abundance?
One must wait for daybreak before going.
If there are sons or daughters of noble family...
Having already received the precepts of fasting,
their minds are set upon the gains and offerings of household life;
they think only of fine food and drink to nourish and sustain the body.
This is like the intention of that cowherd;
he shall not obtain great merit,
nor possess great wisdom.
The second Nigaṇṭha fast consists of prostrating on the ground at the time of the fast on the fifteenth day of the month to receive the precepts,
and paying homage to the various deities within ten yojanas, saying: [as follows].
Today, observing the fast, I dare not commit evil.
I do not regard my wife, children, or servants as belonging to me. They are not mine.
When the next day arrived,
it was as those Nirgrantha non-Buddhists had said:
they did not obtain great merit.
It is not the wisdom of great illumination.
Regarding the third Buddhist Dharma fast:
disciples of the Inner Way observe the eight precepts on the six fast days of each month.
What are the eight? First, regarding the precept:
for the duration of one day and one night, maintain the mind so that there is no intention to kill.
With compassionate mindfulness toward all sentient beings, one must not harm even the smallest crawling creatures;
this is the pure precept practiced with single-minded devotion.
The second precept:
for the duration of one day and one night, maintain a mind free from greed;
contemplate giving and turn away from the intent of stinginess and craving.
Just as one practices pure precepts with a single-minded focus,
the third precept is to maintain a mind free from lustful intent for one day and one night.
He does not dwell on matters of the chamber;
he cultivates the holy life and does not engage in perverse desires.
He practices with single-mindedness according to the pure precepts.
The fourth precept:
for one day and one night, maintain the mind so that there is no false speech; contemplate with utmost sincerity, ensuring that words are not deceptive and that heart and mouth are in accord.
Just as pure precepts are practiced with a single-minded focus,
the fifth precept is to maintain the mind for one day and one night by abstaining from drinking alcohol.
To avoid becoming intoxicated, deluded, or heedless,
one should practice with a single-minded focus as if it were the pure precepts.
This is the sixth precept.
For one day and one night, maintain the mind without seeking comfort;
do not attach to flowers or incense, do not apply ointments or powders, and do not engage in singing, dancing, or entertainment.
Practice with a single-minded focus according to the pure precepts.
The seventh precept:
For one day and one night, maintain the mind without seeking comfort;
do not lie upon fine beds, but instead use low beds, mats, or straw bedding; renounce sleep and rest, and contemplate the Way of the Sūtras.
Just as pure precepts are practiced with a single-minded focus,
the eighth precept consists of maintaining the mind and honoring the Dharma for one day and one night, refraining from eating after midday.
Just as pure precepts are practiced with a single mind.
