Chapter Eighty-Seven: Receiving the Precepts. Section Six:

The Ten Wholesome Actions (89). This section is divided into five parts: Exposition of Intent, Repentance, Receiving the Method, Characteristics of the Precepts, and Efficacy. Section One: Exposition of Intent. First, as for the Exposition of Intent: Now, the Path of the Sages is remote and difficult to aspire to.
A pure mind is easy to approach yet easily deluded;
the foundation of a mountain begins with a single basket of earth,
and Buddhahood arises from the first thought of enlightenment.
Thus, the conquest of ten thousand *li* cannot be achieved without taking the first step; so too, the merit of the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* [cannot be attained without the initial resolve].
It is not that one achieves it without beginning with the mind;
thus we know that the practitioner, from the very first step, must always walk this mind.
To instruct beginners, one must show them that they must revere the ten wholesome paths of action.
Now that the five turbidities are intermingled and chaotic, and transgressions are increasingly manifest,
it is better not to act at all; if one acts,
the consequences will be extremely grave.
Using this as a measure of their condition, how could one possibly slight them?
For example, the sixteen thousand years of a person who has committed a grave offense in this Jambudvīpa is equivalent to a single day and night in the lifespan of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven.
By this long day, their lifespan is sixteen thousand years;
compared to the days and months of Jambudvīpa, this amounts to nine hundred twenty-one billion and sixty thousand years.
In the Avīci Hell, if one remains stubbornly unfaithful to the Buddhist scriptures,
then one should rely on the *Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi-sūtra*.
The transgression of killing eighty-four thousand parents and others is so profound and grave that it is difficult to calculate;
it cannot be eliminated.

Recently, I have observed that among both monastics and laypeople on the days of fasting, while they may receive the five precepts, the eight precepts, or the three sets of pure precepts (*śīla-skandha*), there is absolutely no one who undertakes the ten wholesome actions (*daśa-kuśala*).
This is truly due to the fact that the monastic community has concealed the sacred teachings.
Because this would fail to propagate [the Dharma] and result in a loss of one's share of the Path, the *Adbhuta-dharmaparyāya-sūtra* states:
"The lower grade of the ten wholesome actions refers to even a single moment of thought."
The medium grade of the ten wholesome actions refers to the duration of a single meal; the superior grade of the ten wholesome actions [refers to a longer period].
This refers to the period from dawn until noon;
during this time, because one’s mind contemplates the ten wholesome deeds and refrains from the ten unwholesome deeds,
the jackal likewise contemplates the ten wholesome deeds in its mind.
By not eating for seven days, one may be reborn in Tuṣita Heaven.
Furthermore, the *Ūrdhva-janma-sūtra* states:
"After my parinirvāṇa, the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings..."
If one wishes to be born in the fourth heaven,
from the first day until the seventh day,
one should maintain mindfulness of that heaven and uphold the Buddha’s prohibitive precepts.
Contemplate the ten wholesome actions and practice the ten paths of wholesome conduct.
Dedicate these merits toward the aspiration to be reborn in the presence of Maitreya Buddha;
by recollecting this, one will be reborn accordingly.
Regarding the phrase "seven days," this is discussed by way of the proximate; even so,
one still attains that celestial realm.
How much more so, then, that one does not achieve it even in a single lifetime?
It is asked:
"The superior rewards in the heavens are inconceivable."
"How is it that one receives such great merit in merely seven days?
He replied,
"Though the wholesome cause may be minute, the fruit obtained is exceedingly great."
Just as a small torch can burn a great mountain,
so too can a single good deed destroy great evil;
it is also like a small lamp that can dispel thick darkness.
The light of the sun can dissolve heavy dew;
a tiny seedling can grow into a great tree.
Such is the nature of worldly affairs.
How much more so for those with virtuous power!
Section Two: Repentance. The commentary states:
Recently, I have observed that foolish people are unwilling to accept repentance.
He utters false speech, saying:
"I merely refrain from doing evil;
that itself is what constitutes goodness."
"Why must you cause me to undergo repentance once again?
He replied,
"The Great Sage’s establishment of the teachings is like two tally-sticks meeting in perfect accord."
If one does not practice accordingly, there will be no verification;
therefore, one must make vows and offer prayers not to commit any evil,
and by acting in accordance with those vows, one may attain realization.
Just as a bull, though possessing the strength to pull a cart,
must have a driver to reach a destination;
if one does not prepare in advance but acts impulsively, even if good thoughts arise, they will lack internal guidance and restraint.
Later, encountering conditions for transgression, they continue to commit them without ceasing;
because they previously lacked aspiration, they have created manifold evils.
The Great Sage, knowing their capacities, causes them to receive the wholesome.
If you claim that not committing evil constitutes goodness,
then your failure to perform good deeds should likewise be considered evil.
If one does not kill oxen, horses, donkeys, or mules,
is that necessarily virtuous?
This state of mind is actually indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Since there is no karma of neither-merit-nor-non-merit, one must give rise to mindfulness,
with a focused mind and profound earnestness.
Only then is the course of action (karmapatha) fully established.
As it is said in the *Adbhutadharmaparyāya Sūtra*:
"At that time, there was the wife of a non-Buddhist Brahmin."
Her name was Tiwei. After her husband died, she became impoverished;
reproaching herself for her solitary misery, she wished to immolate herself as an offering to the heavens to seek blessings for the future.
At that time, there was a practitioner named Biancai (Pratibhāna) who instructed the woman Tiwei, saying:
It is like a cow that, being weary of the cart, wishes for the cart to be destroyed;
yet when the front cart is destroyed, it immediately obtains a subsequent cart,
which yokes its neck.
Because their offenses have not yet been exhausted,
it is the same for human beings;
even if one were now to burn and destroy hundreds of thousands of millions of bodies.
The causal conditions of their sinful karma continue in succession without ceasing;
just as in the Avīci Hell, where all sinners are burned,
they die eighty thousand times and are reborn eighty thousand times within a single day.
Only after the passing of one kalpa will that sin finally be exhausted;
how much less can there be any principle by which you might now seek to extinguish your sins by burning your body once?
Tive said, "What means should be employed to cause these offenses to be extinguished?
Pratibhāna replied:
The evil committed by the preceding mind is like clouds covering the moon;
the good arising from the subsequent mind is like a torch dispelling darkness.
One naturally possesses the skillful means to extinguish and eliminate calamities and transgressions.
"One will find peace and security in this life and be reborn in a favorable realm in the next.
Having heard this, Tiwei was filled with great joy;
his anxiety and fear were immediately dispelled.
He immediately led more than five hundred members of his household, including servants and relatives, who surrounded him,
prostrated themselves with their heads to the ground,
and joined their palms in reverent salutation.
He addressed Bhadra-pratibhāna, saying:
"Venerable One, regarding the causes for the extinction of sin that you have previously explained,
I pray that you will further expound the methods for the removal of sin."
"One should practice in accordance with the Dharma. Biancai replied,
"The causes from which offenses arise are the body, speech, and mind."
Unwholesome physical actions consist of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct;
unwholesome verbal actions consist of false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous speech;
unwholesome mental actions consist of envy, malice, arrogance, and wrong views.
These are the ten evil deeds, which bring about the retribution of suffering for one who commits them.
Now, you should with single-minded sincerity repent.
Whether in the past or in this present life,
whatever such transgressions there may have been, I now confess them all.
To emerge from and extinguish transgressions,
one should make a vow to rescue and deliver one's kin and relatives by repenting on their behalf.
Whatever merit and goodness one cultivates, one should bestow it upon all sentient beings who suffer, so that they may attain happiness.
"May I take upon myself the transgressions of all sentient beings.
By virtue of this, may I receive a body until I attain the path of Buddhahood.
Having finished the repentance, [he said:]...
Furthermore, I bestow upon you the remaining virtues;
you should diligently practice them.
May you receive the Dharma of the ten wholesome paths with eloquence.
It is as set forth in the following rules. Section Three: On Receiving the Precepts. The commentary states:
If one wishes to receive the precepts...
One must receive [the precepts] before a group of five ordained persons.
Having fully cultivated the proper deportment,
one kneels on the right knee with palms joined and requests a precept master, saying:
I, [Name], now request the Venerable One to act as my preceptor (ācārya) for the ten wholesome precepts.
May the Venerable One act as my preceptor for the ten wholesome precepts.
"Relying upon the Venerable One, I shall receive the ten wholesome precepts.
"Out of compassion, [I grant them]," thus it is said three times. Although there is no textual record for this, [it is established by tradition].
However, according to the principle of requesting a preceptor when receiving the full ordination (*upasampadā*),

there is no error in proceeding even without such a request; yet, while the ordination is still accomplished, it does not produce as much wholesome merit (*kuśala*) as it would through the formal act of requesting.
However, these ten wholesome actions are the foundation of the Three Vehicles and the excellent medicine for humans and devas; through them,
one attains and receives wondrous fruits.
This truly stems from the teacher’s instruction;
how could one not request it?
Even if one requests it all at once before the great assembly, it is likewise permissible. Furthermore, there are two general principles for receiving this Dharma.
First, one receives the precepts in the presence of another person;
later, one receives the dharmas by oneself.
Regarding the initial reception in the presence of another, I shall briefly cite two passages from the sūtras.
Furthermore, according to the *Adbhuta-dharma-sūtra*:
"You should now, with a sincere heart, take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṃgha of Bhikṣus.
Thus it is said three times.
From this day forth, for as long as life lasts, I shall observe the ten paths of wholesome action.
I, the disciple [Name], from now until the end of my life, shall refrain from killing, refrain from stealing, and refrain from sexual misconduct.
These are the wholesome karmas of the body.
Not speaking falsely, not engaging in double-tongued speech, not using harsh words, and not indulging in frivolous chatter—
these are the wholesome karmas of speech.
Not being envious, not harboring anger or malice, not being arrogant, and not holding wrong views.
These are wholesome mental actions;
these are what are called the ten precepts of wholesome conduct.
Second, according to the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra*.
One receives the ten wholesome dharmas (*daśa-kuśala-dharma*). These ten wholesome [precepts] are identical in text to the ten precepts for the renunciant *śrāmaṇera*.
However, the intent of this sutra also applies to lay bodhisattvas.
They may also receive it together.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is taking refuge in the Buddha?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī,
"As for taking refuge in the Buddha:"
One should speak thus:
"Venerable sir, I, [name],
take refuge in the Buddha until I reach enlightenment."
"Up until awakening, I take refuge in the Dharma.
Up until awakening, I take refuge in the Saṃgha. Thus he says three times: "I, [Name], have already taken refuge in the Buddha;
I have already taken refuge in the Dharma."
Having completed the taking of refuge in the Sangha, this is repeated three times. Next, regarding the characteristics of receiving the precepts:
"Venerable Sir, I uphold the Bodhisattva precepts."
I, [Name], from now until enlightenment, shall not kill sentient beings and shall remain free from the thought of killing.
Until enlightenment, I shall not steal and shall remain free from the thought of stealing.
Until enlightenment, I shall not engage in unchaste conduct and shall remain free from the thought of unchaste conduct.
Until reaching enlightenment, they do not speak falsely and remain free from the thought of falsehood.
Until reaching enlightenment, they do not drink any intoxicants and remain free from the thought of drinking them.
Until reaching enlightenment, they do not wear perfumes or flowers, nor do they give rise to thoughts of doing so.
Until reaching enlightenment, they shall not engage in singing, dancing, or music, remaining free from the thought of such performances;
until reaching enlightenment, they shall not sit or lie upon high, wide, or large beds, remaining free from the thought of such grand furnishings.
Until reaching enlightenment, they do not eat past midday, remaining free from the notion of eating past midday;
until reaching enlightenment, they do not handle gold, silver, or raw precious objects, remaining free from the notion of handling gold, silver, or raw precious objects.
Up until the point where one shall be fully endowed with the six pāramitās and great loving-kindness and great compassion.
Second, the clarification of receiving the precepts for oneself:
if there is no ordained person available to receive them from, [one may proceed as follows].
On the day of the fast, before the Buddha image,
having performed sincere repentance, one should personally make virtuous vows and solemnly pledge to receive [the precepts], saying:
"I, [Name], take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṃgha. Thus it is said three times. "I, [Name], have finished taking refuge in the Buddha;
I have finished taking refuge in the Dharma;
I have finished taking refuge in the Saṃgha. Thus it is said three times. Next is the ritual for receiving the precepts.
I, [Name], for as long as life lasts, toward all sentient beings,
making no distinction between ordinary persons and noble ones, shall practice great loving-kindness;
until I attain enlightenment, I shall not give rise to a thought of killing.
Up to and including not giving rise to wrong views— reciting this three times— I, [name], for as long as life lasts, toward all sentient beings,
making no distinction between ordinary persons and noble ones, shall practice the mind of great loving-kindness.
"Up until the attainment of Bodhi, I shall not give rise to the thought of killing," and so on,
up to "I shall not give rise to wrong views"— thus it is recited three times.
Although receiving [the precepts] before a person based on this [formula] is not the formal text, it is permissible as long as one conforms to its intended meaning.
Section Four: The Characteristics of the Precepts. According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, fascicle 473, it says: "One personally undertakes and maintains the ten paths of wholesome action."
He also exhorts others to uphold the ten paths of wholesome action.
He unerringly praises the dharma of upholding the ten paths of wholesome action, and with joy he extols those who uphold them.
The five precepts, the eight precepts, the monastic precepts, and so forth, are all likewise undertaken by him personally and exhorted in others.
Furthermore, the Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra states:
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying,
"How many kinds of supramundane precepts are there?"
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"If one discriminates with the mind regarding male, female, or neither male nor female,
this bodhisattva commits a pārājika offense."
If one discriminates with the mind among animals, ghosts, spirits, devas, men, women, or those who are neither male nor female,
this bodhisattva commits a pārājika offense.
If one acts through body or speech in a manner unworthy of attaining the Three Vehicles and fails to give rise to a heart of compassion, [this also constitutes a grave transgression].
Such a bodhisattva commits a pārājika offense.
If, through physical or verbal action, they are incapable of attaining the three vehicles; or if, regarding another's property, they give rise to the thought of theft, they commit a pārājika offense.
If, through physical or verbal action, they are incapable of attaining the three vehicles; or if they give rise to the intention of false speech, they commit a pārājika offense.
Furthermore, the Brahmajāla Sūtra states:
The Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas, saying,
"I now recite the Dharma-precepts of all Buddhas every half-month."
All you bodhisattvas, including even those bodhisattvas of the ten stages,
shall likewise recite these precepts.
It is the source of all Buddhas and the root of the practice of Bodhisattvas.
If one receives the precepts...
Kings, princes, ministers, and high officials;
bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs;
and the eighteen Brahmā heavens and the six heavens of the desire realm.
Commoners, eunuchs, lecherous men, lecherous women, slaves,
the eight classes of spirits and deities, vajra-gods, animals,
and even those who have transformed themselves into human form.
However, according to the Dharma Master’s explanation,
all who have received the precepts are called the foremost pure ones.
The Buddha addressed the sons of the Buddhas, saying:
"There are ten grave *prātimokṣa* precepts.
If one has received the bodhisattva precepts but does not recite these precepts,"
"He is not a bodhisattva;
he is not the seed of a Buddha.
I also recite it in this way.
All bodhisattvas have already studied it;
all bodhisattvas shall study it;
all bodhisattvas are now studying it.
The characteristics of the Prātimokṣa have been briefly explained;
you should train yourselves to respectfully uphold it.
The Buddha addressed the sons of the Buddha:
Whether one kills oneself, teaches others to kill, employs means to praise killing, rejoices upon seeing it being done,
or even kills through incantations— these constitute the karma of killing,
the dharma of killing, the cause of killing, and the conditions for killing.
Furthermore, one must not intentionally kill any living being.
This bodhisattva should give rise to a mind of constant compassion, a mind of filial piety, and employ skillful means to rescue and protect them.
Yet, with a self-indulgent mind and a dissatisfied spirit, he takes life.
This is the first *pārājika* offense for a bodhisattva; "pārājika" is translated here as "an extremely grave offense."
If a disciple of the Buddha,
personally steals, teaches others to steal, or employs the means of stealing—
the karma of stealing, the dharma of stealing, the causes of stealing, and the conditions of stealing.
Regarding objects under the protection of spells, spirits, or ghosts, or those belonging to thieves and robbers—
any such property, even a single needle or a blade of grass— one must not intentionally steal it. Furthermore,
the Bodhisattva gives rise to the Buddha-nature, filial piety, and a heart of compassion.
One who constantly assists all living beings in generating merit and happiness,
yet instead steals the property of others—
this is the second *pārājika* offense of a bodhisattva.
If a disciple of the Buddha,
whether acting for oneself or instructing others to engage in sexual misconduct— even with any woman— must not intentionally commit sexual acts. This includes the causes of lust,
the karma of lust, the methods of lust, and the conditions of lust.
Even if one engages in sexual misconduct with female animals, female devas, or female spirits,
or through improper paths,
the bodhisattva gives rise to a mind of filial obedience, rescues and delivers all sentient beings, and bestows the pure Dharma upon them.
On the contrary, they instead give rise to all manner of sexual desire toward human beings,
making no distinction even regarding animals;
they commit incest with their mothers, sisters, and other close relatives, acting without any heart of compassion.
This is the third *pārājika* offense for a bodhisattva.
If a disciple of the Buddha speaks falsehoods themselves, teaches others to speak falsehoods, or employs skillful means to speak falsehoods.
False speech arises from the cause of false speech, the karma of false speech, the nature of false speech, and the conditions for false speech;
it extends even to claiming to have seen what one has not seen, or claiming not to have seen what one has seen—
this is false speech of body and mind.
Yet, while Bodhisattvas always give rise to right speech and also cause sentient beings to give rise to right speech and right view,
they conversely further give rise to all the wrong speech, wrong views, and wrong actions of sentient beings.
This is the fourth *pārājika* offense for a bodhisattva.
If a disciple of the Buddha sells alcohol themselves or teaches others to sell alcohol.
Regarding the selling of liquor: due to the act of selling liquor, the method of selling liquor, and the conditions for selling liquor—one must not sell any kind of liquor whatsoever.
Such liquor is the causal condition that gives rise to transgression.
A bodhisattva should give rise to the wisdom of clear penetration regarding all sentient beings;
yet, if they instead further give rise to the perverted minds of sentient beings,
this is the fifth pārājika offense of a bodhisattva.
If a Buddha’s disciple personally speaks of the faults and transgressions of lay or ordained Bodhisattvas, Bhikṣus, or Bhikṣuṇīs,
or teaches others to speak of their faults and transgressions.
Due to the causes of transgression, the karma of transgression, the nature of transgression,

and the conditions of transgression, when a bodhisattva hears non-Buddhists, evil persons, or those of the two vehicles speak of what is neither Dharma nor Vinaya within the Buddha-dharma, [he remains unshaken].
Constantly giving rise to a heart of compassion,
he teaches and transforms these wicked people, leading them to develop wholesome faith in the Mahāyāna;
yet the Bodhisattva, on the contrary, speaks of the faults and transgressions within the Buddha-dharma himself.
This is the sixth *pārājika* offense for a Bodhisattva.
If a Buddha’s disciple praises themselves and disparages others, or likewise instructs others to praise themselves and disparage others.
When others disparage him by disparaging his causes, disparaging his karma, disparaging his Dharma, or disparaging his conditions,
the Bodhisattva instead accepts these on behalf of all sentient beings;
he intensifies their insults and misdeeds upon himself and gives his own good fortune to others.
If one extols one's own virtues while concealing the good deeds of others,
thereby causing others to suffer defamation,
this is the seventh pārājika offense for a bodhisattva.
If a disciple of the Buddha is themselves stingy, or teaches others to be stingy—
whether through the cause of stinginess, the karma of stinginess, the dharma of stinginess, or the conditions for stinginess.
When a bodhisattva sees any poor person coming to beg,
they provide everything according to that person's needs;
yet, the bodhisattva harbors no evil mind or angry mind.
They do not give away even a single coin, a single needle, or a single blade of grass; nor,
when there are those who seek the Dharma,
do they explain to them even a single word, a single verse, or a fragment of the Dharma as small as a mote of dust.
Yet he instead reviles and insults him;
this is the eighth *pārājika* offense for a bodhisattva.
If a son of the Buddha...
One who is angry oneself and teaches others to be angry creates the causes of anger, the karma of anger, the phenomena of anger, and the conditions for anger. Yet,
a Bodhisattva should give rise to roots of goodness and non-contention toward all sentient beings, constantly generating a heart of compassion.
On the contrary, they further revile and insult all sentient beings— even those who are not sentient beings— with harsh speech; moreover,
they strike them with their hands,
and attack them with knives and staves.
His mind still did not cease;
though the other person sought repentance and offered sincere words of apology,
he remained angry and would not relent.
This is the ninth pārājika offense for a bodhisattva.
If a disciple of the Buddha slanders the Triple Gem themselves...
They teach others to slander the Triple Gem—
slandering its cause, its karma, its dharma, and its conditions. Yet,
when a Bodhisattva hears even a single word of slander against the Buddha from a non-Buddhist or an evil person, [he is deeply distressed].
It is as if three hundred spears were piercing one's heart;
how much more so when one personally slanders [the teaching] with one's own mouth, failing to give rise to faith or a mind of filial obedience,
and instead further assisting those who do evil.
If those who hold wrong views slander this bodhisattva,
it constitutes the tenth pārājika offense for one who is well-trained in the precepts. If there are those who study the teachings well...
These are the ten *prātimokṣa* rules for a bodhisattva;
they should be studied.
Among them, one must not commit even a single transgression, not even as much as a speck of dust.
How much more so for one who fully violates the ten precepts?
If there is such a violator, they shall not be able to give rise to the bodhicitta in their present body,
and they will also lose their status as a king or a universal monarch (cakravartin).
They also lose their status as bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs;
they lose the ten stages of departure, the ten stages of nourishment, the ten adamantine stages, and the Buddha-nature—the eternally abiding, wondrous fruit.
They lose everything and fall into the three evil realms.
For two or three kalpas, one may not hear the names of one's parents or the Three Jewels;
for this reason, you must not commit any of these transgressions individually.
You all—present bodhisattvas, those currently training, those yet to train, and those who have already trained—[must heed this].
These are the ten precepts.
You should train in them and uphold them with a reverent mind.

After one has extensively studied these ten precepts as explained in the "Chapter on the Eighty Thousand Modes of Deportment," there are furthermore forty-eight minor rules (*laghu-dharma*) that must also be studied; however,
they are not described here due to their voluminous nature, and the student should consult them elsewhere.
Section Five: On Function. As stated in the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, the Buddha said:
"O virtuous ones!"
By abstaining from taking life, one obtains ten kinds of merit. What are these ten?
First, one attains fearlessness toward all sentient beings.
Second, they attain a mind of great loving-kindness toward all sentient beings.
Third, they sever evil habitual tendencies.
Fourth, they have few illnesses or afflictions and are decisive in their actions.
Fifth, one attains a long life span.
Sixth, one is protected by non-human beings.
Seventh, one is peaceful and secure both awake and asleep, free from all evil dreams.
Eighth, one is free from all enemies and adversaries.
Ninth, one does not fear the evil realms.
Tenth, upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, one attains rebirth in a favorable realm.
"O virtuous ones,
these are called the ten merits obtained by resting from taking life.
If one can dedicate these roots of goodness toward unsurpassed enlightenment..."
Before long, when this person realizes unsurpassed wisdom and attains bodhi,
that land will be free from all killing,
and long-lived beings will come to be born in that country.
The Buddha said:
"By abstaining from stealing, one obtains ten kinds of merit. What are these ten?"
First, one achieves great karmic fruition as a matter of certain resolution.
Second, all one's wealth and possessions are not shared with others.
Third, one is not subject to the five calamities; fourth, all people love and respect one, never tiring of it.
Fifth, he travels in all directions without encountering obstacles.
Sixth, he comes and goes without fear.
Seventh, he gives with joy.
Eighth, one will naturally and swiftly obtain wealth and treasures without seeking them.
Ninth, one will not lose the wealth one has obtained.
Tenth, at the dissolution of the body and the end of life, one will be reborn in a favorable realm.
"O virtuous ones,
these are called the ten kinds of merit obtained by resting from stealing.
If one can dedicate these roots of goodness toward unsurpassed enlightenment..."
Before long, when this person attains enlightenment,
that land will be fully endowed with various kinds of flowering and fruit-bearing trees, forests, garments, necklaces, and articles of adornment.
Rare and precious treasures were filled therein without exception.
The Buddha said:
"By abstaining from sexual misconduct, one obtains ten kinds of merit."
What are the ten? First, attaining the restraint of the sense faculties as the decisive resolution of one's task.
Second, abiding in the purity of detachment from desire.
Third, not causing affliction to others;
fourth, being a source of joy for all people;
fifth, being a source of delight for all people to behold.
Sixth, they are able to arouse diligence;
seventh, they perceive the faults of birth and death;
eighth, they always delight in giving.
Ninth, one constantly and joyfully seeks the Dharma.
Tenth, at the dissolution of the body and the end of life, one attains rebirth in a favorable realm. O virtuous ones!
This is called resting from sexual misconduct and attaining ten kinds of merit.
If one can dedicate these roots of goodness toward unexcelled bodhi,
that person will before long attain unexcelled wisdom and reach the state of bodhi.
In that land, there are no means of birth,
nor is there the female organ;
sexual desire is not practiced.
All are born through transformation.
The Buddha said:
"By ceasing false speech, one obtains ten kinds of merit."
What are the ten? First, the words of the person are guaranteed by all people and are entirely trusted.
Second, wherever they speak—even among the devas—their speech is always moderate and appropriate.
1. His breath emits a fragrance like that of the utpala lotus.

2. He alone serves as a witness among gods and humans. 3. He is loved and revered by all people, who are freed from all doubt. 4. Among gods and humans, he alone acts as a witness. 5. He is beloved and honored by the multitude, being free from all doubts.
Sixth, one always speaks truthful words.
Seventh, the mind and intentions are pure.
Eighth, one is always free from flattery, and one’s speech invariably accords with the needs of the listener.
Ninth, one will frequently experience joy.
Tenth, at the dissolution of the body after death, one will be reborn in a happy destination.
O virtuous ones!
This is called the ten kinds of merit obtained by resting from false speech.
If one can dedicate these roots of goodness toward unsurpassed enlightenment, that person will before long attain unsurpassed wisdom; when they reach enlightenment, [they shall abide therein].
In that land there are no material possessions for sustenance;
various exquisite jewel-fragrances constantly fill the country.
The Buddha said:
By refraining from divisive speech, one obtains ten kinds of merit.
What are these ten? First, the body becomes indestructible and impartial.
Second, the equality of the indestructibility of retinues;
third, the equality of the indestructibility of spiritual friends;
fourth, the equality of the indestructibility of faith.
5. The equality of the indestructibility of the five dharmas;
6. The equality of the indestructibility of the six modes of deportment;
7. The equality of the indestructibility of śamatha.
Eighth, the equality of the indestructibility of the eight samādhis;
ninth, the equality of the indestructibility of the [nine] patiences;
tenth, at the dissolution of the body and the end of life, one attains rebirth in a happy realm.
"O virtuous ones,
this is called resting from divisive speech and attaining ten kinds of merit.
If one can dedicate these roots of goodness toward unsurpassed enlightenment,"
Before long, when this person attains unsurpassed wisdom and reaches enlightenment,
all their kinsmen and retinues in that land, as well as all Māras, adversaries,
and hostile factions, [shall likewise attain it].
It cannot be destroyed.
The Buddha said:
"By ceasing harsh speech, one obtains ten kinds of merit."
What are the ten?
First, attaining gentle speech;
second, clear and distinct speech.
Third, speech that is logical;
fourth, speech that is beautiful and smooth;
fifth, speech that always hits the mark.
Sixth, straightforward speech;
seventh, fearless speech;
eighth, speech that does not dare to slight or disparage others.
Ninth, one’s speech will be pure and eloquent.
Tenth, at the dissolution of the body after death, one will be reborn in a happy destination. O virtuous ones!
This is called resting from harsh speech and attaining ten kinds of merit.
If one can dedicate these roots of goodness toward unsurpassed enlightenment, such a person will before long attain unsurpassed wisdom; when they reach enlightenment, [these merits will be realized].
In that land, the sound of the Dharma pervades everywhere,
and all harsh speech is eliminated.
The Buddha said:
By refraining from frivolous speech, one obtains ten kinds of merit.
What are these ten? First, one is loved and respected by devas and humans.
Second, people rejoice in them;
third, they always delight in reality;
fourth, they are not disparaged by the wise and dwell with them without separation.
Fifth, they are able to comprehend what they hear;
sixth, they constantly receive respect, love, and veneration;
seventh, they always find joy in dwelling in forest hermitages (āraṇya).
Eighth, one delights in the noble silence of the sages.
Ninth, one distances oneself from evil persons and draws near to the noble ones.
Tenth, at the dissolution of the body after death, one attains rebirth in a happy destination.
"O virtuous ones,
this is called resting from frivolous speech and attaining ten kinds of merit.
If one can dedicate these roots of goodness toward unsurpassed enlightenment,"
Before long, when this person attains unsurpassed wisdom and reaches enlightenment,
sentient beings who are upright and handsome will come to be born in that land;
they will possess strong memories and never forget, and they will delight in dwelling in detachment from desire.
The Buddha said:
"By resting from sensual desire, one obtains ten kinds of merit. What are these ten?"
First, the physical faculties are unimpaired;
second, verbal karma is pure;
third, the mind is undistracted.
Fourth, one obtains superior karmic retribution;
fifth, one attains great wealth and nobility;
sixth, all people delight in beholding one.
Seventh, the karmic rewards and retinue one obtains shall be indestructible.
Eighth, one will constantly meet with wise and enlightened persons.
Ninth, one will never be separated from the sound of the Dharma.
Upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life,
one will be reborn in a happy destination.
Noble sirs, these are called the ten merits obtained by resting from sensual desire.
If one can dedicate these roots of goodness toward unsurpassed enlightenment,
that person will before long attain unsurpassed wisdom; upon reaching enlightenment,
they will dwell in a land free from the enmity of Māra and all non-Buddhist paths.
The Buddha said,
"By ceasing anger, one obtains ten kinds of merit. What are these ten?"
First, being free from all anger;
second, delighting in not accumulating wealth;
third, being a source of joy for the multitude of sages.
Fourth, one constantly meets with sages and noble ones.
Fifth, one attains beneficial matters.
Sixth, one’s countenance becomes upright and handsome.
Seventh, seeing sentient beings happy, one gives rise to joy.
Eighth, one attains samādhi.
Ninth, one attains a luster, harmony, and suppleness of body, speech, and mind.
Upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life,
one will be reborn in a happy destination.
Noble friends, these are called the ten merits obtained by resting from ill-will.
If one can dedicate these roots of goodness toward unsurpassed enlightenment,
that person will before long attain supreme wisdom; at the time they attain enlightenment,
for all sentient beings within that land—
They all attain samādhi;
when they are born in that land, their minds become utterly pure.
The Buddha said:
By abandoning wrong views, one obtains ten kinds of merit.
What are these ten? First, one’s nature becomes gentle and virtuous, and one’s companions become noble and upright.
Second, having faith in the existence of karmic retribution, they do not commit any evil acts even when their lives are at stake.
Third, they reverently believe in the Triple Gem; even for the sake of sustaining their livelihood, they do not place faith in celestial deities.
Fourth, they attain right view and do not regard strange or miraculous events as significant, nor do they select auspicious days or favorable times.
1. The five constant virtues give birth to human and celestial realms and cause one to leave all evil paths behind.
2. The six constant virtues bring joy in merit and virtue, and one is praised by wise men.
3. The seven constant virtues involve discarding worldly etiquette and constantly seeking the holy path.
Eighth, one abandons the views of annihilationism and eternalism and enters into the principle of dependent origination.
Ninth, one constantly encounters those who have correctly set out with the right aspiration.
Tenth, at the dissolution of the body after death, one attains rebirth in a favorable realm.
"O virtuous ones,
this is called resting from false views and attaining ten kinds of merit.
If one can dedicate these roots of goodness toward unsurpassed enlightenment,"
This person will swiftly fulfill the six pāramitās and attain perfect enlightenment in a pure buddha-field.
Having attained bodhi, [they...]
Sentient beings adorned with all roots of goodness, merit, and wisdom from that buddha-field come to be born in that land;
they do not believe in celestial deities and are free from the fear of the evil realms.

the waters of meditative concentration flow and fill it.

although the roof and rafters are not yet complete,

Part Two: Section on Loss and Gain. According to the *Necklace Sūtra* (*Āṭānāṭīya-sūtra*), it says:
The Buddha said:
"O Son of the Buddha,
I shall now establish for all bodhisattvas the root of all precepts."
This refers to the three clusters of precepts.
O Son of the Buddha,
once one has received the ten inexhaustible precepts, the recipient—
It overcomes the four maras and transcends the suffering of the three realms.
From birth to birth, one does not lose this precept;
it constantly follows the practitioner until the attainment of Buddhahood. As the Brahmajāla Sūtra says:
The ten inexhaustible precepts are:
first, not killing;
second, not stealing.
Third, refrain from sexual misconduct;
fourth, refrain from false speech;
fifth, refrain from drinking intoxicating liquors and spirits.
Sixth, not praising oneself or disparaging others;
seventh, not speaking of the faults of lay or ordained bodhisattvas;
eighth, not being covetous.
Ninth, not being angry;
tenth, not slandering the Triple Gem.
These are called the ten inexhaustible precepts.
O Son of the Buddha,
if all sentient beings of the past, future, and present do not receive these Bodhisattva precepts,
they cannot be called those possessed of consciousness.
They are no different from animals;
they cannot be called human beings.
They are forever separated from the ocean of the Triple Gem.
They are not bodhisattvas;
being neither male nor female,
they are called animals.
They are called people of false views;
they are called outsiders;
they do not accord with human sentiment.
Thus, one should know that the Bodhisattva precepts have a method for receiving them but no method for abandoning them.
Even if they are transgressed, they are not lost and persist until the end of the future.
If there is anyone who wishes to receive the Bodhisattva precepts:
The Dharma Master first provides an explanation to inspire their joy and devotion,
and only then does he receive [the precepts] from them.
Furthermore, the Dharma Master is able [to do so] within all lands.
If a Dharma teacher converts a single person to leave the household life and receive the Bodhisattva precepts,
their merit surpasses that of one who constructs eighty-four thousand stupas;
how much more so if they convert two, three, or even up to a hundred, a thousand, or more people.
The meritorious retribution is immeasurable.
As for that Dharma Master, husband,
wife, and their six kin may mutually serve as teacher to one another.
Those who receive it enter the ranks of the bodhisattvas within the realms of all Buddhas and transcend the suffering of birth and death for three kalpas.
Therefore, it is better to commit an offense while remaining within existence than to remain free from offense while dwelling in non-existence;
furthermore, one who commits such an offense is called a bodhisattva.
Those who do not transgress [the precepts] are called outsiders.
For this reason, those who receive one portion of the precepts are called "one-portion bodhisattvas," and so on up to those who receive twenty,
thirty, forty, or all portions, who are called "those who have fully received the precepts."
Therefore, when the mind is exhausted, the precepts are also exhausted;
because the mind is inexhaustible, the precepts are also inexhaustible.
This applies to all sentient beings within the six realms who receive and attain the precepts.
However, if one understands the language, one obtains the precepts and does not lose them.
Furthermore, the *Śraddhākaravarman-sūtra* states:
"There are two causes and conditions by which the bodhisattva precepts are lost."
First is the regression from the bodhicitta;
second is the acquisition of a supremely evil mind.
One should remain free from these two causes and conditions.
Even unto future lives,
among the realms of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts,
they shall never lose their precepts.
If one later receives the bodhisattva precepts again in a future life,
it is not called "newly obtaining" them;
rather, it is called "revealing and polishing them to purity."
Furthermore, the Brahmajāla Sūtra states:
"At that time, the wise one, facing the Buddhas of the ten directions, shall chant the *karmavācanā* for the person receiving the precepts."
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions,
seeing this person from afar, conceive thoughts of him as a son or a younger brother;
they all extend their compassionate hearts to pity and protect him with mindfulness.
Because the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas protect and keep them in mind from afar,
those who have received the precepts find their merit increase and do not lose the wholesome dharmas.
When the person receiving the precepts experiences their entire body— from the crown of the head to the soles of the feet—
tremble with awe as if a cool breeze were entering their frame,
one should know that the recipient possesses the signs of the precepts within the darkness of the mind.
At that time, there must be Buddhas of the ten directions who,
with the eye of the True Dharma, behold this practitioner’s genuine and true mind.
Thus, Śākyamuni Buddha, amidst the assembly of noble ones—
One should chant these words,
announcing to the great assembly:
"In that world, in such-and-such a land, there is such-and-such a bodhisattva."
"I request the Bodhisattva precepts from the wise person [Name].
This person has no teacher;
I shall act as their teacher."
Out of compassion.

"O Son of the Buddha."

one is excluded from receiving the Bodhisattva precepts only if one has committed the seven heinous offenses;
these consist of the five heinous offenses with the addition of killing one's preceptor (upādhyāya) or teacher (ācārya).
All kings, princes, ministers, and officials;
bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs;
and faithful men and women.
Adulterous men and women;
the eighteen Brahmā heavens;
those without sexual organs, those with two sexual organs, eunuchs, and slaves.
All ghosts and spirits, vajra deities,
animals, and transformed humans—
provided they understand the words of the Dharma Master— all may receive the precepts.

so as to distinguish them from those of the non-Buddhists.

"If, O Sons of the Buddha,
a crown prince wishes to receive the position of king..."
When assuming the rank of a Wheel-Turning King,
or when receiving office as one of the hundred officials,
one should first receive the Bodhisattva precepts.
All ghosts and spirits shall protect the person of the King and the persons of his hundred officials;
all Buddhas will rejoice.

the bodhisattva instead gives rise to arrogance, delusion, and pride, failing to rise to greet them,
escort them, or pay them homage.
Each [of these] is not in accordance with the Dharma.

one should sell one's own body.

however, among these seven assemblies, the bhikṣu is the most superior.

The first is the bodhisattva who shares the same Dharma.

Section Four: Repentance. Regarding the fourth section on repentance:
one who wishes to receive the pure Dharma must first cleanse the inner mind before being fit to receive it.
The defilements that stain the mind consist solely of delusion and obstruction.
Delusion refers to slandering the non-existence of the Triple Gem;
obstruction refers to the extensive commission of the ten unwholesome actions.
Now, those who teach the practice of repentance are correctly repenting these two.
Furthermore, according to the Brahmajāla Sūtra:
"If one teaches a Dharma Master of the precepts..."
Upon seeing a person who wishes to receive the precepts,
one should instruct them to request two masters.
The two masters— the Upādhyāya and the Ācārya— should then ask as follows:
"Do you have the seven obstructing offenses?
If you currently possess the seven obstructing offenses in this present body,
the teacher will not grant you ordination."
One who has not committed the seven obstructions may receive [the precepts].
If there are those who have violated the ten precepts,
they should be instructed to perform repentance.
Before an image of a Buddha or Bodhisattva,
recite the ten precepts and the forty-eight light precepts six times every day.
If you pay homage to the thousand Buddhas of the three periods of time, you shall behold auspicious signs.
Whether for one week, two or three weeks, or even up to one year,
one must see an auspicious sign,
such as the Buddha coming to touch one’s head with his hand.
If one sees various extraordinary signs such as radiant light,
one will immediately attain the extinction of sins;
however, if no auspicious signs appear, even though one performs repentance, it will be of no benefit.
Even if one manifests in this body, one cannot obtain the precepts.
This applies whether one has previously received the precepts or has violated the forty-eight minor precepts.
The opponent's transgressions are extinguished through confession;
this is not the same as the seven *ānantarya* offenses.
Furthermore, when one wishes to receive the precepts:
He asked: "Does he not manifest in this body the commission of the seven heinous crimes?
One may not confer the precepts upon one who has committed these seven heinous crimes."
The seven heinous offenses are:
first, shedding the blood of a Buddha;
second, killing one's father.
Third, killing one's mother;
fourth, killing one's preceptor (upādhyāya);
fifth, killing one's teacher (ācārya).
Sixth, disrupting the *saṃgha* by overturning the turning of the wheel of Dharma through illegal formal acts (*karmavācanā*).
Seventh, killing an *ārya*.
If one possesses these seven obstructions, one cannot attain the precepts in this very body.
All other people may receive the precepts.
According to the dharma of those who have left the household life, one does not prostrate to kings,
nor does one prostrate to parents.
He does not prostrate before his six relations,
nor does he prostrate before ghosts or spirits;
he understands only the words of the Dharma Master.
If there are those who come from a hundred or a thousand *li* to seek the Dharma,
yet the Bodhisattva Dharma Master, out of an evil mind or a mind of anger,
does not immediately bestow the precepts of all sentient beings upon them.
I, your disciple [Name], have committed a minor offense.
I reverently address the Buddhas of the ten directions.
"Disciple, from the beginningless limit of consciousness until this present body,
you have either lacked faith in the Triple Gem yourself,
or have taught others not to have faith in the Triple Gem."
Or they see [others] performing acts of sympathetic joy;
or they themselves disparage the Triple Gem;
or they teach others to disparage the Triple Gem.
Or seeing [others] do so, they rejoice;
or they themselves cause injury to the Triple Gem;
or they instruct others to cause injury to the Triple Gem.
Or they see [others] committing them and rejoice;
or they themselves commit killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct;
or they instruct others to kill, steal, and engage in sexual misconduct.
Or they see [others] committing them and rejoice;
or they themselves engage in false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous speech;
or they instruct others to engage in false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous speech.
Either seeing [others] act and rejoicing in it,
or being greedy, hateful, or deluded oneself,
or teaching others to be greedy, hateful, or deluded.
Or they may see [others] committing [such acts] and rejoice in them;
they feel no shame or remorse regarding these various transgressions,

Now, before the Buddha, I repent with utmost sincerity.
May all transgressions be forever severed without remainder.
With a resolute mind, pay homage to all Buddhas once; it would be even more virtuous to do so three times.
5. The Section on Receiving the Dharma. This fifth section has four parts:
first, determining one’s spiritual lineage (*gotra*);
second, determining one’s generation of the resolve (*cittotpāda*).
Third, one determines whether the process is gradual or immediate.
Fourth, one formally administers the precepts.
First, the question is asked as follows:
"You, [Name], son of good family or daughter of good family—Dharma-sister or Dharma-sister—listen! Are you a bodhisattva?
If they answer, "I am," the preceptor may ask while either sitting or standing; both ways are permissible.
The reason one may sit is that the preceptor is elderly and lacks physical strength;
the reason one may stand is—
Because the preceptor is junior in age yet possesses great power,
the name "So-and-so" is merely a title bestowed by one's parents, teachers, or elders.
This does not mean that one should adopt the titles of His Imperial Majesty or the Prefect;
even if one were to adopt them, it would not constitute the issuance of a precept.
It would merely be a case of turning one's back on the Dharma to pursue worldly passions.
This was not out of respect for the ritual of the Way.
The second question asked whether he had made the bodhisattva vow;
he replied that he had already done so.
The vow of a bodhisattva is precisely another name for the mind of the Way.
The third question concerns its gradual and sudden aspects.
According to the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra*,
Upāli asked about the bodhisattva precepts:
"How does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva who has accomplished the dharma of the precepts benefit sentient beings?"
First, one must fully train in and perfect the Upāsaka precepts, the Śrāmaṇera precepts,
and the Bhikṣu precepts. It is impossible that one could obtain the Śrāmaṇera precepts without having perfected the Upāsaka precepts.
It is likewise impossible for one who is not fully endowed with the śrāmaṇera precepts to obtain the bhikṣu precepts;
if one is not fully endowed with these three kinds of precepts, [it is impossible].
It is likewise impossible to obtain the bodhisattva precepts [without this sequence].
It is like a multi-storied tower with four levels arranged in succession.
It is impossible that one should not proceed from the first stage to the second;
it is likewise impossible that one should not proceed from the second stage to the third.
It is likewise impossible for one to proceed from the third stage to the fourth stage without [passing through the intervening stages].
According to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra*, it says:
If one wishes to receive the śrāmaṇera precepts, one must first receive the five precepts of an upāsaka;
if one wishes to receive the full bhikṣu precepts, one must first receive the ten precepts of a śrāmaṇera.
It is like a person entering the ocean, proceeding from the shallow to the deep.
Those who enter the great ocean of the Buddha-dharma should likewise do so.
However, if there are circumstances of difficulty that prevent one from receiving it gradually, [one may receive it all at once].
A bhikṣu who receives the full precepts all at once also obtains the three types of precepts; however,
the one who confers them incurs a minor offense, as in the previous case of the bodhisattva.
It should also be understood in this way.
According to the *Dìchí lùn* (Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra),
it is also permissible to directly receive the Bodhisattva precepts by suddenly generating the Mahāyāna mind.
The fourth [step] is the actual conferral of the precepts.
The preceptor asks:
"You, son of good family (kulaputra) or daughter of good family (kuladuhitrī),..."
If you wish to receive from me all the bodhisattva precepts—
namely, the precept of restraint (saṃvara-śīla) and the precept of gathering wholesome dharmas (kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla)— then [listen].
The precept of gathering in sentient beings.
These precepts are the precepts in which all bodhisattvas of the past, future, and present abide;
all bodhisattvas of the past have already trained in them.
All bodhisattvas of the future shall study this;
all bodhisattvas of the present are now studying it.
Are you able to receive it?
He replied: "One is able to recite it three times. The current mention of 'good men and women' refers to a single person;
if one is addressing many people,"
Thus it is said: "So-and-so," and so forth.
Second, regarding the method of receiving [the precepts] through mental reflection (*manasikāra*):
if there is no person of virtuous conduct available to serve as a recipient, [one may proceed in this manner].
This practitioner should maintain proper dignified demeanor and approach the Buddha image. Having prostrated before the Buddha,
they should kneel with the right knee on the ground and say:
I, [Name], inform all the Buddhas of the worlds in the ten directions and the assembly of Bodhisattvas who have entered the Great Stages:
I now receive all the Bodhisattva precepts before these Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
These are the precepts of restraint,
the precepts for gathering virtuous dharmas,
and the precepts for gathering sentient beings.
These precepts are the precepts in which all bodhisattvas of the past, future, and present abide;
they have already been studied by all bodhisattvas of the past.
All bodhisattvas of the future should study this;
all bodhisattvas of the present are now studying it. As the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states three times:
"If one receives [the precepts] from a teacher without relying on an auspicious sign (*lakṣaṇa*)."
Because the lineage of precept masters has been transmitted through successive generations and possesses great power,
if one were to receive the precepts by making a personal vow before an image of the Buddha,
it is necessary to invoke a favorable sign (*lakṣaṇa*) before the ordination can be obtained.
Because one has not received [instruction] from a teacher and lacks personal power,
it is necessary to request the empowerment of the Sage.
This applies when one is in meditative concentration.
Whether in a dream or while awake, one may experience auspicious signs.
Only that which accords with the holy teachings is valid.
As for the recipient of the precepts,
it is sufficient that they personally express their vow and commitment through the formal procedure of the ritual words.
This is just as one receives the Dharma from a teacher.
Section Six: Requesting Verification. Once the precepts have been received, one must immediately request verification.
First, one requests the Bodhisattvas.
Regarding the subsequent invitation to the Buddha and the initial invitation to the Bodhisattvas:
the latter refers to the bodhisattvas of the great earth.
The "Great Ground" refers to the Stage of the Spiritual Lineage (*gotrabhūmi*), the Stage of Practice through Understanding (*adhimukticaryābhūmi*), up to the tenth stage;
these are [the stages of] Samantabhadra and so forth, down to Bhadramukha.
When the recipient kneels on their right knee, the preceptor rises for them.
They pay homage to the assembly of Bodhisattvas of the ten directions and speak these words:
"I, the disciple [Name],..."
I respectfully address the assembly of Bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms of the earth throughout the ten directions, including Mañjuśrī, Vajradhvaja, Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha, and other Bodhisattvas.
This Bodhisattva [Name], and others, before this image in such-and-such a monastery within such-and-such a world in such-and-such a country.
"Before me, [Name], you have three times received the Bodhisattva precepts; I act as your witness. This is said three times. "Requesting all Buddhas" refers to all the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Furthermore, regarding a single teaching:
from the Buddha Virtuous Virtue in the eastern direction to the Buddha Bright Virtue in the lower direction,
all such Buddhas are the foremost Great Teachers.
Manifestly knowing, seeing, and awakening:
before all sentient beings, I now manifest knowledge, vision, and awakening that such-and-such a bodhisattva, in such-and-such a world, before such-and-such a monastery and such-and-such an image.
I, [Name], have three times received the Bodhisattva precepts in the presence of [Name].
I act as witness for these three recitations because of such a declaration.
Before the presence of immeasurable Buddhas and the Bodhisattvas of the great earth, auspicious omens have appeared according to the Dharma.
There may be radiant light;
there may be cool breezes;
there may be exquisite fragrances.
Because they manifest with signs,
the Buddhas of the ten directions regard this certain Bodhisattva as a son,
and the great Bodhisattvas regard him as a younger brother.
Because they conceive the thought of [the preceptor] as a son or a younger brother,
they possess a heart of loving-kindness and affection;
this causes the bodhisattva, after having received [the precepts], to immediately repent whenever a transgression occurs.
Dedicating oneself to the foundations of mindfulness with steadfastness and without transgression,
one shall never regress until reaching bodhi.
One will be fully endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, all utterly pure, as well as the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses.
The three applications of mindfulness, the three ways in which he needs no protection,
great compassion, the quality of not speaking falsely,
and the eradication of all habitual tendencies.
Fully endowed with the omniscient wisdom of all aspects and the one hundred and forty unique qualities,
he traverses the ten directions by means of great compassion,
extensively delivering sentient beings without ever wearying of the toil.
All sentient beings shall equally share in this benefit.
Section Seven: The Characteristics of the Precepts. Regarding the characteristics of the precepts: the Great Sage’s method for delivering humanity rests solely upon the precepts.
In discussing the precepts generally:
The essentials consist of three parts.
First is the precept for householders,
which refers to the five precepts and the eight precepts.
Second, the precepts for those who have left the household life, which refers to the ten precepts and the two hundred and fifty precepts.
Third, the precepts commonly observed by both monastics and laypeople.
This refers to the three clusters of precepts (*tri-śīla-skandha*).
Furthermore, these three clusters are of three kinds.
The first is the diversity of the nature of the precepts.
The second consists of the precepts, the mind of awakening, and the four immeasurables.
The third consists of the practice of the precepts, the six perfections, and the four means of integration.
Now, regarding these perfections and integrations:
If categorized according to the modes of deportment, they are called the three clusters (*tripuñja*);
if based on the stages of practice, they are termed the seven;
and if considered in terms of the stages of virtue, they are designated as the seven grounds (*bhūmi*) and the thirteen abodes (*trayodaśa-vihāra*).
All such explanations as these concern the differences in the precepts and their methods.
Above, I have briefly outlined the essential principles of the essence of the precepts (śīla-svabhāva).
From here on, I shall explain them extensively for the practitioner.
Once the precepts have been received,
one must recognize the characteristics of the precepts and understand the time of their reception, as well as their relative gravity and the extent of their efficacy;
they should all be recited and maintained so as not to be forgotten or lost.
I, [Name], a disciple of the Bodhisattva precepts,
from the year [Year], month [Month], day [Day],
and hour [Hour], before Master [Name].
According to the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra*,
one receives and attains the Bodhisattva’s Threefold Pure Precepts (*tri-vidha-śīla*). What are these three?
First is the precept of restraining oneself through discipline (*saṃvara-śīla*).
This means being free from all that is evil and giving rise to the practice for realizing the Path.
This is the cause for the virtue of abandonment (prahāṇa-guṇa) and ultimately results in the attainment of the Dharma-body (dharmakāya).
Cessation (śamatha) is itself retention (dhāraṇā).
To act [in such a way] is to commit an offense;
to follow the teachings, practice them with devotion, and exercise caution so as not to do so—
this is the second, the precept of gathering virtuous dharmas (*śīla-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*).
This means that there is no goodness that is not accumulated;
it gives rise to practices that assist the path,
and is thus the cause of the virtue of wisdom.
In the end, this constitutes the retribution-body (sambhogakāya). To act is itself to maintain;
to cease is to transgress.

Third is the precept of gathering in sentient beings, which means that there is no being who is not delivered. By following the teachings and practicing them with devotion, one brings about the perfection of conduct and virtue.
Arising in the practice of the non-abiding path is the cause of this grace and virtue;
it ultimately results in the attainment of the *nirmāṇakāya*.
To act is to uphold;
to cease is to transgress.
This refers to the precept of restraining one's conduct.
In brief, there are only four [points].
First, one must not, for the sake of gain or support, praise oneself and disparage others;
this is the pārājika offense of lack of shame (āhrīkya).
Second, if one intentionally practices stinginess and does not give to another person out of a lack of shame (*ahrīka*),
it constitutes a *pārājika*. Third,
if with a mind of anger one strikes or reviles another person, and that person apologizes and seeks reconciliation, yet one refuses to accept their confession.
Lack of shame constitutes a *pārājika*.
Fourth, slandering the Mahāyāna with a deluded mind constitutes a *pārājika* due to lack of shame.
This comprehensively clarifies the faults to be abandoned within the three clusters.
As for that which has the capacity to abandon them,
it refers to the volition of the actions of body, speech, and mind.
Regarding the precept of collecting wholesome dharmas (*kuśaladharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*):
there is no goodness that is not accumulated.

This refers to the virtues of body, speech, and mind; the three types of wisdom consisting of hearing, reflection, and cultivation; the ten perfections (*pāramitā*); and the eighty-four thousand practices that assist the path.
Following the teachings and practicing them in accordance with them to accomplish conduct and virtue;
as for the precept of gathering in sentient beings:
The four immeasurables are the mind;
the four means of integration are the practice.
As for the four immeasurables:
These are loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
Compassion can uproot suffering until it is exhausted;
loving-kindness can bestow happiness until it is fulfilled.
Joy means celebrating that sentient beings have departed from suffering and are fulfilled by the Dharma of ultimate bliss.
Equanimity means causing sentient beings to practice the conduct of the Buddhas and reach the destination of the Buddhas;
only then does the mind of equanimity arise.
The four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) serve as the practitioner’s [methods].
These are generosity (*dāna*), pleasant speech (*priyavāditā*), beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*), and cooperation (*samānārthatā*).
When a bodhisattva intends to integrate sentient beings, [he employs these].
First, one provides material aid to relieve them from physical suffering;
next, one uses kind speech to awaken their minds,
causing them to have faith and understanding in one's words and deeds.
Regarding "gathering through benefit":
based on the preceding faith and understanding, one next causes the arousal of practice.
Practice refers to morality (*śīla*), meditative concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), and so forth.
Causing others to collectively receive and practice [the teachings] is the gathering through beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*).
As for "common purpose" (*samānārthatā*):
When the practice is perfected,
the transformation of the basis is ultimately accomplished, and the three bodies are realized,
identical to that which is realized by the noble ones.
Therefore, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states:
"Through generosity and kind speech,
one causes those who have not yet resolved their minds to generate that resolve."
One brings those who have not yet matured through beneficial conduct to maturity,
and brings those who have not yet been liberated through common purpose to liberation.
These are the points listed above.
Have the recipient of the precepts recite it,
so that they may know the timing of the reception of the precepts and receive instruction from the teacher accordingly.
This is a brief recognition of what constitutes transgression and non-transgression.
The commentary states:
"Since one has already received the precepts in accordance with the sūtras..."
One must also recognize the six grave and eight secondary precepts.
Regarding the first six grave precepts,
as stated in the *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra*:
Once an upāsaka has received and maintains the precepts,
he must not kill any being, from devas and humans down to even an ant. Having received the precepts,
whether he instructs another with his mouth to kill or kills with his own body, [he commits an offense].
Such a person immediately loses the upāsaka precepts;
they do not even attain the stage of "warmth" (uṣmagata),
much less the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
This is called the first grave offense.
Likewise, one must not steal,
nor falsely claim, "I have attained the contemplation of impurity."
One must not engage in sexual misconduct.
One must not proclaim the faults or transgressions of the fourfold assembly.
One must not sell alcohol.
If one breaks any of these precepts, one loses the upāsaka-precepts;
one will not even attain the stage of "heat" (uṣmagata),
let alone the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
These are called the six grave offenses.
Regarding the second set, the eight grave precepts,
as stated in the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra*:
There are two kinds of bodhisattvas:
first, those who are householders with six grave precepts;
second, those who have left the household life with eight grave dharmas.
If one commits any one of these grave offenses,
one will be unable to adorn immeasurable, unsurpassed bodhi in the present,
nor will one be able to bring the mind to tranquility.
This is what is called a bodhisattva in name only, not a bodhisattva in reality;
this is called a *caṇḍāla* among bodhisattvas.
The minds of bodhisattvas are categorized as superior, middling, and inferior.
If one commits an offense against the lower, middle, or center grades of the latter four grave offenses,
it is not termed an "offense."
If one commits an offense with a superior mind or an evil mind,
this is called "committing a superior offense," namely,
delighting in performing the four matters.
Their minds lack a sense of shame or remorse;
they do not know how to repent,
nor do they perceive their own transgressions.
To praise those who violate the precepts is called the most grave offense of evil intent.
Although a bodhisattva may commit these four root transgressions, [the gravity of the offense depends on the intention].
In the end, one does not lose the bodhisattva precepts. Regarding the eight grave offenses:
they are like the four grave offenses of a bhikṣu, with the addition that a bodhisattva must not, for the sake of greedily seeking gain and offerings, praise his own person, and so forth.
As with the four *pārājika* offenses mentioned previously,
by appending the first four grave offenses,
they become eight grave offenses.
According to the Brahmajāla Sūtra and the Yogācārabhūmi Śāstra,
there are those who receive these bodhisattva precepts;
there are forty-two minor transgressions that must not be committed.
Furthermore, I shall briefly describe three or five essential points;
the remainder is found in the extensive texts. Therefore, the Sūtra says:
O sons of the Buddha,
you should always, with a single mind, receive, uphold, read, and recite these precepts—
even if you must flay your own skin to make paper.
Drawing blood for ink,
using marrow as water,
and breaking bones for pens.
One should transcribe the Buddha’s precepts;
they may be written upon hemp bark, grain paper, silk, or other materials, and should all be maintained as such.
One should always use caskets made of the seven precious gems, priceless incense and flowers, and all manner of miscellaneous jewels.
One should fill the volumes of the Sutras and Vinaya.
If one fails to make offerings to them in accordance with the Dharma,
one commits a minor transgression.
If you are a disciple of the Buddha,
you must not keep swords, staves, bows, or arrows;
nor should you engage in the trade of using light scales or small measures.
They seize people's wealth and goods by virtue of their official status;
with malicious intent, they bind and destroy those who have achieved success;
and they raise cats, wildcats, pigs, and dogs.
If one intentionally continues to maintain them,
one commits a minor offense.
O Disciples of the Buddha!
Because of an evil mind, one should not observe the fighting of men, women, armies, and so forth;
nor should one listen to various musical performances,
nor engage in miscellaneous games such as dice.
To act as a messenger for thieves—
if one does so intentionally,
one commits a secondary offense (light defilement).
If a Buddha’s disciple,
out of an evil mind and for the sake of profit, traffics in men, women, wealth, or sensual pleasures,
or prepares food with their own hands.
Grinding grain by hand and husking it by hand;
divining good and bad fortune through physiognomy;
and incantations and mechanical arts.
The method for training hawks involves compounding poisons;
it is entirely devoid of compassion.
One commits a minor offense of defilement if,
with an evil mind, one slanders the Triple Gem while feigning intimacy and attachment.
Their mouths falsely preach emptiness,
yet their conduct remains within existence.
If they encounter non-Buddhists, any kind of evil person, or bandits, [they will react accordingly].
Selling images of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, or one's parents;
trafficking in sutras and vinaya texts;
and trafficking in monks and nuns.
When the bodhisattva sees this, he employs skillful means to teach and transform them so as to redeem them;
if he does not redeem them, [he commits an offense].
Having committed a minor offense (laghu-pāpaka),
one must immediately prostrate and withdraw once the rules for maintaining and violating the precepts have been roughly understood.
Thus, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śīla-sūtra* states:
Have the recipient of the precepts prostrate once before the Buddha and once before the Earth Bodhisattva.
It does not explicitly state the ritual rules;
however, according to the general principles of propriety,
three prostrations would be more appropriate.
8. The Section on Exhortation. Regarding this eighth section on exhortation, it is stated:
When the Dharma Master has ascended the seat and the time for chanting praises and making offerings has arrived, he shall expound the essential points of the Dharma for the great assembly.
It is only through the empowerment of the Sage that this text can be proclaimed and explained.
May the great assembly simultaneously direct their minds to request the Sage’s empowerment.
May the two assemblies—the ordinary and the holy—throughout the ten directions, both speakers and listeners, [participate].
By applying this to the contemplative mind,
one’s superior wisdom is enhanced within and one’s eloquence in speech is increased without.
Only then can one recognize the faculty of "desire-to-know" (ājñāsyāmīndriya) as it has been explained without error;
furthermore, this applies to the listener as well.
Listen with single-minded reverence and without error.
Thus, a verse in the Āgama says:
"The listener gazes intently as if drinking from thirst, Entering single-mindedly into the meaning of the words."
To those who hear the Dharma with hearts leaping with joy and sorrowful gladness—such persons one may teach it.
Furthermore, they join in requesting all Buddhas to turn the wheel of the True Dharma;
throughout the worlds of the ten directions, they shall become Buddhas.
In every moment of thought, they appear in the world,
transcending all measure and number;
as it was with the preceding thought, so it is with each.
Subsequent thoughts are likewise;
all must wait for an invitation before they speak.
Ordinary beings and sages from the ten directions dwell together in the Hall of the Dharma Realm.
They all entreated him to remain for a long time and turn the wheel of the True Dharma;
for both ordinary beings and sages alike revere people and honor the Dharma,
their hearts being filled with the utmost sincerity.
The Buddhas turn the wheel of the sublime Dharma in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings and in response to their invitations.
"In accordance with" means that when the Buddhas go forth to respond to capacities and accept invitations to turn the wheel of Dharma,
I and the assembly of noble ones are always among those who participate in the stream of offering such exhortations.
There is no passing away in vain.
Why is this? Because one constantly exhorts and entreats [the Buddhas] in every moment of thought.
May all sentient beings hear the Dharma and awaken to its understanding;
may they abandon the false and enter the true, transcending the state of ordinary beings to attain the state of the noble ones.

I purify the karma of defilements as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, accumulated since beginningless time, through teaching others to do evil, destroying the goodness of others, seizing their advantages, and slandering the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha;
yet, once these sentient beings have heard the Dharma, they awaken, enter [the path], and attain realization.
They successively teach and guide all sentient beings,
continuing without interruption throughout the limits of the future.
The *Daśabhūmivibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
I entreat all Buddhas of the ten directions, those currently attaining enlightenment,
to turn the wheel of Dharma and bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings.
I entreat all Buddhas of the ten directions who wish to relinquish their life-span...
I now prostrate with my head at [the Buddha's] feet, entreating him to remain for a long time.
Commentary: The preceding verse requested the Buddha to turn the wheel of the True Dharma.
It increases wisdom and remedies the sin of slandering the Dharma— committed by myself since beginningless time and taught to others.
The subsequent verse requests that the Buddha remain long in the world to receive the offerings of sentient beings.
It increases meritorious karma and remedies the sins of the evil karma of slandering the Buddha— whether committed by oneself or incited in others.
This is the simultaneous practice of both merit and wisdom.

11. Section on Making Vows, Chapter Eleven. First, there are ten great vows.
The following vows from the *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra) are all merely recorded by humans: first, the vow of making offerings,
which is the aspiration to make offerings to the supreme conditions, the field of merit, the teachers, and the masters of the Dharma.
Second, the vow of upholding:
the vow to uphold the sublime and excellent True Dharma.
Third, the vow of turning the wheel of Dharma.
May I turn the unprecedented wheel of Dharma within the great assembly.
Fourth is the vow of practice:
may I practice all the correct conduct of bodhisattvas exactly as it has been taught.
Fifth is the vow of maturation:
the vow to mature the roots of goodness of the sentient beings in this vessel-world through the three vehicles.
Sixth is the vow of service.
May I go to all Buddha-fields, always see the Buddhas, and always be able to serve them respectfully and hear and receive the True Dharma.
This is the seventh vow for purifying the Buddha-field:
may I purify my own land, establish the True Dharma therein, and enable sentient beings to practice it.
Eighth, the vow of non-separation:
may one never be separated from all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas in any place of birth, and may one attain identical practice with them.
Ninth, the vow of benefit.
