On Superiority and Inferiority. Section Twelve on Superiority and Inferiority: There are four types of householders who uphold the precepts.
The first is called inferior;
the second, middling;
and the third, superior.
The fourth is called "the highest of the high.
This refers to practicing for the sake of present happiness, out of fear of ill repute,
or to conform to family traditions and the wishes of others.
If one observes the precepts merely to avoid forced labor or to seek escape from various hardships,

this is the observance of the precepts by an inferior person. If one strictly maintains the prohibitions and precepts for the sake of worldly merit and happiness, [this is the observance of the precepts by a middling person].
This is the observance of the precepts by a person of middling capacity. If,
for the sake of all phenomena being impermanent, one seeks to transcend suffering and attain the unconditioned, eternal bliss of nirvana,
this is the observance of the precepts by a person of superior capacity.
If, out of compassion for sentient beings,
one single-mindedly seeks the Buddha-way, thoroughly understands all phenomena,
deeply contemplates the true mark of reality, does not fear the evil realms, and aspires to summon supreme bliss.
This is the observance of the precepts by those who are supreme among the supreme.
Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Those who observe the precepts at a lower level are reborn among human beings."
Those who maintain the precepts at a middling level are reborn among the six heavens of the desire realm.
Those who maintain the precepts at a superior level practice the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments,
and are reborn in the pure heavens of the formless realm.
Furthermore, through lower purity of precept-keeping, one attains the path of an Arhat;
through middling purity of precept-keeping, one attains the path of a Pratyekabuddha.
By maintaining pure precepts, one attains the Way of the Buddha.
Furthermore, the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states:
"If one maintains the precepts out of fear of the teacher, it is called 'inferior maintenance of the precepts.'"
Holding the precepts out of fear of one’s teacher is called middling holding of the precepts;
holding the precepts out of fear of the evil realms is called superior holding of the precepts.
Section Thirteen: Receiving and Relinquishing. Just as there are three types of Mahāyāna bodhisattva precepts, so too are there three types of receiving and relinquishing.
This refers to the pure ethical discipline (*śīla*) of the three preceding aggregates.
Once this discipline has been received, it is said to be concomitant with the mind;
because the mind has no posterior limit, the discipline is never lost.
Furthermore, the *Śīlasūtra* states:
"There are two causes and conditions by which one loses the bodhisattva precepts:
first, the regression of the bodhicitta."
Second, even if one develops a superior evil mind,
unless these two conditions are met, one will not lose the precepts until the body is cast off and one enters another world as a denizen of hell or an animal.
If one receives them again later, it is not called "newly acquired";
rather, it is termed "opening, revealing, polishing, and purifying," and is thus considered long-term.

If one commits an offense with a weak or middling mind,

What constitutes the superior [offense]?
If one commits any of the four superior [offenses].
Repeatedly delighting in transgressions,

Although a bodhisattva may commit these four supreme offenses,

although a bodhisattva may commit an offense, they can be released from it and receive them again. Therefore, they are not the same.

if there are those who break the precepts, they shall never again be counted among the Sangha.
Furthermore, the Mahāsāṃghika Vinaya states:
At that time, a bhikṣu took a śrāmaṇera with him to visit his relatives; on their way,
they passed through a vast wilderness.
On the road, there was a non-human being who transformed himself into a dragon;
he circumambulated the śrāmaṇera to the right and scattered flowers over him.
He praised him, saying:
"Excellent! You have gained a great and wholesome benefit."
Having left home to enter the homeless life,
he does not handle gold, silver, or money.
When a bhikṣu goes to the house of a relative, [he behaves accordingly].
Having finished his inquiries, he wished to return.
At that time, a female relative said to the śrāmaṇera,
"Now you should go back."
"The road is remote and provisions are scarce;
you may take this money and go to the market to exchange it for what you require.
The śrāmaṇera accepted it, tied it to the hem of his robe, and departed.
While the non-human being was on the path, a novice monk (*śrāmaṇera*) carrying money walked behind a bhikṣu.
The being then transformed into a dragon, came from the left to circumambulate the novice,
and threw dirt upon him.
He said these words:
"You have lost a great benefit;
having left the household life to cultivate the Way, you are walking about clutching money."
The śrāmaṇera then wept.
The bhikṣu looked back at him and asked the śrāmaṇera,
"Why are you crying?"
The śrāmaṇera said, "I do not recall having committed any transgression; why then am I being troubled?
The teacher said:
"Do you have anything in your possession? He replied,
"I have brought this money."
The Master said:
"Discard it. Once discarded, though he is no longer human, one should again make offerings to him as before."
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana was together with the novice Śrīghoṣa;
after their meal, they went to the Anavatapta Lake in Jambudvīpa and sat in meditation.
Then, the novice Śrīghoṣa saw golden sand along the shore of the lake and had this thought:
"I shall now fill this sand and place it beneath the World-Honored One’s bathing vessel.
Having awakened from his meditative concentration, the Venerable Maudgalyāyana immediately ascended into the air by means of his supernormal powers and returned.
At that time, the novice Śrīghana was possessed by a non-human spirit and was unable to fly through the air.
Maudgalyāyana turned back, called for the novice to come,
and the novice replied:
"I cannot go there myself.
I ask you: do you have anything with you? He replied:
"Take this gold sand;
you should discard it. Having discarded it, he immediately ascended into the air and departed.
For these reasons, he reported everything in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
From this day forward, it is not permitted for śrāmaṇeras to handle gold, silver, or money.
Furthermore, the *Śatapañcāśatkakathā* (Hundred Simile Sutra) states:
Long ago, there was a foolish man who raised seven sons.
One son had previously died.
At that time, seeing that his son was dead, this foolish man wished to leave him behind in the house while he himself intended to depart.
Onlookers, having seen this, said to him:
"The paths of birth and death are distinct;
you should quickly prepare [the body] and transport it to a distant place."
At that time, having heard these words,
the foolish man thought to himself:
"If I cannot keep him here, he must certainly be buried."
"It must be that we kill one more son to lighten the burden at both ends;
only then can it be carried successfully.
Thereupon, he killed another son.
He carried it upon his shoulders and buried it far away in the forest wilderness;
those of the time who saw this—
They gave rise to deep derision,
finding it a most unprecedented marvel—
just as if a bhikṣu were to privately violate a single precept.
Out of a sense of reluctance to repent and reform,
they remain silent and conceal their transgressions,
claiming for themselves that they are pure.
Then there may be a wise person who says to them:
"Those who have left the household life maintain the prohibitive precepts."
Just as one protects a bright jewel so that it does not fall or break,
how is it that you now violate what you have received?
Not wishing to repent,
the transgressor said:
"If one must indeed repent..."
He committed the offense once more;
only then did he emerge,
having thus further transgressed the precepts.
Having committed many unwholesome deeds,
he then suddenly emerges,
just like that fool whose only son has died.
Furthermore, he killed one son;
now this bhikṣu is likewise so. Moreover, according to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*:
The Buddha spoke in verse:
"Do not despise small evils, thinking they will bring no calamity; though a drop of water is minute, it gradually fills a large vessel.
Furthermore, the *Śatākavavadāna* (*Baiyu jing*) says:
In the past, there was a king who possessed a fine tree that was exceedingly tall, broad, and large.
It shall produce a superior fruit,
fragrant and sweet. At that time,
a certain person came to the place where the king was.
The king said to him,
"On this tree there are about to grow beautiful fruits.
Are you able to eat them?"
He immediately replied to the king, saying,
"This tree is so tall and broad;
even if you wish to eat it, by what means could you possibly obtain it?"
Even if one cuts down a tree hoping to obtain its fruit,
having gained nothing, one merely exhausts oneself in vain;
later, when one wishes to replant it, the tree has already withered and died.
There is no principle of arising whatsoever.
The people of the world are likewise.
The Tathāgata, the Dharma King, possesses the tree of ethical discipline and cultivates all manner of meritorious virtues.
Failing to understand skillful means, they instead revile the precepts.
It is like cutting down a tree and then wishing to restore it to life; this is utterly impossible.
A person who has broken the precepts is just like this.
Furthermore, the *Jie xiaozai jing* (Sutra on the Elimination of Calamities through Precepts) states:
When the Buddha was in the world,
there was a certain district where all the people practiced the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions.
There was no one brewing wine.
Among them was the son of a prominent family who intended to travel far away for trade and had reached the road.
The parents said to him,
"Diligently observe the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions;
take care never to drink alcohol or violate the grave precepts of the Buddha."
While traveling to another country, he encountered an old classmate.
Overjoyed, he brought out some *pūga* wine and wished to drink it together;
however, his companion firmly declined and would not drink.
The host was so insistent that he could not comply with his request.
Later, upon returning home, he reported the matter to his parents.
His parents replied:
"You have violated my precepts;
this is the beginning of the corruption of the Dharma. You are no filial son."
Having thus obtained the goods, he was driven out of the country.
He then arrived in another land and stayed at an inn.
The host of that inn served three spirits.
It was able to assume a human form, eat and drink face-to-face with him,
and converse with him;
he attended to it for many years.
Their wealth was exhausted,
their family members suffered from illness,
and deaths occurred without end.
We discussed this together.
The ghosts knew the intentions of people,
and they deliberated among themselves, saying:
This man’s wealth has been exhausted;
he has never been of benefit to us,
and now we are weary of him.
"It would be fitting to seek out precious jewels to bestow upon them.
He then went and stole excellent treasures from the royal treasury of another king and accumulated them within his garden.
He replied,
"You have served me for many years with great diligence and toil.
Now I wish to bestow blessings upon you so that you may attain abundance."
The host joyfully entered the garden and beheld the object;
he carried it on a palanquin back to his residence,
where he offered his thanks for the favor received.
The next day, when food was prepared and an invitation was extended,
the spirits arrived at the gate and saw the people of Śrāvastī in the host's house;
they then fled in haste.
The master called out after him.
Having already looked back, the servant asked, "Where are you going?
The spirit said:
"You are hosting a venerable guest;
how could I venture forward?
Once again, I was startled and fled."
The host reflected:
"There is no one else in my house;
it is only this person."
Having finished speaking these words with reverence, he then asked him:
"What meritorious virtues do you possess?
What deity do you serve?"
Fearing his son, he fled.
The guest fully described the merits of the Buddha,
whereupon the host said:
"I wish to uphold the five precepts.
Thereupon, he received the three refuges and the five precepts from the guest.
With single-minded diligence, he did not dare to be indolent.
When he asked where the Buddha was,
he was told that he was at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, in Śrāvastī.
The host went there with single-minded devotion.
As they passed through a pavilion,
there was a woman of beautiful appearance who was a man-eating demon.
The woman had traveled a long distance;
as the sun was setting,
she sought lodging with the girl.
The woman immediately replied, "Be careful not to remain here; you should depart at once.
The man thought to himself:
Formerly, when the people of Śrāvastī were fully endowed with the four Buddhist precepts,
even my spirit feared them;
now that I have received the three refuges and the five precepts, [I am secure].
With a mind free from indolence,
what is there to fear?
He then remained there to stay the night.
At that time, the man-eating demon, seeing the majestic spiritual power of his observance of the precepts,
departed from the pavilion forty *li* away and did not return for one night.
The next day, he proceeded to see that the bones and bodies of the people devoured by the demon lay scattered in disarray.
Terrified and filled with regret, he withdrew and reflected to himself:
"It would be better to take this woman back to my own land and live together as before.
He then immediately turned back.
Because of this, he again requested to stay the night with the woman.
The woman said to the man,
"Why must you turn back?"
The answer is:
Since the practice of calculation does not succeed,
one simply turns back.
He stayed for one more night.
The woman said,
"You are dead."
"My husband is a man-eating ghost.
He will arrive before long;
you should depart at once."
This man was faithless;
he returned and stayed there without departing,
further deluding his lustful mind.
He again gave rise to disbelief and no longer believed in the Buddha’s Three Refuges and Five Precepts;
the heavenly deity then departed.
The ghost returned,
and fearing that the woman would eat this man,
she hid him inside a jar.
Hearing the scent of human breath, the ghost said to his wife,
"Have you obtained some meat?
I wish to eat it."
The wife said, "I will not go; how can meat be obtained from such a source?
The wife then asked the ghost:
The ghost said, "Minister, why did you not return yesterday?
Because of your actions, you hosted a venerable guest and caused me to be driven away."
The man inside the jar became increasingly terrified.
His wife asked,
"Why have you not obtained any meat?"
The ghost said,
"It is solely because you have harbored disciples of the Buddha that the celestial deities have driven me out forty li."
Having slept in the open air and being struck with terror,
I am now ill at ease; therefore,
I have not obtained any meat.
The wife then asked her husband,
"What are the Buddha's precepts?
The ghost replied:
There is a great famine and extreme urgency; bring meat here,
and there is no need to ask about this.
"This is the unsurpassed, true, and correct precept;
I dare not say otherwise," the wife said.
"Please speak it for me,
and I shall give you my flesh.
The ghost then explained the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts for him.
When the ghost first recited the precepts,
his wife would immediately receive them;
this continued until the fifth precept.
Holding it in his mind and reciting it aloud,
the man recognized the five precepts within the jar and received them accordingly.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, knowing that these two men had taken refuge in the Buddha in their hearts,
immediately selected fifty benevolent deities to protect them;
the ghost then fled away.
The next day, the woman asked the man,
"Were you afraid? He replied:
"Greatly terrified, I have received the grace of the Benevolent One;
my mind has awakened and I recognize the Buddha," the wife said.
"Why did the man turn back?
He replied,
"I saw the skeletons of newly deceased and long-dead people scattered here and there."
"I returned only because I was afraid," he said.
His wife replied,
"Those bones were ones I had discarded."
"I was originally a daughter of a noble family.
I was abducted by a ghost.
I have come here to be your wife."
In my wretched misery, I had no one to whom I could appeal;
now, by your benevolence, I have been granted the opportunity to hear the Buddha’s precepts.
Having parted from this ghost,
they later encountered four hundred and ninety-eight people on the road,
and together they went to where the Buddha was.
Listening to the sutras with single-minded devotion,
their minds were opened and their understanding attained; they all became śramaṇas.
They attained the fruit of arhatship.
Now, these two individuals were the former teachers of the four hundred and ninety-eight people when those people were seeking the Way.
One must obtain one's original teacher and virtuous friends;
only then will one understand.
Furthermore, the *Guanding jing* (Consecration Sutra) says:
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"In the past, in the great kingdom of Vārāṇasī, there was a son of a brāhmaṇa named Dhāraṇa."
They were wealthy and of noble lineage,
yet they did not revere the Triple Gem;
instead, they served the paths of ninety-five kinds of heterodox teachers.
In order to seek blessings and protection,
after a long period of time,
he heard that in his country there were a group of virtuous elders.
All who receive the transformative guidance of the Buddha, Dharma,
and Sangha shall attain wealth and honor, experience peaceful and secure happiness,
and be able to transcend birth, old age, sickness, and death.
The Dharma one receives is inexhaustible;
in this life and in future lives, one shall not enter the three evil realms.
Holding fast to this, the elder thought thus:
Rather than setting aside other paths to pay homage to the Triple Gem,
he immediately went to the Buddha and prostrated himself,
placing his head upon the ground.
He paid homage to the Buddha and said to him,
"That which I have served until now was not the truth."
"Therefore, I take refuge in the Buddha alone.
Out of compassion for me, please depart from these turbid and defiled practices and accept the pure Dharma teachings of the Buddha.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One completed the bestowal of the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts.
Having paid homage, he departed.
Thereafter, the elder took up residence and traveled to another country.
Seeing others kill living beings or steal another's wealth;
seeing a woman of beautiful appearance and coveting her with greedy attachment;
and upon seeing the good or evil of others, immediately engaging in gossip and criticism.
Seeing someone drinking alcohol, he immediately wished to pursue them;
his mind was thus unsettled for even a single moment,
and he thought to himself:
He repented for having received from the Buddha the dharma of the three refuges and the five precepts with solemn vows,
and he formed this thought:
"I shall take refuge in the Buddha and the dharma of the three refuges and the five precepts."
He immediately went to where the Buddha was and addressed him, saying:
"The Dharma of the Three Refuges and Five Precepts previously received imposes many prohibitions;
I am no longer able to act according to my original intentions."
He thought to himself, "I wish to desist;
is it permissible for me to cease serving the Buddha or not?
For what reason?"
"The Buddha-Dharma is revered and is not something practiced by ordinary beings.
You ought to return to the Dharma and the precepts.
The Buddha remained silent and did not respond.
Before his words had even ceased,
natural spirits and deities appeared from within his mouth,
wielding iron mallets to strike the elder’s head.
Furthermore, there are spirits and ghosts who strip away their garments;
there are also spirits and ghosts who,
using iron hooks, pull out their tongues from within their mouths.
There are yakṣas who are courtesans;
with knives, they scoop out and cut off one's genitals.
Furthermore, there are other yakṣas.
Molten copper is poured into their mouths;
the various spirits and deities before, behind, to the left,
and to the right vie with one another to tear them apart, take their blood, and devour them.
The elder was seized by terror and trembled uncontrollably, finding no place of refuge;
his face turned the color of ash,
and moreover, a spontaneous fire burned his body.
Seeking life, he could not find it;
seeking death, he could not find it.
The various ghosts and spirits quickly seized the elder, preventing him from moving.
Seeing this, the Buddha felt compassion for him and asked the elder:
"What do you intend to do now?"
The elder’s mouth was closed and he could no longer speak;
he could only raise his hands and strike himself.
He sought mercy from the Buddha, repenting his evil deeds and turning toward goodness.
The Buddha then used his majestic spiritual power to rescue the elder.
When the various kings of the ghost spirits saw that the World-Honored One had used his majestic spiritual power to rescue the elder, they [were moved].
Each stood apart on one side.
Thereupon, the elder found some small measure of relief;
he rose and prostrated himself with his head at [the Buddha's] feet.
He then addressed the Buddha, saying,
"Within my body there are these five thieves who drag me into the three evil realms."
"I sit here desiring to commit a transgression and have violated what I have received.
I pray that the Buddha will take pity on me and accept my repentance.
The Buddha said:
"What you have done with your own mind and speech—
whom else should you blame?
The householder addressed the Buddha:
From this day forward, I shall reform my past ways and cultivate the future.
I take refuge in the Triple Gem and observe the five precepts;
I maintain the six fast days and observe the three long periods of fasting.
They burned incense, scattered flowers, and hung banners and canopies to serve the Triple Gem.
From this day forward, they dared not again violate or break the laws of the refuges and precepts.
The Buddha said:
To speak thus is most excellent.
You shall now receive these Three Refuges and Five Precepts.
Do not again undergo the method of receiving the precepts as before.
To break these returning precepts is called a second offense.
If one commits it a third time, [the consequences are grave].
If they are apprehended by the Five Officials,
they shall assist the minor officials of the Prince; if apprehended by the Recorder, the Supervisor, or the Messengers of the Five Emperors,
their spirits shall be collected and their lives recorded, all according to their original offenses.
For this reason, I have spoken these words to encourage those who receive the refuges and precepts:
they shall be protected and assisted by spirits and deities.
The devas rejoice;
the immeasurable Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Arhats of the ten directions all together praise these faithful laymen and laywomen.
Regarding the time of their death,
the Buddha manifests emanations of his body to go and welcome them,
ensuring that men and women who uphold the precepts do not fall into the evil realms.
If one's precepts are weak, one should increase the cultivation of merit.
A verse says:
Vast and hazy, drifting in confusion day and night; form and mind are stained with attachment.
Unaware that the days grow ever more numerous, the body is perilously subject to decay and exhaustion.
As morning and evening pass by, the vessel of precepts is already shattered; what pure retribution can then be bestowed?
When the seven limbs of conduct are not guarded and the three karmas lose their majesty, the sages and saints all abandon you, while gods and ghosts vie with one another in derision.
The pure assembly does not accept [the impure]; they are expelled like corpses.

Once fallen into the dark paths, one shall suffer for ten thousand kalpas. *Ganying yuan* (Accounts of Resonance and Response). Briefly citing four testimonies: 1. The Jin dynasty śramaṇa Zhu Tansui; 2. The Song dynasty śramaṇa Shi Zhida; 3. The Song dynasty śramaṇa Shi Tandi; 4. The Sui dynasty śramaṇa Shi Huitan. Regarding Zhu Tansui, the śramaṇa of the Xia family during the Taiyuan era of the Jin dynasty: [text follows].
In his early twenties,
he was a white-complexioned and handsome monk of conventional appearance.
Once, while traveling, he passed in front of the Qingxi Temple.
He entered the temple and returned at dusk;
he dreamed that a person came to him and said:
"Will you come to be the deity in my temple? Later that evening,
Xuantan subsequently dreamed that [the deity] asked him,
"Who is this woman?"
The woman said,
"I am the aunt from the Green Stream.
This continued for about a month.
He then fell suddenly ill.
As he was dying, he said to his young fellow-disciples,
"I have no merit, yet I have committed no great transgression."
"After I die, I shall become the deity of the Qingxi Temple.
You gentlemen may go and see for yourselves once you have departed.
After he had died, the young practitioners arrived.
Then the spirit spoke, greeting him with inquiries;
his voice was just as it had been when he was alive.
As he was about to depart, he said:
It had been a long time since he had heard a *bhāṣya* recitation, and he longed to hear one.
His companion, Huìjìn, then performed a *bhāṣya* for him until it was finished.
It was as if he were chanting a hymn of praise, saying:
"Even at a parting on a crossroads, there is still a sense of sorrowful grief."
How much more so this separation,
where body and spirit disperse,
evoking sighs of profound obscurity.
How can these feelings be described?
Thereupon, he sobbed and his grief was beyond restraint.
All the monastics likewise shed tears from their eyes. This is one such testimony, recorded in the *Xu Soushen Ji* (Continued Records of the Search for the Divine).
As for the Song dynasty śramaṇa Shi Zhida:
he was a monk from Suo Temple in Yizhou.
While his conduct was somewhat worldly, he was skilled in the chanting of scriptures.
At the age of twenty-three,
he died of illness in the sixth month of the third year of the Yuanhui era of the Song dynasty.
His body remained warm and was not encoffined.
After two days had passed, he revived;
by dawn on the third day, he was able to speak and look about,
saying to himself:
When he was first in distress, he saw two men,
both wearing yellow cloth trousers and jackets;
one stood outside the door.
A man went straight to the bedside and said, "Venerable sir, you ought to go; you must get down from the ground.
Da replied, "This poor monk’s body is so weak that it cannot endure the journey."
The man spoke again, saying,
"You may ride in a carriage.
As soon as he finished speaking, the carriage arrived.
Once Da had ascended,
his conscious awareness became suddenly vacant,
and he no longer saw his family, his house, or the carriage he was riding in.
Looking out in the four directions as far as the eye could reach,
one saw nothing but wild wastes;
the path ahead was arduous and perilous.
Showing them the path to ascend,
he drives them forward without allowing them to rest until they reach the vermilion gate.
The walls and gates were most magnificent;
he passed through them and reached the area below the hall.
Within the hall, there was—
First was a nobleman,
wearing a vermilion robe and a black cap with a visor, sitting haughtily upon his couch;
his appearance was stern and solemn, possessing a most imposing mien.
There were about a hundred guards on both sides,
all in vermilion robes and holding swords, standing in solemn ranks.
When the nobleman saw Da, he [permitted him to enter].
Thereupon, [the master] composed his countenance and assumed a grave expression, saying,
"How can one who has left the household life commit so many transgressions? Da replied:
"Since the time I first gained consciousness, I do not recall having committed any transgression.
He was asked,
"Do you recite the precepts?"
Dharmada said,
"When I first received full ordination,
I indeed constantly practiced recitation."
Recently, because I have been occupied with the regular affairs of the fasting retreats and the recitation of scriptures,
I have fallen into neglect during the time for reciting the precepts.
He further said:
"A śramaṇa who does not recite the precepts—
how could this not be a transgression?
You should at least recite the sūtras."
Da immediately recited three invocations from the Lotus Sūtra and ceased.
The nobleman ordered the official recording Da’s case to say:
"You may send him away and place him in a desolate place, but do not let him suffer too greatly."
The two men led him away; after traveling several tens of li,
he gradually heard a tumultuous roar like crashing thunder and the sound of boiling fire,
while the path ahead grew increasingly dark.
Next, they arrived at a gate several tens of zhang high,
its color extremely hard and black.
It was an iron gate;
the walls were likewise so.
Da Xin thought to himself:
The Sūtras speak of the hells;
this is precisely what they refer to.
It is truly a great terror.
He regretted that during his lifetime he had not cultivated his practice;
meanwhile, the clamor from within the main gate grew increasingly loud.
Only after listening quietly for a long time did he realize that these were the cries of distress from those people.
Inside the gate, it grew increasingly dark until nothing could be seen again.
At that time, the firelight flickered, sometimes dying out and sometimes flaring up.
He saw several men with their hands tied behind their backs walking forward.
Later, several men seized him with forks and impaled him;
blood flowed like a spring.
One of them then reached his paternal uncle’s aunt.
When they saw one another, they wished to converse,
but someone dragged them along with great speed so that they had no leisure to speak;
this continued for about two hundred paces after they entered the gate.
They saw an object shaped like a rice granary,
approximately one zhang in height;
the two men took up the *da* and threw it onto top of the granary.
Within the storehouse there was fire;
its flames scorched his entire body until half of it was completely charred.
The pain was unbearable.
He fell from the granary to the ground and remained unconscious for a long time.
The two men then took Dà away once more.
He saw more than ten iron cauldrons,
all boiling with sinners;
the people within the cauldrons rose and sank as they were tossed by the bubbling heat.
Beside the cauldrons were people who prodded them with pitchforks;
some even managed to climb out from the cauldrons.
Both eyes bulged out and boiled, and his tongue protruded more than a foot;
though his flesh was completely torn and rotted away, he still did not die,
until all the cauldrons were filled.
Only one cauldron remained empty.
The two men said to Dà, "Venerable sir,
you should enter this one immediately."
Upon hearing these words, Da was so overcome with emotion that his very liver and gall seemed to be smeared upon the ground;
he then entreated him, saying:
"May Your Lordship listen as this poor monk performs a single prostration to the Buddha;
I shall then bow my head with a sincere heart,
praying that I may be spared from this suffering."
Prostrating himself on the ground for the duration of a meal,
his prayers and repentance were particularly earnest.
Shortly thereafter, he looked in all four directions and saw nothing more.
They beheld only level plains and lush trees;
the scenery was clear and bright,
yet the two men continued to guide their way forward.
He arrived at the foot of a multi-storied building.
The structure was tall and small in scale,
and there were people on top.
Having cut it so that it could accommodate his sitting, he said to Da:
"It is truly a cause for rejoicing that a śramaṇa has manifested such a light retribution."
When he reached the foot of the tower, he suddenly became unconscious and returned to his body.
Daqi remains alive to this day and still seeks out the monastery;
his observance of the fast and precepts has become even more steadfast.
His practice of meditation and recitation became even more steadfast. Shi Tandi, a śramaṇa of the Song dynasty:
while still a layman at the age of thirty, he suddenly died of a sudden illness.
Only after seven days did he revive.
He recounted that at the time of his initial death, he saw two men who were driving him away;
there were several thousand of these messengers.
Day and night without rest,
he saw two practitioners of the Way who said, "We are your original teachers of the five precepts," and came to comfort and inquire after him.
He was about to go before the magistrate and said,
"This man is my disciple; moreover,
he has committed no great crime."
Before the calculations were completed,
he was immediately released.
Two practitioners escorted Dian back to his home.
He stayed atop that house and provided him with detailed instructions on the scriptures, saying,

95. Section on the Suffering of Illness (95). Section on the Suffering of Illness, Number Ninety-Five. This consists of six parts:

Part on Stating the Intent, First. Now, the Three Realms are vast and remote, and the Six Paths of existence flourish in profusion.
There is nothing that does not rely upon the four great elements and depend upon the five sense organs to form its substance;
when aggregated, it becomes a body,
and when dispersed, it returns to emptiness.
However, the nature of wind and fire differs from that of earth and water;
each, according to its own portion, seeks its own suitability.
Since the principle of seeking such suitability is difficult to achieve, [conflict arises].
Therefore, it is easy for the harmony [of the elements] to be disturbed.
Suddenly, when one great element becomes unbalanced, all four great elements are impaired.
For instance, when the earth element increases, the physical form becomes dark and coarse.
The muscles become livid with bruising, and tumors and nodules form,
as hard as iron or stone;
if the earth element is deficient, the four limbs become weak and impaired.
Some lose half their bodies;
some suffer from hemiplegia or deformity;
some have their sight destroyed or their hearing lost.
If the water element increases excessively, the flesh becomes hollow and swollen, and the body loses its luster.
The entire body withers and turns yellow, the countenance constantly loses its vitality,
and the hands and feet become edematous while the bladder becomes distended and strained.
If the water element is impaired, one becomes emaciated and skeletal, with veins protruding and the pulse sinking;
the lips and tongue become parched, the ears and nose become scorched and obstructed,
the five viscera are seared within, and the fluids are exhausted without.
The six hollow organs are depleted and cannot maintain themselves.
If the fire element increases excessively, the entire body becomes distressed and parched with heat as if being scorched;
abscesses, carbuncles, boils, swellings, and ulcers break out and flow with pus.
Pus and blood overflow, and putrid stench fills the air.
If the fire element is impaired, the four limbs become emaciated and the internal organs feel as cold as ice;
the chest feels congealed with cold, and the mouth is as if filled with frost.
In the summer heat, he never felt warm even when wearing heavy furs;
his food was undigested, and he constantly suffered from nausea and vomiting.
When the wind element increased excessively, his breath became full, his chest was constricted, and his bowels and stomach were blocked and obstructed.
The hands and feet become limp and weak, and the four limbs suffer from aching and numbness.
If the wind element is severely impaired, the body becomes emaciated and haggard, the vital breath is as thin as a thread, movement is exhausted,
and one draws in the breath with a gasping effort.
Coughing, belching, and hiccups cause difficulty in swallowing;
the abdomen feels oppressed, the back is hunched, and the heart feels as cold as ice.
The tendons of the neck and the vessels of the throat throb and swell with tension.
All such various conditions are caused by the four great elements (mahābhūta) suddenly increasing or decreasing, thereby giving rise to illness.
Once one element becomes frail and weak, then all three remaining elements suffer;
thus they fall ill in succession.
They are simultaneously afflicted by torment;
the mutual upheaval of the four elements is truly due to the retribution of suffering,
for they possess neither shame nor remorse.
They show neither gratitude nor righteousness;
though they are constantly provided with all necessities throughout the four seasons and nurtured day and night, they have never felt indebted for such kindness.
If one fails to provide proper service and support, it will inevitably invite the suffering of illness;

I shall merely seek what is necessary to sustain this body and remove hunger and cold;

Section Two: Citing Testimonies. As stated in the *Buddha-spoken Medical Sūtra*: [text follows].
Within the human body there are originally four ailments:
first, earth; second, water; third, fire; and fourth, wind.
When the wind increases, the vital energy (prāṇa) arises [in disorder].
When fire increases, heat arises;
when water increases, cold arises;
when earth increases, strength becomes predominant.
From these four illnesses arise the four hundred and four illnesses.
Thus, earth belongs to the body,
water to the mouth, and fire to the eyes.
Wind affects the ears;
fire causes a slight chill and makes the eyes dim.
In the first, second, and third months of spring, there is much cold.

In the fourth, fifth, and sixth months of summer, there is much wind; this is because the midsummer in Western countries is characterized by frequent winds and heat, which differs slightly from that of the land of Han. In the seventh, eighth, and ninth months of autumn, there is much heat; in these autumn months of the Western countries, the heat first becomes most intense, which also differs from that of the land of Han. In the tenth, eleventh, and twelfth months of winter, there is both wind and cold.
Why is this? Because in spring there is much cold; since all things are born from the cold, the cold is abundant. Why is this?
Because in summer there is much wind.
Because the myriad things flourish and the Yin and Yang energies converge, there is much wind.
Why is it that there is much heat in autumn?
Because the myriad things reach maturity, there is much heat.
Why is it that there is wind and cold in winter?
It is because all things have reached their end and the heat has departed; therefore, there is wind and cold.
During the months of the third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, and eighth, one may lie down to rest.
Why is this? Because the wind element is predominant, the body is released [from its constraints].
During the eighth, ninth, tenth, eleventh, first, second, and third months, one must not lie down at improper times.
Why is this? Because their bodies contract due to the abundance of cold;
since there is still cold during the three months of spring, they are unable to eat wheat or beans.
One should eat husked rice, clarified butter (*ghṛta*), and various warm substances; these are considered "warm" by the standards of the Western lands, such as wheat and cold husked rice.
During the three months of summer, when wind predominates, one must not eat taro, beans, or wheat.
One should eat bran-rice and dairy products.
During the three months of autumn, there is heat;
one must not eat bran-rice or clarified butter (*ghṛta*).
One should eat fine rice, parched grain flour, honey, rice, and millet.
During the three months of winter, there is wind and cold;
the Yang rises and the Yin joins with it.
One should eat rice with the bran, mung bean soup, and clarified butter.
Sometimes while lying down, wind arises and sometimes it ceases;
sometimes fire arises and sometimes it ceases; sometimes cold arises and sometimes it ceases.
There are ten causes and conditions by which a person falls ill:
first, sitting for too long without lying down;
second, eating without moderation.
Third, sorrow;
fourth, exhaustion;
fifth, lewdness.
Sixth, anger; seventh, enduring excrement;
eighth, enduring urine.
The ninth is the upper wind disorder;
the tenth is the lower wind disorder.
Illness arises from these ten causal conditions.

If any monastics or laypeople see the funeral bier of a preceptor, a monk, or their parents,
and the mourners arriving from outside are fewer in number than the deceased, [they should increase the number].
Upon reaching the site of the corpse, he performed the customary rites;
having done so, he first took the hand of the filial son and silently offered him consolation,
and afterwards went to where the Great Virtuous One was.
He fully manifested his grief,
paid his respects by bowing in condolence,
and also saw foolish laypeople.
They perversely propagate their own teachings and transmit them from one to another,
forbidding the veneration of parents, paternal uncles, other elders, and the spirits of the deceased.
He said: "Since I have received the precepts and they are ghosts and spirits,
it is not appropriate for me to pay them homage."
Fearing that one might break the precepts, this does not accord with the teachings;
on the contrary, it incurs the fault of ignorance.
I humbly reflect that my preceptors and fellow monks have nurtured my Dharma-body,
while my parents, uncles, and paternal cousins have nurtured my physical body;
through their nursing and care, I have grown to maturity.
Reflecting upon this debt of gratitude, it is as vast as the heavens and difficult to repay;
even if one were to recompense this kindness throughout successive kalpas, how could it ever be fully discharged in a single lifetime?
Failing to maintain respect and gratitude,
they instead give rise to arrogance,
following in the footsteps of base men.
How can one be considered a filial son?
Therefore, even the World-Honored One, the Ultimate Sage,
personally assisted his deceased father by carrying his corpse to the funeral site.
How much more so for inferior, foolish commoners who would readily give rise to indolence and arrogance?
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
"One who knows gratitude..."
The root of great compassion is this:
those who do not recognize kindness are worse than beasts.
Furthermore, the *Śuddhodana-rāja-parinirvāṇa-sūtra* states:
King Śuddhodana was in the kingdom of Śākya;
his illness became critical and he was on the verge of death.
He longed to see the World-Honored One and Nanda and the others;
however, the World-Honored One was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain in Rājagṛha,
a distance of fifty yojanas from there.
The World-Honored One was on Vulture Peak Mountain.
With his divine ear, he heard from afar the sound of his father’s longing thoughts;
he immediately ascended into the air together with Ānanda and the others and arrived there.
He stroked the king’s forehead with his hand;
having thus comforted the king,
he recounted for him the Mahāpaurāṇa-jātaka.
When the king heard that he had attained the fruit of anāgāmin,
he took the Buddha’s hand and placed it upon his heart.
The Buddha then preached the Dharma, and [the king] attained the fruit of arhat.
When impermanence confronts them, their lives end and their breath ceases;
they suddenly depart for the next world.
Upon reaching the time of cremation, [the body is consumed by fire].
The Buddha stood solemnly and respectfully before the head of the bier together with Nanda;
Ānanda and Rāhula stood behind the feet of the bier.
Ānanda knelt on his right knee and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I only pray that you will allow me to carry my paternal uncle's coffin.
Rāhula spoke again:
"I only pray that you will allow me to carry my grandfather the King's coffin."
The World-Honored One comforted him, saying:
"In future generations, people will all be violent and cruel;
they will not repay the kindness of their parents who raised and nurtured them."
In order to provide a transformative teaching for those sentient beings who are unfilial,
the Tathāgata personally desired to carry the coffin of his father, the King;
immediately, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways.
All the mountains surged and sank like ships upon the water.
At that time, all the devas, nāgas, and spirits...
They all came to attend the funeral, raising their voices in wailing and weeping.
The Four Heavenly Kings led hundreds of thousands of millions of spirits and deities,
and they all joined together to carry out the funeral procession.
They addressed the Buddha, saying:

"For the sake of those in the future who are unfilial toward their parents, out of great compassion, you yourself wish to personally carry the coffin of our father, the King. Then the Four Heavenly Kings all addressed the Buddha, saying: [the same].
"We are the disciples of the Buddha.
Having heard the Dharma from the Buddha, we have attained the stage of Srotāpanna. For this reason..."
"We should carry the coffin of our father, the King.
The Buddha permitted the four kings to carry the coffin of the father king;
they immediately transformed themselves into human beings.
All the people wept without exception.
The World-Honored One personally took a censer in his hand and proceeded forward to the cemetery.
He ordered a thousand arhats to go to an island in the great ocean to fetch various kinds of fragrant wood, such as ox-head sandalwood,
and to burn them with fire.
The Buddha said:
"Suffering, emptiness, and impermanence are like illusions, transformations, the moon reflected in water, or images in a mirror; once the body has been consumed by fire, all ends.
At that time, the various kings each held five hundred jars of milk.
They used it to extinguish the fire.
After the fire was extinguished, they vied with one another to collect the bones and place them in a vajra casket.
Thereupon, they immediately erected a stupa together upon it and made offerings to the shrine with suspended silken banners and canopies.
The Buddha addressed the assembled multitude:
The Father King Śuddhodana was a pure person;
he was reborn in the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven.
Furthermore, the *Buddhamātṛ-nirvāṇa-sūtra* states:
The Bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī was the Buddha’s maternal aunt;
she could not bear the thought that the Buddha would enter parinirvāṇa after her.
He desired to enter parinirvāṇa first,
together with five hundred *bhikṣuṇīs*, who were *pudgala* women.
As stated in Kang Senghui’s *Fajing jing*:
Ordinary people are defiled by craving for the six sense objects,
just as a starving man craves food without knowing satiety; because the Noble Ones have severed craving and eliminated the famine of the six faculties,
they are called "nuns who have left the home life."
To eliminate his hunger, he rubbed the Buddha’s feet with his hands,
circumambulated the Buddha three times,
prostrated himself, and departed.
Manifesting the virtue of supernormal powers,
he vanished from his own seat and came from the east, performing the eighteen transformations in mid-air.
It was likewise throughout the eight directions, above, and below.
He emitted a great radiance to illuminate all darkness,
shining upward upon the various heavens.
The five hundred *bhikṣus* likewise manifested transformations and simultaneously entered *nirvāṇa*.
The Buddha exhorted the householder to prepare five hundred biers made of hemp oil,
fragrant flowers, and the timber of *candana*, *nangka*, and *tsi*.
There were five hundred of each item;
these exquisite crafts and pure melodies were intended for offering.
Upon seeing them, all ordinary people and sages alike could not help but weep with sorrow.
When the cremation was completed, they carried the śarīra to the Buddha’s dwelling.
Thereupon, two hundred and fifty arhats from each of the four directions arrived by flying through the air with their supernormal powers and prostrated at the Buddha’s feet.
They arrived at the place where the śarīra was,
and all one thousand bhikṣus took their seats together.
The Buddha addressed Ānanda:
"Take the śarīra and place them in it;
then put the bowl into my hand.
Ānanda did as he was commanded.
He addressed the bhikṣus:
"This collection of śarīras was originally a defiled body—
vicious, ignorant, impetuous, and violent."
Envy and intrigue ruin the Way and destroy virtue;
now my mother is able to uproot them and promote the conduct of a man.
Having attained the Way of Arhatship, he passed away with spiritual dignity;
how extraordinary! An imperial decree was issued to establish a temple for his offerings.
Furthermore, the Ekottarika Āgama states:
The Buddha told Ānanda and Rāhula,
"You all shall carry forth the body of Mahāprajāpatī."
"I shall personally make offerings.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra and the Four Heavenly Kings came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I only pray that you do not weary yourself;
we ourselves shall provide the offerings.
The Buddha said:
Stop, stop!
For what reason? Parents who give birth to children derive much benefit from them.
The kindness of nurturing is profound—sustaining one with milk and holding one in one's embrace.
One must repay this debt of gratitude; it cannot but be repaid.
She is the mother of all Buddhas of the past and the future.
Having first attained parinirvāṇa,
all Buddhas personally make offerings to and cremate their own śarīras.
At that time, the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa dispatched various spirits and deities to the Candana forest to gather candana wood for the funeral pyre.
Upon reaching the midst of the wilderness,
the Buddha personally carried one leg of the couch,
while Ānanda carried the other leg.
Flying through the void,
he went to the cemetery.
At that time, the Buddha personally took sandalwood and placed it upon the body of Mahāprajāpatī.
The Buddha said:
"There are four kinds of persons for whom a stupa should be erected and venerated.
The first is the Buddha."
Second, pratyekabuddhas;
third, arhats whose outflows are exhausted;
fourth, wheel-turning sage kings.
Because they all transformed sentient beings through the ten wholesome actions,
the people of that time immediately took up the relics and each erected a stupa to make offerings to them.
According to the *Saṃyukta Āgama*,
the maternal aunt Mahāprajāpatī was the biological mother of Nanda.
Furthermore, the *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
"From among the four assemblies of disciples, taking those from the beginning and the end,
eight individuals are briefly listed."
Among the bhikṣus, the first to attain the Way was like the bhikṣu Kauṇḍinya;
he was skilled at exhorting and transforming others,
and never lost his dignified deportment.
The last to attain the Way was Subhadra,
who entered parinirvāṇa on the very day he attained the Way.
Among the bhikṣuṇīs, the first to attain the Way was Mahāprajāpatī.
The last to attain the Way was like the nun from the country of Dhānakataka;
the first among the upāsakas to attain the Way was like the male merchant,
and the last to attain the Way was like Kūṭadanta.
Among the upāsikās, the first to attain the Way was like the daughter of Nanda;
the last to attain the Way was like the upāsikā Lambā.
Section Four: On Rebirth. Regarding rebirth, it is maintained that the eight consciousnesses sustain [the new existence].
Upon death, the four great elements disperse;
a hundred years pass swiftly, ultimately returning to extinction.
One circulates through the three realms, turning without ceasing.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"That which has a beginning must have an end;
that which has been born must perish."
The holy teachings are not in vain; one beholds them face-to-face for oneself.
Therefore, within these conditions, I shall briefly describe six gates.
In the first gate, regarding the time of approaching death:
Examine one's own body for coldness or heat;
verify its goodness or evil;
and fully know the retribution that follows.
Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"This sentient being is neither form nor mind."
If one were to provisionally designate a "living being," both large and small alike would share the same death, whether gradual or sudden;
so it has been handed down among the various masters.
For one who has performed wholesome deeds, the cold sensations from the lower body reach as far as the navel;
once the warmth is finally exhausted,
they are immediately reborn among human beings.
If the heat in one's head and face is completely exhausted,
one will be reborn in the heavenly realms;
for those who commit evil deeds, it is the opposite.
If the heat from the upper body down to the waist is exhausted,
one is born in the realm of hungry ghosts (preta).
If the heat from the waist down to the knees is exhausted, [one is born in the animal realm].

Those [whose marks] from below the knees down to the ends of the feet are deficient will be born among animals; those [whose marks] from the knees down to the ends of the feet are deficient will be born in the hells.
When a person beyond training enters nirvana,
it occurs either at the "warmth" of the heart or at the "crown" of the head.
However, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"The meaning of *kalala* refers to the very first place of conception,
which is called the 'flesh-heart' (*māṃsa-hṛdaya*)."
"In this manner, consciousness first takes rebirth in this place,
and from this very place it finally abandons it.
The commentary explains:
According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, because the cultivation of goodness arises from below,
one gradually relinquishes [the stages] starting from the lower levels down to the flesh and heart;
only thereafter is the higher relinquishment (*ūrdhva-vairāgya*) explained.
Because one is born into the lower realms due to having committed evil deeds, one first relinquishes [the faculties] from the upper parts down to the flesh and heart,
and only thereafter are they relinquished from the lower parts.
As the Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya states:
When a person is dying,
in which part of the body does the mental consciousness cease?
If the body dies all at once, the sense faculties and the mental consciousness perish simultaneously.
If a person dies gradually, the verse here says:
In gradual death, [the faculties] cease at the feet; consciousness is severed at the heart.
In the *Śāstra on Non-arising among Humans and Gods*, it is explained:
"If there are persons who are certain to go to the evil destinies for rebirth, as well as those in the human realm—
such persons [are included]."
In sequence, regarding the arhat:
this person has severed the mind, mentation, and consciousness.
Other schools state that it occurs at the crown of the head.
Why is this? Because the body-faculty ceases together with the mental consciousness in these locations when a person is actually dying.
This body-sense faculty is like a heated stone in water, gradually shrinking and diminishing,
ceasing sequentially starting from the feet and other parts.
The commentary states:
Since the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* expounds the tenets of the Hīnayāna,
it says that the body perishes together with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) in these locations.
According to the Mahāyāna,
the body-faculty perishes at these locations together with the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).
Second, as for the method of taking rebirth:
According to the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*:
"In order to travel to the place where the path is to arise... [and so forth].
When beings arise in this intermediate state (antarābhava),
by means of the visual faculty produced through the power of their past karma,
even though they abide at the furthest distance, [they perceive].
One is able to see the place where one is to be born,
and therein sees the transformation of the parents; if it is to become a male, [one sees the mother].
If [the being] becomes a male, he immediately gives rise to a mind of desire for the mother;
if it becomes a female,
she immediately gives rise to a mind of desire for the father.
Inverting this mind, one gives rise to hatred.
Within this [state], there are sentient beings;
because of these two, they give rise to an inverted mind.
Seeking sexual play, it goes to the place of birth;
thus, it joyfully attains its own belonging.
At that time, the impurity has already reached the womb.
He immediately gives rise to joy and takes rebirth therein;
from that very moment, the five aggregates (*skandha*) of the sentient being become integrated and solidified.
Within this [intermediate state] there are the five aggregates;
it is only upon their cessation that one speaks of taking birth.
If the fetus is male, it rests against the mother’s left side.
It crouches facing the mother’s back;
if the fetus is female,
it rests against the mother’s right flank, facing her abdomen.
If the fetus is neither male nor female,
it takes birth according to the class of being it desires;
its dwelling therein is likewise.
There is no intermediate state (antarābhava) that is distinct from male or female, as it possesses all the sense faculties;
therefore, one is born and remains [in the womb] as either a male or a female.
Later, while growing within the womb,
one may become a eunuch;
this occurs if one takes rebirth via either the womb or the egg.
The principle is thus:
if sentient beings who wish to undergo moisture-birth go to their place of birth out of a desire for fragrance,
that fragrance may be pure.
Or it may be impure,
depending on past karma;
if one is born by transformation, one goes to the place of birth because of a longing for that location.
If that is so, how is it that hell-beings are born in a place of pleasure?
It is due to the perversion of their minds.
These sentient beings, seeing their bodies tormented by the touch of cold winds and chilly rain,
perceive the fierce and blazing fires of hell as desirable;
desiring the sensation of warmth, they go and enter therein.
Furthermore, they see their own bodies being scorched by hot winds, light, flames, and the like,
such that the suffering is unbearable;
seeing that the cold hells are cool, pleasant, and characterized by a cold touch, they go there to enter them.
The two modes of birth—womb-born and egg-born—give rise to craving through the transformation of the parents' physical elements.

The two modes of moisture-born and transformation-born do not undergo this transformation, as they do not depend upon the union of the male and female reproductive fluids (śukra-śoṇita) to form a body.
Moisture-born beings merely crave and cling to fragrances.
Upon reaching the place of rebirth,
according to the goodness or evil of one's karma,
the fragrances one perceives will naturally be either pure or foul.
Beings born by transformation desire only their place of support.
Although hell is a place of suffering,
sinners still find pleasure there and thus regard it as a desirable place.
One takes birth therein.
Why is this? Because one does not take birth through what is not desired.
The treatise says:
Just as in the past one performed actions capable of inducing such a birth,
so too is the body of one who delights in seeing [it] at this stage.
Seeing those sentient beings in the same way,
one therefore goes to them;
this is what the former masters have said.
If sentient beings, at the age of thirty,
engage in the karma of killing by netting and capturing living creatures,
they will certainly have companions when performing such deeds.
This karma can induce rebirth in hell.

Subsequently, within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), one perceives oneself as being in the same position as when one was thirty years old and engaged in net-fishing; hence the term "position" (*avasthā*).
Furthermore, one sees former companions who have not departed from their past ways;
when seeing the hells,
it is as if one previously saw various companions by the rivers and lakes being led together into them.
Due to this arising transformation, one is reborn therein; subsequently, although many past karmas have been created,
it is necessarily by a single karma that birth in hell is drawn forth—
perhaps having performed this karma at the age of twenty.
Alternatively, having performed this karma during the thirty periods [of time],
one later perceives oneself within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) as being young or old,
just as one was at the time of performing that karma.
He beholds the sentient beings in the hells as being exactly like himself in age;
since their ages are thus identical, [he experiences their suffering].
A transformation arises toward these sentient beings;
one immediately goes to them,
and by virtue of this craving, one undergoes rebirth.
The Sautrāntika masters provide this interpretation.
Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"If one dwells in meager merit..."
When one is born into a lowly family,
at the time of death and at the time of entering the womb,
one hears various kinds of chaotic sounds.
Furthermore, due to their own false views, they enter into thickets of bamboo, reeds,
and rushes; yet those with great merit shall be born into noble families.
At that time, he himself hears peaceful, exquisite, and pleasing sounds,
and he falsely perceives the appearance of pleasing signs such as ascending to celestial palaces.
Furthermore, the Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya states:
"If a person, at the time of death, gives rise to a mind of wrong view,
that person will fall into hell because of the unwholesome deeds previously committed as the cause and the wrong view as the condition."
A certain master of the Abhidharma says:
"All unwholesome states are causes for rebirth in hell;
the remnants of this unwholesomeness lead to birth among animals and hungry ghosts."
Furthermore, due to the intensity of their karmic actions, they fall among the animals.
For example, because of the intensity of lustful desire, one is born among pigeons, sparrows, or mandarin ducks;
because of the intensity of anger and hatred, one is born among vipers, snakes, scorpions, and centipedes.
Because of the abundance of delusion, one is born among pigs, sheep, clams, and oysters.
Because of the abundance of arrogance, one is born among lions, tigers, and wolves.
Because of the abundance of restlessness and frivolity, one is born among monkeys.
Because stinginess and envy were rampant, one is born among hungry dogs; however,
if there is some merit remaining from the virtue of giving even a small portion,
one may experience slight happiness therein despite being born as an animal.
Although the two karmas of body and speech are governed by the mind as their primary cause,
the karma of speech often results in greater retribution.
For example, one who insults others with frivolity and instability is reborn among monkeys, just like a monkey.
If one says that their greed is like that of a crow,
their speech is like the barking of a dog,
and their stupidity is like that of a pig or a sheep.
His voice was like the braying of a donkey;
his gait was like that of a camel;
he was as self-important as an elephant.
Evil is like a runaway ox;
lust is like a small bird;
cowardice is like a cat or a wildcat.
Deceit is like a wild fox;
such various evils bring retribution according to the mouth through which they were uttered.
Yet, these all have the three poisons as their root.
Among the three poisons, craving is the most weighty;
it is like grasping one end of a cloth, whereupon the rest follows entirely.
Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says:
If craving is not severed, craving moistens birth;
therefore, all four modes of birth arise from craving.
As it is said: "Those with excessive desire are born among birds and insects."
Because of excessive craving for flavors,
one is reborn in a latrine;
furthermore, because of lustful desire, one is born from an egg.
Because of craving for odors and flavors, one undergoes moisture-birth;
because of following what one loves,
one performs earnest karma and thus undergoes transformation-birth.
If one with a sincere mind delights in committing sinful karma,
at the time of death one will falsely perceive hell and undergo transformation-birth there.
If one with sincere affection for merit undergoes transformation-birth in the higher realms.
Therefore, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states:
"Just as a tree will continue to grow if its roots are not pulled out,
so too the tree of suffering remains as long as the root of craving is not uprooted."
Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"Why is it that self-love (*ātmasneha*) arises immediately after [birth]? Because one has been attached to and delighted in conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) since beginningless time."
Because it has been permeated by causes;
because it has been permeated by the causes of pure and impure karma,
that which serves as its substratum.
By means of two kinds of causes,
through their predominant influence,
[it arises] from the seed.
At that very spot, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) arises immediately following the maturation (*vipāka*);
at the time of death, it is like the simultaneous rising and falling of the two ends of a scale.
Furthermore, this intermediate state necessarily possesses all the sense faculties (*indriya*), and for those who have committed evil deeds:
The intermediate state (antarābhava) that is attained has a radiance like that of a black woolen cloth;
however, for one who performs wholesome deeds during a dark night,
it has a radiance like that of white cloth.
Or on a clear night.
The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states:
"In this intermediate state (*antarābhava*), one is endowed with the five sense faculties."
It cannot be obstructed by anything such as vajras.
Beneath Mount Sumeru, within a vajra, there is a frog;
[the being] takes birth therein.
Within it there is a subtle material vajra that cannot obstruct it;
this is perceived by those who possess the divine eye.
Being able to see this matter,
he again cites what he has heard as evidence:
"I have previously heard people say..."
He heats iron until it is red-hot,
breaks it open, and sees insects within.
Third, regarding the length of their lifespan:
The Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya states:
"If one is not destined for birth in a particular place,
one may take birth in any other place within this realm."
For example, cows have a preponderance of sexual desire during the summer;
dogs during the autumn;
and bears during the winter.
Horses mate during the springtime,
whereas jackals and the like engage in sexual activity at any time;
at such a time, this sentient being ought to be reborn among cattle.
If it is not the summer season, one will be born among jackals;
if one was destined to be born among dogs but it is not the proper time, then one will be born among jackals.
Furthermore, there are four different explanations among the Abhidharmakośa masters of the Hīnayāna school.
First, some say that after death at the shortest possible moment, one immediately undergoes rebirth into the aggregates (*skandha*).
Second, some say that one remains for seven days.
Once the seven days have passed,
the duration of the intermediate state (antarābhava) is not limited by time;
it may remain for up to forty-nine days until the conditions for birth are fulfilled.
After death, one undergoes rebirth;
this is also not restricted by time or season.
The fourth [point] explains that rebirth occurs according to the conditions for birth.
It may even remain for an entire kalpa without passing away.
Regarding the fifth point, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"If the conditions for rebirth have not yet been met, it remains for up to seven days."
Having died, they are born again;
this continues through seven periods of seven days of death and rebirth.
After this, they will certainly obtain the conditions for birth.
This differs from all four of the preceding [types].
Regarding the fourth, the speed of the supernormal power (*ṛddhi*),
the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states:
This intermediate state being travels through space;
like a person who, upon casting off life, ought to be reborn in a world beyond the immeasurable,
they arrive there in an instant.
The supernatural powers of the followers of the Two Vehicles do not extend beyond a single world-system,
whereas the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) has already reached outside of immeasurable world-systems;
even by the Buddha’s supernormal power, one cannot prevent it from proceeding to rebirth or causing it to remain in another realm.
Because the power of karma is determinate,
regarding the superiority of karmic supernormal powers,
this is based on the superior supernormal powers of ordinary beings of the Single Vehicle.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"As for the excellence of the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), it refers to the swiftness of the Buddha’s supernormal powers (*abhijñā*)."
Fifth, regarding the differences in mutual visibility:
according to the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*,
it is said that those within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) who are born into the same realm of existence will certainly see one another.
If a person possesses the most purified divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), which is a category of wisdom (*prajñā*),
that person can also see their rebirth; however,
if it is a divine eye obtained as a karmic retribution (*vipākaja*), one cannot see it.
Because it is most subtle.
The Sarvāstivādins say:
"If one is to be reborn among the human realm," [the intermediate state] is like that.
It is a fixed principle that those within the intermediate state (antarābhava) of the human realm can see one another.
One cannot see the intermediate state (antarābhava) of other paths.
If a person cultivates and attains the divine eye (divyacakṣus),
this divine eye belongs to the category of that path.
One is able to see the form of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
However, one who possesses the divine eye obtained as karmic retribution (*vipākaja*) cannot see the form of the intermediate state,
because the form of the intermediate state is subtler than other forms.
According to the Saṃmitīya school,
an intermediate state being (*antarābhava*) in the heavenly realm can perceive the forms of intermediate state beings in all five realms;
one in the human realm can perceive those of four realms.
Excluding those in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the heavenly realms, [beings] are unable to see them;
in this manner, each preceding category is excluded in successive order.
This extends even to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the hell realm; however,

Upon reaching the third gate,

At that time, he was still not dead;
he then saw [the man] lighting a fire before the cauldron of boiling water.
Having finished his observation, he returned to the presence of the king.
He saw Zhang Cheng, a fellow villager,
who was also not yet dead.
A certain person accused Cheng, saying that he had destroyed someone's house.
The king dispatched an envoy to investigate it,
who reported back,
"It is indeed so."
Sengcheng said,

the plow broke through his tomb."
"It is not for this reason.
The King said,

He then ordered someone to strike him seven times on the waist with a staff.

release him so that he may return early.

The old mother soon fell ill and died shortly thereafter.
