98. Chapter on the Extinction of the Dharma (98). This chapter consists of nine sections:

Section on Stating the Intent, Section on the Five Turbidities, Section on Time and Season, Section on Ordaining Women, Section on the Buddha’s Alms Bowl, Section on Depravation and Substitution, Section on Breaking the Precepts, Section on Litigious Disputes, and Section on the Wasting of the Dharma. 1. Section on Stating the Intent. First, I humbly reflect:
As the True and Semblance Dharma ages and the teachings flow into their final period,
people become either heterodox or orthodox, and the Dharma becomes corrupted or replaced.
Some rely upon the authentic to construct the false.
Some embellish the false to confound the true;
their borrowed compositions are shallow and disordered in meaning.
Like jade and stone, or crimson and purple, they leave no form unexposed.
Furthermore, as the world gradually became turbid and frivolous and the hearts of people underwent transformation,
delusive thoughts came to dwell within their breasts, and they devoted themselves exclusively to karmic calamities.
The three poisons increased, and they increasingly invited the four evil destinies.
Thus, throughout the vast night of ignorance,
they have no thought of dawn; they take delight in and long for the six sense objects.
Unaware that five swords were following behind him,
fame and profit having already encroached upon him, his sense of self and others grew ever more intense,
leading to the emergence of a faction of malevolent followers.
When light and frivolous, heterodox winds prevail,
those of pure and upright character will from time to time suffer the slanders of the treacherous and sycophantic.
Thus, although the teaching has flowed through Zhendan for over six hundred years,
it has been subjected to three instances of suppression by wicked kings who ruled with tyranny;
yet disaster did not linger, and in every case, the former sages were ultimately vindicated.
Having incurred calamity and punishment, he becomes a laughingstock to the world.
Alas! His future karma is truly a matter for deep lamentation;
it arises precisely because he is entangled by his meager learning, leading him to follow his own mind and make solitary decisions.
The Dharma gradually became hidden and calamities gathered upon his person; yet,
had he originally consulted the diagrams of the Eight Treasuries (*aṣṭapiṭaka*),
he would have synthesized the texts and meanings to achieve clear illumination.
If one investigates the nine consciousnesses and attains a thorough understanding of the delusion and liberation of emotion and wisdom,
then the five obscurations will reach the time of their removal and the end of darkness.
The Three Clarities (trividyā) possess a radiance that surpasses the sun. 2.
The Section on the Five Corruptions (pañcakaṣāya). Second, as stated in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra*:
"That which is called the five corruptions is as follows:"
First is the turbidity of lifespan;
second is the turbidity of sentient beings;
third is the turbidity of afflictions.
The fourth is the defilement of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*).

The fifth is the defilement of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*); this refers to the present age where the maximum lifespan of humans is one hundred years, which is called the defilement of life (*āyuḥ-kaṣāya*).
If sentient beings do not recognize their parents,
nor recognize śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas,
nor their own kinsmen and elders.
They do not cultivate the principles of meaning,
they do not perform what ought to be done,
and they do not fear the retribution for evil karma in this life or future lives.
They do not cultivate the giving of wisdom,
they do not perform meritorious deeds,
and they do not practice the dharma of the fast.
Not upholding the prohibitive precepts—
this is called the defilement of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*).

If these sentient beings increase in unrighteous greed, the giving of swords and blades, the giving of weapons, litigation, strife, discord, flattery, deceit, false speech, and the embracing of false dharmas.
And when other evil and unwholesome dharmas arise,
this is called the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*). If, in this present life, the Dharma is corrupted and the Dharma perishes, [this is called the turbidity of views].
When the Semblance Dharma gradually arises and false dharmas increasingly emerge,
this is called the turbidity of views. Furthermore, when the kalpa of famine arises, [this is also called the turbidity of views].
The arising of the kalpa of diseases and the arising of the kalpa of weapons—
this is called the turbidity of the kalpa (kalpakaṣāya).
Furthermore, the Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya states:
"What are the five corruptions?
First, the corruption of lifespan."
Second, the turbidity of the eon;
third, the turbidity of afflictions;
fourth, the turbidity of views.
Fifth is the defilement of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*). In the future, during the final eon,
the five defilements such as lifespan will become most coarse and most base, having already turned into dregs.
These are called the corruptions (*kaṣāya*).
By means of the first two corruptions, life span and the requisites for happiness are successively diminished;
furthermore, by means of the [remaining] two corruptions, that which assists virtue is diminished.
Why is this? Because of these two defilements,
there are sentient beings who mostly practice the pursuit of sensual objects and the practice of self-mortification.
They are able to impair both householders and renunciants who assist in the cultivation of virtue;
by means of the latter turbidity, they diminish one’s physical stature, complexion, health, strength,
wisdom, mindfulness, right effort, and stability.
Because these virtues have degenerated.
Furthermore, the *Dharanidhara-bodhisattva-sutra* states:
"The Tathāgata has now arisen in an age of the five turbidities."
What are the five turbidities?
First, many people are full of depravity and evil, failing to recognize the principles of righteousness.
Second, the sixty-two types of doubt and false views are so powerful that they do not accept the teachings of the Way.
Third, many people are dominated by desire and worldly afflictions, not knowing how to proceed or retreat.
Fourth, the lifespan is short;
this was the case in ages of antiquity.
Eighty-four thousand years is considered a great loss;
now, with a lifespan of a hundred years, whether longer or shorter,
as the five minor kalpas come to an end, the three calamities shall arise, and there will be none who do not suffer harm.
If there are those who, in this world of five turbidities and evil, are able to believe in and delight in the Buddha’s correct and true wisdom,
this is extremely difficult.
Furthermore, according to the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*:
These five corruptions merely serve to manifest,
in their order of increasing intensity,
the five signs of decay. What are these five signs of decay?
First, the decline of lifespan,
because the duration of time is extremely short;
second, the decline of material requisites.
Because it lacks luster,
the three categories of wholesome qualities decline;
because one takes pleasure in unwholesome conduct.
Fourth is the decline of tranquility,
because mutual opposition leads to clamor and contention.
Fifth is the decline of the essential nature.
Because they are not vessels for supramundane merit,
and because one wishes to sequentially reveal these five types of decline as distinct from one another,
the five turbidities (pañca-kaṣāya) are differentiated.
Furthermore, the *Satyaka-nirgrantha-sūtra* states:
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī, "All Buddhas,
Tathāgatas, possess twelve kinds of supreme and wondrous merits."
Just as clarified butter (*sarpis*) is the most excellent among all flavors,
being the foremost in purity and capable of purifying all buddha-fields,
it is therein that the Tathāgata attains unexcelled, perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
What are the twelve?
First, manifesting the defilement of the eon;
second, manifesting the defilement of the time.
Third, he manifests the defilement of sentient beings;
fourth, he manifests the defilement of afflictions;
fifth, he manifests the defilement of lifespan.
Sixth, the turbidity of manifesting the distinctions between the three vehicles;
seventh, the turbidity of manifesting impure buddha-fields;
eighth, the turbidity of manifesting sentient beings who are difficult to transform.
Ninth, manifesting the turbidity of various afflictions;
tenth, manifesting the turbidity of the confusion caused by non-Buddhists;
eleventh, manifesting the turbidity of Māra.
Twelfth is the manifestation of the turbidity of demonic activities. Good son,
all Buddha-lands of all Buddhas are fully adorned with supramundane merits and are utterly pure.
There are no impurities with such faults;
all these are the power of the skillful means of the Buddhas for the benefit of sentient beings.
"You all should know. Furthermore, the *Sūtra on the Five Great Turbidities* states:
'After the Buddha's parinirvāṇa, there shall be five disturbances.'"
First, there will be bhikṣus in the future who learn the Dharma from laypeople;
this is the first disorder of the world.
Second, laypeople will sit in the seats of honor while bhikṣus occupy lower positions.
There are two corruptions in the world.
The third is when bhikṣus preach the Dharma but do not practice it themselves,
while laypeople preach the Dharma and regard it as supreme.
Regarding the three disturbances of the world,
the fourth is that bhikṣus from the family of Māra arise in the present and regard [their own views] as the true Path and Truth within the world.
The authentic scriptures of the Buddha-dharma are themselves not understood;
they are falsely treated as authoritative.
This constitutes one of the four corruptions of the world.
Fifth, there will be bhikṣus in the future who maintain wives, children, slaves, and servants, and engage in worldly livelihoods;
they will only quarrel and litigate, failing to uphold the Buddha’s teachings.
These are the five corruptions of the world.
Nowadays, one frequently encounters ignorant laypeople who are unskilled in all matters yet falsely claim to understand the Dharma.
To not abandon sexual indulgence while acting as a teacher and model,
using it as a guide for ignorant worldly people,
is to waste one's efforts; though one exerts oneself to the end, it will be of no benefit.
In future lives, one will still not escape hell.
Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"There was once a blind man."
Having not seen the Path himself, he falsely claimed to have seen it,
leading five hundred other blind men to fall together into a pit of excrement.
How can one who remains on dry land save those drowning?
Section Three: On Time and Seasons. As stated in the *Ānanda-saptasvapna-sūtra*: "Ānanda..."
There were seven kinds of dreams that he brought to ask the Buddha about:
first, a dream of a pond where flames blazed up to the heavens;
second, a dream of the sun and moon setting, and the stars likewise setting.
Third, he dreamed that a monk who had left the household life was instead cast into an impure pit or trench,
while a layperson in white robes climbed upon his head and emerged.
Fourth, he dreamed that a herd of pigs came to butt and gore a sandalwood grove, destroying it.
Fifth, he dreamed that Mount Sumeru was placed upon his head, yet he did not consider it heavy.
Sixth, he dreamed that a great elephant cast out a small elephant.
Seventh, he dreamed of a lion king named Huasa.
There were seven hairs upon its head; it died upon the ground.
When all the birds and beasts saw it, they were terrified.
Later, seeing the worms emerging from within its body, they then devoured it.
Having had this evil dream, he came to question the Buddha about it.
The Buddha said to Ānanda,
"As for what you have dreamed..."
"All this is for the sake of the future five turbidities and evil world;
it shall not harm you.
Why do you wear such a look of sorrow?"
Regarding the first dream, in which the flames of ponds and pools reach the heavens:
in the future, the virtuous minds of bhikṣus will diminish while malevolence and rebellion blaze forth;
they will slaughter one another in numbers beyond reckoning.
The second dream, in which the sun and moon set and the constellations also vanished,
signifies that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, all the śrāvakas will follow him into parinirvāṇa and no longer remain in the world.
The eyes of sentient beings are extinguished.
Third, the dream of a renunciant monk who has turned up in an impure pit or trench, while a layperson in white robes climbs upon his head and emerges.
In the future, bhikṣus will be ruined by poison and jealousy to the point of killing one another;
those who shave their heads will be befriended by white-robed laymen,
and upon death, they will enter hell.
The layperson who practices with diligence will die and be reborn in the heavens.
As for the fourth dream, in which a herd of pigs comes to butt and gore the sandalwood grove, destroying it:
this signifies that in the future, laypeople will enter monasteries and temples.
The fifth dream was that he slandered the Sangha, seeking out their faults; he destroyed stupas and harmed the monks.
"One who would not consider it heavy even if Mount Sumeru were placed upon his head:
after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa,
Ānanda shall serve as the master for the compilation of the sūtras for a thousand arhats."
Not forgetting a single word,
he received many awakenings,
yet he did not regard them as significant.
The sixth dream, of a great elephant abandoning a small elephant,
signifies that in the future, false views will flourish and destroy my Buddha-dharma,
such that persons of virtue will all remain hidden and not appear.
The seventh dream, of the lion dying,
signifies that one thousand four hundred and seventy years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa,
the hearts of the disciples of the four assemblies will cultivate virtue.
No evil Māras shall be able to disturb them.
As for the "Seven Aristocratic Families," this refers to events seven hundred years hence.
Furthermore, the *Māyā-sūtra* states:
Māyā asked Ānanda: "Since long ago, you have heard the World-Honored One speak;
for how long will the True Dharma of the Tathāgata remain before it is extinguished?"
Ānanda shed tears and replied, "In the past, I heard the World-Honored One speak of what will happen after the future extinction of the Dharma.

When all matters have been fully concluded,
Mahākāśyapa shall enter the meditative absorption of cessation on Mount Wolf’s Foot; I,
too, shall then attain the realization of the fruit.
They shall enter parinirvāṇa one after another in succession.
You should entrust the True Dharma to Upagupta;
Upagupta is skilled in expounding the essential points of the Dharma.
Just as Pūrṇa extensively taught the means of delivering others,
he further exhorted and converted King Aśoka.
He caused them to establish firm and correct faith in the Buddha-dharma,
and by means of the relics, he extensively erected eighty-four thousand stupas.
After another two hundred years had passed,
There was a bhikṣu named Śīlananda who was skilled in expounding the essential teachings of the Dharma;
throughout Jambudvīpa, he brought twelve hundred million people to liberation.
At three hundred years [after the parinirvāṇa], there was already a bhikṣu named Blue Lotus Flower Eye,
who skillfully expounded the essentials of the Dharma and delivered fifty million people.
At four hundred years [after the parinirvāṇa]...
There was the bhikṣu Ox-Mouth,
who skillfully expounded the essentials of the Dharma and delivered twenty thousand people.
Five hundred years later, there was the bhikṣu Jewel-Heaven.
He skillfully expounded the essential teachings of the Dharma, enabling twenty thousand people to attain liberation.
The eight classes of sentient beings resolved their minds upon Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At this point, the True Dharma was on the verge of extinction.
After six hundred years, ninety-six kinds of non-Buddhist practitioners (tīrthika) will arise,
vying with one another in their false views to destroy and annihilate the Buddha-dharma.
At that time, there will be a bhikṣu.
His name was Aśvaghoṣa.
He was skilled in expounding the essential points of the Dharma and subdued all the various followers of external paths.
Seven hundred years later, there was a bhikṣu named Nāgārjuna who was skilled in expounding the essential points of the Dharma.

The bhikṣus delighted in fine garments and indulged in wanton play.
Among hundreds of thousands of people, only one or two attain the fruits of the Path.
At nine hundred years of age, a male slave became a bhikṣu and a female slave became a bhikṣuṇī.
After one thousand years had passed,
the bhikṣus, having heard the teachings on the contemplation of impurity and mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna),
were overcome by anger and aversion.
Immeasurable bhikṣus—
whether one or two—
contemplated right concentration.
When one thousand one hundred years have passed,
the bhikṣus will act as matchmakers for marriage, just like worldly people.
After twelve hundred years, those bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs who had slandered the Vinaya within the great assembly—
He engages in unchaste conduct.
If he has offspring, his son becomes a bhikṣu.
After the woman had been a bhikṣuṇī for one thousand three hundred years,

then the Naga King Anavatapta will carry them all into the ocean,

Section Four on the Ordination of Women. As stated in the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā-śāstra*:
"Women of middle capacity were ordained."
The True Dharma would have remained for only five hundred years;
however, because the World-Honored One established the eight weighty rules for the bhikṣuṇīs,
the True Dharma was restored to last for a thousand years.
Question: When one thousand years have passed, will the True Dharma be completely extinguished?
Answer: It will not be completely extinguished.
Within those one thousand years, the three types of supernormal knowledge (trividyā) will still be attained.
Furthermore, for a thousand years, they attained the state of an Arhat with the exhaustion of craving, yet lacked the three types of supernormal knowledge (trividyā).
For another thousand years, they attained the state of an Anāgāmin.
For another thousand years, they attained the state of a Sakṛdāgāmin.
Furthermore, during another thousand years, they attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
In total, this amounted to ten thousand years;
during the first five thousand years, they attained the Way.
After five thousand years, people will study but not attain the Way.
Ten thousand years later, all sutras, scriptures, and written characters will have vanished;
there will remain only the appearance of shaven heads and the dharma-robes of the kaṣāya.
Furthermore, the *Vinayamātṛkā-sūtra* states:
"The Venerable Kāśyapa reproached Ānanda for seeking ordination for women to leave the household life."
There were ten matters for which Ānanda was censured.
First: had women not gone forth [into homelessness], the various donors would have constantly each filled a vessel with food and, kneeling by the side of the road, offered it to the śramaṇas.
Second, if women had not gone forth,
donors would have constantly provided robes and bedding,
seeking out the requisites for śramaṇas along the road.
Third, if women had not left the household life,
donors and others would constantly mount elephants, horses, and carriages by the side of the road,
prostrating themselves with their five limbs touching the ground to request that śramaṇas step over them as they pass.
Fourth, if women had not gone forth [into homelessness],
donors would constantly have to spread their hair upon the road and request that śramaṇas step over it as they pass.
Fifth, if women had not gone forth,
donors would always have respectfully invited śramaṇas to their homes to provide offerings.
Sixth, if women had not gone forth...
When various donors see the śramaṇas,
they should always maintain a respectful mind, sweep the ground clean, and lay their upper garments upon the floor to serve as seats for the śramaṇas to sit upon.
Seventh, if women had not gone forth [into homelessness],...
The various donors should always remove their upper garments and wipe the dust from the feet of the bhikṣus.
Eighth, if women had not gone forth [into homelessness],
the various donors would always have loosened their hair and wiped the dust from the feet of the bhikṣus.
Ninth, if women had not gone forth [into homelessness],
the majestic power of the śramaṇas would have surpassed that of the sun and moon;
how much less could any non-Buddhists have even looked directly at the heads of the śramaṇas?
Tenth, had women not gone forth from the household life,
the Buddha’s True Dharma would have remained for a thousand years;
now it has been reduced by five hundred years.
In one hundred years, he attains firm liberation;
in one hundred years, he attains firm concentration;
in one hundred years, he attains firm ethical discipline.
In the first hundred years, one attains firmness in extensive learning;
in the second hundred years, one attains firmness in giving;
in the first century, there is the dharma of firmness in liberation.

while practicing the Path, [attains this].
Delighting in meditative concentration and reducing sensual desire,
he is like a merchant who loathes impure water.
It is also like an infant who, while playing foolishly with impurities,
gradually grows older and abandons his former playthings to take pleasure in other matters;
upon reaching old age, he abandons all those former ways entirely.
One finds delight in the Dharma for oneself;
having attained the path of non-returning, it is likewise so.
One sees that which is enjoyed by all beings within the five realms of birth and death.
Like a child at play,
he redoubled his diligence,
desiring to escape from the cycle of beginning and end.
They take no pleasure in seeking birth.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Just as a small child Plays with filth upon the ground."
As the years passed and he grew to maturity, he abandoned play and took delight in other practices;
likewise, seeking protection, he strove to cross the three realms and,
through diligent effort, fully accomplished the four paths.
Fourth, when the Arhat of No-More-Learning practices the path,
because they are still in the stage of learning, they find no delight; from beginning to end, they have absolutely nothing to delight in.
He does not crave the three realms;
he severs all fetters,
and the three poisons are forever extinguished.

The faculties of mindfulness, concentration, wisdom, energy, and diligence, as well as the factors of enlightenment—seeing cessation as tranquility—is like a king releasing a rutting elephant with sharp tusks; those who encounter it all die.
It is also like a venomous dragon that constantly exhales poisonous gas; those who meet it all perish.
It is also like the venomous viper that constantly harbors poisonous rage and harms all who touch it;
the afflictions of the three poisons are likewise:
whenever they arise and come into contact with one, they cause harm and cause one to fall into the three realms.
Only the ten powers, the factors of enlightenment,
and liberation cannot be severed;
thus one practices with self-reflective mindfulness.
Just as now, he has already become an Arhat,
having attained freedom from attachment.
All outflows are forever exhausted;
the pure holy life has been cultivated;
what was to be done has been accomplished.
Having cast off the heavy burden,
he has attained his own welfare;
birth and death have been severed.
Attaining impartial wisdom and accomplishing the state of no-more-learning,
they cross over from this shore to that.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"The king has released a drunken elephant, Its fierce tusks are exceedingly sharp;
Dragons and snakes harbor venom— Whoever encounters them shall surely die."
They transform all beings, causing them to be tamed; they regain mastery over their minds, and all afflictions are exhausted without remainder.
Dwelling in the stage of training, they practice without fear within the three realms;
remaining unshakable, they realize the Noble Path.
Having already attained one's own benefit, One crosses over suffering and constantly gains peace.
Having severed the five categories [of desire], One fully accomplishes the six supernormal powers.
Having eliminated all defilements, It is like water washing dirt from a garment.
This is called being a true person (satpuruṣa), who follows the sublime and stainless teaching of the Buddha;
therefore, it is called the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣabhūmi).
Section Four: The Four Kinds of Nutriment. As stated in the Ekottarika Āgama:
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are four kinds of sustenance for sentient beings that nourish and sustain them. What are these four?"
That which is called edible food—
whether gross or subtle—
as well as the food of contact, the food of volition, and the food of consciousness.
These are called the four nutriments. What is edible food?
It refers to whatever is eaten by people today that enters the mouth and can be chewed and swallowed.
This is called edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*).
What is the nutriment of contact (*sparśāhāra*)?
It refers to clothing, parasols, canopies, various fragrant flowers, incense, and lamps.
Furthermore, when one gathers with women using fragrant oils and other such things that provide physical pleasure,
this is called the nutriment of contact.
What is mindfulness of food?
It refers to that which is recollected, conceived, and contemplated within the mind,
or expressed by way of speech.
Whether by means of physical contact or through the various dharmas that are maintained,
this is called mindfulness of food.
What is the nutriment of consciousness?
It refers to that which is known by the mind,
beginning with the Brahmā world.
Up to and including the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception,
beings take consciousness as their nutriment;
this is called the nutriment of consciousness.
By means of these four nutriments, one transmigrates through birth and death.
Furthermore, the *Ekottarika Āgama* states that the World-Honored One addressed Aniruddha as follows:
All phenomena subsist by means of nutriment.
The eye has sleep as its nutriment;
the ear has sound as its nutriment.
The nose has fragrance as its nutriment;
the tongue has flavor as its nutriment;
the body has tactile smoothness as its nutriment.
The mind has dharmas as its nutriment;
nirvana has heedfulness as its nutriment.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
Regarding this sublime Dharma, there are nine matters concerning the contemplation of food.
Among humans, there are four kinds of nutriment:
first, edible food consisting of mouthfuls.
Second, the nutriment of contact;
third, the nutriment of volition;
fourth, the nutriment of consciousness.
Furthermore, there are five kinds of supramundane food.
The first is the food of dhyāna.
Second, the food of aspiration;
third, the food of mindfulness;
fourth, the food of the eight liberations.
The five kinds of joyful food are the manifestation of the supramundane.
We should together focus our minds on abandoning these four kinds of food.
Seeking to provide the sustenance for transcending the world.
Furthermore, the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states:
"If there are sentient beings..."
With a mind of faith and compassion, one gives various kinds of food to others;
at the end of life, one is reborn in the Cāturmahārājika Heaven to experience various pleasures,
and at the end of that life, one obtains a human body.
They shall possess great wealth and abundance,
and always practice the True Dharma.
Furthermore, the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states:
If there are sentient beings who, upon seeing those who are ill,
provide them with medicinal decoctions to free them from the suffering of disease, they will,
at the end of their lives, be reborn in the heavens of the desire realm to enjoy the pleasures of the five senses.
If, after their life span ordained by heaven has ended, they obtain a human body,
they will be very wealthy and possess great riches. Yet,
should they see a sick person at the point of death suffering from thirst, [they will feel compassion].
If one gives honey syrup or ice water as an offering, that person,
at the end of life, will be reborn in the Heaven of Coolness and experience celestial bliss.
From the end of their celestial lifespan, they obtain human bodies and are always free from hunger and thirst.
Furthermore, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"If one is the person on monthly duty supervising the food..."

If one wishes to know whether food is raw or cooked, salty or sour, it may be held in the palm of the hand and tasted with the tongue; however, according to the *Ji faji jing* (Sutra on the Rules of Equanimity), tasting with the mouth is not permitted, as doing so constitutes an offense due to a lack of sincere intent and being motivated by greed.
5. Section on Purifying the Mouth. Section Five on Purifying the Mouth. As stated in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*:
"What is meant by rinsing the mouth?
The Buddha said:
Place water in the mouth and rotate it three times;
this is called the method for purifying the mouth.
Furthermore, the Mahāsāṃghika Vinaya states:
At that time, the World-Honored One was preaching the Dharma to a great assembly.
There was a bhikṣu whose mouth emitted a foul odor.
He remained downwind.
The Buddha, knowing this, asked him intentionally:
"For what reason is this bhikṣu sitting alone?"
He replied,
"World-Honored One,
you have established a precept that does not permit the chewing of wooden sticks."
For this reason, fearing that one's foul breath might offend others,
one remains downwind.
The Buddha said,
"I permit the use of tooth-sticks;
they may be at most sixteen finger-widths in length."
It must be at least four finger-widths in length.
When chewing it, one should do so in a secluded place after first washing the hands thoroughly.
Once finished chewing, rinse it with water and discard it.
While chewing, one must not swallow it. However,
if a physician says that swallowing it will cure the illness,
then swallowing is permitted.
If one has no teeth,
one should use ash, earth, brick-dust, gravel, stones, grass, or wood to rinse the mouth. After eating,
or when wishing to offer water over food, one should use pure water.
First wash the vessel for water, and then pour the water.
If your hands are soiled,
you should receive the water using leaves.
When drinking from the mouth,
one must not submerge the lips so that the vessel touches the forehead; rather,
one should drink while supporting the vessel against the lips.
When drinking, one must not drink it all up;
one should leave a small amount behind to rinse the mouth, and then discard it from the opening of the mouth.
The person distributing the water should carefully protect the clean vessel.
If one sees [a corpse] with its lips sunken and adhering to the forehead,
it should be placed in a single spot and marked with a grass banner so that people may know it is impure.
If one consumes non-timely liquids,
it is also according to the aforementioned rule.
Furthermore, the Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya states:
A bhikṣu should wash his hands clean upon rising at dawn.
He must not wash roughly with only the five fingers,
nor should he stop washing until they reach his armpits.
One should wash from the wrist downward until it is clean.
One must not wash roughly or scrub until blood appears.
One should wash the hands using the powder of *kūrcika* grass, or ash, soil, bathing powder, or soapberry.
If one rubs [the hands] so that they make a sound,
or if, after having washed the hands clean, one rubs them against each other again,
it is called impure.
One should wash one's hands again.
Before eating, a bhikṣu should protect his hands;
if he touches his head or grasps his robes, [he must wash them].
If even a bhikṣu must wash his hands again [after such acts], let alone a layperson; the same applies to reading scriptures, receiving food, and so forth—one should follow these rules in practice.
If this is required when the hands are merely impure, how much more so when one kills living beings with one's own hands, drinking their blood and eating their flesh to defile both body and mouth?
Even if one intends to transmit the Dharma, if the mind is impure, it will not succeed.
Furthermore, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:
"At that time, the bhikṣus were troubled by the foul odor within their dwellings."
The Buddha said:
"One should sprinkle and sweep it;
if it still smells foul, one should plaster it with fragrant mud."
Furthermore, if there is a foul odor, one should hang incense at the four corners of the hall.
Moreover, the *Śāriputra Vinaya* states:
At one time, there was a bhikṣu who did not chew a tooth-stick, and his breath was foul.
He informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said,
"I allow you to chew tooth-sticks."
There are five benefits:
first, the mouth does not suffer;
second, the mouth does not become foul-smelling.
Third, it removes wind disorders;
fourth, it removes feverish illnesses;
fifth, it removes phlegm and mucus.
Furthermore, there are five benefits:
first, the elimination of wind;
second, the elimination of heat.
Third, the three tastes;
fourth, the ability to eat;
fifth, clear vision.
Furthermore, the *Caturvargika-vinaya* states:
"There are five faults in not chewing a tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*):
first, the breath becomes foul-smelling."
Second, relishing unwholesome flavors;
third, suffering from feverish biliousness and indigestion;
fourth, not taking food.
The five eyes are not clear.
Furthermore, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"Having finished chewing, one should rinse it and discard it."
They die because they fear being eaten by insects.
Furthermore, the *Three Thousand Rules of Deportment* states that there are five matters regarding the use of the *yángzhī* (willow twig).
1. When cutting, it should be done as prescribed.
2. When breaking, it should be done according to the Dharma.
3. When chewing the end, it must not exceed one-third of the length.
Fourth, there are three teeth in the middle for cleaning the teeth.
Fifth, one should use it for washing oneself with liquid.
There are five matters regarding the scraping of the tongue.
First, one must not exceed three attempts.
Second, if blood appears on the tongue, one must stop.
Third, one must not shake the hands excessively so as to soil the saṃghāṭī robe or the feet.
4. Do not discard the *yānjī* (tooth-stick) where people pass.
5. It should be placed in a secluded spot.
Section Six: On Ringing the Bell. As stated in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya-śāstra* (付法藏經):
At that time, there was a king named Kanishka who was greedy,
tyrannical, and unrighteous; he frequently went on military expeditions,
exhausting the people with corvée labor without ever knowing contentment.
To desire to rule over the four seas and station troops at the borders,
resulting in the separation from one's kinsmen—
such is the nature of suffering.
When shall we find peace?
We ought to be of one mind and together eliminate it; only then shall we be happy.
Because the king was afflicted by a violent illness,
he was subdued by being seated upon it; yet, due to the condition of having heard the bhikṣu Tīṣya preach the Dharma, his life was restored in an instant.
Born within the great ocean as a thousand-headed fish, a wheel of swords revolves and severs its heads;
as soon as they are severed, they are immediately reborn, and are cut again in succession.
Thus it continues in this manner until an immeasurable number of times.
In a mere moment, his head filled the great ocean.
At that time, there was an arhat serving as the *karmadāna* (steward) for the Saṃgha.
The king then addressed him, saying:
Now, upon hearing the sound of the *gaṇḍī*,
this wheel of swords immediately stops;
during that interval, their suffering subsides slightly.
"I only pray that the Venerable One will show compassion and pity.
If the wooden gong is struck so that its resonance endures for a long time,
the Arhat, out of compassion, shall strike it for a prolonged duration."
After seven days have passed, their suffering shall end;
furthermore, this monastery shall exist because of that king.
It has been transmitted in succession,
with the *gandi* being struck for a long duration,
continuing down to the present day.
It remains just as it was originally.
The commentary states:
"Since the meaning of the sūtra has been understood."
To strike the bell and alleviate suffering,
while also assembling the community,
one must have a *karmadāna* (Vina).
Just as one is about to strike the bell,
one should compose one’s countenance, join the palms,
and give rise to the aspiration to benefit all living beings.
Because they focused their thoughts on the wholesome,
their suffering was brought to an end.
Furthermore, the *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
When the bell is struck,
may all the sufferings of the various evil realms cease entirely.
Upon hearing the sound of the bell, one should further recite verses of praise.
One shall be cleared of the heavy sins of birth and death accumulated over five hundred billion kalpas.
Having subdued the power of Māra’s enemies and eliminated all fetters without remainder, one strikes the *gandī* on the open ground; when the bhikṣus hear it, they shall assemble.
All those who wish to hear the Dharma and cross the ocean of birth and death,
upon hearing this wondrous sound, shall all come together here.
(As stated in a verse from another sutra:)
Hearing the bell, one who lies down and does not rise provokes the wrath of the guardian deities of the stupa.
Due to the meagerness of present causes and fruits, the retribution received is that of a snake's body;
wherever one may be, upon hearing the sound of the bell, those who lie down must surely rise.
With palms joined and a virtuous mind, all the noble ones rejoice;
The great bell resounds, awakening all living beings, Its sound pervading the immeasurable lands of the ten directions.
All conscious beings hear and know it universally, As it uproots the suffering of sentient beings in the long night.
The six consciousnesses are perpetually obscured, suffering through the long night; Enveloped by ignorance, deluded sentiments persist for ages.
Hearing the bell, one awakens to enlightenment day and night; With a serene spirit, one attains supernatural powers within the Pure Land.
This is based on the *Record of Miraculous Responses in the Maintenance of the Dharma* by Vinaya Master Xuanchao.
Within the Vinaya Hall of Jetavana, there was a bronze bell weighing three hundred thousand *jin*.
The Four Heavenly Kings collectively forged it with the intention of assembling the holy multitudes of the great trichiliocosm.
Maudgalyāyana struck it using his supernormal powers.
Its sound resounded and was heard from afar.
The platform stood seven zhang high,
and the shape of the bell was like those found in the region of Wu.
On all four sides, there were many images of the sun, moon, stars, mountains, rivers, and seas,
as well as the shapes of measures such as the *dou*, *hu*, scales, and cubits.
Whatever Maudgalyāyana struck, sounds emerged from each object to announce its specific significance.
Whenever a monk strikes [the bell],
it merely produces the sound; furthermore,
within the boundary of the precept platform (sīma), there is also a large bell.
The terrace is four hundred feet high.
Upon it is a golden bell weighing one hundred thousand jin;
its shape is like that of a cup or vessel.
Above is the image of a Cakravartin King,
who likewise has a thousand sons,
each fully endowed with all the requisite attributes.
Furthermore, it is adorned with the various signs of the nine dragons and the eight meritorious qualities of water.
This great bell was fashioned by a Wheel-Turning King at the beginning of the kalpa;
it is when a noble person receives the precepts.
Those who have already attained supernatural powers strike it;
its sound shakes the three thousandfold world system,
and all sages who hear it realize the fruits of their practice.
Those in the evil realms who hear it will remember their past lives.
Within the Jetavana Monastery, there is a separate hall for the masters of Abhidharma,
where there is a bronze bell shaped like a waist-drum.
This was constructed by the Gandharva King.
Above it are images of Brahmā, Śakra, Māra, the Four Heavenly Kings, the eight classes of beings, and male figures.
Should any heterodox practitioners or outsiders come to challenge him in debate, [they would be unable to do so].
Then, he had an arhat with supernormal powers strike it;
its sound shook the three thousandfold world system.
When the various non-Buddhists were about to strike their own gongs, they heard this sound of the bell.
Those whose faculties are dull and hesitant will not dare to speak; yet,
if there are those with virtuous hearts who seek to resolve their doubts,
upon hearing the sound of this bell, they shall awaken to Bodhicitta and attain the stage of non-retrogression.
Furthermore, there was another separate courtyard named the Sūtra Courtyard.
There stood a stone bell in the style of the Wu period,
made of green jade-like material, with a capacity of ten hu.
Upon the nose is an image of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;
its four sides are embossed with gold and silver,
and on the eastern and western faces are large precious jewels.
It was lodged within his belly;
it was as large as five sheng and had eight corners radiating light.
Its shape resembles that of a flower,
and its perimeter is adorned with images of the various Buddhas of the ten directions at the moment of their initial attainment of enlightenment.
This continues until the time the first sun rises.
Upon the bell, various transformation Buddhas preached the twelve divisions of the sutras.
The boys and girls of Śrāvastī all came to listen;
hearing the Dharma, they realized the state of sainthood.
Those who commit sexual misconduct do not hear the Dharma;
the Great General Maṇi strikes them with a vajra,
and the sound [resounds] throughout ten billion worlds.
Within the radiance, one hears all the sutras spoken by hundreds of thousands of Śākyamuni Buddhas.
This bell was cast by Krakucchanda Buddha;
after that Buddha entered parinirvāṇa, [it remained].
The Dragon King Sāgara took it away;
when Śākyamuni Buddha appeared in the world,
the dragon brought it back once more.
When the Buddha had already entered parinirvāṇa, the bell first began to toll, proclaiming:
"In three months' time, he shall enter parinirvāṇa.
Hearing this from the mouth of the bell's clapper, all the devas wept with tears streaming down their faces.
Shortly before the dragon was about to depart,
there was also a bronze chime in front of Ānanda’s room that could hold five sheng.
The four sides of the pedestal were entirely inlaid with gold,
inscribed with the text of the past Buddhas and their disciples;
upon the nose [of the image], nine dragons were fashioned from purple-gold.
Upon its back stands an image of a celestial being,
who strikes it with a mallet;
the sound reverberates throughout the trichiliocosm.
Within these sounds are also spoken the various teachings and admonitions of the Buddha for his disciples.
This gong was fashioned by Brahmā, the King of Devas,
and after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
The Dragon King Sāgara likewise withdrew [them] into his palace within the ocean.
7. Entering the Assembly, Part Seven. As stated in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*:
"Whenever one wishes to enter the assembly, one should be endowed with five dharmas."
First, one should maintain a mind of loving-kindness;
second, one should humble oneself like a cloth used for wiping dust;
third, one should know the proper manner of sitting and rising.
If one sees a senior elder, one should not sit down;
if one sees a junior elder, one should not stand up.
Fourth, when entering that assembly of monks, one should not engage in miscellaneous talk or discuss worldly matters.
Whether speaking for oneself or requesting another to speak;
fifth, if one sees something disagreeable within the Saṃgha that the mind cannot endure,
one should remain silent.
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Because the noble disciples of the Buddha abide in harmony, there are two kinds of dharmas:
first, the speech of the noble ones (*ārya-vāk*)."
The two noble sages now see the place of the assembly for the fast;
they will arrive there later in their next life and have already attained an excellent position. If they see a senior elder or teacher, [they should pay respect].
Whenever he arrives, he never rises to welcome or see him off, nor does he yield his seat;
his profound destruction of the Dharma is truly like that of a youth.
Furthermore, he saw himself entering the homes of the noble and eminent,
or passing through those observing the profound mourning of a recent death,
or performing vegetarian feasts for the distant memorial anniversaries of their parents.
If the monastic community is dissolute, indulging in sensual pleasures, and creating a noisy disturbance that disrupts the assembly,
how can they avoid the worldly reproach of being categorized among "high monks" [in name only]?
The *Sānqiānwēiyí jīng* (Sūtra on the Three Thousand Dignified Manners) states:
Whenever one wishes to ascend to a bed, one should observe seven rules:
first, sit upon the bed with composure;
second, do not crawl up.
Third, one must not allow the bed to make a sound.
Fourth, one must not vigorously sweep the bed so as to create noise.
Fifth, one must not sigh or lament loudly while contemplating worldly affairs.
Sixth, one must not lie down with a pack of dogs.
Seventh, one should rise early according to the proper time.
As the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra* states:

When seeing sentient beings, one should greet them with a comforting and joyful countenance, speaking first with a level gaze and a harmonious expression, while maintaining right mindfulness before oneself.
If a bodhisattva knows that other sentient beings possess genuine merit, [he should acknowledge it].
Out of a mind of resentment, one does not speak of [the person] to others,
nor does one praise them; even when others offer praise, [one remains silent].
If one does not exclaim "Excellent!
(sādhu), this is called a transgression of the assembly;
it is a transgression of many offenses.
Because it arises from defilement.
The *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃgraha) of the Liang dynasty states:
"If a bodhisattva sees sentient beings, he should first speak with a joyful smile before engaging them in conversation."
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"A person who cannot endure [insults] has five faults.
First, they are fierce and violent, lacking forbearance."
Second, subsequent regret;
third, being disliked by many people;
fourth, the spread of an evil reputation.
Five deaths lead to falling into the evil realms.
Section Eight: Seeking the Dharma. As stated in the *Ekottarika Āgama*:
"If one does not accomplish six dharmas..."
Consequently, one cannot distance oneself from dust and defilement to attain the purity of the Dharma-eye.
What are these six? First, not delighting in hearing [the Dharma].
Second, although hearing the Dharma, one does not lend an attentive ear;
third, one does not seek understanding;
fourth, having not yet attained the Dharma, one does not apply skillful means to diligently seek it.
Fifth, failing to properly guard the dharmas that have been attained;
sixth, not achieving the patient acceptance that accords with reality (*anulomikī kṣānti*).
By reversing these six conditions, one can distance oneself from dust and defilement and attain the purity of the Dharma-eye.
Furthermore, the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states:
"There is no layperson who attains the Buddha-way;
one must possess the thirty-two marks."
Having left the household life and donned the dharma robes, his deportment was fully perfected.
The *Samyukta-abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* states:
"Contentment arises in the present moment."
Having few desires arises in relation to the future;
it is difficult not to take even a single coin in the present,
but it is easy not to take [the realm] of a wheel-turning monarch in the future.
Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"Not giving rise to craving for wealth not yet obtained is called having few desires;
not giving rise to craving for wealth already obtained is called contentment."
Contentment is the present;
fewness of desires is the future.
Chapter Nine: Signs of Decline. As stated in the *Vibhaṅga-pratītyasamutpāda-ādya-viśeṣa-dharmamukha-sūtra*:
The World-Honored One said:
"There are five kinds of decline associated with old age.
The first is the decline of the hair and beard."
First, because his beard and hair have changed color and become decayed;
second, because his physical appearance has deteriorated,
as his complexion, strength, and vitality have all declined.
Third is the decline of physical activity:
when speaking, his breath rises and his gasping becomes increasingly urgent; his body trembles and shakes, and he remains hunched over as he stands.
Because his waist and spine were both devoid of strength,
he slumped forward as soon as he sat;
this was because his body was so feeble and weak.
One must carry a staff when walking because the body is weak and frail; furthermore,
one's wisdom and cognition are dull and sluggish, and one's mindfulness is confused and disordered.
Fourth is the decline of enjoyment.
This is because one experiences inferior material resources in the present,
and because one is entirely unable to enjoy all the implements for play and pleasure.
Because they are unable to proceed swiftly, clearly, and sharply regarding the spheres of activity of the various material sense faculties,
or because they do not proceed at all.
Fifth, the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) is impaired;
because the lifespan is about to end and death is imminent,
one cannot endure even minor conditions for death.
The Āgama Sūtras state:
There are four causes and conditions for the hair to turn white.
The first is an excess of fire.
Second, much sorrow;
third, much illness;
fourth, early planting.
There are four causes and conditions for the illness and emaciation of white-skinned people:
first, eating little;
second, having anxiety.
Third, much sorrow;
fourth, illness.
When these four conditions have not yet been regulated, one should not speak of them to others beforehand.
First, white hair;
second, old age;
third, illness.
There are four kinds of death. These four matters can be avoided,
yet they cannot be averted.
All tastes do not exceed eight kinds:
first, bitter;
second, astringent.
Third, pungent;
fourth, salty;
fifth, bland.
Sixth, sweet;
seventh, sour;
eighth, indistinct flavor.
10. Section on Miscellaneous Conduct. The fourteenth sub-section of the *Vinaya* states:
The bhikṣu Upananda was traveling on the road holding a large, round parasol.
When the laypeople saw him from afar,
they thought he was either the king or a high minister;
fearing him, they moved aside to clear the path.
