The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* with Sub-commentary (Wenzi), five fascicles; and the *Qiongtong lun* (Treatise on Extremity and Success). These two works comprise six fascicles in total.
During the reign of Emperor Xiaowu of the Jin dynasty, the śramaṇa Shi Tanshen of Donglin Monastery on Mount Lu composed them; he was a disciple of Dharma Master Huiyuan.
The *Renshi shi yi lun* (Treatise on the Initial Meaning of Human Nature), one fascicle,
was composed during the reign of Emperor Wu of the Jin dynasty by the śramaṇa Shi Fachang.
The Biographies of Eminent and Recluse Śramaṇas, one fascicle, compiled by the śramaṇa Shi Faji of Mount Yang in Eastern Shan during the reign of Emperor Xiaowu of the Jin dynasty.
It contains nine chapters on the Establishment of the Fundamental Treatise and twelve verses on the Pointing to the Goal of the Six Consciousnesses; these two fascicles.
During the reign of Emperor Xiaowu of the Jin Dynasty,
the śramaṇa Shi Tanwei of Shangming Monastery in Jingzhou compiled the following four fascicles:

the *Biography of Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa*, the *Biography of Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna*, the *Biography of Bodhisattva Āryadeva*, and the *Treatise on True Reality* with the commentary of Dharma Master Kumārajīva.
During the reign of Emperor Jin’an of the Later Qin dynasty,
the Dharma Master Kumārajīva of the country of India translated and compiled the following four fascicles:

the *Prajñā-apratigha-śāstra* (Treatise on the Non-cognition of Prajñā), the *Na-ti-zhen-kong-lun* (Treatise on the Non-emptiness of Reality), the *Wu-bu-qian-lun* (Treatise on the Non-transmigration of Things), and the *Niepan-wuming-lun* (Treatise on the Namelessness of Nirvāṇa).
During the reign of Emperor An of the Jin Dynasty,
the Śramaṇa Śīlavarman of Jingzhao composed the *Shi bo lun* (Treatise on Refuting and Discussing),
one fascicle; [this concludes] up to the time of Emperor An of the Jin Dynasty.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Daochang: 1. *Treatise on Goodness Not Receiving Retribution* 2.

*Treatise on the Buddha Having No Pure Land* 3. *Treatise on the Existence of Conditions* 4. *Treatise on Sudden Enlightenment to Buddhahood* 5. *Treatise on the Immanence of Buddha-nature* 6. *Treatise on the Formlessness of the Dharmakāya* 7. *Treatise on the Two Truths* The above comprise seven fascicles.
Compiled during the early Song dynasty by the śramaṇa Zhudao-sheng of Longguang Monastery:

*The Record of the Three Jewels* in twenty fascicles; *The Pure Dweller* in twenty fascicles; *Proclaiming the Manifestations of Verification* in three fascicles; and *The Record of Miscellaneous Meanings* in twenty fascicles—these four works comprise sixty-three fascicles.
Compiled by Xiao Ziliang, Prince Wenxuan of Jingling and Minister of Education under the Qi Dynasty:

*Treatise on the Attainment of Nature through Heaven* (*Chengtian daxing lun*), two fascicles of *The Record of Vengeful Spirits* (*Yuanhun zhi*), and one fascicle of *Instructions on Refraining from Killing* (*Jiesha xun*). These three works are listed above.
Compiled by Yan Zhitui, Grand Master of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices of the Qi Dynasty.
*Shu seng zhongshi lun* (A Discourse on Monastic Midday Meals), one fascicle. The above work was compiled by Shen Xiuwen of the Southern Qi Dynasty.
*Mingxiang ji* (Records of Miraculous Auspiciousness), ten fascicles. The above work was compiled by Wang Yan of the Qi Dynasty.

*Chū-sanzō-shū-ki* (Collection of Records on the Tripitaka) in sixteen fascicles; *Hōon-shū* (Anthology of the Dharma Garden) in fifteen fascicles; *Kōmyō-shū* (Anthology of Propagating and Illuminating the Dharma) in fourteen fascicles; *Sekai-ki* (Record of the World) in ten fascicles; *Sabbattha Shishi-den* (Biographies of the Masters and Disciples of the Sarvāstivāda) in five fascicles; *Shakka-fu* (Genealogy of Śākyamuni) in four fascicles; *Daishū-tō-san-kyō-ki* (Records on Three Sutras including the Mahāsannipāta); *Ken-gu-kyō-ki* (Record on the Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish); *Shū-sanzō-innen-ki* (Record on the Causes and Conditions for Compiling the Tripitaka); *Ritsu-bun-go-bu-ki* (Record on the Division of the Vinaya into Five Sections); *Kyō-rai-Kandai-shibu-ki* (Record on the Four Collections of Scriptures Brought to Han Land); *Ritsu-bun-jū-hachi-bu-ki* (Record on the Division of the Vinaya into Eighteen Sections); *Jūjū-ritsu-go-hyaku-rakan-ki* (Record on the Five Hundred Arhats of the Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya); *Zenken-ritsu-bi-basha-ki* (Commentary on the Samantapāsādikā). These fourteen works comprise seventy-two fascicles.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Sengyou of Jian’an Monastery in Yangzhou during the Liang Dynasty.
This single fascicle contains twenty-one essential dharma verses from various scriptures, compiled during the time of Emperor Wu of the Liang.
Compiled by the śramaṇa Shi Dao-huan.
*Commentary on the Treatise on the Awakening of Faith*, two fascicles. The above work was translated by Dharma Master Paramārtha during the fourth year of the Taiching era of the Liang dynasty.

One volume of an essential compendium of various sutras together with its catalog in eighteen fascicles. This work was compiled by the śramaṇa Śīlamitra and others of Zhuangyan Monastery at the command of the Emperor of the Liang dynasty, at Dinglin Shangsi.
The *Catalogue of the Various Scriptures of the Huilin Buddha Hall* in four fascicles.
This aforementioned catalogue in four fascicles was compiled by the śramaṇa Śramaṇa Sengshao of Anle Monastery, by imperial decree of the Emperor of the Liang dynasty.

*Jīnglǜ yìxiàng* (Diverse Phenomena of Sūtras and Vinaya), one work in fifty-five fascicles, including its catalog; *Míngsēng zhuàn bìngxùmù* (Biographies of Eminent Monks with Preface and Catalog), thirty-one fascicles; *Zhòngjīng gòng shèngsēng fǎ* (Methods for Offering to the Holy Sangha from Various Sūtras), five fascicles; *Zhòngjīng mùlù* (Catalog of Various Sūtras), four fascicles; *Zhòngjīng hùguó guǐshén mínglù* (Record of the Names of Ghosts and Spirits Who Protect the Nation from Various Sūtras), three fascicles; *Zhòngjīng zhūfó míng* (Names of Various Buddhas from Various Sūtras), three fascicles; in the sixteenth year [of the reign], *Zhòngjīng yōnghù guótǔ zhūlóng mínglù* (Record of the Names of Various Dragons Who Protect the Realm from Various Sūtras), one fascicle; *Zhòngjīng chànhuǐ mièzuì fǎ* (Methods for Repentance and Eradicating Sin from Various Sūtras), three fascicles; *Chūyào lüyí* (Essential Discipline), twenty fascicles. Altogether, these nine works comprise one hundred and twenty-two fascicles.
Compiled by the śramaṇa Shi Baoshang and others at Zhuangyan Monastery by imperial decree of the Liang Emperor.
*Sub-commentary on the Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, seventy fascicles. This one work consists of seventy fascicles.
Annotated by the Śramaṇa Shi Huiming of Jian’an Monastery during the Liang Dynasty.
*Yilin* (Forest of Meanings), eighty fascicles.
This one work in eighty fascicles was compiled by twenty great virtuous monks, including the Śramaṇa Shi Zhizang of Kaishan Monastery, by imperial decree of Emperor Jianwen of the Liang Dynasty.
*Neidian boyao* (Essential Compendium of Buddhist Scriptures), forty fascicles.
This single work of forty fascicles was compiled by Yu Xiongji, Secretary of the Prince of Xiangdong; it is largely similar in character to works such as the *Huanglan* and the *Leiyuan*.
Later, he left the household life and changed his name to Huiming.
The *Biographies of Eminent Monks* in fourteen volumes, including its catalog—
this one work was compiled by the śramaṇa Shi Huijiao of Jiaxiang Temple in Kuaiji during the Liang dynasty.
*Famozhao* (Edict on Subduing Māra), one fascicle. The above is this one work, compiled by the monk Senghui of the Liang dynasty.
*Zhuanfalunlun* (Treatise on Turning the Wheel of the Dharma), one hundred and eighty fascicles. The above is this one work consisting of one hundred and eighty fascicles.
Compiled by the Great Virtues and Scholars by Imperial Decree during the Liang Dynasty.
*Brahman Astronomical Treatise*, twenty fascicles. This one work, comprising twenty fascicles, was produced during the Tianhe era of Emperor Wu of the Liang Dynasty.
Translated by the Dharma Master Śramaṇa Dharmaruci of the country of Mo-le (Mālava).
One work consisting of either fifty or one hundred fascicles: the *Subcommentary on the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Annotated by Emperor Wu of the Liang Dynasty.
*Fǎbǎoliánbì* (The Linked Jade Tablets of the Dharma Treasure), 200 fascicles.
The above is this one work by Xiao Gang, Emperor Jianwen of the Liang Dynasty.
While residing in the palace of the heir apparent,
he personally examined the inner scriptures and directed the various domains of practice.
He ordered various scholars to compile and edit them into a continuous work,
similar in scope to the *Huālín biǎnlüè*. This single volume,
titled *Jīngshī tā sì jì* (Records of the Stupas and Monasteries of the Capital), consists of twenty fascicles.

The Discourse on the Immortality of the Spirit (*Shen bumie lun*), one fascicle, composed by the subject Liu Qiu, Minister of the Department of War and concurrently Scholar for History during the Liang Dynasty, as dictated by imperial command.
The aforementioned work was composed by Zheng Daozi of the Liang Dynasty.

*The Biography of Vasubandhu*, one fascicle; *A General Preface to the Various Scriptures Translating Foreign Languages*, seven fascicles; and *A General Preface to the Various Scriptures*, two fascicles—these three works comprise ten fascicles in total.
They were translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇarata of Ujjayinī in Western India during the Chen dynasty.
Chen Fan, known as Zhendi, translated [this work].
It consists of five fascicles titled *Luoyang qielan ji* (Record of Monasteries in Luoyang). This aforementioned work comprises one title in five fascicles.
Compiled by Yang Xuanzhi, Governor of Qicheng Commandery during the Northern Wei Dynasty at the capital of Ye.

The Five Treatises: *Śabda-vidyā* (Grammar), *Cikitsā-vidyā* (Medicine), *Śilpa-karma-sthāna-vidyā* (Arts and Crafts), *Vidyā-mantra-vidyā* (Incantations), and *Hetu-vidyā* (Logic). These are the aforementioned five treatises.
During the reign of Emperor Ming of the Wei dynasty,
the Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghavarman from the country of Pāṭaliputra, together with Jñānayaśas,
translated [this work] at the Old City of Chang’an.
The *Essentials of the Various Scriptures* (*Zhou zhòng jīng yào*), twenty-two fascicles, containing one hundred and twenty dharma-gates.
These two sections, totaling twenty-three fascicles, were compiled by the śramaṇa Shi Tánxiǎn and others at the command of Wáng Yǔwén Hēitài, Chancellor of the Wèi Dynasty.
The *Shilaozi Huahu Zhuan* (The Biography of Laozi’s Transformation of the Barbarians), in eighteen chapters, titled "The Chapter on Difficulties," in two fascicles.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Sengmeng of Yuanguo Monastery in Xin Prefecture during the Zhou Dynasty.
The *Sanhualun* (Treatise on the Scattering of Flowers), eight fascicles.
This one work consists of eight fascicles, compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Huishan of Xixuan Temple in Yangzhou during the Northern Zhou dynasty.

The *Zhidaolun* (Treatise on the Ultimate Way), the *Chundelun* (Treatise on Pure Virtue), the *Qianzhilun* (Treatise on Dispelling Attachments), the *Bushalun* (Treatise on Non-Killing), the *Qushifeilun* (Treatise on Eliminating Right and Wrong), the *Xiukonglun* (Treatise on Cultivating Emptiness), the *Yingyulun* (Treatise on the Simile of the Shadow), the *Fajiebaorenming* (Inscription on the Jewel-like Person of the Dharma-realm), the *Yanshixiangwen* (Text on the Contemplation of Disgust for Food), the *Sengyia Pusa Zhuan* (Biography of the Bodhisattva Sengya), the *Shaofashi Zhuan* (Biography of Dharma Master Shao), and the *YanShanzhishizhuan* (Account of the Efficacy of Good Spiritual Friends). These twelve works comprise twelve fascicles.
During the reign of Emperor Wu of the Zhou dynasty,
the śramaṇa Shi Wangming compiled the *Sanbao ji* (Collection on the Three Jewels) in eleven fascicles; this constitutes one work in eleven fascicles.
Compiled by the śramaṇa Shi Jing’ai during the reign of Emperor Wu of the Zhou Dynasty, based on various sutras.
This single fascicle is titled *Discourse on the Three Teachings*.
The *Xiaodao lun* (Discourse on Laughing at Daoism) in three fascicles, compiled by the śramaṇa Shi Dao’an during the reign of Emperor Wu of the Zhou dynasty. One work in three fascicles.
Imperial Edict from Emperor Wu of the Zhou Dynasty to the former *Sili* (Inspector of the Capital), Mu Jiebo Zhen Luan, to weigh and compare the two teachings of Buddhism and Daoism.
*The Questions and Answers on the Buddha-Dharma by the High Ancestor of Zhou*, two fascicles. One set, comprising two fascicles.

One scroll of the *Wangshi poxie lun* (The Wang Family’s Refutation of Heresy), compiled by imperial decree of Emperor Wu of the Zhou dynasty during his debate with the former monk Rendao Lin of Ye-du; this constitutes one work in one scroll.

During the reign of Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou dynasty, the former śramaṇa Wang Mingguang of Xiangzhou engaged in debates with Wei Yuansong regarding the refutation of the Buddha-dharma. His works include:

*The Treatise on Pacifying the People* in twelve fascicles, *The Treatise on Refining the Spirit* in ten fascicles, *The Treatise on Cause and Effect* in two fascicles, and *The Record of Sacred Traces* in one fascicle. These four works comprise twenty-five fascicles in total.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Lingyu of Daci Monastery in Xiangzhou during the Sui Dynasty:

*Collected Records of Miscellaneous Practices Arising in Response to Faculties*, thirty-six fascicles; *Separate Records of the Three Stages*, four fascicles. The above two works comprise forty fascicles in total.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Xing of Zhenji Monastery in the Western Capital at the beginning of the Sui dynasty.
*Zhongjing mulu* (Catalogue of All Scriptures), seven fascicles.
The above seven fascicles were produced in the fourteenth year of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty.
Compiled by twenty great virtuous ones, including the śramaṇa Śākyamuni Fajing and others of Daixingshan Temple, by imperial decree;
and Śramaṇa Sengmu of Yanghuasi Temple,
and the śramaṇa Yancong of Riyansi Temple.
The sections are divided and meticulously compiled.
One fascicle of the *Ten Mahāyāna Treatises*. The above work was composed by the Śramaṇa Śīlacaṅkrama of Daxingshan Monastery during the Sui dynasty.
*Discourse on the Field of the Three Jewels*, thirty-one fascicles.
This single work consists of thirty-one fascicles, compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Sengkun of Chengdu at Daxingshan Temple during the Sui dynasty.
*The Sixfold Practice of Ordinary and Holy Beings*, twenty fascicles; there are also versions in ten, seven, five, three, and one fascicle. This single work comprises forty-six fascicles in total.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Daozheng of Cangzhou during the Sui Dynasty: *Biography of Dharmagupta*, four fascicles; *Tongji lun* (Treatise on the Ultimate), one fascicle;

*Bianjiao lun* (Treatise on Distinguishing the Teachings), one fascicle; *Bianzheng lun* (Treatise on Distinguishing Orthodoxy), one fascicle; *Tongxue lun* (Treatise on the Common Study), one fascicle; *Record of the Spiritual Friends of Sudhana*, one fascicle; Prefaces to Newly Translated Scriptures; *Futian lun* (Treatise on the Field of Merit), one fascicle; *Sengguan lun* (Treatise on Monastic Officials), one fascicle; *Xiyu xuanzhi* (Mysterious Aims Concerning the Western Regions), ten fascicles. The above comprise ten works totaling twenty-two fascicles.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Yancong of Riyen Monastery during the Sui Dynasty:

1. *Commentary on the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* by Shi Dao’an, 24 fascicles; 2. *Treatise on Preservation and Abolition*, 1 fascicle; 3. *Treatise on the Sorrows of Study*, 1 fascicle; 4. *Treatise on Weariness with Cultivation*, 1 fascicle. The above four works comprise twenty-seven fascicles.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Huiying of Shaivisi Monastery in Chang’an during the Sui Dynasty.
*Jingyi zhuan* (Biographies of Exemplary Marvels), twenty fascicles. This one work consists of twenty fascicles.
Compiled by Hou Junsu, a *xiucaoshi* (excellent scholar) and *rulinfang* (Erudite of the Forest of Learning) of Xiangzhou during the Sui Dynasty.
Composed by imperial decree for Emperor Wen.
*Tongming lun* (Discourse on the Universal Mandate), two fascicles.
This work, comprising one title in two fascicles, was composed by Xu Tongqing, Court Ritual Master of the Jin Prince’s Establishment during the Sui dynasty.
*Wai-nei-bang-tong-biao-jiao-shu-fa* (Methods for Comparing External and Internal Teachings), one fascicle.
The above is this single fascicle, compiled by Liu Ping of Jingyang, a scholar-translator during the Sui dynasty.
*Kaifuang-sanbao-lu* (Record of the Three Jewels of the Kaifuang Era), fifteen fascicles. The above is this one work in fifteen fascicles.
Compiled by Fei Changfang of Chengdu, a scholar-translator during the Sui dynasty.
*Zhongjing fashi* (The Rituals and Methods of the Various Scriptures), ten fascicles. This single work in ten fascicles was produced in the fifteenth year of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty.

Emperor Wen issued an edict ordering the relevant authorities to compile the *Fanyi fashi lun* (Treatise on the Methods of Translating Scriptures) in ten fascicles and the *Zhusi beiming* (Inscriptions for Various Temples) in three fascicles; these two works comprise thirteen fascicles in total.
They were later compiled by the Sui dynasty śramaṇa-translator Śikṣānanda (Shi Mingze).
*Sequels to the Inner Teachings*, one fascicle; *Inner Instructions*, one fascicle.
These two fascicles were compiled later by the Sui dynasty Śramaṇa and translator Śikṣānanda (Shi Xingju).

*The Ambrosia of the Fragrant City*, five hundred fascicles. This single work of five hundred fascicles was compiled later by imperial decree during the Sui dynasty by the Śramaṇa Śikṣānanda (Shi Zhiguo) of the Huiri Monastery, together with the relevant officials.

*Treatise on the Three Virtues*, one fascicle; *Entrance to the Gate of Expedient Means for Entering the Path*, two fascicles; *Mirror Metaphor Treatise*, one fascicle; *Treatise on Unobstructed Dependent Origination*, one fascicle; *Ritual for Tenfold Scripture Recitation*, one fascicle; *Ritual for the Inexhaustible Treasury*, one fascicle; *Origins of the Ordination Precepts*, two fascicles; *Diagram of the Dharma Realm*, one fascicle; *Treatise on the Ten Non-regressions*, one fascicle; *Ritual for Paying Homage to the Buddha*, one fascicle. Altogether, these comprise ten works in twelve fascicles.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Xuánwǎn of Yánxīng Monastery in the Western Capital of the Great Táng:

*Pòxié Lùn* (Treatise on Refuting Heresies), one fascicle; *Biànzhèng Lùn* (Treatise on Distinguishing Orthodoxy), eight fascicles. The above two works comprise nine fascicles. Compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Fálín of Lóngtián Monastery in Zhōngnánshān during the Imperial Court [of the Sui].

*Zheyilun* (Refutation of Doubts) in one fascicle; *Xushiyuan yinghua* (Continuation of the Selection of Flowers from the Garden of Poetry) in ten fascicles; *Zhujingang banruojing* (Commentary on the Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra) in one fascicle; and *Zhujing jiangxu* (Prefaces to Lectures on Various Sūtras) in one fascicle. The above comprise four works totaling thirteen fascicles.
The *Neide lun* (Treatise on Inner Virtue), one fascicle, compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Huijing of Jiguo Temple in the Western Capital during the Imperial Dynasty.
The above one fascicle was compiled by Li Shizheng,
Court Official for Ceremonial Affairs under the Imperial Gate during the Imperial Dynasty.
*Treatise on the Three Teachings through Discernment and Measurement*, three fascicles; *Treatise on the Fourfold Exposition of Chan Meditation*, ten fascicles.
These two works, totaling thirteen fascicles, were composed by the Śramaṇa Shi Fayun of Ximing Monastery in the capital during the Imperial Dynasty.

*Commentary on the Monastic Code for Nuns* (Sengni jieben) in two fascicles; *Sub-commentary* (Shuji) in four fascicles; *Commentary on the Karma-vinaya* (Zhujie mo) in two fascicles; *Sub-commentary* in four fascicles; *Supplemented Rituals of Vinaya Practice* (Xingshi shanbu luyi) in three fascicles;

*Ritual for Repentance as the Orthodox Practice of the Buddhist Community* (Shimen zhengxing chanhui yi) in three fascicles; *Ritual for the Weight of Deceased Property in the Buddhist Community* (Shimen wangwu qingzhong yi) in one fascicle;

*Ritual for Robes and Vestments in the Buddhist Community* (Shimen zhangfu yi) in one fascicle; *Ritual for Taking Refuge and Paying Homage in the Buddhist Community* (Shimen guijing yi) in one fascicle.
*Śrāmaṇera-dharmarakṣa-vidhi*, one fascicle; *Śākya-piṭaka-lüeh*, one fascicle; *Sengji-jianzai-tu-zan*, one fascicle;
*Fohua-dongjian-tu-zan*, two fascicles; *Śākyamuni-fangzhi*, two fascicles;
*Gujin-fo-daolunheng*, four fascicles; *Dada-neidianlu*, ten fascicles; *Xu gaoseng zhuan*, thirty fascicles; *Houji xu*.

*Biographies of Eminent Monks*, ten fascicles; *Extended Collection for the Propagation and Clarification of the Dharma*, thirty fascicles; *Records of the Miraculous Responses of the Triple Gem in the Land of the East*, three fascicles;
*Catalogue of Ximing Monastery*, one fascicle; *Records of Miraculous Responses*, one fascicle; *Illustrations of Jetavana*, two fascicles;
*Responses to the Preservation of the Bequeathed Dharma*, seven fascicles. Altogether, these comprise twenty-two works in one hundred and seventeen fascicles.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Daoxuan of Ximing Monastery during the Imperial Dynasty.
*Chanlin Chaoji* (Notes on the Chan Forest), thirty fascicles.
This single work was compiled by ten individuals, including the Śramaṇa Huaiyin of Hongfu Monastery in the Western Capital and the Śramaṇa Xuance of Ximing Monastery.

In the second year of the Linde era of the Imperial Dynasty, by imperial decree, the Office for the Compilation of Writings at the Western Dragon Gate of the Northern Gate produced a brief excerpt from the entire canon.
This consists of two fascicles of the *Commentary on the Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra: The City of Śrāvastī*. Thus, this single work comprises two fascicles.
The *Record of the Western Regions* in twelve fascicles, annotated by the śramaṇa Xuánzé of Xìmíng Monastery during the second year of the Lín dé era of our dynasty;
and the aforementioned work [the *Great Tang Records on the Western Regions*],
compiled by the śramaṇa Xuánzàng of Dàcí'ēn Monastery in the Western Capital of the Great Táng Dynasty by imperial decree.

*Fayuan zhulin* (Pearl Forest of the Dharma Garden), one hundred fascicles; *Zhujing yaoji* (Essential Collection from Various Scriptures), twenty fascicles; *Dachaoxiaocheng chanmen guan* (Contemplation of the Chan Gates of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna), ten fascicles; *Shoujie yishi* (Rituals for Receiving the Precepts), four fascicles; *Lifo yishi* (Rituals for Paying Homage to the Buddha), two fascicles; *Dacheng luezhiguan* (Abridged Mahāyāna Śamatha-vipaśyanā), one fascicle; *Bianwei xianzhen lun* (Treatise on Discerning the False and Revealing the True), one fascicle; *Jingful lun* (Treatise on Reverence and Merit), three fascicles; *Sifenlü taoyao* (Essentials of the Dharmaguptaka Vinaya), five fascicles; *Sifenlü nichao* (Extracts from the Dharmaguptaka Vinaya for Nuns), five fascicles; *Jingang banruo jizhu* (Collected Commentaries on the Diamond Prajñāpāramitā), three fascicles. These eleven works comprise one hundred and fifty-four fascicles, compiled by the śramaṇa Shi Daoshi, courtesy name Xuanyun, of Ximing Monastery in the Western Capital during the Imperial Dynasty.
The *Yìnyì* (Phonology and Meaning) of the Various Scriptures of the Great Tang, twenty fascicles.
This one work was compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Xuanying of the Great Ci’en Monastery in the Western Capital during the Imperial Dynasty.

The Commentary on the Newly Translated *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*, one fascicle; and the Commentary on the "Preface to the Holy Teachings of the Tripiṭaka Master" by the Two Emperors, one fascicle. These two fascicles were compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Xuanguan of Puguang Monastery in the Western Capital during the Imperial Dynasty.

*Records of the Temples of the Western Capital*, twenty fascicles; *Separate Biography of the Śramaṇa Falin*, three fascicles; *Record on the Non-Veneration of Śramaṇas*, six fascicles. These three works comprise twenty-nine fascicles, compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Yancong of Hongfu Monastery in the Western Capital during the Imperial Dynasty.
One fascicle of the Commentary on the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra*. This one fascicle was annotated by Minzhi, a Court Attendant of the Martial Guard during the Imperial Dynasty.

Forty fascicles of the Commentary on the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*. These forty fascicles were annotated by Li Xuanzhen, the Regional Inspector of Bianzhou during the Imperial Dynasty; he was the younger brother of the Duke Ying.
*Record of Travels in Central India*, ten fascicles. The above work was composed by Wang Xuance, a Chao Sanda Dafu of the Imperial Court.

*Western Regions Gazetteer*, sixty fascicles; *Illustrations of the Western Regions*, forty fascicles. These two works together comprise one hundred fascicles. They were compiled by order of the Emperor’s decree in the third year of the Linde era of the Imperial Court.
*Mingbao ji* (Records of Karmic Retribution), two fascicles. This work was compiled by Tang Lin, Minister of the Ministry of Personnel during the Yonghui era of our dynasty.
*Mingbao shiyi* (Supplement to Records of Karmic Retribution), two fascicles. This work was compiled by Lang Yuling, courtesy name Yuanxiu, of Zhongshan during our dynasty.
Compiled during the Longshuo era.

*Discourse on the Six Realms*, ten fascicles. This one work in ten fascicles was compiled by Yang Shangshan, Court Gentleman of the Left Guard of the Imperial Household and concurrently Scholar of the Hongwen Academy, of the Present Dynasty.
*Xiǎncháng lùn* (Exposition on Manifesting the Permanent), two fascicles. The above two fascicles were composed by Li Xuānjì of the Imperial Dynasty.
*Biànzhēn lùn* (Treatise on Discerning the True), one fascicle. The above one fascicle was composed by Yuán Wànqīng of the Imperial Dynasty.
*Guīxīn lù* (Records of Turning the Heart to the Buddha), thirty fascicles.
The above thirty fascicles were compiled by Xiao Xuanci, Clerk of the Right Guard Commandery.
Section Four: Prajñā. *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Sanskrit original consisting of two hundred thousand stanzas.
Translated into six hundred fascicles, this work comprises four locations and sixteen assemblies, translated by Dharma Master Xuanzang at Cien Monastery.
The first assembly was preached at Vulture Peak Mountain in Rājagṛha.
The Sanskrit original consists of one hundred thirty-two thousand six hundred verses.
This translation comprises four hundred fascicles and seventy-nine chapters as a single complete work.
The second assembly was held at Vulture Peak Mountain in Rājagṛha.
It is said that the Sanskrit original consists of twenty-five thousand stanzas.
The aforementioned translation comprises seventy-eight fascicles and eighty-five chapters, being a re-translation.
Together with the three versions—the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, the *Prabhāsa*, and the *Guāngzàn*—they total eighty fascicles.
Now translated, it consists of seventy-eight fascicles, matching the Sanskrit original.
The third assembly was preached at Vulture Peak Mountain in Rājagṛha;
the Sanskrit original contains eighteen thousand stanzas.
The above constitutes fifty-nine fascicles and thirty-one chapters translated individually.
The fourth assembly was preached at Vulture Peak Mountain in Rājagṛha.
The Sanskrit original consists of eight thousand stanzas.
The above constitutes a re-translation in eighteen fascicles and twenty-nine chapters.
It corresponds to the four versions of the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*: the *Xiaopin*, the *Daofengxing*, the *Xindaofengxing*, and the *Mingdu*.
Now it has been translated into eighteen fascicles.
It corresponds to the Sanskrit original.
The fifth assembly was spoken at Vulture Peak Mountain in Rājagṛha.
The Sanskrit original consists of four thousand ślokas.
The above constitutes one volume in twenty-four chapters translated individually.
The sixth assembly was preached at Vulture Peak Mountain in Rājagṛha.
The Sanskrit original consists of two thousand five hundred verses.
The above is the re-translation in eight fascicles and seventeen chapters,
corresponding to the *Suvikrāntavikramī-paripṛcchā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
It was preached during the seventh assembly at the Jetavana Anāthapiṇḍada-ārāma in Śrāvastī.
The Sanskrit original consists of eight hundred stanzas.
This translation comprises two fascicles without chapter divisions and is a re-translation [of the same text].
It corresponds to the *Mañjuśrī-prajñā*.
The eighth assembly was preached at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, in Śrāvastī.
The Sanskrit original consists of four hundred stanzas.
This translation comprises one fascicle; it is a single, undivided translation without chapters.
The ninth assembly was spoken at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, in Śrāvastī.
The Sanskrit original consists of three hundred stanzas.
This Chinese translation comprises one fascicle, without chapters, and is not a re-translation.
The *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā* was spoken during the tenth assembly, atop the Maṇiratnagarbha Hall in the palace of the King of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven;
it consists of three hundred stanzas in the Sanskrit original.
The above constitutes one fascicle translated as a single work without chapters.
The eleventh assembly was held at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, in Śrāvastī,
where the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) was taught.
The Sanskrit original consists of two thousand stanzas.
The above translation comprises five fascicles, translated as a single work without chapter divisions.
The twelfth assembly was held at the Jetavana Anāthapiṇḍada-ārāma in Śrāvastī.
The *Śīlapāramitā-sūtra*. The Sanskrit original consists of two thousand stanzas;
this translation comprises five fascicles and was translated as a single work without chapter divisions.
The thirteenth assembly was held at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, in Śrāvastī.
Therein, the Pāramitā of Forbearance was taught;
the Sanskrit original consists of four hundred stanzas.
The above constitutes one volume translated as a single work without chapters.
The fourteenth assembly was held at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, in Śrāvastī,
where the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*) was taught.
The Sanskrit original consists of eight hundred stanzas.
This translation comprises two fascicles, translated as a single work without chapter divisions.
The fifteenth assembly was held at Vulture Peak Mountain in Rājagṛha.
This is the exposition of the *Samādhi-pāramitā*,
consisting of eight hundred verses in the Sanskrit original;
translated here into two fascicles, it is a single translation without chapter divisions.
The sixteenth assembly was held at the Bamboo Grove Monastery by the Śāradvatīpūtra Pond in Rājagṛha.
Therein, the Prajñāpāramitā was taught;
the Sanskrit original consists of two thousand five hundred stanzas.
The above constitutes eight fascicles translated as single units without chapter divisions.
This preface to the sixteen assemblies was composed by the śramaṇa Xuánzé of Xīmíng Monastery in Chāng’ān.
Section Five: On the Flourishing of the Teachings. Since the arrival of the Buddhist teachings in China, their capacity to provide salvation has reached its ultimate height.
They have inspired awakening, broadened understanding, and thoroughly cleansed the defilements of the mundane world.
The auspicious omens therein have been fully recorded in previous accounts; here,
several instances are described in detail.
This is intended to guide future students.
Formerly, when Shi Xing sought the meaning of the teachings, his great aspiration lay in the Mahāyāna;
he was about to depart for the Western Regions.
Thereupon, obstacles arose,
and he consequently cast the sutra into the fire;
yet the body of the sutra did not turn to ash.
The fire was extinguished by it,
and he subsequently reached this land;
this is precisely what is known as the *Prabhāsa-sūtra*.
Furthermore, when Dharmakṣema obtained the Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra and arrived in the land of Liang,
a thief stole it at night.
He raised [the matter] but could not bring it forth,
and bowed his head in apology.
This was during the suppression of the Dharma by Emperor Wu of the Zhou dynasty.
When elephants destroyed the scriptures and burned them,
they all saw the Tripitaka rise up together and suddenly enter the void;
such instances were numerous.
It cannot be recorded in full.
Nevertheless, the propagation of the teaching depends on people,
and the state serves as its foundation.
He saved sentient beings by establishing monasteries,
depicting sacred images, and translating scriptures;
at that time, he sought out his associates through mutual agreement.
Therefore, I shall recount its origins to glorify and clarify the Buddha-dharma;
yet prior to the Han and Wei dynasties,
it was certainly impossible to find any mention or record of it.
From the Jin and Song dynasties down to the present, I have briefly compiled this chronological account.

During the reign of Emperor Wu, the Great Ancestor of the Jin, Buddhist affairs were extensively promoted and monasteries were widely established. Emperor Hui of the Jin built Xingfu Monastery in Luoyang, where he regularly provided sustenance for one hundred monks. Emperor Min of the Jin established Tongling and Baima Monasteries in Chang’an. Thus, including both capitals during the Western Jin, there were one hundred and eighty monasteries in total.
There were thirteen translators who produced seventy-three works.
There were three thousand seven hundred monks and nuns.
During the reign of Emperor Yuan, the Middle Sovereign of the Jin dynasty, two temples—Waguan and Longgong—were established in Jiangzuo.
Du Dan-yang ordained one thousand monks; during the reigns of Emperor Suzong and Emperor Ming of the Jin dynasty, he established the two monasteries of Xinghuang and Daochang.
Ji Yixue gathered one hundred monks; during the reign of Emperor Xianzong Chengdi of the Jin dynasty, he established the two monasteries of Zhongxing and Luye.
The *Jiyi xue* (Collection on the Study of Meaning) records that during the reign of Emperor Jianwen of the Jin dynasty, one thousand monks were ordained and images were commissioned;

temples were established, and a wooden pagoda was built at Changgan. During the early Huangtai era of Emperor Wudi, the Son of Heaven of the Jin dynasty, Benqi Temple was founded. Furthermore, Emperor An of the Jin dynasty established Dashisi Temple at the Yuyang Stūpa. Thus, the Eastern Jin lasted for one hundred and four years.
One thousand seven hundred and sixty-eight monasteries were established;
twenty-seven translators produced two hundred and sixty-three works;
and there were twenty-four thousand monks and nuns.
Emperor Wu of the Song dynasty, the High Ancestor, recited the Sanskrit text orally and transcribed the precept sutras by hand;

he established four monasteries, including Linggen and Fawang, where he regularly provided sustenance for a thousand monks. Emperor Ming of the Song dynasty commissioned a golden statue eighteen feet tall.
Upon concluding the fast, he was moved by the manifestation of the Buddha’s relics;
he constructed Hongpuzhong Temple and invited renowned monks.
Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty attended the vegetarian feast and observed the precept against killing.
He founded Chanling Temple.

He constantly provided sustenance for a thousand monks. During the Song dynasty, there were a total of one thousand nine hundred and thirteen monasteries, and two hundred and ten translated scriptures.
There were thirty-six thousand monks and nuns.
Emperor Taizu Gaodi of the Qi dynasty personally transcribed the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and recited the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
On the eighth day of the fourth month, he regularly cast golden images.
On the fifteenth day of the seventh month, he universally established alms-basins at the monasteries and provided offerings for three hundred monks.
He founded Zhiqu and Zhiguan Monasteries; during the reign of Emperor Wu of the Qi dynasty, he established Zhaoxuan and Youxian Monasteries.
There were three hundred monks.

After four years of comparative evaluation among the Three Teachings, the doctrine was finalized during the reigns of Emperors Qi Gaozong and Mingdi, who transcribed all the Buddhist scriptures and commissioned one thousand Buddha statues.
Reciting the Prajñāpāramitā from memory,
constantly upholding the Lotus Sūtra,
and constructing a temple for refuge.
He summoned Zen monks and regularly observed the six fast days; during the Qi period, there were twenty-one hundred and fifteen monasteries under his jurisdiction,
and he translated seventy-two sections of the Buddhist scriptures.
There were thirty-two thousand five hundred monks and nuns.
Emperor Wu, the Gaozu of the Liang dynasty, composed the *Wushi lun* (Discourse on the Five Periods) and other works which were transmitted throughout the four quarters.
He also constructed the Guangzhai and Tongtai monasteries, making five in total.
He constantly provided alms for a thousand monks.

Throughout the kingdom, the six fast days and the eight precepts were universally observed. Emperor Jianwen of the Liang dynasty constructed these two temples, Jingbao and En, and drew his own blood to personally transcribe ten copies of the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
He vowed to observe the fast by not eating for an entire day.
He compiled and edited over two hundred scrolls of records.
His *Fǎbǎoliánbì* (The Linked Wall of the Dharma Jewel) also consists of over two hundred scrolls. Emperor Yuán, the Zhōngzōng of the Liáng dynasty, established the Tiānjū and Tiāngōng monasteries.
He provided offerings to a thousand monks.

He personally lectured on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*. During the Liang dynasty, there were a total of two thousand eight hundred and forty-six monasteries, and two hundred and forty-eight translations of scriptures were produced.
There were eighty-two thousand seven hundred monks and nuns.
During the reigns of the two sovereigns, Emperor Xuan and Emperor Ming of the Liang dynasty, the state was restored.
In Jingzhou, they constructed various temples, including Tianhuang, Zhiqu, and Daming.
Its administration was located in Jiangling.
There were one hundred and eight Buddhist temples in the prefecture,
with three thousand two hundred monks and nuns.
Emperor Wu, the High Ancestor of the Chen dynasty, established the four monasteries of Dong’an, Ji, Huangtian, and Ju in Yangzhou;
he transcribed twelve sets of the entire Tripitaka and cast one million golden and copper images.
He ordained seven thousand monks.
He restored thirty-two old temples. During the reign of Emperor Wen of the Chen dynasty, he had fifty sets of the Tripitaka copied and ordained two thousand monks and nuns.
He renovated sixty old temples. During the reign of Emperor Xuan of the Chen dynasty, he constructed a seven-story wooden pagoda at Taihuang Temple within the palace precincts of Yangzhou.
He also built a spire fifteen *zhang* high at Chonghuang Temple.
Below, he enshrined the Buddha’s fingernail relic.
He commissioned more than twenty thousand golden images and restored fifty old monasteries.
Consequently, one million three hundred thousand images were cast and the twelve divisions of the Tripitaka were transcribed;
ten thousand people were ordained during the forty-four years of the reigns of five successive rulers of the Chen dynasty.
There are one thousand two hundred and thirty-two temples;
the state’s new temples number one thousand seven hundred,
while sixty-eight were constructed by the government.
There are more than three hundred great monasteries within the city walls,
with thirty-two thousand monks and nuns.
Eleven translations of Buddhist scriptures have been produced.
The *Xingdi tu* states:
"In the capital of the Liang dynasty, there were originally more than seven hundred monasteries;
however, during the rebellion of Hou Jing, they were all burned to the ground."
Since the Chen dynasty took control of the state and its subjects, everything has been thoroughly restored and maintained.
Stupas and pagodas stand in rows like stars scattered across the sky,
and the abundance of sutras and sacred images is beyond the power of words to fully describe.
Emperor Daowu, the Taizu of the Wei Yuan clan, constructed a fifteen-story pagoda in the territory of the Rouran.
He also established the two monasteries of Kaitai and Dingguo and transcribed the entire Tripitaka.
He commissioned a golden statue one thousand *jin* in height and gathered three hundred eminent monks for a monthly assembly of the Dharma.
Emperor Wencheng of the Northern Wei dynasty restored Buddhism once again.
Furthermore, he elucidated the gates of the teachings.

In total, he ordained thirty thousand monks and nuns. Emperor Xianwen of the Northern Wei constructed Zhaoyin Monastery and summoned practitioners of seated meditation; Emperor Gaozu Xiaowen of the Northern Wei constructed Anyang Monastery at Ye.
He summoned the Sangha from the four quarters.
The handmaidens of the six palaces observed the six fast days of the three long months,
creating images of the Buddha each month.
He permitted others to leave the household life.
His hands never let go of his scrolls;
whenever he needed something, he would recite it from memory.
On behalf of the late Emperor, he again oversaw the performance of grand funeral rites and offerings, ordaining fourteen thousand monks and nuns.
During the reign of Emperor Xuanwu of the Northern Wei dynasty, the Emperor himself lectured on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* in the Shiqian Hall.
He constructed four ordinary Great Samādhi temples.

He constantly provided offerings for a thousand monks. Emperor Xiaozong (Xiao Mingdi) of the Northern Wei built Dajue Temple in Ye. Emperor Jingzong (Xiao Zhuangdi) of the Northern Wei built five vihāras and a ten-thousand-stone Buddha image. Emperor Wu of the Western Wei built Zhiqui Temple in Chang’an.
He provided for two hundred monks; during the reign of Emperor Daï of the Wei dynasty,
he established Prajñā Monastery to provide for the poor,
while personally reciting the Lotus Sūtra.
The sovereigns of the Northern Wei dynasty, who personally upheld the Buddha’s precepts,
numbered seventeen and reigned for one hundred and seventy years.
During this period, there were forty-seven great monasteries within the state.
North of the Terrace is Chang’an;
there, stone was carved to form a niche.
It is thirty *li* to the east.
There were eight hundred and thirty-nine monasteries built by kings and dukes,
and more than thirty thousand monasteries constructed by the common people;
in total, over two million monks and nuns were ordained.
Forty-nine translations of Buddhist scriptures were produced;
thus did Buddhism flourish as it flowed eastward.
It was only during the reign of Emperor Taiwu that he placed his trust in the sycophantic counsel of the Minister of Education, Cui Hao.
He devastated and brought to ruin the orthodox teaching,
remaining in hiding for seven years.
Later, when he learned that the treacherous and sycophantic Cui clan had been executed, [he emerged].
The light of the Buddha’s teachings was restored and propagated as before.
Emperor Wenxuan, the High Ancestor of the Qi dynasty, ascended the throne through the rite of abdication and received the Bodhisattva precepts from the Chan Master Sengming and Sengchou.
Within the capital precincts, the consumption of meat was prohibited, the drinking of alcohol was forbidden, and the release of hawks and the removal of nets were enacted.
Furthermore, slaughter throughout the empire was banned on the sixth day of the third month each year.
He exhorted the people to observe the fasts and abstain from pungent vegetables in both public and private life, thereby eliminating them entirely;
he saved eight thousand people and, during the reigns of Emperors Xuanzong and Xiaoming, copied twelve sets of the Buddhist scriptures for the sake of the late Emperor.
A total of thirty-eight thousand forty-seven fascicles.

He ordained approximately three thousand monks. During the reign of Emperor Wucheng of the Qi dynasty, he constructed a jeweled pagoda and recited the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*. This was during the twenty-eighth year of the Six Rulers of the Northern Qi.
The royal family established forty-three monasteries.
Fourteen translations of scriptures were produced.
The ordination of persons continued in connection with the Wei dynasty.
Emperor Xiaoming of the Zhou dynasty commissioned a woven image of the late Emperor,
two zhang and six chi in height,
as well as twelve sandalwood images of the same size.
Together with his retinue, he built six monasteries in Chang’an for Emperor Wen of the Northern Zhou dynasty, including Zhiyuan, Zhehu,
and Dacheng; he ordained one thousand monks and also constructed five additional monasteries.
During the reign of Emperor Zhou Xiaozhuang, who honored Master Shi Chan with great devotion and caused the Buddha-sun to shine once more,
over four niches containing more than ten thousand clay statues were constructed,
and three thousand scrolls of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra were transcribed.
The six fast days and the eight precepts were constantly propagated without interruption. This was during the twenty-fifth year of the five emperors of the Northern Zhou dynasty.
There were nine hundred and thirty-one monasteries in total.
There were sixteen translated scriptures.
Not long after Emperor Xiaomin had established the foundation of his reign, [the work began].
The Buddha-dharma was not yet well known;
Emperor Gaosheng Shewu did not believe in the Triple Gem.
As a grave illness manifested as a karmic retribution in this life,
the Sui Emperor Gaozu, Wenhuangdi, in the third year of the Kaihuang era, restored all the monasteries that had been abolished during the Zhou dynasty.
Temples were established beneath each of the famous mountains,
and stūpas for śarīra relics were erected in over one hundred states.
Twenty-three thousand people were ordained as monks and nuns.
He established three thousand seven hundred and ninety-two monasteries and transcribed forty-six collections of scriptures,
totaling one hundred thirty-two thousand eight hundred and sixty fascicles.

He repaired three thousand eight hundred and fifty-three volumes of the scriptures and commissioned one hundred and six thousand five hundred and eighty images; other works created separately are too numerous to detail. Emperor Yang of the Sui dynasty [commissioned these] for Emperor Xiaowen and Empress Wenxian.
In Chang'an, he constructed two meditation halls and two wooden pagodas,
and established ten separate monasteries;
the government provided support for ten years.
He repaired six hundred and twelve *piṭaka* and twenty-nine thousand one hundred and seventy-two sections of scriptures;

he restored one hundred thousand old images and constructed three thousand eight hundred and fifty new images across one thousand sites; and he ordained six thousand two hundred monks. This concludes the record of the two rulers of the Sui dynasty over a period of forty-seven years.
There were three thousand nine hundred and eighty-five monasteries.
Twenty-three thousand six hundred and twenty monks and nuns were ordained.
Eighty-two sections of translated scriptures were produced.
The Great Tang’s High Ancestor, Emperor Taizu, succeeded Yao to occupy the throne of Jin;
he forged his martial foundation upon the legacy of Zhou.
Like clouds rising and dragons ascending, his reign began.
He pacified this world,
bringing it into harmony under a single sovereign to inaugurate a new era;
through his nine unifications, he was joyfully accepted by all as their leader.
Having set out from Sanxu, you have successfully stabilized the capital;
the regulations for the people have already been disseminated,
and the teachings of the codified laws have been further proclaimed.
The five planets were gathered together, their influence extending to the four quarters;
the cords of the earth were restored to their proper alignment,
and the pillars of heaven were re-strung.
From east to west, those far away were brought peace and those nearby were struck with awe; yet,
when the banner of righteousness was first raised, [the situation was as follows].
Passing through Huayin on his way,
he offered sacrifices at the sacred altar from afar,
seeking abundant blessings.
To the right of the shrine,
he constructed a monastery,
which was truly named Lingxian (Numinous Immortal).
Exquisitely fashioned as if by divine artistry,
the golden and azure hues intermingle and reflect one another, while the dragon and water-plant motifs shine in mutual splendor.
Gazing across the entirety of the precipitous cliffs,
one beholds them slanting down toward the pearl-adorned palaces;
the magnificent halls rise up in dense, towering majesty.
Recently, facing Mount Lianfeng,
he produced images and transcribed scriptures,
fully cultivating merit and blessings.
Furthermore, within the capital, he established the Huichang Shengye Cibei Zhenguo Xixian Nisi;
he also donated his former residence to become the Xingshengsi;
and in Bingzhou, he founded the Yixingsi.
The halls and buildings were all brilliantly adorned with images,
and exquisite carvings were displayed.
This was in the first year of the Wude era.
Upon the main thoroughfare south of the Zhuque Gate, a universal site of practice (dochuáng) was established,
where an unrestricted assembly (wūzhā huì) was convened for a multitude of Dharma companions.
When the Vulture Peak was first opened,
eminent guests gathered in great numbers;
it was like the initial assembly at the Crane Grove.
Carriages and horses crowded together;
men and women packed like a dense throng, vying with one another to take refuge beneath the branches of the Bodhi tree.
Furthermore, as if competing in a ritual libation,
he commissioned three life-sized statues made of sandalwood for Emperor Taizu Yuanhuangdi and Empress Yuanzhen.
He modeled the divine countenance of the Ninth Emperor and captured the numinous features of the Forty-Eight [Bodhisattvas].
Through the embellishments of carving and engraving...
Since it is already inferior to King Udayana’s blossoms of gilded gold,
it truly has no cause for shame before these flowers of Śrīnaga.
Furthermore, in the second month of spring of that year,
he commanded forty-nine śramaṇas to enter the palace to perform their devotions.
Consequently, the Brahma-teachings of the celestial palaces once again resounded through the Purple Microcosm,
while the weary scriptures of the royal realm [were revitalized].
Furthermore, he raised his voice from within the imperial carriage.
Thereafter, the practice of veneration and faith did not decline during that era under Emperor Taizong Wenhuang.
He received the vital breath of the Grand Ease and the Grand Beginning;
he was endowed with the spiritual numen of the Celestial Sovereign and the Celestial Emperor.
In the profound chamber, the foundation of Gao Yang was opened.
At Yao’s Hut, the legacy of Chonghua was established;
crimson light flowed through the doors and purple qi surged toward heaven,
manifesting forms with dragon-like countenances and phoenix-like chests.
The auspicious signs of the sun upon the brow and the moon suspended above;
the extraordinary features of the river-like eyes and sea-like mouth;
the marvel of the broad upper body and tapered lower form.
With sagely wisdom and profound insight,
he knows the future and encompasses the past;
he probes the obscure and penetrates the subtle.
Exhausting the divine and exhausting human nature—
whatever is bestowed by Heaven,
its substance is spontaneous.
In the past, he immersed himself in primal virtue and brought order to the world; yet,
as the Sui dynasty fell into chaos, the realm within the four seas was shattered and disintegrated.
The flames leaping from Mount Kunlun and the waters surging across the vast ocean were both driven by the intent to pursue the deer.
This is the ritual for naming and opening the transgressions.
Since the time of the region west of the Yellow River,
those like dragons and snakes have perished.
In the lands of the Central Plains,
jade and stone were burned together;
thus, the earth was overturned and the heavens hung low.
Everywhere there arose sighs for a restoration of prosperity;
from the capital to the remote provinces,
the people were filled with grief as they packed their belongings and prepared to depart.
Our Sovereign, being a close kinsman of the Imperial Son,
has received the mandate of Heaven’s decree and is sternly executing the nine ranks of the army.
He commanded the six armies,
which all dissolved like ice melting and crumbled like grass bending before the wind;
as he presented his victory with songs of triumph, there was none with whom to compare his merit.
Soon thereafter, the miasmic vapors were cleared away and the realm was unified under one rule.
The High Ancestor concentrated his spirit to nurture his sagely nature, directing his thoughts beyond the misty clouds and mists.
In the past, when the myriad regions were submerged in darkness and the hundred deities were deprived of their sacrifices,
you humbled yourself to emulate the lofty spirit of Yingyang.
He rescues all under heaven from drowning;
the common people receive the virtue of being restored to life,
and all creatures bear the grace of his creative transformation.
He did not set his heart on the yellow-canopied carriage;
rather, he looked down with concern for the common people,
harboring the resolve to cast off his sandals like a discarded slipper.
Do not let [this] be forgotten within the treasury of the spirit;
release the aspiration for poverty so that it may manifest in the clarity of dawn.
I rejoice that the ancestral sacrifices at Di and Jiao may be recorded;
I am delighted that the divine protection has a presiding lord.
I examine the seasons and select the auspicious days.
The Great Treasure was transmitted to the Crown Prince.
Since he first received the mandate to oversee and pacify the realm as the regent of the Eastern Palace,
he has diligently followed the three virtues.
Thereupon, he brought the myriad states to stability.
When the world was reopened and the precious calendar renewed,
he presided over the land of the Red County and made a solemn and majestic vow.
He comforted the common people and extensively promoted their welfare;
he opened the sun of the Four Immeasurables,
its light shining everywhere like the clouds of Yao.
He raised the wind of the six perfections and spread the rain of Shun’s benevolence.
In the first month of spring, in the first year of the Zhenguan era.
By imperial decree, all the monks of the capital who were renowned for their virtuous conduct were ordered to enter the inner palace to practice the Way,
each for a full seven days.
The officials in charge of provisions were diligent in ensuring the supply of the finest quality.
By the third year, the Emperor feared that the harvests might fail;
his anxiety and compassion for the people occupied his thoughts.
Thereupon, an imperial decree was issued to select individuals of refined sincerity and long-standing virtue, along with fourteen attendants,
to pray for rain at Tianmen Street for seven days.
Sustained by the mysterious aid of the Sage’s power,
the crops grew double-furrowed and the fields yielded a harvest of ten thousand chests, bringing abundance to every household.
The state possessed resources sufficient for nine years' worth of provisions;
from that time onward, there has been constant abundance without interruption.
Previously, when the banner of righteousness was first raised, the divine army vanquished [the enemy] amidst arrows and stones.
Fearing that vengeful spirits might be formed,
in the winter of that year, he ordered the monks and nuns of the capital to perform ritual circumambulations for seven days,
providing all their clothing from his own donations (*dāna*).
Relying upon these superior causes, I have exhausted my sincerity in repentance and purification;
at the sites of the battlefields, monasteries were established,
including more than ten temples such as Zhao-ren and Deng-jue.
In the spring of the third year,
he again received an imperial decree ordering that monks and nuns perform ritual practices and recite the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* and other scriptures on the second and seventh days of every month;
the government provided the offerings for these meals, establishing this as a permanent practice.
Furthermore, he issued an edict to the Tripitaka Master Wuxing (Bopuo),
who was proficient in the three teachings and fully versed in the ten categories of Buddhist scholarship.
Shi Huisheng and nineteen others translated [the scriptures] at Xingshan Monastery,
and also [served] for Emperor Taizu.
He established Longtian Monastery on Mount Zhongnan and sent six life-sized statues of Emperor Wu and others there to serve as perpetual objects of veneration.
Furthermore, he built Hongfu Monastery for Empress Dowager Mu.
After the monastery was completed,
the Emperor personally visited it.
Jizhen himself bestowed extremely generous offerings and invited ten virtuous monks (bhadanta) to come in person for discussion.
At that time, Daoyi, the abbot of the monastery, spoke.
When these words were spoken, the Empress Dowager was overcome with grief;
